General meeting of the Sosnowiec „Maccabi“

(Ch—ski) Last Sunday an extraordinary general meeting of the Sosnowiec „Maccabi“ took place in its own premises.
With 200 members present, Mr. Kromołowski[?] opens the meeting and proposes electing Mr. Szarf as chairman. Mr. Szarf takes the chair and invites Messrs. Langer and Feldman as assessors. Before proceeding to the important items, the memory of the member and Zionist activist Y. M. Weigreb[?] [Weinreb] is honoured by standing.
The report on activities is given by Eng. Kromołowski, who points out the difficulties under which he had to work in order to bring the association to its present state. In the short time he succeeded in recruiting 150 new members, introduced discipline among the members, and founded the sections 1) ping-pong and 2) boxing section, which are developing very well. After the discussion, in which Messrs. Feldman, Langer, Priwer[?], Horowitz and others took part, the following board is elected: Eng. Kromołowski, Dr. Trapojer[?], Dr. Kowalski, Lancman, Liberman, Landau, Herzberg, Gutowski and Grynblat. Deputies: Chmielnicki and Bajtel. Audit committee: Goldberg, Feldman and Binkowski.
Under any other business it is decided to plant a tree in the Herzl Forest in the name of the late Y. M. Weinreb.

In the coming days the sensational trial of the brothers Wojdaw[?], who manufactured 10-złoty banknotes, opens at the Sosnowiec district court.

Auditor Michelson on the Artisans' and Small Traders' Bank in Sosnowiec
This week an audit (lustracja) was carried out at the Artisans' and Small Traders' Bank by the auditor of the Auditing Union, Mr. Michelson.
In connection with the present situation of the cooperative banks, the writer of these lines turned to Mr. Michelson for his opinion about the above-mentioned bank.
In the past year — says Mr. M. — the bank was reorganised, and today it is counted as one of the most sound cooperative banks in Poland. Its management is solid; the collections have doubled in number.
One of its greatest merits is that at the head of the bank stand respected, honest people who support the bank both materially and morally.

Notes of the Week

[Notes of the Week — abroad and Poland; Będzin — kehilla; economy; Sosnowiec — Zionism.] During a performance by Jonas Turkow in Chełm the balcony collapsed. There are many injured.
—o—
In Lemberg [Lwów] a gathering of Jewish scouts was attacked by a Communist bojówka [fighting squad]. As a result there are many injured.
—o—
A storm occurred on the Baltic Sea. Several Latvian ships have sunk. There are human casualties.
—o—
In the Lublin region several rivers overflowed and flooded large areas.
—o—
Anti-French demonstrations took place in Syria. The police used weapons; there are masses of dead and wounded.
—o—
In Bielsko [?] Endek students smashed the windows of the Jewish shops.
—o—
In the textile factory of "Wegner and Peter" in Łódź a great fire broke out. The damage is very great.
—o—
For a few days Jews had rest..
The Christian population celebrated its holidays.
On Friday, Saturday and Sunday all shops and workshops were closed; all sources of income were forcibly shut not only for the Christian but also for the Jewish population.
Many a Jewish family was without a penny in recent days and suffered hunger and cold, being forced to "rest" for three days.
But on the other hand the Jewish population also had a certain rest during these three days of the Christian holidays.
The Jew-devouring press did not appear; therefore no one incited against the Jews, insulted or attacked them.
No boycott actions were carried out.
There were no visits from the merciless sequestrators with demands to pay the unattainable tax sums.
The notaries [rejenci] protested no bills of exchange, and the komorniks [bailiffs] did not sell the last bit of belongings for debts that cannot be paid, because the constant [?] economic extermination has brought the Jewish population to enormous want.
That is precisely what the rest of the hungry and desperate Jewish population consisted of.
For a few days it was not tormented.
—o—

Account Books for Retailers.
Among the retailers great interest has been aroused by the newly adopted clause to the law on turnover tax, which introduces account books for retailers.
This law is already coming into force and will apply from the New Year.
Soon the Ministry of Finance will issue implementing regulations, in which it will be specified exactly what bookkeeping the retail merchants will have to keep in order to benefit from the turnover-tax reduction.
The bookkeeping for retailers will be greatly simplified, so that one will not need to have a bookkeeper; every shopkeeper will be able to keep it himself. The Warsaw Chamber of Commerce is preparing a draft of such simple bookkeeping, and the Ministry of Finance is working out a plan of such bookkeeping.
As we learn, the bookkeeping for retailers will consist of 2 books. It will be absolutely necessary to keep all invoices for goods purchased. One book will be for daily transactions, in which the goods purchased and the articles sold will be entered, with the sum of the daily takings at once in one entry. The second will be a stock book.
Retailers will not be compelled to keep the account books, but every retailer who wishes to pay a lower "obrotowy" [turnover tax] will have to keep account books. Such retailers will pay one quarter of a percent less in 1932. The other retailers will continue to pay 2 per cent. Every year the turnover tax will be reduced for retailers with books, whereas for retailers without books the reduction of the turnover tax will begin only in 2 years' time.

Preparations for a Great Jubilee Bazaar in Sosnowiec
The bazaar question, which at all of its committee meetings was a subject of discussion, ultimately failed to create the proper human apparatus for the undertaking.
Thanks to the WIZO organisation, headed by Mrs. L. Rosman [?], the best and most industrious forces of our national camp have been concentrated — and the first real steps have already been taken.
Thus the finest premises in the town centre have already been obtained entirely free of charge, as well as all the necessary fittings free of charge.
These days letters are being sent to the industrialists and merchants of the larger towns in Poland, and especially in Zagłębie, regarding their exhibits and kiosks.
From some firms news has already been received about their participation.
"Totzeret HaAretz" [produce of the Land] will occupy one of the finest pavilions and will be stocked with all kinds of Eretz-Israel produce, including the artistic works of the "Bezalel" school.
In general the work is being prepared with feverish speed, so that the imposing opening may take place at the beginning of February.
It is to be hoped that the Jewish population of Zagłębie will co-operate to ensure the success of the first Eretz-Israel bazaar, whose proceeds are designated for the redemption of the Land.
A. Fromer [?].

Persecution of the Jewish traders and pedlars in Upper Silesia.
As we have already written, a delegation of Jewish pedlars from Upper Silesia intervened at the Ministry of the Interior concerning the persecution and harassment of the pedlars. In this connection the Central Small Traders' Association submitted a memorandum to the Minister of the Interior, setting out a series of facts: thus the municipality (magistrat) of Gawowiesz [?] issued an ordinance applied only to the Jewish traders, who are forbidden to come to the markets there. When a Jewish trader wants to trade at the markets, he must take a Christian partner.
The delegation also demanded that the antisemitic periodicals "Do Czynu" and "Drwęca" [?], which call for boycott and terror, be stopped.
The representative of the Political Department declared that the Ministry of the Interior will suppress with all its strength every attempt at hooligan attacks on the Jewish population; as regards the persecution in Upper Silesia, the Ministry will investigate and then take a favourable position on the question.

In the premises of the Katowice District Court, the municipal court last Tuesday dealt with the application of the management of "Huta Pokój", which requests a court supervision (nadzór).

Theatre notes.

"Over Graves" ("Iber kvorim"). A drama in 5 acts by A. Wolfsztat, staged by the Będzin "Muze" under the direction of the author.
On Monday evening the dramatic circle "Muze" in Będzin staged the premiere of "Over Graves" by A. Wolfsztat.
The author made use of a long-familiar theme, one of the countless sad experiences that happened in wartime, when the Jew was the scapegoat at every upheaval [?]. Only the author peppered the fact with several effects, for example the singing behind the curtain, a cemetery and, above all, the finale — the wedding in the cemetery. In our view the wedding canopy did not have to take place precisely among graves, but if the author wants it so, there is surely no point in asking questions...
The plot: three Tsarist subjects burst in on a Jewish family; the Jew gives them food and drink, and when their limbs are warmed, passions awaken in them and they want to dance with the wives of the partners Moshe and Shlomo. Moshe resists and is shot for it. The same end awaits Shlomo too, but his wife saves him by agreeing to dance with the Russian hooligan.
From this dancing a male child is born, and because of it Shlomo's wife is hated and persecuted by her husband and by the whole town. Shlomo's wife seeks a way out of her disgrace and smothers her illegitimate child. Even by this step she is not rehabilitated, and she receives a divorce (get) from her husband.
The third act already takes place in the cemetery, where Shlomo's former wife sits at the grave of her child. At that moment she learns that in the same place the wedding ceremony of her husband with the murdered partner's wife is taking place; in revenge she sets the town on fire.
— The acting in general was not up to the mark. Of the participants, the official Ivanovich (Bushevski) and the town madman (Khaleva) were satisfactory at moments, especially in the second act. About the other players we would rather give the floor to the director, who declared after the performance that "the play was rehearsed altogether in the course of a meagre 2 weeks". That was indeed evident...
Sha—el.
Olkusz. — Constitution of the new kehilla board.

On Sunday evening the constituent meeting of the new kehilla board took place. On the agenda there was 1 item: election of a chairman. Present were 7 board (dozór) members, 5 from the National Bloc and 2 Agudists. The Rabbi, may he live long, also came at the appointed hour. After the meeting was opened by the old chairman and the secretary read out the election procedure, the representative of the "Agudah", Mr. A. Paluch, declared: "Since elections must be free and independent, and at this moment that cannot be, because the National Bloc is bound by an agreement among themselves, under ban and prohibition (!), to vote for the candidate for chairman designated by themselves, he therefore demands that the elections be postponed until the agreement is annulled, for otherwise the elections will not be in accordance with the law of Moses and Israel"...
Messrs. M. Szwarcberg, Sz. Sztark and A. Glikstein replied that formally and juridically their agreement is permissible, and demanded that the elections proceed. In protest A. Paluch, B. L. Kahan and the Rabbi left the meeting. After that the elections were carried out, and Mr. Szymon Sztark was elected kehilla chairman. The participation of the Rabbi in the elections in general, and in the constituent meeting in particular, is regarded by the National Bloc as an assault on the majority of the Jewish population...
As reported, the "Agudah" has lodged a protest with the starostwo (district office) concerning the elections.

Let Jewish Society Awaken

[Będzin — education; polemic.] A. Gottesdiener[?].
(A reply to Mr. R. Let).
In No. 50 of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", Mr. R. Let, in his article "Crisis and Teachers", touched on the question of the school budgets in Będzin, advising the school boards of trustees (kuratoria) to keep pace with the times and to learn the secret of retrenchment.
I understand that Mr. Let meant all non-state schools; I, for my part, however, feel obliged only to sweep before my own door.
Times are very bad, but the deepest ruin of the crisis is borne by the middle class. He who already stands in the "poor" column may indeed have gone through a terrible decline, but once lying in the abyss he has it easier than one who is still in the midst of falling; however paradoxical this may sound, it remains a psychological truth. The lot of the falling, of the declining — that is today the majority of Jewish burghers, and that is the root of the fear that today dominates Polish Jewry. Those lying down groan; those falling are terrified. And this very terror makes the decline even more terrible and accelerates its pace.
A retreat from an economic battlefield must take place in good order, just like a retreat from a military battlefield; otherwise it ends in total defeat.
There are positions in life that must be defended to the last drop of blood, because they are positions that cover the retreat and protect the retreating from the exhaustion of their last strength, with which one will have[?] to build the future.
One of those positions is the education of youth. This position must be defended unconditionally, with all one's energy and in the best order. I have the courage to admit that sending children home from school for money is a crime against the child. It is not merely a matter of losing a few lessons, or even a few school days; it is a matter of something more important: that the child feels hurt in his dignity, that the child sees the noblest spiritual fruit of Torah and wisdom growing on the dirty branch of — money.
But who is guilty of this crime? People are used to moving along the line of least resistance, and so the whole blame is thrown on — the teachers. The school administration is surely not guilty, for if the teachers did not demand any salaries, it, the administration, would not be so hard-pressed. Hence the easiest advice is to tell the teachers: give up part of your salaries, the punctual payment date, and go along with the times.
But what then, when the teachers have already gone along with the times and have already taken the medicine called "reduction" and are still not cured? And one must not forget the situation of the private-school teachers after working for years, when they lose their strength at work, when they grow old, sick, weak — what is left for them to do? I beg you, take a look at such a situation!
And even while he works: imagine the situation of a person who owns nothing but his throat, with which he works 6—8 hours daily, not as a cantor, but as a teacher, with full attention, with all 248 limbs of his soul.
[—] to be a guest in the home of a teacher, and by chance I happened to witness a small incident: my host suddenly felt ill. The great fright that appeared at that moment on his wife's face told me far more, and far more clearly, than all the "zhiaukes"[?] together.
"If he dies — the great fear[?] told me — I remain with my children destitute — and the illness goes its way, and there is no money to get cured."
We are not a state and we cannot create a pension (emeritura), but a people we surely are, and we must not treat as useless the people to whom we entrust the education of our children.
There are in the Jewish community various officials who often fulfil their functions less, or not at all, and nobody has any complaints against them.
In short, I hold that one must look for another way out, one that does not go through the hungry stomachs of the teachers, but through the open hearts of Jewish society and through the organisation of the parents.
The parents must organise an aid fund that will take upon itself the regulation of the payment of tuition fees (sekhar-limud), so that one need not be importunate concerning the payment day, concerning the payment date, and Jewish society must help itself mutually.
When a Jewish child remains without schooling, it is a question not only of that child, but a question of all his fellow children. And I will permit myself to say that the education of youth is one of the most important questions of the Jewish future, and it deserves no less self-sacrifice, attention and offerings than other Jewish questions.
One thing must be clear to us: the ruin of the so-called private schools, over which Jewish society has great influence, will throw our children into such schools where we will be powerless to say our word, and they will be lost to us — lost.
Let Jewish society guard its children and their educators.
Goldkarn's Picture Exhibition

The artist is a graduate of the „Higher Institute of Fine Arts“ in Antwerp.
That he has not yet entirely freed himself from the influence of the Flemish school is attested by his portrait „A Negro“, which is kept in a calm, warm tone; the colour range is not a broad one, but the transitions between the colour tones are very subtle.
In the remaining pictures, however, the influence of the French school is already very prominent. This is especially visible in his large picture „By the Rivers of Babylon“, which the artist conceived in a modernist way. It depicts a group of women in mourning. Woman is meant — according to the artist's conception — to be the bearer of eternal mourning. He has therefore eliminated the man, for whom mourning is only a passing phenomenon.
But what interests us is not the literary side of the picture but the painterly one, and from that standpoint it has a decorative character, already because of its large size. It is a bold step for a young artist to measure himself against large canvases, yet Goldkarn has succeeded in creating a fine, harmonious colour composition, and this proves that he masters well the technique of filling large surfaces.
Very good are the copper engravings, which demand a special technique; they are very successful both in drawing and in composition.
The female nudes are painted broadly, the patches of colour laid down confidently, not overworked, and they therefore breathe freshness.
Especially successful is the picture „A Cow in the Studio“, which is treated in a primitive form. This is one of the most difficult problems in modern painting; the artist has managed to obtain such luminous colours that one gets the immediate impression that they phosphoresce.
Goldkarn is still a young painter, yet one already feels in his works the attempt to seek his own path. His drive towards individuality is very prominent, and this gives a guarantee that he is on the right path, which should lead him to his artistic career.
Sh. R.
—
On Sunday morning, in the hall of „Piast“ in Będzin, in the presence of a large number of invited guests, the picture exhibition of the young artist Abraham Goldkarn was opened.
The opening speech was delivered by the patron, Dr. Wasercug, who outlined in brief strokes Goldkarn's talent already as a pupil at the „Yavneh“ gymnasium, his successfully completed studies at the Royal Institute in Antwerp, and wished the young artist further success in his field.

The New Year's Dream...

[Feuilleton — the civil New Year.] Reuven Flaman.
I am asleep and all kinds of dreams float through my head. Dreams of a finer and happier tomorrow for us Jews. Before my eyes whole crowds of figures drift past, music plays all around, at the side various women's figures whirl, human tongues do not rest, couples in an ecstasy of love, "Bacchus" on the tables.
What is the wonder here? What do these little lights[?] mean, the full glasses, the whirling "blazent"[?], the merry women, the loud but empty music? Eh? You don't know — a figure tells me — why, today is a holiday, the holiday of the New Year, Silvester! At twelve at night the old year parts from us and there arrives — the year 1932!!
And Jews celebrate Silvester too? Is that a crime, then? Are they not human beings, does the sun not shine for them? And indeed I become possessed[?] by the Silvester night, I revel in pleasure — you know, a year of activity has passed, a year of progress!.. I take the glass in hand and drink to our health and to the happiness of the New Year, to its bright future.
Meanwhile the strains of "Bubliczki" are heard, delicious "Bubliczki". True, "Bubliczki", the latest hit of the season! And here I rejoice even more! Involuntarily the thought comes to me — our activity, our efforts, our progress. Here is the fruit of our labour, of our mental exertions: Rafałek, Black Bottom, Charleston, broken feet, Bubliczki, Wanda, Warszawianka, wide trousers, short tailcoats, long... dresses, phenomenal discoveries, such as "Kazimir" powder and the prominent "Larnie"[?]. These precious fruits of our labour allow us to make merry, drink, enjoy. If we live — let us live.
Let us go forward, always forward; this hard work, the inexhaustible power of human energy is already improving our situation, it has won us rights; we are people equal to others, more than that, we are a nation. Revenues flow in, land is bought in Eretz Israel, people speak of the survival of Judaism, of our life in the East — is that not progress? Honour to us, we have even lived to see a "bulletin" about our hard material and spiritual work..
Let us live and make merry! — Wait, you clown [pajac], jester [błazen] of the 20th century, it is not always the time to chase after that[?]! — Father Abraham interrupts me. This is not your way, this is not what you were created for, son of Israel. You should rather weep, not rejoice! Don't you know what awaits you?
— Foolish Abraham, leave me alone; what is past will not return, today we have new times before us. Our name, the roads we have travelled together, the fruits of our history which we lived through together in one language, do not let us go forward with the current of today's times... — The abashed Abraham uttered only the words: — You will perish — and vanished.
The words "you will perish" all but killed me. I want to go on being merry and I can't; something presses and torments, and the dancing goes on[?]! No, I can't! I am unhappy! — What is it, what happened to you — with these words my friend approaches me. Leave me alone, leave me by myself.
In a corner, away from the noisy entertainment and drunkenness, I fall asleep exhausted. And now it seems to me that the day of deed and effort is approaching. With boundless strength I strive and act. I stand on a platform and speak to a great crowd: Brothers! A New Year is coming! Abraham has stood for centuries in one place and does not heed the calls to go forward with progress; brothers, the "Abraham" in you must be awakened so that he goes. He must be shown what suffering and pain he causes himself if he goes on remaining so stubborn. On the other hand we must take care that the younger generation, whom the various kinds of upbringing and education separate from our masses, does not drift away from us. In other words, that Isaac too should go, but should not forget his holy duties. Abraham and Isaac must go together, united, and strive jointly toward one idea and goal.
But my dear brothers! In order to reach harmony, so that divided minds can refresh hearts, for that one must first of all have a heart, in order to gain lively, warmer feelings for the poor — not everyday ones, something higher, more understanding for spirituality.
Let each of us take up his position and fulfil his duties like an obedient soldier. Let each of us show more activity, and then the conditions hitherto will become quite different. Every donation for popular education, every school that brings up a productive Jew — that will be the sowing that will bring a blessed harvest.
Let us go together, brothers, cast off every thought of fragmentation; let us go united, and with all that is good and just, and with all who strive for it. But not hand in hand with those who await our ruin and downfall, who cannot bear either Abraham or Isaac, and who would spare no means to destroy them.
Only quiet, practical and systematic work, far from fantasies, can improve our situation and send a new ray of happiness onto our lives. I finished; at the tumult of the ovations I woke from deep sleep.
And what did I notice? Again the same grey reality. It was only a sweet innocent dream, a New Year's dream.
To you, my brothers, I entrust the dream of my life.
A Year after the Death of Moshe Apfelbaum

[Będzin / Katowice — In memory of an artist; editorial.] A year has passed since the life-loving and original Moshe Apfelbaum [Mojżesz Apfelbaum] is no longer among the living. Moshe Apfelbaum was always original — both in his painting and in his private life. It was a rare thing how modest the man was: for himself he needed nothing, and as soon as he had a gulden in his pocket he did not give a whistle for the whole world. He used to sell pictures only in order to buy paints, and as soon as he had the material — once he had bought himself paints and canvas — the world could turn upside down, it did not concern him at all; he would then sit down and paint, forgetting when the day passes and when the night arrives.
In summer he would set off over the mountains of Cieszyn Silesia [Śląsk Cieszyński] and catch the beautiful landscapes there, and when rain caught him he would huddle into a peasant's hut and spend the night there.
It often happened that on a fine bright day Apfelbaum vanished; nobody knew where he had escaped to, and he never wrote. But those close to him [?] could already guess that he had managed to sell a picture, had bought himself the necessary painting materials and had cut himself off from mankind. At such times [?] he wanted to be alone — alone with nature, alone with the sun, with the fields, with the mountains and with the flowing stream that wound down so gloriously in zigzag form from the mountains into the valleys.
When after a while Apfelbaum reappeared in town and people would fall upon him with questions: Where have you been? Where did you disappear to for so long? — he would answer with contentment: I painted, I created, and the imagination — he would declare — is so rich that I would go on creating without pause; the creative thread draws itself out of the great ball of yarn, which apparently [?] will never come to an end. And saying these words he would shine with joy and contentment, as if the Divine Presence rested upon him.
The man was extraordinarily friendly, naive and modest, and he had optimism without limit. A man who was forced, on a large scale, to go hungry very often, possessed a great dose of optimism which was incomprehensible to those close to him.
When he earned a gulden, he shared his morsel. And in his single little room in Katowice he would always [?] invite guests; and when an artist, a writer or an actor came to Katowice from Warsaw, he was Apfelbaum's guest, and there, in the small room that was at the same time his studio, his guests felt more at home and more comfortable than in the big rich salons, which were not foreign to his guests.
Many art critics characterised Apfelbaum as a seeking and researching spirit. He wanted to discover something new, something original in art; he was never finished with himself — he would paint and smear it over. After he had completed a work and later came to conceive it differently, he would stand up again with the brush in his hand and create another picture, in which the idea was conceived quite differently.
With rare joy and enthusiasm Apfelbaum used to capture the little houses in Będzin that stand below the hill [the castle hill]. He often said: We must quickly capture these original old-fashioned little houses that have not yet entirely collapsed; we must immortalise the little cottages in which our grandfathers lived, because thereby a piece of history that is being lost before our eyes will be saved. And Apfelbaum hurried to immortalise them. He also sought out and rescued the oldest tombstones in the Będzin cemetery, and he went about with the plan of publishing an album of them.
Who does not remember with what enthusiasm, with what reverence he painted the Będzin synagogue [the "shul"], how much strength and power he put into its walls. Once, when he was already completely finished with the eastern wall and the scaffolding [rusztowania] had already been taken down, it occurred to him: No, the wall cannot remain like this — and the work was taken up anew: the plaster ["cement"] was torn off, the wall was smoothed back down to the raw surface, and the work was begun again from scratch. And when he had finished it the second time, he said to the writer of these lines: Now I am satisfied with my creation; what came out is what my imagination had pictured. Now my monument has been immortalised, and I can close my eyes with a quiet conscience.
Our Będzin may be proud that it received the finest and richest legacy of the late talented painter, who was torn from us so early and so suddenly. We may be proud of it because we are so poor in the field of art, and had the synagogue not been painted by such artists as Apfelbaum, Ziegler and Hanft, we would not possess this beauty either.
And now, when a poet like Bialik or a historian like Prof. Bałaban [Majer Bałaban] comes, they first of all go to see the synagogue, which they leave satisfied. Is that not a gain for Jewish Będzin? Can we not boast of the rich legacy that we were fortunate enough to receive?
• • •
A year has flowed by since the deceased has lain in the earth, and the artist has no tombstone in the Katowice cemetery, and the widow with the child he left orphaned has not been provided for either.
In the European world the people takes care of such personalities. The artist becomes a public concern, his works become the property of the community, and the community provides honourably for everything connected with the artist.
Here too one is obliged to take care in such a way of an artist who has left behind a fine and honourable name.
Zagłębie and Upper Silesia are obliged to do everything so that those left behind by the deceased receive an honourable future, and that a tombstone such as he deserved be set up for the deceased.
A year ago, upon returning from the Katowice cemetery, a committee was formed in Katowice which was supposed to take up the matter.
It cannot be denied that the Katowice admirers knew how to appreciate the national loss, and even when it was a matter of saving the deceased, they spared nothing. But now what is needed today has not been done, and therefore a sacred duty lies upon the admirers in Upper Silesia and Zagłębie to undertake this sacred work, which will bring them much honour when they know that they have fulfilled their duty.
L. Szpigelman.
One of the Holiest...

I did not write about Apelbaum at the time of his death, because by nature I hate eulogies while the dead man lies before one's eyes.

Apelbaum belonged to those deep ones whom one could not dismiss [?] in a minute with a few tears. He was one who worked in depth, who entered the heart without a "why" — a simple, good man of the people with deep intuition, good will and verve... He could take to a person and grow fond of him for a lifetime, and in just the same way one could love him all one's life; and whoever was not close to him lost out — he was not loved by a simple, warm-hearted and deep person.

Yes, Moshe Apelbaum the man is a special page in the history of a Jewish artist, a special figure of a martyr for Jewish art: Moshe Apelbaum in London, in Paris, in Będzin and in all the towns and shtetls.

For who did not know him, this good-natured Apelbaum, always in good humour.

There are even opinions that say that man and artist are two separate things.

I am of the opposite opinion: that the artist lies hidden in the man himself, and that is what Apelbaum was — the man among artists. That first of all.

And just as the man was, so were his creations; although even today it is not [known] what he was as an artist or to which trend in painting he belonged, one thing was always clear to me: that his works came from a flowing, deep spring, and in them there always lay the simple Apelbaum, with the world and with people, the ever-affectionate [?] Apelbaum.

"I do not want, my friend," Apelbaum once said, "you to draw conclusions about which regiment of the army of artists I belong to. But I want you to know that I am a soldier of Jewish art." And that is what he was: the faithful worshipper of Jewish art.

* * *

I shall therefore leave the professional side of Moshe Apelbaum's work to the experts and give here a bundle of memories of, and encounters with, him, for Moshe Apelbaum's life was closely bound up with Zagłębie; yes, for a good many years the land of black diamonds held Apelbaum in its arms.

Katowice was his favourite corner; here he lived his life to the full and here he grew greatly.

Several years ago Apelbaum invited me to visit him in Katowice.

I entered a wide, unheated room. On the table lay paints and two or three palettes in disorder, a few rolls and herring, and paper. Apelbaum walked about with bare hands, rubbing them and blowing on his fingers; every now and then he snatched a piece of roll with herring for a bite, and painted, and with every stroke of the brush he said joyfully:

"Yes, now I am happy, I have a room to work in." Yes, after long years here in Katowice he had at last lived to have a room, and how good it felt to him, the big child, when he already stood in his homely corner and painted diligently. We spent several days together, and in those days it became clear to me that Apelbaum — the one who always complained about his luck — had become cheerful: the room had saved him.

Now came the most important thing: Apelbaum loved the mines [kopalnie]; the character of his painting lies precisely here, in the coal pits.

It was a winter's day; white snow had covered the dark earth, and the black spots of the cable-cars travelling over the Dąbrowa wires looked like standing wings.

We — that is, I, the one who proposed the plan, our friend Szpigelman and Apelbaum — went to the shaft of the "Rechnitzes" [?] in Dąbrowa. I must admit that I alone was the coward; both of them began to adapt themselves to the situation, changed clothes, took lamps — and forward.

For two hours I waited in suspense to see what impression the treasure from below would make on Apelbaum.

And when he came out he seized me by the lapels and scolded me:

"Ah, you man, you are to be pitied, very much pitied. I, at any rate, am glad that I got to know the Zagłębie earth in its depth: the deeper, the more beautiful it is." He could say this boldly, for having come to know the Zagłębie earth more deeply he indeed gave us the most beautiful charcoal drawings and the most splendid pictures.

* * *

Several years have passed, and the dear face of Moshe Apelbaum has remained with me something like the vision of a saint.

Yes, so I thought of him and so I think of him today: he was — one of the holiest.

Joel Mastbaum
Political Letters.

For the weekly portion: "And they made their lives bitter."

To my dear friend, the distinguished scholar, our teacher Rabbi Binush, may his light shine!

Such, it seems, is our fate: wherever the world begins to stir [?] anywhere, be it even beyond the Mountains of Darkness — the blood libel; it is on us that they make the first trial "for analysis" [?]...

It is of course very sad that in the Far East a war is now flaring up: firstly, the heart aches for the thousands of human victims falling there; and secondly, a war in our days is a very dangerous thing... It is just like the plague [?] epidemic hundreds of years ago... it starts in one corner of the globe and at once spreads over the whole world... The same can happen with the Chinese-Japanese war... Russia and America will probably also get mixed up in it, and then it will go "like a psalm", for dynamite has been prepared in quite a fair amount, and the human beast, wrapped in all kinds of "veils of peace", is also wicked and bad enough, so that nothing is lacking for the bloody spectacle.

But it is not about the red blood of the yellow [?] people that I want to talk with you now... That is, so to speak, a "lawful" bloodshed... Mankind has got so far with its "progress" that it has found a permission for bloodshed... That, it seems, is how the commandment "Thou shalt not kill" is interpreted: thou (in the singular) may indeed not shed blood, but you (in the plural) may... The same, it seems, is done with the commandment "Thou shalt not steal"...

But I want to talk now about another "war", a war that took place only recently in a number of cities in Poland, Germany, Austria and also in America. I mean the hooligan attacks of the students on the innocent Jews.

This, my friend, is quite a different kind of war... It does not begin, as in other cases, with prior diplomatic preparation... The two sides have no dealings whatever with each other; there is no quarrel over a piece of territory (true, when one thinks it over well, one can say that territory does play a great role here, for if Jews really had their own territory they would not have had to suffer such humiliations and shameful attacks). There is no dispute over state interests... It is a simple matter: one part of the country's population — (luckily only one part) — cannot bear that another part breathes the air of its country, treads on the soil of its land, and lives at all on God's earth.

So the Esaus of today came and argued: how so? In your Torah, Jews, it is written explicitly that Esau must live by his sword; how then can we, the great-great-grandchildren of Esau, not fulfil an explicit verse of the Torah?

For the sons of Esau understand the verse thus: "And by thy sword shalt thou live" — thou shalt live, and when one wants to live, another, his opposite party, must die...

And as is known, it was mainly Polish students who took part in these attacks... And it is quite understandable, for who else should make pogroms if not students? The simple masses are sunk in an abyss of worries about a livelihood, taxes, the trouble of raising children and other sufferings; but the studying youth — the ones on whom a country is built, the future of a nation — they can with a free head strike at other heads...

They, the students who study human rights, have arrived at the conclusion that one has the right to kill defenceless and innocent Jews... for an enemy one may kill by all opinions according to today's morality. One need only see to it that the attack is directed against a large number of enemies, so that it should resemble a war... Well, and so they indeed do, the antisemitic students everywhere... They pick out centres where many Jews live, and kill them, put them to death, rob their goods and property...

True, the country where such disgraceful deeds take place gets no excess of satisfaction from it, for there are still people in the world who are shocked by pogroms, and ask questions, and raise an uproar in the press against the hooligan lawlessness; but everyone already knows from practice that those stay at shouting and... and what they did, they did... done [?] and lost...

Yes, my friend, a fine blessing father Isaac left to his son [?] Esau, a blessing which has been turned for us into a curse... But what can we do? Protest? Against whom and before whom? Against bloodthirsty beasts spitting antisemitic poison? Protest before that part of mankind which has not yet lost its image of God? But we know well, and have already seen it many times, that this part of mankind has almost no weight... And if Japan, for instance, wants by all means to wage war against China and shed rivers of blood — can anyone stop her and ask: what are you doing?

And if tomorrow, God forbid, a war should break out in Europe, will there not float up anew, just as fifteen or sixteen years ago, the same clumsy so-called patriotic cries, calling: Give, give! More and more blood must be shed!

To our deep regret, it is for the time being very hard to uproot the evil instinct in man that strives for bloodshed.

And in the name of that same so-called patriotism the Polish antisemites are now also performing their deceitful deeds...

And meanwhile, my friend, there is no joy at all in the heart.

The "and they made their lives bitter" sits well in our bones everywhere.

Yechiel Melamed
How Does the Zagłębie Merchant, Shopkeeper and Artisan Live?

[Zagłębie — economy and trade; interview with a shoe dealer.] What does a shoe dealer say?
I came to the shoe dealer at the time after “Bata” had opened a shop in Katowice.
And indeed, right at the start we talked about “Bata.”
— If “Bata” had opened the shop in Katowice 3 years ago, the dealer argues, we would not have paid any attention to it at all.
Sosnowiec depended mostly on the provinces; a big wholesale trade went on here, but with the provinces one can no longer trade today, because 90 per cent of the shopkeepers have gone bankrupt; the shopkeeper looks only to the town turnover, and that is why we have now been hit hard by “Bata.”
— What was the situation before?
— In the past year the trade was ruined for the following 2 reasons: first, goods fell by 40 per cent, and so every shopkeeper had to put money on top of the stock he had in the shop; the second reason is that the fashion in women's shoes suddenly changed. Instead of light colours people began to demand dark ones. Now all the shopkeepers are sitting with their bundles. Shoes that cost 20—25 zł. themselves are now sold for 15 zł., and even at that price there are still no buyers. These 2 blows have laid the shopkeepers flat on their shoulder blades. The situation is very sad, and as is foreseen [?], from the New Year a number of shoe shops will be liquidated.
— What are the prices?
— There used to be 3 categories of shoe shops. First category: “tovl” [pressboard/cardboard?] work, that is, the top and the sole of thick [?] board, the uppers [cholewki] of imitation leather and the whole “spód” [bottom] of board. That kind of shoe is sold today: for ladies — 6.50—7 zł., a pair for men — 10—11 zł., even of patent leather.
Second category: made entirely of leather.
The third category: special workmanship.
Today the third category no longer exists at all. The public demands cheap; it does not pay to pay the shoe dealer more for the workmanship than one pays the dealer of the second category. So a pair of good shoes now costs 20—25 zł. (Suede) ladies' shoes — 18—20 zł.; of chrome (box) leather they cost somewhat less still.
What is the turnover?
— Shoes are bought, of course, according to the times. If the times are good, people allow themselves to buy several pairs of shoes a year. But today we are quite far from good times, and one feels it very well in business. People do not allow themselves to buy more than one pair of shoes a year, and others contrive to put it off till later; they “go under” [?] — they put on another pair of soles, and so they get by.
Now, above all, “Bata” has made an assault on even this little turnover.
— — —
The next conversation — with a paper dealer.
Y. R. S.
He Has, She Has

[Feuilleton — serial story, conclusion.] Chats and chatter of a gossip-monger.
Rendered by A. D. Egoz.
A week ago Friday I remained in your debt, having left off in the middle of the story "He Has, She Has". Do you care to hear the end? Here you have it.
Listen, and take pleasure — or perhaps revenge — in that old fool who bought himself the "maftir", and what a maftir: worse than the Tokhekha [the portion of curses].
Where were we? We were at the point where the old widower had barely finished the thirty days of mourning and already staged a wedding with a young widow, on whom he spent almost his entire fortune, thinking good luck had befallen him. In the end that luck turned — may it befall the enemies of Israel — into a noose.
The old man assumed that his little wife was a quiet one, a little dove. The fact that she did not snatch him up at once, and haggled with him and got a fat ketubbah [marriage contract] out of him, he did not take as a flaw — on the contrary, it proved she had brains. After all, he is an old man and she a young thing, so she wanted to secure herself. And once she had secured herself, he thought, he would be her god, and she would stand on tiptoe before him. After all, he had raised her from poverty to riches — she would appreciate it.
But soon after the wedding canopy he realised he had been mistaken in his reading. The supposedly quiet little dove, he quickly [?] found out, had a tongue — one of the genuine tongues.
He saw that she had cheated him of his birthright, and right after he put the wedding ring on her finger, she began to give him pepper to smell [to make his life bitter].
She began to "study Balak" with him [to curse and berate him], and in the loftiest style.
Everything he gave her was too little for her, and she always demanded more; she wanted the little plate from the sky [the moon], and she was literally the death of him.
The flat, she said, was no good for her; she was afraid to sleep in a house where there had been a "bar-minan" [a death].
She dreams, she complained, bad dreams — and she wished the bad dreams onto his head.
He had to give in and rented a flat as she wanted.
Then began a whole saga of furniture. She screamed, squealed and raised a racket that such furniture was fit for "that other woman", but not for her.
He did not want to become a laughing-stock to people, so he gave in to her on that too.
Did he have a choice, the old wretch? Having waded in so far, he waded on.
She had no desire, from the very first minute, to be a housewife at home. She wanted a maid from the start, and without a maid she did not want to cook.
He argued: really, who can afford to keep maids? She answered: did you take me for a cook? I wish you deep in the ground.
So they began to go and eat in a restaurant, and he ruined his stomach; once he was a minute away from death and they barely saved him.
After that he got used to the troubles. What else could he do? Starve?
She even began to nag him about an automobile with a chauffeur, but that she did not manage, and she had to let it go.
Other things, however, she achieved. She wanted clothes, hats and other luxuries — and the old man let himself be milked. She took the reins into her hands and drove the old horse. He who has the hundred has the say, and she made a monkey of him.
And if that was not enough, the young wife began going to dancings and coming home at dawn. When the old man protested, she laughed at him. Don't fool yourself, she said, with birds in your bosom; what do you think — that I'll go around with an old nag like you?
That is how she dealt him "snuff" [snubs] at every opportunity, and he suffered in silence. What better could he do? She has him in her paws, not he her.
And as she began, so she carries on to this day. She has already wrung him dry, brought him to poverty, and he has "neither cap nor penny" ["ni shapka, ni hroshi"].
Until now the old man was ashamed to pour out his bitter heart to anyone — what would it help him to confide his sad secret? Would anyone sympathise with him? They would tell him: whose fault is it? As you made your bed, so you must lie.
But now his patience has burst; he no longer has the strength to endure, and he has cast off the shame and begun to reveal the secret — what a bitter, dark affair he is going through.
He admits that he erred from the start, and he has a thousand regrets over his foolish deed.
Whoever has God in his heart — he begs — should have pity on his old years and help him crawl out of the trouble.
He did, he says in tears, a thing he should not and must not have done; he has already paid a hefty tuition fee, and he is no longer able to pay any more.
With this ends the story "He Has, She Has", which can and should serve as a lesson, as a moral, for others.
Perhaps you have some advice for that Jew who darkened his own old age? Perhaps you know a way for him to wriggle out of his tangle? Keep it in mind.
—

Oneg Shabbat. Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.]
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemot
The Portion
a) "Now these are the names of the children of Israel" (1:1)
"Because of four things Israel was redeemed from Egypt..
because they did not change their names..." (commentary).
"Called by their names upon the earth"
That is what they call themselves: Otto, Andrzej [?] or other non-Jewish names; only "upon the earth" — when they are about to be laid in the ground, when a tombstone is set up on their grave, when an "El male rachamim" is said for them — does one learn that their names were really Reuven, Avraham...
Luach Erez (Rav Moshe Sofer).
—
Why do our "Yahudim" [assimilated Jews] call Reuven — Otto?
Because the Midrash says that at the resurrection of the dead people will be awakened according to the alphabetical order of their names: Avraham, Binyamin, Gad, etc. They do not want to wait until their turn comes, until "Reuven!" is called. After all, R is one of the last letters; therefore they call themselves Otto, whose first letter is Aleph, so as to be the first to rise at the resurrection of the dead... Asam beshem [?].
b) "And the children of Israel were fruitful and increased abundantly" (ibid. 7)
Actually it would have been a curse, an addition to their sufferings: six in one womb, so many children in such bad times... The point, however, is "and waxed exceeding mighty" — that on top of it they were rich (me'od — mamon, money). Well, to the rich many children do no harm. Kli Yakar.
c) "Therefore they did set over them taskmasters" (ibid. 11)
The tax itself could still have been borne. The trouble lay only in the tax-masters — in the [?] bailiffs and tax officials, who constantly had to be given bribes in order to "buy oneself off"... Imrei Shefer.
d) "To afflict them with their burdens" (ibid.)
Not "to afflict them" but "to afflict him" — in the singular.
Because it means not only the Jews but Pharaoh too. He was also tormented... Collecting and grabbing money is indeed no small [?] torment...
And therefore the treasure cities that Pharaoh built from Jewish taxes were called "arei miskenot" — misken also means poverty, for there is no greater pauper than one who collects and grabs from the dead and the living. He always lacks, his coffer is always empty, and one must grab ever more to fill it... Olelot Efrayim.
e) "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied" (ibid. 12)
Because they were tormented, they multiplied and became a great Jewish people. Had they not been persecuted, they would have assimilated, and out of them would have grown a great Egyptian people... Rav Shlomo Kluger.
f) "Moses was grown, and he went out unto his brethren" (2:11)
When Moses went out among his brothers he sees "an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, one of his brethren" — an Egyptian beating a Jew, and around stand many Jews; "he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man", and not a single Jew stands up for his beaten brother. At first he thought this was from not knowing how to fight. But going out into the street the next day, he sees "two men of the Hebrews strove together" — Jews quarrelling and brawling among themselves; he is astonished and says: "Surely this thing is known" — ah, now I know your misfortune: heroes you are only when you brawl with your own brothers; but if one has to defend oneself against an Egyptian, you all become cowards and step aside... Binat La'itim.
g) "Put off thy shoes from off thy feet" (3:5)
1.
"Put off thy shoes from off thy feet."
Take off your locks (man'ul) from your habits [pun: na'al/man'ul, raglekha/regilut]; do not look with the eyes of everyday routine and habit, and you will see that "the place whereon thou standest is holy ground" — that wherever you turn and face there is only holiness. Our greatest enemy is habit.
Rabbi Moshe of Kobrin.
2.
"Put off thy shoes from off thy feet" —
Whoever walks in shoes does not feel the little stones lying in his way. Barefoot, however, one is sensitive even to the tiniest stumbling-blocks. That is what Moses was told: go barefoot through the world, feel the smallest stones beneath your feet...
Olelot [sic] Efrayim.
h) "Draw not nigh hither" (ibid.)
The Midrash says that Moses asked God for kingship ("that thou hast brought me hitherto"), and God did not give it to him, because "draw not nigh hither" (halom — this is kingship).
Over Jews one must not rule by force, by power... Rav Berish Meisels.
Haftarah.
i) "And ye shall be gathered one by one" (Isaiah 27)
"For nothing you were sold, and for nothing you will be redeemed" (the Midrash's words)
"For nothing you were sold" — because of baseless hatred you were sold, driven into exile. "And for nothing you will be redeemed" — and only through another "for nothing", through baseless love, through love and true (selfless) brotherhood will you live to see the redemption. If "ye shall be gathered one by one", then "in that day" will come. Ahavat Yehonatan.
j) "Before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jeremiah 1)
Once someone asks a beggar boy:
— How old are you?
— Seven.
— How long have you been begging?
— Eight years.
— How is that possible?

Jeremiah, too, was already a prophet in his mother's womb. Et Ratzon.
Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov (instalment 5)

Historical novel by Boris Maksimov
5
For readers who have not read the beginning of this historical, gripping novel, we give a summary of the chapters printed so far.
In the house of the banker Dimentshteyn in Petersburg a circle of rich Petersburg Jews gathered for a meeting. To the meeting came also the Jewish Baron Ginzburg, who passed on a confidential piece of news. That a divine service should be held[?] in the Great Synagogue for the health of the Russian naslednik [heir to the throne].
During the meeting the banker reports that shortly[?] [—] a harsh "an-talie"[?]: all Jews are to be expelled from Petersburg. The enemies of Israel say in [certain] circles[?] that if all the Jews are expelled, the naslednik will recover.
At the meeting it is decided to give gifts wherever needed, in order to buy themselves off from the decree, and the banker's daughter Sonia is delegated — she is friendly with the court lady Vyrubova, who should be able to [—] with the chief priest Feofan, the chief initiator of the decree.
At that moment Sonia comes in, bringing the news that the heir to the throne is seriously ill and that a "miracle-worker" has been brought in, the Siberian muzhik Rasputin.
Sonia takes the mission upon herself, and it is settled that a divine service be held in the Great Synagogue and that at the same time Sonia will meet Anna Vyrubova...
A week earlier, before the meeting assembled[?] in the house of banker Dimentshteyn, a strange wanderer came into the Petersburg monastery[?]. This was the Siberian muzhik Grigori Rasputin. The seminarists put various questions to him about the Godhead[?] and the "Trinity"[?].
Now read on:
Among the assembled seminarists there arose a quiet but noticeable excitement. Everyone's eyes were now turned to the wanderer. All were curious and eager to hear what on earth the wanderer would answer to the questions, which are highly complicated and for which one needs a theological education to find one's way in them. Would this simple peasant be able to answer the questions?
Rasputin, the muzhik from Siberia, remained calm. He sat quietly and with peasant attentiveness listened to the words of the young seminarist. His small eyes looked shiningly at the questioner, and not the slightest embarrassment could be noticed in him. He waited patiently until the other had finished everything he had to say. After the other had finished, he remained silent for a while. It looked as if he were going over in his mind the other's words, which he had just heard. And then came his answer. The answer was brief, contained only a few counted words; and what he answered appeared interesting and conventionally correct.
All were surprised; no one had reckoned that this simple muzhik, as he looks, would be able to answer so skilfully and correctly.
Now the attitude of the young seminarists toward the wanderer changed completely. Before, they had only made fun of him; now all felt a kind of respect and esteem for the man whom nothing could embarrass, who had a simple, serious and correct answer to everything he was asked. Now they no longer put questions to him to embarrass him, but because they very much wanted to hear his answers.
The students were so absorbed in their conversation with Rasputin that they did not notice how their senior teacher, the rector of the academy, "Father" Feofan, came up to their group, stood still and listened to the conversation going on.
The old archimandrite stood quietly and with his somewhat dreamy dark-blue eyes he observed the wanderer. Then his voice was heard. All fell silent at once. The students waited with tremendous curiosity to hear the conversation that would take place between their rector and the wondrous muzhik.
"Father" Feofan turned modestly to Rasputin:
— I want to ask you only one question, if you, little father, will permit me...
Rasputin raised his eyes and with kindly glances looked the archimandrite straight in the face. The archimandrite asked Rasputin's opinion about a verse in the Christian scriptures. Again Rasputin was silent for a while and then answered calmly and with assurance. He was not in the least embarrassed that the grey-haired archimandrite stood before him. His answer was again a clear and a fitting one. The seminarists saw clearly that the wanderer's answer had made a strong impression on "Father" Feofan. The archimandrite nodded his grey head and said:
— Correct, little father!... So it is, you have spoken correctly.
Then the archimandrite asked further questions. And Rasputin answered them in the same way as before. So they talked until they came to the problem of sin. The archimandrite wanted to know the wanderer's opinion about sin... In a very cautious, quiet tone he asked him:
— You have said, little father, that one must serve God through sin. But how is that possible? It is well known, after all, that our "Redeemer" and all our great saints of the Orthodox Church condemned sin, because it is the work of Satan?
This time Rasputin answered at once, without thinking even a single second. A strange expression appeared in his pale-blue eyes: submissiveness, assurance and skill. He answered:
— Certainly, little father! Our "Redeemer" and all our saints condemned sin, because it is Satan's work. Correct. But how, little father, can one drive Satan out of oneself if not through remorse and repentance? And how can you feel remorse and repent of your sins if you have not sinned? Ha[?], how?
He paused for a while. His eyes lost the submissiveness that had been in them until then. Then he began to speak again [sic punctuation]. But no longer as calmly and amiably as before. Now he spoke louder, more tumultuously, more vehemently and even with reproach. His words became angrier and angrier, until he finally cried out in anger:
— Leave alone your "holy" scriptures! "Holy" scriptures!.. I warn you, little father! Cast off from yourself the vain, useless work of always brooding in books and in the "holy" scriptures! Cast it off and you will stand close to God! Take life as it is. For: life itself alone is a gift from God... And let me tell you this: stop being afraid of sin. Stop preaching about how much a person must pray and how long he must fast in order to free himself of sin. Stop it! Sin. If there is in you a lust to sin — only by sinning will you overcome sin! Sin, and then you will feel remorse and repent of your sins and in that way drive Satan out of yourself... As long as you carry sin hidden inside you and, fearing sin, want to cover it up with fasting and prayer and talk about the "holy" scriptures — so long will you remain a hypocrite and a good-for-nothing. And that God hates! The impurity must be torn out, do you hear, little father? Sin must be sinned out to the end and Satan — driven away! That is the way to God! So God demands!
The students looked in fear at their rector. This wild talk, what the wanderer had said in such an angry tone without any respect for the old archimandrite, outraged them terribly. How does this muzhik dare to speak like that in the presence of their rector?... They were ready to throw themselves at the wanderer. But Feofan was silent. He remained quiet, surprised and lost in thought. He looked with wide-open, bewildered eyes. It seemed that he was thinking what to answer. Then the students too fell silent and waited with the greatest impatience for the archimandrite to give the Siberian muzhik a proper, sharp rebuff.
(To be continued).
The "Cooking Ladle" — in honour of the New Year

by Ben Amotz

New Year (a hymn).

Like a little
angel
comes to us
the New Year;
prettily dressed up,
and winged,
with a head
of curly hair.

It carries a smile
in its eyes,
carries within it
a greeting of comfort,
and its lips
entice
like a young woman's
to a kiss.

And the children of men
rejoice,
drunk with joy
amid the ringing of bells;
all go out
to meet it
with noise
and song.

Like a guest
from enchanted worlds
the New Year
comes along,
like the snow
that falls from heaven
without a speck
and pure.

At laid-out,
handsome tables
a crowd sits
in a café,
and the ear
is torn apart
by the noise
and shouting.

And the bellies
stand ready
to gulp down
every dish.
Suddenly there grows,
as if out of the earth,
an old
grey greybeard.

He stands quietly,
hunched over,
with his eyes
red from weeping,
looks in
on the merry tumult,
as though he
had heard nothing.

He wrinkles
his furrowed brow,
nervously strokes
his grey beard,
as if he were
a work of art,
marble-mute
and without a word.

Waiters carry
the dishes
and silver tableware
rings in time;
and with fat
chicken-corpses
stomachs
are stuffed.

All are
busy now;
each shows there
what he can do.
The gang stuffs
their gobs
with enthusiasm
and ardour.

And the old one,
as if frozen,
still stands
just so by the door.
Suddenly the New Year
cries out
insolently to the old one:
"Out of here!"

And the old one
twists his lips,
speaks like one
who speaks in his sleep:
"Wait, you insolent one,
nineteen thirty-two,
the very same end
as mine awaits you!"
A. L. Wolfson.
Prophecies for the Year 1932

by Amotzl.
If the "Agudah" [Agudat Yisrael] manages to win a majority in the Zagłębie kehillas, the newly elected kehilla councillors will rise in "resurrection of the dead" — if not, "I shall rule [rządzić] and business [?] will sit at home"...
—
This year there will be no bankruptcies, because there will no longer be anyone left to go bankrupt...
—
The Sosnowiec "Merchants' Association" on Piłsudski Street will once again sink into a sweet sleep, and at Kowalski's [street or place unclear] they will busy themselves with "stawki" [stakes/bets?]...
—
This year there will be a great bumper crop of... new charity societies, "recruitment months" [fund-raising drives], flower days and other calamities...
—
This year there will be a strong building movement. Jews will build... castles in the air, and the Kashrut Committee will busy itself with building the mikveh...
—
This year fresh accounts of debtors will be opened, the borders will be opened — pardon, I mean various academies — only the hearts of the Zagłębie magnates will once again be "closed"...
Have you heard?...

That the "Torah-loyal" in Będzin, seeing that the golem-public is getting wise to their "righteousness" over the Talmud Torah — have taken to their heels...
—
That a group of young people with big appetites said "kol chamira" [i.e. cleared it out like chametz] over the buffet at the "Hitachdut" ball and forgot to pay...
—
That kohanim may not walk on Kołłątaja Street in Będzin or on Modrzejowska Street in Sosnowiec, because in the shops there there are a lot of "corpses"...
—
That the Endeks [National Democrats] are boycotting Jewish shops, and our "intelligentkas" are doing the same...
—
That the "Muza" has reached its final goal and spread its art "over graves"...
—
That — and this is the main thing — from "all these things there is nothing to make Shabbat with"...

—

—

"Excuse me," the waiter says to him, "you can sit down, you know."
"Aha, if I had wanted to 'sit' [in prison]," the merchant answered, "I wouldn't have needed to run away from Sosnowiec..."
Return of a Lost Item.

Last Wednesday the president of the "Linat HaCholim" society, together with its entire board [zarząd], "got lost" in Sosnowiec; whoever has any information about the "lost item" should notify the gabbaim of the Sosnowiec Chevra Kadisha [burial society]...
—o—
Notice from the "Merchants' Association".
We have the honour to inform our esteemed members, male and female, that the lecture on tax matters, which was to have been given on Sunday, 27 December, at the general meeting, will probably take place at the next general meeting, which will be held in 3 years' time, i.e. in the year 1934...
The Board of the "Merchants' Association" in Będzin.
Będzin

Will we have new kehilla elections?
[Będzin — kehilla, elections.] This Sabbath [sic; apparently last Sabbath] a rumour spread through the town that the previous kehilla elections would be annulled and that new elections would take place.
As we learn, the news is still premature. The fact is that a decision has been taken among the Agudah leaders that, if they do not succeed in obtaining control, they will work actively towards having the elections annulled.
—o—
A small child saves the whole family from danger
[Będzin — carbon-monoxide accident.] Last Saturday at dawn a small child of the Sandzer[?] family in Unger's house began to cry. When the maid went over to the cot, she suddenly collapsed and remained lying unconscious. When Mrs. Sandzer and her sister saw this, they ran to the maid to rescue her, but the same thing happened to them too and they lost consciousness.
Luckily the child did not stop crying, which woke Mr. Sandzer from his sleep. Seeing the 3 women lying unconscious, he, already half-poisoned himself, flung open a window and began to call for help.
At the alarm neighbours came running and revived the three women.
As it turned out, the women had fainted from the dangerous fumes (carbon monoxide) that had escaped from the stove.
—o—
Daring theft in the town centre
[Będzin — theft.] On the night from Friday to Saturday thieves got into the shop window of Ptasznik's business on Kołłątaja Street and took out several pieces of merchandise.
—o—
Suffered a haemorrhage in a bathtub.
[Będzin — mikveh, accident.] Last Friday a young Christian woman rented a bath in the municipal mikveh. When the attendant saw that the Christian woman did not come out of her room at the appointed time, she became suspicious and forced open the door. Then she saw a terrible sight: the woman lay unconscious and blood was flowing from her mouth. At the attendant's cries many people came running, who tried by various means to stop the bleeding, but without result. Luckily Dr. Wasserzweig happened to be in the street at that moment; he gave her the necessary aid, and afterwards the patient was taken to the local hospital.
—o—
New Year greetings for the President of the State and the Government.
[Będzin — authorities.] In the office of the local starosta, the vice-starosta Mr. Izydorczyk will receive today, Friday, from 12 to 1 p.m., New Year greetings for the President of the State Mościcki and the Government from representatives of social and municipal institutions and organisations.
—o—
A gang of thieves and their accomplices arrested.
[Będzin — police.] The local police have uncovered the theft committed 2 weeks ago at the tobacco and cigarette wholesale warehouse (hurtownia) on Malapawska[?] Street. Together with the thieves, the receivers [of the stolen goods] were also arrested, among them some of "our brethren, the children of Israel".
—o—
From the general meeting of the "Merchants' Association".
[Będzin — Merchants' Association.] After a break of several years the board of the "Merchants' Association" called a general meeting of its members for Sunday, 27 December [1931]. It had been reckoned that in the holiday days, at the time when the Jewish merchant makes his reckoning of the soul, he would come to a meeting at which questions concerning the merchants' interests were to be discussed. It turned out quite otherwise: again the "small fish" came, and the "carp heads" — did not...
The meeting was opened by Mr. Rubinlicht, who invited Mr. M. Grundman to chair it, Messrs. Ch. W. Sztajghart[?] and P. Felzensztajn as assessors, and Mr. Rechtman as secretary.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, Mr. Rubinlicht took the floor and gave reports for the years 1928, 29, 30. According to the reports the association stood at the proper level, was always on guard and defended the merchants' interests before all the relevant authorities. Mr. Rubinlicht also said that the activity could have been much greater, but the blame lies with the members, who treat the Merchants' Association with apathy.
The report of the audit committee makes clear that the association has a deficit of almost 3,800 zł., and the committee puts forward the following proposals: 1) the old monthly pledges should be collected, 2) a debt-collection (vindication) bureau should be opened, and 3) the members should be charged a one-time levy.
On the 2nd proposal a discussion for and against developed. Mr. Kapłowicz is in favour of the proposal. Such a bureau — he says — will bring new life into the Merchants' Association.
Mr. Rubinlicht speaks against the proposal. It would be — he says — a moral decline for the association if such a soul-snatching bureau were opened.
Mr. Sandzer[?] moves that the matter be taken off the agenda, because there are several merchants present in the hall who regard such a bureau as a "salvation" for their debts; the proposal is referred to the new board.
Under the item "free proposals" Mr. M. Lewin[?] again presents his proposal that an aid fund for the members be created at the "Merchants' Association".
The proposal is referred to the board.
After the new budget of 8 thousand zł. was adopted, elections were held to replace 3 board members and 3 representatives.
As a result a small change took place. On the board, Mr. Markus Gertner was elected in place of Mr. M. Tenenbaum. As representatives, Messrs. Szaul Fridler and Majer Serkowicz[?].
—o—
General meeting of the "Gemilut Hesed" fund.
[Będzin — interest-free loan fund.] Next Wednesday, the 6th of this month [6 January 1932], a general meeting of the local G"Ch (gemilut hesed) fund will take place. As everyone knows, the fund plays an enormous role at the present moment. Hundreds of families are saved from ruin thanks to the fund. Therefore it is every person's duty to come to the meeting, at which questions concerning the further activity and expansion of the institution that bears the name — gemilut hasadim — will be discussed.
—o—
Lecture by Dr. Gottesdiener.
[Będzin — lecture.] This Saturday evening Dr. A. Gottesdiener will deliver, at the "Mizrachi" premises, the second lecture of the series "Maimonides and his book 'Mishneh Torah'".
—o—
From the League for Labour Palestine.
[Będzin — Zionism.] The new committee has constituted itself as follows: Sz. Rotenberg — chairman, Sz. Liwer[?] — vice-chairman, J. D. Majerowicz — secretary, and A. Hampel — treasurer.
The committee has embarked on a large membership campaign, which will last until the end of January this year.
—o—
General meeting of "Hachnasat Kalah" in Będzin.
[Będzin — bride-dowry society.] On Saturday night the annual general meeting of the "Hachnasat Kalah" society was held at the Talmud Torah premises. The president, Hersz Ber Goldblum, opened the meeting with about 90 members present and handed the chair to Mr. Jechiel Zauberman. Mr. M. L. Sendyszew[?] read the report, from which it emerges that during the year the society supported 61 brides with a sum of 2,415 zł., besides prayer shawls (talleisim) for 190 zł.
Then the following board was elected: Hirsz Ber Goldblum, Chawele Unger, Noach Ojazd[?], Herszel Sztajnkeler, Chaim Wekselman, Majer Ber Zyndorf, Fajgele Salcberg, Zelig Ajzenberg and Trane Fiszer. Representatives: Jehoszua Nunberg[?], Joel Lejb Jeżi[?], Jakob Ber Fiszel, Mendel Ropszyc and Jekel Rozenholc. Audit committee: Jechiel Zauberman, Fajgele Telner and Etsze Lejzowicz[?].

Sosnowiec — On Appointing a Temporary Rabbi / General Meeting of the Gemilut Hasadim Fund / 50 Poor Families Receive Clothing / New Commissioner of the Sickness Fund / Mass Meeting of Fruit and Colonial-Goods Merchants / Mass Meetings of Artisans / Stayed the Night... / Inspection in the Kehilla / A Tragic Incident

[Head of the Sosnowiec section; Sosnowiec — rabbinate, kehilla, relief, trade, artisans, accidents.] Sosnowiec
On Appointing a Temporary Rabbi
As we are informed, the local Agudah leaders have approached the voivode [provincial governor] with a request that Rabbi Englard be appointed temporary rabbi.
General Meeting of the G"Ch [Gemilut Hasadim, free-loan] Fund.
On Saturday night [26.12.1931], in the "Sala Angielski", under the chairmanship of Mr. Fridman, the annual general meeting of the local "Gemilut Hasadim" fund took place. The meeting aroused sufficient interest; about 150[?] members were present.
The report on the activity was given by the chairman, Mr. L. Wendel, who pointed out the great role of the fund, through which hundreds of families have been and are being saved from ruin.
The fund's report shows a surplus of 2000[?] zł. The administrative expenses amount to less than last year.
After the speeches[?] of the members[?] Zalcman[?], Weinreb and Hamburger, the report is debated. In the discussion sharp words are said at the address of the local "pnei" [notables], who stand aloof and do not show the slightest interest for the benefit of the institution.
After the budget is adopted, the existing board is re-elected, according to the wish of those assembled.
50 Poor Families Receive Clothing.
The women's section of the local "Dobroczynność" [charity society] has undertaken a sympathetic campaign: collecting old clothes and distributing them to poor families. The clothes collected so far were distributed this week to 50 families. But the number of needy grows from day to day. Therefore, whoever has old clothes should notify the wife of Dr. Grudziński.
New Commissioner of the Sickness Fund.
The current commissioner of the sickness fund, Mr. Wąsowicz, is leaving his post. In his place the general [G.] revision commissioner of the sickness funds in the Częstochowa and Sosnowiec districts, Mr. Tabolski, is being appointed.
Mass Meeting of Fruit and Colonial-Goods Merchants
A fresh misfortune now hangs over the heads of several hundred Jewish merchants: there is talk of a new monopoly, to be introduced on the import of fruit and colonial goods.
In this connection the "Merchants' Association" (Kowalska 2) is calling a mass meeting, which will take place next Sunday [3.1.1932] in the afternoon. Merchants from the surrounding towns and townlets, who because of the monopoly are threatened with losing their livelihoods, are to take part in the meeting.
Mass Meetings of Artisans.
This Saturday night [2.1.1932] a meeting of the tailors' guild will take place in its own premises.
Next Wednesday, the 6th of this month [6.1.1932], the long-awaited annual general meeting of all members takes place.
At the meeting important questions will be dealt with, among others also the founding of a mutual insurance fund for the members.
Stayed the Night...
In the evening an old Christian woman came in to the Marski family in Czeladź and asked to be allowed to spend the night there. Mrs. Marska granted her request, and the old wanderer lay down to sleep. The next morning the old woman was found dead on the bed.
Inspection in the Kehilla.
This week the vice-starosta, Mr. Mandyszewski, carried out an inspection [lustracja] of the kehilla books.
A Tragic Incident.
On the first day of the holiday [Yid. "chaga" — apparently Christmas, 25.12.1931] the following tragic incident happened here: the Będzin resident Zientek, walking home from his brother-in-law's, where he had not begrudged himself a glass of vodka, fell on the pavement. The fall was so unfortunate that Zientek was left dead.
Dąbrowa — 3 Days Before the Wedding the Groom Said "Nie pojadę"...

[Head of the Dąbrowa section; Dąbrowa — family life, matches, rabbinate.] Dąbrowa
3 Days Before the Wedding the Groom Said "Nie pojadę" [Polish: "I won't go"]...
Several years ago the young man G. went off to military service in Warsaw. There he got acquainted with a Jewish girl, with whom he began a romance, and between the couple a hot love flared up.
After finishing his military service the young man went back home to Dąbrowa. On taking leave he again swore eternal love to his beloved bride and promised her that he would write her letters often.
The Dąbrowa "powietrze" [Polish: air], however, cooled the groom's "hot love" a few weeks later, and he began to look for luck elsewhere...
When several weeks had passed and his bride in Warsaw had received no letter from her groom, she became uneasy and, together with her younger sister, decided to travel to Dąbrowa to her groom.
When she came to Dąbrowa the groom received her with great joy: "I had only just wanted," he said, "to write to you that you should come here; here we will settle down and live like a pair of little doves."
The bride agreed to this and began to prepare for the wedding, which was fixed for last Sunday [27.12.1931].
In the house where the wedding was to be held everything was boiling as in a cauldron; food and drink were prepared fit for a king — naturally at the bride's expense.
But it happened otherwise: 3 days before the wedding the groom suddenly vanished — "gone and no more".
After a long search the bride found out that her groom had regretted it at the last minute and had gone off to Będzin, where a "lucky match" is being arranged for him...
It goes without saying that the wedding did not take place. The bride, too, no longer wants such a groom, who has second thoughts at the last minute, and she now wants to be rid of him.
The matter has already come before the Będzin rabbinate, but no result has yet been reached, because the Dąbrowa groom keeps running away...
Donations Section for the Będzin Charity Society

[Będzin — charity; donations.] Donations Section
for the Będzin Charity Society.
The family of Dr. Potok donated 25 zł on the birthday of their daughter[?].
The family also arranged a supper for the children of the "ochronka"[?] [children's shelter / kindergarten].
Industrialist and Merchant!

[Sosnowiec — Zionism/trade.] Do you want your products and goods to be well advertised? Reserve a kiosk in good time at the great Eretz Israel Bazaar, which is taking place in Sosnowiec.
