Very Heavy Penalties for Employing Clerks and Workers Longer.

[Poland — labour law.] We draw attention to the fact that since 25 Listopad [November] a new law on working hours in commerce and manufacturing has come into force.
The new law introduces very heavy penalties for employing clerks and workers beyond the permitted time.
If it is found that a shop or establishment is active longer than is permitted, it will be punished the first time with 200 to 1.000 zł. or arrest of up to three months. If it is found a second time working and trading longer, one will be punished with unconditional arrest of 2 weeks to three months.
From now on the labour inspectors will check whether people are employed longer in commerce and manufacturing, and the penalties will be imposed by the labour courts.
The labour inspectors have already begun checking the shops and workshops to see whether people are working longer than is permitted.
We draw attention to the fact that under the new law one may not even employ the workers and clerks after closing time (fayer-ovnt) and pay them for it. For this too there is a heavy penalty and unconditional arrest. If one nevertheless wants clerks or workers to work after closing time, one must obtain a special permit for it from the labour inspector.

Lecture by Prof. Anisfeld at WIZO.

[Będzin — WIZO, lecture.] Next Tuesday, 5 January, at 8.30 in the evening, a social evening will take place in the Będzin WIZO's own premises with a lecture by Professor Anichfeld [sic; headline: Anisfeld] on the theme "The Destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish Fighters".
Admission is also permitted for non-members (women).

Ball of the Jewish Academics.

[Sosnowiec — academics.] On the 5th of this month the Sosnowiec "Ognisko" of the Jewish academics is holding a ball in the "Arlekin" hall.
The events held so far for the benefit of the Jewish academics have been duly supported by the Jewish public.

[Culture — amateur theatre.] The dramatic circle of the evening-courses society is staging tonight the well-known drama "Di Neveyle" (The Carcass) by Peretz Hirschbein.

Arrest of a Co-operative Manager.

[Bobrowniki — crime.] On the order of the prosecutor, the manager (kierownik) of the workers' co-operative in Bobrowniki has been arrested.
The manager is accused of committing embezzlement to the sum of 20 thousand zł.

From the Katowice Ice Rink.

[Sport — ice hockey.] On Sunday and Tuesday two interesting hockey matches took place at the Katowice ice rink between "Canada" and "Poland". Annual meeting of the Będzin Gmilus-Khesed (free-loan) fund

Last Wednesday the annual general meeting of the free-loan (G״Ch) fund in Będzin took place in its own premises.
Among those assembled one could for the first time see several householders from among the so-called „pney“ („notables“) of the town. There is a supposition that the „big ones“ too are afraid of tomorrow and are ready to work for the benefit of the institution, which is an important factor at the present moment.
The chair was handed to Mr. M. Lewin, with Messrs. Wygodzki, Gitler, Krakowski, Weisenberg as assessors and M. Landau as secretary.
Mr. Bończykowski[?] delivered a report, from which it emerges that the number of members who pay the „vonungs[?]“-instalment (repayment) has shrunk enormously, and in general the prestige of the institution has fallen among the well-to-do members. Mr. B. points to a series of reasons that led to this situation. As one of the „reasons“ [!] he also counts „the opposition of the Zaglembier Tsaytung to the institution“.
At the item „report of the audit committee“ a sharp discussion began around the motion of Mr. Wygodzki, who declared that the meeting was not legally competent because the majority of the audit committee had not signed the minutes of the audit.
The discussion took on a stormy character, and sharp criticism was voiced of the dictatorial management of the chairman, Mr. Bończykowski.
In the end Wygodzki's motion obtained a minority and the meeting proceeded to the further items.
The fund's report was delivered by the secretary, Mr. Montag. It emerges that in 1931 the fund granted loans to 744 members for a total of 149,079,62 zł. The general capital grew during the year by 790,30 zł.
A discussion on the reports followed, in which Messrs. Liwer, Szpigelman, Frachtzweig, Rozensaft, Hampel, Fajgenblat took part, as well as the president of the Sosnowiec free-loan fund, Mr. Zendel, who spoke about the fund and put forward a motion that in future the fund should give no charity handouts.
After adoption of the provisional budget of 23.000 zł., the elections to the board took place.
The result is as follows:
Board: L. Bończykowski, M. Hampel, M. Rozensaft, J. Rozynkier, L. Rubinlicht, J. M. Kurland, Z. Lemberg, B. Rembiszewski, J. Goldfeld, A. Trapawer[?], Ch. Ch. Steinhart, J. Wygodzki, A. D. Bolimowski, B. Aronow and J. Granek.

This Year's Sylvester in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — society.] This year's Sylvester (New Year's Eve) in Zagłębie stood under the sign of the severe crisis.
The youth, which used to travel year in, year out to Katowice in order to spend the "holy" Sylvester holiday merrily — this year had its "holiday" disturbed because of the ban by the Katowice authorities, who forbade every public entertainment.
According to "tradition" the Sylvester celebrations were held this year in a modest way in private apartments, where friends and acquaintances gathered and made merry[?] for several hours over a glass of drink.
In the streets one could notice an interesting phenomenon: Jewish passers-by wished one another, no less than — to make the distinction — at Rosh Hashanah, "May you be inscribed for a good year".
The Będzin "Hakoach" kept up its tradition and arranged a Sylvester celebration for its members, even if not with all the "rules", for in a pinch one makes do without masks too...
In Sosnowiec the Sylvester "holiday" was celebrated in a number of private homes, or, as the modernists call it, "bibkes" (parties).
At one such "bibke" it even came to a brawl between the "in-laws" [i.e. the hosts] and the moralizers.
It happened like this: into the apartment of Mr. M. came several members of the Sosnowiec "Hashachar" with the aim of collecting money for the Keren Kayemet.
"Excuse us, young people," declared one of the Sylvester "in-laws", "this is a private 'bibke', and therefore it is not permissible to collect money for Zionist purposes."
The members of "Hashachar", however, took no notice of this argument; on the contrary — they said — if you are celebrating Sylvester, we must fulfil our mission at just such a Jewish festivity.
From the exchange of words they passed to deeds, and one "treated" the other in honour of the holiday...
The Fighting Methods of the "Agudah" around the Kehilla (A Letter from Olkusz)

[Olkusz — kehilla.] As your correspondent has already reported, new kehilla elections took place 2 weeks ago, in which the National Bloc received 5 mandates and the "Agudah", together with the rabbi's side, only 2 mandates.
Owing to this, the "Agudah" together with the rabbi again used[?] their earlier fighting methods against the majority, but the new means surpass every expectation and arouse strong agitation and almost disgust in the whole town.
The same person who had tried hard to invalidate the first elections keeps sending "little letters" full of lies, even to invalidate the elections, or eventually to break up the strong National Bloc.
Last week the first meeting took place, with the aim of electing a chairman. The "Agudah" with the "rabbi's man", seeing that they were in the minority, did indeed leave the meeting "demonstratively" together with the well-known rabbi, declaring: "Do widzenia [see you] at the starostwo [district office]!" And so indeed it was. The very next morning the writer of these lines was summoned to the starostwo, where it was explained to him that, since the National Bloc is bound by an "issur" (ban), the new kehilla members will not take over the kehilla as long as the "issur" exists, and so it must be.
This "fine" deed stirred up the whole town even more, because the g[aon] rabbi, by his "demonstrative" leaving of the meeting, clearly showed his consent to such a settling of Jewish affairs; whereas when a case occurs where one must intervene on behalf of a Jew who was innocently punished with 7 days' arrest, then the g[aon] rabbi does not find it his duty to intervene. Yet that is his obligation! Must a rabbi choose only the "Agudah" in order to gain power over the majority?!
Householders of Olkusz! Now the word on this matter is yours!
P. Sh.

Just Don't Let Ourselves Sink! — The state of the Jewish hospital. — What does it look like? — What is being done at the present serious moment?

The state of the Jewish hospital. — What does it look like? — What is being done at the present serious moment?
For some time we have not heard in what state the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec finds itself, and since we hear nothing, it is a sign that things are good and everything is going properly, and that what can be done remains, of course, satisfactory.
But now cries of despair have reached our ears that the situation there is not rosy[?] and that material help is needed as quickly as possible, so that things do not approach a catastrophic state. Put simply, this means that money is needed as quickly as possible in order to continue the normal activity of this necessary institution for the sick.
It would be worthwhile to take stock and to want to understand that a hospital cannot be compared with any other charitable institution, which can measure its expenses according to the income it receives. So that as soon as it has less income, it immediately reduces its expenditure, and fewer people receive support. Quite different is it [printed: „in“] at the hospital. Here there can be no talk of reducing expenses. For as soon as a sick person is admitted, he must receive his cure; all means must be applied to keep the patient alive. Here one cannot take into account that there is a shortage of money, so that the operation, which costs so-and-so much, should not be performed on the unfortunate person from whom the hospital administration gets nothing, or at best gets so little that it has to add to it from its own. After all, this concerns the life and fate of human beings, on whom no irresponsible experiments may be made.
We are not familiar with the foundations on which the hospital now exists and how the institution maintains itself. But one thing is enough for us, which cannot impress us, and that is the system of taking the collection box [pushke], running around with it from door to door and knocking everywhere: dear Jews, give money! Merciful sons of the merciful, help the poor sick, do not let them fall and do not let the big padlocks be hung[?] on the doors of the hospital building! This slogan is a sickly one and we must not let it prevail. Such a manner of management, this system, is rotten and outdated through and through, and we must see to avoid it, because it would amount to begging and humiliation, which befits neither the management nor this kind of institution. Such a manner of management would mean walking on crooked paths, on paths overgrown with thorns, on which it is easy to slip and break one's neck. And we must take care not to allow, God forbid, this catastrophic level to be reached.
On the contrary, quite the contrary: we must take all possible means to support our charitable institutions, which are necessary to us; only the support must be such that it does not bring shame upon us, that it does not degrade the honour of the society and of its leaders.
The Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is, so to speak, a good brand; it enjoys sympathy not only among Jews but also among non-Jews. It is known that the patient is treated there conscientiously and that care is taken that he recover as quickly as possible. We, the Jews of Zagłębie, have no other such hospital in our whole region, and therefore it is indeed no news that Jews come here to be cured not only from our region but even from more distant towns and townlets. This is therefore the best proof that there is sympathy both for the directing doctors and for the managing authority, who understand that a hospital is not some little shop whose premises one can change every day. As said, the leading elements know what responsibility they bear, fulfilling their responsible tasks.
So the hospital is properly established, and people also have confidence in it; it is surely a pity that it should have to be degraded to the kind of begging that has unfortunately become so very fashionable.
If we have awareness, if we understand at what height an institution such as a people's hospital must stand, we must fight with every possibility not to let it be degraded to a sad state.
Today, for example, we are content when we see how well-to-do people are operated on there for money together with the poor, who are maintained at the expense of the town or of the hospital. The poor patient is then sure that he is looked after equally with the well-to-do patient, because he knows that he has the same doctor and surgeon and nurse as the well-to-do Jew who pays for everything. The poor unfortunate then has the belief that he is in an institution that can heal him and make him well. And that means a great deal, a very great deal.
The Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is therefore one of the most essential necessities, so that we must see to it that it has the possibility to function normally and does not have to appeal at every opportunity to the Jewish citizens: merciful sons of the merciful, we are about to go under, we need your support, we demand that you save us from a catastrophe. It is precisely this alarm-raising that makes us sickly and abnormal[?]; we must not treat in such a way institutions that must exist among all normal peoples and in every normal country.
And therefore we must begin to take care that the hospital be provided with a normal budget, so that year by year provision is made in good time as to where the means to cover the expenses will come from. A hospital must not stand on chicken legs, and that it should exist on miracles and on the wind is no calculation either.
We do not want now to enter into debates and say whether the hospital should be maintained by the Jewish kehilla, or by obligations[?] of the town's citizens, or perhaps even by the magistrate [municipality]. It is not about this that we want to say our word today. Now we want to establish only one thing: that the hospital's budget must be fixed in advance for a whole year, so that one should not have to run with the collection box after money at the most pressing moment, and so that, as soon as one does not manage to obtain the support that had been foreseen, ruin should [not] threaten.
We understand that there may be a year when there are more well-to-do patients, from whom the hospital earns, and conversely such patients on whom the hospital loses. But more or less one can surely calculate all this and know on what budget it will be necessary to work.
One of the most important things, then, is to work under normal conditions, and the town must know the responsibility it must bear towards its institution for the sick; it goes without saying that there are no two opinions here, that the institution must be supported with dignity — only one must know in what manner.
It would therefore be advisable for the hospital administration to convene, at the first opportunity, a general meeting at which it would give a report of its activity, and at which a resolution would also be adopted on the mode in which it should continue its useful work. This is one of the most important things that ought to be done for the benefit of the institution.
It is important that the public should see what the institution accomplishes both for the well-to-do patients who need medical help and for the poor patients who must be cured at the public's expense, and that a decision should indeed be taken there on the manner in which the hospital is to secure its future budget.
A normal institution must be established on a sound foundation. That is what is important both for the healthy and for the sick.
Dr. Papuri.

Heard and Seen.

[Będzin — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

At the trial...
I was at the trial. Not the "Centrolew" trial [the Brest trial of the opposition leaders], but the trial in which we too are in-laws. We too "sat" on the defendants' bench and heard out the indictment, the defence and the main thing:
— the verdict...
Sitting in the courtroom I was forced to wage a stubborn fight with my eyes and with the sensation[?]...
My eyes in fact wanted to be shut... They do not want to see — so they argued — how "grown-up children play", and my imagination wanted to carry me far, far away, into a children's world...
After a longer "fight" imagination prevailed and "carried" me off to a large courtyard. A great many children were gathered there (in any case more than at the trial), passing their free time with various games.
Of the games, the one that interested me most was the game called "Emperors"...
The greatest "emperor" was a boy barely 12–13 years old. This little "tsutsik" [kid] commanded his friends and handed out titles among them: you, Moshe, will be the Russian emperor; you, Chaiml — an Austrian emperor; Gimpel — a general; Shmelke — a judge [sendzhe, Polish sędzia?], and so on and so forth.
Then a "great battle" took place between the "kingdoms", but without victims and without cripples. On the contrary: after the war each "emperor" gave a two-grosz coin ["tsveyer"], and with the capital collected they bought themselves sweets.
I got my normal senses back precisely when the defence counsel was speaking, and when I heard the verdict I was again reminded of the anecdote:
A matchmaker wanted to match the son of a rich butcher with the daughter of a Hasidic Jew, but one who had come down in the world, poor man.
— What does the in-law do for a living? — the bride's father asked the matchmaker.
— He deals in cattle.
— Live ones or slaughtered ones?
— Sometimes, when times are hard, he sells meat too.
— Then say so straight away — cries the bride's father — say it, then, that the groom's father is a butcher.
— Why rob simple Jews of their Sabbath rest with trials[?]? Why put on comedies[?] in the "form" of judges, prosecutor, experts, defence counsel — just say openly what you want, namely:
— "The whole Jewish press from right to left should go under, and only an organ should appear that will serve the interests of the Left Poalei Zion"...

"Gevalt", a stool...
— What is new at the Talmud Torah? Is anything substantial being done by the "Sanacja" [reorganisation] commission so that the situation of the Talmud Torah should improve? With this question we turned to one of the members of the commission.
But instead of a practical answer to the questions he tells the following:
At the time when the society "Mefitsei Haskalah" [Disseminators of Enlightenment] became active, a rabbinical conference took place at which it was discussed how to save Judaism, which is being burned[?] by the free-thinking elements, by the sinners who hide under the cloak of "Mefitsei Haskalah"...
At the assembly there was also a rabbi who suffered badly from the "Jewish illness" [a euphemism for haemorrhoids], and while the chairman was delivering a fiery sermon that Judaism was in danger, the rabbi was seized by severe pains and cried out:
— Jews, save me, gevalt!...
— What, Rebbe, does Judaism hurt you so much? — the chairman asks him.
— Judaism-shmudaism, give me a stool here quickly, gevalt, it hurts...
From the same "illness" — says my informant — suffer also the several "Torah-loyal" ones, who raised an alarm that "the Philistines are upon you, Israel", that the Talmud Torah is in great danger, that the sinners, the free-thinking elements, want to seize the institution and introduce there the study of Chumash bareheaded...
But no sooner had the gentlemen succeeded, by such cynical means, in getting power into their hands than they grew tired of the work, so that now it turns out that with all that squealing they were only after the same thing as that rabbi: to get quicker
— a stool...

The wanderers...
On Friday at dusk you meet them, the "wanderers", the na-ve-nadniks...
For decades they "wandered" in the town synagogue [the Shtotishe Shul]. They held very fine functions there, were attached to it heart and soul, drew all their spiritual delight from the "small sanctuary" of the synagogue. Sometimes they refreshed themselves with a good sermon, fine singing and the like.
— Where are you going? You are, after all, a regular worshipper at the synagogue — I ask one of the na-ve-nadniks...
— Where? To a minyan. It even costs me money and health, but in the synagogue it is already impossible to pray. The lawlessness there has already gone beyond all bounds... The old-time decency is gone; the "prostak" [Polish: boor] who did not dare utter a word out loud — is today the one who sets the tone, voices opinions on every question; even when the shammes announces a notice from the rabbinate, the new strongman says "no"...
Listening to this, I recalled the words of the Agudah parnas [community councillor of Agudat Israel], who at a session of the Będzin kehilla council shed crocodile tears over why the kehilla had assigned a sum of 40 thousand gulden [złoty] for painting the synagogue...
Only today do I understand the meaning of that criticism: the parnas was far-sighted; he understood already then that it was not worth having the painting of the synagogue cost so much money, because "the synagogue worshippers are to be dragged thereby into the homely brawl, into the hypocritical fight being waged for the sake of the righteous victory...
And the prophecy has come true: long-time worshippers are leaving the synagogue and seeking a remedy elsewhere. This was foreseen, because "what one whitewashes[?], that one cuts"...

By this merit...
On New Year's Eve [Sylwester] I suddenly heard the sound of a shofar.
— What is this? Nowy Rok [the civil New Year] is surely not Rosh Hashanah, so who is blowing the shofar?
Later, when I went out into the street, I found out that my neighbour Menachem Mendel was celebrating Sylwester.
— What connection does the shofar have with Sylwester? — I ask him, Menachem Mendel himself.
— I am — he explains to me — a pious Jew, but last Rosh Hashanah I was more pious than ever; I tore the heavens apart with my prayers: — perhaps He will have mercy. And the outcome you can see for yourself: it is already four months since the Days of Awe, and things have never yet been as bitter for me as now, and... on the other hand, the Jews for whom Sylwester is also no trifle ["not a dog"]... they are actually doing not at all badly. So I thought to myself — one has to try doing the same... But since I am no great scholar in the laws of Sylwester, I did it the Jewish way:
— A new year is coming? Blow the shofar; perhaps things will get a little better, perhaps
by this merit...
The Cause of the Economic Decline of Polish Jewry

[Poland — economy and the Jews; article.] By Docent Dr. J. Rosenblatt.
The world is already living in a new calendar year. In every field a balance sheet of the past year is being drawn up in this connection. Everywhere and for everyone the balance turns out bad.
We Jews would have had no complaints at all against fate, had the past 12 months not been kinder to us than to others. One lives in the same world, and one must[?] be subject to the changes that take place in it. When things are bad everywhere, they must be bad for us too. When things are good for everyone... it is precisely here that our peculiar situation really begins, which consists in this: that we are always worse off than everyone else, and [when][?] even everyone else is well off, we are still badly off.
The last years have been rich in such unusual events that it is especially hard to understand what is actually happening in the world. The most famous scholars, the greatest politicians, the cleverest practical minds no longer find their bearings in current events. People argue about the causes of the present decline and cannot find the means that are capable of removing it. On one point all agree, namely, that people have been seized by a psychosis, i.e. a certain state consisting of boundless pessimism. It is clear that in such a situation the weaker suffers most; since we are everywhere and always the weakest of the weak, we feel the catastrophe more than anyone.
The situation of the Jews has lately become bad in all countries. It grows worse from day to day. The process, taking place since the war in almost all countries, of pushing the Jew out of his economic positions has now taken on a lightning-fast tempo and is assuming ever more threatening forms, the closer one gets to Eastern Europe.
The situation of the Jews in America and in England has become bad; in Germany it is still worse; and in the countries lying on the eastern side of Central Europe it is no longer bearable. This is not only because antisemitism is stronger here. We must in general beware of ascribing all our troubles to antisemitism. That only obscures reality for us and takes away the possibility of assessing the situation clearly. Whoever has no possibility of giving himself a clear account of what is happening now will find it harder to find the right way.
Self-evidently, hatred of the Jew plays a very important role in our life, but this hatred is today only a consequence of the social and of the economic situation. Our means of livelihood, the possibilities of earning a piece of bread, are being taken from us not only because we are hated; rather, we are hated because we occupy — in the opinion of our enemies — economic positions that belong to them alone.
There no longer exists today the former religious or unconscious antisemitism with which the masses were once brought up. There is no longer any so-called emotional antisemitism. Today we are dealing with a coldly calculating, conscious antisemitism of the head.
None of us is so naive as to persuade himself that the Endek [National Democrat] hates us more because his heart and soul are different from those of the other Poles in the country. The Endek only says it out openly; he is not ashamed to say aloud that he wants to push us out of all economic positions in order to take them over himself.
Toward the other nations in Poland one does not behave this way, because they are stronger than we are. Them one fears; us nobody fears, because there is nobody who would stand up for us.
This is the main cause of the events that took place in the past year in Poland.
This is the reason for the boycotts that one is now trying[?] to carry out. Herein also lies the reason why, at the trials concerning the recent student excesses, we are the first to be seated in the dock.
The prospects for our economic future in Poland are even worse because the present ruling factors consist of elements with a socialist worldview in the economic sense.
Monopolies, étatisme, the taking over by the state and municipal administrations of ever more branches of the economy from which the Jew was able to draw his livelihood — these are all elements of the socialist program. After all, all of today's decisive factors once belonged to the Socialist Party.
The disputes between the two sides are more political in character. In the economic field, however, Moraczewski and Daszyński still stand today on the same platform.
When one states the catastrophic situation of Polish Jewry, which in the past year assumed the most horrifying forms, one must take into account the actual conditions mentioned, in which we live. Therein consist the peculiar, specific conditions of Jewish life in Poland.
The business situation may undergo various changes; the present economic state will surely not last forever. But the basic conditions that lead to the pauperization of Polish Jewry will not disappear so quickly. Who knows whether in time they will not assume forms still harsher for us.
Only from this standpoint must the Jewish situation be considered. Clearly. And without illusions.
Only in this way can one try to find a way out of the difficult situation. Only in this way can one seek means of radically changing the hopeless situation and of resisting the complete economic ruin of the broadest strata of the Jewish people.
How Do the Zagłębie Merchant, Shopkeeper and Artisan Live? — What Does a Stationer Say?

[Zagłębie — economy and trade; interview.] How do the Zagłębie merchant, shopkeeper and artisan live? What does a stationer say?
"Bad, bad" — that is what every shopkeeper answers right at the start of the conversation. The only difference between one branch and another is that the causes of the bad business conditions are different everywhere.
Here is what a stationer (paper dealer) told me:
Our branch kept itself going on single-item retail ["eyntsl-prin" — doubtful reading]. A child, a pupil, would come in to buy an exercise book, a pen nib, a pencil. True, the takings were in groszy, but grosz upon grosz — and something was left over for the shopkeeper.
Lately this trade has been pushed out. In all the "powszechne" schools [state elementary schools] and even in the private gymnasia there are "little shops" of their own, where the pupils are sold all kinds [?] of writing materials.
The pupils have to buy in these little shops, which prepare everything to a fixed pattern, as the teacher orders.
"Where is the merchandise for these little shops bought?"
"No Jewish shopkeeper gets any trade from it, because the writing materials are supplied to the schools by the 'Polish Teachers' Cooperative Bookshop'. The critical situation of the private shopkeepers is very serious, and many of them have had to suspend payments."
"How are sales of other articles?"
"Apart from the said writing materials for the school youth, commercial ledgers once took second place in the paper trade. But today these sales too have fallen to a minimum. That is understandable, because there are few big businesses, and there is nobody to keep official account books; even the smaller kinds, such as notebooks and account booklets, sell very little.
Luxury articles, such as writing sets, fancy albums and the like, find no buyer at all, because the public cannot afford any luxuries today.
The paper trade also suffers from the fact that other haberdashery (galanterie) and tobacco shops also sell various paper products and writing materials."
"What is the situation in the wholesale trade?"
"The competition is tremendous; the local shopkeeper cannot withstand the competition of Warsaw and Kraków."
"What about prices?"
"The big paper manufacturers have formed a syndicate [cartel]; so prices compared with last year have not fallen much.
On the whole prices have been reduced by 10–15 per cent; wrapping paper has become cheaper by a full 30 per cent.
In this branch the bill of exchange (weksel) dominates even more strongly: although the manufacturers demand part in cash, the shopkeeper has to borrow entirely on bills."
At the end of the conversation the shopkeeper added that it is worth mentioning two articles that are still in strong demand: playing cards and bill-of-exchange forms.
Although because of the raised excise a pack of cards has become dearer by 2–3 zł., demand nevertheless remains the same.
Y. R—t.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'era)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Va'era
The Portion
—o—
a) "And I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac and unto Jacob" (Ex. 6:3)
"Alas for those who are gone and are no longer found; I have cause to lament the death of the Patriarchs" (Rashi).
Someone once boasted of a certain town that buried in it lay the Taz, the Magen Avraham, Rabbi Akiva Eger and other great men. People looked at him in astonishment: the Taz is buried in Lemberg [Lwów], the Magen Avraham in Kalisz, Rabbi Akiva Eger in Posen [Poznań].
The man answered: No. In Lemberg they still study the Taz, in Kalisz they still study the "Magen Avraham", but here with us the Taz lies buried — nobody looks into him, nor into the Magen Avraham, nor into Rabbi Akiva Eger's books; so they lie buried here with us...
"If you do not walk in the ways of the Patriarchs," God argued to Moses, "then they are indeed buried... Alas for those who are gone... Whoever leaves successors behind never dies, for his spirit lives." Arono shel Yosef.
—o—
"This is the law, when a man dies in a tent" (Num. 19:14).
A tzaddik is likened to a Torah scroll, which everyone kisses and embraces[?], because it stands quietly in the Holy Ark and demands nothing of anyone, says not a word... A tzaddik too is beloved "when he dies in a tent" — when he rests in the "ohel" [tomb], when he is already in the World of Truth and can no longer rebuke anyone; then he is revered by all...
—o—
b) "And I will rid you out of their bondage" (ibid. 6)
To be a slave to a rich master is only half a misfortune. But you will be slaves to poor nations who will want to grow rich only off you... and that is the worst misfortune of all. "Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the Lord shall send against thee, in hunger and in thirst, and in want of all things" (Deut. 28:48): your enemy, under whom you will be, will be in want of everything, and he will want to build himself up out of you...
Bina le-Itim.
—o—
c) "And I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel" (ibid. 5)
"Be gracious unto me, O Lord, for I cry unto thee all the day" (Ps. 86:3).
We argue before God: after all, we will weep and cry to You so long that in the end You will have to listen to us, "for I cry unto Thee all the day" — You will not get rid of us anyway; therefore "be gracious unto me, O Lord": help us soon, then, and spare us tears...
Arvei Nahal.
—o—
d) "These are the heads of their fathers' houses" (ibid. 14)
God ordered Moses to turn to the Jews, that they should prepare for the Redemption. Moses answered Him: "Behold, the children of Israel have not hearkened unto me" — the Jews are still impure[?], they are not yet elevated and refined enough for Redemption. God says to him: "These are the heads of their fathers' houses" — the trouble is that the heads, the leaders themselves, are also not elevated enough for Redemption; and even Phinehas, who reached the highest level of a leader, lacked something! With him the "shalom" had a broken vav, chopped off a little... And so it is no wonder that the children of Israel did not want to be redeemed...
Mi Shalah.
—o—
e) "And he cast down his rod... and it became a serpent" (7:11)
"Any Torah scholar who does not avenge and bear a grudge like a serpent is no Torah scholar."
The brazen serpent united in itself two opposite qualities: it healed, and it also bit when necessary. And a Torah scholar too must possess that quality.
Moses was pure kindness [hesed], goodness. That is why his first miracle was with a serpent — to show that he could sometimes bite too. Not only hesed but also gevurah [severity]...
Degel Mahaneh Efrayim.
—o—
f) "And the blood was throughout all the land of Egypt" (ibid. 21)
"From the plague of blood Israel became rich" (Midrash Rabbah).
The Gemara says in "Bava Batra": "Poverty in a man's house is harder than fifty plagues." Well then, even if one counts like the Tannaim and finds that the Egyptians received in Egypt a full fifty plagues, it is still no worse than Jewish poverty... Therefore the Jews had to become rich, so that it should not be said that they were smitten equally with the Egyptians...
Zera Shimshon.
—o—
g) "And the flax and the barley were smitten" (9:31)
Coins have in Hebrew the name "dinarim" [dinurim], which also means: "di-nur" (of fire), because money is like fire. One cannot manage without it — one must have it. But if one comes too close to it, one gets scalded...
"And fire flashing up amidst the hail"...
"Flax and barley" — these are the hard ones (see Rashi), and usually the rich are meant by that. They did not want to give in easily, therefore they were broken altogether. The late crops, on the other hand — the low, poor masses — bent easily and gave in; therefore "they were not smitten": what is pliant never breaks...
Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
Haftarah
h) "When I shall have gathered the house of Israel from the peoples" (Ezekiel 28)
The Jews among the nations are like the heart among the limbs of the body: the sickest of all and the healthiest of all.
Kuzari.
—o—
Lord Beaconsfield (Benjamin Disraeli) presided over the Congress of Berlin in the year 1879 [sic], which was convened to make peace between Russia and Turkey. Lord B. proposed that in the countries freed from the Turkish yoke the Jews should receive equal rights, pointing to how good it is in England, where Jews have equal rights. To this a Romanian delegate replied that one cannot compare English Jews with Romanian ones, who are not worthy of equal rights.
To this Disraeli replied:
"There are no bad Jews and good Jews at all; every country has such Jews as it deserves"...
—o—
i) "And I will put hooks in thy jaws" (ibid.)
The loudmouths will be struck; they will not be able to bark so much... for the barking against us from all sorts of "Egypts" hurts[?] no less than the bondage.
Misgeret Hashtar[?],
Pini Ba'al Lashon. “Re-smelted Coins”.

[Feuilleton — morality, charity and old ideas in new form; the column "Pini the Wordsmith" (Pini Ba'al Lashon).] Pini Ba'al Lashon.
What does one do with worn-out coins, the kind nobody wants to take in hand any more, that no longer have the value they once had?
Such coins, as everyone knows, are taken back to the smelting house and re-smelted into the newest forms, and are let out into the world again, and they go round once more, until they grow old again, become worn out.
And after that the same will be done with them again. The old metal in new forms!
But make no mistake, my friends, I am not going to talk to you here about plain coins, about money.
It is really not fair to talk to a blind man about light, or to a deaf man about music; and penniless as we are now, it is simply a sin to start talking about coins.
Although the old Hasidim once had a different custom: when there was no brandy, they at least talked about brandy; but we cannot rise to their level!
No, we are not talking here about any money, but about something higher.
We are talking about concepts, about values, about ideas.
Just as we delight in brand-new, shiny coins that come into our hands, and we do not know that these may be the old, worn-out coins of former times that we ourselves once threw away, and that they were re-smelted into new forms, — so we also often delight in new concepts and ideas that we hear, and we do not know that these are the very same old ones of former times that we threw away, and that they were re-smelted into new forms.
———
And here we have yet another new invention of recent times, which is also no new one, but an idea re-cast in a new shape.
They have now invented a kind of machine that will be able to distribute charity in such a way that the giver and the receiver will not need to meet eye to eye.
He who can give will be able to fill the machine with food or with money, and he will set it for certain hours of the day; and he who needs to take will go up to the machine, give a handle a turn, and get what he needs.
The idea of charity is, after all, a very old one. Only the Hebrew name is almost the most beautiful that has been fitted to it. "Tzedakah" means justice. And the true concept of justice, even according to the latest social commentators, is that he who has something must give a part to him who has nothing.
That does not mean that one must give out of pity, because one cannot bear to see someone suffer. No, that is egoism, because by it one only wants to ease one's own heart. One must give, according to the old Jewish concept, out of "justice". For when someone has something to give, it is no longer his own, but the other's, who has not, — and therefore he must "give it over"; that is what "tzedakah" means.
But the pious of former times understood that giving charity publicly is not the right way. For the giver earns honour for himself by it, and the receiver suffers humiliation [lit. "bloodshed", i.e. shaming] by it, and so out of the good deed comes downright evil. And the receiver, who really cannot humble himself[?] and cannot bear the shame, does not take, and goes on suffering.
And that is why the idea of "matan beseter" [giving in secret] arose, giving concealed, so that the giver and the receiver should not see one another. And among us that was the finest virtue of giving charity in such a manner.
And how many beautiful tales we have about such kinds of charity, in which great tzaddikim would disguise themselves in the middle of the night as peasants and go, "as it were", to buy food and heating for poor people on credit..
And how many legends were created among us about "Elijah the Prophet", who came to poor people and brought them all good things: and that was merely the work of true "secret givers", who did not want to shame the receivers...
And that is why we say that today's new invention of the machine, through which one will be able to give charity without seeing the receiver, is the old, former idea of "matan beseter" in a new, modern form.
And how fine it will look when the old-new invention spreads among the broad public everywhere.
And if the inventor wants to hear my advice, I would advise him to give his machine a name: "the matan-beseter machine".
An old idea re-smelted into a new form!...
———
And just recently the greatest doctors gathered at a conference, surgeons, those who cut up the human body into pieces and seek to find out why man departs from the world so quickly.
And the greatest impression on everyone was made by one professor, who said that man himself is to blame for undermining his own life.
A person, he says, must be able to keep himself in hand, to master himself.
Worry and envy, and the lust to grab the world for oneself alone, and begrudging others, — all this saws away at one's health, and the person falls, like a tree sawn through at the base.
An old concept re-smelted into a new, scientific form.
After all, our old rebbes [cheder teachers] taught us already as children, every summer in the "Perek" [Pirkei Avot]: "Envy, lust and honour drive a man out of the world!"
Only the rebbes interpreted it in their own way: "that envying, lusting after what is others', and running after honour drive a man out of the world — he loses his 'world-to-come'", while today's scientists say simply that all these things shorten a person's life...
As a rule, we today, in the civilised world, are ashamed of the word "musar", of learning morals, how to live in the world.
This teaching was long ago thrown out of the schools, and even out of our Jewish schools. People laugh at it; it is now called backwardness, obscurantism, conservatism.
In literature they have even disqualified such works as have somewhat of a moral-educational purpose, and they are not counted as works of art.
It was not so long ago that Tolstoy came out with his moral works; the world seized upon them, people read them and delighted in them.
And even our own Jewish maskilim [printed "mashpilim"] idolised Tolstoy, not knowing that in our smallest little musar book there is more morality than in all of Tolstoy's works put together.
But this was, after all, Tolstoy, no less, and he wrote in Russian, not in the old, backward Hebrew language, — so they licked their fingers.
And in the last few decades they have already forgotten even Tolstoy; he too has already become backward for the times. "Supposedly" people have already gone much further than his ideas.
But now along came Mahatma Gandhi, the Indian prophet, and the world is making a fuss over him. And what, for instance, is all this pedigree with Gandhi? Is he not simply a moralist, who has bound himself in moral chains, as he understands morality?
He pleases the world because people feel that now, in this savage time, one needs a little morality. But a world leader Gandhi cannot be. He is too small for that and too "Indian"...
And that is precisely why the professor made such an impression with his few words of musar, that everyone talked about it.
Respect for science the world still has a little. But, as we have said, that bit of professorial musar lies here in a little corner of an old "Perek".
An old word re-smelted into a new form.
As Peretz, the free, the revolutionary Y. L. Peretz, once said:
"In royal crowns you will not find such diamonds, the sea does not possess such pearls, as we have from of old... Leaf through the little Tanakh and see, and hear the words of the prophets — do they not accord with your mightiest hopes, your broadest and farthest dreams? And open the little siddur — does it not pray your prayers?... You want to be free? Is not imposed heresy a compulsion, a yoke, just like imposed piety"?...
— — —
Who, who, but we, are in great need of the "re-smelted coins": we have enough "metal" to re-smelt, and we can become spiritually rich beyond measure.
Jews in Upper Silesia. (From the Polish press)

(From the Polish press).
In connection with the report in the Jewish press about the intervention of a delegation of the Jewish Small Traders' Association at the Ministry of the Interior concerning the harassment that the Jewish peddlers have to endure in Upper Silesia, we find a very characteristic article in the Chadecja [Christian Democratic] organ "Polonia" (no. 2595):
"Of any terror or harassment against Jews in Upper Silesia — writes "Polonia" — nobody here has heard. We are only now learning of it from "Nasz Przegląd". The report of the intervention caused great astonishment among us, because at a time when the Christian population in almost all of Poland adopted an anti-Jewish stance, complete calm reigned in Upper Silesia; not a single Jew lost a hair of his head, no demonstrations whatsoever took place (?)
Having settled accounts with the well-known Jew-hater Mach (read it backwards), the editor of the inflammatory "Do Czynu", who incidentally receives a moral lesson from "Polonia", the Chadecja organ moves on to the position of the Chadecja party on the question of Jewish trade in general and the Jewish peddlers in Upper Silesia in particular:
"As regards our position on the Jewish question, it is as follows: we recognise full rights for the Jews, and we are against using, in the struggle against Jewry, means that do not accord with Christian ethics; but under no circumstances can we agree to give Jews concessions in economic life, because Jewish competition does not think much of the commercial ethics that bind every Christian merchant. This is especially noticeable among the Jews who have come here from the East.
The Polish Jews who came to Silesia after Upper Silesia was taken over by the Polish government found here not only a livelihood and bread, but also knew how to exploit the good opportunity: at the time when we were fighting in the uprising and later working during the plebiscite, the practical Jews did good business and bought up the houses from the Germans. True, in the first years several antisemitic attacks took place, exclusively in Katowice, but for some years now the local population has behaved with reserve towards the Jews.
A great plague for the Upper Silesian inhabitants are the Jewish peddlers. In our economic life, thanks to the fact that communications are well developed, the peddlers are a superfluous element here; they are entirely superfluous middlemen who have pushed their way into our economic life."
The writer of the article goes on to relate how the Jewish peddlers exploit the Upper Silesian inhabitant, pushing on him goods he does not need at all, and taking bills of exchange for them. The number of Jewish peddlers, he says, is growing into the thousands and reaches the point of export[?]. And that forbidding the peddler to trade has nothing to do with any religion.
"The Jews' position in this matter is impermissible, both legally and morally."
In the memorandum that the Jewish delegation handed to the department director in the Ministry of the Interior, it is demanded that the government shut down the pogrom sheet "Do Czynu". About this Korfanty's organ writes as follows:
"The Jews very much dislike Mr. Mach and his organ "Do Czynu", and we too dislike the organ as well as its methods of struggle; but to demand that the "newspaper" be shut down and the editors be held legally responsible does not accord with the binding laws. Here nobody can shut down any publication. If one wishes to sue the editor, there is a penal code, there is a prosecutor and a court. In this case the Jews wanted to have a special privilege."
A strange thing: to demand of a government to shut down a sheet that spits poison at Jews week after week means touching the law; but to incite the feelings of one part of the population against the other with the help of such hate sheets — that is nothing, that is allowed; that is how "Polonia" understands it. In general "Polonia" finds itself in an unpleasant position. It would like, poor thing, "the wolf to be sated and the sheep whole", since it does after all have a few Jewish subscribers and above all Jewish advertisers. Well, one must be a little restrained, one must also throw the Jews a little bone, for otherwise this cannot be understood with clear reason.
At the end we find the following further hint:
"A bad adviser is whoever told the Jews to intervene at the Ministry, because Polish public opinion will react against it. One cannot call the Jewish intervention anything other than a provocation. True, the broadest Jewish masses are, after all, strong supporters of the Sanacja system."
Yes, how such a reaction on the part of Polish public opinion — even merely from the Chadecja press — may look, we can imagine. It would indeed be worthwhile for our local communal workers to give some thought to this painful matter, which concerns several hundred Jewish families.
S. Szach
A Little Feuilleton. My prophecies for the year 1932

My prophecies for the year 1932
Together with the stargazers and prophecy-tellers of the whole world, I too permit myself to utter a few prophecies about the new year.
They — about the whole world and about particular kingdoms; I — about one little corner of the world — Będzin.
In the year 1932 the Magistrate will submit a budget of 5 million new złoty. Nobody will look at it, nobody will audit it and nobody will ask any questions; Jews will pay taxes and get the fever [i.e. nothing].
The Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce will deliver 10 pood of communiqués about the meetings of its three[?] commissions and send the "opinions" to the ministers. There they will be laid away in the archive, and when the happy hour comes they will be dispatched to the place where the millions of postcards lie which the population of Poland "voluntarily" sent last year to Piłsudski on the island of Madeira.
The "illegal" workshops will be fruitful and multiply like the "outside meat" after the agreement between the butchers and the kashrut committee.
The kehilla administration will go on, as hitherto, caring for the welfare of the community: in summer it will talk about coal for the poor, and in winter — about ice cream ["lody"]. The cemetery employees will demand fairness and a pension from the kehilla administration, and the shochtim will threaten a strike.
The cooperative movement in Będzin will develop tremendously. In every Jewish house there will be at least one little grocery shop and two banks, but "they" will have only 2—3 credit cooperatives.
The Sosnowiec Jewish hospital will receive a circular from the Magistrate that Jewish patients are to be treated only with dry cupping glasses. "Sao"[?] will faint only once a month. The Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin will undertake[?] to pay in 25 percent on account of the pledges which its students — the future rabbis and geniuses — are preparing to take from Jewish magnates — abroad. The philanthropic societies will hold "flower" sales in the streets only three times a day. And I, the little feuilletonist, will earn myself a new bit of sympathy from the readers and a new bit of hatred from the "top people".
Yankele.

But that did not happen. The rector began to speak calmly, quietly, and tried to answer Rasputin's words. But when he glanced at the muzhik [Russian peasant] he became flustered[?], repeated himself[?], fell into embarrassment and could barely mumble a few words that did not hang together. His eyelids drooped over his eyes; he was confused...
Rasputin's two burning eyes were sharp and piercing. The muzhik meanwhile went on talking, and his words beat down on the archimandrite like a hail of little stones, so that the old pedagogue too began to tremble. He could barely stay on his feet... Some strange power had mastered him, and he did not know what was happening to him...
The archimandrite quickly came to himself, recovered[?]... Now there was no sign of anger on Rasputin's face... now his eyes were friendly. His voice was now soft, melodious, and his words — simple and sharp-witted, so sharp-witted that the rector again felt respect and admiration for the wanderer[?]. Again he fell under the muzhik's influence... He summed up his questions to the wanderer, and the students noticed that after every answer Rasputin gave, after every single word of his, the archimandrite nodded his big head and agreed:
— Right, little father! That is correct... that is how it is...
He was under the spell of the "holy" wanderer, who had mastered him...
Meanwhile it had grown late in the evening, and the archimandrite had to go to sleep. He approached the wanderer and raised his hands to bless him. Rasputin looked him straight in the eyes, and some strange power acted so that the archimandrite's hands dropped, and from his lips fell the words:
— You bless me, little father!
Rasputin raised his hands and blessed him.
Somewhat ashamed, the archimandrite set off with quick steps to his room. But already standing by the stairs that led up to his room, he stopped, turned round and called out to the wanderer:
— Come, little father, to my room tomorrow early in the morning... Bishop Hermogen will be there, and I want him to make your acquaintance and talk with you.
That night the students of the Theological Academy went to bed late: they talked a great deal about the strange incident and about the wanderer, who appears to be a "saint". Many of them fell into doubt: what use can the days and years they spend here studying be, if a simple muzhik can come closer to the truth than they can?
Archimandrite Feofan too was restless that night. He lay in bed, entangled in a net of doubts, and for a long time could not fall asleep.
In vain did the old priest torment himself to free himself of his doubts. What does it mean, after all? And — is the wanderer really a "saint"? If so, what do the blasphemous words about sin that he spoke mean? Are those words right too? Or perhaps he is no saint at all but an emissary of Satan who has come down into the world to lead people astray from the straight path and to confuse the minds of pious folk? Who, then, is the wanderer?
He therefore waited for Rasputin's meeting with Bishop Hermogen: this pious, learned man, who understands people well — he, so he hoped, would be able to tell him who Rasputin is. Is he really a "saint", or is he an emissary of Satan?...
• • •
The next morning, early, the Bishop of Saratov knocked at the door of his friend Feofan and came into his room. The rector, still agitated by what had happened the day before, immediately began to talk about the extraordinary muzhik from Tobolsk whom he had met the day before and who had made such a strong impression on him. He spoke fast, in one breath, and since he had no teeth his words came out almost unintelligible, and the bishop had to ask again every so often:
— What happened, little father? Tell me again... What took place?
But before "Father" Feofan had managed to tell everything about his meeting with the Siberian muzhik, the door of his room burst open and Rasputin came in with noise and tumult. He stopped for a while at the threshold, looked around, examined the two men, drew the air in through his nose and came up close[?] to them, as if he wanted to sense the smell coming from them. Then he turned to the corner where the "icon" hung, bowed to it once, a second time and a third time, crossing himself as he did so; after that he went up to the table, planted himself there and called out to the archimandrite:
— Here I am, little father!
Then he fixed his eyes on the bishop, on whose lips a contented smile was playing. The bishop was a tall, broad and fat man. He was sitting on the leather sofa that stood by the window, and with contented curiosity he studied the strange muzhik who was looking at him.
— Is this your bishop that you spoke about yesterday? — Rasputin asked Feofan.
The archimandrite, a little embarrassed by Rasputin's behaviour, nodded his head yes. That is him, in other words.
Rasputin at once ran up to the archimandrite, embraced him firmly and kissed him three times, first on the right cheek, then on the left and again on the right... and, almost falling upon the bishop, embraced him too and kissed him three times. This happened so unexpectedly, and Rasputin did it with such wild impetus, that both — Feofan and Hermogen — were thrown into confusion.
The bishop exclaimed, laughing:
— Little father! Little father! You'll crush me!
From the very first minute the bishop took a liking to Rasputin. He liked him for his simplicity, his merry, lively eyes and above all for his plain speech and peasant skill, his deep voice and Siberian dialect. Rasputin, too, at once took a liking to the bishop. It did not take long before both found the right tone and talked to each other as if they were old friends. In the middle of the conversation Rasputin seized the bishop's hand, pressed it warmly[?] in both of his and exclaimed:
— I like you, little father! I like you very much!
Hermogen burst into merry laughter and looked at Rasputin with friendly glances.
"Father" Feofan tried in vain to steer the conversation to what interested him: the questions of godliness and sin, so that the bishop might acquaint himself with Rasputin's views on sin and pronounce his judgement on them.
The bishop was not so enthusiastic a nature as the rector. He was not at once influenced by the Siberian muzhik to the point of regarding him as a new "saint". Rasputin's theological skill and his views on religious matters did not interest him. But he greatly liked the shrewd and clever muzhik, his manner of speaking and the ability he possesses to make a strong impression on his listeners. It occurred to him that this muzhik could be used for a very important purpose.

Suicides.

[Essay — society and the crisis.]
There is no longer any doubt in anyone's mind that suicides have taken on an epidemic character. Day after day the chronicle records dozens of suicides, embracing the most varied strata of the population: women and men, old and young, poor and well-to-do, religious and freethinkers — in a word, it is a mass psychosis that dominates all parts of society.
The causes that lead to suicide seem to be of a purely economic character, but that only appears so at first glance. True, the bad economic situation is a strong factor that pushes a person to make an attempt on his own life, but an even firmer [?] impulse driving to suicide is the psychological crisis that dominates the masses.
The tragedy of today's person should not be sought only in material poverty [?], but also in hopelessness and in resignation as to any improvement. History knows strong economic upheavals, and yet the suicide microbe never managed to spread so violently as now, because in every crisis one could always make out the contours of a better tomorrow, and that gave courage and strength to hold out. But what honest person will dare say today that under the present social and political conditions he believes it is possible to find a way out of the accursed magic wheel that is called crisis?
With its last strength the capitalist world is trying to save itself from going under. Conferences and consultations are often held on how to get out of the swamp in which a heavy, worn-out body, no longer capable of life, is sinking; but after the negotiations end, everyone leaves exactly as wise as before the start. It looks as if some invisible prankster were watching over everything and at the last minute brought all plans to naught.
Can the latest government conferences, which are nothing more than a pretence to dazzle the eyes of the masses, bring any result whatsoever? Certainly not. Otherwise such barbaric deeds would not have been possible as pouring hundreds of thousands of gallons of condensed milk into the Hudson River, burning millions of bales of cotton in Kansas and destroying sugar plantations for purely selfish speculative motives — at a time when millions of poor children all over the world fall ill with rickets because of bad and deficient nutrition, and therefore grow up (if they live to grow up at all) physically and mentally inferior. What can one call such world madness, if not degeneration in its hopeless stage?
Such an order must be destroyed, an order that tolerates such delusional deeds, of which perhaps even a Nero and an Ivan the Terrible would not have been capable.
Is it any wonder, then, that in such a time of despair, of resignation and loss of every hope, death comes and persuades with its frosty, poisonous breath that it, and it alone, is able to release man from his daily misery and pain? Is it any wonder that at such a moment, seeing in death a supposed rescue, a person leaps into its arms?
True, no one will build his existence on hope alone. But just as surely it is impossible to do without it. Millions of slaves and serfs in antiquity and the Middle Ages, who were fated to live for hundreds of years in inhuman conditions, would have perished in the shortest time had the hope of being freed not lived in them. Whole peoples that were long enslaved would have vanished had they not believed in a better future. What moves tens of millions of people in the world to play the lottery, despite the fact that from a mathematical standpoint the chances of hitting the main prize equal zero — if not hope? Reason can point a thousand times to the illogic of gambling, and yet the illusory hope mostly wins, because there are moments in life when a person wants to be fooled and feels quite fine in such a situation.
Can one imagine what tragedy people must live through — people who sometimes slave away a whole life for the most minimal possibilities of existence, just to keep themselves on the surface of life — if they decide to tear the thread of their life, to lower the curtain in the middle of the spectacle called the drama of life? And is the human mind capable of grasping what revolution must take place in the psyche of a deeply religious Jew (and there are many such among the suicides), who knows what punishment awaits him for "one who destroys himself knowingly" [hamabed et atsmo leda'at]? Such a person must, after all, before he commits murder upon himself, first perform harakiri [?] on his conscience; he must first unconditionally sever every tie with his God, for otherwise it would not have been possible for him to commit suicide. What can one call such a psychic cataclysm? A tragedy? Too pale a term.
Also contributing to the intensification of the tragedy of our generation is mechanization in every field, the tearing out of life of every trace of romance. Life has therefore become too grey, too faded [?], and there is no greater misfortune for man than eternal greyness and monotony. Nowadays one can no longer speak of civilization, because such no longer exists; one can at most speak of a mechanical culture, which has seized everything, and it seems that man is running at a fast pace towards a point in time when he will himself turn into a golem before he manages to create one by mechanical means.
It is hard to deny that deep [?] truth which Schopenhauer expresses in his "Wisdom of Life": "Imagine — he writes — that the act of begetting children were neither a need nor accompanied by lust, but a matter of pure rational deliberation. Could the human race then still have survived? Would not every person rather have had so much pity for the coming generation that he would have preferred to spare it the burden of existence, or at least would not have taken it upon himself to lay it upon it in cold blood?"
But why even quote Schopenhauer to prove the nothingness of human life? "Better not to have been created than to have been created" [tov shelo nivra mishenivra] is an older, indisputable truth, which no one — not even the "happy" — will dare deny. The greatest optimist will not be able to convince anyone that it was worth being born. Even if ideal happiness reigned in the world — not to mention that true happiness does not exist at all, it is merely a "fata morgana" that does not exist in reality.
This, however, by no means justifies suicide. Certainly it would have been better for man not to have been born at all, but once that has happened, it is nonsense to desert from life. The suicides would have shown greater heroism if, instead of voluntarily leaping into the grave and leaving their nearest in still greater despair and want [?], they had rather taken their place in the front-line combat positions of life, and together with the millions of suffering and tormented helped in the struggle to create a new society, in which suicides for material reasons will not be possible — a society that will be based on the foundations of justice, humanity and labour.
S. Rozenberg.

Będzin: (G.) Cantor Żupowicz Takes the Kehilla Administration to Court / One Must Not Tell Tales Out of the Cheder.. / New Members of the Assessment Commission / Regional Conference of „Tse'irei Mizrah[i]“ / A Robbery Attack in the Middle of the Town / News from the „Merchants' Association“ / Vanished on New Year's Eve / They Came on Leave and Made Their „Fortune“..

[Będzin — kehilla, trade and crime; eight short news items under the heading „Bendin“.]
As is known [?], the former cantor Mr. Żupowicz is claiming from the kehilla administration a debt of several thousand zł. from unpaid pensions. After various interventions Mr. Żupowicz received from the kehilla barely a few hundred zł. in bills of exchange, which were protested.
This week Mr. Żupowicz came here again from Kraków and turned to the kehilla president about the debt. The president then declared that the cantor could do whatever he wanted.
After such an answer cantor Żupowicz went to one of the best lawyers and handed him the lawsuit against the Będzin kehilla administration.
Besides the pension, the complaint also includes a claim for 3 months as compensation.
—o—
One must not tell tales out of the cheder..
The local Polish press reports that all the magistrates (municipal offices) in Zagłębie have received a circular (okólnik) [?] not to give the press any information whatsoever concerning the last population census.

New members of the assessment commission.
On the proposal of the local office (urząd) and with the consent of the Chamber of Commerce, Messrs. K. Koplowicz, D. Gitler, J. M. Kurland, H. Stachlic and D. Gutensztajn have been nominated by the Kielce [Treasury] Chamber (Izba) to the assessment commission and [?] turnover.

Mr. Grinberg (Warsaw) and Mr. Eiges (Vilna) took part in the conference.

A robbery attack in the middle of the town.
On Tuesday at 6 o'clock in the evening an unknown Christian ran up to Mrs. Gitel Kimelman, who was walking along Małachowskiego street, and tore from her hand a handbag containing 65 zł.
At Mrs. Kimelman's cries a policeman arrived and caught the attacker at the Old Market.

Vanished on New Year's Eve.
The cashier of the „Elektryczność“ factory in Ząbkowice [?] left his home on New Year's Eve (Sylwester night) and did not come back. On the next day the family received a letter from the missing man, in which he writes that, because he had been dismissed from his post, he sees no other way out than to put an end to his life, and that „the fitting day to bid farewell to the world is only on New Year's Eve“.
—o—
They came on leave and made their „fortune“..
In the course of last week a series of thefts was committed in Zagłębie, among them at Mr. Aroszel [?] in Dąbrowa and in the Russian (Orthodox) church in Sosnowiec.
The latest thefts have been uncovered by the police. The thieves, together with the buyers of the stolen goods, are already in prison.
The theft at Mr. Aroszel's was committed by two soldiers who had come on leave.
At the investigation the soldiers declared that they had committed the theft because they had no money for the journey back.
Sosnowiec: Young Mother Jumps from the Third Floor and Is Killed

[Sosnowiec — tragedy; suicide.]
On Sunday at 9 o'clock in the morning Jewish Sosnowiec was shaken [?] by the terrible news that the 21-year-old Chava Ostrowiecka had jumped from the 3rd floor on Prezydenta Mościckiego street and was killed on the spot.
Two months ago the suicide had given birth to a boy, and since then she had suffered nervous [?] attacks.
At the critical moment she put on her fur coat and her hat and told her mother that she was going to a (woman) broker about a wet nurse.
When she left the house she showed no sign at all of abnormality. But instead of going out into the street she went up to the 3rd floor and from there carried out her terrible plan.
The tragic suicide sent a shudder [?] through the whole town. Thousands of people took part in the funeral.
A Meeting of Merchant-Importers

[Zagłębie — trade; meeting of fruit importers.]
On the initiative of the „Merchants' and Industrialists' Association“ (Kowalska street) a large meeting took place in its own premises last Sunday afternoon, devoted to the new import restrictions on oranges and other fruit.
Taking part in the meeting were representatives of the Katowice, Sosnowiec and Kraków Chambers of Commerce, the president of the Polish Merchants' Association, councillor (radny) Mr. Wierzbicki, and representatives of the merchants' associations in Zagłębie, Częstochowa and others.
The meeting is opened by the president, Mr. Kwiatek. After the greeting he explains the reasons and the tasks of the meeting, and with the consent of all participants the chair is handed over to Mr. Wierzbicki. Invited as assessors are the vice-president of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce Mr. Gruszczyński, the importer Mr. L. Zendel, and as secretary the councillor [sic] of the Chamber of Commerce Mr. Aliner.
The floor is given to the vice-director of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Garamski, who delivers a detailed lecture on the government's attitude to the importers' question.
After the lecture a matter-of-fact and serious discussion develops, in which Messrs. Kwiatek, Kabak, Tencer, Aliner and others took part, and the following resolutions were adopted unanimously:
1) The meeting of importers declares its readiness to import fruit from abroad exclusively through the port of Gdynia.
2) [It] protests against the privileges which foreign importing firms receive in importing.
3) [It] expresses readiness to take an active part in building the port in Gdynia.
After the close of the meeting a supper was given for the delegates, at which there was also broad discussion of the need to improve trade and friendly relations between the Jewish and Polish merchant communities.
The Mine Workers' Wage Agreement Terminated.

[Zagłębie — labour; coal mines.]
This week the local labour inspector received a letter from the Council of the coal mines in Zagłębie announcing that on the 31st of this month [January 1932] the agreement on the wages in force until now is being terminated.
The inspector passed the news by telephone to the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare.
According to rumours, the Council intends to cut wages by 10 to 15 per cent.
As we learn, next Monday, the 11th of this month, a conference will take place[?] at the Ministry of Labour in Warsaw, at which the question of how to settle the newly arisen dispute between the industrialists' and the workers' unions will be discussed.
The news of the wage cut and of the reduction of working hours has caused alarm in workers' circles.
A Son Killed His Own Mother.

[Sosnowiec — crime; murder.]
On Sawrajja[?] Street the 66-year-old Żulczyńska lived in an attic room together with her 28-year-old son. The latter is employed as a „customer-catcher“ [a tout pulling customers into shops], and he drank away all his earnings.
Last Saturday night Żulczyński came home late at night in a drunken state and, as always, this time too he „honoured“ his mother with the lowest abuse and curses.
When the mother opened the door, the son began to strangle her by the throat and then threw her down the whole flight of stairs.
The old woman suffered a brain concussion, and death came instantly.
The murderous son was put into prison in chains.
A Big Scandal Trial in the Local District Court.

[Sosnowiec — courts; sick fund.]
Soon the trial will take place in the local district court against the storekeeper of the Central Sick Fund [Kasa Chorych] in Warsaw and his assistant. Both are accused of buying cheap medical articles and charging very high prices for them.
Dozens of witnesses have been summoned to the trial, among them a large number of doctors.
Bill Forgers Arrested.

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
On the order of the Investigation Office several persons have been arrested who, with the help of forged bills of exchange, swindled a sum of 727 zł. out of the credit fund.
Fell Victim to Swindlers...

[Sosnowiec — crime; fraud.]
Mrs. Sosnowia[?] from Nowy Bytom came here on business matters. Walking along President Mościcki Street, she was approached by an elegantly dressed young man, who struck up a conversation with her, asked her where she was from, what she had come here for, etc.
During the polite conversation the young man picked up a small packet from the pavement, examined it and then said to the woman:
— „I've found money; don't tell anyone. We'll share it.“
The woman, hearing of the „find“, promised the finder that „she would tell no one about it“...
A few minutes later a person came running up and went straight to the woman, saying:
— I lost money on this very spot, and from a distance I saw[?] how you picked up a packet; so give me the money, otherwise I'll call the police.
The frightened woman defended herself, saying she had not found the money; „I have money on me,“ she said, „but it's my own.“
— Show me your money, and I'll see whether you're telling the truth, said the young man.
The woman, without any suspicion, showed him her purse; after examining it the young man declared that he had suspected her for nothing and, saying „przepraszam“ [sorry], the second young man left. Soon afterwards the first acquaintance left too.
Later the woman noticed that during the „inspection“ 200 zł. had vanished from her purse...

On 3 Maja Street the 54-year-old Bibryk, in a hurry, wanted to jump onto the tram that was going to Będzin.

A „Dentist“ Sentenced to Two Years in Prison.
A few months ago a certain Jan Szwarc was arrested who, on the basis of forged documents, had obtained a post in the Sosnowiec sick fund as a dentist and practised in the sick fund's outpatient clinic in Dąbrowa.
The swindler was unmasked a short time later, and the investigation established that the real name of the „black dentist“ [a pun on the name Szwarc] is Apolinary Brausz[?], born in Lemberg [Lwów], and that he had already plied this trade in a number of towns.
This week Brausz stood before the Sosnowiec district court, which sentenced him to two years in prison.

Telephone connection from Łódź with Katowice, Prague, Vienna, Berlin.

On Sunday “Two Worlds” Will Meet at the Premises of the Będzin Kehilla

[Będzin — kehilla.]
Next Sunday a meeting of the old and the new kehilla administration is to take place at the Będzin kehilla, in order to find a peaceful way out between the two fighting sides, in order to save the gmina [community] from a catastrophe.
The meeting has been called on the initiative of the secretary, Mr. Frylich.
Annual Meeting of the Sosnowiec Artisans

[Sosnowiec — artisans.]
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Jaskierowicz the annual meeting of the Sosnowiec artisans took place on Wednesday evening[?].
After the reports of Messrs. Jaskierowicz, Szajer and Goldkorn a discussion developed which led to stormy moments. The “fight” took place between the members of the old administration and the present sanacja[?] [reorganisation] commission.
Owing to the late hour the meeting was broken off. The continuation will take place next Sunday.
Which Artisans Need Not Hold Cards?

[Taxes — artisans, turnover tax.]
In the amendment to the law on turnover tax, the privilege that small artisans are exempt from turnover tax has been abolished.
Every artisan who must hold a patent [trade licence] must pay turnover tax. Artisans who work with one worker, even with a family member, must already pay turnover tax.
All artisans must now hold patents.
All artisans who hold artisan cards will pay only one and a half percent turnover tax.
Exempt from holding artisan cards are only the artisans who work alone or with the help of one family member. They too, without cards, will pay only one and a half percent obrotowy [turnover tax]. This does not concern soap-boilers and butchers, who must indeed hold cards.
If, however, one keeps one outside journeyman, one must already hold an artisan card in order to pay one and a half percent. Without such a card the artisans will pay 2 percent.

Meeting of the Tailors' Guild in Sosnowiec
[Sosnowiec — artisans, tailors.]
