Report on the 2nd General Meeting of the Cooperative Bank in Dąbrowa
[Dąbrowa Górnicza — cooperative bank.]
Last Sunday a general meeting of the Cooperative Bank took place in Dąbrowa.
The meeting was opened by Mr. Nachum Granatman, who explained its purpose. Mr. Iser Cykrowski was elected chairman.
The former president and manager of the bank, Mr. Grünbaum, also came to the meeting; he was given the floor and pointed out that the meeting was not legally competent. To this he received the answer from Mr. Granatman that the meeting was taking place according to the instructions of the Auditing Union.
Mr. Grünbaum again took the floor and declared that today's meeting was not competent because the balance sheet was not on the agenda. In reply the president and manager Mr. Chaim Lewi read a letter of the Auditing Union of 12 April last year, in which it is said: “The previous audit carried out by me on 16 December 1930 then confirmed that, owing to the dictatorship and management of the former president Mr. Grünbaum, the state of the cooperative is ruined both financially and morally. The damage amounts to 14.687,37 zł.” The report is signed by the inspector of the Auditing Union, Michelson.
Mr. Lewi also declared that Mr. Grünbaum had been handed over to the public prosecutor for 6.500 zł. of embezzlement[?], with the consent of the general meeting and of the Auditing Union.
Mr. Grünbaum took the floor in his defence and said: “There is a great prophet in India, Gandhi, and I am the second. I foretold that if I left the bank, the bank would not exist.” Mr. G. reproaches the auditor Mr. Michelson that he is not fit to audit the bank, of which he himself had been president, and that all the accusations against him are sucked out of thin air.
Mr. Szmuel Grinberg comes out in a sharp tone, making sharp accusations against Mr. Grünbaum that Mr. G. materially wrecked the institution.
Mr. Grünbaum remarks in his reply that all those who are against him today could be[?] [—] for him. To this Mr. Granatman answers: “You, Mr. Grünbaum, set yourself up as a prophet just like Gandhi; but here is the difference: from day to day Gandhi gains more followers — while your followers are running away from you.”
After the stormy discussion a liquidation commission is elected and the chairman closes the meeting. S.

[Będzin — societies and community.] In the year 5592 [1832] the Nos'ei ha-Mitah society [pallbearers' society] was founded in Będzin. But from the moment the Chevra Kadisha was reorganised under the Jewish community board, especially when a hearse was bought, the society gave up its activity and remained only in name:
— Chevra Nos'ei...
Several years ago the society built itself its own premises on the Talmud Torah square, where people pray and make merry.
The society's 100-year jubilee was celebrated with great pomp. It was a celebration with all the trimmings [„pitshevkes“]; a pity only that the "Hachnasat Kallah" society [for dowering poor brides] did not use the opportunity — if only a poor couple had got married at this celebration...
The jubilee began last Saturday. In the society's own premises, which had been nicely [printed "ver shayn"] renovated and painted for the occasion, there came to pray Messrs. the dayan [moreh tsedek] R' Chanoch David, H. Gutberg [?], A. Trapwier [?], Y. Higadzki [?], M. Rosensaft and others.

In the evening the cantor Mr. Piotrkowski and a choir held a memorial service for the deceased members. Before the memorial the appropriate chapters of Psalms were recited.
Later the banquet took place. To the sounds of an orchestra the public enjoyed itself. Mr. S. Winer gave a "speech" in which he criticised the persons [?] who allow themselves to insult the members, who "sacrifice themselves" for the existence of the society...
The floor is taken by Mr. Higadzki, who stressed that on the day of the jubilee the members must take stock of themselves and not forget that a part of human life must be given for the good of all humanity and for the future of the Jewish people.

Give Back the Dowry! (From Today's Divorce Stories)

[Rabbinical court — divorce.] In the rabbinical court room stands a Jewish couple, pleading their case.
From the pleas we learn that the couple married several years ago. The young man tried to do business. But nothing he did had any luck. Perhaps the bad times were to blame, and perhaps he is simply no good at any business. Be that as it may, one fine morning the young man realised that he had "squandered" the whole dowry and was left with nothing. Because of this there could be no more domestic peace, and now the husband demands that his wife accept a divorce from him.
The wife pleads: so be it, let there be a divorce, you cannot hold on to a husband by force — but where is fairness? Her husband received a fine dowry from her, so as soon as there is a divorce he must give back the dowry.
The husband acknowledges that his wife is right: it is her dowry and she must get it back. But what is he to do when he has no money. For that, however, he says, he has a plan for how to return her dowry.
How? — the rabbis ask with interest.
Since there are now many girls looking for bridegrooms who are therefore ready to give a large dowry, let his wife meanwhile accept a divorce from him; he will then be able to take a dowry a second time, and from the new dowry he will give her what is due to her.
The rabbis ruled that if the husband wants to divorce his wife he must give her back the dowry; if he has none, let him look for it. The wife is not obliged to trust his word that he will return her dowry later. As for the husband's "plans" to marry again and take another dowry — that has nothing to do with the matter. He must first return the first dowry, and until then he may not let anyone talk to him about a match, nor even think of taking a dowry again...

Neither alive — nor dead

On what foundations does the Będzin "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim Fareyn) stand? What benefit does it bring the public, and what next?
Not long ago we here in Będzin had the opportunity to attend a general meeting of the "Merchants' Association" on the activity of the above-mentioned institution for no more and no less than 4 (read: four) years, i.e. from 1928 to the end of the year 1931.
Among [other] people, out in the wide world, it has been understood that waiting a year for a report is too long for a lively public institution, and the system was reformed in such a way that general meetings are called every 6 months; and one cannot say otherwise — we too make reforms: right on the eve of the year 1932 you are handed a report for the year 1928, and that not from some charitable institution or other that does not interest the public and the broad strata of the population. After all, it is nothing more and nothing less than a commercial institution, which plays no small role in Jewish economic life.
Say what you will, but when one reflects on what the merchant class here has borne on its shoulders from 1928 until today, what defeats and death blows it has suffered, one is beside oneself at having to state that, for all that, such a nerve-centre of an institution has had nothing to say to its members over such a run of years.
Yes, with us anything is possible: a people that is through and through bound up and knotted with trade need not have its own association to care for the good of its members, for the welfare of those who belong to it. It is characteristic, by the way, that the Jewish merchant class cannot sustain even one single cheap trade publication, while others have several, and expensive ones at that, journals.
All this is a reflection of how mature the Jewish merchant is and of how far he understands his tasks. Well, it is self-evident: if the members of a "Merchants' Association" had any understanding for their professional association, they would have had to do one of two things: either liquidate it if it does not fulfil its proper tasks for the benefit of the members, or, if not — if it will no longer take an interest in improving the members' situation — the members would have had to storm it. Otherwise it cannot be understood. Otherwise it remains a riddle. What does it mean: an institution exists for me (every member must understand that the institution exists for him). I pay for it, keep it up, and get nothing from it. But here too it is the same: one does not take stock of the matter, one does not want[?] to understand that not a single grosz may be given to a public purpose if one has no benefit from it. One must know once and for all: if one has to have this or that institution at all, one must use every means so that it brings benefit to the members, and if it does not, one must act so that it does. Here, however, nobody takes stock, and people reckon: what do I know — for now, fine, the gulden plays no role — so one throws in the monthly dues. And if things go badly, as they do nowadays, no penalty will be written down if one does not pay the monthly dues. That is where the trouble lies: people do not want to understand that the whole evil consists in taking the public problem lightly, in regarding it as a kind of charity and not as a kind of duty that must be fulfilled like a law.
Had such a professional institution as a "Merchants' Association" been properly appreciated, it would never have come to such a state that for 4 years not a single general meeting is convened at which one has the chance to speak one's heart out about both the sorrows and the joys in which the Jewish merchant class is so rich.
Is it a trifle what has happened in the country over the last four years in the field of commerce?! Everything has been turned upside down; rock-solid, well-founded large firms have been completely ruined and had to leave the commercial arena — and in such a terrible situation, amid such an enormous panic, a commercial institution really has nothing to say, neither to members nor to non-members? Is that comprehensible? Does it mean that we really have a trade association, or does merely a firm, a signboard, exist? It is ridiculous to play such a role for so many years just so that outsiders will think something is being done in the association.
The only characteristic thing is that the president still had the nerve to declare publicly that the association had always[?] stood on guard and at the proper height, and that it would have stood even higher and achieved more if only the members had not treated the association with apathy. Say what you will, but one needs more than nerve to say those words when the institution is in so low a condition.
The institution could have achieved more if the members had understood their tasks. That is true, one hundred percent true — but who is to blame for it, the members or the management? The management is, after all, elected from the best, most capable, most energetic people, so that its task is to raise the members up, so that they understand their tasks; and if the members do not understand this, the blame lies in the first place with the leadership, with those who run the institution.
Incidentally, let it be said openly: what have you given the members, what did they get from the association that should have drawn them to it? The fact that someone got an appeal (rekurs) written for him has nothing to do with the association as such — any petition-writer would have done that for him. And that is supposed to be the aim of a merchants' institution? Is it not a disgrace that leaders should be so short-sighted, or pretend not to see? And is it any wonder that the members have so little understanding for the institution, when the leaders themselves in person do not know what tasks a merchants' association should have — so that people dare to come and demand, and confirm[?], that the institution actually be turned into a debt-collection (windykacja) bureau?! That is how deep one falls, how far one degrades oneself, when one does not stand at the proper height.
Those people would have done better to see to it that from the outset no goods be given to such as take them with the intention of not paying; would it not have been more sensible to uproot the lawlessness from the very beginning, rather than to look afterwards for means of recovering what is, incidentally, already a lost cause? Why, then, fool ourselves and mock others, what is all this needed for? Whom do such establishments benefit? Surely they do harm, because many think that something exists and in that case rely on the institution. Afterwards it turned out that, thanks to this reliance, people suffered losses.
Such a life is no life; it is called: neither lived nor died. An institution that has to be as active as a "Merchants' Association" among Jews — it would be better either to breathe a spirit of life into it, so that temperament and a healthy spirit may be found in it, or, if not, it is wiser to liquidate it altogether, and then the merchant class will know that such an institution simply does not exist. Neither alive nor dead is the most harmful thing there can be. That is what needs to be said once and for all, openly and sincerely[?].
R. Let.
"Ahasver Smiles".

[Feuilleton — Spain and the revocation of the 1492 expulsion; the fate of the Jews.] By Dr. A. Saralnik.

Somewhere, in the far distances, among mountains, on narrow paths, strides Ahasver, the Eternal Jew. From somewhere. He himself no longer remembers from where. He himself does not yet know whither. He knows only one thing — he must go. Here superfluous, there thrown out. Pushed out, nowhere a welcome one [?]. He is just now coming from the land where people say it openly: you are a burden to us. For us and for you — there is no room on one earth. And even when they do not say it, in every gesture of theirs, every look, every wink — an insult.

And somewhere, between the Andes and the Cordilleras, Ahasver goes his age-old way — from somewhere to somewhere.

And on this road a tiding suddenly reaches him, the first time in a long, long while. The first time — good tidings. And a smile appears on his face.

He reads: a gate has opened, a hand has been stretched out — Spain has officially, in a state formula, lifted from the Jew the edict of 1492. The expulsion by the "Catholic Monarchs" Ferdinand and Isabella. Spain has opened its door [printed: "him"] to the exiles of long ago. What the Spanish liberals and radicals of the nineteenth century dared to ask quietly and with a wink, what Castelar, the grandson of Marranos [?], wanted to carry out and had no time for, what his [?] Ángel Pulido [?] and the other friends of the Jews in Spain preached over the last decades — the Republic of Spain, under the leadership of Manuel Azaña, has done it.

And Ahasver remembers. It was not long ago — only four hundred and thirty-one years. All in all, no more than a few generations. Through the streets of Castile and Aragon, of Andalusia and León, people went about — and wept. Eight hundred thousand people, every hour. Leave-taking — every day closer to the end. Tomorrow, the day after — onto the road. To be pushed out of one's home — and how beautiful and how sweet the home was! How blue the sky of Seville. And how bewitching the fragrance of Alicante. They look around them — here their cradle stood, here they grew up, dreamed, suffered, worked — Pepita and Sancho, Alonso and Diego — friends of their youth, they played together. How they hate them now — how they persecute them and draw their blood day after day. It is not enough for them that all the Jews have been driven out — they still want to rob them, suck the blood out of them, take everything away, leave them naked and empty.

And Ahasver remembers further the day before the emigration. They went off to the cemeteries, the expelled. And there they threw themselves down on the tombstones of their fathers and mothers, grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers. Those who built Spain, those who helped create the language, build the culture, spread knowledge, sing songs. Was not Rabbi Shem Tov of Carrión [?] one of the first — and greatest — Spanish poets? Are not his "Dances of Death" — and his "Moral Proverbs" — pearls of the Spanish language? There was envy and hatred. But the envy grew, and with it the hate, the enmity, which burned its way in like a fire, ate its way in like a poison. And poisoned the whole Spanish organism.

Only recently a Spanish woman writer, Fernán Caballero, wrote such a thing in her novel "La Gaviota". It is told there how "Aunt María and her brother Gabriel take a sick stranger into their house". "Who is he?" — asks Brother Gabriel — "perhaps even a Jew?" "God preserve us" — Aunt María crosses herself in fright — "No. Not possible. If he were a Jew — he would surely have a tail".

That is how Spain thought in its popular masses — only a few years ago. And perhaps still so today.

And yet — historic justice has triumphed — Spain has removed the stain from itself.

Is it worth it?

Perhaps not. But how beautiful. The first time in many years. — The only time, — that someone repents, that a people bows its head in humility and says: "Jews, we — our grandfathers — have sinned against you. Come back, be with us — forget what has been. Jews had, it is true, already been invited a couple of times — once in Poland under Kazimierz, the second time in Turkey under Bayezid. They were useful, it was politics. They were invited — in order to lock them up at once as in a cage, so as to have someone from whom to draw money.

But no one has yet begged them to come back.

Is there perhaps after all still something like "conscience" among people — is the Jewish dream of justice not entirely a feverish one? Now they want to be rid of Jews in the whole world. Six million Germans are sharpening their knives, straining to destroy the Jewish community in Germany, which is older than the German state itself, in any case older than Prussia. They will perhaps soon obtain power — and an end to German Jewry. No less barbaric, no less brutal than in the former land of the Catholic Monarchs.

And let the Kremlin only give a shake — the peasants of Ukraine will hurl themselves like wolves upon the Jews — and strangle them, impale children, and drive out all the Jews on a road of blood. Everywhere they lament, everywhere they gnash their teeth: "Jews, a calamity, Jews a plague from God". And from all sides a sigh: how does one get rid of the Jews?

Then, unexpectedly, comes Spain and gives hope. Without a social revolution on the Moscow model, without a regime of blood and iron, solely through culture, through humaneness, solely through conscience.

Quixotism? Possibly. But when Don Quixote exists in the world again — that is surely already a spark of consolation, too. That alone is already a beginning.

Today Spain — tomorrow perhaps Germany, and further, who knows.

The first time. Jews have been given rights, they have been taken into "society", they have — officially — been emancipated. It seems to him for a while — he sees a way.

But a thought flashes like lightning through his head: miracles! But the one miracle did not happen, did it?! When the Jews fled from Spain — did anyone promise them anything? Did they hope for anything?

But how they hoped at another expulsion! Do you remember the legends that gathered around it? "And when Nebuzaradan led the Jews into exile — a voice was heard on high — Rachel wept for her children, and another voice answered her: a time will come when the children will return home!

And the "children" waited for the miracle. They pictured it to themselves so touchingly childlike, so orientally naïve: the mother sits and waits, she hopes and longs. A land waits for its children. Earth for her children, and for two thousand years on end [?] — the hope: the land of the beginnings will become the land of the "End", of the completion, the end of the road. And always the hope: the Land of Israel will call back the people of Israel.

And precisely there, where the faith was so firm — precisely there the greatest disappointment. The only land that "does not call back", that does not open, that fights with all its strength, and ever more strongly as time goes on, against the return — is precisely the land that is bound up in the people's longing — with the promise, with the song of return.

Spain begs the Jews to come back — the Land of Israel pushes them back. What a remarkable, what a tragic irony!

Ahasver smiles bitterly — and strides on along his aimless way somewhere among the wild mountains.
Jews, Do Not Lose Heart!

Jews in Poland are now going through a three-storeyed crisis: a world-wide one, a Polish one and a Jewish one. The world-wide crisis arose soon after the war and keeps growing sharper the further it goes, chiefly for the following reasons: 1) overproduction 2) the unequal distribution of gold among the various states of the world. 3) the enormous expenditure on armament built up beyond [their] strength. 4) the greatly reduced consumption of the Russian domestic market together with the strong and steadily growing Russian export. 5) the too great sum of customs barriers, etc.
The causes of the chronic Polish crisis, which has become so much sharper of late, are chiefly: 1) the loss, after the war, of the boundless Russian market for the purchase of raw materials and for the sale of finished Polish goods. 2) the bad organisation of labour in Poland, which makes it almost impossible for Poland to compete on the world market with the Western European states and with America. 3) a shortage of capital, which arose not only from the post-war devastation but also from an étatism unsuited to Poland, which, unable to obtain any foreign long-term investment loans, carried out the huge necessary investments with the money that flowed in from taxes, sucking the last remnant of liquid capital out of the country. 4) the military budget, large beyond [the country's] strength. 5) the too great and bad taxation. 6) the too rapid growth of the population. 7) the closing of the emigration countries to the surplus of the Polish population, etc.
The third and heaviest storey of the crisis is, for the Polish Jews, the Jewish part of the crisis. The causes of this crisis are: 1) the almost complete absence of the right to work among Jews, 2) the social and the state boycott of Jewish labour and Jewish goods. 3) the too narrow field of work among Jews, which étatism on the one side and antisemitism on the other have narrowed down to the extreme. 4. The Jews of the Kresy [Poland's eastern borderlands] feel the loss of the pre-war markets more heavily than anyone: they lie as in a sack that is open only towards Congress Poland, which has no need of their products...
This three-storeyed crisis presses heavily on all of Poland, but more heavily than on anyone else, for the reasons mentioned above — on the Jews!
If one adds to this the pogrom and boycott undertakings newly organised throughout Poland by the dishonourable Endeks [National Democrats] — not only does the whole catastrophic situation of the Jews in Poland become clear, but it also arouses in every person a strong astonishment: how can the Jews endure it? Surely, it seems, they should have gone under long ago!... The answer to that is: Jews still hold on somehow, because — they are Jews!...
Jews do not lose, and must not lose, their courage even in the most unfortunate conjuncture now prevailing in Poland! Let us try to give ourselves a more exact account of this situation.
As to the world-wide crisis: economists, starting from different world-views, have tried to find their way through the tangle and the chaos now reigning in the world's economy, but so far they have not succeeded.
It seems to me that the World War dealt a very heavy blow to the capitalist economic system. Because of it a chaotic state arose, out of which the new evolutionary form of the world economy has not yet had the necessary time to crystallise. Even its main contour-lines have not yet shown themselves clearly enough. The new form will not be a purely capitalist one, but perhaps not a purely socialist one either — a "transitional form"? All forms of life are transitional forms. Let us not occupy ourselves here with guessing or prophesying!... In any case one thing is certain: the world will not go under! Little by little the situation will clear up and the crisis, the world crisis, will pass.
As to the Polish crisis:
The economic life of Poland shows ever more clearly and plainly, to those who are able to see at all, the truth — what danger would threaten Poland if the foolish Endek policy of extermination regarding the Jews were truly carried out! Already now, when only part of this policy has been carried out, it has ruined the whole Polish state! In general, the entire Endek plan of annihilation regarding the minorities must be changed completely!...
In connection with the excessive armaments, the possibility of a war — given the destructive power of such a war — is for the time being, at least as it seems to me, very small. One must hope that when Polish foreign policy changes a little, Poland's situation, both internally and externally, will change for the better.
In general, the purely Polish crisis can be liquidated in the near future in one way or another.
The situation regarding the purely Jewish crisis looks much harder.
The sharpness of this crisis will, however, be considerably blunted when the government begins to protect Jewish life and property more energetically against the attacks of street hooligans of every kind.
Further, when the general prosperity of Poland rises, the Jewish crisis, with weakened competition, will also diminish.
That alone, however, is too little: the Jews in Poland must wage a constant and obstinate[?] struggle for their equal rights in the Diaspora and for their future in the Land of Israel. The struggle must be waged with a united front, from which must be excluded all the traitors among the assimilated, who join every movement where they can warm their hands at a kehilla fire...
In any case, the present situation in Poland is not as hopeless as it seems from afar! It would become hopeless only if Jews fell into despair and let their hands drop. That we must not allow, and it will not come to that!
Jews! Do not lose heart!...
Dr. Jakub Wygodzki.
The Week of the Jewish Academic

[Będzin — students and self-help.]
Seven years have already passed since the moment when the Association of Jewish Academics was founded in our town, Będzin; that was at the time when the first Jewish gymnasium graduates left Będzin for the university cities in order to continue their education there. But together with the growth of the ranks of Jewish students from Będzin, the tasks of the union also grew; it conducts vigorous self-help work among the academics, both in the material sphere and in other fields. The financial situation of the Jewish student body, however, has recently worsened considerably in connection with the prevailing crisis. The Jewish academic, who not long ago stood up with dignity to the brutality of the Endek [Polish nationalist] youth, demonstrated his will and his right to study, and defended the honour of the whole people, must — besides the contempt he meets at every step — very often fight financial difficulties on the path of his studies. Therefore "The Week of the Jewish Academic" was recently proclaimed, in order to increase the income and strengthen the self-help work of the Jewish academic associations among the broad strata of the studying intelligentsia.
The Będzin academic union is also taking part in the campaign and has published an information bulletin about its seven years of activity to date. From the bulletin one gathers that the association has fulfilled its duty within the limits of its possibilities.
The income for this period amounts to up to 20 thousand zł. Of this, a sum of over 10 thousand zł. was granted as loans, which are secured by promissory notes of the borrowers. The notes are paid by the academics after finishing their studies. So far the Będzin association has granted over 60 loans. Among them are 15 persons who, thanks to the association, were able to complete their education: 2 physicians, 1 pharmacist, 5 gymnasium teachers, 3 lawyers, 1 engineer and 3 graduates with commercial diplomas.
The Będzin union also contributed greatly to building the academic hostels in Warsaw and Kraków, paying in a sum of up to ten thousand zł. The association draws all its income from various events, such as balls, concerts, lectures, etc. The most important item, however, is the monthly membership fee, because it is a stable and periodic income on which the budget can be built. Therefore the association is now conducting a campaign to increase the number of its members. Besides the self-help work in the material field, the union also carries on fruitful cultural activity. Thanks to the initiative of the board, concerts by famous artistic talents are often held, and lectures by such personalities as Yitzhak Grünbaum, Dr. Schiper, Mark Arnsztajn, Leo Belmont, Julian Tuwim, Dr. Weinzieher and others. The union organises rest colonies in summer and winter in the Beskids and in Zakopane, and very many excursions.
This, in brief outline, is the activity to date of the Będzin academic association. Now, when because of the bad economic situation among the students the duties of the union have increased, it is setting about strengthening its work for the benefit of the Jewish academic and of Jewish society. But in order to carry this out it must meet with general recognition, assistance and understanding for the humanitarian tasks it fulfils. It is a social duty of every former academic, and of everyone who understands the important role and significance of the young academic vanguard, to join the association and to take an active part in its development.
Eliyahu Gertner.
He Makes a "Piatiletka" [Five-Year Plan]...

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; the economic crisis.] (As told by a Sosnowiec merchant)
Retold by Graf Kali.
"What are you so lost in thought about?" my wife asks me, seeing how I sit there sunk in deep thought, constantly wrinkling my brow.
"Eh," I say, "nothing, it's a trifle!"
"But still, what?" my wife grows curious and won't let me be. "When a person thinks, he surely has something on his mind."
"It's nothing," I say, "it's not worth talking about. I'm thinking: how does one get hold of a thousand dollars these days?"
"And that's a trifle to you!" my wife cries out with a laugh. "Do you know, you pauper, what a thousand dollars means in today's crisis? I'd guess that even Dietel and Gamper don't have a thousand dollars in cash in times like these..."
"And yet," I say with a chuckle, "if you, my little dove, only wanted it, I could have a thousand dollars and perhaps even more..."
"Me?" she says in astonishment. "I only have to want it? By all means. Tell me, my dear husband, how can you do it? I'm ready to take upon myself everything you tell me to, as long as we are delivered from our bitter poverty."
"If so," I say, "you're a clever one. Well then, listen: I have a solid plan for how we can get set up [?] and come into a fortune... Let's make a 'piatiletka'."
"What's that?" she stares at me with a pair of astonished eyes. "What kind of calamity is that?"
"Well... a 'piatiletka', how shall I put it? Just like in the Soviet Union... Haven't you heard of the Russian piatiletka? It seems even babies in the cradle talk about it."
"No," she says, a little ashamed that she doesn't know such a small thing. "What sort of thing is it?"
"Well, how shall I explain it to you properly? It's a thing that has to be built for five years, and after that you are blessed with every good thing. You live as in Paradise and you lack nothing, not even bird's milk... Well, do you understand? But what of it? During the five years the plan lasts, one must abstain a little from certain luxury articles, such as meat, butter, milk, eggs, sour cream, cheese, sugar and other such trifles. In short: you must take the following upon yourself:
Five years to suffer hunger and cold,
No making noise, no sulking,
Five years not asking me for money,
Not crawling into the trousers [?]...
Five years not going to a summer cottage,
Five years — no children born,
Five years not demanding clothes
And eating krupnik [barley soup] only in due order..."
"Do you understand now?" I say with a triumphant look. "What a piatiletka means?"
"No," she says, "I still don't understand how we can come into a fortune from such a piatiletka."
"What don't you understand? Listen carefully, use your head: how much meat do you buy every day for dinner? Two kilos? Well, from today on you'll buy a quarter kilo... and the rest will go to the piatiletka.. Now tell me, my dear little wife, how much butter do you buy a day? A quarter kilo? Well, you'll buy five dekagrams of butter, or save on butter altogether... For where is it written that one must eat bread with butter? Is bread with tea bad? Here I was a soldier and ate bread with tea for three years running, and I wish I had my former health today.. Now imagine that every day we save not much from the housekeeping, just three złoty. A year has three hundred and sixty-five days. So we have, it's established, eleven hundred złoty a year, and over five years we have saved almost six thousand złoty on food alone; and what about clothing, the cinema? A summer cottage? Concerts and other indulgences?
In short: a thousand dollars I guarantee you, and maybe a dash over... Well then, my wife, do you now understand the solid plan of the piatiletka? In Russia they too made such a piatiletka, and the plan worked out so brilliantly that they are already thinking of a second... piatiletka.
For what are five years, after all? A summer, a winter, a summer, and once more a winter — a summer. A summer — a winter, and done... You get through it, and now you are provided with every good thing for your whole life...
So, my dear little wife, do you agree to begin such a piatiletka? How much, for example, do you get from me a day for housekeeping? 12 złoty? Well, from tomorrow you'll receive 4 złoty a day."
"What are you saying?" the wife cries out, frightened. "How will we be able to live on four złoty a day? Why, bread and rolls for breakfast cost me two złoty 50 groszy."
"Who tells you to buy rolls?" I shout angrily. "In a piatiletka one doesn't eat rolls; in a piatiletka one eats razowy [wholemeal] bread with 'shtdoy' [?]. Do you know what such a thing as a piatiletka means?"
"Yes," she grows a little softer, "but a litre and a half of milk for the children one must have?"
"Have you gone mad?" I start banging my fists on the table. "In a 'piatiletka' you want to buy milk? Why, that's a real bourgeois article..."
"But what does one do about the children?" she tries to protest a little more. "Well, I'll manage somehow, without meat and without milk, but the children are to be pitied; who knows whether they'll hold out five years of such a life in want?"
"When one must carry out a piatiletka, there's no pity; then it is 'no mercy in judgment'. But for that [?], afterwards, God willing, when the piatiletka succeeds, what will we lack then? We'll be mighty rich men.. Only then will we dress ourselves, as it should be, according to the latest Paris fashion. And you, my wife, will learn to dance the 'dumba' [presumably 'rumba'], and perhaps then you'll be quite another hit?.. First of all I'll send you off to Krynica, so you can fatten up a bit and get the look of a bourgeois lady... and meanwhile I'll pop over a bit to Zoppot [Sopot]: for among the rich it isn't done for husband and wife to travel together; among the rich they love each other from afar... Then we'll open a shop in the very centre of Modrzejowska Street... and perhaps then [?] we'd better begin a 2nd 'piatiletka', because nowadays it's the safest business: you don't have to pay any taxes, you're exempt from the patent [trade licence], income tax [dochodowy], property tax [majątkowy] and other troubles."
"So, my little wife, remember [?]: from Sunday, with good luck, our first piatiletka begins..."
25 Years of Activity of „Linas Hacholim“. (A Short Survey for the Jubilee Celebration).

[Będzin — welfare and health institutions; 25th anniversary of „Linas Hacholim“.] By S. Lewkowicz.
At a time when the highest ideals are trampled underfoot, when the words justice, compassion and humane feelings have lost their former lustre and dignity, when „kol d'alim gaver“ [whoever is stronger prevails] holds the upper hand — the jubilee celebration of an institution whose whole task is to relieve and help suffering and poor people may perhaps not be understood by a certain part of the population — as a necessity of the present time. Nevertheless we consider it important to devote this article to the jubilee celebration, in order to learn how and by what means a „Chevra Mishmorim“ [society of night-watchers at sickbeds] was created 25 years ago, out of which grew a mighty, strong philanthropic society.
It was in the year 1904. At that time a certain Moshe Goldszmidt fell ill in Będzin. No „Chevra Mishmorim“ existed then (the Bikur Cholim society only occupied itself with giving medical help and milk). So the members of the jeweller's trade [„yuviler-fakh“], who to this day are still members of the board of „Linas Hacholim“, Messrs. Moshe Nuta Szwimer, Józef Langfus, Abraham Bolimowski and Moshe Montag, spent the nights at the sick man's side and attended to him.
While fulfilling the office of night-watchers, and seeing the great benefit that night-watchers bring the sick, they decided to found a Chevra Mishmorim.
They held the first meeting in the watch shop of Kalman Kornfeld, of blessed memory, on Dąbrowska Street, and from there they went to the tavern of Mr. Moshe Rozenblum, to whom they handed over the plan of founding such a society.
In the tavern, as usual, there were several more people, who signed up on the spot as members, so that a few days later the Chevra Mishmorim counted some seventy-odd members.
Mr. Rozenblum took an active part in the society: he recruited members and called meetings, so that the entire activity was concentrated in Mr. Rozenblum's tavern.
After a few months had passed, when the society already needed premises of its own, a delegation went to R' Reuven Liwer, of blessed memory, with the request that he give them a room for the society.
R' Reuven Liwer agreed, and besides his donation of 25 rubles he gave the society the room where the Wolbórz shtibl [„Volborzher shtibl“, a Hasidic prayer room] is today.
A minyan was set up in the room. And when the Tsarist police prevented the „illegal minyanim“ from being open, the „Linas Hacholim“ minyan was untouchable.
The society's popularity really grew in the month of Tishrei; at that time an epidemic raged, the so-called „cholerinka“ [mild cholera]. The members were active, and at every call they were ready to give help according to the doctors' instructions. Non-Jewish patients, too, received the necessary help; there were cases where some board members did not go home to their families in the nights of both of the first days of Sukkot, but were busy with patients.
At that time the „notables“ of the town appreciated the usefulness of the society and also signed up as passive members.
The authorities, too, were very well disposed toward the society, and in 1905, when a ban was issued on being in the street after 10 in the evening, the active workers of the Chevra Mishmorim received identity passes with permission to go about all night in all the streets.
The board later broadened its activity. Realizing that it was not enough for them to fulfil their duty as night-watchers, but that at the same time the sick must also receive nursing care, the society then took the name „Linas Hacholim“ and began to dispense medicines, milk (from its own cows), etc.
Nevertheless the society, already under the name „Linas Hacholim“, was not legalized, because of the great difficulties on the part of the Piotrków governor, who under no circumstances would grant legalization even to an institution engaged in philanthropic activity, and for a number of years the society existed as a section of „Dobroczynność“ [the charity society].
But the board of „Linas Hacholim“ was not happy with this match. They were always regarded as „stepchildren“ by the board of „Dobroczynność“, which consisted of the intelligentsia. Disharmony reigned between the two boards, and from almost every meeting the „Linas Hacholim“ board left in a huff...
Suddenly the match was broken off. It happened at a meeting at which the question was discussed of holding the first flower day [a street flower-sale fundraiser], with the proceeds to be shared, i.e. for „Dobroczynność“ and for „Linas Hacholim“. But the representatives of „Linas Hacholim“ felt insulted, left the meeting, and the very next day they had the permit to hold a flower day exclusively for the benefit of „Linas Hacholim“...
After the rapprochement with „Dobroczynność“ had been dissolved, the board began taking steps to obtain proper legalization.
In this connection the board turned to the Rabbi, the great Gaon R' Yissachar Berish [Graubart] of blessed memory, with the request that he help with the legalization.
The Rabbi, of blessed memory, did not refuse; he immediately travelled to Piotrków and came back with the legalization. This happened on 14 May 1911.
[Photo:] The building of „Linas Hacholim“.
At the first legal meeting the said Rabbi was also present; he was honoured as honorary president of the institution, and he said the following words to the board:
— If you want „Linas Hacholim“ to exist as it should, then let there be on the board not a single Hasid and not a single „Daytsh“ [a modernized, Western-dressed Jew]...
— Rabbi of Będzin, why? — asked the assembled public.
— From a Hasid you will get nothing, and from a „Daytsh“ nothing either. Even if you do persuade a Hasid to go to a sick person, he will first of all want to know whether the patient prays in his shtibl... And from the „Daytsh“? You will always get the answer from his Christian servant that:
— „Pana nie ma, pan śpi...“ [Polish: „The master is out, the master is asleep“]. So listen to me, children — said the Rabbi of blessed memory — and keep away from the pedigreed. People like you are needed; you are always and at every moment ready to help the poor man...
In just this way people from „the folk“ gathered around the society; they also took part in every civic question and dictated their decisions. This showed itself most prominently during the rabbinical elections, which took place after the death of Rabbi Graubart of blessed memory.
For the rabbinical seat there fought: 1) the Sochaczew [printed „Tochaczew“] Hasidim, for the Rabbi of Wyszogród, today the Sochaczew Rebbe, the great Gaon R' Dovidl, may he live long, and 2) the „Linas Hacholim people“, for the deputy [of the late rabbi], Rabbi R' Yekusiel Zalman, now a rabbi in Brooklyn.
The struggle between the two sides was a passionate one. Each side even had a newspaper „of its own“. The Sochaczew side received moral support through the „Moment“ [Warsaw Yiddish daily], where Mr. Yoshzohn [?], as a friend of the Sochaczew candidate, campaigned for the Rabbi of Wyszogród. „Linas Hacholim“, on the other hand, conducted its campaign in the columns of the „Częstochowa Tageblatt“.
Once, just before the elections, in a Friday issue of the „Moment“, Mr. Yoshzohn devoted a warm article in favour of the Sochaczew side.
When Graubart's side, the so-called „Linas Hacholim people“, saw this, a meeting was called at which it was decided to buy up all copies of the „Moment“...
And so it was. All the copies were bought up from all the newspaper sellers and sent back by post to the „Moment“ editorial office as a sign of protest: when the Będzin „Linas Hacholim“ conducts an election campaign, the „Moment“ must not come out against it...
After the election victory „Linas Hacholim“ grew stronger still, already counting up to 2000 members, and the board members now had the courage to threaten the dozór members [community board] of that time that if any one of them should be against the society, their „little benches“ in the gmina [Jewish community council] would „fly into the air“...
In 1916 the board bought the house on Podzamcze Street, where „Linas Hacholim“, the „Moshav Zekenim“ [old-age home] and the maternity home exist today.
The purchased building was occupied by poor tenants, mostly porters, but with the help of a few kegs of beer [?] the tenants voluntarily left their dwellings, and the board set about rebuilding the entire building and at the same time built the one-storey outbuilding [oficyna] for the old-age home.
During the construction some of the board members worked intensively, did manual labour and themselves carried bricks and stones.
Fruitful activity was carried on during the war years, especially when the typhus epidemic raged in a severe form; then a rescue committee was formed, which collected food products that were then distributed among the families whose only breadwinners were in the hospitals for infectious diseases.
Besides this, a convalescent home was set up for those who had left hospital and needed good care.
The rescue action lasted several months. Only in the course of time was the action wound up.
The board, fearing that the premises of the nursing institution might be requisitioned by the German occupiers, opened a maternity home.
The opening of the institution in 1922 was received by the town's population with great satisfaction, and within a short time the institution became popular even beyond Zagłębie.
In the course of this time, i.e. from 1922 to the end of 1931, 2052 children were born in the maternity home (including 22 twins). Of that number — 1056 boys and 996 girls.
Women in childbirth: Jewish 1838, non-Jewish 192. The latter are sent by the Magistrat [municipality] and by the health-insurance fund.
In the same year the „Moshav Zekenim“, which had existed in R' Yechiel Winer's house, was moved into the „Linas Hacholim“ building.
At first the old people were accommodated in the room that today serves the domestic staff. Later an independent building was built for this purpose.
— —
In the course of time the number of societies in our town has multiplied. The greater the crisis — the more philanthropic institutions are created. This is one of the main reasons why the income of the „Linas Hacholim“ society is today considerably smaller than formerly, and since the expenses are the same as in the „fat“ years, perhaps even greater, the society has a deficit of close to ten thousand gulden [złoty]...
From time to time the society used to be supported by the Będzin landsleit in Chicago and New York, whose fathers, grandfathers and grandmothers spend their old age in the old-age home.
According to news received from New York, the Będzin society there [„Bendiner Ferayn“] is preparing a large entertainment, and the entire proceeds are designated for „Linas Hacholim“.
— —
The jubilee falls next Sunday. In its honour an „academy“ [festive assembly] with a rich programme will take place. The head of the „Mizrachi“ school, Mr. Gotesdiener, has announced his participation; he will give a lecture on the Jewish virtue of compassion compared with other peoples.
The concert part should also be interesting: young musical talents, but of great ability, will perform a series of musical numbers.
A pledge (nedarim) campaign has also been proclaimed, i.e. everyone called up to the Torah this Sabbath should pledge a donation for the benefit of the institution.
In the premises of „Linas Hacholim“ memorial prayers will be held for the deceased board members.
The memorial prayers will be conducted by the cantor Mr. Żupowicz [?], who is coming here specially from Kraków in order to contribute something in honour of the jubilee.
It is to be expected that the broad Jewish masses will take part, in order to help [?] the institution both materially and morally.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (7)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin; installment 7.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

For readers who have not read the beginning of this suspenseful historical novel, we give a summary of the chapters printed so far.
In the house of the banker Dimenshtein in Petersburg a circle of rich Petersburg Jews gathered for a meeting. Also present at the meeting was the Jewish Baron Ginzburg [Günzburg], who passed on confidential [?] news that a prayer service should be held in the Great Synagogue for the health of the Russian heir to the throne.
During the meeting the banker reports that at the imperial court a strong agitation is under way to expel all the Jews from Petersburg; the enemies of Israel are persuading the Empress that if all the Jews are expelled, the heir will recover.
The meeting resolves to give gifts wherever necessary in order to buy themselves free of the decree. [?] It is delegated [?] to the banker's daughter Sonia, who is a friend of the lady-in-waiting Vyrubova, to try [?] to get acquainted with the [—] priest Feofan, the chief instigator of the decree.
At that moment Sonia comes in, bringing the news that the heir to the throne is seriously ill and that a "miracle worker" has been brought — the Siberian muzhik Rasputin. Sonia takes the mission upon herself, and it is settled that a prayer service will be held in the Great Synagogue and at the same time Sonia will meet Anna Vyrubova...
A week earlier, before the meeting took place in the house of the banker Dimenshtein, a strange wanderer had come into the Petersburg monastery [?]. This was the Siberian muzhik Grigori Rasputin. The seminarians put various questions to him about the Godhead [?] and the "Trinity" [?].
Rasputin gave them an answer, but the answer caused agitation among the seminarians and especially with the rector of the seminary; yet all remained silent and amazed that the archimandrite [—] the muzhik a proper rebuff [?].
But the archimandrite did not answer him on that; he only told him to come to him in his study the next morning.
The next morning, when Rasputin came to the archimandrite, the latter presented him to Bishop Hermogen. Rasputin pleased the bishop, who soon used [?] him from time to time [?] for various purposes.
Now read on:

It was then the time when revolutionary winds had begun to blow over great and broad Russia, when the idea of freedom and uprising was being carried there from Western Europe. Hermogen, who was a representative of the Russian cloister [i.e. Church], fought those ideas, and he at once sensed in Rasputin a great force that could have an effect on the masses, above all on the peasant masses, whose language he spoke and whose manners were his manners. To such a one the peasant masses will listen; he will strongly influence them, and the help he can give the clericals in their struggle against the freedom tendencies forcing their way into Russia is beyond estimation. He is the true type of a muzhik, and the masses will listen to him as to one of their own; they will believe him, they will have great trust in him...
While the bishop sat and listened to this wanderer speaking, he was busy thinking how to exploit this effective, strong power of Rasputin's for his political ends. He felt that this was a force he must not let slip out of his hands.
When Rasputin fell silent for a while, Bishop Hermogen turned to "Father" Feofan and said that they must at once take the "starets" (holy man) to the famous monk Iliodor, and to Rasputin he said:
— Little father! You will go with us to Iliodor... we will introduce you to him.
They all went off at once to visit the "Black Monk" Iliodor.
Iliodor, the monk of Tsaritsyn, was famous as the greatest orator the Russian Orthodox Church possessed. He was a young man of medium height, with broad shoulders and wild, burning eyes; his voice — sharp, unpleasant — had a great deal of power in it. He was a wild fanatic and led a strict ascetic life. People feared him, and at the same time the common masses idolized him. Thousands upon thousands of peasants were drawn to him, came from distant regions to hear him; even the Tsar listened to his speeches.
When he set out from his monastery leading a religious procession that wound along the banks of the Volga, thousands of peasants followed him. He walked under a white "baldachin" (a kind of canopy) decorated with many fresh flowers. He was surrounded by gold-adorned "icons", and wherever he appeared the crowds of peasants knelt and all, as with one voice, began singing religious hymns. After Iliodor came the monks of his monastery. They sat in carriages that were drawn by girls and women. When he came near the kneeling people, they cried out in ecstasy: "Holy knight of the Heavenly Kingdom!"
Iliodor wanted to build a large monastery in Tsaritsyn. But he did not have enough funds for it. So he climbed up a hillock that was in the town. Thousands of people at once gathered around the hillock, and he began to speak to the assembled. He spoke with fire, his eyes burned wildly, and in the middle of speaking his sharp voice began to thunder down from on high:
— Whoever among you owns a plank he does not need, let him bring that plank to me as a gift! And whoever among you owns a rusty nail that he has no need of, let him give that nail away! And those of you who own nothing — let them volunteer themselves and help dig the earth!
The result of this speech of his was that the entire population of the town began bringing together boards, bricks, beams and various other materials needed for building; hundreds of workers came and offered their labour for free. Very soon a large monastery rose up in the poorest district of the town, which with its size put in the shade many other monasteries in Russia, and the "Black Monk" became very famous through it. His following grew steadily. Thousands upon thousands came to his cloister from near and far to attend his "services" and listen to his flaming speeches. His influence and power over his admirers grew stronger from day to day.
Iliodor was a hundred-percent monarchist and a dark reactionary. In his countless speeches he agitated with ardour for the absolute rule of the Tsar, who is anointed by God to rule over Russia. He joined the "Union of the Truly Russian People" (the "Black Hundreds") and became the leader of that Black-Hundred organization. It was an organization of embittered antisemites and political reactionaries, which at that time had great power in Russia.
At the same time as this "Black Monk" agitated for the absolute power of the Tsar, he nevertheless did not refrain from coming out sharply against the rich, privileged classes, and that made him popular among the broad Russian masses.
With an embittered hatred that had no equal, he agitated against the Jews. A wild hatred of Jews burned like a black fire in all his limbs. At all his "services" he incited with poison and gall against the "Zhids", who are the "children of Satan", who suck the marrow of the poor Russian man and bring want and misfortune upon the land. He called the Jews the most terrible names, awakened in the masses evil hatred and cruelty toward them, and called for their extermination. His sharp voice clamoured wildly:
— Exterminate the "Zhids", and "Holy Russia" will be saved from Satan and from misfortune!
— Destroy the godless, and God's grace will descend upon you!
And once, on a Sunday, when thousands were gathered in the cloister and around the cloister, Iliodor set out with a procession. All the icons and the "holy" banners were carried out of the cloister. Iliodor himself took his place under a white baldachin. In his hand he held a large golden cross. The procession formed and lined up, and suddenly all those assembled stared in astonishment and wonder: at the front of the procession there appeared a gigantic doll that looked like a Jew. The doll was dressed in a Jewish kapote, with a yarmulke and with sidelocks... The procession got moving, moved slowly, and religious hymns were sung. The doll with the appearance of a Jew was carried ahead on a pole. Great crowds of people followed. The procession wound through the streets until it came back to the cloister. Then they stopped, a great fire was laid, and with great solemnity the doll was burned..
Iliodor himself threw the doll into the fire with his own hands, thundering as he did so:
— So shall all the "Zhids" be exterminated!
In front of the monastery that Iliodor had built there hung a large picture showing Jewish lawyers and journalists at the head of a camp of sinners condemned to eternal hell. The picture portrayed the Jews as such sinners that it aroused hatred and malice toward Jews.
(To be continued).
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bo
The Portion
—o—
a) "Behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into thy border" (Ex. 10:4)
Among the locusts there reigns an unparalleled unity; unlike other creatures they have no king over them ("The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands"). United and brotherly they live; that is why Moses warned Pharaoh of the plague of locusts (although he had not been asked to do so). For he knew that the downfall of the Egyptians would come through internal frictions, through "and I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians" — which is the main cause of the fall of every people. That is what the plague of locusts hinted at. Mei Shiloah.
—o—
That is why God had to use so many plagues: not every one is affected [?] by the same plague. For one, say, blood is the worst; for the second, the frogs; and for the third, actually the lice... To cater to everyone's taste, all kinds of plagues had to be used. Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
A Jew burdened with eight grown-up daughters asks his brother for support, and when the latter is in no hurry to send it, he writes to him:
"I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Het (= 8), and if thou refuse to let go, behold, tomorrow I will bring four into thy border"... [pun: Het = the letter ח = 8; arba "four" for arbeh "locusts".]
The brother takes fright at the four daughters and quickly sends money. A folk jest.
—o—
b) "I will see thy face again no more" (ibid., 29)
Moses did in fact meet Pharaoh once more: at the plague of the firstborn.
But Moses told no lie when he said "I will see thy F A C E again no more": with such a face I no longer want to see you. At the plague of the firstborn Pharaoh had an entirely different face — a terrified one, a face of mortal fear... Imrei Shefer.
—o—
c) "Speak now in the ears of the people, and let them ask" (11:1 [sic])
"I pray you, ask of the Egyptians, so that that righteous man [Abraham] shall not say: 'And they shall serve them and afflict them' He fulfilled in them, 'and afterward shall they come out with great substance' He did not fulfil in them" (Berakhot 9).
And if that righteous man does not come with a complaint — is God then not bound to keep His word? What is this "so that he shall not say"?
The Jews actually did not want to borrow from the Egyptians. They had renounced the money. Higher goals of redemption now stood before them. So they waived the promise of "great substance". But God feared that Abraham would argue: "And they shall serve them and afflict them" — the Jews did not want that either, yet You carried out the decree by force; so fulfil the promise of "great substance" by force too, even though they do not want it... Mei Im.
—o—
"And they lent them" —
The Egyptians themselves urged the Jews to take gifts from them, just so they would finally leave Egypt... Kli Yakar.
—o—
d) "The man Moses was very great... in the sight of the people" (ibid., 3)
Providence decreed that Moses be raised in Pharaoh's house, then go away to a distant land and come back a stranger. Otherwise he could not have been great "in the sight of the people". The people do not revere one of their own, a homely familiar. "The poor man's wisdom is despised": the wisdom of one to whom one is accustomed (hasakhan) is worth nothing, has no importance. Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
Rabbi Akiva Eger once came to Warsaw, where he was received with great honour. Present at the reception was also the "Hemdat Shlomo". He asks him:
"Rabbi, you are surely as great a gaon as R. Akiva Eger. Why do the Warsaw householders not honour you so?"
The "Hemdat Shlomo" answers him:
"When 'Unetaneh Tokef' is said, the synagogue is packed, Jews weep, the Holy Ark is open, a shudder [?] runs through everyone. Whereas the 'Vehu Rahum' of Monday and Thursday is no longer said so earnestly, although it is no lesser prayer. Why is that? Because 'Unetaneh Tokef' is said once a year, and 'Vehu Rahum' — every Monday and Thursday..."
—o—
e) "This month shall be unto you" (12:1)
"Mine and yours is the redemption... let your joy be complete, even one who is poor" (Perush).
Had the Jews been redeemed by their own merit, because of their piety — well then, only the pious would have been the in-laws [the celebrants]. But because of our piety the redemption will not come; only for the sake of the Shekhinah, which is in exile. Well, then you are all equal in-laws: pious and not pious, young men and old together... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
f) "In one house shall it be eaten" (12:46)
"In one house" — not divided into groups, together, like a family, because thanks to that you were redeemed. "Because they did not change their language" — because they did not speak with the tongue otherwise than they thought in the heart, did not go about talebearing. Olelot Ephraim.
—o—
g) "With unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it" (ibid., 8)
In the Haggadah there is a version: first maror, then matzah. The Torah too says first "and I will bring you out" (redemption) and only afterwards "and I will rid you out of their bondage" (exile). For only once they were redeemed did they feel the former taste of exile, of maror. In Egypt itself they did not feel it... Tiferet Uziel.
—o—
h) "That the law of the Lord may be in thy mouth" (13:9)
"The mouth of strange women is a deep pit."
There is no worse deep pit than when the mouth is a stranger to the words it speaks... Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin.

What's New in Zagłębie? Będzin: A New[?] Change in the Newly Elected Kehilla Council. / Each Will "Keep Shabbat" Separately. / The New Presidium of the Gemilut Hesed [Free-Loan] Fund. / The "Peace" Negotiations Have So Far Produced No Result Whatsoever. / The Magistrat Makes Savings... / From "Hakoach". / The Question of Compelling Landlords to Install Running Water. / Mr. Gottesdiener's Lecture Cancelled. / Notices for Merchants. / Died of a Heart Attack. / Instead of 10 Groszy — 370..

[Będzin — kehilla and municipality; eleven local news items.]
A New[?] Change in the Newly Elected Kehilla Council.
Dafner and Helgrin Lose Their Seats.
At the time when 1 seat was taken from the Zionist list and allotted to the "Agudah" (the seat went to Mr. Dafner), the Zionist list's authorised representative, Mr. Abraham Lizer, lodged a complaint about it with the voivode [provincial governor].
This week Mr. Lizer received from the starosta [district head] a written decision of the voivode, which annuls the starosta's earlier ruling and establishes that lists 1 (Dafner) and 2 (Helgrin) remain without seats. That is: Dafner's seat goes back to the Zionists, and Helgrin's — to the "Agudah".
By this count the "Agudah" now has 5 seats (because Mr. Lagra is, as is known, in opposition to the "Agudah"), and the Zionists — 7.
—o—
Each Will "Keep Shabbat" Separately.
A few weeks ago a conflict arose between the Council of Commissioners and the provisional administration of the Magistrat [town hall]. The conflict consisted in the provisional administration's refusal to recognise the Council's authority to audit the Magistrat's activity.
The matter was sent to the voivodeship, and this week an answer was received that the Council of Commissioners has the right to supervise and to deliver a report on the activity.
At the last session of the Council of Commissioners a discussion about it developed again, and in the end a resolution was adopted that both the Council and the provisional administration are to work out the report on the activity to date.
Messrs. Rechnitz, Gutenstein and Zalski joined the Council's committee.
—o—
The New Presidium of the Gemilut Hesed [Free-Loan] Fund.
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Lewin, the first meeting of the new board of the G"Ch fund in our town took place on Tuesday evening.
Only one item was dealt with at the meeting: electing the institution's presidium.
Before proceeding to the vote, R' Mendel Rosensaft takes the floor and makes a warm appeal to the board to spare the honour of Mr. Boszykowski and hand him the office of president again.
Mr. Rubinlicht replies that Mr. Rosensaft's intervention is not tactful when the person concerned is present.
The election produced the following result: by 9 votes to 6 Mr. Rubinlicht was elected president. Vice-presidents: Messrs. Boszykowski and Goldfeld; chief treasurer A. Trakojer[?]; second treasurer Mr. Rzhinker[?]; and secretary Granek.
—o—
The "Peace" Negotiations Have So Far Produced No Result Whatsoever.
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Jakob Gutman, a meeting was held on Sunday evening in the kehilla office with the participation of the "old" and the "new" members of the kehilla board and council.
The meeting was called on the initiative of the secretary, Mr. Freilich, who set out in a series of facts the catastrophic situation of the kehilla. The treasury stands empty, all revenues have stopped, the officials are not getting any salaries; even boards [for burials] — says Mr. F. — are no longer available...
After the sad report, dozor [kehilla board] member Mr. Rinski proposed an armistice, i.e. that both warring sides conclude a temporary peace and —
— and peace upon Israel...
The floor goes to dozor member Lizer, who points out that it is thanks to the deeds of the Agudah dozor members, with president Lizer[?] at their head, that such a sad state has been brought about. If you are not capable — says Mr. L. — of running kehilla life, then go away and let others, more capable than you, take over. But when you come with your righteousness about peace, I declare to you that the Zionist group will not touch such chaos.
Dozor member Aron[?] Hampel brings a proposal that first of all care be taken that the officials receive their salaries, whereas with the salaries for the clergy who have side incomes, potatoes and coal should be bought, to be distributed among the poor population.
The Mizrachi dozor members, as always, put forward a proposal that the negotiations be postponed to another date.
And so, this Saturday night the "continuation" of the "peace negotiations" takes place...
—o—
The Magistrat Makes Savings...
As we learn, several officials of the local Magistrat are being cut. The entire staff of the health department has also been given notice. All this is being done for the sake of economy. For the same reason the telephone in the municipal establishment[?] has also been cancelled.
— Is the financial situation of the Magistrat really so critical that an expense of 20 złoty a month plays a role in a budget of millions...
In our opinion, many 20-złoty notes are spent in the course of a month on purposes that are not as important as a telephone in a bathhouse...
—o—
From "Hakoach".
In connection with the Maccabiah in Eretz Israel, elimination trials are taking place in Warsaw. The local "Hakoach" will be represented by a larger number of women and men gymnasts, who are travelling to Warsaw accompanied by several board members.
This Saturday night an entertainment evening takes place in the club's own premises. The proceeds are for the benefit of the gymnasts without means who will take part in the Eretz-Israel Maccabiah.
—o—
The Question of Compelling Landlords to Install Running Water.
At the last session of the Council of Commissioners the question of compelling landlords to install running water [mains] was considered. Various proposals were put forward on the matter. The proposal adopted was that the sanitary committee should take up the question: if the committee finds that the water in a given house is not fit for use, running water will be installed in that house compulsorily.
Messrs. Hampel and Zalski were co-opted to the sanitary committee.
—o—
Mr. Gottesdiener's Lecture Cancelled.
The continuation of the lecture series on Maimonides will not take place this Saturday night, owing to the lecturer's poor state of health.
—o—
Notices for Merchants.
There is time until 15 February [luty] to submit declarations of turnover for the year 1931.
At the Merchants' Association information is given on bringing in goods from abroad, and all kinds of applications concerning imports are handled.
—o—
Died of a Heart Attack.
While hunting in the Kresy [the eastern borderlands], the pharmacist Beer suffered a heart attack and died.
—o—
Instead of 10 Groszy — 370..
This week Mr. Szancer[?], a resident of Czeladzka Street, paid 3 złoty 70 groszy in penalty on an old tax debt that amounts to... 10 groszy.
Sosnowiec — Kehilla Representatives Have “Opened Their Eyes” and Seen That the Local Jewish Population “Eats Treyf Meat”

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, kashrut.]
By order of the starosta [district head] the kehilla council was convened to a session to fix the new kehilla budget.
The session took place on Monday evening under the chairmanship of the vice-president Mr. Lejbisz Szwajcer. Present were the Agudah dozors [kehilla board members] and their sympathizers. The Zionists, Mizrachists and artisans did not come[?] in proper number.
In the middle of the session one of the parnassim took the floor and declared: “Since in the town very many pitfalls have arisen in buying poultry and meat from the outside slaughter, the council shall appoint Rabbi Englard as supervisor of kashrut matters. For this a salary of 12 thousand zł. shall be assigned to him for his pains”...
As it turned out, the parnassim had already been informed in advance that such a proposal would be brought in. For there was no strong opposition to the proposal. Only “amendments” were brought in. For example, parnas Mr. Cycemski[?] was of the opinion that “only 10 thousand zł. is enough”.
In principle the proposal was adopted, only the question is, on Mr. Cycemski's[?] motion, being referred to the board.
In connection with this several parnassim of the Mizrachist camp sent in a motion to reject the project, which was considered in a non-legal manner at the Monday session.
At the session parnas Mr. Dawid Feldman proposed that the subsidy for the “Linas Holim” society should be paid out only when a representative of the kehilla is elected to its board.
—o—
73-Year-Old Jew Under a Lorry
[Sosnowiec — accident.]
A serious accident occurred on Tuesday evening on 3 Maja Street.
The 73-year-old Kalman Patlaniek[?] was walking along the street, led by his grandchild. At that moment a lorry drove at high speed into the old man and the grandchild.
Both were taken to the Jewish hospital, where it was established that the old man had several limbs broken and altogether his whole body was badly injured. The grandchild was only lightly injured.
—o—
Sensational Affair at the “Bank Zagłębia” — Embezzlements Exceeding Half a Million Złoty
[Sosnowiec — banking, crime.]
At the local “Bank Zagłębia” large embezzlements have been discovered, amounting to over half a million zł. The director Żuchowski[?] and the [vice-?]president of the board A. Wieczorek[?] have been arrested.
The affair made a strong impression in town.
—o—
“A Heart That Yearns” in Sosnowiec
[Sosnowiec — theatre.]
The management of the Kraków Jewish theatre, headed by Kadisz and Kasz, has invited for a series of guest performances the famous artists Szoszana and Laste[?].
The plays the artists are staging there are having an extraordinary success. The local press is enthusiastic, and the public too greets the actors with stormy ovations.
The artists Nechama, Kadisz, Kasz and others are already popular with the Zagłębie theatre public, so that every performance is received with warmth.
Tonight, Friday evening, the troupe will play at the Sosnowiec municipal theatre the well-known play “A Heart That Yearns”, which makes a very strong impression on everyone.
—o—
The Artisans Have a Tongue...
[Sosnowiec — societies.]
Last Sunday the continuation of the annual general meeting of the Artisans' Association took place for the second time.
For the discussion on the reports some 5[?] dozen “speakers” put their names down. Because of this the meeting was again broken off and will be continued next Sunday.
—o—
Meeting of the “Mizrachi”
[Sosnowiec — parties.]
Under the chairmanship of Rabbi Hager the annual general meeting took place last Saturday night. After the reports a discussion developed which lasted several hours. Because of this the remaining items will be dealt with at the second meeting, which takes place this Saturday night.
—o—
Sensational Trial at the Local District Court
[Sosnowiec — courts.]
In the near future the trial will take place at the local district court against the railway cashier Bernacki[?] and his assistants, who several months ago carried out the planned raid on the cash office of the Dąbrowa railway station.
Some 50 witnesses have been summoned to the trial.
—o—
Dead Body Pulled Out of the “Przemsza”
[Sosnowiec — events.]
This week the dead body of a young man was pulled out of the “Przemsza”. It later turned out that this was the 20-year-old Pietkiewicz, who had jumped into the “Przemsza” several weeks ago.
—o—
Conference Between Employers and Employees
[Zagłębie — labour, mines.]
In connection with the fact that the agreement on wages in the coal mines of the Zagłębie and Kraków districts has been terminated, a conference will open tomorrow, Saturday, at which the question of the new wages is to be dealt with.
—o—

What will the lump-sum (ryczałt) turnover tax look like?
[Taxes.] By 31 March 1932 every taxpayer will receive an assessment order (nakaz) for the lump-sum turnover tax (ryczałt obrotowy) for both years 1932 and 1933.
The lump-sum tax will be payable in 4 small instalments: on 15 April (kwiecień), 15 July (lipiec), 15 October (październik) and 15 December (grudzień).
If one does not pay by the deadline, an execution (distraint) will be made on the instalment that was not paid.
All payers of the lump-sum turnover tax will be able to submit an appeal (odwołanie) to the appeals commission (komisja odwoławcza) by 1 May 1932. We point out, however, that an appeal may be submitted only if the taxpayer was placed in the wrong group because the tax office (urząd) made a mistake in calculating the average turnover, and also if the lump sum is applied to merchants and artisans who are not subject to the lump sum.
It will not be possible to submit appeals for transfer to another lump-sum group because turnover has decreased, or for other reasons, because one would want the turnover tax reduced. As long as the office correctly calculates the average turnover for the last three years, no appeal at all can be made.
If within two years the turnover decreases, the lump sum cannot be reduced.

[Będzin — theatre.] „200 000“, a comedy in 3 acts by Sholem Aleichem. Direction: Y. Y. Rotbaum, music: Henech Kon, song lyrics by M. Broderzon, performed by the „Vilna Troupe“.
On Wednesday we in Będzin had the honour of seeing Sholem Aleichem in a fresh creation. It is only a pity that Sholem Aleichem did not have the privilege, in his lifetime, of seeing the great success of a theatre piece of his.
The director Y. Rotbaum approached „200.000“ with a new adaptation, and he indeed succeeded.
The whole ensemble of the so-called „Vilna Troupe“ performed their roles diligently.
The music, Broderzon's songs, everything so heartfelt, so „folksy“, that the troupe earned the applause it was given.
Particularly distinguished were Mr. Landoy (Mele Soroker), Y. Rakow (Solovaytshik the matchmaker), Vitaliga (Eti-Meni), R. Nera[?] (the flour-shopkeeper), Goldenberg (Bielke), Rozenblum (Yokheved[?]) as well as Messrs. Vaynshtok, Kats, Videtski, Levenshteyn, Dagim, Melnik, Pasashinski and others.
Incidentally it must be noted that from the constant overacting, especially by our fellow-townsmen, and the commanding from off the stage — one sees that the troupe lacks the strong hand that would watch over the discipline and uniformity which play a great role in any serious theatre production.
Ben Avrom.

How Hundreds of People Were Swindled by a „Bank Director“.
A few months ago a „branch“ (filia) of the Kraków Credit Bank for Officials was opened at 64 Piłsudski Street in Sosnowiec.
At the time an advertisement of the „bank“ appeared in the local press, saying that everyone had the opportunity to obtain loans on very good terms, only officials, who must provide good guarantors (żyranci), have priority.
The announcement naturally had great success, and already on the second day dozens of people came [?] for exact information on how to obtain the loans.
Mr. „Director“ explained to everyone that first of all whoever wants a loan must enrol as a member and pay in 10 gulden [złoty].
The public believed, paid in the 10 gulden and waited for the promised loans.
But the „director“ was not yet satisfied with the 10 gulden; he hired agents whose task was to recruit members in the surrounding area.
The „business“ developed very well. Day by day the number of clients, who were already waiting impatiently for the loans, grew larger.
Finally the „bubble“ burst. When the clients who came to collect their loans no longer found the „director“, only then did they understand that they had been cheated, and handed the matter over to the police.
After a thorough investigation it turned out that the „director“ is a professional swindler.
The „director“ has been arrested.

„Whoever Does Not Buy the Holy Agudah Organ Is a Troubler of Israel“...
Mr. Mordechai Hirsch Danziger reports the following fact to us:
On Wednesday during the day he bought a „Hayntike Nayes“ [Today's News, a Warsaw Yiddish daily] from the newspaper seller Shtayer. At that moment a young fellow ran up to him and said to Danziger:
— „You may as well bury your face in the ground“.
Danziger, who is known as a calm man and a pious Jew, regarded the youngster as not normal and therefore did not react to the abuse. Only when the same fellow went on cursing did Danziger say to him:
— Get away from me, madman.
Thereupon the insolent fellow only then let loose with his tongue and shouted at the top of his voice:
— „You sinner of Israel, you troubler of Israel. Buy the „Tageblatt“! [Dos Yidishe Togblat, the Agudat Israel daily in Warsaw]
Only later did it become clear that the impudent fellow is the representative of the Agudah organ and had taken upon himself the mission of standing on guard and watching who buys a different newspaper...
