Zygmunt Turkow's 15-Year Jubilee

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — theatre.] Jubilee evenings in Będzin and in Sosnowiec.
Zygmunt Turkow — only 35 years old altogether, and how much the man already has to his credit. A total of no fewer than 3,500 performances, 250 roles, nearly 50 productions over 15 years of life on the Yiddish stage.
But there are things that get forgotten: alongside the laurel wreaths of enthusiasm, recognition, gratitude and applause, one must also mention pain and troubles, sleepless nights and hungry days, which are no rarity among Jewish artists.
In honour of the jubilee, committees have been formed in all the larger towns of Poland with the aim of marking before the Jewish public the date of 15 years of activity of the famous actor.
The lovers of the Yiddish artistic word in Będzin and Sosnowiec, too, have taken upon themselves the initiative of organising festive jubilee performances.
This initiative deserves to be welcomed, because the jubilarian Zygmunt Turkow belongs to the few Jewish actors who stand out for their intelligence and truly artistic talent. Zygmunt Turkow's famous creations are still in our memory.
The jubilee performances will take place next Thursday, the 28th, in Będzin, and the following day, Friday, in Sosnowiec.
The committees formed have accepted the following programme, consisting of: an introductory address by the actor Icchak Grudberg, who is coming here together with Turkow; 2) "Uncle Moses" by Sholem Asch, fragments performed by the jubilarian; 3) "The Thought" by Andreyev, performed by Zygmunt Turkow; and 4) greetings.
It is to be hoped that Jewish Zagłębie will receive the jubilee performances warmly and thereby show its attitude to the artist who builds and plants a serious Yiddish theatre.
All friends of the Jewish stage art, everyone to whom the living artistic Yiddish word is dear, will pay tribute to Zygmunt Turkow, the founder of "VYKT", one of the finest and most intelligent Jewish actors and directors.
Zygmunt Turkow has earned it honestly and fairly!
We warmly congratulate him on his jubilee and wish him to continue his valuable work for the Yiddish theatre with renewed strength.

[Sosnowiec — human interest.] A bride in a sack.
A sensational story took place these days here in Sosnowiec.
The son of a rich Jewish householder some time ago became acquainted with a poor Jewish girl, a seamstress, whom he liked very much.
The young man began going about with her and spending whole evenings together.
This went on for over 3 years.
In the end the girl's father called the young man in and began talking to him about "intentions" [printed "tfeyles" for "takhles"].
The young man declared that he would marry the girl, only one must have a little patience.
Lately, however, the young man began showing himself to the bride more and more rarely; the girl grew uneasy about this, and one morning she fell in tears on her mother's neck and told her that she was in a different condition [i.e. pregnant]...
The parents turned to the young man, that he should at once set up a wedding canopy with their daughter. The young man, however, gave no clear answer.
Seeing that the story was taking an unpleasant turn, the girl's father hit upon a ploy.
On Saturday night he took a sack and went together with his daughter to the flat of the groom's parents. In the entrance he told his daughter to crawl into the sack and, taking the sack on his shoulders, he rang for the master of the house.
When the maid opened the door for him, the father went with the sack into the dining room, set the sack down in the middle of the room and, without saying a word, left the flat.
When the family and the groom opened the sack, they saw to their horror that inside it was the groom's bride.
The end of the story: soon, with good luck, a wedding according to the law of Moses and Israel will take place between the young man and the bride.

[Zawiercie — cooperative movement.] Visit of Dr. Silberstein and Moshe Shalit in Zawiercie.
At the invitation of the Zawiercie Cooperative Bank, which is one of the oldest Jewish credit institutions in Poland, distinguished guests came on a visit last Monday: Dr. Silberstein, president of the directorate of the Jewish Cooperative Societies in Poland, Moshe Shalit of Vilna, and editor Prawalski of Warsaw.
At the station they were met by members of the council and the management; afterwards the guests went to the bank's own splendid building, where, acquainting themselves closely with the bank's activity, they expressed their appreciation for the splendid achievement in general and in particular for erecting such a building by its own efforts.
Over a glass of tea the guests were greeted by Mr. Gustaw Bernstein on behalf of the management and Mr. Berl Zielonka on behalf of the council.
Dr. Silberstein and Mr. Shalit replied to the greetings, discussing at length the present economic situation in general and that of the Jewish cooperative movement in particular.
Then a 3-hour conference was held, at which Messrs. Cwajgel, Zajman, Beser, Ratmensz and Zielonka reported on the economic situation of our town, which suffers from a specific structural crisis; yet the bank, which has a purely public character, has served 700 members from all strata of the Jewish population and is a support precisely in the present critical time.
The guests, acquainting themselves closely with the balance sheet and with the bank's activity in general, noted with satisfaction the important activity of the institution and promised the fullest support within the limits of their possibilities.
The visit of these leading figures in the field of cooperative affairs made a good impression in the town.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — labour and industry; short news items.]
The Situation in the Coal Mines Grows Sharper.
Tens of thousands of workers awaited with great impatience the decisions of the congress of the ironworks (huty) delegates, which closed on Sunday in Katowice.
320 delegates came. The conduct of the industrialists was attacked with enormous sharpness. There was tremendous agitation. The lockout that had been prepared was described as a "provocation, violence and injustice".
The delegates pointed out that if reductions were to be made, one ought to have started with the directors. 170 directors take salaries of 1,700,000[?] zł., while 100 thousand workers receive 20 million zł. Each director earns on average 10 thousand zł. a month, each worker barely 200 zł. a month.
The congress adopted a resolution which states that the workers energetically oppose the reduction of wages, that the iron magnates are ruining the industry, and that the workers demand state control over production. The resolution states that the workers will fight with all means against the attack of the industrialists.

Public Problems and Party Shops — Why do influential parties remain fragmented in the Jewish street?

(Why do influential parties remain fragmented in the Jewish street?)
When it comes to elections to any institution whatsoever, the artisans come along on one side and prove to you by every sign that they are the majority of the people and that one cannot manage without them, and therefore they demand the majority; and on the other side we again see the same thing with the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel]. Them too we must believe blindly that they are the top of the town, that they are "the majority in number and the majority in substance", and that nobody may[?] have even the slightest doubt about it.
Yes, at elections we see their strength, at elections we hear their mighty breath. At just such moments we hear them resound and ring and roar and clamour and turn worlds upside down, so that, willy-nilly, we come to the conviction that these two elements are the quicksilver of the people, the most living nerve in everyday life.
And yet, when all is quiet, when life is monotonous and the soul is troubled and the heart is sad, then we do not feel at all that the said elements are to be found in the ranks of the Jewish people, that they exist and act together with all the other strata of the Jewish population. When life is quiet and sad and poor, we do not know at all whether the said elements are distinct shades, whether they have special demands and needs.
And what has brought this up? Why, we know that times today are unbearably bitter; "catastrophic" is too mild an expression; it is simply impossible to grasp with the mind how the average and the poor person lives and exists, how he can continue his way of life in a dignified way, in a decent manner — and therefore such a life is now a rarity. People languish in the garrets, simply die of hunger, and there is no way out; one does not see "whence my help shall come", how help can come, from where and in what manner salvation can appear — and in these very moments we do not see one coming to the aid of another, one taking an interest in the other's sorrows and joys, in the other's grief and pain.
Why, we know how bitter it is in the artisans' ranks, how much want and hunger they suffer, and yet we do not see what their organization consists of, how they could or would help one another. It seems that not long ago they were still organized rock-solid, so that they ought to have had some chances or other to help their oppressed fellows; meanwhile, what do we see? We see that they have fallen apart and crumbled, and only when need begs for mercy — have pity on us! — do the artisans in Sosnowiec begin to organize, and, as Sosnowiec loves, one must of course storm and clamour; everyone wants, as usual, to show off his erudition, and meanwhile there is noise and the main thing is forgotten: that now is no time for handing out honours or waging quarrels; it is forgotten that now there should have been no need to stand at "aleph" again, and at best it would have been a blessing if they now organized themselves so as to be able to do something for those who are starving.
Why fool ourselves — better to say clear and open words: should not, for instance, the Sosnowiec artisans have been organized, so that in a time of trouble they would be prepared[?] to help those of their fellows who need help? Could they not have been for their fellows the same as they were when it was a matter of carrying out public obstinacy? Why did they know how to spend all their energy just to push their own way through, and now, when economic interests demand an organized mass of artisans, it has vanished and has to be created anew, as if it had never played any role in the Jewish street.
That is how it is when one does not want to foresee the future, when one acts without a system and without any calculation. Public activity, economic order must be conducted according to a certain order and calculation; otherwise a failure must ensue, and it is not out of the question that one ends up hanging in the air, as has unfortunately happened to the artisans in almost all towns.
Of course, had there been a little more order and had public activity been more crystallized, the artisans' organizations would not have fallen apart like this — from which the artisans suffer doubly: once from the crisis and a second time from the ruins of their institutions, owing to the fact that they were left standing helpless, with nobody to ask for advice or to receive material help from.
Had the artisans' institutions understood their tasks, they would today occupy one of the most honoured places in the Jewish street, and the artisans would moreover be the strongest in the material sense.
Things are no better with the Agudah elements: they, who occupy every corner of Jewish life, they, who know so well how to worm their way in among all strata of the population and know excellently how to exploit everyone, cannot, for all their tricks, go on running the kehilla life in Będzin, so that before capitulating [printed "kapitalirn"] they want, if you please, the "Daytshn" [the modernized, "German" Jews], the sinners, to drag them out of the deep swamps into which they have sunk so deep.
Upon my life, it is a joke with these fellows: until now they let nobody come near them — "we must ride the kehilla nag in all its length and breadth, we may let nobody in there, we must dominate it through and through" — and suddenly a turnabout: as if out of the blue a heavenly voice came forth from the Agudah nag, begging with glazed eyes: "Come here, whoever wishes, and prove that you want to save the honour of the Jewish kehilla, which we have so excellently managed to degrade and disgrace. Now you are kosher and welcome guests; you sinners and Daytshn can save the honour of the Jewish kehilla with your money."
Yes, that is how it is: they are the ones who need to take and "[—]"[?], and the people have to give; and since now times are bad and there is no longer anyone to milk, they invite to the table also those who until now were[?] treyf.
That is how it looks when one has no sense and responsibility for Jewish life and for all strata of the population, when one is only one-sided and seeks only to turn public problems, which ought to belong to the whole people, into petty party shops that are to bring benefit only to "our own people".
R. Les.
A Few Words about the "Keter Torah" Yeshivas.

[Article — the "Keter Torah" yeshivas; Sosnowiec and Będzin.] By Rabbi J. M. Blumenfeld, Warsaw.

During my visit to my brother, the great Rabbi Blumenfeld, rabbi in Königshütte [Chorzów], I was invited by the president of the "Keter Torah" yeshivas, the great Rabbi Moshele Rabinowicz, may he live long and happily (son-in-law of the Radomsko Rebbe), to come with my brother to the Sosnowiec "Kibbutz Gavoha" [advanced yeshiva]. And in truth I must declare that I saw more than I had hoped.

Many well-known rabbis (one of them the Chicago rabbi, Rabbi Pardes) examined the students in the most difficult passages of "Zevachim" and "Eruvin". All of them displayed a skilful [?] sharpness and astonishing erudition, and made everything understood with a marvellous explanation.

My heart rejoiced greatly, because here I heard the true voice of Torah and saw with joy that the light of Torah has not been extinguished. Nor is there any lack of people who sacrifice their wealth and property for its honour. The same can also be said of the Będzin yeshiva, which I visited, and of all the yeshivas that belong solely to "Keter Torah".

Nevertheless all this is done quietly, very modestly and without fuss. The Rebbe of Radomsko, may he live long and happily, supports the yeshivas, and his son-in-law, the president, watches over the spiritual state.

The yeshivas have many great heads of yeshiva, well-known Torah scholars and outstanding rabbis.

How beautiful such an undertaking is among Jews; it is truly a crown of Torah "without paint or powder". And everything is done quietly and modestly, without noise: no one takes photographs and no one makes speeches and the like. Thanks to this it is to be hoped that only through them will the Torah be revived again, in the old-new form of "words of Torah in secret" — "for out of them shall go forth Torah, and the word of the Lord to give rulings in Israel".

The Fifteenth [of Shevat].

[Short story — Tu BiShvat.] (A story). By Shaul Sapir [Szaul Safir].

This year's Fifteenth of Shevat leaves Ester-Beyle somewhat disappointed: it falls right on the Sabbath. This time she will not be able to hand out the Fifteenth fruits to the Talmud Torah children, as she was used to doing years ago.

A few days before every Fifteenth, old Ester used to buy carob, "shatalen" [?], dates, figs and almonds, go to the Talmud Torah, and personally hand every child a little packet... The children's little eyes shone, their little faces beamed and their little hearts pounded... and when all the children said "Shehecheyanu" all at once, Ester-Beyle's face glowed and her heart pounded with happiness and joy.

Her thoughts carry her away, years back, to her little shtetl.

The Fifteenth of Shevat. Her dwelling, which consisted of only one room, is tidied up, festive. The windows are decorated with all sorts of flowers that the month of Shevat itself painted with its cold breath; a pleasant warmth pours into every corner... Ester-Beyle takes out a few copper coins, counts them carefully... wraps herself in a shawl and goes to buy Fifteenth fruit. She cannot buy much for her few saved-up coins. So she buys five pieces of carob, five dates and five figs... She counts them over and measures the pieces of carob: the biggest piece she will give to Dovid; he is the eldest, and already studies in the yeshiva!... The second piece is for Moshele; he doesn't even want to study, but he is so clever, and his eyes — a flame of fire!... Yes, this one is for Berele, this one for Sheftele and this one for Khaimele. She wraps up the Fifteenth and hides it carefully on the top shelf... She sees the pleasure and happiness that the Fifteenth will give her children tonight... They are, poor things, so greedy... the whole year no fruit enters their mouths. With what impatience they look forward to the Fifteenth of Shevat!... Had she not saved those few copper coins, she certainly could not now buy the Fifteenth for the children. There were days when she had nothing with which to buy bread for the children, but the saved-up Fifteenth money she did not touch... to her it was holy money... the children could, God forbid, be left without the Fifteenth...

Her eyes fall once more on the place where the Fifteenth is hidden.. It smells so strongly to her... she herself would also like to taste it... But she decides: no, she will manage without it; may the little children be healthy, they will enjoy it this evening...

In the cheder the rebbe announced to the children that in honour of the Fifteenth of Shevat they would study half a day in the cheder... and to those who stayed in the cheder he would tell a fine story about the Fifteenth... Hearing "a story", the children did not want to budge from their places. The rebbe's beautiful stories drew them like a magnet: they would never have tired of sitting day and night listening to his stories...

Moshele, however, remembered the Fifteenth and could no longer rest... He quietly stole out of the cheder... ran home breathless... At home nobody was there... He is sure that Mother has already got it ready. But where has she hidden it?... He won't touch it, he only wants to look at it with his eyes.. he will [?] put it back afterwards.. He searches and turns over the whole house, in the wardrobe, under the chest of drawers, under the pillows... He looks up at the shelf... yes, it must be there... He sets down a chair, onto the chair... he has it in his hand... He opens the little packet, looks at it and wants to put it back at once... he is dying for it... nothing more than one lick with the tongue... He notices that one piece of carob is longer than the others.. he will even it out... he bites off a piece... he tastes the taste of Paradise... he has shortened it too much... he will have to even out the other pieces to match that piece of carob. He bites again. Now these have become smaller. [He] sets about evening them out again... until he noticed that of all five pieces of carob nothing at all was left... A trembling seized Moshele... what will happen this evening when Mother starts handing out the Fifteenth...

The blood rushed to his head, his eyes began to swim... and with a great impetus he jumped up onto the chair again and took down the rest of the "Fifteenth"; he quickly began to gulp down first the five figs and then the five dates... For a while he remained standing in the middle of the room... and suddenly he ran to the door, opened it in haste and ran away...

In the evening, when the children came back from the cheder, Mother asked them: "Where is Moshele?"

— Moshele left earlier than all of us — they answered.

Mother immediately ran to the shelf, began to grope, to search, and let out a scream: "Woe is me, he has gobbled up the whole 'Fifteenth'!..."

There was weeping in the house... the brothers cursed and swore to get even with him...

But Moshele did not come home to sleep any more.. he vanished as if into water...

For eight years nothing was heard of him... Mother already counted him as dead... every Fifteenth was a day of mourning for Ester-Beyle... Suddenly she received a letter from her Moshele... he writes that he is in America and makes quite a fine living...

Every Fifteenth, when she comes back from the Talmud Torah, where she has handed out the "Fifteenth" to all the children, she tells the whole story of how her Moshele gobbled up the "Fifteenth".

And the mother's eyes fill with tears of joy.
The Ryczałt (Lump-Sum) Tax for Small Traders

Shortly the Sejm is to pass the government's bill on a ryczałt (lump-sum) tax for small traders.
*
The term "ryczałt tax" had a different content in previous years than it has now. Back then it was decided that the turnover tax should be levied not individually, on individual merchants, but collectively, on whole trades. The apportionment of the tax among the individual merchants was to be carried out by the economic organisations themselves, which know every member and know how to assess[?] his business correctly. That plan was shelved, and another kind of ryczałt came up.
Under the present ryczałt plan the tax is fixed individually, for each merchant separately. However, one does not assess the merchant's turnover in the current tax year; rather one takes his turnover for the last three years, 1928, 1929 and 1930, works out the average, and fixes the tax from that.
The bill is intended only for smaller livelihoods: in Warsaw and Łódź for businesses with a turnover of up to 35,000 zł., and in the other towns of Poland — up to 25.000 zł. turnover.
All categories, up to that maximum, are no longer — according to the plan — to be subject to any measuring-up, any assessment, any appeal, and the tax rate is half of what it was before: instead of two and a half per cent, only one and a quarter per cent.
This bill was sent by the Ministry to the central office of the chambers of commerce and to the central office of the small-traders' associations, to give their opinion on it. The latter agreed in principle to this ryczałt, but in their memoranda they demanded that the turnover ceiling falling under the ryczałt be raised — for Warsaw to 50 thousand zł. and for the other towns to 40 thousand.
This demand is now being considered in the Ministry, but with that[?] the matter is not yet exhausted[?]: it turns out that the small shopkeeper will not so quickly be rid of the eyes that peer with magnifying glasses into his business corners, looking how to pump ever greater taxes out of them.
Here is how:
There is in the bill a paragraph 10, which says that if the tax office has received confidential information that a shopkeeper made, in the current tax year, a turnover more than 50 per cent larger than his ryczałt shows, then an additional tax may be imposed on him.
The government regards this point as very important, because otherwise the big merchants could register their turnovers in the names of small customers and thereby wriggle out of taxes.
But this point destroys the whole illusion of the reform[?]. For in order to obtain information about individuals one must, after all, have agents who will investigate everyone, and once the fence is broken there is again room for all sorts of chicanery and harassment on the part of the local petty satraps, just as it was before.
The economic organisations therefore argue in their memoranda that, at bottom, in the present terrible crisis one must expect turnovers to shrink, not grow, and the whole ryczałt is for the state merely an armour against a fall in the tax altogether[?]. But if an exception is introduced for increased turnovers, then an exception must surely also be made for the shopkeepers whose turnover has shrunk by 50 per cent.
And if there is fear of falsifications, penalties for abuses can be laid down, but the small merchant must not be handed over to every petty agent.
Further, there is a question regarding appeals. For example, someone will be assessed a certain ryczałt, based on the turnovers of the three past years. But it may well be that in one of those years he was assessed too high. He lodged an appeal which has not yet been considered, and the ryczałt did not take this into account — so the tax inevitably comes out wrong; in such a case the taxpayer can appeal again. But how is the appeal to reach the table? The plan says that an appeal is granted on the proposal of the naczelnik [head of the tax office]. The economic organisations, however, demand that the commission members too be allowed to submit proposals on this.
Again, there is a paragraph 3, which says that for small businesses paying up to 100 zł. turnover tax the commission may remit the tax entirely, if it finds that although the merchant made the turnover he is nevertheless a pauper and cannot pay the tax. But the proposal on this must come from the naczelnik.
This paragraph represents a considerable relief. True, the same possibility of remission existed before too. But formerly, with the two-and-a-half-per-cent tax, it worked out that only a turnover of up to 4,000 zł. could benefit from this relief. Now even a turnover of up to 10.000[?] zł. will be able to benefit.
The economic organisations reckon, however, that if one is to wait for the naczelnik's grace, one will never live to see it.
They therefore demand in their memoranda that only the consent of the naczelnik be required, as in other tax[?] questions, but not his initiative.
How the government and the Sejm will relate to the above-mentioned and other demands of the economic organisations we shall soon learn.
As for artisans, the new plan provides that a craftsman who works alone, or with one worker, need not undergo any measuring-up or any assessment, but must pay 27 zł. a year. In this all are equal.
M. Suksman.
Fifth Anniversary of the Będzin "Gordonia"

This coming[?] Saturday night, the fifteenth of Shevat [Tu BiShvat], the Będzin "Gordonia" is holding a festive members' evening in connection with the organisation's 5th anniversary.
The local Zionist organisations, national activists, the local cultural societies and the Zagłębie Jewish press have been invited to the "celebration".
Taking part in the concert section are the young violinist Mr. Lejbek Rechnic and Gordonia's own choir, which will perform the latest songs of Eretz Israel.
Greetings have arrived for the celebration from Eretz Israel and from many organisations in larger cities in Poland.
— This week a conference of all the active members of the Zagłębie "Gordonia" took place in Będzin. The "Moetza" (council) worked out a uniform work plan for Gdud Alef (scouts).
Brazen Bandit Raid beyond Ojców[?]

On Saturday night into Sunday armed bandits attacked the Walczak family in the village of Brzozówka[?], beyond Ojców[?], and, breaking down the door, they got into the dwelling. From there the bandits carried off bedding, pillows and feathers.
At the alarm raised by the occupants, the neighbours of the victim came, and a regular battle broke out between the bandits and the peasants.
There are wounded on both sides.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Beshalach
The Portion
—o—
a) "The pillar of cloud departed not by day" (Ex. 13:22)
The pillar of cloud, which led the Jews through the wilderness, is a symbol of the Jewish leader. The pillar of cloud absorbed into itself all the arrows that were aimed at the Jews; the leader, too, must spread his shoulders before the ballista-stones aimed at the people and take them upon himself lovingly... The pillar of cloud levelled the mountains with the pits; so too, for the leader, poor and rich, great and small must be equal... Olelot Efraim.
• • •
"Jerusalem was destroyed only because they did not rebuke one another."
The misfortune that brought about the destruction of Jerusalem was that the leaders and the Torah scholars did indeed [?] rebuke the people, the masses, of whom they had nothing to fear; but "they did not rebuke one another" — they passed over with indifference the crimes that their colleagues, the leaders, committed...
Bina le-Itim.
—o—
b) "And he pursued after the children of Israel" (Ex. 14:8)
"The Merciful One does not strike at lives first" [misprinted "ba'al arachamim poge'a"] — when God exacts payment from a sinner, He first exacts it from his property before He comes to lives.
And therefore "they that trust in their wealth and boast in the multitude of their riches" — therefore the rich have no fear of God, knowing that in the worst case they need only fear for their money, while in body they are insured... So why should they give charity so that God will not punish them, if even in the worst case it will cost only money? Therefore: "None can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him"... The poor man, on the other hand, who has no money — on him vengeance is taken at once, in his body...
Pharaoh, seeing that although he had enough money, God nevertheless chose to lay His plagues on his body, cried out that this is not God's nature and that the plagues were not from God but sorcery, since with the rich God goes first of all for the money... Beit Shmuel Acharon.
—o—
c) "And behold, Egypt marched after them" (ibid., 10)
A man sometimes wants to run away from his sufferings, from his "Mitzrayim" (his straits), but "Egypt marched after them" — the sufferings are already seeking him out and chasing him... like that crazy woman in childbirth who screamed that they should drive her away from her labour [?] pains... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
• • •
The two holy brothers, Rabbi Elimelech of Leżajsk and Rabbi Zusha of Annopol, wandered for years in exile from village to village, from settlement to settlement. Once they happened to spend the night in a gentile tavern. Both brothers sleep in one bed, Rabbi Elimelech by the wall and Rabbi Zusha on the other side [?]. Gentiles gather, have a round of drinks, and, carousing [?] drunk, they notice the two Jews. They drag the first one, Rabbi Zusha, out of bed and give him a good beating. After another round of drinks it happens a second time, and so on, many times.
Rabbi Elimelech says to his brother: "Zusha, sweetheart [Polish 'serce'], you lie by the wall, and I will take a few blows now. After all, you are already tired." His brother obeys him and they turn over unnoticed by the gentiles.
Going again to take the Jew for a beating, the gentiles say to one another: "Let's take the Jew lying by the wall; that one has already had enough blows..."
And again they drag out the rebbe, Reb Zusha..
Rabbi Zusha cries out while they beat him:
"You see, Melech sweetheart, when it is decreed that you be beaten, it's lost — no tricks help..."
—o—
d) "Wherefore criest thou unto Me?" (ibid., 15)
Jews cry to God that the Messiah should come. But does it depend on God? He wants "in its time" [?] that the Messiah should come... "Wherefore criest thou unto Me?" — why are you crying to God? "Speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward" — it depends only on the Jews, that they should want the redemption.. Niflaot Chadashot (Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk).
—o—
e) "Who is like unto Thee among the gods, O Lord" (15:11)
When swindlers pass themselves off as a certain personality, it is a sign that that personality is famous. When various ones tried to present themselves as gods, it shows that the Jewish God is accepted and renowned... and this imitation need not annoy Him, for it proves His fame.
But when a lame man or some other cripple passes himself off as a certain personality, that is already a reason for the other to be vexed by the crippled imitation...
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
f) "The enemy said: I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil" (ibid., 9)
The enemy, the Evil Inclination, says to the pious man: "I will overtake, I will divide the spoil" — I will share in your mitzvot and in your Torah... Imrot Tehorot.
• • •
"There are even rebbes who are of the root of 'a root that beareth gall and wormwood'... In today's evil generation one must beware (of travelling to a rebbe), for most 'travel' because 'lawlessness suits them' — to throw off the yoke of Torah and commandments; and once he gets merely the name of Hasid, his impudence already allows him to cast off the yoke entirely... Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov said that in the footsteps of the Messiah there will be rebbes like locusts, who will delay the redemption, because they will cause baseless hatred and division of hearts and will not teach their Hasidim not to speak ill of other tzaddikim"..
— so writes Rabbi Eizikl of Komarno.
Otzar ha-Chaim.
—o—
g) "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand."
Miriam said the same song as Moses; she merely repeated Moses' words. An old womanly habit, to rechew other people's speech... And so that people would not hear how she was merely repeating Moses' words, they began to drum and make a din... Folk jest.
—o—
h) "And they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter" (ibid., 23)
They do not want to drink of the waters of Torah, "for they are bitter" [pun: "they are Marim" — masters], because they consider themselves masters of the Torah; certain Torah scholars hold themselves above even the Torah..
Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin.
—o—
i) "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you" (16:4)
"Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and He shall sustain thee."
A rich man is driving along the road in a britzka and picks up a poor man on foot who is carrying a bundle on his shoulders. The rich man sees that even in the britzka he does not take the bundle off. So he asks him:
— You are sitting, uncle, in the britzka; why are you carrying the bundle on your shoulders and not putting it down in the britzka?
— It's enough that your britzka carries me; why should it carry my bundle as well?
— Fool! Even if you hold the bundle on your shoulders, the britzka carries it by carrying you...
The moral:
In carrying you, God carries your bundle too...
The Jubilee Celebration of the "Linat ha-Cholim" Society

[Będzin — charity and health institutions.] As is known, the "Linat ha-Cholim" society in Będzin celebrated the jubilee of 25 years of its existence.
In honour of this the jubilee committee worked out a varied programme, such as a pledge (nedarim) campaign, an academy (festive evening), etc.
As always, the campaigns were supported by the Jewish masses, whereas the so-called "notables" [?] and the "fine Jews" stood "at a distance", and the whole matter lay for them "in the left side-lock" [i.e. they did not care at all]...
———
The official celebration began on Sabbath morning with the pledge campaign proclaimed by the Będzin rabbinate. A large number of people from the town were invited to the prayers at "Linat ha-Cholim". Only a few individuals came. The "patented" donors and benefactors of our town — and from the rabbinate, too, not a single one came.
The prayers before the lectern were led by the specially invited cantor Mr. Żupowicz [?], who enchanted the large congregation with his praying. Each time Mr. Żupowicz, with his splendid nusach, touched the depths of the soul, the worshippers said: "Oy, and such a cantor we let go from Będzin"...
After the Torah reading, in solemn silence, a memorial prayer was held for the great rabbi R' Yissachar Dov of blessed memory, who throughout his life was the honorary president of the institution, and for the deceased board members.
After the end of the Musaf prayer the walls shook with the cries:
— Long live cantor Żupowicz!
———
Very imposing and festive was the academy in the "Nowości" cinema. The hall was packed full with all strata of the Jewish population. Almost all social and philanthropic institutions delegated representatives to the academy, except for our highest institution, the Jewish kehilla, whose representatives once again showed how far their social maturity reaches, and did not find it necessary to be represented at the academy.
The beautifully decorated stage was occupied by the first founders and also the present board of the society.
When the curtain opens, the orchestra of "Hakoach" plays the Polish and the Jewish anthem, and the president of the society, R' Yeshaya Rosner, declares the academy open.
The chair is handed over to A' [sic] M. Lewin, who gives a short introduction on current affairs, and the floor is given to Mr. Henech Kornfeld, who reads a written greeting from the Rabbi, who at the same time regrets that he cannot take part in the celebration.
Then come the greetings: on behalf of the Magistrat [town council] the inspector Mr. Janiczek [?] and the member of the Council of Commissioners Mr. G. Rechnic greet. "Tzeirei Mishmorei [?] ha-Cholim" is represented in greeting by Mr. M. Fajgenblat, who stresses that the association he represents declares itself ready to work together with the board of "Linat ha-Cholim" for the good of the suffering Jewish masses.
On behalf of the "Malbish Arumim" society Mr. Sh. Zamder [?] greets; on behalf of the new Artisans' Association — Mr. D. Zylbergeld [?]; on behalf of the "Merchants' Association" and of the "Gemilut Chesed" fund — Mr. Rubinlicht, who declares that at the time when he sat in the Magistrat as vice-president he regarded with the greatest sympathy the institution, which maintains a maternity home and an old-age home ("Moshav Zkenim"), which are of colossal importance for the poor masses of the people.
On the importance of the maternity home speaks its director, Dr. Ferber, who points out the usefulness of the institution. Still lacking, says Dr. F., are very many instruments, but with the help of the society it is to be hoped that the institution will be perfected and enlarged.
The speaker gives statistical figures, from which it emerges that in the course of 10 [?] years, since the maternity home has existed, more than 2000 children have been born there.
A powerful speech, interwoven with sayings of the Sages, is given by Mr. Yitzchak Hirsch Winer (a native of the town, only he lives in Katowice), who speaks with enthusiasm about the people who stand at the head of the institution and who are all devoted to one single idea: to help the poorest part of the population.
The chairman sums up everything that was said in the greetings and speeches, and when he stresses that the Jewish kehilla did not find it necessary to take part in the jubilee celebration, cries are heard:
— A disgrace, this is base..
The orchestra plays a march and the first part of the academy is concluded.
The second part of the academy had artistic value. The performance of the young musicians H. Bernblat (piano) and S. Wajgberg (violin) had an extraordinary moral success. After every number, especially after playing "Eli Eli", the hall shook with applause, and they had to play as an encore ("bis") "Gypsy Dances".
The "appetite" [printed "apetis"] for music flared up in the audience, and when the musicians had finished their programme the audience began to clamour that Mr. Żupowicz should sing something.
The latter, though not prepared for it, satisfied the audience with 2 numbers. Żupowicz sang "La-El Baruch Ne'imot Yitenu" and "Al Chet" by R' Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev.
The festive academy, which left a very good impression, was concluded with a march played by the orchestra of the Będzin "Hakoach".
———
In the evening a banquet took place in the large hall of the "Hotel Grand".
The banquet, too, had a different character. A company of 60—70 men of various tendencies and groupings spent several hours pleasantly, discussing lively plans for the future work: how to enlarge the old-age home, to broaden the activity of "Linat ha-Cholim", and the like. Incidentally they also enjoyed food and drink (naturally from their own cash).
The spiritual part was carried out by Mr. Żupowicz and by some of the guests present.
[—]... number from each room weekly. — It is necessary that the Jewish population of Zagłębie should remember this and support the institutions vigorously and with warm interest.
L. D.
Interest-Free Loans for Trade

Aims and tasks of the Zagłębie relief committees.

The significance of interest-free loans for small trade and artisans is — if one reckons it „cleverly“ — so unimportant that people do not even take account of it, for what does the small amount of interest on a loan amount to compared with the large business expenses such as the shop, taxes („podatkes“), lighting, staff and other various administrative costs[?]. In truth, however, the question of interest in business is a very important one. When the Western European merchant, who runs his business with his own capital and pays interest only on a very small part of his turnover capital — and, compared with our conditions, quite small interest, from 6 to 8 per year — feels the interest paid as a heavy burden on the business, we can already understand how hard it is for our merchant to pay interest, when the interest amounts to 3 to 4 a month and one pays it not only on a part of the turnover capital but even more — on the entire capital, i.e. also on the deficit sum that is missing in the business.

When we further take into account the fact that the merchant in the Western countries works with a minimum profit fixed in advance, while our merchant earns very little, we must come to the conclusion that interest is an enormous burden on the business, and dominates[?] („hershtam“) especially under the present conditions.

It is a fact that one of the main causes leading to bankruptcy and liquidation is the high interest that the business pays.

It goes without saying that the small merchant and artisan is in no case able to pay interest out of his minimal earnings from a small turnover, and therefore it is no wonder that lately the applications of merchants and artisans for loans have been multiplying at the local interest-free loan fund. Interest-free loans also have the advantage that they are repaid in small weekly instalments. The manner of repaying the loan is thereby quite easy for the merchant and craftsman, because with small instalments he pays off larger loans without special effort.

The fund, whose task is to support the impoverished merchant and craftsman with a loan so that the borrower can earn a livelihood for his family, finds itself — because of the many applications from petitioners — in an especially critical situation, because for a long time the fund's capital has not grown much in proportion to the many applications. This is also because the „Joint“ is not increasing the loans and is even collecting repayments on the sums allocated earlier.

In view of the enormous want that prevails especially in the Jewish street, and of the crisis that has lately befallen many Jewish banks — which above all makes it hard for the impoverished merchant and craftsman to obtain the necessary credit — the interest-free fund must strain all its strength and see to it that applications for loans are settled positively as quickly as possible.

It goes without saying that the funds must keep watch over their sources of income, such as the repayment of instalments on the loans issued as well as the collection of the 20-grosz- [—]
A Little Feuilleton.

With the new year one has to be content.

So we have already travelled, that is to say, a few weeks into the new year, 1932, and for the time being one cannot yet complain about it, as people say: „a night — a year“[?] („a nekht a yor“)...

On the contrary, by all signs it is shaping up to be a decent year. A minister here has already assured us that an end has been put to the student anti-Jewish riots of the year 1931, and these words are, after all, holy of holies, for it is clear as day that in the year 1931 no more anti-Jewish riots will take place...

From the neighbouring states, too, we hear good greetings for the new year:

In Germany President Hindenburg in his own exalted person delivered a speech full of consolation and hopes for the German people, and about us Jews he did not say a bad word; precisely[?] — in Germany they are now forgetting the top man Hitler, who holds that the German people can be consoled only through repressions against Jews.

And if Hindenburg did try in his speech to stray[?] from the straight path and hint at „other times“, a „heavenly voice“ at once interrupted him in the middle and muddled his thoughts...

In Russia, on the other hand, the new year has brought very important news — the Soviet government has permitted[?] the Jews there to eat matzah on Passover, and indeed Manischewitz, which it, the government itself, will supply.

True, it is even a question what the Jews there will eat until Passover?

Well, and are you already provided for until Passover? If yes, you must surely be content, and even if not, you still can have no complaints against the new year — most likely you are still hungry from last year...

And until the year after next God is still a father and 1932 is a year — He can yet give us more than once a chance to taste the taste of... food.

Onkelos.
Theatre Notes

"Broytmil" [The Bread Mill] ("Der' toyber" — The Deaf Man), a play in 3 acts by Dovid Bergelson. Direction: Yankev (Jakub) Rotbaum, sets: Pragashki[?], performed by the "Vilna Troupe" ("Vilner trupe"), dir. Mazo.
Bergelson adapted the play from a story of his own, "Der toyber" (The Deaf Man), which he wrote some 20 years ago.
In the play the author shows us the struggle between the mill workers in small-town poverty on the one side, and the mill owner Shimen Bik and his family on the other.
The director Y. Rotbaum, who is under the influence of the modern Russian theatre, has taken pains to bring out the class moment in the play. In Bergelson the conscious class struggle is not poster-like enough; it is rather a spontaneous anger roused in the exhausted, starving mill workers than a conscious class struggle. Only thanks to the direction does one feel in the play the fighting spirit of the workers, who do not resign themselves and are not frightened off by any obstacles.
Bergelson also shows us the moral decay of the bourgeois[?] family, in which a pseudo-morality in fact reigns, where everything is permitted when money is at stake.
Precisely at Rosh Chodesh Elul, when a Jew like Shimen Bik, who regards himself as a pious man, ought to examine his deeds a little — just then he finds it necessary to reduce the already meagre wage of his workers and at the same time to raise, without any doubt[?], the price of flour, knowing full well that neither his workers can live on such a small wage nor the small-town Jews are able to pay higher prices.
The same Shimen Bik and his wife seek by every means to get rid of their maidservant, whom their son has brought to ruin (seduced).
Rotbaum did very well not to stress the "deaf man" in particular, as Herman did in his production, for after all he is no more than a worker, just like all the other mill workers. What matters above all is the whole of the thing, the struggle between the workers and the bread-givers [employers], and not only the "deaf man".
The acting:
Sh. Lagovi[?] (the deaf man) was excellent in the role. His mask, voice and movements brilliantly personified[?] the "deaf man", and his acting had a thoroughly[?] artistic effect[?].
Y. Rakov (Shimen Bik) was considerably weaker. He did not bring out[?] all the nuances that can be drawn from such a role.
Of our Będzin "Porets" [squire], Pashashinski distinguished himself (Yosele Babtsies). His facial expression and movements were restrained. He did not fall into caricature, and that is no easy task in such a role.
B. Melnik (Schulz) satisfactory.
T. Levenshteyn (Mendl) is a talented actor, but this was not his role, and therefore he was too pale, not plastic enough. We would rather have seen him in the role of "Comrade Tsali", who, by the way, was played weakly by the actor Db"im[?].
The whole female cast was very good.
Naturally first place goes to Frim Orleska (Esther). The timbre of her voice and her dramatic tone have a strong effect and call forth artistic emotions. Hearing Orleska one recalls the golden era of the real "Vilner".
The sets by Pragashka do not work. One feels in them a certain disjointedness, a disharmony. But we are sure that this is not the fault of the famous set designer, but rather of the transport difficulties. It is truly hard to take everything along on the road. One must also remember that sets are made specially for a particular stage and the construction is calculated with a precision down to a centimetre, and when they are transferred to another place they lose their whole effect.
On the whole it is a clean, well-made performance, worth seeing.
Sh. R.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (8)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin and the monk Iliodor; installment 8.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Months and months later the "Black Monk" Iliodor led religious and political processions across all of Russia and also across the "Cherta osedlosti" [Pale of Settlement] (the regions where Jews were permitted to live in Tsarist Russia), and a mortal terror would seize the Jews when they heard that the "Black Monk" [printed "shvayartser"] was approaching their town or shtetl.

The Jews then lived as if on a fire-spewing mountain and trembled that at any minute the fire might erupt and the thousands of peasants who followed Iliodor would make a bloodbath of them.

Gates and windows used to be barred in Jewish houses and shops when Iliodor's procession appeared, and long after the procession had gone the Jews could not recover from the fright.

In his speeches Iliodor also came out against high officials whom he did not like. He did this to show the masses that if they suffered, it was not the Tsar who was to blame, but the bad officials. The Tsar himself is a good, faithful father to all his subjects. He wants everyone to be well off; only his officials are to blame for all the troubles. In his speeches he often came out sharply with grave accusations against highly placed persons. At the same time he would revile them with the vilest and filthiest curses. But his reputation as "the great fighter for monarchist ideas" protected him, and nothing could be done to him.

He [printed "r'hot"] began to come out sharply against the high officials and against the whole administration of the Tsaritsyn guberniya [printed here "Tsaritsiger"]. He shouted wildly and kept screaming: "The administration of the Tsaritsyn guberniya is in the claws of Satan!" He thundered against the chief of police and reviled him with the most terrible curses. When the police chief learned of this, he sent for him. Iliodor came. The police chief received him courteously, showed him the "report" he had received about his speeches, in which he had called for disobeying the orders of the officials, and asked him: "Have your speeches been reported correctly? Hasn't a mistake perhaps been made here?"

Iliodor did not think for a single moment. He answered at once and proudly: "Correct! In the 'report' everything is reported correctly! That is what I said, and I do not take back my words!"

When the police chief pointed out to him that such public pronouncements were not permitted, Iliodor burst out shouting and declared that his task was to protect the people and the Tsar from incompetent and dishonest officials...

The police chief had to keep silent. Iliodor's following was so great, his influence on the masses so strong, that no one dared do anything against him. Thousands would have laid down their lives for him.

When Iliodor's fame reached Petersburg, the Tsar and the Tsarina took an interest in him, and he was invited to Tsarskoye Selo. During the time Iliodor was there, he became close friends with Bishop Hermogen and with Archimandrite Feofan, to whom the Tsarina used to make her confession.

The three now worked hand in hand. They led the monarchist movement and the agitation against the Jews. All three were sworn enemies of the Jews. And now Bishop Hermogen wanted to draw into their campaign the Siberian muzhik, Grigori Rasputin, who, as he thought, could be of great use to them.

Could it ever have occurred to him that this very muzhik would not only not help them, but would even get in their way!

That did not occur to him.

The black monk Iliodor was sitting quiet and calm when suddenly there was a knock at the door of his room. Instead of answering, he silently rose from his seat, went with quick, quiet steps to the corner where many icons hung on the wall, lit by oil lamps burning above them, lowered himself to his knees and began crossing himself and bowing to the "holy" images.

Again there was a knock at the door. And when a while had passed and no answer came from the room, the door opened very carefully and quietly, and with quiet steps there crossed the threshold: Bishop Hermogen, Archimandrite Feofan and the Siberian muzhik Grigori Rasputin.

The room was half dark and very quiet. The monk did not look round, as though he had no idea that anyone had entered the room. He lay in the corner before the icons as though deeply sunk in prayer and wholly possessed by pious ecstasy. He whispered quietly with his lips, crossed himself every so often and bowed so low that he touched the floor with his forehead.

For a while those who had entered stood motionless. The darkness in the room, the red little flames of the oil lamps and the pose in which the monk was found made a strong impression on them. Soon they approached the corner where Iliodor was kneeling. All three lowered themselves to their knees, crossed themselves and also began bowing to the "holy" images.

Archimandrite Feofan — who was a great fanatic — as soon as he felt the light of the oil lamps on his eyes, fell at once into a state of deep religious ecstasy. He closed his eyes and began to mumble a prayer. The bishop, however, was a little restless and waited impatiently for Iliodor to finish his prayer, so that he could talk over with him the matter for which he had now come: taking the Siberian wanderer into their company and using him for their purposes.

But Iliodor was in no hurry. He remained all the while in the pose in which they had found him. He crossed himself, bowed and mumbled. He behaved as though he were alone in the room. The bishop had no choice but to remain kneeling and wait... Disturbing the monk at his prayer he did not even dare to think of...

Rasputin remained perfectly calm and patient. From the endlessly wide Siberian steppes from which he had come, he had brought with him a firm calm and an iron patience. He knew how to wait... Nothing could throw him off balance. He was even pleased with the quiet scene. It gave him the chance to observe from close by the famous monk, whom he was seeing for the first time, and to gauge his importance with his sharp peasant instinct.

He waited patiently, standing on his knees, until — Iliodor had finished one prayer, and before he had begun another, and — to the enormous astonishment of the archimandrite and the bishop — Rasputin stood up, went up very close to Iliodor and exclaimed:

— Brother!... My brother!...

Iliodor sprang up like an enraged, wounded beast. A wild fury flared up in him against the unknown dirty peasant who had dared to disturb him at his prayer. His eyes blazed with fiery anger. His lips were already trembling with wild murderousness. "Father" Feofan and the bishop became terribly flustered, expecting a dreadful outburst of abuse and curses. Iliodor raised his hand, caught his breath and was ready to hurl himself at the unknown peasant with furious shouts, but then [?; printed "nor do!"] —

With great friendliness and ease Rasputin laid his right hand on Iliodor's shoulder, broke into a smile and looked into his blazing eyes. Rasputin's pale little eyes looked sharply and smilingly, with a strange tenderness and kindness. And in a voice that was soft, very melodious, and at the same time strong as steel, he exclaimed:

— You are a good prayer [?], brother!

And strangely: Iliodor remained dumbfounded. Rasputin's eyes mastered and subdued him. His simple bearing confused the monk; his anger was as if paralysed, his fury was extinguished, some strong force overpowered him... He began to look at the stranger with great amazement.

Rasputin said:

— Enough of you tormenting God with your prayers. Even God sometimes wants rest... These two here — he pointed to the archimandrite and the bishop — need to talk something over with you.

Iliodor stood hypnotised by Rasputin's sharp and smiling glances. In his heart there was still anger at the stranger who had shown him so little respect. But he was powerless, feeling the muzhik's hypnotising eyes upon him. He felt that some strange weakness was mastering him. In vain he strained his strength to say something; he was unable to bring out a single word. So he remained silent, was very pale, felt lost and looked on with confused eyes.

— Give me your hand, brother! — Rasputin exclaimed, stretching out his hand to him and smiling as he did so with rare calm and ease.

Iliodor took Rasputin's hand and gave it a friendly squeeze.

He was mastered... and he now looked at the Siberian muzhik with both fear and great admiration.

Then they sat down at the table and a conversation began.

— — — — — — —

Feofan spoke with enthusiasm about Rasputin as about a "saint", and praised Rasputin highly to Iliodor. Hermogen acquainted the monk with his plan to use the Siberian muzhik [for] their political purposes... Rasputin himself sat modest and silent and did not join the conversation with a single word. But all the while he did not take his eyes off the monk's face. They kept looking with sharpness and kindness. And strangely: Iliodor constantly felt that those eyes had a strong power over him, that they held him as if captive. And — regardless of the fact that he constantly felt disgust for the muzhik; regardless of the fact that he found him very repulsive and his instinct warned him against him — he nevertheless caught Feofan's enthusiasm, also began to believe that Rasputin was a "saint" who stands close to God... and agreed with Hermogen's opinion that Rasputin was a strong force that could be used by them. He supported Hermogen's proposal that the Siberian wanderer be presented to the committee of the "Soyuz Russkogo Naroda" (Union of the Russian People, a monarchist-reactionary and strongly antisemitic organisation on which Tsarism relied. This organisation constantly incited pogroms against Jews, and at that time it played a large political role in Russia) and that he be taken into that committee.

New inventions made recently

[Economy & technology — the Leipzig Fair; special report.] Special to our paper, by Z. Haber, Vienna–Leipzig.

The economic crisis is without any doubt, for the most part, a result of technical development. The more technology spreads into all areas of daily life, the more people are pushed out of their source of livelihood. In Vienna, for example, an experiment was made in building two larger municipal houses. At one house two hundred workers were employed to dig out the foundations; at the other house a machine was set up which dug the foundation. Eighteen people were employed at the machine. It turned out that the two hundred workers needed sixteen days for the foundation, while the machine dug out the same area of foundation in six days. That 82 people were then left without work goes without saying.
It is exactly the same with all the machines that modern technology devises everywhere; all over the world one feels how the machine displaces man and makes his work superfluous.
Nevertheless, industry does not sleep and technology does its part. Year in, year out, the great technical fair in Leipzig shows what technology has devised in the past year, and the whole world watches the creations, the inventions, which spread from Leipzig to the four corners of the earth.
Apart from the big machines there are also small, very small articles, which are exhibited in Leipzig in a pavilion of their own, the "Inventors' Pavilion", and which together amount to a whole revolution...
Of such small inventions, which will be exhibited at the coming Leipzig Fair, which opens[?] in March of this year, I can already announce today:

Boxes made of cardboard.
A big German paper factory has now succeeded in making cardboard sheets from which boxes can be made for packing all kinds of goods and sending them by rail or by ship all over the world. At the Leipzig Fair such boxes will now be seen for the first time, in all sizes and for all kinds of goods. The advantages of these boxes are as follows:
First of all, anyone can make them at home — one cuts the cardboard sheets to whatever size one wants. Whereas with a wooden crate one can pull out individual boards, take out goods and nail the boards back or put in other boards, with these boxes that is not possible; here one must tear the box open if one wants to take something out. The main thing, however, is how much one saves on freight. Wooden crates are heavy and cost a lot of freight, while the cardboard sheets are very light. These cardboard sheets are so strong that one can throw such a box as much as one likes and it does not[?] break — whereas with a wooden crate the boards break when it is thrown about on the railway or on the ship.

Soldering vessels.
When some vessel of tin-plate, copper, iron or another metal breaks in a household, it has to be soldered, that is, one has to carry it to a skilled craftsman, who heats up and solders the broken vessel. At the coming Leipzig Fair a kind of paste will be exhibited for the first time, which one smears on where the vessel is broken or holed. This cold paste seals all holes better than the hot zinc. In every home it will be possible to repair all vessels without any craftsman.

Bathtubs[?] that can be carried from place to place.
Not only in the smaller towns, but even in the big cities, most people have no possibility of bathing at home; there is nowhere to keep bathtubs, and people ruin their health carrying them from one room to another. At the Leipzig Fair a tub made of rubber will now be shown, which can be set up wherever one likes. After bathing one can fold it up again and keep it even in one's pocket.

Artificial ostrich feathers.
In ladies' fashion feathers are now being used again. Not only for little hats — today feathers are also used to trim dresses. Nowadays there are artificial feathers of all kinds of birds in the world; only ostrich feathers, with their natural colours and sheen, could not be imitated. One had to take genuine feathers, which only wealthy women could afford. Now, at the Leipzig Fair, artificial ostrich feathers will be exhibited for the first time, made so skilfully that one can hardly tell that they are not genuine. In this way it will be possible for women who are not rich to wear ostrich feathers too, for which until now one needed a fat purse.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Będzin — local news.]
Order of the Starosta to Elect the Presidium of the New Kehilla Administration.
On Wednesday the gmina [municipality] received the decision of the voivode concerning the distribution of mandates in the new kehilla council.
According to the decision, Messrs. Damber [?] and Welgrin are stripped of their mandates, which they had received on the strength of a resolution of the starosta [district head].
At the same time it is ordered that within 7 days, i.e. by next Wednesday, the elections of the new kehilla presidium are to take place.
—o—
Accident on the Road to Lelów.
On Thursday evening a group of 26 persons travelled by car from Będzin to Lelów, to the yahrzeit of R' Dovid of Lelów, of blessed memory.
On the way, some 15 kilometres from Lelów, the driver lost his way and went onto another road. The passengers had to get out of the car and walked about 2 kilometres on foot.
While getting back into the car an accident befell Mr. Glitman, who slipped and broke his left leg.
Glitman was brought back here in the same car, and the other passengers set off on foot to Lelów.
—o—
From the New Artisans' Association.
On Sunday an extraordinary general meeting of the new Jewish Artisans' Association took place in the "Piast" hall in Będzin.
At the meeting a report was given on the amendment ("novella") to the law on the turnover tax for the year 1932.
With 300 members present, the chairman, Mr. Grosman, opened the meeting and gave the floor to Mr. Efraim Klajman, who read out an order of the local tax office (Urząd Skarbowy). After the whole amendment to the law had been read through, all artisans were called upon to come next Sunday to the general meeting of the "Bank Spółdzielczy" [Cooperative Bank].
—o—
Died in a Lavatory.
In the lavatory of the house at Małachowska [Małachowskiego] 16 a Christian woman, a resident of Potocka [Potockiego] Street, died of a heart attack; that very day she had been washing laundry for one of the tenants of the said house.
—o—
Meeting of the "Cooperative Bank".
Next Sunday a general meeting will take place in the City Council hall, at which the question of the bank's further fate will be discussed.
—o—
WIZO Is Creating a Library.
The board of the women's association "WIZO", which looks after the cultural needs of its members, has set about creating a library containing, besides Hebrew, Yiddish, Polish and German books, also a series of "Judaic studies literature".
Of the books already donated to the library, worth mentioning is the fine gift of Mr. Jakub Gutman, who presented the library with 24 volumes of "Ha-Tekufah".
—o—
From the Będzin Merchants' Association.
We have been asked to announce that, in the matter of filing appeals against the incorrect assessment of the road tax (which is levied at the rate of 15 percent of the price of the trade patents), [those concerned] should report to the secretariat of the Merchants' Association.
—o—
General Meeting of "Maccabi".
(Ch–ski) In the "Maccabi" hall, under the chairmanship of Mr. Eng. Inhold, the annual general members' meeting of "Maccabi" Biliz [?] (Bielitz?) — Będzin branch took place.
The report on the activity to date was given by Dr. Rechtschaft. The report shows that the Będzin section has generated lively activity: 4 "dry" courses and 7 propaganda lectures were organised. The section now [?] numbers 200 members. Recently a special film is being made, which will be completed on the 7th of February [luty] in connection with the race taking place that same day.
Mr. Lichtenstein gave the treasurer's report, which shows that after all expenses and income there are 190 zł in the treasury.
After the discussion, in which Erlich, Hirsch, Dr. Rechtschaft, Eng. Inhold, Hiner [?] and others took part, a vote of discharge (absolutorium) was unanimously granted to the outgoing board.
Elected to the new board were: Dr. Rechtschaft, Harry Hirsch, Płatek, Eng. Starker, Eng. Inhold, J. Lichtenstein. Deputies: Plesner and M. Lichtenstein. Audit committee: Kramałowski, Lasker, Inhold.
Under "miscellaneous", on the proposal of Dr. Rechtschaft, the general meeting expressed thanks to the editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" for their support of physical education among Jews.
—o—
On the Eve of the Merger of the Two Landlords' Associations.
There are in our town also 2 associations of house-owners. Both parties have the same interests, the same troubles — and yet there has to be a split...
But, as we are informed, the boards of both associations have already realised that the split does harm to the house-owners, because each association "makes its own Sabbath", and this week the first preliminary conference took place on the question of merging.
—o—
Because of Reckless Speeding.
On the highway from Będzin to Czeladź the passenger bus of the "Feniks" works in Będzin went into a ditch and was wrecked. Luckily nobody was travelling in the bus except the driver, who was miraculously saved from death.
The disaster happened because of the driver's reckless speeding.

Sosnowiec — The Power Station Is to Lower the Price of Electricity / He Wanted to Travel to His Son — and Suffered a Heart Attack at the Station / A Motor Accident with Human Victims / The Artisans' Association Already Has an Elected Board / Lectures for Merchants / Joy from One's Children... / Three Suicides in One Day / 75 Groszy for a Kilo of Rolls / A New Financial Institution / The Gerer Rebbe Passes Through / Sosnowiec Loses a Secondary School / „The Big Win“ in Sosnowiec / Political Arrests in Zagłębie / From the Sosnowiec Keren Kayemet Committee / Of 110 Members, Barely 11 Came...

[Sosnowiec — electricity and taxes.]
The Power Station Is to Lower the Price of Electricity
As is known, from the 1st of this month [1 January 1932] the law on the tax (podatek) on electricity came into force, i.e. to every bill for electric light a further 10 per cent will[?] be added for the government.
In connection with this — as we are informed — the management of the power station (elektrownia) in Sosnowiec intends to lower the price by 30 per cent, i.e. so that a kilowatt of electricity will cost only 44 groszy.
The discount price is being introduced so that the consumers should not restrict their use of electricity because of the new tax.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — mourning; Ger Hasidism.]
He Wanted to Travel to His Son — and Suffered a Heart Attack at the Station
As is known, a certain Mr. Palman, at the departure of the Gerer Rebbe for the Land of Israel, suffered a heart attack at the Warsaw railway station and died.
As it turned out, the suddenly deceased Palman had wanted to travel on the same train to Sosnowiec to his son, the well-known engineer Palman.
The news made a shattering impression in the town.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — accidents.]
A Motor Accident with Human Victims
On Friday at midday, not far from Mikołów, an accident occurred to a lorry that was travelling from Bielitz [Bielsko] to Sosnowiec.
The accident happened in the following circumstances. The driver wanted to avoid a cart, and as a result the vehicle ran at full speed into a tree, and the outcome was a grave one. The vehicle overturned into a ditch and crushed the driver, the porter Paliwoda and the forwarding clerk (expeditor) Mr. Zachari' Federman, both from Sosnowiec.
The driver and Paliwoda were taken into the Mikołów hospital, where it was established that the driver's condition was grave, and Paliwoda's left leg had been broken. On the following day the driver died.
The third victim, Mr. Federman, began to feel unwell on coming home, and the doctor who was called out stated that Federman had suffered a haemorrhage from the heart.
Mr. F. is in the Jewish hospital.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — artisans, associations.]
The Artisans' Association Already Has an Elected Board
Last Sunday a meeting of the local artisans' association took place for the third time.
This time the meeting was valid[?] (printed „moldige“), and at last a board was elected, consisting of: M. Y. Artman, Ch. Gawrilowicz, Sh. N. Langer, A. Apatowski, M. Sztern, L. Libner, Y. D. Braner, D. Szajn, B. Aszpic, A. P. Jaskierowicz and Iczę Gliksman.
Deputies: Y. Sh. Horowicz, P. Wajdenfeld, Zilberszlag and M. Cymberknopf.
Audit committee: Ch. Binkowski, M. N. Bergman and M. Goldkorn.
After the elections the topical question of founding an insurance fund, which is to support the members in urgent cases, was discussed.
It was decided unanimously that the fund should begin operating as soon as possible, and for this purpose a committee was elected consisting of Messrs.: Braner, Wajdenfeld, Fajgenblat, Kasirer and Y. D. Langer.
On Tuesday evening the first board meeting took place, at which the following presidium was constituted:
President — Shlomo Nachum Langer, vice-president — Avraham Apatowski, honorary secretary — Jaskierowicz, treasurer — P. Sztern.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — commerce.]
Lectures for Merchants
At the last meeting of the local Chamber of Commerce it was decided to renew the lectures for merchants on various commercial matters.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — crime.]
Joy from One's Children...
Several Jewish young men, children of respectable householder parents, wanted to carry out a theft in the colonial-goods shop of Mr. Rozenes.
The young men were arrested at their „first“ „guest performance“ (gastrol).
—o—
[Sosnowiec — suicides.]
Three Suicides in One Day
The 23-year-old Majka, having no means to live, drank a small bottle of vinegar.
The 59-year-old Mrs. Adamczyk, not being satisfied with her life, drank vinegar essence. On the way to the hospital she died.
The third candidate for suicide was Taragasz; he did not content himself with drinking vinegar, but cut his wrist[?] veins with a razor.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — prices.]
75 Groszy for a Kilo of Rolls
The price commission at the local Magistrate has lowered the price of rolls (Semmel) to 75 groszy.
Today, Friday [22 January 1932], the commission will hold a meeting at which the hitherto high price of milk will also be considered.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — economy, banks.]
A New Financial Institution
In place of the liquidated branch of the Łódź „Bank Handlowo-Przemysłowy“, a financial institution has been created, at whose head stands (printed „sstayt“) the former bank director Mr. Hartman.
At the founding meeting the following board and supervisory council were elected.
On the council: Messrs. P. Gerard (president), Y. Majtlis (vice-president), H Tomczak, Y. Klas, Maurycy Drajer, and A. Śligowski.
On the board: Messrs. director L. Hartman, A. Kramer and Henryk Zinger.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Ger Hasidism.]
The Gerer Rebbe Passes Through
On Monday evening hundreds of Hasidim gathered at the local railway station to greet the Gerer Rebbe, who was travelling to the Land of Israel.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — education.]
Sosnowiec Loses a Secondary School
As we are informed, from the 1st of February (luty) the vocational secondary school for women is to be transferred to Katowice.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — theatre.]
„The Big Win“ in Sosnowiec
Today, Friday, at 9 in the evening, the „Vilna Troupe“ will stage in the municipal theatre Sholem Aleichem's hit play „200,000“.
The play has been performed everywhere with great success.
—o—
[Zagłębie — political arrests.]
Political Arrests in Zagłębie
In the night from Thursday to Friday mass searches were carried out in Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza]. 37 men were arrested, of whom 6 were released after the interrogation, and the rest were put into the Mysłowice prison.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Zionism, JNF.]
From the Sosnowiec Keren Kayemet Committee
According to the traditional custom, „Land of Israel fruit“ will be distributed on Tuesday in all schools, organisations and among the Jewish population.
The KKL committee in Sosnowiec calls on all members to help in the campaign of Chamisha Asar BiShvat, the New Year of the Trees, the festival in which the redemption[?] of the Land and our hope are expressed.
On this day it is a duty to plant trees in the Herzl Forest, and one must buy the fruit of the Land of Israel.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — commerce, associations.]
Of 110 Members, Barely 11 Came...
Last Sunday the members of the Merchants' Association (on Piłsudski Street) were called to come to the annual general meeting, at which the question of reviving the association at the present moment was also to be discussed.
But of the 110 registered[?] members no more than 11 (read: eleven) came, and that already together with the board members...
It goes without saying that because of the members' disregard the meeting did not take place, and thanks to this the hitherto chaotic (tohu-vavohu) situation has been reinforced even more...
—o—
Revisionists and Sympathisers!

Other people's goods and household effects may not be taken for taxes.
2 important rulings of the Supreme Court.
Disputes constantly arise between the tax authority and taxpayers over other people's goods or household effects which the offices [urzędy] list in distraints for taxes [podatki].
Until now enormous difficulties were made over goods found in a shop on commission, as well as over articles, household effects, furniture and machines taken for a usage fee, on lease or on commission for sale — the tax officials would take nothing into account. Whatever they found in the shop or in the dwelling of the tax debtor was listed and seized.
The tax officials considered themselves especially entitled to act this way after the Supreme Court issued a ruling 2 years ago that even commission goods are liable for turnover tax, and that what is found in the dwelling of the defaulting taxpayer is his property and may be seized.
The jurists, however, were convinced that it must be understood differently. Therefore the Supreme Court has issued 2 new rulings, which have changed the earlier practice.
One ruling says:
"Articles found in the enterprise or dwelling of the tax debtor may not be listed in the distraint [zajęcie] for overdue turnover taxes, even though they are on the premises of the enterprise that owes the tax."
This ruling is of 27 March 1931, number "C." [?] 3, section 2 432-30.
A second ruling of the Supreme Court says it even more clearly:
"Articles that are the property of a third person, even though they are used by the tax debtor, are not liable for the podatek obrotowy [turnover tax] which the tax debtor must pay." (Ruling of chamber [izba] 3, section 2, of the Supreme Court of 8 May 1931, number "C." 42-31).
As one sees, other people's articles used by the tax debtor may not be taken for his overdue taxes.
It is, however, absolutely necessary to make sure that there is no doubt whatsoever that the articles belong to a third person.
For that one needs a notarial deed [akt rejentalny] stating that the articles — furniture, household effects — were taken from that person for a usage fee, for a period of 2 years. The deed must state the amount of the usage fee, and that if part of the articles is spoiled, compensation of a precisely fixed amount must be paid.
In this way it will be ensured that in distraints no one can take other people's household effects or commission goods.
Adv. G. Gr.
