The presidium of the Będzin kehilla board elected by 6 votes

The presidium of the Będzin kehilla board has been elected by 6 votes.
As our readers know, the starosta ordered that the election of the presidium of the kehilla board in Będzin should take place.
To the sitting, which was fixed for last Wednesday evening, there came 5 Aguda dozors [board members] and the Rabbi, who took part in the election procedure.
A few minutes after the appointed time the president, Mr. Liwer, opens the sitting and says:
— Let us vote.
When the kehilla (gmina) secretary draws his attention to the fact that there is no quorum — Mr. Liwer answers:
— „But they are inside“...
In the presence of 6 members the election takes place.
Suddenly the dozor A. Liwer comes in; he runs up to the president with the words:
„There will be no voting“, and with that he tears the ballot slips out of the president's hand.
When dozor Liwer leaves the meeting hall, an election takes place for the second time, which brings the result:
By 6 votes Mr. Dawid Skoczylas is elected president, and Mr. Bunem Banhart vice-president.
The minutes of the election were drawn up and sent by the Aguda to the competent authority.
At the same time the president A. Liwer applied to the starosta with a complaint against dozor Mr.[?] Liwer, who had brutally attacked him, and he asks that the authorities take a position on the matter.
The Rabbi's attendant (shamash) has also been named[?] as a witness.
The election victory called forth great joy in Aguda circles.

The Retail Merchants Will Pay Turnover Tax Twice This Year.
[Economy — Taxes.] From well-informed sources we learn that the retailers and artisans who will be taken into the ryczałt [lump-sum] taxation will have to pay two kinds of turnover tax in the present year.
First of all, their turnover for the year 1931 will be assessed, and in April they will receive payment orders to pay the turnover [tax], after deduction of the advances paid in.
At the same time their ryczałt turnover will be assessed, and already in the present year they will have to pay the 4 instalments for the year 1932.
It will thus turn out that in the course of 4 weeks' time, between 15 March and 15 April, one will have to pay the first instalment of the ryczałt and also the assessed turnover [tax] for the year 1931.
This is what will happen with the merchants and artisans whose turnover in the year 1930 was not greater than 30,000 [?] zł.
For these merchants and artisans this will be a considerable burden. In the present situation it will be hard to pay off within a short time the turnover [tax] for this year and for last year.
It is therefore most necessary to make efforts, in whatever way, to ease for the merchants and artisans the transition from the old assessment system to the ryczałt.
The best thing would be if the turnover [tax] — as one sum [?] — were spread over smaller monthly instalments, to be paid off in the course of several months.

After this reply Mr. Rechnic declared that Jews are not vengeful or grudge-bearing and will vote for the item.

A Reply from the Będzin Merchants' Association

[Będzin — commerce; letter to the editor.]
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We ask you to print in your newspaper our reply to the article by Mr. Les [R. Les] in No. 3, entitled 'Neither Alive nor Dead'.
The fact that the general meeting of our association was not convened for two and a half years gives Mr. Les material for depicting the activity of the Merchants' Association [Sochrim-Farein] as 'neither alive nor dead'.
True, we agree that an annual general meeting is very important for the members of every association; it is the highest authority of an association, where everyone can speak out on the most pressing questions touching the association concerned. We do not deny its importance, but that still cannot be a reason for writing an article in which the writer displays an estrangement from the institution.
The exceptionally difficult situation of the merchant class in the year 1930, the struggle around the city council, the organisational work around the Chamber of Commerce and the like made it impossible to convene in 1930 the regular annual meeting for the year 1929; that is how it came about that the general meeting in 1931 heard a report for the years [19]29, [19]30 and two months of the year 1928.
Had Mr. Les been a little sincere, he would have had to admit that the report delivered at the meeting (4 pages of typescript) is of great significance for the Jewish merchant. From that report every objective listener surely saw what a widely ramified activity the board carried out during the period under report. Truly imposing figures are to be found there.
12 sections, dozens of sittings, countless interventions in almost all the offices in Zagłębie, Katowice, Kraków, Kielce and Warsaw. The board's sittings are the source of the initiative for projects that were later realised, for instance the construction of the new station and post-office building, the new premises for the municipal court; over 6500 [?] certificates were issued by the association in that time. Can one imagine how many difficulties were removed thereby? About 700 letters on matters of first-class importance, [such as?] to the tax offices, the Treasury Chamber [Izba Skarbowa], the Chamber of Commerce, the railway directorates, the Starostwo, the courts, and the Kielce and Silesian voivodeship offices, were sent out in that time; besides this, 36 memorials were drawn up on matters that concerned the whole town: the investment tax, postal matters, licences for pedlars, and others.
Over 500 pieces of legal advice were given by the association's lawyer in the course of that time. It is impossible within the frame of an article to convey everything that was created through the association.
The success of the work and the realisation of the projects that arose in the association are the best witnesses to the fruitful activity of the previous board.
The 'Merchants' Association' has the fullest proofs of recognition and trust from the whole Będzin merchant class — namely all the elections that took place during that time. In all those elections the lists of the Merchants' Association, or those on which the association's candidates figured, won well-deserved victories with a moderate, un-noisy campaign. The calm, solid and planned work was evidently the best advertisement. The board of the association held the standpoint that it is not hullabaloo, advertising, meetings, demonstrations and the like that are proof of activity, but rather systematic, fruitful work.
In the whole of Mr. Les's article no concrete reproach whatsoever is actually raised; we could have passed over it to the order of the day, but we consider it our duty to react against incomprehensible and unfounded pronouncements. For such pronouncements one needs 'more than courage'.
Respectfully,
The Board of the 'Merchants' Association' in Będzin.
—o—
'More Than Courage'.
Yes, one needs more than courage; one must be honest and sincere in order to tell the truth to the face of such an institution, which is close [?] and dear to the writer of these lines.
We keep on rousing the merchant class, again and again, to have their own association, one able to represent the merchant in all his greatness and breadth; he should be sure that his association is doing things for him and brings him benefit by word and deed. We have said more than once that every merchant, whoever he may be, without exception, must be a member of his association, and that his not being a member hinders the institution from being properly represented. It must have the possibility of intervening in the name of the ENTIRE merchant body. We say that the more members the institution counts, the surer its activity is on the road to success. But one must, after all, be consistent: just as the merchant is required to be a member, so we have the right to come and require of the institution that it give the member something — and that 'something' ought to consist of a somewhat larger dose.
True, we made no concrete reproach against the board, but what do you need one for? Nor did we say that you did nothing at all, just as we did not say that you did EVERYTHING. You also relate that, because of the great organisational work bound up with the 'Merchants' Association', you were unable to call a general meeting in the course of several years. We understand it differently: precisely when there is much work and intensive activity, general meetings ought to be called as often as possible, and often even extraordinary meetings — all the more so when we take into account what hard periods the merchant class has gone through in the course of recent years.
R. Les.
On Guard Before a Catastrophe. V. (Consequences of the Times and of Not Standing on Guard. — Harmful and Useful Deeds)

[Editorial / society — the crisis, suicides and beggary.] From all sides bitter groans are heard; from everywhere sad greetings arrive. Misery and want reign everywhere, and among the greater part of the citizens poverty occupies the most honoured seat at the head of the table.
One must not fool oneself and think that only here in Poland is the situation bitter and grave. From all corners of the world sad tidings arrive, so that the lamentable tunes and the fearsome storm-waves reach us as well.
It goes without saying that it is much easier to solve a local or even a national crisis than a world crisis, which, incidentally, is acquiring chronic symptoms. The difference, however, is that elsewhere people at least make some effort to hold things back, so that the dangerous storm-waves should not pour out far and wide over the citizens' heads, whereas we do not dwell on the dangerous situation with full awareness. Before our eyes the terrible picture is not seen in its full, fearsome size. We give ourselves no account at all of the terrible impetus with which the tragic scenes are developing among us, how nimbly and colossally they spread and how contagious they are; after all, they spare no one: one suffers more and another perhaps less, one is struck by the misfortune directly and another indirectly, one somehow manages to clutch at the edge with all his strength and for the time being saves himself, and another has no strength for that and falls in an instant down into the abyss, so that his strength gives out at once.
Dread seizes one when one casts a glance backwards and looks at what has become of well-to-do citizens who stood on a respectable level and who employed hundreds of people around them; and now not only are their people perishing[?] of hunger, but the bosses themselves — either they go hungry, or, if not, they have long since become mere shadows.
A man, as long as he does not go through various things in his life, as long as he does not go hungry, as long as he does not fall ill or go through other grave periods, which incidentally cost much effort and strength — so long he does not know how strong he is, how steadfast he is, how great is the power of suffering, the power of courage. The human, and incidentally also the animal, a man sees in himself only when he has to torment himself, when he has to toil, when he goes through the supernatural — that which he could never have imagined he would be able to bear on his weak shoulders, on his sensitive human body, which is so singular, so mysterious: so many burdens, so much superhuman suffering and pain, aches and feats of strength[?].
As is known, there are differences of opinion among the thinkers. Many say that one must have a rare strength, a strong intuition, in order to carry out a murder upon oneself; then others come and say that he who commits suicide is weak, broken, he has no courage to continue life as it is, he cannot suffer, he has no strength to torment himself, to toil; strong, on the contrary, are those who accept with love the troubles that come upon man and that pour down on human heads.
But about such a question one could polemicise once upon a time, when a suicide was a rare thing in general and among us Jews in particular. Today, when the question has become so topical, when suicides have taken on an everyday character not only among other peoples but also among us Jews, this must be reacted to properly; one must not merely seek the causes of the suicide epidemic, but one must find means of how to stop them, how to hold them back.
It must be established once and for all that we are living in exceptionally hard conditions. One must not, after all, forget that we live in Central Europe in the 20th century, so that each of us must earn comparatively much, because everyone must go dressed like a human being, eat like other people, bring up his children in a decent manner. In short, the broad strata of the population find themselves in almost the same conditions of life as the rich, so that as soon as things go a little badly for them, as soon as things get somewhat thinner — may God have mercy. Then one has to move worlds in order to fulfil the duties one has taken upon oneself, only it does not work. So one must go over or under. "Red or dead" — that is how it comes to suicides. One is ashamed before people, one does not want to put on the cap of shame, and one makes an end of the life one has come to loathe.
One must not forget, however, that not all characters are alike; there are also such elements that can suffer, and indeed suffer without limit. Thus, for example, the sufferings have reached the most loathsome, the most humiliating. Those who do not take their own lives have no other way out than to stretch out the hand and come to beggar's bread. Certainly for the greatest number of the humiliated it is no tasty thing to stretch out the hand for alms; more than one has his blood spilt at this "occupation". But however unpleasant it may be, however hard this "livelihood" may come to him, with time he becomes hardened, and stretching out the hand becomes for him a trade like all other trades, a livelihood-business like all other businesses that have a daily taking. Yes, yes, people become poisoned, and with time you will not be able to prevail upon such a one to occupy himself with something else; yes, such a property, such a kind of destructive power has the stretching out of the hand. Just as at the beginning it comes hard to them to stretch out the hand for alms, just so one will later be unable to prevail upon these elements to take up something else, regardless of the fact that from the proposed livelihood he would be able to live in dignity. That is how it is: in stretching out the hand he becomes a sluggard, no longer wants to work and does not want to know at all whether he would be better off with the livelihood offered. The worm has already got into the horseradish and you will do nothing with him. Alas, alas, this is a bitter truth.
Among us no one takes an interest in seeing that these people should not be allowed to lose their balance — the people who are later condemned to be professional schnorrers. On the contrary, our charity societies, the benevolent associations, remain content with it, because then they have no obligation towards the elements that have gone off the rails; they are likened to the animals, which must seek their sustenance by themselves.
And therefore it is a gladdening phenomenon when we hear that in Sosnowiec and in Będzin cheap kitchens have opened, where food will be given out to the unemployed. This will help to prevent, on the one hand, people going hungry and languishing in the darkness, and, on the other hand, the manufacture of new professional schnorrers. As soon as an unemployed man knows that for 5 groszy he gets a midday meal, he will not want to blacken his face. And therefore the whole attention must be directed to the oppressed and the unemployed, so that they may be saved and so as not to allow the schnorrer family to be enlarged by them.
We welcome the cheap kitchens that have arisen in Zagłębie and we wish to see such in as great a number as possible. There are no funds — let them be created by the municipal authority and by the Jewish kehillas. The government too will come to help popularise the idea of creating new cheap kitchens for the broad strata, both for the Christian and for the Jewish ones.
Such an activity is desirable; that is real, productive and useful support, which does not corrupt and does not poison a man's soul.
L. Szpigelman.
The Crisis Reaches Doctors and Lawyers Too

[Poland — Economy, the liberal professions.] The crisis, which is growing ever sharper, has begun to tell heavily on the material situation even in those professions where until now it was almost unknown. Doctors and lawyers, for example, who until now used to earn very well, have lately also been complaining a great deal. The number of sick people has not actually become smaller — rather, much larger; but the very same poverty that is the cause of all kinds of illnesses, epidemic and non-epidemic, is also the reason that people have nothing with which to get themselves treated. Many of those who, although they were entitled until now too to benefit from the Sick Fund [Kasa Chorych], did not use to avail themselves of it, now have no other choice. This has forced many doctors to come down from their previous prices: and one can now already find doctors who go to the patient's home for 3 and even for 2 złoty.

Lawyers too feel the crisis strongly. Here too, it would seem, there is no lack of trials: the summary courts have enough work — arrests every little while, excesses, protested bills of exchange, bankruptcies, blackmail and swindles, more and more as time goes on — and yet the material situation of the lawyers has become considerably worse.

It now often happens that if a lawyer does not ask for [his fee] down to the last grosz in advance (not all can do so, and it is not always possible — the competition, after all, is great), the lawyer never sets eyes on the client again, even when he has won the case.

Worst off of all, as is known, are the lawyers in Galicia, where this species is in no short supply... A town like Drohobycz, which does not even have a district court, only a municipal court, has no fewer than 86 [?] lawyers, while Katowice, which is 10 times as large, has only 44 lawyers, and Toruń only 19. Incidentally, the lawyers in the formerly Prussian part of Poland have one more chance: they often perform the functions of a notary.

Altogether there are 4074 lawyers in the whole of Poland, of them in the district of the Warsaw Court of Appeal 847, the Lemberg [Lwów] one 1628, the Kraków one 763, the Wilno one 195, the Katowice one 130, the Volhynian one 178, the Poznań one 238 and the Toruń one 97. As can thus be seen, more than half of the total number of lawyers is to be found in Galicia.
The Pride of Poverty

[Feuilleton — the economic crisis.]
Chaim Hurwitz.
That poverty is no disgrace — this paupers proclaimed across the world long ago, and it turns out they were not at all wrong, for things are already coming to the point where not only shall destitution be no shame, but it shall actually become a matter of pride.
People will walk about the streets and boast of their poverty. Each will strive to outdo the other with his destitution. A prize will be announced for the greatest pauper. But the prize will not be allowed to be money, because if it is money, that will already make him an ex-pauper, and so he will probably not want to take it anyway.
Already now people go about letting everyone know how broke they are. Many make it up and want to persuade the public that they once had millions, so that their collapse should look much mightier. It is not so much what one lacks now, but what one had and lost. The [more] a man has lost, the more cause he has to boast. And conversely, there are plenty who still do have, but in order to keep up with the fashion they too cry that they have lost. Nobody wants to show himself a good-for-nothing. At a time when the biggest bears [?] have gone broke, little people will surely be ashamed to admit that they are shlimazls who have not gone broke.
The vanity of vanities, human foolishness, usually drives a man to look for something to be proud of and to boast about. Well, can anyone come out nowadays and boast that he has made great fortunes and lucky speculations? He would surely be taken for a madman. And altogether it is no longer any distinction; the sign of the times is to be broke.
And the shares of the poverty-market keep on rising.
* * *
The more one hears of broken men who have lost their treasures, the more one begins to wonder who has found those treasures.
After all, it did not sink in water. It came about mostly through "legitimate" dealings, in which money passed from one person to another.
There must surely be some explanation for it.
And perhaps not one but several explanations, at least three.
First, perhaps there never was as much as people reckoned. Not even half of it. People carried around various securities which represented enormous sums and which later turned out to be worth only a small part of that, or nothing at all. It was an empty dream, an unfounded speculation. People reckoned and calculated just like that peasant who was about to catch the squirrel and had already worked out that little by little he would earn more and more through it, until he would become a very rich man — and in the end even the squirrel vanished. Big figures in an over-excited imagination, which never rested on a firm basis. It was fine as long as the fantasy held. No sooner did people catch sight of reality than the fantastic treasures melted away.
Second, real wealth is indeed also diminishing. On the one hand overproduction; on the other hand perhaps half of the people fit for work do not do a stitch of productive work; nothing is produced and yet people consume — some living at their own expense and some at another's, all consume and meanwhile reduce what there is. When millions of people lose the opportunity to earn enough for their own needs, this must reduce wealth in general, no matter where it is to be found. Goods become cheaper and many articles of consumption have to be distributed entirely for nothing, as is now the case with the immense treasures being spent by private, communal and government relief, although it is still not enough. All this is, after all, a part of the general property that is being spent and in a certain sense squandered, because no other is produced [?] in return for it.
And third, it is indeed the new fashion which has brought a kind of pride in destitution. A fair bit is still left, but everyone complains of being broke — whether because they fear the evil eye, or the taxes, or the charitable institutions, or quite simply because they enjoy complaining.
Circumstances change the behaviour of [printed: "and"] people and alter the songs they sing. So too the object of their pride changes. Formerly it was money; now it is destitution.
Let Us Free Ourselves from the Slavish Nightmares

[Opinion — Jewish rights in Poland.]
It is, it seems, high time that our Jewish communal leaders woke from their slumber, shook off dreams of every kind and began to wage a sober struggle, with all their strength, for our elementary rights in Poland.
To begin anew, from the beginning. Not to accept as axioms the arguments of our opponents: that things are bad for them too, and that after all one cannot go against the crystallised will of the masses; that there really are too many Jews in Poland; that the Christians in Poland are going through a migration from village to town, are taking up commerce, industry and crafts, and so they simply “must” push us out; that once, hundreds of years ago, when they needed us to develop trade in Poland, they received us with open arms, and now that we have fulfilled our historical task they can manage without us; that no one is to blame if the new social reforms, and the altogether changed conceptions of life, are pushing us out of our positions of livelihood.—
All these “axioms” we must cast off, and demand for Jews the elementary right to work and bread.
Who has the right to remind us of the fact that 800 or more years ago we were strangers in Poland? Under every constitution in the world a foreigner is naturalised within a few years — all the more so the tenth and the twentieth generation! “The tenth generation” — beyond that even the Bible knows no further path of separation, not even for peoples who are enemies unto blood!
Had we lived in Poland on territories of our own, like the Ukrainians or the Belarusians, that too would have been only a plus, not a minus. But we did not run any separate economy: we built Polish towns, developed Polish trade, crafts, industry, wove ourselves with a thousand threads into the economic life of the state, became bone of its bone and flesh of its flesh — what sort of strangers are we, and why are all the roads of life barred to us?
Why do we meet in the street only Christian policemen, in all the offices only Christian officials, in all the courtyards only Christian caretakers, in all the state factories almost only Christian workers?
Why has it already become an axiom among us, which no one even tries to dispute, that if some branch of livelihood is turned into a monopoly, the Jews will at once be pushed out of it and Christians will come in their place?
Everyone talks about it, Christians and Jews — the former without shame, the latter without anger — as though it were a natural phenomenon, a kind of force majeure, that Jews have nothing to do with matters of government, that “kingship” is a gentile affair. Why is it so?
In the institutions that administer themselves, such as the municipal ones or the sick funds, where there is no government commissioner, a Jew has in recent years still been able to fight his way to a piece of bread; here too a hard, bitter struggle goes on, and here too Jews feel somehow ashamed, like people admitted on sufferance, as if they were eating someone's bread of charity. But as soon as the institution is not autonomous, as soon as it lies directly under the government, the Jew no longer has the nerve even to think of obtaining a post there.
And it is strange. Our government is absolutely not antisemitic; on the contrary, its organs look for various opportunities to establish contacts — moral ones, of course — with Jews; to declare their love — Platonic, of course — for Jews. But we ourselves have already developed within us this lowliness, this inferiority complex, of not allowing ourselves to raise our eyes to those holy places that are called government offices.
To blame for this is the feeling of rightlessness that has been forcibly implanted in our consciousness and from which we cannot free ourselves! As from a heavy nightmare — although we long ago fought out our rights, and we even speak often in the name of those very rights. But it is spoken only from the lips outward; deep in our hearts we still feel like slaves. That is why we love to dream and fantasise about “little plates from heaven”, while the little plate is in fact standing on the ground, and one need only have the courage to stretch out one's hand to it.
We must free ourselves from all slavish nightmares, begin to feel like free men and demand our rights with a full mouth, without any brackets or quotation marks.
And we must make the other side feel that it should not point us to “a fair in the sky”, that we have no other prospects whatsoever and need have none. Here, in Poland, our forefathers were born, lived and created and found their graves; here we live and here we must live out our lives.
But before we go and say this to the other side, we must feel it ourselves with every fibre of our Jewish national soul.
P. K.
The difference between a “Shir HaMa'alot” and a trade licence (a little feuilleton)

[Feuilleton — the obligation of artisans to buy a "patent" (trade licence).]
(A little feuilleton.)
Dear readers, do you know what the difference is between a "Shir HaMa'alot" and a patent? You don't know — so I will tell you.
When you walk into a home and see a "Shir HaMa'alot" hanging there [the amulet sheet hung in the room of a woman in childbed], you should know that in that home a human being has been born. But when you walk into some premises and catch sight of a patent [a trade licence, Polish świadectwo przemysłowe] hanging there, you should say "Blessed be the true Judge", because in that house a petty trader or an artisan lies dying, and today or tomorrow the burial society will come with the wagon.
In Nikolai's [the Tsar's] times Jews used to let it cost them thousands in order to get a patent of a higher category. Szereszowski, when with great "protection" he obtained his first guild, gave a great ball. At that banquet so much schnapps was drunk that all our Zagłębie petty traders and artisans would wish to own no more than the corks of the empty little bottles.
A patent of a higher category once brought very great benefit. Having such a patent, a Jew had the right to stay in Petersburg and could see the Emperor; today, however, when an artisan buys a patent he at once sees the sequestrator [the tax bailiff].
So I really was not surprised that the patentless artisans, who learned that this year they will have to take out patents, did not dance in the streets for joy, did not throw balls like Szereszowski once did, but held lamentations.
A patent is the same thing as the enrolment fee in a society. When you buy a patent, it means that you are admitted as a member of the fellowship of taxpayers. The patent itself is, at bottom, a trifle. When a poor artisan has to buy a patent he gives himself a squeeze, gives his wife and children a squeeze, and there it [the patent] already hangs on the wall. The main thing here, however, is not the enrolment fee but the membership dues: the subsequent taxes, the little bastards, the little "zaliczkas" [advance tax instalments], and so on and so forth.
Poor artisans: you must know that God himself is a pauper, an even greater one than you, and his technique of creation is not yet so developed that a person should come straight out of his mother's womb with a cheque-book in his hand. God has no money of his own; he only takes from one and gives away to another.
This time you, poor artisans, are the givers! If you had gone up to the tax office you would have seen that the money you will spend this year on patents is not lost: people make a living off you; around you feed sequestrators, writers of appeals, carters who cart your things from home to the market, and a living is also made by the rope-dealer, who sometimes takes in from you the price of a bit of rope.
And now that you already have a patent, sit yourselves down on the threshold of your workshop and wait for the sequestrator.
A. Za—ski.
Our Panorama

[Feuilleton / satire — "Our Panorama": from the neighbouring localities.]
(A remedy for the affliction. — A gabbai who came to grief at Musaf. — Einstein's "comrades" in Zawiercie. — A society[?] that suffers torments from a "kwoka". — A war "for the sake of Heaven" in Dąbrowa.)
Pogroms against Jews in Germany, an Endek boycott of Jews in Poland, several young Jewish men shot dead in Romania, Jewish livelihoods going under — all these tidings of lamentation melt away before my eyes when I turn to the "mail" from our neighbouring localities. "Health into their little bones!" — I feel like crying out with joy; a refreshment, a deliverance they are, after all, from our day-to-day troubles...
Take for instance Piaski — a community of all told a dozen members, corresponding to the twelve tribes; nevertheless things seethe there no less than on the battlefield in Manchuria. The only difference is that in the Balkans [sic] people kill one another over towns and villages, while in the holy community of Piaski they do themselves to death over — the prayer-leader's lectern...
The gabbai there, still a young fellow, took a fancy to lead a Musaf service on an ordinary Sabbath. Well, up to the Kedushah he somehow still got through in peace, but when he let himself go further "on the road" and "drove into" "Tikanta Shabbat", the gabbai came to grief and came out of it battered[?]...
After such a "verdict" he vanished in a huff from the beit midrash and threw up the gabbai's office...
And he "prays" elsewhere, with fervour; in his "prayers" he relates that the beit midrash ought to be closed, inasmuch as there is no permit for it...
What will come of it, it is still too early to say; meanwhile 2 sides are fighting — the gabbai who resigned and the congregation — and the third side — is writing protocols...
* * *
Piaski has become "famous" in the "whole world" through its gabbai, and Zawiercie — through the "Tze'irei Emunei" [the Agudah youth]. Truly, such brilliant comrades as the Zawiercie "Tze'irei Emunei" possess you will not find even in the capital, Warsaw.
There died in Zawiercie a certain Yisroel Grinboim. He died on Friday, only for various reasons the burial took place not until Sunday before noon.
The delay, however, was a great gain for the Zawiercie "Torah-true" youth, because exactly at the same hour when the funeral took place, the lecture of Deputy Grünbaum [Yitzhak Grünbaum] was due to take place there.
So the "Tze'irim" did indeed make use of the opportunity and pasted up death notices [klepsydry] in the prayer houses, that at the appointed hour "the funeral of Deputy Grinboim" takes place...
Well, should young people like these, with such "brilliant brains", not become famous?...
* * *
Good tidings we have also received from the community called
— the holy community of Niemce, near Grabocin...
Generations have passed and the rabbinical seat in Niemce was not occupied. If someone happened to have a question [of religious law], he had to go to Strzemieszyce. But the year 5692 brought a redemption to the inhabitants of Niemce and granted[?] them
— a rabbinical seat...
The business outlook is not a bad one. In Strzemieszyce there is still no rabbi. The newly elected rabbi of Jaworzno has not yet been confirmed; well, how can one possibly allow a flock to be without a shepherd? So a wink was given "from above" that a "grandson" [a scion of a Hasidic dynasty] should first of all occupy Niemce...
Ah, Strzemieszyce protests? The rebbetzin, widow of the deceased rabbi, does not receive her pension? But whom does that interest? The main thing is only that
— "Niemce already has a rabbi of its own"...
* * *
In Niemce a rabbi has "settled", and in the Będzin Chevra Tehillim [Psalms society]
— a "kwoka" [a clucking brood-hen]...
It is already several years since a "kwoka" got into the society and has been causing its members severe pain...
Between Minchah and Maariv, every evening, the "kwoka" comes in, and at once the crowd is bewitched and they begin
— to "cluck"...
Several of the "kwoka-ites" come to us with a request that we should put the "kwoka" into the paper — then she will stop her "apostate tricks".
So they assure us, the "delegates" of the Chevra Tehillim; therefore we fulfil their request and we appeal:
— "Throw out the kwoka"...
* * *
"When a misfortune is fated, it comes right into the house." The Dąbrowa dozors [kehilla board members] have, instead of "kwoka troubles" — teacher troubles...
The school inspector turned to the Jewish kehilla for its opinion regarding a teacher of religion in the "szkoła powszechna" [public elementary school] there.
The candidate, incidentally one with the proper qualifications, was approved by the kehilla representatives, and there would have been peace upon Israel, were it not...
Were it not for the "Agudah", which raised an outcry that the engaged teacher "wants to teach the Jewish children Peretz's Chumash"... and what is more, there are eyewitnesses who saw with their own eyes how the teacher went strolling with the Dąbrowa Zionists... Therefore such a "dangerous" person must not be a teacher of religion in a public elementary school; rather the post must be taken by "one of ours", a young fellow who has none of the qualifications of a teacher at all, but he belongs to the party that fights for the "strengthening of religion", he belongs to the "Agudah"...
Couriers run there and back, ultimatums are sent to the dozors, who for the time being have not said their last word; they do not know, poor things, what to do: on the one side the inspector and on the other side the Agudah...
— Yes, how does the saying go: when a misfortune is fated, it comes right into the house...
* * *
The Ksawera community, too, is under the impression of the "heavy misfortune" that has befallen it.
It happened at a Friday twilight. One of the worshippers wanted, at "Lekha Dodi", to show off his "musical abilities" in coloratura. The congregation greatly "enjoyed" it and for sheer delight positively rolled about with laughter...
The "cantor", on hearing what was going on behind his back, grabbed the lectern and
— out of the beit midrash...
— Perhaps you know, dear readers, where the Ksawera cantor with the lectern is to be found?...
Ben Amotz.
An important clarification about “wyłączenia” (excluding belongings from seizure)

[Law — legal advice: seizures and execution proceedings.]
Nowadays it often happens that a komornik [court bailiff], at the demand of the holder of a court judgment [wyrok] or of a writ-of-execution clause [klauzula], carries out a seizure [zajęcie] on a tenant for the sub-tenant's debt, or the reverse. At first it seems a very easy thing to annul the incorrect seizure, but in truth the matter is very complicated and requires an exact knowledge of the execution procedure.
First, the wronged party must remember to obtain from that same komornik a copy of the list of the seized things (odpis zajęcia) and, enclosing it, to apply to the court (up to 1000 zł — the municipal court [Sąd Grodzki]; larger sums — in the district court [Sąd Okręgowy]) with a claim (skarga powodowa), suing the real debtor and the claimant [creditor] who had the things seized.
In the petition the petitioner must explain that the seized things belong exclusively to him, and indeed confirm this with witnesses or documents. Further, one must ask the court:
1) to recognise the seized things (enumerate them exactly according to the komornik's copy) as his property; 2) to release the seized things from the seizure and to annul the auction [licytacja]; 3) in order not to let those things come to sale, to ask to secure the debt [i.e. the claim] (zabezpieczyć powództwo) with an attachment [areszt] for the same sum on the seized things.
I must add that the municipal court seldom issues the above-mentioned attachments, especially when the request is not substantiated by any documents.
Further, one must ask that the trial concerning the exclusion [wyłączenie] of the things should take place before the auction. The latter is always taken into account by the court at the demand of the plaintiff.
So, as we see, one must be very careful with a "wyłączenie", in order not to lose money and fall victim for the sins of others.
Yaakov Ratner.
Festive Jubilee Evening at the Youth Organisation "Gordonia"

[Będzin — youth / Zionism.] The pioneering "Gordonia" of Będzin held a celebration last Saturday night in connection with the organisation's 5-year jubilee.
A numerous youthful audience came to the jubilee evening, along with representatives of all the local organisations, prominent Zionist activists and the press. The large hall was beautifully decorated, illuminated and adorned with greenery. The eastern wall stood out in particular: it was furnished with fitting inscriptions, pictures and fine statistical drawings executed by the Gordonia member Tz. Magerkewicz [C. Magierkiewicz].
All the Gordonia members of all the "gdudim" [troops] and "kvutzot" [groups] appeared in their pioneer and scout dress. At the presidium table stands the "Gordonia" banner with a guard of honour. The blare of trumpeters and the roll of drums are heard as a sign that the festival is beginning. "Hatikvah" is sung.
The "mesibah" [gathering] was opened on behalf of the jubilee committee by Motek Hampel, who delivers a longer Hebrew and [?] spirited speech. The speaker talks about the difficult situation of the Jewish and Zionist world, about the origin and development of "Gordonia", about the spiritual guide of the Eretz-Israel working class, A. D. Gordon of blessed memory, whose 10th yahrzeit fell in these days (his memory is honoured by rising), and about the Fifteenth of Shevat as the spring festival in Eretz Israel.
The "Gordonai" — says Mr Hampel — is the pioneer, the champion in the front line, who goes to Eretz Israel, and despite all difficulties his strong will has nevertheless remained unbroken. The gates of Eretz Israel are closed — continues Mr H. — but with our youthful ardour, faith and work we shall break open the gates for the pioneer who wants to build his land and rebuild his people.
After the opening speech come greetings. On behalf of the Zionist Organisation the greeting is given by the president of the kehilla council, Mr J. Wigodzki; on behalf of Keren Hayesod a matter-of-fact greeting is delivered by Mr Nute Londner; "Hitachdut" — Dawid Liwer; "Tarbut" — Prof. Bornsztajn; the JNF (KKL) — secretary Cwi Kurc; the parents' patronage — Mrs Czarnocha; the League for Labour Eretz Israel — Grojer; "Hechalutz" — J. Anulewicz [?]; "Hashomer Haleumi" united with "Herzliya" — Horowicz; "Hashachar" — Klajner. The Gordonia hakhshara group in Olkusz — Introligator; on behalf of the Gordonia members in Belgium the greeting is given by Dawid Liberman (Brussels), who briefly describes the Jewish life of the Jews in Western Europe; on behalf of the "Gordonia" organisations in Zagłębie — Mr Penkowski (Sosnowiec); and finally the dozor [kehilla board member] Abraham Liwer, who speaks with sympathy and appreciation of the work of the pioneer youth.
The chairman of the banquet then reads out a series of various telegraphic and written greetings that arrived for the celebration. Greeting in writing are: the hakhshara kibbutz named after Borochov [?] (Będzin), the regional leadership (Hanhagah Glilit) of "Gordonia" in Brześć (Brisk), the head office of "Keren Kayemet" (Warsaw), the Central Committee of "Tarbut" (Warsaw), the head leadership (Hanhagah Rashit) of "Gordonia" (Łódź), Kvutzat Aliyah B (Łódź), the comrades from Eretz Israel, Mrs Lea Widrowicz (delegate of the JNF head office in Jerusalem), the hakhshara group in Zagnańsk (near Kielce) and many more "Gordonia" organisations in Poland.
The Będzin sports club "Hakoach" writes in its greeting, among other things: "We have the task of educating the Jewish youth both spiritually and physically; we must, however, admit that we neglect the first field, believing that in the ranks of Gordonia the youth receives the proper spiritual and pioneering education."
After all the blessings comes an interval, which is at the same time the material part of the evening. Over a glass of tea and at beautifully laid tables, furnished with fruits of Eretz Israel and "mamtakim" [sweets], the audience spends the fine evening in a festive and youthful mood.
An interesting violin concert was given by the young violinist Lejbek Rechnic, who thanks to his fine playing is stormily applauded and called back several times for an encore ("bis").
The recitations also went off successfully. The likeable little Blima Wajsbart recites (in Polish), with great success and applause, "It Happened" by the poet Abraham Shlonsky. At the audience's request Miss Wajsbart [printed: Majsbart] further recites "The Sons of Hulda" by the poet Yehuda Karni.
A. Felberg recites a poem, "You, Earth", by the Hebrew poet Yaakov Fichman (Eretz Israel), whose 50th jubilee the Hebrew literary world is now celebrating.
The vocal numbers of the "mit'oreret" Riwa Warszawska were also fine, and then the organisation's own choir performs several new Eretz-Israel songs.
At the close of the celebration Mr Hampel gives a short report on the 5 years of existence and work of the Będzin "Gordonia". From the report one can see growth, development and expansion in all fields of Zionist-pioneering work. The speaker also discusses the future work of the organisation.
With "Techezakna" and a "hurrah" the "chagigah" [celebration] is closed quite late, after midnight.
A. R.
Our Women — and Our Philanthropic Institutions

[Article — women and charity.] There were once times when women stood at the head of the work in various philanthropic institutions. They, the Jewish women, knew that they, just as much as anyone, bear duties towards the orphan, the aged, the sick. They knew that they had to take an interest in all those who are forced to rely on the help of others — to support them, to care for them.
Nowadays this type of woman has almost vanished from the Jewish street. If there are in Zagłębie a handful of women who occupy themselves with charitable work, who take an interest in everyone oppressed, hungry and needy, they belong to the older generation and are looked down on, or perhaps even laughed at, by our modern women. In a mocking tone they are labelled with the names "gabaites" [lady almoners], "nashim tsidkaniyos" [pious women] and the like. For them, for our modern women, it is not fitting to occupy oneself with such a thing as philanthropy, or, as it used to be called once — "tsdoke" [charity].
But this is so only among us, among the "wise and understanding people". When at the same time we cast a glance elsewhere — at the people that did not have the merit of being crowned with this title, "a wise and understanding people" — we see quite a different phenomenon. Here in Będzin there exists, on the Polish street, a special women's association which has set itself the task of taking an interest in all philanthropic work. And in this very association we meet women from the very heart of the Polish intelligentsia, from the cream of society.
Among us, however, all the philanthropic institutions are going through a crisis — not only a financial one but also one of people. There is no one there to come to the aid of these institutions in their various tasks, which are necessary in order to maintain their existence; for our women it is not fitting to occupy themselves with such things.
One will certainly answer that at the present day the situation of the Jewish woman is quite different from that of the non-Jewish one: she, the Jewish woman, helps her husband in his hard struggle for his daily existence. On her lies the yoke of earning a living equally with her husband, and one cannot demand of her that she should also occupy herself with communal work; the non-Jewish woman, on the contrary, is secure in her existence, she has no worries about a livelihood such as the Jewish woman has. In this answer there is a large share of truth. But not the whole truth. After all, there are still women among us who do not help towards the livelihood and who are left with enough free time in the day. If our communal institutions nevertheless do not succeed in drawing these women into any activity whatever, this is again a sign of the present-day trouble, in which the feeling of helping one another has weakened among us.
Oneg Shabbat — Parashat Yitro

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion — collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Yitro
Portion
a) "For Moses and for Israel His people, that the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt" (18:1)
"For Moses" separately and "for His people" separately, because Moses hoped for one kind of redemption and the Jews for another. There are degrees in grasping the essence of redemption. For one man it is "from subjugation to redemption" — not having to do physical labour for the gentiles. A higher conception is already "from slavery to freedom" — a liberation from spiritual servitude. The Moseses, the chosen few, see in redemption "from darkness to a great light" — the great divine light that will drive away the darkness of exile.
Noam Elimelekh.
—o—
b) "And all the people stand about you" (ibid., 14)
"Nitzav" means standing up to do battle ("the Lord stands up to plead"), because that is the lot of a judge: the whole people hates him and everyone suspects him of taking bribes. But only the rich have the courage to suspect; a poor man believes everybody...
Therefore "judge the poor and the orphan": if you judge between two parties, one a poor man and the other an orphan — "do justice", both will acknowledge that the judge is right... Only the rich man cannot believe that anyone[?] decides a din-Torah without personal gain.
Arvei Nachal.
—o—
c) "Able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain" (ibid., 21)
By "able men" the rich are meant, and among such one must look for those who will also be "God-fearing", for most wealthy men lack a little piety.
By "men of truth", in turn, Torah scholars are meant ("the Torah of truth"), and among such one must look for those who will be "haters of gain", for many scholars, living constantly in want, lack the hatred of money...
Mat'amei Yitzchak.
* * *
"Hating gain" —
"Bitzua" means a settlement, a compromise. And "bitzua" in Hebrew also means: robbery. It seems these are identical things... That is why "men of truth" are haters of "betza", for truth tolerates no compromises and concessions...
"Betza" also means self-interest (not only money), and there are those who preach the truth precisely out of self-interest... Therefore what is required are men of truth who love the truth not out of self-interest, but who are haters of gain.
Divrei Shaul.
* * *
"Men of truth."
In the Kovno community there was once a struggle between the freethinkers and the pious. R. Yitzchak Elchanan [Spektor] said that he was sure the freethinkers would win. They ask him:
"How can that be, Rabbi?"
"Because the truth must win," the Gaon answers.
"Is the truth really with the freethinkers?" they ask him in astonishment.
"Yes — the free ones are all truly free, whereas the pious are seldom truly pious..."
—o—
d) "Rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties" (ibid.).
It appears that even the "men of truth" are not all equal either. There are those who have a higher percentage of truth in them, and there are those who have little truth. Truth, like all of God's attributes, is likewise not a limited thing.
Likkutim Chadashim (Rabbi David of Kotzk).
—o—
e) "And Moses sent his father-in-law away" (ibid., 27)
Jethro, as soon as he arrived, began asking hard questions and carrying out reforms. Moses was afraid that when the Ten Commandments were given he would raise questions about them too and try to reform them. Therefore he sent him away before the Giving of the Torah.
Or Yesharim (Rabbi Moshe of Kobrin).
—o—
f) "They came to the wilderness of Sinai" [printed "Sni"] (19:1)
"Wilderness" is a hint at ownerlessness. Preparing to receive the Torah, they made themselves as if ownerless. They lacked nothing any more, they no longer needed anything. Up to this point it was always told "and the people murmured against Moses" — now they needed[?] meat, now something else. Now they already had everything, because they needed nothing.
"Trust" does not mean that one believes God will send; rather, one feels secure because nothing is lacking...
Chashavah LeTovah (Rabbi Henekh of Aleksander).
—o—
g) "And you shall be My own treasure [segulah]" (ibid., 5)
A "segulah" is the name for a thing that has no reason and no clear sense. Although it is bitter and bad, it nevertheless has a property that can take effect. God's love for the Jews is also a kind of segulah like that. Although they are bad and bitter, He still loves them without reason or sense...
Mei Shelach [as printed; = "Mei HaShiloach"?] (from[?] the "Holy Jew").
* * *
Among the pointing signs there are a segol (∵) and a segolta (∴). The only difference between the two signs is that what is below in the one is above in the other.
"And you shall be My segulah" — like a segol and a segolta. Both the lower ones and the upper ones among you should need one another and change places...
Degel Machaneh Ephraim.
* * *
A segol, even when it is turned upside down, is still a segol (a segolta). A Jew, even when he turns himself about, also remains a Jew...
Rabbi Dovidl of Lelov.
—o—
h) "In heaven above and on the earth beneath" (20:4)
Usually in spiritual matters people look below themselves: that fellow is less pious, studies less. And in money matters people look upward: that fellow possesses more money, is richer. But it ought to be the reverse. "In heaven above" — in heavenly matters, look ahead of yourself and envy those who are more upright; and "on the earth beneath" — in wealth, look below yourself: see that there are still poorer people and greater sufferers than you.
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
—o—
Haftarah.
i) "As a terebinth and as an oak, which when they cast their leaves..." (Isaiah 6)
The common people are likened in the Talmud to leaves that cover and guard the trees. And if the leaves become fallen foliage and drop off the trees (the chosen ones, the intellectuals), the trees remain naked and forsaken...
Ahavat Tzion.
Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov (instalment 9)

[Serialized novel — “Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress”, a historical novel by Boris Maksimov; instalment 9.]

On the evening of that same day a meeting took place of the Central Committee of the “Soyuz Russkavo Naroda” [Union of the Russian People], to which Rasputin was brought in order to introduce him and take him into the committee.

All the members of the Central Committee were assembled. The famous antisemites and reactionaries were there, rich people and highly placed personages. Rasputin sat withdrawn to one side, sat quietly, patiently, and listened to everything that was being said. Only there did he become convinced how important Iliodor was and what a great role he played. Everyone looked at the monk with respect and with awe. Everyone listened to his words with the greatest attention. They talked about the tasks of the organisation, about combating the revolutionary agitations that are directed against God and against the Tsar, about sending agitators out through the villages to raise up in them the faith in God and in the Tsar...

Then Iliodor stood up. Everyone fell silent. In the hall one could hear the slightest rustle. Iliodor's face became suffused with wild hatred, his eyes blazed, venom spurted from them. He shouted wildly and clamoured, cursing with the wildest curses the heretics and the revolutionaries who dare to set themselves against God and against His anointed, the “holy” Tsar... He called for a merciless fight against the unbelieving intelligentsia, which wants to bring into “holy” Russia the customs of Western Europe. Suddenly a hot rage seized him like a black flame and he began to thunder:

— And first of all we must settle accounts with the accursed “Zhids”! They are to blame for all the troubles! They spread revolt and insurrection against God and Tsar! They are the emissaries of Satan! With their lives let them pay!... In their blood Satan must be drowned! Pogroms! Make pogroms against the Jews and it will become quiet in the land!... Exterminate the Jews and Russia will be saved!

He shouted it with savagery, his lips trembled with bloodthirstiness. He called for slaughtering Jews, for torturing Jewish women, for tearing Jewish children to pieces. His shouts inflamed all those assembled with savagery, and he cried out:

— Do you remember, a few years ago? Right after the Japanese-Russian war?

A rebellion arose in the land against God and against the Tsar... Satan had already rubbed his hands with joy, already thought he had gained dominion over the “holy” Russian people... And what did we do then? We then organised a series of pogroms against the accursed “Zhids”! We carried out massacres across Jewish towns and townlets! In the blood of the unbelievers we drowned Satan! Now Satan is raising his head again... The “Zhids” rob the Russian man, bring him to poverty and want, incite him against his faith and against his Tsar! So the same thing must be done again: slaughter the Jews!

And Iliodor spread out his hands in wild prayer and in a screeching voice cried out:

— Russian people! Why are you silent? Exterminate the “Zhids” and Satan too will be exterminated! Drive the “Zhids” out of the towns and the Russian people will breathe more freely:

He finished, and a wild clapping of hands broke out. Something like a madness fell upon all those assembled; they shouted “Bravo”! Everyone's blood was boiling. The faces were flushed red, and from all eyes wild hatred spurted.

Rasputin sat the whole time calm, patient, only a little bewildered: he had never seen any Jews and did not understand why everyone felt such hatred for them... He lightly wrinkled his forehead, had knitted his brows, and meanwhile was thinking: what are these Jews, then, that they are to blame for all the troubles? And since in Siberia there are no Jews — does the poor muzhik live well there? Do the Siberian muzhiks not suffer want and hunger? And why does such murderous fury seethe in Iliodor? With his peasant instinct he felt that Iliodor was a wild demagogue and careerist, but — he also understood that he must now agree with the black monk, that it was very important for him to win his trust, and when Iliodor finished, Rasputin too clapped his hands and shouted “Bravo”...

Iliodor turned his head to the side where Rasputin was standing. He felt Rasputin's eyes upon him, and again he had the feeling that the eyes of the dirty muzhik were confusing him and having a strange effect on him. Again there was in him a mixture of different feelings: disgust, fear, anger and admiration...

The assembly was seething after Iliodor's inflammatory speech; there was tumult and noise. Everyone had some proposal against the Jews. They talked about sending agitators out through the villages to incite the muzhiks against the Jews, about organising gangs in the towns that would attack and beat Jews, about turning to the Tsar and obtaining from him that all Jews be sent out of the Russian capitals and their property confiscated, about interceding with the appropriate ministries so that Jewish doctors and lawyers be forbidden to practise...

Iliodor sat like a victor and with concealed pleasure listened to all this talk. He was greatly pleased with the impression his speech had made on those assembled.

When those assembled had calmed down, the “holy” wanderer from Siberia was then presented to them. It was Archimandrite Feofan who presented him. When Rasputin stood up, those assembled smiled slightly to themselves. At the first moment he made no impression on them. But Feofan called him a “starets” (holy man), spoke of him with enthusiasm. He said that this wanderer, who comes from Tobolsk, is a “man of God”, that he stands close to God, that God's word speaks through his mouth and that he is able to work wonders.

Out of respect for the Archimandrite those assembled did not smile now, but it was easy to recognise in their faces that they believed very little in the holiness of this muzhik.

After that Bishop Hermogen took the floor. He endeavoured to explain to those assembled how important Rasputin could be for their organisation and proposed that he be taken into the Central Committee. But to his great regret he sensed that his words had no effect. His explanations were heard out in indifferent silence, and he noticed from the expressions on the faces that most of those assembled were against taking the Siberian muzhik into their ranks.

When Hermogen had finished speaking and everyone was silent, Iliodor suddenly jumped up; regardless of the fact that he himself, deep in his heart, agreed with those assembled, he flared up with anger against those who dare to doubt the holiness of the Siberian wanderer. He was terribly agitated, and in a thundering voice he began to shout and openly declared that into the ranks of the “Union of the Russian People” too the devilish ideas of Western Europe had crept — those lawless thoughts about freedom and rebellion that seek to undermine the faith in God and in the holiness and chosenness of the Russian people.

— Yes! — he clamoured — I say it to all of you to your faces, that into the ranks of our “Union” too Satan and the spirit of unbelief have crept!

With flaming eyes and with foam on his lips he flung into the faces of those who dare not to believe in Rasputin's holiness that the “Antichrist” had crept into them; that their patriotism is worth no more than the patriotism of the unbelieving Zhids, lawyers and journalists who believe in nothing. With raised hands he cried out:

— Woe! Woe and alas for poor holy Russia, if among the “faithful sons of Russia” unbelief has crept in! After that Iliodor appealed to the “clear political sense” of his listeners and tried to demonstrate how important and useful it is for the aims and purposes of the “Union” to acquire so strong a force as Grigori Rasputin. He endeavoured to prove to those assembled that the “Union” must strain all its powers to win the trust and the support of the people, in order to be able to bar the way to the ideas of freedom and unbelief that are pushing in here from Western Europe. Therefore, in his opinion, the Russian peasant must be put forward before the people as the representative of a “God-fearing people”. And Grisha, the Siberian muzhik, is the suitable person for that. He is a “holy man” and a simple one. He will have a very great effect on the people with his plain and sharp-witted words, with his simple cleverness and fear of God. Everyone will listen to him!

Iliodor caught his breath and added:

— And one more important thing: what will it be worth, that we shall have the possibility, when an important resolution has to be adopted, of having for it the assent of a “holy man” through whose mouth God Himself speaks?! Everyone who does not want to set himself against religion and the country will have to recognise as right every resolution that has the assent of such a “holy man” as Rasputin...

(To be continued.)
A Festival of Culture in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — theatre, jubilee.] (On today's jubilee evening at the Municipal Theatre.)

This Friday evening it is, in its turn, Sosnowiec's part to celebrate the festival of one of the greatest Jewish stage artists. It is not a festival in the ordinary sense of the word; it is rather an expression of 15 years of extraordinary exertion, of migrations and wanderings, physical and spiritual, by a man who simply sacrificed himself in order to raise Jewish culture in the field of theatrical art.

Fifteen years of playing Yiddish theatre — and playing it in such a way — is perhaps, in quantity, quite a modest figure for ordinary, average people; and if such a sum of years contains[?], even for such people, very often a whole era of various trials and diverse stages of life — how much more so for temperamental and deeply gifted people, for whom life is an eternal struggle of seeking and inquiring, in whom the thirst for perfection is always like an unbridled storm — for such people of genius that number of years is certainly a great and important date in the course of their lives. Here quantity goes together hand in hand with quality, so [that] the number of years and the content and quality of those years both form an epoch of great significance.

This epoch, stormy as the Sambation and at the same time rich in spirit, belongs to the renowned and brilliant Jewish artist Zygmunt Turkow. His 15-year jubilee is being celebrated by the whole Jewish cultural world, by all those to whom everything created for Jewish culture and art is dear and precious. It is not a personal, individual festival of one man. Zygmunt Turkow's jubilee bears a general, popular Jewish character, because through his colossal achievements and wonderful accomplishments over the 15 years he has contributed much to the treasury of Jewish theatrical art, enriched it and raised it to such a level that we have ceased to be ashamed before others. Only then did we catch sight of ourselves and cease to be so lowly in our own eyes in the field of artistic creation. With Zygmunt Turkow we began to show ourselves before Europe and began to take pride in him.

Fifteen years — that is a hard martyr's road for a Jewish artist. We are not even speaking of the material side; that is a sad chapter in itself. While among all nations [artists] are maintained, or at the very least supported, by the governments, by the self-governing bodies and simply by great financiers, the so-called patrons of art, the Jewish artist is thrown upon his own resources. He is a wanderer. He must fight hard and bitterly for his existence and at the same time work on himself, seek, inquire, study and learn; even on the road of his wanderings and in abnormal conditions of life, when he is simply struggling to keep himself alive from day to day, he may not for one minute forget to create new values, to go forward — because, first, if he is truly gifted and possesses artistic feeling, it gives him no rest. Within him something like an inner, hidden genius strains towards perfection, towards bringing out as many new revelations as possible; that is the first driving force. The second stimulus is that the Jewish artist must come to his audience constantly with new stage works and always give it premieres. How this is done, how and with what self-sacrifice it is created — of that we do not wish to know. We, the Jewish spectators, are strict, and we demand of the Jewish artist something new, only new achievements.

With whomever it is the other way round — with us it is turned upside down. Among the nations of the world the people helps to create culture and art. The whole people takes part in their growth and development. The bearers of culture, the intellectuals and artists, find to a certain degree a prepared and grateful soil on which to continue[?] their creative process. With us it is different: the public stands at a distance, and the work of culture has to be carried on the shoulders of a chosen few. Besides the spiritual baggage, these few chosen ones must carry the clay and the bricks to lay the first foundation of the edifice of culture and art. We want to come to what is ready-made. Yes, in one thing we do excel: we have demands, and high demands.

To these artistic chosen few Zygmunt Turkow belongs without any doubt. His 15 years of activity on the stage are a splendid page in the history of the modern Jewish theatre.

We hold that Zagłębie belongs to the circle of Zygmunt Turkow's admirers. Indeed 15 years ago — it would be, if we are not mistaken, in the year [19]17 — Ester Rachel Kamińska played[?] here with her ensemble, in which Zygmunt Turkow already was at that time (he then became engaged to Ida Kamińska). Those were his first steps on the Jewish stage, and we saw him in Kobrin's and Peretz Hirschbein's plays, and above all his artistic star shone forth in the Ibsen repertoire. People who understand theatre foretold already then that in Zygmunt Turkow a force was growing. Those experts and connoisseurs were, it appears, not mistaken. Today the same prophets meet Zygmunt Turkow again; but what a colossal road of triumph Zygmunt Turkow has travelled in that time.

We greet the celebrant of the jubilee and wish him long and good years, that he may be able, in comfort, to continue and develop his artistic work on the stage for the good of the modern Jewish theatre.

P. T.[?]
What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Zagłębie — local news; Będzin.] What's new in Zagłębie?
Friday, 21 Shevat 5692 — piątek 29 stycznia 1932 [Friday, 29 January 1932].
—o—
In a time of crisis even that is good...
Thieves got into Elementary School [szkoła powszechna] No. 2 in Czeladź and took a few school exercise books, rubber stamps and several groszy...
Because the "business" did not "pay off", the thieves, as revenge, overturned the tables and did other damage.
—o—
Będzin
From the Commissar's Council.
At Thursday's sitting of the Commissar's Council it was resolved to ask for a prolongation of the short-term loan of 50 thousand zł. which the Magistrate [city administration] owes the Communal Bank in Warsaw.
At the sitting councillor Mr. Szwajcer handed in a written declaration that, because the item of the surcharge on the state tax on immovable property is again on the agenda, he is leaving the sitting in protest. For lack of a quorum the sitting is broken off.
—o—
Mr. Rubinlicht — nominated commercial judge.
On the basis of a decree of the Ministry of Justice Mr. Rubinlicht has been nominated commercial judge [sędzia handlowy] at the Sosnowiec District Court.
The nomination is valid for 3 years.
—o—
The road tax reduced.
On the basis of an intervention by the new House-Owners' Association the temporary City Commissar has agreed to reduce the road tax [podatek drogowy] by 20 per cent.
Only those house owners who lodged an appeal against the assessment of the above-mentioned tax [podatek] benefit from the reduction.
—o—
Będzin in figures.
The last census established, as we are informed, that in the town of Będzin there are 28,116 souls, in Ksawera — 6,770 [?], Koszelew — 3,565, Warpie — 3,956, Małobądz — 3,071 and Gzichów — 2,887 souls.
According to the statistics 26,843 persons gave Polish as their "język ojczysty" [mother tongue], the rest — Yiddish and Hebrew.
The oldest woman in Będzin is Blimele Gutman. She is — no evil eye — 106 years old.
—o—
Sugar for schoolchildren.
The Main Committee for the Support of the Unemployed has also allotted sugar for the poorest children of the elementary schools, of the Talmud Torah and of the orphanages.
—o—
From the Merchants' Association
we are asked to communicate the following:
1) All kinds of scales and measures must be legalised every 2 years, i.e. a scale that was legalised in the year 1929 must be stamped again at the end of the year 1931.
2) All scales and measures are subject to legalisation, even when they are used in premises that are not a public place of trade.
3) The Jewish Agency has undertaken to organise an excursion to Palestine, with the participation of merchants and industrialists, with the aim of getting acquainted with the trading conditions there.
Exact information is given in the secretariat of the "Merchants' Association".
—o—
"The Jews had light"...
Messrs. Sz. Waldman and A. Berkowicz have been brought to judicial responsibility for carrying out unpermitted manipulations on the electricity meter, thanks to which damage was caused to the municipal power station [elektrownia].
—o—
On the unification of the house-owners' associations.
The negotiations between the house-owners' associations are not yet concluded. The main sticking point is the demand of the new House-Owners' Association that the seat of the united association should be in their premises.
Next Sunday a conference of both sides will again take place on this question.
—o—
Concert of the Folk Choir in Będzin.
The Folk Choir [Folks-Khor], which was created a few weeks ago in Będzin, is already appearing with a concert on Thursday the 4th of February [lutego].
As we are informed, the concert should be a very interesting one; among other things the most beautiful Yiddish folk songs will also be sung.
Besides the Folk Choir, which numbers about 40 persons, the pianist Mrs. Til-Fogelgarn [?], the singer Miss Pojarska [?] and the chief cantor of the Katowice synagogue, Mr. Dembitzer, are also taking part.
In Jewish circles the concert has aroused great interest.
—o—
A little factory of false 2- and 5-złoty coins discovered
Beyond Oytsev [?; perhaps Ojców] a little factory of 2- and 5-złoty coins has been discovered.
The "manufacturers" are well-known names in the prisons...
—o—
Lecture by A. Gottesdiener.
The lectures of Mr. A. Gottesdiener, which were interrupted for reasons beyond control, are being renewed.
This coming Saturday night the next continuation of the cycle "The Life and Work of the Rambam [Maimonides]" takes place.

"A Wedding in Upper Silesia".
Next Monday the folk play called "A Wedding in Upper Silesia" [Wesele na Górnym Śląsku] will be performed in Polish in the cinema "Kapitol".
The performance takes place in the presence of the author, Professor Yanelini [?].

A car crushes a chauffeur to death.
The chauffeur Adamowski of Groytse [?; perhaps Grodziec] was repairing a car. In the middle of the work he fell down under the car and was crushed to death.
Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — local news.]
Memorial of the kehilla representatives to the starosta.
On Sunday the kehilla board held a meeting at which the changes in the budget made by the kehilla council were considered.
Because of the differences of opinion as to whether the kehilla board has the competence to reject the resolutions of the council, it was resolved that a delegation of the dozors [board members] Zendel, Reznik, Nachemia, Wajnsztok and secretary Lewenhof should turn to the starosta to hear his opinion as to whose decision is authoritative, the council's or the board's.
The delegation was received by the vice-starosta, who declared that the deciding party is only the council.
At the same time a memorial was handed in, in which a series of facts is pointed out concerning the unlawful resolutions passed by the council.
—o—
A stubborn suicide.
On Tuesday before noon the mentally ill Zakrzewski [זאקשעווסקי] threw himself under the tram. Thanks to the fact that the motorman managed to stop the tram, Z. was saved from death.
A few minutes later the same person again threw himself under a second tram. This time too he was saved, only the police took him under their protection.
—o—
Concert of Gershon Sirota.
Next Sunday the music-lovers and lovers of song in Zagłębie will have the opportunity to hear the famous world cantor Gershon Sirota.
Gershon Sirota is reckoned today in the cantors' world as the greatest cantor of the present time and also a great singer and composer, for above all his splendid singing and the cantor's voice[?] that he possesses have no equal whatsoever and make a tremendous impression on the listeners.
Sirota's Sunday concert contains a rich musical programme, consisting of the finest cantorial motifs, Jewish folk songs and also opera arias.
Together with Sirota his daughter also appears, the gifted lyric singer Helena Sirota, who will perform splendid pearls of the vocal repertoire.
At the piano, his son Naftali Sirota.
—o—
The suppliers of the Sick Fund have received a heavy sentence.
Last Saturday the trial was concluded in the local district court against Mr Stanisław Żywna [זשיוונא], "g." [probably: former] manager of the medicines store of the Sick Fund, and Mr Szpinak, who supplied the articles.
The accused were charged with having supplied cheap articles and taken high prices for them.
Sentenced were: Żywna to 18 months and Szpinak to 6 months of prison.
—o—
A litre of milk is to cost 35 groszy.
So the price commission determines.
The price commission at the Sosnowiec magistrate considered the milk prices at its last meeting. Until now there were two milk prices: milk straight from the cow cost 45 gr. (in fact the consumers paid more[?] according to this price) and "kalye" [spoiled, inferior] milk 40 groszy.
The commission abolished the hitherto existing sorts of milk and fixed one sort of milk at the price of 35 gr. per litre.
The price comes into force on the 1st of February [luty], i.e. from next Monday.
—o—
Meeting of the Jewish metal guild.
Next Tuesday a general meeting of the Jewish metal guild will take place in the premises of the Artisans' Association; very important questions will be dealt with and elections of a new board will take place.
—o—
From the district court.
At Wednesday's session of the local district court there took place, among others, the trial of the young man Rozmaryn, who was charged with communist activity.
Rozmaryn was punished with 3 years of prison.
—o—
3-year-old boy kills his 2-year-old brother.
In the village of Marczynaja[?] [מארטשינאיא] such a tragic case occurred:
In the home of a local inhabitant there were two little boys, one 2 years and the other 3 years old.
The children, being alone in the house without any supervision, passed the time in games, during which the 3-year-old found a rifle, which went off and killed the younger brother.

Mine workers ready for the fight for their existence.
In the course of the week mass meetings took place in a number of places in Zagłębie, at which the project of reducing wages by 25 per cent was discussed.

Personal.
The hitherto prosecutor at the Sosnowiec district court, advocate Henryk Rajchman [רייכמאן], who made himself popular through conducting the trials and in particular won renown in the recent Rosenberg trial, has now opened a law office in Sosnowiec at Małachowskiego 10 (the house of Mr Zweigenhaft), and receives clients daily from 8 to 9 in the morning and from 4 to 7 in the evening.
