Constituent meeting of the new kehilla board.

On Sunday the second constituent meeting of the new kehilla board took place. On the agenda there was only: election of a president. Present this time were 6 dozors [board members]: 5 of the National Bloc as well as the Beit-Midrash candidate Mr. Reuven Dafner; the 2 "Agudists" did not come. The meeting is opened by the old president Mr. Ch. B. Ajbeszyc, who read out the order of the starosta that before the election every member of the National Bloc must declare that the "issur" [ban] has been lifted. Against this declaration Mr. M. Szwarcberg protested sharply, and in a lengthy speech censured the conduct of the small group (Agudah), which makes use of the ugliest and most shameful methods, which are contrary to morality and ethics and make things harder[?] for the Jewish [sic — a word seems to be missing] outwardly, and brings ruin and demoralisation inwardly. After the declarations that the ban has been lifted were attached, the election was proceeded to. With 5 votes of the National Bloc Mr. Szymon Sztark was elected anew as president. After the election Mr. Sztark made a statement that, despite all the efforts of the opposing side to have the election annulled again, he will endeavour to satisfy all strata and to thwart the harmful work of all kinds of "strongmen"...

After the meeting a consultation of all 6 dozors took place at Mr. Glücksztajn's; they resolved to call upon the Rabbi, shlita, to transfer the kehilla's plot of land from his own name to the name of the kehilla.

—o—

Campaign for the artisans' relief fund.

On Saturday night an entertainment evening took place at the "Artisans' Association" for the benefit of the relief fund for unemployed craftsmen. The board took pains that the evening should turn out very festive and bring in a larger income. It splendidly decorated the new artisans' premises and lit them with a sea of electric lights; all the Jewish institutions were represented. On matters of the day spoke Messrs. E. Kożma[?] and M. Sz. Szwarcberg, who described the bitter distress prevailing among the Jewish craftsmen, who receive no support from anywhere, and called on those assembled to support the relief campaign by every possible means. The evening brought in an income of 200 zł.

A. B.[?]
On the concert of the 8-year-old little cantor Nachuml Epsztajn

[Będzin — music and cantorial art.] This coming Saturday night the second appearance of the 8-year-old little cantor ("chazndl") Nachuml Epsztajn takes place in the "Kapitol" ["קאפיטאל" — hall].
Nachuml Epsztajn is a wonder child, a phenomenon; it is astonishing to see how such a small boy carries himself freely on the stage, sings heartily and with relish; every gesture of his is excellently accented, and he refreshes the listeners with his soft, lyrical tones.
Almost the entire Jewish press in Poland has responded warmly to the concerts of the little, likeable Nachuml. In the review in the "Lodzer Togblat" we read:
"Nachuml Epsztajn is one of those star-children who fall from heaven in a golden cloak. When you close your eyes and listen to the sweet prayers that pour from the platform over the hall, it seems to you that here before you stands a prayer-leader (shliach-tsibur) who expresses the groan of the wandering congregation of Jews."
The well-known music reviewer Mr M. Kipnis writes in "Haynt":
"Nachuml Epsztajn sings like a child; what makes one marvel in the 'child' is his musicality; he sings very rhythmically, more rhythmically than other, old cantors, keeps splendidly in key, calm and composed — not like a child, but like a composed cantor with a little paunch... If a great cantor is ay-ay-ay, then a 7-year-old little cantor is a whole sensation, and for fathers and mothers of small children — certainly and most certainly."
—o—
Great victory of the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" at the elimination contests in Warsaw.
[Zagłębie — sport.] To the elimination contests in Warsaw 60 people travelled from Zagłębie, 15 of them standing for the competition.
We left Będzin at 2 o'clock at night. In spite of the late hour, a crowd of 130[?] people came to the station to see us off.
In Warsaw nobody was waiting for the sportsmen of Zagłębie, and here the World Union "Maccabi" deserves a great reproach. After an hour's waiting the general secretary, Mr Dikes, finally arrived; he took an interest in the guests and quartered them in the comfortable emigrants' house of "JEAS".
On Saturday morning the elimination contests began in the premises of the Warsaw "Maccabi". From the very start it was noticeable that Zagłębie was playing first fiddle, as the members of the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" Maks Trajster and Josl Sztajnic proved to be without rivals in Poland in the field of gymnastics.
Zagłębie attained 6 prizes out of 10 possible. The technical result is as follows:
First prize — Maks Trajster (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 147½ points
Second prize — Josl Sztajnic (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 137½ points
Fifth prize — Cytryn (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 114½ points
Sixth prize — Chaim Prachtcwajg (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 111½ points
Eighth prize — Heniek Melach (Hakoach Będzin) — 96 points
Ninth prize — Icchak Gożykowski (Hakoach Będzin) — 88½ points
Among the women too Zagłębie played a dominant role. Out of 6 possible, Zagłębie attained 4. The result is as follows:
First prize — Mania Gelbhard (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 58½ points
Third prize — Jadzia Pinkus (Hakoach Będzin) — 51½ points
Fifth prize — Jadzia Kurcfeld (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 39½[?] points
Sixth prize — Lola Grajfer (Maccabi Sosnowiec) — 34½ points
The joy of the Zagłębie crowd was beyond measure; greater still was the joy of the sportsmen themselves, who kissed one another and wished each other "God willing, in the Land of Israel at the Maccabiah".
The next day, Sunday, at 12 o'clock noon, a great gymnastics festival took place in the largest Jewish theatre of Warsaw, the "Nowości", with the participation of sportsmen from: Sosnowiec, Będzin, Bielitz [Bielsko], Płock, Włocławek, Warsaw and others. Here too it was noticeable that the gymnasts of Zagłębie set the tone and that they will make up the largest part of the representation of Polish Jewry at the Maccabiah in the Land of Israel. At the close there was a march-past with the banners of all the participants. The orchestra of the Warsaw "Maccabi" played. The march-past left a good impression on all those present, who were delighted with the sportsmanlike conduct of the men and women gymnasts of Zagłębie.
In the afternoon an excursion was made round the sights of Warsaw, such as: the Belweder, Łazienki, the Sejm. The editorial offices of "Haynt", "Moment" and the "Sport-Tsaytung" were also visited; everywhere the sportsmen were received in a friendly manner by the chief editors of each newspaper.
At the departure from Warsaw the committee of the World Union came in a body to take leave.
To the Zagłębie sportsmen for their victory — a hearty "yasher koach" (well done).
A. W—ski.

The united Zionist youth organisations „Ha-Shomer ha-Leumi“ and „Ha-Tselia“[?] are developing broad activity in Zagłębie. Szmitana[?] opened the course and pointed out in a few words the enormous importance of the instructors' course, which helps to educate Jewish youth in the national spirit.

Questions of the Day: It Is High Time

The time is approaching when the turnover tax is assessed, and fear takes hold of the merchant. All his toil and efforts to stay in existence will be cut off at one stroke if he is assessed at more than he is able to pay.
The worse the situation of the merchants becomes, the more serious grows this fear of excessively assessed taxes. There is nowhere to take from, nothing to pay with. In previous years people paid from their own property and from goods bought on credit; now nobody gives goods or money on credit, now the taxes are paid from the very last pennies. If they now assess more than one is able to pay, it will bring inevitable ruin upon the merchants.
How large, in general, was the overall turnover in the year 1931?
This question is answered clearly and plainly by the official figures.
In the year 1931 the metal industry produced 50 percent less. Leather production — 40 per cent less. The textile industry — 32 per cent. The ready-made clothing branches reduced their turnover by 25 per cent compared with the previous year.
If the turnover is reckoned not by the weight and measure of the goods but by price, then the money turnover in industry and trade in 1931 was smaller by no less than 50 percent compared with 1930.
As regards transport, the official figures show that in 1931 the railways carried 25 per cent less goods than in 1930.
The credit statistics show nothing better. Bank Polski last year approved credit amounting to 1 milliard and 55 million, but only 670 million zł. of discount credit was used, simply because the manufacturers had no takings and had no bills of exchange.
From this one can plainly see that the whole economic life has shrunk enormously [?]. This is a fact that strikes the eye; one need not even prove it. The 530 thousand unemployed and the 300 thousand workers who are almost unemployed, since they work only one or two days — all this speaks and cries out in clear words.
In accordance with this sad balance, this year's turnover tax must be assessed for everyone at half of last year's. That is how one must act, unless one wants to crush what remains of trade and industry.
One must stop being mistaken that when the merchant is impoverished, only he alone suffers; because of this false opinion the crisis here is sharper than anywhere else. If the merchants are overly pressed with unjustifiably high taxes, industry too is stifled. That drives fresh tens of thousands of workers out of the factories and workshops, and so drives them into unemployment and want.
Now is the highest time for it. Practice has already taught us that the intervention work must not be left for later, when everyone has already been assessed and all have already been pushed to despair — after the fact nothing helps any more.
This must be done in good time!
G. Ch.
Greetings from Będzin and Sosnowiec Compatriots

In November 1930 a society was founded by some Będzin compatriots (landslayt) living in Berlin. The purpose of the society is to hold all compatriots together and to support them in case of need, and to give social and legal help. Gold and Leo Grunwald as secretaries, M. Grunwald and J. Kleinman as auditors. Messrs. Palimade[?] and Yisakhar Szwarcbaum as board members (assessors).

On the Eve of the Opening of the Eretz Israel Bazaar in Sosnowiec

We are already on the eve of the opening of the grandiose Eretz Israel bazaar in Sosnowiec, whose proceeds are destined for the redemption of land for the Jewish people in Eretz Israel.
What actually is a bazaar? An exhibition in miniature: it embraces more or less the production that every country possesses, popularises its products among the broadest strata of the commercial population and draws the attention of its many visitors to the creations of the given country.
The task of the local bazaar here must therefore be, besides popularising every branch of trade, industry and all kinds of home products, to serve at the same time as a demonstration of our will, strength and devotion to the lofty idea of building the Land.
At the centre of general attention during the exhibition will undoubtedly be the Eretz Israel pavilion, occupying the most prominent place at the exhibition and arousing admiration among the numerous [?] visitors.
True, the production of Eretz Israel cannot appear before us in the lands of the Diaspora in all its many-coloured richness, with all the branches of creation that Eretz Israel puts out.
But we are proud that at the greatest international exhibitions Eretz Israel has won its reputation as a land in which Jewish creative power finds expression, showing what we are capable of creating under objective conditions.
The bazaar, which will be opened in Sosnowiec in the month of February, demands, even on the eve of its opening, a great deal of work and intensity; it is indeed no wonder that all the committees created for this purpose are working with their utmost effort to satisfy all visitors, consumers, customers — those who will come in the evening hours to spend time over a glass of tea, a drink and music, and even to dance a „tango“, a „rumba“, and simply to pass the time cosily in a warm Eretz-Israel atmosphere, which is created in the course of its eight-day exhibition.
A. Frommer.

They Want to Create Educated Craftsmen — A Bill on 3 Types of Vocational Schools

[Poland — vocational education and crafts.]
The Chamber of Commerce has received from the ministry the draft of a law on the school system, in particular on vocational schools.
Two kinds of vocational schools are to be created: one type of vocational school is to give young people theoretical and practical preparation for a trade, which will be divided into 3 levels, depending on the various functions in the trade concerned.
The vocational schools of the lower type will have a pronounced practical character. Their curriculum will build on the first level of the curriculum of the elementary schools and will be [—], depending on the trade, 2 and 3 years. The vocational schools of the gymnasium type will give, besides practical, also theoretical preparation and a broader general education.
Finally a type of vocational school (lyceum) is to be created, which will build on the curriculum of the general gymnasiums and give deeper vocational knowledge. Pupils who complete the lyceum-level vocational schools will be able to enter institutions of higher learning.
The Chamber of Commerce will soon give its opinion on the bill.
The representatives of the Jewish craftsmen in Zagłębie must take care in good time that the Jewish craftsmen too will be able to benefit from the new laws (ustawy).

On Guard Against a Catastrophe (VI)

By L. Szpigelman.
(Harmful substances must be radically uprooted!)
When a person is frightened, every trifle bothers him. The slightest movement agitates him and he cannot come to himself. He then finds himself in abnormal conditions and loses his balance, until it reaches the level of helplessness and abnormality.
It is precisely this phase that many citizens reach in the present critical time. The struggle for a piece of bread is getting harder and harder. Moreover, the economic conditions of existence nowadays are simply unbearable. If one wants to trade honestly and earn something on whatever article it may be, that is a dream, a utopia, because, first, one will not [find] a customer just for one's bright eyes, and second, he [the customer] gets it cheaper than it costs [the seller] himself — how is that possible? About that it is better not to ask, because people, merchants, all kinds of craftsmen nowadays devise various combinations, and the whole combination is this: that one should not let the other earn; and first and foremost this very combiner is himself the scapegoat ("kapore"), because the whole trick consists in not earning. It is, after all, an old Jewish rule: a Jew does not ask himself what will I earn on this, he only thinks: how much will I lose here. In this way one does not let the other live, and the end is that one has nothing oneself and makes the other unhappy.
Now the situation has reached the most helpless phase: people do not trade because they lose money, and those who do trade mostly add [their own money] to their businesses, thanks to the fact that the basis, the foundation, the whole system of trade is a rotten one, rotten through and through. So that nothing can be repaired, nothing improved, nothing changed in order to continue the course of a normal existence.
In the war a "pasek" [black-market profiteering] began to spin. The public began to profiteer; however much one earned, it was too little. Like a hungry wolf, like a lion, the profiteer ("paskarz") wanted to swallow everything; however much he earned was too little for him. The whole world became too narrow for him, he had too little of everything. He acquired beastly appetites. He reckoned with nothing and with no one. Each of them strove to become an unlimited ruler over capitalism, and this arose on the ruins of the people; they rode over the backs of the oppressed working strata. To possess the whole world — all the palaces and factories and houses and villages and estates — was too little for them. And then, when people looked around, they saw the danger and began to organize usury offices ("lichwa" offices) which were to curb the unlimited appetites of the parasites that had sprung up in all countries; but the stifling air was poisoned everywhere, it became harder to breathe, the atmosphere became unbearable — until the catastrophe came. Profiteering, which made working humanity so unhappy, dissolved like a soap bubble, and it is characteristic that, just as no one knew where the "pasek" got the strength to maintain so firm a rule, so no one knew how its downfall came at so fast a pace.
We are already far away from that time; there can be no talk of profiteering now. On the contrary, the "pasek" was uprooted by itself so radically that one no longer believes it was supposed to happen in our generations — so far a distance are we from it, although not long ago we were living here in that unbearable atmosphere.
Now we find ourselves in entirely different conditions. It is the opposite: just as earlier people became hungry for capital and greed for money played first fiddle, so now people have become hungry for a piece of bread; they stopped dreaming of palaces and of grabbing the richest; today one wants no more than security for a piece of bread. Truly one wants no more than not to starve in the literal sense of the word.
In the period of usury and the "pasek" one could not stem the current that was to limit the appetites for profits; just so it is now the reverse: one cannot understand how people can allow themselves to produce and sell goods below the price and, at best, without profit.
How can people, poor hungry citizens, allow themselves such a luxury? And in the end one will come to the conviction that, just as the system of profiteering was dangerous for the world, so the not wanting to earn is dangerous. And just as one had to fight the former, so one will have to fight the latter.
One need not go deep at all to see the harmful consequences. The lawlessness ("hefkeyres") and the refined grabbing of money and all kinds of shady operators ("aferistn") arose, after all, thanks to this not wanting to earn; for a firm that barely — that does not earn, and has expenses both for the business and for household needs, and pays taxes, had of course to go bankrupt. When one does not earn, and one has to live, and one trades all the same — one must take the other man's goods, or at best "eat them up"; that is a matter of course. But thanks to this system people went further still: it led to deliberate bankruptcies, which should not have been permitted.
No one bears any responsibility any more. A kind of grabbing has arisen: whoever manages to ride the horse and has the nerve to mock the other devilishly[?] — that is, unfortunately, how it has become. And this is harmful, extremely harmful, because in this way people become reckless, gamble with other people's money and drag with them whole rows of innocent honest firms, which would gladly have earned something and remained in place as solid firms, as honest citizens, as decent people.
One must know once and for all that selling below cost ("keren", the principal) or even without profit is just as harmful as "pasek" speculation, because in the end the former take the other man's hard-earned groszy; for no one can work for the sake of Heaven alone, and if he does so anyway, he is harmful to society, to the community, to the country and to every single person.
We understand that one firm contents itself with a smaller profit and another with still less; but in no way can one agree to work without profit when one must[?] pay all kinds of taxes and has, even at the least, the most minimal business expenses. We know, after all, that no miracles happen in our generations, we possess no thirty-six righteous men, and no one receives manna from heaven either. So the question arises: how can one live and trade honestly and pay the other party when there is no profit at all? Such trade is just as much a swindle as all the other refined swindles, which must not be tolerated.
Trade, industry and the crafts must be logically founded, honestly reckoned, well calculated; otherwise it is not honest, and from the outset it stands on chicken legs and on rotten foundations, to which no healthy firm and no honest citizen will agree.
— That is what must be radically uprooted.

Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

Little denunciations...
A very marketable article. The harder the crisis, the more the number grows of
— "tellers"...
They, the gentiles, know everything exactly, what goes on among us. Jews tell —
they tell who travels to the baths, who has handed over[?] his child "in honour", who submitted a false declaration ("zeznanie")[?] about turnover, and they tell
— "which Jew ought not to get any coal from the Citizens' Committee"...
— If only you knew what Jews are capable of! — one of the Jewish members sitting on the committee for the support of the unemployed tells me, — my face floods with blood as I hear out the content of the shameful anonymous little letters that are sent to the committee.
— What do they write? — they ask me.
— They write denunciations: that Yekl ben Todros ought not to have got any potatoes, since his wife has just bought herself a pair of new shoes... that Beila the market-woman ought not to get any coal, because her daughter was seen last Sabbath dressed in a new coat...
And the gentiles take delight in the Jewish "open-heartedness" — "a viler garv"[?] are your Zhidki — they say — they tell everything, even about those who benefit from the Citizens' Committee...

"Untouchability"...
There are people and also institutions that are untouchable...
To the first category belong Sejm deputies, great men, and to the second category — institutions with old traditions, such as museums, antiquaries and
— the Sosnowiec "Linat HaHolim".
An old institution, — the "mother" of the Będzin "Linat HaHolim", a "rich" past. All around, nothing but
— lineage and holiness...
Untouchability is therefore strictly guarded; the "vessels" that the institution owns — are not profaned by "strange hands", "thou shalt not lift up any iron upon them", no craftsman's hand is laid upon them, and the lineage — pardon, the rust, we mean — grows and grows...
A society exists, a minyan too, members pay, collectors write, and the subsidies get taken.
And when the "people" begin to murmur — "let us bring the book and see". Let us take a look at what the activity looks like, let us acquaint ourselves with the work for the kehilla elections (oh, excuse us, made a mistake again, we mean — for the poor Jewish population...), the answer from above is
— "nye nado" ["no need", Russian]...
Crowns fall, kings are deposed from their thrones, only one "fortress" has not fallen as yet
— the "fortress" of the Sosnowiec "Linat HaHolim"...

"Sought" and "found"...
The Będzin "Tseirim" [Agudat Israel youth] set themselves a great task: the task of searching for sins in the head of the "Mizrachi" school (printed "shu"a")
— in Dr. Gottesdiener...
They, the "Tseirim", could not stay calm hearing, and perhaps seeing, how the name of the "Mizrachi" school is raised very high thanks to its new head, and wins sympathy not only among the "free" elements, among the nationalist Jews, but also
— in Agudah circles...
And because of that — "come, let us deal wisely", one must set to work, one must find such sins as would defile the honour of the "Unknown Soldier", who keeps taking positions in the Jewish life of our town...
The work was from the outset no easy one. Had he, Dr. Gottesdiener, been a rabbi or a Mizrachist communal leader, the matter would have gone more easily, quite literally: a few trustworthy witnesses would tell that "the rabbi's wife buys butter in the market on Sabbath afternoon", or that they themselves saw cooking done at his home on the Sabbath...
But "nothing stands in the way of the will", nothing is hard for the "Agudah"; when the "Agudah" wants, no "kaverushe"[?] [tricks?] are needed; when the "Agudah" wants, the "veygers"[?] [perhaps: clocks] stop in the opposing camp; and when the "Agudah" wants, there have already been found a few of the "Tseirim" who heard with their own ears (with their side-locks tucked down...) how Dr. Gottesdiener "blasphemed the honour of the Rambam"...
Yes, the work of the "Torah-true youth" was a hard one, but when you seek you find, and they did indeed
— "find"...

"Warsaw has lost"...
Such alarming news we read in the sports papers. In big "Kiddush Levana" letters the great tidings were announced, that "Warsaw has lost" and
— "Sosnowiec has won"...
Do not think, dear readers, male and female, that this concerns "the big prize" that Sosnowiec won in the lottery; the whole matter concerns only sports fans, among whom it caused indescribable joy that:
— Sosnowiec has won.
The joy, too, is not out of love for Mordecai but "out of hatred for Haman": Warsaw, the city that has so many central offices, which regard the provinces as step-children (except for fund-raising...), had to bow its head before the Sosnowiec "Maccabi".
The initiative came from Warsaw. There, elimination exercises were held, at which certificates were given to those who would take part in the Eretz-Israel Maccabiah.
Among the participants there also signed up the gymnasts of the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" and the Będzin "HaKoaḥ".
When the Zagłębie gymnasts arrived in Warsaw — so the gymnasts tell — none of the chief "in-laws" took any interest in them. And indeed, it is hardly fitting that the leadership of the Warsaw "Maccabi", of the city that has so many central offices, that members from the "stolica" [capital] should have any kind of association with provincial young lads. And with provincial "feydlekh"[?] [girls?] — why, that is beneath one's dignity, hem... hem...
At the official reception it had such a "face" — just look at the heroes — the "Galut-people" of Warsaw joked at the expense of the Sosnowiec and Będzin gymnasts, men and women: with mere Warsaw steam they would knock them out...
And so it "really was". Only a little differently. When it came to the "knocking out", Sosnowiec and Będzin began to "blow", and
— "Warsaw went out with a tooth and an eye"...
We — explains a Będzin gymnast — ought to have received all the points; only out of pity for the Warsaw "Maccabi" did we allot them a few shares, after all [they are] the chief in-laws...
Hearing this out, we are again obliged to repeat the long-voiced opinion that in many fields the Warsaw big shots ought to take lessons in the provinces...
How Do Things Look in the "Happy" Countries?

Compiled especially for our paper by Z. Haber, Vienna.

Only about a year ago one could read in all the newspapers that there were several countries in the world where people live happily, there are no unemployed, there is no crisis — in a word: all is well and fine...
The Leipzig Fair Office is, of course, very interested to know what is happening in those countries, since the exhibitors after all want to do most of their business with the merchants of those very countries, where there is still a possibility of being able to sell something and to see some money.
It is therefore interesting to take a look at the reports now coming from those countries. We shall try to give the content of the reports country by country — the countries which only a year ago knew of no crisis or want.
France: No exact statistics of unemployment are kept in France. In the parliament there it was announced that only one third of the workers are employed full time, two thirds work only by the hour. More than 2 million workers are employed only half the time compared with before; 8½ per cent of the workers are unemployed, and their number is estimated at 650 thousand.
Meanwhile the government has informed all offices that they must order nothing from abroad without the government's consent. The government has demanded the same of the railway administrations, which in France are private.
Portugal: In the country itself a crisis reigns as everywhere, but Portugal has lately secured in its African colonies the introduction of a high duty on all goods not coming from Portugal.
Until now Germany and England supplied most of the goods to the Portuguese colonies. Today the duty on German and English goods is so high that only Portuguese things can be brought in. Especially in Angola, a large Portuguese colony in West Africa, where a somewhat modern life prevails, business has lately been very good, and for the time being people there know nothing of any crisis, any economic want or any unemployed.
Yugoslavia and Greece: In these two countries the great world crisis is for the time being still least felt. Yugoslavia has too much foodstuff and exports it to neighbouring Greece, which in return supplies it with many products, mostly textile goods. In Greece a strong industry has developed lately, which for the time being is well employed. In Athens and other Greek towns streets and houses are being built and workers have plenty to do. The port of Piraeus is being greatly enlarged; large warehouses are being built there. And one can say that no want prevails there; in addition, in both countries people live very thriftily, need little and content themselves with the smallest sum they earn.
Tunis: In the French colony of Tunis the situation has lately grown much worse; every day large firms go bankrupt; because of the new high duty nothing at all can be bought from abroad; besides that the banks have stopped credit, so that the larger merchants are literally being strangled; on top of that, Arab firms do not understand that bills of exchange must be paid at once, and under the local law they go bankrupt as soon as a single bill is not paid within one week at the latest after the protest.
Chile: The new government has issued foreign-exchange regulations — since the local money, because of the shaky political situation, has suffered badly on the American market, the government wants to save itself by various restrictions[?], which make all trade almost impossible. No bills may be drawn on foreign currencies, no foreign goods may be brought in without a permit, and so it has gone so far that in Chile all trade has now come to a standstill.
Australia: Only there does one know nothing of any crisis; in the past year business went very well, especially manufactured goods (textiles), machines, paper, chemical fuel[?] oil. Dairy products sold more than twice as much; only wool and grain sold less than a year ago.
The only happy country in the whole world, where nobody knows anything of all the troubles and sorrows from which the whole world now suffers.

How Jews Earn a Living in Zagłębie

What does a leather merchant say?
The leather trade already has its brilliant days behind it. Only pale remnants are left, which in no way recall their bygone leather trade as it looked in former years here in Zagłębie.
The leather merchant with whom I struck up a conversation about the situation in this branch gave his explanations almost in the chant of the Book of Lamentations (Eicha).
— As recently as 1925 the leather trade flourished here, so much so that hundreds of Zagłębie Jewish families were employed in this branch, whereas today not even a third of them is left. The rest have been washed off the surface by the crisis and bad business conditions.
The rubber industry dealt the leather trade a heavy blow. Both summer and winter people wear a great many rubber goods. With that they already save on using leather shoes. And this hits first of all the leather merchant; for the peasant, who was a big buyer and a good customer, has almost disappeared; instead of the peasant, as in better times, going into a leather shop after selling his produce at the market and picking out goods for a pair of boots from beginning to end, farm produce has today fallen so much in price that the peasant allows himself to buy almost nothing in town; it really looks terrible to him that after selling a cow he can barely afford a pair of boots; so he buys himself any old pair at the market, the cheapest one, and avoids the leather merchant altogether.
This circumstance has taken from the leather merchants a customer who over the year brought in a very large turnover, of which a negligible minimum now remains.
A customer has been lost — the soldier.
Before the war whole camps of "nowobrańcy" [new recruits], before being drafted into the army, used to besiege the leather shops, where they would buy goods for boots. On being released from the army, too, they used to make similar purchases. And today [printed "מיינט"] this kind of customer is entirely gone.
— What are the terms of buying and selling?
— The leather merchants have to buy goods, with payment in cash. This was brought about by the bankruptcies and liquidations of many leather businesses. But when we sell the goods retail, we give them on credit, otherwise it cannot work in our trade, and in such a situation it is today a common phenomenon that a lot of money is lost.
I took this as enough to illustrate the situation of the leather shopkeepers.
What does a ladies' tailor say?
The ladies' tailor with whom I talked about the situation in this trade began by recounting that before the war ladies' tailors made a fine living. There was plenty of work, and on top of that one paid no taxes either; now, in addition to all the bad circumstances created by the crisis, there has come great competition, because the trade has grown and spread very much. Whoever knows how and whoever doesn't have all become masters, and people work simply for nothing, so that the truly qualified ladies' tailors are going under.
— How is the current season with you.
— In September and October there was a little work, but now it has almost come to a standstill. At a time when the present month was always the best month for ladies' tailors; on these two months one has to live a whole winter until before Passover, that is, until the second season.
This situation of the ladies' tailors can be explained 1) by competition, 2) by the crisis.
— Do you hand out your work without money, and do you pay debts?
— There is no other choice. One must give without money. One cannot quarrel with any customer; some pay and some don't. A bit of money gets lost; the ladies' tailors have already several times made an attempt to agree among themselves not to give without money; it brought no result whatsoever.
— What kind of customer sews most now, and from which fabrics — expensive or cheap?
— One notices now a middling customer; rich customers one doesn't see at all, and for the most part people have worn clothes turned ("nicować").
He ends his conversation thus:...
— In general ladies' tailors find themselves in no better position than men's tailors.
P.
Ba'al-Melokhe and — Hantverker (Craftsman and Artisan).

For some years now there has arisen among us a very important and interesting movement in Jewish social-political life: — the Jewish — — ba'al-melokhe [craftsman]!
This element — mostly backward culturally and socially, yet a significant one in Jewish society — suddenly roused itself from its lethargic sleep and turned into a Jewish — — hantverker [artisan]!
With aspirations to occupy an important and worthy place in Jewish social-political life!
Firmly organised artisans' associations sprang up in all the towns and townlets, and the Jewish craftsmen — these — — humiliated and — insulted by our crippled social psyche — quickly left their place by the — — western wall! [the low-status seats in the synagogue] and strode off with giant steps to the very top, to the — — east! [the eastern wall, the seats of honour] of our social-political life.
In all the social organisations and institutions the artisans pushed through their representatives, and often even in a — — larger number! than was their due [?], thanks only to their firm organisation and discipline of unity, amid the enormous — — fragmentation! of the other parts of the Jewish population.
And there were people who, already then, at the very start of the movement, said that this sudden leap from the — — western wall to the — east! is unnatural and already carries within itself the elements of the coming destruction.
That just as unjust and unnatural as the generations-long social degradation and enslavement of the Jewish — — ba'al-melokhe! had been,
so too it is unnatural, and not justified by our social conditions of life, that the Jewish — — artisan! should suddenly occupy the very top of our social-political life.
And now barely a few years have passed and we already see the complete social-political — — collapse: of the whole Jewish artisans' movement.
The artisans' organisations, in the centre as well as in the provinces, having sensed their — — victory: unexpected even by themselves, on the political-social arena of the fragmented and crumbled Jewish life, did not trouble themselves to rise to the height of their real tasks.
Instead of fulfilling their actually proper task — to develop a broad and intensive activity in order to strengthen and secure the economic positions and raise the cultural level of the backward Jewish — — ba'al-melokhe! in order truly to raise him into a self-aware Jewish — — artisan! proud of his work and knowledge;
instead of reviving in the Jewish social psyche the ideology, lost by us, of — — work and — knowledge!;
instead of taking up these important and useful tasks, our artisans' organisations set off on the false road of — — high politics!
And very soon after their founding we already see the artisans' organisations, mighty and strong with their inner discipline and unity, transformed into an — — army for — hire! [literally "an army for earning"] in the political struggle of various parties.
Here we see the "foreign army", under the command of its general, engaged in battle in the Folkist camp against — — Zionism!
A couple of years later we find the same "foreign army", under the command of the same general, in the — Zionist camp fighting against the — — Agudah [Agudat Israel]!
And a couple of years after that — the game turned around, and we find the same "foreign ar-my" [misprinted "ari-dee"], again under the command of the same general, in the — Agudist camp, in fierce struggle against everyone and everything that bears the name — — national!
That is — against all its former allies.
And so there took root [?] in the psychology of the artisan masses an unbridled — — idea-lessness! An ideology of the unprincipled, servile and sold-out [?]. — — What more do you want?!
Which is [?] exploited, with the greatest and easiest success, by the first-best — — careerist!
Who has not even any connection whatsoever with artisanship, but — who needs, or simply wants, to show somebody that he has — — accomplished something!
And when you happen to meet an artisans' leader at closer quarters, he gives you the impression of a certain type of American — — politician!
Without principles, without any conviction whatsoever, without the slightest understanding of or concern for the economic and cultural needs and hardships of the artisan class, but only — with one worry: — how to get — — ahead of — somebody else! along the well-trodden but sure path to the — — back door [?]! that so enchantingly beckons.
Through which one can sometimes later go far, far along the road to — — splendour and — glory!
And unwillingly one must come to the sad conclusion that the artisans' organisations, with their incessant play at — — high politics! have brought no positive benefit whatsoever to the economic and cultural interests of the — — ba'al-melokhe and — artisan!
They have merely transformed the former backward — but for that very reason honest, modest and sincere — Jewish — — ba'al-melokhe! into an incessantly noisy, politics-playing and unprincipled Jewish — — artisan!
Emes [pen-name, "Truth"].
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (10)

[Serialized historical novel — Tsarist Russia, Rasputin; installment 10.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Iliodor spoke with such force that when he had finished he could see at once that his words had had a strong effect on all the listeners, that he had drawn [?] them all over to Rasputin's side, and that they now recognized the importance of the muzhik from Tobolsk [printed "Sabolsk"]. All of them nodded their heads slightly, and their faces expressed agreement.
Iliodor sat back down in his place. Then the priest Vostorgov rose from his seat and, with submissiveness, expressed to the monk, in the name of all those assembled, gratitude and admiration. He assured Iliodor that with his arguments he had convinced the whole committee how important Rasputin was for the organization, and that the committee would adopt a resolution according to his wishes. He asked to be allowed to add from his side that he himself, travelling about on a propaganda tour in the Tobolsk region, had become convinced of the importance of drawing representatives of the muzhiks into their work, and that he had submitted a report about this to the Central Committee of the "Union". His report, however, had not been given the proper attention.
Now he thanks the honourable persons, Archimandrite Feofan, Bishop Hermogen and especially the highly esteemed Iliodor, thanks to whom his report is receiving the proper attention.
He also related that, travelling about the Tobolsk region, he had heard a great deal about Grigori Rasputin, who was renowned throughout the whole region as a "saint" and a "miracle worker" (baal mofet).
Now, while the priest Vostorgov was speaking, the colours changed on Iliodor's face. Hearing how the priest spoke of Rasputin as of a "saint", Iliodor felt that he held the opposite opinion — that he believed Rasputin was nothing more than a cunning hypocrite, a false "saint", no more than a dirty muzhik. What spirit, then, had driven him to speak against his own intuition? [?] Anger at himself now burned within him. But to take back his words — that was not in Iliodor's nature. He was one of those people who, once they have told a lie, will use all their strength to uphold the lie and defend it consistently.
And so it came about that Iliodor, against his will, helped Grigori Rasputin enter the high circles, become a member of the Central Committee of the "Soyuz Russkogo Naroda" [Union of the Russian People] and acquire a name as a "saint" and "miracle worker" through whose mouth God Himself speaks...
The session of the Central Committee ended in complete success for Rasputin. "Father" Feofan and Bishop Hermogen were very pleased. Hermogen at once went up to the archimandrite and proposed to him that he, being the Tsarina's priest, should bring Rasputin to Tsarskoye Selo and introduce him there to the imperial family... Iliodor remained silent, and anger burned quietly within him. He felt that by helping the Siberian muzhik to be taken into the Central Committee of the "Union" he had brought danger upon himself. He was greatly agitated, he felt fear. But it was already too late...
— — — — —
And on that evening, when the meeting took place at the house of the banker Dimentshteyn, on that evening Rasputin [printed "Rakhputin"] was brought for the first time to the salon of Countess Ignatova [?] [probably Ignatieva]. He was brought there as a "saint" and "miracle worker", in order to introduce him to the high-placed persons who were present there...
There Rasputin first set eyes on the Jewish daughter Sonia Dimentshteyn, to whom he was introduced.
Her wondrous beauty, her graceful figure and the health that radiated from her body attracted and enchanted Rasputin [printed "Rakhputin"] very strongly. When he stood beside her, held her delicate hand in his and looked into her pure face, he felt his heart being squeezed with longing, and in his hot blood the lust for her flared up...

Chapter Three.
The Consolation.
It was around eleven o'clock the morning after the meeting. The banker Mr. Dimentshteyn was already ready to go to the synagogue, where a divine service would be held and prayers would be said for the health of the Russian heir to the throne [printed "Tronfolger"]. Sonia was already ready to drive to the lady-in-waiting Anna Vyrubova.
Sonia came into her father's study.
Now she was dressed in a black silk dress. Her face looked a little pale and her large eyes were pensive.
Her father stood up, took his daughter's head in both hands, kissed her tenderly on the forehead and asked:
"Are you already going to Vyrubova?"
"Yes, father. I have already ordered the carriage to be harnessed."
"Good, daughter, I am already going to the synagogue. The service is set for exactly twelve o'clock."
He fell silent for a while. He was thinking about something, and his face was serious and there was a little worry in his eyes. Then he said:
"I think, daughter, that you should not go empty-handed. Have a few bottles of the best wine taken out of the cellar, and in the street you will buy a fine bouquet of flowers."
"I will do so, father."
"And I am going now."
He took leave of her, tenderly pressed her hand:
"Go, and may you succeed..."
The banker left the house and went off to the synagogue. Sonia had a few bottles of wine brought up from the cellar and put into the carriage, and she drove off to Vyrubova. In the street, in front of a flower shop, Sonia told the driver to stop. She went into the shop, bought a large bouquet of the most expensive flowers, came out and drove on.
An hour later the carriage stopped in front of a small palace in which Vyrubova lived.
Sonia rang, holding in her hand the bouquet of flowers wrapped in silk paper. Behind her stood the coachman with the bottles of wine.
A servant opened the door, took the bottles of wine from the coachman, and showed Sonia into a small but splendidly beautiful reception room.
It did not take long before Anna Vyrubova — a slender lady of middle age — came into the reception room. She exclaimed in a friendly way:
"Sonia Oskarovna! Is it you?"
Sonia bowed, smiled good-naturedly, and, greeting Vyrubova, handed her the flowers.
"Flowers!" Vyrubova exclaimed. "Thank you!"
She at once unwrapped the paper from the flowers, broke into a smile of satisfaction, and her dark-brown eyes lit up. She exclaimed again with delight:
"What splendidly beautiful flowers! Sit down, Sonia Oskarovna!"
"And how are you, Sonia Oskarovna?" Vyrubova asked in a relaxed [?] tone of voice, and she too sat down not far from Sonia.
"Thank you for asking," Sonia replied.
"And may I ask you what has brought you here now?" Vyrubova asked in a friendly way.
Sonia began to tell her what it was about. Her face was serious; she spoke calmly, in clear words, in a soft, tender voice in which a little worry could be felt. She knows that Vyrubova has a good, humane heart, that she is very friendly to Jews, and so she has come to her to ask for her help, and she is sure that she will not refuse her in this... Let her bring her together with Archimandrite Feofan. Sonia will speak with him and will ask him not to be so bad to the Jews. Can it really be possible that the archimandrite truly believes that by torturing innocent people and good citizens the naslednik [heir to the throne] will be healed? Does he really believe that God wants quiet, peaceful people to be tormented and persecuted? She will talk with him, she will appeal to him...

Parashat Mishpatim
The Portion
a) "Now these are the ordinances which thou shalt set before them" (Ex. 21:1)
1.
"'And these' adds to the former ones: as the former were from Sinai, so these too are from Sinai" (Midrash Rabbah).
Those who arrange the laws — the leaders — must symbolically resemble Sinai, which is the lowest mountain in the Land of Israel, and that is why the Torah was given upon it. The previous portion, too, ends with the verse "Neither shalt thou go up by steps unto Mine altar", on which it is expounded: "A warning to the leaders that they should not tread over the heads of the holy people." Tiferet Yehonatan.
2.
"Which thou shalt set before them — like a set table" (Rashi).
Every Jew must bear his bundle of sufferings, of "judgments", in this world. If someone is a great man, he is given not material torments but spiritual, ideal ones. For instance, when someone has to become a rebbe, sit at a "set table" and conduct a tish... these too are sufferings, judgments. Tiferet Shlomo.
———
A village Jew (yishuvnik) once comes to Rabbi Gershon Henekh of Radzyń. Rabbi Gershon Henekh sits drinking porter, and he treats the yishuvnik to a glass of it too. The yishuvnik tastes a little, screws up his face at the bitter porter and spits out: brrr... br... and looks at the rebbe, who has drained a full glass. "So it is, my child," Rabbi Gershon Henekh says to him, "being a rebbe is not easy; a rebbe must drain three such glasses every single day..."
3.
First it speaks of "gods of silver" and now of judgments. — A warning not to appoint rabbis for the sake of money. Baal HaTurim.
b) "And he that smiteth his father [printed: 'Aviv'] or his mother... and he that curseth" (ibid. 15; 16 [?])
Striking is a lighter sin than cursing, and the punishment is lighter ("the smiter by strangling, the curser by stoning"), because "the words of a whisperer are as dainty morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly"; intrigue and slander are worse than blows, for blows harm only the body, while the blows of the mouth penetrate into the soul...
Shaar Bat Rabim.
c) "Ye shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child" (22:21)
1.
The whole portion speaks in the singular; only here is the plural used. Because not only may one not torment — one may not even stand by and watch while another torments the unfortunate. One must not allow it. Kadmonim.
2.
"For if they cry at all unto Me" —
For what more can the unfortunate do than cry out?.. What more can he do in a world where the rule prevails: "might makes right"? Divrei Shaul.
d) "If thou lend money to any of My people" (ibid. 24)
1.
Having spoken of the rich man and the poor man, the warnings about charity and "Thou shalt not revile God" follow at once, because both the rich man and the poor man are put to the test. The rich man — whether, being rich, he will also give charity; and the poor man — whether, suffering want, he will nevertheless not blaspheme God.
Rav Shaul of Loyshbakh [?].
2.
"If thou lend money to any of My people" — you go to a wealthy man to ask for an interest-free loan — "the poor with thee" — he answers you at once that he is as poor a man as you... And he really is that poor, because "he who has a hundred wants two hundred"...
[By] Rabbi Yehoshua'le of Dzików.
———
Most rich people are stingy and wicked, for otherwise the Almighty would not have entrusted them with so much money. He must be sure that they will not distribute it to poor people... "There is wealth kept by its owner — why? — to his hurt": because he is so wicked, he was entrusted with such wealth. But in truth this wealth belongs to some other poor man; it was merely given to the rich man as a deposit. Matgefei [?] Oraita.
e) "And ye shall be holy men unto Me" (ibid. 30)
Holy men — humanly holy shall you be...
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk.
f) "Neither shalt thou favour a poor man in his cause" (23:3)
When a poor man quarrels with God and has complaints against Him, people are inclined [?] to justify the judgment against him: he probably deserved it. "Serves him right." But do not so readily declare God right and the poor man wrong...
Ohel HaTorah (the Seer of Lublin).
———
Of Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdyczów, who always had complaints against God, Rabbi Akiva [?] of Medzhybizh said: "According to Rabbi Levi Yitzchak, the Blessed Name has not yet fulfilled His duty towards a single Jew"...
g) "Keep thee far from a false matter" (ibid. 7)
"Truth springeth out of the earth" — truth lies in the ground.
And if such a precious treasure lies on the ground, why does nobody pick it up?
— Because people are too lazy to bend down...
[By] Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov.
———
When Truth was against the creation of man, who would be a liar, it was cast down to the earth ("and it cast down truth to the ground").
For here, on earth, it will see that it is impossible to get along in the world with truth alone...
Asam Beshem [?].
h) "And on the seventh day thou shalt rest" (ibid. 12)
"Thus [?] saith the Lord unto the eunuchs that keep My sabbaths" (Isaiah 56).
The author of "Machaneh Levi" once said that the reason Torah scholars are not honoured nowadays is that people are afraid of the reward for it. The reward for honouring Torah scholars is: to have children who are Torah scholars (Shabbat 23). That is what people tremble at... But the childless, who no longer have that "punishment" to fear, surely ought at least to look after the Torah scholars ("Shabbat" means Torah scholars)...
Haftarah
i) "And I will make you a horror unto all the kingdoms of the earth" (Jeremiah 34)
"Keep me as the apple of the eye" —
The eye is the only organ that cannot bear even the slightest touch. So we pray that the nations should not even touch us — not even to kiss and caress us...
Measef Derashot [?].
The Eternal Victim. (On the new excesses in Vienna and Berlin).

[Essay — antisemitism; history.] They beat Jews in Warsaw, they beat Jews in Wilno, they beat Jews in Lemberg (Lwów), they beat in Kraków, they beat in Vienna and in Berlin and in many other cities. The enemies of the Jews everywhere, when they are angry, throw themselves upon those from whom they can expect less resistance, in order to vent their anger on them. Thus the base cowards, the Endeks, picked the Jews as a victim on whom to vent their anger. But we need not be impressed by this at all, and it must not cast us into any despair. In our bloody two-thousand-year exile we have had many such cases; if one were to write them all down, many thick books would come of it. I will therefore mention here only one similar case, which happened in the not so distant past.
In the year 1819, when as a result of the wars of that time Germany fell under Prussia, a German Christian student, Karl Zanek [sic; Karl Sand], killed the Prussian commandant Kotzebue. The Prussian authorities therefore issued various decrees against the German revolutionaries. The Germans were therefore greatly agitated and, being unable to take revenge on Prussia, they vented their anger on the Jews. Students in Hirschberg began with "Hep Hep" and "Juden-Verrecke" [death to the Jews].
And then they fell upon the Jewish shops and began to plunder and throw all the goods into the street. And when the robbed Jews stood up against them and began to throw stones at the robbers, they carried out a real slaughter of the Jews. Many Jews were killed and wounded, so that soldiers had to be brought in to quell the pogrom; otherwise all the Jews would have been butchered. Afterwards the burghers of Hirschberg also turned to the authorities to expel all the Jews, and the authorities fulfilled their demand.
Thus, throughout our bloody exile, we have been victims for the sins of others. But meanwhile we have outlived many of those who made us their victims, and on many of them we have lived to see revenge. Many of them have long since been wiped off the globe, and we live. Yes, yes, we live, we live. Standing on the high mountains we saw burning Rome, before the mad emperor Nero. We have seen many kingdoms and peoples being born and perishing, and we shall live to see this too in our present enemies.
Yakov Kohen.
What Every Tenant Must Know.

[Legal advice — tenants' rights.] 1) Repairs.
In this article I want to make clear how one can legally compel the landlord to carry out the necessary repairs.
Under the Tenant Protection Act the tenant has the right to demand and compel the landlord to repair the flat so that it is fit to be lived in. Besides this, article 1719 of the Civil Code says: whoever lets a property for habitation is obliged to keep it in order, so that it has the [proper] appearance and is suitable for the purpose for which it was let.
Under the Civil Code the tenant can demand from the landlord a repair that is necessary because of the age of the flat, or on account of natural damage. In all these cases the landlord must, at his own expense and within a short time, carry out the proper repair.
The only question is: what does one do when a landlord is obstinate and will not willingly acknowledge the repair?
Well then, the first thing to do is: apply in writing to the Sanitary-Building Commission (Komisja Sanitarno-Budowlana) at the Magistrate [city hall], requesting an inspection (wizja) to establish the necessary repair, and at the same time call upon the landlord to carry out the repair. If despite this the landlord still refuses to repair the flat, one must obtain a copy of the decision of the said commission, turn to the court with a suit, and demand:
1) that the court send the landlord a demand (nakaz egzekucji — enforcement order) that he willingly carry out the established repair within 8 days;
2) that the court at the same time also authorize you, after the deadline (8 days), to carry out yourselves, lawfully, the necessary repair in your flat.
Only on receiving this authorization does one have the right to carry out with one's own money the repair established in the decision and to deduct the amount from the rent, or to recover it from the landlord through a komornik [bailiff].
It is worth adding that the law also permits the tenant to carry out a repair in his flat without formalities and court decisions, but only in urgent cases, when there is danger to life, for example: when a floor caves in, when a water pipe bursts, etc.; but even then one must remember to call upon the landlord to prove the damage before witnesses.
All this is fine when the landlord is a tough litigant and lets himself be driven into costs, since in the end he must carry out the proper repair anyway; for the most part landlords do it right after the inspection by the Sanitary-Building Commission.
I must stress that wrong is the conduct of those tenants who withhold the regular payment [?] of rent, thinking that in this way they will compel the landlord to make the repair, or in the end they pay court costs when the landlord files a claim against them in court.
The same applies to subtenants towards the tenants, when they occupy a separate room.
2) Assessing the rent.
The Tenant Protection Act gives whoever rents or lets the flat the full right to have the premises assessed when it is hard to prove how much the occupied property [fetched] before the war, in the year 1914.
The procedure is conducted by the "Urząd Rozjemczy" [Arbitration Office] for tenancy matters (dla spraw najmu) at the Magistrate. There the tenant concerned [?] must apply in writing, requesting a commission to inspect the condition of the flat in order to establish the correct value of the rent. In the request one must remember to state the amount of the rent in roubles — how much the occupied flat is worth in the opinion of the petitioner. One must also state all the defects of the occupied dwelling (broken floor, damp walls, etc.) that lower the value of the rent.
In its inspection the commission takes 3 things into account: 1) the aesthetic appearance, 2) the location in town, 3) the purpose for which the flat is used. In any case one must remember that poverty cannot be any ground for reducing the rent. On the basis of the inspection carried out, the "Urząd Rozjemczy", at a public session, assesses the legal rent in roubles, which on payment is reckoned at 2.66 zł. If the interested party is not satisfied with the decision of the "Urząd Rozjemczy", he has the right to file an appeal with the District Court. It must be noted that the dispute cannot be any reason to stop paying the rent regularly. The tenant must therefore, until the matter of the assessment is settled, send the landlord by post the rent in the amount stated in the petition to the "Urząd Rozjemczy".
As we see, the procedure is not complicated; it is therefore better — in order to avoid misunderstandings between tenant and landlord, which sometimes end in an eviction — when the tenant feels wronged by paying too high a rent, to request an assessment inspection by the "Urząd Rozjemczy", so as to establish the amount of the rent once and for all.
Now that we have discussed the 2 rules a tenant must know concerning repairs and rent assessment, there remains to discuss the most important question, which is called: eviction. Eviction, or the forced vacating of the flat, is nowadays the fate of thousands of families who tremble at losing the roof over their heads.
How one can guard against an eviction, and by what legal means one halts the course of an eviction — in the next issue.
Jakub Ratner.
Foolish Little People.

[Feuilleton — the world crisis and the talk of war.]
(Just chatting...)
And so, day in, day out, and so for years now, desperate cries for help are heard; "from one end of the world to the other" a wailing and lament is heard: S.O.S.! Save us! S-a-v-e u-s!
Millions of people walk about without work! Millions of people are starving! A world is going under! S-a-v-e u-s!
The millions of hungry rebel, shout and threaten out of despair: what will be? What will the end be, after all?
They rebel, and shout, threaten and... still hope for the "bright" tomorrow, but how much longer?!
And the world, the great world of mighty states and countries, with the kings, presidents, ministers, diplomats and plain "cooking-spoons" [busybodies], sit in constant unrest, sit like blockheads, helpless, and wrinkle their foreheads at the hundreds of sessions, consultations, conferences and congresses, searching[?] for advice, a way out of such a terrible situation and, when one searches[?], one finds:
— War! War! comes the decisive answer to all questions and doubts. What of it that millions of people walk about without work? What of it that millions of people are starving?
— War! Yes, a nice little war...
— Then the world will be merry, orchestras will play, regiments of soldiers will march singing to the beat and... tr'... r'... r'... ta.. ta... boom! boom!...
— And hands and feet will fly. Bellies and heads will be smashed, towns and villages will be wiped off the face of the earth and.. and... br'... r'...
And then the hungry masses will come to an end. An end to unemployment, and not[?] then will come the days, the so long awaited days of well-being and plenty, days when milk and honey will flow in the streets...
And then...
— War! Little war! Where are you?!...
— Foolish little people!...
Ajzyk Rimuz.
The Festival of National Deed.

[Zionism — the Jewish National Fund; the blue box.]
(Sent in by the Keren Kayemet headquarters in Warsaw.)
During this year's great celebrations in honour of the double jubilee — 50 years of Hibbat Zion and Bilu and 30 years of the Keren Kayemet — the modest blue box must not be forgotten — the chief instrument for collecting the people's groszy for the redemption of the Land.
The 30-year history of the people's efforts for the redemption of land in Eretz Israel is in fact the history of the blue box. It is chiefly to it that we owe the more than 300 thousand dunams of land in Eretz Israel; its merit is the Emek [Jezreel Valley], its achievement are the dozens of village settlements where the pure, vibrant national life is being created.
The pennies of the box helped create the national property, brought the people back to the soil, and turned thousands of fateless Jews into proud, building people.
In the finest corner of every Jewish national home stands the blue box, which has been the symbol of our liberation movement.
That is why it is so beloved by every man of the people, that is why it has become a refreshing part of Jewish life.
The Jewish child has always bound his dreamy soul to the beautiful deed of our liberation movement. In the most intimate corners of his child's world he wove himself images of the heroic halutz, and in the blue box the young Jew found the embodiment of all his dreams of the new Jewish life.
In the history of the Jewish renaissance movement the blue box will, without a doubt, occupy one of the finest places.
During our jubilee celebrations we shall therefore also celebrate the jubilee of the Keren Kayemet box. Rosh Hodesh Adar I is the date of the jubilee emptying [of the boxes].
The box-holders will be visited by the most respected and most responsible activists of all shades. The box-holders will multiply their donations to the Keren Kayemet. The jubilee emptying must be the record emptying of 5692 [1932] and must make it possible to redeem as quickly as possible the land area needed for founding the two new villages in Eretz Israel — Hibbat Zion and Bilu.
We are certain that in honour of the festival of the blue box the box-holders will support the redemption of land in Eretz Israel with increased readiness for sacrifice.
Today's Bridegrooms.

[Humour — satirical monologue; the dowry in times of crisis.]
(Monologue of a father of several daughters).
There is no wisdom and no counsel against today's bridegrooms... It has become a world, so to speak[?], nothing to talk about, a world with little worlds, bridegrooms with little bridegroomlets. They walk about, "patsetn"[?] [dandies], dressed up à la chic without worries, never putting a hand in cold water; who cares about a livelihood, what livelihood, who cares about a crisis, what crisis — it concerns them about as much as their left sidelock, it moves them like last year's snow... A trifle! After all, today they are an article of first necessity and great aristocrats, "mensh-tsizge"[?] diamonds, and they turn up their noses [lit. throw back their heads], just like a count [hrabia]. And when you want them to settle, they know no measure at all... You think, honoured lady [pani szanowna], that they are talking about hundreds? Begging your pardon, you are mistaken; they are talking precisely about thousands of dollars. So I ask you, may you be well and live long days and wives [sic, for "years"], do they deserve this? You should know that I have, no evil eye, diamond daughters, pretty and fine, educated in all seven sciences, and I simply cannot marry them off... "Haz parias"[?] you ask me; you know what is going on today with the male sex: I cannot give them a dowry. I tell you, today's bridegroom-lads are unbearable. You know that all trade lies deep in the ground today, the world is sinking into poverty, businesses are being liquidated, factories are being shut, and with them it is all "joy and gladness", lively and merry, all they know is going to balls and polishing their nails. They are organised: this one a Halutz, that one a Shomer, that one a Gordonist and that one a Revisionist. It has become a world of parties and little parties, Shomrim and little Shomrim, Halutzim and little Halutzim, and I, Naftali-Hersh, slave away like a horse in bloody sweat, I don't get enough sleep and don't get enough to eat, and save groschen upon groschen — and all for whom? For these little "patsetlekh", who go about "bareheaded", who don't lay tefillin and don't kiss the mezuzahs and are "pal-bu"[?]... No and no... If I knew that my maidens would, God forbid, may that hour never come, be left on the shelf, I would give them, the lads, a dowry — a plague... They can't even be bothered to know about a crisis, about bad times, about taxes, trade licences, agents, bailiffs, inspectors. What do you think? The world is a free-for-all! Their licence must come to an end; a general meeting must be called of all parents who, poor things, have daughters, and they must come out with a protest against the impudence, against the conduct of today's lads. Any old lad [lada] wants a thousand dollars — help! It's cruelty to animals towards the girls; there's no approaching them ["ani przystęp"], it's a scandal, "as I love God" [jak Boga kocham]!
An easy word to say in today's crisis times — a thousand dollars. And they want it precisely in cash — "gotówką" [in cash], they shout — have you ever heard such impudence! And where and from where does one take so much money? And why do they deserve it? Ask them whether they have ever earned a thousand dollars in their lives! I tell you, if no remedy is devised against them, it will, God forbid, be very nasty [paskudne]... No weddings will take place, rabbis will earn nothing, klezmers will not play, and the commandment of "be fruitful and multiply" will, God forbid, perish; one must not keep silent, there is a duty on all Jews in general and on our Sejm deputies in particular. First of all taxes must be imposed on the lads — then they will hurry to marry; and all the parents to a man, whom the Almighty has blessed with the luck of maidens, must register and found an association named "Anti-nadragova"[?] or "Struggle against today's bridegrooms", and our "turgudige"[?] little lads will willy-nilly have to come down in price, and there will be an end to the heated and tangled dowry question, and salvation will indeed come to the girls.
So then, gentlemen [panowie], "parents of girls" [rodziców dziewcząt], from word to deed, to practical work — don't sleep, for the hour is urgent.
Address
Yeshayahu Wasserstrom.
What’s new in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Będzin — seizures; the gmina.]
Heading of the local page: „What’s new in Zagłębie?“ Friday, 28 Shevat 5692 (28) — piątek 5 lutego 1932 [Friday, 5 February 1932].
Będzin

„Now — ‘be-agala’ [by wagon / speedily] and soon..“ [a pun on the Kaddish phrase „ba-agala u-vi-zman kariv“, „speedily and soon“; here „agala“ = a real wagon]
On Monday a sequestrator from the local office (urząd) came with the „wagon“ and wanted to take away everything to be found in the office of the gmina. This, however, was not permitted. The sequestrator, having received an instalment of 500 zł., drove on...
To be freed from paying a 16-groszy „tax“ one must submit a petition..

[Będzin — taxes; the magistrate.]
Mr. Lipa Openheim tells us the following characteristic fact:
Last Wednesday he went to the magistrate (town hall) to pay the road tax (podatek drogowy) on his patent [trade licence]. At the same time Openheim wanted to pay the tax for his son-in-law, who had not received any payment order (nakaz).
When[?] the sequestrator Mr. Milsztejn had looked out the payment orders, Openheim asked him that Mr. M. should note that the cash office should accept the tax without a fine (kara).
Mr. M., seeing that the fine amounted to a few paltry groszy, granted Mr. Openheim’s request and noted it on the payment order.
This „sin“ of Mr. Milsztejn was noticed by chance by the head (kierownik) of the tax department, who revoked Mr. Milsztejn’s decision and categorically demanded that Mr. Openheim pay the fine in the amount of... 16 groszy.
In this connection Mr. Openheim turned to the inspector, who, after hearing what it was about, declared that the matter had to be „clarified“ („wyjaśnić“) and told Mr. Openham [sic] to apply to the magistrate with a written request that he be exempted from paying the 16 groszy...
Right after Havdalah the landlord crawls through the window to his tenant..

[Będzin — landlords and tenants.]
In Zandberg’s house on Kościelna street lives the tenant Kowalski, who last Sabbath was in Sosnowiec and had[?] locked the flat. The landlord, taking advantage of the opportunity, got into Kowalski’s flat „by a miracle“ and set up a workshop (pracownia) there. The neighbours informed Kowalski of this by telephone; he brought the police, and the landlord had to clear out the room he had seized.
Found a resting place in Będzin

[Będzin — charity and relief.]
This week a Jewish family of 8 persons arrived here travelling on a cart [—?] from Kalisz.
Several young people took an interest in the poor family, providing them with food and drink, and the butcher Mr. Markowicz gave the family a flat in his house.
On employing a larger number of journeyman bakers.

[Będzin — labour and unemployment; bakers.]
On the initiative of the labour inspector Mr. Peferman a conference was held in the premises of the local Artisans’ Association with the local master bakers, to whom the inspector appealed that the working hours of the employed journeyman bakers be reduced, in order to give work to the unemployed journeyman bakers.
The inspector’s proposal was taken note of, and a commission was elected to carry out the proposal.
Accident involving two soldiers.

[Będzin — accidents; the army.]
On Monday morning an artillery detachment of the 23rd regiment set out for exercises. While driving along Małobądzka[?] street a tram came towards them, at which the horses took fright and bolted with great force.
The result was a grave one. Two soldiers, Jakub Szczadra[?] and Jerzy Kamiński, fell off the wagon. Szczadra broke his right arm and Kamiński was seriously injured. Both were taken to the local hospital.
A „guest“ through the ceiling..

[Będzin — thefts.]
Z. Szenberg, coming into his flat on Mandzhever [Modrzejowska?] street on Sunday evening, was startled to see a man hanging on a rope in a hole in the ceiling.
S. called the police, who caught the „devils“. As it turned out, the thieves, taking advantage of the opportunity when nobody was in the flat, had hacked a hole in the ceiling and with the help of a rope got into the flat, where they took various articles and valuables.
After carrying out the theft the men wanted to get back out through the ceiling, but at that moment Mr. S. came into the flat and caught them red-handed („in the hot minute“).
Strike at the „Strem“ Factory

[Strzemieszyce — labour.] On Monday morning the 70 workers employed at the „Strem“ factory in Strzemieszyce went on strike.
The cause of the strike is the announcement [?] by the management that they are abolishing the 100-percent supplement for work on holidays.
After Emptying the Bottles of Vodka They Took to Axes and Knives

[Czeladź — crime.] On Sunday evening [?] a celebration [?] (an engagement or wedding) took place at a Christian family in Czeladź. When the guests had already emptied several bottles of vodka, they began to fight with deadly weapons. One of the guests was cut [?] to pieces.

From the League for Labour Palestine
[Zionism — lecture.] Today, Friday evening, in the premises of „Hitachdut“, the guest from Eretz Israel, member of „Gdud HaAvoda“ (the Labour Battalion), Yehuda Kopelewicz, will give a lecture on the subject: „Light and Shadow in the Reality of Eretz Israel“.
Sosnowiec — A False Accusation against a Jewish Merchant of Buying Stolen Turkeys

[Sosnowiec — court.] In the month of December (grudzień) of last year several turkeys were stolen from a rich Christian. A few days later the thief was arrested; at the inquiry he declared that he had sold the turkeys to the forwarding agent Landau on Sargawa [?] (Targowa?) Street in Sosnowiec.
On the basis of the thief's statement Mr. Landau was arrested, taken under strict guard to the police station, where he sat for 2 days under police supervision.
Last Saturday the trial took place in the local district court. The witnesses summoned established that Mr. Landau is one of the most respected forwarding agents; then Advocate Kahn delivered the speech for the defence, pointing out that this was a plain false accusation against Mr. Landau.
The court withdrew for deliberation and afterwards issued the verdict that Landau is recognised as innocent. The thief was sentenced to 3 years in prison.
Mr. Zendel Resigns as Kehilla President

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] In connection with the events at the last meeting of the kehilla board, Mr. Zendel has sent a letter to the starostwo (district office), in which he announces that he is laying down his mandate as vice-president of the kehilla.
Notices on Reducing Wages

[Sosnowiec — labour.] At the last conference on the dispute between the industrialists and the workers' delegates it was decided to continue negotiations on the question, so that the workers did not lose hope that the dispute would end in their favour.
In fact, however, the situation is different: the industrialists have issued notices that from the 1st of this month wages will be reduced by 8 percent.
The notices caused chaos in workers' circles, and the workers already wanted to throw down their work. Only after the delegates reassured them that, regardless of this, the negotiations would continue, did the workers return to work.
Medical Aid from the Jewish Kehilla

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] To the credit of the kehilla's activity one must note a very important function in the field of providing medical and social aid to the poor Jewish population.
Despite the difficult state of the kehilla treasury, a sum of 31.752 zł was nevertheless spent in the course of the year 1931.
Out of this sum patients were maintained at the kehilla's expense in the Jewish hospital, for whom the gmina paid 15,699 zł; doctors 4,013 zł; for medicines 9,430 zł; support for convalescence (cure) purposes 1,255; and free [?] advances 1.355 złoty.
Warsaw burglars on “tour” in Zagłębie

Friday evening, at a time when nobody was in the flat of Mr K. Rajner on Teatralna Street in Sosnowiec, thieves got in there and began to make themselves at home.
The thieves gathered up jewellery (bijouterie) and other articles worth 2 thousand złoty. When they were already about to leave the flat, the maid arrived and raised the alarm. One of the gang was caught; the others ran away.
The arrested thief is a resident of Warsaw; he had come with his partners on “guest performances” (“gastrole”) in Zagłębie.
Burglary at a drapery shop

In the night from Sunday to Monday a wall of Gleitsman's[?] drapery (manufaktura) shop on Targowa Street was broken through, from which the thieves took out goods worth several thousand złoty.
The next morning the police discovered the theft and put the thieves in jail.

General meeting of “Linat ha-Holim”
Next Sunday the continuation of the institution's annual general meeting will take place at the “Hotel Polski”.
The meeting is important if only because it is being called by a special commission, which took the initiative to reorganise and revive the institution, so necessary in the present time.
On the agenda is also the election of a new board. It is to be hoped that the Jewish population will take part in the meeting in sufficient measure and elect such a board as will be capable of putting “Linat ha-Holim” on its proper level.

On 20 April (kwiecień) of last year a crowd of unemployed gathered in front of the local magistrate (town hall), who wanted to force their way by violent means into the magistrate's premises.
