City Council Elections in Olkusz
The elections to the Olkusz city council have been set for the 28th of this month. Until Tuesday the 9th inclusive one can check whether one is properly entered in the voters' lists. Candidate lists are to be submitted from the 15th to the 17th during office hours. Appointed from among the Jews to the main electoral commission are Messrs. Y. Lender and M. Tolerman, and to the district commissions Messrs. Berish Wajselfisz, Avrahamele Paluk, Reuven Damber, Avraham Parasol, Avrahamele Kerner and Kalman Wajselfisz.
The city council consists of 24 councillors and 12 deputies. In all there are 4720 voters; of that number fifteen hundred are Jewish. In the previous elections there were 40 percent Jewish voters. Recently a few neighbouring villages were annexed to the town (possibly for the very purpose that the Jews should have no influence on the town's economy), so that if the Jews go to the elections split up (as party men [?]) they will have a very small representation in the city council and not a single representative in the magistrate. It is therefore the duty of the leading Jewish circles to create a united Jewish list of candidates, in order to secure a larger number of representatives in the city council and the magistrate.

Successful Evening of Miriam Orleska.
On Tuesday a recitation evening was held in the premises of the Będzin "WIZO", performed by the well-known actress of the Vilna Troupe, Miriam Orleska.

Reorganisation of the "Dobroczynność" [charity society].
On Sunday evening a joint meeting was held in the kehilla premises of the kehilla leaders M. Szwarcberg, R. Dafner, B. L. Kohn and the board of the "Dobroczynność", with the aim of reorganising the institution. Mr Szwarcberg explained that because of the gmina's [community's] lack of money, and also because of the authorities' order not to give any support to anyone until the overdue[?] debts to the kehilla employees (the rabbi and the shochtim) have been paid, the kehilla is at present unable to give any support whatsoever.
Taking into account, however, the hard and bitter situation of the poor, the gmina decided to reorganise the "Dobroczynność" in the following way: to attract more members, to call a general meeting and to explain the situation that has arisen. The present board, together with some of the dozór members, is to deal with this matter. It was also decided to apply to the authorities for support from the unemployment fund.
It is worth noting that many rich men pay nothing at all, and one of the richest sent the "Dobroczynność" a notice that because of the crisis he is reducing his weekly grosz contribution by 50 percent.

Picture Exhibition of Jewish Painter-Artists

[Sosnowiec — art; relief for the unemployed.] [Picture; caption:] "A Jewish [—]ip[?]" [probably "type"], painted by Brodower[?].
On the initiative of the Citizens' Committee to Support the Unemployed, a picture exhibition of works by a group of Jewish painters from Kraków has been opened in the premises of the Sosnowiec Merchants' Association, Kawalska[?] 2.
The opening, which took place on Sunday, was performed by the deputy starost Dr. Mioskowski[?], who greeted the initiators of the exhibition.
At the exhibition there is a series of successful pictures by the painter Józef Brodower[?], above all "The Unemployed Man", "The Menahem Mendel Type", which characterises so well a Jewish type who "turns worlds" with his little stick... and others. One sees that Brodower[?] has a fine sense of colour, thanks to which his pictures catch the visitor's eye.
Important places at the exhibition are taken by the works of Prof. Joachim[?] Kahane (metal sculptor) and Szymon Miller (watercolour), especially the "Chuppah Lamp" (Kahane).

Miriam Orleska. (On her second recitation concert tomorrow at "Wiza")

[Culture — recitation evening; Miriam Orleska.] Few today are the sceptics who still doubt whether Yiddish is a language. Asch and Bergelson alone [Sholem Asch and David Bergelson] are enough to remove every doubt. But even the most stubborn deniers[?] would admit that Yiddish is not only a language but even a very beautiful and sonorous one, if they heard it from the mouth of Miriam Orleska. With her the language is refined through the filters of her wonderful diction; it becomes many-coloured passing through the prism of her great talent. With her voice she brings out the most varied nuances, from the lyrical, caressing, girlish tones to the sorrow-soaked[?], melancholy widow-chords that recall the spirit motifs of "Peer Gynt".
She is incomparable in the social motifs, painting plastically the rhythm of labour and movement. She works with her artistic word and rouses more intensely to struggle, a thousand times more strongly than dead printed proclamations.
Social redemption would have come sooner if, instead of talentless demagogues, the ideas of freedom were spread by artists of such stature as Miriam Orleska.
She is an artist of great scale. She embodies the beautiful girl. Her bearing and her rhythmic movements bear witness to a great artistic culture; she acts suggestively[?] already at the first contact with the listeners.
Only a few are endowed by the gods with that wonderful fluid which calls forth such higher, spiritual emotions. To those fortunate [—] belongs[?] Miriam Orleska.

First death sentence of the summary court in Katowice.
On Monday the first summary court (Standgericht) sat in Katowice. In the dock sat the 22-year-old Skudło [?], who in the course of a robbery had killed 2 people.
Interest in the trial was great. In front of the court building stood a large crowd, which followed with curiosity every single item of news from the trial. The entrance to the courtroom was strictly controlled. Without tickets no one was let in.
After long deliberation the verdict is announced, according to which Skudło is sentenced to death by hanging.
At the same time the court declares its support for the defence counsel's proposal to apply to the President of the State for clemency.
After the verdict the murderer behaved very calmly. He only asked to be given cigarettes (papirosy) and black coffee.
After 20 hours had passed and no answer had come from the President, preparations for the execution began.
Among other things the hangman Maciejewski was summoned by telephone from Warsaw. As time was short, the hangman came to Katowice by aeroplane.
But at that very moment an answer arrived by telephone from the President of the State that the death sentence is commuted to life imprisonment.

Winter Is Here.

[Zagłębie — weather and daily life.]
The first two months of winter passed in very mild weather, and people who have no stocks of coal already thought that one would somehow push through, just as things are, until spring.
But last week the wheel turned quite differently and it became cold, and no joke. A wind truly blew from the north, and the frost together with the considerable snow brought the real winter.
True, winter is no loss for everyone. Drapery and fur dealers, knitwear and shoe dealers may perhaps snatch back at least part of what they lost because of the failed winter season. The [?]- and sleigh drivers are now in seventh heaven. After all, they could barely wait for the bit of snow that heaven has sent down to us [?].
But all those who have to buy a cartload of coal are not to be envied.

Forms of Existence in Our Century

[Article — economy and trade; Polish Jewry.]
(Economic interests and needs, formerly and today — how they were understood in Russia, and how in Austria and Germany.)
From time to time we find ourselves arguing about the immaturity of the Jewish citizen, who has so little grasp even of the economic field from which he has to draw his livelihood.
The citizens of Congress Poland and of the Kresy [the eastern borderlands], that is, those who were brought up under the Russian government, did not have the opportunity to mature either in the socio-political field or in the economic field. The Tsarist government was strongly interested in the people living in darkness and knowing nothing, and insofar as it did not succeed in this with regard to other nations, it applied it with full energy against us Jews. For us there existed the so-called "cherta osedlosti" [the Pale of Settlement], so that we Jews were not allowed to be in the greater part of Russia. Besides that, we were, after all, not admitted to the schools; all this hampered the process of development, and the Jews of Congress Poland and the Kresy remained backward compared with their brethren in the other countries.
Before the war, when we lived within our own four cubits, when we did not mix with people from other countries, we perhaps did not see it, and certainly, certainly did not feel it. But now that the map has changed and Poland has become independent, we see the colossal loss we suffer thanks to [i.e. because of] our backwardness.
[—] We are today citizens of free, independent Poland, which is taking shape on republican foundations, and more than once we see that we are not suited, not adapted, to the free order. Today, after all, we find ourselves under one roof with the inhabitants of Poznań, Galicia and Upper Silesia, and then we see what a colossal distance there is between these and those citizens.
If we look at how, in those places, not only a factory or some other larger enterprise looks, but even a quite ordinary merchant or craftsman, only then do we see by how many heads we stand lower than they, how little orientation we possess, how undeveloped we are in the line from which we draw our livelihood.
With us, in Congress Poland and in the Kresy, people trade so that the other fellow should think that I am earning. Here we do business with the slogan: "What do I lose on the deal?" He does not reckon what he will earn as soon as he makes the deal; he is merely satisfied that he will not lose, while in fact he is already losing on the deal as soon as he earns nothing on it. That is one thing, and there is a second thing besides: that he is, in general, a bad calculator; he cannot calculate, he cannot work things out for himself. He does not know how one must reckon in order to add in all the expenses he has on the goods and products he has bought, and since he does not add everything in, it seems to him that he has earned, while in reality he is actually losing.
If he kept books — if such an average citizen kept a ledger, debit and credit — he would see at the end of the year how he had fooled himself in his accounts. And that would have been a lesson [literally: tuition money] for the future. He would have become convinced that he deceives himself in his accounts, miscalculates, and he would have known that the shortcomings must be corrected; but the trouble is that no books are kept, and consequently not [?] ..., so that unknowingly one digs a pit for oneself, into which one finally falls.
Moreover, everyone of course persuades himself that he is an expert in the line, or that he has already "eaten up" his time on this article, that he was born and raised in it.
So it is with merchants and small traders, and it is interesting that the latter think the craftsman is well off, because he can work out how much his labour costs, while in reality it is even worse with the latter. They cannot calculate at all and do not know in the least how to work things out. They work a great deal and toil day and night, just like the merchant, without a stop, and get nothing from their work. One must not think, however, that they get nothing from their work because they earn little — no, that is far from the case; if they get nothing from their hard labour, it is only because they cannot calculate, they are very, very poorly oriented in their line, and have no intention at all of carrying out any reforms that would, on the one hand, improve their situation and, on the other, let them train themselves further in their trades.
We, then, the citizens who lived under the Tsarist government, are overworked and worn out day and night without a stop. Each of us is always immersed from head to foot in his business, in his trade, and in the luckiest case one brings in the most necessary expenses. When one works for 3 people, one has a piece of bread.
Quite differently live the citizens who were under Austrian and German rule: they were brought up on parliamentary foundations, they had access both to secondary schools and to the universities, and they have indeed arranged their lives differently.
If we look, for example, at the tiniest little shop in Katowice, Poznań, Bielsko, we see what a difference there is between it and ours. Not to speak of larger shops, which are provided with a staff of people and with bright [?], aesthetic, modern shop windows that draw the customer into the shop; and when he receives something new, fresh, he knows that he cannot do without the newspaper, that he must advertise his article, and everyone wants to be the first, every merchant wants to announce it to his customer sooner, everyone wants to show that he was the first to take care of the customer. On the other hand, when the time comes to close the shop, he forgets about everything. Then he belongs to himself. Then he is a husband, a father, a visitor to the theatre or the café-confectioner's; he knows that he must rest, and he has nothing whatever in common with the business, as if he did not need to live from it.
The same goes for the craftsman: he too has his rest and working time divided; with him it is reckoned that on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such an hour, he is to finish his article and at that very second deliver it to you, wherever you like [?], to house and yard. Whereas with us, when you start going to a craftsman — even though the expert must not let him out of his sight — you grow tired of walking, and in the end the article becomes loathsome to you, and quite often you even let it go to waste; and this at a time when the craftsman is hungry and is waiting for a bit of work.
It goes without saying that this is thanks to [i.e. because of] the fact that both the merchant and the craftsman lack education, not only in the social sense but also in the professional sense. If he wanted to learn, if he wanted to progress, he would have chances of reaching the point of becoming the educated craftsman and merchant whom we need so badly in the twentieth century, for after all we must be able to adapt ourselves to the times, if we live in the [20th] [?] century.
That is what one ought to think about in earnest, if we want to have a right to exist.
R. Let.
Inventions.

[Satirical feuilleton — inventions.] (A small feuilleton).

Germany has, as always, set a record this time too.
For the year 1931 it invented quite a few things that are truly astonishing.
I think, however, that human imagination has not yet drawn up the final total with this. It will probably go on working in this field.
Meanwhile, though, I want to try to note down a little programme in the field of inventions, and I hope the world will heed my demands.
In the field of technology the following ought to be invented:
1) A mother-in-law who talks only when one presses such a button on a special device.
In time it may perhaps be possible to perfect this invention also with regard to ordinary women, i.e. not only to mothers-in-law.
2) An umbrella that serves only public figures and employees in certain institutions. This umbrella has a property that allows it automatically to cover up all kinds of "disappearances" [embezzlements] and thefts.
At the same time, however, it has the property of opening itself up whenever an opportunity turns up to pull something off with one's fingers.
3) A pocket watch that shows precisely when, with whom and how one can have a bill of exchange protested without suffering any material damage thereby.
4) A microphone to be used especially by speakers on social and literary topics. This microphone has the property of catching only the lecturer's foolish talk and keeping it to itself, so that the audience will hear only the clever words.
5) A little machine that dispenses gemilut chasadim [interest-free loans] mechanically at any time.
6) An apparatus that censors sealed letters and newspapers without the help of paid officials.
This apparatus will surely be intended especially for those countries where freedom of the press and of speech exists.
7) A little machine that curses superbly in seventy languages; such a machine would come in handy for parliaments, party congresses, "dozory" [kehilla boards], etc.
8) A little purse[?] that warms other people's pockets.
9) A movable market. It will spare one going to the market.
In short, there are still plenty of things one could think up, but one cannot talk about them all at once.
Rebus.
Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton; communities and synagogues: Dańdówka, Dąbrowa, Strzemieszyce, Zawiercie.] (Jews have nothing but complaints. — Trading on the Sabbath. — Sins sold[?] for 5 bottles of beer. — A "republic" in one synagogue. — Jewishness grows stronger. — Kehilla board members who speak no foreign languages and dress in alpaca coats).

It has long been a well-known thing that we always have nothing but "complaints"; we are not content with the various concessions we receive, we have grievances against the English government concerning its obligations towards the Land of Israel, we have grievances against the tax offices, against the government bodies, that Jewish livelihoods are being undermined — and in the end it turns out that all these grievances and complaints "are unfounded"...
Here before us lies a "document" from Dańdówka[?] that Jewish trade is "flourishing" there. People trade in everything the world stands on, not only on the six days of the week but
— on the Sabbath too...
The handful of Agudah members in the village of Dańdówka, in order "to enlarge the business", have introduced a "revival" in the zemirot of the third Sabbath meal [shalosh seudot]. The "revival" consists in the zemirot being sold. The prices are even affordable: for one bottle of beer anyone can buy a zemer...
The "business" has already developed so well that not only zemirot are being sold but
— sins too...
The first "sin transaction" was made last Sabbath at shalosh seudot. A young man came into the beit midrash, and the zemirot seller turned to him asking him to buy a bit of "merchandise"...
The young man, who is no great lover of buying zemirot, proposed a different deal to the seller:
"If you buy from me the sins I have committed from Yom Kippur until today, I'll give 5 bottles of beer"...
The zemirot seller, hearing of a deal that could bring a profit of 5 bottles of beer, agreed to it, and with a handshake the deal was concluded on the Sabbath at twilight...
Well, as long as people complain that there is a crisis and Jews are without employment...
———
The same "joy" is provided by the report of the goings-on in the Dąbrowa synagogue.
In the Dąbrowa synagogue — the kehilla president tells us — Reb Lawlessness has seized the seat of honour and lords it over the place[?]. It is a natural phenomenon. Since the rabbi cannot come and the kehilla representatives do not come either, as a matter of course "the common folk, scissors and iron" [i.e. the tailors] have the say, and every Sabbath it is
— "la-Yehudim"-like [as merry and rowdy as Purim]...
The main cause of the goings-on is the "strategic position"[?], i.e. the synagogue borders on the beit midrash, where two separate "republican governments" exist which do not live in peace with one another; they trip each other up, one disturbs the other's financial income, for no sooner does a gabbai of the "8 o'clockers" give a kiddush of brandy and honey cake than the gabbai of the "9 o'clockers" gives brandy, snacks and in the afternoon
— a little glass of beer...
And when both "kingdoms" reach the stage of "and the children struggled together within her" — the synagogue turns into a hullabaloo[?], a confusion; one does not hear what the other says, for when the synagogue cantor sings "Hakol yoducha" — from the beit midrash come the voices of
— "Mele'im ziv"...
In such a situation the president is helpless. "What is to be done?" he asks; perhaps close the synagogues[?] altogether... "The beit midrash, where the 'republicans' conduct their politics, I have already closed," says the president, "but where does one take the strength to uproot the lawlessness in the synagogue, so that the prayer stand should not be a 'free tribune' for anyone who can throw a punch..."
———
In Strzemieszyce the "political situation" is already better. The local kehilla majority creates special "little kingdoms" for rabbinic "courts", which receive temporary titles
— "wierniki" [trustees, supervisors]...
The task of a "wiernik" is to stand on guard and see to it that the stomachs of the Jewish population of Strzemieszyce should not, God forbid, digest a single piece of "treif" meat...
The first to be privileged with such a "wiernik" were the Jews of Niemce. As long as the rabbi was alive, Niemce was in a state of kashrut, but since the rabbi passed away Niemce has been eating "treif" meat, until salvation came and Niemce now has a rabbi of its own... A "wiernik" it is called.
But there is in Strzemieszyce a large part of Jewish "inhabitants" who resent the "wierniki". We have — they say — elected the Jaworzno rabbi, who is to take over the rabbinical seat in the very near future. Also the obligations towards the widow, the rebbetzin, have not been fulfilled to this day. So why take upon ourselves a fresh burden of pensions and other worries?
So argues the minority, those who want "to eat treif meat"; but "speak to the trees and the stones" — never mind logic, never mind fairness, the main thing is: there is a seat! And whoever is to sit down on it is also here[?], so who cares about the interests of a widowed rebbetzin. "He who sits on the horse rides it".. And if a dispute flares up? The air is charged with "gunpowder"? That is not their worry either. No matter; to supply "Jewishness" all means are kosher, even insulting the Jaworzno rabbi...
———
A true "idyll" reigns among the new kehilla rulers in Zawiercie. The local "shepherds of the flock" are far from all the "pranks" that happen in Warsaw or in Sosnowiec. No, at the meetings of the Zawiercie dozory [kehilla board members] nobody throws chairs, not even stones; rather, peace and tranquillity reign, simply "messianic times". Every meeting is regarded as a holiday; all the board members come to the meeting dressed in new alpaca coats, their little beards nicely combed, and the meeting is conducted in the old manner. One is not allowed to use any "foreign word" whatsoever; for example, the word "Feuerung" [firing] must not be mentioned, because in the gmina sit dozory, after all, not a "straż ogniowa" [fire brigade]...
— If only in all kehillot there were board members with alpaca coats who would use no foreign words in their speeches...
Ben Amotz.
The Short-Sighted at the Present Moment

By Efraim Kapłan.
„If one does not give to Jacob, one gives to Esau“ — so runs an old Jewish folk saying.
The generations of old believed with perfect faith in this saying. They were truly convinced that if someone is stingy and will not give charity, he will sooner or later pay dearly for that stinginess.
So, to this day, the very pious Jews also believe — those who give charity for every good cause, as far as their means allow.
The freethinkers do not believe in it. They regard it as an absurdity, a superstition, a great foolishness. They think it has not yet been proven that one must give either to Jacob or to Esau. It is fine to give to neither of them, and then the few złoty really stay in one's own pocket...
And those of them who do give charity do not do so because they fear punishment, but because they possess a good heart by nature and pity the sick, the wretched and the helpless.
But the truth is just as the pious believe.
There is a punishment for those who care only for their own bodies, for those who do not concern themselves with others.
Our little world is simply so arranged that not giving at all is impossible.
A man may lock himself behind ten locks of self-love — it will not help him at all. Sooner or later a storm of evil circumstances will arise that will drag him out of his egoistic fortress and punish him severely for neglecting his duties to the community.
For every one of us is a link in the great chain called „society“. He is forged to it by force and cannot tear himself away from it and exist as an entirely separate link.
We live in society and we are a part of it, bone of its bones, flesh of its flesh. When something hurts us, it must feel a part of our pains. Conversely, we must feel and suffer pains when something hurts it, when it is not all right.
When someone is a millionaire and lives by the best rules of hygiene, he is not safe from consumption as long as there are, in other districts of the town, unfortunates who are afflicted with this plague[?]. Those unfortunates walk about in the streets, in the trams, and they poison the air with their sick breath and sow the seeds of the accursed, contagious disease wherever they come. These seeds can sometimes take root even under the millionaire's feet...
It is therefore in everyone's interest to help fight this disease. One must see to it that the healthy do not fall ill for lack of food and airy dwellings, and that those who are already ill are admitted to sanatoriums.
When one comes in person to someone to ask for a donation to help a poor family that is starving without bread, he may be ever so hard-hearted a soul — but if he has any sense and calculation at all, he ought to give the largest donation he can, in order to still the hunger of those poor people, because the nests of hunger are also the nests of all contagious diseases. The fewer such nests there are, the safer it is for him, as for everyone else, to live and be healthy.
The commandment „Love thy neighbour as thyself“ we must fulfil ourselves, quite apart from the World to Come, from piety or goodness. We must love the other and care for his health and his comfort precisely for the sake of our own benefit.
When we care for our neighbour, we care for ourselves: when we help our „friend“ or even our enemy with bread and clothes, we help our very selves. But if we let the other suffer, we thereby bring suffering upon our own heads.
If we do not give to Jacob, we must give to Esau...
• • •
Poverty and want bring not only physical illnesses but mental ones too. A large percentage of thieves and robbers were driven into their underworld „profession“ by poverty.
Robbers are the children of your neighbour — who is in fact an honest man — who once stretched out his hand to you and asked you to help him in need. His children are dying of hunger. You turned down his request. What do I care about his children, you thought, as long as my own little ones have enough to eat.
Hunger drove your neighbour's boys out into the street; all their senses begged for food. Suddenly they caught sight of bread. They watched for the moment, snatched a loaf of bread and ran away.
That step led them onto the road of theft. They became professional robbers and began to rob even when they were full.
You are guilty of their downfall. With your closed hand you pushed them onto the bad road. Had you seen to it that your neighbour's children were fed, they would not have become what they are today, and you would not have had to complain at all about the great loss you suffered through their robbing hands.
But something far worse can still happen. It can happen that you receive a greater sentence for your[?] hard-heartedness. It can happen that your neighbour's children, who were driven by hunger and need to become thieves, will by various manoeuvres catch your children in the net of their demoralising influence and draw them into their gang.
• • •
The trouble with most of our people is not so much that their egoism is so great, as that their intelligence is small and they do not grasp that precisely because one loves oneself dearly, one must share the bite from one's mouth with the other... For as long as the other is hungry and greedy[?] for a piece of bread, you cannot be sure of your own satiety...
Here are millions of people going about without work; they starve and their families ache with hunger.
What, then, can the result of such a situation be? The result can be manifoldly sad. Some of the hungry may fall ill in body and with their illness infect the well-fed too. A second part of them may be stricken with mental illnesses, may sink into demoralisation, become criminals and take revenge on those who refused to help them. And a third part may be provoked to revolution, to world-overturning. Then those who today swim on top will be hurled to the bottom. True, the overturners too, the topplers of the present capitalist „order“, will not make themselves better off; they too will remain lying on the bottom, as is the case in Russia. But that is, of course, a scant consolation.
The main thing that must be remembered is that the three dangers enumerated above threaten our society at this critical moment, and that people must open their eyes and see and admit that the road on which they are now walking is strewn with gunpowder...
If they, for their part, do not want to open their eyes voluntarily, their eyes must be torn open with forceful instruments of logic.
The old method of moral preaching has outlived its time. It is useless to appeal to people's nobler sentiments, for we see that little is achieved that way. One in ten thousand responds; the others stay silent, as though they were not meant.
The old formula of the appeal for charity has completely lost its force. It must be changed. One may no longer go bent in three asking for alms. One must demand — demand not as a favour, but as a debt that everyone must pay first of all to himself, because if he does not give to the unfortunate, he will hurl himself into the abyss of misfortune.
If someone does not give, he is not merely a robber towards the other but also a robber towards himself; his not giving will sooner or later bring him to ruin.
And if someone does give, he is owed no thanks, he is owed no title of donor or philanthropist. He is guarding[?] his own skin...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Terumah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Terumah
The Portion
—o—
a) "And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying" (Ex. 25:1)
"Why was the portion of Terumah given after Mishpatim? — It is as written (Psalm 119): I have done judgment and justice." (Midrash Rabbah).
"He hath not dealt so with any nation; and as for His judgments, they have not known them" —
Suppose an ill-bred street urchin came along and wanted to learn elegant manners and salon etiquette — would it not be ridiculous? Isn't he still far from etiquette? — In just this way the nations go in need of all sorts of laws and "refined" statutes, while they still lack the simple "Thou shalt not steal", "Thou shalt not murder"... Even their virtue[?] stands[?], too, on a foundation of injustice.
Among Jews, however, justice is above everything. Charity and justice are synonyms. Charity that comes from dishonest sources is hateful to God. That is why justice is always mentioned before charity: "I have done judgment and justice" — first Mishpatim and then the portion of Terumah. Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
Charity is great. It is the best insurance for a person's property. It guards a person against damages and robberies — but which charity? —
Like the man who wanted to cross a forest inhabited by robbers. He took along an armed gentile to guard him. But the gentile was himself a robber, and while he was guarding his companion the robbers winked at him: you're one of ours, after all. And it goes without saying that he no longer guarded his companion...
Charity that itself comes from robbery cannot protect against robbery... Kol Yeshurun.
—o—
b) "That they take for Me an offering" (ibid., 2)
"That they take" — even from the collectors themselves they should take...
Collecting and demanding contributions is indeed a good thing, but the collectors themselves must be an example...
This applies also to the collectors and demanders of fear of Heaven and piety: they themselves must also be an example... Divrei Yosef.
—o—
c) "Of every man whose heart maketh him willing" (ibid.)
"Terumah" also means separating oneself from "gold, silver and brass", from the lust for money. But usually a person says: for the time being I will gather a little more [—][?], until I have enough already. Only then will I separate myself from the lust for money...
That is why this symbolic offering is called "nedavah" (freewill gift), because "nedavah" means an immediate gift — "behold, this [is given]" ("neder", a vow, means for later); and this gift too — from the lust for money — must be a one-time[?] one, not for later... Magor veShemesh[?].
—o—
d) "Gold, and silver, and brass" (ibid., 3)
The best sign that they mean it honestly will be if they bring the first thing at once: gold. At once the most valuable. For usually the giver of a donation starts by giving the skimpiest, and only after long work is he brought up to giving something more valuable. Be'er Yitzhak.
—o—
e) "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (ibid., 8)
In Midrash Mishlei it is said that for going to the study house to listen to words of Torah one's sins are forgiven.
Because — those who listen earnestly to the words of Torah and reflect on them are forgiven their sins as a matter of course. Those, on the other hand, who cannot bear to listen to words of Torah, but must come into the study house only for the sake of honour and "stand on pins" — they have, after all, suffering there, and "sufferings scour away a man's sins", so their sins too are forgiven... Olat Hodesh.
—o—
f) "Within and without" (ibid., 11)
A Torah scholar must be the same within as without, as pure inwardly as outwardly... But first of all the weight lies on "within", on inner purity — first the inwardness. Kiflayim leTushiya.
—o—
Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever once stayed in Vienna together with a Polish Hasidic rebbe of the well-known sort. The rebbe, feeling himself free of his Hasidim, proposed to Rabbi Shmuel that they go to the Imperial Viennese theatre to amuse themselves a little. Rabbi Shmuel answered him:
You indeed feel free here because your Hasidim are not here; so here you are no rebbe and may do whatever you please. I, on the other hand, as a rabbi, am a rabbi wherever Jews are found, even in Vienna; and just as in Mohilev[?], so in Vienna too I will not go to the theatre.
—o—
The "Seer" of Lublin once sees a plain pious Jew, and says to him:
— A holy Jew. Should the "Seer" of Lublin not wash his fingernails [the morning hand-washing], there would be an uproar: a rebbe doesn't wash his nails... Should he not put on tefillin, there would be an uproar: a rebbe doesn't put on tefillin!... So he has to be pious. But you, a plain Jew, whom nobody watches, and you still put on tefillin — you are honest after all — you are truly holy!...
—o—
g) "One beaten work of pure gold" (ibid., 36)
"One beaten (mikshah) work" — there is one hard (kasheh) thing in the world: "pure gold" — that a person should own pure gold, without robbery, without theft... that someone should acquire a fortune only through clean, honest means...
Rishfei Esh (Rabbi Mordechai of Neschiz).
—o—
A characteristic excerpt from the "Talks" of Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav:
"Now, in these times, it is very, very hard for an upright man to own money, because one must undergo a very great descent before one acquires money. And even when one has already descended in Jewishness, one still does not get money so quickly... for even the wicked have no money either. But for an upright man it is truly hard to have wealth... Wealth has fallen into the depths of the husks (kelipot). 'And she came down wonderfully (pela'im)'. 'Pela'im' has the letters of 'alafim' (thousands). The thousands one can nowadays[?] have only when one is a spiritual descender"...
—o—
"Length of days is in her right hand".
The Gemara asks about this: "Length of days" — yes, and riches and honour — not?
The Gemara answers: length of days, and riches and honour all the more so.
But it remains only an "all the more so", an a fortiori; but explicitly, in cash, they don't have it... Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka[?].
—o—
Haftarah
h) "And they two made a covenant" (I Kings 5)
Even while making a covenant they remained "two"... Hiram and Solomon, even when they conclude peace, remain nonetheless "the two of them" — separate... Torat Simcha.
—o—
i) "And King Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel" (ibid.)
To build a sanctuary he took penny donations from the whole people, although larger donations from individuals would have sufficed. He wanted all Jews to have a share in the building of the Temple. Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
j) "And the Lord gave Solomon wisdom" (ibid.)
God offered Solomon: wealth or wisdom. Solomon chose wisdom. God said: if so, I must give you wealth as well, for wisdom without wealth has no value; in the world there is no [esteemed] poor sage... "And the poor man's wisdom is despised". Divrei Hefshiya[?].
Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov (instalment 11)

[Serialized novel — “Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress”, a historical novel by Boris Maksimov; instalment 11.]

Vyrubova [Anna Vyrubova, lady-in-waiting and confidante of the Tsarina] listened calmly and quietly to Sonia’s words; nothing of what Sonia had told was news to her. She knew very well about the spiritual agitation that the Archimandrite [Feofan], supported by the bishop and by Iliodor[?], was conducting at the imperial court. She herself had been against it. She had always advised the Tsarina not to listen to Feofan’s words. Between her and the Archimandrite there was therefore a quiet, hidden hatred. And Vyrubova answered:

“I know about everything... But I do not believe that one needs to meet Feofan now... Besides: I am not the suitable person to bring you together with him.. He and I are not on good terms...”

“So what is to be done?” Sonia asked, and worry showed on her face.

“I believe that for the time being you need do nothing at all,” Vyrubova said meaningfully.

“May I ask what you mean by that?” Sonia asked.

Vyrubova was silent for a while. She thought and then said:

“What I am going to tell you now, Sonia Oskarovna, is for the time being a secret; I want you to remember it.”

“Surely I will remember it,” Sonia exclaimed.

“Then I will tell you: I am certain that any day now changes will take place at court and the Archimandrite will lose his influence..”

“Really?” Sonia exclaimed.

Vyrubova nodded her head:

“A great ‘holy man’ has appeared... a ‘miracle-worker’; he will cure the naslednik [the heir to the throne] and will take Feofan’s place..”

And Vyrubova added:

“He has never met any Jews.”

“He does not know any Jews at all?” Sonia “answered”.

“No. He does not know them. He comes from a region where there are no Jews. He has never seen them and he has nothing at all to do with them.”

“Who could that be?” Sonia wondered.

Then Vyrubova smiled and said:

“Why, you, Sonia Oskarovna[?], know him. You have seen him.”

“I have seen him? Where, when?”

“You saw him yesterday evening, in the salon of Countess Ignatieva. He was introduced to you and — you made a good impression on him...”

“You mean the muzhik? The Siberian muzhik?”

Sonia’s voice trembled. She now remembered how that strange muzhik had looked at her. How his pale-blue eyes had been sharp and tender... Again she felt a cold dread in her heart:

“You mean him?”

Vyrubova nodded her head. Pious ecstasy appeared on her face and with fervour she said:

“This muzhik is a man of God. He is a ‘holy man’ and he can perform very great miracles... He possesses a heavenly power, and I myself — I owe him my life.”

“Your life?” Sonia asked in astonishment.

“Yes... He saved me from certain death.”

She spoke with tremendous admiration, with great reverence for this “holy man”, and she told how it had been barely a year before; she was then in Siberia and had travelled to visit a famous monastery situated in the region of Pokrovskoye[?], where Grigori Rasputin comes from. At the last railway station the Pokrovskoye[?] postmaster was already waiting for her with a britzka harnessed to two horses. He had been informed of her coming in advance. And the postmaster himself had waited for her in order to drive her to the monastery. She got into the britzka, the postmaster urged on the horses and off they went.

“It was in spring,” Vyrubova related, “and the day was a fine one. The horses were well rested and ran easily. When we were already not far from Pokrovskoye, the horses bolted and began to run wild. The britzka began to bounce violently and I had to hold on with both hands so as not to fall out. The postmaster pulled hard on the reins, strained all his strength to hold back the horses and could not manage it. The horses grew even wilder, more enraged, and tore along like devils. White foam flew from them. They left the road and tore along at a terrible gallop across the fields. From great fright I could not even scream; a cold sweat broke out on me and the blood froze in my veins. My life was in great danger. The horses dashed back towards the road. Along the road grew trees, and at any moment the britzka would smash into a tree and death awaited me...”

Vyrubova closed her eyes for a moment as she said this and her whole body trembled, as though she were now seeing death before her eyes. Sonia sat bewildered and stared with great frightened eyes. Vyrubova caught her breath and began to speak more calmly and in a quiet voice:

“Suddenly a tall, broad-shouldered muzhik appeared on the road. He was walking from Pokrovskoye. He strode with calm steps and was deep in thought. On seeing him I cried out with all my strength: ‘Help! Save me!’ The man stopped and raised his head. Seeing how the horses were tearing like an arrow from a bow straight at him, he crossed himself, stretched out both his hands and in an unwavering[?], firm and clear voice he cried to the horses: ‘In God’s name! Stop!’ And a miracle happened. The horses heard the muzhik’s cry, at once began to slow their run and to calm down, and before you knew it the muzhik was already holding the horses’ bridles with both hands... I saw this miracle with my own eyes... The horses were still panting heavily, but they already stood with lowered heads, submissive[?] to the muzhik’s supernatural power — and my life was saved...”

Vyrubova now drew her breath with relief. Her face brightened.

“It is easy to imagine how frightened I was. I could hardly breathe. Here — the muzhik let go of the horses, which were already standing quietly, and he came up to the britzka. He began to look at me with his eyes. He looked with such gentleness and tenderness that I at once came to myself and grew calmer. I wanted then to get down from the britzka; I was afraid to drive on. But the muzhik made the sign of the cross over me and said: ‘Have no fear, [?]“par veyser”, no harm will come to you.’ And as he said it, I felt that I could rely on his words. The fear left me completely. I thanked the stranger, took the cross I was wearing from my neck and gave it to him as a gift. He took the cross, made the sign of the cross over me once more, bowed and went his way.”

And Vyrubova continued:

“The postmaster also came to himself... He again gave a tug at the reins and we drove on. The horses were calm and let themselves be guided by their driver. I asked the postmaster who that was: ‘That is Grisha the holy man.’ He told me that this muzhik is famous in the whole region as a ‘holy man’, that he often performs great miracles. Sometimes it happens that he disappears for a while and wanders about the roads of Siberia. When he is in Pokrovskoye, it often happens that at night he goes off into the deep forest. Believing women and girls follow him and stay with him through the nights in the forest. There they light great bonfires, they sing ‘holy’ songs and dance ‘holy’ dances. They serve God and spend the time in prayer... The postmaster also told me that we had had great luck in meeting him. Otherwise our britzka would have been smashed to pieces and we would no longer be alive. With the divine power he possesses he stopped the maddened horses and saved our lives..”

Vyrubova’s face flushed slightly with enthusiasm and joy as she related:

“Yesterday I come in to the priest Vostorgov and find there a stranger who looks like a simple muzhik. Vostorgov says to me: ‘Anna Vyrubova, make the acquaintance of a “holy” man. This is’ — he points out the stranger to me — ‘the starets [holy elder] Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin.’ I come closer to the stranger, look at him intently, and it seems to me that his face is very familiar to me. And he — looks at me in such a way as though he knew me. For a while we looked at each other like that. Suddenly he began to smile. His eyes became gentle and tender and he asks in a soft voice: ‘Don’t you recognise me?’”

The Prague Fair

From our correspondent there, S. Lagsztajn [?].
Without any doubt the Prague fair will be the most interesting of the fairs to be held now. Taking into account that Czech industry has lately done everything not to be pushed out of the world market, it will be interesting to see how the industry has reworked its whole production so as to be able to compete with the entire world both with good goods and with cheap prices.
At the present Prague fair a separate fair for hotels and restaurants will be held for the first time. Every country strives to attract as many foreigners as possible. It shows off its particular beautiful places, the natural and artistic characteristics that the country possesses. Certainly one must have the means to receive strangers and to honour them with the best, as they are accustomed to at home.
It is clear that all the hotels, inns and guesthouses existing until now, which were sufficient for commercial travellers, must be changed as soon as travellers come there who want to enjoy their journey.
At the present Prague fair one will be able to see how the old hotels and restaurants can be reworked on the model of world-class hotels, so that everyone may have an idea of how to do it at home.
Besides this there will be a separate exhibition, "Tea and Coffee". The biggest social gatherings are nowadays held only over tea or a coffee. The greatest and most important part of our life is played out there, and so it is important that not only hotels and restaurants but housewives too should know by all means how to arrange this so that everyone feels comfortable over a "glass of tea". The "electric kitchen" too, which today offers hundreds of possibilities and conveniences for every housewife, will be demonstrated there in all its details, and in this way it will attract the interest of the whole international world that will gather at the Prague fair, which opens on 13 March of this year.
South America and China Need Goods

Specially for our paper, by Z. Haber.
The reports now arriving from all over the world at the Leipzig Fair Office give a clear picture of the economic possibilities that exist at present in the four corners of the earth.
From South America a great many buyers will now come to the Leipzig fair, because a great shortage of goods prevails in those countries.
Thus, for example, Ecuador needs — as the Leipzig Fair Office learns — a very large number of optical articles, spectacles, field glasses and the like, but also musical instruments and radio sets, which are paid for there literally in gold. The exhibitors of these articles at the present Leipzig fair will do good business.
Colombia, Bolivia and Mexico need many articles from Europe: medical articles, new electrical appliances, machines, all kinds of artistic works and many other articles that are not manufactured in those countries.
A particularly good customer is Peru; there is no unemployment in that country. There are few railways in the country and everything is done with carts; the government is now striving to build good roads so that one can get there by automobile. So far 12 thousand kilometres of roads have been completed. Ten thousand kilometres more are now being built, and a further ten thousand kilometres will be built soon. — In the country itself there is enough work, and there is a need there for various articles which people now want to buy at the Leipzig fair. Besides this, Peru will need automobiles of all kinds, for passengers and for freight, and since the customs duty there is not high, it will be well worth doing business there.
Moreover, one must not forget that in Peru conditions for colonization are very good: while in Germany, for example, 133 people live on one square kilometre, in Peru four people live on the same area, and so it is with everything else — the country is very backward by our European notions.
One can travel to Peru on 25 shipping lines, founded in 9 different states.
It is worth looking more closely into the country of Peru, in order to find out thoroughly whether there are possibilities for trade or for colonization in that country.
China too urgently needs all kinds of goods, especially ironware. No machines whatsoever have been imported into China until now, and it is a rule that a country cannot develop as long as no modern machines are brought there. Thus it could happen that although last year the harvest was so good as China has not remembered in the last 25 years, nevertheless 16 percent of the grain still had to be brought from other countries to cover the needs of the country.
This year the government ordered that all authorities and private institutions should bring in modern agricultural machines in order to improve the produce of the soil. Besides this, China now wants to build iron works, which do not exist there. China now needs some 70 thousand railway wagons every single year in order to build out its railways and factories, which have lately been built there continually.
In China there exist two great coal mountains, from which nothing can be transported for the time being, because a railway must first be built to them. The Chinese government has now decided to develop all the neglected areas of the country.
It goes without saying that there is now an opportunity to sell thousands of articles needed for daily life which are now lacking in China, where for the time being there is neither crisis nor unemployment.
The coming Leipzig fair will make it possible for merchants from all over the world to begin trading with the Chinese market, which has always been a great consumer and which now wants to free itself from English and American economic dependence.
The Sosnowiec Jewish Hospital and Its Significance

One of the greatest virtues of the Jewish people has been, and still is, the commandment of "bikur cholim" (visiting the sick). In this field there are always people who shed their day-to-day affairs and devote themselves to the work of helping and relieving the Jewish sick person in all his needs, such as doctors, medicines and also money support. For this purpose special institutions were created, which fulfil their tasks towards the sick according to their means.
Later it turned out that the main thing is not yet that the sick person receives help; the chief role belongs to special healing institutions. Hospitals were founded, among them also the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec, founded in the year 1910.
At that time there did not exist so many Jewish parties in the Jewish street, and such strong antagonism did not yet prevail. Only a few rich Jews of Sosnowiec, such as Reicher, Oppenheim and others — some more, some less — gave with an open hand, and so the building of a Jewish hospital was erected.
In the memorial book are found the names of the donors; only one is missing — missing is the person who, as far as I know, gave his very soul and devoted his whole energy for the benefit of the hospital: that is Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory, whom I unfortunately did not find among all the names that were inscribed for remembrance. What is more, I searched all the hospital rooms for the portrait of Dr. Perlman. I was sure that his name was engraved in golden letters, but nowhere did I find his portrait...
In a quiet, unlively street, behind the town, stands the building of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec. The building, which stands in the middle of a small garden, is not easy to reach until one gets there. One needs enough strength before the "walls"[?] (probably a misprint for "sounds") of the bell reach the ears of the watchman...
The hospital is arranged according to all the rules. Besides special wards for women and for men — an operating room, X-ray, also a chemical laboratory, a maternity clinic, etc.
One must also dwell particularly on the proper staff of doctors, feldshers and nurses; but the soul of the hospital is Dr. Weinzieher, beloved by all, who is devoted heart and soul to relieving the sick in their suffering. Mention must also be made with gratitude of the surgeon Jankowski, of Dr. Weiss, devoted to the sick, of the likeable Dr. Teichner and of Dr. Mittelman.
As far as I know — better said, from what my own eyes have seen — I saw how the walls weep and through the ceiling one can see the new moon to bless it... But one must take into account the present severe crisis. One may not judge our brethren harshly, who remember after all that there exists a Jewish hospital which must be supported. Nevertheless it is very desirable that there be founded 1) a committee whose sole task would be to help the Jewish hospital materially, and 2) a women's committee that would look after the hygienic side and also devote time for the benefit of the sick sisters and brothers.
H. Szer.
What Every Tenant Must Know

3.
Eviction.
In the present crisis, when thousands of families are perishing from hunger, when people struggle with terrible want, the dwelling is the only thing they possess. Therefore it often happens that people do not eat their fill and do not drink their fill in order to save up the few złoty for rent.
Despite this, for many tenants it is an impossible thing to guard themselves against eviction, especially when a larger sum of rent accumulates.
The tenant-protection law gives the landlord the possibility of evicting his tenant in the following circumstances:
1) When the tenant does not pay rent for half a year. 2) When by his immoral conduct, or through quarrelling, he makes living unbearable for the other neighbours. 3) When he hands over his dwelling without the landlord's consent. 4) When he wilfully damages the rented premises. 5) When the dwelling is very much needed by the landlord himself. 6) When the dwelling is badly ruined and requires rebuilding.
The most topical case is point no. 1, which speaks of owing rent, the landlord obtaining an eviction through the court. Yet tenants without means who occupy dwellings no larger than two rooms must know that there is a special amendment to the Tenant Protection Law which makes it easier to stay an eviction already issued by the court.
The amendment says that every tenant who has run into debt for rent because of unemployment, and against whom the landlord has obtained an eviction, has the right, upon obtaining work, to pay off the debt in instalments of up to 25 percent of the amount of the normal rent. The instalments must be paid together with the current rent, i.e. when an unemployed tenant owes 100 zł. for 2 quarters' rent, he must, for the new current quarter, pay in 50 zł. and at the same time an instalment of 12.50 zł. for the old debt. The money must be sent to the landlord by post, and the postal receipt enclosed with a petition to the same[?] court where the eviction was confirmed, requesting that the eviction be stayed.
It must be noted, however, that missing an instalment cancels the privilege, and the eviction can be carried out.
Against poor people no eviction can be carried out in the winter months, from 8 November to 31 March.
As regards point 2, this means tenants who keep illegal houses of ill fame, or salons of "intimate" ladies, especially near a synagogue, church, etc., as well as tenants who are drunkards, adventurers, etc.
Point 3 is clear to everyone, and it is superfluous to explain it here.
But on point 3 [sic; read 4] one must dwell. Tenants must be warned to be careful and not wilfully damage their dwelling by chopping wood indoors, damaging walls, stairs, etc.
As concerns points 5 and 6, the landlord must provide the tenant with a suitable dwelling. Above all in point 5, which is very complicated, because the law demands clear proof that the dwelling is vitally necessary for the landlord.
It is worth knowing that all agreements and contracts with the landlord that are contrary to the Tenant Protection Law have no legal value whatsoever.
Music Notes.

(After the first performance of the People's Choir.)

On Thursday the People's Choir (Folks-khor), which was founded here a few months ago under the direction of Mr. Prof. Barowka [?], appeared in a concert at the "Na-vashtshi" [Nowości] theatre in Będzin.

Also taking part in the concert were: Miss Bajarska, Mrs. Til-Fogelgarn, Mr. Dembitzer and Mr. Barenblat.

The programme consisted of a series of songs by Mendelssohn-Bartholdy, Otman [?], Moniuszko and others, as well as Jewish folk songs.

The first thing we would point out is that a Jewish people's choir ought to open a concert with a Jewish song and not with a song in a foreign language. In general, the number of Jewish songs should at least equal that of the others.

We will not dwell here on each song separately, because the choir is still very young and the programme did not consist of any difficult works. We shall therefore confine ourselves to a general assessment.

The choir lacks women's voices, which should make up about sixty per cent in mixed choirs. The women's voices give the choir its proper colour and subtlety.

The tenors, too, must be completed; they were heard very weakly, even at moments where they should be heard most strongly.

Best of all are the basses. They have fine voices, and it is also evident that they have a musical sense.

On the whole the attempt was a successful one. If the above shortcomings are removed, one can predict that the choir will develop and in time will be able to perform serious musical works.

Miss Bajarska has a beautiful soprano; since her last appearance she has improved considerably. In the "Bell Song" ("aria with the little bells") she displayed quite a fine technique. Her coloratura range, too, was broad enough, and her modulation plastic.

Mr. Barenblat accompanied very well.

Mr. Dembitzer (Katowice) has a strong tenor voice, which is very sonorous in the upper register as well as in the middle range; in piano, however, a dullness is felt — it lacks the metallic ring it has in the upper notes.

He sang the opera arias considerably more strongly and better than the songs. The latter demand a great musical culture, a subtle interpretation, which Mr. Dembitzer does not possess to any great degree.

Mrs. Til-Fogelgarn (Katowice) accompanied very subtly. It is evident that we are dealing with a pianist who has a brilliant command of the keyboard.

It was no easy task for the conductor, Mr. Barayka [sic; = Barowka], who managed within a bare 4 months to train a choir out of elements that had no notion of solfège — to the point that they can read music at sight. Only so capable a teacher as Prof. Barowka could have achieved this; he is, incidentally, very popular in Upper Silesia as the director of the most important choirs.

It is therefore desirable that the public should take more interest in so appealing a cultural phenomenon as the People's Choir, which — given normal development — can bring about the creation of a permanent musical public.

Sh. R.
The Life-Path of Great Men

Careers like tales from the Thousand and One Nights!
The fisherman — MacDonald.
In a small Scottish village Ramsay MacDonald, the present Prime Minister of England, was born. His parents were poor fishermen who could give their son neither food nor education.
When he grew up, a longing for a better life awoke in him: he wants to study. But where does one get money for it? His parents cannot give it to him.
Then he went to a neighbouring estate owner to dig potatoes. Half the day he would work and the other half of the day he would study; all the money he would spend on school supplies and books, and he himself always went about hungry and ragged. With great effort he managed to finish school; he went to London, where he attained the highest government post in England. He travelled the road from the poor fisherman's hut to the London government palace.
The shepherd — Teodor Masaryk.
Masaryk was born in a remote Slovak village; in his childhood he was the village shepherd. Early in the morning he would drive out the cattle, tend them a whole day in the meadow and bring them back. But at the same time Masaryk would buy books with his last groszy and study, and precisely because of that the cattle got lost more than once.
In the end the inhabitants of the village considered that they had no need of a scholar, and dismissed him.
Then he left the village and for long years wandered in hunger and want through various towns.
Today he is the President of the Czechoslovak Republic.
The beggar — Benito Mussolini.
In an Italian village Mussolini was born. His restless spirit pushes him out into the wide world. He wanders from village to village and begs from the peasants — a midday meal, a night's lodging; more than once gendarmes would detain him and take him off to prison for illegal begging, but Mussolini was not frightened.
He came to Geneva and moved in the circles of the socialist students. He lived on what the richer among them would toss him.
Now the man whom gendarmes used to arrest for begging is the Prime Minister and dictator of Italy.
The privy cleaner — Herbert Hoover.
In an American village an orphan was born. He was brought up by his poor relatives. He would do all the menial work in the house; among other things it fell to him to clean the privy in the yard where he lived.
But such work did not satisfy him. He dreamed of becoming an engineer; looking at the high mountains of his native region, he would say to his friends:
— One day I will still lay railway lines over the mountains.
— You will do it — his friends would laugh at him — first learn to clean the privy properly.
But little Herbert reached his goal, he became an engineer.
Now he is the President of the United States of America.
The shoemaker — Stalin.
In a small town in the Caucasus lived a Georgian shoemaker; he had a son whom he also wanted to make a shoemaker; he sat him down at the workbench and said:
— Work, my son; I am a shoemaker, be a shoemaker too.
But the son was not drawn to shoemaking; he wanted to become a priest. After truly superhuman efforts he managed to get into the theological seminary.
But the Greek [Orthodox] seminary was for him an antechamber to... the Bolshevik party.
Today he is the General Secretary of the Bolshevik party and the dictator of Soviet Russia.
The smith — Lloyd George.
When Lloyd George's parents died, he was still a child; a smith, a friend of his father, took him in as an apprentice.
But Lloyd George does not want to work; his master would beat him mercilessly and not give him food, but it did not help — he did not manage to stifle little Lloyd George's stormy spirit.
In secret from his master he would read books; when the master caught him at such "criminal" work, he would give him a good beating.
But he reached his goal and became one of the greatest politicians in England.
The coachman — Pierre Laval.
In a peasant cottage Laval was born. When he was twelve years old he became a coachman on a cart that every morning carried provisions into town; sitting on the coach-box he would study Cicero's speeches and do mathematical exercises, and precisely because of that his horses overturned the cart more than once.
He was dismissed from that job and left home to seek his fortune; he went through a whole hell before he achieved anything.
Now he is the Prime Minister of France.
• • •
This is the life-path of the greatest politicians of our time, who rose from the very lowest social rung to the highest.
Their careers sound like tales from the Thousand and One Nights.

The Sad Situation of the Melamdim of the Talmud Torah
Some weeks ago, when the starving melamdim [teachers] of the Talmud Torah stopped teaching, the Talmud Torah trustees undertook a relief campaign for this purpose. The campaign was organised with great noise and commotion. The best forces were mobilised, who appeared in the minyanim and shtiblekh with sermons, crying that „the Greeks[?] [i.e. the secularists] want to seize the Talmud Torah“...
At that time a rehabilitation committee was also created, with the task of finding means so that the existence of the important institution would be maintained.

Dr. Wolfgang von Weisl. (On his visit to Zagłębie).

As recently as 10 years ago he played a role in Vienna as ideologue of "Tzeirei Mizrachi". But when the latter had [unclear word] their ideology, Dr. Wolfgang von Weisl went over to the Revisionist camp.
As a man of enormous abilities he brought Zionism great benefit. Delegated by the 2 great newspapers "Neue Freie Presse" and "Vossische Zeitung" as correspondent in the Far[?] East, he published in the said newspapers a series of articles on England's anti-Zionist plans regarding Eretz Israel; every article was a real revolution, and it is no wonder that the world press reprinted the articles. In the same newspaper on which Herzl was a staff member and could not write about Zionism, Wolfgang von Weisl published over 60 articles on Zionism and on the development of Eretz Israel.
All this no doubt helped a great deal to propagate Zionism in the Western countries. Settling 7 years ago in Eretz Israel, Wolfgang von Weisl placed himself at the head of the Eretz Israel Revisionists, was editor of "Doar Hayom" and of "Haam", which was closed down by the English government because of his sharp articles against the English Mandatory power. During the events of Av [1929] Wolfgang von Weisl was the first to defend the honour of the Western Wall, where he was struck with a knife by an Arab and lay for over a year on his sickbed.
Dr. Wolfgang von Weisl left Eretz Israel half a year ago; he made a journey through the East and a number of countries in Europe. He has also published a book, "In the Struggle for the Holy Land", and is about to complete a scientific medical book.
Ben-Porat.
From Sport / Meeting of the Free-Loan Fund in Ząbkowice

[Będzin — sport; boxing.] For the first time the boxing section of Będzin's "Hakoach" appeared last Sunday, before a packed hall in the "Światowid" theatre, against the vice-champion of Poland "B.K.S."; the match ended 6:4 for "B.K.S."
The "Hakoach" boxers proved to be good material, but for the time being they are still too weak to come out against so strong an opponent.
Brumer, Patak and Gitler have the chance of becoming good boxers. But they must still train a lot, a great deal.
The Jewish boxers deserve special praise for their ambition. Such ambition in fighting is seldom seen in other boxers.
The course of the match was as follows:
In the first pair Brumer–Cimerman fought — both from "Hakoach". Brumer proved to be the better technician; he had the upper hand in all three rounds and also wins high on points.
Then the match proper begins. In the bantamweight Pois ("B.K.S.") meets Wajntrepau ("Hakoach"). In the first round Wajntrepau has a slight advantage. In the second round Wajntrepau, because of poor covering, takes a hard[?] blow to the jaw and loses by a "knock-out". In the featherweight[?] Biskup ("B.K.S.") met Werdiger ("Hakoach").
After a fairly interesting fight Werdiger, who in the third round was already completely exhausted, loses on points.
In the lightweight: Buchalik (B.K.S.), Gitler ("Hakoach"). Gitler too, who had the upper hand in the first round, loses the fight because he could not keep up the tempo in the remaining rounds. Gitler must pay more attention to his feet.
Then Fik (B.K.S) meets Patak ("Hakoach").
This fight was very interesting. Patak could have won the fight by a "knock-out" had he not kept wanting to clinch the opponent with his arms. In all three rounds Patak had a strong advantage; he was also technically much better than his opponent, and wins high on points.
In the welterweight: Gruszka (B.K.S.) — Moszkowicz (Hakoach). Moszkowicz was specially borrowed for this match from the Sosnowiec "Maccabi". This fight had a tragic course. In the first round Moszkowicz has a strong advantage. In the second round Moszkowicz takes a hard blow in a forbidden place, so that he is unable to fight on. Because of this the opponent is disqualified and Moszkowicz wins by "walk-over".
The referee, Mr. Kacyr — not energetic enough.
Next Sunday morning an interesting boxing match will take place in the "Światowid" theatre between the strong Katowice "Police Club" and "Hakoach" Będzin. This match has aroused great interest in Zagłębie sporting circles.
Shortly a large gymnastics festival (Turnfest), organised by the local "Maccabi", will take place in Sosnowiec. The festival promises[?] to be very interesting, because the champions of Poland Trichter, Steinitz and Perl, Mania[?] are taking part.

General Strike

[Zagłębie — general strike; coal mines.]
In the Zagłębie and Kraków coal mines.
The negotiations conducted between the industrialists and the workers' delegates concerning the plan to reduce wages were broken off on Wednesday afternoon.
On the morning of the same day the Central Workers' Union had addressed the Council of Industrialists by letter, demanding that the industrialists' claim be withdrawn; their answer was expected by midday.
At the same time a conference of delegates and shop stewards of the workers' unions was called.
Because the industrialists ignored the workers' union's letter, the conference adopted the following resolution:
„Those assembled at the conference on the 17th of this month resolve to proclaim a general strike, to begin on Thursday the 18th of this month at 6 o'clock in the morning.“
The news of the strike spread through Zagłębie with lightning speed.
Yesterday passed quietly. In the smaller coal mines work went on normally.
The strike committee has resolved that if, because of the industrialists' stubborn attitude, the strike is prolonged, every effort shall be made so that the strike breaks out, at least partly, in Upper Silesia as well.

Katowice National Activists and Their "Activity" for the Youth

[Katowice — Zionism and youth.] What have our gentlemen the Zionists in Katowice given the youth in the field of culture — that lawlessness grows among the youth from day to day.

If the Katowice Zionists gave a little thought to the Katowice Jewish youth movement in general and to its cultural condition in particular, their faces would turn red with shame; they would see that the youth, whom they have abandoned in the field of culture, is falling into an entirely different life...
The large youth, which in Katowice amounts to almost 50 percent of the general Jewish population, has no path, no ideal in life. Because there is no leader, no cultural educator, who would teach in the field of national consciousness. At present there is in Katowice not a single Zionist social premises (lokal) where the youth could live itself out culturally, and the result is that the youth falls into the night-clubs, into the dance-whirl of life, and again part of the youth goes away from us and enters the premises of communism, where ignorance and demoralisation grow.
For example, the German-Jewish youth has premises where cultural work is carried on at the so-called "Jugendbund", but their cultural work is far from the spirit of our nationalism.
And who is to blame for this? Yes, our gentlemen the General [?] Zionists in Katowice. They have lost all contact with the youth. They have for themselves the "B'nai B'rith lodge", where various topics are discussed, and the youth is left to the "shrim" [?] dance...
3 parties exist in 1 premises (in the Merchants' Association): that is the women's organisation "WIZO", which is led by Mrs. Halpern. Thanks to her strong will and energy, current lectures take place every week; then there exists a right-wing [—] [?] Zionist youth, where cultural courses take place twice a week; and the Revisionists under the leadership of the energetic Hebrew teacher Koralnik — it, however, is without youth...
3 [?] years ago there existed in Katowice a "HaTikva" organisation under the direction of Józef Weisberger; every day various lectures took place. The youth found itself in a warm milieu. But today Katowice is, in this field, a cemetery.
When the writer Yoel Machtboim [probably Joel Mastbaum] was in Katowice, he, together with the writer of these lines, took the initiative to create a cultural organisation in Katowice, and we began to work on the matter. But our gentlemen the General [?] Zionists did not show the necessary interest.
Therefore I appeal to the Katowice Zionists: remember that the youth is going away from our paths and falling into a swamp of demoralisation, and only you, gentlemen Zionists, bear the moral responsibility for the sad consequences for the youth, which is being lost in the "shrim" [?] dance in the night-clubs...
Huda Kaner.
Nine of them there were.

[Będzin — sketch, charity.] Picture a little scene.
In a house a wedding is taking place.
The piano plays klezmer, couples dance; in the other room, at the long table, people feast. It is wedding-merry.
Suddenly someone taps at the window. Silence falls. Who could be knocking so late?
— Let us in, Jews!
— Who is there?
— Let us in, outside the frost is burning!
— But who are you?
— Nine Jews are we; our teeth chatter in our mouths from the frost. Let us in!
— This is no hostel for wayfarers [hakhnosas orkhim].
— This is a wedding, we know. But we are no strangers; we are locals and we come precisely to you... only the door is locked...
— What do you want?
— We are collectors, nine collectors from nine societies.
Yes, nine collectors stood under the window: from Linas ha-Kholim, Hakhnosas Orkhim, Hakhnosas Kalo, Moshav Zkenim, Talmud Toyre, Beys Lekhem, Menakhem Aveylim, Ahavas Akhim, Malbish Arumim.
They go to all weddings and other celebrations, collecting small change for their institutions. But here the door was locked.
Inside they danced, feasted, sang, made merry. Outside the frost crackled, and the collectors stood, waited and...
dispersed.
Each one went off to his own institution to warm himself — — —
Arg.
—o—
Dreadful murder for robbery in Olkusz.
Last Friday the [—]3-year-old Piechowicz, owner of a sausage shop in Olkusz, was murdered.
Piechowicz received word that thieves were breaking into his ice cellar. P. at once went there with his workers to catch the thieves. But when he reached the spot he was met with revolver shots, from which P. fell dead on the spot.
The burglars were caught. Under strict guard they were taken to the Będzin prison.
The death penalty awaits them.
—o—
The Dąbrowa Jewish butcher shops will be furnished with "kosher signs".
The rabbi of Dąbrowa decided to introduce in the butcher shops, too, the same regulation as exists in Będzin, i.e. a butcher shop that is under the rabbi's supervision shall be furnished with a sign. Because, however, the rabbi intended to make restrictions in this matter, so that not every butcher would have the privilege of obtaining the kosher certificate, the butchers declared a strike.
In connection with this, on Tuesday at one [o'clock] [?] a meeting was held at the rabbi's with the participation of kehilla representatives and butchers. At the meeting the strike was liquidated, so that in all butcher shops where kosher meat is sold the "kosher signs" will be found.

The visit of Dr. Wolfgang von Weisl to Zagłębie.
On Thursday, Friday and Saturday the president of the Revisionist executive in Eretz Israel, Dr. Wolfgang von Weisl, stayed in Zagłębie. In his lectures on the theme "The decline of Jewry and Zionism", the speaker described the dreadful [?] situation of Jewry in Europe and the tasks of waging an open struggle against the Mandate power in order to obtain a Jewish majority in Eretz Israel.
On Saturday evening the distinguished guest spent several hours at the premises of the Będzin "WIZO", where he expounded in a splendid manner the state of general world politics.
—o—
An urgent campaign, in which the whole Jewish population of Sosnowiec must take an active part
We are in a situation where almost every day various fund-raising campaigns for various purposes are undertaken, but to the campaign of which we speak here one must take a different attitude, because it is an urgent matter which, unfortunately, touches every person, one sooner, another later; but in the end everyone's term falls due...
The campaign we are touching upon here consists in this: Jewish Sosnowiec no longer has a cemetery, and things have already come to the point that if, God forbid, a death should occur, the deceased would have to be taken to Będzin or elsewhere...
In connection with this situation a committee has been founded, which is already negotiating to buy a plot of land of 1500 pręty [Polish land measure] on very good terms.
The formal side has already been settled; now the fate of this important matter lies in the hands of the Jewish population, which must have its say in the fund-raising the committee is conducting.
Let the Jewish population of Sosnowiec understand the great responsibility it takes upon itself should the plot, God forbid, not be bought. That would be "a wrong that cannot be righted". Do not allow the disgrace that the Sosnowiec kehilla should have no cemetery, and let everyone who receives the contribution slip from the committee fulfil his duty at once.
—o—
Trumpeldor Academy in Dąbrowa.
This Saturday the "League for Labour Eretz Israel" in Dąbrowa is holding, at the premises of the "Folks-Hoyz" [People's House], a festive Trumpeldor academy devoted to the 12th yahrzeit of the fallen heroes of Tel Hai, with the participation of Mr. Yehuda Kopelowicz [?] (Eretz Israel), a former personal comrade of Joseph Trumpeldor, who together with him defended Tel Hai against the attacks in 1920.
Mr. Kopelowicz will describe in his lecture his personal experiences during the battles around Tel Hai, in which the hero Joseph Trumpeldor also fell.
The programme also includes stagings performed by the artist Mr. Lewensztajn, pioneer scenes and Eretz Israel songs performed by a specially rehearsed choir.
