[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
A Big Swindle at the Katowice Commercial Bank
A person appeared at the branch of the Commercial Bank (Handlowy Bank) in Katowice with 2 bills of exchange for 6 500 Dutch guilders, asking the bank to accept the bills for collection (incasso).
The bank accepted the bills for handling and sent them to an Amsterdam bank. After some time word was received from the Amsterdam bank that the bills had been redeemed and that a sum of 13.000 Dutch guilders had been credited to the Commercial Bank's account. On the strength of this notice the Commercial Bank paid out the whole sum to the person concerned. But a few days later the Commercial Bank received a notification that the bills were forged. In this way the Katowice Commercial Bank became the victim of the swindle.
—o—
Terrible Car Disaster.
Not far from Wielkie Strzelce [Groß Strehlitz?] a terrible car disaster occurred, which claimed human victims.
The car, in which the director of the insurance company of Stuttgart and the merchant Keller of Oppeln [Opole] were travelling, was, while going over the level crossing (przejazd), [hit] by[?] a train, which smashed the car and killed the director. The second passenger was seriously injured.
—o—
Disaster in a Coal Mine.
The fire in the „Gotthard“ coal mine has led to a great disaster.
At a depth of 450 metres the accumulated gases exploded and the mine was engulfed in flames that shot upward.
Fortunately the workers saved themselves through a side exit.
A rescue operation was undertaken at once. As reported, the fire in the mine will continue for another 7 days.
The damage is colossal.
Because of the fear of new explosions the mine will have to be closed for several months.
1590[?] workers lose their jobs.
In the „Nikisz“ coal mine too an explosion broke out; 1 worker was killed and 7 workers were injured.
—o—

The director of the Friedenshütte [Huta Pokój] informed the demobilisation commissioner that in the present situation the works cannot employ all the workers, and 2,100 men must be cut.

Film „Stars“ and „Starlets“[?] Sue the Director of „Empe-Film“.
At the Katowice District Court the trial took place against the director of the film school „Empe Film“ in Katowice.
The director was sued by his male and female pupils, who had longed to become „film greats“[?] and had paid a hundred zł. tuition fee for it.

The “Opportune Moment” (Shaat ha-Kosher).

We do not write about the Jewish communities in general, and about the Będzin one in particular; we do not write — not because there is nothing to write about; we do not write because everything is rotten through and through, sick. We do not react to the most disgusting deeds, to the most ridiculous episodes and to the most comical phenomena that are played out before our eyes.
It is a rule that when some institution or other is criticised, that is the best sign that, at the worst, there is something useful, something desirable[?] there. Worse is when one does not dwell on an institution at all. Then one knows that it does not exist, or need not exist, for society, and that the public need not concern itself with it.
When an institution reaches this sad state, society stops taking an interest in it, does not pay the monthly[?] few-groszy[?] contribution, and that is the best sign that it does not exist for the public and thus becomes dead for public opinion and for the broad masses, with whom a public institution must, willy-nilly[?], reckon.
So it is with all sorts of our public institutions. Quite different, however, is the situation with regard to our kehillas, already in that we must maintain them whether we want to or not. Whether it is sympathetic or antipathetic to us — there we must pay; and therefore it must not be assumed, since we pay the tax with which we have been burdened by our kehilla representatives, that the institution is sympathetic to us and that we regard it with appreciation. We pay because we must; we pay because a yoke[?] has been laid upon us.
It goes without saying that none of this is news. Every one of us knows how degraded, in the eyes of the public, the kehilla representation has become — the body that should have occupied the top place in our Jewish world and should have been the tone-setter for the Jewish citizens.
What is vexing, and what truly hurts, is only this: that, dragging itself through the deep swamp, it not only does not want to scramble out of it, but does the most inhuman deeds and the most incomprehensible acts, so as to sink ever deeper, down to the abyss.
It is characteristic that in last week's issue of our paper we come across a notice telling us that the light was cut off there, i.e. there is no longer anything to pay the few guilders for lighting. It would seem that the honour of our kehilla representation has fallen far enough when one has to speak of such trifles, of such absurdities. But that is nothing yet. That is not yet all; worse is when one does not see and does not feel the shame, when one accepts the most degrading absurdities as understandable, healthy deeds, without which one cannot manage, without which one cannot exist.
And it is interesting that in the same issue, and even on the same page, we also see a second notice, which tells us neither more nor less than that means and ways are being sought for smuggling in a fifth shochet. Well, is this understandable? Do these people know what is happening to them? Do they give themselves any account whatsoever of their unheard-of deeds? Has such a liquidation — or, better said, such lawlessness — ever been heard of? Have we anywhere been shown[?] that as soon as an enterprise does not prosper as it should, when it cannot cover its expenses and there is no income even for the staff, one should then come and enlarge the staff further and create still more expenses? Is that understandable? Is it possible to grasp? Is it done with sound, logical reason? But about this nobody will doubt. Every one of us knows, after all, that combinations are being made here, that here one is waiting for an “opportune moment” in order to smuggle in someone who needs a livelihood.
We do not want now to enter into debates on whether Będzin needs another shochet, although everyone knows perfectly well that this expense is as useful as the fifth wheel on a wagon. We therefore only want to ask those concerned: if they will reckon with nothing except the young fellow who, poor thing, needs a livelihood, then the question arises — is now really the “opportune moment” for smuggling in new officials, at a time when the employees are starving and every Monday and Thursday the office furniture of the Jewish kehilla is being seized? Is this not more than lawlessness, more than indifference, more than helplessness? What can one call this? What name does one give such a behind-the-scenes manoeuvre? Will Jewish Będzin really not hold anyone responsible for the unheard-of deeds that are to be committed precisely in the present bitter time? True, a Jew needs a livelihood, and it would surely, surely have been a mitzvah to do him a favour; but is this Jew such a rarity? Are there today so few Jews for whom one would need to provide a livelihood? And if so, if this Jew is not unique, why should he be exempted from the rule?
After all, we know what Jewish livelihoods look like now, how bitter the Jewish situation is and how terrible the Jewish poverty. Perhaps these persons would have taken upon themselves the initiative of helping the Jewish people (Klal Yisrael), surely through the Jewish kehilla, if they understood that it is so strong and so healthy — on the contrary, nobody would have been against that; but the public is against the crooked [lit. “left-handed”] smuggling, calculated on combinations and on secret agreements.
(Whom does one want to “do favours” for — individuals or the public? — What do the veiled secrets look like?)
It will on no account be permitted that ever heavier burdens be loaded onto the weak kehilla-nag, regardless of the fact that even now it cannot drag itself along.
Possibly the calculation is this: who knows what may yet happen in these times; possibly we will not be at the helm — so let us leave them “last money”[?]; let the new ones come to an ever bigger budget and an ever bigger deficit; let them have a wheel to turn that will not come easy to them. One knows, after all: when a nail is knocked in, it sits firm and nobody will be able to move it any more; and if not[?] — as soon as they do hold on, that is surely, surely good; perhaps[?] one will have as many of one's own people as possible and will surely be able to count[?] on the favour. Possibly one wants to exploit this very “opportune moment”?
It is a well-known thing that nowadays the public is not reckoned with, that whoever rides the horse does what he wants and as he pleases. But still, still there must be a limit to everything; every thing must after all have some calculation or other — not a logical one or indeed a logical one, not a well-founded one or indeed a well-founded one — but one must have something; some basis or other must in any case exist. And what do we see here, in this combining tactic? We come up against nothing but incomprehensibilities, mysterious, veiled secrets, to which no ordinary mortal (basar va-dam) can get through, and for a simple person it is a kind of “sorcery-wheel” to which the broad strata of the population have no access.
But be that as it may, and whatever pretences may be made to blind the eyes of the citizens of Będzin, one must nevertheless dwell on the unheard-of, grave, critical situation in which the citizens find themselves today. One must consider: is anyone whosoever permitted, at such hard moments, to make the situation harder for the Jewish people only because one wants to do someone or other a favour — or perhaps one is after something more?
In any case we have the right to demand accountability from the people who do not reckon with the public, regardless of the fact that they themselves are living witnesses and have the opportunity to see how hard the situation of the Jew is, with what self-sacrifice and by what miracles he survives each day.
And therefore we say that those who lend a hand to worsening the internal Jewish situation, those who do it consciously, even covertly, preparing excuses for later — they remain responsible and shall be held[?] to their word for their future deeds.
R. Let.

Don't forget to stamp your invoices.
For several days there has been a bit of a stir among the merchants because the tax office (Finanzamt) has suddenly begun carrying out inspections.
Officials visit offices, shops, workshops and private offices, as well as local-government offices, and carry out a thorough inspection of all invoices, checking whether they have been duly stamped.
In cases where unstamped invoices are found, fines of 10 and 20 times are imposed.
Because many merchants do not keep proper books, many unstamped invoices are found with them.
Many persons have already received penalty notices.
Heard and Seen.

[Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton; Sosnowiec.] By Ben Amotz.

The hands are the hands of Jacob...
The humanity of this century makes constant progress. New cultures are[?] created, new movements, which "beautify" and "modernize" the new life and change the old dogmas that "darkened" human life for thousands of years...
Here[?], for example, we always believed that "the voice is the voice of Jacob and the hands are the hands of Esau"; consequently we Jewish [—] were afraid of Esau's hands and hated with utmost hatred the bestiality[?] and bloodthirstiness that we see among all other peoples.
When a Jew walking in the street saw one child attack another child, he hurried to put an end to the fight. Many times it happened that Jews broke up fights among gentiles[?]...
But what "follies" existed in those "dark" times, when culture still lay in swaddling clothes, when Hasidic young men [—] tore[?] themselves over the difficult sugyot of Abaye and Rava, when romantic youth devoured every new work[?], when humanity debated ideals, which concepts, principled opinions about philosophical systems...
Today, however, in the "epoch of culture and civilization", when the whole[?] [—] [—] [—], new "cultures", new people are created, they too prove that — "the hands are the hands of Jacob"...
The hall of the "Światowid" cinema is packed full, not only with young people but also with older people, who, as they themselves explain, have come to see how a boxing match takes place. "I have come," my neighbour tells me, "for the first time to see how people box; my son gives me to understand that boxing is nowadays the hit sport in Europe, and 'when a [—] manages to land one on somebody's jaw, it is truly a delight to watch...'"
The match begins.
The referee signals[?], the seconds prepare buckets of water and "empty buckets for blood". The fighting area is fenced with ropes (apparently so that if one of the fighters rolls over, he should not fall off the stage...)
A signal is heard, and they begin to hit; like roosters[?] they leap at one another, and whoever is "stronger" (here one truly sees that the hands are the hands of Esau...) deals a heavy blow, until the opponent falls...
But with that the vanquished has not yet done his duty. Immediately he receives refreshments, is sent back into the fight, and after taking several[?] blows to his face he loses consciousness and falls again...
Such a procedure must be gone through as many as 3 times; then the referee declares that the "avodah" and the "korim" [as in the Yom Kippur service] are finished... and the spectators applaud "bravo" — (naturally, from the winner's side).
In truth, I confess that I was the only one who applauded with all my strength, most vigorously. In great ecstasy my imagination carried me all the way to Spain, where I became acquainted with the ceremonies held on the national holidays, during the bullfight...
And a feeling of consolation came over me: blessed be the twentieth century, which has raised humanity to a new era, to a bright future and to the new epoch of
— the hands are the hands of Jacob...

The power of will...
In the cheap kitchen in Sosnowiec.
On entering, at first I could not believe that I was at the right address. A small room filled with thick steam, so that it is impossible to see one another... I only hear how the ladies, who are toiling to get the lunch ready, ask the cook whether the food is ready yet, because the doors[?] of the kitchen are already being stormed by the guests.
I run out of breath, I flee out of that inferno... How can people — I ask the proprietor of the premises — endure such bad conditions?
"If one wants to, one can," the gospodarz [manager] of the "Maccabi" premises answers me. "Do you know who the woman is who cut the hundreds of portions of bread? That is the wife of Dr. Jungster. Every day, at 8 o'clock in the morning, she comes here to work in such conditions until 2 o'clock in the afternoon, and often even later...
"She is a woman of tremendous energy; true, she also[?] has helpers, first of all Mrs. Dr. Grudzińska[?], who registers the poor, and afterwards they are sent here into the kitchen; also Mrs. Dr. Mittelman, Mrs. Binder, Mrs. Kleiner and others. But the soul of the kitchen is Mrs. Jungster."
Yes — I agree — these[?] women have surely never before gone through such hard kitchen work; but if that energy were used in other fields, perhaps we would have been spared from opening cheap kitchens...
We possess enough people with great capabilities, but in normal circumstances one does not see them; they have withdrawn from the field of social obligation, and in them has congealed[?]
— the power of will...

Sound the alarm...
He comes into the editorial office with a demand:
"Sound the alarm!"
"About what matter?" we ask.
"About the new fashion, about skating..."
Well, if we parents provide this pleasure for our children, it can still be understood; it has some connection with sport, with physical development; but when mothers of children take up the craft, the newspaper must not be silent and must come out
— with an alarm...
"What do you mean? Speak plainly..."
And he pours out his bitter heart to us.
"Recently," he says, "coming home for lunch, I find my missus angry; every word that comes out of her mouth is a lump of fire, every glance — a grenade...
"I thought to myself: if it were the month of May now, I would have taken the 'spasms' as a preparatory lesson regarding the dacha [summer house], but we are only now in the real frosty winter — what can it be?
"'What is the matter?' I ask cautiously. 'Something wrong with everyone[?]? Perhaps call a doctor?'
"'What? Doctors, for me of all people? [unclear phrase, possibly Polish]... I need something else that will improve my health.'
"'What?'
"'A pair of foreign skates...'"
"Well?" we ask.
"You ask what the end is? Come to my home and you will see how my wife lies with a sprained foot; her sufferings are indescribable, but I may not say a loud word. I have only come to you so that you should do something about it — that in the newspaper you should
— sound the alarm..."
The Twelfth Hour Has Already Struck for Polish Jewry!

Let us take a moral lesson from our German brethren

German Jewry has taken a step which ought also to serve as a model for the Jews of other countries, especially for Polish Jewry.
The growth of antisemitism in Germany, the intensified anti-Jewish agitation conducted by the Hitlerites, has forced German Jewry, without distinction of tendency or conviction, to seek common means of defence. Without long arguments and debates a conference was held in Berlin on 1 February with the participation of the most important Jewish organizations in Germany, headed by the "Central-Verein". And at this very conference a working community (Arbeitsgemeinschaft) for the economic questions of the Jews in Germany was founded. This is a body which, with united forces, will seek and perhaps actually find practical means of alleviating [?] Jewish economic distress through planned action and occupational restructuring. Special experts have been drawn into the working community.
Already at the first conference a work programme was adopted. Thus, for example, it was decided to establish permanent contact both with employers and with employees of all branches of the economy, in order to ascertain the prospects for Jews.
The question of expanding the Jewish employment-agency system was also discussed. It is not merely a matter of placement, but also of finding and creating new jobs. A centralized employment office for Jewish university graduates will be created. At the next session the project of how to combat economic bankruptcy will be discussed. A plan was also outlined for creating public means for productive Jewish economic work (credit cooperatives, colonization, etc.).
We see that German Jewry, at a moment of general danger, understood how to set aside all internal differences of opinion and to find a common language and a joint platform in order to fight — more correctly, in order to defend itself — against the external enemy.
In German Jewry various tendencies fight one another, just as in Polish Jewry. Especially sharp and bitter is the struggle between the Zionists and the assimilationist "Central-Verein". But German Jewry possesses culture and has an understanding of the needs and commandments of the hour. They understood that at the present moment, when the whole of Jewry in Germany is in danger of losing all its political, cultural and above all economic positions, one must set aside all internal differences and march united. And they immediately turned this understanding into a fact. The working community has already been created; it already exists.
Here in Poland, where the economic situation of Jewry is incomparably worse than in Germany, and where the process of ousting it from its economic positions has been going on for a number of years and has lately been especially sharp, people at most discharge their duty by tossing out [?], once in a blue moon, such an idea, by voicing the wish to create a concentration of all Polish Jewry, at least on the economic front — a wish which, however, remains a mere wish that nobody takes seriously.
Is it not high time that we too should proceed immediately to create such a working community and, at a moment of common danger, at least go a stretch of the road together?
The example of Germany must serve us as a model not only in this respect, that in the present hour of danger we must go together, but in that we must immediately give form to the idea of a united economic front of all Polish Jewry and at once set about creating this front.
The clock has truly already struck twelve for Polish Jewry. One cannot wait any longer, and one must not.
Ben Moshe.
Heaven, Earth and "Rumba".

(A little feuilleton).

"Rumba!" —
You are surely amazed: what have I, Paltiel Yosl Apteyre, whose head and day are not enough to deal with the bills of exchange, protests, prolongations, little interest-free loans, trade patents, advances [?], taxes, distraints with [—?], what has a Jew like me to do with the new dance "Rumba" — hush, hush, why do you stare at me with such a pair of eyes? One of these days you will have to put in the paper that a Jew, God save us, hanged himself because of the "Rumba".
Day and night, without stop and without pause, there is "rumba-ing" only in your [sic; read: my] home: my sons with the daughters and with a couple of gallants who come to see them keep on studying the difficult doctrine of the "Rumba", and even my wife with the mother-in-law [?] have already caught this it's-heaven-earth-and-"Rumba".
My head is so dizzy from this new article that I am really bewildered. And so I had to write to a soap manufacturer in Częstochowa to send me a few boxes of soap — I wrote that he should send me a few boxes of rumba.
The fellow thought I was making fun of him. He answered that he had already come to an understanding with the hospital administration that they should reserve a bed for me in the lunatic ward.
Well, how do you like that? Soon I won't be able to show my face in the street.
I come home. A fine young fellow sits there, strumming on a stick — supposedly it's a fiddle — and both my daughters are spinning around the middle of the room, making strange movements with their hands and feet, wiggling — pardon the expression — their bellies, and similar crazy impudences[?].
So of course I get angry:
— Your father barely crawls along on his belly [barely makes a living], and you have to wiggle your bellies as well!
— What do you mean, papa, this is a symphony of movements, it's “rumba”.
— A great find you've hit upon, it's “rumba”; as if your father brought home at least 5 gulden every night.
So I slam the door and run into the kitchen — and there, a real calamity!
My wife stands with a “wiecheć”[?] [dish-rag] in one hand and a little pot in the other, turning around the kitchen and humming: tidl-ridl, lidl-zidl, rumba, rumba!
And I have to sit down and do a bit of accounting — not how much, God forbid, I earned, but how much I put in out of my own pocket. I walk straight into the tiger's mouth: I decide to go in to my mother-in-law in the little room[?].
And there is my mother-in-law warming herself by the stove, knitting a sock and humming to herself to a tune from the “Teitsh-Khumesh”: rumba, rumba, rumba, rumba.
You might as well pack up and run away from home.
And so it goes, day in, day out, from early morning till late at night.
And I'm afraid I'll now have a court case on my hands as well, because I had to issue someone a bill of exchange [weksel]. I was so confused that instead of “Płatil[?] Josel Aptajde[?]” I signed “Płatil Josel Rumba”.
I'm sure I'll yet have a case for a forged “podpis” [signature].
Not-rumba'd be they — tfu[?], I mean: not-to-be-mentioned be they [“nisht gedakht”]!
Ploni ve-Khehi (So-and-So). — To Be Reincarnated as a Goy.

[Feuilleton — reflection; the Jews and the Christian world in the crisis.]
Do you know, Jews, what I would like today? I would like to die for one single hour and be reincarnated as a goy, l'havdil...
But don't goggle your eyes, don't shrug your shoulders and don't rush to pronounce that I have either gone out of my mind, become a hater of Israel, or crawled off the Jewish path.
This notion does not come, God forbid [?], from madness, nor from youthful bravado [?], heaven preserve us [?]. It [?] comes [?] precisely from a genuinely Jewish sentiment.
You see, lately I have been going around with an embittered heart. I am bitter, agitated, boiling against the goyim — and not simply because they are goyim and serve the God in whom they believe, God forbid! There is no Jew in the world who would be such a fanatic; on the contrary, every Jew is in his essence steeped in the sublime prophetic liberalism of 'let every man walk in the name of his god.' None of us cares that others go in the ways of other faiths. Let them go in good health. You have the proof [?]: we have never engaged in soul-snatching and never chased after converts. Many of us go even further and display a far greater 'liberalism' — they do not even seek to bring Jews back to Judaism. They do not care at all [?] about the souls of their own children...
So, at least on the first point, I am no different from all Jews. The goyishness of the goyim does not bother me in the least.
What then? I am angry at them quite simply because lately they have sat down far too heavily on my years and on the years of the whole of Israel. For it is not enough that we suffer more than enough from the general depression — they also seek to devour us, to press and choke us and to make our existence literally impossible.
And I say 'they' without making any exception, because one does not see and does not hear now a single goy with the countenance of a Righteous Gentile — a goy who would come forward as our defender, who would raise his voice against the Endek [Polish National Democrat] wickedness, against Hitlerite antisemitism and against the whole antisemitic bacchanalia.
Well, I was on the point of reaching the conclusion that the whole non-Jewish world is wicked through and through, that all non-Jews are far from being righteous.
But right in the middle I remembered the stern warning of our ancient sages: 'Judge not your fellow' — that is: do not judge your fellow until you stand on the same place-of-circumstances on which he stands. But this I have always considered an absolute impossibility, for how can one stand on the same place where someone else stands?... There, on the little patch of ground where his feet stand, your feet surely cannot stand. The matter is clear, isn't it? What then — there is no choice left but to crawl right into him [—], and only then, when you are completely melted into him, into that 'fellow,' will you stand exactly where he stands.
And for this very reason a desire awoke in me to die for a while and be reincarnated as a goy, to crawl into his psychology boots and all, to weave my 'I' into his, and in this way to place myself on the same standpoint where he stands.
And I want it precisely now, because it seems to me that never — not even in the [?] time of the war — has the rottenness of Christian civilization revealed itself as it does today.
Whatever you may say about us Jews — certainly we are no angels either. Of the ten measures of egoism that came down to the earth, we too took a share. We have not renounced it altogether, truth is truth; but we become egoists especially when we grow too fat in the feathers, when fortune begins to smile on us too strongly. As you say: 'Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked.' When Israel grows fat, his heart becomes overlaid with fat and he ceases to feel the other, the lean one...
But when that same Israel is struck, may it not happen to anyone, by emaciation and begins to suffer want, his Jewish heart begins to feel and to feel with those who suffer more than he. In short, 'poverty becomes Israel' — poverty and troubles suit the Jew, that is, they make him a finer human being, they bring out in him the finest traits of his stock, of his people.
The Christians, however — for their egoism there is apparently no cure at all. They oppress you when they are fat and do the same when they are lean. Poverty suits them just as vilely as wealth.
Just look, out of curiosity, at today's situation. The crisis rages literally like a plague, may it not happen here. The further it goes, the deeper it gets into everyone's bones. Everyone suffers, everyone is tormented — not only the unemployed and the truly poor, but even those who are for the time being sated and rich; they are tormented by the fear that any moment now the heavy wheel will reach them too and run them over as well.
At such a moment one might at least have expected that human feeling would quiver, that the heart would soften a little, and that the great common misfortune, the general world catastrophe, would awaken an urge to draw closer to one another — people to people, race to race — that they would begin to huddle together and seek jointly to protect themselves from the common enemy; for even animals forget at such moments their old instinctive grievances and huddle together...
But with them it does not even begin. Every Monday and Thursday they have travelled together, they hold [?] conferences and supposedly seek to save themselves. But no practical result comes of it, because every conferee [?] has only one thing in mind — himself and himself. Everyone wants to save only his own skin; the other's worry does not interest him in the slightest [lit. does not lie in his left heel]. And as a matter of course [?] all of them lie in poverty [?].
Is this not simply stupidity and idiocy? Whatever you may say — the nations concerned are not idiots. At least the better among them have culture, have science, have wisdom. But the trouble lies in their savage egoism. It is against their nature to care truly and sincerely about the fate of others. So far is it against their nature that one is ready [?] to tear out one of one's own eyes, so long as the other loses both eyes...
But in spite of all this they go about boasting of 'Christian civilization' and of Christian love.
I begin to think that perhaps it is so because I look at them through my Jewish spectacles. Perhaps all of us, children of Israel, have a twisted logic, and that is why it comes out to us that everything we see in the non-Jewish world is twisted and crooked and full of strange distortions?
Who knows, perhaps we are the crooked ones of the earth, and all the other nations are the straight ones, and what seems to us their crookedness toward us is in truth as straight as happiness [?] itself?
Perhaps it is indeed straight to shout with the mouth: love, love — and with the heart to hate like death everything that is not 'I,' that is not my own body?...
That is why I would like for a while to be reincarnated as a goy and to grasp the art of [—] and to love people with the tongue and [—] with all the fibres of the soul...
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (12)

[Serialized historical novel — Tsarist Russia, Rasputin; installment 12.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Hearing his voice, I recognized him. Why, this is the one who saved my life. And I cry out: "I recognize you! Why, it was you who rescued me from certain death near Pokrovskoye [printed "Pakrovski"]! Why, you are the "holy" Grisha!" He was very glad to see me and said: "And I wear on my neck the gift you gave me. Your gift is very dear and precious to me." It immediately occurred to me: God himself has sent the "holy miracle-worker" to Petersburg now, when the imperial court needs his help so badly. It is already the fourth day that the "naslednik" [Russian: heir to the throne] is ill. He suffers terrible pains and the professors cannot help him. I believe with all my heart that the "holy man" from Siberia, with the divine power he possesses, will make the "naslednik" well.. This very day I will bring the "starets" [Russian: holy elder] into the court, and I am sure that he will help the sick boy.
Vyrubova fell silent. She lightly wrinkled her brow and her eyes shone with triumph. Apart from believing that the Siberian muzhik was a "holy man" and capable of working miracles, she had a particular aim in this: for a long time already there had been a quiet mutual hatred between her and Archimandrite Feofan, and each intrigued against the other. The archimandrite, who regarded Vyrubova as a sinful woman and a friend of the Jews [printed "and a fo' a friend"], whom he hated, had tried from time to time to influence the Tsarina to have her removed from the court. Vyrubova in turn sought to weaken the archimandrite's influence and, if possible, to get rid of him altogether. Until now she had not succeeded. But now she was certain that by bringing a new "holy man" into the court she would be able to accomplish it: she believed that Grigori Rasputin would help the "naslednik". Through this he would win the Tsarina's trust and would take the place of Archimandrite Feofan... In this way she would be rid of the one who intrigued against her. And Rasputin in turn would be eternally grateful to her and would never forget that it was she who had brought him into the court.
Sonia broke the silence and asked:
— Forgive me, Anna Vyrubova! So you think it is not necessary to see Archimandrite Feofan?
Vyrubova answered with certainty:
— Absolutely not necessary... His influence at court will be cut off this very day. I am almost certain that tomorrow at this time Feofan will have been removed from the court. A greater power will take his place... But for the time being this must remain a secret... You understand, Sonia Oskarovna [printed "Oskarova"]?
— Of course I understand — Sonia nodded her head.
Vyrubova glanced at the clock, stood up at once and said:
— You will excuse me, Sonia Oskarovna!
That meant that the visit was over, and Sonia too rose from her seat.
On taking leave Vyrubova pressed Sonia's hand in a friendly way, thanked her warmly for the beautiful flowers and assured her once again that there was nothing more to fear from Feofan's agitation against the Jews; that this very evening the archimandrite's influence at the imperial court would be finished; that a new, greater power was coming today which would take his place, and tomorrow at this time Feofan would already be completely removed from the court.
— In any case — Vyrubova concluded — wait a day or two... If one does have to see someone after all, it will not be the archimandrite but another... And with that other — Sonia Oskarovna — I will be able to bring you together.
Sonia understood that by the word "other" she meant the Siberian muzhik, and she again felt fear in her heart at the thought that she might have to meet him...
Sonia thanked Vyrubova for her friendliness and left her. Coming out of the palace, she at once got into the carriage that was waiting for her and ordered the coachman to drive as fast as possible. She was hurrying to get home to her father, who was surely waiting for her with the greatest impatience, and [printed "in"] to tell him that Archimandrite Feofan was about to fall and lose his influence at the imperial court...
* * *
When the banker, Mr. Dimenshtein, entered the Great Synagogue of Petersburg, he already found a large crowd of Jews assembled there. Those gathered stood in little circles and talked quietly among themselves. Their faces were serious and worried. Everyone felt that some great calamity was approaching the Jews, that a harsh decree was about to descend on the Jewish inhabitants of the capital. They felt it with their Jewish instinct, although most of those gathered did not know exactly what it was about.
Mr. Dimenshtein went up to the eastern wall, where Baron Tsinberg [?] [so printed; later "Tsunberg"] and the city rabbi were sitting. He greeted them and sat down next to them.
The baron asked quietly:
— What's new? Is there any news, Mr. Dimenshtein?
Unfortunately there is no news at all for the moment — the banker answered. — The situation is the same as it was. The "naslednik" is still no better, and the Jew-haters are not keeping quiet; they are straining their forces and want to exploit this against the Jews by every possible means. The danger is great..
The city rabbi asked:
And your daughter, Mr. Dimenshtein? She wanted to see someone, didn't she?
— My daughter has driven off to Vyrubova. I believe that this lady-in-waiting, with whom my Sonia is on good terms, will help her get to Archimandrite Feofan.
— And I fear — said the baron — that the whole effort to get to the archimandrite is a futile one.
— Why do you think so, Mr. Baron? — the banker asked.
Because, as it seems to me, nothing will help to soften the archimandrite's heart. Today I met with a highly placed person with whom I am friendly, and as I learned from him, the archimandrite is a fierce enemy of the Jews, and nothing will move him to stop his agitation against the Jews...
The banker gave a slight shrug of his shoulders and made no reply at all to this. For a while all three stood silent, and there was great worry on their faces. They felt that they were powerless and that there was no way to avert the decree approaching all the Jews, unless some miracle were to happen... The baron raised his eyes and looked over the great crowd of Jews gathered in the synagogue. There were Jews there of all classes and strata. There were rich and poor, distinguished personalities and simple artisans. And he thought with pain: who knows what will happen to all these Jews in a day or two? Who knows what lies ahead of them? It is quite possible that all these Jews will be driven out of the city like outcasts, with wives and children; that they will be driven by gendarmes and have to wander lonely and crushed along the roads, seeking a night's shelter for their exhausted bodies. When the baron thought this, his heart contracted with pain and pity, and he sighed heavily.
Then the rabbi spoke up:
— Let us nevertheless not lose our hope. Let us hope to God that He will not forsake us and will help us... It is not the first time that danger hangs over Jewish heads. Jews are already used to great dangers. Many times already we have found ourselves in great troubles, and it seemed that no help would come from anywhere, and nevertheless God helped and we escaped from the troubles. Let us then now too rely on God, and He will help us. My heart tells me that God will not forsake us, that His help will come at the right time.
In the synagogue it suddenly became very quiet; the crowd began to move silently. It was exactly twelve o'clock, when the divine service had been set, and into [printed "in in"] the synagogue came the Petersburg gradonachalnik [Russian: city governor] accompanied by two of his adjutants. The crowd made way for them, and they — jingling their spurs — approached the eastern wall, where the notables [printed "der pney"] of Petersburg Jewry sat.
They came up to the place where the baron, the banker and the city rabbi [printed "shtot-ros" [?]] were sitting. These stood up. The gradonachalnik greeted them politely and said:
— I reckon we can begin now.
— We are beginning at once — the baron answered.
The rabbi with the gabbaim, among whom were Baron Tsunberg [so printed] and the banker Dimenshtein, as well as the gradonachalnik with his two adjutants, all went up onto the bimah. The shamashim lit many candles, and a festive, divine mood came over the synagogue. The assembled Jews became very quiet, stood with bated breath, with agitated faces and eyes, and in everyone's heart there was fear.. The presence of the gradonachalnik had struck dread into everyone..
Two Torah scrolls were taken out of the Holy Ark and brought up onto the bimah. The rabbi wrapped himself in a tallit; his face was radiant and pale; he turned to those assembled and called out in a pious voice:
— We have gathered here in the synagogue in order to pray for the health of the heir to the throne.. We are all very worried that our "naslednik" is ill, and from the depths of our hearts we will ask our God to send him a cure at once and that he should recover, for we all wish him health and long years...
After the rabbi had said this, the baron gave a short speech. His speech was patriotic and expressed Jewish loyalty to the Tsar and his heir [printed "Tronfolger"]. The baron understood quite well that everything he would say here would be passed on to "the high windows" [so printed; i.e. to the highest circles]. Indeed one could notice how one of the gradonachalnik's adjutants held a notepad and wrote down everything he heard — and the baron was therefore very careful with every word he uttered. He intended his words to make a good impression and hoped in this way to avert from the Jews the decree that was being prepared [?] against them.
The baron had a warm Jewish heart, cared deeply for his community, and now he spoke with a force that could have an effect. He spoke of how the Jews are devoted and faithful to the country in which they find rest and protection [printed "rest in protection"], that Jews are grateful for everything that is done for them, and that the Jews are very worried about the health of the naslednik. In the name of all Jews he sent his blessings to the Tsar and to the heir to the throne and said: the Jews are faithful, devoted subjects, and we will all now pray for the health of our "naslednik" [printed "naslidnik"].
(To be continued).
Now One Travels Free to the Leipzig Fair

[Leipzig — economy and trade; the international fair.] By Z. Haber, Leipzig.

In former times a journey to the Leipzig fair was quite a difficult affair; people used to drag themselves there in little carts over bad roads. Later, of course, it became easier. Merchants who ran larger businesses knew that they had to travel to the Leipzig Messe, because there they would become acquainted with all the newest goods, with the manufacturers and with all kinds of merchants, and they would have the opportunity to revive their businesses.
Today — in the time of the most severe economic crisis — a journey to the Leipzig fair has again become a very difficult and important matter, although the journey to Leipzig is itself very easy. One travels there by luxury trains and by aeroplanes, but one small thing is missing — the expenses of the journey... Many merchants, who know very well that in Leipzig they could find new articles to trade in, good agencies, cheap goods, find it hard today to lay out money on expenses; it is not easy "to lay the living upon the dead" [idiom: to risk real money on an uncertain thing], to spend money and travel to look for something. Perhaps one will not find what one needs, perhaps it will not pay...
The Leipzig Fair Office [Messeamt] has therefore hit upon a new invention: it refunds the expenses of the trip to Leipzig and back, according to how much one buys at the Leipzig fair.
The fair office has arranged [?] with all the exhibitors that they pay one percent of their takings into the fund. From that percent the fair office refunds the travel expenses of all merchants who show that they have bought at the Leipzig fair.
Everyone who wants to go to Leipzig receives from the Leipzig fair representative in his district a card, on which the exhibitors confirm how much he has bought; on this card one gets the travel expenses back in Leipzig.
Besides this, everyone receives the fair catalogue free of charge. The catalogue contains some eight thousand addresses of the exhibitors with all kinds of their goods.
Listed there are 850 manufacturers of metal goods, household and kitchen utensils; 650 manufacturers of glass and porcelain, 600 manufacturers of furniture and lamps, 800 manufacturers of leather goods and travel articles, 600 manufacturers of gold and silver objects and of all kinds of jewellery, 800 manufacturers of toys and sports articles, thousands of manufacturers of paper, writing articles, pictures, books and advertising articles, seven hundred manufacturers of textile goods, a hundred manufacturers of musical instruments, three hundred manufacturers of chemical and cosmetic articles, 150 manufacturers of photographic articles, some two hundred manufacturers of chocolate and the like. All these articles are exhibited in 37 palaces in the city itself.
In addition, machines and apparatus of all kinds, from the smallest to the largest, will be exhibited in eighteen halls and on the grounds around the halls; the catalogue lists some sixteen hundred such firms.
Apart from this, larger nations will exhibit in Leipzig in their own pavilions: Soviet Russia, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Italy, France, Spain, Japan, Canada, India, Denmark and Turkey, which will show there what these countries have produced in the past year. The English government too will exhibit there the produce of its lands, probably also from the Land of Israel.
The catalogue, which always cost two dollars, will now be obtainable free, so that buyers should have no special expenses at the Leipzig fair.
One sees, then, that the Leipzig Fair Office has found new methods of attracting as many customers as possible to the Leipzig fair, and will refund to everyone who buys something at least part of his expenses, in order in this way to help revive international trade.
Three Years of the Dąbrowa City Council and the Merits of President Dr. Madejski

The term of the Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] city council has ended. The "little benches" that we still occupy in the city council we hold only as an "extra favour". I therefore consider it my duty to give a brief outline report of our activity. Let at least the Jewish mass of voters be informed about what has been done until now and what the future activity in the economic sphere of the city of Dąbrowa consists of.
Our activity in the city council dates from 23 September 1929. On that day the Jewish councillors' club concluded the agreement with the B. B. W. R. club [Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government], which of course forms the majority of the present city council. Before we concluded the agreement, whose purpose was to win the Jewish votes in electing the presidium of the city administration, we held a conference with the presidential candidate Dr. Madejski, to whom we put the question of his position regarding the Jewish postulates. In his reply Mr. Madejski stressed several times that he recognises no Jewish question; all citizens must enjoy equal rights, and this — he said — I will sign into my programme declaration.
Dr. Madejski's words made a good impression on us Jewish councillors; we saw that the candidate for president is an outspoken democrat, that we would not be disappointed in him in the future, and with the Jewish votes Dr. Madejski was elected president and Mr. Każuk [Kożuch?] as vice-president.
The work of the new city council and of the city administration was very hard. It was at the time when the economic crisis began to develop. From the previous socialist city council there remained... an empty treasury and, as a bonus, the well-known Ulen loan in the amount of 275.000 dollars, that is, as is established, two and a half million zł...
The Ulen loan was taken on very hard and unfavourable terms. Many towns in Poland which Ulen "blessed" with his loans will have long years "to sing and tell" of it. Dąbrowa too was "privileged" to receive this "gift". The socialist rulers, not reckoning with the conditions of revenue and the means of the citizens, took the loan of 275 thousand dollars for a term of 21 years with the obligation to pay 25 thousand dollars every year. With the loan the sewerage and waterworks were carried out at the time.
The local inhabitants now feel the consequences of the loan. From the moment the magistrate charges a fee for water, constant protests are heard: how can it be? To pay for water, even[?]! In the present severe crisis must the population be burdened with yet another tax?
Truly a just complaint, but the magistrate and the city council simply had to introduce the water fee, for when a capital of two and a half million zł. of city money lies buried in the ground, one must see to it that the work bears proper fruit; otherwise the city treasury would have come to the point of — bankruptcy!
Proceeding from this standpoint we decided to charge 1 zł. from every dwelling. We admit that the fee is perhaps a heavy and a maximal one, but one must not forget that the fee was introduced as a trial, for 6 months in all, in order to amortise the money invested in the waterworks. It is worth noting that persons without means are entirely exempt from the water fee.
The introduction of the water fee also came about because of the liquidation of the servitudes of the coal mines dating from 1908.
By order of the then Russian Governor-General the owners of the coal mines undertook to supply water to the inhabitants of Dąbrowa. The quantity was 50 litres per soul. The water was, as is known, in a number of places very dirty, harmful for use. At best one had to stand in "ogonki" [queues] until one managed to get a little water; so that with the putting into operation of the waterworks the servitude rights were abolished, and the population has clean, healthy water for its use.
A second important municipal achievement is the agreement with the Małobądz power station. Under the agreement a kilowatt of electric light will cost only 50 gr. (until now 60 gr.); the streets will be lit by 80 lamps entirely free of charge. Besides this the city treasury receives 10 groszy from every kilowatt, shares worth 60 thousand złoty and 1 representative on the supervisory board. Thanks to this agreement Dąbrowa is the only town in Zagłębie where light is cheap.
In the field of the municipal economy we have to record a number of further facts which illustrate that President Dr. Madejski has passed his examination. Among other things much care was given to the school youth, for whom a splendid school building was built; a children's library was opened, as well as a municipal lecture hall where lectures are given by the intellectual forces of Zagłębie, etc.
Taking into account the time of crisis, this year's budget has been considerably reduced compared with previous years.
What do the Jewish subsidies look like?
In 1930 subsidies were given to the cheder "Yesodei ha-Torah" (1,500 zł.), a summer colony for Jewish children (1000 zł.) and "Tarbut" (100 zł.)... Certainly these are not sums that can satisfy our needs. One must, however, take into account that 1) had there still existed legalised Jewish institutions, they would no doubt have been subsidised (according to an official declaration of the chairman of the B. B. club, Mr. Kaczkowski), and 2) the system of reducing the budget on all items also caused the above-mentioned subsidies to be cut even further this year.
How the magistrate's work plans for the future are envisaged, and what the president's attitude to the Jewish population is — in the next issue.
Councillor B. Rechnic.
When Does a Bill of Exchange Lose Its Value?

The well-known German jurist Lezer[?] writes in his work "that if a bill of exchange is to be current like silver, the bill-of-exchange law must be strong as steel"...
For this reason the law on bills of exchange is the harshest law, and it does not allow any compromises. The only check in the bill-of-exchange law is prescription (przedawnienie).
Article 70 of the bill-of-exchange law says: "A claim on a bill-of-exchange debt lapses by prescription after 3 years with regard to the drawer, after 6 months as between one endorser and another, and, in the case where the second endorser has had the bill protested, after one year with regard to the first endorser". It follows from this that when a lawful holder of a bill neglects to demand and claim the debt within these terms, the debtor has the right not to pay later. The running of prescription can be interrupted only by:
1) filing a court claim;
2) lodging [the claim] with a bankruptcy estate.
It must be noted that when the court costs have not been paid, the privilege is not valid. It often happens, however, that the holder of a bill has let the term pass through an oversight; especially when the debt is a large one and can damage his fortune, the bill-of-exchange law provides the right to sue the debtor up to 3 years from the day of prescription on the ground that he has been enriched through the damage of the bill holder (niesłuszne zbogacenie — unjust enrichment). The procedure, however, is very complicated and requires firm proof that the debtor bought himself something of value with the bill sum, such as a house, a plot, etc.
Incidentally, it must be stressed that preserving the right from a prescribed bill does not come on the judge's initiative, and the wronged party must demand it himself.
From this it can be seen that one should not delay in claiming a bill-of-exchange debt through the courts, especially as the court procedure is very much simplified[?] and accessible to every bill holder.
Yaakov Ratner.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tetzaveh
The Portion
—o—
a) “And thou shalt command” (27:20)
Wherever the subject is a loss of money, taking money from Jews, it is said in the language of command [tzav], because this requires special zeal... Baal HaTurim.
—o—
“And upon the moments of the earth, words of deceit shall be reckoned” —
How much a man cheats throughout his life! With how many lies and how much falsehood he serves himself in the chase after money! And all of it for a moment, for an instant. After all, he does not gather money for the past. And as for the future — is one then already sure of acquired wealth? Yes! So all these are “words of deceit”. The whole devilish chase after the golden calf — all for the “moments of the earth”, for the instant, for the moment... Pesher Nifla'ot (Rabbi Mendel of Kotzk).
—o—
“He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver” —
Where does this devilish chase after money come from, that the more one owns, the more it always seems that one has nothing at all!
— A man always feels that his fortune is not his own; he never feels secure with it, because he did not acquire it with honesty and decency. It only seems to him that it is slipping out of his hands. Instinctively he feels that it is not his, and therefore he chases after more, after fresh money... Torat Emet (Rabbi A.Y.H. of Apta).
—o—
b) “That they bring unto thee” (ibid.)
What is truly a mitzvah — that the evil inclination does not allow. He is even ready to let the rich give charity, but only for dishonest purposes, not for matters of mitzvah: for the Calf — yes, but not for the Tabernacle...
Therefore God did not say as a commandment “and they shall give” but “and they shall take”, so that it should indeed not be a mitzvah — then perhaps the Adversary will not hinder the rich from donating to it...
Rav Aharon HaKohen (the rabbi of Petah Tikva).
—o—
c) “Pure olive oil” (ibid.)
“Oil” symbolizes wisdom. And in order to attain wisdom, a higher truth, one must approach it “pure” — clean and without prejudice.
Wisdom is also likened to a sister: “Say unto wisdom, thou art my sister”. On this the Talmudic sages expound: “like your sister, who is forbidden to you”. The truth should be forbidden to you for benefit. You will reach it only if you do not want any self-interest from it.
And further: just as the closeness with a sister changes when she marries a man, so too your kinship with wisdom is destroyed when it loses its maidenly purity and wholeness. — Kol Yaakov.
—o—
d) “And take thou unto thee” (28:1)
A leader must not stand lower than the people, nor higher. Therefore Moses was not chosen as priest, because he was much higher than the people and was not able to descend to them. Aaron, however, could descend to the people, understand them and be with them. Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
“...for I am a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit...
— go, prophesy unto My people Israel” (Amos 7)
Not the saint who is far from and above life can be the prophet, the people's admonisher, but only he who is a gatherer of sycamore fruit and knows the “boker” — the time in which he lives. Me'asef Derushi.
—o—
“Thou hast made him but little lower than God — and hast crowned him with glory and honour” —
With glory and splendour we bestow only on him who “is a little lacking of God” — him who lacks a little fear of God. Precisely such people Jews like to make their leaders... Rav Yisrael Salanter.
—o—
e) “And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, for glory and for beauty” (ibid., 2)
The garment, the rabbinic mantle, is indeed for a man for glory and for beauty. But only when an Aaron dresses in them... A rabbinic mantle in which an ordinary man dresses has no holiness at all and evokes no respect whatsoever... Be'er Yitzhak.
—o—
f) “Two each day continually” (29:38)
The Rabbi of Lissa was once in Brisk and lodged with R' Leib Katzenellenbogen. R' Leib was so absorbed in learning that he never ate at the proper time and never slept at the proper time.
On taking leave, the Rabbi of Lissa wishes R' Leib: “and the two continual offerings according to their order”.
— What do you mean by that, Rabbi? — R' Leib wonders.
— The Shulchan Aruch begins with the words: “I have set the Lord always [tamid] before me” and ends with the words: “he that is of a merry heart hath a continual [tamid] feast”. These two “tamids” a man must not mix up. When it is time for learning — one learns, and when it is time for eating — one eats...
—o—
g) “And I will dwell among the children of Israel” (ibid., 45)
Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Heschel of Apta once came to a town. Two Hasidim asked him to lodge with them. One was pious but arrogant, and the other an easygoing, unassuming man — only not so pious. The Rebbe chose to stay with the latter.
— Because — he said — of the arrogant man God says: “I and he cannot dwell in one abode”, and if God does not want to dwell there, I don't want to either... Whereas of one who is not pious God says: “I am the Lord that dwelleth with them in the midst of their uncleanness”, and if God dwells with a sinner, I may surely dwell there...
—o—
h) “And overlay them with gold” (30:5)
All the vessels of the Tabernacle were only o v e r l a i d with gold. Except the Ark-cover and the Menorah, which were gold t h r o u g h o u t — even on the inside.
Because the Tabernacle vessels allude to the structure of the human body. And the Ark-cover signifies — the heart.
All the limbs may be o v e r l a i d with gold; even thought may be gold mixed with wood; only the h e a r t must be pure, without any admixture...
Mei HaShiloah [?].
—o—
Haftarah
i) “Show the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities” (Ezekiel 43)
When we look at the Jewish home, how it looks today, how everything that smacks of Jewishness and tradition is driven out of it — we can only be ashamed...
Doresh Tov LeAmo.
—o—
j) “This is the law of the house” (ibid.)
“The brazen-faced to Gehenna... may it be Thy will that the Temple be rebuilt” (Avot)
People say: the bigger a synagogue is, the greater the brazenness it holds. Well, for today's brazen-faced, given their great impudence, even the biggest synagogue is too little. One really needs to build the Temple for them...
From the people's mouth.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The State of the Kehilla 'Improves'

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 12 Adar [I] 5692 — piątek 19 lutego 1932 [Friday, 19 February 1932].)
Będzin
The State of the Kehilla 'Improves'..
On Tuesday afternoon the electric current of the beth midrash was cut off. The same was to be carried out at the synagogue, but the men sent by the power station (elektrownia) found the synagogue locked...
—o—
The Bridegroom Runs Away from under the Wedding Canopy.
On Sunday evening a scene took place on Modrzejowska[?] Street that caused great merriment among the local residents.
A resident of the street, a poor Jewish woman, was holding her daughter's wedding. When the in-laws began to get ready for the chuppah, they realised that 'the lad is gone' — the bird had flown.
One can easily imagine what an impression this made on the bride and on the in-laws of the bride's side, and a search began throughout the whole town; only late in the evening did some wild young fellows catch the 'bird' near the depot (remiza)..
Under threats the bridegroom was led off to the wedding, where he finally said the 'harei at' [the betrothal formula]...
—o—
A Tragic Accident while Sledding. — A 12-Year-Old Boy Killed.
On Sunday around noon a group of children were sledding on the hill near Podzamcze Street.
At a certain moment the sled on which 12-year-old Frażak[?] was riding fell into a pit full of stones.
Frażak was seriously injured and died that same day in the evening.
The tragically killed boy was his parents' only son.
—o—
Hooligan Attack on a Young Jewish Man.
Binyamin Szwajcer, walking on Sunday evening along Piłsudskiego Street, saw 3 young hooligans molesting a Hasidic Jew. When Szwajcer reacted against this, the hooligans threw themselves upon him and with knives inflicted several wounds on his head and hand. The Hasidic Jew, instead of raising the alarm, ran away and left his defender in the hands of the hooligans. Disregarding his wounds, Szwajcer chased the bandits, and with the help of the police they were caught and handed over to the investigation office (Urząd Śledczy) in Sosnowiec.
It is very important that the Hasidic Jew come forward so that he can serve as a witness in the trial against the attackers.
—o—
Merchants' and House-Owners' Associations against the New Tax for the Water Works
A short time ago the commissarial council, without the votes of the Jewish members, passed a resolution to impose on the population a new tax (podatek) amounting to some twenty-odd thousand złoty. The tax is being levied to cover the costs of installing the water-supply system.
According to the statute a commission must be elected, which has the competence to assess the taxpayers at its own discretion.
To set up the commission, the provisional town administration called a meeting last Wednesday. The boards of the merchants' and house-owners' associations sent notices that, since they are against the unjust tax, they will not take part in the commission.
—o—
Took His Father-in-Law's Fur and Vanished.
A few weeks ago the tailor Mr. K. in Czeladź married off his daughter to a young man from Kraków. There was domestic harmony between the couple, and the family took pride and joy in their little son-in-law.
This week, however, the 'gem' vanished, taking with him also a fur garment that his father-in-law had finished making for a customer.
—o—
They Are Waiting for Salvation to Come from Warsaw..
On Saturday night the shochtim [ritual slaughterers] went on strike because they are not being paid their salaries (pensje). When the rabbi learned of it, he wrote the shochtim a letter in which he demanded that they break off the strike at once — if not — the rabbi warned in the letter, he would immediately send another shochet to the slaughterhouse.
The shochtim accepted the request and returned to work. A few days later, when the shochtim again began to demand to be paid what was due to them, they were asked to have patience[?] for a few more days until word comes from Warsaw that the new Agudah president [of the kehilla] has been confirmed.
—o—
The Recitation Concert by Miriam Alska[?],
which did not take place last Saturday because of the artist's illness, will take place next Saturday, the 27th of this month, in the WIZO hall.
Tickets already purchased are valid.
—o—
'Shabbetai Tzvi as Messiah'.
This Saturday night Dr. A. Gottesdiener will deliver at the 'Mizrachi' the second part of the lecture series on the Sabbatean movement.
—o—
A Place for the Insane and Idiots.
The magistrate has rented a large hall in Gzichów[?], where calm mental patients and idiots will be accommodated, who do not need to be isolated in special mental hospitals at all.
The premises are to be opened in the month of March of this year.
—o—
A Sanatorium for Lung Patients.
The magistrate has bought a building in Siewierz[?], where patients suffering from lung disease will be accommodated. For the time being there is room for 14 patients. But next summer the magistrate will build a larger new building.
—o—
A Concert of the Living Word.
This Saturday at noon the artist-reciter Herman Löwenstein will appear at 'Nowości' in a concert of the living word.
On the programme: Shakespeare, Andreyev, Leivick, Halpern, An-sky and others.
—o—
Lecture by Prof. Suchacki.
The Society for Regional Studies (Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze) is holding this Saturday evening a lecture by Prof. Suchacki entitled 'Impressions of Norway'.
The lecture takes place in the hall of Public School no. 2, Krakowska 14.
—o—
Meeting of 'Ezrat Menachem Avelim'.
This Saturday night the annual general meeting of the society 'Ezrat Menachem Avelim' [comforting mourners] will take place in its own premises on Modrzejowska Street.
The young institution has, during the short time of its existence, won sympathy among the Jewish population, as one sees ever more the usefulness of the society, especially in the present hard times.
It is therefore important that the meeting be well attended.
—o—
The 'Chuppah Concession' Is the Property of the Czeladź 'Bikur Cholim'.
Last week a wedding took place at the Rozenholc family in Czeladź. When they began preparing the chuppah, the local rabbi sent to the gabbaim of the 'Bikur Cholim' society asking that they give the chuppah poles. The messenger, however, came back without the chuppah, saying that the society demands a fee of 25 zł. Needless to say, the fee was not paid, and they made do with a parochet [ark curtain]...
Because of such conduct, the guests from Sosnowiec and Będzin refused to give any support whatsoever for the benefit of the Czeladź institutions.
It is only a wonder that the rabbi, who was present at the chuppah, did not react to the society's irresponsible conduct.

Sosnowiec
57-Year-Old Hasidic Jew Commits Suicide.
On Monday morning Jewish Sosnowiec was shaken by the news that the well-known grocer ("colonial" goods merchant) Mordechai Dawid Bajgelmacher had committed suicide by poisoning himself.
Nobody could believe that the quiet Hasidic Mordechai Dawid had taken such a step, but unfortunately it turned out to be a sad truth.
As his mother-in-law related, the late Bajgelmacher got up very early on Monday, sat down to recite Psalms, and then lay down in bed and drank a sizeable portion of vinegar essence.
In a grave condition Bajgelmacher was taken to the Jewish hospital, where he died during the night.
The suicide caused mourning among the entire local Jewish population.

Strict Measures to Collect the Debts of the Gemilut Hesed Fund.
At the last board meeting of the G"Ch (interest-free loan) fund the question was discussed of combating the negligence of the debtors, and of the guarantors in particular, which has led to the fund having 160 overdue ("zaległe") debts, which paralyse the fund's existence. It was therefore decided to use the most far-reaching measures against the debtors, and even more [?] against the guarantors, and not even to shrink from holding auctions.
—o—
With Fresh Strength the "Linat HaCholim" Society in Sosnowiec Begins to Be Active.
While some philanthropic institutions are inactive and are simply waiting for a formal funeral, a group of people in Sosnowiec have placed themselves at the head of the stagnant "Linat HaCholim", which is now starting a new, young, energetic and useful activity.
At the first meeting of the new board the following presidium was constituted: Mr. Icchak Goldkorn was elected chairman; vice-chairmen — the feldsher Jakub Tajchner and Josel Lenczner; treasurer — Mr. Cygler; and honorary secretary — Mr. Urbach.
At the meeting new plans [?] were worked out, intended to bring to life the newly rebuilt "Linat HaCholim" society. Taking into account the difficult situation of the Jewish masses, the board got in touch with a number of well-known doctors, who will give help to members of "Linat HaCholim" for only 1 zł. Activity will be carried on in the field of [?] medicines, milk, etc.
In a word: "Linat HaCholim" has been completely reorganised, and since the relief action involves large expenses, it was decided to collect monthly pledges and one-time donations. It is to be hoped that the Jewish population of Sosnowiec will help, so that "Linat HaCholim" can fulfil its necessary functions.
—o—
Mr. Zendel's Resignation Will Be Decided by the Voivode.
As is known, the kehilla president Mr. Zendel tendered his resignation because of the events at the session on the new budget.
As reported, the starosty has sent the matter to the voivodeship.
—o—
Sad State of the "Merchants' Association".
The "Merchants' Association" on Piłsudskiego Street, which once played an important role and was the lifeblood of the local merchant community, is in a moribund state.
To the meetings called several times in order still to save the institution from collapse almost nobody came — not only of the members, but even most of the board did not come either...
This week the health insurance fund (Kasa Chorych) placed a distraint on the association's furniture and office equipment, and if the debt is not paid the distrained equipment will be sold at auction.
— Will the large number of merchants allow it to come to this?...
—o—
"He Didn't Know That This Is Not Allowed"..
Before the local district court stood a house administrator who, in the absence of the tenants, threw their furniture out onto the street.
To the judge's question why he had done it, the administrator defended himself saying that "he didn't know that one is not allowed to throw out [?] other people's things"...
For his deed the administrator will serve six months in prison.

"The Shabbetai Zvi Movement".

[Zagłębie — culture; lectures at the Mizrachi.]
Dr. A. Gottesdiener lectured on this subject at the "Mizrachi". He has, however, barely given the introduction to the subject, because his lectures are not continuous, connected treatments; rather, every subject and every problem that Dr. G. lectures on and discusses he builds up according to his historical research, and gives his listeners an all-round survey of the problem or historical event.
In the introduction he explained the transition from the philosophical period among Jews to the kabbalistic period. In a very easy form he made understandable the way of thinking [?] and learning Torah of the kabbalists, their outlook on life and the variety of letter combinations (tseirufei otiyot) and gematrias in the Kabbalah. With easy and poetic examples he made the difficult parts of the hidden wisdom comprehensible. He made comprehensible the distinctions between the false messiahs who arose after the destruction of the Second Temple, who were more realistic than false messiahs such as Shabbetai Zvi and others who arose in a later period, because of the economic ruin of the Jews in the exile countries concerned.
It is quite understandable that Dr. Gottesdiener's lectures are so well attended, since the place for these lectures ought to be at a university, before an audience able to appreciate the value of the novelties he introduces [?] in the course of history.
The further lectures will be divided as follows: 1) Shabbetai Zvi as Messiah (his personality), 2) the Shabbetai Zvi movement, 3) Shabbetai Zvi in literature, where Dr. Gottesdiener will discuss the various conceptions of Shabbetai Zvi by the most important writers such as Zangwill, Sholem Asch, Żuławski and others. For learned men and maskilim it is a spiritual delight to hear the lectures. The hall is a bit too small, so the crush is too great. It would be desirable for the organisers to see to better order and a more comfortable hall for the lectures. —L.

Coal strike intensifies / 19-year-old youth sentenced to 4 years in prison / Będzin kehilla budget approved / Local tax must be paid according to the 1914 rent / Echoes of the Będzin kehilla elections / On the eve of the opening of the Eretz Israel bazaar in Sosnowiec / 3rd propaganda exhibition in Katowice / Meeting at the Co-operative Bank did not take place / Against the secret sale of alcohol / Man of 105 dies in Olkusz / Sudden death of advocate Gurbiel

Yesterday several pits in Upper Silesia went on strike.
In the general strike situation there has been, as we write these lines, no change whatever. The strike continues almost in the coal pits [sic]. The smaller industrialists already even agree to give in to the workers' demands; only out of solidarity is the strike being kept up.
On Wednesday afternoon the funeral of those killed during the events took place in Będzin and in Czeladź. The funeral, arranged with all Christian ceremonies, was attended by thousands of people of the working class. The mood was very tense. At the cemetery the priest spoke first, and then a delegate of the workers.
It passed off calmly. Strong police patrols kept order.
In Nowy Bytom a demonstration took place. The police ordered it to disperse; when this did not help, a volley was fired into the air. Whereupon the crowd began attacking with stones and pieces of iron. During the further [?] action one of the crowd was killed.
The general strike in Upper Silesia has not yet been decided. Yesterday the workers of 4 pits went on strike. In Jaworzno a meeting took place at which it was decided to strike.
In general the situation in Upper Silesia is getting worse from day to day.

Local tax must be paid according to the 1914 rent.
Since in some cases landlords have of their own goodwill raised the rent, the question arose whether the local tax is calculated according to the present state, or according to what was paid in 1914.
A circular of the Finance Ministry of 25 January puts an end to the various interpretations: the local tax is levied according to the amount of rent in 1914.

On Sunday the Jews of Olkusz face an exam.

(On the new town-council elections in Olkusz.)
As is already known, next Sunday, the 28th of this month, new elections to the town council take place (for the third time in a year). In the matter of elections Olkusz can have no complaints any more — the matter has lately not come off the agenda. Hardly is one finished [?] — something is not in order in the series [?] of elections, and soon comes a new edition; so it is with the town council, and also [?] with the kehilla elections. So the Jews of Olkusz are not unemployed.
But whoever observes how the matter of elections is understood and handled by the Jewish public [?] of Olkusz — that the more one sees [?], the stronger the lawlessness — darkness falls upon the soul.
True, Olkusz has never belonged to those towns where political methods prevail, or a social communal life. True, Olkusz also does not possess so many devoted, sincere public workers, and in every election campaign lawlessness and demagogy reign to a great degree. The political parties sleep soundly; even the election alarm does not disturb their rest, because the custom of Olkusz is that one need not necessarily obtain a seat through the party — it is enough to have the "will" and one is helped. The only parties demanding mandates are just the "Maccabi organization" and [a list] in the name of the "beit-midrash public".
Politics, programme, or even an election platform have no place in Olkusz.
It was hoped that at long last the situation would improve thanks to all the failures, and the Jews of Olkusz would no longer be an object of scorn and derision even in the eyes of our Polish neighbours.
But the present election campaign was again conducted in the old Olkusz manner. The "providers", for whom all year long the public interests lie in the left corner [?] [i.e., matter nothing to them], came together (God forbid, they did not have the courage to call [a meeting] themselves), divided the places among themselves, provided the town with 2 lists — everything in the best order.
The Jews of Olkusz will "vote" ("glosiren") and the mandates are secured.
Later people will shout, make noise, and have complaints against themselves.
But, Jews of Olkusz! It will be, as always — lost...
You can improve the situation only when you have the courage to remove the "seat-grabbers" — and nothing stands in the way of will...
M. Sh.

What's new in Upper Silesia?

On Monday a coal strike is to break out in Upper Silesia.
The central union of mine workers in Upper Silesia has decided to call a convention of delegates from all Upper Silesian coal mines for next Sunday, the 28th of this month [?]. At this convention the coal strike is to be proclaimed, which is to begin the following day, Monday.
Strike [?] of tram workers in Upper Silesia.
On Monday and Tuesday meetings of tram workers took place in Wielkie Hajduki [?]. The meetings were very stormy because of the coal strike in Zagłębie. The speakers called on those assembled to show solidarity with the strikers in Zagłębie.
In the end a resolution was adopted that together with the strike of the metalworkers in Upper Silesia the tram workers should also go on strike.
The chief hero of the swindle at the Handelsbank arrested.
In the previous issue of our paper we reported the fact of the swindle that was carried out at the branch of the Handelsbank in Katowice.
This week the Katowice police succeeded in arresting the chief hero of the swindle, a certain Janicki of Katowice, who is known for postal manipulations.
The arrested man confessed that he had also taken part in the swindle of 26,000 zł carried out at the International Bank in Katowice.
109 boys in the dock.
Before the juvenile court in Katowice stood 109 boys accused of not having come to school.
The accused declared that the main reason is that they have no shoes and clothes. Some, in turn, defended themselves saying that their masters do not want to release them to attend the evening courses.
The judge released all of them from punishment, except those who behave badly at school during lessons.

The cry of woe of the many poor people has finally moved [hearts]. At the meeting held at the rabbi's, may he live long, a committee of householders was formed, which collected a few hundred zł, which were distributed for coal.

Because the gmina [municipality] did not pay the Talmud Torah teacher his starvation salary for a few [?] months, the teacher went away, and about 30 children have nowhere to study.

The Wolbrom town council, which consists of 13 Jews and 11 Christians, constituted itself as follows: elected president was Mr. Paborek [?] (Christian), and vice-president the Jewish pharmacist Mr. Rozenbojm. From the election front.
This Sunday the town-council elections take place in Olkusz; in general apathy reigns on the election front among all parties and especially among Jews, so that this must be avoided [?]. And all Jewish voters [should] [?] take part in the elections.
