Important Resolutions at the Merchants' Convention in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — economy; trade.] Over the last several months the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce has organised district conventions in a number of towns of the Kielce voivodeship; these merchants' conventions took place in Kielce, Częstochowa, Radom and, last Sunday, in Sosnowiec.
Taking part in the convention were representatives of the starostwo [district authority], the municipal administrations, deputies, the press, economists and about 600 merchants from Zagłębie.
The convention was opened and chaired by the president of the Chamber of Commerce, Eng. Gnadamski [?], who invited to the presidium the local presidents Dr. Likiernik and Gruszczyński, board member Mr. Rybinglichs [?], the representative of the Central Union of Small Traders Mr. Zygadlewicz [?] and others.
The first to speak was the local president of the Chamber of Commerce, Gruszczyński, who reported on the Chamber's activity for the benefit of the merchant class.
Councillor [Ratman] Mr. Kryczak [?] came forward with a long and matter-of-fact lecture. With a series of examples he illustrated the government's economic policy towards the merchant class, which suffers heavily because of the system of etatism [state intervention in the economy], export, import and above all because of the cartels.
On behalf of the Central Union of Polish Merchants in Warsaw, the editor Szczerbiński spoke about the importance of using domestic goods. The speaker expressed his wish that both the Jewish and the Polish press should help restore friendly relations between Jewish and Polish merchants.
After the lectures a lively discussion developed, in which councillors Papier [?], Tencer, Adler, Kabak, Bachura [?], Jagielewicz [?] and others spoke, and they submitted the following resolutions:
1) A post-office building should be built in Sosnowiec, and parcels should be delivered to the addressees.
2) At the Bank Polski bills of exchange should be protested on the 3rd day after the due date.
3) To reduce the charge for the telephone subscription.
4) To reduce the price of electric light and, after 3 years, no longer to charge a fee for the meter.
5) To reduce the percentage [charged] for executions [distraints], and also that sequestered goods be kept under proper supervision.
6) Imports should be conducted through the port of Gdynia.
7) The municipal administrations should buy their [printed "vieire"] articles of consumption from domestic firms.
8) The magistrate's coupons, on which foodstuffs are issued, should also be redeemable in all shops, not only through the cooperative stores.
9) Protests should be lodged from the first sources.
In conclusion Messrs. Zygadlewicz and Kucharski expressed thanks to the Chamber of Commerce for organising the convention.
To the Jews of Zagłębie Who Are Going to the Land of Israel

[Zagłębie — Land of Israel; immigration.] On Saturday night after the Sabbath of the portion Terumah [13 February 1932] the following olim [immigrants] from Zagłębie living in Tel Aviv gathered in the apartment of Mr. Shabtai Weiss: Messrs. Shabtai Weiss, Zisha Sandzer, Shmuel Krysztal, Nachman Bajtner, Eshka Wajman [?], Leibel Warszawski, Avigdor Wiener [?], Endel Bajtner, Shlomo Wajberg [?] and Shalom Meir Feigenholz [?], with the purpose of organising a committee that would assist the tourists and olim who will now come to the Land of Israel from Zagłębie.
All those present unanimously recognised the necessity of assisting them throughout [?] [their stay], so that they need not suffer from various difficulties and possible losses of money.
In the course of the conversation it was stressed that all means must be employed to avoid the mistakes that were made at the time of the "Fourth Aliyah", because on coming to the Land of Israel they did not find the proper institutions and people who would assist them with advice and deed, so that they should not fall victim to their unfamiliarity with the conditions and reality in the Land of Israel.
These bloody mistakes must not be repeated now. Those who now come to the Land of Israel, whether as tourists or those who intend to invest money in Eretz Israel, must find here a homely, warm atmosphere, a faithful brotherly hand that will guide them and guard them against false steps.
The assembled therefore elected Messrs. Shabtai Weiss, Zisha Sandzer and Eshka Wajman [?] to the committee, which will receive the tourists and olim who come to Eretz Israel and will help them in all matters that they will need.
All tourists and olim from Zagłębie are asked to apply for information to the address:
Hitachdut Olei Polania [Association of Immigrants from Poland], Tel Aviv, [?] Montefiore St. 25, for Mr. Shabtai Weiss.
A Word About Competition From Our Own (A Letter to the Editor)

[Będzin — sport; letter to the editor.] For years sport was almost the only field in which one knew nothing of particularism and fragmentation.
But lately "personal ambitions" have begun to appear here too, and "our own" sports clubs are being created.
First place was taken by Będzin, where a small group dissatisfied with the democratic character of "Hakoach" has created a "Maccabi Garden Association" [?] and is waging a competitive struggle with "Hakoach".
The most piquant thing is that the "new" Kremlin is led by the honorary president and several members.. of "Hakoach"!
New presidents, secretaries, premises and other expenses — at a time when "Hakoach", because of unemployment and the general situation, is going through a severe crisis.
It is also worth touching on the ball that the "Nartsa-oshes" [?, perhaps narciarze — skiers] recently held, from which about 600 zł. was designated for building a storey for Będzin in the building on "Hala Boracza" in the Beskids.
We do not wish to question the goal itself, but must Będzin alone — when dozens or hundreds of associations are interested in the construction — spend 600 zł. in present times; was it expedient to draw 1200 zł. gross out of the town so that the ambitions of a few individuals from Będzin and Bielsko [Bielitz] might be fulfilled?
Especially when the only gymnastics and sports association, which has existed for 8 years, is struggling hard for its existence!
Będzin's "Hakoach" must absolutely take certain steps in order to remove the harmful competition on the part of... our own.
A friend of "Hakoach".
—o—
[Dąbrowa — religion; kehilla.] The Stormy "Kabbalat Shabbat" in the Beit Midrash at Kolonia Reden in Dąbrowa
Last Friday evening a storm broke out in the beit midrash at Kolonia Reden in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] over a sermon that was to have been delivered by Rabbi R' Moshe M"Tz [moreh tzedek?] Klein, delegate of the Mesivta [yeshiva].
Rabbi Klein wanted to deliver the sermon before Kabbalat Shabbat. When the young congregants protested against this, the preacher turned to the youth with the following words: "I did not come here to speak to you; after all, you want to burn our Torah."
At these words a protest broke out from almost all the worshippers, also from the "pnei" [?, front rows], and the end was that Rabbi Klein delivered no sermon at all.
Even after the prayers the congregation did not calm down and spoke with bitterness about the insults the speaker had hurled at the religious-national youth who were at the prayers.
As we are informed, the youth of Dąbrowa is very "downcast" because of the declaration of this old shochet, who assured them that if "the world learns of this, nobody will want to make a match with a young man from Dąbrowa"...
—o—
[Dąbrowa — kehilla.] For the Second Time the Presidium Elections of the Dąbrowa Kehilla Annulled
Last Monday the gmina [Jewish community] received a notice from the starostwo that the ministry has annulled for the second time the presidium elections of the kehilla board in Dąbrowa.
At the same time it is ordered that within 8 days elections of the presidium are to take place for the third time.
What Is Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
The Majority Is Against a Coal Strike in Upper Silesia.
On Sunday a consultation of delegates of the Central Union of Coal Miners was held in Katowice. Taking part in the consultation were representatives of 30 Upper Silesian coal mines, of the Dąbrowa coal district, and a delegate of the Czech coal miners' association.
Deputy Stańczyk delivered a report on the strike situation, saying that because of the impossibility of proclaiming a solidarity strike in Upper Silesia, the Dąbrowa and Kraków coal workers are determined to continue holding out in the struggle.
After a lengthy discussion a vote took place, which gave the following results: 16 mines declared themselves for a strike, 12 — against, 2 voted for a conditional strike, 11 mines sent no delegates at all to the consultation.
Because of this result the delegates declared that under such conditions it is impossible to proclaim a strike in Upper Silesia.
—o—
9 Coal Mines Are to Be Closed.
The crisis in Upper Silesia is deepening. A grave impression was made by the industrialists' proposals that 9 coal mines be closed. If this happens, another 14 thousand workers will lose their bread.
—o—
Kehilla Elections — Confirmed.
Since no protest whatsoever was lodged against the kehilla elections within 2 weeks, the elections are automatically confirmed.
—o—
On a Uniform System for Upper Silesia and Zagłębie
At the Katowice Chamber of Commerce a conference was held with the participation of industrialists on the question of introducing a uniform system of automatic telephones over the territory of Upper Silesia and Zagłębie.
Also taking part in the conference were the president of the Katowice post and telegraph office, Eng. Kowbek[?], and the president of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, Dr. Garamski, who took part in the discussion, and it was resolved that the automatic system be introduced, so that subscribers may receive faster and more convenient telephone communication.
—o—
A Terrible Tragedy Caused by Want.
In Siemianowice an unemployed man shot dead his wife, his 11-year-old daughter, and then himself. The cause of the tragedy is that the family had suffered from want for a long time.
—o—
Half a Million Złoty for the Unemployed.
At Tuesday's session of the Silesian Sejm it was resolved that the half million złoty provided in the budget for construction purposes be used for the benefit of the unemployed.
Olkusz

[Olkusz — municipal elections; trade; relief.]
Result of the City-Council Elections.
The result of Sunday's city-council elections is as follows: out of 4720 eligible voters (among them 1300 Jews), 3142 valid votes and 25 invalid ones were cast. The percentage of Jews and of Christians [who voted] was this time equal, i.e. 67 percent. The quota was 129 votes. The individual lists received the following numbers of votes and mandates: No. 1 (Sanacja) 139 votes — 1 mandate; No. 2 (P.P.S.) 269[?] votes — 2 mandates; No. 3 (Endeks) 588 votes — 5 mandates; No. 4 (Workers and Artisans) 134 votes — 1 mandate; No. 7 (Chadeks) 1163 votes — 9 mandates. Of the two Jewish lists, No. 5 (National, Youth) received 220 votes — 1 mandate, Yekutiel Kruk (it lacked 8 votes for a second mandate); No. 6 (United Jewish Bloc) 628 votes — 5 mandates: Adam[?] Blum, Avremele Kerner, Avraham Glikstein, Mendel Kerner and Berish Zilberberg.
Election day passed completely calmly, with the exception of a few small incidents between the Jewish election canvassers.
—o—
Confectioneries Forbidden to Be Open on Sunday.
According to an order of the starosta, all confectioneries must be closed on Sundays and holidays and must close daily at 7 in the evening (until now they were open until 11 in the evening). A few dozen Jews will suffer from this order.
It is therefore the duty of the competent Jewish circles to intervene in this matter.
—o—
Registration of Jews Without a Livelihood.
The "Poalei Agudat Israel" organisation has applied to the municipal unemployment committee concerning support for Jews without work and livelihood.
The committee resolved to grant this on condition that the Jewish community also supports the committee.
To the general Citizens' Committee were delegated: Berish Weislfisz, Pinchas Trajman and Icchak Feliks; 170 Jewish families numbering 700 souls have already registered.
A. B.
Musical Notes

[Zagłębie — music and culture.]
The Kipnis–Zeligfeld Concerts.
After a break of several years, lovers of the Yiddish folk song again had the opportunity to hear the popular folk singers Zeligfeld-Kipnis, who appeared in concerts in Dąbrowa, Sosnowiec and Będzin. The concerts had a moral success. The repertoire even consisted partly of some well-known songs. Still, they are always pleasant to hear when they are sung by such well-known singers.
—o—
The Second Recitation Evening of Miss Orleska
at "WIZO" this time too had an enormous success. After the fine introduction by Mr. Moua[?], the artist Orleska recited "At Night in the Old Market", "Dos krefke yingele" by Peretz, and others. A special yasher koach to the esteemed artist for the numbers "The Dance" and "The Jazz"[?], which were performed masterfully.
—o—
Concert of the "Hakoah" Orchestra.
On Sunday[?] the second concert of the "Hakoah" orchestra took place at "Światowid" under the direction of Mr. Icchak Barenblat. In the course of one year the orchestra has made great progress in this field. Certain defects are still noticeable in the playing, but one must admit that the orchestra has a future. We hold that this is the main post (placówka) in which the "Hakoah" board must invest, so that the orchestra may be enlarged and perfected. Ten boxing matches are a mere "kapore" [not worth] even one "Florentina" march...
Among other things "Kol Nidre" was performed, no easy thing for a brass band; nevertheless the number was a successful one.
As an encore ("bis") the Modzhitz niggun was played..
To the conductor and the participants — bravo!
Our Financial Institutions.

[Sosnowiec and Zagłębie — Jewish banking; article.]
(The time of blossoming — their weakening and the collapses. — How can they be saved?)
When the Jewish credit institutions began to appear on our horizon, when the banks began to develop well, credit became easier. The Jewish merchant, small trader and artisan, who had no access either to Bank Polski or to Bank Handlowy, only then began to breathe freely; they gained access to our financial institutions, got their bills of exchange handled there, and in this way became more creditworthy. Only then did one see how useful one's own financial institutions are, how necessary they are for the people, for the broad strata of the population. We saw the benefit. We felt the colossal development, and we simply beamed with pride and took delight in the useful popular work that had taken such firm hold in our everyday life and in our homely world.
And here we must not forget one thing: that it could be good only for so long. The institutions could bring benefit to the population only as long as people treated them seriously, as long as they held them in awe and respect — derekh erets, that is — as long as it was an ideal, as long as the ideal was not exchanged for small change. But as soon as people began to let themselves go, as soon as they began to give up prestige, we immediately pointed [?] to the first mistake being made, and in a series of articles we illuminated the financial question from all sides and came to the conclusion that we must not count on the fact that our financial institutions are flourishing, and that merely for that reason [people] will break away from them.
We said then that the stronger our public financial institutions become, the more honour they will bring us, and the more honour we have from them, the more chances we have of gaining benefit from them. But nobody took anything into account and nobody wanted to know anything, so that things reached the level at which people had unconsciously aimed, and what in the end (printed "kof kol sof") came about.
It was, after all, self-evident that as soon as people began to tear surplus [?] away from every bank, it would come to the point that every Hasid would have his own "bankl" [little bench/bank] and every minyan its own little shop, so that then [?] the great ideal, which had been built up like an edifice, began to turn into tiny toys — already then a more far-sighted view had the chance to see the prospects that had arisen.
It is a mistake for people to think that the collapses of the institutions arose because of the strained situation in which we find ourselves, because of the prevailing crisis. That is far from true. The institutions were rotten through even before things got bad. From the moment people began to look at the institutions as a little shop, they approached them with disregard — and therein lay the trouble. Founding a bank in the same way as a colonial-goods grocery should not have been allowed. First of all, people did not take account of two things: first, that this is not a private institution but a public one; and second, one had to remember that apart from being public it is also a financial institution, which must be treated with the greatest caution, because as soon as a financial institution acquires the slightest blemish in the street, that is already damage of the greatest importance.
And it is self-evident that because of this fragmentation people completely forgot that these are public financial institutions, so that, to our greatest shame and pain, people pushed their way in there who seized the institutions and exploited them for their own purposes, and in this way the people's money was squandered [?], and the guilty were not even called to account.
Yes, as soon as the diamond began to be exchanged for an imitation, for a glass stone, it had already lost its value, regardless of the fact that the glass had the same fire as the real diamond. The process thus played itself out before our eyes on entirely normal grounds: the smaller the bank became, the more lightly and disdainfully it was treated, the cheaper it became in the eyes of the population, until it came to what it had to come to. One should therefore not be surprised that none of us has any trust even in such a bank that looks good.
But one must not forget that, apart from the cheapening of the institutions in the eyes of the street, of the community, the institutions on the other hand also [?] cost dearly, and precisely because of their small scale, for such a bank had almost the same expenses as a large bank. And one knows, after all, that if in any enterprise whatsoever large turnover plays a great role in cheapening the goods, at a bank it is one of the most important things. A small bank that had a small turnover had the same expenses as a large bank that had large turnovers.
The method [?] (printed "marus") of splintering the financial institutions has thus gone bankrupt along the whole front, so that there is no chance that they can hold out normally. Here and there a will for unification, for agreement, is noticeable. Thus in Sosnowiec they have already understood that instead of two small "banklekh" it is more logical and more rational to create one bank, and to that end [?] the new "Kasa Urojałowa" [?] was created. These deeds of agreement and unification are therefore to be welcomed. It is an old rule that splintering and crumbling are weak and worthless, and society does not take it into account; on the other hand it is known that unification strengthens. Everyone knows the slogan that in unity lies our strength.
We therefore want to believe that now, after so much damage has been suffered, after so much Jewish property has become a heap of ruins, people will come to the realisation that we must be a little more careful with our financial institutions.
The Jewish People of the Book is at the same time also the people that reckons and counts and calculates and trades by all sorts of systems, and for all that it cannot manage without its own financial institutions.
Perhaps, therefore, it would now be a plan [?] to take stock and to save the institutions that are still holding on somehow in our financial world? Perhaps one would try to repair the edifices that have not yet collapsed and can still be saved?
The merger of the two Sosnowiec institutions into one large one, into one healthy one, has presented [?] the certificate of understanding and maturity; and now, if they run the institution in a professional manner, so that it brings benefit both to itself and to the Jewish community, they will perhaps have the merit of having been the first to understand the responsibility towards society, whose duty it is to guard the Jewish groszy, which at the present moment must not remain ownerless for all and sundry.
We have, after all, somehow been crowned with the name "a stiff-necked people". Let us in this case remain stubborn and obstinate and set ourselves a motto: not to take our hand off the heart [?] (printed "tartsn") until we have saved our financial institutions.
R. Les.

A bloody brawl over the "black diamonds".
[Zagłębie — labour and coal.]
Near Niwka a bloody brawl took place between a group of workers and peasants. The latter will not allow the so-called secret "coal pits" to be opened on their fields. The brawl took on a serious character. Several seriously wounded were taken to hospital.

Glassworks in Zawiercie closed.
[Zagłębie — industry and unemployment.]
This week in Zawiercie the glassworks, where 450 workers were employed, was closed for a period of 3 months. During this time the management will try to obtain new export markets and to obtain long-term loans.

Tragic death of a 3-year-old child.
[Königshütte — accident.]
Mrs. Richter of Königshütte (Chorzów), while doing the washing, put a kettle of hot water down on the floor. At that moment 3-year-old Klara was passing by; she fell into the kettle and scalded herself so badly that within a few hours the child died.
Upbringing

[Feuilleton — antisemitism and upbringing.] Itzkus.
"You will by no means convince me that the worst Endek [member of the Polish nationalist National Democrats] or antisemite wants his son, too, to be a hooligan. Wickedness was always leased out to grown-up people, while the children were given an upbringing. People sought to plant all the virtues in the little children, while they themselves were poisoned with envy and hatred — and that is why the latest antisemitic outbreaks all over the world will help to educate a little the older enemies of Israel too."
With such a long preface my friend, the researcher, greeted me — he who always has a habit[?] of interpreting events in his own way and has a strange inclination to draw a moral from everything that happens under God's sun.
But this time I decided that I would not let myself be provoked. Through the thick cobweb of my friend's round and polished[?] aphorisms I nevertheless caught a conversation about the very latest Polish-Jewish relations.
"You have, it seems, lately," he remarked with a venomous little smile, "developed a fair sense of humour. When you speak about Polish-Jewish relations — where have you lately learned all these diplomatic tricks, where have you picked up all these liberal, mild words[?]: 'relations', 'excesses'? You think that when one tears out a Jew's beard, one consoles[?] him by explaining to him that he was a victim of 'excesses' and not of pogroms? And when female students are thrown out of the university windows — are these such 'relations'? But don't be alarmed, I do not want to talk about the matter itself. Pogroms are no news among Jews, thank God, and the Jewish people, who better, is an expert in pogroms. With the word 'excesses' no pogrom wound has yet been healed, nor any pogrom shame wiped away. In the dictionary you cannot find any mild words of consolation for hooligan tricks."
My friend, the researcher, got heated, and it took a good while until he calmed down so as to be able to rise to his usual[?] philosophical height, where there is no hatred and no revenge, but only the sharpness of the human mind flashes.
"But you must admit," he went on, "that the latest wild tricks of the Endek students in Poland, of the swastika-men in Austria-Hungary, will in the end have to sober up the antisemitic beast — precisely because it is young students who have taken up the hooligan trade."
"You understand," he began drilling into me, "Polish democracy is ashamed now, and that is a good sign. And why is it ashamed? It is easy to guess. Go into a house, take a look at the little children, and you will know by yourself who the parents are. Because little children have the childish nature of betraying their parents by their behaviour. That is why the pedagogues try so hard to educate the children. With upbringing one wants to smooth over and hush up one's own faults, which cry out so openly through the children. We, the grown-up generation, have made ourselves civilised, but what does one do with the little children who blurt out everything they have inherited from us?
"That is why the Polish antisemites are now ashamed, and that is a sign of the times. The Polish Endeks waged a systematic struggle against the Jews. It was a policy of extermination and annihilation. The whole Jewish people was reduced to beggary, but that was 'policy', 'relations', as you say; when, however, young students underline that policy with pogroms, then it is, upon my life, fie, a shame and a disgrace. Poland's noblest and most educated children forgot their 'proszę pana' [Polish 'please, sir' — polite manners] upbringing and showed the world the face of the whole policy against the Jews."
My friend, the researcher, stroked his fine silver little beard and screwed up his warm, deep, Jewish eyes.
"It is good like this — that all over the world the greatest louts now are the young students; the fine products of our culture have run wild[?]. The fathers drilled the New Testament into them for so long: love for the world, love for the neighbour, love for the friend, love for the enemy, love and love and love. They refined their children's senses, they refined their tastes, and they themselves were poisoned with hatred, with brutality; they themselves declared wars, shed blood, they themselves invented the wildest spiritual and physical tortures for Jews — and they thought that the children they had reared would keep silent about it, would not blurt out to the world what fine people their fathers are."
The researcher lit a cigarette and began blowing the smoke up to the ceiling.
"It is good like this," he went on throwing out words while puffing[?] the smoke, "let them bury their faces in shame. The students have shown the complete bankruptcy of Christian civilisation; the walls of the universities are rotten through with medieval hatred like the walls of the Inquisition dungeons. Let them rage[?], for it will have to crack, because even the most hardened pogromist will not pinch the cheek of his only son when he comes back with a bandaged head.
"When a 16-year-old gymnasium pupil shoots his 12-year-old sweetheart and kills himself too, the grown-up heroes of love must reflect whether the whole business of love is no more than a children's game," the researcher began explaining by way of a parable, "and when students take up hooliganism, grown-up pogromists must reflect and be ashamed.
"And let them indeed be ashamed, for Einstein, too, was once a student. Einstein is the symbol of our student body, and in his whole fruitful[?] life he never touched a fly on the wall, never once offended anyone's honour. And if in the course of his whole life he did make a mistake for a quarter of a moment, he will correct that mistake within a year or two with a new note to his theory. But the error of the antisemitic world student body cannot be repaired so quickly. It is the crooked mirror of the whole Christian world. Take a look, dear friends, and be ashamed!"
My researcher began wrapping himself in thick walls of smoke from his cigar and fell silent.
Without Credit — the Merchant Class Is Going Under

[Economy — trade and credit.] Jakub Adler.
The necessity of immediate help — why the P.K.O. [Postal Savings Bank] grants the merchants no credit — whereas [?] the P.K.O. after all makes its turnover with the capital of trade and industry.
In the Polish journal "Tygodnik Handlowy" [?], which appears in Warsaw, the well-known councillor [ratman] of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Jakub Adler, [—] an article on the "unconditional [?]" necessity of cheap long-term credit for the merchants. Because of its topical and interesting content we are reprinting the article in our paper as well.
The collapse of trade in the provinces already embraces such circles and reaches so deep that we are in fact already facing a complete catastrophe and the complete destruction of trade.
The extraordinary impoverishment of village and town, the distortions in tax policy, the bad enforcement (distraint) regulations threaten the merchant class with extermination.
The village does not buy even 10 per cent of what it really needs, and of what it was buying until not long ago. The village customer has turned, for us, into a tale of long-past years.
Town dwellers limit their needs to the minimum. This is because they do not want to incur expenses that they would later be unable to cover. And their means of covering expenses are so small that trade has altogether become a wholly superfluous thing for them.
But meanwhile the distraints for private and public debts, which weigh mercilessly on the merchant class, are, by their number, taking on destructive forms.
These distraints are becoming the grave of the merchant class. The public and private creditors of a merchant often carry out distraints in order to [collect] sums that are not large, and at the same time they do it so ruthlessly that the merchant's property, worth several tens of thousands of złoty, is sold at auction for a few thousand zł.
More than once it happens that the auction barely covers the court and distraint costs; sometimes it covers the tax arrears, and the strict creditor who conducted the auction receives barely trifles — or else the auction has destroyed for good the merchant and his independent workshop.
We regularly read about the concern that the chambers of commerce, the legislative bodies and the economic organisations have for protecting the lender (creditor), and it seems to me that today one should really be thinking of protecting the sinking borrower.
We are going under, and this is happening because we do not receive appropriate credit.
The provincial merchant class knows absolutely nothing of such credit. The Bank Polski grants only in petty amounts a credit for two and a half months, which is absolutely insufficient [?] for the merchants.
Moreover, these credits are becoming ever scantier and fewer.
The "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" does not concern itself with trade. The private banks think of themselves and not of trade, on which they after all live to a great extent.
And finally:
The P.K.O. (Pocztowa Kasa Oszczędności) has completely forgotten that its entire turnover and its earnings rest first and foremost on the capital of the merchants and industrialists.
This capital, which remains at the P.K.O.'s disposal for at least 3–4 days, means strength and power for it. How its turnover would shrink if trade and industry stopped making their deposits and payments [?] through the medium of the P.K.O.!
Under such conditions the merchants' demand is therefore understandable, that the P.K.O. should consider the means and possibilities of putting certain credits into operation for trade.
The P.K.O. cannot and must not look on indifferently at the distress of trade and of the merchants in their unprotected decline, for this decline may drag it down too.
I am not putting forward any detailed project here. I am not talking here about a particular system that ought to be applied. I am only underlining the tragedy of trade, which has been robbed of credit, and I am only pointing to the possible source.
I am a modest merchant in the provinces who thinks about the totality of our interests. I therefore consider it a sacred duty to sound the alarm and to point to the possibility of help.
Time is pressing: let the P.K.O. answer, and let the chambers of commerce take up this important matter as quickly as possible, so that they do not end up facing a fait accompli, when trade and the merchants are already on the brink of ruin and already completely lost.
The Needle, the Knife and the Poor Man

Three of them stood before the Heavenly Court: two as defendants and one as plaintiff.
The first two were these: the pedigreed needle and the kosher khalef [slaughtering knife], and the third — the poor man.
And this happened long ago. Quite a long time ago — back then, when there still were [sic] in the world the great inventions, such as radio, electricity and Sabbath-observing Jews...
Against the first two the prosecutor came forward with these words:
— Great Creator! Strong complaints (in today's language they would be called — protests) are heard on earth against the two aristocrats: the needle and the knife. Everything that comes from steel and iron, starting from the washbasin by the synagogue door down to the little nail-knife, strongly resents that You have granted those two so great an honour.
— Meaning? — the prosecutor is asked.
— In that the khalef-knife has more merit than all the others. Pious ritual slaughterers occupy themselves with it, and great meticulous rabbis watch over it so that, God forbid, it should have no flaw in it; hundreds of blessings are said over it, and every Thursday or Friday, when every Jewish woman prepares the meat and fish in honour of the Sabbath... Besides all this, You have given this knife one more rank, of very great and important significance — You entrusted it with carrying out one of Your greatest commandments: bringing all eight-day-old Jewish males into the covenant of our father Abraham...
But an even greater honour You bestowed on the needle — it is used to embroider all the precious, lavish[?] Torah-ark curtains and silk mantles[?] for Your holy Torah. With its help all the white garments of the kohen are sewn, and besides that it has in itself even greater power than the khalef-knife. When it takes a fancy to settle in a chicken's gizzard, then one must take the trouble with it (together with the gizzard, of course) [to go] to the rabbi to ask a ritual question, and more than once the whole chicken is declared treyf because of it, without even regarding the fact that the khalef had not a single flaw in it...
And before the prosecutor had even finished his speech, the poor man leapt up and shouted in his hoarse voice:
— And why am I so lowly? So small, smaller even than the knife and the needle in the gizzard? Nobody pays me any attention, gives me no importance whatsoever, no honour at all — why am I worse than everyone?... I too want some symbol, an honour; I too am Your creature, Master of the Universe!
— Right! — a voice was heard from the Heavenly Court. All are right: both the complaints against the needle and the knife, and the complaints of the poor man, poor thing...
And therefore:
— From this day on the knife and the needle shall also be given a flaw, a degradation, that will somewhat take down their importance. The khalef- and circumciser's knife shall also become a razor for Jewish beards, through which it will lead to sins and nuisances. The same goes for the needle. It too shall be used for making profane things, such as trousers, low-cut dresses and costumes for masked balls...
— And what about me, Master of the Universe?... the poor man cannot restrain himself — what will become of me?
The heavenly retinue is left at a loss. What indeed is to be done with him? Were he too a piece of inanimate matter — of steel or of iron — I would already have found some honour for him too; but he is, after all, of flesh and blood — what shall we make of him, really?

Between Themselves

[Literature — a sketch of the times; the economic crisis.] By A. Goldzberg.
(A picture of the times.)
They sit, the two of them, husband and wife, and argue. He is a silent man by nature, speaks little. He does not let himself be drawn into any long conversations. She, on the other hand, talks for herself and for him, well, and for the children, may they live.
Sometimes he used to have a short answer: don't worry, it will still get „better“... In this sentence[?] lay his whole optimism; here lodged the whole meaning of the deep hope...
And when she pestered him, got talking to him about the „situation“, he would answer her short and sharp — „Don't worry, it will still get better, God does not forsake“...
Such an answer not only calmed her, but sometimes also stirred her imagination. What they would do when „it gets better“: first of all she herself would nurse[?] him a little, weak as he is, poor thing; she wants no more than to be able at least to make an omelette, now and then a good dinner, to remake the dress that has gone out of fashion, and to keep sending the children to school — more than that she wants nothing. Quite „skromne“ [modest].
And when she had reckoned up her tiny little list for him, he would optimistically „draw on“ a Hande cigar and lovingly calm her. „Don't worry, it will still get better, better“... Like fragrant olive oil, like a balm, it poured through her limbs, and he had avoided the worst thing for him — getting dragged into a long conversation.
That is how it is in the world. When things are good, she is silent and he talks — for why, does one need to ask him anything? One buys by oneself, one provides by oneself, one becomes a „briye“ [a capable person] — a „state of emergency“ is declared along the whole line, and he — talks, poor man... If, God forbid, things are worse — he is silent and she talks. It is a kind of questioning, an investigating, a searching — exactly as in the state: when things are bad a commission sits and investigates the economic conjuncture. She too began to investigate the conjuncture. But he — the worse each day, the shorter each day his words, dazed, worried[?]...
And she talks... Do you hear, let there at least be enough to pay the small expenses, let there at least be enough to pay for the new pair of shoes. Let me at least have something to put on, at least to repair last year's ball[?] dress... [garbled in print] — she breaks down and whimpers, and frets[?], and sobs, so that it grips one at the heart... „Don't worry. It will get better“... — he says.
— For almost a year now you have been feeding[?] me with your little sayings, and at home it is like after a fire. I no longer ask you what will be; when will I too finally know something of life?...
When he saw that, with the shrunken livelihood, hope[?] was like a „freylekhs“ [a merry dance] at a funeral, he decided to change front. When the conversation again turned to worries of livelihood and he had hastily drawn on a „Wanda“[?] — he says to her, just quietly — do you hear, it will still be... it seems to me, worse...
— Why do you salt the wounds, I beg you...
— That is how it is, my dear: when it goes worse after better, it goes worse, worse... better, better... a pleasure — but, he twirls his finger philosophically, when it goes „better“... a little better... worse, worse — it must simply become nasty[?]. Only you don't want to understand it.
The philosophical idea of rise and fall, presented quite graphically, had such an effect that she fell silent...
And when her old complaints were repeated once more... — And what is one to do? What will be the end? It must surely come to an end — he again „drew“ on his smoke and calmly answered — „What are you talking about, it will get even worse“.
At this answer she became somehow differently disposed. In place of the earlier certainty[?], hope, a strange feeling began to penetrate, which replaced the „list of complaints“. The husband behaved like a doctor, acting gradually[?] as with narcotic remedies: each time a stronger dose... She slowly began to talk to herself, to talk with the children, to pour out her heart to them, to complain, to do accounts and now and then throw in a word or two at his expense — but his remedy worked like opium.
— Well, what do you say? — she asks once when he comes in from the street.
— What, what, what should I say? I say it will get even worse...
She became distraught[?], bit her lips and quietly murmured against him. Inside she was seething — not, God forbid, because she must deny herself the smallest things, simple needs[?] — not for herself, God forbid, but for the poor children... But what can one do, if perhaps, as it were[?].. „it may yet really get worse“...
He became completely silent: silently ate, silently sat, silently spoke, silently answered.
She still went on talking; every time the will to talk broke through again — no longer to „unburden herself“, but at least to ask again what „after all“ the end would be...
And once, when he sat lost in thought, chewing a piece of dry bread, she did no more than ask him a quiet question, short, and not in her usual manner, God forbid...
— Just tell me. I don't want any dresses, I don't want any balls, I don't want any shoes, I don't want any theatre, I don't want the children to study — but bread, will... will... we... have?...
He hunched himself up, „drew“ on the cigarette (papiros) and blurted out: „Worse it won't get any more“...
And then they were both silent.

Sonia smiled to herself. She felt with all her senses that Leon Ziniberg was very much in love with her, that he was always thinking of her, and this made her heart feel warm and joyful. And thinking of him thus, she remembered: it had been a week ago. It had been a week ago [sentence printed twice]. It was at night, and Leon had taken her home in a carriage after they had spent time together in a café... The night was cool and fresh. He sat close beside her, nestled shoulder to shoulder, held her right hand clasped in his hands and spoke in a warm, tender voice that trembled slightly... What did he speak about? Ha? — about her, in fact, he spoke. He was greatly enchanted by her beauty, admired her wisdom and intelligence... He spoke with enthusiasm, and she felt on her cheeks the warmth of his breath... It was good for her to feel his nearness and to hear his words. In her heart something sang, quietly and wondrously... She sat silent, holding her breath, sensing his ardent love for her. She expected to feel his lips on hers. She still [printed "yokh" for "nokh"] longed for it, and at the same time she liked very much that he did not dare to do it... So she did not encourage him, and he indeed did not dare... When she was already standing ready to go into the house and held out her hand to him in farewell, he stretched [sic] her hand to his lips. His lips clung, as it were, to her hand, and she felt a warm tremor run through her whole body...
She thought: how good it would be if he were beside her now... how pleasant it would be for her now to hear his tender voice and to feel upon herself his loving, longing glances... Ah! Should she perhaps call him [printed "ir" — her?] on the telephone? She will call him and say: "Do come, I am waiting for you"... Has no more than one week gone by since she saw him? No more? It now seemed to her that a very long time had already passed... Ah! So perhaps she should really call him?
There — and someone knocked at the door of her room. Sonia remained lying motionless.
— Come in! — she called out.
The door opened. The servant came in and announced:
— The young lady is requested at the telephone.
— I am being called to the telephone? — Sonia gave a start up [literally "gave a jolt up"] who is calling?
— He did not give any name, — the servant answered.
— It is a gentleman, the one calling?
— Yes... a gentleman — the servant nodded his head.
Joy leapt up in Sonia: could it be Leon? Warmth flooded her heart. Her eyes lit up and a colour rose to her cheeks; she sprang up at once and rushed impetuously to the telephone. She took the receiver [?] in her hand:
— Who is speaking?
Hearing the young baron's voice, she exclaimed:
— Leon? — and at once caught herself — is it you, Mr. Ziniberg?
— Yes... it is I...
— I was just thinking of you, — said Sonia.
His voice became saturated with joy:
— Really? That is very fine and I thank you very much... And how are you, Sonia Oskarovna?
— Thank you for asking... and how are you?
— Quite well... My father told me about the important news which you passed on today and — — —
Sonia interrupted him:
I think it is better not to talk about it over the telephone...
— You are right, Sonia Oskarovna!... So perhaps you will allow me to come to you and express my appreciation to you in person?
Sonia smiled and asked playfully:
— Only for that, in order to express your appreciation to me, you want to come? Only for that?
His voice became tender and gentle:
— No, not only for that... You know, Sonia Oskarovna, how pleasant it is for me in your company. And I have not seen you for so long.. a whole week has already passed.. I want very much to see you..
— You speak as though you had been longing for me...
For a while he was silent. Sonia waited, smiling, for his answer, and her heart beat faster within her. Then he asked:
— Shall I be frank with you?
— Please! Be [?] so!... if you can.
— It is true, Sonia Oskarovna, I long for you... I long very much.
— Even very much? — Sonia exclaimed mischievously, and happiness shone on her face and in her eyes.
— Yes... I long for you very, very much... Does it annoy you?
— Oh, no, it does not annoy me, on the contrary. It makes me glad!
— Sonia! Do you mean it? Do you really mean it?
— Of course I mean it. Did I not tell you that I had just been thinking of you?
— How good you are to me! — his voice now rang out. Sonia could feel that he was overjoyed. She breathed more quickly:
— And do you know what it seemed to me?
— What, then?
— It seemed to me that a very long time has already passed since I saw you and... I want very much to see you.

Sonia took leave of him [printed "of her"], hung up the telephone receiver, stood for a while radiant and happy, feeling how in her heart the love for Leon, now come to ripeness, was singing, and resolved to herself: today she would receive him warmly, informally, at ease, and would encourage him to behave more closely towards her... She would no longer hide her feelings for him and would allow that he too [the word "he" is missing in print] should reveal his feelings to her.
In the room it was already dark, but Sonia did not notice it. In her eyes there was brightness.
For a while she stood thus. Then she broke into a merry song and with brisk [? printed "shteyfe"] steps strode off to her room to change and to get ready to receive the young baron Leon Ziniberg...

Chapter Four.
The Sick Heir to the Throne
The Russian heir to the throne Alexei, who was the only son of Tsar Nicholas, was then about six years old. He was a merry, lively boy with a round little face and golden-blond hair, physically well developed and tall for his age. But the boy's life had been, ever since he was born, a long chain of heavy suffering and pain. He suffered from a terrible incurable disease called "haemophilia", and every slightest blow or careless movement was a great danger to his life. If he knocked a foot or a hand, a haemorrhage would at once begin inside his body which no doctor was able to stop. The place of the blow would swell up bluish, and the boy's pains were dreadful.
This terrible disease made the life of the heir to the throne unhappy and embittered the life of the Tsar and the Tsarina, who loved their only son extraordinarily and were constantly in one single fear lest something should happen to him.
Alexei was always under the supervision of the sailor Derevenko, who never took his eye off him and constantly watched him closely so that he should not romp, not jump, not run and not even take too quick a step. At the slightest movement the boy made, he would at once hear the voice of the sailor warning him:
— Careful, Alexei! Watch out! You'll hurt yourself yet!

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayakhel)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayakhel
The Portion
—o—
a) "And Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel" (Ex. 35:1)
The root of impurity is division; the root of holiness is unity. The Jews made the [golden] calf, sank into impurity, which causes division and strife, and now God wished to lead them into the world of holiness — and that could come about only through "Vayakhel" ("and he assembled"), through unity.
Nachalat Yaakov.
—o—
Thereupon the Torah immediately says:
"These are the things which the Lord has commanded that you should do"
Unity God commanded for all generations. Later leaders should learn from the Tabernacle that a holy thing cannot be accomplished without unity. Likkutim Chadashim.
—o—
b) "A Sabbath of solemn rest to the Lord" (ibid., 2)
The Sabbath is called "the most coveted of days", the best of the weekdays.
But there is such a thing as a head of a yeshiva and a head of thieves. Both are heads. The first, however, is a head of Torah scholars, and the latter — a head of thieves.
Whatever days a person spends, of them the Sabbath is the head. If they are days of honesty, then the Sabbath's headship[?] is to be praised. But if they are days of theft and robbery, then the Sabbath is "the most coveted" of dishonest days.. Ofalim le-Tushiya.
—o—
"Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates; they are a burden to me" —
God has opened a credit for those who keep the Sabbath: "Borrow on My account and I will repay." God pays for the Sabbath expenses. But only when the Sabbath is used for God. Not when it is "your new moons and your feasts", not when it is merely your own holiday, for eating and drinking. Then "they are a burden to me" — you burden God for nothing, that He must pay off your debts...
The proof that you are not celebrating only your own Sabbath is when you see to it that the poor man, too, has the means to keep the Sabbath. Then "He who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him his deed"; then God pays your debts together with what He owes you for the poor man... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
c) "For whoever does any work on it shall be put to death" (ibid.)
A freethinker once asked the Malbim to devise some permission to smoke cigarettes on the Sabbath.
The Malbim answers him:
— There is a permission: by way of a change. That is, you should hold the cigarette reversed, with the burning end in your mouth...
—o—
It was once told of a well-known rabbi, who was a great impractical dreamer, that a certain Jew had opened his shop on the Sabbath. He did not want to believe it and went himself to see for himself. Arriving there, he indeed sees the shop open, but customers there happened to be none. Says the rabbi to him:
— You fool, why do you keep the shop open at a time when you may not sell anyway? ..
—o—
d) "You shall kindle no fire in all your dwellings on the Sabbath day" (ibid., 3)
This speaks of the fire of strife. Usually on the Sabbath, when everyone has time, quarrels and brawls flare up in the Jewish communities, in the synagogues and houses of prayer...
Akedat Yitzchak.
—o—
e) "And all the women that were wise-hearted spun with their hands" (ibid., 25)
Those who are "wise-hearted with their hands" — who have their heart in their hands, who rule over their traits — of them it is said: "they spun and brought"; they indeed also brought. Whereas of the others, "whose heart stirred them up", whose heart ruled over them, who were not in control of themselves — of them it is said only "they spun the goats' hair"; they only spun. And when it came to giving — there the heart no longer let them... Yalkut ha-Urim.
—o—
f) "And He has filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom" (ibid., 31)
In the Midrash "Shocher Tov":
David asked God: why should there be rich and poor people? Why should there not be only rich?
God answered him: "Appoint lovingkindness and truth to preserve him" — who would do charity and kindness with whom?
One asks: how does the word "truth" also come into the answer? Kindness, fine — perhaps it refers to him, or the rich must take care of him[?]. But how do they come to truth?..
But David asked about both things: why do some have only money without wisdom, and the others, conversely, only wisdom without money... To this God answered him: "lovingkindness and truth to preserve him". But now the rich trade with the wise: they give the wise money, and the latter give the rich wisdom...
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
Moses Mendelssohn worked in his youth in a bank for a rich Jew who was, besides, a coarse man. A friend once remarked to him:
— It is not just on God's part: you, such a sage and scholar, and you must work for such a coarse soul.
Moses Mendelssohn replied to this sharply:
— God knows what He is doing, for had He made it the other way round, that the coarse fellow should work for me and I should be the banker, what would I have done with such a coarse fellow?...
—o—
g) "All the wise men that wrought all the work of the sanctuary" (36:4)
A rabbi was once asked why he flatters the town's wealthy men. He points to an explicit saying: "A cantor is permitted to flatter the congregation." They ask him again: how so? Here it speaks only of a cantor. The rabbi replies:
— A cantor is a fool, therefore one has to tell it to him explicitly; on his own he won't understand. A rabbi need not be told — he will understand by himself what he has to do...
—o—
h) "And they brought yet unto him freewill offerings" (ibid., 3)
"And they" — the collectors, the gabbaim (those who "received from Moses") — they too gave their donations...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
—o—
Haftarah: Shekalim.
i) "Moreover they reckoned not with the men... for they dealt faithfully" (II Kings, 11 [as printed; actually 12])
Suspecting certain communal workers of stealing and misusing the kehilla's money — this is loved precisely by those who are themselves not honest.. Those who "deal faithfully", who are themselves honest and faithful — "they reckoned not with the men": they check up on no one and suspect no one..
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
j) "And [Jehoash] did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord" (ibid.)
A pious man was Jehoash. And nevertheless it is told in "Chronicles" that he made himself a god. He considered himself so pious that he was already a god.. After Ahavat Yehonatan.
There Is Still Time...

[Sosnowiec — economy; banking.] (On the Sunday general meeting of the Sosnowiec "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank])
Next Sunday, the 6th of March, the annual general meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" in Sosnowiec takes place. For this reason I consider it my duty to inform the honoured members of the "Bank Kupiecki" and to present in brief strokes the general situation of the bank at the present moment.
5 months have passed since the "Bank Kupiecki" in Sosnowiec collapsed because of the prevailing economic crisis — at the moment when the bank stopped its activity — the bank owed about 53 thousand złoty for bill and freight [?] collections, and 110 thousand złoty — deposits. — Those were hard 5 months for the few individual members of the management and the council. But we have passed the test, and with pride I must say that during these 5 months much has been achieved. In the first place we have paid off the collections completely, down to a minimal sum — that is to say, the 53 thousand złoty of collection debts are almost settled. With the deposits, too, we have achieved a great deal, so that at the present moment the "Bank Kupiecki" in Sosnowiec still owes about 30 thousand złoty for deposits; this is, it seems, a colossal achievement of the management and council in office until now.
The bank still has a debt amounting to some twenty-odd thousand zł., which the management and council have brought over to a longer term without interest. On the other hand, the "Bank Kupiecki" has to collect from its members a sum of 183 thousand zł.
The debts have been examined by a special commission, which established that if we agree to such a "surgical experiment" as striking off 112 thousand zł., which cannot be realised for the time being — one must wait for a better business climate — there still remain over 71 thousand zł. of debts, which are secured by mortgage entries [?] and good guarantors, so that the 71 thousand zł. can be counted as live capital. It is also important to stress that the premises are paid in advance for a whole year. The whole inventory, the entire equipment also represents a value of a couple of thousand zł.
So the conclusion of my short characterisation is to tell you: honoured members of the "Bank Kupiecki" in Sosnowiec! The fate of the institution, which still has sound foundations and rests on firm bases, now lies in your hands. With good will and a small effort you can raise your bank back to its standing, to become again the bank which the Sosnowiec merchant community needs so much.
In a few days the bank can be opened for you again — the bank which served you for 8 years soundly and conscientiously — for 8 years the bank stood guard over your day-to-day worries.
So — a little bit of effort — and your financial institution — is saved.
President Natan Abramczyk.

[Law — court decisions; taxes; sickness fund.] On goods belonging to third persons — even though they are located in the enterprise of the tax debtor and are used by him — no "zajęcie" [seizure] may be made for taxes.
(Decision of the Supreme Court number 42/31).
• • •
If a worker or an employee has not been registered with the sickness fund at all, one can be fined up to 5 times as much as the unpaid "składka" [contribution] amounts to. If, however, one did register them, but declared too little, the sickness fund has no right to demand the "kara" [penalty]; it may only demand the difference with interest.
This follows from Art. 10 of the sickness-fund law.
• • •
If a deed contains a clause that all disputes must be settled by an arbitration court, this is binding on both parties. If one party does not want to choose an arbitrator, the court can do so.

Not registering a worker or an employee with the sickness fund does not deprive them of the right to make use of all its facilities, i.e. even if they were not reported, they may demand medical help, etc.

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 26 / 26[?] Adar 5692 — piątek 4 marca 1932 [Friday, 4 March 1932].)
Będzin
Echoes of the kehilla elections.
As our readers already know, Mr. Efraim Kleiman sued Messrs. T. D. Rudzin and L. Brama[?] as those responsible for the insults published against Mr. Kleiman in the one-day publication during the election campaign for the Będzin kehilla.
The epilogue to this was played out last Monday at the Sosnowiec district court, before which all the filth that had settled on the fringes of the local artisans' association was stirred up.
On Sunday evening, in connection with the trial, negotiations took place between the two artisan sides. The negotiations led to an agreement that peace would be made, and its first practical result would be that the trial would not take place. The next morning, i.e. Monday morning, — as we are told — the agreement was broken by Mr. Kleiman, and there was once again a "state of war"..
Twenty-five witnesses were summoned to the trial by both sides.
For the prosecution stood the advocate Mr. Kowalski. As defence counsel — Mr. Farelli[?].
Very characteristic and interesting was the hearing of the witnesses, which lasted almost a whole day. On the one side several witnesses presented Mr. Kleiman as a fighter for the "eynsl"[?] and "that is why the Zionist artisans are conducting a campaign against him", and the other side laid before the judge's table facts about malversations committed by Mr. Kleiman while he was running the artisans' association.
The "star"[?] (printed "figal"[?]) of Mr. Kleiman's witnesses was the shoemaker Mr. Braner, who presented himself as a Piłsudskiite and friend of the Sanacja. To which advocate Farelli remarked ironically: "Just look at this Sanacja fighter — a pity you do not yet have the title of a director or some other high office."
After the hearing of the witnesses advocate Kowalski spoke, pointing to Mr. Kleiman's popularity as a public figure. The best proof is that in the kehilla elections he received a larger number of votes than the artisans' list.
A sharp speech was delivered by advocate Farelli, who censured Mr. Kleiman as a public figure. All that — he says — which the witnesses declared today proves clearly that the publishers of the publication had factual material for accusing Mr. Kleiman.
After deliberation the court pronounces the verdict that Mr. Kleiman's suit is dismissed.

A woman's revenge on her husband
[Czeladź — crime.] Five months ago Mr. A. D. Rozenblum of Małobądz married Miss Kiukawicz[?] of Sosnowiec. After the wedding the couple settled in Czeladź, where they opened a drugstore (apteka-skład). But between the couple there were "silent tragedies". The husband — according to what the neighbours tell — treated his wife badly, and recently he threatened her that he would shoot her. The fear of being shot grew even stronger when she saw a revolver in his possession. The woman went to the police station, where she said that her husband wants to kill her; in passing the woman also informed the police that her husband keeps false business books, from which the Treasury (Skarb) suffers loss.
After these revelations the police carried out a search of the flat, confiscated the business books and other documents, and then sealed the flat and the shop.
What will come of it is not yet clear. Meanwhile Czeladź has been "blessed" with a "sensation".

A new kind of swindle.
[Będzin — crime.] Into the grocery (colonial goods) shop of Mr. Abramczyk on Mandzheyer [probably Modrzejowska][?] Street came a Christian, who bought a packet of tobacco for 60 groszy and handed over a banknote of 20 złoty.
When Mr. Abramczyk had given him change, the customer stepped aside in the shop and [checked][?] whether. In the change there are no counterfeit coins [so printed; evidently: "checked whether there were no counterfeit coins in the change"]. Soon afterwards he turned to Mr. Abramczyk with the claim that among the money there were 2 counterfeit 5-złoty coins. Mr. A., realising that he was dealing with a swindler, called a policeman, who drew up a report against the Christian.
As we are informed, a number of similar cases of such swindles have already occurred. One must therefore be careful with such "customers"...

About the food parcels to Russia. The money can also be paid in Sosnowiec
The Federation of Jewish Relief Organisations in London has concluded an agreement with the Soviet government on the issue, from the state stores called „Torgsin“, of food parcels according to fixed types and at special reduced prices.
There are 4 types of food parcels at a price from 2.40 dollars to 17.35 dollars per parcel.
In addition, orders are accepted for special Passover parcels, of which the most expensive costs 3.70 dollars. Such a parcel contains: 18 kilos of Passover flour, 4 kilos of sugar, 100[?] grams of tea and a litre of vegetable oil.
A smaller Passover parcel costs 1.80 dollars.
In order to make it easier for the inhabitants of Poland to send these parcels to their relatives and acquaintances in Soviet Russia, the London Federation has entrusted the Cooperative Bank in Warsaw (Nalewki 2) with accepting payments and orders for these parcels.
The parcels are delivered even in the most remote corners of Soviet Russia.
One should know that the whole campaign of the London Federation of relief societies is of a philanthropic character and that the Cooperative Bank charges no special fee for its trouble or for the money transfers, since all costs are covered from the Federation's funds.
More detailed information is given by the Artisans' and Small Traders' Bank, Targowa 9.

For how long may one issue a cheque, and when must it be protested?

[Economy and trade — cheque law.] In merchant circles there is no clarity regarding the time limits — for how long one may issue a cheque.
Article 15 of the Polish Cheque Law explains the matter in question precisely:
According to the said article, cheques are divided in this respect into domestic and foreign ones.
The domestic ones are further divided into those issued in the same place, or in the area of another town of the state.
As for foreign cheques, they too are divided into European and worldwide ones.
European are called such cheques as originate from a European state and are drawn on a banking institution in Poland.
As worldwide, on the other hand, are considered those cheques which originate from a country situated in one of the other parts of the world and are to be cashed within Poland.
Thus, cheques of the first category (payable on the spot) may be issued for a term of ten days; cheques of the second category (payable within the territory of the state) for a term of twenty days; cheques of the third category (originating from Europe) for a term of thirty days; cheques of the fourth category (outside Europe) for a term of sixty days.
When one speaks of the term for which a cheque may be issued, what is meant is the term within which the holder is obliged to present it at the institution concerned.
All the terms listed above begin to run from the date on which the cheque in question was issued. The day on which the cheque was issued is in no case counted.
If the preclusive day falls precisely on a Sunday or a holiday, the binding term for presenting the cheque is moved to the next day.
At the moment the cheque is presented and it turns out that there is no cover for it, the banking institution makes an appropriate annotation on that same cheque. Such an annotation has the legal force of a protest.
As soon as a cheque has not been presented within the stated term, the existing endorsements (giros) and guarantees lose their validity.
As for cheques originating from Poland and to be cashed abroad, in the said particulars they are governed by the binding regulations of the place where they are payable.
—Ld.

The Coal Strike Goes On

[Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — the coal strike, economy, crime and community; followed by eight further news items.]
The loss in wages already reaches 3 million złoty.
The situation of the coal strike, as we write these lines, is as follows: at the „Czeladź" and „Reden" mines work has stopped entirely. At „Renard", „Flora", „Kazimierz", „Juliusz", „Niwka", „Klimontów", „Saturn" and „Mars" the number of those working amounts to up to 15 per cent.
On Tuesday evening the workers at „Flora" went to work. They were, however, held back by a group of women of the unemployed.
In the Kraków district the strike continues at almost all the mines.
In „Groyce"[?] [perhaps Grodziec] and at Piaski the police did not allow the planned demonstrations to take place.
The situation of the striking families gets worse from day to day. Hunger and want reign in full measure. The loss in wages over the period of the strike is estimated at 3 million złoty.
—o—
Today, Friday, the fate of 15,000 Upper Silesian miners will be decided.
In connection with the fact that 10 coal mines in Upper Silesia are to be closed, a special delegation has gone to Warsaw to intervene at the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Labour.
The delegation will be received today, Friday, at 0,30[?] by the Minister of Commerce.

The watchman of the „Bloki" persecutes Jewish traders.
A Jewish girl used to bring baked goods every day to the Jewish tenants in the „Bloki" houses. When one of the tenants complained[?] to the administrator about the watchman's conduct towards Jewish traders, the administrator merely drew the watchman's attention to the fact that he should not do such things any more.

The cashier of the Ząbkowice[?] railway station sentenced to 2½ years in prison, his assistant — to 4 years.
On Monday and Tuesday the trial took place at the Sosnowiec District Court against the cashier at the railway station in Ząbkowice[?], Mr. Bernarski, and his assistant Olszewski, who at the time carried out the „affair" of 50 thousand złoty. Bernarski took the sum, but to cover his tracks he pretended that bandits had attacked him. Mr. Olszewski helped[?] in the affair.
22 witnesses were summoned to this sensational trial. After the speeches of the defence counsel, amid the greatest tension, the court delivered the following verdict: Bernarski is sentenced to 2½ years in prison and loss of rights, Olszewski — to 4 years in prison.

„Agudah" in Czeladź „cares" for poor children.

In the course of the week dozens of Jewish residents of Czeladź have come to us, indignant that in these present hard times, when the poor man struggles for a dry piece of bread, the Czeladź „Torah monopolists", those who seized the Talmud Torah as „a spade to dig with", should make the situation of poor Jewish parents still worse and bring it about that their children are brought up in the street...

Rent Must Become Cheaper!

[Będzin — tenants and rent; article.] (On the Sunday [?] meeting of the Będzin Tenants' Association).
The town citizen is already ruined to the highest degree. Not only is he terribly impoverished and pushed out of his former economic position — he is also inwardly [?] disappointed and full of despair and bitterness; he stands downcast, in trembling expectation of the almost [?] prospectless tomorrow.
And when hunger and need drive the despondent citizen out into the street to look for where to earn a groschen to support himself and his family, and there is almost nowhere to earn — he must, whether he wants to or not, cut all his expenses down to a minimum. Today it is no longer a matter of luxury goods; that is a subject for empty phrases and "fat bellies" — it is simply a matter of a bite of bread and nothing more.
But here, besides the various state and municipal taxes under whose yoke the citizen has been groaning for years, come also the terribly inflated prices of such articles of primary need as electricity and housing. The high prices for the bit of light and the roof over one's head now lie on the poor townsman like a heavy indirect tax that draws the last marrow from his bones.
But the citizen has already come out of the dull passivity into which need and despair had [?] driven him, and he is beginning to fight against the usury practised at his expense. What is the strong, lively wave of "electric strikes" in a number of larger towns in Poland, if not an expression of the accumulated bitterness against the owners of the electric power stations, for their unwillingness to understand the critical situation of the ruined electricity consumer and their wish to go on stripping a "strap" [of skin] off him?
No less important for the citizen is the question of rent prices, which have already been screwed up far too high.
The landlords themselves make efforts wherever necessary, knock on the doors of the ministries and the big banks, so that their taxes on immovable property be reduced, so that far-reaching concessions be made for them, etc. — and what is their attitude to the tenants?
Just let a tenant try not to pay the rent on time — the landlord does not wait and immediately obtains an eviction. It does not interest him in the least whether the tenant sometimes fails to pay the rent because he has not even a spare gulden [złoty] to eat a midday meal; it matters little to him whether the tenant and his family are not sometimes freezing from cold because he has no wood — just give the rent, and at the full inflated price — and if not, if not, it's eviction...
Now it is still winter, and under the tenants' law it is somewhat difficult for the landlord to throw the tenant out onto the frosty street. But as soon as the spring sun sends out a ray, evictions will come pouring, and hundreds, if not thousands, of declassed and utterly ruined citizens will be left without a roof over their heads...
This danger, which lurks quite seriously over the heads of many, many thousands of impoverished citizens, is so real, so conspicuous against the background of frightful poverty and... screwed-up rents, that the groan of troubles, the worry about a roof over one's head at accessible prices — is today a burning question on the agenda of our painful life.
A broad-scale tenants' campaign must be undertaken at once so that rent becomes cheaper, and one would like [?] to believe that the decisive state factors in Poland too will meet the just demands of the tenant masses, numbering millions, which have been dictated by the pain and need of our hard and bitter life.
G.
Struggle for Cheaper Light in Łazy, Zawiercie and Dąbrowa.

[Zagłębie — consumers and electricity prices.] In Łazy a meeting took place, attended by 150 consumers, on the question of making the price of electric light cheaper. At the meeting it was resolved to demand from the management of the power station: 1) to reduce the price to 45 groszy per kilowatt, and 2) that the meter should belong to the subscriber after 3 years.
In case the demands are not granted, the inhabitants of Łazy are to join in solidarity with the campaign that is to begin in Zagłębie.
In Zawiercie a committee has been formed, which has drawn up a series of postulates to be submitted to the management of the power station.
At the general meeting in Dąbrowa it was resolved to turn to the government and the Sejm so that a law be issued concerning cheaper prices for light, tram tickets, and the products of the state monopolies.
Finally a resolution was adopted that if the power station does not, within 2 weeks, reduce the price of electricity to 40 gr., the consumers will come out on strike.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
A Bloody Demonstration.
On Tuesday demonstrations of the unemployed took place in a number of localities in Upper Silesia, among others also in Orzegów[?], where it came to bloody events.
About 1000 unemployed gathered in front of the gmina [municipal] office. At a certain moment the premises of the office were pelted with stones. The same happened when a police patrol arrived. One of the policemen used his weapon, whereby one of the demonstrators was seriously wounded. There are also some lightly wounded.
Similar demonstrations took place in Świętochłowice, Szarlej and Lipiny, where the demonstrators shouted: „Give us bread, down with the fascist dictatorship“. A large number of women took part in the demonstration, carrying baskets[?] in their hands.
—o—
Preparations for a General Strike.
On Tuesday a conference of workers' delegates took place in Katowice. At the conference the question was discussed whether a general protest strike should break out in Upper Silesia on the 16th of this month.
In connection with this, a large workers' congress is taking place in Katowice this Saturday, at which the question will be decided.

Trial for Printing an Article Entitled „Jews and Brest“.
In the dock of the Katowice court sat the responsible editor of the „Polonia“ for printing the articles: 1) „At the gates of Brest waves of revolution are rising“ and 2) „Jews and Brest“. In that article the writer stated that the Jews in Poland had taken upon themselves the responsibility for Brest and would have to render an account for it.
At the trial the prosecutor withdrew the charge concerning the first article, but upheld the charge regarding the article entitled „Jews and Brest“.
The court acquitted the editor of every charge and annulled the confiscations.

Great abuses have been discovered in the Katowice prison, on account of which the state treasury suffered a loss of 75 thousand zł. The chief culprit is the official Szykarski[?], who committed the swindle with the help of false documents. A number of persons from Sosnowiec are also involved in the affair.
In this connection a special commission has arrived from Warsaw and is conducting an investigation.
