The Price-Reduction Course

The difficult situation in the country has led the citizens to the most exact calculation and to the most varied computations. Nobody wants to enlarge his budget any more; everyone today works out how to carry less of a yoke on his shoulders.
Yes. It used to happen quite often that people quarrelled[?] over why it is so easy to squander money at a time when one works comparatively hard enough for it. True, we now live in such conditions, where people have stopped being petty and where the grosz need not play any role. But the fault is this: when the times changed — as soon as days without a livelihood arrived, mass unemployment — the course should already then have been changed; already then one should have considered how to save so-and-so much, how to arrange oneself so as to ease the conditions of life; but no one even thought of it. One had in mind — what do I know: the storm will pass and things will be as before. But the trouble is that the storm does not pass, that it keeps on lasting, and meanwhile people did not spend less, could not pay their debts, until it led to recklessness and irresponsibility.
This order has meanwhile been shaken[?]; it has toppled from the pedestal the guilty and the innocent alike, and people came to the realisation that to go on running such a lamentable economy means annihilation, ruin. Only then did people begin to seek a way out that would save the difficult situation. People began to think seriously how to reduce expenses, in what way to draw up the most minimal budget. It goes without saying that it is not good for the country, as for the citizens, when one begins to economise down to a minimum, just as it is no good throwing money about too much, because in the minimum neither the citizens nor the government's coffers earn anything, certainly; but when there is no other way — it is lost; surely it is more restrained and wiser to be a minimal spender and to know that the grosz one takes out has been earned, than to squander maximal expenses that one does not earn. Conscious, honest and modest European citizens will, believe me, always live with the scales in hand; they will always see to it to maintain the balance. Here, unfortunately, people are not used to such calculation, and therefore the catastrophe in Poland came in quite a different mode. Here no one had a farther view, or did not want to have one; we always looked through short-sighted glasses, and therefore the catastrophe came upon many in an incomprehensible way, by an inconceivable system.
But thanks to the hard state, thanks to the catastrophic situation[?] in which we find ourselves, people have been raised — or lowered — to the level where they began to carry out a revision. Yes, today every responsible person carries out a revision of himself: whether he can allow himself the expenses or not; and when he saw that after cutting back he does not have even for the most necessary, that he does not manage with what he earns, the question arose in him: yes, the times are bad, everyone earns less, everyone must be more calculating — so why should many monopoly expenses not be reduced?
From various regions of Poland reports reach us that the population has begun to strike against the suppliers of lighting; they do not want to take any current [prąd] from the power stations [elektrownie] as long as they do not reduce the price, so that it follows anyway that in the present "good" times current costs us 10 percent more, since the government takes a tax of 10 percent from every consumer. Therefore the citizens ask themselves: since every single one lives in hard conditions, why should the big ones not feel it too? How can it be that the smallest — the poor worker, the wretched artisan, the tiny shopkeeper and every average merchant and small industrialist — must cut their prices and earnings and even so cannot stay afloat, while the big ones, the concession-holders, want to know nothing of anything?
It is therefore understandable that the merchants' convention called in Sosnowiec by the Chamber of Commerce adopted various price-reduction resolutions, such as lowering the price of electric light, and that after 3 years the customer should no longer pay for the meter. And why, for example, should such a thing not be carried through? The power station hangs a meter in our homes which we do not need — only the enterprise needs it, to measure the light — and we are responsible for the object all the time; so why should we pay for it and never finish paying it off? Is it not rational, when the citizens come into such a hard time, that they demand relief on articles of prime necessity?
Or, for example, many readers turn to us with the question whether the telephone company intends to reduce the subscription price of telephones; if not, many of them will be forced to give up their telephones. Many firms that have separate telephones in the business and in the home are beginning to economise and cut down to one telephone, and those who have only one are about to give up that one too. Moreover the expense has risen indirectly, because the disinfection also costs money every month.
Here too the question arises: should the telephone directorate not meet its subscribers half-way and reduce the price? It is to be understood that it will gain more from the reduction than from holding on to the price, because already now we see that the number of subscribers is shrinking, and in the case of a reduction every subscriber will try[?] not to give up this useful object, so that the company will suffer no loss here.
The same goes for the disinfection. Either the price must be reduced to a minimum, or else everyone who[?] can should be allowed to carry out the disinfection himself; after all, it is only a matter of disinfecting, and as soon as the disinfection is done, everything is in order.
And there is one more pain on which one must dwell, and that is the housing question. The rent, too, must be reduced. We are no longer able to pay the high rent in such hard times. The tenants' associations are obliged to stand on guard and to protect the people's interests.
Also all sorts of tax matters, which press so heavily on the body of the citizenry, must be radically reformed; otherwise the present, and still more the future, will be sad, and the further on, the more catastrophic.
A system of price reduction must be carried through on all fronts of our existence, in its whole length and breadth.
It goes without saying that reductions of expenses and incomes are no great virtue for the government or for the citizens, but at the present moment there is no other way; a course of cheapening, of calculation, must be carried through, so that we can continue our living existence in a normal way. One must think and consider and combine, so as to keep step with the times, so as not to fall into the abyss.
Nevertheless one must not forget that it will not always be so, and that things will not keep getting worse for ever; sooner or later the hard situation will end, and then, when the bright moment comes, we should not be extinguished shadows, without strength and without marrow in our bones.
Care[?] must be taken now that the citizens can return to the bright era in a normal state, and that the body of the citizenry still has flesh and skin on it.
R. Let[?].

Homely Letters

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton; kehilla, mikveh and Chevra Kadisha.] B"H, for the portion "asher pakad Moshe" (Pekudei)...
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
Several months have already passed since we last wrote to each other. The main reason for it is that one does not feel like it, and has no appetite, to chew over again and to repeat the same questions that we have already dealt with many times. It is already more than [?superfluous] to talk about the everyday matters, even about this. If the Będzin "Agudah" gets back its rule over kehilla life, it is no longer worth even talking about the institution that bears the title — gmina...
And that is exactly why this time we shall set aside our conversation so far and deal with a matter which will no doubt arouse satisfaction in you too.
The matter is this: the majority of our brethren, the Children of Israel (except for Wacław's [?] comrades...) always complain: why are we not equal in rights, why do we not enjoy the same privileges as other minorities, why are we only the givers and others the takers, etc. etc. I, for my part, do not agree with those who only look for grievances and make a [?fuss] over every smallest matter: even when students want to have a little fun...
You see, R' Shlomo, I am very far from the line supported by those who want to set up a "państwo w państwie" (a state within a state). My reason dictates to me that one must be grateful to the "kingdom of kindness" for its kindnesses towards us. One sees plainly how they take an interest in our affairs: even the matter of the school system they want to take under their supervision too, to carry on themselves the whole burden of our private schools... Now just look at the privileges we receive on every holiday: if one of our people wants to greet his rebbe on the holiday, he enjoys railway reductions and the like.
But all this is only a miniature of the rights we have received through the kehilla budget, which, thank God, has come back koshered according to the law of R' Avraham and R' David...
Yes, R' Shlomo, I put my hand on my heart and swear that the budget has taken a heavy stone off me, which had tormented me for months. Just imagine what the Będzin kehilla administration allowed itself! It went and earmarked a sum of 2,000 złoty (gilden) for setting up a cheap kitchen for the Jewish victims of the crisis. Right at the start this made me very angry at the kehilla representatives: how is this possible? How dare you do this? How can one display such disloyalty as to open a special Jewish kitchen? Isn't the magistrate's "tania kuchnia" (cheap kitchen) enough for you — I wrote to them?... What for, all of a sudden, separate kitchens? We ought to be grateful that we get a bit of cooked food there. What remedy would we have had — I wrote to them, to our kehilla representatives — if the "Komitet dla biednych" (Committee for the Poor) were to introduce a "numerus clausus" in its "kuchnia"? [?Then] you would have run [?] to Yitzchak [probably Sejm deputy Yitzhak Grünbaum] to make an interpellation in the Sejm. A fine face we would have shown to the world if we demanded special kitchens for our poor people...
And indeed the minister did not want to blacken us before the outside world and struck out the budget item of 2,000 złoty that had been earmarked for opening a cheap kitchen at the kehilla.. And as if that were not enough, the minister himself, in all his glory, raised the pensions for the shochtim, so that they should be honest Jews and not look for any side earnings... And the consequences will be that the klei kodesh (religious functionaries) will suffer material damage...
Now, R' Shlomo, I want in this way to talk over with you a very important matter, on condition that you do not make it public to the wide world, because it could cause the "order of the world" as it has been until now to be changed, God forbid...
The matter is as follows: as you know, a mikveh is being built in Będzin. The building proceeds according to the "same system" as Noah's ark before the Flood. The difference is only that Noah's ark was finished before the Flood came, whereas the Będzin mikveh has already lived through several "floods" and
— they are still only at the beginning...
And since "the sorrow of carrying is so great" that all sources of income have already been exhausted, the mikveh committee began to look for new revenues. And "I laboured and I found" — whoever searches, finds — the committee understood that, since a mikveh has, after all, a close connection with the other world, and since every mortal must sooner or later pack up and move over there, the committee should therefore sell plots (karka'ot, burial plots)... Properly speaking, the concession for plots belongs to the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha, but since several "deals" had already been made without reckoning with the Chevra Kadisha, the "trade" became legal and took on wide dimensions... For example, until now the committee sold plots for men, but since the crisis has had an influence on this "article" too, and there are no buyers, the committee hit on a plan to deal in
— women...
Ordinary women cannot enjoy this privilege; to reach this "rank" the "klientka" must have certain merits for the sake of religion, possibly for Agudah purposes... and above all — several thousand zł. for the plot..
The trade has raised a storm among the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha, because it concerns women who want, after a hundred and twenty years, to lie next to their husbands... The gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha are against the new reform which the mikveh committee together with the Shomrei ha-Dat want to introduce in the Będzin cemetery...
The matter has flared up badly, quite simply: it is about getting, for such a little plot, a sum of 8 thousand zł. Notes are flying, intercessors (shtadlanim) are sweating. But the Chevra Kadisha gabbaim are fighting against it. The matter is not yet settled; God willing, in my next letter I will write to you who prevailed — the power of money or the power of truth. Meanwhile, have a good Shabbat, wishes you your
Ben Amotz.
We Are Returning to the Times of Our Great-Grandfathers.

[Poland — economy; press review.]

We must win back the domestic market, rediscover it, deepen and broaden it! —

This, holds the "Ilust. Krak. Kurier" [Ilustrowany Kuryer Codzienny, Kraków], must at the present moment become the slogan and the command of the hour in Poland, which supplies foreign countries with cheap sugar, coal and other articles and does not care at all about the domestic market.

It is no paradox and no mere play on words, but a sad truth: Polish industry fences itself off from the domestic market with high barriers, chokes it and strangles [?] it, thereby sawing off the very branch on which it itself sits.

Our industry treats the domestic market as a field of exploitation, as a means serving other goals: the goals of export. A veritable export fetishism has arisen among us, which may no longer be tolerated, because it is beginning to suck out the last drop of blood of our economy.

Touching on the high premiums which the government gives to all kinds of exporters, the paper writes:

If export fetishism was still justified in the era of "open doors" in the world, nowadays it is a senseless thing [?] and must — if it goes on like this — lead to the ruin of the country. Our export runs with ever greater deficits and costs ever more sacrifices. And meanwhile, running up in export against impenetrable walls, our industry is losing its natural sales market. The only way out of this is to turn back to the domestic market, to treat this market as the first and last goal and not merely as a means of forcing the deficit export.

And if there is no other choice, the paper says, it is even better to close, gradually [?] to reduce to a minimum our borders to imports; rather than give away to foreign countries almost for nothing the products of our labour — it is better to give these products at the export price to the domestic market.

If we were to send our coal, or oil, cement or iron at export prices to the eastern Kresy [Poland's eastern borderlands], or if we were to sell them — to agriculture and the processing industry — only then would it be established whether we were really incapable of producing such goods whose export would pay without paying extra for it. Our domestic life would revive. Unemployment would decrease. New consumers would be added, etc., etc.

Then it would turn out that our overall export has not decreased at all, only it would have acquired a different structure, a far healthier one than now. It would turn out that one can export without losses, and not as now — adding to every article at the expense of the domestic market.

It is surely an absurdity that an economy of 32 million should export only at a loss; it surely cannot be that Polish industry does not possess a single branch which has natural conditions to make its way in [?]. Such branches surely exist, only they are beaten down by the false structure of prices, by the false approach of economic policy and by the false orientation of our industry, which brings it about that Poland becomes a hewer of wood and drawer of water for other nations, and that for ridiculously low prices which do not even cover our own most primitive expenses.

Such a situation, holds the author, may not last any longer; it threatens ruin. The village is gradually weaning itself from all kinds of industrial products, which have simply become inaccessible to it because of the high prices.

Instead of kerosene, people already use resinous pine splinters; instead of coal — wood; instead of shoes and cloth — bast shoes and rags; iron and cement, artificial fertilizer are disappearing entirely from the village, and the same goes for salt and sugar, yeast and rice; in transport the railway is gradually being pushed out by the peasant cart [furmanka]; the too-expensive postal tariffs have called into being the private letter-carrier, who is becoming an ever stronger competitor to the post office; the same goes for the samogon [home-distilled vodka] factories, of which in Eastern Galicia alone no fewer than 40 were discovered in the month of January.

But not only in the village — in the town, too, this movement has already set in. A rebellion of the urban consumer is arising, whose incomes are shrinking more and more because of the crisis and the [wage] reductions, and who is unable to pay as much as in the times of the favourable boom.

The high prices of electric and gas lighting are gradually forcing him to abandon these achievements of civilization and to return to the primitive means of heating and lighting. It is no longer news that some town dwellers burn kerosene lamps or candles.

In a number of towns in Poland strikes of electricity consumers, for whom electric lighting is becoming a luxury, have already broken out, and in Warsaw, Lwów, Łódź and also Sosnowiec they are about to break out.

In a word, a general "barbarization" of economic life is taking place; we are returning to the primitive forms of economy.

And as a result — ever greater unemployment and an ever stronger devastation of our economic life. And therefore the slogan of the day must now be: "Away with export fetishism! Face the domestic market!"

Our industry must rediscover and win anew the domestic market by supplying the citizen with cheap goods, which will revive the dying economic life and bring money and goods into circulation. The domestic consumer must be treated not as an object, but as a goal, as a client, who must be served honestly and matter-of-factly and not be skinned alive.

M. G-n.
My Uncle and His 5 Daughters.

[Feuilleton — the crisis, matchmaking and the Maccabiah.]
A dear, but tragicomic, guest I had this week: my uncle, the scholar and maskil, came from the shtetl. "I even wanted to put the trip off to another time," my uncle told me in a whisper, "but your aunt, may she be well, made a scene [lit. 'worked deeds']: the whole world is looking [?] for advice, running to save itself, and you don't budge from the spot... you should have gone already!..."
— Probably again [?] some little tax! — I try to guess my uncle's constant plague. But he shakes his grey, finely chiselled head sadly.
— This time, little brother, you didn't guess at all... It is not a matter of money law here now, but of life and death [dinei nefashot]... Marrying off a daughter nowadays [?] is a matter of life and death, and I have, as you know, five, no evil eye... one after another, marriageable girls [?]. Go and lead them under the wedding canopy...
— So you [?] have come here, that is, about a match?...
— That, you know, I really did not expect of you... You have become a true mocker of the poor!... How could I come here about a match when I haven't a broken penny to my name?... And who, I ask you, can in times like these think about that at all?... Beggars' sacks! A world of beggars' sacks... Do you remember in Graetz [the historian Heinrich Graetz], in the history? In former times, he tells, Jews in Germany could not marry off their children because of a royal decree. Now the same is happening in Poland, though there is no decree... So what does one do after all? Jews look to save themselves in various ways. Now girls are travelling to the Land of Israel for the "Maccabiade" [the Maccabiah], and in the heart a hope glimmers: perhaps a chalutz will fall in love with them there and marry them... It goes without saying that things have not yet come to young men snatching dancing [?] girls in the vineyards, as it was once before the Destruction... But all the same we have there the finest of our youth, idealist young men who do not look at money... With them there are no tricks! "Cheshkah nafshi" [my soul desires] — says a chalutz to a girl — meaning I love you, and let's go write the betrothal contract... Pure, true love, just like Amnon and Tamar in "Ahavat Zion" [Mapu's novel]... So we lie in our beds, I and your aunt, and plan [?] it out: first we will send Beshke, the eldest, to the "Maccabiade", as is the custom [?]. There she will find her true match and later will bring over Mashke; Mashke will pull Baylke over, Baylke — Fesl, and at the very end Fesl will drag over Asnale, the youngest, just like in the Had Gadya... Then we'll remain alone, I and your aunt, "an old man with his old woman" [Polish in the text: dziad z babą] — and draw joy from afar...
I took a look at my uncle — he was all radiant [?], flying in the higher worlds... But suddenly, it seems, he remembered something and sighed:
— Only it's bad that there is no money for expenses... How does one borrow when nobody has any?... So I've really come to sniff around whether it can't perhaps be done on promissory notes, or even on instalments?... After all, the whole world runs on instalments today!...
He tried to smile, this uncle of mine, but no smile came out — instead some painful grimace twisted his ideal, scholarly face. Seas of sorrow poured from his black Jewish eyes, the sorrow of a whole nation, it seems, which toils with its last strength to maintain its existence in this ugly, mangy [?] world...
A. B-ezinski [?]
Two Kinds of Tears.

Saturday morning, as soon as I had got up, a neighbour from the same street came in to me, dressed in a plush jacket, a black silk shawl on her head, a big "Korban Minchah" prayer book under her arm, and, wishing me a broad "Gut Shabbes", she sat down.
"I have come to you, Reb Shiele, knowing that you are a man who writes in the 'gazettes'; I must pour out my bitter heart to you.
I want the whole town to know it. But since it is now the Sabbath, I want to tell you, and right after Havdalah you shall write it up."
I begin to get curious. But I have a rule: women and children must not be pulled by the tongue — so I wait.
The neighbour unties the shawl, lays the Korban Minchah prayer book on the table, takes off her snow boots and, after a good cough, she begins:
"You may believe me, Reb Shiele, that since yesterday noon I have had nothing at all in my mouth. You surely think that I lack, God forbid, 'forbidden pork' [i.e. that I lack something]: I myself bought for the Sabbath a good live little carp, my bride-to-be daughter prepared it — I can tell you, a husband will have a sweet life with her. Golden hands, a successful thing, only a little more luck. 'Sate'[?] in 'chimlen'[?] and a good bit of plums I prepared — fit to serve the emperor — delicacies, baked a good lot of biscuits, made a little cherry brandy with spirits, and after all that, food will not go down. I cannot sleep whole nights, my children ask me: 'Mamele, why do you groan whole nights?' Well, can I tell them? May they be healthy for years and with luck. I have 3 girls, successful children — only to lead them to the wedding canopy in a lucky hour. What would I have lacked? A livelihood, thank God, I do not lack — may it be said of all Jewish children — and from America they also send a few dollars. So what would I have lacked? There remained a dowry; my elder son deposited it in the 'Ch. Ger'[?] bank. My heart, a mother's heart, rejoiced, I was happy, everything was already prepared, it was just then a good match, a man of pedigree, from a fine family, a handsome person, a breadwinner — and here you have such a crash, with a bank of all things. My grandfathers and great-grandfathers lived out their years and did not know of the plague of banks-shmanks, may the sickness fall on them! It cuts me to the heart — 500 dollars, a fortune! My child's happiness, my child's future —" here she wiped away a tear with her batiste handkerchief — "the devil talked me into putting the money into the bank, a dark hour it was; better I had not lived to see it, and 'jumped back'[?]; who could have expected this? It seemed so very fine and good: every month my son used to bring the interest from the bank; we thought we would become happy, since from the interest came yet more interest, a joy — and here you have such a misfortune: they will take away my child's dowry, my happiness, my fortune, my heart. Is this how people act — simply take from another? Bandits act so, free-loaders, swindlers, robbers! I will show them, I will not keep silent." And she started to curse and to weep, so that I could barely calm her. I promised her that right after Havdalah I would describe her misfortune in the 'gazette', and let everyone know and judge.
As soon as the neighbour had left my room, the door opened again and in came a woman of middle height, pale, emaciated, with a kerchief on her head, in a badly worn coat, leading a little boy, also pale, who was coughing sickly. Humbly she said "Gut Shabbes" and apologised many times for coming to trouble my head on the Sabbath.
"What shall I do," she says quietly, "in the middle of the week I have no time. Now, as I am coming with my child from the 'Kropla Mleka' [infant milk station][?], I decided to come up to you."
I asked her to sit down.
She began: "I myself come from a poor home; something was always lacking[?], never eaten my fill, never slept enough, never been warm. I always worked, my life was full of suffering, because my parents died early on me and I had to provide for myself. And when I married, life changed for the better for me: we saved up a little money and my husband started travelling to 'Ślonsk' [Silesia] and earned not badly. On top of that my husband took a loan from the bank, in order[?] to buy a little more merchandise. Meanwhile, however, times became even worse, there was nothing more to earn; still my husband paid no heed to all this, worked hard and bitterly himself and paid the bank the interest out of that money, just to push through the bad times. The child was already there then —" she points at the little boy with the sickly face — "he is a very fine child, a clever one; the doctor tells me to give him fatty things, cod-liver oil to drink and lots of fruit, oranges. Well, I ask you, can I even think of such things, when such a misfortune lies in wait for me? It is already a year that I have not paid any rent.
The landlord wants to throw me out of the flat, out of the 'grave'[?], for after all the damp runs down the walls, the rain comes in; and now, as if this were too little for me, the bank now demands the loans back from us. I already have a notice from the bailiff ['komornik']; he has listed for seizure the last bit of property that I still have at home [—]. On top of all that my husband has lately been unwell, may it not happen to you — he has begun to suffer from his lungs, he coughs whole nights and I cannot sleep. I have become nervous. In the morning the landlady makes a 'market' [a scene] at me because I do not pay her rent; she scolds and shouts with deadly curses. Now I go about the whole day in mortal fear lest the bailiff come and take from my home the last bit of poverty — I shall no longer have where to rest my worn-out bones — and today[?] the disgrace! They still point their fingers at me, that I grabbed money from the bank and do not want to pay, and the guarantor does not keep quiet either; and the main thing is my sick husband — he may, God forbid, get a 'napad' [a fit] and fall in the middle of the street!"
Her eyes filled with tears. The little boy too, looking at his mother, burst out crying.
Weeping she said: "God is my witness that I did not want to take anything from anybody. What shall I do, when I have become so impoverished that I simply have nothing to get through the day with? If I did not have the child, I would have put an end to my dark life. I beg you, Mister Writer, write it down — perhaps people will have pity and not deal so brutally with fallen people; perhaps there is still [—] pity in people."
I see them both out and describe it. Who is more in the right — you shall judge for yourselves..
Shiele.
The Portion — a) "As they were counted according to Moses" (38:21)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion (Pekudei); first part of the column.]
The Portion
a) "As they were counted according to Moses" (38:21)
"As they were counted according to Moses" —
That is to say: it was not the Jews [?] who demanded of Moses an account of the gold and silver spent on the Tabernacle. Moses did it himself; he himself pointed out every penny that he had spent out of public money. Although it would have occurred to nobody to suspect him of misuse, he did it as a path for all later leaders.. Torat Moshe (Alshich).
—o—
Rabbi Yose said: May my portion be with the charity collectors; and Rabbi Yose further said: May my portion be with those who are suspected without cause. (Shabbat 118).
It appears that this is one and the same thing: if one is a charity collector, one must already suspect him, even if sometimes without cause... Sichat Chachamim (M.H.).
—o—
b) The Tabernacle of the Testimony (ibid.).
"A testimony to Israel [?] that the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave them for the deed of the Calf"..
For the gold that was given to the Calf no account was taken, because it was donated without accounting, in agitation. A proof that the motive for giving was an abnormal, a sickly one — agitation. For the Tabernacle they already gave with an account; it already sprang from natural generosity of heart. Kiflayim Letushiya.
—o—
c) "And with him Oholiab... of the tribe of Dan" (ibid., 23).
Bezalel descended from the most distinguished tribe, Judah, and Oholiab from the lowliest: Dan.
So too the Temple was built by Solomon of the tribe of Judah and by Hiram of the tribe of Dan.
For before God there is no lowly class and no class of pedigree. "The small and the great are there." Tzror HaMor.
—o—
d) "And they brought the Tabernacle to Moses" (39:33)
"It happened that Rabbi Abbahu, as he was departing from the world, saw all [?] the good being prepared for him in the World to Come; he began to rejoice and said: All this is Abbahu's? And I said: I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought and vanity." (Midrash Rabbah)
There was once a poor man whose rich brother was making a wedding. So he starved himself for three days beforehand, in order to be able to "enjoy" such a wedding on an emptied stomach...
The third day comes, hunger gnaws under his heart, but no messenger from the brother is to be seen. The hunger is great, impossible to bear. So our poor man takes bread and onions and eats his fill, as after a three-day fast. When he has already filled himself with the onions, the messenger arrives: the brother invites you to the wedding...
Well, one goes. But when the carp's head is served and he touches it with his fork, the smell of onions rises up, and he no longer feels any taste in the fish.
And so he pushes away all the dishes: not good, not good...
The moral:
The same happens to all those who approach the Torah when they have already filled themselves with horseradish and onions. Can they then smell the taste of truly better dishes? After all kinds of trash and abomination, can one then feel a taste for the higher, the more spiritual?
"I have laboured in vain" — the whole effort must first be to cleanse oneself of "chaos and vanity". Then one can attain something of the World to Come... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
e) "And he set the laver" (40:30)
The laver which served for washing was made of the mirrors of the serving women, of mirrors.
For cleansing and washing oneself one does not do [on one's own]; only when one sees oneself mirrored in the other [?]... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
f) "And Moses finished the work" (ibid., 33).
In the Midrash:
"From what was left over from the Tabernacle they made a Tabernacle of Testimony."
?
That which was left over. The fact that Jews [?] were always afraid that they had not yet made the Tabernacle as it ought to be, that they had not yet fulfilled everything — this very feeling is the Tabernacle of Testimony, the Holy of Holies of the Jewish soul... Imrei Tzaddikim (R. Y. M. of Bełz).
—o—
Also a Midrash:
"'And his banner (vediglo) over me is love' — do not read vediglo but vedilugo [his skipping]" — that is to say: a Jew's skipping during his prayer, saying "ve'ayavta" instead of "ve'ahavta", is dear to God. Why? —
Like that guest to whom the innkeeper handed a bill saying that he had drunk 10 little bottles of wine at 5 zł. and 10 little bottles at 10 zł. The guest opens his eyes wide:
— But I drank no more than 10 little bottles altogether, at 5 zł. And how can a Jew have such "Jewishness" — if you already want to steal, to put the invented bottles down at 10 zł.! You could at least have set [?] them at 5 zł., since in truth I did not drink them at all...
The innkeeper, a clever Jew, answers:
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion (Pekudei) and haftarah; column heading and continuation.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Pekudei
[continuation of the innkeeper's answer:]
About what you really did drink one may say that you drank ordinary wine at 5 zł. But what you did NOT drink can surely be at 10 zł. too...
A Jew, when he prays badly, prays badly, of course. But what he skips can surely be good as well, valuable... Therefore: "and his skipping over me is love".
Rabbi Yaakov Kranz (the Dubno Maggid)
—o—
g) "For the cloud of the Lord was upon the Tabernacle" (ibid., 8)
In the Tabernacle where God rests, it is shrouded in smoke from above, hidden by a cloud — and the divine fire: "and fire was in it by night", only at night. When no one sees, the inner flame shows itself. "And walk humbly with the Lord thy God."
Sha'ar Bat Rabim (R. Y. L. of Wolkowysk).
—o—
A rich Jew comes to R' Itchele Peterburger to complain about his pious son-in-law:
— The whole day he sits and studies. He prays until twelve, fasts, recites the midnight lament. In a word: this is not a human being!
Says R' Itchele to him:
— What is the fuss? [?] I too do the very same, exactly the very same.
The rich man answers:
— You do it for a living, of course, but the fool, my son-in-law, does it for real — — —
—o—
The Haftarah
h) "The things which David his father had dedicated... he put among the treasures of the house of the Lord."
(I Kings 7)
Solomon did not use David's treasures for building the Temple because David had gathered the treasures in a time of famine, and God said to him: My children are dying of hunger and you gather gold and silver to build a Temple? I swear to you that Solomon will not make use of them. Midrash.
—o—
In the Sanz synagogue there was a gabbai, R' Reuvele, a man of standing with the Sanzer Rebbe, but people murmured something about him, that he "forgets" to hand over the communal money he had collected.
Everybody hated him and wanted to depose him, but the Rebbe would not allow it.
Once he was caught in open theft; Rabbi Boruchl of Rudnik goes in to his father: now R' Reuvele must surely resign.
But the Sanzer Rebbe goes on protecting him:
"You know, my child, that in Heaven there is a chair for those who faithfully occupy themselves with communal needs. Until now the chair is still empty. Well, do you want, my child, that R' Reuvele should be seated on that chair? — Let the chair remain empty...
Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov (instalment 15)

[Serialized historical novel — Tsarist Russia, Rasputin; instalment 15.]
It was a great torment for the boy to sit whole days here, quiet and still, when he was so strongly drawn to romping, running about and all kinds of games. This made him very sad and dejected. He mightily [?] envied other children, who were allowed to jump and run about. He saw how his own sisters played tennis, chased each other in the park by the court, romped and laughed, and only he alone remained almost motionless. The childish heart in him often clenched with pain and vexation... What would he not have given to be able, even just once, to run about as his heart desired and not to have to hear the voice of the sailor warning him:
— Be careful, Aleksei! Watch out!
Very often, when the heir to the throne would come to his mother, the Tsarina, to ask her for something, she, the mighty Tsarina and devoted mother, had with great pain in her heart to refuse his requests:
— Mama! I want to have a bicycle — the boy begged hard — I want so much to ride a bicycle!
And the mother was compelled to answer:
— You can't have a bicycle, Aleksei... You know that riding a bicycle is dangerous for you... You might fall off and hurt yourself.
— Mama! I'll learn to play tennis... My sisters play tennis and I want to play too
— You know, Aleksei, that you are not allowed to play tennis — she again had to answer.
— Mama! I want to run about a little in the park!
— No, Aleksei... You mustn't run about.
— Why are other children allowed to run about?
— Others may, but you, Aleksei, mustn't... You might fall and give yourself a knock, and you know: that is dangerous for you.
The child would then burst into bitter tears. The tears ran in hot streams down his cheeks and he lamented:
— Why? Why am I not like all the other children? Why may everyone chase about and romp, and not me?
The mighty Tsarina stood helpless, listening to the boy's words. Her heart bled for her child; tears choked her throat. Her heart was torn with pain and anguish. But what could she answer him? With what could she console him? She was helpless and could not ease the child's pain.
For the heir they bought the most expensive toys. His room was full of all kinds of splendid, costly playthings. What was not there? There were railways on rails, and dolls sat in the carriages as passengers. There were signal towers set up with stations. Whole camps of tin [lit. zinc] soldiers, ships that sailed on water. Factories with dolls as workers. Coal mines with coal miners, houses, monasteries, and everything was precisely imitated. All these things moved mechanically by means of devices. The heir had only to press a button, and the trains began running over the rails. The workers in the factories and the coal miners in the mines began to work. The signal towers began to blink with variously coloured little lights. The little bells in the monasteries rang and the soldiers began to march.
But all these toys gave the heir no joy. He was a quiet, dejected child. He wanted to jump, shoot, run — but the sailor Derevenko watched over him constantly and he did not dare any mischief.
And so it was, one morning. The sky was clear and the sun was shining. The day — although it was the beginning of winter — was mild and fresh, and the sailor Derevenko took the heir out for a walk in the park. The boy stepped carefully, as he had been warned; the sailor followed him and did not take his eyes off him. The boy felt very well and had a longing to break into a run, but — he did not dare. Every moment he heard the sailor's voice:
— Careful, Aleksei, watch out!
They strolled leisurely among the tall trees, which already stood bare, without leaves. The bright rays of the sun played among the branches and on the ground. The heir breathed the fresh air deep into himself and felt merrier. His eyes shone mischievously and a rosy colour appeared on his cheeks. He walked upright and with stiff steps. Suddenly he noticed: not far from him a bird was standing on the ground. He was overcome by his mischievous impulse and broke into a run, to chase the bird away. Before the sailor even had time to cry out — the heir caught his right foot on the ground, fell heavily on his knee, let out a terrible groan and fell full length on the ground. The misfortune had happened. In the knee a haemorrhage began at once.
The sailor too let out a groan, ran at once to the heir, bent down and cried out in fright:
— Aleksei... Aleksei!...
Aleksei lay motionless and badly doubled up with great agony. His face was very pale [printed "very straight", sic] and expressed pain. His eyes were closed. He was almost unconscious and did not answer the sailor's cries.
The athletic sailor Derevenko lifted the heir from the ground and, holding him in his strong arms, walked with him to the palace and carried him inside.
When the Tsarina saw the sailor carrying her son, she stood as if paralysed. She heard the sailor stammer out: "He broke into a run and fell", and she understood at once what great danger her child was in. She opened her mouth, wanted to let out a scream, but she had no voice. Her head began to swim and her eyes went dark. She swayed and stretched out her hands, seeking something to hold on to. People ran to her at once, caught her, and she fell into a deep faint.
— — — — — — — — —
The heir was laid on his bed. He was carefully undressed, and then they saw on his right leg the blue swelling, which was a sign that a haemorrhage was taking place in the leg, which is so dangerous to his life.
The boy now lay as if lifeless. He was badly worn out [?] by the great pains, and he held his right leg drawn up to his body. His face was now yellow as wax and his nose was very pointed, as is the nose of a dead man.

Ryczałt (the lump-sum tax)

[Taxes — merchants and artisans; the ryczałt tax.]
This word is heard more and more often today in merchant and artisan circles. The public does not know whether to rejoice or to complain. One thing everyone says: that it is no salvation. Everyone interprets the word according to his understanding, everyone makes up his own theory. But what it actually means, nobody knows. The truth is that in the very next few days the public of taxpayers will [printed "מעט", ?] receive a brand-new "nakaz płatniczy" [payment order] for two years, i.e. 1932 and 1933, and will meet the ryczałt [lump-sum tax] face to face.
But to receive such a guest one must be properly prepared, because otherwise quite unpleasant surprises may come out of it, and those who will receive it, or will not receive it, will have plenty to sing and tell about it.
So we want not to let our readers wait until the "guest" arrives, because he may, God forbid, find the taxpayer unprepared for it, and then it may be too late.
In Dz. Ust. [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws] No. 14 of 26 February 1932 there appeared an ordinance of the Finance Minister concerning the ryczałt tax on turnover for certain enterprises. The provisions of the ordinance are so complicated that more than one jurist will have to work hard before he chews through them. Worse still, however, is the matter for our small merchants and artisans, who will in no way begin to know who falls [?] under the ryczałt tax and who [printed "מער"] does not. Like all ordinances, this one too is worded in such a way that the tax authority always has the possibility of springing various surprises on the taxpayers. Therefore, first of all, every merchant and artisan must acquaint himself with the content of the said ordinance, so as to be able to defend his interests successfully.
Taking this into account, the undersigned has taken upon himself the responsible work and translated the ordinance into Yiddish in a very easy form, so that every interested person will be able, without any difficulty, to find his way at once in the labyrinth of provisions. The translation is already available in booklet form at the very cheap price of 50 gr. [groszy]. Subscribers and regular readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" will be able to obtain this booklet at the special price of 25 groszy, as a premium.
Every merchant and artisan should therefore, in his own interest, buy the booklet, because in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" we will give every week, in the form of "questions and answers," detailed explanations about the ryczałt tax.
In the next issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" I will give an exact treatment of the law, illustrated with examples of the way the ryczałt tax is calculated, as well as instructions on the direction in which the defence against injustices must be conducted.
M. Kaner.
An Appeal to the Jewish Public in Zagłębie

In our present hard and bitter time, when we Jews are being pushed out of all economic positions, when we are all occupied with the question of dry bread, when there is not a single Jewish home that is not being broken by the terrible crisis, which undermines our economic existence more and more as time goes on — in this difficult period we come to you, Jews of Zagłębie, brothers and brethren, with the call to join the Hebrew World Union, whose aim is to unite all friends of Hebrew culture throughout the whole world.

It is not the first time in our history that precisely in hard times of Jewish national life, precisely in periods of economic and political upheaval, when the Jewish people struggled with all its strength for its existence — precisely then the people began to take a greater interest in its spiritual life and its cultural treasures, bound itself more strongly to the values created in the national culture and literature, and also created new spiritual values, thereby enriching everything that had already been accumulated as our spiritual capital over hundreds of generations. In these creations the people found consolation in its hard experiences; spiritual creation made it easier for it to bear the unbearable yoke of the bitter time.

True, we still have enough strength and power to continue our national struggle on the whole front, which stretches from one end of the world to the other, from the fields and towns of Zion to every remote corner in other lands. The Eternal One of Israel will not lie [Netzach Yisrael lo yeshaker], and just as in all generations and at all times we have come through various catastrophes and upheavals, so we shall also prevail today in our struggle, the struggle of an ancient people against the mightiest and strongest of the world. And in the end we shall renew our national life both in the Land of Israel and in the lands of the Diaspora. Meanwhile, however, in this difficult transitional period, amid today's depressed mood, when with one hand we must protect our national existence and the positions we have won, and with the other hand strengthen and fortify our great national edifice. Meanwhile let us also fortify our spiritual treasures. Let us help all those who occupy themselves with the affairs of Hebrew culture, literature and education, without which our national renaissance is impossible.

The Hebrew World Union was created in order to place the problems of the Hebrew language, culture and education — the problems of the Hebrew education of the young Jewish generation — at the centre of our renewed national life. And on whom, if not on our brothers in Poland, lies the great task of taking their place in the ranks of the first builders? On whom, if not on Polish Jewry, which has shown so much self-sacrifice and devotion in maintaining hundreds of schools and hundreds of institutions for Hebrew culture — so it is on the long-tested Jewish public in Poland that the duty lies to lay the cornerstone of the highest tribune of the Hebrew movement, the Hebrew World Congress.

At the Hebrew World Congress there will gather all those who stand at the head of Hebrew literature and art, all the activists of Hebrew education in all its forms and currents, from all the countries where Jews live and create, in order to seek means of raising and renewing our national culture; how to save hundreds of thousands of Jewish children in the East and in the West, in the North and in the South, from the terrible danger of assimilation and national extinction; how to bring the whole Jewish people, in its millions, back to its cultural independence, which is to be built on the sources of its history and on its one national language — the Hebrew language, the language of our past, the language of our prophets; and we, the friends of Hebrew culture. Where assimilation penetrates unnoticed into every corner of Jewish life, where hundreds of thousands of Jewish children in Poland are brought up without Jewish knowledge, without Hebrew culture; where great Jewish masses become estranged, consciously or unconsciously, through indifference or through lawlessness — we, the friends of Hebrew cultural affairs, must raise a great outcry before the broad Jewish world and sound the alarm about the great danger that threatens the great Jewish public in Poland, if there is not a great effort for a great cultural campaign and help in creating the World Union for Hebrew Culture.

The first step towards the World Congress is the "sela" [the Union's membership token, like the Zionist shekel]; the sela paves the way to the Congress, and it will lead the emissaries of the Hebrew movement to the highest tribune for the affairs of Hebrew culture and all its values. We call on you, comrades and friends, to prepare for this Congress, which will convene in the near future; therefore every Jew, every Zionist, every member of the national youth organizations, every teacher and educator, every pupil of a national school — all of you are called upon to buy the sela of the Hebrew World Union and to become partners in the creation of the Hebrew World Congress. Hebrew culture, which we have guarded throughout our entire history, which we cherished in days of joy and of mourning! They cry out to us loudly and beg us to rescue them from the great world mixture, from the terrible confusion of minds in Jewish life. It depends on us whether we shall go on spinning the golden threads of our history and preserve the cultural treasures already created, and also create new values that will give us courage and strength to endure the hard struggle we are now living through in all countries.

You, Jews of Zagłębie, who have always shown your devotion to our national affairs — show now too, in these hard times, your understanding for Hebrew culture, and buy, without exception, the sela, which gives you the right to take part in the elections to the Hebrew World Congress.

The Committee "Lema'an ha-Sela" [For the Sela]
in Będzin
Authorized representative: N. Lundner.
You, Men, Make Us Nervous!

[Women's column — essay.]
From a woman to women.
By Bella Blank
Very often lately we hear of men who run away from their homes and leave their wives at God's mercy.
When you ask them why they ran away from their wives, no fewer than nine out of ten would answer with the same refrain:
— I can't live with her, she is terribly nervous.
"She is terribly nervous."
Possibly.
But who, dear men, is to blame that your wives are nervous? Have you ever given [?] it a thought?
Perhaps, dear men, you yourselves are to blame for your wife's nervousness? Perhaps she is nervous because you are nervous?
Men forget that a woman is ill a third [?] of every month with an illness for which one cannot even call a doctor, because he can do nothing to help. The woman herself, with her own strength and her own nerves, must sit out her monthly illness quietly by herself, in secret, so that no outsider should have the slightest notion of it.
Does the average man take much account of this condition of his wife? Well, just let her show at such a time a little weakness, nervousness (a thing to which, because of her "illness", she is fully entitled) when her husband comes home from work; let her receive him with a groan, with a sharp word, or fail to prepare the proper supper for him — and you will soon hear with what a "gut yor" ["good year", i.e. a curse] the husband will answer such a "gut shabes" ["good Sabbath"].
And if it happens, besides, that he himself also comes home nervous and irritated (and such a thing happens very often with men), then it is simply dangerous for the woman to feel weak, or tired, or nervous. When her dear despot does her the favour of coming home to eat the good supper she has prepared for him and to sleep in the soft bed she has made up for him.
He, the healthy "mansbil" [Mannsbild, he-man], may come home nervous and pour out on his wife and children all the troubles and vexations he has had from his boss, from his partners, from his employees, or even from his — sweetheart; but she, the sick, weak, suffering woman, must not be nervous; she must be stronger than iron.
"I can't live with her, she is terribly nervous," men often reply.
Yes. Many of us are terribly nervous. We are what men have made of us.
Every married woman is entitled to a little nervousness. The whole of married life is for a woman a source of mental torments and nervous upheavals. The engagement, the wedding, the wedding night, the pregnancies, the childbeds, the nursing, the weaning, the raising of the children — all this is bound up for the woman with hard physical and mental experiences and nervous shocks. And when a woman comes out of all this with only a small, ordinary weakness of the nerves, she is a heroine and deserves a monument.
If men understood this and met the woman with tenderness, with love, with consideration, especially at the times of her periodic illness, she would have been [?] only a little nervous, a little capricious, and it would not have mattered; domestic peace would not have been destroyed on that account. After all, it is a woman's privilege and a bit of an adornment to be a little capricious; it lends her a certain charm, a truly feminine trait and grace.
But many, many men are themselves terribly nervous. They come home angry, boiling, and want to know of nothing. Taking nothing into account, they come home with a slam, with a growl and with a grumble [?], and they dance on their wife's weak nerves so long and so wide until her small nervousness turns into a great nervousness, and the capricious woman who pampers herself becomes an agitated, distraught woman who quarrels, who curses, who loses all control over her nerves.
Such "terribly nervous" women exist beyond measure, but almost all of them are the results of the malice, egoism, depravity or nervousness [?] of their husbands. With a good, faithful and civilised [?] husband the woman is never "terribly nervous".
According to the statistics the number of nervous women is much greater than the number of nervous men.
True, we do not deny the statistical figures, but neither our own experience: mostly it is the men's fault that we have so many nervous women in the world.
You must not forget that one nervous man can make ten women nervous. A "madman" makes nervous not only his wife, but also his mother, his mother-in-law, his sisters and his sisters-in-law — all the women in his family. He makes nervous even the maid and the women neighbours in the house where he lives and shouts and quarrels with his family. I myself know many such "dimenstne" [?, perhaps "demonic"] men, on whose account the whole street is up in arms.
You make pogroms on our nerves, sweet men, and then you complain that we are "terribly nervous".

Będzin — Changes in the Kehilla Budget for 1932

[Będzin — kehilla.]
All last year's subsidies struck out.
As we have already written, the kehilla budget for the year 1932 came back these days, approved by the Ministry of Religious Denominations.
The following changes were made in this budget:
All subsidies for cultural and philanthropic institutions that had been estimated and approved in the budget of 1931 were struck out.
From this year's budget were struck out: the item of 5000 zł. for the orphans' home, the subsidy for „Hachnasat Orchim“, the sum of 2000 zł. for opening a cheap kitchen at the kehilla, 600 zł. for Froebel schools [?] (kindergartens), 200 zł. for academics (university students), subsidies for the yeshivas „Keter Torah“ and „Beit Yisrael“, „Bnot Mizrachi“, „Icha“ [?] for the courses at the artisans', and „Tzeirei Mizrachi“, and 150 zł. for tea and sugar for the office employees.
On the other hand the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) were favoured: they have been granted the full salary of 8.500 zł. a year; and the subsidy for the „Bnot Agudat Yisrael“ was kept.
The increase for the shochtim is justified on the grounds that they, the shochtim that is, should not carry out any illegal slaughter.
The reason why the subsidy for the „Bnot Agudat Yisrael“ was approved after all is not known to us...
The Talmud Torah to Be Closed for 3 Months

[Będzin — education.]
A proposal by one of the trustees.
The situation of the „Talmud Torah“ is getting worse from day to day. Together with the „sinners“ („poshim“), who no longer have any control over the 400 [?] poor children, the income has fallen considerably.
So the trustees met for a session and began to deliberate how to improve the situation of the institution. Various projects were put forward on this question. But the „most realistic“ proposal is this: that the Talmud Torah be closed for 3 months, and afterwards a new Talmud Torah be founded..
It would be interesting to know, however, whether „sinners“ will after all be admitted to the future administration of the new Talmud Torah or not...
A „Bear's Favour“ for Tenants

[Będzin — housing.]
The management of the „block“ houses has, because of the crisis, reduced the price of rent. At the same time the management has considerably raised the charge for water and sewerage.
This „favour“ has, of course, aroused discontent among the tenants.
Inspection at the Magistrate

[Będzin — municipality.]
In the course of the whole week a special commission of the Kielce voivodeship office carried out an inspection (lustracja) in all departments of the local magistrate (town council).
The result of this inspection is not yet known.
Because of Little Jewish Denunciations..

[Będzin — welfare.]
We have already written several times about the fact that the Citizens' Committee for the support of the unemployed and the poor is flooded with little denunciations, in which „our brethren, the Children of Israel“ point out which Jewish families should not receive any support from the cheap kitchen. As we are informed, the denunciations are having great „success“, so that thirty-odd families have been struck off the list for receiving support..
The Division Has Been Made..

[Będzin — religious education.]
The subsidy of 3,500 zł. which the magistrate grants to the religious schools has finally been divided in the following way: the Talmud Torah receives 1,300 zł., „Mizrachi“ and „Yesodei HaTorah“ 900 zł. each, Beit Yaakov 400 zł.
The struggle over the „division“ was a fierce one, because the „Aguda“ (Agudat Yisrael) demanded for „Yesodei HaTorah“ the same sum that the Talmud Torah receives.
Keren Kayemet Evening at WIZO

On Saturday, the 19th of this month, in the evening, the traditional evening in aid of the „Keren Kayemet“ [Jewish National Fund] will take place in WIZO's own premises. The organisers are making efforts for the evening to be interesting, with a varied programme.

The Jewish Society for the Propagation of Fine Arts is organising in Warsaw an exhibition of paintings by the already well-known young artist Abraham Goldkorn. The exhibition opens this Saturday in Warsaw, in the premises of the above-mentioned society.

Next Sunday the annual general meeting of the House-Owners' Association will take place. At the meeting, among other things, the question of uniting both house-owners' associations will also be discussed.

Next Sunday the local Tenants' Association is holding a meeting, at which the topical question of reducing rents will be discussed.
Explosion of a Motor in the „Mars“ Mine
On Saturday evening, in the „Mars“ coal mine in Łagisza, the 100-horsepower electric motor exploded. The investigation has not yet established who is to blame for the explosion.

The committee of the striking workers of the „Flora“, „Reden“ and „Paryż“ coal mines has posted appeals all around, in which the public is asked to support the striking workers.

Under the chairmanship of Mr. Rozman the annual meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank] took place in the "Hotel Polski".
The main point at the meeting was the question of continuing to exist or liquidating. Several of those assembled spoke on this, and afterwards it was decided that the meeting be adjourned for a month; during that time the reorganisation [sanacja] committee is to negotiate with the Jewish councillors of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce that they take the management of the bank into their hands.

In the premises of the Revisionist local group (o"g.), the first Eretz Israel bazaar in Zagłębie will be opened tonight, Motzei Shabbat, at 7 o'clock in the evening.

On the Automation of the Telephones in Zagłębie

As we have already reported, a conference took place in Katowice on introducing automatic telephones in the territory of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia. The automation is to cover Katowice, Będzin, Dąbrowa — 11 towns in Upper Silesia.
In a memorandum to the Post Ministry the local Chamber of Commerce added that the automation should be introduced in Zawiercie and in Częstochowa as well, because both towns are in constant contact with Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.

From Artisans' Life.
On Sunday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Rozenbaum, a general meeting of the hatmakers' and milliners' guild (tsekh) took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association.
After hearing the reports on the activity and the treasury, a discussion developed in which Messrs. Hajszeryk[?], Cimerman, Miss Bajtner and others took part.

The meeting includes: shoemakers, shoe-upper stitchers, saddlers, bookbinders and upholsterers.

Decided to Continue the Strike.
Tuesday was the most decisive day regarding the strike situation. In the course of the day huge workers' meetings took place at almost[?] all coal mines, at which it was discussed whether to continue the strike or to return to work. The tendency of the speeches at the meetings was to continue striking, and the resolutions were adopted in that sense.
At the mines "Flora" and "Jakub" the workers declared that if the majority of workers come out against the strike, they will at any moment be ready to return to work.

On the Increased Local Tax
As is already known, the local tax has been increased by 12 percent for flats of 3 rooms with a kitchen and up.
Cases occur where artisans who hold 2 rooms as a flat and 2[?] rooms as a workshop are sent by the Magistrate a tax notice for 12 per cent, counting it as a 4-room flat.
This way of handling is not legal, especially[?] when the workshop is separated from the flat, i.e. the workshop is located in an outbuilding (oficyna) and the flat in the other one; or the workshop is on one side and the flat on the other.
In such a case the person concerned must, within 14 days of receiving the tax notice, obtain a certificate from the landlord that he occupies in that house 2 separate flats of 2 rooms each, one as a workshop and the other as a dwelling, and file an appeal with the Magistrate, enclosing the certificate.
At the same time it must be noted that workshops located in buildings that have the character of factory buildings are entirely exempt from the local tax.
For a Secure „Today“ and a Better „Tomorrow“

(On the visit of Deputy Yitzhak Grünbaum to Będzin).
At the present moment, when such a terrible crisis reigns in the Jewish street, when the struggle for the daily existence of every individual becomes ever stronger and harder, at a time when the Jewish people as a whole finds itself in a truly catastrophic situation, when from day to day we Jews are pushed out more and more from our economic positions, at a time when the Jew, both as an individual and as a community, feels helpless, is dominated by terrible apathy and a mood of despair, loses his faith in the just struggle, and little by little his power of resistance is weakened, he is swept along with the current and lets himself be ruled by the various upstart careerists on whose banner is written „servitude, submission, baseness“, and with this triple sign[?] they want to confuse the Jewish forces and dull the Jew's will to fight for his individual and national existence — on the other hand, when [we see] lately among the broad Jewish masses a great interest in Eretz Israel, and it is already evident that we stand on the eve of a great aliyah — witness the success of the various organised excursions to Eretz Israel, which everywhere arouse admiration and joy; one could not believe that at such a hard time such undertakings would succeed. This proves best of all that the Jewish faith in our national renaissance is still deeply enough rooted in the hearts of the Jewish people — at such a twilight time, when the historic struggle takes place between the grey reality of „today“ and the bright „tomorrow“ that beckons to us from Zion, one truly wants to hear the strong, daring word of the Zionist leader, the old, well-known fighter Yitzhak Grünbaum, who is the symbol of Jewish dignity, pride and courageous struggle, who is able to drive away the terrible nightmare that presses and oppresses so hard, able to revive the smouldering[?] sparks in our hearts that are about to go out, and to pour into us drops of hope and faith in the struggle for a secure „today“ and a better „tomorrow“.
N. L.

Wednesday's One-Day General Strike in Zagłębie and Silesia
The general strike that was proclaimed for last Wednesday [16 March 1932] partly succeeded in Zagłębie.
In the mining industry 8785 workers struck in the morning; in the afternoon the number of strikers decreased.
In the works: Staszic, Renard, Dietel, the zinc works — all workshops struck. Smaller was the number of workers (on strike) at the Milowice, Katarzyna, Fitzner and Gamper works. At Huta Bankowa and at Huldczyński's [?] factory work went on normally.
In the street, movement was normal. The trams and buses ran normally; order was nowhere disturbed; only in Kazimierz did the police intervene, when a larger number of women attacked the workers who were going to work.
Yesterday a rumour spread that the workers' union would today still appeal to the workers to return to work.
In Upper Silesia the proclaimed strike was a failure: of 42 mines, [some] struck partially, i.e., of 120 thousand workers barely about 13 thousand struck.
On Wednesday afternoon in Żywiec [?] there was a bloody clash between unemployed and police. The result of the events: 3 of the crowd were killed and many wounded. On the police side, too, there are 4 wounded.
Because of the events, military and police reinforcements arrived in Żywiec [?].
In the afternoon the Sosnowiec needle-trades union held a meeting in its own premises on Czysta Street.
The meeting was dispersed by the police, and 45 people were arrested.
—o—
Königshütte as Partner of the Będzin Hospital
The municipality of Königshütte [Chorzów] has decided, for reasons of economy, to send its sick to the Będzin hospital, where the treatment costs are comparatively cheaper than in the Upper Silesian hospitals.
As the Upper Silesian press reports, the municipality of Königshütte has bought a part of the Będzin hospital [?] for a sum of 100 thousand złoty.

Registration of Artisan Cards with the Purchased Patents for the Year 1932
In connection with the demands of the tax offices that all artisan workshops holding artisan cards and patents (trade licences) of the 6th, 7th and 8th category for 1932, as well as enterprises holding patents of the 8th category whose turnover did not exceed 45,000 zł., (register) by the 15th of this month in order to benefit from the ryczałt (lump-sum) payment — i.e., instead of 2 per cent of turnover, only 1—1/2% — a delegation of the Sosnowiec Jewish Artisans' Association intervened with the inspector of the Sosnowiec tax office to extend the deadline, and also that the registration might be carried out by the office of the association.
After an agreement with the Ministry of Finance, the artisans' association was yesterday permitted to carry out the above-mentioned registration until the 20th of this month.
All members are called upon, in their own interest, not to be late in registering at the secretariat of the association, Targowa [?] 9, in order to benefit from the ryczałt payment.

A Large Smuggling Affair Uncovered
In Königshütte a large store of smuggled goods was uncovered at the forwarding firm Franciszek Błach [?], which belongs to four brothers; a great deal of silk, stockings, saccharin, etc. was found.
The trail of the smuggling store was picked up because of an arrest [?] in Warsaw on 3 March. During the search a slip was found on them with the inscription: „286, Królewska Huta, Brank“.
The investigation established that this is the telephone of the said firm in Królewska Huta.
The firm Franciszek Błach ran a large smuggling operation. The smuggled goods used to be taken across the German border in a special motor car. All 4 Błach brothers have been arrested.

An appeal to the members of the assessment commissions of the turnover tax.
Since the assessment of turnover for the year 1931 will begin shortly, and to our great regret the small traders are very weakly represented in the assessment commissions — in particular the grocery („colonial“) and food trades were disadvantaged[?] in the distribution of seats in the assessment commissions at some of the tax offices.
The situation of the small traders in the past year was very critical, and many of the supposedly[?] strong merchants went under, or at best were turned into small shopkeepers.
This comes precisely at a time when the economic crisis has ruined everyone from the greatest to the smallest. Consumption has shrunk, [there has been] a cheapening[?] of all goods; the regrouping from yesterday's big [traders] to today's small ones, from yesterday's textile dealer to today's grocer, i.e. to a small trader, is quite understandable. So that instead of 10 food shops in one street, 20—30 have sprung up in the same place. The question arises: how can the food shopkeeper of 2—3 years ago now make the same turnover as before, and what of the competition that has arisen because of this, in which one eats up the other? That is in general; now the specific conditions in the grocery trade, where there is no calculation at all. So it is true that on selling a sack of sugar the shopkeeper earns only the sack the sugar came in, on a case of soap — only the case. Whereas in assessing the turnover the head („naczelnik“) of the tax office relies on so-called „information“ that so-and-so bought 8 sacks of sugar this month at a total value of 1240 zł., i.e. 14.880 zł. over the year for one article. And where are the other articles? But according to the method of calculation shown above it turns out that he indeed sold that much sugar, but earned only the value of the sacks...
That, gentlemen members of the assessment commissions, is how turnovers look in reality.
It is therefore desirable that in assessing the turnover tax for 1931 the actual situation[?] described be taken into account.

Exhibition of paintings by Maurycy Gottlieb in Kraków.
At the National Museum in Kraków the opening of the exhibition of paintings by the brilliant Jewish painter M. Gottlieb, who died in the year 1879 at the age of 23, took place not long ago.
The opening took place in a most festive manner in the presence of the elite of Polish and Jewish society.
The paintings of the brilliant Jewish painter who died young, the pupil of the greatest Polish painter Matejko, arouse the greatest admiration in all strata of Polish and Jewish society. Thousands of people from all parts of the country and from abroad visit the exhibition daily.
The Society for Knowledge of the Country (Polskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze) in Zagłębie is organizing an excursion to Kraków to visit the exhibition on the 29th of this month. On this occasion other sights of Kraków will also be visited.
One can register at the secretariat of the Society in Będzin, 3 Maja Square 4, daily from 6-8 in the evening. Tel. no. 85.
