From the Festive Opening of the Eretz Israel Bazaar in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, Keren Kayemet.]
In the new[?] large hall of the Revisionist organisation in Sosnowiec, the festive opening of the Eretz Israel bazaar, whose proceeds go to the Keren Kayemet (Jewish National Fund), took place last Saturday night.
For the opening there had been prepared a large choir of the pupils of the Jewish girls' gymnasium, an amateur orchestra, a buffet, decorations, etc.; only one thing, the main thing, was missing —
— order... The bazaar committee paid no attention to that "article", and consequently the celebration made the impression of a small-town wedding: hubbub, din; the ladies' choir wandered in and out for 2 hours, never got to perform in the end and had to leave...
———
After a delay of almost 3 hours the celebration is opened with a short introduction by the chairwoman of WIZO, Mrs. Rasman, and the first word of greeting on behalf of the Zionist Organisation in Będzin goes to Mr. Tygadzki[?], who points out the significance of the bazaar's opening at the present moment.
A fine greeting in Hebrew and Yiddish is delivered by Mrs. Ratner (Będzin), who points to the self-sacrificing work of the Sosnowiec WIZO in arranging the bazaar; she appeals to Jewish women to take up work for the Zionist ideal.
On behalf of the Keren Kayemet committee in Będzin a matter-of-fact greeting is given by Mr. A. Liwer[?]. On behalf of the Sosnowiec Betar — Mr. Ch. Triger. On behalf of the Sosnowiec "Dobroczynność" (charity society) and of the "Keren Hayesod" committee — Mr. B. Tencer.
Written greetings are also read out: from the starosta (district head) of Będzin, who stresses that for official reasons he cannot take part in the celebration (the Sosnowiec police commissioner, Mr. Kuszniak, left the hall because of the late hour); from the Central Committee in Warsaw, from the Central Office (Lishka Merkazit) in Jerusalem, and from A. Klarman (Warsaw).
Accompanied by several Mizrachi activists, Rabbi Hager enters and delivers an inspired speech on the building of the Land. In his speech the rabbi stresses that, just as at the building of the Tabernacle, so too at the building of the Land one must recall the blessing "May it be His will that the Divine Presence rest among you". We do not build the way all other nations build their homes. You — the rabbi calls out to the youth — must not desecrate the holiness of the Land of Israel, which will be built "not by might, nor by power, but by spirit".
The floor is then given to the distinguished guest, a member of the C.C. of [?] (Ts.K.P.Y.[?]), Mr. Frejd, who, as one of the first of the Hovevei Zion movement, gives a longer speech in which he outlines certain epochs of the Hibbat Zion movement and the activity of the Keren Kayemet to date.
Mr. B. Rasman honours Rabbi Hager with cutting the silk ribbon on the door leading into the bazaar.
Getting into the bazaar takes self-sacrifice, because a large part of the youth present treated the celebration with disdain — better said, with licentiousness. This caused the first impression to be weakened and the mood to become a "Bavarian" (rowdy) one...
———
On entering the bazaar the impression is a good one, full of atmosphere. The first pavilion is taken by the Keren Kayemet with all its "jewels": all the undertakings and publications of the Keren Kayemet are exhibited here. A splendid impression is made by the flower pavilion of the Goldberg brothers.
To the side stands the pavilion of "Hashomer Hatzair". The eye cannot get its fill of the carving and painting work done by the members themselves; diagrams of the world Shomer movement and of the area of the Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel.
Then pavilions of "Helios" lamps, paper and book products of the firm S. Langer, and next to[?] the beautiful pavilion of the Sosnowiec WIZO there is, upstairs, the pavilion of "Totzeret Haaretz" (produce of the Land of Israel), furnished with splendid pictures and Bezalel work.
The bazaar is also equipped with special "bazaar numbers", such as a lottery at which you cannot lose, a screeching gramophone, callers and noise-makers who "create atmosphere"...
———
On Sunday evening Deputy Yitzhak Grünbaum visited the bazaar. Mr. Grünbaum stressed that he likes the bazaar better than all the bazaars he has visited recently in a number of towns in Poland.
———
On Sunday during the day a ball for children took place in the hall adjoining the bazaar, but a "miracle" happened, and the grown-up "young men" "became little children" and were the first to take the seats... Thanks to that "miracle" the [actual][?] children stayed outside and "fulfilled their duty" with the fact that the grown-ups had fun...
———
In the course of the week performances and concerts organised by the bazaar committee took place every evening.
———
The bazaar will be closed on the 20th of this month with a great event the like of which has not yet been seen in Zagłębie (so the organising committee assures). Tonight, Saturday night, at 10 p.m., a great blue-and-white Purim ball will take place at the "Arlekin" with various attractions, such as contests, prizes, a dialogue of Queen Esther with King Ahasuerus, etc.
On Sunday afternoon, in the same hall, a children's performance for the second time. The committee is taking all measures that guarantee order at the children's ball.
The musical part was performed by the amateur circle: Messrs. M. Ziskind, Sosnowiec (violin), B. Goldsztajn, Będzin (piano), B. Patak (Będzin, cornet), Ch. Ziskind (jazz[?]).
The guard at the entrance to the bazaar was kept the whole time by the Sosnowiec Betar under the leadership of Ch. Triger.
Kol Dikhfin… [“Let All Who Are Hungry…”]

[Będzin — Community and relief; ahead of Passover. Opinion piece.] It is an old rule that “thirty days before Passover one studies the laws of Passover”, and usually people really begin to see to matzot and Passover needs only after Purim, because there is then still enough time to buy flour, to see to the kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour for the poor], etc. Quite different, however, is the situation in today's hard times, and especially because of the sad circumstances and specific conditions of the local Jewish kehilla [in Będzin].
To the Aguda [Agudat Israel], and no less [?] to our “dardeki de-vei rav…” [little schoolboys of the rabbi's house], we owe the sad state of the kehilla, which they have brought to a condition of “neither alive — nor dead”: the old kehilla has not gone and the new one has not come. At the present moment our kehilla finds itself in a state of twilight [bein ha-shmashot], and that in the fullest and worst sense of the word.
This abnormal situation of the kehilla, at a time of such a tremendously severe crisis, when the number of the needy has risen so much while the number of givers has shrunk so much — this is what lays upon us a much greater duty. We must not sit carefree and indifferent with folded hands and put off the Passover campaign until the last moment. We must by no means look the fact [?] in the eye and rely on miracles [so printed; the intended sense is apparently: we must not ignore the fact and rely on miracles]. Precisely because of the hard, abnormal times we must already now, while there is still time, begin organising the Passover campaign. With all our energy, with redoubled effort, with the Jewish self-sacrifice of old we must, in good time, set about the tasks that weigh upon us in practice, because it will be enormously harder this year than in any other year — for we live today in a time of “kol dikhfin”, when everyone is in need.
Yes, everyone is in need today. Everyone, everyone; only rare individuals are in a better situation. Therefore the campaign must be conducted in such a direction that everyone, the formerly well-to-do middle class too, should not face the question “how does one make Passover” as a difficult problem.
We must firmly take it to heart that at the present time, when many of the former givers, the kimcha donors, are no longer in the fortunate material situation of the past, when the majority of the local Jewish community is in a crushingly difficult material condition — care must be taken, and indeed the whole weight must be laid on this, that this middle class too should not be burdened in the ways that have been customary until now.
We do not intend to enumerate here all the impermissible practices, the senseless payments and Passover groschen [?] which are a plague for the community and from which only individuals profit. This is not the place, and now is not the time for it.
In view of the hard times we only wish to point out that a case such as this — that the Passover flour should be paid for at 20 per cent more, after agreement on the price had already been reached and the purchase had to be cancelled solely over the question of “payments” — must not happen.
Today such facts must not be repeated. Care must be taken for [illegible word] relief of the population. At the present hard moment no senseless “contributions” [levies] may be imposed on the population, supposedly on account of kashrut, which in reality, however, have absolutely nothing in common with “compromises” [pesharot — so printed, apparently for kashrut].
It is the duty of the Jewish population to provide for our poor brethren. It is the duty of the future matzah committee to care for the middle class, which can still only barely get by with its livelihood, so that it should not be crushed under the screw of the kashrut tax.
The slogan must be: relief, relief in the broadest measure. Every single złoty plays an important role today in the budget of every family. If money is given, it must be exclusively for the poor population, but by no means for individuals. Care must be taken that the Passover products should not become dearer for no reason at all through the procedure of “kashran ha-pesharim” [so printed] and above all through the payments.
The Jewish population can by no means, at the present hard moment, pay a fresh “contribution”. Today is not the time to burden the Jewish population with “hekhsher podatki” [certification taxes].
Relief! And that in the broadest measure. Everything must be cheap! We are living now in hard times, in a time of kol dikhfin… when everyone is in need.

A Będzin Young Man Is “Sequestered” Before the Wedding Canopy

[Częstochowa — A wedding; a curious incident.] We are written to from Częstochowa:
A very characteristic case occurred here these days with a bridegroom from Będzin, whom they hid in a wardrobe before the wedding canopy.
The Częstochowa householder Reb Henich married off his youngest daughter, in a good hour, to a young man, an “esrogl” [little citron — a pampered, delicate youth]. A “tsatske” [a “jewel”, ironically] from Będzin. A certain L., a lad with a fine yellow beard.
So the groom came, travelling with all his bachelor friends, to whom he had given the expenses for the journey here and had promised them that the expenses for the way back the bride's father would surely give.
It is already 11 o'clock in the evening [?]. The dayan [rabbinical judge] with the shammes [beadle], with the canopy poles, stand and wait. The marshelik [wedding jester] has already “sung over” the bride, and they are waiting only for the groom — and “the lad is not there” [Gen. 37:30], the groom is missing. So they run over to the young man with a complaint: How can it be! How long is the measure of fasting? [the groom fasts on his wedding day] But the groom does not answer. Instead, one of the bachelors stood up and spoke thus:
If you want the groom — the in-law from the bride's side [?] must pay for the bachelors' expenses and for the wine they have drunk. A “kayma lan” [a fixed ruling] of 80 zł. And if not, we will not hand over the groom...
But the in-law is a tough Jew, so he raised an outcry that he was being robbed, that he would not let it pass — robbers! bandits! hand over the groom! And before anyone can look round there is a quarrel, an uproar, and Jewish caps are mixed up with shtreimels, glasses with bottles. And when the crowd had at last been calmed down, people look round and do not see the groom — he had vanished, and after a long search he was found hidden in a wardrobe...
In short, negotiations began and at last they came to a compromise that the bride's father pays the bachelors 30 zł. and a festive meal. And only then, after one o'clock at night, was the groom — who could barely stand on his feet after such a long fast — led, in a good hour, to the wedding canopy.
Important for Those Who Have Relatives in Russia

[Relief — food parcels to Soviet Russia; ahead of Passover.] Passover is approaching, and dozens of local Jewish residents are already thinking about sending parcels of food and provisions to their relatives in Soviet Russia, who certainly need them.
Sending provisions, however, is very expensive and also involves great difficulties. The Jewish relief society in London has taken note of this and has set up large food stores in several dozen towns in Soviet Russia, and has made the sending of provisions easier in such a way that one can pay in, in Poland or in other countries, a certain sum of money, and on the strength of the transfer to the relief society the designated person in Soviet Russia receives his parcel of food and provisions.
The agency for Poland has been taken over by the Warsaw bank Udziałowy [Bank Udziałowy]. The agency for the Będzin district has been obtained by the Bank of Artisans and Small Traders in Sosnowiec, Targowa 9.
The prices of the Passover parcels are as follows: when one pays 1 dollar 80 cents, the designated person in Russia receives 6 kilos of white flour, 1 kilo of sugar, 100 grams of tea and half a litre of oil
For 3.05 dollars one receives 12 kilos of flour, 2 kilos of sugar, 100 [?] grams of tea and 1 litre of oil, etc.
The arrangement is a very good one, because the products work out much cheaper than if one were to send them from another country.
The procedure of sending is thus a very easy one.
Payments are accepted by the bank every day during office hours.

"The wheels go round"... — An encounter from recent days.

By Pini Baal Loshn.
At the little window of the ticket seller at the new station stands a Jew of fine appearance, not badly dressed, in his sixties judging by his face, and he keeps pleading with the cashier:
— Believe me, my friend, I haven't a single grosz in my pocket! Do a person a kindness and give me a ticket — after all, I want to go home and rest my tired feet!...
And the cashier answers him coldly:
— No, no, without money you can't travel!
I paid for the Jew, took a ticket for him, and we both got on the train to Sosnowiec...
The Jew didn't even say thank you, as though that was how it should be; he sat down right next to me and began with a bitter little smile:
— Did you hear what the cashier told me? Without money — he says — you can't travel, brother! A clever goy, upon my life a philosopher, as surely as you see me a Jew!
— What can you blame him for? — I answer on the goy's behalf — if he were to let everyone through without money, his salary wouldn't be enough to cover it!
The Jew smiles another bitter smile and says to me:
— God forbid, I don't blame him; I only mean [?]: did you listen to his words? Without money you can't travel, brother! Yes, to you, it seems, these are simple words? But to me they say a lot, a great, great deal!...
And the Jew turns his face to me, looks into my eyes and speaks quietly, in a tone of despair:
Yes, my friend, I say so too: with money you travel on, but without money you can't travel on. Stop! When I was on the horse, it was worth travelling, and now, when I have lost everything, it is neither possible to travel nor worth travelling... You understand? Without money — off the market, go your way and don't get under the world's feet!...
And he raises his head toward me and his eyes flash:
— Do you know what it means to be a rich man? No, as I can see in you, you don't know. You have not yet tasted that taste. And imagining it is very hard. The one who actually lived through it cannot be compared to the one who merely pictures it...
To be a rich man, my friend, means to feel yourself the chosen one of Fortune, the darling of luck, the pampered child of success.
You feel that you and only you are what matters, and no one besides you. You know and are convinced in yourself that the world and everything in it exists not for anyone else's sake but for yours — it is owed to you!...
When you see that you are growing, that you are getting richer and richer and you yourself don't know where it all comes from, you begin to believe that wherever you step, the legendary shretele hovers over your head — the creature that brings luck and rakes in treasures for you — and that it will go on raking and raking without end, because once you've caught the "shretele" that's that, it stays with you forever!
And you are ready to destroy the whole world, so long as your good fortune isn't diminished by a hair.
And indeed, tell me yourself, how could I have thought otherwise, when from the first minute everything went my way, through every door and every gate.
Do you know what I started with? I started with two wooden wheels that I turned myself, and I rose to thousands of steel wheels that the electric angels of destruction turned for me in my "shpeter" [?] and mills, and so I climbed high and higher, until my head was spinning. I could no longer even take a look down to see what was going on below...
And as the little song goes: "The wheels go round, the years go by" — and one forgets where one is in the world.
But now, since the wheels have stopped and have long not been mine — the years too must stop; they too are no longer mine... What for? Who needs them, who? Perhaps [?] it may be that others need them — yes, the foolish years, I mean. Well, then I wish them many years, and may they delight in them, if they can. But I, the former rich man, certainly don't need them...
* • •
Several months have passed since then. The Jew's words rang in my ears. His image stood before my eyes the whole time. I very much wanted to know what had become of him.
A man stood at the edge of the world — what was his last step, this way or that?
My curiosity grew from day to day; somehow he became ever closer to me, and I took an interest in him as in one of my own, wanting to know his fate. But he was gone, vanished, as though into water.
But I did not lose hope; I began to inquire, inquire among textile (manufaktura) merchants I knew, searched and rummaged so long until I found him.
And... I recognised him at once! Not at all the same person — a man reborn. Calm, with a shining face, with a sweet little smile.
— So what are you doing now?
— Ah, my friend, I have started all over again from the beginning, with a pair of old wheels! And because I do it myself, it is sugar-sweet to me... And believe me, my friend, it is much better when I turn the wheels than when the wheels turn me...
Pe-be-be-e-e..
Who Is to Blame for the Present "High Cost of Living"?

With protests against the so-called "high cost of living" [yoker], against high prices for electricity, the question of the world crisis will not be resolved. The consumer imagines that if electricity costs no more than 60 gr. [groszy] a kilowatt, he will be well off. He is, with all due respect, mistaken. If things go on for him as they do today, he will not be able to pay even 40 groszy a kilowatt. In the Talmud a Tanna (R' Yochanan) relates: he remembers times when four se'ah (wheat or flour) cost no more than one sela, i.e. there was great cheapness, and nevertheless many people lay in Tiberias then, swollen from hunger, because there was no money with which to buy the cheap products. And there lies the dog buried.
The cause of the world crisis lies in the existing state system. Mankind pulled today's state "costume" on itself thousands of years ago. In the places where the costume burst from age, it put on a patch, darned, mended. Instead of a theocrat they made a king, a republic, a triumvirate, an autocrat, consuls, parliaments, etc. But the time has come when mankind has entirely outgrown the old costume. Today it is too short for her, too narrow, too tight, and is tearing at all the seams.
If one is to protest against high prices at all, the world must first of all protest against the unbearably high prices that the upkeep of the state mechanism costs the population today. Were it not for the high taxes, which sap the juice out of agriculture, trade and industry, we would not have become so impoverished, and the crisis would in any case not have taken on such acute forms.
We here can sign such a protest with both hands. They have cut the map of Europe into patches and created new little states; every state is a hefty spender and pumps its expenditures out of the population without any mercy. To protect its currency, every state protects exports and puts blocks [obstacles] in the way of imports, thereby making the standard of living dearer at home. For currency reasons our state burdens international traffic. The foreign passport hobbles the tourist's feet as if with chains, at a time when the whole cultured world supports, sustains and expands tourism — if only because tourism teaches, develops and makes a person capable. Even animals that enjoy free movement are more gifted and more capable than animals that always live in one place. Fruit is reckoned the most nourishing and vitamin-richest product and is energetically recommended by medicine to be eaten. For currency reasons such products as oranges, lemons, grapes are burdened with such a duty that not only the poor worker but even the middle-class consumer cannot allow himself to enjoy them.
When a worker buys an orange in a shop where he is known, the shopkeeper asks him with pity who is ill at home. Usually the tax burden presses harder on the small states than on the large ones. But the large states, too, have plenty to "sing and tell" about, and the troubles of the small states echo on the large ones.
There is one means capable of leading the world out of the chaos, out of the tangle in which it finds itself, and that means consists in the unification of the states. Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, Charles the Great [Charlemagne], Napoleon the First once strove for this goal; but they wanted to reach their goal with the help of force, and therefore they did not succeed. Today, when the dynastic obstacles have for the most part been removed, and [printed "az"] after the upheavals in Russia, Germany and Austria the great-power aspirations have shrunk, there are no insurmountable difficulties to carrying out the unification in a good way, with general consent. There is no need at all to wait for the realization of the idea of European states; it is enough that at first no more than two or three states unite, for example Germany and France, as they were in the time of the Carolingians. The neighbouring smaller states would join them within a short time, and it would not take long before the peoples of the other states forced their governments to enter the union. The states in Asia, America etc. would follow Europe's example, and in time a league of all mankind on our globe would arise.
The limits of a newspaper article do not allow one to dwell at length on the blessings that the unification would bring the world; but that is not necessary either. Suffice it to say that thanks to the unification the world will be rid once and for all of wars and militarism. The expenditures that the states lay out on their military budgets, on their upkeep, would be applied to free education, to raising the welfare of the impoverished, to giving every family the possibility of building itself a home. The question of the homeless ["bedless"?] would cease to exist, because the globe is big enough and every unemployed person could receive enough land from which his family could live. Every state will produce the articles for which it is geographically and ethnographically best suited, and the market for general production will be the whole world, without borders, without duties.
One may tell us: this is a fantasy, a utopia. I will not, however, answer this with Herzl's winged reply: "If you will it, it is no fantasy, and if you do not will it, it is a fantasy." No — whether we will it or not, this is no fantasy; it is the only means that can lead mankind onto the level road, and every cultured person is obliged to write, to speak and to do what he can in order to popularize and spread the idea of unification.
The period in which mankind strove towards differentiation, in which high mountains, the greatest forests, wide lakes and great deserts divided mankind and constantly created new nations with new languages, is gone. Today we live in a period in which even the great ocean is not able to divide mankind. Two people who find themselves at the two poles talk to each other as though they were in one room, and we are not at all far from the two people being able, while they talk, also to see one another (television).
Today mankind is undergoing a process of re-mingling. If the states do not carry out the unification by way of mutual understanding, the unification will come anyway, but only after the world has lived through cataclysms and experiments for which mankind will pay dearly.
Avraham Tiktin.
Save on yourself — but not on charity.

The whole world is now talking about saving. Thrift is without doubt one of the finest virtues; even in the best of times it is desirable and necessary, especially for us Jews.

At all times we must refrain from luxury so as not to catch the eyes of our enemies, who are always looking for pretexts and libels in bad times.

To live thriftily, to dress modestly, to be thrifty even at weddings and ordinary celebrations, is a command of reason: first, so as not to reduce oneself to poverty; and second, so as not to shame poor relatives and friends who cannot keep up with the 'show' [shtat] — and very often they are forced into it, because it is not proper for them to lag publicly behind their rich relatives.

Thrift is especially necessary for people who live beyond their means. Have few people been reduced to beggary through their wasteful living? But it is not saving on charity that can make anyone rich, and the other one, who gives charity with a full hand — can it, God forbid, reduce him to poverty? — for the charity budget is in general a small one. Our sages already said: the more one gives, the more wealth. And as that poor man said to the rich young man, who before his wedding used to give him 5 zł. a month and after the wedding only 4 groszy, with the excuse that 'before getting married I had other means' — the poor man came out with the complaint: 'So you want to get married with my money?'

Already in my childhood years I heard people reproach certain persons who, in a crisis, were the first [?] to cancel the 'shtibl boy's' 'eating day' [?]; they were openly scolded and shunned.

Today we live, after all, in an age of progress and advancement, but the bad qualities have remained with most of the population.

Starting with the 'pnei' [the community notables], those who ought to be our guides to good conduct, down to some rich men and 'gentlemen' — they save on charity. Most of them have reduced their annual contributions to charitable societies and institutions, and not a few of them have stopped paying their monthly dues altogether.

One asks: where is their sense and their honesty? Precisely in such a critical time everyone, whatever his situation, must account to himself for what he saves by cutting his payments to the charitable societies, and at the same time reckon what damage and misfortune he may thereby cause to others. First, he undermines the existence of the charitable societies; he cuts the livelihood of dozens of collectors of the institutions, who live in want even in the best of times; and who knows how many death sentences he issues against poor people and the needy... Are there few people who commit suicide because of want and hunger?..

Therefore one should save on oneself. In every household there are expenses which in a time of hardship one can do without, so as to be able to support the needy and the relief funds all the more. But one must not save on charity!

B. A. Gliksman.
Man Is to Blame

Reflections

By A-gus.

I sit and think: what will become of us after all?

People always said that the war destroyed human culture and turned us back to barbarism. Now they say that peace is destroying culture and turning us back to barbarism; and, as it turns out, it is neither war nor peace that is to blame, but man. He himself has evidently gorged himself on culture, on civilization — gorged himself, vomited it up, and remained emptied of everything, a barbarian.

Copper and brass he once found in the earth; first he made a little mirror of them, saw his own face and began to wash himself, to have his hair cut, to dress up and clothe himself, to make himself cleaner, handsomer. His earthenware pots he exchanged for copper ones, in which the cleanliness of the food was better kept; with shining door-handles he adorned his doors, and in various corners of his dwelling the mirror-like gleam of brass and copper glittered [?]. And artists cast their most sublime works of art in this noble metal. Peoples inspired with musical enthusiasm built musical instruments of it, poured their souls into heavenly melodies, and in copper bells the religious enthusiasm of thousands rang out.

Then man gorged himself on the broad tranquillity of his life, on the joyful elevation of cultural achievements, and forged them all into bullets, rifles, tanks and cannons, to chop [?] human heads like straw. And with these weapons of destruction he smashed and broke all the works of art that had stood as witnesses of the former civilization.

And when the battlefields were already strewn with millions of dead and mutilated bodies, when hundreds of settlements were already utterly destroyed, when bled-white mankind no longer had the strength to lift the instruments of death that had fallen from its hands and go on murdering [?] and slaughtering one another, and peace had to be proclaimed again — then —

then the senseless hatred was left in the hearts; people turned away from one another, set up barbed wire between [?] themselves, tore apart the connections that civilization had created, and brought it about that the achievements of culture again became impossible to use.

And just as primitive men each had his own idol at home, which he served, knowing no universal, single God, so twentieth-century man has created his own idols, idols of chauvinism; he kneels before them, serves them, brings sacrifices on their altar, and for their sake he drives out every trace of all-human, world-wide culture and civilization.

Once it was said that precisely war is the factor of culture, of progress, for war is movement, dynamics, a march forward, a levelling of borders and fences. And what is peace? Stagnation, sitting still, 'every man under his vine'. Very well — if only the vine, from which the fragrant drink drips [?], were not surrounded by a high [?] fence through which one cannot even see the bright light.

Wars, uprisings, revolutions — these were always the storms [?] that carried the seeds of culture from one place to another, kept widening the horizons of the human gaze, and drove out the household idols before the sight of the great divinity of universal man.

And it was thought that after thousands of years of wars the day had at last come when the goal had been reached, man had come to know the world, he would now wash the blood from his hands and return to his vine — but without the dark, 'fatherly' [?] fences.

But no: man has proved incapable of preserving the cultural heritage of his fathers and grandfathers; he has thrown it off his shoulders, trampled it underfoot, ground it into dust, and feels more comfortable in the wild barbarism of his great-great-grandfathers.

People talk of the decline of Europe and the rise of the East, of the yellow race, which has indeed been stirring [?] lately; of the bankruptcy of materialism and the building of idealism — but the brass door-handle and the bronze sculpture, who will give them to us? How shall we keep the brilliant light of electricity, by which we could read books and study wisdom? Who will give us spacious flats with all conveniences, so necessary for our physical culture and hence for the elevation of the soul? How shall we keep the ease and freedom of communication, which has brought us all closer into one family? Why did our matter have to expel the ideal? Why has man no room in his soul for both?

And what will it matter if Europe goes under? Does not the East go along its very same paths? Does it not use its means? Does it not set itself the same goals? Does not Gandhi fight against English material exploitation, and does not Japan want to seize the Chinese [?] market? Does she not fight with the same American and German cannons and aeroplanes? What can one expect of the pupil, if the master had such an ugly end?

Man, man is the guilty one in everything. Not war, not peace — man is to blame.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (16)

[Literature — serialized historical novel: Rasputin and the Tsar's court; installment 16.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

A great commotion arose in the palace. It seemed as though some heavy cloud were hovering over the splendid rooms. At the Tsar's command the most famous doctors to be found in the capital were summoned at once. The doctors came running to the palace in great haste. They examined the sick heir to the throne, tried various remedies, held a consultation (consilium) among themselves, then examined the patient again and again conferred among themselves, and finally they had to admit that they were powerless and could not help the patient... that only a miracle could save him...

When the Tsarina came to from her faint, she went into the room where her sick son lay, and from then on she hardly stepped away from it; days and nights she spent in that room. For hours on end she stood on her knees before the icon that hung in a corner, and prayed to God... The mighty ruler of great Russia was now no more than a broken, chastised [lit. "punished"] mother, terribly despairing over the fate of her child. The sick boy moaned bitterly without pause in a weakened, pitiful voice, and his moaning tore her heart to pieces.

And besides the Tsarina's despair over her child's gruesome pains, she suffered especially from knowing that she was the one to blame for her child's suffering: it was she, she who had brought from her family the terrible disease with which she had infected her child. An uncle of hers, a younger brother and two nephews had died of the disease (this terrible disease, "hipofilia" [= haemophilia], is passed on by inheritance, but only [printed "gar"] to males. Females do not contract the disease; they only carry it over to the boys they bear), and she had carried the disease over to her son... And this awareness weighed her down heavily and broke her...

Three days and three nights went by. All that time, in the monastery at Tsarskoye Selo, they did not stop praying and pleading for the health of the heir ["naslednik", Russian for heir]. Several times a day "Father" Feofan came into the sick boy's room, made the sign of the cross over him, sprinkled him with "holy" water, knelt before the icon and recited [?] a prayer. But no miracle happened. The patient did not get better. His sufferings were not eased. He kept moaning in his weak, pitiful voice. And "Father" Feofan tried to influence the Tsarina to have the Jews driven out of the capital and thereby lift God's wrath from the imperial court...

The Tsarina listened to the archimandrite's words to the end, but [printed "gar"] she made no answer to him at all; she looked at him with fixed [lit. "standing"], sad eyes, her face was motionless, and it seemed that she did not understand at all what he was saying to her... But the archimandrite did not tire of repeating it every time he was there:

"Follow my advice, do the will of our 'Redeemer': drive out the Jews, the unbelievers, from the holy capital, and God's wrath will depart from your child..."

And when the Tsarina did not answer this, he said in the pious voice of a chastiser:

"Reflect, great ruler of 'holy' Russia... and know this: where there are unbelievers, there Satan holds sway... So drive out the unbelievers, and Satan too will be driven out..."

The Tsarina still looked at him with a motionless face, with fixed eyes. She breathed heavily, listening to her child's moans. Feofan then asked:

"Will you reflect on it, great ruler [printed "ersherin"]?"

She nodded slightly and the archimandrite left the room, sure in himself that he would get his way... The Tsarina would in the end listen to his words and follow his advice. If not today, then tomorrow... The Jews would be driven out of the capital...

During the three days and three nights that had passed, the heir to the throne had not only not got better but the reverse: he had grown worse and worse. His pains grew with every day, became heavier and more agonizing [?]... Before, when it happened that he lay sick, he had had moments when the pains let go of him, and then he used to talk to his teacher or to his governess... This time, however, the pains did not let up on him for a single moment. The boy wept and moaned constantly, without a break, writhed from the gruesome torments, and his mother sat by his bed with an anguished heart, with wrung hands, and her suffering was very great.

From time to time Alexei sank into silence and lay unconscious. And the heart in the Tsarina died of fright. She thought the end was coming, that death was snatching her child away from her; but it passed. The heir came to again and once more began to weep from great torment and pain.

And the Tsarina sat and kept watch over him; the servants did not dare come near the patient's bed.

The Tsar often came into the room to see how the patient was and what the Tsarina was doing.

Once, when the Tsar came in, he silently took his place by the bed and looked with sad eyes at his sick son, who now lay sunk in unconsciousness, and his heart was wrung with great pity. For a while he stood motionless; then he stretched out his hand and laid it tenderly on the boy's forehead — and the boy came out of his unconsciousness and opened his eyes. For a while he looked at his father, then he stretched out his little hands. The Tsar bent down, the pale little hands embraced the Tsar's head, and the sick boy whispered into his ear in a soft voice:

"Father... if I die, you must bury me outdoors... in the park..."

Tsar Nikolai, the mighty ruler of Russia, felt all his limbs trembling, his heart fainting within him and hot tears choking his throat. He carefully freed his head from the boy's arms and hurried out of the room, and before he had even managed to close the door behind him — he burst into tears like a little child...

— — —

It was already the fourth day since the heir had fallen ill. Tsarina Alexandra sat motionless by the patient's bed. She held her hands convulsively clasped together and was terribly worn out by her suffering. She sat dejected, her face somewhat drawn; she was very [printed "ver" = "zer"] helpless, but in her heart a hope still smouldered; she was still waiting for a miracle. She no longer prayed; she was certain [?] that God did not want to hear her prayer. Nor did she have any strength left to pray; three days and three nights had already passed in which she had not undressed or lain down. She was neglected. Her hair was uncombed [?], her beautiful face was pale and wrinkled like the face of an old woman. Her eyes, which had always shone, were now extinguished and dull, reddened and dry. It seemed she had wept out all her tears, that not [?] even a single tear was left in her.

Oneg Shabbat

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
(collected and edited by [—] Yehuda [?])
Parashat Vayikra

The Portion

a) "When any man of you brings an offering to the Lord" (1:2)
A remarkable Midrash is found on the quoted verse: "Ten things are called precious: the Torah, prophecy and folly (foolishness)"...
So in what does the preciousness of foolishness consist?
— Someone [?] lost an object of little value; he searches for it and does not find it. But while searching for the object he stumbles upon a precious treasure that had been hidden there. —
The little bit of perfection that a person lacks, the bit of folly, moves a person to search and to study, and this very searching is the greatest blessing for a person, because on the way of that search he stumbles upon the great treasures of knowledge.
Ohel Yaakov.

* * *

The Rebbe Reb Bunem used to tell the story of Reb Eizik Reb Yekel's:
The famous Reb Eizik Reb Yekel's of Kraków dreamt that under the bridge over the Vistula there lay a great treasure. So he hangs about the bridge. The sentry asks him what he is looking for. He tells him the dream. The soldier smiles: and I — says he — dreamt last night that in the house of a Jew, Reb Eizik Reb Yekel's, there is a treasure under the floor... Bah, dreams!
Reb Eizik understood that the whole dream had come only so that he would learn, at the bridge, that the treasure was in fact at his own home. And so it was. The treasure lay under his floor.
The moral:
A Hasid travels to the Rebbe to seek the treasure, the meaning of the world, in order to learn there that the treasure is with him, in his own heart...

b) "And they shall sprinkle the blood" (ibid. 5)
Blood heats a person. Fat — cools. And both are offered to God. For a person must offer his heat — to good, and his coolness — to evil.
But man likes to swap the roles, and mostly he is cool towards good, and hasty and hot towards evil...
Panim La-Tushiya [?].

c) "And if his offering is a burnt offering of birds" (ibid. 14)
The bird, the poor man's offering, is symbolic of its owner:
"And he shall wring off its head" — and such, after all, is the poor man too: his head is bowed, his face to the ground, and all the persecutors [beset] his scrawny neck...
"And its blood shall be drained out on the wall of the altar" — the poor man's blood is "drained", sucked out, exhausted [?]...
"He shall not divide it" — the rich man, if he does some good, it is divided [?]: only with the hand and not with the heart.. The poor man, on the other hand, the little he does — he does with body and soul...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).

d) "If a soul sins... of any of the Lord's commandments" (4:2)
"And does one of them" — if a person knows that he has done a good deed, if he feels it and lets others feel it — he is thereby a sinner...
Kedushat Levi.

"And they that handle the Torah knew Me not" — (Zechariah [actually Jeremiah 2:8])
Those who touch [?] Him, as it were, with their hands — they do not know Him...
Rabbi Shmuel of Karov.

e) "When a ruler sins" (ibid. 22)
"Happy is the generation whose ruler takes it to heart to bring atonement for his unwitting sin" (Rashi).
When an ordinary flesh-and-blood person repents of a crime of his, it is no great wonder. But if a ruler admits that he has sinned — happy is a generation that has such leaders, for it is rare that a leader should acknowledge a sin of his own...
Shemen ha-Tov.

A curse in the Admonition!
"So that you shall be driven mad by the sight of your eyes which you shall see" —
If one is mad oneself — never mind; every madman thinks after all that he is who-knows-what a worldly sage, so he hardly feels his misfortune.
But if "the sight of your eyes", if "the eyes of the congregation", the leaders and guides, are, God forbid, not in their right mind, then the misfortune is a double one: you, the led, feel the misfortune, you see that your leader is going astray, and you must also imitate his disorderly [?] deeds... The greatest grief is this: to see oneself led madly and to have to go along with it...
Maharia Engel [?].

* * *

At Reb Yoshe Ber's (the Rabbi of Brisk) a meeting of the town leaders took place about a communal matter. Well, they quarrelled and argued, and no one knew what the other wanted. Reb Yoshe Ber bites his lips and watches the foolish palaver [?].
Suddenly a Jewish woman comes in. She has something to ask the Rabbi. She dreamt that her son had gone mad.
— Be calm — Rabbi Yoshe Ber interprets her dream — it shows that he will be a rich man and a leader of the town...

f) "Then the congregation shall offer a bullock" (ibid. 14)
"So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips" —
Just as the bullock, which served as an offering to atone, but itself understood very little of what it was serving for and what was being done with it... — so too prayer, the davening, which is in the sense of "so will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips". Many worshippers too know as much of what they do with their lips as those bullocks... The mouth babbles, but the heart —
Toldot Noach.

g) "He is guilty before the Lord" (5:19)
When it is only "guilt before the Lord", when one sins against God alone, an offering helps, repentance. But when one "deals falsely with his neighbour", when one sins against a person, it means one has at the same time sinned against God too, and for that it is of no help at all that he repents before God; he must make amends to the wronged fellow.
Reb Yaakov Kranz [the Maggid of Dubno].

h) "And deals falsely... in any of all these that a man does, sinning therein" (ibid. 22)
The first thing: "deals falsely", being dishonest in money matters. And once the evil inclination already has a person at that point, it goes further; it already leads to all kinds of other sins and transgressions.
Imrei Shefer.

Haftarah for Parashat Zachor

i) "Though you were little in your own sight, were you not head of the tribes of Israel" (1 Samuel 15)
"Though you were little in your own sight" — if you consider yourself small and do not want to be too clever by half [?], then you are indeed worthy to be the head of the tribes of Israel.
Reb Eliezer Iram [?].

j) "But Saul spared" (ibid.)
Saul had pity on Agag, Amalek's king, yet "Nob, the city of the priests" he slaughtered entirely. Toward his own people, toward Jews, he was merciless, but when it came to gentiles he suddenly became merciful...
Ahavat Yehonatan.

(Folk motif)

Purim is a holiday,
a holiday, a fine one,
the greatest pleasure
from it is had by children.

It is a great joy,
a holiday without a “but”[?],
apart from it there is not
a single proper[?] one.

A bit of fun;
why, it is hailing money —
whoever has a mask
is a great hero.

Boys and girls are merry,
singing, hopping and doing a “koushelke”[?]:
who is Ahasuerus the king,
and who — Esther the queen.

Children go about together,
in and out,
and sing a little song
in every house:

“Today is Purim,
dear people,
tomorrow it is already over
— you understand?”...

L.[?] Shikman

How to Free Oneself from Worries.

[Humour — Purim page; economic crisis, satire; followed by three short pieces: “My Purim Eve”, “A Rare Phenomenon”, “Declaration!” (Sosnowiec).] (From a submitted project.)
Since millions of people go about whole days complaining about the crisis, groaning, sighing and moaning about the bad times, worrying about a livelihood, bills of exchange, payments and other matters — which takes up so much of the population's time and is an utterly unproductive, useless labour — therefore in every town a few persons should be hired, a flat taken for them, their board provided, wages paid, and they should do this work. One should weep over the crisis, a second should groan over poverty, a third should worry about paying a bill of exchange, a fourth should fret about the bitter times, about the shortage of money, and so on and so forth. As a result the rest of the people will be freed from this unproductive labour and will be able to occupy themselves with useful and productive work, which in turn will drive away the crisis.
Eh, what — if the hired “worriers” get a pension, they will stop worrying? Then their pensions should be reduced, or possibly not paid at all — then they will worry anyway.

Lectures on public hygiene.
The Sosnowiec “TOZ” [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population], which shows special activity in the field of school hygiene, has worked out a regulation on the importance of hygiene for schoolchildren.
We consider it our duty to give a short summary of this regulation:
Jewish parents, if they want to have healthy children, must leave the damp dwellings and the dark, wet cellar-rooms. Every Jewish family must have at least 5 rooms with a kitchen and a bathroom. The walls must be painted in oil paint, the floors must be polished every day. The linen must be changed twice a week; every woman must have two maids, one for cooking and one for cleaning.
Every child must sleep in a separate bed. Great attention must also be paid to the food given to the children; every day there must be different dishes, so that the children do not grow sick of it, which, God forbid, could spoil their appetite.
By observing these rules — the regulation assures — healthy children can grow up.

Where Can One Do Business Today?

Compiled at the Leipzig Fair by our special correspondent Z. Haber.
The Leipzig Fair (Messe), which has just been held, has published a report on where exhibitors can do business and in which countries one can sell despite the various difficulties that now exist.
This report is worth writing about — in the whole world there are only three countries which have lately made no difficulties at all, either on account of foreign currency or on account of customs duty; these are: Albania in Europe, Peru and Paraguay in “North America”. In all other countries there is a catch (hook)...
Into Belgium and Luxembourg no goods of bone meal[?], “pamet”[?] or plush are let in. Into Bulgaria one cannot bring oil, textiles, minerals and paints. After the goods enter the country one may request that the government allot foreign currency to pay for the goods. The allotment takes at least three months. For the most part it is not granted.
Into Germany, Austria and Denmark one can bring everything, but foreign currency is granted by the National Bank only very rarely. Into Estonia and Finland one cannot bring leather goods, electrical articles, sewing goods[?], wool, textiles, carpets, lace and ornaments. To obtain goods from abroad one needs a permit from the National Bank. Into France one may not bring toys, radio sets, machines, household and kitchen utensils, wood, tools, copper, leather and glass; on shoes and electrical articles, too, there is a very high duty. Greece: one can bring in everything, but payment may only be made in Greek money. England: the ban on foreign currency has been lifted. There is quite a high duty on porcelain, glass lamps, furniture, steel, radio, textiles, typewriters, linoleum, paper, cosmetic articles and photographic cameras. Italy: the duty has been raised sharply, especially on radio and on films. Foreign currency is not obtainable. Likewise no foreign currency can be obtained in Yugoslavia and in Portugal, where, however, one can import everything without[?] a high duty. In Latvia one gets no foreign currency, and a special import commission decides on the necessity of importing goods from abroad. In Lithuania the duty has been raised up to a hundred percent. In Holland the import of shoes and all kinds of textiles is restricted. In Norway the duty has been raised up to 20 percent. Payment can only be made in local money. The same applies to foreign currency in Sweden, where there is a very high duty on films, cosmetic articles, paper, pictures, clocks, pianos, gramophones, toys, radio and automobiles. In Romania the duty on paper has been raised; no currency difficulty exists there. In Poland, too, there are no currency difficulties, but the duty has been raised sharply on radio, machines, bicycles, paper, oilcloth, printed matter, books and pictures. Furthermore, no shoes, gloves, wire, wallpaper[?], electrotechnical articles, bicycles, paper[?], textiles and tools can be imported there. In Switzerland one needs a permit to import wood, furniture, luxury articles, textiles and motors. In Spain, Czechoslovakia and Turkey special government permits are required to bring in foreign goods. Many articles cannot be brought in at all, and on many articles the duty has been raised sharply. Also, the permit to pay for imported goods is obtained only when the government has previously given permission to bring the goods in.
Special difficulties are also made in all non-European countries. Everywhere the duty has been raised by 15 to 20 per cent, and the governments of North and South America, as well as of Africa, give no permission to pay in foreign currency. Thus, for example, one cannot bring into Eretz Israel any sole leather, silk and artificial silk, because the duty on them is now so high that it does not pay to import them. In all the countries of the world the gold standard has been suspended[?].

Będzin
Decision to rehabilitate the Cooperative Bank.
On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Cooperative Bank took place in the hall of the Artisans' Association. Given the mood now prevailing in the artisans' ranks, it was expected that the most embittered struggle between the artisan camps would be waged at the meeting; but it is gratifying[?] to note that sound instinct prevailed and the meeting proceeded seriously. Evidently the popular masses are beginning to understand that "it is easy to destroy and hard to build"...
The meeting was opened by Mr. Regierer, and the chair was handed to Mr. Kamiński.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, Mr. Jakub Erlich gave a report on the actual state of the bank. The report shows that the bank's present situation is almost the same as 2 years ago. During the time the present management has been in charge, the bank has been left with a debt of 7 thousand zł. The previous management, by contrast, has "dead debts" amounting to nearly 170 thousand zł.
After the report a discussion develops, conducted on the premise that the bank — the oldest financial institution in our town — should be rehabilitated and resume its activity.
This view was further reinforced after Mr. Jakubowicz declared in Mr. Fürstenberg's name that he is ready to give support once the bank is rehabilitated.
After the discussion a resolution was adopted that the members should increase their shares[?] fivefold, in order to spare themselves the large sums of money the members would lose should it come to liquidating the bank. Then a new board and a supervisory council were elected.
Board: Sz. Hampel, Ch. Jakubowicz and Abraham Liwer. Deputies: A. D. Bolimowski and M. Szpigel.
Supervisory council: Sz. Fürstenberg, M. Gotfryd, M. Gerszner[?], M. Kajzer[?] and L. Brama. Deputies: M. J. Frankscwajg[?], S. Frylich and Ch. G. Goldblum.
The new board and council ask us to point out that every member must help in rebuilding the bank, which is being reorganised on the system of a people's institution.

Who will and who will not be included in the ryczałt?

In response to the various inquiries about the ryczałt [lump-sum turnover-tax assessment], we shall give a series of explanations concerning the most important doubts.
Persons who hold two separate patents (trade licences) for separate enterprises will not have their turnover added together; rather, the turnover of each enterprise will be assessed separately, and they will have to pay two turnover (obrotowy) ryczałts.
Thus, for example, there are merchants who have patents for their shops and separate patents for trading at fairs. Bakers have two patents: one patent for the bakery and one for the shop. Many have workshops and separate shops. In all these cases, where until now two turnover taxes (podatek obrotowy) were paid, separate turnover taxes will now also be set under the ryczałt.
Shops which during[?] the last years held patents in different names, and which in 1930 had a patent not in the same name as in 1929 — for those no ryczałt will be set; their tax will continue to be assessed at 2 percent.
If the business was handed over to an heir owing to the death of the previous owner — in such cases the enterprise will be taxed under the ryczałt. But in these cases the matter will have to be clarified.
If the patents in 1929 and 1930 were in different names, no explanations and no appeals (odwołania) will help. That means new businesses, and 2 percent will have to be paid.
If in 1929 the patent was taken out later than New Year, even in the middle of the year, such enterprises will indeed be counted under the ryczałt.
If, adding up the turnovers[?] of the three years 1928, 1929 and 1930, or if the business was later moved in the years 1919 [sic] and 1930, it turns out that the assessed turnover averaged 35 thousand and 10 złoty — they will no longer belong to the ryczałt but will pay turnover tax at 2 percent.

Open Letter to the Będzin Rabbinate
(Concerning the question of machine matzot).
[Będzin — letter to the editor; Passover matzot.] The festival of Passover is approaching, and I [—] it a duty to raise in the columns of the newspaper a matter which must be settled in favour of the broad Jewish masses of Będzin.
Everyone knows that for several years now the town of Będzin has been an exception among all the largest towns in Poland as regards the baking of machine matzot. Not to speak of the small shtetls — even in Kraków, Sosnowiec, Częstochowa etc., where world-famous geniuses and authorities occupy the rabbinical seat, machine matzot are also baked.
The writer of these lines already turned to the Będzin Rabbinate before Passover last year with the question: why is it forbidden to bake machine matzot? Are machine matzot not as kosher as the matzot kneaded by the Christian women from Ksawera?... Does the matter of kashrut stand so high in Będzin that one is afraid to permit the baking of machine matzot? After all, we know very well that kashrut affairs here are unfortunately not as much in order as in other towns; so why should the poorer part of the Jewish population suffer from such a "groundless prohibition", which is not practised in any town at all? The better-off obtain machine matzot from elsewhere anyway; only the poor man's lot is to have to buy the "bread of affliction" that is worked by various dirty creatures and vulgar riff-raff...
Well, I shall not dwell on this, since everyone knows and understands the great injustice done year in, year out to the broad Jewish masses by not permitting the baking of machine matzot. But all the more[?] [lit. "kol zman"], in the present hard times, when every Jewish grosz drips blood, the Będzin Rabbinate must change its decision to date and permit the baking of machine matzot, since after all tens of thousands of kilos of machine matzot are brought in from outside. In any case it is far better that "they be unwitting sinners rather than deliberate ones"...
A Będzin householder.

The Constitution of the New Municipal Administration.
On Thursday the first session of the new town council took place. On the agenda was the election of the municipal administration. The session was a festive and joyful one on the part of the Right, over its victory over the Sanacja (as is known, the right-wing parties together have 15 mandates and the Sanacja only 1 mandate). After the united Christian parties put up candidates for president and vice-president, the representative of the Jewish club, Mr. Adam Blum, made a rather long and successful speech and set a categorical condition: if both candidates make a declaration that they will treat all citizens of the town equally, without distinction of class, religion and nationality, the Jewish club (6 men) will also vote for them. After both candidates read out such a declaration, the elections were held. As a result Dr. Majewski (moderate Endek [National Democrat]) was elected president with all votes (except 2 of the PPS), and Mr. Fr. Zbieg (Padek [?] — perhaps Chadek, Christian Democrat) as vice-president. As ławnicy, by agreement, 2 Christians and 1 Jew were elected: Messrs. Kipiński, Juszczyk and M. L.
