Only Jewish Workers Must Be Employed at the Matzot!

We are entering the pre-Passover season. Never before has the pre-Passover period been as sad and as lean as this year. Shopkeepers and artisans do not expect much from this season; the tailors will not be busy with work. The haberdashery, ready-made clothing and shoe shops, and even the grocery („colonial“) shops, are not counting on any particularly large takings. Everyone will spend on the holiday only on the barest necessities.
Only one thing every Jew will have to have — matzot. He may at least[?] economise on this article, but without matzot no Jew can remain. Matzot one must buy.
Several hundred people are employed at the matzot, besides the regular bakery workers.
And here one must remember:
Hundreds of Jews have been left without any employment. These Jews do not enjoy the relief benefits, as non-Jewish unemployed do.
These Jews have been living for months on a little soup that they receive in the free kitchens. They are ready to do any work, just to earn something for their families for the holiday.
It is therefore the duty of the bakery owners to enable these hungry Jewish masses to get employment at the matzot.
Nothing extraordinary is demanded of the bakers. They need not make any sacrifices. They do not pay the Jewish worker more than the non-Jewish one. One can therefore rightly demand of them, at no loss to themselves, that they come to the aid of the Jewish unemployed.
All Jewish bakers who will bake matzot must take on for the work exclusively Jews. This is demanded by the elementary Jewish and human[?] duty!
Kh.
An Academy in Honour of the Opening of the Maccabiah in Tel Aviv

On Monday morning the Będzin „Hakoach“, in connection with the opening of the first Maccabiah in Tel Aviv, held an academy [festive assembly] in „Shvitarid“[?].
The celebration of the sports festival began with a march through several streets of the town with the participation of Zionist youth organisations with their flags at their head; the procession, led by the powerful „Hakoach“ orchestra, called forth a festive mood, and great crowds of people accompanied the marchers to the theatre hall.
The honorary president of „Hakoach“, Dr. Rechtschaft, opens the academy and invites representatives of Zionist organisations to the presidium; the orchestra plays the Polish and the Jewish anthem, and one proceeds to the first part of the academy — the lectures. Here it turns out that of the half-dozen advertised speakers not one has come... so that it gave the impression of an annual general meeting, where the presidium waits for someone from the „audience“ to take the floor, to criticise — just to speak... And indeed Mr. Wigodzki[?] took the floor „willy-nilly“ and said a few words on current affairs.
Dr. Rechtschaft reads out a written greeting from the Starost, Mr. Bosa[?], who regrets that he does not have the possibility of taking part personally.
A Jewish celebration must, after all, have a „bitter drop“. In his report on the participation of the Będzin „Hakoach“ in the Maccabiah, Dr. Rechtschaft told of the disregard of Jewish society in general, and of our patrons in particular, towards the sports club. „The upshot is that „Hakoach“ is facing liquidation...“
With this lamentation-speech the first part of the academy ended.
The situation was saved by the second part. The performance of the „Hakoach“ orchestra and the gymnastic exercises performed made a strong impression on the visitors.
Maurice Lampe and Shoshana on Tour in Zagłębie

The well-known artistic forces Maurice Lampe, Shoshana and their ensemble are on tour in Zagłębie with their new sensational play entitled „Song[?], Love and Punishment“.
It is a play that possesses a great baggage of singing, weeping, laughing, and at the end one gets the impression — just as Lampe sings: „I thought it was day, and in the end it is actually night“...
The plot: a pious shoemaker is visited by his brother, who is a great devotee of touring[?]. While he is staying at his brother's house, a love develops between him and his brother's wife, who decide to remove the honest „genius“[?] husband from the world. „Fortunately“ they do not succeed, and as punishment they commit suicide by poisoning themselves.
In the production one sees how Lampe plays his role willy-nilly, as it is not of his genre. The same is evident with Shoshana (especially in the last act). A well-rounded type is created by Mr. Shapiro (as the shoemaker's apprentice); not bad is Mr. Kurtz (the learned brother).
On the whole the performances are having due success. But we would like to see Lampe and Shoshana in better, more serious plays.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

Zionist kehilla board in Siemianowice.
The Silesian voivode Dr. Grażyński has appointed as the provisional kehilla board Messrs. Dr. Pillersdorf, Herman Oksenhendler, Abraham Zelwer, Maksymilian Rozencwajg, whose task is to take over the management of the kehilla at once, to draw up statutes and to hold elections. It is to be hoped that the above-mentioned gentlemen, who are incidentally well-known public workers, will bring a little order into the neglected actual state[?] in which the kehilla affairs have found themselves until now.
—o—
Passover campaign in Siemianowice.
For the said Passover campaign a Purim ball was held. The programme consisted of a theatre performance: the local amateurs staged Gordin's well-known play „The Jewish King Lear“ under the direction of M. Ajrman. — The ensemble played brilliantly; especially distinguished were Messrs. Sofer, Buchszrajber, Rozmaryn, and of the women Mrs. Rus, Szwajcer, Bernsztajn. The moral success was great. This is the first time since Siemianowice has existed that in one of the largest halls of the town a [—] Jewish performance was staged in the Jewish language [Yiddish]. After the performance the audience enjoyed itself until morning.
Ish Yehudi [„A Jewish man“].
—o—
„And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast“.
During a holiday party at a resident's home in Königshütte [Chorzów] a quarrel broke out among the guests; from words they passed to deeds, and the end was that one of the guests was murdered.
—o—
Shoot-out between the border guard and communists.
The border guard near Nada-Wieś[?] [perhaps Nowa Wieś] noticed 4 suspicious persons carrying large packs. In answer to the guards' call to stop, they opened heavy fire from revolvers and rifles on the members of the border guard. The guards began to answer with fire from their carbines.
A regular battle developed, lasting more than 2 hours. In the end the smugglers were forced, after one of them was wounded, to surrender.
On close investigation the smugglers turned out to be communist couriers. Two German carbines with bullets and 2 pistols were found on them; the packs they carried were full of communist proclamations.
The 4 persons, who come from German Upper Silesia, will be brought before the summary court that will soon sit in Katowice.
—o—
Another 500..
With the consent of the demobilization commissioner, 500 more workers of the state factory in Chorzów will be laid off today, Friday.
—o—
Fight for cheap electricity.
In Katowice a committee has been formed which is starting a campaign to make the Katowice power station lower the price of electric light.
In Katowice a kilowatt of electricity costs 1,05 [złoty]; this is the only town in Poland where the price of electricity is so high.
As reported, the committee is calling a meeting of all consumers.
Zionist District Conference in Będzin. Visits of Mr. Natan Asz in the Zagłębie Region.

The Central Committee of the Zionist Organization in Poland has decided to convene in Będzin on the 24th of April this year (Chol HaMoed Pesach) a district conference of all Zionist societies in the Będzin—Częstochowa region. This region comprises the following towns and places: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Pogoń, Modrzejów[?], Niwka, Dąbrowa, Zagórze, Strzemieszyce, Sławków, Olkusz, Wolbrom, Miechów, Sasznica[?] [perhaps Charsznica], Żarnowiec, Ząbkowice, Łazy, Zawiercie, Kromołów, Pilica, Myszków, Żarki, Grodziec, Czeladź, Częstochowa, Kłobuck, Krzepice, Przyrów, Mstów (Amstov), Radomsko etc.
To organize the conference the Zionist C.C. delegated Mr. Natan Asz to Zagłębie. In Będzin a special organizing committee and a regional secretariat under the direction of Mr. Asz have been set up. The Zionist committees and activists in the places listed above must immediately get in touch with the regional secretariat, which is located in the apartment of Mr. A. Liher[?] on Sanczewska[?] Street.
With the participation of Mr. Asz several meetings took place in Będzin, at which various matters connected with convening the conference were considered. The local committee has already set about carrying out a broad registration and recruitment campaign for the Zionist Organization. A special committee will take care of the technical arrangement of the conference. In Sosnowiec, after Mr. Asz's visit, they set about reorganizing the local organization, which had been weakened for a long time. A suitable premises for the organization is being rented there, and the provisional committee is carrying out a broad registration and recruitment campaign. In Dąbrowa a re-registration of the local members of the organization is being carried out and the general members' meeting, with the participation of representatives of the C.C., is being prepared. In the other places too, which Mr. Asz is now visiting, the preparatory work for the conference is being carried on lively. Special activity in the work is shown by the united youth organization „Herzliya“ (which is quite strong in the Zagłębie region) and „HaShomer HaLeumi“. After re-registering, the members receive their membership cards for the year 1932, without which they[?] will have no right to vote at the conference.
As rumoured, the conference will also be attended by the honorary president of the Zionist Organization in Poland, Deputy Y. Grünbaum [Yitzhak Gruenbaum], [„mart“ — unclear word] before his leaving Poland.
Olkusz.

The gmina gives up baking matzot
Because of differences of opinion the gmina [kehilla] has given up buying the holiday flour and has leased[?] Kals's[?] oven to the baker Moshel Waldman. Next Monday baking will begin at 2 bakers' — the flour for machine matzot. The „Dobroczynność“ [charity society] wants to levy kimcha [de-pischa] of a couple of złoty on every sack of flour; the rabbi too demands (by established right) 2,50 per sack.

Theft of 1,200 zł. from a beggar
In a lodging-house[?] at Israel Morgen's, 1,200 złoty were stolen from a beggar. The thief, also a beggar, has vanished.

General meeting of „Maccabi“
On Saturday night the general meeting of „Maccabi“ took place, at which the following board was elected: Abraham Hoferman (chairman), Jakob Machner[?] (vice), Lejbl Glajtman (secretary), Lipa Fridman (treasurer), Jekusiel Kruk (commander), Judel Trapojer[?] (manager [gospodarz]) and Szlomo Frenkel (deputy).

[Będzin (?) — collapse and treasure.]

A House Collapses on Podzamcze Street.

Yesterday[?] afternoon an old house on Podzamcze Street suddenly collapsed. Fortunately not a single person was present at the time of the disaster. When they began clearing away the collapsed walls, they found a walled-in strongbox deep in the ground.

The place where the treasure lies is guarded by the police. Today, Friday, at 11 in the morning, a special commission is coming from Kielce, which is to establish the cause of the disaster and to whom the treasure must[?] belong.
Those who poison the air. (We may no longer tolerate [it] — the seriousness of the situation.)

Because of little Jewish denunciations. As we read in our paper not long ago, the citizens' committee for [?] the support of the unemployed in Będzin has stopped giving relief to some thirty-odd Jewish families. The committee is regularly showered with little letters from our brethren the children of Israel, saying that so-and-so son of so-and-so receives relief he does not deserve; needless to say, reasons are not lacking. Shmerl — so the little letter says — has [?] money, and Berl has rich relatives in America.
One must not forget that the committee sits at the magistrate [town hall], so the Jewish representatives who occupy themselves with this charitable work are certainly cautious. It therefore goes without saying that once people have barely managed to obtain the relief, there is no doubt that they need it like life itself, since every application is, after all, closely investigated.
So how do those representatives, who recognise the need, look when these "little letters" arrive afterwards? What sort of face do they have then? Does it not make on the Christians the impression of "swój do swego" ["each to his own", the slogan of the anti-Jewish boycott]? Do they not reckon at such a moment that one Jew wants to support another not because he deserves the relief, because he needs it, but only because he is a brother, a Jew? And in that case, of course, the Jewish representative is in the wrong towards his Christian fellow committee members, for it then gives the impression that he carries no weight, that he cannot represent our poverty.
This kind of conduct, the writing-in of the denunciation letters, makes a dreadful impression, and it must by no means whatsoever be allowed. Besides, one must not forget one thing: as soon as the "writers" see that their scribbling has had an effect, this kind of activity becomes popular in the extreme, so that it is not out of the question that special bureaus will be set up to make a living from it.. With us, after all, everything is possible. No kind of abnormality, of lawlessness, is ruled out with us, as long as in the field of obstructing and overturning, destroying and tearing apart there is enough courage and energy. If only this were used among us for fruitful activity — to create and to build. One would then know that much that is useful is being created and built, which would be an honour and a glory for the Jewish people, and would bring us enormous benefit in every field of our life.
Therefore the question quite often arises: what shall we choose? Shall we let life go on as it goes, with all the ugliness and baseness that corrupts everyone inwardly and outwardly at every step, or shall we strive to uproot the bad, to drive out the unworthy, and in its place apply all our energy to what is useful and positive — to creating and building, to beautifying and enriching our so very poor life, both in the social-political field and in the communal-philanthropic sense.
It goes without saying that there are no two opinions about the need to take up useful activity; but one must not forget that these are nothing more than fine words, threadbare phrases. One need only look at the course of our life, and then the prospects are not at all cheerful, not at all pleasant, for we see that the course of our normal life is to wreck, destroy and ruin both what exists and what is on the way to developing.
Let us not deceive ourselves: is it only one poor man who informs on another in order to get a free dinner? Does the danger of informing not reign in every field of our life? In every stratum of the Jewish population? Does Shmerl not inform on Berl merely because the former sees that the latter makes a living? Does one man not see to it that the other spends money merely so that he should break his neck and nape and never again be able to rise, not even at the resurrection of the dead? Does one man not trip up the other so that he should be completely ruined? Does one competitor not quietly cause the other such damage that he will remember it forever and ever?
What more is needed: formerly, when such "little letters" reached the authorities, the treasury [skarb], it was believed that the writer was a patriot seeking the good of the government; later, however, people became convinced that this is [?] not so, and that one is out for nothing more than to destroy the other, to remove him from his place. What is even more painful is that the denunciations have reached such a level that often it is not even a matter of competition — envy alone is enough. One man envies the other even though he does not have the same business as the other and the other does not get in his way; he simply begrudges him, because he lives and does business. That alone is already enough to write "little letters" wherever needed, so that he be watched, that an inquiry and investigation be conducted against him. Such are the satisfactions one wishes to live to see in another.
These lawless deeds have reached such a level that from individuals, from single outcasts, they have been raised to the masses, to the broad strata of the population, and often reach the community as a whole. We do not see the colossal "progress" being made in this field because we have already been dragged into it too far; by force the community has been dragged into the sad indignity that we nowadays call life.
No attention is paid to this danger. People do not notice it, or do not want to notice it, and perhaps many citizens do not have the possibility of noticing the harmfulness of this unworthy activity, which thoroughly destroys the community. After all, at the present time it is hard to fight for one's existence, for the daily piece of bread. Incidentally, it is only called "for bread" at a time when, before one gets to the piece of bread, the obligations are so great that one sweats hard until one arrives at one's own piece of bread.
However far the course of informing may have progressed in every field, beginning with the greatest and ending with the smallest, we hold that the highest time has come for the question to be treated more seriously and more sincerely; it must be approached with full attention and strictness. By no means may we let ourselves be destroyed because we cannot adapt to the conditions of a terrible [?] life that corrupts our whole system.
One must begin to think up advice and means of how to exterminate that which is beginning to cause so much harm in every corner and in all strata of our population. The government, too, does not want such individuals to hover in the air and poison it. The government wants honest citizens who fulfil their civic obligations towards the country and the government; on the other hand it must not have professional informers who occupy themselves with their "business" as with a trade to which they have been called.
The highest time has come to stop looking at the question through one's fingers. We must treat it seriously in its full magnitude. We must dwell on its danger and harmfulness, which take on ever worse forms and lead to catastrophes.
It makes no difference — it is already so bad, so bitter and hard, that one can say with a clear conscience: the great "credit" for our dangerous situation, which keeps unfolding in our little world, belongs to the system of informing. Thanks to the form of informing, the broad highway of lawlessness came into being. One man began knowingly to snatch [?] goods from another, and so another thought to himself: they ruined me for nothing and again for nothing, so I will do the same to whoever lets himself.
We must therefore look at the dangerous situation with open eyes. We may no longer let ourselves be done to death while still alive. If we exist, if we live, if we act, one must see to it that our existence, our life, our activity be carried on in a dignified way, and for that it is necessary to remove the dangerous elements that make ugly and exterminate our life, our present and our future.
Let us remove the whole leprosy from the broad highway, which has spread over all our paths and does not allow us to lead a healthy, normal and honest life.
We may no longer tolerate, and look on with apathy at, the poisoned air that has settled like a thick fog on our horizon.
R. Let.
Letters from Home

[Będzin and Zagłębie — feuilleton in letter form: kehilla, housing, economy, elections; an April Fool's piece.]
With God's help, the week of the Torah portion "do not make yourselves abominable" [Shemini]... in the minor reckoning.
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
The long grey winter has had to give way to the beautiful, splendid spring, which poets sing of year in, year out. Once, when "mankind was bloodthirsty," every spring brought great battles and offensives. But in the present century, when the idyll of "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb" is gradually being realised, when state budgets allocate a minimal sum for maintaining armies, when munitions factories are being converted into school buildings — spring is a double salvation for mankind.
With us too, R' Shlomo, our well-known miscellaneous[?] affairs will this time take their stand. When outside it is spring in God's little world, when the trees regain their lustre and splendour, one does not wish to rehash wintry grey matters. Let them go to their rest together with the winter. This time we will chat about cheerful things, from which you, R' Shlomo, will surely derive satisfaction...
We shall make the beginning with our kehilla life, which is now taking on a new face of revival and vigour. Good sense has prevailed among the hitherto parties — the "Aguda" and the Zionists — who have at long last come to the conclusion that such a regime[?] as until now could lead the kehilla to bankruptcy, and have concluded an agreement between them, under which the Zionists receive the chairmanship of the board and the "Aguda" — the chairmanship of the council. As for the further distribution of mandates, it depends on the various factions. The agreement was received by all parties with great dissatisfaction. There is only a doubt whether the authorities will ratify the agreement. The "Aguda", which is vitally interested in the Zionists obtaining the office of kehilla president, is taking action and applying means of patronage so that the authorities give their consent. There is also a conjecture that today, Friday, Deputy Mincberg is coming here specially on this matter, to intervene so that the starostwo [district office] should not be against the union...
Be that as it may, the moral merit of this union is an unexpected one. All the parties and associations, seeing that such bloody enemies have united and made peace between them, decided to follow the example. As is reported, a conference took place last night at the premises of the Będzin Small Traders' Association, at which it was decided to create out of both merchants' associations one merchants' institution, to be run by a council of 3 persons. In general, the system of unification is very topical with us. A union of both artisans' associations is also in the offing; out of a union of the Jewish banks and all philanthropic institutions one institution called "Tsedakah Gedolah" is to be created... Instead of a board, a provisional body is to be set up for the time being, which is to stand under the control of the board of the "Gemilut Chesed" fund.
Spring has also brought with it a law that eases the hitherto heavy yoke of the poor tenants. According to the new law adopted, tenants who occupy 1 room will pay no more than a quarter of the rent according to the year 1914. Those who occupy 1 room and a kitchen will pay 50 percent according to the normal rent, and for larger flats the rent is reduced by 12 and a half perc.
A revival is also noticeable in industry and in the business world. The factories are supplied with colossal orders; above all the ironworks in Upper Silesia have received orders from Russia worth hundreds of millions of zł. Thanks to this, the previously announced workers' layoffs have been held back. In the commercial world too things have become livelier; merchants want to explain it by saying that the large turnover is connected with the approaching holiday, but be that as it may, the money crisis among merchants has ceased[?] to such an extent that it may happen[?] that barely 50 percent of merchants still seek an interest-free loan...
No smaller joy will probably be for you, R' Shlomo, the news that the commissarial councils in Sosnowiec, Będzin and Zawiercie are being dissolved. And already this month preparations begin for the elections to the town councils in the above-mentioned towns. Although the exact election calendar is not yet precisely known, consultations are already taking place on creating a single list of candidates of all parties and factions. The initiator of the unity list is the universally known peace-pursuer ("rodef-sholemnik"), councillor Lewin... As foreseen, a united list will easily be created, for since peace now reigns on the kehilla ground between Zionists and "Aguda", no great differences of opinion will be met in this important matter either.
The same opinion may also be voiced regarding the town-council elections in Sosnowiec. The first "signal" of this is the kehilla budget: as you know, almost all budgets of the Zagłębie kehillas have already been approved, except for the budget of the Sosnowiec kehilla, which is still not a "living child". The reason was that the kehilla representatives firmly believed that the kehilla elections would be invalidated and new elections would take place... This week, however, "their faith melted away" with the special notice that was received, that the kehilla elections have been approved and the new budget must be ready within 2 days.
The strict order had its effect, and almost without any discussion the new budget was determined by the council and the board. No important changes were made in the new budget. Only the proposal of the Aguda representatives that 5000 zł. be provisionally set aside for the rabbinical competition which is soon to be announced by the Sosnowiec kehilla...
I still have to write to you about very important things that would have made your heart overflow with delight, for example about the proprietor[?] of the Będzin mikveh, about the Małobądz power station, which has reduced the price of electricity to 40 groszy a kilowatt, and the like. But I must cut it short, because I have been called by telephone to a meeting of the tramway management, which has finally decided that from the first of April Jews are to be taken on as tram conductors...
Yes, R' Shlomo, as they say: "The good is not forever and the bad is not forever either" — and yet we have lived to see a bit of consolation in our dark little world. Would that from today on salvations and consolations begin for the whole of Israel, as wishes your
Ben Amotz.
P.S. I have a small request of you, R' Shlomo: do let me know when you received this present letter; I am very curious to know whether you will receive it today, on the first... The above.
There Is No Public Opinion.

If it is true that every country has the government it deserves, it is truer still that every "esteemed public" ["wertes Publikum"] has the plagues and afflictions it deserves.
If you find too many nudniks [pests] in a population, blame the population, not the nudniks, for they, poor things, are not to blame. It, the population, produced them. It brought them into the world, and they, poor things, have no other choice than to be in the world and — to nag[?].
If you meet many idiots in a region, censure the region, not the idiots, for it begot them. They came out of its belly, and they, poor things, have no other choice than — to act the idiot.
On a lean, neglected, overgrown field grow coarse, bitter, loathsome fruits. It is not the fruit that is responsible for its coarseness and bitterness, but the field, or its lazy, negligent owners.
For this reason [Aramaic "mehai ta'ama"] I am inclined to judge favourably every nasty ["paskudne"] phenomenon in local Jewish life — what fault is it of the poor phenomenon that it seems nasty. The guilty one is life. It is its father, its mother. Against it I am a prosecutor; it I would tear apart mercilessly, like a herring.
And when I walk in the street and meet wild ignorance [am-haratsus] and lawlessness [hefkeyres], I do not get angry at these two ugly, miserable fellows, and I have no heart [to] grab a stick and split their heads. What, I think, are they to blame for, poor things — just as a horse is responsible for being a horse and walking on four legs, or is a donkey perhaps guilty of being a donkey and not a knight?...
I am therefore indignant at the street; against it I am fire and flame. It is the father and the mother, the grandfather and the grandmother of these sad twins, ignorance and lawlessness. As the Gemara says there: "lo akhbar ganav" — it is not the mouse that is the thief, but the hole, nothing more. The trouble is that you cannot drag a hole into court. Go and litigate with an empty void.
So[?] — thus it is "also" with the street, with the Jewish street. There is nobody to talk to, nobody to argue[?] with. It is an empty void. Many times I have tried to talk and to plead and to protest to the street, but each time I became convinced that I was only making a fool of myself, that I was talking to thin air...
That is why I disagree with the well-meaning but naive readers who often write us letters and demand of us why we keep silent about this vile deed or that vile deed, this scandal or that scandal, this "terrible affair" or that "terrible affair". They think that all we need to do is raise an outcry, and the "villainists" and the scandal-mongers will tremble and shudder so badly that they will swear off[?] doing such deceitful deeds. But we know the truth: our writing will help like a compress on a corpse; all we can achieve is to wear out[?] our throats, become hoarse as the wall, and have no chance of being hired as a cantor for Musaf, not even for Shaharit, on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur...
And our crying out will not help, because there is no "da'as ha-kohol", no public opinion, before which one could accuse those who sin against Jewishness or humanity. And when there is no one before whom to accuse, nobody need be afraid if he is put in the pillory. He makes light of the shame and whistles at the pillory.
Here, for example, lies before me a letter from a reader, which in itself is very nicely and intelligently written. But the writer of the letter ["ba'al abriol", misprint for ba'al-ha-briv] tells us[?] about an injustice by a Jewish institution and adds: if you do not raise a hue and cry against such an outrage in Israel and do not publish the names of the perpetrators of the scandal, it will be a sign that your newspaper is no more than a "noeh doresh" [one who preaches well] but not a "noeh mekayem" [one who practises what he preaches].
Well, it is certainly a "scandal", a wild, scandalous thing, if the affair as told in the letter really happened exactly so. And let us tell you that we are inclined to believe that it really was so. But the worthy[?] writer is apparently still a greenhorn when he demands of me that I "raise a hue and cry", because he does not yet know the secret that here there is no "public" ["olam"], and so there is no one to stir up. [—]
For affairs similar to the one in question have already been told more than enough in our newspaper, and we too have more than once "raised a hue and cry" against them, whether in serious articles or in feuilletons, by mocking the "heroes" and making fun of them. But nevertheless nobody was frightened off by it.
That is because lawlessness rules and reigns here ["shaltet un valtet"], and there is no Jewish public opinion before which to have respect, before which to feel ashamed.
On the contrary: people will come who are well acquainted with the conditions in the institution mentioned in the letter, and although they will not be able to deny the facts touched upon — for they know of far worse — they will nevertheless not come out against the wrong, nor blame those who caused the wrong, but rather those who brought it out into the open; for unfortunately there are very many here who think that the core, the innermost part, may be rotten through, as long as it has an outward gloss.
L. T.
If I Had Been Given the Floor...

[Będzin — trade, feuilleton.] A Trader's Little Letter.
Conveyed by Yosef (Józef) Perlmuter.
My friend! Recently I attended a conference at the Minister of Commerce's, which had been convened specially in order to find a way out and the means how to rescue trade from ruin. Various delegates came, representatives of all the traders' associations, Jewish and non-Jewish, and in the end, after nine measures of talk, in which everyone poured his heart out, people went away with the same thing they had come with...
And truly, what could the conference have achieved? Already after the first speech by the minister himself, right at the opening of the session, that he indeed considers the situation in trade very dangerous and catastrophic, and that this is precisely why he found it necessary to convene this conference, in order to consult with the representatives of commerce what is to be done, what to do, so that trade should not die out entirely. But... the minister drew attention to one thing, namely, that the traders' representatives should not expect that salvation can come at the expense of the government treasury (skarb), because the treasury is at present not in a position to meet demands of that kind...
Naturally, nothing was left for the Jewish representative to do but to thank the honourable minister for the initiative of calling a conference of traders' representatives, and also for the good will to help trade, as he put it when opening the conference, and — that was that...
But you see, my friend, it is a pity, a great pity, that I, the humble one, was after all not given the floor. First of all I would have told the minister that among us there is a saying from the Gemara that "will alone accomplishes nothing" — with mere will one can do nothing at all. True, I believe you that you have the best will in the matter, but as long as you do not open the purse and hand out credits — to make the distinction — as with us the aliyot to the Torah: first the Kohanim, the big industrialists, then Levi — the smaller manufacturers, and then Israel — simply that lone trader who still clings to his little business — nothing will come of all these conferences, with all the good wills and all the fine speeches...
And secondly, I would have told a well-known story of Sholem Aleichem's and asked: what did you need to inflict such severe wounds for, with such unbearable experiments? So that now you have to look for doctors with prescriptions to heal the wounds — did you really not understand that if you monopolize all articles of prime necessity, so that no trader should have any access at all; and if one tightens a tax-screw that squeezes out all the little life there is in trade, and in the end also kills the last nerve — reduces consumption to a minimum, so that ninety percent of the population cannot afford even the most necessary of the necessary, and the whole of trade has turned gangrenous and already lies in its death throes — so why now call us to conferences, so that we should help... Where were you when we cried with all our strength that we cannot pay for such experiments? We were tearing our hair out [lit. throwing ourselves off the storeys], we closed the shops, and you took none of it into account. You just went on doing your own thing. And now, esteemed Mr. Minister, if you truly mean, with heart and soul, to help us and to set us back on our feet, and soon, you must do all these experiments the other way round, exactly the opposite... First of all, free all articles of prime necessity, so that there can be free trade in them... Then, as soon as we traders feel the true taste of trade again, soon, trade will surely revive so much that all the factories will be swamped with work, and the worker will earn so much (it costs me nothing if he earns even four and five times as much) that he will be able to afford to wear a smoking jacket with patent-leather shoes on weekdays and in the evening to sit in a fine café, so that every single person will have a penny in his pocket and everything will be bought at full price — and not, as you have brought about, that everything costs half for nothing and there is nothing to buy with...
Let everything be expensive, it does not matter at all... and better let everyone earn, rather than give things away as cheaply as possible.
And the main thing. You see, taxes (podatki)... that yes, the treasury needs money and that must be paid, it makes no difference, it would bother us as much as the gragger bothers Haman. The motto must be: trade, earn and pay...
That, you see, my friend, is how I would have explained the situation, and I ask you, write me an answer straight away whether you would have accepted it, because with the Zagłębie people I am somehow never sure...
Your friend, Yosef.
Before the Holidays

[Feuilleton — scenes of merchant life.] (From mercantile life.)
For whole days on end R' David, the haberdashery (galanteria) merchant, sat through the rains and snows without taking in a single grosz. If during the day one złoty ("gilden") of takings came in, it was barely enough for the dry piece of bread.
He had borrowed and run into debt, as they say, up over his ears.
His whole hope was that the Almighty would help and that "in the days before the holidays [?]" something would be sold; then he would pay off all his debts and also "take a look" at himself and the family [i.e. see to their needs]: buy himself and his wife shoes with new galoshes, make the children new warm little coats, lay in a cartload of coal.
He counted the days and hours until a "road" would at last set in for a market day. Finally R' David lived to see it: snow fell with frost, there was good sleigh-road in the street, and he reckoned that on Wednesday some takings were bound to come in. He assured everyone that on that day he would pay them all off, down to the last bit of earnings.
That day R' David woke up earlier than usual and took a look outside — beautiful weather, the sky clear as crystal, and he thought to himself: "I am not worthy to mention His name" — He will help. It will be a good market day. He went straight to the beit midrash, prayed with the first minyan, and from there into the shop: tidied up, put things a little in order, stoked the little iron stove and took his place by the door to wait for the "początek" [the day's first sale].
He did not wait long; a customer appeared and gave him the first złoty to take.
With special satisfaction R' David contemplated the złoty, spat on it [for luck] and put it in the table drawer.
Right after that a couple [came up] to him, very finely dressed up, their eyes still sleepy, and pinned a little tag on the lapel of his fur jacket; he threw a few groszy into their collection box.
R' David had barely felt that he had earned something when he wrapped up the parcel, counted over the money and sent it with the child, who had already been waiting at the side, so that mother could go to the market.
Up turns the watchman (stróż), who sweeps the street: "Panie [Mister] David, I'm due for the month, today is market day. Pay me."
"True," answers R' David, and pays.
After the watchman in comes the washerwoman, who does not say a word but only gives the master of the house a look, and he already understands from the hint what she wants. He hands her 2 złoty and swears that he has no more; when she comes back from the market he will give her the rest.
After her several customers come in at once: an old squire (dziedzic), two peasant women, a schoolboy. R' David answers each one separately and keeps an eye out that no loss should occur.
A good market day is shaping up.
He lets no customer out of the shop, even when they offer "below cost." "In the drawer it all gets mixed together," thinks R' David.
In the middle of it a policeman springs up and notices that the spittoon is not at all in order and not washed out. R' David promptly receives a fine slip and pays 2 złoty with a groan.
Meanwhile a few more customers come in, and with them a collector from an institution, who demands the monthly dues for 3 months. He stands to one side so as not to disturb R' David. R' David notices him and has a receipt written out for the whole debt. The collector takes his leave — and the shammes of his beit midrash arrives: he had pledged 3 złoty, and the shammes demands the pledge. "It's for Torah, after all," thinks R' David, and pays.
A few minutes later the collectors of the Gemilut Chasadim fund, of Malbish Arumim [clothing the poor] and of Linat HaCholim [care for the sick] turn up, demanding payment for a couple of months. Yes, answers R' David, important institutions, one must pay — and has receipts written out. The clock strikes 12. His wife appears, bringing him a bite to eat, and tells him he should pay the baker the whole debt, and the butcher's wife only 5 złoty, because she has an account to settle with her. Meanwhile he notices that it is already half past one, snatches a [note?] down from the wall and cries out: "I've still got a bill of exchange to pay today at the 'Bank Polski'; I need a hundred złoty and I have no more than 20."
With these words R' David runs out of the shop and goes round the neighbours to get an interest-free loan to pay the bill. It was not easy for him to get hold of a hundred from a neighbour, by 7 o'clock [?]. And, out of breath, he went off to the bank and redeemed the bill. Coming back from the bank he finds several customers in the shop whom his wife cannot cope with; he promptly answers each one separately.
R' David takes his place by the door; 2 respectable householders come up and ask him for "a very important donation." It simply did not befit him to refuse, and he hands over half a złoty.
In between he sold something more; the baker's wife turned up, handed him a bill and fussed that she would not budge until he paid the debt.
After her came the shoemaker, who had mended the children's shoes; he has to be paid — a poor man with children.
To the butcher's wife he gave nothing more and sent her to settle accounts with his wife.
The last creditor was a neighbour from whom he had borrowed a few złoty to buy out the trade licence (patent) for the new year.
When he returned home, the whole household surrounded him and each one separately demanded something of father. But, alas, he only heaved a great sigh and reckoned up to them the whole list of debts that he had scheduled for today's market day.
For tomorrow he again wondered where to get money to give his wife for the market.
About shoes, a summer garment for the daughter, the children's school fees, buying a cartload of coal — about that he no longer even wanted to think. That is what remained to R' David after the great market day on the eve of the "holidays," which he had been hoping for for several months.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (18)

[Serialized historical novel — Tsarist Russia, Rasputin; installment 18.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

"This is the very same 'holy man', and now he is in the capital..." Vyrubova caught her breath and at once went on talking and telling with great ecstasy: with full certainty she can say that this Siberian muzhik surpasses in his 'godliness' and 'holiness' even the holy John of Kronstadt... The 'holy' John himself admitted it: it happened two days ago. In the monastery of the 'holy' John a great crowd had gathered. The most distinguished ladies were there, the aristocratic women of the capital. The monastery was full right up to the doors. And this is how it happened: 'Father' John had finished the divine service. He had preached wonderfully... Afterwards he called out as usual: 'Draw near to me, believers, bow to God, and let the holy water cleanse you of all sins'... The richly adorned ladies began pushing closer to 'Father' John, in order to bow to God, be sprinkled with the 'holy' water and be blessed by him. But then a strange thing happened: 'Father' John took a few steps forward from the 'altar', stood still with very bright, burning eyes and a radiant face. He raised his right hand and in a mighty voice cried out: "Wait! Today we have among us an important 'holy' man! And let him be the first to approach [?] and bow to God!.. It is the simple wanderer who stands there among you!"

He pointed with his hand at a plain muzhik who was standing near the door, where the beggars, the blind and the lame usually stand.

Everyone turned their heads to see who it was... at whom Father John was pointing.. And they saw — it was an ordinary muzhik, dressed in a sheepskin coat, with heavy, dirty boots on his feet. In his hand he held a wanderer's staff, and on his shoulder hung a sack of coarse linen. But — as Countess Ignatova [Ignatieva] told me — everyone immediately noticed what wonderful eyes the muzhik had... He has extraordinary eyes... And his bearing was quite extraordinary: one might have thought he would lose his composure or be a little ashamed at the great honour Father John had bestowed on him... at the fact that the eyes of the most distinguished ladies were turned on him... But the wondrous man remained perfectly calm. He was not at all taken aback. He was not ashamed, did not feel uncomfortable a hair's breadth... Quiet [?; printed "shpiler"], upright, he stepped with measured steps up to the icons, crossed himself, bowed; and then — not 'Father' John blessed him, but the reverse: he blessed 'Father' John! All those assembled were left dumbfounded; all felt that this muzhik is a great 'holy' man!

Vyrubova's face glowed with enthusiasm as she told this. She expressed her enormous regret that she herself had not been present. That day she had intended to go to 'Father' John's monastery. But at the last minute, when she was already ready to leave her house, a visitor came to her and she could not get away. Ah! How terribly sorry she is!

Be that as it may, the incident caused a great sensation among all the distinguished court-ranking [?] ladies who were present... In the salon of Countess Ignatova people began to take a keen interest in the strange wanderer... They immediately began to inquire who he is and where he comes from... It turned out that he comes from Siberia, that his name is Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin, and that the Archimandrite Feofan had already spoken about him in the salon.

Vyrubova [printed "Vyrubovanhat", a misprint] kept talking with great enthusiasm, feeling that the Tsaritsa too was catching the enthusiasm and that her interest in the wanderer was growing with every minute. And Vyrubova told how Archimandrite Feofan had met the wanderer from Siberia in the monastery where the wanderer had come for a night's lodging, and how he had been tremendously struck by the muzhik's speech and bearing. The next day or two days later the Archimandrite came to the salon and told of the impression the Siberian muzhik had made on him, on Bishop Hermogen and on the highly esteemed monk Iliodor... All three are convinced that he is a 'godly' man... that he can perform great miracles.. that God speaks through his mouth... And not only the high clergy were astonished and enchanted by his profundity, his 'divine' knowledge and innate wisdom, but also people of sober understanding and logical mind, such as professors, lawyers and senior officials, who met him at a session of the central committee of the "Soyuz Russkovo Naroda" [Union of the Russian People] (the well-known Black Hundred organization), held in the capital. They too were greatly enchanted by Rasputin. They too are convinced that he is a great 'holy man', that he possesses a wondrous 'divine' power, and he was unanimously accepted as a member of the central committee of the "Soyuz".

Bishop Hermogen, who is tremendously enthusiastic about him, brought him to Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolayevich in the palace. And the Grand Duke too was enchanted by him.. A deputation of the "Soyuz Russkovo Naroda" asked that he bring the new 'holy man' to Tsarskoye Selo and present him to the Tsar and the Tsaritsa. They believe with all their heart that through the mouth of the Siberian muzhik speaks 'the voice of the Russian soil', the soul of the 'holy Russian people'. And they hold — and rightly so — that never before has it been so necessary and important to listen to the voice of the Russian people as it is necessary and important now, when the revolutionaries are conducting a mighty, broad agitation among the people and are undermining the pillars on which the throne and the 'holy' Church rest... The Tsar and the Tsaritsa are surrounded by false courtiers, who deep in their hearts incline [?] toward the free, heretical ideas of 'Western Europe'... And it is therefore very necessary and important that at court the voice of a representative of the true Russian people be heard.. And — Grigori Yefimovich is the representative of the true, pious Russian people..

Here Vyrubova stretched out her hands as if in prayer and, rising, cried out from the heart:

"Dear Alexandra Fyodorovna, I feel that in the person of Grigori Yefimovich the Almighty has sent you a loyal, devoted friend! With his arrival at court everything will change! You will be loved, respected and esteemed by the whole Russian people, for whom your heart holds [?] so much love! With his appearance all those who intrigue against you will be put to shame! A time of wondrous happiness is coming for all Russia. The 'holy' man who has been sent to you by God will lead you in God's name along the right paths."

Vyrubova sat down again; she saw how the Tsaritsa's face had brightened, understood that her words were having the proper effect, and went on talking:

The people of the "Soyuz Russkaya Naroda" are, after all, the most loyal and devoted supporters of the monarchy. They care, after all, for the integrity and security of the dynasty. And if they propose something to the Tsar, there is surely no doubt that they mean only the good of the monarchy, which is so dear to them, and one must listen to them.. Grigori Yefimovich is a genuine Russian... He comes from the people and knows very well what the people think and demand.
