A Chat with the Reader.

[From the editors — the Passover issue.]
Although, together with the whole Jewish press in Poland, we too are going through a severe crisis, we nevertheless strive to make the reading matter of our paper interesting and to have it reflect Jewish and general life in Zagłębie.
We devote special attention to the holiday issues of our paper. This year's Passover issue too will be rich in varied reading matter. Besides articles and feuilletons by the permanent members of our editorial staff, we have received for the Passover issue: an article by Pini Baal-Loshn entitled „Once Upon a Time“ — a characteristic picture of how the preparations for the Passover holiday once used to begin months in advance. A feuilleton by Dr. A. Gottesdiener entitled „Elijah the Prophet's Cup“, a treatise on why precisely the cup was raised to greatness; selected Torah sayings by Ye'ura, the compiler of „Oneg Shabbat“; a historical legend by the well-known historian Mr. Moshe Feinkind entitled „Nine Days of Passover in Prague“. A special section for culture and literature entitled „Ears of Grain“ [Zangen]. This section will include works by young Jewish writers and notes on cultural matters.
In this issue we give a summary of the thrilling historical novel „Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved“; the novel is a reflection of that epoch when Rasputin „the holy man“ played a role at the Russian tsar's [court].
Besides this, a special Haggadah with modern commentaries, translated by Ben-Amotz.
Our Poor Are Provided For. (Must We Tolerate the 'Order' Prevailing Until Now in Our Homely Little World?)

The economic situation in the country is enormously difficult. The crisis, which has entered a chronic phase, is no longer a temporary, passing phenomenon. The wound is too strong and too deep to be able to heal so quickly. It has penetrated into the very bones, so that the body is, for the time being, damaged [?] to its foundation.
There is nothing to do. Unemployment in every field takes the upper hand, and there is nothing by which to earn. People wander about the streets like shadows, looking for work, looking for something by which to earn a groschen, but it comes hard. So hard is it in the present time to lead a clean, dignified, honest life. People have not earned a single groschen for months on end, and it is simply impossible to understand how they keep on their feet. It looks legendary, just as if one had survived the time by miracles.
Yes, that is how bitter and bad it is. No one ever imagined that one would [?] be able to hold out so long, to stand on a paper bridge and not fall into the water. Of course many, many fall into the abyss, everything is systematically destroyed, but be that as it may, it is a wonder and incomprehensible with what strength those who have not yet been washed away keep going. For the conditions of existence are enormously hard. In the field of [financial] obligations a terrible disharmony has set in, lawlessness has already reached its culminating point, and that is the reason why many cannot remain honest, because against their will [?] they are swept along [?] by the dangerous current, which grows ever bigger and stronger.
It is often said, and we also see it plainly, that today there are no idlers, that today people stop at nothing. People are willing to carry stones up onto the walls, as long as they are given work; one is hungry, and as the proverb says: need breaks iron. Yes, true, so it is. The hard time, the bitter situation and the terrible crisis have taught humanity a lesson: the fastidious, the wavering, those who cannot adapt to everything, that they must be reduced [?] to everything in order to fight for the 'hard existence' (das schwere Dasein), as the German says.
And if this was a lesson, and a hard lesson at that, for the common people, for the middle class and even for the upper part of the middle class, it did not at all touch the lowest strata of the Jewish population, those who made some sort of living, and when the crisis broke out they, true, were the first to suffer, as people say: the first kapparot-chicken is the poor man; but they made little of it. As it were [?], they got the opportunity to stretch out their hand, and so within a short time they became professional beggars. Here it must be said to our credit that we are merciful sons of the merciful, and at all times we give alms to an outstretched hand. Among us people dislike getting into arguments over whether this is right or not; one holds that it is a mitzvah, and what Jew will renounce [?] a mitzvah? That, in short, is the story of our painful beggary, which has unfortunately blossomed so quickly in various forms.
Not long ago the Jewish population in Zagłębie appealed through our newspaper to the bakers that, when baking matzot for Passover, they should take on our poor people, so that they, as the appeal said, could earn from the work on the matzot for Passover; and it was indeed tried, in the hope that this work would help many poor people, and they would thus earn something for Passover. Unfortunately, however, we hear from the bakers that, regrettably, no Jews come to them, so that they must employ non-Jews for the work. Of course we are not against non-Jews also earning in such a hard time. But why should our own poor people not also be able to earn for Passover by helping to bake matzot? Is that a small wrong? Has it ever been heard that, having the possibility of earning with one's own hands, one would rather go begging? But we are, after all, merciful sons of the merciful. Among us people give to the right and to the left. Whoever stretches out his hand gets alms tossed into it, without reckoning that the number of takers keeps growing all the time and, conversely, the number of givers keeps shrinking. But however hard that may be, will a Jew then refuse to give alms?
And the takers: why should they give up stretching out their hand, once they have weaned themselves from every kind of work? That is the scandal, that is the unheard-of thing. On no account may we support with alms those who can support themselves by work, those who have the possibility of getting work. We hold that just as one must not let a brother fall because he has nothing with which to get through the day, so one must not bestow alms on him when he has the possibility of getting work and making a living from it.
Many poor families have the possibility of getting work at the matzot; why do they not use the moment? Why do they go around the doors at that time? Is it not more fitting to earn for the holiday in a dignified way? Is it not more pleasant and more comfortable when one earns honestly and decently for the holiday, and even for after the holiday, than to drag oneself from door to door with outstretched hands?
And is baking matzot the only way to earn for Passover? Can women not earn now by cleaning flats and shops? Do we not remember that every year at this time there is a shortage of Christian women, and housewives literally quarrel over a Christian woman? Can certain [?] of our own women not also take up this work? Do they not go after alms at the very time when they could earn quite nicely at this work and make Passover from it? Can one tolerate, and may one tolerate, such wrongs? Would the situation among us not improve to a certain extent if there were not so many idlers, or, better said, if we ourselves did not help them become idlers and beggars, all kinds of charity-box rattlers? What do we make in such a case of healthy people full of vitality, when by giving alms we push them toward the loathsome bread of beggary?
Granted, we understand that they must be supported when there is no other way out, when we have nothing to do with this contingent of people; but as soon as there is another possibility, another way out, must not everything in the world be used in order to achieve, even from time to time, a desired goal, a lofty economic ideal? It is an old rule that a Jew cannot get into a factory, nor into an office, nor as a labourer into rough work; therefore [?] it ought to be sweet as sugar when topical work turns up from time to time, especially when it is not used at all on our part.
Usually, when times are bad, people gladly grab hold [?] of whatever there may be. But among us people do not think of it even in a bad time, while others do so all year round. Do we see many of our brethren, the Children of Israel, going to rough work? We see no Jewish coal carriers and no washerwomen, and the number of servants, too, keeps shrinking, regardless of the fact that a Jewish servant girl today is not treated as in the past and is not so hard worked, and yet she is ashamed to take a post as cook or cleaning woman. How many Christian cleaning women, the so-called 'obsługaczki', make their living from Jews; is there at least a minimum of Jewish cleaning women or washerwomen? Where do you see a Jewish washerwoman? Would it not be high time also to give some thought to doing something in this field, in order to relieve need on the one hand and to reduce beggary on the other? Is it right that in such a hard time people among us give to the right and to the left, thereby pushing healthy people into beggary, so that they are torn away from practical, honest work?
In this serious, bitter time it would, it seems [?], only be fair to consider all this, to dwell on it, and also to do something substantial and real.
R. Les.
Heaven, Earth and Poverty...

[Feuilleton — the plight of Jewish shopkeepers; distraint for taxes.] It was a gloomy day. On the white-spread heaps of fallen snow a thin rain was falling. The thawing snow had made deep puddles, in which the passing peasant carts cut deep ruts. In front of the shops the merchants stood, pale[?], with longing eyes, looking out for a customer. But the street was empty. From time to time a few single passers-by dragged themselves along, marking their steps in the dirty, grey, wet snow.
It was already one o'clock in the afternoon. The merchants had long given up hope of seeing a customer before their eyes. Suddenly, with a clatter, the "wagon" drove up on Modrzejowska Street [printed "Mandzhever"]. The skinny, wasted little horse lazily dragged its legs, pulling behind it the heavy, broad platform.
The crowd, which by the way was already used to these guests, regular visitors, was this time badly frightened at the sight of the "wagon", knowing that there was not a penny in the pocket.
The "wagon" dragged itself from house to house, from shop to shop. Now they loaded broken household odds and ends onto it, now again they dragged out of a shop goods that had filled the empty shop shelves, and the little horse dragged on, further and further. The load grew ever heavier for it. Under the pressure of the load the wheels of the platform cut ever deeper into the soft snow, leaving a deep track.
Dozens of eyes, sad, full of grief and pain, followed the "wagon" with their gaze, the wagon that carried on it all their goods and chattels. Merchants wrung their hands and sent after it desperate, hopeless looks and heavy sighs, which echoed in the empty space of the street.
The "wagon" drove on further. Suddenly everyone stood as if turned to stone. The "wagon" had stopped in front of a poor little shop. The whole street knows this poor Jewish shopkeeper, whose entire little property consists of about a kilo of sausage, a few rolls, a jar of marinated herring, two broken little tables, two stools and a pair of scales. The sequestrator [tax bailiff] went into the little shop. I went in after him. Outside, meanwhile, people had gathered, who exchanged astonished glances: Is it possible? How can one demand taxes ["podatki"] from a Jew who is simply dying of hunger?
In the shop stood the owner, a short, emaciated man with a yellow, wrinkled parchment face and two[?] red eyes. At the sight of the sequestrator the Jew began to tremble all over. His pale face turned whiter still. His red eyes clouded over as if with a mist. He swayed all over, on the point of falling.
"You are paying," the sequestrator broke the silence.
"I pay..." the Jew repeated in a trembling voice, "I would pay, I would gladly pay, but I simply don't have it. Look, this is all my property. Altogether it is worth perhaps 10 złoty, and on that I have to keep a whole family. Do you know what goes on in my home? How great the need is? How many days we have not eaten our fill — not, God forbid, of delicacies, but of dry, tasteless potatoes, with which we still our hunger? I simply don't have it!" — and he burst into loud sobs like a little child.
"You are not paying," the sequestrator demanded coldly. "If not, I'll take everything from you."
"But I don't have it," he repeated in a trembling voice, aching with tears. "I am so poor, so poor..."
I looked, moved, at the weeping Jew. He, a shopkeeper, a former[?] big merchant, now stands broken and weeps that he has nothing, that he is perishing of want — and [they] don't believe him! Is not his property a witness, a mute witness, crying out heartrendingly loud: Look at me, don't my figures say that he has nothing? And the face, that yellow parchment face, is it not the best witness of his poverty, of his terrible destitution? Ah, how it cries to heaven, when a grown man stands before you and weeps, shouts that he has nothing — and he is not believed...
"You don't pay? Then we take everything from you," the sequestrator said, and he began to carry out the little bit of poverty [misprinted "aripkeyt"] from the little Jewish shop, which altogether consisted of 2 broken little tables, 2 stools and a pair of scales.
The Jew stands as if petrified, he says nothing, only his tear-filled eyes, full of great sorrow, look on so strangely, saying very, very much...
Those gathered in the street were stirred with pity; in some, tears came to their eyes.
A few Jews went into the shop, collected among themselves the few złoty and then handed them to the sequestrator.
He [printed "er hot er"] took them, coldly wrote out the receipt, adding on [a charge] for the "wagon" and for his own fee.
"Here's your receipt, go, take your things," said the sequestrator, handing the Jew the receipt.
But the Jew stood as if frozen, did not stir, took the confirmation with indifference and stuck it deep into his pocket. He wept, wept bitterly in silence, but his eyes said, full of meaning: What will be tomorrow, the day after tomorrow?...
And there came to my memory a little story of an old, sick melamed [cheder teacher], whose wife and children had died, and he was left in the world a lonely man with a little sheep, which he had been raising for many, many years. The little sheep was his only provider: he drank its milk, ate its cheese and dressed in clothes of its wool. The little sheep was raised and raised, and fed its old, sick master. Until one morning, when the melamed went to see how his little sheep was doing, he found it with glazed eyes and stretched-out, stiffened legs. It was dead. The melamed beat his head against the wall, wept and cried out: God, why have You killed my little sheep? My only provider?
And the melamed looked with tear-filled eyes upon the great injustice that had been done to her. God, what will be today, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow?..
L. Fajgenbaum.
The Economic Front Must Be Strengthened.

There are truths that everyone knows, yet no one dares to utter them as long as they have not been heard from an authoritative mouth.
Just such a well-known truth was revealed to us by Yitzhak Grünbaum in his farewell speech. He said that what now confronts the Jews in Poland is not the problem of national rights, but that of equal rights.
This does not mean, of course, that we may renounce our national rights. It means that Jewish national-personal autonomy, with which we opened the first page of our Jewish history in renewed Poland, is not so much an object of external struggle as a matter of internal "foundation-building".
In the whole of the past 14 years of our work, only the general, permanent contours of a Jewish autonomy have barely emerged, and they are still very far from a building. We have built up a school system which can in no way be called national, but at best party-based, because every group has its own school. In a twilight state we have developed a Jewish social welfare system, which holds itself up by the force of inertia. But no one can know which institutions of this kind have a right to exist and which do not.
In both these fields the internal struggle is immensely embittered, and it is still very far from consolidation and synthesis. Therefore we ourselves do not yet know how we should make use of these parts of our national autonomy, which ought to be the most important foundations of our public life in Poland.
The field of Jewish religious life, too, is still entirely uncultivated. Not to speak of the religious parties fighting among themselves for hegemony in the Jewish street — a quarrel that acts destructively on Jewish spiritual life — we are still altogether very far from knowing what place the religious bodies should occupy in our communal life; the boundaries of the concept "religious needs" are so blurred among us that everyone puts up the fence wherever he pleases, and no general agreement on this has yet been reached.
The cement of national autonomy, the organized Jewish kehilla, was at the outset built by us partly on secular foundations; by the government it was narrowed down to a religious congregation. But there is no doubt that, just as the latter satisfies none of us, so the former, too, was not yet sufficiently crystallized and perfected, reaching for such prerogatives as do not belong in its programme. And it is our own task, over the course of years, to put into this vessel the content suited to our aspirations and capabilities.
On the whole, the national autonomy proclaimed at that time was merely a kind of "Ten Commandments", from which there must still develop a Torah with its 613 commandments and with a proper Shulchan Aruch.
The situation of our civil rights is different. In the economic-political sphere we are wholly dependent on external factors. Here, too, our structure must undergo a complete rebuilding, adapting itself to the new conditions. But at every step and turn we run up against the hardest external obstacles, which block our road to progress.
All our fighting forces ought to have been concentrated on the economic-political front. Our entire intelligentsia ought to have thrown itself here into the service of the masses, worked out the strategy and the tactics, and led to victory. But the intelligentsia had not yet made this elementary truth clear to itself; it did not want to profane itself with everyday struggles, leaving the hardest and most responsible positions in the hands of the masses themselves, to defend them — without a plan, without a perspective, without an understanding of the general, the whole, the future — fighting for a morsel of bread instead of for the national economy, and defending a handful of sand instead of the national battlefield.
The Jewish political leaders, the great as well as the lesser, must beat their breasts in contrition for having abandoned the most vital interests of the Jews in Poland, for having pushed into the background the economic struggle, the problems of our civil rights.
And let them, at least now, after the word has been heard from an authoritative mouth, revise their attitude to Jewish problems and throw themselves into the work with refreshed forces and with full clarity that our greatest national effort must now be turned to the front of our civil equality.
P. K.
Remember, Help Is Urgent!

[Appeal — Passover wheat money (maot chitim).]
When we call to mind what is now going on in the Jewish street, what terrible poverty reigns among us Jews, the blood freezes in our veins. Many respectable Jews toil all year long to earn a dry piece of bread for themselves and their families. But for the holiday of Passover, whose increased expenses are unavoidable for them, a man is in no way able to help himself, and with a cry of "gevalt" the poor fellow runs to a close friend of his for help.
At so terrible a time everyone must give his "maot chitim" with a generous hand; it is too little to give according to one's means — one must exert oneself with all one's strength and give beyond one's means.
In more than one home the seder tables will glisten with tears, and many will recall with heartache their seders of years past, when their table was laid with every good thing, and now the poor man must conduct [the seder] at empty tables.
It is true that at such a time we are not able to relieve the want that reigns in the Jewish street, but we are obliged to do what we are able to do; we may on no account shirk the duty that lies upon us to help our poor brethren for Passover.
Do not delay! In the last few remaining days every Jew must show his feeling of compassion and come to pay his "maot chitim" to the matzah commission at the Jewish kehilla.
Remember, help is urgent.
Sh. H-s.
Sun, Air, Greenery and Water

[Sport — the gymnastics societies in Zagłębie.]
(For the attention of the gymnastics societies in Zagłębie.)
The thousands of gymnasts and sportsmen are leaving the gymnastics and sports halls and are now going out onto the green field. Spring and summer are the time which, with systematic work, can be properly used for the benefit of the sportsmen.
Sun, grass and air, the greatest treasures of nature, must be used for the benefit of our youth. Only the gymnastics and sports societies can do this — but not in the form of taking part in various championships and in various games for points. We are speaking here of the great masses of [—] [?] and [—] [?] youth who do not engage in sport as an occupation and cannot put their whole mind into it, but of those who must, for at least an hour a day, tear themselves away from the stifling factories and workshops after their hard work; of those who must, for at least an hour a day, stop breathing the dreadful "Zagłębie air" amid the most dreadful housing conditions here in Zagłębie.
For these thousands of young and older Jews the Jewish gymnastics and sports societies must now do the work. No especially large budgets are needed for it; a vacant ground is enough: nature gives air, sun and greenery free of charge; a little organization and good will on the part of a few instructors are enough. No special training of the thousands for records or competitions is needed. What is needed is to make the lungs healthy, to straighten the shoulders, to make the faces cheerful.
No special discipline is needed, no special apparatus; what is needed is to arrange sports games in the fresh air, to accustom [people] to water, to swimming, to try for one hour to become a child again.
The enormous benefit of this no one can estimate, but the gymnastics societies too will be able to draw their own benefit by searching out special talents for their outward representation.
The gymnastics societies in Zagłębie must take up this mass work at once; it is the most rewarding task. Make use of the treasures of nature: sun, air, greenery and water.
S.
“Echo Żydowskie”...

[Feuilleton — Jewish press in Polish; Agudas Yisroel.]
"Echo Żydowskie" ["Jewish Echo"] — that is the name of a new weekly that appears in Warsaw in the Polish language. In the goyish tongue it is called a "tygodnik" [weekly]. The paper is printed on Friday — "w piątek". In our tongue — erev Shabbat kodesh. It is sent out — who knows when... Some Jews get it just in time for eating the cholent. And those whom fate willed to be, poor things, removed [?] from Warsaw by a two-day train journey must "niestety" [unfortunately] wait another half day and receive the paper only at the third Sabbath meal, delighting themselves with a [—] [?] of Polish literature by various holy men, rabbis, rebbes and great men of the generation.
Well, so another paper has been added. It has after all become a "bread article". Whoever has merely a hand and a pen produces nowadays, in the blink of an eye, newspapers, becomes an editor, a full-fledged journalist, and from that moment on you [?] must reckon with him seriously, because if not, he may smear you in his "little sheet"... Because of the heading "Żydowskie" I actually bought myself such a little gazette. On Shabbat after the midday meal, when I am accustomed to take a Jewish holy book in hand, I lay down at ease on the sofa and began to contemplate the new "Żydowskie" [—] [?] in the Polish language.
Envy — I thought to myself, while I was deeply busy drawing the moral from the paper — what are Jews not capable of doing; [?] a Jewish "kishke" probably thought: if a "Nasz Przegląd" is a [?] thing, and a "Nasza Sława" [?] is altogether the very height, then why shouldn't there be another paper "po polskiemu" [in Polish]?.. A knock for that one, a pinch for you — and a little livelihood for me...
— "Poseł Rab. Lewin" [Deputy Rabbi Lewin] — is the first thing that struck my eye — and after he settles accounts with Grünbaum for his last sharp protest in the Sejm against the Gerer Rebbe, and "przedstawia" [?] [presents] the "czcigodny [?] rabin Alter z Góry Kalwarii" [venerable Rabbi Alter of Góra Kalwaria, i.e. the Gerer Rebbe], who has already for the fourth time travelled in a luxury carriage for a thousand dollars [?]-money "w pielgrzymce do Ziemi Świętej" [on pilgrimage to the Holy Land], and what "dziesiątki tysięcy [?]" [tens of thousands of …] Hasidim he has, and what a Torah scholar he is, and what geniuses his Hasidim are, and that he, "Rabin Lewin", would always answer Grünbaum thus for his "podłe obelgi" [vile insults], only he is often "przeszkodzony chwilową niedyspozycją" [prevented by a momentary indisposition]...
— Brrr! — I turned the paper over to the last page and went on searching, for from the first page I had realized that the paper smacks of Ger Hasidism in Polish...
— "Kącik dla pań" [Ladies' corner] (the women's gallery, in the vernacular) — there stood displayed [?] great letters, like those of the blessing of the new moon, so that they poked my eyes out. "Postacie kobiece w Talmudzie" [Female Figures in the Talmud] on the right-hand side, and on the left — "Echo mody" [Fashion Echo], and in the middle "Poradnik dla gospodyń" [Housewives' Guide]...
— Oy — I had already bitten my lips from agitation — such a profanation! And who? Holy and pure men put it together! And for whom? For their [—] [?] "Hasidic [—]" [?] — ha-ha-ha! "Female Figures in the Talmud" and "Fashion Echo" together, hard by one another [?]! When Rabbi Akiva's wife "Rachele" is described there — what a splendid female figure she was, and how she married Rabbi Akiva without her father's knowledge, and how she is finally driven out of her father's rich house and lives with her husband in great straits and want — "Dokończenie nastąpi" [Conclusion to follow]. Pure [?]...
And further on the left: "efekty dwukolorowe" [two-colour effects] are much desired; a white spódnica [skirt] with a dark jacket, smooth, with a basque-flare [baskinka-klosz]; a "smoking-style or [?] [—] [?] cut" and blouses of white satin are also in fashion. In front little cockades with pearl buttons. Also very much in fashion are "kozaczki" [?] and various other troubles and "cultures" [?] of which I understand nothing at all...
The "Poradnik dla gospodyń" I no longer had the strength to read through. I had had enough without it, because for so weird a surprise I had not been prepared and had not expected it. Greatly agitated, I flung the comical paper away and did not even read the articles of Motel Leibele Mincberg (fully two in one issue — out of great enthusiasm), nor the novella "Ślepy grajek" [The Blind Fiddler], nor even a feuilleton about Zionist "króliki" [rabbits] and Mizrachist "[—]" [?].
Yes — they started with "Tanu Rabbanan" in the kloyz, sneaked one by one over into politics and crawled onto an "Echo Żydowskie" with a "Kącik dla pań", under the strict supervision of the very greatest gedolim and of "zacnych [—] [?] rabinów" [honourable … rabbis], which appears "w piątek" [on Friday], to give Jews oneg Shabbat with a little Torah in the vernacular on the great and holy day, when all Jews ought to rest and occupy themselves with Torah, mitzvot and good deeds.
Lux.
Yitzhak Gruenbaum the Pioneer — On His Leaving Poland

[Article — Zionism; Yitzhak Gruenbaum.] By L. Gutgeld.
(On his leaving Poland.)

The crown-stones[?] of every movement are always those men who serve it not only with their brilliant thoughts, which flash up in noble minds in the great hours of experience, but who also give themselves over to it, as a faithful mother to her children, day after day, with honest devotion, even to the point of self-forgetfulness and self-annihilation. It is they who, by kindling their own heart into a torch to light the half-dark roads on which the bearers of the movement must tread, thereby at the same time light great torches in the masses around them — and the horizon grows brighter, the steps firmer and the goal nearer. Nothing affects people so much, nothing carries them away so much, as the sight of great self-sacrifice, of enthusiastic self-offering for the ideas that one preaches. Friends must then follow, and enemies must stand dumbfounded and full of reverence.

I do not know who made the great upheavals in the world — the individuals in their studies with their lofty theories and predictions, or the stormy masses with their needs and sufferings — but it is clear as day that the lion's share[?] of the credit for the great social changes in the world belongs to those very men who, in their extraordinary[?] devotion to the ideas, were themselves the fluttering banners of a new tomorrow; and they called the masses to them, inspired them and made heroes of them.

The Zionist movement is the movement for the great Jewish upheaval. The present day is so grey that only in moments of deep concentration are we able to grasp the great, luminous changes that we want to carry out in our life. Therefore, like no other movement in the world — with the exception of the socialist one — Zionism demands almost[?] superhuman efforts, stubborn endurance and strong minds. It is not a movement for which it is enough to toy with its ideas in the salons. It is no poetry for twilight hours and no spiritual bread for sated souls. Zionism is the movement of the Biluim, of the heroes of the "Yizkor book" and of the new Maccabees. They are few, for their number is only in the thousands and the tens of thousands, and we need the millions... But people admire their heroism more and more[?], marvel at their devotion and little by little draw ever closer, until... they are carried away by their idealism. Then the number of builders grows, who sacrifice not only cheers of hurrah, enthusiastic speeches or złotys for the Keren Kayemet, but themselves, wholly, body and soul, with all the fire in their eyes and all the faith in their hearts — and it becomes the camp of the millions.

Not for nothing is chalutziut preached throughout the Zionist world in the broad sense of the word, that is, binding one's personal life, in the form of burning[?] sacrifices, to the idea of Zionism. Only in this way shall we become more than we are, and our strength will be greater than that of average flesh-and-blood, and in honest spiritual intoxication we shall perform those very wonders that are needed to reach our final goal.

One of the first of the few men in the Zionist movement who tread the path of chalutziut is Deputy Yitzhak Gruenbaum. As for a half-legendary medieval knight, Zionism is for him the only beloved, whom he serves in all the hours of his day, with all the chambers of his mind and with the whole love of his heart. For more than thirty years, since the hottest days of Sturm und Drang, he has been her constant troubadour, her singer. He is the first to be full of fear at every shadow that falls on her dearest face, and is always ready to draw the sword against anyone who wants to make her feet stumble.

Great and many are the heroic deeds of this Zionist knight. He is one of the finest strings of pearls the Daughter of Zion has ever received. In Moscow as in Helsingfors, in Warsaw as in Zurich — everywhere her faithful companion. Also in the struggle for national rights in the lands of the Diaspora, in the struggle for the secularization of the kehilla, in the struggle for the Minorities' Bloc in the halls of the Sejm — everywhere he sees before his eyes the road to Zion. At the same time he is fearlessly ready to be the first to go onto the barricades and take all the arrows. Indeed, when the number of open enemies of the Jewish renaissance is great, and still more its hidden enemies, and the bullets fly at him from all sides, then he becomes even more rock-firm, even stronger and even more devoted. Oh, when enemies lie in wait for him and he and his camp are in the minority, then he has no equal among the most splendid Zionist spirits. Then he is the mighty leader of the weak, the guide of the few — and yet the strong man of faith. And remarkably, his strictly controlled thoughts do not hinder him in the temperamental devotion of his heart. The one perfects the other, the one complements the other, and a splendid harmony is created between the radiant ideas of the mind and the warm self-sacrifice of the heart. He looks like a symbol of great strength[?] and ethical perfection.

And if a movement such as the Zionist one has in its ranks such personalities, such knights of chalutziut, it is a sign for the Jewish world, as for the wider world, that Zionism is a lofty idea and will also be realized. People give themselves over to it body and soul. Can[?] there be a greater proof that a great faith in its realization lives in them? That faith then infects others too, and the camp grows larger and more loyal. The millions come — and the work grows stronger.
Telephones (Notes)

[Feuilleton — Zagłębie, economic crisis.] (Notes)

If you want to examine the economic and cultural condition of any town at all, first of all take the telephone book of that town — a telephone book is a kind of barometer.

Leafing, for example, through the Zagłębie telephone list, which is included in a book together with a series of telephone lists from the surrounding towns and townlets, you can easily guess which of them are bigger, richer, more developed, etc.

The top place in this telephone book is occupied, of course, by the town of Sosnowiec with its nearly two thousand telephone numbers by now.

There was a time, not long ago at all, when Sosnowiec had some six hundred telephone numbers. The economic situation in the town was then "a little" better, and people scrambled to have telephones installed. But with that old-fashioned telephone system (when one had to turn the crank for hours on end to connect with another number) the telephone exchange [—][?] was not able to accommodate everyone, and one needed great pull with it...

Dozens of applicants waited for one subscriber to give up his line, just as one waits for the death of a rich uncle.

By the time Zagłębie was helped to a modern telephone system, the subscriber network had grown in length and in breadth and...

Here we come only now to the main point — to the decline: the town is turning into a townlet, and the network into a little network.

Outwardly everything is, for the time being, still as it was — in the telephone book the few thousand numbers are in their places, just as in the town the thousands of houses are in their places; but just try to ring this one or that one, and you will keep hearing the telephone girl's answer: "Disconnected", there is no such number any more...

It goes without saying that it is not out of well-being that people give up the telephone they had grown so used to.

What did twenty gulden [złoty] a month matter in former times, compared with such a convenience as a telephone; for many it was the main foundation of their business; truly a question of life. But once the main foundation has been undermined, the twenty gulden have become a fortune.

We leaf through the telephone book, the barometer of Zagłębie, and constantly stumble upon dead numbers — upon gravestones, under which lie buried ruined livelihoods...

Izydor.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Metzora, Shabbat HaGadol)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Metzora
The Portion
—o—
a) "This shall be the law of the leper" (14[?]:1)
"This is what is written: 'But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes'." (Midrash).
Not by studying Torah can one buy off the sin of tale-bearing, on account of which leprosy comes upon a person, for such study is not for its own sake (shelo lishmah), and it is said:
"Hear, for I will speak of princely things (negidim)" — words of Torah are likened to nobles. Just as a noble can bring to life and put to death, so too words of Torah. If they are not earnest[?] — they become a deadly poison, for the greater a person is, "the greater his evil inclination." Well then, if someone studies Torah — and the evil inclination is no trifle — when the study is not for its own sake, his evil inclination grows greater too, and he certainly has no reward from that not-for-its-own-sake study. So he is left only with the enlarged evil inclination..
Beit Shmuel Aharon.
—o—
b) "The plague of leprosy" (ibid., 13)
In Ben Sira it is said: "A bad wife is leprosy to her husband."
For leprosy comes because of evil speech — and who is more given to that than those who have taken over his measure of talking...
Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
Ben Sira compares the husband of a bad wife to a leper, because "a leper is considered as dead"...
Well[?], why does he not compare him to a blind man, who is also "considered as dead"? Because it would indeed have been better for him to be blind and not see her deeds...
Milin de-Rabbanan.
—o—
c) "And I put the plague of leprosy in a house of the land of your possession" (ibid., 34)
Through the plagues of houses the Jews — according to the Aggadah — became rich, because the former peoples of Palestine had hidden money in the walls "in itst"[?]. With the plagues the houses were torn down, and the treasures were "torn down" [sic; probably: uncovered].
So what, again, is the punishment for it?
The punishment is to get rich through plagues..
Imrei Shefer.
—o—
d) "When ye be come into the land of Canaan" (ibid.).
"This is what is written: 'The Lord is good unto them that wait for Him.' Could it be to all? — Scripture says: 'to the soul that seeketh Him'." (Midrash).
God asked King Solomon what he wanted: wealth or wisdom. He asked for wisdom. And therefore he was given both: wisdom — because he asked for it, and wealth — because he did not ask for it...
"To the soul that seeketh Him" — if someone pursues only spirituality, he has both spirituality and wealth, for money likes to cling only to him who runs away from it.
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
A [—] village Jew (yishuvnik), who had become an upstart rich man and bought himself a new house, made a celebration. The melamed Weiger[?], being tipsy, was making merry. The villager asks him:
— Why are you dancing so much, [?] is it your house, then? Your term will pass and you won't be here any more.
— So what? — answers the melamed — and when Y-O-U-R time passes?.. So don't you rejoice because of that?
—o—
e) "And if he that hath the issue spit upon him that is clean" (15:8)
"Rabbi Yochanan used to proclaim: Beware of the flies of those afflicted with ra'atan."
This means those afflicted with ra'atan — those who see only the bad in people; the flies, the insects that always land there where there is some unclean sore, and which one does not see on any clean place...
Kli Yakar.
—o—
f) Shabbat HaGadol and Parashat Metzora.
Shabbat HaGadol mostly falls on Parashat Metzora. This hints that the essence of redemption depends on uprooting our old fault of tale-bearing and evil speech. If because of it we were driven out of the Land of Israel, how shall we be redeemed while we still possess this very fault?
Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
g) "Draw out and take you lambs" (for Shabbat HaGadol).
The road to redemption could only lead on when the Jews were so courageous and bold that they dragged the sheep — the Egyptian idols — through the streets, slaughtered them publicly and [roasted?][?] them. Such a people, so courageous — is worthy of being redeemed. In this lies the miracle of Shabbat HaGadol, the miracle of the lamb.
Binah la-Itim.
—o—
Haftarah
h) "I the Lord change not, and ye are not consumed" (Malachi 3)
Jews say: God has changed; He no longer performs miracles nowadays. But: "I the Lord change not." God has not changed. He continues to perform great miracles for the Jews, even greater than before, for "ye are not consumed." The fact that Jews still exist to this very day — is that not the greatest heavenly miracle?
Kokhav mi-Yaakov[?].
—o—
i) "Remember ye the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded them [sic] in Horeb."
The Torah was given at Horeb, in a desert, to show that it is not subject to any climate, nor to any time. Desert-raw[?] and desert-eternal is the Torah.
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
—o—
j) "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers."
Jerusalem was destroyed because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza — because of the friction between old and young. And the coin of Jerusalem bore David on one side and Solomon on the other. Father and son on one coin — that is the symbol of Jerusalem rebuilt[?].
Yalkut Peninim.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (20)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin at the Tsar's court; installment 20.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Some more time passed. They agreed on which entrance the new "miracle-worker" should be brought into the palace by. If he were brought in through the reception rooms, it would take too long. He would have had to pass through three guard-posts; he would have been stopped — like everyone else who wished to be received by the Tsar — at least twenty times, and asked why he wanted to see the Tsar. His name would have been entered in twenty different books... They would have telephoned the palace commandant ["nachalnik"] and asked what to do. The commandant's answer would have had to pass through several people before the visitor was allowed to approach and be received by the Tsar. Various spies would have watched him, looked him over, stopped him and asked him various questions... All that would have taken too long, and they wanted the "holy man" to reach the sick "naslednik" [heir] as quickly as possible. It was therefore decided that Vyrubova should bring Rasputin into the palace through a side entrance that was always kept locked, used by no one and guarded by no one. That entrance would bring him straight into the private rooms of the Tsar and Tsarina. He would not have to pass any guard at all, and no one would notice him...

It was agreed that Maria Vishnyakova, the loyal and devoted governess of the heir to the throne, would wait for them at the side entrance, lead them through dark corridors and up the various stairs, and bring them into the Tsar's rooms. Rasputin would come in Vyrubova's carriage, and the few guards hanging about behind the palace by the driveway would not be surprised to see Vyrubova's carriage drive up, for Vyrubova was a very frequent visitor at the palace and everybody knew it...

After everything had been agreed, Vyrubova took leave of the Tsar and Tsarina, walked out of the imperial palace with quick, stiff steps, and drove off to fetch Rasputin, with whom she had arranged only the day before that he should wait for her at the house of the priest Vostorgov...

The carriage ran fast. Vyrubova breathed deeply and her joy was great. Now she was sure of her victory over Archimandrite Feofan, who had intrigued against her and sought to have her removed from court... She believed in Rasputin, was sure that he would work a miracle and heal the heir to the throne. Feofan would be removed from court, her position at court would be strengthened, and the Tsar and Tsarina would be grateful to her.

When Vyrubova had left the palace, the Tsarina went into the room where the sick boy lay. She found him lying and groaning in a bitter, weeping voice. His face — pale as a dead man's. His legs drawn up to his body; and in spite of all this she felt much lighter at heart. Now she hoped that everything would yet be well...

She remembered what the "holy" Ioann had once foretold her: that God would send her a "friend" who would protect and guard her from every evil. And now, having heard from Vyrubova about the "holy" Rasputin, she thought: and perhaps... perhaps the time has already come... God has sent her a "friend" who will help her in everything?... Perhaps...

Chapter Five.
The New "Miracle-Worker"

It was already nearly nine o'clock in the evening, and the Tsarina was counting the minutes with the greatest impatience, awaiting Rasputin's arrival. Several times, when she had run to the door, stood and [hoped?] to hear footsteps, she ran over to the big writing desk at which the Tsar sat and exclaimed in agitation:
"He is coming!... He is coming!.."

But she was mistaken. The minutes crept by. It was already nine o'clock and Rasputin still had not come. The Tsarina was terribly restless. Her heart was constricted with great impatience and expectation. She breathed hurriedly and was very nervous. The large, finely carved, gold-covered clock had already struck nine, and Vyrubova and the "godly" man were still not there... Where were they? Why didn't they appear? Anna had said, after all, that she would come with him at about nine o'clock?

The Tsar too was restless and nervous. He sat at the writing desk, which was littered with various documents and reports. He tried to read the papers, but in vain. He was so flustered that he did not understand at all what was written in them.

On the desk lay "rapports" about new resignations of high-ranking officials, about murderous attacks on tsarist servants, about uprisings and revolts; there were orders placing certain parts of the country under martial law, which had to be signed by the Tsar. But the Tsar was not capable of doing anything.

Tsar Nicholas in general hated the work of reading papers. Affairs of state did not interest him. Listening to his ministers' reports, being occupied with politics — he had always regarded this as a heavy burden on his shoulders [printed "their shoulders"], one he would have liked to be free of. The lives of the millions of people of great, wide Russia, over which he ruled, did not concern him. He took no interest in what was happening in the country. The country was living through hard and tragic times. In various regions thousands of people were dying of hunger and of epidemics; in times of war the Russian people bled rivers of blood and suffered great defeats, and he — the Tsar of the land — remained indifferent to it all. He had only himself and his family in mind... he thought about cruises on yachts and about passing his time merrily. To everything that did not touch him personally he remained cold. Being occupied with matters of state was for him the greatest torment, and on that evening — while he waited for Rasputin to come and stop the heir's suffering — he was entirely incapable of attending to his official "work" of looking through and signing various documents and orders.

Outwardly he kept calm, so as to soothe the Tsarina as much as possible, but inside him there was unrest. He too was very impatient, waiting for Rasputin. Everything Vyrubova had told about the wonderful muzhik who had volunteered to cure Alexei had left a strong impression on the Tsar. Where was he, then, this wonderful man? Why was he not here yet? Anna had promised, after all, to come with him at about nine o'clock...

Every minute dragged on for the Tsar and the Tsarina as long as an hour. The Tsarina was very nervous!

"Where is he? Why isn't he coming?" she kept exclaiming in fear.
"He will probably arrive soon," the Tsar answered.
"But it's already past nine!"
"He will probably be here soon."

"Oh, if only he would come!... If only he would come!" — the Tsarina wrung the fingers of her hands in agitation.

The Tsar rose from his seat, went over to the Tsarina, laid his hand on her shoulder and said in a seemingly calm voice:

"Calm yourself, Alix dear... He will come... Be calm."

Suddenly the door flew open all at once, as if torn open by the wind, and Grigori Yefimovich, the Siberian muzhik, appeared. With his heavy boots he strode over the threshold and, without the slightest embarrassment, walked into the Tsar's study and stood still. He was dressed in a long black "kaftan". His big beard was dishevelled, the hair on his head — uncombed, and he looked around with a yawning gaze.

After him came Vyrubova, her face beaming, and after them came Vishnyakova, who had led them in through the side entrance.

Vishnyakova was surprised and bewildered by Rasputin's appearance and by his having opened the door so hastily without knocking first. She stood with her hands folded on her breast, her eyes wide open and her mouth half open. She was so bewildered that at that moment she forgot she was in the presence of the Tsar and the Tsarina.
For a while silence reigned...
(To be continued.)
Livelihoods... (From a matchmaker's archive)

[Humorous feuilleton — matchmakers' letters.]
(From a matchmaker's archive).
By Y. Weinstein [J. Weinsztajn].

1.
My esteemed friend, Reb Osher Chaim!
How are you? Well, as for me, things go as they wouldn't go for a cripple even in a dream... If all clocks ran like this, the watchmakers would have grown rich like Korah before the crisis... But praised be the Blessed Name, we have not yet lost our little scrap of hope.
Listen then, my friend, to what I want to propose to you here.
I have a pair here, i.e. a young man and a maiden, who both want to marry, but each separately, i.e. the young man wants a different girl, not the one I have on my list, and she, likewise, also wants a different young man...
Perhaps it would be only fair for you to join as a partner in the business, and we'd marry the two of them off and earn a few złoty.
She is a very fine child...
Firstly, she is no older than 28 (by the new calendar) and already has almost more than half a head of grey hair... (you surely know that nowadays grey hair is very much in fashion)... Secondly, she has a certificate from which it can be seen that already 10 years ago... her brother finished the gymnasium, and now he is already, it seems, somewhere an engineer or a doctor, God spare us...
As for beauty... I have no interest in it, of course, but I must tell you the truth: "none that go unto her return again" — whoever just comes into her home and sees her mother no longer wants to leave so quickly... Well, and about pedigree I need hardly tell you... a brother an engineer, a father — a former millionaire, the mother descends even from near Pińczów... In short, she is no simple girl..
As for wisdom, you can rely on me... let that be the only obstacle...
About the young man I shall write in the second letter... Let us first finish with the girl...
From me: Shmuel Itzi.

2.
My friend Reb Shmuel Itzi!
Your letter I have received... It is simply a matter of Providence, I tell you. Because just when you came with your maiden, a young man came my way — a real gem... It will be a match made in heaven.
He is a very great Hebraist.. speaks the Holy Tongue like water, so that I understand one word in ten...
Besides that [printed "chutz lia"] he is a wizard at Sholem Aleichem... when he reads a Sholem Aleichem piece one could burst with laughter...
But all this is still nothing... In today's times, you know, one wants above all to provide a child with a livelihood... So he, the young man in question, is provided for in that respect too for all his years, because he is one of the greatest singers in our little town.. He possesses a voice that melts into all your limbs... And then his [?] sweetness, his trills... Just 2 years ago a famous cantor wanted to take him along to America, but because of the quota both of them [?], the cantor as well as he, had to stay here...
As for education, there is no need to drag it out: firstly he finished the evening courses, and secondly he very nearly passed the "examination", had there not been a little hitch — his elder sister was, God spare you, suddenly left an agunah [a "chained" wife], and he had to provide her with bread...
He is not looking for a big dowry... It may be only ten thousand dollars, as long as the capital is real capital.
Yes, about your young man you are keeping something quiet, and it is precisely he who would be very useful to me here.
From me: Osher Chaim.

3.
My friend, Reb Osher-Chaim!
I see [?] that we shall, God willing, eat fat kneidlach... One only has to put one's shoulder to it, as they say, and a speck of luck should play into our hands.
I have talked it over with the maiden's father and it is on a good path, i.e. he consents to the match, but he sets a condition that the groom must not be a cantor. Because cantors, he says, he already has enough of in his family... they all stick in his seventh rib. When a holiday comes round, or just a little celebration, they start showing off their tricks, so that one has to run away from the house... And besides, he simply doesn't like this profession, because a cantor must always be afraid of catching cold, and precisely in summer, when [?] it is warm and one catches cold less, they don't pray then, the cantors...
And I will reveal to you another secret: the maiden's father was himself once a cantor, so he knows well that cantors are all (except perhaps the clever ones) great fools... Ah, how can he say that about himself? Well, he really did stop being a cantor...
In short, the match will go through; you only need to see to it that the cantor stops being a cantor... Let him be whatever he likes: a merchant, a bankrupt, a teacher, a card-player, a shopkeeper, only not a cantor... What does it matter to you anyway?
As for the dowry, you may tell him, that Hebraist of yours, that nowadays dollars don't lie about in the street... Even pawning has become hard lately... The main thing, after all, is the capital, and precisely about that he may rest easy... Even at sixty he won't regret the match...
From me: Shmuel-Itzi.

4.
My friend, Reb Shmuel-Itzi!
I see [?] you are a stubborn Jew? Several times already I have asked you to write to me at length about your young man, and you keep pushing the maiden on me... "Were there no graves in Egypt?" [printed garbled]? You take me, apparently, for a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor? So what, do you really think that your maiden, who in your opinion is no older than 28 and has a pretty mother with an educated brother, will take all the local young men by surprise?
No, my friend, "keep the goods for yourself" — the girl you may sell off even with the Passover chametz; and your young man, if he is any good at all, you can give to me, and we'll sugar-coat him somehow...
You see? For him I have a bride [?] here — one of a kind... pretty, educated, clever, [?] ["baleon"], a wondrous creature...
True, she is a little hard of hearing, that is, hear she does, but whoever talks to her has to shout a little; but all that is nothing at all... The deaf live longer than the hearing... And besides, a [local?/young?] professor has thought up a means by which the deaf will hear even better than those who aren't deaf.
On the other hand, she descends from genuine pedigree: nothing but rabbis, ritual slaughterers, rabbinical judges and the like...
True, her brother-in-law is a bit of a — one might say — scoundrel [?]; he was badly caught in that affair, but who nowadays can vouch for a brother-in-law?
In short, drag your young man over here, I'll take on my maiden, and with the help of the Blessed Name we'll pull it off...
From me: Osher-Chaim.

5.
My friend, Reb Osher-Chaim!
You've missed the mark...
I am a good judge of matchmakers like you...
You have such a maiden as you describe just as much as I now have [provisions] for Shabbat and for after Shabbat... But what then? You think, apparently, that you've caught some little snail and will turn his head... Know then that I have no wish to do business with you, so leave me alone... Bargains like yours I can get at any time.
From me, who asks you to write no more: Shmuel-Itzi.
Cantor Żupowicz's Claim before the Sosnowiec District Court

[Będzin — kehilla; court.] As our readers know, the Będzin cantor Mr. Żupowicz [?] has submitted to the district court in Sosnowiec his claim against the kehilla board, for a sum of 8 thousand złoty.
Last Monday the case came up for the first time. No witnesses are summoned to the first "procedure"; only the interested parties appear, and the court proposes a settlement to them.
On behalf of Mr. Żupowicz appeared attorney Kowalski, — on behalf of the kehilla — attorney Teitelbaum.
Attorney Kowalski presents the contract which the kehilla board signed at the time with Cantor Żupowicz, and supports the money claim with it.
Against this argument attorney Teitelbaum speaks out, relying on the first notice-of-dismissal date which the board gave Mr. Żupowicz; and if — says Mr. Teitelbaum — Mr. Żupowicz went on performing his office, he did so "without the consent of the community"...
Since the two parties do not agree to any settlement, it was decided to summon the witnesses named, and the case is postponed to a second hearing date.
Good Prospects for Jewish Workers to Get Work

[Będzin — economy; employment.] This week we received a report that at Fürstenberg's zinc works the Jewish workers who were laid off at the beginning of winter are being taken back.
On the strength of this report the writer of these lines turned to the president of the zinc works, Mr. Fürstenberg, with the question whether the report corresponds to reality, and whether it is not possible to employ more Jewish workers, who are starving together with their wives and children.
To this Mr. Fürstenberg declared that first of all the laid-off Jewish workers have been taken back, but in the near future 160 new workers are to be taken on.
We therefore point out that manual [?] workers, married [?], who have several children should report immediately after reading this notice at Fürstenberg's zinc works in order to be taken on for work.
A Fire at the Małobądz Power Station

[Będzin area — fire.] On Sunday evening a fire broke out, from an unknown cause, in the power station (elektrownia) at Małobądz. Firemen from the neighbouring towns and also from the "Mysłowice" [?] steelworks (huta) were called to the fire.
The damage from the fire is not great.
On the Hygienic Conditions of School Youth When Bathing

[Będzin — municipality; health.] In connection with the notice in the previous issue of our paper under the title "How the Magistrate takes care of the hygiene of the school youth", we have received the following from the head (kierownik) of the Health Department, Dr. Wasserzweig:
1) the traffic of sick people in the Health Department is only in the morning hours; 2) the schoolchildren bathe in the afternoon hours, i.e. from 1 to 5 p.m.; 3) the premises where the children bathe are separated from the premises where the sick stay; and 4) the bathroom is intended only for schoolchildren.
Passover — A Great Gymnastics Festival of "Hakoach"

[Będzin — sport.] On Sunday, the 2nd day of Chol Hamoed, the local "Hakoach" is arranging a great gymnastics festival, in which all the women's and men's groups will take part; also, for the first time in Będzin, various gymnastic exercises and rhythmic dances will be performed by children aged 4—5 years.
The technical committee is taking every measure so that the gymnastics festival will be imposing. On the day of the festival there will also be a march through the town with the orchestra at its head.
The Activity of the Delegate of the "Yachin" Society

[Będzin — Zionism; settlement.] The delegate Mr. Y. D. Beth-Halevy has succeeded in interesting a number of respected persons of our town in middle-class colonization. A plan has arisen to create in this very colony a group of Będzin Jews, who will settle in and live together as neighbours.
In the next few days a consultation of the group will take place.
The delegate is soon concluding his activity in Zagłębie.
A detailed treatise on the significance of "Yachin" — in the Passover-eve issue.
The Municipal Bathhouse before the Holiday

[Będzin — municipality.] We are asked by the Magistrate to announce that on account of the holiday the municipal bathhouse will be open on Monday and Tuesday from 2 p.m. to 10 p.m., and on Wednesday, the eve of Passover, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
—o—
Theft in a Cooperative
[Będzin — crime.] In the night from Wednesday to Thursday a theft was committed in the cooperative on Kościuszko Street. The damage amounts to about 3 thousand złoty.
—o—
Buried Alive
[Będzin — accident.] The 62-year-old Kuchciński, while working at his building on 1 May Street, a wall collapsed and buried the house-owner. When he was found [?] later, he was already dead.
—o—
He "Treated" His Bride to a Knife
[Będzin — crime.] Teofil Gruszanek, while out walking with his bride (fiancée), came to a sharp [?] exchange of words with her, during which the bridegroom seriously wounded his bride with a knife; she was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
To Spite the Wife..

[Będzin — accident; suicide attempt.] The sewage-cart driver [?] Twardowski, having no domestic peace, drank a hefty portion of vinegar essence; in a serious condition the would-be suicide was taken to hospital.
Sensational Arrest of an Engineer

[Zagłębie — espionage, arrest.]
The charge is espionage.
The investigative authorities (security police) recently got on the track of economic espionage being conducted for the benefit of a neighbouring state. The aim of the espionage was to cause damage to industry in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia.
After careful observation, the engineer Paks [?], who is suspected of the espionage, was arrested in Ząbkowice.
After questioning, engineer Paks was sent to Warsaw, where the authorities placed him in Mokotów prison.
Sosnowiec — The Kehilla Budget to Be Approved Without the Consent of the Dozorcy

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, budget.]
Because of the situation that has arisen in the kehilla [of Sosnowiec] concerning the new budget, which to this day has not been approved by the dozorcy [members of the kehilla board], the opinion has been put forward that the budget should be approved without the consent of the dozorcy, within the framework of last year's budget.
The Attackers of Kalman Fuks Sentenced to 18 Months in Prison

[Sosnowiec — robbery and trial.]
On the evening of 22 December (grudzień) 1931 two bandits broke into the flat of Mr. Kalman Fuks, where, under the threat of revolvers, they robbed him of 700 zł. and bills of exchange worth 400 zł.
Thanks to the physical [?] resistance of Mr. Fuks the bandits were caught, and last Saturday they stood before the local district court, which sentenced them to 1½ years in prison.
For Running Over a Child to Death — a 100-Złoty Fine

[Będzin — accident and trial.]
Last summer, while the Pfeffer family of Będzin was staying at a summer residence in Siewierz [?], the 3-year-old Pfeffer was run over and died a few hours later.
This week the carter stood before the local district court, which sentenced him to pay 100 zł. or 10 days' arrest.
The Board of the "Maccabi" Football Section

[Sosnowiec — sport, "Maccabi".]
The football section at "Maccabi" was recently reorganised, and a new board was elected, consisting of the following persons:
Alek Herzberg (kierownik — head), Avraham Triger (1st vice-head), Shlomo Majerszajn [?] (2nd vice-head), Rotensztajn (secretary), Shimon Tajtelbaum (treasurer), Avraham Ziskind, Yaakov Rakowski, Zanwil Finsztok [?] and Yosef Piekarski.
The board is carrying out very intensive work.
Regional Conference of the Revisionists in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, Revisionists.]
The regional committee (Va'ad HaGlili) of Brit HaTzohar [Union of Zionist Revisionists] in Sosnowiec has sent the following circular to all branches of Brit HaTzohar, Betar and Masada in the Kielce voivodeship:
In accordance with the resolution of the 5th All-Polish Conference, the Central Committee is organising regional conferences whose aim is to strengthen Revisionist activity and enlarge the ranks, as well as to create close contact for cooperation among all Revisionist branches. By decision of the Main Committee the conference has been set for 24 April, i.e. Sunday, the 2nd day of Chol HaMoed Pesach.
At this conference, besides various current questions, lectures will be held on: the situation of Jewry in Eretz Israel and in Poland, the situation in Revisionism, Keren Kayemet, Keren Tel-Hai, Keren Hayesod, youth problems, "Brit Ivrit Olamit", the transfer (resettlement) cooperative, Totzeret Ha'aretz, the Zionist women's movement, the work in the city councils and in the kehillot.
The regional committee, which will be created, will have to organise all branches in the Kielce voivodeship in order to carry out the above-mentioned tasks.
As the secretariat of the conference informs us, over 30 delegates from 20 towns have already registered.
According to expectations, over 70 delegates will take part in the conference. On behalf of the Central Committee (C.C.) the following will take part: the president of the Jewish academics, Adv. Elchanan Lewin, Dr. Y. Drolicz [?], Miss stud. Shulamit Drolicz and Y. Bielebrow [?].
—o—
"Herzl and His World-View"
On this topic [?] Mr. Yehuda Kruk will give a lecture this Saturday afternoon in the premises of the local Betar.
Dąbrowa — City Council Meeting / In May Work on the New Post Office Building Is to Begin / A "Shul-Kult" Committee Formed / A 14-Year-Old Girl Raped / The "Mining School" to Be Moved to Katowice

[Dąbrowa — municipality; post office; education; crime.]
On Monday the continuation of Saturday's city council meeting [in Dąbrowa Górnicza] took place. At this meeting there was already a quorum, and the magistrate [town administration] was given authorisation for a short-term loan of 100 thousand zł.
At the meeting an interpellation was submitted on the question of hastening to obtain the concession for an own electric power station.
In connection with this it was decided that the president [mayor] Madejski [?] together with the members of the presidium should intervene at the Ministry of the Interior.
—o—
In May work on the new post office building is to begin.
The question of building a post office is moving forward. The new post office building will stand at the corner of Sobieska and Kościuszki streets. The first floor will be occupied by the post office, and on the ground floor there will be private shops. The cost of the building, amounting to 350 thousand zł., is covered by the Ministry of Posts.
This week the agreement between the applicants for the private shops and the town administration was signed at the magistrate.
Work on the shops is to begin as early as May.
—o—
A "Shul-Kult" committee formed
In connection with the financial campaign proclaimed by the "Shul-Kult" central office [Yiddish school and culture organisation] and the forthcoming first All-Polish conference of Shul-Kult branches, which is to take place in the coming months, a local committee has been formed at the Poalei Zion party, consisting of comrades Tenenbaum, Kożuch, Wajsalc [?], Knobler and Bras.
The committee has set about active work.
—o—
A 14-year-old girl raped.
The 30-year-old worker Krawczyk raped his servant girl, aged 14. The scoundrel has been handed over to the investigative authorities.
—o—
The "Mining School" to be moved to Katowice
The central authorities have worked out a plan for the local "Mining School" (Szkoła Górnicza) to be moved to Katowice. The plan has aroused bitterness, and it was decided that the magistrate together with all public institutions should use every means so that the plan to move the school is not carried out.
Historic meeting of hundreds of Zagłębie activists in Katowice.

[Zagłębie — Zionism; Katowice.] In the very near future a festive academy and meeting of hundreds of activists from Zagłębie and Western Galicia will take place in Katowice, in honour of the 50th jubilee of "Hibbat Zion" and of the first conference of the "Hovevei Zion" in Katowice.
—o—
The preparations for the district conference in Będzin.
As has been announced, on the 24th of this month (the 2nd day of Hol ha-Moed Pesach) a conference of the Zionist associations of the Będzin–Częstochowa district will take place. In all the localities the conference covers, the Central Committee's representative, comrade Natan Asz, is completing the campaign of registering and recruiting members for the year 1952 [?] (active and passive voting rights will be held only by holders of membership cards for the year 1932, issued by the Zionist Central Committee).
The youth, organised in "Herzliya" and "Ha-Shomer ha-Leumi", is also taking an active part in the registration and recruitment campaign.
The conference will hear lectures on the situation in Zionism, on the situation of the Jews in Poland, on kehilla affairs in the city council [sic], on youth questions, etc. The festive opening of the conference will take place on Sunday the 24th of this month at 12 noon.
—o—
Sensational trial before the district court in Sosnowiec.
On the 20th of this month the sensational trial concerning the murdered estate owner Stecki, near Skała, will take place at the Sosnowiec district court.
In the dock sits the former police commandant in Skała, who is accused of having conducted the investigation to the bandits' advantage.
—o—
Peasant from Sławków swindled out of 1000 francs.
Mr. Stryk of Sławków came to Sosnowiec to exchange 1000 French francs for Polish złoty.
In the corridor of the "Bank Zagłębie" Stryk met an unknown person who struck up a friendly conversation with him. In a short time their friendship went so far that Stryk handed his chance friend the francs to exchange.
Soon the "friend" came back and handed Stryk a full envelope, telling him that the złoty were in the envelope.
When the "przyjaciel" [?] (friend) had gone, Stryk saw that instead of złoty he had an envelope with scraps of newspaper...
—o—
Jewish university students to Jewish society
The "Ognisko" of the Jewish university students in Kraków has proclaimed a "Help Week" for the Jewish student youth, beginning on the 10th of this month.
The same appeal is also addressed to Jewish society in Zagłębie. It is to be hoped that the appeal will not remain a voice crying in the wilderness, and that the Jewish students, who suffer so much as Jews, will be supported in this campaign.
—o—

Today, Friday, "The White Lady".
Saturday the 16th, "A trug [?] oyf a meydl".
In German:
Sunday and Monday "Faust". Monday the 25th, "Grand Hotel".

Appeal against the election of the Będzin kehilla presidium rejected

As is known, a few weeks ago the new presidium of the Będzin kehilla administration was elected with 6[?] Agudah votes. D. Skopilas[?] was elected president and B. Banawert[?] vice-president.
The other factions lodged an appeal, in which they pointed to several illegalities in the elections that had taken place.
This week the community (gmina) received a reply from the starosta, who announces that the appeal against the elections has been rejected by him.
—o—
Hitler's visit to Beuthen.
A mass meeting took place in Beuthen [Bytom], at which the well-known Hitler spoke. Several hours before the meeting began, thousands of people had already [—] gathered on the station square[?]. Up to 10 marks were paid for a ticket to Hitler's lecture. Hitler spoke for about 20 minutes. He ended his speech by telling his listeners that „one must fight until victory“.
—o—
Jewish soldiers in Żory[?] will not be released for Pesach.
This week the Będzin kehilla administration received word from the colonel (pułkownik) that the young Jewish soldiers serving in Żory will not be released for Pesach this year.
In this connection Messrs. Goldsztajn and Bogusz-kaski[?] were delegated to the Katowice kehilla, so that the soldiers who were not released would be provided with Passover food.
The Katowice kehilla accepted the proposal, on condition that the expenses for the food be borne by the Będzin kehilla.
The younger soldiers who[?] serve in Będzin received permission to be in the town under the supervision of an escort.
—o—
From Brit HaTzohar in Dąbrowa.
On Monday, the third day of Chol HaMoed Pesach, „Brit HaTzohar“ [Zionist Revisionists] in Dąbrowa is arranging a festive academy in the hall of the Artisans' Association, dedicated to the 50th jubilee of the poet Dr. Jacob Cohen.
Lectures on the topic „Jacob Cohen, his life and work“ will be given by advocate Elchanan Lewin, Dr. Drolicz, Mrs. Shulamit Drolicz and Y. Klerman.
—o—
They tried their „luck“ in Kraków.
The police in Kraków arrested several Christian youths from Będzin who had intended to commit thefts in shops in Kraków.
—o—
„Oneg Shabbat“ at the „Tze'irei Mizrachi“ in Sosnowiec
The Sosnowiec „Tze'irei Mizrachi“ has set about active work. During the holidays a series of lectures on national topics will take place.
Next Shabbat the opening of the „Oneg Shabbat“ will take place with the participation of Rabbi Menachem Hager.
—o—
The municipal subsidies fixed for 1931 are to be cut in 1932.
On Monday evening a meeting of the Będzin council of commissioners was held. The main point of the meeting was the magistrate's proposal to cut by 25 percent the subsidies approved in the 1931 budget.
The total sum of the subsidies amounts to 26 thousand zł. Of this sum about 11 thousand zł. have already been paid out to various institutions (not Jewish)...
Councillors Hapel and Rechnitz[?] opposed the magistrate's proposal, arguing that the proposal should have applied to all institutions and societies, „but we cannot agree — they said — to adopt now a decision from which only those institutions will suffer which to this day have not received the sums allotted to them“.
A lengthy discussion arose over this, and the result was that it was decided that the voivode should decide the matter.

A Maidservant Wounds Her Mistress with a Knife.
In the dock of the Katowice district court sat the servant Sokołowska, who out of revenge threw herself at her employer with a knife and seriously wounded her.
Sokołowska was sentenced to half a year in prison.

Conferences on the Situation in Upper Silesian Industry.
In connection with the situation of industry in the Upper Silesian area, the head of the industry department in the Ministry of Commerce, Eng. Lewandowski, came to Katowice and, together with the chief labour inspector Mr. Klat, held conferences on the tense situation.

2 Years in Prison for Killing His Own Wife.
The district court in Königshütte [Chorzów] heard the trial of the 22-year-old hairdresser Hartwig, who killed his 19-year-old wife.
The murderous husband declared before the court that domestic peace in his home had been disturbed after his wife gave birth to their first child; from that moment on — he says — she refused to do housework, so that after his hard working day he had to wash laundry, cook, etc. Because of this there were frequent quarrels, especially when he found out that his wife was also unfaithful to him, which led him to murder her with an axe.
The murderous husband was sentenced to 2 years in prison.

To all friends of the Jewish school and culture in Będzin.

Under very hard conditions it became necessary to build the school and culture association "Szul-Kult" in Poland. The severe economic crisis threw the Jewish masses into apathy and indifference towards the most spiritual cultural tasks of Jewish national life, and cleared the way for assimilation and ignorance (am-haaratzut). The attempt to ligvern[?] the cultural assets in Jewish popular life ran up against a wall of indifference and apathy. And yet, despite all the obstacles and difficulties that "Szul-Kult" has met on its way, one can state with satisfaction that during the short time the association has existed it has managed to accomplish important, substantial work. More than 50 schools and children's homes have been founded; central libraries, reading rooms, evening schools, people's universities and other cultural and educational institutions are affiliated to the "Szul-Kult" association.
They never took lightly the great and heavy burden they assumed when setting out[?] to build the movement, but, imbued with a deep sense of responsibility for the fate of Jewish national survival, they carried within them the belief that however hard the work might be, the Jewish masses would find the ways to defend the positions of their national struggle.
And indeed thousands of parents and friends of the Jewish cultural movement have constantly helped in the hard work, and only thanks to the devoted and self-sacrificing work of Jewish teachers, parents and school activists was it possible to erect the great cultural edifice that links thousands of Jewish children with the treasures of Jewish cultural creation.
The severe economic crisis, which is shattering Jewish life and day by day undermining the existence of thousands of Jewish families, has hit the Szul-Kult institutions very hard. The poverty of the parents whose children attend[?] the schools has taken from them the ability to pay tuition fees. The kehillot and municipal councils have struck out their subsidies or reduced them to a minimum. Without help from abroad, and given the state's indifferent attitude to the cultural needs of the Jewish working and popular masses, the institutions' existence is threatened.
We therefore turn, in the present difficult hour for the movement, to all Będzin friends of the Jewish school and culture:
Do not let the Jewish cultural positions, built with so many sacrifices and such self-sacrifice, fall!
Będzin, warm-hearted Będzin, which always helps worthily in various campaigns, will not lag behind this time either, and for the first time in our town will help in the rescue campaign for the Jewish school and culture!
Strengthen and consolidate the Jewish secular national cultural edifice!
Carry out the "Szul-Kult" campaign!
Organizing Committee of "Szul-Kult" in Będzin.
