Elijah's Cup

[Passover — essay; reflection.] By A. Gotesdiner
Of all the 18 [?] prophets the Jewish people possesses, none has merited the honour on the Seder nights — the two most beautiful nights the Jewish people possesses — but Elijah: the non-literary prophet, the mysterious man of the desert, who arrives in his fur and leather girdle, with his long hair and his club [?], like a living piece of desert in the beautiful streets of Samaria. No one knows where he comes from. One can tell that he comes from afar, from very far, from an entirely different world and an entirely different time. He does not bow to "Baal," does not kiss "Ashtoreth," he does not see the spires of the tall palaces, the cloud-scrapers of Samaria, he does not gape at the fine shop windows of the big city, he does not smile when he sees Ahab's horsemen performing tricks on their military horses — in his heart a fire glows, flames shoot from his eyes, and when a Samarian couple meets him on their stroll, the hot blood freezes in their veins. Not to them has he come; he has come to the very top of society, to the priests and to the king. Not to warn has he come, like his colleagues, like other prophets, but to punish — to punish injustice and sin, with hunger and want, with the ruin of death. No rain and no dew falls any more on the fields of Samaria. At Elijah's word the earth dries up, and plants and people. Ahab's strongest soldiers are burned to coal and vanish.
Ashtoreth, the goddess of fertility, has not even once in her Jewish kingdom so much green grass as would suffice for a wreath around her head. She loses all her worshippers. Only her priests remain to her, who live off her.
Now it is not the prophet who seeks the king, but the king who seeks the prophet; he seeks him in all the lands and among all tongues.
But it is not the king's envoys, not his detectives who bring the prophet — he comes of himself at a divine call; misfortune has made the king's heart soft and wide, and the prophet can now sow God's word there.
But the priests of "Baal" stand and laugh. Our god — they say — bestows strength and might, power and wealth; Elijah's brings want and hunger. And Elijah demands a trial.
It turns out bloody for the priests of Baal. The only time in the activity of our prophets that it comes to bloodshed.
[But?] the impression is a great one, an eternal one — not only on the king, but indeed also on the prophet. The king becomes more pious, the prophet becomes softer [?]; his heart fills with compassion, his gaze carries a ray of the spring sun, his word brings only consolation and good tidings. Now he hears God's word not from the fire, not from the storm, but from the quiet, secret-of-secrets whisper of the breeze.
He will one day come again to his people, but for a different mission — not hunger, not want will he announce; not fire, not water will he bring. He will come — to still the storm in the hearts of fathers toward children and of children toward fathers; he will come as the herald of the great day.
And Jews sit on the "Night of Watching" and listen for his steps. A cup stands ready for him. He comes from a far, far road — we open the door for him:
— Come, Elijah the Prophet, and announce the tidings of the great day, of eternal peace — which shall reign even between fathers and children; we all look out for you, fathers and children alike — come!
But Elijah does not come. He does not come, because through the door that is opened for him gentiles burst in to search for blood among the Jews; he does not come, because there, beneath the door, they stand with a sack, with a corpse that they themselves murdered, in order to plant it on the Jews. He does not come, because people mock "Kol dichfin" ["Let all who are hungry"]; he does not come, because people mock "Next year in the Land of Israel." He does not come, because the whole world keeps fulfilling our "Pour out Thy wrath"!
Yes, we composed the prayer, but with the prayer we discharged our duty; others composed prayers like white doves, but they discharged their duty with poison gases. We too tell of liberations, of the Exodus from Egypt, but in our war of liberation we never fired a single bullet. Not at the redemption from Egypt, not at the redemption from Babylon. We only keep our "Night of Watching," we only listen for the steps of Elijah. We pour him the cup.
Ready on our table stands the cup for him, flung wide open before him stands our door, we all look out for him — if only others do not block the way, and he will come.
A Great Invalid Is to Be Found in the World.

[Essay — reflections; the world crisis and antisemitism.]
In times of crisis, when the organism of society in the human world begins to feel not quite itself, all sorts of unhealthy and unsightly spots begin to appear on the surface, on the skin of the social body; some portents and signs of the most internal disorder — then the "doctors", the politicians, the leaders of the human world-community, also become busy: they search, they examine, they hold all kinds of "consiliums", they try to guess and mostly make mistakes; they put forward hypotheses and promptly deny them — in a word, things become "lively and merry" around the great apathy and "depression" that has seized the world, and they look for stratagems how to save the world before the illness takes on serious forms, before the established form of life bursts out and over into — formlessness.
In such times everyone feels that some great invalid is to be found in the world, that some illness is eating into it. Or it has long since eaten into it and now breaks out in signs of plagues, troubles and leprous sores. That the world is not healthy is a "well-known thing"... Evolutionists, however, believe that it, the world, is still only a child, and — a child is exposed to all sorts of illnesses and ailments. True, one must not keep silent, one must rescue, and those who regard themselves as the father and mother of the world indeed do not keep silent in this matter; nights go sleepless, Psalms are recited... spells are muttered and all sorts of charms are "performed". Yes, when one looks at the sort of "ratunek" [Polish: rescue] with which the leaders of the world, its doctors, rescue it, one must agree with the evolutionists that we are still at the very earliest childhood of mankind, and to heal the child's illnesses we still use incantations and old wives' remedies.
At a time when death has become for us such a highly civilised general, when it has become through and through the symbol of the highest achievement of civilisation — and the militarists will have to agree with me that they, exactly like me, a thoroughgoing pacifist, see, in my imagination, death hung and decked[?] with the highest decorations that a military "thinker" could ever devise; and at the very same time of such a civilised exaltation of death, life still goes about, more than three parts of it, torn and swallowed up, for even from the beautifully furnished dwellings into which the dwellers in darkness, yesterday's poor of the "low" residence, have moved, hungry children's eyes peer out, and father and mother look for buyers for the beautiful piano they bought in the good times for the child who showed musical talent.
On the one side life suffers from over-sugaring, from a surfeit of sweetness and well-being (nature's revenge), and honey and milk, so that the blood begins to turn into — sweet water, into syrup; on the other side half the body of the world wastes away; the blood turns into water, into bitter, gall-filled water; this half of the body dries up and weakens from lack of blood, while the other half of the body bursts with a surplus of blood, becomes so heavy of itself and is sick from causes opposite to those from which the first half of the world-body suffers, and —
The doctors?
The doctors experiment, every moment, with another, a new instrument, with other medicines and above all with — incantations. The greatest wonder is how today's diplomats have taken over the methods of the spell-casters of old. It is almost astonishing how the whole of world politics is transformed overnight into that legendary forest hut among tall, dark oaks, and there, when one gets there, by seven-times-seven twisted and crooked roads and paths, until one climbs up the last seven stepped little paths leading up to the hut, where the sorceress of diplomacy sits by her "eywele"[?] [perhaps: little stove] and ponders — how to save the world —
And the air is full of the smells of illness, of medicine bottles, of powders, dust, etc. And among the symptoms of disease on the body of the world there grows, plague upon plague, also the ugly, loathsome blister of antisemitism. This [?] "growth" spreads around itself a terrible, musty stench; country after country becomes "intoxicated" by its loathsome smell, and the air in the world grows tight for us, we do not know where to turn, and above all it makes itself felt there, in those places where the "spirit", culture, had settled, and where we, in our rootlessness, saved ourselves into these cities of refuge of the spirit; we become confused and lose ourselves, and in our great bewilderment we do things perversely, often clumsily, out of our fear and inferiority complex, and perhaps only for frightening, dark and despairing reasons, we begin to seek back-ways into the world; we crawl with bowed faces and bowed spirits through the cracks of "leber"[?], like creatures of the night in the locked palaces of the enemy.
Perhaps it is put too bitterly, but it is very hard to watch how, among all the sores that grow in a time of crisis, the ugly "scab" breaks out on [printed: "and"] our own body; the plague of: Jews without — Jews. One no longer even speaks of "Jewishness without Jewishness". That is already a normal ailment among us, with which half a peace has already been made. The trouble with the Jews who seek by every means to distance themselves from their own is still, for the time being, fresh and bleeding, and it stings the eyes all the more when it comes at a time when the gentile casts it off from us with a deep grimace of disgust.
J. Sigal.
Sholem Asch on the Jewish School.

[Education — the Jewish school; "Shul-Kult".]
The old Jewish school preserved us through the past; the new, modern Jewish school is the only guarantee for our future. Without touching on the existence of other school systems, which each part of the Jewish population creates for itself according to its spirit and conscience, I find that the type of school which "Shul-Kult" [Szul-Kult — a network of bilingual Yiddish-Hebrew Jewish schools in Poland] has created is capable of educating worthy Jewish people, who will be prepared for the hard struggle that lies before them in life, both as human beings and as Jews.
I hereby call on all Jewish-minded and right-thinking people that, as long as we have not won our just struggle for the Jewish school from the government, whose duty it is to maintain the Jewish school system, — to support the schools of "Shul-Kult" and to put shoulder and hand to the honest and holy efforts being made by the builders of the Jewish schools.
Sholem Asch.
Faith (from the series of folk legends: "Once Upon a Time in Poland")

[Literature — a folk legend from the series "Once Upon a Time in Poland"; by Yehuda Yafet.]
Why he, Moshe, found such favour with the poritz [the Polish landowner] — he himself does not know. A thorough villain, yet to his Moszke he is so kind, so good. His whole livelihood, after all, comes from him. Go and understand the whims of a poritz! Just as he has fallen in love with a monkey, on which he spends hundreds of rendlach [gold coins]...
What is more: he never dares to make sport of his Moszke. How could he? A poritz gives Moszke fine rendlach week after week, and would never once "invite" him to dance a bear-dance at a court ball? He, Moszke, can sing so beautifully, his prayers [?] are so heartfelt, and he would sing a "Ma Yafit" so nicely! And as for dancing — he dances in exemplary fashion!
It may be that the poritz, too, more than once had it in mind to invite his Moszke to a bear-dance, but when he glanced into his eyes, into his Jewish-sad yet at the same time free, courtly [?] eyes, his desire melted away [?]... The weak-charactered poritz more than once felt himself mastered and enslaved by Moshe's somehow superhuman looks.
Moshe lived only off the poritz, off the rendlach that he gave him from time to time. But Moshe did not bow himself double [?], he did not kneel and did not lick his bread-giver. When the poritz handed him something, he took it, and at the same time made a face as though he were doing him, the poritz, a favour by consenting to take alms from him... And the poritz felt it, flared up [?] a little in his heart, and — went on giving.
Moshe also had an official occupation: he went around the villages buying up small hides [?] and hares from the gentiles. This occupation brought him no income at all. But a man must do something, and the poritz should not think that without him he would have died of hunger...
Moshe loved this occupation of his. Ah, how good it is in summer to stride along the roads from village to village. As soon as the morning star rises, Moshe takes his sack over his shoulders, puts in his tallis and tefillin, and — off on his way. A new day is born. The sky takes on a fresh, reddish face. Birds rise with song, twittering; a juicy freshness is poured out over everything, and Moshe takes out his little book of Psalms. Ah, his dear, beloved little Psalter! Yes, it was no different: King David, too, composed his Psalms when on summer mornings he wandered over roads and fields grazing his sheep, just as he, Moshe, wanders now. On such mornings there sang within him:
"The pastures of the wilderness drip,
and the hills gird themselves with joy...
and the valleys are covered with corn;
they shout for joy, they also sing..."
[Psalm 65:13–14, in Hebrew in the original]
Coming home in the evening, Moshe is mostly empty-handed. He was more filled with divine song than minded to trade in anything. But he did not come back sad. Livelihood! — the crazy poritz will surely send him something. He will surely send him a few rendlach through his lackey. And here is such a glorious night! Ah, he feels the divine stillness, the stillness of eternity, of a deep [?] everlastingness. The pale moon, dotted with so many little stars, goes ahead of him, and in his mind lofty [?] thoughts are woven, conversations from the Zohar and other holy books.
* * *
One spring evening, at night. The poritz drives out for a ride with a guest. From afar Moshe's figure stands out, his staff thrust forward and his little sack hanging below. The poritz shows his friend his Moszke, who is not at all like all the other Moszkes — a bent shoulder, true, but still no dog, and that is why he loves him and showers him with rendlach. The poritz relates that his Moszke is a real rabbi, an "uczony Żyd" [Polish: a learned Jew], and in order to show off to his friend how much good he does for his Moszke, he stops him as he passes and asks him:
"Moszke, when will your Passover be?"
"In a week, Your Excellency."
"Do you already have [what you need] for Passover?"
The poritz believed that Moszke would answer: "Surely the gracious lord will deign to give me for Passover, as every year" — he wanted such an answer to come in his companion's presence, but he soon sensed for himself that "not with Moshe."
"I hope [?]," answers Moshe, his eyes fixed on the sky, "that His dear Name will provide for me..."
The poritz flares up in anger:
"You dog's blood! Always you thank and still hope to God. I would like to see whether, if I did not give to you, you would not die of hunger? If you were not Moshe, I would have you flogged for such an answer... Get out of here! You won't get another grosz from me — let's see whether you will have [anything] for Passover..."
"Well, we shall see..." answers Moshe proudly.
* * *
Days go by. One evening the poritz sets about polishing his treasures of rendlach. He takes each gold rendl into his mouth and breathes on it, so that it should polish up well.
His monkey, his favourite, which he took along with him everywhere, watches this, and a desire seizes it to imitate it.
When the poritz steps out for a moment, the monkey quickly runs up and swallows quickly, quickly rendlach. It thought the poritz was swallowing them... Well, by the time the poritz comes back, it had swallowed a full belly of rendlach..
A few hours later. The monkey, the poritz's favourite, suddenly dies of suffocation. Nobody knows what has happened to it...
The poritz is upset, and finally says to his lackey: "Take the monkey and throw it into Moszke's house — let him have a roast monkey for the holiday..."
* * *
Sheindl Leah quarrelled with Moshe for insulting the poritz: "Well, what will you do now? You know very well that what the poritz does not give you, you do not have — how can one insult him so? We won't have even for matzos... A fine thing you've done, you schlimazel..."
"You'll see, Sheindl Leah, that God will provide for us, to spite the poritz."
"To spite the poritz," Sheindl Leah mimics him, "if the poritz doesn't give to you, you'll get a plague. I'm going to beg his pardon, I'll fall at his feet, he'll have to forgive you — I'll weep for as long as it takes."
"Heaven forbid, don't go, for God's sake..."
"Of course I'll listen to you... of course..." And Sheindl Leah snatches a kerchief to run to the poritz. She opens the door and — the poritz's lackey flings in the roast monkey and runs off with ringing laughter..
The monkey burst open, and rendlach began to pour out...
— — — — —
Passover night. The poritz calls his lackey and tells him to go and see what is happening at Moszke's. Now he will taunt him: "Well, since I didn't give to you, did God give to you?.."
The lackey comes back with the answer that at Moszke's all is bright and merry, a table laid like a king's...
The poritz does not want to believe it; he turns pale up to his ears, his heart pounds... No, it's a lie, he must go himself to make sure...
He stands beneath Moshe's window: what grandeur! what riches! Everything goes dark before his eyes...
He cannot restrain himself, bursts into Moshe's house and embraces him: "Tell me, Moszek, where did you get [the means] for Passover?"
"God sent it to me..."
"But surely He did not throw it down to you from heaven.."
"How do you know He didn't? Perhaps He did after all..."
"You must tell me, Moszek, I beg you, I beg you."
"If you promise me that you will do nothing to me."
"I swear to you!"
"By the hands of your lackeys a monkey full of rendlach was thrown in to me from heaven..."
"Aha..." mutters the poritz...
At a Serious Moment.

[Article — Będzin, orphans and relief.]
"Happy are they that keep judgment, and he that doeth righteousness at all times" (Psalms 106)
"This is one who raises an orphan boy and an orphan girl in his home." (Ketubot 50 [printed נ׳/ג׳])
"...whoever raises an orphan in his home, Scripture regards him as if he had begotten him." (Sanhedrin 9 [sic; should be 19])
All civilised peoples are governed by a strong feeling of compassion for poor, miserable children in general and for orphans in particular. It lies in the very psyche of mankind and in the blood of every single individual to share in the sorrow and to take part in the sufferings of the helpless souls whom fate has punished, taking from them their providers and their educators. Tolstoy once said: better that all cultures perish than that one child should have to shed tears. Above all, distinguished from time immemorial by its strong feeling of compassion towards orphan children has been the Jewish people, which regarded the raising and feeding of orphans as one of the greatest mitzvot. Our Sages regarded the raising of orphans as the highest expression of tzedakah, as we see from the Talmud quotations cited above, and thereby the upbringing of orphans came to be counted among the Jewish people as a sacred duty, as a mitzvah, which every Jew must fulfil and from which he may in no case exempt himself, and for which he bears the full responsibility, exactly as for his own children. And that is precisely what the saying "whoever raises, etc." means: that he who raises orphan children does not thereby perform any act of charity, but fulfils a sacred duty, because it is "as if he had begotten him", because orphan children are counted as our own children, whom we — whether we want to or not — must raise!
As we see, there rests upon us a very heavy and great responsibility, from the religious, the moral and the humane point of view alike, and had we failed to fulfil our duty we could never wash ourselves clean of the great sin against the helpless and innocent victims of fate, which tore their parents from them, whereby they lost not only the warm and loving atmosphere of the family nest, and not only the reverence and tenderness with which parents surround their young children — but thereby they also lost their providers and educators, lost their piece of bread, in the literal sense of the word! But to our good fortune there are in our town a few devoted individuals, "fanatics" in this field, who work with true self-sacrifice and superhuman effort like real, faithful parents, in order to raise the orphan children properly, and at whose head stand the famous "mothers": the "mother" of the thirty orphan boys, Mrs. A. Szajn [?], and the "mother" of the thirty-seven orphan girls, Mrs. Dr. Weinzieher; and these few individuals relieve all of us of that great and heavy responsibility.
At the present moment, however, the orphan institutions face a very hard and serious problem; the situation is truly catastrophic: the sources of income are shrinking and growing smaller and fewer, both private income and the subsidies from the public institutions, such as the Magistrat [municipality], the kehilla, etc., whereas the expenses, which have in any case been cut to the minimum, cannot be cut any further, and thus the existence of such important institutions is gravely threatened; therefore each of us must give himself an account of the seriousness of the situation and of the sad consequences to which such a situation may lead.
And this situation casts upon us very serious obligations, from which no one can and no one may exempt himself; rather, all of us together must carry the heavy burden on our shoulders and save the poor, unfortunate, forlorn, "roly-poly"[?] orphan children; that is the command of the hour and our most elementary duty at this hard and responsible moment.
And although we all find ourselves in a desperate economic situation, we are economically broken and are living through a moment of despair and depression — we must nevertheless not let our hands drop with regard to our most sacred duty, and we must always remember that the orphan children are our own children, and "if I am not for myself, who is for me?".
We must therefore also welcome and support with open hands the initiative of the orphan administrators, which consists in introducing[?] in our town the so-called "Orphans' Week", which is being held simultaneously throughout Poland. In the course of the "Orphans' Week" various events will take place for the benefit of the orphans, and then the so-called "One Kilo Campaign", which is to be carried out right after Passover.
The holding of campaigns of this kind is actually nothing new; in the Western European countries various philanthropic institutions use this means from time to time, because the benefit of such campaigns is twofold: besides the immediate material benefit, it also serves at the same time as a means of propaganda to popularise the institution concerned among the broad strata of society and to acquaint them with its activity.
And it is precisely such a campaign that the "Charitable Society" [Wohltätigkeitsverein] wants to carry out this year in Będzin for the benefit of the orphans. The campaign is to consist in delegates of the societies going round from home to home and from house to house collecting donations in kind, a minimum of one kilo, whether it be foodstuffs or textile goods, leather, haberdashery, etc., because everything, absolutely everything, is necessary and is needed for the orphan children.
We are sure that Jewish Będzin will know how to appreciate properly the importance of the so-called "One Kilo Campaign", and we Jews, who have distinguished ourselves from time immemorial by the quality of "merciful sons of the merciful", will support the campaign generously and thereby pass a maturity exam at the present responsible and serious moment.
Y. Wygodzki.
Common Work and Mutual Help

[Będzin — economy, cooperatives.] (On the general meeting of the Będzin Credit Bank).
The cooperative movement in Poland is now going through difficult moments. Of the large number [?] of cooperative banks that were scattered all over Poland, barely a small part has remained; the rest have collapsed, dragging down with them many merchants' livelihoods, which cannot go on existing without the bank's help. Cooperation, which precisely in the present hard times should have brought its constructive help to the economically weakened Jewish population, is not only incapable of helping — on the contrary, the movement itself now needs help. In a word: cooperation, which served as a base of operations in the hard struggle for the merchant's livelihood, has itself failed to withstand the first test of battle and has collapsed.
What has happened? Where do the causes of the collapse lie? Is cooperation really condemned to destruction? Has the mighty cooperative movement really lost its right to exist? No! Cooperation is an idealistic movement that has struck deep roots in life, and its existence cannot depend on passing economic upheavals or other caprices. Cooperation today, amid the enormous process of re-stratification of the Jewish population, is the only economic form that allows the declassed Jewish population slowly to rebuild its economic structure and adapt itself to the changed conditions of life. The shake-up in the cooperative movement was caused by external psychological factors. The young Jewish cooperative movement in Poland, having no sufficient working capital of its own and not enjoying state credit in adequate measure, became entirely dependent on the depositors. The upheaval of economic life is felt throughout the whole world. The collapse of the largest financial concerns weakened the public's trust in its financial institutions. On the contrary [?], panic seized the whole population, which withdrew its deposits from the banks en masse. In such circumstances, having no financial centre able to serve it with credit, the whole Jewish cooperative movement in Poland had to stop its credit activity, aggravating still further the credit shortage, which had already been very severe before. The situation became even harder because the Bank for Cooperatives collapsed and the whole movement was left alone, with no one to lean on.
The second, most important but invisible cause of the crisis in Jewish cooperation was the unserious attitude of the members themselves towards their own cooperatives. The whole movement in Poland had no proper ideological foundation.
The leading bodies of the cooperative movement, both at the centre and in the individual localities, paid little attention to the educational side of the cooperative members; constantly waging a competitive struggle against other auditing unions and against other cooperatives, they taught the members to regard the cooperative merely as a competing shop and not as an ideological outpost [?] that is to play a great role for the Jewish people in the future. And that is the cause of the collapse.
The economist who has just died, the greatest expert in cooperative science, Professor Charles Gide, said: "If a cooperative is only a commercial enterprise, it is always a bad enterprise; when a credit cooperative is only a bank, it is certainly a bad bank."
A cooperative is not merely a business enterprise with short-sighted business calculations. A cooperative must be one of the institutions that rebuild life on entirely new foundations: on foundations of caring oneself for one's own fate, on foundations of common effort and shared enjoyment, of creating one's own institutions with one's own means and by common work — and not making oneself dependent on outside persons or institutions.
A conscious member of a credit cooperative understands that in his cooperative he has 2 functions to fulfil: the function of a borrower and of a lender. He is the one who borrows money and the one who lends money to another member. And if as a borrower he takes care that he can satisfy his credit needs at his bank, he must also, as a lender, think about the bank being able to satisfy its members. These are the main principles of cooperation; these are the cornerstones of mutual help and common effort.
With us, however, the cooperative movement went an entirely different way: instead of unification came fragmentation. The liberal cooperative law gave every political group, every mercantile faction, every individual the possibility of creating separate institutions, which waged a competitive struggle against the other banks, destroying one another economically and morally.
Bank inflation led to credit inflation. The merchant, being a shareholder in all the banks at once, drew credit everywhere, exceeding his creditworthiness. Besides this, the member's interest in and ideological attachment to his cooperative were completely weakened, since he was after all a member of all the cooperatives. These working methods brought the cooperative movement to the sad state in which it now finds itself.
The members, overburdened with large credits, had no possibility in the present severe crisis of repaying the credits to all the banks; and having no particular sentiment for any institution, they repaid the borrowed money to no one, regarding the institutions like all other creditors, whom one should pay as little as possible and from whom one should ask as long a repayment term as possible.
The result is that at the hardest economic moment the cooperative institutions are unable to fulfil the natural functions for which they were created.
———
The present general meeting, which takes place on Sunday of Chol HaMoed Passover, must take stock of the situation that has arisen and find a correct way out of it;
moral pressure must be exerted on those who wilfully seek to undermine the cooperative institutions.
Lawlessness and demoralisation must be removed from our ranks. The sense of responsibility of all members towards their institution must be renewed.
We must make it clear to ourselves that the great struggle for existence now taking place throughout the world, that the great pauperisation occurring among the Jews in Poland, compels us to rebuild our economic structure on new foundations — and the only way to do so is cooperation, the principle of common work and mutual help.
Moszel Tenenbaum.
We Are Going to Geneva

[Feuilleton — political satire, Geneva conference.] (A short feuilleton).

So, we are going to Geneva [Genève; the Disarmament Conference].
There we shall witness a very interesting play, in which the greatest — one may say — artists of word and deed will take part.
There will naturally also be many extras there, bystanders, who come to take a look at this rare world concert.
I too have decided to go to the Geneva conference. I have taken along a whole sack of luggage.
You are probably curious to know what I have taken with me in the sack?
Diplomatic correspondence I do not have, of course. All my diplomacy is to be found in a small corner of my head.
And in any case they will probably not give me the floor. For making speeches there are greater artists there than me, and besides [printed "chutz lot", for "chutz lezeh"], I think very little of speeches altogether. I hold that one of the main reasons why mankind suffers is — speeches.
And the proof: before every calamity to befall mankind there first comes a conference, or a congress, where they talk so long that they part with exactly what they came with.
So what, then, am I carrying with me?
Firstly, a bundle of grievances against the world.
Between one conference and the next a great deal of material usually piles up which could have been put to use, but there is not always an opportunity for it.
Secondly, I carry with me a kind of spyglass through which one can see a person not only from his outer side, but also his inner side, his inner self.
I think such a spyglass may come in very handy at a conference where peace is being talked about.
Thirdly, I have with me a pen of a special kind, which writes automatically, but it possesses a quality that is very useful for journalists during a conference, especially when disarmament is being discussed there.
My pen writes only what agrees with reality. They may talk as many lies as they like — the pen will record only the truth.
With this luggage I set off for the Geneva conference.
What I heard and saw there — in the following letters.
Rebus.
The Maccabiad.

[Eretz Israel — sport; letter.] (A letter from Eretz Israel)
The "Maccabiad" has ended and its participants have already dispersed — some with a defeat and some with a victory, some in triumph and some in disgrace; and however the results of the first "Maccabiad" turned out, all the "Maccabees" are accompanied by a feeling of longing for Eretz Israel, which intoxicated them with the beauty, strength and youthfulness of the land that is building itself.
By the time this letter reaches the reader, the outcome of the first Jewish Olympiad will already be known to all, and more than one Jewish champion will no doubt be strutting with a silver cup and a medal ["zhetón"] adorning the lapel of his garment as the reward for his distinction at the "Maccabiad".
For the first time since our wanderings in exile, thousands of Jewish young people came together in Eretz Israel and proved by deeds that we are not merely an "am ha-ruach" [a people of the spirit] — a people of intellect, of soul — but also a people of a healthy body and strong muscles.
The various matches and contests held on the great "stadium" ground and in the closed halls were interesting and drew a large public, which followed the course of all the various events. At this "Maccabiad" there was no chase after medals, one did not feel the antagonism we always see at similar international sporting events, because all the participants in this Jewish sports festival were brothers of one people and members of one organization. There were no victors and vanquished, and the first and the last alike were received with the same recognition, knowing that today or tomorrow they may become citizens of Eretz Israel.
The "Maccabiad" is closed, and only now is the summing-up ["résumé"] being made of the "battle" that took place in the great "Maccabiad" days in Eretz Israel.
Almost all European countries, America and the whole East took part in the "Maccabiad". The Polish delegation numbered up to 70 men from all branches of sport, except winter sports. The football section numbered 16 men, among them Gottreich from Upper Silesia and Nunberg from Będzin; the swimming section — 7 men, most of them from Bielsko [Bielitz]; the boxing group — 8 men, all from "Yarden" (Warsaw) and Gross (Lwów); heavy athletics: Zing [?], Morgenstern (Łódź); tennis: Hitman (Katowice) and Dr. Lubling (Kraków); the gymnastics group — 6 men, among them: Treister, Prachtzweig and Steinitz (Stanowitz [?]); the light-athletics group numbered 4 men, among them Meirczyk from Königshütte [Królewska Huta / Chorzów].
On this occasion I may be permitted to make some critical but principled remarks addressed to this delegation: the Polish sportsmen did not present themselves properly in outward appearance in the parade at the stadium and in the closing march-past in the streets of Tel Aviv. Other groups from other countries distinguished themselves by order and discipline, which was precisely what the Polish delegation lacked. There was no organizing hand [?] to lead the Polish sportsmen, and therefore the group's participation in the parade in honour of the festive opening of the "Maccabiad" came out pale and weak. I believe that this friendly remark, made in passing by many Eretz-Israel friends of the Polish "Maccabi", will improve the organization of this delegation at the next Olympiad.
The results are as follows:
In the swimming competition the following distinguished themselves: Austria with 183 points, Czechoslovakia — 136 points, America — 58 and Poland — 79 points. In the 1500-metre swim first place went to Alfred Guth (Austria).
In water polo between Czechoslovakia—Austria against Poland, the Polish team won 0:2.
In football too Poland won. The second match between Eretz Israel and Poland, held in Petah Tikva, ended 3:2 in favour of the Polish football section.
In tennis Czechoslovakia won and took the championship. Poland lost. The match between Klein (Czechoslovakia) and Dr. Lubling (Poland) ended 0:3 for Klein, and the match between Hecht (Czechoslovakia) and Hitman (Poland) gave the result 1:3 in favour of Hecht.
In the shot put and discus throw the championship was taken by the American champion Harry Schneider.
In the running races first place at 5,000 metres went to Stir [?] Maamer (Egypt) and at 1,500 metres — Flaxman (America).
In the high jump: Martin Pirin (New York), who jumped a height of 1.80, and in the long jump, 6 metres: David Weiss (America).
In the discus and shot put in the women's group Miss Frida Berson (Warsaw) distinguished herself. Miss Kaf [?] Zibel distinguished herself in running and jumping. In the high jump she clears a height of 1 metre 40 cm.
In boxing Austria won; Poland took second place, followed by Egypt. The well-known boxer Gross of Lwów, who became famous after the tragic fatal accident during his bout with Godlewski in Lwów, was not lucky this time in Eretz Israel, being defeated by Lauf(en) [?] of Vienna. Grabosz of Warsaw, thanks to his light movements and fine combinations, defeated Grinshtein of Jerusalem. Wysocki, Birenzweig and in general the whole Warsaw "Yarden" group represented themselves well.
In the relay race the winners were: Czechoslovakia and the British Eretz-Israel police.
———
The first "Maccabiah" was a splendid sports holiday such as we had never seen until now. The initiators and organizers of the "Maccabiad" deserve true recognition for the successful event, which will surely be neither the first nor the last.
The "Maccabiah", under the patronage of the High Commissioner Sir [Arthur] Wauchope, was closed with a fine march-past in Tel Aviv. Once again thousands of "Maccabi" and "Hapoel" [?] members demonstrated to the sounds of many brass bands and under dozens of blue-and-white flags, filling the streets with the noise of the song "Am Yisrael Chai!" [The people of Israel lives!]
The flag of Będzin's "Hakoach" was this time indeed unfurled, and it was carried by the excellent "bramkarz" [goalkeeper] Nunberg, who is the only envoy of such a strong and recognized Zagłębie sports club. In this respect the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" showed more organization, activity and alertness.
Matek Hampel.
The Tasks of the „Yakhin“ Company

[Palestine — agricultural settlement; special report.] Special for the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ by Yisrael Dovid Beit-Halevi, Tel Aviv.
In the year 1926 the cooperative „Yakhin“ for agricultural enterprise was legally registered in Eretz Yisrael, with a share capital of 6,000 (six thousand) pounds.
The tasks of „Yakhin“ are: 1) Anyone who wants to plant an orange grove (pardes) and is not himself an expert must turn to a contractor on whose professional knowledge and honesty he can rely; those who live abroad and want to plant a grove need this especially.
The advantage that „Yakhin“ has over other contractors lies in the fact that, working on a country-wide scale, it is able to study various kinds of plantations from its own experience and to employ the best professional agronomists, who direct all its works and keep them under constant supervision and cultivation.
No less important for the employer is the advantage „Yakhin“ has over all other contractors in the financial respect as well, in that it takes on all the work on its own responsibility — from preparing the soil and installing the irrigation system up to planting the trees until they already bear[?] fruit. „Yakhin“ is responsible for the total sum that the contracted work will cost according to the contract, and so the employer knows in advance how much the grove will cost him and how much money he must prepare.
2) The main obstacle to the vocational training of the Jewish worker in the colony was that the work is not permanent and not secure for the morrow. The work system of „Yakhin“ has improved this situation[?], in that it hands the work over to work groups, under a contract for a fixed period, under the supervision of agronomists and with the workers themselves responsible for the quality of the work. In this way it avoids all sorts of labour conflicts and assures its workers steady work for a certain period. The worker, who works in one place and goes through all branches of the work, has the opportunity to perfect himself and to multiply the productivity of the work. And the system has proved itself in practice to be the best, in that output has risen without increasing wages.
3) There are many Jews abroad, of the middle class, who strive to settle in Eretz Yisrael but cannot liquidate their businesses and gather at once the whole sum needed to set up a farm and to live until the fruit comes. These Jews can enter into an arrangement with „Yakhin“, which will prepare the farm for them and in general help them to settle — individuals as well as groups organizing for this purpose, both in the old colonies and in new settlements — according to a plan and payment terms fixed in advance.
To show the course of development of „Yakhin“ it is worth giving a few figures.
In 1927 „Yakhin“ cultivated 195 dunams, in 1928 — 905[?] dunams, in 1929 — 1414 d., in 1930 — 2140 d., in 1931 — about 3000 d.
In 1927 the monetary turnover of „Yakhin“ amounted to 8,043 pounds, in 1928 — 17,314 p., in 1929 — 23,590 p., in 1930 — 31,523 p., in 1931 — about 40,000 p.
„Yakhin“ is equipped with the most modern machines, buys large quantities[?] of the necessary materials at the right time, runs [—] a rational and economical enterprise, and thereby it is truly able to calculate the cheapest prices for the work and to deliver the highest quality and full success in the works it undertakes.
Despite the present severe crisis, people are making the greatest efforts and taking advantage of the present opportunity, which is offered by the Keren Kayemet and carried out through „Yakhin“, because precisely in this critical time one must remember the saying „better one hour earlier“.
„Yakhin“ has also already made a name for itself in Poland, and this explains the success of this campaign to recruit members in Zagłębie for the colony being founded by „Yakhin“.
In Honour of Passover

[Passover — humour and homilies on the Haggadah.]
Witticisms and anecdotes around the Passover Haggadah.
Collected and styled by: Yehuda.

Ha lachma anya
Is it not a mockery that we eat "the bread of affliction" in memory of our former slavery, at a time when we still languish in bondage no less than once in Egypt?
To answer this, the author of the Haggadah adds: "Next year in the Land of Israel." That is: we are in fact already redeemed. We hold a promissory note (wechsel) for it — a divine promise. Only the note's due date has not yet come; it is not yet payable. But holding so safe a note one can already count the redemption as cash, as "money in the till"..
Emet le-Ya'akov.

"And you too shall set his teeth on edge"
Why does the wicked son not receive such a verdict in the Torah? Why is the author of the Haggadah stricter with him than the Torah?
Because the Torah says: "And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you" — that speaks of the many, of many wicked ones, and when the wicked are many — keep your hands to yourself... Whereas when the wicked one is alone, as in the Haggadah ("The wicked son, what does he say?" — singular), give it to him in the teeth..
By Rabbi Tzvi Yechezkel Michelsohn.

"Had he been there, he would not have been redeemed."
In Egypt, on the night of redemption, God commanded that blood be smeared on Jewish doors so that the Destroying Angel would do no harm there. Well, the wicked one would surely have been ashamed to mark his door with a Jewish sign so that everyone would know a Jew lives here. So the Destroying Angel would not have known of him, nor God — only death would have redeemed him...
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.

"And afterwards they shall go out with great wealth."
The Jews did not want to leave with possessions; God first had to ask them to. "'Na' is nothing but a term of request" — because the Jews did not understand: what does "great wealth" mean? After all, the more money one has, the greater a pauper one is...
"Great wealth" could only mean: contentment, being able to make do, being "happy with one's lot."
Lachmei Todah.

"The spoil of the sea" means: they despised the money, were disgusted by it...
Tiferet Shlomo.

"The Jews did not want — says the Talmud — to borrow money from the Egyptians 'because of the burden,' for money, wealth, is a burden; it weighs down the road to redemption, the will to be redeemed; it is a 'graves of craving,' a swamp from which it is very hard to get out.
Olelot Efrayim.

"And the Lord brought us out of Egypt."
Pharaoh argued to the Jews: don't think that God is bad only to me, striking me with plagues. When He is done with me and redeems you — He will turn bad to you too. "So be the Lord with you" — God will be as bad[?] to you — "as I will let you go" — after[?] I send you out. That is simply His nature: to strike..
Binah la-Itim.

"With matzot and bitter herbs shall they eat it."
Maror is a memorial symbol of bondage, of the bitterness of exile, but it must be eaten together [with the matzah], with the remembrance of redemption — to remember while in exile, and at the same time to remember in redemption...
Rabbi Yitzchak Krenitz[?].

"Praise Him, all ye nations, for His mercy is great toward us."
Why should the gentiles praise God for being merciful to the Jews?
Because we ourselves perhaps do not know our miracles. They, the gentiles, know what terrible decrees they had planned against us and from which ones God saved us — they themselves know our miracles best...
Shemu'ot Tovot (R. Yitzchak of Volozhin).

Elijah's Cup.
Every year we set a cup at the Seder for Elijah the Prophet. We open the door, Elijah comes, and does not taste from the cup at all[?]... Why?
Because he does not want to rely on the kashrut of the wine, not even on the certifications of our rabbis...
Otem Bosem[?].

"To You, yea, to You."
A preacher (maggid) once dropped in on a company of scoffers. One of them asks him:
— Why are the Ten Plagues written in the Haggadah and not in "Vayiten lecha" ["May He give you"]?
The maggid answers him:
If the plagues were in "Vayiten lecha," it would only be "may He give you" (and with that he pointed at the questioner). But since they stand in the Haggadah, it comes out: "To You and to You, to You, yea, to You, to You, also to You" (and with that the maggid pointed at each one separately)...

The Passover Seder is concluded.
With Jews there is never any order (seder). Once a year they do have a "seder" — and that too is a topsy-turvy one: horseradish before the meal, eggs before washing the hands, etc.
Folk saying.

"Then came the Holy One, blessed be He, and slaughtered the Angel of Death."
Once there was a question of reinstating a disqualified ritual slaughterer, and R. Shlomo Kluger was against reinstating him, because —
why did God have to slaughter the guilty Angel of Death? He should have brought the innocent slaughterer back to life, and that would have been enough. It must be, then, that a slaughtered slaughterer, even one slaughtered innocently, may not be brought back to life...
Zangen [Ears of Grain] — The Jewish Beggar

[Literature — translated poem; the "Zangen" supplement.] Supplement for literature and culture matters.
Julian Tuwim.
The Jewish Beggar.*)
Rendered in verse from Polish by: Menachem Eisenzweig [Menachem Ajzencwajg].

In the courtyard a little boy stands singing,
a Jewish beggar, wrapping himself in rags.
Chased by people, his head well muddled by God,
the long exile has dulled [?] his speech.
Scratching himself and dancing, he weeps and laments
that he is lost and that a pain torments him.
The gentleman from the first floor looks at the madman:
Brother, look at your brother, whom sorrow oppresses.
From the great world, ground into little pieces —
where has it led us, where has it driven us?
The one [printed "tsar"] from the first floor, your mad brother,
with his hot head, dances through the world, a weary one;
the gentleman from the first floor has become a poet:
his heart, like a penny, he soberly wraps up.
Through the window he throws it, let it break,
so that you may trample it, so that you may stab it to death!
And afterwards we shall go, each his own way,
wandering on in our old chain of wandering;
no rest shall we have in the weary struggle,
we singing Jews, mad Jews...

*) With this poem we begin a series: "Jewish motifs in young Polish poetry." The first in the series is the well-known Polish poet Julian Tuwim, whose Jewish descent and its influence on his poetry is now a subject of polemics in a certain part of the Polish press. The Editors.
The "Buda" Is Falling Apart.

[Literature and press — opinion piece; the writers' union.] Thus the poet Segalovitch [Zusman Segałowicz] grieves before us. Yes, the Jewish Literati and Journalists' Union is falling apart. It has already lost its prestige by the mere fact that things have come to this stage. It could not even have occurred to people that such an institution might fall apart — just as it cannot enter one's mind that all at once the press and the book and the culture of any healthy, normal people should perish. And just as that could not happen, so too one could not believe that the culture-makers and word-builders should ever lose their centre, which is as necessary to them as water to fish.
The writer cannot create when he does not have his spiritual centre; he must have his atmosphere, his air, his point of inspiration — and where can he find it if not in his literary circle, in his centre of comrades?
Yes, among normal peoples it could not have come to such an absurdity. But we do not belong to the average normal peoples. We are much, much better and much, much lower than average people, and that leads to abnormality, to incomprehensible things.
It is characteristic: on the one hand our Literati Union placed itself on the highest pedestal, so that many of the men of the pen could not reach it; when one stretched out a hand to it, the hand remained hanging in the air. And on the other hand everyone who had merely a certain dose of chutzpah and insolence pushed his way into it; it did not even matter that he had no connection at all with the literary world, or that the little connection he did have brought his colleagues not only no honour but only humiliation.
The institution as such did not know how to take under its authority the honour of the printed word; it did not try to take under its protection the press, which in this way became ever more lawless.
Whoever wished to see himself in print created a newspaper for himself, regardless of the fact that he was neither here nor there [lit. "neither chopped nor ground" [?]], that he could not even take a pen in hand; and like a boy he went around with a correspondent's card, with which he perpetrated all the follies in the world in the name of his newspaper.
It is not good that the union has turned into a "buda" [a shack, booth; Polish buda — a shabby den], whose aim is only to do harm and to ruin everything that was created with so much effort and diligence over a series of years.
If one wants the institution to exist and to bring honour to the Jewish writer, one must first [?] of all remove the "buda" and destroy the dangerous growths that have accumulated and that do harm to the Jewish writer and poet.
Only then can a union bring benefit and honour to the Jewish writer, to the book and to the press.
L. Szpigelman.
Literary Trifles

[Literature and culture — short items; Warsaw, Będzin, Zagłębie.]
Toward the Founding of a New Jewish Writers' Association in Warsaw.
A group of young Jewish writers who [?] belong to the left camp have taken upon themselves the initiative of founding a new writers' association, around which the Jewish writers of socialist orientation are to organize.
And as is the custom among Jews, there is already even a name for the not-yet-born creature: „Soshrayf“ (Sotsyalistisher Shrayber Fareyn — Socialist Writers' Association). A statute has also already been worked out, according to which the task of „Soshrayf“ is „to make the masses ripe for the great revolutionary ideas of socialism“.
—o—
Among Others and Among Us.
Mr. J. Czempiński [?] complains in the „Kurjer Warszawski“:
„It is hard to believe that in a country in which the population spends hundreds of millions on alcohol and cigarettes, there should not be found even a few thousand people who would spend, at least once a month, as much on books as they spend daily on cigarettes and bars [?]“.
And what shall we say to that?
Our population may not spend hundreds of millions on alcohol, but the „People of the Book“ certainly puts no other people to shame with its attitude toward the Jewish book and toward our culture...
—o—
Goethe's Drawings.
In Germany this year there is a bumper crop of Goethe literature in connection with the hundredth anniversary of the death of the great German poet. Among other things, an interesting collection of 30 drawings by Goethe has appeared in Leipzig from the „Insel-Verlag“. The book has appeared in a luxury edition and in multi-colour print.
—o—
A Branch of „Shul-Kult“ in Będzin.
In connection with the campaign [printed: „section“] conducted by the „Shul-Kult“ society in Poland, an organizing committee has been set up in Będzin, which includes representatives of several organizations and friends of the Jewish school and culture at its head [?].
The first task the organizing committee has set itself is to create in Będzin the branch together with a Shul-Kult institution, as well as to carry out properly the proclaimed relief campaign.
For this purpose the general secretary of the head office, Mr. A. Grodzeński [?], is coming to Będzin; in his presence consultations will be held on the further organization of the „Shul-Kult“ branch in Będzin.
—o—
Young Jewish Poet from Romania Visiting Zagłębie.
Staying in Zagłębie these days is the well-known young Jewish poet Naftali Herz Kon from Romania. The above-mentioned poet made his debut some years ago in the German journal „Literarische Rundschau“, published poems and articles in the German press for a long time, later went over to Yiddish and published in various Jewish literary publications in Romania. Kon came to Poland as a scholarship holder of the Jewish community of Czernowitz, to study the materials of YIVO in Vilna and to become acquainted with Jewish cultural life in Poland, such as schools, seminaries, etc. The poet also spent a longer time in Warsaw, where he made himself known with his poems in the „Literarishe Bleter“ and the „Vokhnshrift“; the poems in the „Vokhnshrift“ and those the poet read at various evenings were very well received.
The poet is coming to Zagłębie in order to become acquainted with Jewish workers' life in general, and he will visit the coal mines.
The poet will also give lectures and will read his newest works.
Dreams (A Sonnet)

[Poetry — sonnet; a poet from Sosnowiec.]
Leyzer Shikman, Sosnowiec.
Blind night has wrapped me in nightmares: —
As if I am somehow not myself, the cripple cast out by God and man...
O [printed „A.“], how good, how splendid is a healthy life,
Though I am just some hungry bohemian somewhere.
And now something flings you far back:
When you were still a child, full of the happiness of empty weavings [?],
And when Mother would rock you to sleep, blessing you:
„Leyvke, my son, happiness and joy will accompany you in life...“
And soon after that you picture yourself
In another, ugly, repulsive shape:
A homeless, crippled and lice-ridden man,
Bent over threefold and terribly old,
So you drag yourself on a dark, frosty night along nobody's roads —
And the black road comes toward you — — —
Forest Dawn

[Poetry.]
From the book „Dawn“ [Bagines].
In a garment of pure azure the forest stood deep in thought.
And drops of pearl still from the fresh night
Rested [?] quietly on tree and leaf.
Only deep up in the forest, like a piece of gold, glowed
The young day accompanied by the sun, and with spears
It cut across branch and tree and tall giants,
Hundred-year-old trees, [?] renewed with gold of [„roym“ — ?].
And every branch, leaf and tree
Woke gently from a sweet dream.
But all at once the forest became full of sound and song,
And sweet tones without measure rang out through the giant forest,
As many birds as there are in the forest all sang loudly, each on its own,
Called, asked, awakened; in a sea of pure joy
The forest rocked itself in its greenness.
N. Sternberg.
Press Voices on the Artist-Painter Abraham Goldkorn

[Art — press review; a native son.]
The Jewish Society for Fine Arts in Warsaw has organized an exhibition of paintings by several young Jewish talents, among them also a native son of our town, Abraham Gold-korn by name.
In the critical assessments in the Polish-Jewish press we read the following about the young artist-painter.
„Nasz Przegląd“.
Goldkorn finds himself in the fortunate position of having been under good guidance from his earliest youth.
As a boy he fell into the hands of the highly cultured painter Henryk Gotlib; later he studied for several years in Antwerp, where he learned the science of painting on the splendid models of Flemish painting, and at the same time he had the opportunity to meet distinguished [?] representatives of present-day modernism. Hence comes the new plastic conception in Goldkorn's pictures, and the problems the young artist paints stand at a European level.
A certain rawness can still be felt in the colour composition, but this is a transitional period which he will overcome in the course of his development, because he possesses talent, which foretells an artistic future for him. Already today the young artist has pictures at the exhibition that show the ability to look at the world with his own eyes.
„Nowe Słowo“.
Goldkorn's exhibits — this is the story of his struggle to find a distinct and decided painterly conception.
He has reached quite a high level in drawing and in composing the reality surrounding us, as can be seen from his latest works (landscapes, architectural fragments).
In his landscapes we sometimes see a deep and apt understanding of the meaning and optical weight of the coloured patch, which Goldkorn practises as a constructive element, achieving unheard-of effects by eliminating incidental things, which are very characteristic of the artist's free approach to work; he shows the concrete face of a thoroughbred colourist. (Sh.)
A. B. Wertheim
A Lost Dream

[Poetry.] A Lost Dream.
Today spring has already knocked at all the windows, doors[?],
like a quietly listening dove in the bluish dawn,
only I am encircled by such a cold, like a rusted hoop.
And I seek a way to the sun —
like a stray little lamb — a little path to the well.

The trees have already opened all their buds,
and on their branches dances such a quiet, green joy.
But to my heart the tidings somehow have not reached,
and the eye still languishes in the fog, like an un-bedewed[?] flower.

Hey, my youth, spread out your hands and catch back in a net
the dream of my life, which has hidden itself somewhere,
for today I stand bowed, like a pauper at the door,
and still there is a longing for a little joy in the sunny morning. — —

Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (21)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin; installment 21.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Summary of the preceding chapters.

In the house of the banker Oskar Dimentshteyn a narrow circle of rich St. Petersburg Jews gathered for a meeting to which the banker had summoned them.

The Jewish Baron Tsinberg [so printed; probably Ginzburg] arrives and relates that a high official came to him and handed him an order: the Jews are to be assembled in the Great Synagogue and a service is to be held for the health of the Russian heir to the throne, who is gravely ill.

The meeting opens and the banker reports that at the imperial court a strong agitation is under way to expel all the Jews from Petersburg. The agitation is led by Archimandrite Feofan, the chief priest, and he is supported by Bishop Hermogen and by the rabid enemy of Israel, the monk Ilidor [so printed; = Iliodor]. Because the "naslednik" [the heir] is ill, the agitation has grown stronger. The priest persuades the Tsarina that in order to drive Satan out of the court, the Jews must be driven out of the capital, and then the sick heir will recover.

The meeting resolves that every influence in the high circles must be brought to bear. Gifts must be given wherever necessary, in order to avert the evil decree that is approaching. Above all: someone must be found who can get to Archimandrite Feofan and buy off the decree from him...

But who will be able to get to him? The banker then declares that he believes his only daughter Sonia will manage to do it. She is friendly with the lady of the court Anna Vyrubova, who is well disposed toward Jews, and Vyrubova will bring Sonia together with the Archimandrite.

Meanwhile Sonia arrives. She is a wondrous beauty. She comes from the salon of Countess Ignatieva, where her father had sent her to find out what is going on at court. She brings the news that the heir is very ill. She also tells that she has had a fright: to the salon of Countess Ignatieva a new "holy man", a "miracle worker", was brought today. This "holy man" is a Siberian muzhik [peasant] named Rasputin. When he was introduced to her, he gazed deep into her eyes and said that she had a beautiful, pure soul... She felt that any moment he would draw her to himself and embrace her; she tore her hand out of his and drew away... but her heart was badly frightened.

Her father laughs at her fright. He tells her about everything that was said at the meeting, and what was settled: tomorrow a prayer service is to be held in the Great Synagogue for the "naslednik's" health, and Sonia is to meet Anna Vyrubova tomorrow and through her reach Archimandrite Feofan.

A week earlier, before the meeting took place, this had happened: in the monastery attached to the Petersburg Theological Academy there appeared a young wanderer who had come from Siberia, and his name was Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin. He looked like a simple muzhik and spoke like a "holy man". There he met Archimandrite Feofan, on whom he made a strong impression as a new "holy man". The Archimandrite introduced Rasputin to Bishop Hermogen, who was one of the leaders of the reactionary antisemitic "Union of the Russian People", which incited against the Jews; and it occurred to him that this sly [printed "piterer"; probably "khitrer" = sly], clever muzhik could be used for the political aims of the Black "Union" and help to conduct antisemitic agitation among the muzhiks. At that time there was in Petersburg the rabid enemy of Israel Iliodor, who stood at the head of the "Union" and led a savage campaign of incitement against the Jews. He called on the masses to make pogroms against the Jews, and in this respect worked hand in hand with Hermogen and Feofan. Bishop Hermogen invites Rasputin to go with him and Feofan to Iliodor, and all three went off to visit the black monk Iliodor.

They find Iliodor lying before the "icons", crossing himself, bowing and praying. Rasputin interrupts his prayer. Iliodor [a stray word "son" precedes the name in print, apparently a misprint] becomes very agitated, leaps up like an enraged [?] beast, ready to fling himself on the muzhik with the worst curses. But the muzhik's eyes master him. He becomes as if hypnotized by Rasputin's gaze, and finally he greets him, pressing his hand.

Against his will, but under the influence of Rasputin's eyes, Iliodor agrees to Hermogen's proposal that Rasputin should be taken into the central committee of the "Soyuz russkovo naroda" [Union of the Russian People].

With Iliodor's help Rasputin is introduced into the highest reactionary circles grouped around the monarchist "Union", and Rasputin is accepted as a "holy man" and as a member of the central committee of the "Union". And on that evening when the meeting took place at the banker Dimenshteyn's [so spelled here], Rasputin is brought for the first time to the salon of Countess Ignatieva. There he meets the Jewish daughter Sonia Dimenshteyn, and a great lust for her awakens in him.

Sonia drives to Vyrubova, and Vyrubova tells her that changes are about to take place at the imperial court and that Archimandrite Feofan will lose his influence. She tells Sonia: a great "holy man" has appeared; he will cure the "naslednik" and will take Feofan's place...

Sonia asks who the new "holy man" is, and when Vyrubova tells her that it is the Siberian muzhik Rasputin, she again feels a cold fright in her heart... Vyrubova, who has an interest in Archimandrite Feofan losing his influence at court, speaks of Rasputin with enthusiasm. She is sure that he will cure the naslednik, and she assures Sonia that tomorrow Feofan will be removed from the imperial court.

In the Great Synagogue of Petersburg the Jews hold a service for the health of the naslednik. The gradonachalnik [city governor] is present, and the service makes a good impression on him... After the service the banker Dimentshteyn, Baron Tsinberg and the city rabbi drive to the banker's home. Sonia arrives and tells them the good news that the Jew-hater Feofan is about to fall and lose his influence at court. The rabbi then exclaims:
"Thank God! Our prayers really have helped!"

Sonia stays alone in the house. She longs for the young Baron Leon Tsinberg, whom she loves very much. Leon telephones her and she invites him to come to her.

The Russian heir to the throne suffers from a terrible incurable disease called "haemophilia". Every blow is dangerous for him; he is closely guarded, but he is not always guarded well enough. He goes for a walk in the park, falls, strikes the knee of his right leg, and a haemorrhage begins in the leg at once. The leg swells and his sufferings are terrible. The doctors cannot help him. The Tsarina does not leave the patient's side. She is terribly broken. The Tsar too is broken. The heir suffers terribly. Every moment they expect death to carry him off.

The Archimandrite advises the Tsarina to drive the Jews, the unbelievers, out of the capital, and God's wrath will depart from the patient.

Every day he repeats the advice. On the fourth day — since the naslednik fell ill — the Tsarina sits utterly exhausted from three days and nights without sleep. She thinks perhaps they should follow the Archimandrite's advice... But just then Vyrubova arrives and says she has brought the Tsarina good news: a "miracle worker" has appeared in the capital. He must be brought to court and he will cure the naslednik...

Vyrubova succeeds in interesting the Tsarina in Rasputin, telling her many wonders about him. She also tells her that she told Rasputin about the naslednik's illness, and he bade her tell the Tsarina: "Let her weep no more, worry no more; I will cure the naslednik. The naslednik is a soldier, and he will have red, healthy cheeks." The Tsarina, who is extremely pious and superstitious, comes to believe that Rasputin has been sent by God to help the naslednik.

The Tsarina is cheered up; she tells the Tsar about it, who is no less superstitious than she. Vyrubova repeats before the Tsar the wonders of the Siberian muzhik, and it is decided to bring Rasputin into the court; so that he should not [printed "he he", a doubled word] have to pass all the guards, he will be brought in through a side entrance that is never used and therefore — is not guarded. Vyrubova drives off to fetch Rasputin; Vishnyakova, the heir's governess, waits for them outside in order to lead them in through the side entrance into the palace.

Rasputin is awaited with great impatience, and at last he enters the Tsar's study. He comes in noisily and boisterously, without the slightest embarrassment. Vishnyakova is astonished at Rasputin's appearance and at the fact that he flung open the door into the Tsar's study so hastily and did not even knock. She stands with wide-open eyes. For a while silence reigned.

And now read on.

Rasputin looked around, contemplated for a while the room in which he found himself, turned his head toward Vishnyakova, saw how she stood greatly surprised and dumbfounded, and called out to her, baring his teeth in a grin under his moustache:
"My good soul, what are you standing here gaping for?"

Vishnyakova started at the way Rasputin addressed her. She immediately collected herself and her face flushed red, so ashamed was she. She bowed deeply and at once left the room.

Then — and Rasputin, with a radiant smile and with sharp, shining eyes, went straight up to the Tsar and Tsarina, who stood somewhat bewildered, freely and without ceremony embraced the mighty ruler of all Russia and planted a juicy kiss on his cheek. Then he embraced the Tsarina, kissed her too, and exclaimed with assurance:
"Take me to the sick naslednik... I will drive the pains out of him! Take me to him!"

His face shone and his eyes gazed hypnotically, compellingly...

In the room where the sick heir lay, another sleepless, hard night was expected, and the attendants had made various preparations for it. Alexei lay groaning all the while. His face was pale as death and badly contorted with pain. He held his right leg drawn up against his body. One of his governesses came close to the bed and asked in a devoted voice:
"Alyosha dear, how do you feel?"

But the sick boy was in a stupor [?], did not answer and did not make the slightest movement. He only groaned in a quiet, weak voice...
"Answer me, Alyosha!" the governess pleaded. But the boy did not stir. It seemed as if he did not hear at all that he was being spoken to. The governess sighed quietly and her face expressed sympathy and pity.

Suddenly the door opened and into the room, with quiet soft steps, came Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin. After him followed the Tsarina and Vishnyakova. The faces of both were as if frozen and full of curiosity and expectation to see what would happen. Would this "holy man" really work a miracle? Would he really drive the pains out of Alexei as he had promised?

Rasputin, as soon as he entered the room, went straight to the corner where the icons hung and the "lampadas" [icon lamps] burned, lowered himself to his knees, crossed himself and began to pray in a quiet whispering voice, bowing every moment so that his forehead touched the floor. The room was very still. The patient was not groaning now, and the Tsarina and Vishnyakova stood with bated breath, waiting with great patience to see what would happen here...

Rasputin prayed for a few minutes in all. Then he stood up, approached the bed with cautious steps, bent over the patient and made the sign of the cross over him once, a second time and a third time. As he did so he murmured something in a soft, sing-song voice.

The sick boy opened his eyes and gazed in wonder at the strange stranger with the big beard who was smiling at him with such gentleness and kindness. The gaze of Rasputin's pale eyes was tender, yet so sharp that the boy shrank a little under it, as if he had taken a slight fright. But at once Alexei felt that the stranger did not mean him any harm and that he need not be afraid of him.

"Don't be afraid, Alyosha!... You have nothing more to be afraid of... You will not suffer any more pains..." said Rasputin. His voice was very pleasant and melodious, strong and at the same time very tender. The feverish boy began to listen with great attention.

Rasputin began to stroke the boy's body. From head to feet he stroked him. His magnetic eyes remained fixed on the boy all the while, and he went on talking:
"See, Alyosha!... I have now driven the painful aches out of you... Nothing will hurt you any more... You see... the pains have already gone from you... It no longer hurts you... And tomorrow, Alyosha, tomorrow you will already be healthy and strong... And the two of us will play all sorts of merry games... We will romp together and it will be such fun..."

Talking thus, Rasputin kept stroking the boy's body. The caressing movement of the big coarse hands gradually revived the heir, and he began to smile... And Rasputin continued talking, speaking in a louder and louder voice:
"Listen to me, Alyosha!... When I was a boy as big as you are now, I used to play very beautiful and wonderful games, of which you surely have no idea. I will teach you those games... and I will play with you."

And Rasputin began to tell about various games he used to play once; about various pranks he and his friends used to get up to; how he and the other peasant boys used to spend their days in their Siberian village.

He spoke about Siberia, told him that Siberia is a big country. It is so big that no man has yet reached the end of that wonderful land! And this great land belongs to Alyosha's father and mother, and later on, in time, when Alyosha is healthy, strong and grown up, the land will belong to him... Siberia is a very beautiful land... There are great forests there... broad, distant, endless steppes... And the people there are entirely different, not like the people in Petersburg.

Rasputin sat down on the edge of the bed, took the boy's little hand in his big peasant hands and stroked it tenderly.
