The Modern Haggadah — The Order of the Haggadah.

[Zagłębie — Passover satire, kehilla, economic crisis.] Published in honour of Passover with a hechsher [certificate of kashrut] from Ben Amotz.
Sweaty from too much idle walking before the holiday, we sit down on the reclining bed to conduct the Seder. It's no use, no clever tricks will help — one has to put on the airs of a prince, a ben chorin [free man], a “free person”, and recite the Haggadah.
So then, ben chorin, call in your household, order them to sit around the laid table and tell them about the miracles of old that Jews lived through; perhaps it will give them courage to survive today's troubles:
Put on the kittel and begin:
Kadesh [sanctify]. Whoever on the bazaar committee still has something left of the “vanished” little bottles of wine — must make Kiddush...
U-rechatz [and wash]. If you have had the merit of getting a nadzór [state supervision], then wash your hands and do not say the blessing “al netilat yadayim”.
Karpas. Take the Finance Ministry's promises that Jewish merchants will get credit from the “Bank Polski”, and the present love of the “Agudah” [Agudat Israel] for the Land of Israel, dip them both in salt water and say the blessing “borei pri ha-adamah”...
Yachatz [break]. Take three Jewish cooperative banks of Zagłębie, break off a piece of them and hide it for an afikoman...
Maggid [telling]. Take in your hand the list of the impoverished and the failed merchants and say:
Ha lachma anya [this is the bread of affliction]. This piece of bread, sweet Father, of a whole year is covered with blood and tears; and now this lachma anya which we eat like princes[?] has surely come to us with death-sweat[?]. Oh, how much Jewish blood has been diminished, how many Jews have let their faces be “washed” [have been put to shame] so as to receive the bread of affliction...
Ha lachma anya — how many Jews still gave kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour relief] a year ago, and today they figure on the list of recipients...
Kol dichfin [let all who are hungry]. Who is hungry? It seems that only a very small percentage of people are full today... Hashata avdei [this year we are slaves], next year — if, God forbid, the situation does not improve — b'nei chorin: we will already be free of everything, even of the bailiffs [tax distrainers]...
Mah Nishtanah? [Why Is It Different?]

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — Passover satire, kehilla, taxes.] Since it is now a season of reduction, we too will reduce the questions by 25 percent...
Mah nishtanah. Why is there such a way of running things in the Sosnowiec kehilla? She-be-chol ha-leilot [on all other nights] — in Będzin and in Dąbrowa the kehilla budgets have already been approved, and in Sosnowiec the budget lies in the chicken coop[?]?
She-be-chol ha-leilot we eat other vegetables — we have never lacked troubles; ha-laylah ha-zeh [this night], but this year — it is all maror [bitter herbs], it is so bitter after all
She-be-chol ha-leilot, in all years, whether sitting or reclining, there were among the tax assessors “sitting” ones and “silent” ones; ha-laylah ha-zeh, but this year we all recline — they are all as if asleep....
Avadim hayinu [we were slaves]... Slaves we were to Pharaoh, and to this day we cannot tear out the slavish souls of our representatives, the benefactors and providers of Klal Yisrael...
The story of Rabbi Eliezer. It was at the time when the new president of the Będzin kehilla had to be elected: Rabbi Eliezer had “guests” and came late to the meeting. Until his disciples came — the Agudah dozors [kehilla board members] spoke up, va-amru, and they said: rabboteinu, the time has come — the time has come to proceed to the election even without a quorum...
Said Rabbi Elazar: behold, I am — I am after all an expert in parliamentarism and have never yet heard of electing a president without a quorum, until Ben Zoma expounded it. To this Rabbi Nechemia says: lema'an tizkor [so that you remember] — you Zionists will remember all the days of your life, your whole life long, that you did not vote for your own[?]...
Baruch. Blessed is He who has given us four sons in the commissarial [appointed] city council; no small job they have at every meeting answering the questions of the wicked son, who asks “Mah zot? What is this for?”...
What are the evening courses good for? Worse still with the one who does not know how to ask, as it is said, to whom one must always say “ba'avur zeh” [because of this]: this must be done for the taxpayers, at a time when 80 percent of the municipal revenue comes from Jews...
Be-yad chazakah [with a strong hand]... With a strong hand they pull the marrow out of our bones; u-ve-mora gadol [and with great terror] — a shudder goes through one's bones when the bailiff appears in the doorway; u-ve-moftim [and with wonders] — this is the blood: it is a wonder and a miracle that the blood does not congeal.
Elu eser makot [these are the ten plagues]. These ten plagues exist, of which one cannot rid oneself, and these are they:
Obrotowy [turnover tax]
Dochodowy [income tax]
Majątkowy [property tax]
Ryczałtowy[?] [lump-sum tax]
Drogowy [road tax]
Nieruchomościowy [real-estate tax]
Bezrobotnowe [unemployment levy]
Wodociągowe [water-supply charge]
Lecznicowe [hospital charge]
Mieszkaniowe [housing tax].
Rabbi Yehudah called the plagues by an abbreviation:
Kasper-Melchior-Baltazar [the Three Kings; printed “Kasper-Meycher-Baltser”]..
How Many Good Favours

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — Passover satire, kehilla, municipality, culture.] Ilu [had]: had the Eretz-Israel bazaar in Sosnowiec passed without dancings — dayenu [it would have sufficed us].
Had the commissar governed the Będzin magistrate [municipality] without his brother-in-law — dayenu.
Had there been no representatives of the “masses” in the tax-assessment commissions — dayenu.
Had the Sosnowiec “Bnos” [Bnos Agudath Israel girls] read only the “Togblat” [the Agudah daily] and not acted in the theatre — dayenu.
Had the “Muza” been content with the “Old Market” and not gone “into Polish” — dayenu.
How much more so must we give praise that the bazaar committee arranged dancings, and in the Będzin magistrate we have a commissar and a brother-in-law, in the tax-assessment commissions we have “honest” representatives, Agudah daughters act in the theatre, and the “Muza” has sat down “in Polish on the chain”. To atone for all our sins...!
Rachtzah [washing]: if you still hold to the “regulation”, then wash your hands and say “al netilat pekl” [over the taking of a bundle]...
Matzah: take an olive's bulk of matzah kneaded by the shiksas [gentile girls] of Ksawera, read through the “kosher appeal” [odezwa] of the rabbinate and say “le-shem yichud”...
Korech [sandwich]: on top lay a parnas [leader] from the new kehilla council — underneath the future kehilla president — in the middle put the minutes of the last presidium election, and say “zecher” [a remembrance]. This is a memento of the Sejm elections, to fulfil that which is said. As it was promised that the “men of loyal citizens” would eat it up with bitterness...
Who Knows One?

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Passover satire, kehilla.] One I know: one person governs the Będzin kehilla.
Who knows two? Two I know: there are two artisans' associations which need a [?] craftsman...
Who knows three? Three I know: all three banks suffer from one disease...
Who knows four? Four I know: of the four Jews in the commissarial council, two sit at home...
Who knows five? Five I know: there are five rabbis in Sosnowiec, and the Agudah cries that “the public eats treif meat”...
Who knows six? Six I know: six votes are nowadays enough to elect a president...
Chad Gadya, Chad Gadya... [One Little Kid]

[Zagłębie — Passover satire.] The author of the Haggadah thinks that this year one should not mention the Chad Gadyas at the Seder, because if one were to tell what is being done nowadays for “trei zuzei” [two zuzim]... one could expect to become a candidate for the real Chad Gadya...

From the Sick Fund
The local sick fund asks us to announce that today, Wednesday, the eve of Passover, all members must report to the "Kasa Chorych" (sick fund), where the dentists will examine the condition of the teeth of every single Jewish member and note it in the books, because the sick fund cannot be responsible for treating after Passover the "żydowski" (Jewish) members who have broken their teeth gnawing the kosher matzos and also while saying the "Haggadah"...
—o—
And It Came to Pass at Midnight
If you want a favour from the tax assessors, you come to them — at midnight.
Yiddish theatre starts playing — at midnight.
Merchants wait for one złoty of takings until — midnight.
The municipal council adopted the budget — at midnight.
To get an interest-free loan of 10 gulden you have to search until — midnight.
—o—
Then and Now
Once, when the Jews were freed from the Egyptian exile, they were left with 4 questions and 1 answer.
In today's exile the Jews have many questions to ask, but they will not get any answer...
Once, in the Egyptian exile, the Jews toiled hard and in the end they came out with great wealth.
Today they toil hard, the wealth is taken away from them, and they go out empty-handed...
Leib Stabinski.
—o—
A Question to the Rabbinate
— Rabbi, since I possess half a minyan of grown-up marriageable daughters, I ask: may I fulfil my obligation at the Seder with them instead of maror (bitter herbs)?
Leib Stabinski.
—o—
After Passover It Will Be Better
— How is business?
— Bad, nothing to do.
— Don't worry, after Passover it will be better.
— Why?
— You'll be able to catch flies and kill them...
What Does a Jewish Pupil of a State Gymnasium Tell about the Jewish Religion?

[Humour — "The Modern Haggadah", Passover.]
So he, the rabbi, came into the classroom and told us that on Passover we Jews must not go barefoot, because it is a fast of Abraham's, because God gave the Jews the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai...
Then he told us about the ten plagues with which Moses struck the Egyptians with a stick, and they turned into a lump of salt, like Esther... And God ordered Noah to build a sukkah, so that the water of the Flood would not leak into the house, and that is why we drink salt water at the Seder, on Passover night...
One must not cut one's nails regularly, only when a leap year falls on Pharaoh...
What Does a Jewish Girl Pupil of a State Gymnasium Tell about the Jewish Religion?

[Humour — "The Modern Haggadah", Passover.]
The Jewish religion teacher told us that in order to be kosher a Jewish daughter must say the blessing over the etrog when the shammes comes, and make challahs in the mikveh...
The moon is made of brass and is chametz all year round, only on Passover it becomes meaty; one sticks it into the earth with a pareve knife, and one lights the candles three times on the table; after that one eats Purim latkes and plays dreidel until Shavuot...
An Appeal Concerning Kashrut for Passover

[Humour — "The Modern Haggadah", Passover.]
A group of local Torah-observant Jews have turned to us with the request that, since they, the pious, poor things, cannot look on while there is no exact supervision of kashrut, they ask us, for Heaven's sake, to publish in our newspaper their "Kol Kore" (proclamation) with the following important warnings, to remove a stumbling block and keep people away from the forbidden.
a) Tailors' journeymen who on the eve of Passover or on Chol Hamoed bring the garments to the customers must not accept any "beer-money" [tip], because beer is absolute chametz...
b) Women and maidens who powder themselves all year round with... flour should remember today, on the eve of Passover, to leave themselves, for all 8 days of Passover, the necessary quantity of holiday flour.
c) Hasidic daughters who belong to "Bnos Agudath Israel" must powder themselves with "shmurah" flour.
d) Mature maidens older than thirty mostly turn chametz, and one must therefore sell them to a gentile.
(The remaining warnings we will give next year on the eve of Passover, if we live to see it.)

What's New in Zagłębie? — Jewish Workers Have the Opportunity to Get Work

[Head of the local page; Zagłębie — employment.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Wednesday, 14 Nisan 5692 — Środa 20 kwietnia 1932 [Wednesday, 20 April 1932].)
Jewish workers have the opportunity to get work.
In the previous issue of our paper we pointed out that the president of the zinc factory, Mr. Fürstenberg, had declared to us that if physically healthy people in their thirties came forward, they would be taken on for work.

[Sosnowiec — charitable institutions.] Quietly, without noise or fuss, a splendid building named "Moshav Zkenim" (Old Age Home) has been erected in our town. [Będzin — Zionism.] On Sunday, the 2nd day of Chol ha-Moed, the Zionist district conference convenes in Będzin, as has already been reported in our paper. The conference embraces the Zionist societies in the following places: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Mogan[?], Modrzejów[?], Niwka, Dąbrowa, Zagórze, Strzemieszyce[?], Sławków, Olkusz, Wolbrom, Miechów, Charsznica, Żarnowiec, Ząbkowice, Zawiercie, Kromołów[?], Pilica, Myszków, Żarki[?], Grodziec[?], Czeladź, Częstochowa, Kłobuck, Krzepice, Przyrów, Mstów, Radomsko and others.

All those who are now in Eretz Israel confirm that, despite the bad political situation, the Yishuv in Eretz Israel is full of joyful awakening and constructive energy. They are right: in spite of everything and everyone, these hard years will be remembered in Zionist history as a period of aliyah and not of yeridah, a step towards victory and not a step into disappointment. And I hope that in the same spirit of confidence and with an offensive drive your district conference will open, proceed and conclude. Our movement is growing and strengthening from day to day; within about 2 years the Revisionist movement will lead the whole Jewish people, on one condition: U N I T Y. Unity based on mutual feelings of respect. The Revisionist movement is not a party. The Ha-Tzohar is the people of Israel in miniature, containing all kinds of shades: the shekel-payer and the opponent of the shekel; the old Jew and the Betari, the moderate and the revolutionary; all of them in the Revisionist ranks, that is, in the fighting camp for the Jewish future. In short — if they will go on the road that we marked out at Calais — the road of an inner agreement, which shall serve as a united attack outward — then we shall fulfil our historic task, for there is nobody [now?] in Jewry besides us who could fulfil it.

Who Can Benefit, and How, from the Suspended Evictions.

In connection with the decree of the President of the State on suspending evictions of the unemployed, we find it necessary to give our readers the following 6 explanations:
1) Evictions already issued earlier by the court are not automatically suspended, neither by the court nor by the komornik [bailiff]. If the interested party wants an eviction judgment that has already been issued to be stayed under the President's decree, he must apply about it with a special petition to the appropriate court.
2) Only evictions of unemployed persons occupying 1- and 2-room flats are suspended. But the interested party must fully prove before the court that he is indeed unemployed; without sufficient and certain proof of unemployment the eviction is not stayed.
3) As proof of unemployment may serve a certificate from the State Labour Exchange (the mere red identity card, however, is not enough), or a certificate from the police. The court also takes into account statements of witnesses.
4) Regarded as unemployed are not only wage workers who have lost their job, but also those who work on their own account and have lately had no work.
5) Evictions from larger flats too (of 2, 3 and even 4 rooms) are in many cases postponed by the courts for a period of 6 months, if the tenant can prove that he is not paying rent because of his very difficult situation.
6) Sub-tenants too who do not pay rent to the main tenant cannot be evicted from the flat, if they meet the conditions stated above.

On Guard Against a Catastrophe

[Editorial — the economic crisis in Zagłębie; after Passover.]
L. Szpigelman.
VIII. The holiday is already over — what will happen next? May one remain indifferent at such a moment?
Hard, very hard it was this year for the Polish Jew to bring Passover into his home. True, from time immemorial this has been the hardest of our holidays; for weeks ahead [?] one toils to bring it into the home, and one feels thoroughly worn out by the time the very eve of Passover arrives; but however hard it always is, this time the holiday was bound up with special difficulties, with extraordinary self-sacrifice and with enormous toil and suffering.
For the bitter times had never yet reached today's critical state. For the crisis had never yet knocked [at the door] in so large a dose as we have seen it now, during the Passover days.
Among us provision was made for the professional beggar and for the supposedly „respectable" pauper of many years, who could have earned quite well for the holiday had he only wanted to. If we were not obliged to care for him, he would then have known that he need not be ashamed to work, just as the one who feeds him works, the one who comes to his aid in his hard need. Only no provision was made for the one who has just fallen, for the one whom people in the street still regard as an earner, for the one who is still assessed as owning so-and-so much, and whom the Treasury (the „Skarb") still assesses as having had a turnover of tens of thousands of złoty. That is whom no one provided for; that is the element which did not even enter the minds of the people engaged in public philanthropy.
Yes, it must be stated that people, whole families of this very category, had nothing with which to make Passover; more than that, there were some to whom people came to collect for the kimcha [de-pischa, the Passover flour fund], while they themselves had nothing with which to make Passover.
Nobody knew about them — and had one known, could one have helped them much? That is a question that must be seriously considered. At best one would not have gone to them to collect kimcha, but one could have helped them only very, very little, because — let us not fool ourselves — are there not nowadays more receivers than givers? And can this small, weak handful of givers sustain the great contingent of receivers? Are they so strong in today's hard times? Is not every obligation thrown onto the one who is still holding on today and does not know what his tomorrow will look like? Is it [?] a small responsibility when one keeps reaching the stage where the moderately well-off man falls only because on the one hand he has too many obligations and on the other his assets are in other people's hands, and because of the slightest change the capital he has handed out is suddenly ownerless and lost? Must this question not be taken into serious consideration?
It is possible that the leftist elements, the working strata, will come and bear a grudge against the writer of this article. Aha, they will say, he is defending capital, he weeps crocodile tears, he is afraid the rich man will be impoverished — but it is wrong when one thinks so, when one wants to solve the problem in such a way. One must not forget that we are not speaking here of the big industrialist who exploits the workers with all his might. We mean here only the small industrialist, the merchant and the artisan, who barely stand on chicken legs and whom the slightest wind turns into a heap of ruins forever. We therefore hold the opposite: that care must be taken that these elements remain standing on their feet, because around them are concentrated larger masses of people who live and earn their livelihood thanks to their existence, thanks to the fact that they have not yet fallen. And for them to fall no great [?] is needed; any movement can bring about that risky step, and then we shall have a whole people of impoverished, crushed human beings. True, we present [?] [ourselves] as an ideal people, with feelings of compassion, with ideal hearts and with much love and sympathy for the sufferer; but what can we do with our feelings of compassion when we are crushed through and through, when we are broken and impoverished? Does one get much from the poor man's kind-heartedness? True, he is good and his compassion is immensely great — but whom can he help with it? And what good can he bring his impoverished fellow?
Yes, one must look more far-sightedly at our hard economic situation; one must consider it with the fullest seriousness and sincerity. One must begin to think how to stem the tide of impoverishment, which is making such giant strides forward; one must not allow things to reach the terrible state in which the whole Jewish people will be impoverished and there will be no one to help anyone, no one to take pity on anyone.
In all of Poland things have been bad for a long time [?]; with us it has until now still been bearable — after all, our Zagłębie corner is regarded as the best-situated corner of Poland; but the terrible crisis has already begun to break in on us too, and for some time now it has been showing the true signs of its rule. One must therefore reckon with it and seek means of how to tear oneself out of the dangerous situation.
How bad things are can be shown to us by the latest fact: that there were in Zagłębie many well-to-do Jewish people, firms, who had nothing with which to make Passover. This is not just said into the air; these are facts, living proofs. People came who confided it to their acquaintances in the deepest secrecy.
That the truth of these facts is confirmed is also proved by the fact that this year far fewer goods were brought in for Passover than in all previous years, and yet nothing was lacking; on the contrary, of all goods a larger quantity remained unsold. And that is the best proof of what the prevailing times are like, when people could not prepare even something to eat for Passover.
Today we are already after Passover — and what will happen now, with what will all sorts of unemployed people help themselves? From what will they draw their livelihood? The situation is very, very hard, the state of affairs is very, very strained — so what will one turn to now? How and in what manner can the forms of existence now be continued?
One must not remain indifferent to this question, which must decide how to save the existence of those who have not yet been completely crushed, and to help those who are drowning [?], those who are ready to cling to a straw just so as not to fall into the abyss.
The time is hard, the situation is extraordinary, the state of affairs is well-nigh unbearable — and yet, and yet one must not lose courage, [one must] be clear-minded and not lose one's balance. One must seek means of how to save oneself and others, how to lead oneself and one's fellow back onto the normal road of existence. To leave things as they are now is in no way permissible; by doing so one commits a crime against oneself and against the Jewish community as a whole.
When a misfortune affecting the whole community draws near, one must not remain indifferent; then one must stand on guard and take care that it does not come to the catastrophe.

A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

He kept looking the boy in the eyes, smiling kindly, and he promised Alyosha that when he was completely well, he would take him along to Siberia and show him a great many beautiful things there... He would lead him around villages and fields there and show him such interesting things as nobody besides him — besides Rasputin — had ever seen. The boy listened to Rasputin's words with great curiosity. The boy's eyes grew bigger and bigger and began to shine with quiet joy... The heir to the throne had by now completely forgotten that he had only just [?] been ill; he no longer thought of his pains and did not feel them. His right leg, which all the time had been drawn up against his body, gradually straightened out, and he now [?] already held it fully stretched out; he raised his body, pushed himself higher up on the pillows, so that he remained almost sitting, in order to see better the face of the stranger with the big black beard.

The Tsarina had all the while been standing to one side, standing silent and watching with bated breath. When she saw the heir move, she started in fright and lunged closer to the bed, afraid that the boy might hurt himself again, and she cried out:
— Careful, Alexei! You know you must be careful and stay calm!
Alexei answered the way a person answers when he is disturbed:
— Leave me in peace, Mama! I want to listen!
And turning to Rasputin, who had also fallen silent for a while, he exclaimed with childish curiosity and eagerness:
— I beg [?] you... I beg you: tell me more...
Rasputin smiled and nodded his head good-naturedly:
— Right [?], Alyosha! You need not be afraid of anything anymore... Nothing can harm you now... No evil can befall you while I am here with you... Nothing bad can happen to you...
— Tell me more... tell me — the boy pleaded.
And Rasputin again began to speak and tell about Siberia. Then he began to tell fantastic tales. He told of hunchbacked horses, of riders who have no eyes. And the boy listened with great attention and rapture.
Rasputin spoke of the various flowers that grow on the wide Siberian steppes; he told that in Siberia the flowers in the fields and the old trees in the forests also have souls, and they can talk among themselves... The animals there also have a language, and he himself, when he was a child, had learned to understand the language of the horses. He understood what the horses in the stable were saying to one another...
The boy turned his head to Vishnyakova and exclaimed with enthusiasm:
— Do you hear, Maria? I always told you that animals can talk, but you are so silly and know nothing about it... You said they don't... that they can't talk...
Vishnyakova, who had herself been listening with great curiosity to Rasputin's words and had been gazing at him with admiration all the while, nodded her head in agreement.
The naslednik [Russian: heir] smiled mysteriously at Rasputin and said:
— But we both know that beasts and animals can talk... And you will tell me everything you have heard from the horses... Isn't that so? You will tell me, won't you.
It was already late at night, and so Rasputin answered with a smile:
— Not now, Alyosha!.. That will be enough for today. Tomorrow... tomorrow I will tell you more things.
— And why not now? — Alexei asked.
— Because it is already late now and you must sleep.
— I want to listen like this! — Alexei exclaimed imploringly. He no longer felt any pain now, and he could have sat like that and listened a whole night.
— Tomorrow, Alyosha!.. Tomorrow you will hear.
Rasputin stood up. But the boy would not let him go. The Tsarina came up close to the bed. She assured her son that the good "Father" Grigori would come back tomorrow evening; she had to assure him of it many times before the child agreed to let Rasputin go.
Rasputin took his leave and started out of the room. As he stood at the door, Alexei called after him:
— Don't forget to come tomorrow, "Daddy"! I won't go to sleep until you come!
Rasputin turned his head and answered:
— I will come, Alyosha! I will surely come! Now go to sleep and sleep well... Tomorrow I will be here again. Good night, Alyosha!
— Good night, "Daddy" — Alexei called out.
Rasputin left the room. The Tsarina saw him out.

— "Holy Father"!

One Must Not Pin Too Great Hopes (On the Concessions on Overdue Taxes)

[Economy — taxes and trade.] In the last few days a ray of hope has shone for the merchants: an ordinance has been issued with very important tax concessions. The old taxes will be extended (spread out), and whoever pays them within 3—4 months will receive a reduction of 25 to 50 percent.
It is necessary, however, to make clear that one must not pin great hopes on the tax concessions, because, as far as one can know the situation, perhaps only a handful of merchants will benefit from them at all. The great hope and the disappointment that may follow it are more harmful than dispelling the hope right at the start.
We already have experience of what tax concessions look like when they depend on the local naczelniks [office heads]. We have seen many times how genuinely large concessions made by the Ministry of Finance remained, regrettably, only on paper, because the application of the concessions was made dependent on the opinion and discretion of the heads of the tax offices.
On this occasion, by the way, it is worth recalling the important "concession" on patents [trade licences] that the Ministry of Finance made.
A few weeks before the last New Year the Minister of Finance issued a circular with the following extremely important concessions on patents:
1) Merchants of the second category who had a turnover smaller than 30 thousand zł. may buy out a third category.
2) Merchants of the third category who had a turnover of less than 10 thousand zł. may buy out a fourth category.
3) Merchants of the 4th category whose turnover is less than 2 thousand zł. are to be exempted from a patent.
A great concession indeed, and all merchants rejoiced, seeing in it a good beginning of a better attitude toward the merchants and toward trade.
Only one small detail was added: one must submit applications. And thousands upon thousands of merchants submitted applications.
Now they have all, perhaps almost all, received notices that the applications have been rejected and that within 7 days they must pay [the balance on] the patent.
Thus a fine hope for a concession on patents came to nothing...
And therefore one must not fall into great raptures over the present "concession" either, because —
In the ordinance on the tax concessions there is a clause under which the whole concession will depend on the opinion of the head of the tax office.
In the ordinance there is a clause that:
The concession is not to be granted to those "who have systematically failed to keep the payment deadlines of the taxes". And who knows whether a few merchants will be found who, because of this clause, will be privileged to benefit from the important tax concession.
The campaign of the economic circles to make it easier for the merchants to pay off the old taxes has thus not yet ended. With the new ordinance on the concession, the requested relief has still not been achieved. One must therefore not cease the efforts with the government to obtain the concessions.
On the contrary, it is precisely now that the economic circles must, with redoubled energy, point out to government circles the necessity of enabling the merchants to pay the old taxes over a year and a half, as was done wholeheartedly for agriculture.
G. W.
Coty and the "Agudas Yisroel"

[World — antisemitism.] As is well known, the famous French perfume manufacturer Coty is conducting an antisemitic campaign in his newspapers "L'Ami du Peuple" and "Figaro".
An interesting "Jew-expert" article we find in the latest issues of his papers, in which Coty defends himself, saying that he is not going to conduct any antisemitism; he only wants to expose to the world the guilty Jews, the Jacob Schiffs and similar Jewish bankers (who did not want to introduce his shares on the New York stock exchange... — the Ed.), but against the people as a whole he has nothing.
And the proof that he is right, writes Coty, is that even a large part of the Jewish people agrees with him and condemns these bankers — for instance the organisation "Agudas Yisroel", which consists of 800,000 members and was founded in 1912 in Katowice. "This organisation," writes Coty, "has always been on bad terms with the 'Jewish Agency', which only yesterday was presided over by Felix Warburg, a son-in-law and co-owner of the bank Kuhn, Loeb and Co."
"At the time when the 'Jewish Agency', which has in fact seized the Zionist movement, is giving the latter an almost openly revolutionary turn — at that same time the founders of the 'Aguda' hold that the Jewish race must on no account leave the religious ground, which nobody even thinks of fighting. They hold that the political adventures will set all the nations against the Jews.
The 'Aguda' regards as a grave imprudence the formation, among the nations, of Jewish political minorities, which bombard the League of Nations with constant and insolent appeals against the nations among whom they live.
"And still more the 'Aguda' regrets the brutal declarations of war by certain Jews, such as for instance the declaration of Doctor Vladimir Jabotinsky, who said in Warsaw at a congress of a Zionist group that if England does not hand over to his kinsmen the administration of Palestine, the Jews will be the dynamite that will blow up the British Empire."
The "Aguda" fears that this "Jewish wildness", which the Roman historians already sharply condemned, may in the end provoke repressions from which the whole Jewish race will suffer.
Coty underlines that the members of "Agudas Yisroel" who express such fine opinions are the most pious people of the Jewish race, and they hold, just like him, Coty, that the bank "Kuhn, Loeb and Co." is guilty of all the troubles of the world. Since one surely cannot accuse the "Aguda" of antisemitism, one cannot accuse him of it either...
That is how Coty babbles and twists with his tongue — Coty, who apparently is nevertheless afraid that Jewish daughters will not stop using his cosmetic articles.
The fear is groundless!...
B.
A Little Feuilleton — Thrift.

[Feuilleton — humour.] Thrift!
That one word has eaten its way deep into our bones.
All my acquaintances, relatives and neighbours, and just plain people, have snatched up that word and won't let go of it.
Now, I know a Jew. He is truly crazy about that word. He is so muddled that he no longer knows which world he is in.
When he wants, for example, to travel to Katowice, he goes to Sosnowiec instead, because it costs less.
Thrift! One must be thrifty, he says.
Every year he used to throw his mother-in-law out of the house five and six times, and this year he threw her out only three times.
Thrift!
When my neighbour used to quarrel with his wife, he would smash a plate worth 60 groszy, and today, when he wants to throw a plate on the floor, he first buys a plate for 30 groszy.
Thrift!
Once, when he wrote letters, he used to write his address on the back; today he no longer does it.
Thrift!
One must economize.
In the good old days, before the crisis, my neighbour used to pray three times a day: Shacharit and Mincha and Maariv. Now he has dropped [?] Shacharit. One must, he says, save as much as one can.
My aunt Gnesha, in the good old days, used to go to every funeral and faint twice. Now — shoot her, slaughter her — she won't faint for you more than once, even if the funeral is one of the biggest.
And if times don't get better, she says, she won't faint that one time either!
Thrift!
And my cousin, Yona Sender, already wears trousers with one crease and one pocket — thrift.
"My wife always used to have twins; for the last couple of years she has had only one child," — so says Yona Sender.
One must be thrifty!
"My uncle always used to cough 5 and 6 hours a day, and now he gets it done in 2 hours."
"Thrift," says Yona Sender.
"My father always used to go to the steam bath every Friday, and now he goes to the bath only once in 6 weeks."
Thrift! — says Yona Sender.
"This year my father held only the first Seder; the second one he saved."
Bad times!
B. Kahner.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Acharei Mot)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Acharei
The Portion
—o—
a) "After the death of the two sons of Aaron" (Lev. 16:1)
"For they did not take counsel with one another" —
Nadab and Abihu looked forward to the death of Moses and Aaron so that "you and I will lead the generation" — so that they would become the leaders: one a High Priest in Aaron's place and the other a king — in Moses' place. But even in this they were not of one mind: each of them reckoned that he would be the High Priest...
Shemen ha-Tov.
• • •
The wording of the Torat Kohanim implies that only Nadab said this to Abihu. But because Abihu heard and kept silent, he too was "punished". The listener is as good [i.e. as guilty] as the speaker...
Nachal Kedumim.
—o—
b) "The two goats — lots" (ibid. 8)
The "goat for the Lord" — if the Jews were worthy — always fell to the right-hand lot [?]. But when the Jews were sinful, the "goat for Azazel" fell on the right — (Yoma).
The good inclination likewise occupies the right side of a person's heart, and the evil inclination — the left. But the misfortune is that today they swap places. The evil inclination settles itself precisely on the right... Here it is the pious one; it urges one only to mitzvot: a mitzvah to inform on the wicked, a mitzvah to uproot one's fellow, and similar mitzvot...
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
• • •
The evil inclination is according to its generation.
Our generation says one thing with the mouth and another in the heart, and today's evil inclination too is in disguise: it says one thing with the mouth and another in the heart..
Beit Shmuel Acharon.
—o—
c) "For the life of all flesh — its blood" (17:14)
"The life of all flesh", the soul of every person — "its blood" [damo; damim = money], is his money...
Or Penei Moshe.
• • •
"Deliver me from blood-guilt [damim], O God" —
Save me from money becoming my god...
Paren Resh"t [?].
—o—
d) "Like the doings of the land of Egypt" (18:3)
The essence of the Egyptian exile, the chief cause of Jewish misfortune in all the exiles, is that the Dathans and Abirams are forever asking the Moseses: "Who made you a prince and a judge over us?" It is against this Jewish insolence, picking on every leader, that the Torah warns here...
Ma'or va-Shemesh.
—o—
e) "And live by them" (ibid. 5)
The mitzvah should leave a person's hand alive, whole, not crippled...
Nifla'ot Chadashot.
—o—
f) "To uncover nakedness" (ibid. 6)
Rabbi Hershele Berliner [R. Zvi Hirsch Levin, rabbi of Berlin] once said in a sermon about the difference between German and Polish Jewry:
"Most of them in robbery and a minority in sexual transgression" — in Poland the Jews are a bigger community (most of them), and their main fault is: in robbery, too little honesty. In Germany the Jewish community is small (a minority) — in sexual transgression: the purity of family life is less [?] at the proper level — mixed marriages, etc.
A rich man who was present told him that he had been in Poland and had seen that there too family purity was not at its best. The Gaon answered him:
— Didn't I say that they are not honest, that their failing is the trait of robbery? Well, so they have also robbed the German Jews of their levity in family purity...
Zvi la-Tzaddik.
—o—
g) "To any of his near kin" (ibid.)
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk, as is known, became through his second marriage the brother-in-law of the Chiddushei ha-Rim. Under the wedding canopy Rabbi Mendele says to his brother-in-law:
— There is a doubt [?] about the betrothal: your sister-in-law accepts the betrothal because she thinks I am a rebbe, but in truth...
The sharp-witted Rabbi Itche Meir answers him:
— But she doesn't think that you are a rebbe; all her pleasure comes only from the fact that people call you "the Kotzker Rebbe", and in the eyes of the world you are indeed "the Kotzker Rebbe" even if in truth you were not..
—o—
h) "That the land not vomit you out" (18:28)
The Land of Israel has a quality: whomever it does not want there is repelled by it... When the Land of Israel does not want someone, Providence puts into him a disgust for the Holy Land, so that he should, God forbid, have no desire to settle there. And that person then speaks ill of the Land of Israel. But he does not know that what is speaking out of him is the Land of Israel's hostility towards him...
Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer.
—o—
Haftarah.
i) "They have taken bribes in you" (Ezekiel 22)
Of a rabbi who took bribes, Rav Eizel Charif said:
He says "Tzidkatcha tzedek" for (a) mincha... (for a gift).

Festive Opening of the "Moshav Zkenim" (Old-Age Home) in Sosnowiec
On Sunday, the second day of Chol HaMoed, Jewish Sosnowiec experienced a communal celebration. The opening of the "Moshav Zkenim" building was celebrated — a building erected thanks to tireless work and energy.
The interest was very great. Although the building stands on a site far from the town, a large crowd came to the celebration. Also taking part were the entire Va'ad ha-Rabbanim (rabbinical board) of Sosnowiec (except Rabbi Englard); Rabbi Dr. K. Chameides of Katowice, accompanied by the kehilla representatives Director Cytterman [?] and Dr. Rapaport; the Deputy Starost Mr. Mandyszewski [?]; the Municipal Commissioner Mr. Kuźniak [?]; delegations of the Sosnowiec and Będzin kehillas, of the Będzin "Moshav Zkenim", of the Będzin "Dobroczynność" (charity society), of the Sosnowiec "Dobroczynność", of the Sosnowiec "Merchants' Association", and others.
The building is beautifully decorated both inside and out, and the mood is festive.
The ceremony began with the affixing of mezuzot, performed by Rabbi Hager. Then the reception committee, rabbis and delegates gathered in the special synagogue in the "Moshav Zkenim"; the cantor Mr. Lejchter and his choir sang "Ma Tovu", "Mizmor Shir Chanukat", a prayer for the President of the State and Marshal Piłsudski, and the Polish and the Jewish anthems.
Then the official part of the opening took place in the large dining hall. On the presidium sit the first founders, Messrs. Gronem Sater, Jehoshua Pachter, Chaim Józef Zając, Maurycy Rajner, Moryc Mitlis, Kwiatek and others.
The chair is taken by Mr. G. Sater, who declares the celebration open and, after honouring the deceased members and donors Herc Lipszyc, Izaak Ber Walman and Israel Mosze Wajngreb [?] (in whose name his wife Lea established the synagogue in the Moshav Zkenim), Mr. Sater gives a short survey of the founding of the institution and appeals to the Jewish public to continue helping, so that what has been created can be kept going.
The first speaker is Rabbi Hager, who gives a speech rich in content, in which he discusses the whole meaning and significance of old age among human beings, draws an analogy concerning humanism among other nations and among Jews, and unfolds all the dark epochs the Jewish people has endured in exile, down to today's Hitlerites and Cuzists [followers of the Romanian antisemite A. C. Cuza]. The conclusion of Rabbi Hager's speech is that the Jewish protest against all these injustices must be nothing but compassion, righteousness and philanthropy, and he appeals for further support.
The speech made a tremendous impression.
In the further greetings took part: Commissioner Kuszniak on behalf of the Sosnowiec Magistrate (municipality); Dr. Chameides on behalf of the Katowice kehilla; for "Dobroczynność" — Dr. Herzman; for the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association — its chairman Kwiatek; for the Będzin "Dobroczynność" — Dr. Weinzieher; for the Będzin "Moshav Zkenim" — Mr. M. Lewin.
The large crowd then visited the splendid halls and the facilities, which were built according to the latest requirements.
—o—
Annual General Meeting of the Credit Bank [printed "Sredit"] in Będzin
On Sunday, the second day of Chol HaMoed, the annual general meeting of the "Bank Kredytowy" took place in the hall of the "Merchants' Association". The meeting drew the interest of some 150 members.
The bank's director, Mr. Tenenbaum, opens the meeting with a short introduction in which he points to the difficult economic situation that has caused the pauperisation of the Jewish merchant element, and states that with strenuous cooperative efforts the merchants' situation can be improved.
Mr. Tenenbaum also addresses sharp words to the members. At a time when — says Mr. T. — members of the board and council showed understanding and readiness for sacrifice, lending the bank a sum of 50 thousand zł., the members who are debtors of the bank did not show the slightest will regarding their obligations towards the bank.
The chair is handed over to Mr. Michał Lewin. As assessors, Messrs. Salomon Gutman and Bornsztajn; secretary N. Fiszel.
The report on the activity to date is given by the vice-chairman of the board, Mr. L. Rubinlicht, who characterises in the light of figures the bank's activity in the year under report. Mr. Rubinlicht stresses that the bank has, as usual, fulfilled its obligations towards the depositors, the bank having punctually paid out a sum of nearly 400 thousand zł.
In his further report Mr. R. explains that because of the withdrawn capital the bank was forced to conduct a limited credit activity.
The report of the supervisory council is given by Mr. M. Gold. The reporter states that the balance sheet presented by the board is correct according to the books, but the balance sheet — says Mr. Gold — has been drawn up too optimistically, because in the present situation various losses may occur which the board did not seriously take into account when compiling the balance. Especially as this balance sheet was ready 4 months ago and in that time the situation has become much worse; therefore Mr. G. proposes that the general meeting resolve to send the balance sheet back to the board, so that it may draw it up anew according to today's actual situation, and afterwards convene a general meeting again to approve the balance sheet.
A discussion develops on this proposal, in which Messrs. Grünwald, Bornsztajn, Pinkusson [?], Najmark, Fridman and Krajzler took part.
After Mr. Tenenbaum's reply the proposal is adopted unanimously.
The meeting also dealt with the question of merging all the cooperative banks in Będzin.
This item was adopted unanimously without discussion, and the board and council were authorised to conduct negotiations in that direction.
Owing to the critical situation, this year's budget was reduced by one quarter compared with 1931. The bank's entire budget for 1932 amounts to 18 thousand zł.
The supplementary elections brought no change whatsoever, and the members serving until now were re-elected.

the following presidium is elected: Hofer (Parwicer [?]), Szwarcbaum (Będzin), Kornfeld (Miechów), Krak (Częstochowa), Miss Pardes (Zawiercie), Unger (Olkusz), Rozencwajg (Sosnowiec); secretaries: Blat (Miechów) and Rozenberg (Zawiercie).
The following papers are delivered: Keren Tel-Hai — Józef Dafner [?]; Keren Kayemet — Chaim Szriger [?]; youth problems — Efraim Jasny; Totzeret ha-Aretz (local produce) — Dawid Feldbaum; and on the [—] and the emigration cooperative — Białobrów (Warsaw). The last paper aroused great interest, because according to the "plan" emigration to Eretz Israel is made possible for the middle class, the artisans and the youth.
A. Landner (Będzin) gives a longer paper on "Keren Hayesod", calling on the conference to intensify work for the fund.
After the papers, reports were given by the individual branches and discussions were held on the papers delivered. Taking part in the debate were: Turner (Będzin), Unger (Dąbrowa), Kornfeld (Miechów), Rozenberg (Zawiercie), Śpiewak (Strzemieszyce), Rajzman (Sosnowiec) and others. In the evening there took place the
festive academy
before a packed hall. The head of Keren Kayemet in Poland, Mr. A. L. Bloch, gives an interesting paper on land policy in Eretz Israel, on the village economy and middle-class colonisation. He appeals to the delegates to follow the example of Sosnowiec, where Betar and the Revisionists hold first place in Keren Kayemet work. Miss Szulamit Dralicz [?] gives a substantive paper on the task of women in social and political life and on the Jewish woman in the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. The speaker holds that the Jewish woman must not remain indifferent to the political situation in Zionism; she therefore proposes creating Revisionist women's circles. Mr. Klarman speaks on the Hebrew movement in the Diaspora and in Eretz Israel and on the institution that encompasses the whole Hebrew movement, and appeals for enrolment in "Brit Ivrit Olamit" by redeeming the "sela" (membership shekel). In an elevated mood and with the singing of Hatikvah the academy was closed.
Late at night the last session took place, at which various resolutions were put forward and a plan was worked out for broader activity in the Kielce region, covering Totzeret ha-Aretz, the emigration cooperative, Keren Kayemet, Keren Tel-Hai, Brit Ivrit Olamit, Betar and others.

Suicide of a Young Couple.
The 23-year-old Szczepiński in Sosnowiec was in love with the 21-year-old Miss Flak [?]. Because Szczepiński had been laid off from his work, the couple had no possibility of setting up on their own. Last Tuesday the couple in love went for a walk in the Ząbkowice forest. After a long conversation they agreed to commit suicide. The bridegroom, who, as it turns out, had come prepared for this plan, took two small bottles of vinegar out of his pocket; one little bottle he offered to the bride, and the other — to himself...

Paid 14 zł. for a Parcel of "Forverts".
A certain Sosnowiec resident of Ciasna Street received before the holiday a notice from the post office to come and collect a registered-value parcel. When he came to the post office, however, he was told that he had to pay 14 zł. customs duty for a piece of linen contained in the parcel.
The Jew, no small pauper, barely managed to scrape together the 14 zł. by borrowing from acquaintances and went to collect the gift from his American uncle.
But when he opened the parcel, everything went dark before his eyes. There lay several dozen copies of the "Forverts" [the New York Yiddish daily], wrapped in a piece of linen.
The customs office had assessed the whole parcel not as paper but as linen.
Now the Jew complains — when he could have borrowed a couple of złotys for the holiday, he has used up his credit on this loan.

Take Advantage of the Reliefs When Paying Tax Arrears.
As is known, the Ministry of Finance has issued a circular (okólnik) which provides reliefs of up to 60 per cent on tax arrears; taxpayers also enjoy reliefs with regard to interest and enforcement costs.

“In polish oyf der keyt” (“In the Vestibule, on the Chain” — a kloyznik's dream), dramatic poem in 3 acts by I. L. Peretz. Staged by the Drama Society “Muze” in Będzin. Staging and direction: Nachum Melnik; set design: Y. Cigler; dances: Dvora Rozenblum; music: M. Kaner.
Drama occupies an important place in Peretz's work and years of laborious effort. Nevertheless Peretz's dramas were not crowned with the same success as his novellas, ballads and poems. Peretz's greatness, which consists in expressing the sharpest idea in a 50-line novella, in saying the sharpest thought in a few polished words free of every kind of florid phrase, did not, despite the greatest efforts, enable him to write a larger novel. More correctly put: he could not spin out[?] the content. Understandably the drama suffered from this, which demands endurance and time; with Peretz it came out overloaded with ideas, and its main idea basically runs counter to the ABC of building a drama. A drama demands one main idea, a backbone, a ground line from beginning to end, which should be the axis around which ideas of secondary importance can be brought forward[?].
Of all Peretz's dramas the exception is “In polish oyf der keyt”, which has a fundamental idea from beginning to end, aiming at sexual liberation, with a secondary idea of liberation from capitalism and religion.
The content: a kloyznik, one of the great mass who dream of air and free sexual movement[?], falls in love with the daughter of the town's rich man and moneylender, Reb Berakhia. The love is mutual. Berakhia knows nothing of it and makes a match with one of his own kind. On the wedding day, when all the guests have already gathered and the in-laws with the groom are ready for the chuppah, the kloyznik bursts into the synagogue and proclaims that he and Berakhia's daughter are a destined pair, bound by what is called love. A tumult breaks out. The in-laws and the groom go home. At that moment Berakhia's daughter comes running and denies what the kloyznik has said (for her father's sake). For staining the name of a pious Jewish daughter the kloyznik is punished by being chained[?] for a day and a night in the vestibule, on the chain. Householders and artisans oppressed by Berakhia come to free him. They do not free him. In the middle of the night Berakhia's daughter comes and says:
Forgive...
For a moment I denied you
Because of father's white head
Because of mother's sick heart,
And frightened by shame and disgrace!
Sinner, answer:
No!
Berakhia's daughter:
Where to?
I have left my husband's bed,
Gone away from my stepmother's[?] house...
The sinner:
To the river, to the river...
Try[?] to wash yourself clean
Try[?] to wash yourself clean.
Berakhia's daughter drowns herself in the river. The kloyznik is freed by a person spat upon, insulted like himself — the woman of the street. Thus comes sexual liberation together with revenge for desecrated love. Interesting here is that the madman does not let the rabbi put the chain on him, but rather the town madman, who appears in the play as a vanguard of the exploited mass.
* * *
Alongside the main idea of sexual liberation, the idea of liberating the burghers (householders and artisans) is brought in[?]; protests[?] are heard which end in mere words.
* * *
What is director Melnik's conception?
Melnik blurred Peretz's basic idea of sexual liberation and brought forward (rightly) the more important idea of social liberation. The conception was properly[?] worked out, and what came out of it was a liberation of the petty bourgeoisie. Besides that, Peretz's main theme, sexual liberation, became strongly blurred and led in some[?] scenes to a lack of clarity in the direction. With Melnik it is also not understandable why the kloyznik lets himself be locked in chains by the madman and in the end the same madman frees him from the chains — a moment which in Peretz is quite clear.
* * *
The debut of “Muze” turned out on the whole quite successful. Although there is much to reproach in the direction of the first act, which was thrown together chaotically and is poor in composition. Mr. Melnik was out of place in the role of the kloyznik, [—][?] and stiff. The same can be said of a considerable number of participants. On the other hand Mr. Palewa[?] Szymon (the madman), Krakowier, Lala[?] Fiszer and [—] were successful. And the dances of Dvora Rozenblum were aptly fitted in; the sets of Mr. Cigler — more than modest; the music of Mr. Kaner — successful.
On the whole a performance of high seriousness and artistic value. It is only a pity that the performance was staged by amateurs and in... Będzin. The Będzin “better” theatre public, especially the proletarian one, meets its artistic aspirations with “Binke Pinke”[?], “Pintele Yid” and other “pintelekh”.
Yisroel Tojman.

Regulations of the Będzin Kehilla administration concerning order in the synagogue.
1) Whoever has no seat on the Eastern Wall has no right to occupy any seat [there].
2) Every father must keep his child beside him.
3) No talking during prayer. Whoever does not obey will be led out.
4) The aisle in the synagogue must be kept free.
5) Nobody may go up onto the bimah, except those who keep order.
6) Nobody has the right to call [anyone] to lead the prayers[?] except those on the commission confirmed by the Kehilla administration.
7) Whoever does not pay for pledges (nedarim) will not receive an aliyah...

What every taxpayer must know about appeals against the turnover tax.
The last deadline for filing appeals against the assessment of turnover tax for the year 1931 expires on 15 May of this year.
Before filing the appeal every taxpayer should apply to the tax office and request oral (or also written) explanations of the grounds on which the turnover in question was assessed.
The amendment to the law, in force since 1 January 1932, provides this right to interested taxpayers in Art. 80.
In the appeal every taxpayer concerned may demand, on the basis of Art. 98, to be summoned[?] before the appeals commission to give oral explanations when his appeal is considered.
If any taxpayer has not received the tax assessment notice (nakaz), he must turn to the tax office about it at once. The responsibility for this rests solely with the taxpayer, who will thereby miss the deadline for filing an appeal in case he is penalised[?].
The final deadline for paying the assessed tax expires on 15 May of this year. Within 14 days, until 29 May, one can pay without costs (interest) for the delay. Distraints (zajęcia) can indeed be carried out by the tax office within these 14 days.
Every taxpayer can also submit a request to limit the enforcement to the sum he stated in the appeal, until the final settlement of the appeal.
*
As we are informed, the turnover-tax assessments for 1931 are higher than for 1930.
In this connection the economic organisations are collecting material; on the basis of all the material collected and concrete facts, a memorandum will be drawn up to the Fiscal Chamber. It is therefore desirable that all taxpayers concerned turn to their associations as soon as possible.

A Bloody First of May in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — May Day.]
2 killed. — Many wounded, among them 17 policemen.
The First of May in Zagłębie passed stormily. From early morning it was evident everywhere that mass demonstrations were forming.
In Sosnowiec the communists, 600 strong, demonstrated on Piłsudskiego Street, from where they went on to Teatralna Street, where they wanted to hold a meeting. Foot and mounted police soon arrived and dispersed the crowd.
Later a communist procession formed at the railway station. When the police reacted to it, several revolver shots were heard from the side of the demonstration, fired at the police; but thanks to the quick action of the police no bloody events occurred. One of the senior police sergeants (przodowniks) was hit in the face by a stone, from which he fainted. Several dozen persons who took part in the demonstration were arrested.
In Będzin, the Right and Left „Poale Zion“ demonstrated in larger masses. The latter marched through the town to the sounds of their own orchestra. The demonstration passed off quietly. When a speaker of the Right P. Z. began to speak Yiddish at a meeting, heckling shouts of „Do Palestyny!“ [Polish: „To Palestine!“] were heard from the crowd.
Serious events with human casualties took place in Dębowa Góra (near Niwka). After the police had broken up a communist demonstration, the communists Borda and Parszyk[?] were found killed in their dwellings. A certain Stanisława Naga was also seriously wounded. Several policemen were slightly wounded.
In Strzemieszyce, too, it came to bloody clashes between demonstrators and police, which had the following results: several of the crowd were seriously wounded. There are wounded on the police side as well.
In Olkusz a workers' demonstration took place, as every year. An Open Letter to the Będzin Rabbinate and Kehilla Leaders.

[Będzin — the old cemetery; an open letter.]
During the last Chol HaMoed of Passover, when the historian Dr. Schiper visited our town, he expressed his wish to visit, among other antiquities, also the old local cemetery. Wishing to fulfil his wish, I took him to the cemetery „under the hill“. But as we came close to the walls, everything went dark before our eyes on seeing its lamentable, sad outward appearance. The walls — as if after a bombardment by heavy artillery — crumbling[?] ruins; then every few steps an artificial passage leading inside, which is used for their dirty purposes by all kinds of outcasts of the underworld. But all this is as nothing [lit. „as the peel of garlic“] compared with what goes on inside. We stepped through an artificial passage and had barely gone a few steps when we stood stock-still in astonishment and a shudder went through us, seeing the terrible, sad picture, and we simply did not believe our own eyes.
Hear and be amazed! On the hill above the cemetery there is a channel through which all kinds of filth flows, and the opening of this channel is turned directly towards the cemetery, and the filth pours onto the graves with their tombstones, so that it is almost impossible to walk across this area.
The question arises: how can such a desecration of the holy be permitted? Where is the rabbinate, where are the kehilla leaders and where is the Chevra Kadisha? Can we imagine that among any nation and tongue such a thing could happen? And especially among Jews, for whom a cemetery is called „the pure place“, and above all in such a „city and mother in Israel“ as Będzin?
Why, only a short while ago we protested vehemently and raised an uproar when Romanian hooligans desecrated a cemetery and when Hitlerites defiled tombstones — and here we ourselves allow such a terrible desecration and defilement of a cemetery where the bones of thousands of Jews rest, among them rabbis, tzaddikim and martyrs. Woe for that shame and woe for that disgrace!
And one more question to the rabbinate: the law is, after all, that „one who enters a cemetery recites the blessing ‚Who created you in judgment' etc. etc.“ — and with God's name and kingship. So how may one recite a blessing in such a place, and can there be any greater „mocking of the poor [i.e. the dead]“ than this? On the contrary — rule on the question!
Finally, a few words to the Herciger family.
You, whose grandfather was the Rabbi of Będzin and whose bones now rest under the „ohel“ in this very cemetery — how can you tolerate that he who should be your honour and pride should have his bones resting in a place where filth constantly pours?...
Y. Wygodzki.

The Zionist District Conference in Będzin.*)

[Będzin — Zionism; district conference.] On Sunday of Chol HaMoed [Passover; 24 April 1932] the Zionist conference of the Będzin—Częstochowa district was opened in Będzin. The conference was opened by Mr. Yitzchak Wygodzki[?], who greeted the delegates and especially the guests from the Central Committee (C.C.) in Warsaw, Messrs. Dr. Schiper [Ignacy Schiper], editor Goldberg and Ch. Bloch.
The conference was greeted on behalf of the Będzin kehilla, the KKL [Jewish National Fund], "Tarbut" and "Hakoach" Będzin, the Sosnowiec kehilla, the Zawiercie kehilla, Keren Hayesod, and the Częstochowa and Zawiercie Zionist associations. A telegram of greeting was also sent from Paris by Deputy Grünbaum [Icchak Grünbaum], which read: "From afar I wish you fruitful work."
After the greetings Dr. Schiper takes the floor and delivers a very rich two-hour lecture on the situation of the Jews in Poland. He gives a survey of the development of the Jewish question in Poland from the emergence of the new Poland to the present day, and of the attitude of the Sanacja to the Jews, and in particular to the Wiślickis and Mincbergs. "We," says the speaker, "were ready to support the government, but we demanded deeds, proof that the attitude to the Jews had changed. We do not want to be put off with the answer that the government is afraid of public opinion. People who had the courage to cross the Poniatowski Bridge must not be afraid either to step down from the paper bridge of fine words" (loud applause).
In conclusion the speaker calls on the assembly to continue the stubborn struggle for Jewish rights.
Then editor Goldberg gives a lecture on the Land of Israel. The speaker touches on the yearning of the Jews of the Diaspora to be able to come to the Land of Israel. The most important point is therefore[?] the question of aliyah, of emigration possibilities for the broadest Jewish masses.
The afternoon session opens with the election of a presidium. The following are elected: Messrs. Rozman (Sosnowiec), Gutman (Zawiercie), Kestenberg (Niwka), Gelbart and Liwer (Będzin), and Mr. Fajgenbaum (Częstochowa) as secretary.
Dr. Schiper gives a major lecture on kehilla affairs. The speaker remarks that it is a characteristic phenomenon that precisely at a time of political decline the kehilla problem has become as gripping as a novel — and that is no accident. Jews are waging a hard struggle for their existence. To make them forget that struggle, they are supplied from outside with a gripping kehilla spectacle.
When we fight the Aguda [Agudas Israel] we must remember that we are aiming our arrows further, right up into the high windows. It is no secret to anyone that the Aguda represents no force whatsoever; it is the tool with which the attack against us is being waged. And we must withstand this attack, which is directed at clericalizing the kehillas.
We are being "favoured" with various kehilla laws and new ordinances that turn the whole kehilla into a heap of ruins and make its existence impossible. Even the ringleaders of the Aguda are now running to the "poretz" [the lord, i.e. the authorities] with an outcry, asking that the ordinances not be introduced.
No wonder, then, that in such a situation the question of our withdrawal from the kehillas is constantly topical. It was resolved to convene a special meeting of Zionist kehilla councillors (parnasim) in order to take a position on this question.
Messrs. Asz, editor Goldberg and Rogoziński also speak on the youth and organization question.
Mr. Rogoziński complains about the attitude toward the youth. The youth department develops almost no activity at all. Mr. Natan Asz complains strongly about the state of the organizations in the Będzin—Częstochowa district. He demands that more attention be given to this problem and that the importance of the organization be understood.
On the same matter editor Goldberg speaks again, saying that as many people as possible must be drawn into the Zionist ranks in order to be able to create a Jewish state.
After Mr. Bloch's lecture on the upbuilding of Eretz Israel and the KKL, the delegates give reports on their organizations. The reports are very sad; everywhere neglect of the work prevails.
A discussion develops in which all the delegates take part.
The proposal to create a regional committee is, because of the difference of opinion, handed over to the C.C. to decide.
With the singing of "Hatikvah" the conference is closed at 5 in the morning in an elevated mood.

Luxury Pensions and Hunger Pensions / The Gesture of the Zawiercie Rabbi — the Course Must Be Continued

[Opinion — the economic crisis and pensions in the kehillot; followed by a short item from Dąbrowa.]
... and the times are bad, and about the prospects for the future it is better to keep silent; one does not want to think about them, for not a single ray of light appears; everything is so veiled, shrouded in a thick fog that shows only signs of hardship and darkness and enormous suffering.
And worse still is that we do not see how, and in what way, an improvement could come about. The "whence shall my help come" is heavily clouded; not the tiniest ray of light breaks out of the deep darkness. This grave situation fills mankind with fear, for whom it is so hard to win for itself a secure and finer tomorrow, in which it would know the purpose of life, the purpose of a peaceful existence.
It is not only we Jews who find ourselves in such a state, and not only in the country where we live; everywhere the situation is so strained and everywhere mankind suffers. Since the war one has still not managed to get onto the straight line, and not only can one not reach it — the nearer[?] one seems to be to it, the further away it is. Quite often we thought that now, any moment, the goal had been reached, that now, any moment, we had made our way to the right line — and meanwhile it was no more than a dream, an illusion.
And as badly off as mankind is throughout the world, worse still — it goes without saying — are we Jews, who like every weak creature are the first to begin suffering immediately[?], for the slightest wind can overturn us, the calmest little stream can wash us off the surface.
It is therefore no wonder that our inner Jewish life is so poor in every field, that the greatest, most impossible impossibilities are possible among us, and however fantastic and legendary they may look, they are everyday real phenomena to which we at once grow accustomed and which give the impression of the most self-evident things.
Thus, for example, it is impossible to understand how our Jewish kehilla administrations can run such an abnormal, reckless economy. No account is taken of the fact that the members are ruined and broken and are in no position to pay the burdensome taxes; and barely — whoever must be done a favour for the sake of politics, it is right to smuggle in another shochet, another moreh hora'ah and another ne'eman; whether it serves the cause is of course beside the point. And of course on that account the budget will later have to be increased, the slaughter fees will have to be raised, new sources of income will have to be sought. For when one enlarges the [body of] religious functionaries, one must surely also, when the time comes, be able to give them pensions; and with that, with that one takes no account of the hard times, of the critical situation; there is barely any money in the till — one turns where one must, and of course after such interventions the pensions must be paid out without any "why".
And therefore, when we read a few days ago[?] a note from Zawiercie that the local rabbi had asked that, because of the crisis, his pension of 600 zł. a month be reduced to 400 zł., this is a fine deed — all the more so when we bear in mind that the pension is not such a large one to begin with. Such a phenomenon is to be welcomed; here we see good will to help ease the economic system in the Jewish kehillot. The deed shows us that the rabbi shares the hard situation of the masses and is set on not allowing the prestige of Jewish kehilla life to be debased; he is willing to sacrifice himself, if only to save the economy, which is meant to be maintained by the whole Jewish community.
When one sees[?] that it is dark and hard and no way out appears as to how it will become light — precisely at such a moment one must sacrifice oneself, in order to bring in a little revival, a little cheerfulness.
The world says: one swallow does not make a summer. Of course that is so, but this is a fine gesture by a spiritual leader, and others may follow his example; it is possible that this will, even if only minimally, ease the difficult situation in our kehilla life — and that is already a great thing.
Let us thereby show the authorities that we help ourselves according to our possibilities, according to our strength, and this may lead others to follow the example too. And a course will be set of cutting back, on our own, unnecessary expenditure, whereby the life of the broad strata of the masses can be eased.
First of all our public officials must come forward — those who have excessive pensions, and of whom there are enough[?] in various fields — and as an expression of sympathy with the masses they must demand that their high pensions be reduced, so that those who have no more than a piece of dry bread for themselves and their households need not be harmed. Instead of cutting back such people, who would then have to take their own lives, it is surely wiser that they should find their work, for which they would be paid out of the reduced excessive pensions.
There are factories where the directors draw legendary pensions, and these very directors harm the workers, who are driven to take their own lives because they have nothing with which to support themselves and their families. So why should the directors not say to themselves: we will give up a lavish life and come to the aid of thousands of workers, so that they may be able to provide for their families.
And then let the government come and let it too carry out a revision of its own house and help ease the life and existence of the citizens, at a time when such a dreadful crisis prevails and no prospects appear of how it might be alleviated.
It too must carry out a course of reductions, and [in] its monopoly articles, which belong to the basic necessities — and let it show that it is thinking about and taking measures to come to the aid of its citizens in the prevailing worst situation in which the whole country finds itself.
All public institutions that deal with economic questions must set about organising courses of reduction — not by making the citizens unemployed, but by giving them the opportunity to earn and to spend little. To this end the prices of light, water, housing, taxes and all other public expenses must be reduced; the official and semi-official bodies too must set about carrying out the necessary projects, which will undoubtedly bring relief in the economic field.
Nowadays there is surely no need to say how terrible the situation and the system are: whoever is unemployed obviously earns nothing, and the others, who trade and work on their own account, earn nothing either, because without cash one can do nothing; so that when one sees[?] that a gulden costs [dear], one sells at any price, and since one earns nothing on the goods it is self-evident that one eats up the few gulden, and there is no more money for other goods.
Therefore there is no other way out than to change, to economise the system of present-day life: one should spend less, earn less and be responsible for every transaction, so that no further recklessness sets in — things are demoralised enough already.
Measures must be adopted by which the question of reducing excessive pensions will be regulated, so that people need not have their bread-pensions reduced.
R. Let.
