He blushed with shame — Historical understanding. Antiquities and sanctities. The responsibility of the rabbinate and the kehilla councillors

Historical understanding. — Antiquities and sanctities. — The responsibility of the rabbinate and of the kehilla councillors.
Last week we had the opportunity to read in our newspaper an open letter to the Będzin rabbinate from councillor (parnas) Wygodzki, who tells us that when Dr. Schiper was here in Będzin not long ago, he happened to visit an old cemetery, and it was a disgrace for the historian to see in what a sad and shameful state the cemetery is.
Comrade Wygodzki relates several dreadful facts which must not be tolerated, and comes to the conclusion that the rabbinate and the Chevra Kadisha must take an interest in the question and must see to it that our martyrs and our forefathers can rest peacefully in their graves.
Councillor Wygodzki blushed with shame when he wanted to show his guest our historic sanctities. Of course it is a disgrace and a pain to look at the conditions under which our historians have to work and from what sources they must draw their material, which is being perpetuated for coming generations. But it is a rare thing how naive Mr. Wygodzki is when he demands that the rabbinate should fulfil this mission. What interest do they have in this matter, what connection do they have with what is already past? What material benefit can it bring to the present?
Yes, for him it was a disgrace, when he had a guest and wanted to show him something; only then was he disappointed — and what should we say, who very often find ourselves in such unpleasant situations? A Jewish writer, a thinker, an intellectual, a man of science comes to Będzin; first of all he wants to tour the town — to whom does he turn? Naturally, he takes his first step into a Jewish editorial office. If there is a Jewish editorial office, a newspaper — so we hear from these persons — they come to us, and from us, after all, they have the right to demand what they need. Yes, we are already used to blushing with shame during our 'visits'. Of course we often want to wriggle out of this very unpleasant situation, but we rarely succeed; it only looks as though the writer of these lines is unfriendly to his guest, and in the end his request must be fulfilled.
[Anumelt(?)] such a Jew has a complaint: Good heavens, you are a murderer, a pen-bandit! When I finally come for once, for the first time in my life, to a town like Będzin, a very old town, a 'city and mother in Israel', which I have so longed to see, and to view everything you have — all your riches and sanctities, historic and present — you treat all of this with so much apathy, with such levity? It is unheard of to show such unfriendliness to a person who is interested in all this, who has so much love and respect and holiness and reverence for all of it.
Go and tell such a Jew with what a heavy heart one has to make such visits, and what a grim impression it makes on the visitor.
Yes, we know what these visits smell of, and what a verdict we catch afterwards from the visitor, how disappointed he becomes, when an hour earlier he had a different opinion of the town and of the people. If we manage not to show such a guest the town, he still leaves with the same illusion and with the good opinion he had before; but wriggling out of such a visit is, to tell the truth, a very rare thing — and you understand, of course, that the holiness is then profaned and the beautiful illusion turns into a soap bubble.
And what do we have to show of which one need not blush with shame? Do we have a beautiful antique, or a modern hygienically equipped mikvah — which our rabbinate perhaps really should have cared for in the first place, and which has already cost the town so much money — do we possess such a building? Of course not. But to tell the truth, it is not right when we say that we do not possess one. If we had no mikvah at all, private people would come and build such institutions from a business standpoint, and there would be somewhere to go; but as it is, everyone keeps thinking that the municipal mikvah is about to be completed — so neither does anyone do anything himself, nor is the possibility given for private individuals to build such an institution.
Shall we show such a guest this 'antique' mikvah of ours? Or shall we show him our Talmud Torahs, shuls and batei midrash, and in what a sad state they are — with the exception of the town synagogue?
Yes, and one is reminded of this every time one merely happens to speak of the Będzin synagogue: under what conditions it was renovated and what stumbling-blocks were laid in the way of the 'clean-shaven beardies' by the Agudah people. Who does not remember how they turned worlds upside down then; terrible things happened then, so much did the renovation of the synagogue hurt them — the synagogue which today is an ornament not only for Będzin but for all of Poland. When connoisseurs come here, at least they have something to look at and to express their opinions about.
Those very people who trembled so much lest the 'sinners' finish the synagogue so that it would look like a holy place — it did not bother them at all that when a holiday came and the children of the schools were taken into the synagogue, we were ashamed to tell our children that this ruin was a holy place and that representatives of the authorities had come there; each time our heart was surely stained with shame. But they, the true Jews, the 'Jewish Jews', did not care about any of it, and the rabbinate certainly, certainly not; and that it does not concern them in the least one can see from the fact that the mikvah which they took on lease they have been building for years, and to this day it is an egg not yet laid...
And in what condition is the beit midrash today? Is it not a real ruin? Is it not dark and filthy there, so that it drives one out? A holy place belongs, after all, to the Torah-faithful, in whose hands the rabbinate is — so why should they desecrate its holiness? Is a beit midrash not a holy place? Is this not a [sin?] for 'Jewish Jews'?
Yes, what we see at every step, what pricks our eyes day in, day out, councillor Wygodzki saw once, when he had a guest, and then he was ashamed; he blushed with shame — while for us it is an everyday phenomenon, we meet it in our everyday life.
Of course it is comical when a councillor says this to the rabbinate, while in reality our councillors bear no less obligation than the rabbinate. But if they come and say: we have been disarmed, they do not let us do anything — that too is an incomprehensible answer for kehilla councillors. In that case it must be one way or the other: either one becomes active, or, if not, one dissolves oneself. To remain helpless and to stand there like a statue is certainly not consistent.
Councillor Wygodzki's appeal to the rabbinate, that he blushes with shame, sounds paradoxical in the ears of a simple Jewish citizen. From anyone else we might have heard the said accusation, but by no means whatsoever from a councillor, who should have no fewer duties than the rabbinate.
R. Les.
Clever, Clever — and Fools Himself!...

By Pini Baal-Lashon.

In Yiddish they say:
"Clever, clever — and makes a fool of himself!"
In the language of the Gemara it says:
— "Lefum ḥurfa shabeshta!" [The sharper the wit, the greater the blunder.]

And if all these sayings were said about ordinary people, then they fit us, the seed of Abraham our Father, even more than anyone else.

For why should we deny it: we are, after all, a clever people, a "seasoned, shrewd people" — but when it comes to something real, we make fools of ourselves.

We always want to show that we love the whole world so much; only ourselves we do not love.

We always have more respect and give more honour to a "small gentile" than to a "great Jew" — and not just to one great Jew, but to many great Jews.

So it was in our old "backward once-upon-a-time", and so it is in our new "progressive today".

* * *

It really is a remarkable thing with us:

All the world's questions we Jews try to answer. For all the puzzles of all the nations on earth we try to find solutions. We devote to it our best strength and brains. And only when it comes to our own questions — we are left outside [?]!

For everyone we have sense, and only for ourselves there is nobody at home.

Need one go looking far? — Here is the very old question that the world asks:

— Why is our people hated more than all other peoples? Certainly, nations and tongues in general do not love one another. One doesn't even need signs or proofs for that. What one nation wishes the other is that it may fall into the sea.

But when it comes to our people, it seems all the nations would form a partnership so as to be able to hate us more strongly — just as once upon a time Midian and Moab made peace in order to strike at the Jews.

Usually, one must admit, there are degrees of Jew-hatred in every nation. With one it is at a low degree, with another at a higher one, and with another at a very high one. But all of them, from the most civilized to the most backward, hate us.

An old question, you say? — Yes, certainly!

But where is the answer? The wise think that as long as we do not all try to understand and remember the right answer, the question will remain forever new.

Some trifle! A little word to draw [?]: that from Pharaoh's times to Hitler's times it is all the same story with "Come, let us deal wisely" [Exodus 1:10].

They hate us and hate us and seek means to drive us off the globe, which the gentiles have talked themselves into believing belongs to them alone.

Yes, people have pondered enough and found explanations: religion, nation, race, economics, social status and suchlike — because we are different from others, and therefore we cannot be tolerated.

But it doesn't hold! That is not it!

The hatred toward us began with Jesus and did not end with Trotsky...

But never mind: what the nations are guilty of here, they are guilty of; them we cannot change — unless the Messiah comes and brings the true portion of sense, and "the earth shall be full of knowledge" [Isaiah 11:9]...

How can we expect anyone else to love us when we do not love ourselves? How can we please others when we are not pleased with ourselves? What is our own is no good in our eyes, and what is foreign has a thousand charms for us!

And therefore we do not seek to beautify what is ours, but throw it away altogether and grab at what is foreign.

One of ours, a Jew, will disguise himself even as a Red Indian, so long as nobody recognizes the Jew in him...

One of ours, a Jew, will torture himself to speak even Gypsy, so long as nobody hears his Yiddish...

A whole congregation of Jews among us can fall on its knees before one gentile, and they will all torment themselves "voluntarily" to speak his language.

Even where the gentile does not torment us, we torment ourselves for the gentile's sake.

When Jews celebrate any happy occasion whatsoever, the invitations are sent out not in Yiddish. And the speeches are not in Yiddish either! And why, do you think? Just because of a couple of gentiles!

Now here is the question: has it ever happened anywhere in the world that gentiles celebrating an occasion of their own would speak Yiddish because a couple of Jews would be present? Never!

With them it won't happen — foolish gentiles! With us, though, it happens often and practically always — clever Jews!

* * *

A nice anecdote is told about a Jewish censor in Russia in former times.

The Jewish censor wanted to show the government how patriotic he was, so he would not pass a single Jewish book with the word "goy" in it. Wherever "goy" stood, he replaced it with the word "akum", meaning "idolaters of old".

Meanwhile they brought him prayer books to censor. The Jewish censor looked them over and found there the terrible words: "Guardian of the holy nation [goy], let not the holy nation [goy] perish" — at once he grabbed the red ink and wrote there: "Guardian of the holy idolaters [akum], let not the holy idolaters [akum] perish"...

And so he satisfied the "goy"...

* * *

And for those to whom the censor anecdote is too harsh, I'll tell another, a little softer one, from our own shtetl.

The rich man's daughter got married. He intended, as the custom is, to invite all the Jews of the town; but there were also in the shtetl a pristav [police chief] and an aktsiznik [excise official]. So the rich man hit upon an idea: if he printed Hebrew "tickets" [invitations], as all Jews do, the two gentiles would not understand — so he went and printed the invitations in Russian: "Po sluchayu brakosochetaniya" [On the occasion of the marriage] and so forth.

And literally the whole shtetl was offended by the gentile invitations and refused to go to the wedding.

But he did satisfy his gentiles!

* * *

Yes, my dear Jews and colleagues, we are a clever people. And that is why we make fools of ourselves so often.

Why shouldn't it happen so, as it happens.

Upper Silesian Economic Sketches

[Upper Silesia — economy and trade; article, part 1.] By Dr. Abraham Szajer [?], Katowice.
1) Trade.
From the time of the "good" inflation and after the inflation years, Upper Silesia had the reputation of an economic paradise. And indeed, from the moment Poland took over Upper Silesia until the year 1929 things were very good in Silesia, especially in Katowice — not only did people not feel the crisis that was beginning in the other parts of the country, but business was genuinely good.
As in other industrial centres, here too the crisis arrived suddenly. Without a mild autumn came the dreadful winter — the severe crisis in its full force. Incidentally, the same thing happened in Łódź after the inflation years.
Proof of the good business of the earlier years in Silesia was the well-developed "instalment trade" as well as peddling. Thousands of people travelled about with all kinds of goods through the workers' colonies, through towns and villages densely inhabited by miners ("górnicy") from the various smelting works [huty] and zinc works [cynkownie] and other giant enterprises that employ thousands and even tens of thousands of people. All goods sold in bulk, and on the first and the fifteenth of every month the instalments flowed in punctually. Eventually, in many cases, the instalments were deducted straight from the worker's earnings at the "wypłata" [pay-out] for a minimal commission, which the collector received. The so-called "raciarze" [instalment dealers] were, in the wholesale trade of all branches, the best customers, and since they paid quite large sums for the goods they bought, they gradually built up large credits and even bank credits.
But with the growing unemployment in heavy industry, on which this whole branch [?] of trade relied, the non-payment by the cut-back ["reduced"], or lower-earning, workers and employees begins, the result of which is that the "raciarze" have stopped paying.
—·—
The retail shops in Silesia, and chiefly in Katowice, are fitted out with an elegance and luxury unmatched in all of Poland, with splendid and beautiful display windows. That is precisely why they feel the crisis much more strongly than in other parts of the country, because the costs of trade are much greater here. A retail merchant, no matter in which branch, does not understand how one could fail to change the decorations in the window thoroughly at least once a month. He installs costly display fittings, electric lamps of hundreds of candlepower, equipped with reflectors; he engages a decorator, a specially trained one, who subscribes to foreign trade journals — and so he sets up splendid display windows which here take up almost as much space as a whole shop in Sosnowiec or in another Polish town.
Rent here is horrendously high: 15 and even 20 thousand złoty a year. The accessories for the novelties [?] and trained staff, paid according to the rate fixed by the trade unions, are also no small expense. It is therefore no wonder that the existence of the businesses is very hard today, because even while cutting expenses it is hard to bear them on account of the small turnover of goods, the small profit and the unheard-of high tax burden.
———
Wholesale trade, which before Poland took over Silesia was developed one-sidedly — that is, only those branches that had a connection with the local industry (chiefly supplies for the smelting works and coal mines) — only developed when [printed "שען"] Katowice and other large towns here acquired — through the creation of the Silesian Voivodeship — greater importance, which concerns first and foremost Katowice as the Silesian metropolis.
So a whole series of wholesale houses [hurtownie] of all sorts of branches came into being, larger import enterprises, employing whole crowds of dispatch clerks and officials. Wholesale trade here, however, has no specific character at all, except perhaps a more modern organisation on the Western model than in the other parts of the country. But many respected firms have been brought to ruin by the crisis. Non-payments and "bites" [?] have become normal, and various liquidations are unfortunately on the agenda.
———
Even today Silesia gives a visitor who is not acquainted with local conditions the impression of a land flowing with milk and honey, a land full of life. The movement is truly enormous, the tempo of life — American, and Katowice, the capital of Silesia, develops and grows at a very fast pace. Having had, after the Polish takeover, somewhat more than 50 thousand inhabitants, Katowice now counts over 130 thousand people. That is, in 10 years an enormous influx of people. All of Silesia, as well as the neighbouring "Dąbrowa Zagłębie" [Zagłębie Dąbrowskie], travels to Katowice. The intercity trams are always overcrowded, and the railway station, situated in the very centre of the town, spews out whole crowds of people all day long, coming to the proud capital of Silesia.
The movement grows chiefly in the morning, at midday and in the evening, when the pupils, office workers, stenotypists etc. arrive or leave for the neighbouring places. Unfortunately, though, amid all this bustle the shops stand empty; only the confectioneries [cukiernie] and the places of entertainment are always overcrowded with guests from the surrounding "provinces", eager for amusement.
———
So much for the outward appearance of trade. About the innermost relations, about the less joyful and more painful questions of Silesian trade — in the second article. (Sz.)
Katowice, in May.
Sounds of the Day

[Feuilleton — everyday life in Zagłębie; economic crisis.]
Sefirah Days.
The holidays are over already — the Jewish, the international and the Polish-national ones. The grey, long, monotonous days and weeks are beginning. For Jews it is now the Sefirah period: no celebrations may take place now, one may not put on new clothes. Days of mourning. And yet precisely the Sefirah days always awakened so many hopes. The beginning of spring. And in perspective?
A long summer. Now it is gloomy, very gloomy. Times are getting worse from day to day, one doesn't see a penny of takings, not a stitch of work, and the outlook is weaker still, gloomier still.
Once, after Passover, every well-to-do Jew of Zagłębie would think about where to rent a summer place, where to spend a few weeks' holiday. The women had their heads full of worries about their summer outfits; the dressmakers, seamstresses and milliners were swamped with work.
Today the dressmakers sit idle and strain their eyes in vain for their faithful clients; the women look for quiet, peaceful corners in town where the children can catch a little fresh air, and the men rack their brains over how to pay the taxes, how to stock up on a few necessary pieces of summer goods so that they will have something to sell when a customer does turn up, where to find money for the rent, for the promissory notes, for the household's living.
Gloomy in the heart and empty in the pocket.
True Sefirah days.
A 3-Day Working Week.
In America and in Germany they are thinking of introducing a 5-day working week. We in Poland are already much further ahead: here a three-day working week has already been introduced. Take last week, for example. Monday, Wednesday and Friday were working days; the remaining days were holidays: Sunday is Sunday, after all; Tuesday a national holiday [3 May, Constitution Day], and on Thursday we again had a religious holiday [Ascension Day, 5 May 1932].
Whatever else, we certainly cannot complain of a shortage of holidays here.
When it is not a holiday and one may work, one rests quite comfortably as well. Neither the craftsman, nor the worker, nor the merchant has anything to do. If a holiday means not working and not trading, then we have a holiday all the time. The Jewish merchant and small trader no longer remembers when he last had some relief [?], when he last had any takings.
The problem of reducing the number of working days in the week has already been solved in Poland. For the Jew, certainly.
Only one small thing is missing: that on the days when one may work there should be something to work at, and on the days when one may trade there should be something to trade with and someone to trade with...
Kahal.
The Second Exhibition in the East.

[Eretz Israel — the Levant Fair in Tel Aviv; notes.] By Z. Katler.

Small notes on a great undertaking.
(Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").

The exhibition in general
"The Second Exhibition in the East", which has been opened in Tel Aviv, is in all respects a great success.
Already just in comparison with its older sister, "The First Exhibition in the Orient" in the year 1929, it is a great success in that it shows very clearly the rapid and brilliant progress of the Jewish upbuilding work in the land of our future!
The first exhibition occupied an area of only 7,000 square metres; only one single government took part in it o f f i c i a l l y — the Palestinian (Eretz-Israel) one; and it had only 19 pavilions, with only 309 exhibitors.
The present second exhibition, by contrast, occupies an area of a full 52 thousand square metres; 10 governments take part in it o f f i c i a l l y and with their own separate pavilions. And it has 70 separate pavilions with 1,200 exhibitors.
Surpassing its predecessor by its present [size and breadth?], despite its short interval of barely three years, this second exhibition thus demonstrates very strongly and clearly the wonderful rapid success of Jewish strength and brains in Eretz Israel, through whose effort and energy it, too, was created.

The purely Jewish creation.
Much more strongly and clearly still, however, the success of Jewish strength and brains is demonstrated by the purely Jewish manufactures, works and creations which are displayed at this exhibition in a special large pavilion named "Totzeret Ha'aretz" [Produce of the Land].
Of the 1,200 exhibitors at this exhibition, a full 300 are purely Jewish, Palestinian, that is: manufactures and products that are manufactured and produced in Eretz Israel with Jewish capital, strength and brains, in all fields of culture, health [?], industry and agriculture, in the village as in the town, with private means and on private land, and even more with national means on national land (of the Jewish National Fund).
Mark this: a full three hundred exhibitors! From the most necessary, to the desirable, and even the downright luxurious: for the mind and body of the modern living person, for the modern family, for the complete furnishing and arrangement of the modern house, the modern city and modern society.
All kinds of food and drink; all sorts of printing and art work: dishes, furniture, weaving, fabrics, clothes, ornaments, jewellery.
In short: everything that a person, a family, a society, a room, a house, a hotel and the like need, even the downright luxurious, such as an electric kitchen, expensive liqueurs, etc. — all this you can now already get in Eretz Israel, and precisely of our own, p u r e l y  J e w i s h invention, p u r e l y  J e w i s h manufacture and work.
And all this has been created in such a short time, and in Eretz Israel which not long ago was utterly desolate, and with such a severe lack of money and experience, such a lack of confidence in our upbuilding work in that very land.
No wonder that on entering the "Totzeret Ha'aretz" pavilion and seeing in it the wonderful creation of purely Jewish strength and brains, an old Jew — one of the Old Yishuv, at that — became so enthusiastic that he literally shouted at the top of his voice:
— Jews! Why, here one truly sees God's wonders! Let us say "Shehecheyanu" together! No! What am I saying, "say Shehecheyanu"? Let us say "Al ha-nissim ve-al ha-nifla'ot" [for the miracles and the wonders]!..

And the other pavilions.
I stroll with the great crowd of visitors from pavilion to pavilion and note down their short remarks.
Well, how do you like the pavilion of Stalin's kingdom (Bolshevik Russia)?
— Like a creature on one leg!
— What do you mean by that?
— You see, in the field of material creation Russia has distinguished itself mainly [?] with 4 things: vodka (schnapps), samovars, borscht and kvass. And of all four of its creations it has exhibited here only the samovar...
— But to make up for it, it has such a giant flag on its pavilion!
— I believe that this is really all it was after with its pavilion: to display its big red flag!
—————
— Here, let's sit down and rest a little! — one Jew said to another as they entered the pavilion of the Romanian government.
— God be with you, what are you saying? I barely escaped from Romania with my life, and I'm supposed to rest here again?!
— Then let's go into the Luna Park; we'll sit down in the wheel, sit and spin around at the same time!
— I've spun around enough in my life; the whole purpose of my coming here was finally to stop spinning!
— But I'm already so tired that I can't drag my feet any more.
— Then come into the pavilion of the Jewish National Fund: i n our own, o n our own and a m o n g our own — here we can rest properly and well, and at the same time see something interesting, instructive and encouraging.
— And after that, where shall we go?
— Home! In one day you can't see such an exhibition from "Aleph" to "Tav".

Can There Be No Unity Among Jewish Merchants?

[Sosnowiec — merchants and their organizations; article.]
Sosnowiec has no fewer than three merchants' organizations — either all of them will go under, or one will at long last create a single powerful organization! — the command of the present critical hour.
It would seem that in our times one need not prove to anyone the necessity of unity and organization. Everyone knows that in order better to defend one's economic interests one must be organized in a group that embraces all who have the same interests. The greater the number of those who have joined together in one organization, the more it is reckoned with as a social factor. This needs no proof; it is clear to everyone.
That is precisely why the workers and artisans have their trade unions. Merchants all over the world have their merchants' organizations, which constitute a power the governments must reckon with.
We must, however, unfortunately state that the Zagłębie merchants are an exception to this rule. They have not understood the matter of organization, or, to put it more correctly, they have understood it badly. We have here plenty of "organizationally capable" people among our merchants, but what have they achieved?
Instead of reaching an understanding, coming together and jointly raising up a powerful organization that would represent the whole of the Będzin or Sosnowiec merchant class, each one worked separately. The result of this is that several merchants' organizations were created.
It is worth noting that in Warsaw there exist altogether two merchants' unions, and that suffices there too..
At a time when the members pay their contributions so irregularly that there is darkness in the till, the merchants' organizations — each with its own board and with its own president and vice-president at its head — must keep their separate premises. It is hard to pay the salaries [printed "pensions"] of the employees, but rent for the premises — that there must be.
But that is not yet the worst. Imagine: a delegation travels to the Minister of Commerce to present the bitter plight of the Jewish merchants. Thanks to the intervention of Deputy X they succeeded in getting all the way to the minister.
And here is a little scene in the minister's office:
The minister: "Witam panów [Greetings, gentlemen], tell me, I beg you, how can I serve you; forgive me, be brief, for I am very busy."
The delegation: "We have come to you, Panie Ministrze [Mr. Minister], as the representatives of the Sosnowiec Jewish merchants. The need is great, the merchants are ruined. The last is being squeezed out of them. We wanted to ask that the distraints be stopped. We have brought here a memorandum with details and proposals for how the need can be relieved.
The minister takes the memorandum from them and says quickly: "I thank you, gentlemen, I will study the memorandum. Do widzenia [Goodbye]."
The next day, the same office of the Honourable Minister: a group of Jews, happy that through the intervention of Senator Y they are being received by the minister himself.
The minister: Tell me, I beg you, how can I serve you, only forgive me, be brief, for I am very busy.
The delegation: We have come to you, Panie Ministrze, as the representatives of the smaller Jewish merchants, etc., according to the previous formula..
The minister (astonished): But, gentlemen, you were already with me yesterday!
The delegation: Yesterday you had the delegation of the large merchants' association "X". We, however, as the representatives of the merchants' association "Y", are the true representatives of the Sosnowiec Jewish merchants..
The minister (less friendly): "Dobrze, panowie [Fine, gentlemen], give the memorandum to my referent K. Żegnam [Good day]!"
With the third delegation, from the small traders' union, only the referent spoke, because despite all their efforts they did not manage to get through to the minister. The referent promised to talk their matter over with the minister and took over memorandum number 3 from the delegates.
The delegations (it goes without saying that delegations must be sent to Warsaw) were received by the referent's secretary. He took the memoranda from them and laid them on the shelf, where those three memoranda were already lying, and they are probably still lying there, quite covered in dust, to this day...
I too would certainly have laughed at this story, if it did not contain the blood and tears of thousands of Jewish families who are perishing of want!
Is it then really necessary that, because of the personal ambitions of individual public workers, the interests of the community be sacrificed?
Could one not unite all the unions in one institution, which could do something more quickly for the poor, oppressed Sosnowiec merchant?!
My dear presidents and vice-presidents! Is it honour and titles you are after? Fine, that can be arranged: one can form a collegium of presidents and vice-presidents, and the first chairman shall be determined by lot. The chairman can be appointed for half a year, after him another can come in turn, so that everyone can have the chance to become the first chairman of a truly great and powerful institution!
In Berlin, at the beginning of 1930, under the pressure of the crisis and owing to the necessity of consolidating, the "Deutsche Bank", with a capital of 230 million marks, and the "Disconto-Gesellschaft", with a capital of 180 million marks, merged. In this way the united bank, under the firm name "Deutsche Bank und Disconto-Gesellschaft", became the strongest bank in Germany. When a year later, in June 1931, all the largest banks in Germany began to totter, the above-mentioned bank stood firm as a rock. Each of the two banks had some 200 branches with directors, presidents [?], etc. When the boards of both banks met, there was a gathering of over 400 persons, so that the newspapers wrote that the bank "parliament" was "seting" [?]... The merger saved them from collapse.
Make an effort, honourable board members of the Będzin and Sosnowiec merchants' organizations, to come together and resolve to unite as quickly as possible.
The crisis does not understand jokes, and before you look around it will smash your weak organizations and make a heap of ruins of them.
But when you unite — how many important, urgent and fruitful tasks there are to be carried out by capable people... One could create sections for each branch of trade, chaired by experts from that same branch, so that every member could see for himself [?] that he gets truly sound advice and guidance when he comes to the association.
The standing of the Zagłębie Jewish merchants would grow both with the local authorities and with the government in Warsaw, where their demands would be given more consideration.
If, however, because of personal motives (I see no others) the associations cannot merge, then a delegates' commission of all the merchants' organizations must absolutely be created, which shall jointly handle all questions requiring intervention with the government.
It must no longer happen that each association makes its own "pilgrimage" to Warsaw separately...
Y. P-ashker [?].
New and Amended Laws

[Law — new legislation; survey.]
In the course of the last two weeks a whole series of new and modified laws has been published in the Dz. Ust. [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws].
We shall report the most important:
1) On combating contagious diseases among cattle and domestic animals.
The said law, printed in number 26 under item [poz.] 229, amends the binding regulation of 22 August 1927 to the effect that, in case the owners do not immediately notify the local authority and do not carry out precisely all the legal provisions, the contagiously sick domestic animal or head of cattle may be subjected to compulsory treatment at the expense of those owners.
On the other hand, if the owners of contagiously sick cattle or domestic animals do notify the competent authority in time and comply with the regulations, they can, in case the animal or domestic animal dies, receive a cash allowance amounting to from 1 third to 3 quarters of the assessed value.
2) On relief in court distraints for agricultural owners
This law is published in number 25 under item 219.
The moratorium in the said law consists in this, that the local courts will be permitted to suspend the auctioning of the farm for private debts, for a period of 1 year, insofar as it concerns farmers who have fallen into difficulty of payment.
A. G.
Oneg Shabbat — Parashat Emor

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Yehuda.
Parashat Emor

The Portion
a) "Except for his kin that is near unto him" (21:2)
The sons of Aaron, the holy vessels, pride themselves on their piety. But that is only because of "she'ero". ("She'er" sometimes also means livelihood; Onkelos renders "she'erah" as "zinah" [her food].) Because their livelihood is "near unto him" — because their livelihood is brought to them right into the house. Because they ride so pleasantly on the mare ["klatshe"]... That is why it is easy for them to be pious... (No'am Megadim)

b) "For his kin that is near unto him"
The "Pnei Yehoshua" had a wife who was blessed with every virtue: lame in one foot, hunchbacked, and with a cataract ["blane"] on one eye. To someone's question why she was so "blessed", the Gaon answered that it is because she descends from a family of great pedigree. His only misfortune is that she did not have more people of pedigree in the family.
— ?
— When it was proclaimed in Heaven forty days before birth — said the "Pnei Yehoshua" — that she would be my wife, her grandfather, a great gaon, came and argued that it was beneath his dignity that his granddaughter should be my wife. So God answered him that she would be lame. So he had no choice but to agree. A second grandfather came, a greater tzaddik, and again did not insist on the match; he was answered that she would have a hump. The third was placated by her having a cataract on the eye...
— But — the Gaon concludes — had she had one more distinguished ancestor in the family, and on his account she would have had to have one more defect: become mute — at least I would not hear her screaming...

c) "Neither shall they take a woman put away from her husband" (ibid. 7)
In Austria there once was a case in which a Jewish magnate, a kohen, desired to marry a divorcee who had divorced her husband, and the rabbis naturally refused to perform the chuppah and kiddushin.
The magnate, who was close to the government, denounced the rabbis to the authorities and argued his complaint thus: the reason the Torah forbids a kohen to marry a divorcee is that if she was divorced, she is a castoff and not worthy of a kohen; here, however, the case is that she divorced the man.
To the inquiry from the higher government circles a rabbi answered: Actually, we do not find in the Torah that a wife may divorce her husband. There is only an enactment of the Sages to compel the husband in many cases to give his wife a get when she demands it. Well, if the said magnate wishes to marry the divorcee without taking the Sages into account, and if he believes only what is written in the Torah, then she is no divorcee at all, but a married woman... (Responsa Chatam Sofer)

d) "He shall not defile himself among his people" (ibid. 4)
"This excludes a met mitzvah" (Torat Kohanim)
A met mitzvah means a deceased tzaddik, because mostly he dies on account of the mitzvah — he falls a sacrifice to it... (Olelot Ephraim)

e) "And the priest that is highest among his brethren"
His greatness should come only from his brethren having made him great, and not from a foreign power... From Jews he should take his gifts, and not from strangers... (Tiferet Yehonatan)

f) "Howbeit on the tenth day of this seventh month" (23:27)
On the eve of Yom Kippur, eating is as good as fasting. It is a fast of eating. But such a fast does not atone... "Akh be-asor" — "akh" is a "limitation". (Kli Yakar)

g) "And they stoned him with stones. And the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses" (24:23)
Just as the air of a sick person is harmful, so the atmosphere of a sinner is spiritually harmful. Only when the sinner had been stoned did the Jews become better. Sin is contagious. (Tiferet Shlomo)

h) "Speak... and say" (21:1)
"To warn the great concerning the small" (Yevamot)
To warn the great that they should be small, humble, in their own eyes... (Alei Zayit)

Haftarah
i) "That kept the charge of My sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray from Me" (Ezekiel 44)
That is the wonder: to be pious at a time when the surroundings are corrupt. (Kokhav mi-Yaakov)

Avot
j) "Anyone with whom people are pleased, God is pleased with him" (Chapter 3, 12)
The "Noda bi-Yehuda" was brought a rabbinical appointment letter from Prague, and he did not want to accept it. Later he learned that a Prague scholar, R' Zerach Eidlitz, wanted to become rabbi, although the city did not want him. Only then did the "Noda bi-Yehuda" take up the rabbinate. Asked why he had changed his mind, the Gaon answered:
— For two reasons it is worth becoming a rabbi, although it is not a pleasant thing: 1) in order to infer that if people are pleased with him — if people like me — it is a proof that God too is pleased with him; and 2) so that one's sins be forgiven: "Whoever rises to greatness, all his sins are forgiven".
— Now, for the first reason alone it is enough to know that the city wants me, but I still need not become a rabbi. Now, however, when R' Zerach wants to become rabbi although the city does not want him, although "people are not pleased with him" — it must be that only the second reason holds, and that one takes up the rabbinate only for the forgiveness of sins. Well, for that reason knowing no longer suffices — one really has to be rabbi...
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (24)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin and Anna Vyrubova; installment 24.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

She also thought about how the Tsar still loved her very much, even though some time had already passed since he had grown distant from her. How fiery, how madly wild he had kissed her when she was left alone with him. Even now she feels on her face, neck and lips his hot kisses, and on her body — the touch of his hands...

The carriage with the rubber wheels rolled smoothly along the road, and she sat quietly and listened to the passionate longing that the Tsar's kisses and caresses had awakened in her blood. It seemed to her that she could hear the longing crying out within her... Suddenly she felt Rasputin's strong arm take hold around her shoulders and the fingers of his hand press passionately against her right shoulder. She also felt his sharp glances sawing across her face. She raised her eyes to him and saw: his eyes were burning and glowing like phosphorus in the darkness of the carriage. She felt his glances piercing deep into her...

He pulled her more strongly to himself, brought his face very close to hers, and she could see a deep pallor covering his face. He was breathing hurriedly, with a hot breath that sent fiery streams over her cheeks.

For a while he looked at her like this in silence. The Vyrubova got the feeling that she was being overcome by religious ecstasy, as God [?] too was silent. Then she heard his whispering, soft voice:

— My good soul, dear Anyusha! Where are you taking me now?

His voice was saturated with passion and with tender intimacy [?]. The Vyrubova felt heat in her body and a strange softness in her heart, and she asked, also whispering, in a soft voice:

— Where, "Father," shall I take you?

His fingers pressed more strongly against her right shoulder. His arm became as if "grown onto her shoulders. His eyes still glowed like phosphorus and looked deep into her face. And he whispered in a seductive, dreamy voice:

— Listen to your own heart...

— To my heart? — she asked again.

— Don't you hear how your good heart bids you take me home with you? You do hear it... So take me home with you... You'll give me supper... I want to eat... and I want; you should give me something to eat...

And strangely: it seemed to the Vyrubova that her heart really did bid her take him home with her. So hypnotized was she. She drew a deeper breath and said:

— Good, "Father"!...

And she told the coachman to drive to her home.

— Anyusha-sister! — Rasputin exclaimed, great joy now in his voice — you have a wonderful soul!...

He took his arm off her shoulder, moved his face away from hers and at once became calm. He got back his usual pious, melodious voice and began to talk like a "holy man." He spoke of the ways that lead to God, of how a man must serve God, of purifying the soul and cleansing oneself of sin through repentance and remorse in order to come close to God... As he did so he held his head to one side, as priests do when people make confession to them. His words were pensive, softly sing-song. And so he talked until the carriage stopped by the Vyrubova's palace.

— So this is where you live, good soul? — Rasputin asked in a fatherly voice, glancing at the little palace.

— Here, "holy Father," — the Vyrubova answered.

They got out of the carriage. The Vyrubova led him into the reception hall. Rasputin at once threw off his black coat with the lambskin [?] fur cap and remained in a white linen shirt girded at the loins with a broad leather belt. Meanwhile the Vyrubova ordered her servants to lay the table. When the table was ready she led Rasputin into the dining room.

Rasputin approached the table and looked over the various dishes; on the table there were sliced bread, smoked fish, cheese, meat and a bottle of wine. Rasputin rubbed his hands, as a peasant does when he sees tasty dishes before him, sat down at once, crossed himself and began to eat with great appetite. He ate noisily and fast, used no fork or knife, but ate with his hands. The Vyrubova sat silent and watched him eat.

— And you, good soul, don't you want to eat? — Rasputin asked, chewing with a full, crammed mouth.

— I am not hungry, "Father"! — the Vyrubova answered.

— But drink you shall, with me! — Rasputin exclaimed.

He poured two glasses of wine. The wine was red and strong; he pushed one glass over to the Vyrubova.

— Drink! The wine is good for you!

They clinked glasses. Rasputin emptied his glass in one gulp, grunted with pleasure and wiped his moustache with his sleeve. The Vyrubova drank only a little, but Rasputin fixed his sharp eyes on her and exclaimed:

— Drink it up! The wine is sanctified by me! Drink it all up!

And he did not take his compelling gaze off her until she had drunk the whole glass, and Rasputin exclaimed with satisfaction:

— That's it, my soul! That's it!

For himself he again poured a glass of wine and emptied it in one gulp. Again he wiped his moustache with his shirt sleeve. His face was now somewhat flushed, and a pleased smile played on his lips. Then he got up, took a few steps away from the table, stood still with his head slightly bowed, stuck both hands into his leather belt, began to sing a folk song that sounded like a monastery chant, and began to sway calmly back and forth to the beat and the song; he raised his eyes to the Vyrubova and exclaimed:

— Help me sing!

The Vyrubova also got up and began to sing. Rasputin began to take firm steps, stamped with his heavy peasant boots and began to dance. Their singing grew louder and Rasputin's dancing — faster. He danced in a circle, every moment casting a hot glance at the Vyrubova, who clapped her hands as she sang. For a while he danced like this. But suddenly he came close to the Vyrubova, wound his right arm around her waist and exclaimed commandingly:

— Dance with me!

He pressed her tightly to himself. She did not resist. She had no strength at all to resist, and both of them, singing, moved in the dance. This went on for a while. Suddenly — and the song died away on his lips. Now they moved silently, and Rasputin's face was very close to hers. His face grew pale and paler... His eyes — sharper and more burning; passion boiled in him and beat with heat from his body. His breath scalded her cheeks and neck, his glances bored deep into her face; she felt that she was wholly mastered by his hypnotizing glances and by his will... Her breath became short, broken and hot. A leaden heaviness poured into her legs.

The Problem of Physical Education

[Physical education and sport; article.]
Every new idea meets with stubborn resistance among the masses of the people — not only among us, but even among the most culturally developed nations; so what wonder is it that work for physical education is still pioneering work and still does not find proper understanding in the broad circles of society? True, the idea we are speaking of here is not entirely new. The ancient Greeks and Romans already put forward[?] the slogan: "Mens sana in corpore sano" (a healthy soul in a healthy body); with these words the ancient peoples expressed the truth about the equal value of the two factors, body and soul, for the healthy and normal development of both the individual and the community — that body and soul are indivisibly bound together, and that to neglect one of them means to harm both.
The migration of peoples, however, buried in ruins the once-mighty nations and, together with them, their lofty culture. And when the Renaissance came again, it remained only a renaissance of the spirit. Europe rose spiritually, yet remained — thanks to the crippled medieval idea of asceticism — in its vile contempt for the "sinful" body. This medieval curse pursues us to this day. To this very day it is a stumbling block for those who spread the idea of physical education.
The clumsy[?] folly about the inferiority of the body in the ethical sense took an especially heavy toll on the Jewish people. Shut up in the narrow and stifling ghettos, without light and without air, condemned to a life of want, persecuted and tormented by various bloodthirsty enemies, the Jews were brought to bodily degeneration and with it to the decline of many spiritual virtues — first of all of courage and even of personal dignity. And when, under the hammer of the French Revolution, the ghetto walls fell, and later other no less important historic days were repeated many times, the Jews became like birds whose wings had been clipped and who were then told... to fly. Like a curse, physical degeneration hung constantly over the Jews. It was to a great extent the cause of their unpreparedness, of their inability to make use of often important historical situations, because it was the cause not only of the shameful cowardice, unworthy of a human being, as expressed in Bialik's "City of Slaughter", of passivity and apathy[?] in times of wild storms and national defeats, but also of the difficulties — incomparably greater than anywhere else — in organizing and consolidating for great joint public undertakings. This was grasped by the people who stood at the head of the national renaissance movement, and, understanding that there can be no talk of a full national revival without a simultaneous renaissance of spirit and body, they raised the old slogan of the Greeks and Romans: "Mens sana in corpore sano".
This appeal found an echo among the youth, which began to found sports clubs and gymnastic organizations. The youth did this and does it fully aware of the seriousness of the task it takes upon itself and carries out; but the older generation of society still largely regards the efforts of the youth with ignorance and often with cynicism, seeing in them merely "child's play" and "a waste of time". Therefore the sports and gymnastic organizations, besides their work of physical education among the youth, must also take upon themselves the burden of propaganda and enlightenment among the broad strata of Jewish society. We shall not tire of knocking at the hearts and minds of Jewish society until the plain truth that has already conquered the world — the truth that without bodily health there is no mental health — is absorbed into the blood and becomes the building block[?] of our society, which gets many times more use from a person who knows less but is healthier and has more endurance than from an educated epileptic[?]. A sick person is only a burden to society. That is why immigrants must undergo medical examinations at the border of a new country. That is why the ancient [Spartans?] (printed "[—]-ger") used to throw their crippled newborn children down from Mount Taygetus, and in the Spartan[?] gymnasia — from which the name of our present-day secondary schools derives — bodily culture was cultivated first of all; and the people whose youth this was laid, after all, the foundation of our entire civilization. That very people, which devoted so much time and care to the culture of the body, was a people of philosophers, poets and artists unsurpassed to this day.
"Physical education is the foundation on which alone moral and intellectual [values] can blossom" — these are the words of the committee which the King of Sweden appointed in his time to give its opinion on the matter of physical education, and which consisted of eminent personalities: "If we invest great capital in agriculture, mining, the processing of building materials and intellectual education, we must not forget that all this will lose its value if we neglect health and strength. Those who [work?] the field, bring up the treasures from the mines, process the building materials and cultivate their minds — they are the human material of the country. If we do not protect it against harm and exploitation, sad prospects open before us for the future and for the fate of the country."
And the English educator William Stead[?] states: "The power and might of the British Empire lie in the strength of character of each individual Englishman, and I am convinced that nothing owes this strength its steady year-by-year growth so much as the love of sport and of play in the open air, which finds expression among all classes of the English people."
And whoever is not moved by arguments of a national and social character — to him we shall make our way and drill[?] into his mind by other means. To him we shall appeal in the name of his children and his relatives.
The wrong done to our youth through the lack of physical education and sport is beyond measure. Our society does not account to itself for the enormous damage its passive attitude causes. Among the large percentage of the physically weak, in the number of those whom tuberculosis cuts down year after year and brings prematurely to the grave, an enormous [sic — the sentence is incomplete as printed]. But the most important means in the fight against tuberculosis is to strengthen the resistance of the organism through sport and through games in the sun and in the open air.
Sport is also a powerful brake on the growth of alcoholism, card-playing and venereal diseases; in Western Europe, and especially in Germany, there is ample experience in this respect.
To understand the weight of what has just been said, one must mention the most important data on the so-called social plagues. Alcohol is the cause in 5 per cent of mental illnesses, in 70 per cent of murders and crimes, and 11–19 of suicides. As for tuberculosis, the diseases make up 14 per cent, mortality 15 per cent of all deaths; tuberculosis reaches 1,3 [probably: one third] of all infectious diseases taken together. Twice as many people die of tuberculosis as of all diseases in general.
Institutions of physical education are the most important weapon in the fight against all these social ills.
What Is Heard in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Meeting on Kashrut Matters

[Zagłębie — Local News: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa.]
What Is Heard in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 7 Iyar 5692 — piątek 13 maja 1932.)

BĘDZIN

A meeting on kashrut matters.
Last Sabbath the local rabbinate issued a public proclamation (kol kore) calling all worshippers of the minyanim and shtiblekh to come to the Great Synagogue, where the rabbi delivered a sermon on the sad state of kashrut matters in our town.
After the rabbi's sermon, R' Yitzchak Meir Lewin, the rabbi's son, spoke and appealed to those present to help his father in his work in religious affairs. In his speech Mr. Lewin said: "You possess[?] in this town a diamond, a man full of holiness and purity, the great lover of Israel — so help him in his work."

The magistrate does not pay out the subsidies for the Jewish schools.
In last year's budget a sum of 3,500 zł. was granted as a subsidy for 4 Jewish educational institutions, namely the Talmud Torah, the Mizrachi school, "Yesodei HaTorah" and "Beis Yaakov". But to this day, despite the schools being in a catastrophic situation, the sum has still not been paid out...
When the representative of the Mizrachi school, Mr. Bugmeitz[?], explained to the commissioner that the school was threatened with closure if the subsidy was not given, the commissioner was not in the least moved and answered: "Let the school be closed"...

Meeting of artisans.
On Sunday a general meeting took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association at Kołłątaja 45.
The chair was handed to Mr. Kamiński. The report given by the outgoing president, Mr. L. Brama, was not accepted, on the motion of Mr. Goldsztajn.
Then the following board was elected: L. T.[?] Brama, T.[?] L. Goldsztajn, Icchak Fürstenfeld, Mosze Wolf Kamiński, Józef Kac, Noach Ajzner[?], Beryl Goldwasser[?].
Deputies: H. A. Cukierman, M. J. Prutzowicz[?] and Kilsztok.
The meeting also elected an arbitration court of Messrs. Plbojm[?], M. Gotfryd[?], A. Błochacz, Sz. Wignański, Lustiger and A. Berner.
On Tuesday the first session was held, at which Mr. Goldsztajn was elected president and Mr. Brama vice-president.

Conscription of the 1911 class begins on 3 June.
We are informed by the magistrate that the conscription (pobór) of the 1911 class will begin on 3 June (czerwiec) and will last until 15 June.
The conscription will take place, as before[?], in the premises of the ochronka[?] on the "Góra Zamkowa".
During that time the classes of 1909 and 1910 must also report.

A temporary notary appointed.
In place of the late notary Mr. Schröter[?], Mr. Wacław[?] Polender[?] has been temporarily appointed and is already performing his office.
As we are informed, the vice-president of the Court of Appeal in Warsaw, Mr. Raczkiewicz, is to be appointed as the permanent notary.

Parents' meeting about the summer colonies.
Under the chairmanship of Mrs.[?] N. Ratner, a meeting was held on Saturday of the parents whose children are members of "HaShomer HaLeumi" united with "Herzliya".
The meeting discussed the question of the summer colonies being arranged by the organization in the Beskids[?]. The parents showed a strong interest in the problems of the organization in general and in the particular colonies specifically.
A patronage committee was elected, made up of Mesdames Pfeffer, Gertner, Miałka, Naparstek, Szpilman and Mr. Diamant. The patronage committee has the task of organizing the summer colonies.

Help for working Eretz Israel.
In the coming days the great May[?] campaign will be conducted. According to letters arriving from Eretz Israel, the Histadrut is awaiting the outcome of the present campaign with impatience. With the new[?] aliyah the work of the Histadrut institutions has expanded, and the need for material help is growing ever greater.
In several larger towns the campaign has already been carried out and, even in the present crisis, has given considerably better results than in previous years.
It is also to be hoped that the Będzin friends of working Eretz Israel will this time too respond warmly to the call of the workers[?] of Eretz Israel.

The attacker was mistaken...
On Kościuszki Street an unknown person snatched a handbag[?] from Miss B. The bag contained in all 9 groszy...

Owner of 2 houses eats at the cheap kitchen.
At the cheap kitchen for the unemployed in Czeladź the local Christian house-owner, owner of 2 buildings, Mr. B., came forward and asked to be given a little food for his family.
For a long time the house-owner's family had been living on horse meat[?].

SOSNOWIEC

Newly elected presidium of the kehilla council and of the board.
As our readers know, the presidium elections of the council and of the board were recognized as not legal, and the starosta demanded that elections be held a second time.
The elections took place last Sunday. The council's presidium was elected in the morning and that of the board — in the afternoon.
At both sessions declarations were read in the name of the national groupings and the artisans, that since the present elections are a further continuation of the agitation and secret agreements between the parties of Rabbi Englard and Rabbi Frommer, they would not take part in the elections.
After the reading of the declarations by Messrs. Mendel Szapiro and Lewi Jungster, the representatives of the Zionists, the "Mizrachi" and the artisans left the session.
The council session was [chaired — verb missing in print] by vice-president Mr. Lejbisz Sznajcer, and that of the board — by Mr. Lejbisz Zendel.
Elected as president of the new council was Mr. Mosze Mordechaj Hajgsztok[?], as vice — Chaim Jungster; on the board: as president Mr. Mendel Klajner, vice — Lejbisz Grylak[?].

Dispute between employers and workers.
Negotiations took place at the labour inspector's over the dispute that arose between the owners of the smaller coal pits and the workers.
The dispute consists in the pit owners wanting to reduce wages by 7 per cent, to which the workers' union will not agree.
The inspector proposed a compromise of 6 per cent. This compromise too was rejected. Consequently the negotiations were broken off.

Bread has become dearer.
The price commission at the Sosnowiec magistrate has raised the price of bread to 45 gr. a kilo.
The new price still has to be confirmed by the Voivodeship.

Legal advice for artisans.
The board of the local Artisans' Association has engaged, for the benefit of its members, the advocate Mr. Brandt, who will give legal advice to the members in the association's premises.

More papal than the Pope...
At the board meeting of the Polish Red Cross, Dr. Karl Rider honoured the memory of the late priest Plenkiewicz and at the same time proposed that the portrait of the late priest be placed in the Red Cross office.

The appeal against the elections of the board and council — not considered.
In its time an appeal was filed against the elections of the new kehilla board and council. This week the signatories of the appeal received an answer that, since the appeal was not filed within 14 days after the elections, the appeal will not be considered at all.

From the meeting of the Bank for Artisans and Small Traders.
Sunday's meeting of the members of the Bank for Artisans and Small Merchants aroused wide interest. The best proof is that at the start of the meeting some 300 members were present, most of whom took the questions on the agenda seriously and voiced various opinions on the bank's further existence.
The meeting was opened by the president of the board, Dr. Herzman[?], who characterized banking in general and in our area in particular, and stressed that thanks to the sound, non-risky operations, what happened to other similar financial institutions did not happen to the bank.
At the general request the chair was taken by Mr. Kabak[?], with Messrs. Artman and Fridman as assessors and M. Lancman as secretary.
Reports on the year's activity were given by Messrs. Dr. Herzman[?] and Fürstenberg, and for the Auditing Union — inspector Michalon[?]. The reporters again emphasized that the bank conducts a systematic, responsible activity.
After the reports a discussion developed in which, as is the custom, personalities were attacked.
After the reply of the bank manager Mr. Fiszel Lewi, the board and council were granted the absolutorium.
The budget for the current year was reduced by 5,000 zł.
Then a series of resolutions was adopted, among others that all losses to date be covered from the reserve and share capital, while the members must again increase the share capital to its former level.
The composition of the existing board and council was not changed; however, Mr. Dawid Rozenfeld was elected deputy on the board and Józef Artman deputy on the council.

The "unfortunate" dollar-holders in Zagłębie.
The "panic" over dollars. The reports from America that it had been decided there to devalue the dollar by up to 60 per cent of its present value set off a "panic", which drew a scare[?] in Zagłębie too.
Although[?] dollar devaluation is still very far off, there are nevertheless "sharp operators" who took the opportunity to coax out the hidden dollars and exchange them[?] for other, "safer" money.
On Friday one could buy dollars very "cheaply". People looked for buyers to "get rid of" the dollar. There was buying and selling. A real problem was had, and is still had, by those who do not want it known about their dollars. They looked for a quiet corner to sell them — even if[?] more cheaply...

Tax demands of the Chamber of Commerce.
In order to be informed on a series of tax questions concerning income and turnover tax, the local Chamber of Commerce called a conference regarding[?] the above questions. Also taking part in the conference were the head of the Izba [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce and representatives of merchants' organizations in the district.
After the address by Mr. Szekański[?], the following demands were put forward:
1) To limit enforcement actions for turnover tax until the appeals are settled.
2) The appeals should be considered as quickly as possible.
3) To recognize trade books that have already once been approved.
The head declared that he would try to have the demands settled as wished.
At the same time he appealed to the representatives of the Chamber of Commerce to spread among the broad public that the reliefs for paying tax arrears (zaległe) should be taken advantage of.

Mourning flags after the loss of the French president.
On the building of the Dąbrowa magistrate and on the factories of French companies, mourning flags were hung out as a sign of grief over the loss of French President Doumer.
Shavuot

[On Shavuot] one does not eat such heavy foods as in winter, for we are already drawn to the spring novelties such as vegetables and salad, together with lighter meats, poultry and fish. As sweets, the tastiest and best-loved on the holiday table always remain the easily digestible [?] puddings and creams, which can be prepared in an easy and convenient [?] way from a packet [?] of pudding powder from the well-known firm Dr. Oetker.

Usually nothing special is baked on Shavuot [the print has "הערט" for "ווערט"], so the choice of pastry must be left to the housewife, who sometimes decides on the universally beloved cheesecake.

Good instructions for baking cheesecake are to be found in Dr. Oetker's recipe booklet, editions C and F.

Ungar's Artistic Visions

[Sosnowiec — music; concert review.] (Reflections on his Saturday concert at the Sosnowiec "Palace").

Someone said that Ungar [Imre Ungár] does not play, he prays. I think it would be more correct to say that he "duchens" [gives the priestly blessing], just like the kohen with the tallit drawn over his head. He looks into himself, sees there a world of harmonious sounds, which he draws up in an ecstasy of awe and bursts out into the void, arousing in the audience an almost religious enthusiasm.

When he appears on the stage with his closed eyes and approaches the piano, his head thrown back, one recalls the biblical "falling down, but having his eyes open" [Num. 24:4]. What a world of mysterious visions must reveal itself to him then. He — the clear-seer, and we — the blind! He floats in a sea of melody, where every little drop is for him a new angelic sound, a special chapter of song [Perek Shira], and we, the blind, grope in the dark, take in the dry echo of that mysterious song, and yet grasp its soul!

Are we to be the connoisseurs of the heavenly sound-combination of Bach — Ungar, Chopin — Ungar, Liszt — Ungar, Schumann — Ungar! Are we to pass judgement on the artistic interpretation of those works of genius! How can we, and how may we?

Whoever's heart had trembled beforehand lest the physical defect, the blindness, should stand like a partition between the virtuoso and the instrument, saw his error at the very first sounds. The artist does not look at the piano with physical eyes; he sees the notes with his spirit: just as he does not need to look at sheet music, so he does not need to look at the keyboard either. That is the first achievement of every pianist, even before he attains virtuosity. But Ungar is, after all, a first-class virtuoso! With him, it seems, the being-shut-off [?] from the surrounding world is yet another advantage, a push toward inner concentration, toward immersing himself in his own esprit.

And since his soul is entirely wedded [?] to the instrument, for us listeners the possibility of dry analysis vanishes, because there pours out to us the noblest song, which seems to come not from dry little bones [i.e. keys] with human fingers, but from some hidden wellspring of melody.

It is not a dry piano with separate keys that plays for us, but a fiddle, a cello, a string with tones flowing into one another, in wonderfully tender vibrations. It can weep like a child, hum like a dove [?], storm like a [—] sea. But the divine is not in the storm, not even in the biblical "still small voice". However great Ungar's power in forte, however caressingly his pianissimo may work, when the key is barely, barely touched and yet he draws a sound out of it — the main thing is the art of crescendo and decrescendo, of whipping up the sounds into a storm and stilling [?] them. A moment ago a thin little pipe trilled, and now a full orchestra is already thundering — all through the magic of this young maestro, who does not see the world around him, only his inner world of sound-harmony!

Is there, then, no greater player than him? Who has the audacity to compare between good and good? He bewitched us right at the beginning, after all, and took away our power of judgement!

It was thought beforehand that he would show his greatest wonders in Chopin, for whom he had, after all, received the master's title. But already in Bach, especially in the fugue, we were enraptured; Beethoven's sonata was like a sweet dance of angels, Schumann's playfulness electrified, Liszt's rhapsody was a grandiose symphony, and Chopin's greatness showed itself exalted in the Polonaise.

Each piece was more beautiful than the one before, each more enchanting and bewitching than the other. It was the highest level of art!

Chanan.

From Wednesday the increased stamp duty is obligatory
[Poland — taxes.] On Wednesday the 18th of this month the new law on the increased stamp duty came into force. According to the new law, every petition submitted to a state institution must bear a stamp for 5 złoty (until now only 3 złoty).
The duty has not been raised for court certifications, nor for documents attached to the petition, for which one will pay 50 groszy as before.
On the other hand, the fee for a licence (concession) to run an enterprise is sharply raised, from 20 zł. to 40. Permits to organise concerts, even charitable ones, will cost 50 złoty.
Copies and extracts of notarial deeds will cost 50 groszy per page (until now only 20). The minimum duty on receipts is raised from 20 groszy to 25.
In a word: one has to see to having fresh money.

The Jewish Public in Będzin Is Called to Fight Against Football.

[Będzin — Education; sport.] For years now this branch of sport — football — has captured the whole of the youth. There is no place where this sport does not take first place.
Lately this sport has also drawn in the schoolchildren, who have given themselves over to the game with full ardour. On almost every empty lot one can see children of 8–10 already busying themselves with this dangerous sport. The harm is great: the children neglect their schoolwork, and it often leads to sad results as well. For example, this very week football claimed another victim — a 15-year-old pupil of class 7 of Public School No. 2, who met his death while playing football on a stranger's ground.
Public School No. 2 has long endeavoured to combat football-playing among the school youth; the school authorities, too, banned the game long ago, but it has already taken such root that it is almost impossible to eradicate it. Nevertheless the management is striving to continue the work and turns to the entire Jewish population to help it in the work of eradication. Let every father and mother influence their children, by fair means or foul, not to play football; let every single passer-by turn his attention to the matter; let us with joint forces strive to root out football among children, which so often claims such terrible victims.
The Management of Public School No. 2 in Będzin.
Great Fire with Human Casualties in Szczekociny

[Szczekociny — Fire; relief.] 150 families left without a roof over their heads.
On Sunday at 8 in the morning a fire broke out in Szczekociny on Kraków Street [ul. Krakowska], in the house of Hershl Goldsher. The fire spread lightning-fast to the neighbouring streets, so that the whole town stood in blazing flames.
An hour later the firemen from Pilica, Zawiercie, Włoszczowa and elsewhere arrived and, together with the civilian population, conducted a vigorous rescue operation. Only at 5 in the afternoon was the fire brought under control. Some 70 buildings went up in smoke, and 200 families, mostly Jewish, were left naked and destitute. The fire raged so fiercely that a large part of what had been rescued burned in the street and in the field.
The fire also caused human casualties. The 47-year-old Nute Shtiblman and an elderly Christian died suddenly of fright; a 4-year-old child was also burned to cinders.
The damage is very great. The fire victims were quartered in the prayer rooms (minyanim), synagogues and the beys-medresh requisitioned for them.
In connection with the great catastrophe that so terribly struck hundreds of Jewish souls in Szczekociny, a relief committee has been founded to collect donations.
As Mr. Yekl Grosfeld of Sosnowiec informs us, the committee will also come to Zagłębie, where donations will be collected for the fire victims, especially among the Szczekociny „landslayt“ [townsmen] now living in Zagłębie.

Reb Leibish Diamand, of Blessed Memory

[Będzin — Obituary; black-bordered.] One generation goes and another comes — a generation goes, a generation comes, but the face of each generation is different. Ever fewer becomes the generation of Jews who are Torah scholars, and especially of Jews who are enlightened Torah scholars, of scholars who are also fighters for the national ideals of the Jewish people.
When will Będzin again have a Jew like Reb Leibish Diamand, of blessed memory? His whole life he spent at his work; at his daily work he forgets neither the Book nor the People of the Book. A Jewish word is his lifeblood[?], a good word his delight, a Jewish matter — his own, a national question — his personal one.
One of the first Hovevei Zion, Reb Leibish Diamand remains the eternal, faithful soldier of the Zionist idea. It goes without saying that by his whole essence he later belonged to the „Mizrachi“. In the „Mizrachi“ he wants to see the true „spiritual centre“, the true standard-bearer of Jewish culture. In his last few months he took a keen interest in the „Oneg Shabbat“. Why — he used to argue — is there anything more important than a word of Torah? When work was needed again, a struggle for a national cause, Reb Leibish Diamand, of blessed memory, stood once more in the front ranks, yet never did he budge a hair's breadth from the truth. He had a special sense for the truth, and only thanks to it was he able to leap with Hasidic fervour into the Zionist movement and into blazing Zionist work, while standing with both feet on the old ground of Hasidism.
No, such Jews are not born today; Jewish Będzin has suffered a great loss with the passing of Reb Leibish Diamand, of blessed memory, and one can truly say: Alas for those who are gone and are no more to be found. Peace to his ashes! A. G.
—o—
A large crowd, admirers and friends, accompanied the deceased to his eternal rest on Monday.
In the courtyard of his home he was eulogized by the rabbi and director of the „Mizrachi“ school, Mr. Gotesdiner. In several thoughtful reflections, interwoven with sayings of the Sages, Mr. Gotesdiner pointed out the greatness of the deceased as a strictly religious Jew and an ardent fighter for the Zionist ideal.

Holding bills of exchange without a fee.

The well-known merchant activist Mr. Jakub Adler of Radom has submitted the following two proposals to the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce.
The banks should introduce the same system as in the P.K.O., namely: bills of exchange may be held over to the morning after the due date, until 12 o'clock, without any fee. Besides that, on the day the bill falls due [the banks] should be open from 8 to 12 and from 3 to 6 p.m. That is, the management, the staff and the bank administration in general should work as usual until now; only the cash desk should be open a few hours longer in the afternoon.
Mr. Adler calculates in his proposal that the 15 groszy paid for holding a bill — be it even for the smallest sum — amounts to a large percentage, which for many bill-payers is too great an expense.

Theatre notes.

(On the "Art" guest performances in Zagłębie).
After a rather long interval we again had the opportunity to see the small-art [cabaret] theatre "Art" here.
The 2 programmes "Celebrations among Jews" and "Laughing at the World" contain numbers that are true pearls of small-art creation, e.g. "Tempo, Tempo", "In the Tavern", "Checkmate", "In the Beth Midrash", "Szarabanda" and "Human Struggle".
As for the last number, which is perhaps the best and strongest in form, one must say that one is disappointed listening to the words. Outwardly one gets the impression of a strong protest against social inequality, but listening more closely, it turns out to be some lukewarm, bourgeois-pacifist bigos [hodgepodge] that says nothing.
One must point out that such scenes as handing someone paper with a few groszy so that he may go and attend to a physiological need are in no way permissible; it is very shocking and considerably weakens the good impression of the whole.
The acting of the artists was excellent. We could have singled out individual performers in first place, but we deliberately do not do so, because we do not want to favour anyone. It does not matter whether one plays a little weaker or stronger; the main thing is that in "Art" we have a brilliant ensemble performance, and no one strains to become a star. Everyone is in his place and strives to give the maximum.
The sets, costumes and music are well suited and harmonize with the whole.
It is gratifying that at a time when almost the entire Jewish theatre world here is sunk in shund [trash], when great actors lower themselves and play in American shund plays, "Art" has managed to maintain its artistic level, and for that it deserves a yasher koach.
Sz. R.
