On Tangled Roads — The grave, unbearable situation of the present. — What are the prospects for the future?

L. Szpigelman.
The situation in the country has become such that one no longer stops at all to consider how dangerous it is, and the trouble is that we have been blinded. We have grown used to the most terrible catastrophes; the aches have penetrated deep into the marrow of the bones and the pains have ceased to be felt; even the most "oysgveynigster" [doubtful word] has already grown used to the sick man and no longer regards him as sick. And when we do see that the sick man is sick, when we begin to analyse all this, when we do not want to fool ourselves — then we come to awareness, then we must admit that things are not as they ought to be, that once it was different. But people have grown so used to the bad that one does not notice that it is getting steadily worse, as the saying goes: when you get used to suffering, you live with it in joy.
In Poland things have been bad not since today and not since yesterday. The situation was catastrophic already several years ago, but people still would not believe it; they wanted to persuade the public that it was only a pretence [?]; "the devil is not as terrible — they said — as he is painted." The population could barely catch its breath; people groaned and grew bitter, but those who did not want to open their eyes to see the bright light wanted to persuade the masses that it was no more than an illusion, a fantasy. And so people kept persuading themselves even then, when the situation was already very, very dangerous, very, very bitter.
People came here to us from every corner of Poland, and all of them stated that we were living here in the best conditions compared with other regions, and to tell the truth we too could see it: when someone, a person from our parts, travelled outside Zagłębie or Upper Silesia — as soon as he stuck a foot out, poverty and want appeared before his eyes in all their size and breadth, and then he could truly establish that here in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia was the best-situated corner of all Poland, although a large percentage of our inhabitants never saw that "good fortune".
Now we, the "rich", have also become great beggars; here begging already goes on today on a very large scale; workers go hungry and the unemployed go begging; people do not have the means to get through the day — and one does not see it, one does not feel it, or better said, one does not want to see it and does not want to feel it. And so the catastrophic process advances ever deeper and deeper; no one takes into account that the wounds have entered the stage of a chronic disease and are thereby causing dangerous ruin in the economic sphere.
Here we have witnessed an interesting phenomenon: in Czeladź a Christian, the owner of 2 houses, turned to the free kitchen asking to be provided with a few lunches for his family. For some time now, he related, he has been feeding his household on dog meat.
Sensitivity has vanished among us; we have become "hardened", we have become indifferent to everything. Once people would have stopped at such a news item; readers would not have skimmed through it in such a way that later they would no longer remember what they had read; our fellow writers too would have devoted several articles to such a question — and today it passes by with the cigarette smoke. After all, we live in the 20th century, when everything runs and flies and races like an arrow from a bow. One lives quickly through the few years, torments oneself with them, and before you know it everything is over: quickly lived, quickly died, quickly worn out. So people drop like flies, and nobody tries to think how to remedy the dangerous situation into which we are being hurled by force, with terrible impetus.
Well, one knows that things are bad now not only here in Poland; a world ruin has poured out over everyone who lives in God's world; everywhere want, hunger and unemployment reign; the present pains are still wartime sufferings, wartime complications, which should really have been over long ago; but the system has become so incomprehensible that the world cannot grasp it, and the faster one reckons to get out of this tangle, the deeper one gets caught in it.
Thus, for example, "economists" persuaded us that the situation in the world was bitter because products were too dear and the population could not afford them. Then things went bad again and everything began to fall, so that for a few groszy people began buying fortunes; and then one sees that this is no good either: an ox for a grosz — but there is no grosz. Again people realised that this too was no good, and began to shout that the world was becoming miserable thanks to cheapness; and when last week some products began to rise, people swelled with pleasure, although they had not had [the money] even for the cheap products. "Let it be dearer," people wished — perhaps in this way the world will be helped; better that it be dearer and one earns, than that it be cheap and one hasn't the grosz. With joy and enthusiasm people greeted the rise in the price of goods. "On the contrary," people said, "let something stir, let there be demand for goods; today there is nothing at all, today everything is dead, nobody needs anything at all."
One must not forget that the system, the economic order, is no good. Thus, for example, we know that in many countries cotton [?] and grain were burned and thrown into the water, because those countries had too much of them and could not get any prices, while at the same time in other countries people starved and froze, [perished?] from cold, having nothing to put on.
Is this morass [?] then understandable, which like a spell has clamped itself over the heads of our horizon? Can any regulation come about under such an economy — in the sense that in one country products are burned while at the same time people in another country starve and take their own lives because they do not have those very products for themselves and for their little children?
We do not know in what way the world will regulate itself after us, but one thing we do know: the future historian will have a sea of material when he sets about describing our present era, and later people will surely be unable to understand how their grandfathers could live in such abnormal, strange times, to which we adapt ourselves so neatly and which already look to us as if it could not be otherwise, as if it need not be otherwise.
Yes, our feelings have already been blunted; we no longer see the most terrible deeds being played out before our eyes; we do not feel the sufferings and the strange pains which cause so much trouble to mankind as it exists.
Our grandchildren, when they study the history of our generations, will reckon [?] us heroes of the age; the historian will then stamp us as martyrs, as saints, for having had so much endurance and patience to adapt ourselves to all sorts of world caprices, and for having had it so hard to fight for our poor, stubborn existence.
At the present day, in our current present, we find ourselves in a foggy condition, in a raw state, and we do not know in what way life will crystallise; now it looks as if everything were beginning anew, from Genesis. And those who are now departing from the world are surely curious to know in what way the world will take shape; for just as at the time of the World War people wanted to live to see the end, so as to know what the world would look like after the war, just so, and perhaps even more, people now want to see how the world will crystallise after us; for all who have even a somewhat deeper gaze see that the present order and system has no future, and that new forms of life, new prospects, are already on the way, which will have to, willy-nilly, bring in a new outlook and fixed rules for the ways of human life.

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton, trade.] A Merchant's Letter
By Y. Perlmutter.

My friend! When there is no luck, then of course there is no success either, and when there is no success — it is hard[?] and very bitter. I was sure, and all the signs pointed to it too, that this summer season would turn out not bad at all and that things would be a little livelier than until now. Here at home too, in Zagłębie, a mood took hold: there, things are getting better... First, enough seasons have already gone by in which nothing was sold, and in the end there simply has to be some turnover. People won't, after all, go about naked and barefoot, and that is exactly why everyone talked themselves into believing that this season would no longer disappoint.
But, good brother, when there is no luck, there is no wisdom and no counsel and no calculation and no energy, and nothing helps... As the sages say: in "a year of drought, the food spoils in the bowels" — even what you have already swallowed and is already in your guts becomes cursed too, so that it brings no benefit.
And just so: when we prepare for the summer season and hope for fine, warm days, with all the fine, good prospects — it turns really cold and all hopes freeze over like ice, and [—][?] something, when luck says "no"...
In general, lately everything here has somehow gone to ruin and all calculations fail. In the old days, when someone opened a new shop on Kołłątaja Street, he had a calculation; one of the two — if the business went well and there was turnover with a living, all well and good; and if, God forbid, not — then it would have to be done according to the "intention"[?] — take, turn, turn over again, and above all, a chance to save oneself, may no trouble come, was always there, so as not to be left bare. But now everything is nothing; the calculation is no calculation, because there is no turnover. It should be warm — it's cold; it should be cold — it turns warm. And when nothing sells, since the Almighty is a "changer of times", the merchant wants to throw himself on the second means — the "intention" — to become a "changer of the seasons" [a play on the blessing "who changes times and alters the seasons", i.e. postponing payment dates]; and now it turns out that the intention is no good either, simply because nobody lends today, so it is neither this nor that.
And as long as the times don't return when whoever opens a shop has the two chances I counted out above, no new businesses will spring up, because "no man places his money on a deer's horn"...
Do you know, my friend, what the whole trade looks like to me today? — Like that fellow who once went off to look for luck...
A man in a small town once read[?] in a newspaper[?] that in the big city someone walking in the street struck it lucky: he found a purse with a lot of money and became a great rich man. And further he read that in that same city a rich widow looked down from a window and fell in love with a poor porter, and the porter became very happy for the rest of his life... Without thinking long, the reader decided to travel to that city to try his luck, and one of the two — so he thought to himself — either he would find a purse of money or he would come upon a rich widow...
No sooner said than done. Arriving in the big city, he lies awake at night and ponders what to do first: whether to walk with his head down and look for the purse, or with his head up, toward the high windows, and look for the rich widow?... In the end he concluded that first he must look for the purse of money, because once he has money he will of course be able to make a rich match, and that's that... First thing in the morning he went out into the street to search.
Walking all [?] the time with his head down, his head spun more and more, and by evening he was already running about like a madman. One he shoved, another he knocked over, and so on at length, until he was "invited" into Sha'are Rachamim [a mental asylum]...
Lying like that on the hard bed at night, unable to shut an eye, and considering the situation well, he decided that as soon as he went out again into the street he would no longer search on the ground but up high.
And so it was: as soon as they let him out, he went out into the street with his head held high, looking into every window where any living woman appeared. Sure that in the end he would find what he was seeking, he stopped everywhere and looked up, until he was completely drained and worn out from running around a whole day. At last he noticed that a woman was standing at a window looking down at him. His imagination ran wild: this is just what he is looking for. And he pulled the newspaper out of his pocket and began to study how that other fellow had behaved... He began signalling up to her with his hands and winking with his eyes; she, on the other hand — a simple maid who was washing the windows — seeing such a pest, did not think long, grabbed the bucket of water and poured it over him from head to foot [misprinted "dpgegosn"], and on top of that had him taken off to the "Chad Gadya" [jocular for the police lock-up]...
Arriving at Sha'are Rachamim for the second time, the superintendent began to question him: "Ma tovu?" — what does he want here and what is he doing here? He told the whole story: that he had come to look for luck, and that he is sure that everything written in the paper is true — only he himself is a shlimazl...
Truly, both things he read in the newspaper exist in reality — money does roll about in the street, and rich widows do look out for their destined match. But what then? He, poor soul, has no luck: when he searches the ground and keeps his head down, a rich lady stands right at the window looking out at him — and he doesn't see her; and when he holds his head up high, the purse with the money is rolling right between his feet — but he doesn't notice it...
For everything you need luck, and when you have luck you hit on exactly what you need.
Here too, my friend, things have somehow been swept away and there is no luck: you have goods — you have no customers; you have customers — goods are lacking; you have both — the customers have no money to buy with... You need warm weather — cold spells come; so that we can in no way hit on the right thing.
But, as they say over there where you live[?]: the top acorn must also come out some time. One must, after all, hit it right some day too, and may the Almighty grant that it be at least before the soul departs, because our strength is really giving out..
Your friend Yosef.
Upper Silesian Economic Sketches

[Article — Upper Silesia, economy.] Dr. Avraham Shayer, Katowice.
2) Retail trade.
As we already mentioned in the first article, one of the most painful questions in retail trade is the very important item of business costs, which are required by the level at which this kind of trade stood before the war and at which it has maintained itself and developed after the war as well.
The minimum of luxurious fittings and the larger capital that such a business requires have, however, the advantage that they unintentionally hinder the rise of poor undertakings without capital, which cannot afford all this and whose existence is doomed in advance to collapse; that is why there is no pauperisation in retail trade, as there is in other parts of Poland. The causes mentioned above thus hinder the rise of competing firms with smaller business costs, which thanks to this would lower [?] the average prices in the place.
And speaking of competition, one must especially mention the dangerous competition that threatens Upper Silesia — since Poland took it over — from Sosnowiec and its surroundings on the one side and from Beuthen (Bytom; German Upper Silesia) on the other. Sosnowiec, a town of over a hundred thousand inhabitants, lying right by the former German border, has, like all border towns incidentally, a very developed retail trade. A very important factor in the competition with Silesia is that here no luxurious businesses are set up; the shops are in unkempt front premises, in gateways or in flats, and the merchants are not used to the proportionally large profits which the Silesian merchants must, for the reasons already mentioned, add to the goods. That is precisely why Sosnowiec has the name of a cheap town, and the Silesian workers buy almost everything in Sosnowiec. The trains and trams bring whole masses of shoppers from Silesia, who come here to buy cheaply and go from shop to shop picking over and looking for the lowest prices. A special class of street brokers has arisen here, the so-called "lapaczes", who stand in groups at every train or tram and drag in the Silesian customers with various promises. On the only shopping street, on Modrzejowska Street, there reigns all day a "quiet" [?] bustle and a crush, and a newcomer who is not familiar with the local conditions has at the first moment the impression that some meeting or demonstration is taking place here. The public drags itself along the pavements, which, dating still from the times before Sosnowiec was given sewers, are 40 centimetres higher than the middle of the street. People also jostle in the middle of the street, and one hears a hubbub as if one were at an Oriental fair. The shops are full of customers examining the goods, and of brokers waiting for their minimal commission "per piece". While in Silesia the principle of fixed prices has been adopted, here the "bidding" (asking higher prices) has taken root among the merchants, and the customers know it, so they haggle in a very comical manner. The difference between the asking price and the price finally reached [?] is enormous. Everyone persuades himself that one must haggle, and that after a longer bargaining he has snapped up a bargain. The writer of these lines himself witnessed a merchant asking 175 zł. for a lady's coat, and the customer offered… all of 35 zł. And after an hour's haggling and a few more "threats" to walk away, he bought the same coat for 65 zł.
The Sosnowiec competition makes itself strongly felt by the Silesian retail merchants; it grew stronger still from the moment the trams that connect all of Silesia with Zagłębie began running. Especially affected by the competition from Zagłębie are the branches: ready-made clothing, shoes, linen, butter and colonial goods (groceries).
Of a quite different character is also the fairly strong competition from Beuthen and other German border towns; and despite the stepped-up border inspections, the competition there has taken almost all the wealthier customers. The consumers are accustomed [?] to articles in the German "taste", so they travel to Beuthen, where one can get everything one could wish for. The urge to buy in Germany grew stronger from the moment the tariff war with Germany broke out, which — as is well known — has lasted from June 1925 to this day, and since the Silesian (Polish) merchants sold off all their stocks of German goods, and no fresh goods can — because of the ban — be brought in. One must add, however, that local industry is trying with all its strength to satisfy the local market as well as the taste of the customers.
The introduction of the Polish language has created a whole series of new livelihoods here in Silesia. The merchants mostly know the Silesian dialect (Po ślunsku) from before the war, but only rarely do they know the Polish language in writing. So a huge number of writing offices has sprung up here, translation offices, bureaus for interventions with the administrative authorities and the tax office or in court, which is very important for the retail merchants. Very many merchants keep no books, but hand the work over to the special offices, which keep their accounts for them, draw up balance sheets and submit tax returns. There are over 70 such offices here; many are even run by qualified lawyers who — for various reasons — cannot devote themselves to the bar. The offices have developed very well here, and many employ a whole staff of clerks and have a very rich clientele; and for their growth they have above all to thank the unheard-of high taxes with which the merchants are burdened.
Despite all the difficulties with which local retail trade has to contend, there exist respected and well-appointed shops of various branches, which are a "fat morsel" for the country's wholesalers and manufacturers because of their proportionally strong and creditworthy position.
On wholesale trade — in the next article. (Sh.)
Lag ba-Omer — Women's Day for the JNF (KKL)

[Zionism — Jewish National Fund.] The Head Directorate in Jerusalem, together with the WIZO centre in London, at the time proclaimed Lag ba-Omer as the day of the Jewish woman throughout the world for the Keren Kayemet. On this day all Jewish women must manifest their participation in the work of redeeming the soil in the Land of Israel.
On this day the Jewish women will spread the idea of the redemption of the land (Geulat ha-Aretz) through various events and undertakings, bring the ranks of women closer to the ideas of the Keren Kayemet, and collect money for the purposes of our Fund.
Hadassah in America, too, in connection with the custom of "Mother's Day" in America, has designated this day as "Hadassah Day" for the Keren Kayemet, and in honour of the Jewish mother trees are planted in the homeland on the soil of the Keren Kayemet.
In these days the strong bond between the work of the Jewish woman in the Diaspora and in the Land of Israel and the idea of the redemption of the land should be emphasised. Jewish women must understand that their work for the Land of Israel can only succeed if the soil of the homeland [?], which is the foundation of our work of construction, is transferred into the possession of the whole people. Only when one understands the significance of the national and social principles that the Keren Kayemet realises in its activity will Jewish women draw from it enthusiasm and devotion for our great tasks and for the eternal values of our work.
There is no doubt whatsoever that our active and energetic workers, men and women, will devote great attention to "Women's Day", and new camps of devoted and self-sacrificing women workers will grow for our noble and holy work, the redemption of the land.
Lindbergh's Tragedy

(How much is a child worth?)
Like lightning in a dark night, which tears off a piece of darkness and in a second throws light over distant expanses, so certain events throw a bright light on everyday life.
Facts take shape — single, separate, sometimes, it seems, without any connection to one another, making no particular impression on you; but as soon as you connect facts with facts, events with events, every occurrence acquires a meaning, and the essence of human fate and of social struggle becomes clear to you.
Just as dynamite explodes at a certain temperature, just as thunder arises under certain conditions of electric charges and the closeness of clouds[?], so the eyes of the blind are torn open, so the ears of thousands of deaf are opened, when one shows them razor-sharp, clear, stark, chain-linked facts of today's society, when one makes them hear the voices that accompany the events...
Among such occurrences of recent times belongs the tragedy of Lindbergh's murdered child.
Millions of eyes strained every day over the newspapers, searching for the fate of Lindbergh's child; millions of hearts feel with the unhappy parents, to whom a wrong has been done.
What is
In the United States someone stole the child of the famous aviator Lindbergh from a splendid villa. Staffs of agents and policemen were set on their feet. They searched all of America, combed the ports, inspected ships in mid-ocean. Special detectives were sent to Europe to look for the stolen child. All the countries of the world (Poland among them) received telegrams asking them to help search for the child. Every day the newspapers brought new telegrams on how the investigation stood, and printed reports: "The child is on a ship in mid-ocean, it is healthy, eats normally every day." "The child's mother is on the verge of going mad." "The child is in a European port." "The bandits are ready to return the child to its parents for the sum of 50 thousand dollars." "Lindbergh is paying one hundred thousand dollars." "Lindbergh's child has been found dead." The ransom sums grew. The bandits stood firm, the telegrams kept running, ears were pricked, the affair became sensational, perhaps[?] a little exaggerated. In America everything is possible, people think; be that as it may, a whole world was stirred up over the tragic fate of Lindbergh's child.
Fact number one.
Now I read in the same newspaper this small notice: "Good people, have pity on my one and only child. Out of want I must leave it in the street. May good hearts take pity on my child." Such a note was found pinned to the little dress of a 2-year-old girl who was found in the gateway of...
Fact number 2.
Now, dear reader, tie the two facts of life together and see how the whole chaos of today's world is mirrored in them, the "truth" of our time, the "happiness" of people...
Which of the two mothers is more unhappy? That does not concern us in this case. Whose grief is greater? But the sensational facts of today's reality do strike the eye.
I leaf further through the big-city newspapers and read: "Yesterday afternoon the police picked up four abandoned children who were lying wrapped in rags. The eldest is 6 years old. People hurried past in the severe frost and did not notice the children. The eldest child relates that the father has been unemployed for a year already, the mother runs around doing various jobs and does not get any. Everything at home has already been sold off. The children did not want to give their name and address. The police took the children to the foundling home."
I read on: "Yesterday at dawn the woman... 32 years old threw herself down from the fourth floor. Reasons: want and despair. The suicide left 3 small children. Her husband went off weeks ago to look for work and nothing has been heard from him."
Here another report crops up that strikes the eye: "Here the 23-year-old (name and surname) was arrested on suspicion of abandoning a child. The arrested woman confessed her crime and explained her deed by want: she cannot find work anywhere and could not bear to watch the child's suffering; in the foundling home — she explained — the child will have food and a clean home."
Facts pile up upon facts. One's head is already spinning. I try to set the occurrences against each other.
On one side, parents are ready to ransom their child from strangers' hands for hundreds of thousands of dollars, a world mourns their misfortune and... at the same time thousands of children perish for a piece of bread; at the same time thousands of parents want to get rid of their children because they cannot satisfy their most minimal needs; at the same time mothers commit suicide, unable to watch their children perish in want and grief; at the same time...
Lindbergh's tragedy lights up hundreds of facts, throws a searchlight's beam on them, and the chaos of today's life becomes clear. The abysses that divide the poor from the rich become visible; the voices that press[?] in the depth of the abyss become audible...
And a question pecks: "How much is a child worth?" How much? In our time it depends — "on which child?" Children of palaces and children of want have different prices. There is no comparison between their worth. Here children have the worth of millions, and here children do not have the worth of pennies (groszy)...
It is not the worth of children that is valued today, but the pedigree of social standing. Children of poor parents, who must already work from their earliest years, have at the factory owner's the worth of pennies, while his own children of the same age spend thousands of złoty („gilden“) on themselves.
And not only children — what is the price of a working man with "high-pedigreed" proprietors? A fraction of their own [worth], sometimes the worth of a horse and sometimes even less. Therefore let us not appraise the worth of a child under today's conditions.
Let us stand in the light of Lindbergh's tragedy and behold the thousands of tragedies that come not by chance through bandit attacks, but grow up in the folds of today's order as the inevitable consequence of the "justice" and "truth" of the conscientious robbers in white gloves...
Let us stand in the light of the human struggle and behold the white tomorrow...
H. Ring.

Antisemitism Against the Community and Against the Individual.

[Editorial — Poland, antisemitism and government policy.] We are reproached quite often that our oppositional mood stems not so much from reality as from our habits of the old Tsarist times.
If there is a little truth in that, we must at once point out that the malice of some of the lower state agents also stems from old habits — of looking upon the Jew as an inferior creature. Were those elements psychologically imbued with the spirit of the Polish Constitution, our struggle for the realisation of our constitutional rights would be much easier.
In truth, however, our situation today is considerably worse than before, and very often we find ourselves sighing over "we remember the fish" [Num. 11:5]. And this not because there is a general crisis, or because we no longer have the old sales market, but for quite another reason.
In Tsarist Russia a wild antisemitism reigned, which in the last 35 years of the Romanovs was carried out with fearful consistency. But there the forest was so big that one could not see the trees, and when a decree went out against the community as a whole, the individual could nevertheless think: "I shall have peace."
In other words: the savage persecution of the Jews had a political, not an economic character — an aim "to destroy and annihilate", but not to starve, not to take away the morsel of bread from so-and-so.
Here, even the antisemitism of the Endeks [National Democrats] could not take on such a character as in Russia, because in the end the enemies of Israel stood face to face with a Constitution that equalised the Jews in their rights with all citizens. They could make the Constitution "harmless" by braking and delaying its effect, but to erase the particular paragraphs from it was not within their power.
And today, since the Sanacja government came to power, antisemitic policy has been taken out of use altogether, and every effort is made to behave towards the Jews tolerantly and loyally. The Jew is not allowed to be beaten, insulted, and... there it stops; more than that they cannot protect us. In the practical struggle for existence antisemitism rages, and for the most part it has bitten precisely into those areas from which the channels of livelihood stretch today — the state spheres.
Even the Sanacja-loyal Jewish BBWR deputy Wiślicki has to admit that the tax offices pursue an explicitly antisemitic policy, which is especially conspicuous in the Pinsk affair, where the new finance director overestimated Jewish earnings many times over.
What then are we to say when we see that suddenly, without any reason, Jewish employees of the sickness fund are dismissed? How can we let ourselves be lulled to sleep by supposed motives of a "conspiratorial" character, when we see that this is a general line: as soon as an institution passes to the government, the Jews are smoked out of it?
If it is not antisemitism, then it is simply a Hottentot notion of "what's mine is yours" — that whoever stands close to the trough may drive away the one further off, not let him eat...
And at times one thinks that perhaps it would have been better to have antisemitism against the community as a whole, which would leave the individual in peace...
P. K.
An Urgent Task.

[Sosnowiec — health and children; an appeal to TOZ.] (Addressed to the Sosnowiec "TOZ" [Jewish Health Protection Society])
With the coming of summer the narrow Jewish lanes in the courtyard[?] begin to swarm with poor children below school age, who roll about all day long in the gutters, swallowing dust and dirt. Only rarely does it occur to anyone that it must not be so, that in summer children should be out in the fresh air, in the forest, in the field — and not alone, without any supervision, but under the guidance of qualified educators.
The question of educating pre-school children does not lose its sharpness in winter either. Then, however, it is much harder to find a solution; to talk of founding Froebel schools [kindergartens] for all these children, who remain without supervision and suffocate all day long in the narrow, stuffy rooms, would simply mean touching on questions that cannot be realised even with the best will: neither can the Jewish population of Sosnowiec provide the means for it, nor are there the appropriate forces that would be capable of fulfilling such a task.
Much easier, however, is it to solve this task in summer. It does not require any enormous means, as people imagine; what is needed is rather a little devotion and interest.
All these hundreds of children whom we meet in the courtyards, rolling about in the gutters, could quite easily be placed in the so-called half-day colonies, where they would spend the time until midday in a nearby forest or garden, get food there, and be under the supervision of suitable educators.
Such a task should without any doubt be taken up by the Sosnowiec "TOZ" (if it exists), which should come to the Jewish population with an appeal to give it the means to fulfil this task.
And if "TOZ" fulfils this task, it will have earned merit for the health of the hundreds of poor Jewish children.
Is It Summer Already

[Short feuilleton — the weather and summer.] (A little feuilleton).
Is it summer already?
May I be forbidden if I know, because always, in the good old times, the weather — like everything else — stood firm in its place and in its time without any fluctuations, like the dollar or the pound; but today nothing stands firmly on its feet, everything is shaky and uncertain, and with the weather it is the same.
In the morning — chilly; later a little hot; before noon lukewarm; in the afternoon a rain, and in the evening you actually start shivering.
I don't know whether it is fitting yet to begin a "left-handed"[?] summer flirt on the cucumber [i.e. in the "cucumber season", the slow summer season], and whether damp summer kisses might not sometimes do no less harm than a winter grippe.
Well, what I don't know — there is a lot I don't know; years ago, for example, by the 20th of May it was already summer with a bang, and — silly, but one remembers; it was then, on the New Market, "on the green carpet" (as the poets write), that I got to know my present wife; that was then no smaller a catastrophe than, let us say, a car catastrophe today. But summer it was! And today? The forest has no intention yet of putting on its green summer overgarment and leading couples astray, although according to the calendar there should already be a real heat, and the beach should already be shimmering with girls in fig-leaf bathing costumes; but apparently the weather too is in such straits that it didn't even have the means to buy itself a calendar, and it hasn't the least idea whether it is now May or October.
You see, yesterday towards evening the real summer arrived for me personally, with the "double-eight" heat:
when my little wife said to me:
— Mendel! You must already rent me a dacha!
I got hot, no less than in the very middle of Tammuz...
P.
Go bathing, but with sense!

One of the best and most useful summer pleasures is bathing. On hot days it is a real delight to refresh oneself in the Przemsza.
But every year many accidents happen while bathing. Mostly this happens through one's own fault — people are not careful enough. If one wants to guard against drowning, or even against catching a chill, one must observe certain rules.
First of all one should in general take care not to stay in the water too long. Someone who can swim may stay a little longer than someone who cannot swim. This is because, thanks to the exertion of swimming, the body stays warm for a longer time. As soon as one feels cold in the body, one must get out of the water at once.
One should never go into the water right after eating. One must wait at least 2 hours. One must never bathe alone in a place where there are no people around. Before bathing one must see to it that the nose is clean, so that one can breathe well. Whoever suffers from the ears, or is deaf, should put cotton wool in the ears before bathing.
When a wind blows from the land, one must not swim too far away from the shore; it may happen that it will be exceptionally hard to swim back. One should never go into the water when out of breath. After bathing one must dry oneself well. Do not bathe in a deep place one does not know, and above all be careful, because every ill-considered step can bring an accident.

A conversation with a factory chimney

I clambered up a factory chimney and struck up a conversation about our industry, so to speak[?].
At first the chimney wanted to whistle at me, but since it happened to be a strike day, it had nothing to whistle with...
— Who is to blame for the strike?
— What do you mean who, — answers the chimney, — the workers, of course; they didn't come to heat the boiler, so the factory stopped.
— But the manufacturers want to cut the wages.
— Then the workers mustn't let them.
— So they are not to blame after all.
— But nowadays times are bad, everything has become cheaper than last year.
— So who is to blame after all?
The chimney threw back its head and pointed me to the sky: you're not far from heaven already, climb up — it says — maybe there you'll get to the bottom of it...
Yosef.

Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin; installment 25.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov. (25)

They stood still. Rasputin's hands began, with overpowering tenderness, to stroke her hair, face, neck and breasts... She stood as if bewitched... Then he laid his hands on her shoulders, kept looking with his sharp gaze into her face, and whispered:
— I see! A great inclination [?] to sin is in you!
She trembled: it was the truth...
And he said in a hot whisper:
— And I tell you: do not stifle the sin within yourself, and let the sin not remain with you... Sin the sin out, and let your soul be purified. That is the way that leads to God! Sin and repent... That is what God demands!
Again his hands stroked her whole body... Her breath was taken away. She was completely hypnotized by his gaze and by his words... He said again:
— The "holy" spirit that is in me commands me. I must be close [?] with you and purify your soul... I, who once saved your body from perishing... who rescued you then, when the horses bolted — I will also save your soul... Sin the sin out!
And he began whispering strange, licentious words into her ear... He spoke about all the limbs of her body... Soon he cried out:
— Undress!... Throw off your clothes!... Do not be ashamed of your nakedness!... For nakedness is from God! Clothes are from men... Undress! Nakedness was created by God! Undress!
She was entirely in his power... She obeyed and began to undress. He did not take his eyes off her, stood with open lips and watched the clothes falling from her...
• • •
When Rasputin had sobered up, he again began to play the role of a "saint". He was silent, pensive, and his eyes radiated piety. He dressed and went straight to the corner where the icon hung, lowered himself to his knees and began to cross himself, bow and pray. Vyrubova too came up to him, knelt at his side before the icon and said her morning prayer.
Rasputin folded his hands on his breast and began to pray aloud. His voice was now soft, melodious and heartfelt. Vyrubova remained quiet, listened to his voice, and again she was overcome by religious ecstasy. His voice was so familiar and pleasant. In her heart she believed in the "holiness" of the muzhik and felt: beside him she is purified and exalted...
When Rasputin had finished his praying and stood up, Vyrubova stood up too. Now he looked at her with fatherly, tender eyes. He made the sign of the cross over her, embraced her [word unclear, "patshlikh"], kissed her three times on the cheeks and exclaimed:
— Now, my good soul, I see: you are cleansed of sin and close to God!
And she smiled with enthusiasm, she believed him, and Rasputin stood drawn up straight, holding his head bent to one side, his eyes half closed, and began to preach. He spoke again about God and about the ways that lead to Him... spoke about how God hates the hypocrite... that it is not by fasting and praying to God that one comes close to God, but by cleansing oneself of sin; through repentance and remorse one enters the gates that lead to God...
He spoke calmly; on his face there was now no sign of passion. And Vyrubova had the feeling that she was in a convent, hearing the chastising and consoling words of the "Redeemer"... And the more she heard the words, the lighter and purer her heart became, the calmer her mind grew. Now she felt a tremendous attachment to this "holy" man. She must have him... She can no longer be kept far from him... It seemed to her that she could stand like this for whole days and listen to his words...
Then Rasputin stopped preaching and said:
— And now, radiant [?] sister, it is time to eat breakfast!
— Good, "Father" — Vyrubova exclaimed — I'll have the table set at once.
— And don't stint on the food... One must not shame the body! Rasputin exclaimed earnestly.
It did not take long, and both were sitting in the dining room at a richly laid table. Again all kinds of dishes had been set out on the table. Rasputin ate with great appetite and with his hands. With his not overly clean fingers he tore pieces of smoked [printed "geroyberte", probably for "gereykherte"] fish, plucked pieces of cheese and stuffed them into his mouth with gusto. Vyrubova ate little and the whole time did not take her eyes off the "holy" muzhik. She talked about how Rasputin must now settle permanently in the capital and be regularly [?] close to the imperial court, which so badly needs his help and his protection... She would also meet with several of his admirers, who had made his acquaintance in the salon of Countess Ignatieva, and within a few days an apartment befitting him would be arranged for him... The Tsarina herself would also help them with it... for the Tsarina would no longer let him go away from her... She herself and several more of his female followers would look after the apartment, would see to it that the "holy Father" should lack nothing... and would provide everything for him.
Rasputin heard out her words, did not stop eating in one breath, and only now and then cast a glance at her with smiling, kindly eyes and nodded his head: he agreed.
At last he stopped eating, wiped his moustache with his sleeve [printed with a doubled "di di"], surveyed the table as if looking for something, and asked:
— Good sister, where is the wine?
— At once! — Vyrubova answered and rang for the servant. The door opened, the servant appeared, and Vyrubova ordered him:
— Bring in a bottle of wine!
— Right away! — said the servant, bowed slightly and turned to leave the dining room. But here — and Rasputin stretched out a hand.
— Wait a moment!
The servant turned his face to the table, and Rasputin turned to Vyrubova:
— Good sister! Tell him to bring the same wine that he brought during the night... That wine is very good, it smells like the Siberian "veygen" [?]...
Vyrubova asked the servant:
— Which wine did you bring in during the night?
— Of the wine that Miss Dimenshtein asked to have brought here — the servant answered.
— Is there still some of that wine?
— Miss Dimenshtein brought ten bottles... there are six left.
Bring in a bottle of that wine.
The servant went out. Rasputin squeezed his eyes shut for a while. Lightly furrowing his brow, he at once remembered who Miss Dimenshtein is... Why, that is she, the wonderfully beautiful girl whom he had met in the salon of Countess Ignatieva. He drew a deep breath and again felt how lust cried out [?] in his blood. He made an effort and called up her figure in his memory. He saw standing before him a tall, slender girl breathing youth and health. He saw her full red lips, her head of thick dark-brown hair, her alabaster neck, her firm breast, to which the dark-blue silk of her dress clung. And the muzhik, from whom a hot spring of eroticism gushed, swallowed heavily, feeling a passionate wave flood his heart. His eyes became half closed, pallor appeared on his face, he breathed faster and fell silent.
Meanwhile the servant brought in an opened bottle of wine with a couple of glasses, set them on the table and went out. Rasputin mastered his passion, which had raged wildly in him, and his face became calm. He poured a glass of wine, gulped it down, and then he asked Vyrubova:
— Who brought the wine, did the servant say?
— Miss Dimenshtein brought the wine — she answered.
— Miss Dimenshtein? — Rasputin asked again — Isn't that the one I met in the countess's salon? Isn't she the daughter of the Jewish banker?
— Yes, "Father"... that's her... She was at my place yesterday and brought me the wine as a gift.
— You are friends with her, then?
— Yes, "Father"...
— She has a wonderful soul!
Rasputin exclaimed this in a pious voice. He nodded his head calmly, remained quiet, pensive, and furrowed his brow... He drew himself up and sat for a while as if he were listening very intently to something... Then he began to speak as if in a dream, to himself:
— I hear! The "holy" spirit that is in me tells me: this Jewish daughter has a radiant soul... and the spirit commands me to help her purify her soul and bring her under the wings of our "Redeemer"...
And he began to speak as though he were arguing with the spirit:
— I am ready to fulfil your command... But who then will bring her to me? Or [?] the purified sister? Good. I will tell her so. Here he opened his eyes wide and began to stare hard into Vyrubova's face. Again his gaze was sharp, mild and commanding — Vyrubova again felt that she was in his power and subject to his will — and he sang it out in his melodious voice.

Which Articles Can Still Be Sold Today?

[Economy — foreign trade and world markets.]
(Specially for our paper, by Z. Haber, Vienna–Leipzig.)
Not only manufacturers but also exporters and wholesalers are today seeking every possible way to produce and sell those articles which customers demand and which can still be marketed somewhere.
The Leipzig Trade Fair Office (Messamt), which is already preparing for the fair that will open on 28 August of this year, is already issuing information on which articles are now in demand all over the world, and with which articles one can do business even in the present time of severe world crisis.
It is worth knowing which articles are now sought in the world.
In Romania: household goods and novelties of all kinds needed in the home are bought not only in the Romanian towns but even in the villages. There are exporters and consumer cooperatives there that employ hundreds of agents who travel from town to town and from village to village selling household goods; mostly smaller practical items sell. One can obtain quite good prices, and it pays to import goods from abroad, which are bought [more readily ?] than the simple cheaper things manufactured in Romania itself. Besides this, one can do big business in Romania by bringing in from abroad all kinds of lamps, fine handkerchiefs, tulle, gloves, and also all kinds of rubber articles, hairpins and combs for women's hairdos. Gablonz [costume jewellery], necklaces are in great demand in Romania today, and one can do big business with them. The duty on them is not high.
Holland: there one can now do good business with used typewriters. In almost every house — even among private persons — a typewriter is used today; but since new machines are very expensive, people look for used machines, which are lacking throughout the country and which can be brought from abroad, because the duty on used machines is very low.
Belgium: throughout Belgium one can easily sell pretty, inexpensive articles of luxury porcelain, all kinds of pretty things of leather and wood, articles for ladies' fashion, for example toilet articles, necklaces [?]; pretty toys and household goods are also in great demand. Besides this there is a large demand for table cutlery of semi-precious metals, copper goods, brass goods, and in general all novelties of every line. The duty on these things in Belgium is not high.
France: good business can be done here with precious and semi-precious stones, art objects of bronze, marble and fine metals, feathers for dresses and ladies' hats, [cigarette] holders of amber and imitation, and advertising articles. Especially children's toys, combs and hairpins of rubber for ladies' hairdos.
England: the country, especially for the colonies, greatly needs lamps and lanterns burning paraffin, furniture and instruments for doctors, rubber goods for medical purposes, cheap electrical novelties, glass and porcelain goods, celluloid, articles for shoemakers, feathers and furs used for clothing, and all kinds of chemical dyes.
In Eretz Israel: there is a great shortage of bicycles, which people there are beginning to use a lot; besides this one can do good business there with machines needed for making chocolate and [—] (…lades) [?].
Egypt: tools are lacking there, iron chains and small iron articles such as locks, bolts, small chains, screws and the like. With these articles one can do good business there.
Africa: many countries in East Africa, such as Madagascar, badly need porcelain, glassware and almost every line. Especially lacking there are drinking glasses and glass chimneys for paraffin lamps, which are still used everywhere there. Enamelware too is much needed there, and there are many exporters who buy these articles for cash in the European countries. But they demand low prices, although in Africa people pay pieces of gold for them.
In America: in America there is now a great demand for cellophane paper — a kind of paper that lets no moisture through. Formerly this paper was used wherever parcels or crates of goods were shipped overseas; today in America it is used for all kinds of purposes: dust coats, raincoats, dust bags for winter clothes — in short, everything is made of it, because the paper does not let through even a speck of dust.
Since this paper is not manufactured in America, the exporters who bring the paper from abroad do a big business; the paper is literally snatched from their hands, and so they raise the prices from day to day.

Będzin: Out of the Conflict between the Butchers and the Shochtim a Fifth Shochet Is “Hatching”...

[Będzin — Kehilla; Ritual slaughter.]
As our readers know, a delegation of butchers turned to the kehilla board with a series of accusations against the shochtim (ritual slaughterers). In this connection a meeting of the kehilla board, together with the rabbinate, took place on Sunday; the shochtim and representatives of the butchers were also present. At the meeting it became clear that the main accusation against the shochtim is that they demand a special payment for slaughtering after the official hours, while the butchers are free to adapt themselves to the official hours of the shochtim. For this matter a commission of the rabbinate and kehilla representatives was elected, which is to decide the question in a favourable manner.
It is interesting that during the discussion of the question the proposal to engage a 5th shochet was unexpectedly put forward...
At the meeting Mr. A. Liwer (Zionist) submitted an interpellation concerning the improper reception given to the rabbi and the kehilla representatives during the 3rd of May celebration. To the interpellation the board member (dozór) Mr. Bożykowski declared that the reception had been a satisfactory one..

The catastrophic situation of the Jewish carpenters.
The new presidium of the local craftsmen's association called the members of the Jewish carpenters' guild to a meeting at which various questions concerning the improvement of the general situation of the carpentry trade were to be discussed.
But instead of taking part in the discussion on the agenda, a large part of those present poured out their bitter hearts and told horrifying facts about the situation of their families. It turns out that among the Jewish artisans tremendous want prevails, children are starving in the literal sense of the word, the despair is indescribable, artisans are selling their last goods and chattels just to feed their families with dry bread.
— Perhaps the craftsmen's activists in our town would at last stop their political dabbling and care more that the only most productive section should not die out! It is surely high time that the internal frictions should cease and the energy be used for real, tangible deeds...

Obliged to be vaccinated are schoolchildren and adults who have so far never been vaccinated, children subject to compulsory schooling, and also those who have not been vaccinated during the last 5 years.

At the general meeting of the members of the “Bank Kupiecki” [Merchants' Bank] it was decided, after a lengthy discussion for and against, to liquidate the financial institution. For this purpose a liquidation commission of 5 persons was elected.
Tag Sale of “Linat ha-Holim”

Next Tuesday, Lag ba-Omer, a tag sale will take place in the town for the benefit of the “Linat ha-Holim” society. As everyone already knows, the present committee of the institution works very actively in its field, thanks to which the hard situation of the poorest part of Jewish society is eased. It is therefore to be hoped that the tag sale will be properly supported by Jewish society, so that the board of “Linat ha-Holim” may be able to carry out its relief programme for our sick sisters and brothers.
Ran Up Debts of 700,000 zł. and Vanished / Meeting of the Leather Guild / For Forged Bills of Exchange / There Was No Domestic Peace...

In the circles of the cattle dealers the news has caused a great sensation that the well-known cattle merchant Niewiarowski has vanished. Niewiarowski owes the Trade Bank (Handels-Bank) and the “Bank Spółek Zarobkowych” a sum of 400 thousand zł. Besides this he owes 380 thousand zł. among merchants.

Meeting of the Leather Guild
Next Sunday a meeting of the leather guild will take place in the local Craftsmen's Association; it will deal with current questions.

For Forged Bills of Exchange
Before the local district court stood a certain Maksymilian Żył [?], who was accused of circulating forged bills of exchange for 3,500 zł. Żył was sentenced to 18 months in prison.

There Was No Domestic Peace...
In the Niemce colony two young women from Strzemieszyce were found unconscious; they had attempted suicide by drinking sizeable portions of vinegar essence. The cause was — family quarrels.

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the local Revisionists will take place in their own premises. A representative of the Central Committee (C. C.) is to take part in the meeting and will lecture on the present situation in Zionism.

These days the president of the Head Committee for Aid to the Unemployed, former minister Klarner, stayed in Zagłębie in the company of the Kielce voivode and the head (naczelnik) of the Social Welfare department, with the aim of acquainting himself with the activity of the local committees for the unemployed.
In connection with this a conference took place in the office of the Będzin starosta, A. Baksa [?], at which the further action was also discussed.

In the building of Mr. Musiałek [?] on Górnicza Street a fire broke out. The house, 2 horses and various inventory implements were burnt.

From the local resident Knobler [?], who was arrested by the Będzin police, 17 kilos of saccharin were confiscated.

An appeal to Polish Jewry.
This year too the Union of Centrals for Orphan Care in Poland, "CENTOS", turns to Jewish society for help in its difficult and responsible work of bringing up the most neglected Jewish child — the orphan.
10000 children are at this moment under the full care of the institutions belonging to the Union!
3000 children are learning a trade!
5000 children benefit every year from health and "apru"[?] colonies!
Hundreds of mentally and physically[?] retarded children are maintained in special institutions!
The severe economic crisis has hit the orphan institutions hard. Into many institutions hunger is breaking in, and danger and ruin threaten them!
Jewish society, which has shown so much understanding and self-sacrifice for its orphans and neglected children until now, will not allow the children in the Union's 137 institutions to remain without care.
We call on the whole of Jewish society to exert all its strength to support the Orphans' Week, which is being held throughout the country by the Union for Orphan Care in Poland.
We call on you to contribute to the local orphan committees, to give larger one-time donations and to support all the events of the Orphans' Week:
The fate of thousands of orphans depends on us:
None of us will shirk fulfilling the sacred duty towards the neglected Jewish child, towards the orphan!
—o—
Exhibition of paintings by Natan Szpigel.
Yesterday the exhibition of paintings by the acclaimed painter Natan Szpigel opened in Będzin, in the hall of the Merchants' Association.
About a year ago we had the opportunity to see the art of the painter Szpigel here; he was then in Będzin with the artist Ignacy Hirszfang. Now Szpigel has come with his new collection of paintings, which captivate the eye with their distinctive language of colour.
Szpigel recently had a colossal success in England. The exhibition in London, which was opened by Nahum Sokolow, attracted the most prominent personalities and art critics. In London the artist sold several paintings to public art institutions and private collectors, such as the well-known Jewish financier Otto Schiff and others.
Szpigel is an artist and an optimist: when he paints the skies of Kazimierz, his colours sing with brightness and light and kindliness radiate from them. It is quite different when Szpigel leaves the sky for the field and paints for us man and our time — man immersed in the grey conditions of his hard, toilsome existence.
Szpigel does not chase after outward colour effects; rather, as a skilled, seasoned artist, he descends into the depths of the objects he paints. Natan Szpigel is very industrious; from time to time he comes into our little Jewish world with his creations and surprises the public with his splendid brush.
His present exhibition is a product of his power: about 100 paintings speak to us from the wall in his distinctive language of colour; they simply captivate the eye, and it is a delight to visit this exhibition.
—o—
Italian guests in Olkusz.
In honour of the anniversary of the death of the Italian colonel Francesco Nullo, who fell in the Polish uprising of 1863 and lies in the Olkusz cemetery, the Italian delegation visiting Poland also visited Olkusz and the grave of their countryman Fr. Nullo. The starosta and the town administration made sure the town had a festive appearance. All the houses were decorated with Polish and Italian state flags. In front of the railway station a parade gate with splendid decoration was specially erected. Thousands of people gathered on 3 Maja Street, along with various military and civilian organisations with their banners and orchestras. At 3 o'clock in the afternoon the guests arrived from Kraków, among them the Italian consuls and ambassadors in Poland and the Italian colony of Upper Silesia and Kraków, in black shirts with fascist pennants. As they passed through the gate the starosta greeted them and the Italian anthem was played.
Afterwards they visited Nullo's grave, where a religious service was held.

At Szlomo Goldfeld's, on ...[?] day, 500 zł. disappeared. He cast suspicion on the house painter who was present, Jankiel Dawid Apelsztejn, and his son Lewi. To clear themselves, the latter, following the rabbi's ruling, took an oath in the synagogue.

Counterfeit 10- and 20-groszy coins
Recently counterfeit 10- and 10- [sic; read 20-] groszy coins have appeared in circulation. The side of the coins bearing the state coat of arms is nickel-plated.
The counterfeit small change is being passed at the markets or in shops. The police are conducting an energetic investigation with the aim of uncovering the counterfeiters.
—o—
Vacation cannot be counted into the notice period
It often happens that white-collar workers who are given notice by their employer [have their vacation] counted into the notice months — into the 3 months of notice [sic; words apparently missing].
According to a ruling of the Supreme Court, however, the employer may not take away the white-collar workers' vacation by counting it into the notice period.
Since the matter is now topical, white-collar workers should know that as soon as they agree to use their vacation within the 3-month notice period, they no longer have the right afterwards to sue the employer in the labour court.
—o—

The board has already begun preparations for the elections.

The Sosnowiec kehilla budget is already on its way...

This week, after long and heavy suffering, the „rozkład“ [apportionment of the community tax] of the establishment (etat) and budget for 1932 was completed.
The „rozkład“ amounts this year to 144 thousand zł., i.e. 17 thousand zł. more than last year.
The budget and the „rozkład“ have already been sent for approval.
—o—
On Monday construction of the post-office building in Dąbrowa begins.
Last Wednesday a delegation of the Ministry of Posts stayed in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] with the aim of finally settling a series of questions concerning the construction of the post-office building.
The delegation held a conference with the [town] president Dr. Madejski, at which the necessary matters were definitively settled.
Next Monday construction already begins. First the commercial premises on Sobieska Street will be finished, and later the one-storey post-office building will be built, which will stand vis-à-vis on Kościuszki Street.
—o—
That one must pay for water...
The Sosnowiec magistrate has installed water taps in several streets, at which supervisors have been posted who sell [water] at 2 gr. a bucket.
The water-sellers are „loyal“ to the magistrate and take care that nobody should enjoy the „living water“ without money.
This week on Pańska[?] Street it came to a brawl because a poor woman permitted herself to take a little more water for a grosz... than the fixed portion...
—o—
100 per cent matura at the Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec.
This year's matura examinations at the Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec brought an unexpected result. 16 pupils who sat the examinations received matura certificates.
The examinations were conducted this time by a [woman] inspector delegated by the school curatorium in Kraków.
The following pupils received the matura:
The first was Eydl[?] Dafner of Będzin, then Feigl Epsztajn of Będzin, Eugenia Folkowicz, Chana Feldbaum, Chana Fiszel, Złata Fiszel of Będzin, Malka Goldberg of Miechów. Felia Szpigelman of Będzin, Lea Krupa, Jocheved Planczner of Będzin, Halina Lancman, Zosia Mestel, Zelde Makower of Będzin, Złata Sztern, Tojbe Szpigel of Będzin and Prima Trajman.
The result of the matura examinations shows that the gymnasium stands at the proper level.
—o—
The last 3 days of Spiegel's exhibition in Będzin.
Friday, Saturday and Sunday are the last 3 days of the picture exhibition of the well-known painter Natan Szpigel.
In order to enable the broad strata of the people to visit the exhibition, the admission fee has been reduced to a minimum.

Meeting of the Będzin „Muza“.
In the premises of the „Muza“ in Będzin the annual general members' meeting took place, at which the following board was elected: chairman Sz. Bojm, vice-chairman H. Orner, secretary A. Najman, treasurer T. Hamburger. M. Kaner, J. Winer and M. H.[?] Mager as board members.
The first task of the board is to found within the society a tourist circle, which will be active in the summer months with the aim of visiting the surrounding area, the industrial centres, and making excursions.

A new Jewish pharmacy in Będzin.
The pharmacy on the Old Market in Będzin is passing to a Jewish pharmacist. The owner of the new pharmacy is Mr. Perec Kahan of Katowice.

Need breaks iron...
In front of the gmina [municipal office] in Lipiny about 300 unemployed gathered, demanding that the relief sums[?] be paid out to them.
Among the crowd there was also a large number of working women who, hearing that the payments would not take place, went off to the market, where they snatched bread from the stalls...

From an unknown cause the clothes of 11-year-old Rozalia Hejda of Radzionków[?] caught fire. The girl was so badly burned that she died the next day.

Your Best Friend Is Your Mother!

[Zagłębie — society; Mother's Day.]
(For Sunday's “Mother's Day” in Zagłębie).
Already in the year 1910 America, the land of sober[?] reason, celebrates a “Mother's Day”. The ever-cold businessman devotes one fixed day in the year of his practical life to honouring his highly esteemed, above-all beloved mother. The example was soon followed by Sweden[?], France, England and Germany.
In Poland “Mother's Day” was celebrated for the first time in the year 1928. At that time “Mother's Day” was also celebrated for the first time in Sosnowiec.
In the first year, within the limited campaign, we contented ourselves with the slogan: everything in honour of your mother, and also of every mother. Today[?], after four years of planned campaigning in the elementary and secondary schools, we go further.
Every mother, without distinction whether poor or rich, carries her child in her heart. Every beggar-woman or queen spends the nights in mortal fear at the time of her child's illness; the mother is the being who understands and feels the joy and contentment of her child; only the mother knows best how to ease the pains and sufferings of her child.
Therefore, remember that your mother is your dearest friend, a friend who does not abandon you in your troubles and dangers; she is always ready to sacrifice herself for your well-being. So be good and gentle, be tender to your mother, do not be ashamed of tenderness and show her your gratitude, love and respect; for only with the mother, rich or poor, does every person feel safe and freely protected, because she never refuses you her help. A mother's heart does not demand, rather it gives more than her weak strength allows.
Next Sunday, the 29th of May, Zagłębie celebrates a “Mother's Day”. On that day every child must give honour to his mother, but that is only a mere demonstration. The chief meaning of the day is — to hold your mother in honour, to value her and always be good to her and think of her with attentiveness.
Bronisława Grudzińska

From Sport.

[Sport — Będzin.]
“Hakoah” — “Maccabi” 0:3.
The match drew a large crowd. “Maccabi” came out to this match with 9 men, “Hakoah” fully complete. Throughout the whole time of play “Hakoah” had a strong superiority and does not let the initiative out of its hands. The “Hakoah” forwards continually bombard the opponents' goal, but owing to the brilliant play of the goalkeeper it is hard for them to score a goal. Only in the 30th minute does Gutman score the first goal with a splendid shot, and 2 minutes later, from a corner, Kalman scores the second goal with a “główka” [header], and a minute later the third goal is already in.
Immediately after half-time “Hakoah” begins energetically to attack the opponents' goal, but in the 5th minute the “Maccabi” goalkeeper is injured and leaves the field. Because of the team's being incomplete the referee Kożybucki[?] breaks off the match with the result 3:0 for “Hakoah”.
Finally, a few words about the match.
For quite some time before the match rumours were going around in Będzin that “Maccabi” wants to pull a stunt [“shpitsl”] for “Hakoah” and give away 2 points without any fight. The rumours later, unfortunately, proved to be true, and “Maccabi” fielded a mixed team of 9 men for the match.
Hakoah is not concerned with what “Maccabi” is after with this, but how can one allow oneself to give away 2 points without a fight?
Unbelievable too is the report that for the second round “Maccabi” is said to have engaged several Ślązaks [Silesian non-Jewish players].
The “policy” with the Ślązaks must finally be brought to an end here among us, the Jewish sports clubs in Zagłębie. In the ranks of Jewish sportsmen there must be no Ślązaks. It is better to lose (by fighting) with one's own players than to win through foreign players.
No, we are not against Christian players playing in Jewish clubs, but not there where one appears as a Jewish national blue-and-white team.
A. Wrocławski.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — miners, crime, Katowice community.]
Congress of the Polish coal miners.
On Sunday a congress of delegates from the coal mines and the coal miners' unions took place in Katowice. The question of a new wage agreement, proposed by the industrialists, was discussed.
The congress adopted a resolution which categorically opposes the industrialists' new agreement. The resolution declares that the workers will stop at nothing in the struggle against the worsening of their living conditions.
More than 200 delegates took part in the congress. The main speaker was the leader of the class union (Klassenverband), former deputy Stańczyk. He gave detailed particulars of the appalling living conditions of the coal miners in Zagłębie and in Silesia. Tens of thousands of workers are forced to live on wages of a few groszy, and their despair may lead to unforeseen results.
The coal miners are ready[?] to strike and not to give in. The long strike in Zagłębie did not frighten them. The only question is whether the N.P.R. and Christian-Democratic unions will once again betray, or whether they will support the struggle of the class union.
—o—
A son murders his 89-year-old mother.
In Świętochłowice a son killed his 89-year-old mother. The mother, who is spending her last years, came to visit an acquaintance in Świętochłowice. When the son learned of this, he lay in wait for her with a blunt iron bar, and when his mother appeared he struck her dead with 10 blows.
The murderous son declared that he had taken revenge on her because she would not give him money for a glass of vodka...
The murderer will be brought before a summary court.

Katowice community budget before the plenum
Under the chairmanship of President Dr. Reifmann a meeting of the community council took place together with the commissarial administration. On the agenda of the meeting was the community budget for the year 1932/33. In drawing up the budget the commissarial administration used the method of 1) cutting and 2) raising...
The cut applies to the officials and the rabbinate, while on the other hand an item of 600[?] zł. a month was entered for new premises for the office. Director Abraham, too, has again kept his salary of 15 thousand zł. a year; only the designation of the item was changed: instead of "director", the same sum is provisionally budgeted for a lawyer.
The council spoke out against the budget as drawn up, above all against the administration's proposal to cut[?] the rabbis' posts.
Accordingly a budget commission was elected, which is to fix the budget within the limits of the present economic possibilities.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bechukotai)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bechukotai *)
The Portion
—o—
a) "If you walk in My statutes" (Lev. 26:3)
"If" — a doubtful, hesitant expression, because every commandment must first be examined as to whether one should perform it. And not every commandment suits everyone — for instance, being sandek, for a coarse young fellow.. That is why the Midrash says on this verse: "This is what is written: 'I considered my ways'" — one must think over every commandment.
Ohel Yitzhak (Rabbi Yitzhak of Warka).
—o—
b) "Then I will give you rain in due season" (ibid., 4)
"A loaf and a rod were given wrapped together from heaven. He said to them: if you keep the Torah, here is a loaf to eat; and if not — here is the rod." (Midrash)
The bread and the stick were sent down wrapped together, bundled up, so that it is hard to tell them apart, and only a person with a good sense can feel which is the stick and which is the bread.. For not all commandments are like bread and not all sins like sticks... Only when you unwrap them do you see their true face...
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
c) "And I will give peace in the land" (ibid., 6)
Rashi explains the verse "the fruit of the land — the children of the righteous." Peace — "the land" means the tzaddikim. It is indeed the greatest blessing that there should be peace among the tzaddikim, that the rebbes should not tear at one another. Oh, what a blessing that is...
Degel Machaneh Ephraim.
—o—
d) "And I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (ibid.)
What keeps a person from sleeping is envy of his fellow. Not because he himself lacks something, but because his fellow does have it. But if "I will give peace in the land" and you will not envy one another, then "you shall lie down and none shall make you afraid" — you will sleep peacefully...
Siftei Tzaddikim.
—o—
e) — "Ten women shall bake your bread in one oven" (ibid. 26)
Abraham Mapu once passed a Jewish bakery in Slobodka on a Friday. He hears the women cursing and swearing at one another over the "shifting" of the cholent pots. Said he: now I understand the curse of the Rebuke: "ten women shall bake your bread in one oven" — because when women bake together they curse each other with curses that are not even in the Rebuke...
—o—
f) — "And also My covenant with Abraham will I remember" (ibid. 42)
Isaac is — worship, Jacob — Torah, and Abraham — acts of loving-kindness (gemilut chasadim).
Why is it with Isaac and Jacob in the singular (not "worships", not "Torahs"), and with Abraham in the plural — gemilut chasadim (not gemilut chesed)?
Because in Abraham's loving-kindness Sarah helped him...
Sippuran shel Tzaddikim.
—o—
The Haftarah.
g) — "Cursed is the man who trusts in God" [sic; the verse reads "in man"] (Jeremiah 16 [sic; 17:5])
It is not Jeremiah who curses him — the one who relies on a human being is himself an accursed, a damned man...
Petach Sha'ar.
—o—
h) "As the partridge that sits on eggs it has not laid."
Money is certainly not a clean thing, certainly does not have a good taste. But — like those impurities that the water carries along: if it is running water that carries the impurities away, it is still bearable; but if it is standing water — such a stench of the impurities rises from it that it is dangerous.
With that rich man from whom the money flows back out to charity and the like — it is still no problem; but if it is standing water from which nobody has [seen] a penny [?]... — it stinks!!
Kochav mi-Yaakov.
