Harmful Upbringing — Do Our Teachers Look After the Children Entrusted to Them? / Communist Activists Arrested in Dąbrowa / Shot "na wiwat"...

[Editorial — education: football and cinema; followed by two short news items: Dąbrowa — police; Góra Zamkowa — court.]
Last week an appeal to the Jewish population was printed in the columns of our newspaper from the management of the Jewish Public School No. 2, which comes out clearly and distinctly before the public, asking it to begin waging a struggle against football.
The bitterness stems from the fact that a 15-year-old pupil paid with his life for the game of football. The wound is thus fresh, the pain is great, and hearts ache over the victim who was so tragically torn from the world.
We did not wait for the catastrophe; more than once we have already touched on the question and pointed out the harmfulness of this newly arisen sport. We did not at all want to wait for victims; for a whole year we warned public opinion not to make light of the football matches, which take from the youth so much strength, time and health. But who, in such times, pays attention to questions that are highly topical and modern in spirit? After all, one must adapt to the times and behave like everyone else.
Well, we would still have understood that one has to take part in this sport, and all that would have been fine if our youth had kept within bounds, if it had known where the limit begins and where it ends. But under no circumstances whatsoever should it have been allowed that they be immersed in this "trade" body and soul, that one should get up with football and go to bed again with football. The under-age boys were bewitched by the game. They chased after the sport as after a card game. And once one had been drawn into this gamble, one was capable of going even as far as murder. How many times have knives flashed in this sport; every perceptive eye could assess the consequences this newest sport will bring in the near future.
Unfortunately, with us people see only when they are struck, only when it hurts. With us one never wants to imagine that nothing of substance can come out of emptiness, that water is, after all, no more than water. Unfortunately, we never want to give ourselves an account of what matters in which we have no confidence can bring.
And now along come the heads of a public school saying that one must fight the football idea, that it must not be allowed to take the place which it has in fact long since taken, and the motive put forward is that a young sprig has been torn from their school. Of course the heart aches when such a catastrophe happens; but why should one not have calculated beforehand that it could lead to such horrifying moments? And had the accident not happened to the child from the school, would that mean that one need not fight against what is harmful and what has been neglected[?]? That it can come to this? It is a rare thing, how short-sighted these people are — and they are the very ones who are always in the company of children, those who study and are immersed in the psychology of the child, in the soul of the children's world.
Of course one must begin a struggle against this dangerous phenomenon, which gives the community nothing and utterly corrupts the child's naive little soul. But in this case we would not want to deceive ourselves. With mere words and long newspaper articles one will not achieve much in a real sense. Why then deceive ourselves — this sport-pain has already penetrated too deep into the bones to be removed so quickly; and therefore the real work must be begun and carried out in a systematic way. First of all we would wish that no one set about tearing out this disease radically, because such a thing cannot work on the youth: it has already penetrated deep into the blood of the bones, so that the youth will miss it like a fish misses water; therefore one must set about the work according to plan, in a systematic way. One must begin to wean the young footballers gradually from this gambling game; it must be done exactly as a mother weans her child from the breast — gradually, slowly, systematically, so that the child does not notice that the breast is missing. In this way one must wean the children from the sport of football; [to do it] all at once[?] — we do not know whether that is desirable, for if one tears him out of the bewitched circle all at once, the element will have to rush off toward something else, and then the question arises whether this "something else" will not be just as dangerous — and who can know whether it may not be even more dangerous than the "football game" from which he has just been torn?
It goes without saying that there is no lack of things dangerous for children in our times. Of course, not everything must threaten mortal danger, and yet it is harmful and poisons the child's little soul from the earliest years on.
Take the cinema — a product precisely not meant for children; and whom does one see there if not children and youth from the earliest years? True, one does not pay with one's life for a film that is unsuitable for a child, but the child's little heart is poisoned before it has ripened, and then we get a whole contingent of broken children's hearts, which remain cripples — spiritual cripples — forever.
And therefore why should we imagine that we have victims only when a child leaves the world prematurely because he becomes crippled at a football match? We hold that no less must we guard our children so that they do not go to the cinemas for programmes unsuitable for them.
More than once we adults turn red with shame when we sit together with children and see what films and live cabaret programmes they come to watch. We are then ashamed before ourselves; so why should the school youth be allowed to attend such films, which for them are deadly poison? Why are they let into such programmes, and why do our educators permit such lawlessness in this field? The cinema can give the child a great deal, but only when it is given films suited to its age, which help it develop spiritually and culturally. On the other hand it is harmful when children crave to see films that are not for them. Those films break the children's naive little souls, which can then no longer be led onto the right path. So why should our educators, our guides, not pay attention and protect the children from all sorts of ways that can break children's little hearts? For the people there is really no difference whether we raise spiritual or physical cripples; in a certain sense spiritual cripples are more dangerous for a people than physical ones, and therefore it would be only right to look seriously into the upbringing of the future generation, of the coming man, on whom we pin so much hope.
Our teachers and educators, for whom the children must be the apple of their eye, must take an interest in their children who are entrusted to them. At every step the teachers must watch over their children, so that they are not brought up wild and free in the street and do not become blind tools in whosever hands, or undesirable individuals.
Youth — that is a tender being, a young little twig that bends in all directions; it is so elastic that one can do with it whatever one wishes, but only in the earliest years, while it is still helpless; therefore we must make use of these years and bring it to the desired goal. Then the dough can still be kneaded as one wishes, and this opportune moment must not be missed; the very earliest years of our children must be guarded like the apple of the eye.
Our educators and teachers must render an account; they must not forget that the people has placed in their hands the upbringing of its children, and they are therefore responsible for everything they do with these children of the people.
We know that in our generation it is not easy to bring up children and make human beings of them, and that is precisely why it is the duty of our teachers to watch every step, so that their work should not go to waste and the people should receive from its teachers future human beings, prepared to make their way later along the road of their future in everyday life.
R. Let.

The Problem of Physical Education

(Children in their first school years).
The years of childhood, in which the child is still free of any study whatsoever, and above all of the burden of spending several hours a day at school, are of great importance for the development of the child's organism and for its whole further life. Those are mistaken who are naïve enough to persuade themselves, or who want to persuade others, that on entering school the child is still a "tabula rasa", a completely blank sheet on which one can still write whatever anyone's heart desires. By that time the child already has an enormously important period behind it, and it comes with a world of concepts, feelings, inclinations and with a treasury of experiences that have left indelible traces on its psyche. Likewise the child also brings along a physical "baggage", on which its later health depends to a great extent.
The transition from free, carefree romping in the friendly [?] home surroundings to life under compulsion and the imposed rules of the school is a rupture in the child's life. This rupture can have a fatal effect if it comes too brutally, if at that moment the proper pedagogical methods and the necessary care for its tender organism do not come to the child's aid. Modern pedagogy therefore demands that the school should, as far as is at all possible, be a continuation of the home.
But even a school equipped in the best possible way pedagogically and hygienically has a bad effect on the health of children in their first school years. It has been established that the child's growth in the first school year is considerably held back. At this tender age, from the sixth to the seventh year of life, the child needs a constant stimulus to grow, vigorous growth and an excellent metabolism. To make these tasks possible, good nutrition and plenty of movement are important — movement that should not be limited to certain groups of muscles but should take in the whole organism and bring about a livelier circulation of the blood. Yet precisely at that time the child must begin to get used to working several hours a day on the school bench. There is not the slightest doubt that this has a harmful effect on the child, first of all on the function of breathing, because breathing on the school bench is limited to the lower parts of the lungs, while the apices of the lungs hardly function and therefore become as if "smoked" [?] or "clogged" [?], and from this a catarrh of the lung apices easily develops. And not only the lungs, but the heart too works under difficult conditions in a child on the school bench. From long sitting on the bench children become accustomed to a bad posture. Considering the child's weak, delicate musculature, it is clear that this often gives rise to hunched shoulders and a curvature of the spine. This happens especially in rachitic and anaemic children.
So no small dangers lurk for the child in its first school years. It has in general been proved that a child who stays outside school develops in the same period two or three times faster than one who is at school.
What, then, is the moral of this?
First of all, every careful mother, before she goes to hand her child over to school, must have it medically examined, and hand the child over only when the doctor finds that the child's state of health and its physical condition are satisfactory. A child that is not properly developed should stay at home a while longer and begin learning later. And on the other hand one must combat all the negative influences of the school and do everything that is necessary and at the same time possible for the normal, all-round physical development of the child. The way to this, however, by no means leads through two to three hours of school gymnastics a week — but plenty of movement and plenty of free, fresh air. That is what the child's health demands.
We said above that the school has a harmful effect on the child's health in the first school years even when it is hygienically and pedagogically equipped [?] in the best possible way — all the more so does a school institution which in the pedagogical and hygienic sense still leaves much to be desired, as for example a school where some sixty children are driven into one class. The gathering of a larger number of people in a closed room pollutes the air, and this air poisons the lungs and through them the whole human organism. That is why children in their first school years are mostly bloodless, anaemic — and all the more so the more overcrowded the class is.
A mother who cares for her child's health will therefore make every effort to avoid such a school for the reason noted above alone, not to speak of the fact that a school where a class is crammed with a crowd of sixty children cannot, even with the best will of the best pedagogical staff, in any way meet the weighty [?] watchword of modern pedagogy — to be a continuation of the home.
The weeks are approaching when parents will have to make a decision about enrolling their children, who have reached compulsory school age, in the schools. They do not always realise the significance of this step — it is a first-rank, fateful decision.
What Do You Say to That?

[Będzin — education; opinion.] In the Zaglembie chronicle we read:
"When Mr. Bufheitz[?] declared to the Government Commissioner of the city of Będzin that if he did not pay out the subsidy for the 'Mizrachi' school it would have to close, the Commissioner answered laconically: 'Let it close.'"
Could the answer[?] have sounded any different, if in a town like Będzin, which has 80 percent Jews, one can approve for a Jewish school with two hundred pupils a subsidy of[?] nine hundred złoty a year, and then one takes the subsidy away[?] and answers nothing: 'Be no uncle to me and give me no slice' [idiom: neither kinship nor favours]. In the same way one may go on to strike out the subsidy and order the school closed.
Honour, personal as well as national, must be guarded in its entirety; otherwise it ceases to be what it is, and one can do with it whatever one likes.
It would be fair to ask the Commissioner how much the Magistrat pays just in rent for the teachers of its own schools!
But go argue with a man of power. A man of power does not reckon with the most elementary demands of justice and social logic. Yes, one does not reckon even with the politics of tomorrow, only with the politics of today, the politics of the present.
But even more short-sighted than the Commissioner is the Jewish community of Będzin. Nobody gives any thought to the situation arising in Jewish cultural life. People are beginning to walk the well-trodden paths of assimilation. Assimilation that costs cheap and assimilation that costs dear. If you stop, say, a Jewish Jew in the street and ask him what he thinks of the materialist world-view of 'lit din ve-lit dayan' [there is no law and no judge] — only a hand, and in the hand bread and sometimes an axe — he will jump back[?] four cubits and spit three times; but if you look closer you will see that in practice people are not so far from materialism at all. It simply breaks your heart to see how, under the blows of the economic crisis, the spiritual-national and even the religious backbone is bending too, while people keep persuading themselves that it is actually for the good of the ideals which they are beginning to deny.
Once — I believe Jews will remember it — the main thing in upbringing, the main thing in education, was Jewish knowledge, Jewishness.
More understanding, enlightened Jews taught their children writing too, Polish too, German too, arithmetic too — all as an 'also', as an addition to the actual Jewish knowledge. The World War, which overturned the worth of many values, brought many changes into the education of the young Jewish generation in Poland too. Many Jews came to the honest conclusion that the children should no longer be left in the old 'vayitrotsetsu' [the struggling of Jacob and Esau in the womb], like Jacob and Esau wrestling in the Torah portion, but that the worlds should be divided between them equally — and a balance set in. People wanted to raise children fit for God and for people. They took education into their own hands. They organised schools themselves, maintained them themselves, cared for them themselves, supervised them themselves, and the Jewish schools formed one of the most important cultural and political-national positions, for which people went into political struggle. The approach was right. I am not at all opposed[?] to the urge of today's youth towards Eretz Israel and the Hebrew and religious-national school and the Hebrew teacher. But in the 'high windows' [the seats of power] they understood this well and created the 'szabasówki'[?] [state schools for Jewish children, closed on the Sabbath]. Had Jews held fast to their school system, they would in the end have found some way out that would have led not to decline but to the further building of the Jewish school system. But Jews soon capitulated and began sending their children to the Polish schools; more than that, they built Polish schools with their own money. From the moment the front was breached, things in the Jewish school system went from bad to worse; finally the economic crisis brought on the 'galopka'[?] [apparently: the final gallop], and dozens of Jewish schools today stand before 'gesisah' [the death throes].
Jews, good Jews, stand at a distance and watch the ruin breaking in, and not only do they keep silent, they already stand ready with clods of earth to fill the grave — the ship is rocking and the mice are already starting to run, and it is all fine. It is even fine that the hand that can give or not give 'nine hundred złoty' can decree whether a large Jewish school is to live or not; it is not needed, there is [a school] for free, and Yiddish will be taught as well, and the old 'Polish too' now sits down[?] on the Jewish rabbinical throne — now it is called 'Yiddish too'. The balance is already disturbed, the border already shifted. Tomorrow will show us its wonders. Dentists may rejoice in advance: many a Jewish tooth will break on a haftarah.
Only one should not goggle one's eyes and say 'le-shem yihud' [for the sake of unification — a pious formula], one should not persuade oneself that one is committing here some 'sin for the sake of Heaven'. Let one have the courage to say: impossible, I don't want to...
Well, that Jews have no money — that I understand; but that the thread runs out precisely at the Jewish zemirot [Sabbath table hymns] — that I do not understand. That Jews love order we all know; but that he should love it so much as to sacrifice this for it — that I do not know.
Not only with money; in general, somehow, many Jews do not feel like doing anything Jewish themselves, and so we have no cause to complain about other men of power who say: we don't live from this, 'lo mi-piv anu hayim' [we do not live by his word], and we won't die from this.
But what do you say, what do you say?
Does your Jewish pulse not beat in your thoughts? Does your heart not stir a little? Do you not think of the morrow and of the face of the coming generation? I know your pocket is tight, on your heart [it is] 'katamosne'[?], but do you no longer even say a blessing over thunder?
What do you say to that?
A. Gotesdiner.
Collect More Strictly!

Drop into the execution (enforcement) department of the tax office in the morning, and you will see how the enforcement officer sends the bailiffs out into the town at exactly 10 in the morning. He literally drives them out of the building. If he were to catch a bailiff hanging around the rooms of the tax office 5 minutes past ten, it is quite likely that the bailiff would lose his post after a single warning.
The officer presses the bailiffs because the tax chief (naczelnik) presses him. The tax chief is pressed by the Finance Minister, and the Minister is pressed by the state budget.
And this week we read that at a conference between the Finance Minister and the tax chiefs, the Minister declared that the taxes must be collected strictly — that alone can rescue and maintain the balance of the budget. That means that until now the taxes were not collected strictly; the tax pressure was too weak. The five years during which the „wagon“ has been going round the houses taking away the last stool from the home and even the smallest trifles, such as lamps, clocks, pictures, curtains, linen — all that is called collecting taxes mildly.
Or perhaps the Honourable Minister thinks that the „wagon“ system has gone bankrupt and that one will have to resort to other „inventions“ for pumping the last groszy out of the population for taxes?
True, the government has now taken over the monopoly on the „wagon“. The magistrates and the sick funds will now no longer get any „prawa judis“[?] (apparently a pun on prawo jazdy, „driving licence“); there will[?] be only one „wagon“. But it turns out that the „wagon“ was a good means only in the first years, right after Grabski invented it. Today it is already a stale thing, as if the automobile had pushed the real wagon aside...
In earlier years, when the public was not yet accustomed to taxes, people did not pay, reckoning that it would blow over. Then the wagon came down, and people used to cry and pay. Today, however, it is quite different. Whoever has money and runs a business pays his taxes at the cash office, so as not to have to pay any superfluous interest and enforcement costs. From the one who has nothing, everything was taken long ago. To the sluggish taxpayers the „wagon“ has after all been driving for 5 years, day after day, and in such a time one could already have emptied the shelves of the shop and stripped the home bare.
That is precisely why the bailiffs have little desire to go round the town; they have to be driven out, because they know that with their going round the houses they will achieve very little, and it is quite likely they will come back to the „office“ (urząd)[?] the next day with empty pockets...
When the Minister said that the taxes should be collected even more strictly, it certainly made no strong impression on those directly concerned, the taxpayers. What can be stricter than the way they have collected until now? Only the bailiffs are surely racking their brains now: what means can be applied that will work even more strongly than the „wagon“?...
J. Abramowicz
At Last I Have Seen a Bright Future Before Me...

[Satirical feuilleton — taxes.] When I felt that my only piece of furniture, the wardrobe, was shortening my years so much — day after day sequestrators [bailiffs] came walking in and kept listing it [for seizure], and I had to pay without limit and without measure — I decided once and for all: enough! I don't need any wardrobe.

And without thinking much, I took my wardrobe on a cart and carted it off to an acquaintance of mine. There — I thought to myself — let it stand there; it won't be like this forever. When times change, I'll take it back.

The moment I moved the wardrobe out of my home, I became a completely different person; a new vitality rose in me. Only now did I feel the taste of life — they come to me, they grope, they search — no wardrobe! So they register me as impoverished, and I'm rid of the whole business.

But my happiness did not last long. Not a few days had passed when my acquaintance came running to me, neither dead nor alive — bad news, he says, Reb Chaim Yankel, hurry and take your wardrobe out of my place, because I expect that any moment now they will list it for my "podatki" [taxes]; with me, too, they have already piled up...

Hearing the story, everything went dark before my eyes. I immediately ran off with a little cart and carted my wardrobe off to a relative of mine on my wife's side, a well-to-do Jew, a merchant, who lives in a flat of five rooms and a kitchen; he permitted me to put my wardrobe in a corner of a children's room. After all, one must do a poor relative a favour, provided it costs no money...

And again I lived happily for quite a long time, until once, on a bright Wednesday, my rich relative from my wife's side comes in to me and addresses me thus: Listen — he says to me — Reb Chaim Yankel, I would advise you to take your wardrobe away right now, and as quickly as possible, because it may become too late. I stared at him wide-eyed. Bless you, I answer him, Reb Yona Grunem! What has suddenly happened to you?

— Don't ask questions — my rich relative Reb Yona Grunem waved his hand — you don't know, times nowadays: money was taken from me, so I had to take it from someone else, and now there's a business with protests [protested bills], with "komorniks" [bailiffs], clauses, "licytacje" [auctions] — hurry and grab your wardrobe out of here...

In short, why should I go on babbling at length: I ran off and grabbed the wardrobe... But where does one take it now? And an idea occurred to me: I would put my wardrobe at Moshe Zelig's, my first cousin's [?], who is a poor Jew, a sort of collector for some society, runs no businesses and has nothing to do with commerce. At his place, I thought, would be the most suitable spot for my wardrobe...

And so indeed it was. For a while it was quiet. But suddenly I see Moshe Zelig come running, out of breath...

— Chaim Yankel! — he grabbed me by the hand — as God is dear to you, hurry and grab your wardrobe. I owe the free-loan (gemilut chesed) fund 50 guilders, and they have taken the bills of exchange to the "komornik".

So you understand that I needed nothing more: I immediately grabbed a porter, and a few minutes later my wardrobe was already lying on a cart. But where does one take it now? Since there is trouble everywhere... And a happy idea occurred to me — to my uncle Moshe Leib's son-in-law! My uncle Moshe Leib's son-in-law is a young married man, half a year after the wedding, does nothing, boards at his father-in-law's, has no "patent" [trade licence] and makes no "obroty" [turnover], eats his lunch and waits for supper — a golden spot...

And so indeed it was. For a whole year it was quiet. Only yesterday his wife came running to me with a cry: Chaim Yankel, hurry, grab your wardrobe!...

And as I ran with the porter and the cart to rescue the wardrobe, I racked my brains, unable to understand why they would pick on a young man like my uncle Moshe Leib's son-in-law. But it turned out that in Poland they don't pick on you for nothing: it turned out that my uncle Moshe Leib's son-in-law owns some sort of "majątek" [property], thanks to which he was exempted from the military, and those exempted from the military must pay a "podatek" [tax]; so as long as he was a bachelor and there was nothing to take from him, they left him alone, but now that he has married, they came to demand "majątkowe" [property tax] from him for 8 whole years..

For 4 hours I drove around the town with the wardrobe and could find no resting place for it by any means. Nowadays, thank God, nobody is safe...

God alone knows how long I would still have been dragging my wardrobe around, had the real, right idea not come into my head...

— Israelke! — I commanded the porter — turn left! That's it, and now a little straight! Open the painted little gate very carefully! Don't scrape it even a bit...

It didn't take more than a couple of minutes and I was standing at the tax office [?], in the office room. "Panie naczelniku" [Sir, chief], I say to him, I am Chaim Yankel Poczewke [?], a men's tailor; I owe some big "zaległość" [arrears], so I have brought you my wardrobe...

For a moment the chief looked at me strangely, but soon he handed me over to an official, and when I saw that my wardrobe was already resting in the storerooms, only then did I truly feel that a mountain had fallen from my shoulders, and I went home like a newborn man, lively, fresh; the spring sun shone on me doubly, and I saw before me a bright future...

Y. L—tsh.

Small Remarks on Big Matters

13 days of rest in one month
Of the great and heavy baggage of days of rest with which we, the Jews of Poland, have been so richly blessed, we had the greatest success in May of this year.
Namely: thirteen days of rest in one month.
All in all it turns out that we Jews rest 129 days a year more than non-Jews; we Polish Jews rest for more than a third of the year.
Ever since the decree of compulsory Sunday rest came out, much effort and energy and much intercession by many Jewish representatives have been spent to ease this heavy burden for us.
But the matter does not budge.
I want to point out here, by way of example, how the matter looks in other countries, in the highly developed cultured countries.
In England, when a Jew rests on the Sabbath he may trade freely on Sunday. In France every single person has the right to choose the rest day that is convenient for him. In Belgium he may work and trade whenever he wishes and on whichever day, Saturday or Sunday. In Vienna a law has now been passed that those who keep their businesses closed on the Sabbath will be allowed to trade on Saturday night until late in the evening, and sometimes also on Sunday.
Very characteristic is the fact that on the island of Rhodes, which is under Italian rule, compulsory Sunday rest has now been introduced, but the Jews are not obliged to observe it. What is more, the Sabbath rest is recognised as the Jewish day of rest: all Jews are required to rest only on the Sabbath, not on Sunday. Even the Jews who until now kept their businesses open on the Sabbath must from now on rest only on the Sabbath.
These are examples of how the progressive countries treat such a painful question of a part of their citizens.
And here, a population of over three million Jews must bear such a heavy, superfluous burden.
We want to work honestly and hard, but thirteen days of rest in one month, 129 days a year, that is, resting more than four months a year — that is already a bit too much, too hard for us... and above all, not normal.
Who buys railway tickets
And indeed we are the most loyal and — I will go further: even the most faithful citizens of Poland. We get nothing, we give everything, or everything is taken from us.
Not long ago I was standing with a friend at a railway station by the ticket window. "Look," my friend says to me, "who buys tickets and who travels for free."
We often pay very little attention to the everyday phenomena of life, which are highly characteristic and in which the whole gamut of political attitudes toward a certain part of the citizens is reflected. And precisely because these facts are an everyday matter, we pay little attention to them.
I began to observe this phenomenon and came to the conviction that full-fare railway tickets are bought only by Jews. Perhaps 40–50 percent of the citizens of the ruling majority buy no railway tickets at all, or at most buy discount tickets. Each of them has some identity card in his pocket, a scrap of paper that gives him the right to travel free or at a reduced price.
Citizens of a somewhat lower rank are the main buyers of railway tickets and the payers of the hundred-percent price.
High prices and wage cuts
When last year the reduction offensive [?] against wages began throughout the country, the government for its part had an excuse: budget deficit, economic crisis; the private employer — bad business in general and... cheapness of products.
The cuts did not bring balance to the state budget, did not mend the crisis in the country and did not improve private business.
On the contrary, when we cast a glance back, from the time the first wage-cut "vaccination" was given until today, a sad picture emerges before us.
Not only has the wage-cut "cure" not added to our health, but since the wage-cut injections have been practised on our sick body, we keep growing thinner and losing weight.
The deficit in the state budget already reaches the official figure of 200 million. (Of the unofficial one we no longer speak.) And this is quite natural when we consider that by cutting wages the average income was in fact cut and the possibility of providing takings in the former proportion was taken away — consequently the turnover of the trading element also had to shrink, not to mention that consumption in the country and the standard of living of the consumers and of those whose pay was cut also shrank; about that there can be no two opinions.
The moral to be drawn from this should surely have been not to apply such "healing methods" against the crisis any further.
It turns out that the government still does not renounce these "healing methods"; it is again applying them in life. Just now it has again confirmed a 10 percent pay cut for civil servants, and, looking to the government, the private capitalists and employers will soon begin to follow suit, although even such a "convenient" excuse as the cheapness of products is now lacking. The spectre of high prices no longer hides tucked away [?] in a sack, but marches cynically and impudently, openly, along the whole line of our life, with bared teeth and sharpened claws.
This time high prices and wage cuts have met together. Both march in partnership. It would seem that at bottom they are opposites, enemies, but apparently there is a time when the two walk arm in arm.
What can come of such an unnatural match?
It is frightening to think.
Growing poverty.
In recent weeks we have witnessed a gradual rise in the prices of articles of prime necessity. Bread, meat and food articles have become dearer, and in parallel the prices of all kinds of foodstuffs are rising.
Meanwhile the rise has not yet stopped. On the contrary, there is a tendency toward a further growth of prices. At the same time the crisis eats ever deeper into the bones of the poorly-off and poorer population. To the same degree as the prices of foodstuffs rise, the prices of goods and wages fall.
Today's hunger wages, of both manual and intellectual workers, the pennies earned by small traders and artisans, barely suffice for dry bread to eat one's fill; of putting aside a few złotys for rent, of buying a shoe and a garment, there can be no talk at all.
Never before has want among the broad strata of the people taken on such a mass character as now; never before has impoverishment on the Jewish street been as catastrophic as now. In Jewish public life a deathly silence reigns. An apathy that comes from despair and, even more, from indifference. There is no public force that would venture on a broad and rationally conducted action to relieve the want.
Dearness of foodstuffs, low wages, meagre earnings and a growth in the number of paupers, who are already quietly sewing their beggar's bags in order to go later from door to door — all this will further enlarge the already large number of beggars, alms-recipients and needy of every kind.
Will no one stir to seek at least a small remedy for the growing want?

The 10-złoty banknotes are being withdrawn from circulation

[Economy — Bank Polski.] From 1 July of this year the „Bank Polski“ begins withdrawing from circulation the 10-złoty banknotes of the issue dated 20 July 1926. These banknotes will remain legal [?] tender until 31 December 1932, and after that date they will no longer be valid for payment.
From 1 January 1933 to 31 December 1933 these banknotes will be exchanged by all branches of the „Bank Polski“, and from 1 January 1934 to 31 December 1937 they will be exchanged only by the issue office of the „Bank Polski“ in Warsaw. After that date the obligation to exchange these banknotes will lapse altogether.

Theatre and Art

[Theatre and Art.] (From the guest performances of the Warsaw Yiddish Dramatic Theatre).
A considerable literature has already been written about Azef. Who has not read something about the great provocateur? It is therefore superfluous to recount the content of the stage reportage by the authors A. Tolstoy and P. Shchegolev [?].
It is hard to believe that Azef committed all his horrifying deeds only for money; we are dealing here, besides a provocateur, first of all with a psycho-pathological type. Azef is grateful material for a psychoanalyst.
As through a kaleidoscope, the greatest leaders of the Socialist Revolutionaries, as well as the most important tsarist oppressors, pass through the play.
Mansdorf is a talented actor; we know him from other roles. As Azef he was not strong enough, somewhat too wavering; even a weaker actor could have played it like that.
Klara Segałowicz (Maria) was excellent in her role. She was not stereotyped and was truly [?] convincing in her revolutionary fervour.
Very good were: Friedländer (Burtsev), Poznański (Devyatkin), Lemberger (Plehve; printed „Plshue“).
On the whole it is a very successful performance, both in the direction (Mark Arnshtein) and in the acting of the artists.
Parnose (Livelihood).
(Musical comedy in 3 acts; direction M. Weichert [?], sets: M. Weintraub, dances: Lea Rotbaum, music Henech Kon).
A worker scrapes together a little money and, together with his wife, buys a grocery shop. They do everything to draw in customers, but it does not help — the reason is that opposite, a beautiful widow also has a grocery, and all the customers go to her.
The worker gets an idea: he will [?] say of his wife that she is a widow and he is her brother.
That helps; customers come. But the couple cannot cope with the excessive abundance, and at the same time people flirt with the young „widow“ and propose matches to her.
Finally the husband can no longer go along with the game; he renounces the livelihood, so long as he can have his wife to himself.
The comedy breathes healthy humour; it is only a pity that the 3rd act somewhat weakens the good impression of the first two acts. The dancing and singing smack of cheap revue.
Also woven into the play are characteristic New York types: a doctor who speaks a dreadful English-Yiddish jargon, a strapping fellow before whom everyone trembles, a lumpenproletarian who uses revolutionary phraseology.
The acting is very good. The troupe consists of first-class, seasoned artists, and therefore it was a fine ensemble performance.
The sets by H. [?] Weintraub are very effective; the painted skyscrapers impress with their giganticness.
Henech Kon's music is well fitted, and there are very beautiful motifs in it.
M. Weichert's direction is good on the whole; it is only a pity that he allowed banality into the third act.
In our poor comedy repertoire „Parnose“ is a significant gain, and it is to be hoped that the comedy will hold the stage for a long time yet.

Natan Spiegel
(From his picture exhibition).
We saw Spiegel's exhibition a few years ago. At that time the artist was still in the stage of searching. His works showed clear traces of the various „isms“.
In the present exhibition we already see Spiegel the individualist, who goes his own artistic way.
Spiegel has discovered the secret that the spirit he was seeking lies within himself, and from there he drives it out onto the canvas; he speaks to us through the language of the line, through its rhythm, its melodiousness and its lyrical precision.
The main qualities of Spiegel's works are expressed in this: in drawing they are naturalistic and in colour expressionistic; thanks to this combination his pictures are varied, even though they are painted according to one unified conception [printed „kondemtsye“].
Spiegel takes from nature pieces of life, pieces of light, and passes them through the prism of his colour-rich palette, unpacking them onto the canvases with such lightness, with such grace, that the viewer is enraptured by the splendid colour chords.
One must admire how Spiegel manages to obtain such a firm, juicy colouring, dripping with so much life. Every landscape of his is a piece of dancing nature.
It is a hymn sung by the bewitching colour chords that the artist draws out with his brush.
Spiegel's subject matter is varied. We see a pair of shoes painted by him that remind us, with so much sadness, of something of Chaplin's tragicomedy; but soon the eye falls on a landscape of southern France, lit with such an abundance of colour that we are cheered and at once forget the sad mood.
For those who love in life mastery of artistic technique, the play of magnificent colour scales and aesthetic taste, Spiegel's pictures are a source of emotion [printed „emanation“], of true joy of life.
Sh. R.

Chapter Six
Who Was Rasputin?
Grigori Rasputin, or, as they called him in his native village, Grisha, was born in distant, cold Siberia, in the village of Pokrovskoye, to the muzhik and carter Yefim Andreyevich, and grew up in the stable, among the horses. As a boy he spent most of his time in the stable. For hours on end he would sit there, looking at the horses with wide-open eyes, and listen with bated breath as they snorted through their nostrils, stamped their feet and shook their hides.
In the street, in the village, Grisha was a wild, unbridled boy. He played all kinds of wild pranks and was the ringleader of all the mischief the peasant boys used to get up to. But as soon as he crossed the threshold of the stable, he at once became someone else: his boyish face grew serious, his eyes filled with curiosity, and he became as quiet as if he were not in a stable at all but in a monastery...
When there was no one in the stable except him, he would approach the horses with quiet steps, stand on tiptoe, stretch out his young body and with outstretched hands stroke the horses' warm bodies. He stroked them with great love and would even groan with pleasure. Toward the horses Grisha showed such deep tenderness as he never showed to his sisters and brothers, nor to anyone in the world.
He would stand like that for a long time stroking the horses. It often happened that in the middle of stroking he would become lost in thought and look toward the door; then he would run to the door and cast a glance out into the yard to see whether anyone was coming. And when he saw no one around the stable, he would run to the trough [printed "kareta", probably "koryto", trough] from which the horses ate. Nimble as a monkey he clambered onto the trough, clutched the horse's mane with his hands, pulled himself up and lay stretched out on the horse's back. With great love and tenderness he nestled against the horse, pressed his hot cheeks to the warm hide and held a conversation with it... He spoke to the horse in a stifled voice, spoke in a language he himself had invented and which nobody except him and the horses understood.
For a long time he lay like that and talked, laughing every now and then, and the horse answered him with a neigh [?]... The horse understood him...
Being with the horses was the greatest happiness for Grisha. Being in the stable and breathing in the smell of dung was his greatest joy...
Once, on a winter evening, when a terrible frost reigned outside and the fierce Siberian winds howled like hungry wolves, old Yefim — Grisha's father — was at home and did not know what to do with himself. So he called Grisha over, told him to sit down beside him on the bench and said:
— I will read to you from the "holy" book.
He took down from the shelf a big book with thick black covers, opened it and began to read aloud the story of how Christ was born.
Old Yefim read very calmly, pointing with his dirty finger at every word and every line. Grisha sat quietly, spellbound, and listened with the greatest attention to every word of the legend. Yefim read in a hoarse, pious voice about "Saint" Joseph, the "Holy" Mary, and about the "holy" child who was born in a stable...
The story made a tremendous impression on Grisha; from then on the stable became a wondrous place for him. Everything in the stable took on a different look for him. The trough, the lantern that hung there and shone with a little red flame — everything was full of secrets for him, which he alone knew about and of which he spoke to no one.
The next day, in daytime, when old Yefim was not at home, Grisha stole into the big room, pushed a chair over, climbed up on it and took the "holy" book down from the shelf. In the book there were many coloured pictures. And he turned leaf after leaf until he found the picture that showed the stable and the cradle in which the Christ child lies. The picture was in bright colours of blue, red and gold.
For a while Grisha stood bent over the book and could not tear his eyes from the picture. He was gripped by a mystical religious feeling. Afterwards he waited [?] with the greatest impatience for evening to come, when he would be able to ask his father to read to him again from that "wondrous" book.
In the evening old Yefim did Grisha's bidding and again read him the stories of Christ. Grisha sat on his father's knees, listened attentively to every word and looked with curious eyes at the coloured pictures in the book.
Evening after evening — at Grisha's request — old Yefim read aloud from the big book with the thick, heavy covers. Grisha sat spellbound and listened intently to every word. And so, by listening and watching how his father pointed with his finger at the words and the lines, he gradually learned the letters and how to put the letters together into words.

The Omer Days (A Historical Survey of the Bar Kokhba Uprising in the Year 132)

[History — the Omer days and Lag BaOmer; by Neta Landner.]
The earth had not yet properly soaked up the spilt blood of the hundreds of thousands of victims who perished in the terrible battles of Titus-Aspinus [Titus and Vespasian] at the time of the destruction of the Temple; the picture of the horrible destruction and of the barbaric deeds of the Roman legions was still fresh in everyone's mind — and yet the people could not calm down[?]. The spilt blood gave no rest; it called out and demanded vengeance on the hated Romans, and once again the dream of uprising and of liberation from the Roman yoke began to be woven. Throughout the land of Judea secret armed camps began, one by one, to organize, and they started to wage a slow partisan war. In secret caves among the hidden rocks of the Judean hills countless weapons were gathered, and from these secret, strategically calculated positions came the [?] attacks on the Roman soldiers marching through. The Roman governor of the time, Turnus-Rufus [Tineius Rufus], tried to suppress the uprising with the well-known cruel methods — but in vain; it did no good at all. The Jewish camps won every time with their well-planned attacks, constantly wearing the enemy down. The Roman rulers realized that they would not succeed in breaking Jewish obstinacy by force, and decided to change their attitude toward the Jewish people; and the emperor of the time, Adrinus [Hadrian], at the intercession of R. Joshua ben Hananiah, gave permission to rebuild the Temple, wishing thereby to win the sympathy of the Jews so that they would not support the hot-headed rebels. But this tendency did not last long: in the middle of the work the order came to destroy the further work, and later the order also came to the governor to have the whole site of the Temple Mount ploughed up, so that no trace of the former Temple should remain, and to erect a [pagan] temple in its place; and as a memorial he had bronze coins specially minted, engraved on one side with a picture showing the ploughing of the Temple Mount and on the other side with the words "Colonia Aelia Capitolina". This shameful act naturally aroused the greatest bitterness among the Jews; the blood boiled in all young hearts, and it served as the signal for the uprising known as the "Bar Kokhba uprising".
The freedom fighters of that time were joined also by the great Tanna Rabbi Akiva, who after the death of R. Joshua ben Hananiah had become the leader of the generation, the spiritual guide of all of scattered Jewry throughout the world. In his heart burned a flaming desire to see the Jewish people once more independent and free of any foreign yoke, and when the struggle for freedom began, Rabbi Akiva did not stand aside but actively entered the ranks of the rebels. Heedless of any danger, Rabbi Akiva undertook the most dangerous journeys through the Land of Israel, Asia Minor and Babylonia, holding conspiratorial meetings everywhere at which he called for war against Rome. At the head of the movement Rabbi Akiva placed his disciples, whose number reached 12,000 men and, according to some opinions, as many as 24,000. His disciples too were imbued with a fiery love of the people; they were the vanguard of the struggle for freedom, and their memory was immortalized in the memory of the Jewish people by fixing the day of 18 Iyar, Lag BaOmer, on which Jewish youth go out into the fields with flags and bows and arrows as a symbol of struggle and freedom.
It was not easy for Rabbi Akiva to persuade the other Tannaim to agree with him as well. Then, too, just as in the time of Titus-Aspinus, there were "Brit-Shalomniks" [advocates of peace and compromise — an allusion to the contemporary Brit Shalom movement] who put up very strong resistance; well known is the saying of R. Johanan ben Torta: "Grass will grow on your cheeks before the Messiah comes" [literally: grass will sooner grow on your cheeks and the Messiah will not come] (referring to Bar Kokhba, whom Rabbi Akiva regarded as the Messiah).
A large part of the Tannaim held that the rule of Rome had been decreed by "Divine Providence", but Rabbi Akiva overcame all these obstacles and the people went along with Rabbi Akiva, who became the spiritual leader of the freedom movement; and he and Bar Kokhba, the military leader, led the inspired masses hand in hand into battle.
About the person of Bar Kokhba, unfortunately, no clear historical sources have survived; even Bar Kokhba's origin is not clear, and what does exist has a rather legendary character. The popular imagination created countless exaggerations around the wondrous hero. Thus, for example, it is told that Bar Kokhba wanted to test his men to see whether they were brave and did not shrink from death, and ordered that whoever wished to enter his ranks must have the courage to chop off one of his own fingers. This test provoked a strong protest even from his followers, who cried out to him bitterly: "How much longer will you go on making cripples of the Jewish young men?!"
They advised him to make a different test, which would consist in being able, while riding a horse, to uproot a fir tree. It was from such heroes that his fighters were recruited, whose number reached as many as four hundred thousand men, who spread over all Judea like fiery lava and took city after city, fortress after fortress. Terror fell upon the Roman legions, and after one year of fighting fifty fortresses and 985 towns and villages in Judea, Samaria and Galilee were already in Jewish possession. The governor Turnis-Rufus was forced to withdraw from the Land of Israel; then Adrianus [Hadrian] sent his best field marshal, Julius Severus, who applied a different tactic: he realized that by storm and offensive he would not overcome the heroic Jewish camps, and therefore remained on the defensive, began to besiege the Jewish towns and let no food be brought in — and this system succeeded for him. One by one the Jews had to give up their acquired[?] positions, and in the end the remaining camps concentrated in the city of "Betar", where Bar Kokhba fortified himself and waged the last desperate struggle of life and death. Wonderful stories are told about the heroic battles around Betar. The war at Betar lasted a whole year, and it would probably never have been taken but for the treachery of certain spies, who betrayed to the enemy the secret area through which food used to be brought in. Through the provocation of a certain Samaritan, the great Tanna R. Eliezer of Modi'in [ha-Moda'i] also perished at the hand of Bar Kokhba, having fallen under suspicion of espionage, and the legend tells that soon after this deed came the defeat of Betar, and Bar Kokhba fell in the last battle.
Thus ended the tragic Bar Kokhba uprising, after which came the terrible Roman reaction, the "decree of persecution" (gezerat ha-shemad) with the Ten Martyrs, among whom Rabbi Akiva too perished by a very tragic death. One of his most faithful disciples, R. Simeon bar Yohai, unable to bear the anguish of the nation, hid in a cave and stayed there 13 years, and according to the Kabbalah R. Simeon bar Yohai is said to have composed the "Zohar" there [printed "Mozer" — a misprint]. In the Land of Israel every year on Lag BaOmer, in the town of Meron, the anniversary of his death is celebrated with a great procession, known by the name "Hillula of Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai".

Sosnowiec — A Gang of Blackmailers Who Extorted Money from Merchants by Means of Terror Uncovered

[Sosnowiec — crime; extortion of merchants.]
A great sensation has been caused in Jewish merchant circles by the uncovered gang — „fine young fellows“ — who by threats and beatings extorted money from a number of Jewish merchants.
The gang's main task was to „settle“ various disputes, especially between debtors. Whoever wanted to take revenge on his bad debtor or on an enemy turned to the gang, which summoned the person concerned to its „court“ [sąd], where he was told: „If you give us so-and-so much, fine; if not, we will teach you Balak“...
At the head of the gang stood a certain Adolf Weisberg, known by the name „Władek“; together with him the members of the gang were arrested: S. Weisberg, Marian Paczarek, Jehonatan Berger, Lejb Kalman Lubelski, A. Zojberman, Z. Binsztok, Stefan Zenbacz [?] and Rejzl Zylberfenig.
Those who suffered from the gang are: Jakow Strasberg, Szmuel Grinbojm, Israel Cuker — whose son was attacked a few weeks ago as he was going to pray on Friday — Icchak Landner, Jakow Szwarc and others.
The local Polish press also dragged Rabbi Frommer into the affair; as we are informed, the rabbi had absolutely no idea of the gang's deeds.

Bloody Family Dramas

[Zagłębie — crime; family dramas.]
This week two family dramas occurred which claimed human victims.
The first drama took place in Dąbrowa Górnicza, in the flat of the Wansow [?] family, where a brawl broke out among several Silesians and one of them murdered another with an axe.
The second drama happened in Środula at the Struch family: an official of the Huta Bankowa used to visit the family as a guest. The official's frequent visits led to close relations developing between him and Struch's wife. When the husband found out about it, he reacted, and thanks to that the wife broke off her relations with the lover [„kochanek“].
The latter therefore decided to take revenge, and with a knife in his hand he went at dawn into Struch's flat and there seriously wounded his beloved and her husband. Then with the same knife he stabbed himself in the heart and fell dead on the spot.

A series of elections in the Będzin community

Among today's chronicle is the report that the starosta [district head], for formal reasons, annulled[?] the elections of the presidium of the Council [the kehilla council] and of the Board.
In connection with this, a meeting of the kehilla Council will take place next Monday evening for the purpose of electing the Council's presidium.
The next day, Tuesday evening, a meeting of the kehilla Board is to take place, which will elect the presidium of the Board.
It is interesting to add that the Council member Mr. Goldsztajn, who is taking the place of Mr. Abraham Hampel, has not yet been invited, because the Mr. Chairman of the Board „does not know“ that Mr. Hampel is in Eretz Israel..
At the Board meeting, held yesterday evening, the question was discussed whether Mr. Goldsztajn should be invited to Monday's meeting or not.
—o—
Events at the „Mysłowice“ coal mine
On Wednesday a sharp incident occurred at the „Mysłowice“ coal mine because wages had not been paid out. The workers stopped work, and a crowd of several hundred men went to the villa of director Breuer on Mikołowska Street. The intervention of the police brought about the dispersal of the crowd.
An uneasy mood was aroused among the workers by the report that the mine management intends to cut 700 workers or possibly to close the mine altogether; the report greatly agitated the workers. One engineer was beaten.

[Zagłębie — taxes and commerce; followed by ten short news items: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Strzemieszyce, Bytom.]
A special conference on income tax took place at the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce.
Taking part in the conference were all the councillors (radcy), the representative of the Kielce Treasury Chamber, Naczelnik Izmanucha [?], and delegates of a number of merchants' institutions in Zagłębie.
At the conference all the painful questions were discussed which result from the incorrect interpretation of the state ordinance on income tax.
Apart from the purely theoretical statements during the discussion, the conference adopted the following resolutions:
1) From Mr. L. Rubinlicht: that Kielce should from now on instruct all heads (naczelnicy) of the tax offices that, in assessing income tax, they must go only by the turnover established for the merchant or firm concerned. On the other hand, calculating income tax according to a new, increased turnover is recognised as unlawful.
And 2) the Treasury Chamber will introduce an order in dealing with appeals. Thus, for example, before an appeal on income tax is considered, the appeal on turnover tax will be considered first.
—o—
Interpellation to the Będzin Kehilla Board Concerning the Shochtim
Messrs. "Dowers" [?] Bauszykowski [?] and Goldsztajn have addressed an interpellation to the kehilla board in Będzin concerning the conduct of the shochtim (ritual slaughterers).
The interpellation stresses: 1) to reduce the salaries (pensje) of the shochtim; 2) to fix their posts [?] in the slaughterhouse; and 3) to abolish the special payments which the shochtim take from the butchers for slaughtering after office hours.
The interpellation was on the agenda of yesterday's meeting of the kehilla board.
—o—
On Certifying Commercial Books
The Będzin Merchants' Association asks us to point out that merchants who keep commercial books must, under paragraph 10 of the Commercial Code, have the books stamped every year.
—o—
A Sensational Communist Trial
Next month a sensational trial will take place at the Sosnowiec District Court against the well-known Communist activist Henryk Haj [?] of Warsaw, a member of the Communist Central Committee. Haj is accused of conducting Communist activity in the Kielce voivodeship.
—o—
When Misfortune Is Fated..
Miss Chagete [?] came at Passover as a guest to her sister in Strzemieszyce. There she met a young man, a married man, and a love affair was knotted [?] between him and the girl.
Last Sunday the "secret" was discovered, when the young fellow abandoned his little wife in Strzemieszyce to her fate and vanished with the Będzin girl.
This fact is passed on to us by Mr. Józef Grünfeld, who asks those who have any information about the young fellow to notify the Strzemieszyce rabbi. His distinguishing marks are: medium height, clean-shaven, by trade — a tailor.
—o—
The Chimneys Start Smoking
In the coming days 2 furnaces (chimneys) will be put into operation at the "Katarzyna" [?] ironworks (huta).
120 workers will be employed.
—o—
"Hakoach" Excursion to Wojkowice
The "Hakoach" gymnastics society in Będzin is organising an excursion to Wojkowice next Sunday. A number of national youth organisations and gymnastics societies from Zagłębie are taking part in the excursion.
Departure from Będzin is at 6 o'clock in the morning, accompanied by the "Hakoach" orchestra at the head.
—o—
Certificates for the Revisionist Organisation
Yesterday the committee of the Będzin Zionist Organisation received word from the Central Committee (C.K.) that a certain number of certificates have been reserved for the Revisionist organisation.
In connection with this, a members' meeting will take place this Sabbath afternoon at the "Ahavat Chesed" hall, at which the matter of the certificates will be dealt with.
—o—
A Strike That Lasts 5 Minutes
Yesterday the workers at the "Renard" mine broke off work as a protest against the plan to abolish the workers' holidays.
The strike lasted 5 minutes.
—o—
A Bytom Team Plays a Match with Sosnowiec "Maccabi"
The football club "09" [printed "9.0"] in Beuthen (Bytom) has accepted the proposal to play a match against the team (drużyna) of Sosnowiec "Maccabi".
The match is to take place this Sabbath.
—o—
Appeal of the Będzin L.O.P.P. Committee
Citizens! The Air Defence League (Liga Obrony Powietrznej i Przeciwgazowej) is an institution that protects the whole civilian population in case of war from the most terrible gas bombs and other dangerous explosives. In order to promote the idea of the L.O.P.P., an "Air Week" is being organised, which will last from the 5th to the 12th of this month. Because the "krig." [?] protects the entire population, one cannot be satisfied with one-time urgent income; rather it is our duty to create permanent, secured income and new organisations of members with standing obligations.
We must rouse the broad masses and convince them that, by being members of the L.O.P.P., we are at the same time helping ourselves to be protected in time of war. It must be remembered that by enrolling as a member of the L.O.P.P. and giving donations and membership dues, we shall show [?] that the success of the "Air Week" is of interest to every Polish citizen.
The Będzin committee of the L.O.P.P. consists of: Dr. Narbit [?] (president), Dr. Salomon Weinzieher (vice-president), Anna Birnblazska [?] (secretary), Stefan Jędrusik [?] (treasurer), Professor Anisteld [?] and Mr. Jan Szulc.

The Duty of the Jewish Population in Sosnowiec Towards the “Gemilut Hesed” Fund

[Sosnowiec — interest-free loan fund.]
As in all towns in Poland, a “Gemilut Hesed” (interest-free loan) fund was founded in Sosnowiec too, in 1927. At first the Jewish public showed due sympathy, and apart from larger donations the income from the modest monthly pledges, starting at 50 groszy, reached a sum of 800 złoty a month. In time the income became smaller and smaller, so that today, when the fund plays a dominant role among the Jewish masses, the monthly payments amount to a paltry sum that does not even cover the administration expenses, even though these are very small and paltry.
Because of such a cold attitude on the part of the Jewish population towards so important an institution as the Gemilut Hesed fund, the board has decided to turn with a printed appeal to that part which still does not understand the usefulness of the interest-free fund, that they should contribute monthly payments, so that the basic capital, which is intended solely to save hundreds of Jewish families from downfall and ruin, should not be diminished on account of some trifles.
It is therefore to be hoped that every Jew who has but the means will not refuse the monthly payments, and will understand that with the small, paltry groszy he maintains the existence of the fund, which is now the only institution in the town that gives real help to the great camp of small traders and artisans oppressed by the crisis.
A Great Fire in Żarnowiec

[Żarnowiec — fire.]
The “red rooster” [i.e. fire] is raging in the small towns. A week ago almost the whole little town of Szczekociny was wiped out by a fire, and already there has again been a fire in Żarnowiec, where 15 houses were burnt down and a large number of Jewish families are wandering about under the open sky.
The fire broke out in the night from Monday to Tuesday.
“Miti”[?] — Excursion of the JNF in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, Jewish National Fund.]
On Sunday the 29th of this month the committee of the Sosnowiec KKL (Jewish National Fund) organised an excursion to “Wysoki Brzeg”, a very beautiful area.
The organisations “Maccabi”, “Betar”, “Gordonia”, “HaShachar”, “Young WIZO”, “Hitachdut” and the Revisionists took part in the excursion.
Some youth organisations did not take part in the excursion because of their private ambitions.
At 6 o'clock the above-mentioned organisations assembled on Theatre Square. After a report had been delivered to the chief commander of the excursion, Mr Chaim Trieger, the procession moved off. The “Maccabi” banner opened the imposing procession, and the banner of the Sosnowiec Betar closed it.
On arrival at the site each organisation settled into its own camp. A very splendid sight was offered by the “Betar” camp with the large “namiot” (tent).
At 5 o'clock in the evening all the organisations assembled in ranks in one place with their banners. Messrs Frommer and Intraligator[?] spoke on topics of the day.
The streets such as Ostrogórska, Modrzejowska[?], 3 Maja, Piłsudskiego and Sienkiewicza, through which the procession marched on its return, were filled with masses of people, who greeted the procession enthusiastically.
On Theatre Square the procession halted and, after the singing of the Polish anthem and “Hatikvah”, the procession was dispersed.

Police Distribute Bread to Hungry Children of the Unemployed

[Olkusz — unemployed.]
A crowd of some 300 people, among them women with children in their arms, gathered in front of the Olkusz starostwo (district office) and demanded support. As the starosta happened to be at the voivodeship office on that very matter, the crowd turned to the cashier of the relief fund with the warning that if they did not receive any support, the crowd would set about looting the shops.
The cashier did manage to calm the crowd, but the crowd, being incited, then went off into the market, where[?] a panic broke out among the inhabitants.
The police, keeping order, bought several loaves of bread and distributed them in pieces to the children of the unemployed; the butchers too gave them pieces of meat. It did not come to any disturbances.
