Where Are You Going, Jewish Academic? — Some Remarks on the Difficult Road Ahead for Our Graduates

[Article — Jewish youth, the universities and emigration.] Some remarks on the difficult road ahead for our graduates.
As every year, a whole host of Jewish graduates [abiturients — holders of the matura] is now beginning to leave the secondary schools. Here in Zagłębie, too, quite a number of Jewish pupils, boys and girls, will leave our gymnasia this year with matura certificates in hand, "ripe for higher education" — each of them a new person who has shaken off the school hierarchy and gone through one of the most important stages of life, and who will now stand on the threshold of further self-improvement, of the further struggle for existence. New dreams, new plans for the future — but for the time being some 3–4 months will pass carefree — a "well-earned" [?] recompense for 8–10 years of toil and exertion.
So it used to be every year, and so it ought to be now.
But this year the situation of the Jewish graduates will be different — and therefore the well-deserved three-month rest must also be used differently.
True, things were not always so good; the Jewish graduate could not always spend the summer holidays without a care; the doors of the university were not always open to all Jewish children — but never yet has the situation been as hard and hopeless as now, in the new school year.
To say nothing of the difficult economic situation in general, and of us Jews in particular, which will mean that the material means to send the children on to further study will simply be lacking, and that the prospects of any earnings from giving lessons or in some other way are very small — a new wave of hardships is rolling over Jewish academic youth.
First, the application of the "percentage norm" [numerus clausus], intensified with every year, will surely be sharpened further this year. The events at the Warsaw and Wilno universities, the grounds of the verdict in the Wolfin [?] trial in Wilno, the latest events in Lwów [printed "Lemberg"], the resolutions adopted at the last convention of the "All-Polish Youth" [Młodzież Wszechpolska] — these are only the first swallows announcing to us the new Jew-baiting agitation now being prepared, new bestial deeds on the part of the "patriots", new restrictions on Jews entering the university. And let us also expect [literally "hope"] that the "Legion of the Young" [Legion Młodych] of intellectual antisemitism will unite with joint forces, and "with a sound body and mind" they will drive the Jewish academic out of the temple of learning.
And when the gates of the universities at home are closed to us Jews, only then will the question arise: where to?
Emigrate, perhaps? — True, we have long had a Jewish student emigration. That emigration looked different before the World War, different 2–3 years ago, and it will look different in the current year.
Whereas in former years the gates of foreign universities were open to Jewish emigration; whereas three years ago Masaryk, the grey-haired Czech president, declared to Nahum Sokolow that the doors of the Czech schools were open to all Jews from all over the world, and after that declaration an increased student emigration to Czechoslovakia did indeed begin; whereas in France, Belgium, Italy and often in Austria and Germany the Jewish student was not put to great difficulties on entering the university — the prospects for the future are now not good at all.
The reasons for this are explained in various ways: in part because of the economic crisis, where there is a fear that the student emigrants will take up other work and compete with the local worker; or else for reasons of a political character, as for instance in Czechoslovakia, where the measures are directed not specifically against Jews but in general against "foreigners", who overfill the German exceptional [?] state universities. Surely the Czechs have no taste for maintaining two German universities, 2 new polytechnics and other German higher schools, which would have been reduced to a small number were it not for the foreign students who stream mostly into the German schools.
And since Jewish youth is the most strongly represented in the student emigration, it is self-evident why this calls forth "antisemitism" among the Czech "Endeks" [nationalists], and the whole campaign against foreigners takes on — for the public, in order to win more support from the socially less enlightened youth — an antisemitic character.
And on top of all this comes [printed "in", read "is"] the new tariff for foreign passports, which recently came into force: under the new tariff a reduced-fee passport for scientific purposes will cost 80 zł. instead of the previous 20 zł., and together with the administrative expenses — about 100 zł. So, a new burden on the Jewish academic, who is driven from the universities at home to somewhere abroad and is then told to pay dearly for it. And if he should still feel like rejoicing with his family on a holiday, or coming home for the vacation, that pleasure, besides the travel expenses, will cost him very dearly, because the passports alone cost him some 300–400 zł. a year.
It is simply incomprehensible what motives moved the government in fixing the prices of the reduced-fee passports. We believe that what was intended was not so much an increase in revenue from the fees, as that this is the first step towards an understanding between the Sanacja and the Endecja regarding the "numerus clausus" — a quiet understanding, the first triumph of the "Wilno heroes".
As we see, then, the prospects for the future, both at home and abroad, are very poor. It is therefore desirable that the graduates and the factors responsible for them take stock in good time, and do not once again find themselves afterwards before an accomplished fact.
L. P. [?]
Jewish Troubles in a Small Country

[Austria — politics; antisemitism.] Of Austria — today's Austria, that exhausted, starved and cut-down little country — one cannot speak as if it were a more or less normal state. When the World War ended, Italy took Tyrol, Hungary went its own way, Serbia took Bosnia with Herzegovina, Romania cut off Siebenbürgen [Transylvania] for itself, Galicia went to Poland, and from Bohemia with Slovakia the Czechoslovak Republic was founded; on the battlefield there remained lying a cripple, without hands and without feet. Only with the help of crutches has the cripple kept itself going on God's earth.
Vienna, once the very important doer and opinion-giver of Europe, the old aristocrat in costly clothes and diamonds but without a piece of bread in her mouth — Vienna has turned into a wailing beggar-woman who has long forgotten the shame of begging. Were it not for the obstinacy of France and other states, with their decision not to permit any union of Austria with Germany, even the begging would not have helped. The country would simply have died of hunger and nobody would have looked round.
These days the Austrian government again turned to the League of Nations with the request to allow it not to pay its international debts, because it is bitterly hard for it. The League of Nations answered with a sharp refusal and told the repeated bankrupt in all seriousness that the debts must be paid punctually and without any further excuse. The refusal caused a real uproar in Vienna. The government feels completely lost and does not know what to do...
We say this here as against that: from such a crippled little state, which has to depend on public charity, one might have expected at least a little fairness towards other small peoples who find themselves in a difficult situation. In Vienna, however, the most malicious antisemitism has blossomed in recent months. Antisemitism private and official. Vienna has become a centre of antisemitism and can lay claim to second rank after Berlin.
The government puts on a show of being against the persecution of Jews, but in fact all these villainies are carried out either with its consent or with a "neutral" attitude on its part.
For the Jewish world there is no reason whatever to rejoice at the misfortunes of this small country, for we know better than others what a time of trouble is. Besides everything, masses of Jews live in Austria. Their fate is bound up with the fate of the country, so one ought to help the country in one way or another. Jews of the whole world would surely have responded — were it not for the incessant, dogged agitation against Jews...
L. G.
Heard and Seen

[Feuilleton — Będzin and Dąbrowa; art, charity, kashrut.] By Ben Amotz.
One came...
The opening of Natan Szpigel's picture exhibition. The time set for the opening is long past; from time to time an "interested party" slips in. The first are from the "masses", later — the intelligentsia, and at last — public figures.
Silence in the hall; the "in-laws" look at the pictures, pronounce connoisseur's remarks and sit down to have a chat about fashion, the crisis and the like.
— When does the opening take place?
— The committee is not here yet — comes the answer.
— There's a committee?
— But of course, what then, a picture exhibition without a committee? There has to be a body to take care of the exhibition's success.
— Who are they?
— What do you mean who? Doctors, directors, prominent activists and, for form's sake — a Zionist too...
The hours run on. The clock already shows that the time of the opening belongs to the past... and God knows how much longer we would have waited for the committee to come, had not one of the visitors given us to understand that the bigwigs of the committee and the invited "notables" will not come, because—
because the exhibitor is called Natan...
— You are surprised?
— It is, alas, a sad truth. Had the exhibitor been one of the Wąsachowskis, Kraszyńskis or other "-skis", our people would have been bustling around him. Ladies would have been making a great stir that the "wystawa" [exhibition] should have "powodzenie" [success], "bo nie wypada" [because it wouldn't be proper otherwise]. It is different, though, when the artist's name is Natan Szpigel. Here all doors and gates are closed to him, for what interest can there be in a "żydowski malarz" [Jewish painter]?..
So they, the committee and the "bigwigs", stayed at home, and to the opening —
— only one came...
The one who came is he who does not style himself doctor or director, but has a warm Jewish heart — Icchak Wygodzki [?] is his name. He entered the hall abashed; in the committee's make-up he is the last — and he came first.
— One came...
A "remedy for the deficits"...
I met an acquaintance, a public worker from Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], and so we struck up a conversation.
— About what? About what not — about everything; we began with the general crisis and ended with our home-grown troubles and burdens.
And once one is talking, one also mentions the sad state of our institutions in general and of the philanthropic ones in particular. The first scapegoats are the philanthropic societies: whoever is angry with the gmina [community], with the rabbinate, even with his own mother-in-law, takes revenge on the institutions and says:
— I don't pay any more for any society...
Yes, where were we? At our philanthropic societies, it seems. We discussed the matter very broadly, thought of ways to ease the crisis of our societies, and —
— I have an idea — my friend cries out — I have a remedy for all societies and institutions so they get rid of the crisis, and there will always be plenty of money in their coffers.
— What remedy?
— Every society — he says — should engage a board member of the Dąbrowa Women's Association...
— What are you saying? Speak plainly.
And he tells:
— There is — he says — in Dąbrowa a women's association, a sympathetic institution, gladly supported by all strata, and above all — thrift...
The collected monies are well guarded; let a "golden head" come and intervene for urgent help — he will achieve nothing with them. At the women's association they say they cannot do otherwise: one must save and "localise" the money in a bank...
And "penny by penny adds up to a large sum". Income there is, expenses — not necessarily; so the capital grows ever larger...
— Take my advice, write about it in the paper. First, let the world learn what "brilliant" public work Dąbrowa possesses, and second, if this system were introduced in the Zagłębie institutions, there would never be any deficit...
— Zagłębie activists! Think it over. Let every institution get better acquainted with the "practical" activity of the Dąbrowa Women's Association, and you can be sure that in the institutions there will no longer be —
— any deficits...
Money answers everything...
The editorial-office door opens hastily and in comes an elderly Hasidic Jew, and after a broad "good morning" he begins:
— I've come to ask you a question.
— But we don't rule on religious questions.
— I know, yet I've come to pour out my embittered heart to you. I can't bear it.
— Why are you so bitter?
— My name is Yeshaye, my livelihood is — cows... for more than twenty years now. I supervise the milking; my milk — that is, the milk of my cows — may be drunk by the most God-fearing man. I myself pay for the Lublin yeshiva, I am a member of all the societies, my father-in-law disputed Talmud with the old Rebbe of Kock of blessed memory — I tell you, kosher milk... And here suddenly such a calamity: the kashrut society demands from me a hechsher for my kosher milk.
— Well, what's the fuss? Take a hechsher.
— What are you saying? — shouts the Jew — I should take out a hechsher? It would mean I am accusing myself, that until now I have been a transgressor in Israel, that for so many years I have sold treyf milk...
— Don't be so angry, Reb Yeshaye — a little Jew standing by calmed him — nobody suspects you that the milk you sell is not presumed kosher; just take my advice and give a złoty.
— For a złoty everything will be kosher?
— Yes, that's how it is: it's not the committee they mean but the dumplings; the main thing is the gulden.
— Money answers everything...
The Face of the World.

[Essay — the world crisis and the state of the world.] By J. I. Sigal.

Even before the economic crisis entered the world in all its terror, people in the world of the spirit were already talking a great deal about a great cultural crisis that was on its way into our life. Books were written about it; it became the question of the day and of the time. Everyone not only voiced his opinion about the present shaken state of the world, but added his own observation, the mood of his mind, his own feeling and grasp of present-day reality. The intellectual person senses the coming and occurring changes in life as sharply and clearly as the sensitive person with a keen sense smells the odour of an object at a distance from himself. It had to take more than ten years before man, who reacts with spiritual senses, could feel the effect of the war on the great mass public that fills the earth, and also its effect on himself, the individual, who can be somewhat more objective in his view of reality and its events.

At the very beginning of "feeling ourselves" as if torn away from a firmly rooted world settlement, which had sat at ease on its established traditional "economy", we looked around us with a wild strangeness: somehow it was not so easy to believe that it was really we who had gone, under our own step, through the great upheaval; that it was really we ourselves who had earned from the gods the right to be such exalted sacrifices on the altar of world history. But it soon became clear that it was indeed we ourselves, by whose strength "History" guided the pen and wrote one of the bloodiest and most glowing [?] of its chapters. The script is brilliantly sharp, and from the words, from the letters not yet dried, there still comes the smell of the pen, and of gunpowder, of the blood not yet dried and the not yet subsided cry of pain of the great sacrifice.

And an even more despairing thing became clear to us after the smoke of the last battlefield fight had vanished into the empty sky — it became clear to us that the ideals, the gods with which they had sought to console us at the time of the great offering of sacrifices — these gods and ideals behaved like every bird that saw that it would in no way "be able" to save all its little young, which cannot move from the nest on the falling roof: it spread its wings over the nest, which had already begun to sink under the red flames, and was burned together with its little ones. The gods, for whom millennia had "toiled" [?] and laboured, climbing from rung to rung and stretching toward them, have "resigned" from their "courtly glories" and given up their majestic "game of gods".

To the deeper eye it looks as though human deifications carry something destructive and unmoving [?] for man. It is not man who destroys the great ideals, which he reaches in thought and attains only to see them through the spyglass [?] of thought, like distant stars on the distant horizon of the future; rather the ideals themselves are destroyed and perish together with the sacrifices brought for their sake, so that one sees before oneself, at times, in a despairing minus — a kind of "other side of the coin" — that there remains no way out of the despair, which lets burst some of its deadly "gas bombs" that poison the air of the world.

We feel the bitter smell of such despair; it burns in our nostrils in the last few years, since the economic crisis began to wage its underground campaign of extermination on earth. I say "underground" [printed "unferdishe"], because formerly it still concealed the [?] of the situation: the mouth is still stuffed, somehow, in the few "people's kitchens", with unemployment relief, and for the time being the impoverished alleys are provided, for bare survival, with a piece of bread, so that the soul may hold out and be able to drag on to the better day, and when the better day comes one will be able to "grab" also a "better future".

Meanwhile, however, the centre of the world is occupied, like a hollowed-out abyss, by the "crisis". Behind it stands its father, the World War, which brought it into the world, and — facing it, ahead, like a fiery comet with a bloody tail, pointing to — yet another cruel morning that pushes its [?] tip out of the yellow eastern horizon and foretells something "terrible and desperate": the conflict between Japan and China, which seemingly played, for world politics, the part of a kind of curious phenomenon in the Orient. Something was undermined with a supposed [?] [?], and what was taking place opposite, people pretended not to know.

"Underground" interests. The diplomacy of the great powers can put on such spectacles that see in the heaps of the slain — heaps of gold and diamonds, and its hardened face, just like its petrified heart, will not stir a single wrinkle. Diplomacy sees the map of the world in a constantly fluid state. Borders shift aside, yielding their place to boundless appetites.

A world war only recently gone by behind us. A terrible, bloody fear of hidden coming ruins, and "in the middle" — a crisis that has set almost three parts of mankind entirely aside as superfluous on the brink of doom; and the dread, the apathy, creeps like a heavy cloud over the despairing world —
The face of the world.
The Trusting Optimist (Baal-Bitochn)...

[Humorous feuilleton — monologue; the economic crisis.] (Monologue of a Jew who has "come down in the world") by Pey-Tof-Shin.
Just as you see me, I am a Jew from "Jordan-land" [a pun: "Yordn-land", land of those who have come down].
I have already been through every incarnation; I have been, as they say, "na koniu i pod koniem" [on the horse and under the horse], ran big businesses, turned the world around, went bankrupt some five times, was regularly arrested, wriggled out and carried on[?] — until God helped and the real crisis came.
Now I have come out clean, as my mother bore me. A great help in getting rid of my bundle was the "urząd" [tax office]: day and night "nakazy" [payment orders], a "sequestrator" [bailiff] for breakfast, lunch and supper. Interest on interest and percentages on the interest, "zaległe" [arrears] and "drogowe" [road tax], i.e. for the wagon — until they set me right.
And now I give praise and thanks to Him whose name I am not worthy to mention, for the great kindness He has done me.
I am fine, well off and in bliss.
Only the wife nags me: — How can it be, Hone-Ber, is this a purpose in life — going around empty and fasting!
— Hush, I say, woman, you have a short mind; we ought, I say, to thank the Creator of the World ten times a day that He made it so.
— Take a look, I say: the world is turning over, volcanoes erupt, mountains of ash pour down on settlements, a world is burning like Sodom and Gomorrah, God save us; magnates, billionaires shoot themselves, hang themselves; Morgan and Rockefeller, the mighty of the world, are already bankrupt too.
And the "lokshn" [noodle — slang, apparently for the dollar] is also lying on the ground; people already stand in line at the "Bank Polski", wanting to push it off as fast as possible and stock up on złotys.
A small matter: little America ["Amerítshke"], the rich lady, the high-born, the provider[?] — she too, poor thing, is becoming a "yoredte" [one who has come down].
And I, Hone-Ber, stand at a distance and enjoy it. What is it to me? This heartache is not my lot; the Almighty has already spared me such distress.
— Foolish woman — I argue with my wife — look, I say, you have a husband in a million. If I owned a fortune ["matnia"[?], probably majątek], I would now have thrown myself from the sixth floor, I would have shot a bullet into my temple, I would have drunk sublimate or inflicted some other strange death on myself... Ha, a fine thing to be a forlorn widow, I say!
And what would you do, I say, if — may that hour never come — I became president somewhere, and along came a murderer like Gorgulov ["Gargele"] and shot a couple of bullets into you — piff-paff, and no more Hone-Ber...
Or look, I say, how the world stormed when Lindbergh's child disappeared. Father and mother went out of their minds, poured out so much money, and in the end found the child dead. Our little kids ["putsakes"], I say, nobody will snatch, because they would get troubles from me, not money.
Oh, I say, would to God, dear Father, that a couple of fellows took pity and stole my over-aged spinster daughters. I swear, nobody would let out a cry, the police would not even let out a peep, and the radio certainly would not search for them.
I am fine, I am well, I laugh at the world, I am the great trusting optimist. The sequestrator comes to me — I laugh and he laughs along; the landlord comes to demand the rent — I show him the new decree — I am the aristocrat.
The kehilla collector comes about the "etat" [kehilla tax] — I get good burial money, the true anonymous charity.
Yes, gentlemen, let the world storm, let everything go to ruin[?]. What do I care? I, Hone-Ber, have great trust; God willing, I shall get through it all.
The Problem of Physical Education

[Health and education — article in a series.] By S. Yuval.
(The age of puberty).
The age of puberty is one of the most important periods in the life of young people. In boys this period begins more or less in the thirteenth year and lasts until the fifteenth year of life; in girls it begins somewhat earlier, around the twelfth year of life, and also lasts about two years. In well-developed children this process begins earlier, in weaker ones — later. It also depends to a certain degree on the climate and on the race to which the children belong. Children of the south mature earlier than children of the north. In our children the age of puberty [printed: "newspaper-age", a misprint] begins a year earlier than in the Aryans, although we live at the same geographical latitude. Just as the growth and development of a plant depend on the soil, the sowing and the later treatment and care, so the growth and development of the child's organism are also affected by climatic conditions; hereditary traits, the social position of the parents, housing conditions, nutrition and[?], to a great degree, also physical exercise.
A rapid gain in weight in eleven- to twelve-year-old children is often a sign that the period of puberty is approaching. In this period the organism grows and develops very fast. This phenomenon is, however, accompanied by a weakening of the mental faculties. This is no coincidence, but occurs regularly. It happens more than once that a pupil who still in his twelfth year of life excelled in learning and justified the greatest hopes shows, in his thirteenth or fourteenth year of life, no aptitude whatsoever for any intellectual work.
It is also the period in which bad, morbid habits and harmful inclinations easily arise, such as kleptomania, mendacity and similar excesses, sometimes also an urge to suicide. The characteristic signs of this period are, as a rule: a weakening of the intellectual faculties owing to the rapid tempo of physical development, a lack of psychological balance and an instability of character, a constant change of moods and a tendency to psychopathic phenomena, which sometimes end in a mental and a nervous illness.
The age of puberty, or as it is sometimes called — the age of transition, usually finds schoolchildren in the sixth or seventh class of the elementary school. If they attend a gymnasium — in the second, third or fourth class of the gymnasium for girls, in the fourth or fifth class for boys.
The period of puberty leaves to a certain degree a stamp on the character and organism of the child and often leaves indelible traces for its future. Supervision of the child must therefore be especially vigilant at that time, and its organism must be especially spared.
If in a whole series of our earlier articles we have pointed out how necessary it is for young people to spend time in the free, fresh air and how important physical exercises are for them, we must in this case, for this stage of young people's lives, underline this necessity especially. In any case — strenuous exercises, football, fast and long-distance running are forbidden; on the other hand, movement games and excursions are to be recommended.
It is the most critical chapter — the age of puberty — in the life of young people. From this recognition there arises a special duty for parents, educators and teachers. It is their duty to come to the aid of youth; the most important help then, however, is — first of all to understand. In an earlier article we already spoke about the overburdening of schoolchildren and pointed to its grave consequences; this overburdening is extraordinarily harmful to children in the period of puberty, and it must therefore be fought here with all our strength.
In the period of transition a child must sleep eleven hours in twenty-four; teachers must remember this and not give pupils much homework. The holidays and the festivals are intended for rest, refreshment and the joy of life, and no pedagogue may forget this. A child in the period of transition must not be overburdened with either intellectual or physical work. The parents must also remember this — not to send the children additionally to extra lessons, such as foreign languages, or keep them for hours at the piano and the like.
In the period of puberty the child is dominated by nervous, feverish moods. It is driven and exhausted by an inner struggle with secret forces, not understood by it and not explained. To overburden the child in these circumstances, to force it under these conditions to strain its nerves, to take from it the opportunity to spend time in the free air, in movement and physical exercise — means to put at risk the mental and physical health of the child and of the later grown-up person.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bamidbar)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bamidbar
The Portion
a) "And the Lord spoke unto Moses in the wilderness of Sinai" (1:1)
"The Torah was given through three things: through fire, through water and through the wilderness." (Midrash).
"Through fire" — Torah must be studied only with enthusiasm, with fervour. But — "through water": water has the nature of running down to a low place; the Torah, too, endures only where it is low... And — "through the wilderness": for the Torah one must give up one's life, "let him make himself ownerless like the wilderness."
"I do indeed like it — said the Rebbe Reb Bunem about this — when a man gives himself up for the Torah, but only himself, not somebody else"... Nifla'ot Hadashot.
—o—
Rav Yosef Engel, of blessed memory, used to say:
At the blessing of the new month we say: "And grant us long life, a life of peace," etc. — to us You would give a good life; but when it comes to Torah and the fear of Heaven, one says: "a life in which there is [lit. in them] love of Torah and fear of Heaven" — they should have the love of Torah and the fear of Heaven; that is given to others.
b) "And with you there shall be a man, a man of the tribe [lit. 'a man below']" (ibid., 4)
The "man below", the lowly Jew, shall be "with you" — equal to you, the heads, because "he is head of the house of his fathers": he is, after all, of the same lineage as you; he too is a grandson of the Patriarchs (of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob)... Tiferet Shlomo.
c) "Every one head of the house of his fathers" (ibid.).
Usually, before someone mounts the seat of honour, he is good and pious and decent. Once he is already sitting on the seat, only then does he take off the mask... Therefore the Torah praises those princes [nesi'im], that "he is" — "they stood in their righteousness from beginning to end": that they remained so honest, although they already held the princes' seats... Dan mi-Daniel.
—o—
"He is head of the house of his fathers."
Because "a leader [parnas] is appointed over the community only if a basket of creeping things hangs behind him" — a parnas is made only from someone of low lineage, so that one can at any moment point at the bundle under him, at his lineage... "Head of the house of his fathers" — according to his descent he may become a head. Harei Besamim.
—o—
"The face of the generation is like the face of a dog."
A dog is insolent. "And the dogs are greedy [brazen]," because it is always sated. A dog is sated for three days from one meal. That is why it is so impudent with its being full. But it is sated because "God knows that the dog's food is scant," so that it should not bark so much...
The leaders, too, think that they are elected because they are sated, rich; but in truth they are elected because "a basket of creeping things is behind them," because they are do... so that they should not bark... Imrei Yafeh.
d) "Ye shall number them" (ibid., 3)
Jews are always blessed "which cannot be measured nor numbered" — they will not be counted. What sort of blessing is that?
When money lies in a full cash-box, it all lies together. But as soon as one starts counting, it turns out that one coin is worn, another is false...
Better for Jews not to be counted... Ohel Yaakov.
d) "So were all those that were numbered of the children of Israel" (ibid., 45)
There are six hundred thousand letters in the Torah and six hundred thousand Jewish souls.
In the Torah one letter must stand apart from the next; one may not touch the other. So too the Jews...
And yet one letter may not be too far from the next, not too far apart... So too the Jews.
The Torah must be sewn together, all in one, one long scroll. So too a Jewish people can only exist as — one sewn-together sheet... Nehmad mi-Zahav.
f) "And thou shalt give the money unto Aaron" (3:48)
Someone asked a Hasid:
— What would have happened if there were no money in the world — what would one then give the Rebbes as pidyonot [redemption offerings]?
The other answered:
— Fool that you are, if there were no money, there would be no Rebbes either... From the mouth of the people.
Haftarah.
g) "And they shall be gathered together... and appoint themselves one head" (Hosea 2).
Ah, the greatest blessing is that Jews will have only one head, one leader... Petah ha-Sha'ar.
Avot.
h) "And the Torah is acquired... through a minimum of derekh eretz [good manners]" (Chapter Six, Mishnah 6)
Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce [Ropshitz] explained it simply: with little derekh eretz... by pushing and shoving one's way to the Rebbe's table in order to hear a word of Torah.
The Eggs and the Hens

[Sketch — family life: parents and children, Yiddish and Polish.]
An overheard conversation, reported by A. D. Egoz.

The other day I was up on the "Górka" [the hill]. It was a warm day, and people were enjoying a little fresh air and warming themselves in the sun.

It was swarming and teeming with older people, younger ones, children and young mothers with babies in cradles.

The little ones ran about, romped, played in the sand [?], played "hide-and-seek" and held conversations in their own fashion.

The grown-ups talked about the crisis, about politics and other important news and events.

Next to me sat two women, an old one and a younger one — a mother and her daughter. The old woman was saying something, carrying on a conversation, but the younger one, it seemed, was barely listening, looking off to the other side, as if to say: talk to the wall.

A little boy came running up in nothing but his shirt ["hemdum pemdum"]: "Mama, jestem głodny" [Polish: Mummy, I'm hungry]; his mother gave him a roll.

"Say a blessing [brokhe]," the grandmother called out, and gave him a pat on the cheek.

"Say a brrrakhe," the boy shrieked mockingly, burst out laughing and ran off. The mother laughed along.

"What a world," sighed the old woman. "The eggs teach the hens; they think they are cleverer than the hens."

And turning to me she said:

"You think it's only the little one? The older ones are the same — they don't understand a word of Yiddish, or don't want to understand, and they mock not only the grandmother but their mother and father too. Why, mother and father, they say, are 'old-fashioned'... What they do is no good, and how they talk doesn't suit them. Yes, the eggs laugh at the hens."

The daughter evidently did not relish her mother's words. She even ground her teeth in annoyance, and the old woman muttered again: "I see how the eggs teach the hens!"

I kept silent; I didn't want to utter a word for fear the daughter would tell me off [?], but I thought to myself that it is a bitter pity, alas, both for the grandmother and for the mother. Among their grandchildren and children they are like hens that have hatched ducklings and go about with them.

And this really is a plague of the land. In many, many Jewish families the same tragedies are played out — the eggs teaching the hens.

Fathers and mothers, grandfathers and grandmothers are supervised by their children and grandchildren. The latter think that they are the wise ones, the experts and the knowers, and they dismiss their parents and grandparents. The young generation considers itself cleverer and more experienced and permits itself to ridicule its elders and to teach them manners.

And why is this so? It is because the parents, the fathers and mothers, bow their heads before their own children.

Eggs must not be left to warm in the sun too early — it is harmful to them; it makes them go bad and acquire a foul smell.

And these spoiled eggs think that the hens that bore them are good for kapores, and they swing them as kapores, and the foolish hens let it happen; they think that this is how it should be and how it must be...

I think the chief troubles and conflicts between parents and children come from language. Children become estranged from their parents because they cannot properly understand each other, because they cannot talk together as they should. The child is brought up in Polish, while most parents use their mother tongue — Yiddish. The parents cluck and the children caw. It comes out like hens with crows. And so the parents are fanatical [?] and the children allow themselves to laugh in their faces.

But if Jewish fathers and mothers taught their children Yiddish from childhood on and made an effort that they too should understand and know our mother tongue, it would be much better. The children would look at them with different eyes, and they would have quite a different standing in their eyes.

But this is neglected. People do not foresee what will happen later, and those who should be taught become teachers instead. "And ye shall teach them to your children" is turned into "and your fathers shall be taught by you" ["ולמדכם את אבותיכם"], and that is no good [to anyone?].

On the contrary: an older child, a sensible one, can grasp more quickly how important it is for him himself to reach better understanding with his own father and mother, to be able to discuss and debate with them freely, and not to look upon them as people from another world.

I still have more to say on this matter, but I shall leave it for another time.

A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

And so he grew up under the influence of the stable with the horses and under the influence of the big book with the coloured pictures.

When Grisha was about thirteen years old, the following happened:

Grisha caught a chill, fell ill and came down with a high fever. It was winter. Sharp, icy winds blew through the streets of the village. The frost was burning, and the warmest place in the house was the kitchen. So they made up a bed in the kitchen and laid the sick boy there. For a few days he lay almost unconscious, burning with fever. Then he felt a little easier, but the fever still had not subsided.

In the evenings, peasant neighbours used to gather at old Yefim's; they sat in the kitchen by the big stove, smoked and talked about various things that had happened in the village. They told one another various news that had reached them from the nearby [?] towns. One evening the peasants gathered at Yefim's in the kitchen were greatly agitated and spoke among themselves with great excitement: the previous night a crime had been committed in the village that had thrown all the inhabitants of Pokrovskoye into the most terrible anger; from one of the poorest peasants someone had stolen his only horse out of the stable, and had made him a wretched man. At daybreak, as soon as the crime became known, the peasants gathered. The whole day they searched and rummaged, but in vain — the horse was not found, and who the thief is, nobody knows. The peasants were in a terrible rage. For Siberian peasants, stealing a horse is the greatest and worst crime, worse even than killing a man... They all seethed and fumed, and Yefim's wife had to ask them again and again to speak more quietly, because Grisha was very ill again that evening; he lay with his face to the wall and was sunk in sleep from the high fever he had.

The peasants tried to speak more quietly, but the anger boiled in all of them; the thief must be found! Such a crime must not and cannot be passed over in silence! Anyone who dares to steal a horse must not be found in the village!

Suddenly the sick Grisha sat up on his bed, looked around with burning eyes and gave a wild smile. In nothing but his shirt he got down from the bed and went up to the peasants sitting by the big stove. His face was sunken and pale as death. His eyes glowed, and the hair on his head was wildly tousled. He looked like a ghost; the peasants were all bewildered and stared wide-eyed, in astonishment.

Grisha stopped, looked for a while with piercing glances, and at once he leapt onto one of them, a giant of a peasant, clambered up and stayed sitting astride the man's shoulders, and then he cried out:

"Ha! Ha! Pyotr Alexandrovich! You stole the horse! You are the thief! You! You!"

Grisha burst into wild laughter and even shook with joy; meanwhile he began to beat with his bare feet on the peasant's chest and shouted again:

"Ha! Ha! Pyotr Alexandrovich! You stole the horse!... A horse thief, that's what you are!... You!... You are the thief!... You!..."

Grisha's voice was so sharp and piercing; his eyes shone with such a strange brightness, that his outcries made a tremendously strong impression on the peasants. It seemed to them that some spirit was crying these very words out of Grisha... They were greatly bewildered, in great embarrassment, because Pyotr Alexandrovich was a highly respected and prominent householder in the village. He was quite well-to-do, and he had been more agitated than anyone over the crime that had been committed. He had seethed more than anyone and demanded insistently that there be no rest until the thief was found and punished without mercy with the harshest punishment. How, then, could one believe such a thing of him?

Old Yefim and his wife were very upset by the incident. Had Grisha not been ill, his father would have "fulfilled the verse" on him properly [i.e. given him a good thrashing], for Yefim was a man who knew how to keep discipline in the house. He dragged the boy down from Pyotr Alexandrovich's shoulders and laid him back on his bed. Yefim's wife apologized profusely to Pyotr Alexandrovich, who was pale, frightened and beside himself with the insult. He should not be troubled by the words of a sick child who is talking from fever. He [sic; probably: she] was terribly sorry about what had happened, but the worthy Pyotr Alexandrovich should forget the whole matter. She begged his pardon a thousand times. Did he not understand that the boy had been talking from fever?

Upper Silesian Economic Sketches

Dr. Abraham Szajer, Katowice.
3) Wholesale Trade.
Our home-grown economists, who after the war sprang up like mushrooms after the rain and whom one quite often finds in responsible positions, hold that wholesale trade is a superfluous link in the chain that runs from the producer to the consumer. Because of this, wholesale trade counts for almost nothing in the state economy, and the decisive circles put stones under its feet, especially when it concerns import as a special branch of trade.
No one who has not had a direct connection with trade can have any idea how much knowledge, energy, quick orientation and also decisiveness wholesale trade in the modern sense of the word demands. This branch of trade is, in the state economy — we mean well-organised and specialised wholesale, along a certain defined path and in specially designated branches. The opponents of wholesale trade under the present economic regime support and favour the larger retail trading houses, consumer societies and cooperatives — that is, those that do not meet the consumer directly and, on the other side, buy from the factories. The statistics I compiled among large foreign department stores assured me that for the most part these stores, or even the giant western[?] cooperatives, buy not from the factories but precisely from the wholesalers, who, buying large lots of goods and warehousing the goods themselves, receive special discounts and are able to forgo the profit they envisage and sell the goods much cheaper than the factory that makes them — not to mention that the choice at the wholesalers, who work with several factories, is a large one, which allows and makes it easier for retail businesses to cover their needs from one source.
Abroad they have long understood the importance of wholesale trade; proof of this is the fact that the most reputable factories do not run their own sales offices but hand their representation over to trade agents or well-known wholesalers.
As I already mentioned in the first article of this series, which characterised the whole of Silesian trade, Silesia had, even from before the war, that is from the German times, a wholesale trade developed at only one point, namely: most wholesalers dealt in selling the products of the local industry, especially of the steelworks (huty), as well as the products of the local mines (kopalnie). Wholesale trade in goods was of no importance because of the hugely developed Breslau and Berlin wholesalers, where retail sales covered their needs. After the war, after Poland took over Silesia and after Katowice was raised to the rank of a voivodeship town, many wholesale houses arose, because the wholesalers of other parts of the country could not satisfy the local market because of the special taste of the region.
So wholesale houses of all branches arose, and a whole series of them, after pushing aside the weaker ones, which had held on only thanks to the competition, developed and attained a dominant importance in the wholesale trade not only of Silesia but of the whole country.
The most important difficulties of the local wholesale trade are the burdens on importation and on customs duty and, most important of all, the absolute lack of any legal protection whatsoever in the present court system, so unfortunately divided[?] along the lines of the partition zones (zabory).
One of the most painful questions is import. Since the time the customs war with Germany broke out, that is from 15 June 1923, so-called import permits and a certificate of origin (Świadectwo pochodzenia) were introduced, which serves to prove[?] that the goods in question do not come from Germany. The import permits are only a formality, calculated to bring revenue to the state treasury, because in principle every wholesaler who fulfils the proper regulations and holds the necessary trading certificates (patent) can obtain an import permit.
Next comes the duty, which is a very high one, and the minimal purchasing power of our consumers is a healthy[?] automatic brake on our import.
Despite the strong opposition, protests and memoranda asking for the duty to be lowered, from the second half of last year the handling fees were increased from 4 to 6 per mille of the value of the goods, as the Polish consulates abroad endorse the factory invoices.
It is clear that the point here is not so much to protect domestic production, which is anyway protected by the horrendous tariff rates, but rather that the decisive factors take every opportunity to burden wholesale trade in general and import in particular. The chambers of commerce and the merchants' associations are powerless here, because such things [come], despite the opinion of these institutions, "from above", and that is binding without appeal. It is, after all, not only a matter of the material side of the burdens but also of a technical one.
One cannot always obtain an import permit in time, sometimes because something is missing in the permit, and so it happens quite often that a merchant who must deliver goods by a certain deadline — the goods have arrived on time, and because of the absence or delay of some trivial formality the merchant must pay contractual penalties and suffers great material losses, not to mention the high warehouse charges he has to pay, through no fault of his own, to the post or customs warehouses. (S.)

A Powder Keg

Between the Sanacja [Piłsudski's ruling camp] and the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] a new conflict has recently broken out, a new storm, around which both sides are going about with burning torches — so they accuse each other — and thereby they may bring about a catastrophe.
By the powder keg is meant here the Treaty of Versailles. And it is connected with the victory of the Left Cartel in France, with Poland's foreign policy and with the... Sanacja regime in Poland.
Deputy Niedziałkowski, who is regarded in the PPS as the "specialist" in foreign policy, has published several articles in "Robotnik" in which he points out that the coming to power of the Left in France must force Poland into a change of its internal policy; other elements must come to power in Poland, so that the democracy of France and that of Poland can work together for the good of both states.
Deputy Niedziałkowski accuses the Sanacja of having invited to Poland, to spite French democracy, the guests from Fascist Italy, so as to demonstrate thereby against the new France.
On hearing such words "Gazeta Polska" came out with an alarm: how so, how dare anyone accuse it of such a thing! None other than its own camp represents true democracy. The Fascist guests were invited to Poland months ago, before anyone even knew of the victory of the French Left. As to the substance of the matter, the Sanacja press points out that the internal conditions in the country do not decide its foreign policy. The Soviets and Italy live in the best of friendship, the same goes for the Soviets and Turkey, and therefore one must assume that the Left in France will reckon with Poland as a state and not with its separate parties.
But another question arises: Italy today is on the best of terms with Germany. The Sanacja press itself openly admits that if Poland is threatened by a danger, it is only on its western borders. Germany, which wants to break the Treaty of Versailles — Italy provokes and incites it to this deed. The Fascists have a formula: "Revision of the peace treaties shall be by war." So how, asks "Robotnik", can Poland invite Fascist guests and rejoice with them? But the opposing side comes and shows that it is precisely the P.P.S. that goes about with a burning torch around the powder keg called the Treaty of Versailles — and here the Polish Left is caught red-handed. "Robotnik" itself writes that socialist circles hold to a formula: "Revise the treaties, but never by war." That is the formula of socialist circles all over the world. "Gazeta Polska" declares that whatever the formula, whatever the government, whatever the balance of forces — Poland will never agree to a revision of its borders, and should it nevertheless come to that, it will lead to the explosion of the powder keg.
Concretely, the matter now is a match with French democracy. "Robotnik" is striving to win the French bride for Poland, warning the Sanacja that there is a danger that the French Left will get in touch with the German Left, and then the situation will become far more serious.
The Sanacja press is unnerved; it suspects that there is a grain of truth in the warning, but what is it to do when the price of this match, the dowry, must be — the liquidation of the Sanacja regime...
—N.
Thrift and Stinginess

How stingy husbands embitter life for themselves and for their wives.
A period of economy is now going on in the world.
In Europe, where the economic crisis has lasted since the World War, this period has been going on for years and years.
Even before the war Europeans lived far more economically and frugally than the American, because in Europe one always earned much less than in America, and so one had to live with calculation and good sense.
The American earned more. So he was extravagant; he allowed himself more luxury and comfort. He believed in getting as much pleasure as possible out of life.
Then the crisis came, and America too sobered up and was forced to take up economizing.
That is why everyone now talks about economy everywhere. Government people, senators and deputies sit racking their brains over how to economize as much as possible in government expenditure.
Large firms do the same — they try to abolish superfluous expenses as far as possible and to guard against waste.
This is often done at the expense of people who are thrown out of their jobs and are left without a crust of bread.
But so it is: this is a time of economy, both in the life of the community and in the life of the individual.
Economy, however, is a good thing not only in a time of crisis.
Above all, economy is important in the life of the private person.
It is a crime when people live only for today and forget about tomorrow.
It is a sin against oneself and against others when one spends all one's earnings and saves nothing for a "rainy day".
Many people who today suffer hunger and want are paying the bitter price for having lived without reckoning, for not having put aside a little money and protected themselves against hard times.
The trouble is only that many people confuse thrift with stinginess.
One must bear in mind that thrift is one thing and stinginess is another.
When someone is stingy and lies on his money, as the Talmud puts it, "like a mouse lying on a heap of gold coins", that does not mean he is thrifty.
And that is precisely the misfortune: stingy people do not know how to be thrifty... They will save a groschen and squander a whole hundred.
Besides, stinginess is simply an ugly trait. And a stingy person is a misery for his family, for his acquaintances and for society in general.
Women who are "blessed" with stingy husbands have a bitter life.
Many family tragedies come about because the husband is stingy and counts out every groschen to his wife, who runs the household.
Women who have such husbands feel insulted and humiliated, and rightly so. For a husband who checks every groschen that his wife spends on running the house and providing all the necessary things for the household — such a husband shows thereby that he has no trust in his wife, in her ability and understanding to run a house; he simply does not believe her.
These husbands think that by their stinginess they are fulfilling the duties of economy.
But that is not right, because, as we have already explained, there is a very great difference between thrift and stinginess.
We know of cases where stinginess has often led to very sad results. Take, for example, this case: a certain Mr. Z. fell ill. He struggled for a long time and did not want to give in. He went about instead of lying down in bed and calling a doctor; he did not do so because he was busy and thought that if he stayed home for a few days his business would suffer. He belonged to that type of people who persuade themselves that if they leave their business for one day, everything will go to ruin and the world will come to an end.
His wife saw that her husband was ill and urged him to lie down in bed and call a doctor. But he would not hear of it, because a doctor costs money, after all, and one has to pay for a prescription.
But the husband had to lie down after all, and when the doctor was brought, his condition was already so serious that afterwards professors had to be brought, medicines applied, and it cost a fortune to keep him alive.
The husband was lucky still that he got up from his bed, although he never again became a fully healthy man.
And, as the doctors explained, this happened because the man had neglected his state of health.
And he had neglected his state of health because he was a miser; the coin was dearer to him than his own life.
And we also know of cases where wives have left their husbands because they could no longer bear their stinginess.
Stinginess is therefore often a curse.
As psychologists explain, stinginess is a kind of mental illness, and the miser is simply a sick person.
But the miser can free himself from this ugly trait.
He need only apply a little willpower and use a little common sense, if he has any at all.
If stingy husbands understood this, they and their families would be much happier and more contented in their lives.
Ch.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Presidium Elections of the Kehilla Council and of the Board Annulled

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 28 Iyar 5692 — piątek 3 czerwca 1932 [Friday, 3 June 1932].)
Będzin
The presidium elections of the kehilla council and of the board annulled.
This week the starosta notified the Jewish community that the presidium elections of the kehilla council and of the board had not been held in accordance with the relevant paragraph, and therefore the elections are recognised as invalid.
At the same time the starosta orders that the presidium elections be held within 2 weeks. First the presidium of the board will be elected, and afterwards that of the council.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Crime.] Suicide of a Sosnowiec man in Siewierz.
In the Siewierz forest the dead body of an unknown person was found.
The police investigation then established that the dead man is a certain Gajda from Sosnowiec.
Gajda went off into the forest, where he committed suicide.
—o—
[Będzin — Kehilla.] Appeals against the kehilla budget.
This week the deadline for submitting appeals against the new kehilla budget expired.
400 appeals were submitted.
—o—
[Będzin — Crime.] A lady's fur coat stolen.
During the absence of the Rabinowicz family on Wspólna Street, thieves got into the flat and took a lady's fur coat.
—o—
[Będzin — Attempted suicide.] He was weary of life...
The 74-year-old Cupiał (Dębowa 34) hanged himself in the lavatory. The residents of the house noticed it, and the old man was saved from death.
—o—
[Transport.] On rubber wheels..
A French firm is developing railway carriages on rubber wheels. Such a carriage has room for 60 persons. The route runs through Będzin. This week such a trial carriage was sent from Katowice to Warsaw.
Instead of Shochtim — Assistants..

[Będzin — Kashrut and Shechita.]
The question of the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) in our town has become topical again, but since the matter is for the time being hard to realise, the plan arose to engage assistants...
The candidates are the "Sighet shochet" and the son of Avraham the shochet.
As we are informed, the negotiations between the butchers and the candidates are on a good path and will probably be successful...
Summer Colonies.

[Będzin — Holidays.]
The Society for Knowledge of the Country (Krajoznawstwo) is organising summer colonies this year in Zakopane and in Kazimierz. In Zakopane it costs 180 zł. a month, and in Kazimierz 140.
The Będzin "Ognisko" of Jewish academics is also organising a summer colony in Poronin. The price is 130 zł. a month.
Heavy Sentences for Communist Activity.

[Będzin — Courts.]
On 15 December last year a group of young communists gathered on Kołłątaja Street and wanted to hold a meeting. The police came to the spot and arrested the young men L. Podliński, K. Gwa, M. Rotenberg, Yissachar Lewkowicz and B. Goldsztajn.
Last Friday the arrested stood before the Sosnowiec district court, which handed down the following verdict: Podliński 4 years of heavy prison, Gwa two and a half years, Rotenberg a year's imprisonment, Goldsztajn and Lewkowicz 6 months' imprisonment. Goldsztajn's sentence was suspended for 2 years.
There Is No Money for the Talmud Torah Children..

[Będzin — Education.]
Next Sunday an outing of the Talmud Torah children was to have taken place to Małobądz, where they had been permitted to spend a few hours in the local garden of the Potok family. Because the community refused to give 50 zł., which are needed to buy food for the children, the "outing" will not take place.
About the Draft of the 1911 Class

[Będzin — Military Draft.]
In connection with the draft (pobór) of the 1911 class, which began yesterday, we are asked to announce that those liable to the draft must present themselves to the commission in clean underwear and washed. They must bring along documents, as well as certificates concerning their education and vocational skills.
For not presenting oneself on the appointed date one can be punished with 50 zł. or 6 weeks' arrest.
If anyone does not present himself for the draft with the intention of evading military service, he will be handed over to the judicial authorities and faces up to 2 years' imprisonment.
Collapsed in the Street from Hunger.

[Czeladź — Destitution.]
On Bytomska Street in Czeladź an unknown woman was walking by, who suddenly fell down on the pavement.
People came running and revived the fainted woman. When the woman came to, she told them that she had been going hungry for two days already.
Koshered Milk and — 'Sabbath' Bread..

[Będzin — Religion; Satire.]
The "Shomrei Shabbat ve-ha-Dat" society in our town is active. Apart from the ordinance on kosher milk, which will surely have an echo "all over the world", the society has accomplished a second thing, which "strengthens" Sabbath observance...
The ordinance consists in this: hechsherim (kashrut certificates) are issued for baking bread on the Sabbath, on condition that labels "szabasówka" are stuck onto the bread baked on the Sabbath... With this ordinance the society intends that the bread should be eaten by Christians...
Members' Meeting of “Tse'irei Mishmerei Holim”

[Będzin — society, care of the sick.]
On Sunday a members' meeting of “Tse'irei Mishmerei Holim” [Young Watchers of the Sick] took place in Będzin. With a handful of members present, the chairman Mr. Yitzhak Fajgenblat opened the meeting and invited to the presidium the comrades Elchanan Małgowicer [?], Icze Meir Ehrlich and Elchanan Piekarski as secretary.
The chairman reads the treasurer's report, from which it emerges that the income from 1 styczeń [January] of this year to the present day amounts to 140 zł. 89[?] gr. The activity report shows that 104 watches [volunteers sitting up with the sick] were sent to 34 sick people.
After the reports it was resolved: 1) to create sanitary [first-aid] courses, so that the watchers can deal with the sick person properly, and 2) to collect a membership fee of a minimum of 25 gr. a month. Then the chairman closes the meeting and proceeds to constitute the presidium of the recruitment committee. The following presidium was then elected: Yaakov Rodaler (chairman). Ehrlich and Rajz (vice-chairmen) and Elchanan Piekarski (secretary).
Who Will Be Able to Get Support from the Unemployment Fund?

[Będzin — unemployment, social insurance.]
The local relief office for the unemployed has been sent a circular from the Minister of Labour in connection with the changes in the “ustawa” [law] concerning those who benefit from the unemployment relief fund.
1) The right to benefit from support belongs to workers who in the course of the last 12 months have worked 26 weeks (until now 20 weeks); 2) those whose main earnings are not from the work from which they have now been dismissed have no right whatsoever to support (on this a special law is still to be issued); 3) the Ministry of Labour has the right to exempt enterprises from insuring their workers who work no more than 6 months in the course of the year; 4) to the insurance fund the employer pays one and a half percent, the worker half a percent. 5) Seasonal workers pay 4 percent: the employer 2 pc. and the worker 2 percent; 6) the amount of support is determined according to the earnings of the last 13 weeks; 7) a worker who has voluntarily renounced it loses the right to benefit from unemployment support.
The new changes come into force from 11 July of this year.
Sosnowiec. General Meeting of Jewish Artisans

[Sosnowiec — artisans.]
On Sunday a general meeting of Jewish artisans took place in Sosnowiec. Before the agenda was taken up, the officer for artisans' affairs, Mr. Lepowski [?], gave a lecture in which he informed at length about the way to combat illegal workshops. The speaker dwells on broader powers for the inspectors, who will also have the police at their disposal. The inspectors will receive special identity papers from the starostwo [district office]. He also mentioned that in the next few days the compulsory guild law will come into force, which will oblige all craftsmen to belong to a guild. Incidentally he remarked that for the artisans this is an important moment.
After the lecture comrade Rotensztajn was elected chairman. After hearing the reports of G.[?] chairman and the treasurer, a lengthy discussion developed.
The election of a new board did not take place.
The meeting resolves to create a board of all the guilds, which is to take over the whole management of the association.
The continuation of the said meeting will take place in about 2 weeks.
—o—
Next Sunday a session of all the boards of the guilds will take place at the Artisans' Association. At the session the question of the committees that will examine the appeals on [the] turnover [tax], of delegating [members] to the assessment committee for income [tax] for the year 1932, of diplomas, and other important artisans' questions will be considered.
Instead of Their Own Association — a Jewish Secretary

[Sosnowiec — house-owners.]
A group of house-owners in our town decided to found an independent association. Against this spoke out those who tremble lest the “porets” [the (Polish) lord] be offended, and the project came to nothing. The “moderates” argue that instead of founding an association of their own, it is better to make efforts with the existing Endek [National Democratic] house-owners' association so that a Jewish secretary should also be engaged for the Jewish members...
Grabbed a Piece of Goods and Ran Off..

[Sosnowiec — trade, incident.]
In the textile shop of Mr. D. Szwajcer a Silesian woman (Ślązaczka) bought several metres of goods. When paying, the customer did not want to pay the price agreed upon. When Mr. Sz. reacted to this, she grabbed a piece of goods and ran off. With the help of a policeman the “paferin”[?] was “invited” back into the shop, where she returned the grabbed goods and took the purchased goods at the proper price.
Thank God, a General Meeting Took Place at the “Talmud Torah”

[Sosnowiec — Talmud Torah, community.]
After a break of 11 years (the gabbaim say it was no more than 6[?] years...) a general meeting of the Talmud Torah members took place last Sunday under the chairmanship of Mr. Tabiasz.
Of 700 members a number of 70 came, but, as we are told, even the number of those present was almost superfluous, since in any case not a single critical word was addressed to the outgoing board, and everything remained
— as of old...
After the most “thorough”[?] “reports” a new board was elected, consisting of: Rabbi Englard, Leib Englard, Szymon Mendel Tabiasz, Gronem Pfeffer [?], Lejbisz Szwajcer, Baruch Sećemski [?], Chaim Josef Zając, Chaim Unger, Mendel Czechowski, Herzke Szczekacz, Icchak Dafner and Moshe Mordechai Wajnsztok.
The Modrzejów[?] Works Have Received Large Orders from the Soviets

[Sosnowiec — industry, economy.]
The Soviet trade representatives in Warsaw have concluded a transaction for 70 thousand tons of iron. The largest part of the order will be carried out by the “Mandzhever” works [Zakłady Modrzejowskie? — Modrzejów, a district of Sosnowiec].
Besides this the Soviets have ordered a large number of machines at the “Poręba” factory.
In connection with the orders the number of unemployed is expected to decrease in the near future.
The Soviet government pays for the goods with bills of exchange, which will be discounted through the “Bank Polski”.
—o—
In May Products Became 2.15 Percent Dearer.
At the local magistrate [town hall] the prices commission held a session at which it was established that in the month of May articles of prime necessity rose by 2.15 percent.
—o—
Into the Trap...
The local police arrested an unknown person who had been watching [?] the shops. At the police station (komisariat) it turned out that the “bird” has been wanted for a long time by the Katowice police.
—o—
On Workers' Holidays
Next week the Council of Industrialists in Zagłębie will hold a conference at which the question of workers' holidays will be dealt with.
—o—
Support for the Unemployed Is Being Reduced.
The relief action for the unemployed in Zagłębie has been reduced from the 1st of this month. Urgent help will be available only in exceptional cases. At the same time the committee is endeavouring to give employment to those who until now received support.
—o—
“Reden” Halts Work.
The “Reden” coal mine in Dąbrowa has notified its workers that owing to a lack of orders work will be halted for two weeks.
At “Reden” 1000 men were working.

Demonstration of the unemployed in front of the Sosnowiec magistrate

[Sosnowiec — unemployment and relief.] The day before yesterday[?] in the morning several hundred wives of unemployed men gathered in front of the Sosnowiec magistrate (town hall) and shouted: "We don't want the midday meals for the poor and the unemployed."
The crowd chose a delegation of 4 women, who went to the commissioner, Mr. Kuszniak.
The delegation declared to the commissioner that they do not want to eat at the free kitchen; rather, they should be given the raw provisions.
The commissioner promised to fulfil the wish after coming to an understanding with the committee for the support of the unemployed.
The epidemic[?] being over, commissioner Mr. Kuszniak has decided to liquidate the free kitchen.
—o—
Echoes of the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec.
In May of last year, when the struggle over the kehilla elections flared up in our town, a leaflet was distributed in which various sins of Rabbi Englard were listed.
On that leaflet Mr. Alter Markowicz figured as the responsible person, against whom Rabbi Englard has now, for a year, conducted a lawsuit.
—o—
Pensions of the Sosnowiec magistrate officials reduced.
The local magistrate has received from the voivodeship office[?] an order to reduce the pensions of municipal officials in accordance with the resolution of the Council of Ministers.
The order already came into force last Wednesday, the 1st of this month.
—o—
Matura at the Real School.
At the Real School in Będzin the following pupils passed the matura: Bernard Szer, Emanuel Finkelsztajn, Zygmunt Baum, Roman Grajcar, Dawid Manela and Mieczysław Lubelski.
—o—
"Mothers' Week" in Sosnowiec.
On the initiative of the wife of Dr. Grodushinski, "Mothers' Week" was [held][?] in Sosnowiec. In its honour celebrations and memorial prayers[?] for deceased mothers took place in the orphans' shelter, the Jewish hospital, the "Beit Yetomim" orphanage and the old-age home; at the Jewish hospital Dr. Weinzieher spoke about the significance of "Mothers' Week", and at the shelter the children gave presents to their mothers.
—o—
Committee to celebrate the memory of Chopin.
A meeting took place at the Sosnowiec magistrate at which a committee was created to organize the "Chopin Days", which will be celebrated throughout Poland in honour of the brilliant Polish composer Chopin.

Extraordinary general meeting of the Będzin "Maccabi".
Tonight an extraordinary general meeting takes place at the "Hakoach" premises, at which a new board is to be elected.

Będzin landsleit send a hundred dollars through the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ for „Linas haCholim“

Some weeks ago an article was printed in our newspaper in which the writer appealed to the Będzin landsleit across the sea not to forget the philanthropic institutions in Zagłębie, which find themselves in a critical financial situation.
The appeal brought the proper result. Our brothers in America responded to our call and contributed to the institutions in the town of Będzin.
Two weeks ago Mr. Yakov Gutman received from the Bendiner Verein 100 dollars for institutions and private persons. The sum has not yet been distributed, because the cheque for the 100 dollars has not yet been cashed.
Besides this, our editorial office received word that the Bendiner Verein in Chicago, on the basis of an intervention, had undertaken a campaign for the „Linas haCholim“, the „Moshav Zekenim“ [old-age home] and the maternity home.
The news has indeed been confirmed. Yesterday 100 dollars for „Linas haCholim“ were received at the address of the editorial office of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“.
We immediately handed the 100 dollars over to the board, which sends the donors in Chicago, through the newspaper, a hearty yasher-koach.
—o—
Meals for Jewish soldiers at Shavuot
Mr. Brafman has prevailed upon the colonel (pułkownik) to release the Jewish soldiers for the holiday, on condition that they be provided with meals in a respectable manner.
The kehilla board, which was approached about this matter, refused. Therefore whoever wishes to give a meal to a Jewish soldier at Shavuot should apply to Mr. M. Brafman, Będzin, Podzamcze 12, or to Mr. Sh. D. Ferens at the timber yard, or at his flat, Mandoszewer [?] 8.
—o—
No „success“...
A Christian thief went to Dąbrowa, where in Kalman Epstein's drapery (manufaktura) shop she stole a piece of linen. The theft was discovered in time and the „customer“ has been arrested.
—o—
Medical help for the needy population
The present board of „Linas haCholim“ has undertaken an important campaign for the needy part of the Sosnowiec Jewish population.
The campaign consists of the following. The board has at its disposal several doctors who have undertaken to give medical help to the sick who hold slips from „Linas haCholim“.
The initiative is very important in the present severe crisis. It is, however, also desirable that the board should find a way for the poor members of the society to be able to buy the necessary medicines at reduced prices.

Appeal of the Charity Society in Będzin.
Esteemed citizens!

Windows Smashed in the Building of the Ogrodzieniec Gmina.
A large number of unemployed came into the Ogrodzieniec gmina [municipal office], shouting that they should be given bread, because they had been hungry for several days.
The next day the representative of the starosty, Mr. Paszyarla [?], came to Ogrodzieniec and declared to the crowd that there were prospects of giving employment to a larger number of workers. The local priest also calmed the crowd with his speech to them. Suddenly voices were heard from the crowd that the starosty's representative should be detained until a favourable answer was received from the starosty.
The situation became bad, and the detachment of police present intervened. At that moment a hail of stones began from the crowd, by which all the windows in the gmina building were smashed.
In connection with this, police reinforcements were called from Zawiercie, and they put an end to the events.
—o—
Result of the Kimcha Campaign in Sosnowiec.
From the Sosnowiec [Jewish] community we have received the following account of this year's kimcha [Passover flour] campaign.
Collected in the town: 5679 zł; from the community — 393 zł. The sum was distributed among 584 persons, at 5 to 30 zł.
This year's kimcha campaign brought in about 1500 zł less than last year.
—o—
Price Lists Must Be Hung Up in Conspicuous Places.
The Ministry of the Interior has issued a circular concerning price lists of articles of prime necessity. The circular reminds the administrative authorities that in food shops, as well as butcher shops and stalls in the markets, in restaurants, railway buffets [?] and cafés, price lists must be hung up in public places so that everyone can acquaint himself exactly with the prices. This regulation also applies to coal and wood depots, which are regarded as articles of prime necessity.
—o—
Décolletés Forbidden.
Overalls buttoned up to the neck must be worn.
In the latest issue of the "Dziennik" of the Ministry of Justice an order of Minister of Justice Michałowski has been published, in which all women employed in the various offices subordinate to the Minister of Justice are forbidden to wear décolletés. All women are ordered to wear overalls of a fixed cut and style. The order specifies exactly what the overalls must look like: the overall must be of a thin black material with a collar, reaching to 25 centimetres from the floor. The overall must be buttoned in front up to the very neck with 8 small black buttons.
In short, women — into the overalls. It is not excluded that inspections will be carried out on the ladies in the offices, to see whether they have complied with the overall order.

What Is Heard in Upper Silesia? / Editor of the "Kattowitzer Zeitung" Arrested / Attacked His Stepmother with an Axe / Czech Deputy Foreign Minister in Katowice / Damage by Lightning / Tragic Death of a Small Child / A New Jewish Bank / Drowned Man Found / Murder and Suicide

[Upper Silesia — short news.]
What Is Heard in Upper Silesia?
Editor of the "Kattowitzer Zeitung" Arrested.
On the order of the prosecutor, the responsible editor of the "Kattowitzer Zeitung", Mr. Szrej [?], was arrested because an article about the question of Danzig and Pomerania had been printed in the paper.
—o—
Attacked His Stepmother with an Axe.
An unemployed man stood before the Katowice district court, accused of having dealt his stepmother several blows with an axe.
Before the court the accused told his life story, his sufferings from the stepmother, who would not let him in to spend the night.
The words of the accused made everyone present in the courtroom weep.
The accused was sentenced to 5 months' imprisonment.
—o—
Czech Deputy Foreign Minister in Katowice.
The Czech deputy foreign minister Dr. Krofta arrived in Katowice, accompanied by the Czech consul in Kraków and the Polish consul in Prague.
—o—
Damage by Lightning.
On Saturday lightning struck a house in Mysłowice. The electric wires were torn down and part of the roof was also damaged.
—o—
Tragic Death of a Small Child.
On Sunday several children were playing in a garden in Königshütte. While playing, a child of a year and a half received a blow to the head from a swing. The child died a few hours later.
—o—
A New Jewish Bank.
The "Bank Dyskontowy" in Sosnowiec, which is developing very well, opened a branch in Katowice this Tuesday.
This branch, too, has good chances of developing here.
—o—
Drowned Man Found
On Sunday the drowned body of the 56-year-old unemployed Szurmer of Siemianowice was found in the Siemianowice river.
—o—
Murder and Suicide.
In the post office at Paniówki, near Rybnik, the 31-year-old letter carrier Janusz Józef shot dead the head of the post office, Sołtysik [?], and then committed suicide himself. The reason for the murder and suicide is that the head of the post office wanted to dismiss the letter carrier from his post.
Important Order Concerning the Claims of Polish Citizens Against the German Insurance Companies

[Poland — finance and insurance; regulation.]
In "Monitor Polski" No. 108 an order of the Minister of Finance has appeared concerning the registration of the claims of Polish citizens against the German insurance companies. The registration covers the claims enumerated in Art. 21 of the Polish-German valorisation agreement, i.e. claims on life insurance in crowns, Polish marks, "krizis-bones" [?] and Russian roubles, as well as from contracts in German marks concluded through the German insurance companies in Austria.
The claims may be filed with the Commissioner for the Liquidation of Life Insurance Companies (Warsaw, Nowogrodzka [?] 40, apt. 1).
The final deadline for filing claims is 30 November 1932. The form of the application has been published in "Monitor Polski".
