The Process of Our Way of Thinking. (Disappointments that arise from the forms of the times.)

L. Szpigelman.

Apart from the prevailing world crisis, which has entered the phase of a chronic illness that can seldom be radically cured — apart from this abnormal phenomenon, it is in general very hard in our generations to continue the course of our existence, of our everyday life. That is to say: even if everything were good and fine, even if we did not have to go through these passing, fairly long-lasting storm winds that tear out deep-rooted rocks[?], even if all these stumbling blocks did not strike against our feet — even then it would not be so easy to go through the process of our struggle for existence; let alone when so many obstacles are laid down that make it impossible to carry through the route that was intended for mankind to work, to plant and to beautify, so that our children should see what was created for them, what their parents shaped for them.

Yes, people interfere who will not let the world go at its ox-pace[?], along its normal, well-trodden path, which can exist only under normal conditions, by a normal reckoning. If various individuals had not laid countless stones before mankind on the straight, paved road that people adorned for themselves by themselves[?]; if all these disturbing elements had not burst in with their explosive materials and had not set up barricades before the eyes of mankind — then mankind would have formed its own unique way of thinking, and a new and fine generation of useful citizens would have arisen, who would have progressed on the globe and would have truly worked wonders for the beautiful world.

Yes, one could have lived and worked and created wonders, had there not sprung up, as if from under the earth, all sorts of destroyers who want to turn the world upside down and constantly seek explosions in order to reach their goal and to be able to fish in troubled waters...

We are often mute witnesses to various phenomena: now it seems to us that a beautiful world is being built, a splendid world. People begin to think humanely, to comprehend humanely, to understand one another humanely — and right in the middle of it [printed "דריגען", apparently for "דרינען"], in the middle of it, while we see that mankind is beginning to climb onto the highest pedestal, there suddenly come evil storm winds that tear with tremendous obstinacy through the thick fog, where they plunder across the beautiful plants, which they destroy, and in their place wild plants appear in disorder, prickly thorns that poison the surrounding air and pollute the normal pleasant scent into a stinking atmosphere that grows worse from day to day and harder to breathe from hour to hour.

Yes, from time to time stinking gases accumulate which must be exploded; with the best will in the world the gases cannot be kept stifled and they must shoot out; they must knock down fortresses and break through walls, and then it is self-evident that everything is destroyed. Of the best and finest there remains a mountain of ash, and in place of useful citizens there arise dangerous individuals, unwanted elements; and with these outcasts the world fills up, and they begin to pollute the surrounding air; they jump up onto the horse and want to persuade the world that they will be [printed "זיי", for "זיין"] the saviours, they will be the leaders, they will be the ones who will build a new world.

But all these are illusions, fantasies, soap bubbles that burst as quickly as they are born; these are merely fashions, a kind of topical gallery pictures that last no longer than the season lasts and vanish together with the fashion magazine. It goes without saying that "world and mankind" cannot stand on such foundations. One cannot come and say that what was created over generations with arduous labour and brought mankind so much benefit is today worth nothing at all.

We would still understand if an object or an outlook had a lesser value today because something new had been created in its place, something that had caused an upheaval; then we would understand that the progressive completely replaces the outdated. But on no account can one throw away the old god at a time when nothing new and important has been introduced.

Some decades ago mankind was brought up according to a different conception. It received an idea from its educators, it was given an ideal, and later its way of thinking was continued according to a certain outlook, according to its own conception. The main thing was that it was given an ideal, and then that ideal was shaped according to various systems.

Now it is completely different. The ideal we inherited from our parents they want to tear out of our hearts by force, and at the same time [printed "און דער צייט", for "אין דער צייט"] we are given no other ideal. We have given our children nothing, and that is why everything with them is so dry. We watch what forms have been adopted among them — and then we are disgusted on their behalf. We see that yesterday's sanctities have today been desecrated among them. Ideals, outlooks, concepts are instantly exchanged for everyday matters. It is enough to point out that what was holy only yesterday is already trampled underfoot today. The finest and best, the most delicate and noblest and most splendid has vanished with the speed of the smoke of a papiros [cigarette].

And say what you will — it is hard, very hard, to get used to it. It is ugly today to spit on what we idolized yesterday. Something drives everything at such a speed — may God guard and save us. Everything is done quickly today. People run fast, travel fast, fly; people live fast through the bitterest time, and quickly digest all bitter feelings.

So it is no wonder: when the bullet races, there is no way out — one must catch hold of the flywheel, which cannot stop in full gallop; and if it does stop in mid-momentum, it wrecks everything, destroys, does damage, damage beyond measure.

The consequences are these: the older people, those who studied and worked before the war, cannot catch hold of the flywheel; it is too tight for them there, they cannot catch their breath there; and the younger ones, those who have only just hatched, cannot adapt to the older elements, and they drift far apart in their differences of opinion.

We would like to be honest and tell the truth, and it is this: never, for as long as the world has been a world, have the older generations been able to come to terms with the younger generation, and that too is understandable: after all [?], outdated concepts — what was once beautiful is today worn out and gone stale.

Well yes, that would be understandable if we saw newer concepts, finer ideals, more refined manners, a genuine, unaffected consciousness. Unfortunately we see none of this.

In the past there were no schools; a gymnasium was a rarity; illiterates there were more than enough — to say nothing of higher schools. Who, of mankind in general and of the Jews in particular, was privileged to get to a faculty and graduate from it? And yet, and yet — we draw a parallel between the past and the present, and only then does one see how deep "the abyss" is, how terrible the course, how far astray things have gone.

Today there are nothing but intellectuals, conscious people, newspapers without number and beyond measure; books appear in masses — but who buys a book? Who takes an interest in a new work? Who reads it, and into whose head does it go? If one does buy a book, it is for show, and if one even reads it through, one does not manage[?] to give oneself any account even of what one has read. One does not manage to digest the book one has read; that is how people rush, and how artificially everything is done — a kind of cheap trash, it is stereotyped work.

And in the past, in the past, when a new book appeared, it was simply a holiday; countless reviews were read for months on end. Lectures took place and discussions were held. The lectures gave a person much more than the reading. We had the book well [sic; a word seems missing], and digesting is more important than eating...

Yes, today everyone gets educated, every single one graduates from a faculty, and in the past there were no schools, ignoramuses were raised; but what a contrast there is between the conscious intellectual of the past and today's superficial intellectual who comes to us with an academic education.

Yes, in the past intellectuals were few and far between, and today the whole community is intellectual; everyone today is educated. It is a kind of record work that must be finished to the minute and the second.

The difference is this: in the past one studied Torah for its own sake, one let oneself develop in education, in learning; and today it is done with the speed of the flywheel. That is why there is such a contrast between the ideals of the past and of today, between the people of the past and of today, who want, in a drastic manner and unconsciously, to overturn worlds and exterminate people.
Time Will Tell...

[A merchant's letter — economy and trade.] (A Merchant's Letter)
By Yosef Perlmutter.
My friend! Ever since our professors and minister have been standing with their little hammers in hand, tapping and studying and holding conferences and various experiments, in order to find the spot where the wound lies that blocks the blood circulation in the grandiose body called the State, and on account of which another limb dies off every day — they have never, it seems, been so close to the truth. They have evidently hit upon the right spot, and they already know how the pulse must start beating again as it once did...
In the end the latest conferences have led to the very idea I have written to you about more than once in my letters, namely: that the main thing is free trade; that all restrictions must be lifted from commerce, together with all those "concessions" [licences] that were so burdensome and so oppressive that almost fifty percent of the trade in Poland lay not in the right hands and was conducted with great difficulty, until it reached its death-throes... Willingly or not, they have therefore had to open their eyes and look around and see that they had crawled too far... The concession schemes must be given up — schemes with which the government was so thoroughly imbued, to which it held so stubbornly, and which it would on no account yield...
Surely, my friend, you have read about the latest government project to remove the difficulties and abolish the concessions that hampered free trade in tobacco products, so that "let all who are hungry come and eat" — whoever has a little money can open a wholesale business [hurtownia] of goods... Even more: whoever proves worthy will even get credit as well... You understand what a breach this is in the economic armour and in the whole political edifice in general, which cost so much money and effort, out of which they wanted to make among us an everlasting "bkhis" [sic; presumably "edifice for generations"] — and to take, or even tear, trade away from us for ever and ever...
That we are more capable of trade, that we understand better how to drive and push business — for that we have this week even received a rabbinical "ordination" from our "friend", the "Kurier".
According to the "Kurier", we have lately had a season such as has not been seen for a very long time... ready-made clothing ran short, because everything was bought up... Mandzhever[?] Street simply "sugared up"[?] literally all the goods, turned everything into money and piled up the wealth of Korah...
Had it really been so, it would have done no harm at all; but all in all, today's season, with its whole shortage of goods, looks to me just like that boy... You know the story:
Once there was a boy who was very fond of beans with dumplings [bobelekh mit kluskelekh]; he was absolutely dying for that dish. Once, sleeping in his bed at night, he dreamt of a whole bowl of beans with dumplings — but alas, he had no spoon to eat it with... The next day, before going to sleep, he took the precaution of providing himself with a spoon under his pillow — but the dream never came again...
The same thing has happened to us in Zagłębie. This season, when nobody had prepared any goods, there happens to be turnover, there are customers — and there is nothing to sell... Whereas in the previous seasons, when we pawned ourselves to the last and prepared goods for the season, no customers came and we lost all the money, because all raw materials became cheaper by a full forty percent.
But the main point is not even that people were afraid to prepare stock; there was simply nothing to prepare it with. Since there are no credits, and with cash alone one cannot run an industry as it should be run — for in all there is in circulation in Poland about a billion złotys; deduct half of it, which is deposited in the P.K.O. [Post Office Savings Bank] and in the banks and also in various institutions, and it turns out that the whole industry together with the whole of commerce is choking on half a billion zł. And how can one cover an industry that must prepare goods for a population of thirty million with such a sum... Cover the head, and the feet stick out; cover the feet, and the head sticks out... And on top of that came an unwritten plague: everyone and everything wants precisely now (because money is so dear) to sell; the whole atmosphere is pervaded by that mood. It will be no exaggeration if I tell you that almost all houses, all estates, all factories, all businesses — I would put it: the whole globe — is up for sale. Just as fifteen years ago every single person thought only of how to get rid of his money and buy some property, today it is exactly the opposite — everything is for sale, only bring the money here...
And this, you know, my friend, is perhaps the greatest point of dispute, the greatest "rock of contention" between the leaders and those who stand at the head of every state individually. One school says: since we have come to this — since with so much effort and material we have brought money to such a level that it has indeed become so dear a thing — every effort must be made to hold the position, for otherwise the trouble with money is that "if you have begun to fall, you will surely fall" [after Esther 6:13; misquoted as printed] and it will no longer be possible to hold it back.
The other side, on the contrary, argues that one cannot and must not strangle industry with all its enterprises, with so many millions of people, just because we keep money at such a high level. It will turn out, they say, that "his gain is outweighed by his loss"... In any case, my friend, what time will do, reason will not do.
Time will tell...
So, have a good holiday.
Your friend, Yosef.
Topical Notes: An Ugly Epidemic / Another Accursed Disease / A Sold Soul

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — editorial notes: informing, card-playing, a corrupt "editor".]
An Ugly Epidemic.
Jewish life has lately been suffering from a terrible disease — informing (mesires). This disease has simply taken on an epidemic character. Its victims grow in number from day to day. There is not a single state office that is not swamped with such denunciations, and the tax office most of all. And were we able to publish even a small part of such facts, we would show[?] that these informers are our own people, our communal workers, our intelligentsia, our "fine Jews".
Horror simply seizes one on seeing what people have come to. If someone wants to defend himself against too high a tax, the first thing is to inform on another and tell that So-and-so son of So-and-so is rich, that he buys his wife a jacket for 789 (tarpat) dollars, that he travels to a warm spa abroad, etc. But this ugly means is used not only to defend oneself against taxes; many use it in everyday life simply to get rid of a competitor.
If once such people were put outside the camp, avoided from afar, and no one wanted to have any dealings with them — today they are found in our own ranks; it is simply "and the ambusher sits in the chamber"; sometimes they even take the seat of honour, and people pay them respect.
Who among us has not yet been a victim of informing? Such a person is already almost a rarity. These victims are many in all strata, among merchants, artisans and among whomever you like.
We are not so naive as to believe that our appeal can have an effect in such cases, and that people who have fallen so low will repent in a single moment. Nor are we able to point to means of fighting this disease. Our task was only to record this ugly epidemic.
—o—
Another Accursed Disease.
From various sides complaints are addressed to us: why does our paper, whose task is to fight harmful phenomena in Jewish life, almost never touch — or only in rare cases — the disease with which ever more hundreds of people are infected: card-playing.
Those to whom it hurts, those who know what ruin card-playing has wrought in their homes, are perhaps right in such complaints. Certainly, who else but a Jewish newspaper should, week in, week out, have torn the mask off such people, who do not lift a finger and have made card-playing their trade, their profession.
Certainly such people — from whom, with all the devices in the world, you will not get a few groszy for a public cause or even a debt, whereas at the card table they do not begrudge tens of złoty — should have been properly reflected, so that their true face might be seen.
Certainly one should have told of facts: how people, having lost the last bit of cash at the card table, resorted to other means, pawned pledges, wrote bills of exchange and went on indulging their passion.
On the other hand, it is no news, nor is it to be hoped — just as with the disease of informing — that a newspaper note will make the card players suddenly good and pious and make them overcome in themselves this passion in which they have been sunk so long. All the more so since every card player — both the loser and the "lucky one", the winner — claims that card-playing is his private affair and nobody has the right to meddle in his private matters.
That is perhaps a "just" claim, and therefore this question must be linked to a public matter: one of the Sosnowiec societies builds its existence on the income from card-playing. This society has turned into a card club, which brings no honour to the members who belong to it.
One ought therefore to raise the question whether such an association, which keeps itself going "by virtue" of card-playing, is worth having.
It would be worth thinking about.
—o—
A Sold Soul.
There appeared in Będzin a "newspaper" whose slogan was "Strengthening of Religion" (chizuk ha-das) — a means to cheat the naive public out of a gulden. More than once we unmasked the gang and showed with facts that these are persons of
— "mockery of religion" (chozek ha-das)...
But every swindle is found out in the end. The Hasidic public saw ever more clearly the blatant lie of the "editors" and one by one stopped paying the monthly guldens...
Their biggest failure was with the section concentrated around the "Agudah" (Agudat Israel). There they became convinced that the chief "editor" is a person who is ready and willing to sell the birthright for a pot of lentils — and they shunned him like a stench...
The upshot:
One "editor", who by the way never had anything more in mind than getting a złoty, became a milk supervisor (mashgiach) and is rid of the business...
The second "editor", however, will not give up his pride; he struts around impudently, knocks at the doors of various associations and societies, which he tries to drag into his harmful net..
And when he did not manage to achieve anything with his co-religionists, he said:
— "Kapore the cap with the horse..." [idiom: to hell with it all]
broke off with the "Agudah" and went off with his plans
— to the Sosnowiec Zionists..
When someone asked the impudent fellow:
— How can it be? You, the enemy of Zion, you, who in your "bargain-sheet"[?] always compared Gruenbaum [Yitzhak Gruenbaum] with Haman the Wicked, you, who never stopped pouring buckets of filth on every Mizrachi rabbi, you, who played the role of the worst antisemite — you now want to become the "editor" of a Zionist newspaper?...
— Yes, so it is — answers the brazen one — ideas change; yesterday an Agudist, today a Zionist; yesterday I was an enemy of Zion — today an enemy of the Agudah... Let's make a "tsatung" [mock spelling of "tsaytung", newspaper]...
— A sold soul...
Tsar Nicholas's sister-in-law sues the Polish government for 10 million zł. in compensation

The widow of Grand Duke Mikhail Romanov, the sister-in-law of the murdered Tsar Nicholas, Countess Brasova, has brought a lawsuit against the Polish government over the return of her 4 estates located near Częstochowa.

The matter stands as follows: in 1895 Tsar Alexander III stayed in the vicinity of Częstochowa and at that time bought a few large estates from a German colonist.

After his death the estates passed by inheritance to his two sons. Nicholas, who received the crown, renounced the inheritance in favour of his brother Mikhail. Meanwhile the prince fell in love with the wife of one of the cuirassier officers — Mrs. Wulfert, whom he later married against the will of his family. This led to his losing his princely title and becoming a private person, while remaining the owner of the 4 estates near Częstochowa.

After the outbreak of the war he returned to Russia, where he got back the title of Grand Duke. Meanwhile events in Russia developed rapidly; the Tsar abdicated and handed power to the Grand Duke. Meanwhile the Bolshevik upheaval broke out and the Grand Duke was murdered. The surviving wife, who had not been recognised by the family and bore the name Countess Brasova, fled from Russia with her young son to Paris, and there she began to take an interest in her estates near Częstochowa.
She met with great difficulties, however, because the Treaty of Riga of 1921 recognised all the estates of the former Tsar that he had owned in Poland as belonging to the Polish state. But she was not deterred by all this, pointing out that Prince Mikhail died in 1918 and from then on she and her son became the de facto heirs, and the Treaty of Riga was made later.

Having no money to conduct the case, she applied to the District Court in Częstochowa to be exempted from court fees. The Częstochowa court rejected her request, but the Warsaw Court of Appeal granted her request and exempted her from the court fees, which amounted to over 55 thousand zł. Then Countess Brasova filed her suit in the Częstochowa District Court for the return to her of the 4 estates, which are worth up to 15 million zł. On behalf of the plaintiff, the former chamberlain of the Russian court — Barinkov — appears in the case. Her lawyer is the former Deputy Marshal, advocate Bogucki, a member of the B.B. [BBWR].

As mentioned, the de facto heir is her son Jerzy, who 2 years ago finished secondary school in Paris and entered university. Her means are limited, but the King of England, as a former friend of the Russian court, pays her a small pension.

Recently, however, an accident occurred which may have a great effect on the outcome of the case: the heir Jerzy, while walking in the street in Paris, was run over by a car and died soon after; the Countess's chances have therefore become almost nil.

In any case, this interesting lawsuit will soon be heard in the Częstochowa District Court.

[In honour of Shavuot — Torah sayings and folk anecdotes; holiday section.]
Short Torah sayings and folk anecdotes
Collected and styled by Yehuda.

a) "Who chose us from among all the nations."
The legend is well known that God first went around with the Torah to all the nations, and only when they did not want to accept it did He give it to the Jews.
If so — one asks — what is the meaning of "Who chose us from among all the nations and gave us His Torah"? After all, at that time it was first peddled around among all the nations, and only when they balked at it was it foisted on the Jews?!
But God knew His people: that they only want to imitate what other nations do. Therefore He wanted another nation to accept the Torah — then the Jews would follow suit as a matter of course, although it is not such an easy thing...
[From?] the author of "Machane Levi".

b) Idlers and moderns at the giving of the Torah.
Where does it come from that the "Germans" [Westernized, assimilated Jews] do not hold by any commandment of the Torah but only by "derekh eretz" (manners)?
— Because when the Torah was about to be given to the Jews, Moses called out: Jews, to Mount Sinai! Well, the Hasidim, the batlonim (idle scholars), did not lose a moment, lifted the skirts of their coats and set off running to the mountain; whereas they, the "Germans", the moderns, preparing themselves for such a solemn act, began doing their toilette, which took quite a while, and by the time they reached Mount Sinai the entire Written Torah and Oral Torah had already been given. They only managed to arrive at the last tractate of the Talmud — the tractate "Derekh Eretz"...
Osem Bosem.

c) The nations and the Torah.
The Gemara says that the nations will later claim: "Give it to us anew and we will do it." God will answer them: "He who toiled on the eve of the Sabbath will eat on the Sabbath." What is the meaning of this dialogue?
The gentiles would have agreed [?] to a Torah, only: "give it to us anew and we will do it" — give us a raw Torah, not yet cut out, and we will cut it to our own measure... But You give us a ready-made, sewn-up Torah, which is not at all to our measure...
God will answer them: "He who toiled on the eve of the Sabbath will eat on the Sabbath." Everything has already been prepared. On the Sabbath one does not cook fresh. If you don't like the food — your loss; you go hungry...
Yad ha-Sha'ar.

d) "Were not Your Torah my delight."
"Were not Your Torah my delight, I would have perished in my affliction."
The Torah was given to the Jews — says the Gemara (Beitzah 25) — because the Jews are impudent by nature and the yoke of the Torah humbles them.
And in "Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu" it is said further that God found no better quality for the Jews than poverty, because poverty humbles and weakens natural pride.
So: two remedies for Jewish chutzpah — either Torah or poverty. The choice is in their hands..
Rabbi Arish of Humna [?].

e) Whose Torah is his own...
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev was once in a certain town. The town's rabbi did not come to greet him. People murmured about this rabbi that he "steals" Torah from others. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak said about it:
The Gemara says that a rabbi may forgo his honour, because the Torah is his own and he may do with it as he wishes. But this rabbi's Torah is not his own... so he cannot do with it as he wishes. Therefore he may not forgo his honour, and must come to me.

f) "We will do and we will hear" and... money.
The "Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu" says:
When the Jews said "we will do and we will hear", God immediately told them: "that they take for Me an offering."
Evidently, whether a person is truly pious can only be tested by the pocket, by the coin... whether, when it comes to the guilder, one is still pious...
Osem Bosem.

g) An anecdote about the "Chofetz Chaim".
When the "Chofetz Chaim" had printed his work, he travelled around with it [to] sell it. He comes to a wealthy [?] young man. The latter mockingly refuses it.
As soon as he learns that this was the "Chofetz Chaim", he runs to apologise to him.
— I have nothing against you — answers the Chofetz Chaim — I am no greater than the Holy One, blessed be He; He too went around with His Torah, and no gentile wanted to take it into his hand...

h) Dairy food on Shavuot.

A pogromist who slaughtered hundreds of Jews comes to make confession at Mount Sinai.

[Article — Land of Israel and the East; travels, Mount Sinai and pogroms in Russia.]
Mount Sinai, the mountain on which the Jews received the Torah. From time to time one hears a greeting from this mountain — scientific expeditions, explorers and scholars travel there. And now we read in the press these very days that from Mount Sinai it will now be possible to forecast the weather several months in advance.

Travellers who have been at Mount Sinai relate in their travel accounts that at night echoes are heard from the mountain, some mysterious voices — this phenomenon repeats itself every night, and it seems as if the echoes are carried from the mountain.

The journey to Mount Sinai is undertaken very rarely, and it involves great hardships and mortal danger. Only a handful of Jewish travellers have explored Mount Sinai. Among them is also the old writer and scholar Tsvi Kasdai, who devoted his whole life to exploring and studying Jewish historical sites and to getting to know Jewish life in distant, remote places. For years Kasdai travelled about; he explored the Caucasus and described his journeys in his book "Mamlekhet Ararat". He travelled across Siberia, Japan and China and printed the travel accounts in a book, "Merkavei Tevel". He was at Mount Sinai and published all the details of the journey in his book "Le-Har Sinai".

Kasdai announced his journey in the press beforehand and corresponded with several Jews, but not a single Jew was found who would be willing to accompany him on his journey.

Interesting is the conversation Kasdai had with the rabbi of the town of Suez.

"I knocked at the door of a house built in the Arab style, in one of the dark back alleys. Out came to me a barefoot, half-naked 'Arab' in wide pantaloons.

— Are you the head of the Jewish community, the 'Hakham' of the town?

— I am the 'Hakham', the cantor and... and who are you, khawaja (my lord)?

— I am a simple Jew, an Ashkenazi, travelling to Mount Sinai.

— An Ashkenazi! To Mount Sinai! What do you need that for?

— To see the mountain in which we all believe.

— Well then, what do you want from me?

— Perhaps one can get kosher food from you, Hakham?

— Certainly, what a question, but as I see, you are surely of the sect of 'Sionists', isn't that so? So why are you particular about kosher food?

— And who told you that the 'Sionists' do not eat kosher?

— I was told that all Sionists eat carrion and treyf, and any ordinary Jew who travels to Mount Sinai is surely a 'Sionist'..."

Very interesting and moving is Kasdai's encounter on Mount Sinai with a pogromist, who revealed to Kasdai his great sins against Jews and made confession (viduy)... I shall therefore translate this episode of Kasdai's book and present it to the reader.

"We made our night camp — Kasdai relates — among the date palms. All around reigned a deep silence, disturbed only by the murmur of the springs. Suddenly a shudder ran through my body. I heard a scratching of nails and the rustle of fingers clambering up the curtains of the tent.

I wanted to cry for help. But at once I heard a weeping voice in Russian:

— 'Son of Israel, God's people.'

— What are you doing here in the middle of the night? I asked the man, and wanted to drive him away.

The Russian burst into sobs.

— Dear Jew, son of the people of Israel, allow me too to come in to you in the tent; I want to tell you a very important thing.

I raised the curtain and saw the tall giant of our group — the giant, a 'Vanya' with broad shoulders and iron arms — fall to the ground, lamenting and sobbing in a heart-rending voice:

— Forgive me, dear Jews, sons of the chosen people. Forgive and pardon me my grave sins, which I have sinned against your brothers, the children of your people and your religion — oh, forgive me.

— What are your grave sins? — I asked the weeping Russian.

— Woe to me and to my soul! — the Russian wept without stopping — I sold my soul to the devil... woe and alas is me... I have sinned, robbed and plundered and killed many Jews in my life. Oh, woe is me, forgive me, sons of Israel!

The Russian fell to the ground, kissed my feet, and wept and sobbed piteously.

— Woe to me and my filthy soul! Cursed be the day and the hour in which I let myself be talked into it by the bad companions who made pogroms on Jews. Oh, woe is me!

Weeping and sobbing he told me that he had taken part in several pogroms and carried out a whole series of murders of Jews.

— I drove nails and spikes into the heads of Jews and their wives, I murdered little children... I killed pregnant women... woe is me... There they are, all the holy souls. They point at me with their fingers...

I glanced at the Russian. His eyes were bulging, and foam was pouring from his nostrils. Suddenly he gave a shudder and remained lying like a log.

When he came to, he went on speaking:

— Calm me, find a word of comfort for me... help my filthy soul... I have already been to the greatest priests and monks and confessed my terrible sins to them; they forgave me all my transgressions, but my soul finds no rest; I doubt their forgiveness... Like a worm it gnaws and grinds at my heart constantly; I always see before my eyes the murdered Jews, I see their eyes begging for mercy that I let them live... I have done everything possible to calm my sinful soul. I was at the 'Pecherskaya Lavra', the great monastery in Kiev, and at the grave of 'Vladimir Svyatoy' [St Vladimir]. I went on foot to the grave of the holy Seraphim and was in Jerusalem at the tomb of Christ, but I still cannot calm myself; I decided to make a journey to Mount Sinai, to God's mountain!..

Oh, dear Jew, son of Israel, son of the chosen people, light of the world! Find some comfort for me! Not out of wickedness and malice did I do it, but I was talked into it.

The Russian again fell to the ground, kissed my feet and would not go away until I stretched out my hand. He kissed it with ardour, with fervour, angrily tore the cross from his neck and cried out:

...I will fall to the ground before every Jew and kiss his footsteps! Dear Jews!.. Children of the people of Israel, light of the world!.. Only you can forgive me for the blood of your brothers that I have shed.

The whole night I could not sleep — Kasdai concludes — the confession of the pogromist on the summit of Mount Sinai shook my nerves, and it seemed to me that I heard the weeping of the whole Russian people, which had come to us to confess for the countless slaughters and killings."

The other peasants also tried to calm the offended man, and at last Pyotr Alexandrovich calmed down, even began to smile, and said:
"Of course I understand that the boy was babbling from the fever... What a pity about Grisha... the poor thing is very sick..."
Later the peasants dispersed, and it seemed that everyone had already forgotten the whole incident.
But there were some among the peasants who could not forget the sick boy's words. One peasant talked it over with his neighbour [?], the second with a third, and when it was already quite dark a few peasants quietly stole up to Pyotr Alexandrovich's farm and began to lie in wait. In the darkness one bumped into another, and so a number of peasants, curious to learn the truth, gathered around the fence that enclosed Pyotr Alexandrovich's yard. They lay stretched out on the ground by the fence and kept watch.
Silent, crouching, they lay like that for a while, until — suddenly they caught sight of Pyotr Alexandrovich. He came out of his house, stopped and looked around carefully to see whether anyone was near his yard. The watchers lay holding their breath, and he could not notice them...
And then Pyotr Alexandrovich went off into a dark corner of his yard, fiddled about there quietly for a moment, and after that, to their great surprise, the peasants saw him lead out the stolen horse and vanish with it into the darkness.
At once a tumultuous commotion arose among the watchers. They began calling out to one another:
"That's the stolen horse!"
"That's him, the thief!"
"Move!"
"Let's chase him!"
"We have to catch the thief!"
The peasants leapt up, split into small groups, and the groups began running in different directions, reckoning that the thief with the horse would not be able to escape from their hands, and a wild chase began in the night...
It took a while, and at last — the thief and the horse appeared in the field. A shouting and an uproar broke out on every side:
"There he is!"
"He wants to get away!"
They set off after him, shouted after him and ordered him to stop. But the thief did not stop; he drove the horse with all his strength and tried to escape. Soon several riders galloped out of the village, racing like an arrow from a bow. It did not take long before they overtook the thief, surrounded him and stopped him. Peasants came running together from all sides. The respectable Pyotr Alexandrovich was dragged down from the horse; he trembled like a leaf and could not bring out a word for fright. They recognised the stolen horse, and — —
Heavy blows began to echo through the night... They beat him with fists, with sticks; they beat him with wild murderousness and kicked him with their feet without mercy. When he was already so badly beaten, lying bloodied and unconscious — only then did they leave him alone, left him in the field, and dispersed.
———
Next morning, right at dawn, the village peasants one after another knocked at the door of Yefim's house. One after another they went in, crossed themselves and told how Grisha had uncovered the thief, that everything he had said was true: Pyotr Alexandrovich had indeed stolen the horse. The peasants wore pious faces, and all were certain that God Himself had spoken through Grisha's mouth; that a "holy" spirit dwelt in Grisha.
How did the peasant boy actually know who the thief was? — It is possible that, lying in fever, his senses were sharpened and he sensed the falseness in Pyotr Alexandrovich's words... It is also possible that, wandering about the stables and knowing what went on in everyone's stable, he had earlier noticed stolen horses in Pyotr Alexandrovich's stable and therefore understood that this time too he was the thief... Be that as it may, the incident set the whole district boiling; the peasants saw in it a great "miracle", and all believed that a "holy" spirit dwelt in Grisha and that he was growing into a "miracle-worker"...
After the incident Grisha recovered, and he often came to feel and notice how the peasants of the village, as well as his own father and mother, looked at him with hidden enthusiasm and admiration... This made him feel exalted and chosen above all the others.
In the course of the following years he developed physically and grew into a strong, solidly built, broad-shouldered muzhik. Together with the other village lads he became a frequent visitor at the tavern; he chased after girls and led a rakish, dissolute life; very often he got thoroughly drunk and spent whole nights roaming about with merry fellows and with women.
When he was some twenty-odd years old, he met at a village dance a girl from a nearby village, who strongly attracted him and won all his attention. The girl was tall, young and beautiful; she had burning black eyes and glossy black hair; she was well developed, slender, graceful and supple; she was dressed very neatly, and she radiated health and earthy joy.
Grisha became acquainted with her; her name was Praskovya Fyodorovna Dubrovina. He fell deeply in love with her. For a while he courted her, and later he married her and settled with her in his father's house. But even after the wedding he did not give up his wild [?], dissolute life. From time to time he would go off to the tavern in the evening, drink until he was dead drunk, and then spend the whole night in the vilest orgies with the village girls, whom he overpowered with his wild lust. In his blood raged a hot lava of seething passion that could never be stilled.
At the same time he was very religious and superstitious; every Sunday he went to church, knelt before the icons, crossed himself at length, bowed and prayed.
Coming home from church he had a quite different look. He was lost in thought, a little pale, and gazed with very pious eyes. He sat in silence and did not say a word to anyone.

A reduction that is urgently needed.

To all the reductions that are being carried out day by day, a new reduction has now been added: the reduction of the salaries (pensje) of state officials. The government, which in last year's reduction spared the army officers, has now been compelled to cut 8 percent of their pay as well. The civil officials of the provinces have now lost 9 percent of their salaries on top of last year's 15 percent.
Among private employees the situation is much worse still. Here the reduction is not 25 30 [sic; presumably 25–30] percent, but sometimes 50 and more. The state official at least has the advantage that his salary — however small it may be — he does receive punctually every first of the month, in advance. Among private employees even this advantage is absent. Salaries are paid with a delay of long weeks and even months. They are paid out in instalments of 5 and 10 złoty. They are paid in bills of exchange, and these are not always redeemed, etc.
Nor can one say that the situation of the Jewish petty trader, of the artisan, is better than that of the employee. Sometimes it is even worse. Of the worker there is no need even to speak. And yet the government has to this day not found it necessary to reduce rents, so as to adjust them to the real "means" — to put it mildly — of the great majority of tenants.
A certain newspaper has rightly pointed out that the state treasury will feel the relief from the reduction only once — on the 1st of June. On the 1st of July the same treasury will already feel the consequences of the reduction — the reduced consumption and, as a result, the reduced state revenues.
It would be different, however, if together with the reduction rents and the prices of monopoly articles had also been reduced. The part of the budget that millions of people would have saved would certainly have been spent on purchasing a whole range of goods, and this would in consequence have brought a certain revival into economic life.
Now, for example, is the dacha (summer-resort) season. It is clear that many of those who still went to summer lodgings last year will not be able to afford it this year. The state railways, the buses, the peasants' carts will suffer from this, and above all, once again, the peasant. The few złoty the peasant used to earn from letting dachas, from charging a higher price for milk, for butter, for eggs, etc. (while in town a litre of milk now costs 25–35 groszy, far from town it costs no more than 10–15 groszy), served him to pay taxes, to buy himself a pair of shoes, a coat, kerosene[?], salt, etc. This year a large part of the peasants will lose the special dacha earnings, and in consequence this will once again rebound on the urban householder, shopkeeper, worker, etc.
As said, only an immediate decree of the President (on the basis of the special plenary powers) could ease the situation — that rents be lowered by several tens of percent, and that at the same time there come a proper reduction in the prices of monopoly and cartel articles.
Ruth, dear Ruth!

(A hymn of praise to the one and only original woman.)
Ruth, O dear Ruth!
I admire you, I am proud that you, daughter of Moab, became one of ours.
Among all women of old and of today, from the most modest to the most modern, you are the one and only — the truly original one.
Which of your sisters, daughters of Eve, does not consider herself more accomplished than her girlfriends? More beautiful, cleverer and better than they? And in truth they are all kneaded from one dough, cast in one mould, and their gazes are turned towards one point.
They themselves do not believe in their originality, but they make others believe in it and rule the world with this power — with the power of seeking novelties.
How much has each of them given away to get her head under a crown?
And you?
You threw the crown off your head and set out on foot across the fields of Moab — to the border of Judah.
You did not seek novelties, but old things: an old people and an old God — "Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
And in the best years of your springtime you saw death before your eyes — "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried."
How divinely these words ring, expressing so strong a love!
And to whom?
To a mother-in-law!
Ruth, dear Ruth, I admire you — you, the only one, fell in love with a mother-in-law.
• • •
And here you are already in the land of Judah.
All roads and paths are free to you, door and gate are open to you.
You could, after all, have made a brilliant career had you got yourself into some newspaper office and begun publishing your memoirs of the land of Moab, the secrets of the imperial court.
As a king's daughter you could also have made a career on the stage, or even become a film star.
But you do not do it — you are too modest to reveal secrets and too modern not to be provocative.
And you go out into the field to glean ears of corn.
And you catch sight of the chosen one of your heart, who kindled a fire in you.
But you do not demand that he quench this fire with bonbonnières and perfume; all you ask for is — a little vinegar to dip your bread in.
And when love flares up still more, you do not wait until he wraps you in velvet and silk and showers you with diamonds and pearls. On the contrary...
• • •
In you awakens the truly modern woman, who does not talk about equal rights but takes equal rights for herself; who does not wait "for him to ask for your hand and fall at your feet, but you pay love for love, and on a dark night you steal to his bed like a ray of light.
You do not even wait for him to sanctify you with chuppah and kiddushin — what is as holy as love itself?
He felt your warm body, touched your [loose?] locks, and trembled.
You, the weak one, were calm, and he, the strong man, took fright.
• • •
Ruth, dear Ruth!
Where are you? I seek you and seek you, and can find you nowhere but in... the Megillah!
Y. G. Steinsapir.

On Shavuot the Clocks Stand Still

[Literature — poetry (Hasidic ballad); Shavuot.]
(On the Baal Shem's passing).
By L. Malach [Leib Malach].

Days of the Omer count — curtains pure,
blue, transparent as through tulle;
gold melted over the rooftops,
and the nights — so blue
as if the whole little town
had been fashioned out of silver,
as if the whole region
were wrapped in sorcery.

Now in those white days,
the days drawing near to Shavuot,
the Baal Shem would walk
alone along the narrow roads,
the sandy, winding ones,
between hills and deep in the valleys,
until he would vanish,
so that no eye of his Hasidim
could reach him.

Meaning hides in the hints,
deep springs in the ideas...
Every year he had a custom:
precisely a day or two before Shavuot
he puts on a "sukmana" [peasant coat],
girds his loins with a rope
and sets off to a village
to seek out some leaseholder,
a dairyman Jew, a simple one,
and to keep Shavuot with him.

People tried to interpret the hint
and to get to the intention.
They approached him:
— "Rebbe, what lies hidden in this?"
He would answer with a smile:
"Not for nothing was the Torah
given to us precisely on Shavuot,
for the Torah is likened
to a tree of life, a tree of living,
and Shavuot is the beautiful festival
when life wells up in every blade of grass,
in every little leaf, and every sprouting
sends its praise to the Creator of the world.
Therefore, since there is such a festival,
I want to be in the field, in the open,
to sing song with the trees,
to praise God with all the grasses".

Having said this he would vanish.
And no one could find out
where, in which "yishuv" [rural homestead] somewhere,
he would keep the festival of Shavuot.
• • •
And when the Baal Shem
did come to a leaseholder,
things would already be astir in the village [?];
neither the leaseholder, nor his wife,
knew of the great guest
who would keep Shavuot with them.
For the Baal Shem was simply
a plain Jew,
dressed, too, not in town fashion
and behaving, too, like a villager;
he went along with the wife
into the cowshed to milk the cattle
and churned butter himself
and helped press cheese,
and went himself to the river
and plucked fresh greenery
and decorated the walls with it,
and when the leaseholder was tired,
and his Jewish wife — more tired still,
and they had fallen asleep
after the first dairy meal,
only then did the Baal Shem
go out into the field,
made himself clearer [?],
and the deep secrets of the Torah
were revealed to him.
• • •
And the Almighty calls to judgment,
once, though, before Shavuot,
he gathers his Hasidim
and says to them thus:
"I am already advanced in days,
one cannot be stubborn
and insist on not going".

The people fell silent,
and they understood his words
and a sorrow began
to cloud over their faces.

And the Baal Shem speaks on:
"It does not trouble me that I am called,
but that there are still so many
wicked people in the world
who must be set right.
Apparently they do not want that in heaven.
Pe-khe-khe, well, I am being called!
I really ought never
to leave my home.
For here I am the mighty one
and would not let the Angel of Death
into my domain, into my precinct.
But since it is a custom
to go for Shavuot to a yishuv,
therefore you shall diligently
say the Tikkun, say Psalms,
until I return".

Hearing this, the people
fell silent ever deeper.
And the Baal Shem speaks on:

"[—?] this will happen,
who can know the moment,
only I know that when the clocks
in the town stop,
then you shall know, Jews,
that"...
He did not finish [?] his word..
Before anyone could look around
the Baal Shem had vanished.
• • •
Eve of Shavuot. The day as always,
as if millions of festive candles
had poured themselves out;
all the alleys, all the houses
are decorated with greenery,
all the rooms, all the windows
are pasted with "roses" [paper cut-outs].

Suddenly — a guest in the town,
a "węgierek" [itinerant 'Hungarian' tinker] has come,
with an odd little hat,
with a golden green feather,
and he stands in the marketplace
and clangs his tin plates
and calls at the top of his voice:
"Clocks, clocks to repair"!

The Jews are startled: oh, perhaps,
perhaps one really, really must
have the clocks looked over,
so that they don't, God forbid,
stop in the middle!
so that there be no mishaps [?]...

And the "węgierek"
with the green little hat,
with the golden green feather,
was virtually welcomed [?] to the town.
Like a deer he leapt,
over houses, over rooms,
"fiddled" with the clocks
and turned, turned the hands,
and did not even take any money...

Before one knew what or when,
he was already at the neighbour's
and from one neighbour to the next
and before night had fallen,
the little "węgierek" was already
no longer in the town.
• • •
It is the first day of Shavuot.
The people are in the beit midrash.
Spring streams in through the panes.
Now — they are already opening the Ark,
taking out the Torah scroll.
Suddenly an echo trembles.
From the old "chain clock"
the "weight" has fallen down.
And the unrest began
slowly, slowly to sway,
as if the clock's strength
had slowly run out.

Then came the tidings:
"All the clocks in the town
have suddenly stopped".

A Hasid cried out:
"The Baal Shem Tov has departed"!
• • •
In the Baal Shem Tov's town
young and old still tell today:
"the węgierek" with the feather
was the Angel of Death.
Had they not let him in,
not let him touch the clocks,
(which in truth, it seems, he actually broke),
the Baal Shem Tov would surely
have lived many, many more years;
there were still so many
sinful souls to set right,
but from Above
they did not want to allow it...
• • •
In the Baal Shem Tov's town there remained
a custom that on Shavuot
all the clocks are stopped,
in memory of the Baal Shem's passing.

The Modern “Ten Commandments”

[Humour — Shavuot; the economic crisis.] 1) “Anokhi” [I am]: there is no “I” any more today.
2) “Thou shalt have no [other gods]”: if you don’t have the “me’a” [a hundred — money], your “de’a” [opinion] is worth nothing.
3) “Thou shalt not take [the name in vain]”: when you are badly off and dying for a grosz, you need not swear — they will believe you even without an oath.
4) “Remember the Sabbath day”: when Sunday comes you should remember that it is already Sabbath again, and look for how to get a free loan (gemiles-khesed) for your wife again for Sabbath.
5) “Honour thy father and thy mother”: you should pay respect to your parents, especially to your wife’s parents, if they receive American dollars.
6) “Thou shalt not murder”: do not kill off your brother when you climb up onto a kehilla bench [seat].
7) “Thou shalt not steal”: a warning to women that they should not steal years off [their age].
9) “Thou shalt not bear [false witness] against thy neighbour”: do not tell the “urząd” [the (tax) office] that your friend is doing well.
10) “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife”: you should not lust after your friend’s wife, because he envies you.
Lejb Sztabinski.
Just as Before the Giving of the Torah

[Humour — Shavuot; the economic crisis.] Our situation now looks as it did before the giving of the Torah:
At the giving of the Torah it is said: “And there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud.” Today too it is the same: every day one hears the crashes of another firm, and voices [shouting] in all the institutions. Today too a heavy cloud is drawn over us, people no longer recognise one another and one doesn’t see a grosz before one’s eyes — “and all the people trembled” — and the whole Jewish people lives in mortal terror. Only, at the giving of the Torah the Jews first said “na’ase” — we will hear [as printed]; today the Jews would also first say “na’ase” — we want to do (to work) — but there is no “nishma” — they don’t want [?] to hear us.
Lejb Sztabinski.
The Scroll of Ruth with a New Commentary

[Humour — Shavuot; the Book of Ruth.] “And it came to pass in the days when the judges judged” — this means that our kehillas are worth a stick [deserve a beating].
“There was a famine in the land.” — Woe and alas, when one looks forward to a rise in prices, perhaps then times will get better.
“And a certain man went” — so it always is: when one has no livelihood, the husband is a — “yelekh” [one who goes off].
“For I am too old to have a husband” — a wonder; after all she could have used paint and make-up.
“It grieveth me much” — apparently there was already a tax office then.
“Thy people shall be my people” — without clauses and without conditions.
“Let me now go to the field… in whose sight I shall find grace” — it is true that women cannot keep a secret.
“And dip thy morsel in the vinegar” — it seems Boaz was a miser; otherwise he would have treated her to a box of chocolates.
“And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry” — he probably had not yet received the “zaliczka” [tax advance demand] for the year 1932.
“And he took ten men” — this is really hard to understand! How can it be? How does one take ten people and not hold elections?!

[Humour — taxes and distraint; the economic crisis.] The bailiffs [tax executors], so it is said, will strip us naked. You have surely already read in the newspapers the newest regulations on how to collect taxes.
The “government” has noticed that the public keeps hidden treasures in the corners of the body, where no outsider can get at them...
So the bailiffs will strip every taxpayer stark naked and conduct a “search for leaven” on him. But what does one do with women? No man, such as the bailiff with the green hat, will have the cheek to order a woman to undress. So now they will indeed engage female bailiffs.
Couples will go round the houses: a bailiff with a female bailiff... The bailiff will take the men into one room and the female bailiff — the women into a second room.
Can you imagine what it will look like?
The bailiff stands and casts an eye on how the taxpayer undresses.
— What, 2 pairs of underpants? One for the “Skarb” [the Treasury]. Double braces with buttons — the spare for the “Skarb”. 2 shirts — the undershirt for the “Skarb”.
The female bailiff will not keep quiet either; she will order the women’s rags thrown into the stove.
Bras, slips, sweaters, luxurious Parisian lace — all this is superfluous and belongs to the “Skarb”.
Only after that will the distraint couple get down to the real work, as the minister orders, and “inspect” the “hidden places”; for that, of course, they will need telescopes.
But the technique of collecting taxes will not stand still; soon it will progress. The distraints will be carried out with X-rays.
Since the taxpayer, male and female, will stand naked, the bailiff or the female bailiff will order the “petent” [applicant] first to clean out his stomach with castor oil, drink a glass of “vier-milk” [? contrast liquid] and then have the X-ray taken, to see whether someone is hiding gold rings in his appendix.
Yosef.
—o—
Pogotowie [Emergency Service].
[Sport — football; humour.] The sub-district [Podokręg] of the football clubs in Zagłębie has decided to set up a “pogotowie” to give medical aid at the matches...
—o—
A Lecture.
[Humour — merchants.] On the first day of Shavuot a lecture will take place at the “Merchants’ Association” on the subject: “How does one come by 50 zł to pay a deposit on a dacha [summer cottage]?”
The speaker will discuss the great importance that a “fifty in cash” has for the merchant class in the year 1932.
All branches are called upon to come.
—o—
Registrations.
[Humour — Będzin and Sosnowiec.] From the 15th of this month the following will be registered: 1) those whose clothes were torn on the barbed wires at the Będzin Old Market, and 2) the victims of thefts in the secretariat of the Sosnowiec Artisans’ Association. Vanished berets, overcoats, pencils, etc. will be registered.
—o—
An Internal Loan.
[Humour — Sosnowiec.] In connection with the present crisis, the members of the “Club” at the “Merchants’ Association” on Kowalska Street in Sosnowiec have decided that, so as not to come to any “bitul Torah” [interruption of study — i.e. of the game], an internal loan should be arranged among the “musicians” [apparently the card players].
For this purpose a commission of experts has been elected, to work out regulations for the internal loan...
—o—
The True Reason
[Humour — Shavuot.] Three days before the giving of the Torah the Jewish people were told to separate from their wives and stay apart. Why? “Rabbeinu Bahya” says about this: had the wives known that their husbands were going to receive a Torah in which it would be said “and he shall rule over thee” — that the husband should rule over the wife — they would never have allowed it; therefore the men were ordered to separate from the wives.
Lejb Sztabinski.
The Voters of the Jewish Kehillas in Zagłębie Are Requested to Come to the Mourning Memorials

Today, on the eve of Shavuot, on the first anniversary of the kehilla elections in Zagłębie, solemn mourning memorial services will be held in the gmina [community] offices, at which eulogies will be delivered for the tragic victims who, God save us, perished on the battlefield in the holy struggle for the sake of religion and Jewish autonomy. The souls of those who, in the course of this year, suffered palpitations of joy and — disappointment, will also be remembered...
The people's choir at the "MOE" [?] will sing several chapters of Psalms, such as: "Happy is the man that hath not walked"... "Hear this, all ye peoples"... "They that trust in the knepl [the button]"... "He is like the beasts that perish"...
Then a specially composed "El Male" will be recited: "Grant perfect rest under the wings of the gmina, in the heights of R' Leybele Ladver, and the soul of our teacher R'.. O"V O"H."
All voters are requested to come to the sad memorials en masse. Everyone must bring along last year's election appeals of his list and group; thus, for instance, the small-trader voters should bring their anti-Agudah appeal entitled [?] "May the mouth of them that speak lies be stopped"...
Each of the "piątka" [the "five"] people shall demonstratively hold the P"Ts in his left hand (the initials of Paragraph Twenty).
May the Blessed Name comfort us all; from today on may there be only joys among Jews, and may a redeemer come to the gmina speedily in our days, Amen.
At Mount Sinai.

Posters and the newspapers announced that tomorrow morning, at 9 o'clock, the great ceremony of the Receiving of the Torah would take place.
Meeting point: at Mount Sinai.
Before that, however, at 8 o'clock, a festive academy will take place on the large square below the mountain, at which Ben Amram will deliver the keynote address.
The German Jews were in no hurry.
A large part of them first went off to the coffee house, where they debated the German political situation... We know — they said — a Jewish 9 o'clock will probably start at ten or at eleven.
The Hasidim all ran off to the mikveh.
The Zionists declared that there was still no quorum, so they went into a side room and waited there for their candidate..
The "Mizrachi" immersed itself — part at home and part in the mikveh.
The "Bund" resolved: out of consideration for Jewish culture, to send its representatives to Mount Sinai.
The Communists resolved to unfurl the red flag and come to disrupt the religious ceremonies.
—
At exactly eight o'clock Moses took his place at the foot of the mountain and began to speak in the Hebrew language:
"My sisters and brothers"!
"Down with the capitalist order", shouted the Communists.
"Down with the monarchy", shouted the Socialists.
"Yiddish"! shouted the Bundists.
But shouts and curses were heard from all sides [?].
Between the "Agudah" and "Achdus Yisroel" a bitter quarrel broke out on the way to the Receiving of the Torah.
The "Agudah" shouted:
"Forget the whole Torah, we need a rabbi"...
—
At exactly 9 o'clock the "thunders and lightnings" began.
The women had all powdered themselves and sat down in the front rows at the foot of the mountain.
A Beys-Yaakov girl brought the news:
"They will give us only three commandments; as soon as we accept the three commandments — we may do whatever we like. What does it matter, three commandments?...
The conversation of the seated women was about the new magazines and the new fashion.
—
Moses went up the mountain and announced.
"Anokhi [I am]", a mighty call was heard.
The crowd stood petrified.
The Communists shouted:
"Down with religion"! and demonstratively left the mountain.
When Ben Amram began the "Thou shalt nots", the "Torah-loyal" began to edge away. "Thou shalt not steal", "Thou shalt not covet", "Thou shalt not take the name in vain" — those they no longer heard.
When Ben Amram said in a loud voice "Thou shalt not commit adultery", the ladylike women stopped up their ears.
The Germans scratched their heads...
By the time Ben Amram had reached the second part of the "Ten Commandments", there was not a soul left at the mountain.

Upper Silesian Economic Sketches

By Dr. Avraham Shayer [?], Katowice.
(Continued from the previous issue)
The customs office is not among the merchant's good friends, despite the fact that the office de facto lives only off the merchant and draws its main revenues from him. Here the merchant is treated like a professional smuggler, and no opportunity is missed to cause the merchant trouble by charging him a higher duty, although for a number of years he used to pay for the same goods at a lower rate [stawka]. On such occasions the customs officials give the merchant to understand that he can lodge a complaint and that, if he proves to be in the right, he will get his money back. In fact one can complain, but only after a few months does one manage [?] to get the money back; this, however, does not in the least prevent the very same story from repeating itself a few days after the victory, because that is how the customs official likes it. At this point the Silesian border guard must also be mentioned, which occupies a very prominent place in harassing the merchant class. On the agenda are raids on the most solid firms by entire 'patrols' of the border guard with the assistance of the police, who take no account of the time, the customers or the season [?]; they close the business for a few hours in order to carry out an inspection, allowing no one to move or to go to the telephone, and in general they treat the merchant like a criminal whose guilt has already been proven.
It must be noted, though, that everything is done with silk [?] gloves and in a very polite tone, but this does not redress the wrong committed by such treatment and by the humiliation of the whole merchant estate. One can understand that a border guard near the border is a necessity, but on the other hand the gentlemen must not forget that the merchant does society no harm; on the contrary, he brings society as much benefit as a senior state official.
—
In this time of severe crisis, which brings with it the shrinking of creditworthiness and the demoralization of merchants, the wholesale merchant suffers especially from [the lack of] statutory legal protection. If someone today does not want to pay, no court will help; neither the public prosecutor nor any power can compel him to pay a protested bill of exchange. Such a bill, which ought to obtain a judgment as quickly as possible so that the debt can be collected, is subject to the same procedure as open debts. Moreover, the acceptor is still allowed to lodge an objection, though all he wants by it is to drag the matter out.
In former Congress Poland, where a 'wyrok' [judgment] with an enforcement clause [klauzula] is easy to obtain, the execution in turn cannot be carried out, because it already depends on the court bailiff [komornik], the 'Mister Judge' or 'Commissioner', whose self-importance recalls a 'Freiter' [i.e. Gefreiter, lance corporal] in the former Austrian army — as everyone remembers, nobody could torment an ordinary soldier the way Mister 'Gefreiter' (the one-stripe man) could.
Entirely without protection [?] is the merchant in the formerly Austrian part of the country. There the creditor no longer has any say at all, and he depends wholly on the majority, which the clever debtor prepares for himself from real or fictitious creditors even before filing with the court, and with which (majority) he pushes through the 'ugoda' [composition with creditors] over two years, quite often at 25 percent of the whole debt — not to mention that in practice one will never [see] a single grosz from such a debtor, and one is moreover forced into unnecessary expenses on lawyer's fees etc., in the very mistaken belief that perhaps something can be done. All this brings the most respected and most honest firms to ruin, and if no radical procedural changes take place, the granting of credit will vanish entirely, and more than one respected firm that employs many people will be turned into a heap of ruins.
This is a matter which the merchants' associations must take up seriously, intervening with the proper authority; and if the procedural changes cannot come about so quickly, then at least it should not be possible to make 'ugodas' and 'nadzors' [?] [court supervision] so easily?
Unfortunately, one cannot write of any privileges with regard to wholesale trade. Let us at least have the confidence that better times will come, that the crisis will weaken, and that with better earnings it will be possible to bear all the chicanery and obstructions that are met at every step by the hard-working wholesale merchant class.
In the next article: on peddling [?] and installment trade in Silesia.
(Sh.)
Smoking Should Be Allowed on the Tram

The newspapers report constantly: here a burglary was committed, there someone had a briefcase stolen, and elsewhere someone had a pocket with a wallet cut open. Usually the policeman comes and, sooner or later, lays his hand on the criminal's shoulder, but more rarely, much more rarely, does the victim get the stolen articles back. Thefts are usually carried out where people gather in larger crowds; there, where there is a crush — something the 'knights of industry' [printed 'hitters'] like very much. Whether it is the cloakroom of the theatres and concert halls, and very often in the trams. Here the criminal exploits one more circumstance — the haste of the passengers, who leave the tram car at once, and then every hope of catching the thief vanishes. For the most part the pocket-heroes 'work' on the platforms of the trams. There is usually a greater crush there than inside the car, because there, on the platform, many men stand in order to smoke a cigarette [papieros]. Men also usually carry a larger sum of money on them than women. Besides that, the jostling of the passengers creates an opportunity for the professional pickpockets.
The result is that the victim only realizes it once his pockets have been emptied, when the pickpocket has also already 'fled' [vayivrach]. If a report is drawn up afterwards, it ends, as is the custom, with the stereotyped remark: the thief is unknown.
There can be no question of everyone stopping smoking cigarettes one fine bright morning. The above-mentioned situation will therefore last as long as smoking is forbidden on the trams. There can surely be no doubt that the tram management is obliged to safeguard the safety of the passengers as well. Could the problem not be solved by introducing a small innovation in the form of special cars for smokers?
It is surely clear that a person sitting comfortably in a tram cannot be robbed, whereas a passenger squeezed into a crush among strangers is at the mercy of his neighbours.
That is precisely why introducing cars for smokers is an urgent matter, which the management can settle without undue difficulties and costs. If it is a question of protecting the non-smoking minority, the freedom to smoke can be restricted to the trailer cars. In this way 'the wolf will be sated and the lamb whole'. Let the tram management think it over.

What's Heard in Zagłębie? / Będzin: A Zionist elected president of the kehilla council for the second time. / Fees at the slaughterhouse and the magistrate reduced. / Prayers disrupted in the Aleksander shtibl over the shochtim question. / Presidium elections of the board to take place on Monday. / The 'Agudah' asks the starosta to confirm the board's presidium elections. / A child under the tram. / A Christian maidservant — a thief. / Cantor Sherman to lead Shavuot prayers in the town synagogue. / Number of children at the summer colony — smaller. / A synagogue committee appointed. / Propaganda for the campaign on behalf of the L.O.P.P. / Meeting of Revisionists. / Already quarrelling over the distribution of certificates.

[Zagłębie — Będzin; kehilla and local news.]
After 10 months had passed, the starosta announced that the presidium elections of the council and of the board were void and that the elections were to take place a second time.
On the basis of this order, the elections of the presidium of the kehilla council took place on Monday evening in the gmina [municipal] hall.
The meeting hall is packed with "interested parties", the mood is tense, but thanks to the "conduct" of the president the public grows calmer...
The meeting opens with councillors of all tendencies except the "Agudah", which is holding a consultation in another room.
The president of the board opens the meeting. After the formal explanations of the secretary, Mr. Fröhlich, they proceed to the voting procedure.
At this point councillor Mr. Ryński comes in from the consultation and hands the secretary a written declaration that, since the elections are not lawful, the Agudah group is taking no part in the elections. Mr. Ryński also hands the chairman a "secret document".
The elections produced the following result:
For the candidacy of Mr. Wygodzki as president of the council 8 votes were cast, 1 vote for Silberfreund, 1 blank ballot, and councillor Feiner did not take part in the vote.
The same result was obtained in the election of the vice-president of the council. With 9 votes Mr. Icchak Meir Kurland was elected.
After the elections the newly elected president expressed his thanks for the confidence shown in him. "I believe," says Mr. Wygodzki, "that the 'Agudah' will again submit a denunciation against me; nevertheless I have the full satisfaction of having been elected by the broad Jewish masses."
—o—
Fees at the slaughterhouse and the magistrate reduced.
An appeal up to 50 zł. is free of fees.
On Monday evening a meeting of the council of commissioners took place. At the meeting the fees under a number of municipal statutes were reduced. Among others, the slaughterhouse fee was reduced. Until now the fee for a head of cattle cost 8 zł.; the fee has been reduced to 6 zł. The fee for appeals, certificates, petitions and the like has also been reduced. An appeal up to 50 zł., for which 2 zł. used to be paid, is entirely free of fees.
The fee of the "Urząd Rozjemczy" [arbitration office] has also been reduced by 50 per cent.
—o—
Prayers disrupted in the Aleksander shtibl over the shochtim question.
As we already reported in the previous issue of our paper, negotiations are being conducted with the butchers to allow 2 new shochtim into the slaughterhouse: Kusserwasser's [?] son-in-law and the unmarried son of R' Avraham the shochet. They have only just come out "of the eggshell", and only with the help of... they want to obtain the licence as shochtim in place of R' Yisrael Moshe the shochet, who is to retire.
In connection with this, last Sabbath after the Torah reading the widow of R' Mordechai the shochet and her daughter-in-law came into the Aleksander shtibl, where they shouted: why do the Aleksander Hasidim tolerate such an injustice and not take up the cause that the son of R' Mordechai the shochet, of blessed memory, who has the proper qualifications, be accepted as a Będzin shochet?
Because of this the prayers were disrupted, and almost the whole congregation went to the rabbi with the said demand.
The rabbi, having heard the delegation's arguments, declared that he would give an answer the next day, i.e. Sunday.
The Aleksander Hasidim did not wait until Sunday but turned to the rabbi right after the Sabbath ended; he declared to them that the decision could not be changed, i.e. that the demand that R' Mordechai the shochet's son be accepted as shochet cannot be fulfilled.
—o—
Presidium elections of the board to take place on Monday.
On the basis of the starosta's order that the elections of the presidium of the board are to take place a second time, a meeting of the board has been called for next Monday at 8 in the evening.
—o—
The "Agudah" asks the starosta to confirm the presidium elections of the board.
At Monday's meeting of the kehilla council Mr. Ryński handed the president of the board a document which he is to pass on to the starosta. In the document Mr. Ryński and his colleagues express the wish that the elections of the board's presidium should not take place a second time, because — it is stressed in the document — the presidium elections were held lawfully and those elected, Messrs. Skoczylas [?] and Banhart [?], should be confirmed.
—o—
A child under the tram.
On Saturday afternoon, on Małobądzka [?] Street, 7-year-old Regina Gutman fell [?] under the tram. By a miracle the child was saved from death; she received only a light wound.
—o—
A Christian maidservant — a thief.
The maidservant of the Mandelbaum family on Sączewska [?] Street stole various goods from a cellar.
—o—
Cantor Sherman to lead Shavuot prayers in the town synagogue.
On Monday evening the former Będzin cantor, Mr. Avraham Yitzhak Sherman, arrived from New York to visit his family.
As we are informed, the distinguished guest will lead the prayers in the town synagogue this Shavuot.
—o—
Number of children at the summer colony — smaller.
As we are informed, the commissioner has decided, for reasons of economy, also to reduce the number of children sent by the magistrate to the summer colonies in Sławków.
Such a thing must not be allowed; one must not rob them of the only bit of freedom they enjoy during the month they spend in the fresh air.
—o—
A synagogue committee appointed.
The kehilla board has appointed a synagogue committee of the following worshippers: Mendel Rapszyc, Szlama Saks, Jakob Goldring [?], Dawid Saks, Lejbil Lanrner [?], Michał Gutman and Jechiel Frachcwajg.
As deputies: Moshe Mordechai Schweitzer, Lejb Szojmer, Eliyahu Mager and Yisrael Laudan.
—o—
Propaganda for the campaign on behalf of the L.O.P.P.
On Sunday a propaganda campaign on behalf of the L.O.P.P. [Air and Anti-Gas Defence League] began in Zagłębie.
On the Sabbath the rabbi delivered a sermon in the synagogue in which he called for support of the campaign.
On Sunday a festive march through the town took place, with the participation of social organizations, firemen and schoolchildren. The procession, headed by several orchestras, assembled at the sports ground of the "Sokół", where the public and the children were "treated" to tear-gas bombs, from which the children did indeed cry...
—o—
Meeting of Revisionists.
On the first day of Shavuot in the afternoon a members' meeting of the Revisionist organization will take place in the premises of "Mizrachi". A number of current matters will be discussed.
—o—
Already quarrelling over the distribution of certificates.
A meeting took place in the premises of "Ahavat Chesed", at which the latest distribution of certificates by the Palestine Office in Warsaw was discussed, in which the Mizrachi people and the Revisionists were badly wronged.
It was resolved to turn to the Office demanding that the distribution be changed; if not, the organizations will draw the appropriate conclusions.
