[Sosnowiec and Zagłębie — local news.]
On Sunday the 5th of this month a meeting took place at the premises of the Metal Workers' Union, with the participation of delegates from the steelworks „Milowice“, „Katarzyna“, „Staszic“, „Raków“ (Częstochowa), „Światowid“ (Myszków) and others.
The meeting dealt with the situation that has arisen in the metal industry, where wages are not being paid.
After the discussion the following resolutions were adopted:
1) The irregular payment of wages, which has already lasted about 2 years, has brought the workers to the lowest level.
2) The assembled turn to the managements of the steelworks [demanding] that, in the wages, they settle the arrears by the 15th of this month. If not, the workers' delegates disclaim responsibility for the calm in the factories.
—o—
His Wife Ran Away from Him, So He Then Carried Her Home in His Arms..
In the household of the couple G. in Wojkowice dramatic scenes used to occur often, which led to Mrs G. running away from her husband and going to live with a neighbour. After a few days the „straw widower“ went to the neighbour with the aim of persuading his wife to come back home. But when the husband approached the house, the neighbour's door was locked and he was not let in. The husband did not want[?] to leave the house and sat down to wait until the door would be opened to him.
Because of this the wife let herself down through the window with the help of a rope and ran away. When the husband found out about it, he ran after her and indeed caught her, but he did not take revenge on her; he only carried her home in his arms in a „courteous“ manner...
—o—
Lecture Before the Minister of Commerce on Credits for Merchants
A plenary session of the commission devoted to granting cheap credits to merchants took place under the chairmanship of the Minister of Commerce.
At the session Mr Józef Safer [Yosef Sofer?], councillor of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, delivered a lecture in which he showed with factual arguments that the only task of the government at the present moment, in order to alleviate the severe economic crisis, is simply to give credits to merchants.
The arguments were accepted by those assembled, and it was decided to apply on this question to the Ministry of Finance.
—o—
Storm over Zagłębie
On Monday a storm with a downpour, accompanied by strong thunder and lightning, passed over Zagłębie.
Because of the heavy rain some low-lying streets were flooded.
—o—
Will Sosnowiec Get Cheaper Electricity?
Several weeks ago, thanks to the proposal of Councillor Aliner, a commission was elected to work towards making the price of electricity cheaper.
The commission drew up a proper memorandum, which was submitted to the syndicate of the electricity companies.
As we are informed, negotiations are taking place about it, and things are heading towards the price being reduced by 50 groszy per kilowatt.
—o—
A Degenerate Sentenced to a Year in Prison
Before the local district court stood a chauffeur from Zagórze who had raped an 8-year-old girl. The degenerate was sentenced to one year in prison and loss of rights.
—o—
A Jewish House-Owners' Association Is Being Founded
In the previous issue of our paper we drew attention, in a short note, to the necessity of founding an association of Jewish house-owners.
The note aroused due interest, and in the coming days a larger consultation of house-owners will take place about realising the matter.
—o—
He Attacked His Wife with a Knife and Shot at His Brother-in-Law with a Revolver
In the local district court the trial took place of a certain Najakowski from Zawiercie, who during a family quarrel wounded his wife with a knife, and when his wife's brother put up resistance, shot at him with a revolver.
The court sentenced Nowakowski to two years in prison and loss of rights.
—o—
Copyright
Mr K. Zajdman of Będzin brought a lawsuit against the local merchant Mr Dafner, who had copied various printed matter compiled by Zajdman.
In the first instance Mr Zajdman's complaint was dismissed.
This week the case was heard at the Warsaw Court of Appeal, which upheld Mr Zajdman's complaint and sentenced Dafner to pay 200 zł. or one month's arrest.

[Będzin — ritual slaughter; open letter.] The fact has not yet been forgotten that "certain bigwigs" wanted to smuggle in "one of their own" as the 5th shochet (ritual slaughterer) in Będzin, thereby burdening the Jewish population with a larger budget. But thanks to our energetic protests the matter did not come about.
But as we hear from behind the curtain, the rabbinate, under pressure from the same bigwigs, has again decided to push through "their own man" as shochet at any price, without taking into account the catastrophic state of our kehilla's finances; and therefore we turn to you, Jews of Będzin! Can this happen at such a time, when the kehilla is sinking in debts over its head and bailiffs (komornicy) and distrainers (egzekutorzy) are frequent guests there?
And if Będzin will have to have a new shochet, then surely the one to be considered is the Torah scholar and God-fearing man well known in Będzin, R' Yechezkel Weitzman [Wajcman], whose father R' Mordechai, shochet and inspector (sh"uv), of blessed memory, his grandfather R' Ishe [Yeshaya] Meir of blessed memory, and his uncle R' Dovid of blessed memory, shochet and inspector, were all local shochtim all their lives, and whom the town knew as honest Jews and treated with due reverence.
Concerning this, last Sabbath a congregation of Jews turned to the local rabbi, may he live long, with the question whether he wishes to rob R' Yechezkel Weitzman of the right of inheritance to the local slaughtering post, which is his by Torah law, who holds certification (kabbalah) from the greatest rabbis in Poland, among them from the Będzin rabbinate, and who sits without a livelihood, God spare us — which is simply a matter of life and death — and is burdened with a large family; the rabbi, may he live long, answered that only "their own man" must be shochet, because thus... he decrees.
Jews of Będzin! If the matter of taking on a new shochet in Będzin should ever come up at all, we must always keep before our eyes the crying injustice that the local kehilla has been committing for years towards the widow of R' Mordechai, shochet and inspector, of blessed memory, the mother of R' Yechezkel Weitzman, who as the widow of a lifelong shochet receives a pension of all of 10 zł. a week... an injustice without equal, for even the wife of a mine worker gets more than this ridiculous sum for her upkeep. Therefore, if the question of a new shochet in Będzin should ever become topical, it must be none other than R' Yechezkel Weitzman, who is worthy of that mantle. In this way we will also give satisfaction to his mother, the widow of R' Mordechai, shochet and inspector, of blessed memory, for the great injustice we have been committing towards her for many years.
A group of Będzin householders
(A series of signatures follows)

Annual general meeting of the Revisionists.
[Sosnowiec — Revisionists.] On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Sosnowiec Revisionists took place. The chairman Mr. Klarman gave the opening speech, in which he surveyed the development of the Revisionist organisation and its prospects for the future. Mr. Dov Jasny was elected chairman of the meeting; as assessors: Friedman, Feldman, Kożuch; secretary — Menashe Ingster.
The secretary Mr. Yosef Rapner delivers a report on the activity, from which it emerges that the Revisionists have lately conducted a ramified Zionist activity in all fields. Mr. Grinfeld delivers a report on the work of the Keren Tel-Hai; on the participation of the Revisionists in the Keren Kayemet — Mr. Triger; and on the treasury — Mr. Feldbojm. After the discussion, in which Messrs. Migus[?], Przerowicz, Pramer, Wandersman[?], Lazenger, Efraim Jasny Feldman, Triger, Dov Jasny and others took part,
Mr. Klarman answers the discussants, and confidence is expressed in the old board.
The new board consists of the following persons: Klarman, Rapner, Grinfeld, Feldbojm, Rajzman, Friedman, Rozencwajg, Feldman and Menashe Jungster. As deputies: Anklewicz, Szarf and Gutowski. Audit committee: Dov Jasny, Żepkowicz and Szarf. In the party court: Gutowski, Szarf and Jasny.
The meeting also adopted a sharp resolution against the Zionist Executive, which does not submit to the Congress decision to change the composition of the Palestine Office, and — against the Palestine Office for its scandalous distribution of certificates.

In connection with this the parents have begun to conduct a fund-raising campaign.

An end to the lawlessness with bills of exchange! The procedure of clauses and bailiffs is to be abolished
[Economy — bills of exchange; legislation.] The bill of exchange has lost its value because the possibility of collecting the sum is a small one. If someone does not want to pay the bill — he will not pay it. That is a fact, and therefore the acceptance of bills has weakened.
Concerning this matter there is a plan to issue a law that is to strengthen the position of those who lend. The long process of enforcement clauses, of bailiffs and of auctions will be eliminated.
A protest will be stamped and noted in the court office, and that will suffice to carry out execution against the debtor. The auction will not be necessary. An appraisal of the goods will suffice for the lender to take goods from the debtor for himself, as is the case in America and in other countries.
Conferences on this matter will yet take place in the Chamber of Commerce.

Accusations against Rabbi Englard and the gabbaim of the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah

[Sosnowiec — community and institutions; Dąbrowa — community; followed by short notices.] Accusations against Rabbi Englard and the gabbaim of the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah.
This week Jewish Sosnowiec got a fresh sensation concerning an affair in which Rabbi Englard and members of the board of the local Talmud Torah have been drawn.
The sensation consists of the following details. Several weeks ago the wedding of Rabbi Englard's daughter took place in Sosnowiec. A large number of guests from a number of towns were invited to the wedding. So that the guests could enjoy railway discounts, a petition was sent in the name of the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah to the railway authority[?], declaring that since a convention of all the Talmud Torahs in Poland was taking place in Sosnowiec, the delegates should be granted the right to a 50 per cent railway discount.
Rabbi Englard obtained the permission, and besides the wedding guests other persons travelling in various directions also made use of the discount.
Rabbi Englard and his son Abraham were summoned to the investigation of this matter. The latter had been occupied with issuing the slips on the strength of which the railway cashier issued discount tickets.
Among others, the gabbai and treasurer of the Talmud Torah, Mr. Szczekacz, and the director of the Talmud Torah, Mr. Pariuer[?], were also questioned.
At the investigation Mr. Szczekacz declared that for the slips issued a total of 140 złoty was collected from the guests for the benefit of the Talmud Torah.
The investigating authority incidentally took an interest in the finances of the Talmud Torah, and it turned out that for years the institution has had no exact account of all its income; for this reason, as we are told, the Talmud Torah's books have been sealed.
The sensation has naturally stirred the whole town, and the further course of the investigation is awaited with great suspense.

The President of the Kehilla Board, Mr. Rubinlicht, on His Work

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
Esteemed colleagues!
Although today it is no honour to be president of a Jewish community (gmina) in general, and of the Będzin community in particular, I nevertheless thank all of you, colleagues, for the trust you have placed in me in electing me president of our kehilla.
I shall endeavour to be active in all the questions that will be dealt with by the board.
I shall endeavour to raise the prestige of the Będzin Jewish kehilla, which until now has sunk so low.
I would like to see the Będzin Jewish kehilla in the future not, as until now, as a "house of the dead", where one comes to arrange a burial plot when misfortune strikes a Jewish family, but as a flourishing institution whose task is to safeguard not only the religious but also the national and cultural interests of the entire Jewish population of Będzin. I hope that you, colleagues of the board, will help me carry out the great and difficult task that the Jewish population of Będzin has entrusted to us, and only this gives me the courage to accept this difficult and thankless office.

Make Use of Railway Discounts

[Tourism — railway discounts; Zagłębie.] The railway discounts, which enable the broad strata to enjoy cheaper train tickets, are of great importance for the development of tourism. It is a fact, however, that not only the broad public but even a large part of the tourist circles do not give themselves an exact account of which discounts one can enjoy, and therefore the discounts do not play the proper role they ought to play.
Besides the so-called group discounts, which can be used by associations travelling in groups of at least 10 persons, we are most interested in the so-called individual discounts, which any person can use individually, regardless of the season.
Individual discounts are available to members of the "Union of Polish Tourist Societies", which groups around itself all the tourist associations in Poland; among them is the Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land in Poland (ŻTK), Zagłębie branch. The "Union of Polish Tourist Societies" issues railway identity cards recognised by the railway authorities, which entitle the holder for a whole year to a discount of 25 per cent off the normal tariff price for journeys for tourist purposes in 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-class carriages of passenger and express trains. On showing the card to the railway cashier one receives the discount ticket only on condition that one travels from a so-called "large station" to a so-called "access station", or vice versa.

Revisionists and Betar Break Off Work for Keren Kayemet and Keren Hayesod

[Zionism — the Revisionists; Sosnowiec.] From the Central Committee of the Zionist-Revisionists in Sosnowiec we have received the following communiqué:
Ten days ago we turned to the Jewish public with an appeal pointing to the great injustice committed against us in the distribution of the latest certificates. The demand of the Revisionist movement in Poland, which counts 30 thousand members, was ignored in an unheard-of manner: of the total number of certificates, 4 per cent were assigned to Brit Hatzohar and Betar in Poland.
Our demands were not taken into account, and we therefore see ourselves compelled to use the last means of defending our rights.
However hard it may be for us, we are obliged to order all our branches and individual members to stop all work and support for the Keren Hayesod and the Keren Kayemet until a just order is established in the composition of the Palestine Office, in accordance with the resolutions of the 17th Zionist Congress. We throw the consequences of our orders onto the heads of the present leftist majority in the Palestine Office, which by its arbitrariness has driven us to use the said means.
In connection with this resolution the Sosnowiec Revisionists held a protest meeting on the second day of Shavuot, at which a resolution was adopted to send back the Keren Kayemet collection boxes.
The next day, Sunday, all the Revisionists sent their boxes back to the Keren Kayemet, enclosing a letter in which they justify their step by the fact that the distribution of certificates was carried out in such a way that only those who had been on winter hachshara thanks to the support of the national funds — which were enjoyed exclusively by the leftist groupings — received certificates. In this way the Revisionists' work for these funds has been turned into a weapon against them.
———
To the invitation of the "Keren Hayesod" committee to take part in the Keren Hayesod campaign, which begins these days, the Revisionist organization replied that as long as its demands are not fulfilled, its members will take no part in the work.

The First Jewish Sports Festival in Czeladź.

[Czeladź — sports, community life.]
Great success of the Będzin “Hakoah”.
Only a month ago, when on the initiative of Mr. Gelbard a gymnastics association named “Bar Kochba” was founded in Czeladź, and the “leaders” of “Chizuk ha-Dat” learned of the great “danger” threatening the town on account of the sports association, they raised an outcry [“va-yitz'aku”], called meetings, and issued bans against the parents whose children had “gone astray” and joined “Bar Kochba” as members. Also on the day of the first gymnastics festival, which took place last Sunday, the “fine” Jews went to work: they posted guards in front of the theatre to watch that no “Jewish cap” should fall into the gates of impurity... But all these stringencies helped little: the theatre hall was packed full [?] with a varied public; even the “snare” [probably a misprint for “fear”] of “Beis Yaakov” did not hold back its “representatives”... And all the more so: even the rebbetzin herself did not withstand the temptation, and while the procession marched through the town, the rebbetzin did not leave her balcony and took part (if only from afar) in the sports festival being held for the first time in Czeladź...
———
The gymnastics festival was organised by the Czeladź “Bar-Kochba”, but the programme was performed by the sportswomen and sportsmen of the Będzin “Hakoah”, led by their orchestra under the direction of Icchak Bargblat.
Before the start of the programme the founder of “Bar Kochba”, Mr. Gelbard, greeted the participants and appealed to the Jewish public to support the newly founded sports association in Czeladź.
On behalf of “Hakoah” Mr. Maniek Plesner replied, stressing the importance of physical education for the young Jewish generation.
The festival took place in the municipal theatre — a comfortable hall, a large and wide stage — which contributed much to the great moral success that the Hakoah people had in Czeladź. After every number the hall shook with incessant, noisy ovations. The Christian visitors [“bal prtm” — unclear] applauded warmly and could not have enough of the fine exercises, especially of the rhythmic numbers performed by the ladies' group.
During the intervals the orchestra performed a series of musical numbers, among them also the melodies from “The Dybbuk”, which went down very well with the Jewish public.
During the exercises Mr. Luszek Barenblat (piano) and a violin accompanied.
Great applause went to the dance in make-up, performed by Miss Pinkus.
After the march-past and the closing words of Mr. Gelbard the gymnastics festival was ended.
Then a procession formed with the participation of delegations, “Bar Kochba” members and the groups of “Hakoah”, with the orchestra at their head.
The procession through the whole town was accompanied by men, women and children. The Szwajcer family honoured the “Jewish military” with... confetti.
At the last tram stop the procession dispersed.

Don't Be Stubborn

[Essay — everyday life; police, fines and the courts.] Surely more than one of you has already had this happen: you are dragging yourself along a respectable street, lost in gloomy thoughts, and you meet a friend of yours or some relative [?]; you won't want to let slip a chance to unburden your heart a little of your troubles, so you stop for a moment in the middle of the passage and start a little chat.
Meanwhile a policeman steals up on you unnoticed; he invites the two of you into the nearest [?] gateway, takes out a little pad and tells you to pay one, possibly two, or even a whole three gulden.
Well, if you are a Jew, a calm, level-headed one, you understand perfectly that there is no getting clever with the police, and although the three złoty are a great loss to you, you have no choice but to open your purse, pay the fine imposed, and be done with the matter.
It is different, however, when such a thing happens to a stubborn hothead: a fellow like that feels like playing the tough guy; paying the złoty or two of his own free will is out of the question, and he won't even want to show his papers. They try to lead him off to the commissariat [police station]; he starts arguing and struggling, and the end of it is that he is finally taken there by force — and on top of that he is charged with resisting authority, for which, as is well known, a very severe penalty is threatened [sic; printed „סדראט“].
In the best case, if he is not charged with resisting authority, a report is drawn up against him for obstructing the passage, and for that one is sentenced to a fine of 20, 30 and sometimes even 50 zł. One must also remember that in both cases the enforcement and court costs come to quite high sums.
So it turns out that, for the sake of digging in one's heels over one złoty or two zł., one later has to pay 25 times as much and perhaps more; one is already registered with the authorities as a troublemaker; and besides [?], the lost time dragging oneself through the commissariats and courts and the torment [lit. "bloodshed"] of arrest are surely worth something too. Perhaps the arrogance of many such stubborn young men comes from their reckoning that from them, as young men who have no homes or property of their own, the fine money can't be collected anyway.
If that is what they think, they are badly mistaken: the bailiffs [komornicy] won't hear of any concessions [?]; they come to the addresses given, home to the parents, and rightly or wrongly they seize the last cupboard or the only table, and the innocent parents, poor things, have to pay in tears the fines for their all-too-impudent little sons.
Likewise: you have to make a trip by train and buy a ticket; in a hurry, however, you sit down in a more expensive class, or you doze past your destination station and ride a little further. The inspector catches you and tells you to pay for a triple-price ticket.
You don't feel like meeting the railway authority's demand of your own free will. You start resisting, and they take you off the carriage and lead you into the office of the stationmaster [zawiadowca], and a report is drawn up against you for violating police regulations.
The trial takes place at the court to which the station where the incident occurred belongs, often dozens of miles from your place of residence; so of course you do not appear at the trial. And if you do appear, you are also sentenced to a larger or smaller fine, and the court and enforcement costs are likewise heaped onto your shoulders.
If you think that the matter is thereby settled, you are mistaken again, for some time later you are again dunned for the civil claim awarded, amounting to a triple ticket price, together with the accrued interest and further enforcement costs as well.
We therefore take this opportunity to appeal to people who are stopped for obstructing the passage, for crossing the street diagonally, or for similar petty offences, to have pity on their dignity, their time and their money, and to pay on the spot, without arguments and wrangling, the ticket fine [mandat] demanded of them, and on no account to let it come to reports.
Y. A.
An Instructors' Course for Women

By Miriam Jakubowicz (Warsaw).
A few weeks ago I became acquainted with sports life in Zagłębie. A region such as Będzin and Sosnowiec interested me greatly, not only from my personal point of view but also as a representative of the women's sports movement in Poland. On the basis of the conferences I held with the representatives of the local sports associations, I came to the conclusion that the physical education of the Jewish woman interests everyone, and that the women themselves, as members, work very hard and could make even better use of their work. I emphasize: the women "could", but they "are not able to". Why? Because along with good will one must also have a certain measure of technical and practical knowledge — and precisely that is what they lack. There is a shortage of well-trained women instructors and women sports leaders. Therefore the Association has undertaken to carry out, with the help of the local organizations, a planned campaign to train women instructors for the Zagłębie district; and it will depend only on the good will and proper interest of the local clubs whether our campaign develops and bears the proper fruit. The first task will be to train women instructors for sports games: volleyball ("Netzball") and basketball ("Korbball"). Such courses last only 5 days and are intended for those who already know the rules of the game but cannot yet lead others. A specially qualified woman instructor is coming from Warsaw to conduct the course.
Such a course will take place in Będzin in the month of June [czerwiec], and also in other towns where there are more than 15 candidates. The second course, in August [sierpień]: the 4-week "camp" [obóz] will take place in Józefów near Tomaszów Maz. On the programme: theoretical and practical instruction in gymnastics, movement in sports games, light athletics and swimming. The fee at the "camp" is about 50—60 zł, already including food, lodging and tuition. The candidates receive an 80 per cent railway discount. Our propaganda campaign consists not only of training instructors but also of cultural work, which we have already begun in Będzin, Sosnowiec and Katowice, where conferences were held with all the sports associations and civic organizations. This summer we shall use to train the instructors, and in the autumn we shall proceed to the further work. The Association is making every possible effort to make the matter of the Jewish woman's health a topical issue, to interest the organizations, and most important of all — to convince the woman herself that without her help it will be hard to achieve anything.
Every woman strives to preserve her health, youth, capacity for work and beauty. Every one of us thinks so, but that is not enough: one must work on oneself a little, so that we do not lack energy — for the understanding we already have. Every time I spoke to women I felt and saw that they all agreed, but in this case I take stock and ask myself: how long will this "flame" last? Let it not be shattered at the first obstacle or by one's own laziness. Every woman must enlarge within herself the measure of awareness and understanding.
We expect from you full understanding and support, and we have no doubt that we shall achieve it.
Woman can play a great role in the sports organization, and therefore one must take an interest in her.
Let us make a start with the training of women instructors and take an interest in the Association's plan of courses and "camps"! Let this be our first step towards working for our physical renaissance!
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

Jews say "mevinus" [connoisseur's remarks]..
The courtyard of the Będzin synagogue is full of people. To get inside is a matter of mortal danger. Not only bearded Jews, but our youth too; if a stranger saw it, he would think nothing else but that today's youth had suddenly become pious...
— What's all the noise about?
— Why, Sherman is leading the prayers! We Jews by nature have more respect for a foreigner, and all the more so when the foreigner is one of our own, with a supplement:
— Sherman, the former Będzin cantor...
Here someone comes out of the synagogue, flushed and sweaty; the crowd pounces on him, wanting to hear an opinion from inside:
— Were you in there? Does he still have the sweetness of old? They say — great wealth in dollars. Are they saying anything in the synagogue about it?
And when the "connoisseur" begins answering all the questions, a buzzing starts.
— Shh! Shh! — he's tossing out tenors, listen...
The crowd breaks off the conversation and throws itself at the entrance, because "they're catching the tenors", "American tenors".
But the quiet is disturbed again: a wave of exhausted people bursts out into the open air.
— Don't push — says one of those "who came back out" — just wait until Musaf and you'll hear an "U-mipnei chata'enu" ["Because of our sins"]...
— Quite right — remarks a second — we need to hear that "U-mipnei chata'enu", because "because of our sins we were exiled from our town": Sherman went off to America, taking with him the unpaid bills of exchange of the Będzin kehilla..
The "advice" is accepted; the crowd waits until Musaf, and meanwhile, between Shacharit and Musaf,
— Jews say "mevinus"...

The dissatisfied..
We, the "Thou hast chosen us" people, are always the dissatisfied ones; we always have nothing but complaints against our neighbours: why aren't we accepted as state officials, why we fancy becoming railway conductors, postmen and other such "degrading" trades? Is it possible? Why are we not grateful for the great "favours" that are done for us?
— This question came into my mind when I found myself in the courtroom of the Sosnowiec artisans' association [?]. My own eyes could not believe that this was reality; on the contrary, tell me yourselves: did a Jew ever dream of becoming a judge in Poland? And on top of that, of conducting the court procedure in the Yiddish language?..
At the top — the judge, Itche, wearing a silk-green sash; on both sides — lay assessors [ławnicy], and in front of them — the accused, who describe the "events" and appeal to the "tribunal" to hand down a milder penalty...
My heart swelled with joy; but when I looked around the hall and saw the spectators, the camp of artisans dressed in their Sabbath clothes, only then did I understand the "bear's favour" that is being done to us... Sunday, the second day of rest, one is not allowed to work, [so] artisans become "risters" [sic; probably a misprint for "judges"]...
They sat there ill at ease, gloomy [?], sulking, embittered and
— dissatisfied..

A great pity...
At a meeting of the Dąbrowa kehilla board. On the agenda a very "important" matter: for the third time — electing a chairman and vice-chairman of the board. The "judges" are in no hurry; perhaps because "over this Kohelet [kehilla] nothing new shines" [?]. Slowly, one by one, they arrive, and an hour after the set time the meeting begins.
The chairman, a great stickler, does not believe the secretary's assurance that there is a quorum; instead every member of the board signs that
— he is present... A question about a fact? A trifle — what today's "dozory" [kehilla board members] are capable of: today he is here and tomorrow he can claim that "he said nothing", "nothing was there and nothing was said"...
Decorum at the table is maintained.. 11 board members: 10 right-wingers [?] and one "leftist"... He, the "leftist", sits bareheaded; the others — in their hats. Even the secretary, who is no great stickler for the commandments, does not take off his hat either... Only when, for convenience, the chairman removes the secretary's hat does the leftist triumph and call out:
— "May you live to a hundred and twenty"...
Parliamentary "rules" are "very carefully" observed at the meeting. The door is open to everyone — not only the body but also the mouth... Every outside spectator takes part in the discussion, for what difference does it make?... And why shouldn't one swear at a Jewish meeting [zebranie]? Pardon, I don't mean swearing, just plainly telling the other fellow a few words, calling him a scoundrel, a liar and a few more "spicy" expressions...
Watching the scene, I greatly regretted that the former Grabski does not trouble himself to come up to a meeting of our communal representatives...
— A great pity...

Go off to cheder...
It is told: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev, of blessed memory, once on Rosh Hashanah, before the blowing of the shofar, threw down the shofar and cried out:
— Let Ivan blow the shofar! For the nations of the world have every good thing, they are not persecuted, they are not tormented — so let them blow the shofar...
The same cry, only with a different echo, has been raised by the Zagłębie Revisionists.
The Revisionist organizations were badly wronged in the last distribution of [immigration] certificates. Well, what's to be done? Take them to court? Before whom? If everywhere they want to "drown the Revisionists in a spoonful of water"... So the Revisionists thought it over and did what Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of blessed memory did:
— "Let Ivan blow the shofar"!
They packed up the collection boxes of all the Zionist funds and sent "the daughter with the children" back home to her father. Spare us your favours — they wrote to them — don't throw us any bones, and
— go off to cheder...

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Naso)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Naso
The Portion
—o—
a) "They too, by their fathers' houses, by their families" (Num. 4:22).
When "they too are of their fathers' houses" — when they too are like their parents, whose lineage they boast of — then "take the sum [lift the head]": they deserve to be given a place at the head. But mere lineage, when the grandchildren live[?] off their grandfathers, is worth nothing. Binah le-Ittim.
• • •
Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh [Międzybóż] loved to pick quarrels with all the rebbes of his generation, for being the Baal Shem Tov's grandson he held that all of them should be subordinate to him. Thus he quarrelled with the Lubavitcher Rebbe, with Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev [Berdyczów], and others.
Once he met the "Shpola Zeide" [Grandfather of Szpoła], and, as was his way, he needled him:
— Why do they call you the "Shpola Grandfather" and not the "Shpola Grandmother"? It seems to me that all your miracles are womanish.
— Because I really am a grandfather, and "the glory of grandchildren is their grandfathers" (the glory of children are their fathers, etc.), and were it not for a fine grandfather, one would not even have heard of the grandchildren['s bones?] (a hint at Rabbi Baruch, the Baal Shem Tov's grandson)...
—o—
b) "And the covering of tachash skin" (ibid., 25).
"Mikhseh ha-tachash" amounts, by a certain gematria (small number with the kolel), to "mamon" — money. For money is a suspicious cloak (tachash), a suspect covering for a person... It is a "covering" with many suspicions. Or Penei Moshe.
—o—
c) "Two thousand, seven hundred and fifty" (ibid., 36).
Rabbi Jonathan Eybeschütz, in his book "Tiferet Yehonatan", makes a kabbalistic calculation of why the numbers were so. Seven hundred — for the seven lights of the menorah; two thousand — for the Torah, which was given two thousand years before the creation of the world; only for the table is the number fifty, a half number.
For the "table", according to Kabbalah, is "ma'ashir" — it makes rich, and as such it can make rich only by half, because to make a man entirely rich is impossible. However much one has, one wants double. A man is always only half rich...
—o—
d) "And every offering of all the holy things of the Children of Israel" (5:9).
The Israelite must give a tithe of his produce to the Kohen and the Levite, and afterwards both rejoice: "And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your sons and your daughters... and the Levite that is within your gates."
Like those two in-laws —
Once two in-laws are dancing at the wedding of a divorced man. One is the present father-in-law and the other the former one, whose daughter had divorced the groom. They ask the latter: why are you dancing at the wedding? He answers:
— The in-law is dancing because he is now getting a groom for his daughter, and I am dancing because my daughter got rid of him...
The moral:
The Israelite rejoices in the produce, and the Kohen rejoices that he is free of such drudgery, that others work for him...
—o—
e) "Thus shall you bless the Children of Israel" (6:23).
Once a village Jew [yishuvnik] came to Rabbi Meirl of Premishlan [Przemyślany] with his two sons to ask for a blessing:
— Rebbe, bless my sons for me.
But Rabbi Meirl wants a pidyon [a redemption fee]. The villager, who knew a little of the "small letters" [i.e. a bit of learning], says to him:
— Rebbe, does it not say "koh tevorkhu" — you shall bless "just so", without money (in the folk idiom "azoy" — "just so" — means without money)...
Rabbi Meirl smiles and blesses the sons for nothing.
—o—
f) "The Lord bless you and keep you" (ibid., 24).
"Bless you — with money; and keep you — from harmful spirits." Midrash.
According to the Gemara (Pesachim 111), even demons show respect to a rich man, and Rav Papa, who was a wealthy brewer, therefore indeed had no fear of demons.
So, if "He blesses you with money", if you will have money — "He keeps you from harmful spirits" — you will be guarded even from demons...
Such is the power of money. Brit Shalom.
—o—
g) "Nachshon the son of Amminadab" (7:12).
Nachshon is not given the title "Nasi" [prince], because a complete man needs no titles. When one says of a finished house that it has walls, windows, doors — it is foolish; but of an unfinished house, if one says that it already has, say, windows — that is to the point.
For a complete man, "man" alone is his title. Divrei Shaul.
The Haftarah.
—o—
h) "And his name was Manoah" (Judges 13).
"Manoah was an ignoramus: for he walked behind his wife."
Because "he walked behind his wife" is proof that he was an ignoramus — for had he also known how to learn, he would have gone after strange women... and talked them into believing that with a chapter of Mishnah he could buy off the sin...
Par [sic] Rabbi Mordechai of Chernobyl [Czarnobyl].
Avot.
—o—
i) "Let your house be open wide" (Avot 1:5).
"Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household."
If you live too lavishly — so the people interpret it — poor people will be members of your household, or rather: the members of your household will be poor people...
The Public Worker

[Feuilleton — communal activism, kehilla.] A little story with a moral.
Once there was a public worker [klal-tuer].
He worked selflessly in all the kehilla institutions, not for the sake of receiving a reward — truly only for the public good.
Whatever institution there was, he stood at its head. Where wouldn't you want? In the kehilla — the real president; in the bank — a ringleader; in the free-loan fund — director; in the hospital — curator; in the town council — councillor; with the volunteer firemen, in the sejmik [county council], in the justice-of-the-peace court — in a word, everywhere, in all the institutions, a ringleader, a real macher.
He lived with his household not badly — one could say well. In the last years he even bought a piano. True, nobody ever played on it, but they did not deny themselves.
Where he got all this from, nobody ever bothered to find out, for really, whose grandmother's worry is it?
Something happens, and in town people begin to murmur about the self-made [samorodny] public worker, whom everyone had always held to be crystal-clean and had never suspected of anything. Nobody knew any facts, but they had plenty to tell one another.
When the public began to ask around among the other "spoon[?] people", they all took mouthfuls of water and kept silent.
The public worker went on working selflessly, for since he is a public worker, he must work.
Until...
Until the public had had enough of it, and the honest public worker was little by little pushed out of almost all the institutions.
It turned out that at the "kehilla door-handles" [klamki] the public worker, with his wife and children, had almost died of hunger, and on top of that had remained a debtor — and not [a"v] for luxury items.
Luckily, a small inheritance turned up from his or her parents, and on that they lived as they lived; thus a Jew lived out his years for the public.
In the last years one could find him at some little celebration singing a song of praise (too delicate a word — let us rather say "Mah Yafit") for a drink of vodka, or for a small free loan.
Moral: from kehilla affairs nobody has yet come out even.
A Zaytiger [An Outsider].
—o—

Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (29)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin; installment 29.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

After the meal he went off to the stable to the horses. There he sat for a long time in the darkness and, by the red glow of the lantern, read from the great "Holy Book" the story of the "Redeemer", who was born in a stable.. He read calmly, pointing at the words with his finger, and as he did so he felt that he too, who had grown up in a stable beside the horses, was one chosen by God... And feeling this way, he would often fall into religious ecstasy...

And then — this once happened:

Rasputin was working in the field. He drove the horse on and walked with calm steps behind the plough, which cut through the [rich?] black, glistening earth. It was a spring day and a bright sun shone down from the blue sky. All around rose the chirping song of the birds, and gentle [?] fragrant breezes blew playfully. Rasputin trudged in his heavy boots behind the plough and thought about the "Redeemer", whose life he had read about yesterday, Sunday, sitting in the stable, and he was gripped by religious ecstasy. When he reached the edge of the field and was about to turn the horse and plough back around, he suddenly heard behind him a wondrous singing. The singing resembled that of the village girls who sang in the choir in church. Rasputin turned round to see who was singing like that and — from great astonishment he let the plough slip from his hands and stood petrified. He saw before him an extraordinary vision: the "Holy Mother" was sitting on the rays of the sun and swaying on them... The air was full of pious song, which burst from the throats of thousands of angels, and the "Holy Mother" sang along...

The vision lasted a few minutes and then everything vanished.

Shaken to the very depths of his soul, Rasputin stood in the field without moving a limb. He stood like that for a while and could no longer go on with his work. He was terribly bewildered and a heavy melancholy took hold of him. He now believed with all his heart that God wished to draw him near and to lay upon him a great, holy mission. At the same time he knew well that, in order to take this divine mission upon himself, he would have to part from the horses, from the tavern, from his father, his wife and the village girls.

He did no more work that day. Towards evening he went into the stable and sat there a long time thinking. It was very hard for him to leave the horses and the village girls, and he decided to keep the whole thing to himself and think no more about the extraordinary vision, and apart from his friend Pecherkin he told no one about it.

But the vision he believed he had seen, and the notion that God wished to draw him near, gave him no peace. He thought about it constantly and dreamed of it at night. Often such heavy sorrow and mute longing took hold of him that he kept silent for whole days and did not say a word to anyone.

Several years went by. Rasputin went on with his father's trade: he was a carter, carrying passengers and all sorts of goods through all [?] the villages and towns, and in summer he worked the field diligently. In the evenings he often got drunk and afterwards spent the nights in debauchery; but he could not forget the "vision", and the notion that God was seeking to draw him near would not leave him and often disturbed his peace.

And finally, when he was already over 30 years old, he suddenly made a sharp break in his life. One morning he got up, left his wife with the children she had borne in the meantime and, without telling anyone where he was going, vanished from the village.

With a bag on his shoulders and a staff in his hand he set off striding along the Siberian roads. He wandered a long time until he arrived in Verkhoturye, which lies among the Ural mountains. He went into the local monastery and stayed there.

The Verkhoturye monastery owned large stretches of fields and gardens around it. Besides occupying themselves with piety and prayer, the monks there also occupied themselves with working the fields and cultivating the gardens, and so for the muzhik Rasputin it was not hard to stay there.

* * *

Having spent some time in the monastery, Rasputin learned that the monks there were divided into two parts. One part — the larger — consisted of those who openly or secretly belonged to sects which the high clergy regarded as heretical. These monks had been sent to the Verkhoturye monastery so that they should repent there, return to the straight path and be brought back under the wings of the Orthodox Church. The other part — the smaller — consisted of those who were supposed to keep watch over the exiles and see to it that they were good and pious.

A little later Rasputin discovered that the monks who were supposed to watch over the exiles, and who strictly observed all the precepts of the Orthodox Church, did so only for appearances, but in truth nearly all of them leaned towards the sectarians and believed in the sectarian teaching, which differed from the teaching of the Orthodox Church.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Presidium of the Kehilla Board Elected for the Second Time

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 13[?] / 13 Sivan 5692 — czwartek 17 czerwca 1932 [Thursday (sic), 17 June 1932].)
Będzin
A presidium of the kehilla board elected for the second time.
On Monday evening the new kehilla board was called to a meeting for the purpose of electing, for the second time, the presidium of the board.
No "interested parties" were admitted to the meeting; even the parnassim did not have the privilege of entering the meeting hall.
The Agudah group, numbering 5 members, submitted a protest against the election, arguing that "they recognise the first presidium election as lawful". After submitting the protest the group left the meeting.
Then the election took place, which gave the following result: Mr. Elazar Rubinlicht was elected president of the board, and Mr. Abraham Liwer [?] vice-president.
Savings Are Being Made at the Expense of the Jewish Children

[Będzin — Municipality; Education.]
As is well known, the "municipal commissioner is a strong supporter of making savings. Be it so — a fair thing, especially in the present economic crisis; but the savings are not made inside, that is to say in the Magistrat [town hall], but outside the Magistrat. Thus, for example, their [?] telephone was removed in the municipal bath-house, the number of children sent to the summer colonies is being reduced, etc.
But that is still too little: the present rulers of the Magistrat have cast an eye on the school premises for the Jewish children who study in the public elementary schools (szkoły powszechne).
Under the slogan of savings the commissioner, together with the school board (dozór szkolny), adopted a resolution that the school premises in the town used until now shall be let out, and with the income school premises shall be rented for the non-Jewish children in Gzichów [?; printed "Grushibov"] and Koszelów.
— And the Jewish children?
— For the Jewish children the hall of "Piast" will be handed over.
And if the hall is too small to take in all the school-children? There is a remedy for that too: some of the children will be at school in the morning and some in the afternoon. Instead of the children enjoying a few free hours in the day, they will have to toil at school until 8 o'clock in the evening... One must also take into account that in the winter months, when Sabbath begins at 4 o'clock, a large part of the children who study in the afternoon will not go to school at all because of the Sabbath.
We believe that the Jewish parents of the hundreds of Jewish children (may they multiply) will not remain indifferent to the outrage crying to heaven that is being planned at the expense of their children, and will start an action so that the resolution is changed without fail.
Great Success of Cantor Sherman

[Będzin — Cantorial music.]
This year on Shavuot our town had a distinguished guest in the person of the former cantor Abraham Yitzhak Sherman, who came a few days before Shavuot to his children in Będzin. It was impossible to get into the synagogue where Sherman led the prayers. Those who came an hour before the time of prayer had the privilege of hearing him. Because of the great heat Sherman was not able on the first day to pray in his usual manner; on the second day, on the other hand, the congregation delighted in Sherman's sweet praying and piyyutim.
Talmud Torah Melamdim Break Off the Lessons

[Będzin — Talmud Torah.]
On Monday 2 melamdim of the lower classes in the Talmud Torah broke off the lessons.
The reason is as follows: a melamed of such a class, where about up to 60 children study, receives 30 zł. a week, but in cash he got 7—8 zł. a week; the rest is set aside [deferred]... This time, however, the melamdim did not get even the 8 zł. Because of this they stopped teaching.
The breaking-off of lessons for 120 children, however, makes no impression whatsoever on the "Shomrei ha-Dat"; apparently, supplying the population with "kosher" milk is preferable to poor children studying...
Number of Children at the Summer Colony Limited and the Fee Increased

[Będzin — Municipality; Summer colonies.]
The management of the department of social welfare at the local Magistrat has considerably reduced the number of children who are sent to the summer colonies in Sławków. Besides this, every child, even the poorest, must pay 10 złoty.
Because of this decree many poor children are threatened with not going to the colony, since their parents are not in a position to give the 10 złoty...
Meeting of the Debtors of the Piotrków Credit Society

[Będzin — Economy; Credit.]
In the hall of the House- and Plot-Owners' Association a meeting was held of the debtors of the Piotrków Credit Society.
At the meeting a series of resolutions was adopted, among others that 1) the interest rate shall be reduced according to the norm of Warsaw and Łódź; 2) further, [properties] shall be put up for auction (licytacja) only when the member owes 3 half-yearly instalments; and 3) an extraordinary meeting of all debtors shall be called.
At the meeting a commission was elected consisting of president Gelbard [?], president Krzymański [?], Kornfeld and secretary Widman. The commission has the task of attending to the resolutions adopted.
Badge Sale for the Benefit of the Summer Colony

[Będzin — Youth movements; Summer colonies.]
After much effort and endeavour "Ha-Shomer", united with "Herzliya", succeeded in obtaining a permit for a badge sale. The badge sale takes place next Wednesday; the proceeds go to the summer colony organised by the organisation, thanks to which dozens of poor children spend a longer time among mountains and valleys.
To Combat Illegal Workshops

[Będzin — Artisans.]
Last Sunday a joint consultation of Jewish and Christian artisans took place in the hall of the Polish Craftsmen's Association. At the consultation the question was discussed of how to combat the illegal workshops.
After a lengthy discussion the programme of work was laid down and the following committee was elected: Dziedzic [?] (president), Shmuel Greitzer (vice[-president]), Zając (secretary), Łubik [?] (treasurer), Obarnik [?], Zaks Feigenblat.
On Distraints, Price Lists, Policies and Tax Reliefs

We have been asked by the „Merchants' Association“ to announce that:
1) The Ministry of Finance has issued a circular (okólnik) on limiting distraints (egzekucje) against those taxpayers whose turnover assessment the appeals commission has reduced.
2) The Ministry of the Interior has issued a circular obliging [printed „per-plistet“] that goods of prime necessity be provided with price lists (cenniki).
3) All holders of German policies must register with the „Merchants' Association“, and
4) those who pay tax arrears (zaległe) in the months of June and July (czerwiec and lipiec) will still receive reliefs of 85 per cent.
Founding of a Jewish Song and Music Society. — A Charity-Society „Ring“ in Będzin. — As You Sow, So Shall You Reap...

Founding of a Jewish Song and Music Society.
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Wajcenberg, the founding meeting of the „Jewish Song and Music Society Będzin“ took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association. Not far from Ząbkowice station a band of several dozen men attacked a train.

[Będzin — Crime; followed by short news: Upper Silesia, local, Będzin, Sosnowiec, Königshütte, Rybnik.]
In Kapuścik's house at 44 Podzamcze Street there lived alone in a room the 23-year-old Kaniewska, an employee in a shop in Dąbrowa.

With One Hand He Begs for Alms and with the Other He Wants to Support a Wife.
Mrs. Rivka A. of Jasna Street relates to us an interesting fact.
A few days ago a young man came to her, crippled in one hand, and begged for alms. Seeing before her such an unfortunate person with a dangling sleeve, she remembered her own bitter lot, her husband, who died a few years ago while a diseased hand was being amputated, leaving her a widow with 4 small children without means of livelihood.
She took pity on him and, handing him her last 5 groszy, asked him in passing how the misfortune had befallen him.
To the poor man's question why she was so interested to know, she told him the whole tragic story of her late husband.
"I feel for you very much, madam," the young man began to console her, "and if it is hard for you, as I see, to make a match, I am ready to marry you."
The woman was dumbfounded by the stranger's brazen frankness and answers him smilingly[?]:
"But how could I marry a poor man who goes begging from house to house, and a cripple into the bargain?"
"Don't fret," the young man replies, "it's not a bad business."
With that he takes out a wallet full of banknotes and shows it to her. He also tells her that nobody refuses him and that he does good business. He himself, he says, is a Varsovian, formerly a shop employee, and if she agrees to marry him he will throw over this profession and take up something else.
To the woman's question how he could be good for anything, being a cripple, without a hand[?], poor thing, the young man at once unpinned his jacket and, to her great amazement, took out... a second, healthy hand, which he had cunningly tucked away and hidden.
The woman could not believe her own eyes and said: "Go, go, I'll think it over!"
"But with what do I leave you, then?" the poor man would not let up.
"With what?" the woman ironically repeated his question. "You came, poor thing, with one hand, and you are leaving, thank God, with both hands..."

An unknown woman came in to Mr. Fojgel in Königshütte and asked that Mr. Fojgel lend her 5 złoty, which she needed for the expenses of travelling to Bielitz. When Advance Payments on the Turnover Tax Must Be Paid
In order to avoid unpleasantness and fines, we bring here the dates of the advance payments („zaliczki“) on turnover taxes.
Traders who do not keep commercial books must pay the advance payments on the following dates:
For the first quarter — by the 15th of July (lipiec).
For the second quarter — by the 15th of September (wrzesień).
For the third quarter — by the 15th of November (listopad).
And for the fourth quarter — by the 15th of March 1933.
One has 14 days after the dates to pay. But one must know that the tax offices (urzędy) have the right already from the 16th to carry out a distraint, and then one must also pay the distraint costs.

New Circular of the Finance Ministry on Income Tax
From a well-informed source we learn that the Finance Ministry has sent a circular („okólnik“) to the Treasury Chambers („izby skarbowe“), that conventions of the heads of the tax offices be called concerning the new assessment of income tax („podatek dochodowy“).
At the conventions the norms will be fixed according to which income tax is to be assessed. The average income norms used until now are too high, since last year people earned less than in the year before.
Thus, for example, in the earlier assessments 8—10 percent of the turnover in textiles („manufaktura“) or leather was counted as income, 6—8 percent in groceries („colonial goods“), etc. Now the need to reduce the average norms is being pointed out, since in the last year people earned less.

A Shameful Libel — Against the Halutz Kibbutz in Będzin

On Thursday the police came to the kibbutz of halutzim in Buszowice[?], where they undergo their hakhshara (training) in preparation for emigrating to the Land of Israel. After a strict search, 3[?] halutzim were arrested — 2 young men and 1 girl. The police ordered the rest to come to the commissariat at 8 in the evening. The arrest was made because of a denunciation by 2 Christian women, local inhabitants, who reported to the police that they had seen the 3 arrested putting up illegal proclamations, and that the whole kibbutz was a nest of nothing but communists.
The 3 arrested were held at the commissariat until Saturday. The various interventions of respected citizens and of representatives of the Zionist groups, who demonstrated the opposite of the accusation, were of no avail, and the arrested halutzim were sent on to the investigating judge in Sosnowiec. He released them at once. But the whole matter was handed over to the prosecutor's office.
It is worth noting that the arrested halutza has been in hakhshara for 2 years already and is one of the most active halutzot. She has already received a certificate and was supposed to go home at the beginning of last week to prepare for her aliyah.
The kibbutz, located in such a Polish area as Buszowice[?], has long been provoked by the neighbours there; they cannot bear that such a holy, pure Polish area has been „Judaized“, and they devised such a shameful and ugly libel. Already some weeks ago the halutzim received an anonymous letter saying that if they did not leave their place of residence there in the course of May, none of them would come out of it well. The halutzim submitted the letter to the police.
The kibbutz is suffering very much moral distress from the local inhabitants, and it is worth taking an interest and moving the kibbutz out of there and creating a place for it in a safer area.
Because of a Wagon Axle the City of Betar Was Destroyed, and Because of the Kehilla Elections the Ger Hasidim in Strzemieszyce Have Split...

The Jewish inhabitants of Strzemieszyce have been given a breath of life... What do we care about the crisis, who cares about the crisis — new kehilla elections are coming...
So „the common folk, scissors and iron“ [i.e. tailors and plain people] put aside their weekday business and took up with great devotion the holy work — the kehilla elections.
Factions were formed. Whoever has a larger family — that is certainly good, and lists were drawn up in such a way that the Strzemieszyce Jewish kehilla, which counts some 300 budget-taxpayers, put up no fewer than — 12 lists...
That too might still have been tolerable — why not? Let Jews enjoy the democratic order and get „little benches“ (seats) in the kehilla. The trouble, however, is that thanks to the lists it came to a split among the Ger Hasidim, or more correctly, within the „Agudah“.
The split came about because the Ger Hasid Mr. L. „rebelled“ and figures on the Rabbi's list. For this rebellion a band of the „Leibishists“ obtained that Mr. L. be disqualified because of his „own sins“, because of — paragraph 20...
The man disqualified by the election commission does not rest either, and is using every means to get back his rights. As we are informed, a Będzin dozor (kehilla board member), the political leader of the „Agudah“, is also intervening wherever necessary so that Mr. L. may become kosher again...
For greater force and vigour, Mr. L. has turned to the kehilla administration with a letter in which he „gives notice“ that if he is not made „kosher“ again, he will prove that the shochet of the opposing side, also a Ger Hasid, has caused damage to the kehilla treasury...
Meanwhile Strzemieszyce is boiling like a cauldron.

Będzin Revisionists Protest

On Saturday a protest meeting of Revisionists, Betar and sympathizers took place at the „Merchants' Association“, chaired by the parnas (kehilla elder) Kisner. After the lecture by Mr. Klarman on the dishonest and unjust distribution of the certificates, the following resolutions were adopted:
1) The assembled Revisionists in Będzin, who received up to 600 votes in the elections to the Zionist Congress, protest against the Palestine Office in Warsaw for robbing our aliyah candidates, who have completed hakhshara, [?]of being given the possibility of aliyah, treating the Revisionist masses — the largest group in Zionism — in stepmotherly fashion by tossing them a bone in the form of 4 per cent of the certificates.
2) The assembly protests against the conduct of the Zionist Executive for not carrying out the resolution on the proportional distribution of the Palestine Offices, which was adopted by the Zionist Congress.
3) The assembly unanimously resolves, as a protest, to break off work and donations for the funds: Keren Hayesod and the Keren Kayemet (JNF).
What's New in Upper Silesia?

Katowice kehilla budget before the kehilla council.
Under the chairmanship of President Dr. Reichmann a meeting of the kehilla council took place in Katowice. At the meeting the budget, drawn up by the administration, was discussed.
In the new budget the administration has provided a salary for only one rabbi, because the administration is in favour of one rabbi being given notice of dismissal from his post.
On this proposal there was a lengthy discussion at the meeting, and it was decided to hand the matter over to a commission which should find a way out so that both rabbis may again remain in their posts.

Protekcja and Our Homegrown Mouse-Nest.

[Editorial — Będzin, kehilla and rabbinate; protekcja and taxes.]

(Private calculation and a grand gesture at the people's expense!)

It is like this everywhere; everywhere we hear one and the same thing: the protekcja system holds the upper hand. If you have connections, whatever they may be, you can push anything through; but if you are no good at the business, if you lack the art of fawning and putting on airs, and do not have, on top of that, a hefty dose of brazenness, then you are lost, then all doors are closed to you, then you find no rights that might protect you; you may be a hundred per cent in the right, everyone may see that you have been wronged — nobody will want to help you, nobody will even look round at you. The worst bitterness, the whole pain, you then have to carry in your heart and choke on them until it is past bearing.

Actually this is no news. It has long been known that each and every thing is decided by the protekcja system, and nobody has the courage to stand up against it, however wrong it may be. The trouble, however, is that today is not like before. Well, when the situation was normal, bearable, when money played no great role, it concerned nobody that thanks to protekcja a private budget was enlarged by a minimum; society did not reckon with such trifles and paid no great attention to it all. It is quite different now, however, in the present time, when a private budget is enlarged with the help of society — even by a minimum — because of the prevailing protekcja system: this is an enormous injustice, an unheard-of crime that must not be tolerated.

Today, when a person is "slipped in" to a public institution only because he is without a livelihood, and afterwards this tells on the people's pockets, it must by no means whatsoever be done. It goes without saying that it is a great thing to give a livelihood to someone who is going hungry. But all this is said when that one person is a rarity and when it does not land on the public's neck. It is quite different, however, when those without a livelihood are a very large number of the citizens, and because of a select few the whole community must suffer, and on everyone who still has the possibility of standing on his feet — on that element — one makes heavier the burdens that were heavy enough until now, as a result of which a systematic decline is plainly visible.

Private firms that want to exist and keep afloat keep thinking and scheming how to cut their budgets, and whatever is at all possible for them is reduced to a minimum. On the other hand, nobody thinks at all, and still less does anything, about the community coming to meet the individual halfway. Let the individual calculate as far as possible how to need less — the community takes no account of it, so that everything is loaded onto the individual's shoulders, and let him toil hard and bitterly, pulling hard and bitterly at the thick ropes that so embitter his life, because of the hopeless prospects.

It is quite different, however, with public institutions: with them we do not see any economy being made, because they know that they draw their income from the community; on the contrary, there they even strive to draw in as many of their own people as possible, and pay no regard whatever to the prevailing hard situation.

The tax question — about which people keep writing that taxes should be reduced: not only are they not reduced, but people keep thinking how to increase them and create new ones. So it is with the government taxes, and it is no better with the municipal taxes. New taxes are created all the time with no regard whatever for the citizens, for whom the municipal authority is supposed to care; they only search out new names, and fresh taxes are born.

In our own homely little world, too, in the Jewish mouse-nest, it is no better. Our broken kehilla representations, with all their shortcomings, help to aggravate the Jewish situation as much as they possibly can. The rabbinate, around which the whole kehilla council revolves, as if there were nothing else in the sad Jewish kehilla life, keeps thinking how to grab as much as possible into its domain and there to work out a special world-view to which all of Jewish life shall have to adapt. The rabbinate in Będzin reckons with nothing; they only keep thinking how to obtain as much income as possible, and since they have no other recourse than to take the Torah to their aid, they come in the name of the holy Torah and cry: little Jews, good little Jews, dear little Jews, beloved little Jews, pious little Jews, be so good as to shell out [lit. "strum the cymbal"] for all sorts of labels that we shall show you, because it is in the name of the Torah, in the name of the little people whom we need on every occasion when there is merely a danger that the transgressors might break in; these "people of our own" we need, so that they guard our interests and stand on watch against every trouble — may none come. But the money, God forbid, we do not ask for nothing: we will reward you for it with various labels — meat labels and dairy labels, red, green and blue labels and, God willing, dyed[?] labels and assorted coloured labels; if need be, there will be all kinds of colours. The main thing is that you should be pious and obey everything we tell you, and then there will be "a redeemer shall come to Zion" and "speedily in our days, amen", so that we shall be protected and have for that purpose people of our own, "anshei shlomeinu".

And besides that you should know that not everything will be made of paper coloured labels; we will go, God willing, ever further and further, and if you listen to us it will be good for you in this world and well for you in the next; then we will add for you our own shochet and our own moreh hora'ah, and so we will go ever further and further... Rest assured that we will then see to it that all your money falls first of all into our hands, and with God's help you will not regret it...

That is how they keep thinking and pondering in the Agudah circles, and with an enormous appetite they want to swallow everything — and this, God forbid, not for themselves or for the "court people" who stand on watch to guard their "Torah interests"; the aim, of course, is nothing more than that Jews should be "true Jews", "Jewish Jews"; and what one is told to pay above all, and the constant enlarging of the rabbinate's budget — this is nothing more than a kind of tax levied[?] in the name of the Agudah Torah for religious purposes.

That is how they think to improve the Jewish situation, how they want to help the Jewish people in its serious, hard situation, how they take into account that Jews are starving in the literal sense of the word and that Jewish livelihoods are being lost from day to day. That all this is done in the name of the holy Torah — it is hardly worth saying.

The question arises, however: may one remain indifferent and watch with an easy conscience with what hypocrisy they want to blind the eyes of the whole community? May we remain indifferent to all this, as if it were not all being done at our address and as if it were not our money it cost? Is today really a time when one can allow oneself to lead a lavish life and not to reckon that one must not throw money away on useless things? Should one not rather reduce what one can do without, just as everyone does in their private businesses and in their private lives? May we stand at a distance, shake our heads and mockingly laugh at everything done in our name — and afterwards we must bear all this at our own expense and carry it on our shoulders? Must we not, in this case, give ourselves a clear account of what crime we commit by our indifference?

It is high time to realise that not a single grosz may leave our pockets when it is not necessary and when we have the possibility of doing without such things.

R. Lem.
