The Results of Immature Activity

[Zagłębie — artisans; article.]

(The most impoverished, most productive part of the Jewish masses.)

There were times when the artisan section played the most important role in our poor public life; wherever one turned, they occupied a most honourable place. In the kehillas, in our financial institutions, in the philanthropic societies — everywhere they had the upper hand; even in the municipal self-government bodies they were broadly represented. Nor was that any wonder, for they had honestly earned the majority: by the power of votes they attained their prestige.

And because of this power of theirs, society entrusted them with the most important functions, and, let the truth be told to its credit, they often knew how to use their public offices for the good of the community and for the interests of the broad strata of the population. And thanks to these privileges of theirs they won the trust of the broad masses, so that the offices entrusted to them were also gladly supported by others, by their sympathisers, and it came about that they acquired friends even among outside elements.

The artisan masses, the working population, then rose to the highest pedestal; they achieved what they had not even dreamt of, and this too was understandable, for they had strength, and they devoted their free time to the good of their brethren. They believed extraordinarily in their mighty power; they believed blindly in everything; never in their lives did it occur to them that they could make any mistakes whatsoever, and when they saw plainly that a mistake had indeed been made by them — which is in fact understandable in anyone — they reckoned [?] that the mistakes they had made were in their own favour and for the benefit of the whole community.

That is how far their short-sightedness, their blind ambition went. Often unforgivable mistakes were made, which we pointed out to them at the time; we told them, and gave logical reasons, that not all their paths were the straight line; but they were strong, touchy, and at once knew how to take offence and raise a storm. Yet our experience did not frighten us off, and we carried out our part methodically: when they accomplished something for the community, we said "yishar koach" to them in the name of society and gave them courage for the future; and when they deserved reproach, they received it from us, without our taking their power and influence into account. We explained to them the mistakes made and told them that toward the community one must bear the broadest responsibility, and that if one is not careful [garbled in print], that is a shortcoming, an unforgettable error for the future work on behalf of their interests.

But once they had risen to the proper height, they forgot everything; they forgot that one does no favours and that one is leading the community astray. Although they had a tremendous experience behind them, they did not stop at the shortcomings that had been committed by them almost consciously, and they did not think of ways to get back onto the straight line on which they had walked at the very beginning; on the contrary, they penetrated ever deeper into the crooked, branching road, so that the population began to feel it on its shoulders, and the Divine Presence began to withdraw from them; their prestige began to fall faster and faster, until disputes broke out not only outside, but frictions, dangerous secessions and quarrels arose within their own inner camps, until it came to splits and dissolutions. Because the disharmony led [printed "dedfirt"] to complete ruin, today, at the present moment, all the artisan institutions are torn apart and dissolved [?], and of their public wealth, which had been accumulated here in Zagłębie in the good times, a heap of ashes remains.

Yes, today one does not even know that they once occupied so honourable a place in our world. Not even any traces of their once fruitful activity remain.

Why do we say this? Why have we mentioned it? Yes — when times are bad, one remembers the good times. It is no longer news that things are bad, bitter, among all strata of the Jewish population; but to the extent [?] that the crisis has struck the Jewish community, it has struck the artisans most of all. The artisan is being ruined from all sides: he has not a stitch of work; the workshop stands covered over until they come to take it from him for taxes. And if the impoverished craftsman is helpless when he stops earning a livelihood, he becomes completely bewildered when he has to defend and justify himself before the authorities. Here he loses all his balance; he cannot defend himself, because he is broken and crushed by the starving days, weeks and months.

Yes, in such a bitter time people will only now [realise] how useful their institutions would have been to the artisans, institutions to which they could turn both for material support and for civil legal advice, which they need in dealing with the authorities.

How many times do we see artisans pay the same tax twice, only because they cannot defend themselves, or they do not have the receipts with which they could prove that the tax or instalment had already been paid by them once. In the matter of paying taxes the artisan is completely helpless: he does not know what he has to pay and what he has paid, so that as soon as the bailiff comes in to him and he has money, he pays; and as soon as he has none, it comes to the point that they sell off his only breadwinner — the machine — and he does not even know whether he had to pay the tax at all, or whether he had not already paid it once.

So much for the civic duties of the artisan. The question is therefore put to his leaders and representatives [printed "postulatn" — doubtful]: were they permitted to abandon their poor, or now impoverished, comrades in such a terrible situation that they have no one to turn to in these difficult tax matters, which they have no idea how to settle? In fact this element pays the most unjust taxes, because he has no bookkeeper to keep his accounts, he has no one to keep the paid receipts for him, or to know how to keep track of the deadlines, so that he ends up paying every time anyone simply demands it of him, without knowing where in the world he stands. In the field of taxes the artisan is completely in the dark.

And in such a critical time, at such a hard moment for the middle class and the petty bourgeoisie in general and for the artisan in particular, all sorts of individuals crawl out as if from their burrows, who supposedly want to rescue their artisan "comrades", and among themselves, without further ado, help — no matter how, directly or indirectly — to destroy this oppressed, impoverished craftsman, who in his despair thinks that anyone is able to help him, that everyone wants to save him from the dangerous situation in which he is already sinking.

The wretched, helpless craftsman does not even hit upon the idea that these harmful elements are out only for their own benefit, and that for the sake of the most minimal material gain of their own they are capable of abandoning the artisan's property and existence.

The artisan, who is crushed, does not realise that in order to get involved with people one must demand responsibility from them on the one hand, and on the other hand one must have sympathy for them and the awareness of carrying out what is entrusted to them; otherwise they remain hanging as if between heaven and earth.

Now as to the economic situation in general. Does anyone know how broken and crushed the artisan class is now? Do we, who are not artisans, feel their terrible condition, when everything stands rusting and when the fingers grow soft from not taking any tool in hand?

Who more than the artisan needed his own representation — precisely in a time of trouble — to which he could turn for advice and assistance, for material and moral support?

Yes, the artisans' representatives ought to have prepared good ground, an organised body that would come to the help of its comrade in a critical situation; and since they did not do so in their time, since they then had no understanding of it, their comrades now find themselves in such a dreadful situation, with no one to whom they can stretch out their hands for help, for support.

These, unfortunately, are the results of immature public activity.

R. Let.
In the Polish Switzerland

[Travel — Ojców and environs; trip sketch.] (From a visit to Ojców).
S. Lewkowicz.
— You've still not been to Ojców? — a young schoolgirl laughs at me; so close and still not been!
— Yes, my child — I answer — I have not yet seen the place that foreigners — not citizens of this country — call the Polish Switzerland. And do you know why, my child? Because among the nations of the world tourism takes first place in private life, whereas we, especially people of the older generation, mock those who go into raptures over beautiful natural scenery..
And in order "to wash myself clean of the sin," I accepted the invitation of "Chachmei"[?] and
— we are off to Ojców...
After a half-hour journey from Olkusz we enter the vestibule of Ojców — Pieskowa Skała, an idyllic village surrounded by tall pine trees and rocks.
On a hill stands a three-storey building, a noble one; there — if we are to believe what the guide tells us — King Casimir the Great lived at the time of the Polish uprising in the 16th century.
We grow curious, and after [—] [?] we receive permission to visit the historic palace. Right at the entrance — figures of Polish knights, the heroic "shapragtses"[?]. They lie comfortably stretched out and "listen" to the praises the guide recounts at their expense...
On the first floor, in the knights' hall [the "Rycerska"], stands an old sofa; this "object," too, is supposedly a relic of the 14th century. In general, a century plays no great role here. There are all sorts of "antiques" from all sorts of centuries. But what interests me most is the "antique" of the last century, a famous[?] Polish patriot who took from the palace everything that had any historic value, and vanished...
Thus we stride from room to room. The guide waits until the whole company of our excursion has gathered and delivers the rest of his sermon, on chivalry, the judgment of God, and presently he shows us how the kings of old used secret powers to get at the truth from the guilty. He takes his place in a corner of a wall, whispers there softly and tells us to put an ear to the other side — and one will hear secret "voices."
The crowd obeys; the girls of the excursion strain their sense of hearing and they "declare" [oświadczają] that — "one really does hear the wall talking"...
———
The road to Ojców is splendid; the fellow-travellers envy those sitting by the windows of the bus, because they can see the beauties of nature along the way better...
The mood in the bus grows merrier. The Jewish-Polish girls exhaust the whole repertoire of the latest Polish hit songs and, at the end — "The First Brigade"...
And no wonder; I myself, having barely set foot on the purely Polish soil, felt a longing to sing the Polish anthem — "Jeszcze Polska nie zginęła," because Ojców and its surroundings must be the pride of the Polish Endeks [National Democrats], not to speak of the fact that nature has grown up here so beautifully; but the Endecja can "boast" that the area has not yet been "grabbed" by Jewish hands... Everywhere Jewish power and Jewish capital have managed to dominate — but not in Ojców; the place is to this day[?] "Judenrein"; you will not meet there a single Jewish business, Jewish restaurant, not even a Jewish dealer... When you stroll in Ojców you forget completely that three kilometres away lies the shtetl of Skała... Everything is Polonized; even when a Jewish housewife in a wig comes to Ojców on a Sunday for a few hours, she too becomes "intelligentsia" and conducts her conversation with Mendel (yes, he wears a hat...) also — "po polskiemu" [in Polish]... otherwise the people around would look at them as at terrible enemies..
———
In Ojców we engage a second guide; he, the new guide, denies and turns into "ash and mud" all the legends that the "Pieskowa man" had told us. The new "Baedeker" is an ardent devotee of King Łokietek, who hid in the "grottoes" during the war with the Czech king Wenceslas, and perhaps that is why the "grottoes" occupy such an important place in Ojców. If someone says he comes from Ojców, the first question put to him is:
— Been in the "grottoes"?
On the way to the "royal place" the eye is captivated by the wondrously beautiful landscapes and picturesqueness. Ah! the guide exclaims, if this region were in "Leipish"[?] hands, what wouldn't there be here? There are also — he says — healing springs, but everything is still neglected; the whole patriotism consists of dropping in for a day and eating lunch at "Pod Łokietkiem"...
Before we enter the "historic cave," each member of our company is provided with a small lit candle; it gives the impression that our Marranos went off with Yom Kippur candles in their hands to a cave for the Kol Nidrei prayer..
We stride through the terrible cave; the crowd cringes with fear, but — we go on... The guide halts the "train" and points: "Right here King Łokietek had his dining room, there — his bedroom, a bit further — was the hall for the knights. [—] We listen and believe — after all, we are in the dark; more darkness — more faith... And indeed, many of us began to "believe" in the resurrection of the dead: that coming out of this ruin in one piece is truly a great "miracle"...
We visited other places too, but there, where nature holds sway, everything is so beautiful and fresh, and wherever a human hand meddles[?] — it is ruined and neglected.
It was truly a pity to part so soon from the beautiful landscapes that Ojców possesses, but when we hear the signal of the leader Plesner[?] — "jedziemy do domu" [we're going home], we must perforce settle ourselves back in the bus and leave the place that has been crowned with the name
— the Polish Switzerland...
Mockery.

[Essay — reflections; the crisis of society and the age.] By J. J. Sigal.

If I should have the privilege — or the misfortune — of living to see the later time, when the "future" historian sits down to write the chapter about our days — if I could slip under his arm and quietly, quietly listen as he ponders a word, a title for the chapter of history, I would murmur to him and advise him to call the chapter — the age of mockery of man. He will realize it anyway when he goes through all the sad and grievous details, all the troubles the present generation has endured. At first it will not be so clear to him how people bore such torments and yet patiently kept silent; but then the human being in him will speak — the one who looks upon the human race as unique of its kind — a phenomenon in the world of creatures that lives out its life and develops in culture and in an environment of a different kind, a civilized life. He will then be no historian but a human being who is "in the game" — but when he begins to sum up, to draw the total, he will understand and — still be unable to forgive, because mockery is the lowest and ugliest trait of cruelty, the expression of a sadism that sucks everyone's blood through a very, very sublimated vessel and means.

From too much abundance and surfeit the holders of power in the world, the very masters of the world, without rendering account to themselves, began to mock and jeer at their own kind. Tormenting has already become a natural function for them; for this they received a right from the gods. Their abilities raised them to those heights and thrones from which all the decrees of oppression came down. Great became the tumult in the world, all lands were mined[?] and all seas, states became great and mighty, and everything, everything was built not on any great goodness and "humaneness", or. Who stopped to dwell on such trifles, when the work for a great, mighty world was not permitted to stop? The "mission" of man became to build up a stormy[?] civilization up to the sky. So all "obstacles" in the way had to be removed and swept aside; people went "forward", onward" — ever further and further...

And — the historical tribal [stage; "shmokhes" — doubtful reading] we have long since passed beyond. Now one can recall it with a proud smile and display the [?"beykhige"] "personality"... with dignity, that one is no longer wild; but that to which one has flown "with railways and aeroplanes" is, it seems to me, another kind of wildness, which may very closely resemble that prehistoric state and perhaps far surpass it. It is the wildness of excess and decadence in the conduct of human life, which points to that [generation] "wholly guilty" before the Messiah comes.

And how does it show itself? — In the malicious mockery that has ruled the sated "pibik[?] of the strong". Satiety has planted itself in a laughter that is the expression of abundance, over the misfortune of those who are the continuation of hungry generations, generation after generation, age after age. People saw before them a new, the newest kind of pleasure; the body began to feel cynical and to puff itself up in the supreme enjoyment of which it had amassed and swilled so much. It began to celebrate its own triumph, and the hymns it sang out were — mockery! Mockery over its fellow men, whom it used as one uses stone and brick, as one uses sand and dust and water. It saw the masses before it as inanimate matter, with which it could do whatever its heart desired. It shovelled them into heaps like sand, poured them and kneaded them, mixed and cast them and chemically transformed them into whatever was needed. And this very achievement, this pliant material, so broadened his heart, and he took a look at the used-up and saw them as the leftover, the straw on the fields, after the grains had already lain thoroughly[?] threshed, and — he burst out laughing with pleasure: this straw comes from the same kind as I, ha-ha-ha-ha! When all the pleasures have worn off, when even the pride in the conquests has grown paler, one must laugh at the used-up, one must trample over them with mockery and sweep them away with one's feet.

This mockery, the indifferent watching as people perish, as hunger rages in homes and cold, like a wolf, threatens to kill the small, badly nourished children in thousands of rooms, the spreading of a thick shadow of melancholy over the gaunt faces of so many wretched and drained people — how else can one call it but mockery! Mockery of those who have been cheated and fooled, mockery of everything that, since men became men, has been spoken and preached from all pulpits and platforms; mockery of the great teachers and teachings, ethics and humanisms, morals and warnings, which passed from book to book and drove people out of the streets and houses — as soon as one had eaten one's fill and slept calmly through a night.

Mockery of everything that was held holy; arts grew up in the shade and light of the religions. And around all this the wings of a demon have now spread — one which, it seems, always hovered [?"hetter"] around and bared its teeth and laughed and derided... It laughed at human earnestness, at endeavour, at good deeds, at the illusion of beauty that made one forget the monotonous grey everyday; it laughed at all sacrifices and all martyrs who raised their lives like a torch in the darkness of human wandering in the wilderness and wildness of history; it laughed at everything and everyone, and now this demon has entered into that sated and calm, self-crowned, sole-ruling "flesh and blood" and bursts out of him with mockery, mockery and mockery.

But it is a bitter pleasure; there is in it a spark of madness, a portent of that dark insanity which creeps from the gloomy caves to suicide. Not the single ones, not the dozens, not the thousands of suicides that have multiplied so frighteningly in our days show the tragedy of the time — not they; they are a terrible portent of a great suicide that is moving and drawing ever nearer: the suicide of an entire social order, which now dances its mockery-dance on the skulls of its victims. It dances and laughs, it dances and laughs, it dances and mocks, it dances and — dances ever closer to the abyss of madness.

The madness of prosperity has given birth to the dance of mockery; the dance of mockery takes place on the edge of an abyss that has been dug for centuries between one man and another, between one people and another. And no one comes who could hold [it] back from the last leap, from the catastrophic fall and disintegration into dust. Still the voice of the great warning does not come, before which the red[?] one, grown dull with satiety, would stagger out of his mockery over the world and — take a step back from the edge of the abyss on which he dances and into which he rolls his mocking, cold, half-insane laughter.
Let the Merchant Catch His Breath a Little!

The only estate that throughout the whole 14 years of Poland's independence has been treated like a stepchild is the merchant class. Its role in the modern apparatus of exchange has not been appreciated. At a time when the state, within the limits of the possible, looked after other estates, the merchant estate was decried as a parasite, a useless element, etc.
Suffice it to mention that at a time when merchants paid, in direct taxes alone, 38 per cent of all taxes, the percentage of credits that reached the merchants amounted to barely 8 per cent. The disproportion is glaring enough and needs no comment.
Nor did the anti-merchant front stop there: new economic theories were created in order to sanction the cartels and syndicates that had been founded, which with their policy of exploitation finished off the merchant. Etatism in its various forms likewise had only one aim: to render harmless the few merchants who are still breathing.
The aim was quickly achieved: solid businesses were turned into ruins; the whole merchant community finds itself on the edge of want and despair, because it is no longer capable of resisting all the attacks upon it.
The resilience of the merchant and the trader is broken; only now has the government seen itself compelled to convene a conference with representatives of the merchants on the situation of the merchant estate. At the conference, held on 31 May, the directors of the state banks and the director of the credit department of the Ministry of Finance took part this time. Credit aid for merchants was discussed. The merchants put forward minimal demands, which do not exceed the bounds of the possible and are at the same time a necessity of state. Perhaps this time the deciding factors will show a drop of goodwill towards the exhausted merchant community?
If trade does indeed feel a change in the state's attitude towards it, if refreshing credits are injected into it and, on the other hand, the heavy tax pressure eases a little, a breathing pause may come for trade, and in that time the merchants will be able to gather a little fresh strength to endure the general crisis.
A breathing pause is capable of sustaining thousands of trading families and at the same time improving economic conditions in the whole country, because the merchant estate fulfils a very important function in economic life: it gives credit to consumption, develops and expands it, and keeps stocks of goods in shops and warehouses at its own expense, which in itself strengthens production and gives people work.
The planned relief action for the merchants comes a little too late, but "better late than never".
By all means — let us see! Z. Malecki.
Troubles from Children.

(Monologue.)
You say: troubles from children... But I tell you, not all troubles are alike... One can talk about troubles from children when the children, for instance, are good-for-nothings, rowdies, spendthrifts, card-players, drunkards and who knows what other shlimazls — well, then you have troubles! And not just troubles, but real disgrace and shame — you can't look a person in the eye. But at least you know why you are suffering: you pinch your cheeks so that the colour, as they say[?], holds up... But successful, decent.. God-blessed children — the kind every father and mother would wish for — and still you have troubles from them — how would you explain that?
You shrug your shoulders? I shrug too...
Many children? God forbid! All in all I have a girl and a boy — two, as they say. Well, the girl — she is a real girl! Pretty, clever, accomplished, sings, plays the piano and the violin and whatever you like: dances superbly — I tell you — a fine child. You might think I praise her because I am her father — I tell you no. On the contrary, ask the neighbours and you'll hear. My son — a couple of years older — is also a dear child: tall as a pine, red and white, well educated, also plays the violin and the piano. And that is just where the dog lies buried — that is where my troubles begin...
You smile? I care very little. You may smile in good health, even laugh out loud, I won't forbid you, but I tell you that if you were the father of such children, you would smile differently. Let me tell you further how one gets troubles from respectable children. Well then, my son plays ball. If I were to tell you that I know what it is and how it is played, I would be a liar. I was told — that is: my son took pains to explain to me what sort of thing it is. "You take," he says, "a ball, a big 'pilka', and one kicks it away to a second, the second throws it to a third and so on, until they all come together, they line up 'rekom'[?], head to head, and someone throws the ball into the middle, then there is shoving[?] and kicking and... Whoever gets to give the ball the first kick out, he is" — I don't know what he is...
Never mind. At first I didn't want my son to go and throw the ball, but when I was told that it is nothing more than a bit of gymnastics, I agreed; gymnastics is good, especially since he, my son, that is, sits properly over his books — it is certainly good for him to have a little movement, to get the blood moving.
Several weeks went by, I was content; he, my son — flourishing[?]. All of a sudden he comes limping. What's the matter? He got a blow on the leg; well, cold compresses were applied, he was treated, doctored — thank God, he recovered. "Perhaps," I say to him, "that's enough gymnastics already?" He smiles: "What does it bother you," he says, "if I spend an hour or two a day?" "Arn[?]," I say, "it doesn't bother me at all; on the contrary," I say, "I am glad you enjoy yourself, but that while enjoying yourselves you kick one another — that I don't like." He smiles again: "There was," he says, "an accident. It's nothing," he says. And he went on playing.
One day I look — woe is me! — my boy arrives in a cab, his whole head bandaged. What's the matter? What happened? "Nothing," he says. "Nothing, and your head bandaged?" "Nothing —"
I take off the bandage — and I nearly died on the spot: his whole mouth covered in blood and two teeth missing! What? How? He caught no more than a single kick in the mug... A series of doctors and X-rays began — and it cost a fortune.
"Well," I say, "an end! No more gymnastics, no more games, no more ball! An end! I am surely not obliged to lose my health and my money." Well, the time he was ill he did not leave the house, didn't play ball and didn't get kicks — and then my boy goes and puts on those certain clothes and begs me to let him go and play. "Players have come," he says, "from somewhere, and he would like to take part. Firstly," he says, "he will be in the newspapers, make a name for himself, you know; secondly, he really needs a bit of gymnastics — he hasn't moved for so long"... And he begs me literally as if I were a robber. I looked at him and saw that he was indeed paler than before and that a little gymnastics would not harm him, so I allowed him, on condition that he be careful and not stay out long. He got dressed and left.
Not an hour had passed when a carriage drives up and they carry him in in their arms! Well, what is there to say? They had beaten him[?]. His face was torn to pieces, you couldn't see either eyes or nose — in short, they crippled him for ever; again a whole "wedding" began with doctors, X-rays, and money flowed like water.
When he was a little better, some of his friends — young fellows — came to visit the sick; they were very sorry for him and said that if not for this, they would have won.
"What exactly," I say to them, "would you have won?"
"What do you mean," they are very surprised, glancing at one another — "what would have been? Had we won the prize, we would not have lost — you understand? And it is all his fault" — they point at my son.
And now[?] you say "troubles from children..."
The Path of Suffering of the Jewish Matura Graduate

[Article — education and higher studies; Zagłębie.]
The Zagłębie gymnasia have now once again sent out several dozen young people with certificates of maturity.
The greater part of them want to study medicine. Jewish parents mostly want their child to be a doctor. But the study of medicine and the related fields (dentistry, veterinary science and pharmacy) is, because of the de facto "numerus clausus," possible only for a select few. That is a fact known to everyone.
But since the Jewish matura graduate does not want to give up — and his parents certainly not; after all they want to have nachas from their children — he decides to go abroad. Studying abroad undoubtedly has its advantages: the universities are good, one learns a European language, one becomes acquainted with Western European culture, etc. But what does this pleasure cost? In today's bad times the parents must be made to understand that if they are not able to send their children abroad a considerable sum of money a year for the whole course of study (six years), they had better give up straight away on having a son a doctor or a daughter a dentist. These are no exaggerations, and one must not imagine that one can earn something abroad — that is out of the question.
And if one cannot send the student the necessary sum of money every month and sends him less, one only does the young person harm: having no money he does not eat much, he goes hungry, and within a short time it tells on his state of health. More than once it has already happened that healthy matura graduates went abroad and a year later came back ill, with ruined stomachs and often with signs of consumption.
And even when the lucky one does get through the whole course abroad and squanders his best years on it, he cannot practise afterwards. Abroad, as a foreigner, he is not permitted to. In Poland he must first have his degree nostrified, i.e. pass all the examinations once again. That can take a minimum of two-three years or even longer. Thus one has to sacrifice almost ten whole years in order then to earn one's bread as a doctor.
Is it worth it!
Almost the same can be said about studying engineering. At the only one, the Warsaw Polytechnic, Jews are admitted in minimal numbers. One goes abroad, especially to France — earning is impossible, money has to be sent from home for 5–6 years; besides, such studies demand abilities. And above all: after finishing it is very hard to get settled. The state and the municipal institutions, which employ the greatest number of engineers, do not take Jewish engineers; private industry and free enterprise do not need many engineers, and even less so when it comes to Jews. That is precisely why dozens of Jewish engineers now go about without a stitch of work and simply die of hunger.
So much for the so-called "practical" faculties. No better are the prospects in other fields of study that a Jewish student can go through in Poland.
The study of law is, from the economic side, easier than medicine. One can quietly study at home and travel to the university for the examinations. But the drawbacks of this study are great. Four-five years one must study, three years one must do an apprenticeship at the court, two years one must do an apprenticeship with an advocate. One thus has to lose 10 years — not counting the waiting for a court apprenticeship — until one manages to become an advocate. Incidentally, the Jews are made difficulties: they are made to wait for an apprenticeship two and even three years, and for the work at the court they are not paid, at a time when Christian apprentices receive salaried posts. Nevertheless the Jewish students, having no other way out, have so filled the law faculties that today an overproduction of Jewish lawyers is already noticeable, and a quiet competitive struggle among them. This will be even stronger in the nearest years, and for anyone who is now beginning his law studies there is a meagre prospect of a livelihood ten years from now.
This summing-up has not been made in order to frighten anyone off, to push the young matura graduate away from the source of knowledge; the point is only that every single one who intends to study further should know exactly what difficulties his studies involve, what he has to expect after finishing his studies, and whether he is able to overcome all that.
Not every matura graduate needs to study. One finishes the gymnasium not only in order to be able to study further at a university, but first and foremost in order to obtain a secondary education. Every graduate must remember this; the parents must remember this. Only the truly able should study at the institutions of higher learning. The others must look for a different path in life, one that can make them no less happy than studying. Yes, we Jews need an intelligentsia, without which the people cannot exist. But one must not allow an overproduction of intellectuals, because that can do great harm to the life of the people.
R. N.
Jewish merchants from Poland two hundred years ago.

[History — Polish Jewry; article.] (A page of Jewish history, specially for our newspaper.)

In the year 1732 a larger number of Jewish merchants who had come from Poland to Leipzig are recorded for the first time in the archives of the Leipzig Fair Office. It is interesting to delve into the various files kept at the Leipzig Fair Office that deal with the Jewish merchants from Poland of that time.

What did they buy and what did they sell? On this there are precise descriptions in Leipzig.

They used to arrive at the Leipzig fair with 40 to 200 large wagons, fully loaded with small pelts, mostly of hares or also of wild animals. These pelts they would sell in Leipzig, and with that money they would buy cloth from the French and English merchants there, which they then carried mostly to Brody, but also to the fairs in Berdichev and in Warsaw, where they were permitted to trade.

But since it often happened that they could not sell all the pelts, they would leave their goods with forwarding agents (expediters), who had then opened in Leipzig for the first time. The forwarders would lend them the money until the next fair, when the goods had been sold.

But there also came merchants with cash to buy goods in Leipzig. Merchants of this kind, however, were rarer, because owing to the unsafe roads people did not dare to carry cash with them.

At first people were unwilling to give the Polish merchants credit; they were considered bad payers. In time they began to give them credit, but the reports of that period state that "with the Polish Jews no good experiences were had"... They did not come again to the next fair, and new merchants came who bought for cash and wanted to settle accounts in place of the old merchants, but the Leipzigers would not come to terms; then, at the following fair, the old merchants came and paid their debts. For years no one would give them credit. Only later, when times grew worse, did they again begin to receive credit. In the report of that time it says: "One must again give the Polish Jews credit, because the Leipzig merchants are dependent on the Polish Jews"...

It was precisely this dependence on the Polish Jews that compelled the Saxon government at the time to grant the Polish Jews various privileges. Such privileges were enjoyed not only not by the Bohemian and Russian Jews, but not even by the local merchants. While, for example, all merchants had to pay weighing fees on all imported and exported goods, the Polish Jews had reductions of up to 75 per cent on all taxes. The government justified these reductions by the fact that Breslau and Frankfurt on the Oder, which lie close to Poland, give the Jews the greatest privileges and are trying to keep the Jews away from the Leipzig fair.

In the year 1747 the Saxon Minister of Trade, Hagen, plainly told the King that experience had shown that "the number of Jewish merchants from Poland, in whose hands the whole of Polish trade lies, is growing smaller and smaller. The reason for this is that while Breslau and Frankfurt treat the Jews with the greatest freedom, in Leipzig they have to pay special taxes. Therefore his opinion is that the Polish Jews should be given exemption from taxes, and he is sure that what the state will lose on the taxes, the merchants will take in ten times over from the Jewish merchants from Poland, who will begin to come to the Leipzig fairs in greater numbers."

And on 8 July 1748 the law was indeed issued that Jewish merchants from Poland receive in Leipzig the greatest reductions, both at the post, at the weigh-house, on excise and on customs.

Two Jews from Dobromil, Wolf Bereth and Josef Lebel, and Moshe Aleksander of Opatów, received on 5 March 1749 the right to stay in Leipzig for several weeks before every fair and several weeks after every fair, and there "to help the Polish Jews in buying and selling their goods."

These were the first Jewish brokers at the Leipzig fair.

A few years later an ukase was issued that "Polish Jews may come to the Leipzig fair without any passports and may stay in the whole Leipzig area wherever they find it necessary and important for their business"...

Z. Haber, Vienna–Leipzig.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shelach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Shelach
—o—
The Portion
A) "Send thou men" (13:1)
"This is what Scripture says: As vinegar to the teeth and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him." (Midrash).
When someone's teeth ache because of vinegar or some other sharp drink, only he himself feels his suffering, which no outsider notices; smoke-reddened eyes, on the other hand — that everyone notices.
The spies, who later turned out to be wicked, were at first also an ailment like a toothache: no one but the sufferer saw it. Later their ailment became a public "smoke to the eyes." Now people realized how they had earlier suffered from them in silence, wrapped as they were in righteousness...
Ohel Yaakov.
B) "Of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a prince among them" (ibid., 2)
When Moses went to choose them, they were simple souls (lemeshkes). "One man" — each regarded himself as plain flesh and blood. "Shall ye send every one a prince among them" — they had stripped the princeship off themselves ("tishlachu" — in the sense of stripping off)[?], poor things. But later, when "Moses sent them," when they had already been chosen and were riding high on their horses, then "all of them were men who were heads of the children of Israel" — then they showed that they were the heads of the children of Israel, that they had power...
Tiferet Shlomo.
C) "And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun Joshua" (ibid., 16)
"He prayed for him: May God save you from the counsel of the spies."
(Midrash Rabbah).
It was for Joshua that Moses trembled most. He, the humble one — the people would believe him; no one would suspect him of arrogance[?]. Should he wish to do harm[?] to the Land, he would succeed best of all. That is why Moses trembled so for him...
Yefe Einayim.
D) "And they told him, and said" (ibid., 27)
What, actually, was the sin of the spies[?] — after all, they told only the truth, only the truth...
But truth does not mean what the outer eye sees. The outer eye can deceive itself; the truth lies deeper. And only in that way can one see the Land of Israel... To the outer eye the Land of Israel is indeed a terror — such neighbours: Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai... the children of Anak... But the higher truth of the Land of Israel lies in God's promise, and striving to find that truth is what is called "telling the truth"...
Nifla'ot Hadashot (Rabbi Mendele[?] of Kotsk).
E) "And they brought up an evil report of the land" (ibid., 32)
Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan, the Rabbi of Kovno, was, as is well known, a Hovev Zion. But he had a secretary, R' Yaakov Lipschitz, who was the enemy of the Hovevei Zion.
Once Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever comes to Kovno and asks his friend Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan to host a meeting of the Hovevei Zion at his home. The Kovno rabbi agrees, but the next day, under pressure from his Zion-hating secretary, he sends him a note in the familiar formula: "Owing to an unforeseen reason, the meeting unfortunately cannot take place at my home, etc."
The next day the Kovno rabbi visits him and invites him to his home for Shabbat, but Rabbi Shmuel declines. Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan feels offended and asks him why he does not accept his invitation.
"Because I am staying at an inn. If I accept your invitation and do not order the Shabbat meal here, but rely on you — what will I do if the next day I receive a little letter from you: 'Owing to an unforeseen reason, the meal unfortunately cannot take place at my home'... I'll be left hungry on Shabbat..."
Ha-Dat ve-ha-Tehiya ha-Le'umit.
F) "How long will they provoke me" (14:11)
"How long will this people provoke me, and how long will they not believe in me."
A strange thing: believe — they do not believe in God, and yet they wage war against Him. If "they will not believe in me," if you, God forbid, do not believe in God, then why "provoke me" — why do you anger me? Does one fight against something that does not exist?...
Bina le-Itim.
The Haftarah
F) "Now therefore, I pray you, swear unto me by the Lord, since I have shown you kindness" (Joshua 2)
No man is ungrateful; everyone feels that for a good deed one must be grateful. But people very much like to persuade themselves that the favour their fellow does them is no favour at all... that it is no good deed on his part, and so they are not obliged to repay him.
That is why Rahab asked the spies only to affirm "that I have shown you kindness" — that they know she did them a kindness. And if only that is clear and certain to them, they will repay her as a matter of course.
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
Avot
H) "And the conversation of children... drives a man from the world" (3:14)
"The conversation of children" — the constant talking about and worrying over the children — that turns a man into a ruin. A man's whole life is filled with worry for the children.
Avodat Yisrael.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (31)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin; installment 31.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Earlier he had gone off to a monastery. He spent many years there, tormented himself with the wildest torments, in order to test his flesh and blood whether they still had anything earthly in them. When he was at last certain that his blood no longer had any power over him, he went off into the deep forest and settled in a little hut. There he lived, entirely close to the "Holy Spirit," free of earthly lusts and desires. And even the iron chains that he had fastened around his emaciated feet were not heavy for him. All earthly pains were far from him. And, as many believed, he could look into every person's fate and know what must and will happen to that person.

Rasputin decided to visit this "holy man" and ask him what to do next: should he return home to his wife and children and to his merry life with the lads and the village girls? Should he return to his horses in the stable? Or should he sacrifice his life to a greater purpose, toward which a "holy" force had drawn him since his youth? He resolved within himself that he would follow the advice of "Father" Makari.

Makari's hut stood deep in the forest. One had to walk a long way over paths and roads before one reached the hut. The hut was poor and small; there was barely enough room in it for one person. In this hut the "starets" lived in great poverty and want, but his face shone with joy and a sunny smile shone from his faded lips. He had a head of tousled, thinning [?] hair and looked altogether wild. His voice was so weak and low that all one could hear was heavy breathing. But in the voice there was a certain homeliness and warmth, as is often the voice of quiet mentally ill people.

When Rasputin came up to the hut in front of which the "starets" was sitting, he threw himself down before him on the ground, seized the old man's hands, on which there were iron chains, and covered them with kisses. The old man looked at him with smiling, bewildered eyes, smiled with a kind of childlikeness and then said:
"Tell me, what is your wish? Tell me, son of God!"

Rasputin remained kneeling before the old man and with tremendous simplicity and frankness told him why he had come to him. He did not need to hide anything. He told of the sinful life he had led, of his sinful thoughts, of his wild passion, which had not ceased tormenting him the whole time he had spent in the monastery, and he also told him of the extraordinary "vision" he had seen. He told of his weaknesses and of the doubts he had; of how he often hears as if an inner voice whispers to him and tells him that he must give himself over to God and take God's mission upon himself — and at the same time he is often overcome by a great longing for his wife and children, for earthly possessions and for the tavern.

Rasputin made his confession kneeling and holding his head bowed to the ground. When he had finished his confession, he raised his head and saw: Makari was smiling at him, looking at him with kindness and friendliness. He kept silent and waited; then he felt on his head the "holy man's" thin skeleton hands and heard his weak voice:
"Rejoice, my son! Rejoice! For out of many thousands God has chosen you alone! Great things await you! Hear my advice, my son! Leave your wife and children, leave your horses and your home [?], hide yourself from people... Go and wander over fields and forests... Go, and you will hear how the earth speaks to you, and you will learn to understand the speech of our holy Russian earth. Then — and not before — you shall return to people, reveal yourself to them and tell them what the holy Russian earth says to them through you... Go, my son!"
"Ah, 'holy Father'!" Rasputin cried out. He was full of ecstasy. His eyes blazed and his face was bathed in radiance. Again he seized the "starets'" hands and covered them with kisses. He breathed heavily and then cried out:
"Bless me, 'Father'!"
The "starets" again smiled a childlike smile, laid his thin hands on Rasputin's head and said in his weak voice:
"Be blessed, my son!"
For a while longer he mumbled something and then fell silent.
Then Rasputin stood up, bowed deeply, took leave of the "holy man" and left him.
— — — — — — — —
Rasputin then returned to Pokrovskoye, took leave of his family and set off wandering.
Setting off to wander and "taking upon oneself exile" [penitential wandering] was at that time very widespread in great Russia. Men of various ages suddenly abandoned their work in the fields, gave up [?] their former names, threw away their former clothes, burned their passports, forgot father and mother, wife and children, friends and acquaintances, and, dressed in rags, with a bag on their shoulders and a staff in hand, they vanished, and no one knew where they were.

Because of the Crisis.

[Sosnowiec — a picture of the times; the crisis and unemployment.] By P. Palier.
(A Picture of the Times).

G., a resident of Sosnowiec, was counted among the best craftsmen. He had always done not badly. He never lacked work. He ran his own independent workshop, in which he employed several people.
G. married for love. He got to know a decent, respectable girl and took her without a penny of dowry. For a long time after the wedding they lived happily. His happiness grew even greater when his beloved, faithful wife bore him, in the course of time, two lovely and well-turned-out children. He, the husband, worked and earned nicely, and she, the wife, kept a respectable household. Their family life went on like a lovely, quiet idyll.
But with the coming of the bitter crisis the idyll was shattered. Unemployment burst into G.'s workshop with its sharp claws and drove out first the employed workers. Then G. too was left without a stitch of work and began to wander, an unemployed man like many, in despair through the streets of Zagłębie.
At first the wife, a great homemaker, tried hard to keep their poverty from being noticed; the want that was already whistling in every corner she would not let out into the street. So they quietly began to sell everything in the house, but it went so far that in the end there was nothing left to sell. They had owed the rent for almost a year already, so they had to cut down from three rooms and move into one room — the smallest little room, where they suffered in great cramped conditions.
But all this did little to save the situation; there was no longer anything with which to buy bread. The little children begged with tears in their eyes for at least a piece of dry bread, and even that was no more. The young, hungry and languishing children, with their young, still unripe little minds, already understood the reason why there was no bread. So with dimmed little eyes and pounding little hearts they asked, one after another: Daddy, when will there be work.
G. stroked his children's little heads and comforted them that today or tomorrow he would get work and then they would buy bread. But deep inside he felt his heart being torn apart; he could no longer bear to watch the suffering of his wife and children, and he resolved on something he himself had not believed he would be capable of.
One evening at dusk he took himself off to a remote back street and stretched out his hand for alms. When it had grown quite late and people stopped passing and the street became empty, G. came home miserable, broken and black as the earth, so that he could not be recognised. He said nothing, only laid down a few groszy. When the wife went out to the street to buy something for the hungry children, G. disappeared again, but he never came home anymore: someone had recognised him standing in that back street with an outstretched hand, and so he could no longer stay in Sosnowiec. He went off to another town, but as bad luck would have it he met familiar faces there too, and he decided to uproot himself from there as well.
But where to?
Nobody knows that anymore. Not even his own wife; even from her he kept himself hidden, for fear that it would become known. Until recently he still sent something home, but lately he sends nothing at all and gives no sign of life. The wife now ponders a great deal: perhaps he again ran into an acquaintance from Sosnowiec and went off still further.
But where to? That the lonely, desperate wife does not know, and she shudders at the mere thought that perhaps he has fled to the place from which one never comes back...
For everywhere he meets acquaintances...
P. Palier.
A Letter from Eretz Israel (From Our Correspondent)

[Eretz Israel — letter from our correspondent.] Mister Steinhändler in Jerusalem, having once counted up his fortune, looked around and saw that he was still not rich enough — there were many people far richer than he — and he "decided" to become a richer man.
But how does one become rich all at once? One fine morning he dressed himself up, boarded a ship and travelled to Europe. First he went to Riga, put up at a first-class hotel, introduced himself everywhere as a great Jerusalem merchant, rode around in motor cars, tipped the servants as befits a rich man, in general led a rich life, and placed large advertisements in the newspapers (at the cash-box's expense...) saying that he had come to buy machines. All day long his door had no rest: agents, merchants, manufacturers etc. came and placed orders; not every merchant had the "privilege" of his buying from them, and with each he settled on 20 per cent cash and the remaining 80 per cent in instalments, and so he bought machines for a handsome few thousand, and the machines were shipped to Jerusalem.
In Jerusalem Mister Steinhändler sold the machines, enlarged his capital and opened a bigger business.
And suddenly, as he sat thus in his office, triumphant over his good deals, in comes a gentleman with a briefcase in his hand and asks: "Are you Mister Steinhändler?" — "Yes, please sit down [?]. Who are you?" — "I am from the police, and I have been instructed to provide you with a 'free' hotel." And here is what had come to light:
The Riga manufacturers, after the date of the first instalment had passed and they had received no money, began writing letters to Jerusalem; at first they politely asked after his health and "in passing" mentioned the instalment. But when they had no answer at all "about his health", they began writing only about the instalments. Mister S., however, apparently begrudged the postage stamp and did not answer at all. The manufacturers, seeing that the merchant was pretending ignorance, hit upon the following device: they wrote about the affair to the Latvian consul in Jerusalem, enclosing all the invoices, and the consul, after a certain investigation, established that the merchant had long since sold the goods and pocketed the money, and handed the matter over to the police.
The merchant was arrested, his goods were auctioned off, and the money collected was sent by the Latvian consul to Riga, to the merchants.
———
In Haifa there recently died the clergyman Sabbatai Rohold, head of the British mission in Palestine, director of the "Bible School" in Haifa and former editor of the English missionary paper "Hope of Israel" in Chicago. And now it turns out that the late clergyman was a former yeshiva student, the son of a rabbi and a grandson of the author of the famous book "Or Nogah", R. Kalmush of Chrzanów. It will therefore be interesting to relate his life story.
He was born in the small town of Wiśnicz [?]; his father gave him a strict religious upbringing, he studied in yeshivas, and already in his youth he began studying a great many Kabbalah books, used to fast and run into the forest to practise solitary meditation (hitbodedut). When he reached the age of 16 his father died, and guardianship over him was taken over by a relative of his, an uncle, Yehoshua Chajes in Brisl [?]. This uncle, a great maskil, began to implant Haskalah in him and sent him to Berlin to study at the rabbinical seminary.
In Berlin he met a distant relative of his, Jedidiah Lucky, a missionary originally from Kraków. Lucky was well known in Berlin for his unusual conduct; he considered himself something of a messiah and went about with the idea of a union of Jews and Christians, and this Lucky had a great influence on Sabbatai and used him as an emissary to spread Lucky's idea.
Later Sabbatai went to Leipzig, and there the well-known missionary Franz Delitzsch baptised him; then he joined up with Pastor Strester [?] of America, and together with Pastor Strester, who had then come to Europe, began to organise missionary activity among the Polish Jews. Later he went off to Chicago, where he edited the above-mentioned paper.
In 1920 he came to Eretz Israel and, together with the Jerusalem apostate Aharon Segal, a rabbi's son (about whom I shall write in a second letter), founded the "Bible School" in Haifa.
About his activities the following is also related: in 1905 he came with Pastor Strester to Warsaw to see for themselves the "work" of their new convert Abraham Rozencwajg, who wore Orthodox dress and was secretly baptised, and about whom it had been reported that he did nothing for the mission and took money for nothing. And as was reported to headquarters, his work consisted of this: twice a year, when Pastor Strester came, he would invite him into a beit midrash to hear his sermon. His sermon was an ordinary one on various "matters", but in the middle of the sermon he would mention "Messiah", "Righteous Redeemer" many times, and since Strester knew no Yiddish apart from the words "Messiah" and "Righteous Redeemer", he was sure that he had given a missionary sermon.
But how Rohold unmasked him, and what became of him — in a second letter.
Under Police Guard

[Będzin — Kehilla; the shochtim.]
The kehilla board decides to engage 2 young shochtim — a hail of stones and glass in the hall of the meeting.
Last Sunday morning a meeting took place in the hall of the gmina [Jewish community], which is bound to take up an important chapter in the history of our kehilla.
At the meeting the "urgent" question of our kehilla life was settled — to engage 2 young fellows, "nowobrańcy" [newcomers to the trade], as Będzin shochtim [ritual slaughterers] ..
The "filling" of the shochtim posts did not come easily; various "forces" worked to have the matter finally settled before the new board comes to power, and at last the "moment" was fixed — at a time of general [?] staff reductions — and the Będzin kehilla has acquired 2 new shochtim; they possess no qualifications, but for that they have handsome dowries...
The shochtim question also had an echo last Sabbath in the synagogue, where a stormy demonstration took place against the community delegates, because the shochet matter is being settled not in an honest way but only by the force of...
As we are told, the storm in the synagogue broke out under the following circumstances: after the Torah reading, the wife of R' Yechezkel Shochet turned from the women's gallery to the worshippers, asking them to react to the great injustice that the rabbi and the kehilla board do not allow her husband, the son of the late R' Mordechai Shochet, to receive the post of shochet in Będzin.
The words had the proper effect on the congregation, and loud protests were heard against those who disregard the just claim of R' Yechezkel Shochet and take the bread away from a family of 9 souls only because the family has no cash...
The storm grew even stronger after the prayers, when the same woman went up noisily onto the bimah and from there addressed the congregation.
The synagogue boiled like a kettle. Seeing such a situation, the rabbi left the synagogue in great haste. But this did not extinguish the "fire". The crowd, men and women, voiced their protests in the street, and because of this the rabbi went to the apartment of Mr. L. Landner, where he waited until the crowd dispersed.
The events in the synagogue spread through the town with lightning speed, and the whole Sabbath day the main topic of conversation was the shochet affair, the unheard-of events in the synagogue, and above all the meeting to take place the next day, Sunday, when the shochtim question was, on the rabbi's proposal, on the agenda.
The night from Sabbath to Sunday was a "leil shimurim" [night of vigil]. All night long negotiations went on with the community delegates, who are to decide with their "votes". That night, as the wags of the generation say, a few "transactions" were concluded, so that the "Agudah" came to the meeting with the victory in its pocket...
The meeting was called for 12 noon. Already at 10 o'clock a police guard stood in front of the gmina hall, which did not allow any larger groups of people to form — curious people who had gathered around the gmina in order to learn as fast as possible the result of the "historic" meeting.
The mood in the street — an "elevated" one; the public forgot for a while its everyday worries and was busy with such a "world problem": supplying the Będzin kehilla with 2 more shochtim.
The meeting had the following course: under the first item the demand of the insurance company in Königshütte [Królewska Huta, Chorzów] that the gmina pay within the next days the debt of 13 thousand zł. was discussed... Having "disposed" of the 13 thousand zł., the letter of the rabbinate was considered, which turns to the kehilla board with a proposal to take on the young Radoszycki and the bachelor-bridegroom Gerlic as shochtim in place of R' Yisrael Moshe Shochet. The pension R' Yisrael Moshe has received until now is to be divided into 3 parts. The proposal is supported by Dr. Ryński; Dr. A. Liwer speaks against it.
The vote gives the following result: for the proposal — President Liwer, Ryński, Plesner; and against — Liwer and Buchheic [?]. Mr. Bauszykowski abstains from voting. Immediately after the vote there is a crash of windowpanes, and stones and bricks fly into the meeting hall. The councillors ("dozórcy") scatter in fear and terror.
The stones and bricks thrown in lay "untouched" until Monday. After the police report was drawn up, "order" was restored.
The Parnassim Are “Flying”...

[Będzin — Kehilla, Agudah.]
As we have already written, the leadership of the local “Agudah” [Agudat Israel] has worked out a new “strategic” plan: having got rid of the candidacy of Mr. Winaducki [?], who had to step down because of his father-in-law Mr. Werdiger, the “traps” were aimed at Mr. Buchheitz. He too will have to step down when his father-in-law Mr. Schönberg enters the list of parnassim [kehilla board members].
— How so?
If the parnassim Kalman Liwer and Berish Liwer resign their mandates, Mr. Schönberg then comes in. But, as it turns out, Mr. Schönberg does not want to harness himself to the Agudah’s “diplomatic wagon”, and he has resigned as parnas. In his place Mr. Berish Jakubowicz comes in.
Because of family kinship Mr. Bunem Banhart must also leave the board, on account of his elder brother-in-law, parnas Mr. S. L. Zylberfrajnd. The latter was sent a warning that if he does not give up his mandate in favour of the Agudah’s policy, “his life as well as the life of his family is in great danger”... But the threats had no effect whatsoever on Mr. Zylberfrajnd, who decided by no means to resign. Because of this Mr. Banhart’s candidacy falls away, and in his place Mr. Efraim Klajnman enters the board.
Owing to the changes, the meetings that were to have taken place last Monday did not take place and have been postponed to next Sunday. Naturally — provided that no new “retreats” occur in the course of these days.

The Great “Power” of the Electric Meters.
They “Run” Even Though the Lights Are Off...

[Będzin — Electricity, consumer affairs.]
Mr. Jechiel Naparstek passes on to us the following interesting fact:
In recent months Mr. Naparstek has been paying larger sums for electric light. Each time he settled the bill it struck him as odd why he was paying so much at a time when he was sparing with the lights. But the “secret” was discovered these days: it became clear that he had been paying for the light of a premises which has already been completely closed for 3 months...
The official of the electricity works, who was called in about the “mystery”, did indeed establish that although no light is used, the meter “moves” forward and shows how many kilowatts have been used.
Sharp Protest by Jewish Parents against a Plan to Eliminate School Premises in the Town

[Będzin — Education, municipality.]
Last Sunday a parents’ meeting took place at School No. 4, at which reports were given: 1) a general report by the management on the state of affairs in the school, 2) by the chairmen of the school self-government, and 3) elections of opiekuns [patrons/guardians].
After the reports, the former headmistress Mrs. Szancer was elected chief opiekun; second opiekuns — Messrs. Zauberman and Tuchsznajder.
At the meeting the large number of parents submitted an urgent interpellation to the headmistress. The interpellation asks whether the report in the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” is true that the magistrate [municipality] intends to reduce the school premises in the town at the expense of the Jewish children, who even until now have not had any comfortable school premises, and now they want to reduce even that for them — at a time when the premises of the Christian schoolchildren are not being reduced.
The discussion about this “injustice crying to heaven” was very stormy. The parents censured the Jewish public figures, as well as the religious representatives, who are indifferent regarding this assault on the Jewish children.
Finally a protest resolution against the proposal was adopted, and it was resolved at the same time to turn with a petition to the competent bodies.
Sosnowiec — The Pledges for Buying a Plot for a Cemetery Will Be Collected by Compulsion

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla, cemetery.]
Several weeks ago a committee was set up at the gmina [Jewish community], whose task is to collect the required sum needed to buy a plot for a cemetery. The committee carried out the collection campaign in the following way: every town taxpayer was sent a notice that he had been assessed proportionally for a certain sum in favour of this important purpose. But, as it turns out, the Jewish population has no understanding of the matter and treats it with the same indifference as any other institution. Therefore the committee has decided that within 14 days everyone must pay in the assessed sum. If not, the gmina is to collect the money through the magistrate [municipality], with enforcement (execution) costs.
Hulczyński’s Workers Refuse to Leave the Factory

[Sosnowiec — Labour, industry.]
The management of Hulczyński’s factory has decided to shut down the factory for a certain time. The workers are against the decision and refuse to leave the factory grounds. In connection with this, a delegation went to Warsaw yesterday, which is to confer about it with the Minister of Labour.
Craftsmen’s Meeting Dissolved for Not Holding the Proper Identity Cards

[Sosnowiec — Craftsmen, police.]
On Sunday a general meeting of craftsmen took place in [their] own premises. On the agenda was the election of a new board.
In the middle of the meeting a policeman, accompanied by a secret agent, entered the hall and asked the chairman whether he knew the surnames of those assembled and whether they held membership cards, according to the regulation which came into force on the 7th of czerwiec [June] of this year.
When the chairman gave no satisfactory answer, the meeting was dissolved by the police.

Summer Colonies of “Herzliya”.
[Sosnowiec — Youth, Zionism.]
The district (galil) of the united youth organisations “HaShomer HaLeumi”, “Herzliya” and “HaNoar HaIvri” is organising summer colonies on the model of previous years.
Taking part in the colonies are the towns of Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie, Częstochowa, Krzepice, Miechów, Chażnica [?], Działoszyce, Wiślica, Katowice, Mandżew [?], Bielsko, Wojkowice, Cieszyn, Kraków, etc. The colonies will take place in two locations — in Bojaków [?] and Milówka.

The work at the colonies will be divided into plugot [units]. A whole series of lectures will be held, and the work will be conducted almost entirely in Hebrew.

The investigation concerning the “religious excursion” in Sosnowiec is continuing, and in recent days a number of persons were summoned for questioning, including melamdim [teachers] from the local Talmud Torah.

A delegation from the 'Chofetz Chaim' (may he live long) in Zagłębie / Those who registered to receive certificates / Summer colony of 'Hashomer Hatzair' / General meeting of the 'Discount Bank' in Będzin

[Będzin — rabbinate and yeshivas; followed by three short items: Zionism, youth movements, economy.]
As is known, the great world yeshiva 'Chofetz Chaim' in Radun, which was founded 60 years ago by the author of 'Chofetz Chaim' (may he live long) and has over that time produced thousands of great scholars and geniuses in all the lands of the Jewish dispersion, is threatened, because of the prevailing crisis, God forbid, with closure. The great support from America, which always supported the great yeshiva on a broad scale, has stopped completely, and the 400 Torah scholars of the yeshiva of great men of Torah and piety, who study day and night, are suffering great want and hardship.
The great Torah centre, which has spread the light of Torah over the whole world over a period of more than a jubilee of years, now finds itself in a difficult material situation, which endangers the very existence of the holy yeshiva, God forbid.
Two weeks ago, therefore, a large assembly took place with the participation of the great rabbis of Lithuania at the home of the 'Chofetz Chaim' (may he live long), and it was decided to undertake a great rescue campaign to save the yeshiva from ruin. The rabbis who took part in the assembly undertook to travel to the larger cities of Poland to carry out a collection campaign for the benefit of the yeshiva.
To Zagłębie were delegated the rabbis: the well-known, famous Rabbi and Gaon Avraham Leib HaLevi Pentelnikov [?] (may he live long), head of the rabbinical court of Derewno, and the great Rabbi R' Dov HaLevi Lejzerowski, one of the closest disciples of the 'Chofetz Chaim' (may he live long).
On the Sabbath the Rabbi of Będzin (may he live long) introduced the distinguished guests to the worshippers in the synagogue, describing the greatness of the 'Chofetz Chaim' (may he live long) and his yeshiva and asking them to help the distinguished rabbis in the great campaign as far as possible. Then the Rabbi of Derewno (may he live long) read out the great letter of the 'Chofetz Chaim', which made an extraordinary impression on the worshippers.
As we are informed, the delegation of distinguished rabbis is received everywhere very well and warmly, and it is to be hoped that the rescue campaign will be crowned with success.
———
On Wednesday evening a meeting took place in the community office (gmina) with the participation of the rabbinate, the parnasim and representatives of the houses of prayer, before which Rabbi Pensielnikov [sic] of Derewno and Rabbi Lejzerowski spoke about the great importance of the yeshiva, from which famous great scholars emerge year after year. The delegates also described the sad material situation of the yeshiva.
It was decided: 1) despite the existing regulation that no one but the local rabbi may speak in the synagogue, to make an exception in honour of the Chofetz Chaim (may he live long) and the delegates, who are famous rabbis, so that they may speak in the synagogue this Sabbath, parashat Shelach, at 5 o'clock in the afternoon, and on Sunday, parashat Korach, at 6 in the evening; 2) to organise a pledge (nedarim) campaign in all houses of prayer, and all pledges made during the Torah reading shall belong solely to the 'Chofetz Chaim' yeshiva.

Next Sunday a joint excursion (haflagah) of the Zagłębie youth of 'Hashomer Hatzair' will take place. As every year, 'Hashomer Hatzair' in Zagłębie is organising summer colonies for its members. In connection with this, a campaign begins next week in the towns of Zagłębie.

General meeting of the 'Discount Bank' in Będzin
On Wednesday the annual general meeting of the 'Discount Bank' in Będzin took place at the 'Piast'.
With 125 members present, the chairman of the council, Mr A. Lidzbarski, opened the meeting and gave an overview of the present economic situation, of the cooperative movement and of banking in particular, stressing that the only salvation is to strengthen the Jewish cooperative banks.
At the general request Mr Jakub Ehrlich took the chair and invited to the presidium Messrs Izaak Ehrlich, Meir Beri, Gershon Rechnic, Nete Landner, and as secretary — Mr Fridman.
Reports on the activity of the supervisory council and of the management were given by Messrs Lidzbarski, Rus and Gutensztajn.
The honorary auditor Mr Pinkus read the balance sheet, which shows that the bank's profit in 1931 amounts to about 9 thousand zł. The sum remains as reserve capital.
After the discussion on the reports, the motion of the chairman Mr A. Trapauer to give 6 dollars to the 'Keren Hayesod' and 100 zł. to the Small Traders' Association was adopted unanimously.
The budget for 1932/33 is reduced by 50 per cent against last year, so that the whole budget reaches up to 30 thousand zł. It was decided that the amount of credit for members can be only up to 3 thousand zł.

On the Sad State of the Będzin Talmud Torah

From several activists of the Będzin Talmud Torah (T"T) we have received the following open letter to the Będzin rabbinate, with the following content:
„We do not doubt that our Będzin rabbinate is well aware that the T"T melamdim have not been teaching the T"T children since last Friday, because apart from their arrears they do not receive even enough for „lechem tsar“ (meagre bread) for their present work, and 400 poor children, orphans, wander about idle and empty in the streets. It is no secret to anyone that the Agudah gabbaim of the T"T want the T"T to be abolished altogether. Above all they have no time now to concern themselves with it, since they are busy with communiqués to Karlsbad and Krynica about Mr. Szenberg's mandate. But you, since you also take part in the shochtim politics, must surely understand that one ought to decree a fast when hundreds of orphans, without father and without mother, Heaven preserve us, are being cut off from „and the study of Torah outweighs them all“...
We must, after all, give an account of this at every single moment — and you did not even find it necessary to come on Sunday to the meeting about the sad state of the T"T?
Therefore we turn to you through the esteemed newspaper with the request that you come to the synagogue this Sabbath, Parshat Korach, and rouse the worshippers with warm words to receive cordially the delegates who will collect the one-time donations for the T"T. After your appeal we shall call a large meeting, at which a committee will be elected of such people as are ready to work with all their heart and all their soul for the good of the Talmud Torah.“
—o—
Struggle over the G"Ch (Free-Loan) Fund in Pogoń
For several months now, since the „secret known to all of Brody“ [i.e. an open secret] was discovered that a rather large sum is missing from the gmilus-chesed free-loan fund in Pogoń [district of Sosnowiec]. The chief culprit was Mr. Fridman, who was the whole „kol v'lakh“[?] [be-all and end-all] of the fund. When several board members, headed by R' Dovid Shochet Cwajgenhaft, demanded an accounting, the system of „a scholar — out of the society!“ was applied against them... Mr. Cwajgenhaft, who has great merits for the fund, was removed from the board, and for the „impudence“ of demanding an accounting a campaign is being waged against him as a shochet.
For this purpose R' Berish Shochet comes from Będzin and slaughters poultry in Pogoń.
The conduct of the Będzin shochet has aroused great bitterness, for he is, after all, depriving another of his livelihood and encroaching on his domain.
