A Letter from the Chafetz Chaim, May He Live Long and Well

[Będzin and Zagłębie — the Radun yeshiva; letter of the Chafetz Chaim.]
To the Jews of Zagłębie.
In connection with the campaign for the Radun yeshiva, the Chafetz Chaim, may he live long and well, has sent us the following letter, in which he appeals to the Jews of Zagłębie to support the campaign.
We therefore print the letter in the original, word for word [the letter is in Hebrew]:
To our dear brethren, the generous of heart, lovers and esteemers of the Torah, pursuers of charity and kindness, and at their head the honoured public workers in the towns of Zagłębie, may the Lord be upon them and may they live.
I hereby express before your honours my great sorrow concerning the present condition of our holy yeshiva in Radun [?], which is in a dreadful and extremely distressed [?] state that cannot be described — it would not be believed if told — for it is now many months that close to four hundred students of the yeshiva, great in Torah and in the fear of Heaven, have not received their meagre maintenance, and they are melting away from hunger, want and terrible pressure; for we have come to such a state that even the most necessary things, the bread and cooked food given to the yeshiva students, we are unable to supply, and the strength to bear it has already failed under the great want and pressure and the yoke of enormous debts of many thousands of dollars that weigh very heavily upon us, and the yeshiva is in danger of hunger and of closing, God forbid.
And for the sake of the survival of the holy yeshiva, over whose survival I have laboured much, and since I cannot bear to see the suffering of hundreds of yeshiva students, great in Torah and in the fear of Heaven, who suffer the disgrace of actual hunger, my friend the rabbi and gaon, the head of the rabbinical court of the holy community of Drewna [?], his honour our teacher Rabbi Avraham Leib HaLevi Pentelnikow, may he live long and well, and my friend the famous rabbi and gaon, one of the outstanding young scholars of the kollel of our holy yeshiva, his honour our teacher Rabbi Dov HaLevi Lewertowski [?], may he live long and well (son-in-law of the gaon, head of the rabbinical court of Siktin [?]), have volunteered to travel to the towns of Zagłębie and there to convey to our brethren, the Children of Israel, our dreadful condition and to ask them to hasten to our aid.
And I hereby earnestly beg the heads of the community, the honoured public workers, the gabbaim and heads of the synagogues, to come to the aid of the aforementioned rabbis in their holy work, for there is today no greater and more exalted mitzvah for us than supporting the remnant of the scholars who have been left to us, few out of many, in this bitter exile of ours, and who are the survivors, the heroes of the nation, from whom the Congregation of Israel will be built and established, and they are the very ones who spread Torah and light to all Israel. Hasten, dear brothers, do all that is in your power to come to the support of our holy yeshiva with its hundreds of students who are melting away from hunger, want and terrible pressure. We must do everything in our power and possibility for the sake of the survival of the holy Torah, that it should not collapse, God forbid, from the magnitude [?] of the terrible want and pressure. And even in the days of the economic crisis prevailing among us it is still in our power to act and to do, if only there is no lack of public workers and helpers who labour faithfully; and it will be accounted to them as a great merit, and the merit of the many will depend on them.
And there is strong hope that the seed of the holy people, who gave their lives for the survival of the holy Torah in every time of trouble and distress, will not stand aloof today either, in such an evil and bitter time for the holy Torah, and with all the strength of their spirit and soul will hasten to our aid; and those individual survivors to whom the Lord has been good and whose economic situation is good will use this opportune moment to "acquire their world in a single hour" by setting aside a certain sum according to their strength and means for the rescue of our holy yeshiva.
And may the merit of the great mitzvah of supporting the Torah and rescuing the lives of great Torah scholars from hunger and want stand by all the honoured public workers and donors, and may they be blessed by the Blessed Name with life and peace and all good, livelihood and abundant success in all their affairs, and may they merit to see the salvation of Israel and the raising of the horn of the Torah speedily.
As is their good soul's wish, and the wish of the soul of the one who honours them and blesses them with all good, who writes and signs for the honour of the Torah and its students, its supporters and upholders,
Israel Meir HaKohen.

The Będzin Rabbinate Decrees a Fast over the Insult to the Rabbi's Honour

[Będzin — Community and Rabbinate.]
Last Friday the following proclamation (kol kore) was distributed in the name of the Będzin rabbinate:
B"H [With God's help]
To our honoured brethren, the Children of Israel, residents of our town, may God protect them.
Last Sabbath, to our deepest sorrow and pain, a great desecration of God's name took place, when the great Rabbi, head of the rabbinical court of this town, may he live long and well, was insulted in an unheard-of manner, with such contempt that "the ears of all who hear it shall tingle." According to the law set out in the Gemara and the Shulchan Aruch, the punishment for insulting a Torah scholar is very severe — all the more so for the town's rabbi, and especially the great Rabbi, head of the court, who is renowned for praise throughout the Jewish dispersion; the matter touches on the desecration of God's name for the whole Jewish people.
We, as a rabbinical court, find it our duty according to the law to protest against this desecration of the holy and not to pass over the matter in silence. We have therefore decided that from all the prayer houses people shall come on the Sabbath to the [main] synagogue to express a protest before the Torah reading, in the very place where the insult was committed against the holy [as printed: "against the insult of the holy"], and that the Torah shall not be read earlier in the prayer houses until after the protest in the synagogue.
Likewise, since we find that for an insult to a Torah scroll one is obliged to fast, all the more so for an insult to a Torah scholar, whose honour is greater, as our Sages said, "These foolish Babylonians…" etc. — we have also decided that on Sunday, the eve of Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, every local Jew shall fast until 12 o'clock, and whoever is not able to fast shall give a redemption (pidyon nefesh) of 18 groszy for the local Talmud Torah.
May the Blessed Name help that the glory of the Torah and the honour of Heaven be raised, and may He in His mercy close the breach of His people Israel.
Będzin, portion Shelach, 26 Sivan 5692.

Half a Million Francs' Worth of Narcotics Found in a Box of Toys

[Crime — Paris–New York; a Będzin native.]
On the 7th of this month the passenger ship "Île de France" brought from Paris to New York a box of toys for the merchant Frenkel. On inspecting the box it turned out that under the various coloured little lamps and other toys there were no less than 52 kilos of narcotics, valued at half a million francs.
The American police began a discreet investigation, confiscating the parcel for the time being. Frenkel in New York was arrested.
The investigative police in Paris succeeded in establishing that the sender was a certain Jakub Polakiewicz, an old criminal in this field, who has already been sentenced in America to 11[?] years of hard imprisonment.
Together with Polakiewicz our fellow townsman, Mr. Moryc Herzberg, was also arrested; a kilo of morphine hydrochloride was also found on him. On Polakiewicz 15 thousand dollars and 325 thousand francs were found.
The French press is outraged and demands that Polakiewicz be severely punished; as regards Herzberg the press is very mild and is seeking mitigating circumstances for him.
As we are informed, Herzberg has been released on bail.

On Guard Before a Catastrophe

[Editorial — economy and crisis; rents and taxes.]
L. Szpigelman.
(XI.) The difficult way out, so as not to sink into the abyss.
There is a Yiddish proverb: a drowning man grabs at a straw, as long as he can save himself. Exactly the same impression is made by all the various proposals and projects for cutting the expenses of the citizen's budget in the present hard time of existence.
People shout that rent for apartments must become cheaper; price lists ("tsennikes" [cenniki]) are being planned for the merchants so that they should not flay the skin off the customer. This looks exactly like the "pasik" [?] [probably: former] times with the anti-usury offices ("lichwa offices"), which ordered the retailer not, God forbid, to overstep the measure; and as soon as someone was caught red-handed, he was taught manners, and more than one was in this way condemned to lose his livelihood.
It goes without saying that we are not out here to defend the actual speculators of that time, just as we do not long for those "pasik" [?] times. But why did they stand so over the neck of the retailer, of the small trader, of the small industrialist at that time, when for the big, heavy factories everything was permitted? Nobody prevented them from setting whatever prices they fancied, and if they received a tax that amounted to a minimum, it turned out to be a favour for them, because in that case they had the opportunity to recover the tax twice over and more. Nobody controlled them, nobody came near them; nobody dared tell them that they were earning too much, that they were overstepping the measure, that they were charging usurious prices, that they were speculating with their products.
That is roughly how the various proposals for the system of price reduction look now. The newspapers shout that apartments must become cheaper; for the merchants they are starting to draw up price lists, so that they should not, God forbid, overstep the measure — at a time when we hold that these small people, the retailers, have long since ceased to overstep the measure in earnings; on the contrary, they overstep the measure in not earning: they wait for a customer as for the Messiah [literally "look out with candles"], and as soon as he appears they let him have the article at any price, just to see money before their eyes. We have pointed out more than once that people sell without profit, and that this is just as dangerous as charging usurious prices, because in that case the merchant's goods become ownerless: he gets rid of the goods, and he has no money to pay for the articles he bought.
True, the industrialists too are now already beaten, and they produce their goods at any price, just to keep the worker employed. Yet there are still such products on which the manufacturers earn very well ["ver gut", probably "zer gut"], and they take no account of the difficult economic situation in the country; so why do our economic experts not see to it that these articles are made cheaper at the manufacturer's, instead of seizing upon the small trader, who waits for a customer as for the Messiah and then sells the article he has stocked [?] at any price, not even counting the most minimal expenses he has?
It is the same with the housing question. We are not at all interested in taking upon ourselves the mission of defending the landlords, but one must after all be consistent. Consistency must nevertheless be demanded. If one wants cheap apartments, one must surely see to it that the landlords have lower expenses, because it has always been known that real estate does not yield an excessive return. True, it would be only just that housing become cheaper in such a bitter time, but how is that consistent when the taxes on real estate are rising, and thus the government and municipal taxes, with which the self-government bodies tax the house-owners, are being increased? If one wants cheaper dwellings, then, first of all one must not raise the taxes — and not only not raise them, but on the contrary, they must be reduced, so that this would give a push to the reduction of prices.
Under the prevailing conditions, however, when the government orders the taxes on real estate to be raised, it surely cannot agree to the citizens' demands to make apartments cheaper; and if apartments are here and there let more cheaply, it is only thanks to the will of the house-owner, who has no choice when he has empty dwellings. But such isolated cases cannot be taken into account; one cannot rely on such occasions, which occur from time to time, to give a push towards solving the question of cheaper housing.
And therefore we say: one must not fool oneself. If one wants apartments to become cheaper, one must first of all see to it that the house has lower expenses; and therefore it would be the task of our tenants' associations, which must fight for cheaper apartments, to fight, together with this campaign, also for lower taxes — both for the landlord and for the tenant. Only in this way can the question be solved for the good of the community, for the good of the broad strata of citizens.
But if one thinks that the housing question — even when prices do become cheaper — will save the general critical situation, one is greatly mistaken. Everything must be reduced systematically, if one really means to save the difficult situation of the citizens.
Thus the government must make efforts to reduce the charges for electric current ("prond" [prąd]), water, telephone, tram and railway tickets, shipment of goods and the like.
Besides that the government must come to the aid of its citizens and set an example by reducing the prices of its monopoly articles of basic necessity, such as: sugar, salt, matches, cigarettes ("papirosn") and the like. The various tax charges, which burden the citizens so heavily, must also be eased. All this could make a lighter existence possible in the present difficult, critical time.
One must therefore not fool oneself into thinking that one trifle will "make the soup fat" and general rescue will come for the citizens, who find themselves in such a catastrophic situation. We have sunk too deep, the population has been impoverished too severely, for the bitter question of want to be solved with the help of trifles.
To solve the hunger question, which already today takes first place in the whole country, it is necessary to carry out reductions on all articles of human use and on all of a person's expenses. Otherwise it does not mean that the question has been solved radically; otherwise it means that one has just "gegart" [?] and talked words into the air, which will help nobody at all.
In the present situation one can simply marvel at how the lower strata of the population live, how the working mass, which is almost permanently without work, exists. It is truly impossible to understand how these elements have the means for the most necessary outlays, for the most minimal expenses. It goes without saying that they barely live, that they barely draw breath, and it is simply a wonder how they keep their children, who are pale, without a drop of blood.
And the question arises: how can one live like this under these prevailing conditions? And how long can one live in such a kind of "life"? Will this not tell in the future? In the near future? Can one raise a healthy generation in such a kind of "life"?
It has been shown to us statistically that the World War produced countless diseases because of the hard conditions in which mankind found itself. And are we now in better conditions? And are there not now great enough chances of new troubles and diseases, which arise because of the hard living conditions in which mankind finds itself?
So why fool ourselves, why go about with illusions for the future, when the prospects in the present are so sad, when no effort is made to have the hard questions of existence solved even for the time being? Can one, in the present dangerous time, really make do with mere empty talk, with hollow, threadbare phrases, which bring nobody any benefit?
If one really means to save the prevailing situation of complete ruin, there is no other remedy than to set about radically helping the citizens, and this can only be done with the help of much understanding and a strong will on the part of the official circles. Otherwise one sinks ever deeper on the road to the abyss.
It's Bitter on All Sides...

[Humour — feuilleton; family life, summer holidays.] M. Mandelzon.
A company of young men were sitting together whose wives were away at the dacha [summer cottage], and they chatted about this and that, until they got round to talking about their good fortune as "straw widowers", and each of them began to tell of his new [?] acquaintances, of his successes ["powodzenie"], of his steady [?] lovers ["kach-unkes" — kochanki?], and in general how he now lives a fine day and a fine night, without fear of his wife's evil eye...
One of the company, however, had kept silent the whole time, and listening to his colleagues' piquant stories, he sighed more than he smiled; and when the gang had already exhausted all their material, the young man gave a bitter smile and began to tell of his own "good fortune":
— Never at all had I intended this summer to transport my wife off to a dacha, because when business has gone to the devil and you don't see a penny before your eyes, a wife should sit at home and not at a dacha. But my wife sniffed out my heretical idea in good time and she planted herself in front of me with a wet cloth [?] round her head, and with groans, shouts and shrieks she proved to me, as surely as two times two is... five, that she can barely stand on her feet, that she can barely take a step [?], and that she must have a dacha, otherwise I am no husband but a murderer, a robber, who has no pity for a living creature, not even for his own wife...
Of course, after such arguments day in, night out, I had no choice but to reconsider: "Oh well. In any case I've nothing left to lose. Things are so bad and so bitter, and when a wife digs in her heels that she wants and must have a dacha, my refusal won't help anyway, even if I stood on my head. So why should I remain a bad fool?" Was I right or not? But where does one get the big money such a dacha costs? And here a happy thought occurred to me: since not far from Katowice there is a village, Jelnica [?], which has peasant cottages with a little wood that at a pinch can be called a dacha, she will go there this summer and I am done with the business.
When my wife heard of Jelnica, she began to list such faults of the dacha, just as if it were her best friend ["koleżanka"]... But I held firm as steel and iron on Jelnica, and I literally talked her into going there, where she would have a fine time ["bawić się"] in the "intelligent society" ["towarzystwo"] of Madame Chatterova, Gossipova, Intrigantova and other "-ovas", among whom she will feel excellent, and with her fiery little mouth she will, God forbid, not be put to shame.
In short, I "packed her off" ["odprawić"] to Jelnica and raised my hands to heaven with thanks and praise that this year I have a dacha for my wife so cheap and so close to town that, whenever I feel like it, I can drive or walk over to her, and the main thing — that in town I am at last a free bird, without a wife, without a cage, without a complainer, without a know-all; in a word, fine on all sides, just like you. And in the very first days I already wanted to set about using the precious free time and enjoying it like all straw widowers who have their heads on their shoulders [i.e. carefree] — when I receive an alarming little letter from her in which she informs me that if I want her to have something to chew and not to perish of hunger, I must take pity on her and provide her with a few provisions from town, because here you can't buy anything worth a penny — you might as well go and gnaw the trees.
Well, she is a wife after all, so of course I immediately sent her a "sprawunek" [a parcel of shopping], a whole warehouse, and thought I would now have peace from her for a while. Not a chance! She got hold of paper and a pencil [misprint: "a a"], and as soon as the muse comes over her, she writes me notes upon notes: get her this here, get her that there, and I — what choice do I have? — must run around the shops, wander around the market with my wife's note in hand, so that nothing, God forbid, is missing; no, upon my life, you needn't envy me!
Just yesterday I received such a note, and listen, out of curiosity ["ciekawe"], to what I have to buy for her today:
Three kilos of challahs, half a kilo of liver without blemishes, a tin of cocoa, ground pepper, two kilos of bread, a kilo of tomatoes, half a kilo of sugar, parsley, a chicken, two kilos of "mantshke" [?] [perhaps semolina], five decagrams of fresh yeast, two kilos of meat without bones, gooseberries, cinnamon, raisins [?], two kilos of "four zero" flour, two tins of sprats, a calf's foot, a few sour sweets, a kilo of salt, two packets of "plutas" [?], half a kilo of beans, two or three herrings, garlic, a couple of bunches of carrots, two kilos of fish, cherries, a kilo of rice, onions, a tin of sardines, pickled cucumbers, a little bottle of vinegar, sweet almonds... — not bad for a note! It's a miracle [?] at least that my mother-in-law, may she be kept apart from me till a hundred and twenty, helps me with the shopping; otherwise, I swear I don't know how I could have managed on my own!
And when I have already got it all in the best order, or I lug it all there myself, do you think she is satisfied? Not a bit of it! Only then does she start to tell the real faults, namely: "This isn't fresh, that's fit to be thrown out", and she honours me with: "A schlemiel stays a schlemiel!" "He's not even fit to do the shopping!" "When you send a fool among the shopkeepers..." — and on top of that, go on, be a hero and endure it all!
Ech — the young man sighed — may my enemies get married and wait for the wife to go away to a dacha! Send her to a "proper" dacha — it costs big money and others even get the pleasure; send her close by, where it's cheaper and you do have control — the husband becomes a shopper, a shop-crawler, a market-goer; then again, send her neither here nor there and ask her kindly to sit at home through the summer months — she gives the husband a taste of real hell, and... eh — the young man waved his hand and ended with a deep sigh — woe and bitter is the married man on all sides, and wherever you lay the sick man, it hurts him...
Upper Silesian Economic Sketches

[Upper Silesia — economy and trade; serialized article, part 5.]
Dr. Adolf Schaier (Katowice).
5.
The press reports laconically that the Finance Minister is to tighten the tax screw further and to issue an order to the tax offices under him to collect, as energetically as possible, the overdue as well as the current taxes from merchants and industrialists. On the other hand, the salaries [lit. "pensions"] of state officials and of military functionaries have been cut by a further 10 percent. Thus the already minimal purchasing power of those elements who find themselves in the fortunate position of still having a certain livelihood and regular income is reduced to the minimum, and their income barely covers the most primitive daily expenses. A vicious circle [lit. "a false wheel"] is thus created: on the one hand they want to increase the already great pressure on merchants and industrialists in order to get still higher taxes out of them, and on the other hand they take away the possibility of doing even the smallest turnover with state officials, since by cutting their salaries they deprive them of the possibility of buying anything except food and clothing themselves in the barest necessities. Where will all this finally lead? The merchant's situation is simply tragic. Respected trading houses with decades of tradition behind them, which have always paid their debts normally, both to suppliers and to the state treasury, have lately been forced systematically to cut staff — thereby increasing unemployment — to exchange their expensive shops and offices for cheaper ones, and when all these reductions do not help, they are forced, as a last resort, to declare themselves insolvent and in the end to liquidate altogether.
In Upper Silesia the situation is even more tragic, because the crisis came later and unexpectedly. Until last year, state and municipal officials received special allowances amounting to as much as 40 percent of salary, i.e. that much more than in the other parts of the country. This created a certain higher category of society, which contributed in no small measure to the prosperity that once reigned here. Almost all the allowances have been taken away from the officials, and at the same time their salaries were cut along with the officials of the other voivodeships. There are cases where an official who a year ago earned 1000 zł. a month earns 600 zł. today, of which another 10 percent was taken away in June.
Most of all, the installment trade, so widespread here, has suffered from all these cuts. This branch of trade lived first and foremost on state officials, who regularly received their full salaries, and on certain days of the month one could count with certainty on the punctual payment of the installments. After the first salary cut last year, the installments that this category of buyers was to pay were not paid, so that the sellers had to extend the installments already due for further months, until the officials [adjust] to the new standard of living and, after adding up all their expenses, have a certain reserve left over to pay the overdue installments. All this brought it about that the installment dealer had no means to buy new goods, and the state official stopped buying altogether, fearing new cuts.
In the wholesale trade, where the installment dealers bought their goods, the crisis had an even more fatal effect: the bills of exchange of the "raciarze" [installment dealers] were not redeemed, for the reasons mentioned above.
What the situation in industry looks like at the time of the crisis — in the next article. (Sh.)
Deeds that are like seeds sown in the earth

[Ethics and reflection — essay.] Among the beautiful legends told in the Midrash about the meeting between the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon, there is a little story about the riddles that the queen — who had come from distant lands to become acquainted with "the wisest of all men" — put to him.

The Queen of Sheba asked King Solomon several riddles and told him: "If you give me the right answer to my riddles, I shall be convinced that what people say of you is true, that you are the wisest of men."

One of the riddles went like this:
"Tell me, if you know: who is the unfortunate one who, before he even dies, is already laid in the earth, and before his breath has even gone out, is already buried; and though he lies and rots, he becomes stronger and more alive, and those who bury him are rewarded a thousandfold?"
To this King Solomon answered her:
"The little seeds that are laid in the earth; the ears that grow up from them afterwards — they will tell you that I have solved your riddle." But from "the little seeds that are laid in the earth," which King Solomon mentioned, one can learn something more; one can draw from them a moral about human deeds.

We often do things from which we have no immediate benefit. We often do things that, on the surface, seem to be not in our own interest but in the interest of others.

But if the deeds we do are good; if the work we do is useful — they can be compared to the little seeds that the peasant sows in the field, from which there later grow tall, flowering ears that bring grain and feed a world full of people, and reward a thousandfold the one who sowed them.

And even if it happens that we ourselves do not enjoy the fruit that we sow, that does not mean we need not sow and plant; it does not mean that we should hold back from doing good to our fellow men and from stretching out a helping hand to those who knock at our door.

There is a second wonderfully beautiful little story in the Midrash that suits the matter very well: the story of an old man who stood in a field and planted an apple tree.

The one who planted the tree was already a very old man: his back was bent, and anyone who saw him could tell that he would not spend many more years in this world. Yet he stood in the field, diligently dug the earth and carefully sowed the seeds from which, years later, a tree was to grow.

Someone passed by the field, saw the old man at work and asked him: "What are you working for, wasting your effort? Don't you know that it will take years until a tree that bears fruit grows from these seeds you are sowing? And don't you know that when the tree begins to blossom and bear fruit, you will long since no longer be among the living?"

The old man raised his head, looked at the questioner with his wise eyes and answered:
"I know, I know; but that makes no difference — I am not sowing for myself. If I get no benefit from the tree, my children will enjoy its fruit."
And in this, in fact, lies the secret of our life and of our work in the world.
And we must also keep in mind that what we do is not only for today, but also for tomorrow. Each of us must regard his life and his work like that old man who stood in the field planting a tree. And just as the one who plants grain or plants a tree sees to it that the seed and the kernels are good, so that the grain or the tree will grow well, blossom strongly and yield good wheat and rye and tasty fruit — so must we, too, see to it that our deeds are good and that they bring good results.

And now is a time when one can recognise how far a person is ready to do good and to help his fellow men. Now, when so many people are in need of warm assistance, of strengthening and encouragement, it is important that as many people as possible stop thinking only of themselves and occupying themselves only with themselves, and instead help those who find themselves in a worse situation.

And the help that each individual gives, as far as his means allow, the warmth that each one shows when someone turns to him for support — these are the little seeds that we sow and that will later reward us a thousandfold.

And our reward will consist in this: that we shall have the happy awareness that we have fulfilled our duty to our fellow men, that we have listened to the voice of our conscience and acted as justice and compassion demand.

And this very awareness is surely the finest reward one can wish for oneself.
Ch.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

To enlarge the business..
You already know my neighbour, you know what sort of man he is: as a rule he is a 'lekish'[?] [a meek simpleton], he wouldn't touch a fly on the wall; on the contrary, every wrong that is done to him he accepts with love and keeps silent.
By contrast, when the public is wronged[?], he burns like a fire of hell, keeps on asking questions and demands an answer.
His first 'victims' are us, for whatever is done, he comes with his complaints straight to us, the representatives of the 'seventh power' [the press], so that we should 'heal the wounds' that he cannot bear...
Such a reception I got from my neighbour last Sabbath. At the break of dawn he came into my home and started banging on the table: why are we silent...
— What is it again, Reb Mendel? — I ask him.
— You still ask? Haven't you seen yet?
— Seen what?
Instead of hearing from him an explanation of why he is so angry, he hands me a proclamation (kol kore): 'Since the Torah was desecrated on the Sabbath, a fast is declared'...
— Quite right — I try to calm him — that is the law: one must decree a fast when the Torah suffers disgrace.
— Yes, — my neighbour starts shouting louder — of course one must react most sharply to disgrace of the Torah, but was the law of decreeing a fast revealed only in the historic time when 18-year-old boys become Będzin ritual slaughterers (shochtim)?.. When one erases 'thou shalt take no bribe', is that not disgracing the Torah?...
Why did those 'who stand on guard and protect the honour of the Torah' not decree a fast when the 'Tze'irei Emunei'[?] disgraced in Tel Aviv, in the meanest, most shameful[?] manner, such a rabbinical authority as Rabbi Kook?... Why were those same 'fast-proclaimers' silent when the late Rabbi of Sompolno, of blessed memory, was spat upon as he was walking back on the Sabbath after prayers from the Będzin synagogue? And when hundreds of Jewish children who attend the 'powszechne' [state elementary schools] grow up ignorant and empty, strangers to the Jewish God, strangers to the Jewish faith — is that not disgrace of the Torah?...
— Calm down, Reb Mendel — we try to influence him — believe me, the gentlemen who produced the proclamation understand better than you that the step is an impudent one. But what are they to do, when the political move to calm the public, so that the 'agitation'[?] should stop, — requires creating a 'mood', so that the 'shochtim concessions' can be legalized...
— To enlarge the business...

With us and with others...
A large stretch[?] of field on the road from Katowice to Sosnowiec is occupied by schoolchildren. In several places the children stand in long rows and enjoy the milk dishes they receive from the Katowice Magistrat [municipality].
Year in, year out, the Magistrat organizes a 'Children's Week'. In the course of the week tens of thousands of litres of milk, sour cream (smetana) and other dairy foods are distributed to the 'tinokot shel beit rabban' [schoolchildren], to schoolchildren poor and rich alike; all of them, the whole children's army, have the privilege of 'and the drinking was according to the law, none did compel' — drink, children, as much as you like...
— And with us? The Sosnowiec Magistrat is altogether far from the 'foolishness' of giving poor schoolchildren the possibility of spending at least a couple of weeks a year in the fresh air.
The Będzin Magistrat too, which does already have merits in this field, becomes thrifty at the expense of the poor children (read: Jewish...), so that the children of parents who are unable to give a few dozen złoty do not merit enjoying the fresh air at the Magistrat's colony...
Every year, when summer comes, we believe that in the field of 'selection'[?] ('pobor'?) regarding sending schoolchildren to the summer colony a logical system will be introduced: that the poorest children should be tended[?] like violets[?], and that their fate in going away should not depend on the caprices of busybodies[?], [—][?],
— on the payments[?]...
But every time we are fooled, and every year we are more disappointed by what our eyes see and what we hear...
Such wicked thoughts[?] awoke in me on seeing the fine action of the Katowice Magistrat, which takes care of the welfare of the schoolchildren:
— With us and with others.

A new 'interpretation'...
'I have[?] an "article" for your newspaper — a new "interpretation" of "Eizehu mekoman": — the whole world — the author explains to us — will only now open its eyes and only now know the true meaning of the Mishnah...'
We try to protest to him that the 'article' is not for our newspaper, but the young Hasid is not impressed, and without our consent he begins, with a Gemara chant, to study 'Eizehu mekoman' with a new 'interpretation'...
— 'Eizehu mekoman shel zevachim?' ['Where is the place of the sacrifices?'] — where is the place of taking on shochtim? — 'Kodshei kodashim' [most holy offerings]: one holds, he says, a so-called meeting about Judaism, about strengthening the faith, but the practical result is to appoint So-and-so son of So-and-so to be a Będzin shochet; 'and the receiving of their blood' — even the taking of the 'klingers' [the jingling coins, the money] is also done 'in a sacred vessel' — in the silk kapotes, 'in the north' [tsafon, i.e. hidden], secretly: nobody sees, even the wives of these people do not know how much the sum amounts to...
The author wanted to go on studying, but a 'miracle' happened: a 'dozor' [kehilla board member] came into the editorial office, of whom the young man took fright, and he stopped studying 'Eizehu mekoman' with the new interpretation...

The Cross of Gold

[Essay — world economy; the gold crisis.] Leo König.
A famous American politician and orator, Bryan, once said a phrase that became even more famous than he himself.
"Mankind — he said — is being crucified upon a cross of gold."
And this beautiful, ringing phrase is also a truth. People always realised it, but now one sees this truth most of all.
Mankind — all the nations — have set up for themselves a golden cross, and they themselves are being tortured and torn upon it.
All nations are now bleeding on their own golden cross, and even the richest nations, those that have amassed the most gold, such as America and France — hang on that cross wholly and half crucified. In America and France too, unemployment and general want are growing, and the golden idol, the golden cross, does not help them with its insolent glitter. People kneel before it, pray to it, raise it up to the very heavens, but it does not help; on the contrary, the higher and more valuable its price, its "mark", becomes, the further the prices of all other commodities fall and sink, and things are coming to the point that the entire present social structure is about to fall apart. And will mankind bleed to death on the cross of gold?
—
And what is also so characteristic of our time is the present revolt against the "golden calf", which is spreading ever wider to all corners of the earth.
One part of mankind, the "mightier", still kneels before the golden cross; the other part tries to overthrow and break it.
And at the same time the cross rises ever higher towards the sky together with its pedestal — the ever-growing mountain of its millions of human victims. The mountain — of fallen, crippled human beings crucified by gold — grows ever higher and larger, and ever higher rises the cross.
It already looks like a symbolic tombstone:
a torn, crippled mankind writhing in suffering, and on the torn mountain of flesh — a golden cross.
—
Even the so very famous bourgeois economists have lately raised an outcry, a voice of revolt against the golden cross.
That is in fact the meaning of the economic conference which is shortly to take place in London. The conference is to work out a plan for raising and stabilising all other values, which keep falling in the same proportion as the price of gold keeps rising.
And many economists now demand that another metal — not gold — should regulate world trade.
Because gold has become concentrated in a few countries — thanks to the war debts and reparations — and has become a rarity, the prices of all other products have fallen so low and have brought world industry and trade to bankruptcy and the brink of bankruptcy.
And the economists therefore demand that silver should take the place of gold.
—
Of course, we cannot enter into the hidden mysteries of economics.
Only professional economists and big businessmen can investigate the question whether abolishing gold and setting silver on its throne will save the world from the present terrible economic crisis.
But what every person is allowed to ask is: and if you set up a silver cross instead of a golden one, will things get better?
And if mankind is crucified on a cross of silver, will the suffering and the torments be smaller?
Various economists can prove that a silver currency (if it could be introduced) would ease the crisis for a while..
But will not the same process ultimately have to be gone through, with the same sum total:
mankind crucified on a silver cross?
—
For the golden cross is, after all, only the symbol of our system, and the system causes these periodic dangerous crises, which become ever more fatal with the growth of technology.
Not gold, but the individualistic striving to amass riches at the expense of the sufferings of the masses is to blame for the present crisis, as for all other similar crises.
On the ruling principle of "cheap labour" the golden cross grew up.
And as long as people seek to grow rich at the expense of others, at the expense of cheap labour, every metal, even the cheapest and commonest, will be turned into a "golden cross".
Whether gold is to blame for the present crisis, and whether silver or tin, or even paper, will help much — that is a question for the specialists, the economists, to answer.
But what plain common sense can already grasp is this: that the hundreds of millions of people who are now dying of hunger must be turned into civilised consumers.
And the earth still has enough fruit to feed all her children equally, and the human mind, human genius, has only just begun to uncover the hidden riches of nature.
Two Letters

[Want and hunger — letters to the editor.] Our editorial office has received two letters; in both letters rises a cry of pain from unfortunate, desperate people who have completely lost the ground under their feet and no longer have anything at all with which to support themselves and their families.
Although the letters are anonymous, it is nevertheless of interest to publish their contents, which illustrate the cruel want and hunger prevailing among the Jewish masses. These people, although they already stand on the brink of ruin, still have in them, it seems, enough shame, and they do not want to reveal their full names, but sign only with initials. It is still hard for them to unmask themselves, and their only request is that we pass their letters on to the public, which may at last give the matter more serious thought and undertake certain steps to rescue people whom despair can drive to the most extreme.
First letter.
"I am a Jew of about 48 years, a Hasidic Jew in long garments, never a great rich man, but I always traded honestly and passed with dignity the years that were destined for me to live. Two years ago a great misfortune befell me. I lay ill for a long time. And from then on hunger began to peer into the house. As is done in such a case, we began to sell the valuable things in the house, but how long could that last for me, my wife and two daughters, who were already grown-up girls whom one has to marry off? Hunger began to torment us; there was no one to help, no one even to give advice. My wife began to fall ill, and the last few pillows were sold for doctors and medicines.
I tried every means, knocked on the doors and thresholds of various institutions. But everywhere I received the same answer: the coffers are empty, we have no support to give.
What was left for me to do? The thought began to cut into my head: suicide; but I cannot do it yet, I feel bitter pity for my sick wife and children. I have decided to turn to your newspaper, that it should write about my terrible fate. Perhaps people will take pity and do something after all for me and for many more such unfortunate people.
I would have signed my full name, but believe me, Mr. Editor, I cannot. That would be too hard a trial for me. Worse than suicide. Do not therefore take it amiss if I sign myself with the mere letter 'T'."
Second letter.
Dear Mr. Editor!
Let me unburden my bitter heart and allow me to print the following words of mine in your esteemed newspaper.
I am still a very young man: a worker, an honest one, who for years worked to earn — — a piece of bread. A year ago I lost my work entirely. All efforts, all endeavours to obtain even the hardest work have not succeeded.
Already almost in the first week since I lost my work I no longer had anything for the first breakfast; with my young wife I wet the pillows at night, we did not eat, so long as our child, our 5-year-old little boy, could eat a piece of bread at least once a day; and that too began to run out, and then my wife and I fell upon a sad thought: to die together on one day and in one hour and to go on living together in the world to come... But our child held me back. But what will happen next? Mr. Editor, awaken the attention of Jewish society, let it do something for those on the verge of suicide; perhaps it will still be possible to save the unfortunate and the desperate.
Respectfully, K.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Korah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Korah
The Portion
—o—
a) "Now Korah took" (Num. 16:1)
Korah may indeed have been worthy of being a leader — after all, he was of noble lineage, rich and clever. The thing is, however, that "Korah took — he took himself": he wanted to take the leadership himself... But by yourself — that one does not take... Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha.
———
"Korah, who was clever — what made him commit this folly?" (Midrash).
From where does the Midrash conclude that Korah was a sly one, a clever man?
Because the other two hundred and fifty men believed the dispute was for the sake of Heaven — Korah had turned their heads; only Korah alone knew how dishonest his aim was, and sinned knowingly.
And this is already an old rule: when Adam had committed only the first sin, eating from the Tree of Knowledge, he had already become a maskil, an enlightened one ("the tree was to be desired to make one wise")... And if Korah committed a sin knowingly, he must surely already have been a clever man, a maskil... Alei Zayit.
—o—
b) "And they rose up before Moses" (ibid., 2)
So it is in every dispute. All you need is two or three bold ones, those who "rose up", who will dare to step forward — then "the men of the children of Israel" join in as a matter of course; they already drag along behind. Or Olam.
———
Korah's dispute is called in "Avot": "the dispute of Korah and his company", and not "the dispute of Korah and Moses", because only Korah quarrelled; Moses, on the other hand, kept silent... Nifla'ot Hadashot.
—o—
c) "For all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the Lord is among them" (ibid., 3)
If "the Lord is among them" — if they do not flaunt their piety outwardly to boast of it, but keep it within themselves — that is a sign that "they are all holy". "Holy" is the highest rung, higher than tzaddik and hasid, and when one reaches it — "and in the midst of the holy ones shall you walk": "in the midst", deeply hidden within... Milin Hartin.
—o—
d) "And Korah gathered [all the congregation] against them" (ibid., 19)
"And Korah gathered against them — with words of mockery." (Tanhuma)
Such is the way of all intriguers and quarrel-mongers. If they have nothing concrete with which to accuse their opponents, they resort to mockery, to ridicule, and want to win followers through frivolous talk. Divrei Shlomo.
—o—
e) "And the earth opened her mouth" (ibid., 32)
Rav Baruch Shedlitser was once asked why everyone envies Korah's wealth. Korah's riches were buried together with him, after all. Who then can know how rich he was?
The thing is — Rav Baruch answered — that this is the custom: when a Jewish rich man is alive, he is reckoned in the thousands, but when he dies and they go to divide up the inheritance, it turns out that he was a pauper. Korah, however, was buried together with his wealth, so everyone can say that he was a great rich man...
———
In Brisk [Brześć] a beggar once died, and a hoard of money was found with him. Naturally there was an uproar in town. Rav Yoshe Ber remarked on it:
"A strange thing: I know so many poor people of Brisk who pose as wealthy men... and nobody makes a peep; but here, one wealthy man who posed as a pauper — and such an outcry!..."
—o—
f) "And put on incense" (17:11)
Of the incense the Sages say that it made [people] rich. But poison lay in it, and whoever did not use it properly was burnt. Wealth too possesses the very same property... Asam [?] in the name of.
—o—
Haftarah.
g) "Whose ox have I taken?" (1 Samuel 11 [sic])
The Jews revolted against the leadership of Samuel's sons because they demanded their share and did not wait until it would be given them. That is why Samuel said to them: "Whose ox have I taken?" I indeed never demanded — well, so indeed I did not have... So what is the wrong of my children when they demand what is due to them? Alei Zayit.
—o—
h) "Your wickedness is great... in asking you a king" (ibid.)
The Jews wanted precisely to be "like all the nations", to have a king; in doing so they encroached on the nations' domain, intruding into a field that did not belong to them. That is why the nations in turn intruded into their field and wrought ruin... Binah le-Ittim.
—o—
Avot.
i) "And be not a head of foxes" (ch. 4)
A fox likes only to look beneath itself... That is exactly what is no good: to look beneath oneself and always see that there are worse ones than oneself... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
j) "And despise not any man" (ibid.)
Not "do not shame" (al tevaze — do not humiliate) but "be not despising" (al tehi baz) — do not hold yourself low before every person. Humility is not always in its place. Magen Avot.

[Children's section — a legend.]
(A legend)

The angels stood before the Creator, and their eyes were shedding tears: drip-drip and drop-drop...
The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: My good angels! What is all this weeping for?
They answered Him: We are weeping because the Jewish children are sad!..
He said to them: What, do they lack bread? I, I will feed them.
The angels kept quiet, and their eyes shed tears: drip-drip and drop-drop...
The Almighty asked once more: My good angels, why are you weeping?
They said: How should we not weep, when the little Jewish ones are sad!..
God looked at them and said: Perhaps they have no clothes — I, I will dress them, I will shoe them!
But the angels did not calm down; they keep standing and weeping...
The Creator shouted at them and said: Cry-babies! When will you stop shedding tears! Rather than sit in heaven and weep, better go down to earth and make the Jewish children merry.
The angels said, weeping: Master of the worlds! Jewish children are not used to joy...
God said: Why not? What is it — have their ships sunk?..
They said: Your people Israel is drowning in a sea of troubles, and the Jewish children suffer along with them...
When the angels said this, the gates of Paradise opened, and Elijah the Prophet appeared, walking and drawing near to the Throne of Glory.
The angels caught sight of the old man and without a word moved aside, stood and bowed before him.
And the Almighty turned to Elijah and said: Elijah, my son! You did well to come to me just now..
Elijah bowed his head and kept quiet.
The Creator said: Elijah, Elijah, Jewish children are wasting away in sadness and you keep silent?..
Elijah kept silent still.
God, blessed be He, said again: Elijah, I have pity on my people Israel!..
Elijah sprang up and said: I will run and announce the redemption to His children; here I am — send me!
The Almighty sighed and said: But the redemption can come only when people are merry.
The angels heard this and rejoiced. At once they went down from the heavens to make Jewish children merry, so as to bring the redemption nearer...

[Children's section — a story.]
B. Prekin.
Fishele and His Little Table.

Once there was a little boy, and his name was Fishele. Fishele had a little table. A nice, small little table. He let no one sit by it, nor touch it, nor even look at it. If a boy glanced at his little table, he began to scream; if he touched it, he got angry; if he sat down beside it, he cried:
— My little table... mine..
His father called him wicked, his mother — little fool, the boys — "Fishele-Tishele", but it did not help. Fishele let no one touch his little table, and wherever he went he carried it along with him.
One time Fishele was asleep.
He dreamt that he was all alone in a garden where there were lots and lots of people; Fishele wants to rest, to sit down on a bench — somebody shouts:
— Get off! It's not your bench...
Fishele gets up and goes over to the sea, wants to take a look at it — somebody shouts:
— What are you looking at, is it your sea?
Fishele goes on and hears music playing; he pricks up his ears and wants to listen too — they won't let him.
— Not your music!
Fishele raised his head to the sky, to the little birds, to the little trees, to the little aeroplanes — they would not let him; everywhere he stood or went they chased him away, shouting: Don't look... don't touch!.. It's not yours!...
Fishele comes home and takes a piece of bread, wants to eat — the baker runs in and snatches it from him:
— Not your bread!
He goes over to the tap, takes a glass of water and wants to drink — again somebody runs up and tears the water out of his hand.
— Your water, eh?
Fishele goes and wants to lie down in his little bed to sleep — a man runs up and blocks his way.
— This little bed is mine!
— — — — — —
Fishele woke up. He remembered everything he had dreamt, and became quite a different boy: he now let others look at his little table, touch it, and even sit and play beside it.
Litman.

Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (32)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin, the wandering sectarians of Russia; installment 32.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

They never wrote a letter, never let anything be heard of them. Years went by, and their families and friends heard not a word from them. They became wanderers, or, as it is called in Russian, "stranniki".

Among all those who belonged to the sect of the "People of God", marriage was considered a crime. For marriage binds a person to a place and to a home, and among the sectarians it was accepted that marriage is a sin against the "Holy Spirit", and every "man of God" is obliged to separate from his lawful wife, or at least to keep far away from her... At the same time, however, the sectarians are permitted to have love affairs with women. Every sectarian may have one or several women with whom he is "spiritually married", and he has relations with them... Such a "spiritual marriage" is blessed by God Himself. For it does not bind the "People of God" to any place or any home. And the women are purified and elevated through their relations with the sectarians...

Thousands of such wandering sectarians roamed across Russia at that time. Many wandered without any goal at all. They merely followed what their feelings dictated to them. Others again wandered with a goal — in order to reach various distant "holy" cities.

In almost every Russian village there were simple peasants who secretly belonged to the "brotherhood" of the wanderers. It was the duty of the peasants to give food and a night's lodging to the wanderers. Every one of the peasants received the "stranniki" with joy. Each of them had a cellar under his cottage, where wanderers who needed protection or rest found a place. There were also whole villages that sympathized with the wanderers. In such a village the wanderer found shelter and rest in every cottage.

The wanderer, who constantly spent his nights and his time in the dark cellars, became a "podpolnik", that is, an underground man. No one knew anything at all about his former life. No one knew his real name, and no one asked him where he came from or where he was going. Free of all earthly attachments, the "podpolnik" lived only for his soul and thereby drew ever closer to God. Little by little people began to look upon such a man as one of the chosen, and the peasants in the villages were very pleased and happy when such a man visited them, and they received him with open arms.

When the wanderer felt that the time of his wandering had come to an end, he settled in a particular place, and then it sometimes happened that he acquired the reputation of a "saint". He became a "mudrets" (a wise man) or a "starets" (a holy elder), and from all over the country believers made pilgrimages to him to ask for his blessing and his advice.

Rasputin became such a wanderer. For several years on end he roamed over fields and forests, hamlets and villages, knocked about in the dark cellars and got to know various kinds of people who, just like him, had abandoned their ordinary [?] lives and become "podpolniki". Coming into contact with followers of various sects and with religious fanatics, he got to know the soul of the Russian people and came to know the true feelings, thoughts and longings of the Russian peasantry.

The sectarians were persecuted by the priests and harshly hunted by the police, and Rasputin, who constantly had to be on his guard against them, learned during the time of his wanderings to understand people, to sense what they were thinking and to notice their evil intentions. This understanding of people developed in him over time to a high degree. Coming into contact with various wandering monks and religious fanatics, often holding long conversations with them and listening attentively to their talk, Rasputin gradually sharpened and deepened his theological knowledge and learned to speak about religious matters and to answer various religious questions skilfully and nimbly.

But the most important thing for Rasputin was that during the time of his wanderings he penetrated deeply into the secrets of the [printed "zey", i.e. "their"?] sect. What he had only heard about in the Verkhoturye monastery he now saw with his own eyes on his wanderings. He attended the orgies which the sectarians celebrated as "holy ceremonies"... He saw what is meant by "mysterious death" and "mysterious rebirth"...

The sectarians held their orgies sometimes in a hidden peasant room, sometimes in a grain barn, and sometimes also in the rooms of the monastery, in which the monks were secret sectarians. Mostly [printed "smerst"] it took place in a simple peasant cottage, and it took place like this:

On Saturday evening people gathered stealthily in a peasant cottage whose owner was a sectarian. They came by side roads and footpaths, and one at a time: first one came, then a second, then a third. Men and women assembled. In the middle of the room where the "ceremony" was to take place stood a white wooden [?] table, and beside the table two chairs. Along the walls stood plain benches.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Election Comedy in the Kehilla

What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 4 Tammuz 5692 — Friday, 8 July 1932.)
Będzin
The election comedy in the kehilla.
Last Sunday the kehilla council was again convened for a meeting at which the presidium of the council was supposed to be elected.
The chairman, Mr. Liwer, opens the meeting and declares that owing to various formal reasons the elections cannot take place, and — the meeting is closed..
The further acts of the election comedy are to take place next Sunday.
A concession obtained for Jewish boys attending public elementary schools.

This week the Jewish press reported that the Minister of Education has issued an order to the school superintendencies (kuratoria) that during the winter months, in Jewish public elementary schools (szkoły powszechne), lessons shall begin half an hour later, so that the boys will have the opportunity to pray.
It is interesting, however, to add that the order was issued thanks to the intervention of the well-known communal activist R' Mendel Rozensaft, who for several years interceded with Hasidic Sejm deputies, with the Central Committee of "Agudat Israel" and with other Orthodox personalities, who raised the question at the ministry until the concession for Jewish children was obtained.
No lessons at all are being held at the Talmud Torah

Throughout the whole week no lessons have been held at the local Talmud Torah, because the melamdim do not receive for their toil even enough for dry bread.
To the meeting that was called last Sunday, not a single one of the "guardians of the Torah and the faith" came.
As it turns out, the business of "installing" a shochet is much cheaper than the neglect of Torah study of 400 children...
The presidium of the "Discount Bank".

On Tuesday evening the supervisory board of the "Discount Bank" held a meeting at which the presidium of the supervisory board was constituted. Mr. A. Lidzbarski was re-elected chairman, and as vice-chairman the former honorary auditor, Mr. Herman Pinkus.
At the meeting the question of collecting bank debts was considered in passing. After a lengthy discussion it was decided that the supervisory board together with the management will apply against the debtors the most far-reaching measures, not even stopping short of bankruptcy proceedings.
A car full of wedding guests overturned.

On Tuesday a car packed full of passengers was travelling from Słomniki to Będzin to a wedding.
Not far from Olkusz the car broke down and almost all the in-laws, together with the bridegroom, fell out of the car.
Luckily all came out safe and sound. Only a few people were lightly injured.

The renovation being carried out at the municipal bathhouse is already being completed, and next Thursday, the 14th of this month, the establishment will already be operating.
A series of technical improvements has been introduced in the bathhouse, such as new showers, increased steam power, etc.

Among the active members of the Czeladź fire brigade is also a certain Yona Gryngras. The latter has for a long time been persecuted by the religious Jews there because he takes part in the drills on the Sabbath.
Last Sabbath, when Gryngras was going home from the drills, he was attacked by a "fiery" Hasid, who began beating G. The firemen came to G.'s aid, and as a result a brawl broke out between the two sides.

The Crash in America Has Divorced a Couple

[Sosnowiec — Everyday Life.]
Two years ago a young man from Sosnowiec came back from America, a widower without children. Here in his old home he has relatives, after all, good friends, companions from his childhood years and, above all, there is money — and with money one is never lost anywhere.
The local friends did indeed surround him on all sides and rejoiced with him. He wrote little cheques right and left, and everyone was very pleased. And truly, why let him travel back — the relatives thought — if they keep the rich relative here, they will be spared waiting for money from afar...
So they spread a net around him and sent matchmakers, until they succeeded in marrying him to a distant relative of his, a widow without children. A wedding was held in one of the local restaurants in royal style, and the old-young couple lived like a pair of doves.
But their happiness lasted only a few short years.
The crash in America brought ruin upon his cheque book; with the torn-out leaves one could no longer buy anything, and pleasures, of course, the American could no longer give his wife. The relatives also turned away from him, and domestic peace between husband and wife was destroyed.
The epilogue of the drama was played out these days in the rabbinical court.
The wife argued that she had married a rich American, but now, since he has no money and is no American either, she does not need him.
The rabbi's arguments — that the wheel may still turn and she may yet see good days with her husband in the land of dollars — did not help. She will hear nothing of it and insists on a divorce (get).

Enough of Dependence and Resignation!

[Zagłębie — economy.] Things are hushed with us, quiet on the economic front. The Jewish economic organizations in Zagłębie wore themselves out in previous years with the numerous interventions, with the various memoranda, with the frequent protest meetings — and now they are resting [?].
Who knows, perhaps there are also psychological reasons for it. Perhaps people themselves have lost faith and trust in all the various interventions and petitions? It is possible that this is so, but it is still no answer to the questions of the day which torment and wear down the Jewish artisan, small trader and merchant.
Many hopes were placed in economic self-government, in the chambers of commerce and of crafts, but the disappointment came quickly: economic self-government has turned into a bureaucratic apparatus, which works worse or better, which collects this or that interesting material, but which has achieved absolutely nothing in the field of the great tax burden.
Today merchants, small traders and artisans are organized in the above-mentioned institutions, and broad and large self-defence actions are no longer undertaken; today the agitated feelings of the great ruined masses no longer find expression in the form of protest meetings and resolutions; today all this is done by the chambers — calmly, coolly, "scientifically", without the methods of the economic plebs.
And what are the results?
The initiative of the Jewish economic organizations has been killed off. Nothing is undertaken to give expression to the "decline" of the economic spheres. People have relied entirely on the mechanized bureaucratic work of the "izby" [chambers], which work without feeling and without soul.
Years ago there were still cases when the economic organizations themselves would come to an understanding in order to carry out a joint action, and one must say that these actions often ended with a certain success. Today they have barricaded themselves in the "izby" and have themselves become passive and dependent.
And the great blind tax machine with its complicated little screws exploits this apathy and increases the ruin from day to day.
At such a moment one must not stand with folded arms; one must begin to think about self-help, independent [?] of the actions of the economic chambers.
All the methods used until now have disappointed. So one must return to the old methods and conduct the struggle directly oneself.
A.

Tobacco Shops in All Localities in Poland
[Poland — trade.] About 45.000 localities in Poland so far have no points of sale for tobacco products, as a result of which the population is forced to overpay for the products, which are brought in by various kinds of middlemen. As we learn, the Finance Ministry, at the request of many interested parties, has now agreed to grant permits to open shops for tobacco products in places where there is as yet no sale of these products — without any formalities and without the obligation to buy a trade licence (patent) for the year 1932.
In rural gminas where there are no suitable premises, the sale of tobacco products may take place in ordinary cottages, but on condition that the products are kept in special cupboards or boxes.
Persons who receive permission to open a tobacco shop in the period from 1 July to 31 December of this year will be exempt from the obligation to buy a licence for the year 1932 if [?], besides tobacco products, they sell only articles needed for smoking, such as matches, cigarette tubes and the like. Tobacco shops whose earnings for the year 1982 [sic, for 1932] will not exceed the sum of 360 zł. — or 30 zł. a month — will be exempt from buying a licence next year as well.
Applications for permits to open shops must be submitted orally or in writing to the competent Office of Excise and State Monopolies.
Submitting the application and obtaining the permit involve no costs whatsoever.

False alarming report of a disaster at the summer camp in Sławków

On Wednesday afternoon, after the rainstorm, a report suddenly spread in Będzin that 6 Jewish children from the summer camp in Sławków had drowned while bathing.
It is easy to imagine what turmoil and panic the report caused; desperate parents, brothers and sisters of the children staying at the camp ran through the streets.
By the minute the report became more serious; all sorts of stories and exaggerations about the disaster were told.
Our editorial office at once got in touch by telephone with Sławków, from where, after an hour's wait, the answer came that the whole story was invented and that nothing at all had happened.
Only then did the desperate crowd calm down and disperse.
Who spread the report is not clear.

Foundation Stone Laid for Jewish Shops on the Dąbrowa Magistrate's Site

As our readers know, the Dąbrowa municipality, by decision of the voivodeship, had to clear the stalls opposite the Kościuszko monument, and on that site the new post-office building of Dąbrowa is to be built.
The decision hit hard the several Jewish merchants who drew their livelihood from the trading stalls, and they began a campaign to soften the decision, so that they should not be directly ruined.
It goes without saying that changing a decision of a higher authority is not an easy matter, but our town is in this respect in a very favourable position, because we have here the hundred-percent democrat, Dr. Madejski, as mayor, and he, like the merchants themselves, was keenly ("bloodily") interested that the difficult question be solved in such a way that "the wolf be sated and the lamb whole". Over 3 years Mayor Madejski intervened with the organs of power and finally succeeded in settling the matter as follows:
The post office will be built on the other side of the same street, and the Jewish merchants are to build themselves shop premises on the government site, on condition that only after 18 years will they pay rent.
After this decision, favourable to the Jewish merchants, the interested parties elected a committee headed by Mr. Jakob Parasol as chairman, and the committee is building the shop premises on a cooperative basis.
Last Monday the first stone of the jointly owned trading premises was laid. Although the matter is a private one, the committee nevertheless, out of gratitude to the town administration, gave a festive character to the laying of the first stone.
Invited were representatives of the magistrate, the town council, the Jewish community, the press and public figures who regard the building question with sympathy.
On behalf of the committee Mr. Parasol greeted the participants; he gave a survey of the time when the matter became pressing, the danger that the Jewish merchants would be evicted from their businesses, and expressed thanks to all who helped remove the stumbling blocks, above all to the mayor, Dr. Madejski.
A greeting on behalf of the Jewish kehilla was delivered by the chairman of the board, Mr. Jakob Mittelman, who stressed that the mayor's deeds prove that he works for the good of all citizens without distinction of nationality, and in the name of the Jewish population of Dąbrowa he wished the mayor further success in his work.
After the reply of the mayor, who thanked the previous speakers and said that the saying "nothing stands in the way of will" is true: as long as there is good will, the hardest question can be resolved favourably, and proof is the present act, which has been settled to the benefit of all sides.
Then the mayor was invited to lay the first stone. To the same honour were also invited the deputy mayor, chairman Mittelman, councillor Bernard Rechnitz and the industrialist Mr. Jakub Rechnitz.
After the ceremony refreshments were served, and with that the ceremony ended.
Terrible Storm over Zagłębie. 5 Victims — 7 Injured by Thunderbolts

On Saturday at about 5 in the afternoon a terrible rainstorm accompanied by thunder and lightning passed over Zagłębie.
In Reyndovke[?] 9 persons had taken shelter in a coal pit; suddenly a thunderbolt struck this pit, and 3 of their number were killed on the spot. The remaining 5 received a number of serious and light wounds. Thanks to quick medical help the injured were saved.
A second thunderbolt struck in Klimontów, in a house that is still under construction. In this house many people had taken shelter from the storm. From the thunderbolt 2 remained dead on the spot and several were injured.
"You Are Our Father, Panie Dyrektorze" — Workers of the "Helena" Pit Call Out to Director Mr. S. Łaznowski

At the labour inspector's in Sosnowiec a conference took place between the director of the "Helena" coal pit, Mr. S. Łaznowski, and the workers' delegates of the pit.
At the conference the question was discussed of closing the pit for a longer time in order to install new technical improvements. And the director, beloved by the workers, Mr. Łaznowski, therefore put forward a series of proposals that give the workers the possibility of having a livelihood during the time the pit will not be working.
The workers received the proposals with great satisfaction and called out to Mr. Łaznowski: "You are our father!" If only the directors of the big mines would follow this fine example.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

Trial over the removal of "manly strength".
At the Katowice district court an interesting trial took place against the doctors of a local hospital, where, owing to a mistake, a patient was deprived of his "manly strength".
A patient, one Wróbel, was staying in the hospital. Some time later another patient, also by the name of Wróbel, was admitted to the same hospital.
The doctors, who held a consultation about the second patient, determined that the patient could recover if his manly strength were removed.
And here the same mistake occurred as in King Solomon's time, and the operation in question was performed on the first patient...
The court, having heard the claims of the "no longer potent male person", could not for the moment determine how much to assess the damage to the male person, and the trial was therefore adjourned.
