The Incomprehensible Incitement — Is It Healthy to Pursue Antisemitism in the Present Hard Times?

[Article — antisemitism; Będzin, Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.] Is it healthy to pursue antisemitism in the present hard times?
A great misfortune has poured down upon mankind. In the world, life is becoming unbearable, existence is becoming an impossible phenomenon. All possibilities have become incredible phenomena in human existence, everything is wrestling with death, all logical certainties have become incomprehensible riddles.
Yes, the world is sick and cannot get well; no cure can be found for the terrible plague that has poured down upon mankind in such a terrible form and in so large a dose. The atmosphere has become so heavy, so unbearable, that it remains impossible to breathe, impossible to carry on the further course of life.
It would surely have been understandable that in such a serious and strained time one should adopt means of solving this difficult problem called existence, which is in truth the further course of life of human meaning, of human life; but instead of wanting radically to solve this question, instead of taking an interest in it so that it should be truly solved, people begin to muddle the brains. And — as happens in such a case — they lose their balance, and then they come to the conclusion that everything would have been good and fine if the Jew were exterminated, if he were cleared off the highway on which, in the antisemites' view, he still wanders about, getting under everyone's feet. A cult has begun to form, to the effect that in the Jew lies the whole tragedy of mankind, and if only he were exterminated, if only he were cleared off the highway, everything would already be saved, salvation would then come to mankind, and then one would be saved from all misfortunes and mankind would be redeemed from all evil; and if there is no other way, if the citizens in the various countries believe that this is the right road, onto which they have blindly launched themselves at a gallop, then in that case one has to say, willy-nilly, amen.
Hitlerism has poured down upon human heads, and a large part of mankind believes that in it lies help, that it will save the world from all misfortunes; and therefore it is no wonder that in all sorts of countries Hitlerism is on the march and its rule becomes ever more popular.
And if the air everywhere is poisoned, if in many countries this "commodity" has taken root as help for mankind, as a radical means of solving the problem called existence and progress, then it is surely no wonder that with us in Poland, too, this course is beginning to become popular.
And indeed, why should the Polish antisemites lag behind their European comrades? It would surely be a disgrace and a shame before the world if our qualified antisemites did not join their comrades and did not carry on the process of development that is forcing its way among people and nations in various countries. And so it is no wonder that we are beginning to see the seeds that were sown — we are already beginning to see their fruits.
Never mind — what more is needed: in Jewish Będzin, in the town where even the Christians are imbued with the Jewish spirit; it does not matter, one may say it openly, for the Christian inhabitants have grown used to living with us, and who knows better than they that "the devil is not as terrible as he is painted"; with us in Będzin our neighbours surely know that the antisemitic tricks are performed only to show that, for appearance's sake, they must not fall behind their comrades and must behave "like everybody else". In truth, however, they know that this is no more than a sort of idée fixe, and therefore it is understood by every one of us that at every undertaking and entertainment [impreza] people come to us asking us to support it, and of course our brethren the Children of Israel never refuse such a mitzvah, however bad things may be. On the contrary, a Jew will sooner not give to a Jewish cause, whereas for our neighbours we have the greatest respect and reverence, and they are always favoured with the finest donations. For ourselves, says a Jew, it is not so important to show friendship and love as towards our neighbours, with whom we have lived together for hundreds of years, and to them we must show true friendship, love and devotion; and therefore we offer them the finest donations when they come to us; we do not even ask for what purpose it is. When they come to us, we give our donation with reverence, beyond our means, because with us it is an old custom that for the other fellow's sake one must pinch one's own cheek so that the colour stays put.
And for this we are repaid. For this such an "international" institution as a fire brigade society can allow itself to arrange entertainments in town whose main themes are interwoven with hefty doses of antisemitism; and this is done not only among themselves at the entertainments — with it they also go out to triumph through the streets of Będzin, where you are told the good news that you will laugh and that, until broad daylight, you will be shown nothing but all kinds of Jewish caricatures, in which they are exceptionally rich, so that they possess the real cream of mockery of Jews.
Thus shame is thrown in our eyes because we know how to support their undertakings; thus sand is thrown in our eyes, and we make nothing of it, as if it were not we who were meant; as if the antisemitic incitements [?] had not been staged in our own town. And for this — because we support all of it — a Jew even gives up his seat at the entertainments with which we are regaled every Sunday.
That is how people here know how to answer the fact that poison and hatred are spread between Jews and Christians, who live together amicably — and this, poor things, gives our antisemites no rest, so that they, poor things, rack their brains how to "demonstrate" the idyllic relations between us and our neighbours.
And one more fact shows how our "kind-hearted" antisemites, poor things, cannot rest when they see that peace and tranquillity reign between Jews and Christians in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, so that they search beneath the bare earth in order to sow hostility and hatred between Jews and Christians.
Thus last week we read a notice in the columns of our paper that the Christian girls from Zagłębie who hold posts in Upper Silesia have applied to the Katowice railway directorate to assign special carriages for them, so that Jews should have no access to them, since until now they have been defiled by the latter.
Of course we are not so naive as to think that these ideas come from the girls; there is no doubt that here, as everywhere, there is a hand that directs all this and strives to give the hostility and hatred a wider scope; the aim is gradually to make the Jew loathsome in our neighbours' eyes to the point of disgust. This is the level to which they want to educate today's Polish youth; this is how they want to make the Jew repulsive to them.
Of course, in the present hard times, when the worker is starving, the peasant has been impoverished and the official has no post, the situation is very grave, and at such a moment the patient hurts wherever he is touched; so that it is very easy in such a bitter time to incite one part of the population against the other — let alone when it is directed against a Jew.
Christian girls are being persuaded that the Jew is dirty and that it is dangerous to sit with him in one compartment; they want to make the Jew loathsome in the eyes of the Christians, they strive to cast disgust upon everything connected with Jewry.
They do not want to know, in all this, that the Jew fulfils his civic obligations towards the country no worse than the sworn "patriots" — and yet they seize upon every trifle as if it were a roast.
The antisemitic clique, seeing that its work has good prospects and that such things can be carried out systematically [?], grows arrogant and strives to take in an ever wider field.
We Jews, as citizens, have the right to demand that our civic rights be protected equally with the rights of all other citizens in free, independent Poland; we must not allow a clique of irresponsible antisemites, for their own benefit, to stir up feeling against us and to make us loathsome, in a disgusting manner, in the eyes of the peaceable Polish citizen.
And it is characteristic that this is being done at a time when the country is struggling so hard with its possibilities of existence, and when the Jew, proportionally, actually brings more revenue into the state treasury in taxes than the non-Jew. But now [?] that the sources [?] are being exhausted, so that there is soon nobody left from whom to collect taxes — of course, during such an economic crisis, which has already lasted so long, one should have had no head for antisemitism; in such hard times it would certainly have been wiser if people had rather pondered how the economic question of the country, which is so depressed, might be radically solved.
Our antisemites could have allowed themselves to indulge [?] in their "ideal" if everything in the country were good and comfortable, if the economic conditions of life were flourishing, if there were no unemployment and if the factories were not broken shards; and so, since there are such light-headed people under the prevailing conditions, it is not enough merely not to be short-sighted — it would have been fitting that such people should not live along with us in our present generations; otherwise the whole incitement remains incomprehensible and inconceivable.
R. Les.
The Dogs' Tails Must Be Docked...*)

[Feuilleton — a satirical fable on the arms race and "disarmament"; translated from German.]

In a certain beautiful and fertile valley there lived as neighbours, one beside the other, brothers, and, as befits brothers, the two of them lived in peace and visited and supported each other.

On the boundary that divided their farms stood a splendid walnut tree, which from year to year bore more fruit, sometimes on the north side and sometimes on the south side — and the brothers, paying no attention to this at all, always shared the fruit equally.

The master of the southern farm — as often happens — had a wife, a stingy one, who, seeing that this year the tree bore more fruit on the south side, argued with her husband: "You really are an idiot! You have more fruit on your side and you give it away willingly to your brother. For years I have been observing that the tree bears more fruit on our side — and where is the justice?!"

In vain did the husband try to convince his wife that for the sake of their mutual, brotherly and peaceful relations it was necessary for the tree to bear more fruit on the northern side, and the inequality would even itself out. But nothing helped; he had to give in to his wife, and without saying a word to his brother he gathered the fruit of the tree from the southern side.

A few days later, as the owner of the northern farm was passing by the tree, he noticed with great astonishment his brother's baseness, and without thinking long he ran to him in anger to rebuke him for the injustice. One word led to another, and the brothers quarrelled and stopped speaking to each other.

The owner of the northern farm, overcome by a feeling of revenge, called together his sons, dug under the tree on the northern side, cut off the branches and the roots, and stripped the trunk of its bark halfway — exactly up to the boundary — and went home. Naturally the tree did not survive this operation and dried up. This worsened their mutual relations and led to a terrible hatred.

Neither of the brothers now dared to cross the other's boundary. The owner of the northern farm even got himself a vicious dog to guard his borders.

The other's wife then badly nagged her husband, and under her influence he acquired two dogs. From then on nobody dared to cross the border without [printed: "in"] danger to his life.

Indescribable was the joy on the southern farm when the dog family grew by four "puppies" [szczeniaki, Polish]. Now the border was truly "walled in". But the northern farm did not fall asleep either. There too they meanwhile managed to breed a new generation of dogs for the border guard. A race in dog-breeding began. Now not only the border but also prestige came into consideration.

It went so far that neither the animals nor the people were safe for their lives. From day to day the dog families multiplied more and more, and a great deal of food was needed for them. The children went hungry; the cattle had to be slaughtered to feed the dogs. You cannot play games with a hungry dog.

And when the situation got worse and worse, truly unbearable, the owner of the northern farm sent messengers to his brother in the south: "Come tomorrow to the border, there where the tree used to stand, and we shall talk about disarmament!" The brother accepted the invitation with satisfaction.

The next day the brothers came to the appointed place with their sons and with their best dogs, so that their negotiations should be more significant and more splendid.

The negotiations began. First of all a proposal came up that all the dogs' teeth should be pulled out. But this proposal fell through: the dogs barked fearfully, as if they had understood what it was about. The proposal to pull out only their fangs [?] also failed to obtain a majority of votes, like many other similar projects.

Suddenly, right in the middle, the son of the owner of the northern farm stands up and says the following words: "We want peace; we want [?] to return the dogs to normal relations, and in place of the dried-up tree to plant a new one and eat its fruit in partnership." It seemed to him that his speech had made a strong impression, for nobody interrupted him. But when he had finished, everyone called him a utopian — it is surely ridiculous to think one can reach an ideal in a moment. And what next? Is there no way out? All sank deep in thought; even the dogs, who rarely think, now became sad.

Suddenly a proposal is brought in — there is a way out! The author of the project stands up: I am of the opinion that we must shorten the tails of all the dogs a little. Bravo! Agreed! — voices were heard from all sides. The dogs did indeed grumble a little, but they were given to understand that they should calm down.

The neighbours went home satisfied, in the awareness that "progress" is a lofty matter — as long as one does not overdo it.

*) Under the above headline a feuilleton by a Swiss farmer, Hans Gisin of Altingen, appeared in the "Basler National-Zeitung". We give this satire in a Yiddish translation.
An End to the Inflated Salaries! A New Means of Easing the Crisis in Poland.

[An End to the Inflated Salaries! — A New Means of Easing the Crisis in Poland.]
The great austerity campaign which the government undertook some time ago consisted first and foremost in reducing as far as possible the administrative expenses of maintaining the state apparatus. As is known, civil servants' pensions were reduced, despite all the protests on the part of the civil-service body, which felt itself greatly wronged; and in this way the government saved a good several million złoty, which was of very great importance for the state budget.
The continuation of this austerity campaign is to be a new draft decree, which is due to appear any day now. Because of the originality of the law, which is in its essence a novelty in Polish legislation, it is worth dwelling in more detail on the question of what this proposed law deals with.
As can be seen from this draft, which, by the way, has already been adopted by the Council of Ministers, the legislator's intention is to create a legal basis for carrying out a revision of the excessive monthly salaries received by the managing bodies of the large enterprises, joint-stock companies, etc., in particular in those enterprises whose cash position has long since ceased to permit the inflated pensions that the directors or other managing persons have fixed for themselves. During the last crisis years it happened more than once that such an enterprise sank deeper and deeper, unable to free itself of these "providers".
It is this kind of larger enterprise, which is simply bending under the burden of the enormous salaries of its managing bodies, that the government wishes to help, and to make it easier, by legal means, for such enterprises to free themselves of guardians of this kind.
The new decree makes the level of salary of the board members of joint-stock companies, limited-liability companies and other enterprises of a public character dependent on the enterprise's earnings and ability to pay, on whether the business is not indebted and has no tax arrears, and also on the level of wages received by the workers employed in the enterprise.
If such an enterprise, i.e. its (managing) body, does not itself take appropriate steps to reduce salaries exceeding 2500 zł. monthly or 30,000 zł. yearly — since only these salaries are affected by the decree — then the Treasury Chamber may come forward with such a proposal if the enterprise has been in tax arrears for over a year; likewise the Minister of Labour may also put forward such a proposal to reduce salaries in the event that payment to the workers is held up for more than 30 days.
What has moved government circles to penetrate into private enterprises in order to regulate their innermost affairs?
The economic crisis, which grows stronger from day to day, has lately brought many enterprises to a catastrophic state. On closer examination of the various causes of the situation that had arisen, what struck the eye were the enormously high administrative expenses, under whose burden the enterprises literally broke down. For lack of earnings the capital was gradually eaten away. "Nadzór" [court supervision] and bankruptcies became a frequent phenomenon. Reducing the administrative expenses, however, was impossible, because the salaries of the managing bodies rested for the most part on agreements concluded in advance for a number of years, which could not be broken.
The only way out that could solve the problem was: to create the legal possibility of annulling these agreements, and that is the task of this draft law.
At the same time a very important point is also indicated, with which the whole question of the above-mentioned reductions is bound up. Limiting the administrative expenses in the largest industrial enterprises will not only make the existence of these enterprises possible, but will also allow a broader development of production. Production costs until now were too high, and because of the expensiveness of Polish production any competitive struggle whatsoever on the foreign market was almost impossible.
With the cheapening of production, however, which will come as a result of reducing administrative expenses, one must expect increased consumption within the country itself, where demand has lately shrunk to a minimum; and above all such a cheapening will enable Polish exports to be competitive on foreign sales markets vis-à-vis other countries, which have lately overtaken us.
In the light of the above-mentioned motives, which, as the government press assures us, are the main reasons for introducing the new law, the new draft law is much more than one of the countless drafts: it grows into an important act of self-defence in a time of crisis, a preventive measure against a danger facing many industrial enterprises, and finally an impetus towards cheaper production, which we after all need very badly.
Mgr. J. Warszawski.
Regulations on Spreading an Adjudged Debt into Instalments.

[Law — debts and payment in instalments; legal column.] The civil court procedure (Art. 136) contains a provision under which the payment of a private-law debt may be spread into instalments.
This institution is of special importance for the masses of debtors precisely now, in the time of general impoverishment and the prevailing shortage of means of payment.
And indeed, if one were to demand all at once a larger debt that has accumulated, be it even for rent, it would ruin more than one householder and in certain cases even destroy him completely. The possibility granted of paying off a debt in instalments thus considerably eases for the debtor the conditions for freeing himself from such obligations.
The concession of spreading a debt into instalments applies to all kinds of private-law monetary obligations. It cannot, however, be applied to debts adjudged on protested bills of exchange.
Likewise one must also remember that spreading an adjudged debt into instalments is not a duty but a right of the court. Therefore the interested party must first make a special request for it.
The motion to spread a debt into instalments must be submitted by the debtor at the actual court hearing, before the verdict is pronounced. In justified cases it may also be done later.
As already said above, every debt, except for the exception indicated, may be spread into instalments, but the said concession cannot be granted to every debtor; under the statutory provision cited, only such debtors are entitled to enjoy this concession as do not possess the means to pay the adjudged sum at once. Qualifying a debtor in this respect depends on the personal discretion of the court. That same court is also solely competent to fix, in proportion to the debtor's ability to pay, the dates and the amount [?] of the instalments granted.
Since we are speaking of the court's right to spread an adjudged debt into instalments and to fix the dates of these instalments, attention must also be drawn on this occasion to the duty of a debtor so qualified to pay punctually the sums concerned on the dates fixed by the court.
For Article 137 of the Code [ustawa] of Civil Procedure provides a certain sanction for abuse of this concession, consisting in this: for failing to pay even a single instalment on the fixed date, one automatically loses the right to this concession, and the remaining sum thereby becomes immediately enforceable — not directly, however, but only on the basis of a special court resolution.
The same rules also apply to spreading accumulated tax debts into instalments.
J. Infeld.

[Chronicle — an adultery affair.] When the Wife Is at the Dacha...
The young merchant G. went off this summer with his wife to a dacha. Of course, it was his wife who stayed at the dacha, while G. himself was in town.
It so happened that out of boredom he carried on a love affair with a Christian young lady — a manicurist — and spent whole evenings and... nights with her.
His wife found out about it and decided to catch her husband red-handed.
On Sunday evening Mrs G. came down to town and began to follow her husband. She watched him as he met the manicurist and went off arm in arm with her to Małachowskiego Street, where they took a separate room.
The wife immediately ran to her brother, and soon they came back and knocked on the door of the room where the couple was.
To G.'s question: "Who's knocking?" the brother-in-law answered:
— Open at once, this is the vice police!
G. opened the door and, to his great surprise, saw his wife with the brother-in-law.
What happened next is no longer important, but there is quite a lot of talk that the story will have an echo in the rabbinical court.
How I Was Turned from a Male into a Female?...

[Feuilleton — humour; a trip to Karlsbad.]
Told by a Jew with a stomach.

Where, you say, am I travelling from? From Karlsbad? I'm not going to Karlsbad any more [?] — not even if you cover me in gold! I'll make my children's children swear never to travel to Karlsbad.
Why am I so angry at Karlsbad? Why shouldn't I be angry? Because of Karlsbad I was turned from a man into a female. I ask you: wouldn't you be angry if someone insisted to you, flat out, that you're a female? It's a scandal, to make a "prawdziwy" (genuine) male into a female — and what a female! A blackmailer!
How I was turned from a male into a female, you want to know? Then listen to me with your head — what can't happen! — so that you'll know how to behave on the train and above all: how one can come to grief because of a name. Hear the story:
As you know, I am — may it not happen to you or to any Jew — a Jew with a stomach.
You think perhaps I have a weak stomach? God forbid! In fact I have a healthy stomach... not a pampered [?] stomach... whatever I give it, it says "this too is for the good" (gam zu le-tova).
Well then, since I have a healthy stomach, why on earth do I need Karlsbad? The excuse is: my son-in-law. Since I have a son-in-law who is still a very young doctor and has no practice, heaven spare you, he practises on my stomach: he groped and searched so long that he found something. He says my liver is "powiększenie" (enlarging)...
So I ask him: what, are you a pauper [?], that I'll have an extra bit of liver? Does it cost you more? It's my liver, it seems to me..
But he is a doctor after all, and gives me to understand, according to the wisdom of doctoring, that the liver has a connection with the heart, and with the heart one mustn't play games.
So I really did pack my tallis and tefillin and set off for Karlsbad (printed "Karlsbar").
But when trouble is laid out for you, it comes right into the railway carriage — and it was in the carriage that I was turned from a male into a female. Hear what happened:
Right before the border there is in the carriage — "for the Jews" — an inspection [?]; they order you to show passports [?], and before you know it they are already standing by me.
— Paszport!
A passport is a passport, and I hand over my pass.
— "Nadnaszcz" [?] — they ask me? Whether I'm "wygodnie" (comfortable)?
— I am — I answer him — very "wygodnie".
— "Jak się pan nazywa?" (What is your name, sir?) — asks me a blonde shiksa in a cap with a shiny visor.
— "Ja się nazywam" — I answer — Elye Rabinowicz.
The blonde fixes on me a pair of eyes that sparkle:
— "Pani będzie łaskawa ze mną" (Madam will kindly come with me).
So I break into a sweat.
— What — I say — my name is Elye; what does it mean, I should go with a strange shiksa?
— "Przepraszam" — I say — "ja nie pójdę, mam żonę i małe robaki w domu" (I won't go, I have a wife and little 'worms' at home) — I have a wife with little worms.
The more I explain to her that I have a wife and children, the more she smiles and makes such strange little eyes at me that I went hot and cold. She looks me straight in the eyes and strokes my beard, looks me over from head to foot — a regular in-law...
But I saw that she was making [?] a whole "shmelke" [?] of me, and then I got angry:
— "Co to jest?" (What is this?) — I ask her — what chutzpah, "przecież ja jadę z mojem wątrobą do Karlsbadu" (I'm travelling with my liver to Karlsbad, after all)...
You think she was terribly impressed by my liver — like yesterday! At the first station she gets up and "zaprasza" (invites) me off the train, leads me into a special room, and here the thick of it [?] begins:
In that room there was already another maiden with a shiny visor, and again they take me apart.
— "Jak się pan nazywa?" Again "Hela" Rabinowicz, again the same groping, groping and stroking, and looking me over from head to foot.
So again I plead the same: "Przepraszam" — I say — "jestem a sickly man with an enlarged liver, jestem urodzony [?] mężczyzna (I am a born [?] man), nie Hela tylko Elia (not Hela but Elia)"...
— "Rozebrać się!" (Undress!) — one of them gives a stern order.
— What do you mean, I say, all a-tremble, what do you mean I should undress? A man among females, "przecież ja mam żonę i małe robaki w domu!" (I have a wife and little ones at home!)...
— "Zdejmować brodę!" (Take off the beard!) — the second one gives a command, and meanwhile she starts groping my beard. She looks it over from all sides, and at every stroke on my "gęba" (mug) my heart grew faint.
I defended myself and they did their thing... they took off my coat, my jacket, my trousers; the shiksas with the shiny visors were doubling [?] before my eyes and my teeth chattered. Two blonde shiksas, and here I stand already as in the bathhouse, to make the distinction... a father of children, a husband of a wife... had it lasted one more minute, God forbid...
Now... now... now...
— — — — —
And then a miracle happened: as I stand like that in my troubles, a young man bursts in with a shout:
— Stop, stop, stop! "Omyłka" (A mistake)!
You want to know the end? The end was: they apologised to me; it had been a small mistake:
On the train they were looking for a woman, a blackmailer by the name of Hela Rabinowicz, who is disguised as a Jew with a beard; and since my name is Elye, they read "Hela". The same name, and on top of it a Jew with a beard — it couldn't be otherwise: I must be the disguised woman Hela Rabinowicz. Lucky still that they caught the right girl; if not, if it had lasted one more minute — who knows? Who knows what faces the two blonde shiksas with the shiny visors would have made.
That is how, on the way to Karlsbad, I was turned from a male into a female..
A—K.
Upper Silesian Economic Sketches

Dr. Arolf [Adolf?] Szajer [?], Katowice.
6.
The situation in Upper Silesian industry does not look much better. Every day we read about the requests submitted to the demobilization commissioner for permission to make further necessary reductions of the clerical and workers' staff. There is hardly a single family in Katowice and in the Silesian province in which there is not some unemployed person, and quite often there are cases where whole families, who once, in the good times, all worked together in a steelworks (huta) or a mine (kopalnia), — are today [?] shut down. Today the unemployed families depend on the small allowance for a dry piece of bread, which is itself barely enough. A few days ago the illustrated magazines carried an illustration showing unemployed people somewhere abroad who take up fishing en masse and later sell the fish at the markets. Here in Upper Silesia such phenomena are quite frequent: the unemployed, who for long years were employed in the pits or in the steelworks, grab at all sorts of trades, if only to have some income and occupation; and, not wanting to fall into the drunkenness that, unfortunately, has lately been spreading more and more, they cannot live [idle], having been accustomed for so many years to regular work.
And from the persecuted trade, which [is harassed] at every step — whether it is a matter of bringing in goods from abroad, or of the hundreds of other regulations and ordinances that spring up like mushrooms after rain — and from the merchant, who can barely catch his breath and who bends under the heavy burden of taxes, under the burden of the various social contributions the law has imposed on him, ever larger taxes are demanded, and the tax offices are ordered to apply the harshest measures in collecting the taxes.
The turnover assessment for the whole year 1931 exceeded the assessments of past years, despite the generally known worsening of the economic situation; and the famous former 'Grabski cart', which takes from the shops not only the goods but also the empty shelves, is again beginning to appear quite often in the commercial districts. Where does this lead?
It is high time that the authoritative circles review all these ordinances, and instead of calling much-advertised economic conferences in Warsaw, and instead of the solemn promises given to the representatives of trade and industry, they should rather attach to their ordinances the postulates put forward by the representatives concerning tax relief: to annul the tax arrears, and to note in the directives to the tax offices that the lamentable state of trade and industry must be taken into account. If the merchant is allowed to breathe a little more freely, if his arrears are struck off — they will never be collected anyway — he will be able to recover his strength, he will be able to find new sources of income, and a healthier and stronger taxpayer will be created, who will not have Damocles' sword hanging over him in the form of constant distraints for old 'tax sins'. He will not have to hide, and he will be able to take up new, fruitful work with all his strength.
Let us hope that the cry of the oppressed merchant will not remain a voice crying in the wilderness. (Sz.)
Assessment Commissions

The year of a loyal citizen is divided into 2 parts: the time when every Jew must remember the turnover tax, and the time when he must stand on guard because of the income tax. On the 15th of February (luty) one must submit a declaration (zeznanie) for the turnover tax. A period of concern with this tax then begins. In order to be protected from unforeseen surprises, one must take careful care that no assessment goes through that could ruin the taxpayer. The members of the assessment commissions then receive visits from a larger number of taxpayers, who give explanations about their material situation. This work lasts until the end of July (lipiec), until the time when the appeals are for the most part settled.
The very same work begins in May, when the income-tax declarations are submitted. Then the members of the income-tax assessment commissions again receive visits with explanations about the taxpayers' income. These explanations are quite good material for the members of the commissions, both for the turnover tax and for the income tax. The taxpayers' explanations, together with the information which the commission members themselves quite often have, are already really quite important in assessing the tax, considering that the rapporteur at the session also has material on every taxpayer, and all of it together already gives a 90 per cent sufficient certainty that there will be no unjust assessment.
It is, however, by no means certain that the members of the commission will take into account the material they receive from the taxpayers during [?] their interventions, and this for a simple reason: it is impossible to remember the details of several dozen persons at each session.
In the course of each series of sessions every member, whatever commission it is, has to remember [particulars] about several hundred taxpayers: what line of business, how many workers, how much equipment the taxpayer possesses, what turnover or income he had, how much average profit is reckoned in the income, etc. All this material is very important, but unfortunately it is impossible to remember it all at the moment when the case of the taxpayer concerned is being considered. At most one remembers only the name and the information that happens to stay in one's mind. But that is really too little to secure the taxpayer a just assessment of the tax.
It has been the custom since time immemorial that the commission member comes to the session empty-handed. All the material, even if he notes it down, he does not take with him to the session. Many members are [?] sure that it is not permitted at all to say from notes what one wants or needs [to say]. In reality it is not so. There is no regulation that would forbid bringing to the sessions the information one collects before the session and which can help to determine fairly the amount of the tax.
In the procedure which the law (ustawa) on income tax lays down [?], for example, it is said quite clearly that the material which the rapporteur collects is used at the session in assessing the tax together with the material possessed by the members of the assessment commissions. It is surely also understandable that the civic element was not placed there in order to perform its duty on the basis of material supplied to it, but in order to know, on the basis of their own information, how high to assess the tax.
Therefore, because of the forthcoming new income-tax assessment for the year 1932, the question of the competence of the commission members is now topical; that is to say, the members should know what they may and what they must not do. A joint conference with proper lectures on the matters mentioned would bring very great benefit to the whole institution of the assessment commissions. Such an initiative cannot come from any economic institution such as a merchants', manufacturers' or artisans' association, because it would not embrace all circles. It is therefore desirable that the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, perhaps after an understanding with the Chamber of Crafts and the Doctors' [?] Chamber, should take over this commendable initiative. We know that the Chamber of Commerce once had a project of publishing a brochure on this matter. But it is much better to convene such a conference of all members of the assessment commissions. Much better and more purposeful.
B. Frejnd.

Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Chukat-Balak
The Portion
a) "When a man dies in a tent" (Num. 19:14)
"You are called 'man' (adam), and the nations of the world are not called 'man'." (Yevamot 61a).
The soul of the Jewish people, the Torah, was created before the Jewish body yet existed — two thousand years before the creation of the world. Therefore even "when he dies", even when the Jewish body dies away, he is still "called man", because his soul lives; it came into being before his birth and can live even after his physical death.
Therefore only the Jewish body can be changed, but not its soul. El Ami.
—o—
b) "Hear now, you rebels" (Num. 20:10)
1.
For these words Moses was punished. Like that father who more than once curses his bad son himself, but when a stranger does so it vexes him. So God was vexed that Moses, in anger, let slip an angry word against the Jews. Arono shel Yosef.
2.
Moses was punished because he spoke too gently to them even while scolding them... "na" ("please"), pleading; patience is not always a good quality. Ktav Sofer.
—o—
c) "You know all the travail" (ibid., 20:14)
How was Moses so sure that Edom knew of the Jewish troubles?
He ought to have known it from the fact that Edom was doing well, for Edom thrives on Israel's suffering: when things are bad for the Jews, things are good for the Edomites... Imrei Shefer.
—o—
d) "And all the house of Israel wept for Aaron" (ibid., 20:29)
"For Moses only the men wept — because Moses would bring judgment to its full truth, whereas Aaron never said to anyone 'you have sinned'." (Yalkut).
Aaron, being a pursuer of peace, inevitably had to deviate from the truth. Truth and peace do not pair together. Already at the creation of the world the truth had to be laid into the earth ("He cast truth to the ground"), so that peace could exist... Siftei Tzaddikim.
—o—
All the suffering of peace comes from truth, for all quarrels stem from everyone shouting: "I have the truth", "the truth is with me". Therefore truth had to be sent down to the earth ("He cast truth to the ground"), so as to become convinced that with it alone one cannot get along in this sinful world... Osem Bosem[?].
—o—
e) "And Balak son of Zippor saw" (Num. 22:2)
A portion of the Torah named after a gentile — because Balak was an honest gentile in that he was such a hater of Israel...
For "it is a known rule that Esau hates Jacob", and if a gentile loves a Jew he is surely a dishonest gentile, untrue to his gentileness, which demands of him to hate the Jew...
Or ha-Me'or (R. Meirl of Przemyślany).
—o—
f) "From Aram Balak has brought me" (Num. 23:7)
Like that preacher who comes from a sinful town to preach morals to another town. People surely say to him: have you already reformed your own town?
The same was Balaam's argument: "From Aram Balak has brought me" — Balak brings me from Aram to curse the Jews for their wickedness. Is Aram not a thousand times worse? Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
g) "And behold, you have blessed them" (ibid., 23:11)
"All that Israel eats in this world comes from the blessings of that wicked man." (Midrash).
For other blessings, Heaven chooses to whom to give them, but Balaam's blessings, which are like a found windfall, are handed out to everyone without distinction... The Maggid of Dubno.
—o—
h) "And the people began to commit harlotry" (Num. 25:1)
Rabbi David of Dynów, staying once at a spa and seeing how people were living it up, how respectable householders from back home were carousing, said the following quip:
The Gemara says that the hot springs of Tiberias remained from the Flood (Sanhedrin 108). One may ask: what was the need for such a remnant of the Flood?
Only that, lest future generations not believe how sinful the generation of the Flood was, the hot springs of Tiberias were left, from which all the spa springs flow, so that there would be spas. And visiting the spas one can indeed believe that the generation of the Flood was so sinful — one can indeed believe that it is possible to fill a world with so much sin...
—o—
Haftarah.
i) "And the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples as dew" (Micah 5)
"The remnant of Jacob in the midst of peoples" — the handful of Jews found among the nations, assimilated, already absorbed into the gentile family — God will have to bring them out "as dew": for rain comes only after a preparation ("and a mist went up from the earth"), whereas dew falls by itself and quietly. Such a return will also be that of the remnant of Jacob — without anyone's preparation, without storm. Abarbanel.
—o—
j) "To do justice and to love mercy" (ibid.)
Mercy one must love. Justice — no, because it is better not to quarrel and not to need to litigate... Hence it is good[?]: "to do justice", but not to love justice. Kuntres Oron[?].
—o—
Avot.
k) "What is the difference between the disciples of Abraham our father and the disciples of Balaam the wicked?" (chapter 5)
It seems that outwardly one really cannot tell them apart, for even Balaam's disciples sometimes wear spodiks and white jupicas (kaftans)... Netzer Chesed (before[?] the Besht).
Yente Tsipa's First Letter from Krynica

[Humorous feuilleton — a letter from Krynica.]
By Fishke the Lame [Fishke der Krumer].

My dear, good, faithful, heartfelt husband Motl — may he live and be well until a hundred and twenty years — amen selah!
Firstly, my dear husband, I come to inform you that I am, blessed be the Name, well, and I wish to hear the same from you and from the little children — may they live.
And secondly I write you that it is not so good at all for a woman who goes for a "kuracja" [a cure] and cannot herself write a letter, neither to her husband nor to the children. I feel now that if one has to be "telligent" [intelligent], it is not enough to be "pan brat" [chummy] with the radni [councillors] of the magistrate — one must really learn to write and read too. So I dragged myself [?] all over Krynica until I found some trailing plague, a "Mandzhev" boor [?], to write this letter for me... and meanwhile he pulls such faces, rolls up his sleeves, opens his shirt, sweats over his whole head until it actually drips — pardon my saying so — from his nose, as if he had to chop a cord of wood or even cut up a slaughtered beast...
But I have landed nicely in a dacha...
"Krynica" — "Krenits" — there you have a "persviete" [?] dacha on my bitter bad luck — me too with a dacha, and supposedly a "telligent" dacha at that. Why didn't my head break — may it befall my enemies — before I took a fancy to "Krynica", me too a dacha-land...
So I took [?] a room in a hotel, just as befits "telligent" people. When I asked the hotel porter [in broken Polish]: "Madam, how much does a little room cost with the honourable sir...?" he first looked me over from head to foot, as if it were a matter of a match, and then said:
"A little room we don't have! We have only big ones..."
Say I: "If the gentleman has big ones, let them be big!"
Meanwhile out moves a coarse, hunchbacked little squire with a twisted little head, whose face is like the question mark in a primer, and says:
"For your rags [szpargały] two rooms won't be enough either."
Say I: Why are your eyes popping out like that at my rags?!
Says he: You must pay for a small room 15 little złotys a day. And he drags it out: "zło-ty-kes"...
Say I: "Pani Fryk [?], why is the business so dear with you? Do you have flowerpots in the business?"...
Says he:
"In our hotel live intelligent people"...
Say I: "I am also a 'telligent' — just ask all the 'telligents' of Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa and Zagórze, and you'll hear what a 'telligent' Madam Yente Tsipa is"...
Says he:
"Ponoch pana po cholere" [garbled Polish, roughly "what the hell did madam come for" (?)]
In short — I had no other choice, so I rented the room in an ill-starred hour.
But hardly do they start unloading all my rags from the cart — the heavens open — all Krynica runs to see my evil wonder [?]. Here a huckster woman, there a market goye, shkotsim and shiksas, old goyes and little children — and suddenly things start flying: now a pot, now a pan, here the noodle board, there the rolling pin — I begin to shout:
"Police! Gevalt! Police! Help! Robbers!..."
But have you ever been lucky enough to have the police come when you need them? — Not a sign! So I'm not lazy, I pick up my feet and run to the police.
I run and the whole funeral procession after me, and when I got into the police station I was whole [?], out of breath [?].
Say I to the przodownik [police sergeant]:
"Pan przodownik, see about making some order [porządek] for me?"
He smiles, the "tistemitic" [systematic] przodownik, and says [in Polish]:
"With madam it isn't orderly... madam brought rags..."
Say I: "What do you care about my rags? I paid for the railway [kolej]; the railway didn't carry me for free, and I wish it had died a strange death before I travelled on it..."
Says he:
"But nothing has been robbed from madam yet..."
"So what" — say I — "do you want to wait until they do rob me?"
Says he: "Don't confuse my head, madam"...
Say I:
"Pan przodek! You should know that I am of the 'Besiakov' [?], the 'telligents', and when I give the honourable poseł [Sejm deputy] Reb Leybele one whistle, he'll come all right and make good order for me."
Says he:
"You may whistle to Poseł Leybele as much as you like, and you may indeed be of the 'Besiakov', of the 'telligentsia', but I can't help you at all.."
So Yente again is not lazy: she picks up her feet and runs to the post office to telegraph to Warsaw, to the poseł, so that he at least should look, he at least should see with his own eyes what a face a [?] Jewish misfortune has. Says the "pochmich" [postmaster] to me: why telegraph when you can telephone...
I stand and wait by the telephone... Says the "pochtmish": "Madam Yente, madam is holding the whole device backwards [?]... What should be put to the ear you put to the mouth — and what to the mouth — to the ear.."
I shout "Hallo".
They shout over there too "Halllo".
I shout [in Polish]:
"This is Madam Yenti Tsipa of the Będzin 'Besiakov', please give me the 'koło' [parliamentary club]..."
Standing there by the telephone is some lickspittle and says:
Which "koło"?
Say I: "The Agudah koło".
Says he: "You are a 'markovitserke' [?], a 'plyasnichke' [?]; Poseł Leybl is busy with the Będzin gmina [Jewish community].."
You hear, Motl, if I didn't fear God, I'd grab the wretched telephone and throw it at his head.
Now you understand my bitter fate [?]..: I am at a dacha without a lodging.. my things lie in the street.
For God's sake, Motl, see that you come over for Shabbat and don't forget to bring the little one. Because I miss him very much.
I greet you, my dear husband, and my dear little children, and I await you with the little one for Shabbat.
From me, your faithful wife.
Yenta Tsipa.
How Children Should Spend the Holidays

[Education and health — article.]
The school year has ended, and the parents' wish is to send their children out of town as quickly as possible, for what can be better for children than spending time in the fresh air!
In the first days in the fresh air the child is truly enchanted by the surrounding nature and devotes himself with great interest to games outdoors. Soon, however, it palls on him; he begins to be bored and cannot find his place. The mother is distressed by this and does not know what to do, but the matter is very simple. For ten months the child had a certain daily plan and did everything by the clock. Suddenly all this has changed, and the child, torn away from his former orderly life, begins to feel unwell.
One must therefore not allow children to spend the vacation time doing nothing. Should they go on studying? Not that. Ten months spent over the book is quite enough; the 2 months of vacation the child should spend in the fresh air, outdoors — but the day must be divided according to a certain order, according to a fixed plan.
The first few days one must give the child full freedom; let him do everything he likes — that gives him great pleasure. But by the third day his day must already be divided in an orderly way: he must eat, sleep and get up always at one and the same time. He must rest, go for walks, take baths ["vane-vanes"], etc. — all at a fixed time. The free hours must be used for practical work: for instance, for boys — whittling, weaving, etc.; for girls — helping the mother with housework, embroidery, etc. If there is a garden, the children should keep it in order, water it every evening, etc. All this must be for the children not merely a game but a real duty, which they must carry out systematically and punctually.
One must know how to occupy children and not let them be bored. One must not let them run things by themselves and do whatever their heart desires. But all this must be done with the proper approach and not with "rugzeh" (anger), as is unfortunately practised by most of our parents and some educators.
Only in this way can the vacation bring the children benefit, both with respect to health and with respect to upbringing.
Dr. S. Kelerman.
On irregular payment of wages.

[Law — Supreme Court rulings; labour law.]
The Supreme Court has considered a very important matter. The question is whether an employee who works for a firm, and whom the firm does not pay his salary regularly, has the right to leave the job and then claim compensation, or not.
The Supreme Court ruled that only in one case does one have the right to leave the job and demand compensation from the employer: if the employer does not pay the salary regularly out of ill will.
If there is no ill will, but the employer simply has nothing to pay with, this gives no grounds for leaving the job and claiming compensation.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved

[Serial novel — "Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved", instalment 33.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.
Everyone was silent and waited.
When the sun had already set, the windows were covered with thick, heavy curtains and the assembled people sat down on the benches. The men sat down on the bench that stood by the wall on the right, and the women — by the wall on the left. One of them, a man, and one, a woman, were seated on the chairs by the table.
They sat calmly and quietly, just as one sits at home resting after hard work. All were dressed in coarse, simple clothes, and their heavy boots were caked with mud. So they sat for a while, and everyone's eyes were turned to the two figures sitting at the table.
Then they began to sing in pious, heartfelt voices. They sang chapters of Psalms and folk songs expressing the yearning and longing of the sectarians that God's spirit should descend from the heavens and settle in a man. Little by little the singing grew more vehement, stronger, merrier and ever more ecstatic. When the ecstasy reached a certain degree, the peasants stood up and, singing, threw off their clothes and shoes, and each put on a white shirt made of white muslin. This was meant to signify that they had cast off the earthly garment and dressed themselves in a spiritual garment, and thereby they had become sanctified...
Then twelve large wax candles were lit, which burned with little red flames.
Dressed in white, by the light of the candles, they went on singing, seated. The singing grew ever louder, stronger and more passionate; so they sang until one of them stood up and began to stride in a circle. Then the rest stood up too. Man drew near to woman, and in pairs they began to move in a dance, striding one after another in a circle to the beat of the singing.
Soon — and the simple peasant dance turned into a dance which the sectarians call "the dance around holy Jesus"; the dance became more violent, noisier, hotter. Ecstasy flooded the hearts. They breathed hastily and the blood cried out from their bodies.
As they persuaded themselves, the sun, the moon, the stars and the whole of creation then danced along with them. They danced so long until "God himself appeared in the circle, sounded a golden trumpet and let the world know that He had forgiven all sinners their sins"..
After that came dances of various kinds. Everything in the room became "holy"... Above their heads rustled the fluttering of the wings of "God's spirit"... The man and the woman who sat at the table became: he — the "holy" Jesus, and she — the "holy" Mother... And then they all began to shout:
— "The Holy Spirit is among us!"
They kept repeating the shout over and over so long that their tongues became paralysed [?]. Then dances were performed. The singing became quiet and heartfelt. The "Chosen One" — the man who had until then sat at the table — stood up and began to speak wild words, and his voice kept changing every moment. Now he shrieked like a beast, now he squeaked like a child. Now the voice wept, now it was flooded with joy. Only the sectarians who were versed in the secrets of the sect understood the meaning of what the "Chosen One" was saying, shouting and squeaking. As they saw it, this man had now been born anew and that was why he laughed like a child... All were flooded with a wild joy; they surrounded the "Chosen One", in whom "God's spirit" now dwelt, rolled on the ground at his feet, crossed themselves and listened to his wild words...
Then they began to dance again. Now the dancing became wild; they stamped their feet, made an uproar and shouted and whirled as if in madness; so they danced until daybreak. When the dancing was at its fiercest, they all stopped and took off their shirts down to the waist. One after another they came up to the "Chosen One", who blessed them.
Then they took to dancing again, and while dancing men and women threw off their shirts; they remained completely naked; here and there someone began to convulse and fell to the ground... Passion began to burn [?]. The candles went out... The women, with loosened hair, fell upon the men, and an unbridled orgy began...

Będzin: The Third Act of the Comedy “Presidium Elections” Has Been Played

Będzin
The third act of the comedy called “Presidium Elections” has been played.
On Sunday morning, for the third time, elections were held for the presidium of the kehilla council and of the board (the “Verwaltung”).
To the meetings “new faces” were again invited. Because of family ties, Mr L. Kacengold entered the board in place of Mr Buchwajc. The latter [i.e. Kacengold] was “attacked” from “the high place” not to go to the meeting, but Mr Kacengold withstood all the temptations and stood firm like a loyal soldier...
The meetings are conducted under the chairmanship of the kehilla president Mr A. Liwer. Mr Nute[?] Landner was elected president of the council, and as vice — Mr Y. M. Kirland.
Right afterwards come the elections of the presidium of the board. Mr L. Rubinlicht was again elected president, and as vice — Mr A. Liwer.
The newly elected president Mr Nute Landner read the following declaration:
“Thank you, esteemed fellow parnasim, for the honour you have bestowed on me in electing me president of the kehilla council. I thank you for the confidence you have expressed in me, and I declare before you, esteemed parnasim, that I will strive, within the limits of my abilities, to safeguard the general interests of the kehilla; and to the gentlemen opponents on the right I also wish to declare that they should not triumph over the so-called victory they achieved by the force of “strong-arm power” in disqualifying the candidacy of my esteemed colleague[?] Mr Wygodzki, for in fact there has only been a change of persons, but never a change of system. I too, as a Zionist, will stand on guard to protect the national-spiritual interests of the kehilla in accordance with the Zionist platform. I hope that the esteemed fellow parnasim, too, will help me carry out the responsible tasks that weigh upon me — to raise the kehilla out of its present lowly state; and with united forces we will overcome all the obstacles we meet, both external and internal, and we will succeed in establishing the kehilla on sound foundations that befit the honour of the kehilla, and it will regain its splendour and dignity for the whole Jewish people.
In the name of the kehilla factions of “Mizrachi” and “Tze'irei Mizrachi” the said Mr Kacengold read the following declaration:
“In the name of the “Mizrachi” and “Tze'irei Mizrachi” factions in the Będzin Jewish kehilla we declare:
Our tactic so far in the field of the kehilla has been a moderate opposition, because its religious-national interests have always been more important to us than the party struggle.
Since the “Agudah” has lately, throughout the country in general and here in Będzin in particular, turned the kehilla into an arena of struggle for its representatives in political machinations, through which the honour of the Torah and religion is degraded, in whose name they wish to make these deeds kosher; in connection with the fact that the Agudah in Będzin allows itself to perform on the ground of the local kehilla various indecent deeds, and especially its fighting against private persons who will not tolerate their deeds (such as the shochtim question), [and that] they have by impermissible means temporarily removed from membership of the kehilla board our esteemed colleague, president Mr Buchwajc — we declare that we are ready to take up the fight, and we will wage it ruthlessly.
We will also apply the most far-reaching means so that Mr Buchwajc, as the one elected by our masses, may remain a member of the local Jewish kehilla board.”
—o—
Mr Szerman accepts the post of Będzin cantor.
On Monday the kehilla board held a meeting at which the question of engaging Mr Szerman as town cantor was again discussed.
It was decided to approach Mr Szerman to take over the office for a “pension” (salary) of 6 thousand złoty a year.
As we are informed, Mr Szerman agrees to accept the office, and this Sabbath the Będzin public will have the opportunity to hear Szerman as town cantor.
—o—
A search at the shochet Wajcman.
A policeman came to the home of the shochet Mr Wajcman, accompanied by the municipal (gmina) official Mr Wekslman, who declared that the municipality had received information that the shochet Wajcman was slaughtering fowl at home without permission from the municipality.
The policeman searched everywhere, but found no “shechita [?]” [literally “shoḥet ḥizl”; doubtful reading].
—o—
Regional conference of the “Gemilut Hasadim” funds.
In the premises of the Będzin “Merchants' Association” last Sunday a regional conference was held of the free-loan (g”ch) funds of the following towns and townlets: Königshütte [Królewska Huta], Katowice, Sosnowiec, Pogoń, Katarzyna[?], Będzin, Dąbrowa, Sławków, Łazy, Strzemieszyce, Wolbrom, Kozłów, Miechów, Częstochowa, Kłobuck, Olsztyn, Szczekociny and Zawiercie.
Also taking part in the conference was the representative of the “Joint”, director Mr Giterman.
The president of the Będzin g”ch fund, Mr Rubinlicht, opens the conference, greets the participants and Mr Giterman in particular, and proposes as chairman the delegate from Częstochowa, Mr Goldsztajn. The latter takes over the chair and gives the first word to Mr Giterman, who delivers the opening address to the conference.
In the opening address Mr Giterman expresses the view that the first task is that the brawls and party struggles around the funds should cease, as they cause great damage to the development of the funds. Also, no fee whatsoever should be taken from the borrower, and as regards the debts, all kinds of means must be applied to collect the overdue debts.
Around the “exposé” a broad discussion develops, in which Messrs Goldsztajn (Częstochowa), L. Zandel (Sosnowiec), Sztark (Katarzyna), Bażykowski and Fajgenblat (Będzin), Liberman (Zawiercie), Jaskierowicz (Miechów), Beri (Sosnowiec), Erlich (Katowice) and others take part, who put forward a series of proposals on the further activity of the g”ch funds.
At the end a series of resolutions is adopted, among others: to double the number of members in every town, and that no fee whatsoever should be taken from those who take loans.

“Hakoach” cycle race.

Sosnowiec: The Kehilla Budget Is on Its Way...

Sosnowiec
The kehilla budget is on its way...
This week the kehilla board received word from Kielce that the new kehilla budget has already been approved and sent to the starostwo (district office).
As is reported, great changes have been made in the budget; above all, the new items that were inserted into the budget this year have been struck out.
Tragic Death of a Couple in Love in the Swimming Pool at the Mysłowice Stadium

[Mysłowice — accident.] On Tuesday, before the eyes of thousands of people, 27-year-old Cygelska and 33-year-old Gawędzki, both of Sosnowiec, drowned in the swimming pool at the stadium in Mysłowice.
Cygelska had come to the stadium accompanied by her girlfriend; later Gawędzki arrived.
During their conversation Cygelska said that she felt like learning to swim. Hearing this, Gawędzki offered to teach her to swim.
At a certain moment Cygelska began to drown. Gawędzki set about rescuing her. But suddenly the crowd of thousands saw both of them drowning.
Several young people immediately went into the pool, but no rescue helped and both drowned.
Plenary Meeting of Jewish and Polish Artisans in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] On the basis of the ordinance of the Kielce voivode on combating illegal workshops — lower-grade craftsmen who do not belong to a guild — the Będzin starostwo (district office) has set about creating a unified (Christian and Jewish) committee of artisans, in order to combat the illegalities in the crafts according to the instructions of the said circular (okólnik).
For this purpose, representatives of all existing guilds in Sosnowiec and the vicinity were called to a plenary meeting, which took place last Monday in the premises of the Polish guilds, chaired by Eng. Kaleński.
After the discussions a board of 7 persons and 4 deputies was elected. From the Jewish artisans 3 persons and 2 deputies were elected, namely: the elder (starszy) of the tailors' guild Szmul Szajer, the elder of the hatters' guild A. H. Jaskierowicz, and from the furriers' guild Salek [?] Drechsler; deputies Józef Rotensztajn and Icchak Czarny.
It is worth noting that the Polish artisans displayed to a certain degree antisemitic tendencies, which were duly repelled by the Jewish representatives.
The joint committee has set to work.
The Rabbinic Seat in the Holy Community of Modrzejów Has "Stirred Up a World"...

[Modrzejów — rabbinate.] For several months a struggle has been going on in Modrzejów (Mandzhev) over the local rabbinic seat, between 2 sides.
One side supports the candidacy of Rabbi Piekarski, who in fact already resides there, and the second candidate is the son of the Ostrowiec Rebbe, son-in-law of Rabbi Englard.
In this connection the Ostrowiec Rebbe stayed in Sosnowiec last Sabbath; he had turned with a letter to the Tomaszów rabbi, Rabbi Brat, a disciple of the previous Ostrowiec Rebbe of blessed memory, asking him to come to Sosnowiec for the Sabbath.
Rabbi Bradt, not knowing beforehand the purpose of the invitation, was ready to travel. But when he was informed what it was about, he declined to travel to Modrzejów for the Sabbath, and the whole plan that he should campaign for Rabbi Englard's son-in-law was spoiled.
To the Attention of the Members of the "Bank Kupiecki"

[Bank Kupiecki — appeal to members.] At the last general meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" (Merchants' Bank) a resolution was adopted that all members should pay an additional 10 and 20 złoty each toward the debts, in order to collect from the members the debts, which amount to approximately one hundred thousand zł. Self-evidently, if even part of the sum is collected, the members will to a certain degree be free of the liability they bear for the bank, which is being liquidated. It is simply a matter of saving large sums of Jewish money, for as soon as the bank is declared bankrupt (upadłość), the members will be forced to pay enormous sums.
Therefore it is our duty to draw the members' attention that they should not be indifferent to this matter; let each of you pay the few zł. imposed on him, in order to avoid very many unpleasantnesses and monetary losses.

The match has aroused great interest in chess circles.

Results of the Kehilla Elections in Strzemieszyce

[Sosnowiec — society; followed by four items: Poland — legislation and residence registration; Będzin — Zionism; Poland — press and hunger; Sosnowiec — courts.]
The “hero” of our story is a shoemaker by trade. He has already forgotten that trade: for a year and a half he served in the army, and after that he took up another “trade” — looking for brides...
Since he is not an ugly fellow, he used to have great success with girls, and catching a bride was as easy for him as — to make the distinction — tacking on a pair of soles.
Nobody would have been interested in the story of his “trade”, were it not that last week the “hero” brought matters to the point where a young Sosnowiec girl attempted suicide out of despair.
This is what happened:
The “bridegroom-lad” got engaged through a matchmaker to a girl in Old Sosnowiec. The girl was naive and believed everything he promised her, so that all the difficulties of making a wedding in such times of crisis were removed, and last week the wedding was due to take place.
Everything was already ready: in-laws, guests, gabbai-women, klezmer musicians, mothers-in-law and a wedding canopy — but before the ceremony the “bridegroom” (no doubt looking for a way to wriggle out) thought things over and solemnly declared that he would not go to the canopy unless they added several hundred zł. more to the dowry.
The bride is an orphan, her relatives are poor people who cannot raise hundreds of zł. among themselves — the “bridegroom” saw this and made a “va-yivrach” [took to his heels].
The bride could not bear the shame and the next day poisoned herself with vinegar essence; but luckily she drank such a large dose, and she was rescued.
Now it turns out that the “bridegroom” had already prepared for himself, in reserve, a second bride in Zawiercie, where he has already gone. But who knows whether the Zawiercie bride is already his final one, because, as neighbours report, he used to promise every bride that he did not love the other one, only “he needs her as a kapore [scapegoat]”, and the naive girls believed him everything...
These very same neighbours came to the editorial office and asked that the “bridegroom” be “described in the papers”, so that people would know to beware of such a “bride-hunter” as our hero, who threw away the cobbler's thread and became a “professional bridegroom”.

Amendment to the Law on the New Registration Regulations
In “Dziennik Ustaw” [Journal of Laws] No. 38 a law has been published amending some provisions of the regulation of 16 March 1928 on the registration and control of the movement of the population.
According to the new amendment, everyone who stays in a given place longer than 3 days must unconditionally be registered within the following 24 hours. The duty to register lies with the owner of the house. In health resorts one is obliged to register within 48 hours of arrival.
As for deregistering from an abandoned place of residence, this must be done within 48 hours, likewise through the landlord.
For failing to comply with the said regulations, a fine of up to 100 zł. or arrest of up to 3 days is threatened.
For falsifying or giving false particulars in connection with registration or passport formalities, a fine of up to 2 thousand zł. or up to 4 weeks' arrest is threatened, possibly both penalties at once.
It is also worth adding that the communal registration offices may not charge more than 60 gr. for a personal certificate. The state offices, on the other hand, are obliged to issue personal certificates for a stamp duty of 60 groszy.
In both cases applications for the issue of personal certificates are free of any fee.
Ing. [signature]

Why People in Poland Go Barefoot and Eat Potatoes
In Paris a weekly appears that prints no articles of its own but only gives excerpts from articles printed in newspapers of other countries.
This weekly, called “Li” [probably “Lu”], already some weeks ago reprinted an article from another newspaper. That article is strongly anti-Polish. It says that it would be just to give Pomerania back to the Germans.
Of course the Polish newspapers came out strongly against “Li”. The paper, however, was not content with its first appearance and has now again reprinted an article from some newspaper in which the terrible hunger reigning in Poland is described.
“The Polish peasants — writes the paper — find themselves in such distress as slaves in Egypt, as the pariahs in India. More than half of the Polish peasants go barefoot and live on potatoes alone.”
Because of this article in “Li”, the Polish Sanacja newspaper “Express Poranny” came out with a big reply and abuses the French weekly for spreading gossip about Poland around the world — things nobody even knows about. “Express Poranny”, however, does not answer seriously what one hears about the hunger in Poland, but tries to make jokes at the expense of the French paper, which comes out not at all dignified or convincing. “Express Poranny” writes:
“What the paper ‘Li’ reports, that half the peasants go barefoot, we must admit with shame. That in summer during field work the majority of Polish peasants really do go barefoot — such is already the custom with us.
As for young potatoes, we eat them with sour milk, and not only the peasants but the w h o l e society. The sauerkraut we have already eaten up; now we eat young cabbage and we boast of it — this too is such a custom with us.”
“Express Poranny” concludes:
“On the other hand worms, which the French eat day after day, we eat only in time of famine; the last time we ate them was during the German occupation. Now we no longer eat them.”
You understand: the poor French have to eat worms because they have nothing to eat. But “we in Poland” eat young potatoes with sour milk, young cabbage and other good things.
With such a “serious” answer the French paper will certainly not be convinced.

[Będzin and Zagłębie — housing and rent; editorial article.]
Landlords must take into account the critical situation of their poor tenants.
Lately lawsuits between tenants and landlords have been multiplying.
Tenants who for many years used to pay their rent every quarter with the greatest punctuality have in recent times become bad payers.
One stays in arrears for a month, two, three; the landlord does not keep quiet, he demands payment, and when that does not help, when the debt does not grow smaller, he files a suit in court.
A lawsuit begins which sometimes lasts for long years. Lawyers are engaged, expenses are incurred, and in the end?
In the end both sides see that it cannot go on like this. The landlord softens and — agrees to reduce the amount of the rent!
This is what must indeed be demanded of all landlords.
The rent is too high, and the tenant masses, today materially almost completely broken, are not able to pay so much.
That is where all the lawsuits come from, and that is where the various „housing tragedies“ come from, which one hears about so often.
Lower the rent! That is the slogan which must be taken up by all.
We are not able to pay today the same rent as years ago. The tenant masses are impoverished and they cannot bear the heavy burden that weighs on them.
Many landlords have understood that things cannot go on like this, and they themselves have agreed to the tenants' demands. In some houses the landlords themselves carried out a reduction of the rent by a larger or smaller percentage.
This, by the way, is understandable.
After all, the landlord would rather receive a smaller rent than have to litigate with the tenants for long years and only in the end do[?] what could have happened right away[?] at the beginning.
The great majority of landlords, however, are people with hard hearts.
They would rather lose everything, they would rather take nothing at all, as long as they do not give in to the just demands of the impoverished tenants.
Against these landlords a joint action of the tenant masses must be undertaken.
One hears of memoranda that have been submitted to the government, but so far we have not yet seen a single step to relieve the distress of the tenant masses.
The tenants must therefore take their fate into their own hands.
Let the tenants' association only take the right initiative, and they can be sure that the impoverished tenant masses will stand in solidarity in the struggle for their rights.
G. B.

Jewish Life in Dąbrowa.

[Dąbrowa — community; shechita, welfare, insurance.]
The fee for slaughtering poultry reduced.
The old kehilla administration in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], headed by its president Mr. Yaakov Mittelman, this week adopted a resolution which should serve as a model for other kehillas in Zagłębie.
It is a fact that for a young chicken (kurczak) costing about 80—90 groszy one pays 50 groszy slaughtering fee, which is a crime in the present hard times.
Proceeding from this standpoint, the following proposal of the president Mr. Mittelman was adopted.
For a turkey or goose — 50 gr. slaughtering fee (formerly 80 gr.); for a hen, duck etc. — 30 gr. (formerly 50); for a young chicken — 20 gr.
The resolution is already in force, and the Jewish population of Dąbrowa need pay slaughtering fees only according to the new tariff.
—o—
A summer colony for poor children.
At the last meeting of the kehilla administration in Dąbrowa the question of sending a larger number of poor children to a summer colony was discussed.
The greater part of the expenses is covered by the subsidy from the municipal budget; the Jewish kehilla, too, has assigned a certain sum for this purpose.
A committee of 7 persons was elected, who are to take care of the summer colony.

Shochtim, ne'emanim and shamashim are exempt from the sick fund
The local gmina [community] has received from the Starostwo [district office] the latest circular (okólnik) of the Ministry of Religious Affairs concerning the insurance of religious functionaries in the sick fund.
According to the circular, shochtim [ritual slaughterers], ne'emanim [kashrut supervisors], shamashim [beadles] and all who fulfil religious functions are not obliged to belong as members to the sick fund.
After 3 Weeks the Workers Left Hulczyński's Factory

[Zawiercie — labour; occupation strike.]
In Zawiercie the management of Hulczyński's factory notified the workers 3 weeks ago that the factory was being closed. The workers, 600 in number, decided not to leave the factory and in this way to defend their jobs. For 20 days on end they lay thus on the iron blocks, on the dirty floors, feeding on the bit of meagre food that their families used to bring in to them, and being guarded day and night by large groups of policemen armed with steel helmets and armour.
Many of the workers became so exhausted in that time that they were taken to hospital.
Only after a series of conferences at the Ministry of Labour, only after the management had promised to pay the workers 15 thousand zł. and a further 5 thousand zł. had been promised from government funds, did the workers agree to leave the factory. The management also gave assurance that none of the workers living in the factory dwellings would be evicted; the workers will also be able to use the gardens on the grounds around the factory.

"Hakoach" — "Maccabi" 0:1 (0:1)
At this match such deceitful doings took place as have never happened before. We saw how Jewish clubs fought each other with sticks and knives, which made a shocking impression on the sport-lovers of Zagłębie, and it is a holy duty of those who stand at the head of the sports movement in Zagłębie to restore the friendly relations that have prevailed until now.
From the start of the game "Hakoach" takes the initiative and carries out several consecutive attacks on the opponent's goal, which however are not exploited because of the "Maccabi" goalkeeper.
