From a Stroll in the Children's Little Worlds. (Greetings from the Będzin Municipal Children's Colonies.)

The day before yesterday, Tuesday, our editorial office received an invitation from the Będzin Commissioners' Council to visit the magistrate's [municipal] children's colonies in Sławków and Okradzionów. It goes without saying that we gladly accept the invitation. After all, it is no worse a mission than inspecting any public activity whatsoever.

Inspector Janiczak explains to the writer of these lines that, since the Commissioners' Council is making an excursion there for a few hours, it wishes to have representatives of the press along; so that we, together with a Christian colleague and 2 Jewish representatives in the persons of the members Messrs. Rechnitz and Hampel, and with the magistrate's steward, Mr. Dziubikowski [?], travel to take a look at what is going on in the little world of the children and how they have been settled there.

On a fine, bright day we tear ourselves out of the heavy, smoky Zagłębie air, and after a journey of about an hour we revive and begin to breathe more freely amid mild nature, glorified by mountain landscapes crowned with tall forest trees, water, shade and other natural treasures. When one escapes into the lap of nature, be it only for a few hours, one begins to feel freer, one comes alive, and it seems that one has become younger; and then one would like to become younger still, and surely to turn back into a child — something one did not know how to appreciate in those splendid years.

———

Before us we see the "Zagłębianka". We are welcomed by the 235 little Sarahs and little Rivkahs [i.e. the Jewish girls], whose little eyes light up with joy. Entering the children's little world, we naturally begin to view and inspect everything.

The head of the colony, Mr. Weisenfreund, gives us the daily schedule and explains with satisfaction that the colony is divided into three groups under the supervision of the teachers Rozencwajg, Bojarska and Klajner. Then the hygienist, Miss Tenenbaum, carries out her mission independently; under her supervision is the colony's pharmacy with all medicines. For this purpose there is also a separate room, intended so that in case of illness the child can be completely isolated. The isolation room was indeed occupied by one child who had come down with a mild angina [sore throat].

Among the teaching staff the children feel like free little birds in the trees: they jump, dance, bathe and make use of the holiday time as far as possible.

The children get food 4 times a day, and, as we are told, they are properly nourished.

Their intellectual life reaches the highest level. Thus they publish "with their own hands" a "colony newspaper", edited by the gymnasium pupil Gotfryd, and it has its own contributors. Upon my life, the newspaper is stuffed with every good thing: there are articles, feuilletons, poetry, riddles, "pupils' learning", a chronicle — in short, a newspaper like all newspapers, even with illustrations.

After we had tasted something, the children begin to entertain the guests. We are enthused by the talents possessed by the little ones of 7 years, such as Róża Pinkus and Szwajcer. The latter truly shows artistic talent, so much so that a future is predicted for her.

Prof. Weisenfreund makes use of the free time and gives the children lessons in anatomy and botany, and teaches them to swim.

Later we inspect the inventory and the storerooms of Mr. Balimowski [?], who, by the way, has a grievance that according to "regulations" the first visit was due to him. Mr. Balimowski is pleased that he has something to be master of and that he can "fatten up" [Polish paść] the children.

The inspector is satisfied both with Balimowski's housekeeping and with the normal relations that have come about. So that we now know nothing — he says — of minority distinctions and race questions.

Sundays — we are told — are simply a hell for the colony. Parents arrive from town with big and small children, not even forgetting to bring babies at the breast; and when such a crowd arrives, no evil eye, there is a tremendous commotion, the children forget the discipline to which they had become well accustomed, and the disorder reaches a frightful degree. The colony is then turned into a tavern.

Besides that, the carters behave there as if "in father's vineyard", and at once they take possession of the utensils and whatever else they can.

The Sławków police inform us that if the lawless deeds of the carters recur, they will react to it as appropriate.

It would truly be desirable for both the parents and the carters to behave somewhat more tactfully. After all, they must remember that this is a municipal public institution, which must be treated with respect. It is indeed a desecration of God's name [chillul ha-shem] to behave so lawlessly, so that one has to resort to the police to establish order.

In general the colony has progressed; the inventory has been enlarged, and the verandas and halls where the children sleep are comfortable and bright. Everything around makes a fine impression, and one can only wish that care be taken to keep progressing steadily and that various defects be remedied.

———

It is getting late, and we begin to hurry on with the march, that is, to visit also the Christian colony in Okradzionów.

Toward evening we arrive there, where we are welcomed by the children and their [female] educators. There too, as in the Jewish colony, is the first group, of girls. But there are already 278 children there, and although the space there is larger, they do not have roomier sleeping quarters.

In general, however, the Christian colony is considerably larger; it is a whole folwark [manor farm] in the true sense of the word. There are gardens with fruit, trees and various vegetables, tended under the supervision of Mr. Dziubikowski, who is an agronomist by profession.

The head of the colony, Mr. Oruba [?], tells the writer of these lines that he notes that from year to year he gets weaker children. Thus this year he has children who actually did not know how one eats meat, so that they did not want to touch that article. They cannot stomach it. And he had a hard job until he systematically taught them to eat meat, which, needless to say, they now relish. But it is a fact that they did not have it at home and could hardly get used to it.

There too the children get food 4 times a day, and the nourishment is about the same.

Attached to the colony there is also an old-age home, which is there all year round. There are 31 old men and women there. The oldest is a woman of 98, with whom one can talk as with a young person. She hears well, walks well, still wears no glasses, and has only one prayer: she wants to become young again.

Thus we spent the time until deep into the night, breathing in the aromas of beautiful nature in the course of the few hours in which we tore ourselves out of the boiling Zagłębie heat-cauldrons.

———

Considering these two colonies, which are the property of the town, it must be stated once again that every good phenomenon must be welcomed at all times. The previous self-government bought 2 estates, and the town benefits from them year after year.

Today, for example, we have no town council, only a Commissioners' Council, in which an autocrat has been installed. Of course, had these colonies not been [the town's] own, no such ones would have been created; but as it is, when everything exists — the buildings stand, everything is arranged, and nature comes to help and begs: "give us the children here and we will welcome them" — there is no other choice; then it is no more than a question of money, which under the conditions that have arisen cannot be set aside [?].

Yes, good deeds will never vanish, and even if no one speaks of them, the silent monuments, the statues, will tell of themselves what the past created for the future and the present.

And therefore let this example be proof that always and at every opportunity useful and necessary things must be created, which will remain as an everlasting memorial, and their deeds will always be crowned with recognition.

Yes, the will is strong and mighty, and one needs only courage and awareness to realize such things at every opportunity.

G. Sz.
May the sick-fund contribution be raised?

The contributions to the sick fund (Kasa Chorych), as is well known, are levied according to the level of wages.
An exception, however, is the contribution for domestic servants, which is levied not according to the wage — since the value of the food must, after all, be counted in — but according to a fixed category, corresponding to the calculated average wage that a servant is supposed to earn.
In today's hard times, when many women go out to "positions" simply out of need, it already happens quite often that the calculated average wage is higher than the actual one.
Now the sick fund intends to move the contribution on servants' wages into a still higher category.
The reckoning is apparently this: as soon as one keeps a servant, one can pay the sick fund a few gulden [i.e. złoty] more.
This reckoning, however, is not correct, since in most households that keep servants it is not a luxury but a necessity — for example, when the wife is busy in the business, or when the family is so large that the housewife cannot manage on her own. In such cases the raising of the contribution will surely be felt very hard.

20 Tammuz 5692.
Twenty-eight years since the passing of Dr. Herzl.
All over the world, from end to end, wherever Jews are to be found, his yahrzeit is being marked — or his "hilula", as the Hasidim call it.
Speakers speak, writers write.
They depict the greatness of the great Jew who passed away.
They recall historical facts about the creator of political Zionism.
They appraise the values of the historic movement.
They tell memories and reminiscences about Herzl the leader.
They sing songs, they throw out flowery phrases about the great dreamer, the great poet, the statesman.
But no one, it seems, will say a new word any more.
Will not say — because one cannot. Everything has already been said, written, sung.
It is worth hearing what the people itself says and tells about its hero, and such a story, from one of the people, I wish to pass on here.
I heard a grandfather tell his grandson about Herzl in these words:
"And it came to pass in those days of Nicholas the Wicked, the Tsar of Russia, and of Wilhelm the Wicked, the Kaiser of Germany, and of other wicked kings throughout the world. Jews were persecuted and oppressed, robbed and slain everywhere; they wanted to wipe the Jewish people off the face of the earth, and no one said a word.
"And there were among the Jews such as betrayed[?] their people, denied their God, and went over to the enemy's camp never to return.
"So the Jews cried out to God, wept and pleaded, and God heard their cry and sent them an emissary to help the people of Israel.
"Dr. Binyamin Ze'ev son of Yaakov Herzl, who had been far from his brethren, suddenly passed by and heard the sighs and groans of the Jews, and saw how they were everywhere oppressed and stifled and tormented in exile. And he stopped beside them.
"As he stopped, he heard them shouting after him from the enemy's camp: 'Hep! Hep!', which are the initials of the Latin words 'Hierosolyma est perdita'! — Jerusalem is lost!..
"His heart was sorely pained, and he resolved to give his life so that Jerusalem would be revived, Jerusalem together with the Jewish people!
"And at once he heard God's voice in his heart, and it said to him thus:
'Go to all the kings and princes in the whole world and tell them that the Jews have a land, and that land lies desolate and waits for them — let the Jews go and rebuild their Jerusalem!'
"So Herzl went, and his majestic figure and his radiant countenance and his piercing eyes opened all doors before him. And the kings heard him out — had to hear him out.
"But when he left them, they inflicted even more troubles on the Jews.
"Then the Jews became angry at Herzl's deeds and cried to him: 'Have we so few troubles, that you have come to add to them? Who asks you for favours? And who sends you as an emissary?..'
"Herzl answered them: 'I am sent to you by God! My brethren, look how you are going to ruin! Do not lie in exile like a worm in horseradish! Act — and the God of Israel will help you!'
"And the Jews still would not listen to him. They dismissed him with the Jewish 'eh! eh!' — 'a new dreamer has landed on our heads'...
"And Herzl prophesied: 'Brethren! Soon there will be a world war, the map of the world will be redrawn, nations will be liberated; do not lose your chance'...
"And only a counted few listened to his prophecies, but the majority laughed at him and embittered his days.
"And Herzl grew sad and prayed to God: 'God, I am tired; it is hard for me to bear the burden and the toil and the intrigues and the complaints of my brethren! Take me from among the living — only give them the redemption sooner!'...
"And God took Herzl to Himself, and let only his soul hover among the stubborn, stiff-necked Jews, and Herzl's soul awakened the Jewish people, and the people awoke from the sleep of exile.
"And Herzl's prophecy was fulfilled. The great World War broke out, nations and lands were liberated — and the Land of Israel was given to the Jewish people as its homeland!
"And only then did the children of Israel understand what Herzl had been to them.
"And Jews mention the name of their 'redeemer' with holiness on their lips!"...
———
That is how the grandfather told it to his grandson.
And this is no legend!...
Credits for Artisans.

[Poland — economy; artisans and credit; article.] The credit question plays a colossal role in economic life. It is quite possible that if it were possible to find a way, in the present hard time of crisis, for trust between man and man in matters of credit to exist, there might perhaps have been no crisis at all. Therefore it is chiefly the big ones who can enjoy credit, because in such cases the trust exists, whereas with small enterprises there can be no talk of it. Nor is this any wonder, for in principle credit is given to one who can be lent to, one who is able to pay back. That is an elementary truth. All the more, then, is it a wonder why the artisan is treated in such a stepmotherly way in the allocation of credit. We do not say that the artisan is in such a brilliant financial condition that he deserves unlimited trust — not that; but the artisan is the one who is able to repay a loan. With him it is not the case as with the merchant, who from today to tomorrow no longer has any stock, and one fine bright day he is no longer a merchant — and go look for him. The artisan stops working only when he becomes rich; stop running his workshop he will not. He will not be able to draw his livelihood from any other source. He will not give up his productive work and become a merchant — with small exceptions, of course, but the exceptions prove that lending to the artisan is a small risk.
Let us now get acquainted with a few figures. In recent years we see a certain allocation of credit sums for artisans through the Bank of the National Economy [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego].
Year | Allocated, zł. | Used, zł. | Used in per cent
1929 | 14664000 | 7599000 | 51 per cent
1930 | 14230000 | 11212000 | 78 per cent
1931 | 8135000 | 8135000 | 100 per cent
We see from the table above that the crafts did not use their sum in the first 2 years. So already in the third year the sum was reduced. Could it be that the artisan does not need credit, and that is why it was not used?
That is an impossible thing. When we take into consideration that in Poland there are approximately 350,000 workshops, we already understand that even if one assumes that half of that number either needs no credit or is not creditworthy, it comes to 80 zł. per workshop if the largest credit sum were used, i.e. the sum that was allocated in 1929. What, then, is the reason why the sum was not used?
Here we must come to the conclusion that there is nobody to take the credits for the crafts from the bank; there is no institution that would demand the allocated sum. That institution does not exist among the Christian artisans, nor among the Jewish artisans.
There exist so-called artisans' banks, which were perhaps the first cooperative credit institutions in Poland. With time, however, they have changed their character, and now they are mostly mixed institutions, and there is no certainty that the sums designated for the artisan will indeed reach the artisan. We quite often see that institutions which have nothing whatsoever in common with the crafts receive allocations of certain sums for artisans from the Bank of the National Economy, as for example the municipal savings banks [Komunalne Kasy Oszczędności], etc.
We must therefore again come to the conclusion we have reached more than once: that the organization of the artisan class is so weak that it is not even able to demand what has already been promised to it. With a good organization and a strongly developed cooperation of the guilds with the central organizations, one could create the kind of institution that would truly be the representative of the organized artisan class, that could approach the proper bodies with just demands and take at least what has already been granted and confirmed for the artisan class. Let the leaders of the artisans reflect and begin to conduct an artisans' policy that will lead to unity and consolidation among the guilds under the supervision of the central unions.
This must happen as quickly as possible. If we merely put the credit question on the table — a vital question, it seems — we must come in the name of a strong, unified organization. Perhaps we shall have to found a network of artisans' credit funds, which would be the connecting link between the artisan and the Bank of the National Economy and which, with the masses behind them, would be able to come forward with the demand to allocate to the artisan at least the credits that were allocated in 1929 and not used by the artisan class.
B. Freund.
A Little Feuilleton: The Torments of Gehenna.

[Feuilleton — a parable on market plenty and poverty.] In the holy books it is written that when a wicked man comes to the other world, he is punished in Gehenna with the very same thing with which he sinned most in his lifetime.
If a person, for example, was in his lifetime a glutton and a drunkard, the prince of Gehenna goes and does one little thing: he seats the wicked man at a richly laid table with the best and costliest dishes, with the tastiest wines. The smell of the tempting dishes strikes into the nose, the sight of the good wines in the golden vessels throws him right into a frenzy — but, alas, the destroying angels tie long forks with spoons to the wicked man's hands. The glutton-and-drunkard spears the fat meats on the fork, his saliva even begins to run in his mouth from the wild lust to gorge — but he cannot bring it to his mouth: the forks are too long...
In this way the wicked man lives through terrible torments. He is hungry, the fat dishes whet his appetite, but he perishes in terrible torments of hunger...
These pictures of Gehenna come before one's eyes in our present time, when one sees how many good things there are around us.
When you go out to the market today, you are simply amazed at the wealth that Mother Earth brings forth in such abundance; you have at the market red and black berries and gooseberries and strawberries and cucumbers and new potatoes and fresh-fresh eggs and good sour cream and milk and radishes and spring onions and lovely little cheeses and delightful butter and wriggling little fish and fowl of all kinds — and what not?
The vendors stand with their lively wares, the goods lie in baskets and spread out on the little tables, the sun pours its lovely rays over it all; it tempts the eyes, it sharpens the appetite — but how many people can touch any of it?
And everything is cheap — dirt cheap — trifling sums: for one or two gulden [złoty] one can buy all good things and refresh oneself and the little children.
But the poor citizen wanders about, like the wicked man in the other world, sees before his eyes so much good, such a wealth of precious fruits — but long forks are stuck in his hands — he cannot reach the things...
M. D.
Post and telegraph to become cheaper from the first of August.

[Poland — post office; economy and taxes.] The government has now finally admitted that its policy of squeezing ever larger taxes out of the population leads to the opposite result: state revenues keep falling.

Meanwhile the government has begun to retreat one step on postal charges. Last year, when state revenues began to fall sharply, the government among other things raised the postal tariff: a letter now costs 30 groszy and a postcard — 20 groszy.

Postal spending over the past year, however, showed no growth at all; on the contrary — it fell considerably. Now a series of reports are arriving that the ministry is preparing to make the postal tariff cheaper: a letter is to cost 25 groszy again and a postcard — 15 gr. This is to happen in the coming months.

The Post Ministry is in general undertaking a major campaign to increase the post's revenues. Minister "Berger" [probably Boerner] called a special press conference on the matter. He declared there that he is going to introduce a cheap commercial tariff. A number of measures will be introduced at the post office which will help make the prices of products cheaper.
My Wife's "Bargains" at the Dacha.

[Feuilleton — summer at the dacha; Rajcza.] Caught and noted down by a dacha-goer.

You surely think that this time I went off to Rajcza on Thursday evening because I got my interest-free loan [gmiles-khesed] earlier, and not as always on Friday evening. I tell you, you are mistaken. Not because of that, but precisely because of the sequestrator [bailiff]. I simply had an auction [licytacja] set for Friday, so I was advised to hang a big padlock on the door, which would say: "The gentleman is not at home."

And he will draw up a report? Let him — what do I care, I have already exhausted every means. I have already obtained extensions, taken other dates, begged, wept, arranged instalments, paid off the bidders, taken the mirror out of the wardrobe... The only means left to me was to lock the door.

So that's what I did, and where does one go so as not to be seen in Będzin? — One goes to Rajcza for Shabbes!

My wife was pleased; heaven forbid she should show it to me — on the contrary, she poured out [?] all her troubles to me:

"What's this," she shouted at me, "a husband comes on Thursday and brings so little money with him — what am I supposed to buy with? What am I supposed to go to market with?"

But outwardly she was pleased after all, because all the women, the neighbours and acquaintances, envied her. On all sides people said:

"Mrs. Rosenthal has a good husband, he doesn't wait till Friday evening. He comes on Thursday, so that the wife needn't torment herself over every grosz at the market..."

I'm telling all this precisely because of the market. After Thursday night my wife said to me:

"You'll see, Chaim, how all the housewives, as they say [?], will burst tomorrow. I'll get up at 3 o'clock at dawn and buy everything from the first peasants who come through from Rycerka. When they come out, I'll already be back asleep and have Shabbes at home — and how much money will I save on it?"

Together with the sun my wife got up too. I couldn't deny myself the pleasure of going along with my wife, hearing how she bargains with every peasant man and woman, carrying the basket after her. After all, one is so free — without a jacket [marynarka], without the yoke [chomąto] on one's neck, in slippers, with no fear of meeting any creditor, any sequestrator.

So out we went together at 3 o'clock at night to wait for the peasants with their wives. I was loaded with a big basket [?] for various "jarzyny" [vegetables], with a small basket for eggs, a plate for butter, a jug for sour cream, a second plate for jagody [berries], a special satchel for hens with kurczaki [chicks] and just something in reserve — maybe we'd manage to buy bargains. So we stand together looking towards the Rycerka side, where the peasants always come from; all around everything was quiet, not a living soul to be seen. We wait like that an hour, two and three — the clock already shows seven.

My wife is already biting her fingers with agitation.

"Isn't it perhaps a [Christian] holiday today?" she asks me.

"No, Dvorele, today is no holiday at all."

Meanwhile one already hears from all sides the shutters being opened, and from everywhere women come out in their "szlafroczki" [dressing gowns], with their maids by their side, hung about and loaded, just like me, if you'll pardon the comparison.

Several women at once turned to mine.

"Mrs. Rosenthal, you're already here?"

"Only 5 minutes that I've been standing here. I didn't even want to come out on the highway at all today, but because of my husband..."

So be it, I thought to myself, what does it matter to me. Several dozen women had already taken up position like this and were chatting; each tried to go as far up into the village as possible, so as to be the first to catch the peasant women, but the others didn't lag behind, and real little races [wyścigi] took place. Suddenly a peasant appeared with a peasant woman, with two baskets in their hands. They fell straight into the midst of dozens of women's tongues, and on all sides people shouted:

"Co wy macie, gosposiu? Co pan ma, panie gospodarzu?" ["What have you got, missus? What have you got, master farmer?"]

The poor peasant was quite bewildered — so many merchants for his bit of goods — and he named [?] prices he had never even dreamed of. The women turned up their noses and didn't buy. But each one was only waiting till the others would go away, so that she could quietly buy up the bit of goods and afterwards say that she paid half the asking price.

Meanwhile peasant carts arrived and the real commotion began. The women began to quarrel and curse.

"I felt that hen first, Mrs. Herszkorn, and you're buying it out from under me."

"I looked at that duck first and now you want to buy it, Mrs. Schneider — how can one be like that?"

"I bought from that peasant woman last week, Mrs. Schuster, and now you're talking her away from me."

"I've already bargained with that shaygets [gentile lad] and settled with him, Mrs. Spitzer — what do you want, that we should share the little he has?"

And so on and on: this one had already felt, that one already had the eggs in her hand, another had already licked the butter — until the women fall out with one another and the peasant women tuck the money into their bosoms. Of course the peasant women won't hand over the goods before the madames pay in advance, before they've checked the money and hidden it away.

"And what will be with fish today?" Mrs. Goldsztajn suddenly said.

"And if one doesn't eat fish for once?" I try to put in.

"You think I need it for myself? But my husband, may he live, is very fond of a piece of fish; on Friday he doesn't eat lunch, so I must give him a piece of fish when he comes."

"And would I have bought sour cream today, if my husband weren't fond of it?" said Mrs. Grinzwajg.

"And what do I need strawberries [truskawki] for?" said Mrs. Parzenczewska.

"And what did I buy a duck for today?" said Mrs. Góralska.

So it turned out that everything they bought — and they bought a lot — was only for the husbands.

Now, when they had all carried their bargains off into the cottages [chałupy], only then did they get ready to go to Gelbard's confectionery [?] to buy young cabbage, cauliflower, yeast for the baking, herring and other things — of course, all for the husbands.

On Shabbes the real wedding [i.e. the real show] only begins, which deserves to be described separately.

Izi.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Pinchas)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Pinchas
The Portion
—o—
a) "Pinchas" (Num. 25:11)
Anecdotes about people named Pinchas:
1.
R' Tzvi Hirsh Segal of Zhytomyr (Żytomierz) had an only son, Pinchas. Later, however, he "went sour" [became a freethinker]: he left the yeshiva for the university, received the title of Doctor of Medicine and the name Piotr Gringarovich [?].
Father and son were at odds. Yet once, at the mother's request, the rabbi invited his son Piotr for Shabbat. At the Shabbat table he sat bareheaded and smoked papirosy [cigarettes]. While the father sang "He who keeps the Sabbath, son and daughter"... — which, however, did not stop him from tasting the Sabbath kugels and relishing their Jewish flavour... After the meal he gets up:
— Oh father, one really ought to reform Judaism a little.
R' Tzvi Hersh boiled over:
— A Judaism that gives you kugels, and fried pork, and the name Piotr — that still needs reforming?
— Well yes, it is precisely because of such "jewels" that Judaism is hard to bear. It is precisely the Pinchas-Piotrs that need reforming... Darkhei Moshe.
2.
In Białystok there was a famous cantor named Pinchas. Big cities used to invite him and pay a great deal of money for his praying. Once one of his choristers (meshorer) set off around the world, passed himself off as the cantor Pinchas and made money.
When R' Pinchas learned of it, he said:
— "He does the deed of Zimri (zemer — singing) and asks the reward of Pinchas"...
—o—
b) "Therefore say: Behold, I give him My covenant of peace" (ibid., 12)
Therefore — because he performed such a heroic deed, because he acted so rightly and well, there is indeed a fear that Jews will hate him and that he will have strife... That is why he needed the blessing of peace. Da'at Zekenim.
—o—
c) "For they harass you with their wiles" (ibid., 18)
Jews persuade themselves: the gentiles hate us because we are pious. It is all because of God. If only we were like all the nations...
Now God shows them: "in the matter of Peor and in the matter of Cozbi, daughter of the prince" — you have already served their idol Peor, already married their daughters, and still — "they harass you", and still they hate you. They hate you no less when you assimilate among them. Divrei Shaul.
—o—
d) "A man over the congregation" (27:16)
"The face of the generation is like the face of a dog."
Like the dog that licks and fawns on its bread-giver to the point of disgust... Such "faces" there will one day be. Lev ha-Ivri.
A dog makes a racket, a noise, barks at the one it attacks. But when that one raises a stick or a stone, it runs back where it came from. On the other hand there are proud creatures that do not shout and do not bark, but quietly wage war on their opponents and are not frightened by any stick.
Our "face", however, in its struggles resembles the dog... Ibid.
—o—
e) "Who shall go out before them and who shall come in before them" (ibid., 17)
A leader who can mix with the people and live among them — and yet one should not invent about him all that's in the cards [all sorts of things]; for mostly, the leader who lives among the people is watched and gossiped about. "And they gazed after Moses." Birkat Shamayim.
—o—
f) "Which have no shepherd" (ibid.)
That the shepherd should not be there for his own sake, but only "for them" — for them and not for himself... Chatam Sofer [printed "Hatam Sofer"].
Haftarah
—o—
g) "I have been very zealous" — kano kineti le-hashiv [?] (I Kings 18)
Elijah stormed: Jews have sinned, they have served the Baal — so they must all be uprooted, all destroyed. He was shown a vision [?]: "The Lord is not in the wind and not in the earthquake." This is not how God treats His Jews — not to annihilate and shatter for every sin, but "in a still, small voice"... calmly, gently, as a father with a child. Kokhav mi-Ya'akov.
—o—
h) "A prophet unto the nations have I appointed thee... I am a child..." (Jeremiah 1)
When God told Jeremiah that he was to become a leader, he began to plead: "I am a child" — I am still young, I still need to live. Or Pnei Moshe.
Avot
—o—
i) "And do not covet honour" (chapter six)
A rabbi was annoyed with the cantor: why did he not wait for him at the Shema until he had said aloud "the Lord your God is truth", whereas at the Amidah (Shemoneh Esreh) he did wait until the rabbi had finished ("gone out").
Asked why he did this, the cantor replied:
— I'll tell you: waiting for "truth" (the Lord your God is truth) from our rabbi is hard... but "go out" [finish praying — and also: expire] he must some day — so I wait..
Remarks. "Good Tidings".

[Zagłębie — the press; editorial remarks.] Crisis along the whole front. There seems to be not a single thing left on which the crisis has not laid its paws. Yet there is still one limb that twitches and cries:
— "I'm alive and will not keep silent"..
In such language there appeared this week "the Committee for Publishing a Newspaper at the "Agudat Israel Organization in Zagłębie"".
The committee, so it says, which no longer has the strength to keep silent about "the injustices committed against the camp", calls on the Agudah activists to help create a newspaper that will combat "the strife in the Jewish street".
It is self-evidently pointless to dwell on the cynical content of the prospectus. Nevertheless we consider it a duty to point out to the Jewish population that this "is the same Yente, only veiled differently": the "editors" of the new Agudah "newspaper" are the same persons from the former "Vayakhel Pekurei" [= Pekudei] organ in Będzin. The same gang that is facing a criminal trial for taking several hundred złoty owing to an error of the P.K.O. [Postal Savings Bank]. These are the louts who, with the help of the "Va'ad ha-Kashrut" [kashrut board], so to speak [?], made themselves a living from the guldens they take from poor Jewish widows, milk-women...
Let Jewish society be clear about this!
We also consider it right to draw attention to a second "cultural tidings" in our street.
With drums and dances the Jewish reader has been told the great "tidings" that a new newspaper is beginning to appear under the name "Zaglembier Yidisher Kurier" [Zagłębie Jewish Courier].
We are absolutely not against it — on the contrary: "the rivalry of scholars increases wisdom". But when one wants to fool the naive Jewish reader, when one wants to talk him into reciting "Shehecheyanu" in honour of the new newspaper, we are morally obliged to clear up the matter of the "cultural tidings".
For several years now a daily paper has been appearing in Warsaw for 5 groszy under the name "Der Yidisher Kurier" [The Jewish Courier]. It is a "child" of "Unzer Ekspres" [Our Express], and since the "Kurier", poor thing, has no luck — in every town it has, the "Kurierek" as it is called, a minyan of readers (not a single reader...) — they look [printed "vokht"] for schemes and tricks how to treat [printed "mezaeh"] the Jewish readers to the "Kurier" delicacies.
The tricks and machinations are as follows:
In every larger town in Poland an "editorial office" of the "Kurier" is set up, and to the street the tidings are announced that in this or that town a paper of its own is beginning to appear. In fact, however, the very same "Kurier" is printed in Warsaw, and only on the 4th page is a "tablespoon" of local chronicle given.
This combination has also been made in Zagłębie. As editor they have appointed [?] the stage director of the Będzin "Muza", Mr H. Lewensztajn..
So this is the "paper of our own" that Zagłębie Jews have been waiting for.
Comments are superfluous...

Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (34)

[Serialized historical novel — Rasputin; installment 34.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Such ceremonies, which ended in the wildest, most unbridled orgies, were held by the members of the sect "God's People" every Saturday night... They believed that when a person sinks into sin to the point of madness, to the numbing of the senses, his own earthly self is extinguished and the person finds himself wholly under the influence of the "Holy Spirit," by which he is ruled..

Grigori Rasputin, the lustful and pious muzhik from Pokrovskoye, while wandering through the villages and forests, took part in these orgies and learned from them to understand what is meant by "mysterious rebirth through sin," which the sect preached. He understood that he could reach the truth of life only by sinning out the whole of the sin that is in him, until he would attain "holy passionlessness." And so he threw himself into the orgies, in order to attain "holiness" through sin... In this way he lived out his lust, and his piety did not suffer from it...

Chapter Seven.
The Wailing from the Cellar.

Year after year went by, and in Pokrovskoye nothing was known and nothing was heard of Grigori Yefimovich. His young wife, who had stayed with old Yefim, did not stop longing for him. Her blood cried out in her with lust and yearned for Grisha. She felt lonely and dejected. From great longing she aged quickly. Her beauty began to fade [?]. Her joy of life shut down [?] and a heavy melancholy took hold of her. She worked hard at the housekeeping, raised a child, but there was no happiness in her. She became quiet and silent.

It happened not seldom that wanderers passed through the village and asked for a night's lodging in old Yefim's house. Whenever such a wanderer appeared, Praskovya Fyodorovna became talkative again. She would sit down by the stranger and start questioning him whether he had perhaps somewhere met such-and-such a man... who looks so-and-so... She always hoped to receive some news of her Grigori.

In the first times, right after Rasputin's disappearance, it did indeed happen that from time to time one of the wanderers would declare that he had really met a man such as Praskovya described; some even remembered that they had talked with him and had wandered together with him for a while. One told that he had met him in a monastery in the Ural Mountains. Another told that he had met him on the road leading to Kazan; others believed they had come across him in the forests not far from Pokrovskoye, on the other side of the river Tura. But there was never any certainty that the strangers were really speaking of Rasputin, because none of them had ever called him by name...

Later, however, Praskovya no longer received even such meagre news of him. Wanderers came [printed "received"] who stayed the night in old Yefim's house; Praskovya described her husband's figure to them, gave them various signs, but her inquiries were in vain — they had not met such a man nor seen him anywhere.

In the third year after Rasputin's disappearance, various rumours began to circulate among the peasants of the district about a "strannik" (holy wanderer) who performs many wonders. Among the peasants there was much talk and telling about the "miracles" this wanderer performs. People began to tell various stories about him.

It was told:
The "wondrous man" first appeared among the fisherfolk who live by the river Tura. He spent many days with them, helped them haul in the nets, taught them to sing chapters of Psalms and other hymns. To the fisherfolk he revealed that he had been sent by God, and that in him [printed "in her"] rests the "Holy Spirit," which had descended from heaven in order to be among men...

Others told:
The "holy man" first appeared among a group of men and women who were working in the field. Through the days he helped them in their work: cutting the grain, binding the sheaves and carting the sheaves to the barns. In the evenings he called together the men and the women and preached to them. He told them that the priests of the monasteries had forgotten the right paths that lead to God, that they do not remember the true words of [?] the "Redeemer" and have become estranged from His commandments... The priests do not know that all sins can be forgiven through repentance and remorse, and that God loves the one who has gone astray [?] more than all others.

It was further told that this wondrous wanderer holds strange services in the depths of the forests. He and his followers make their way deep into the woods; there he makes crosses out of branches, sets them up, and he and his followers pray to them. After he finishes the prayers, he embraces the women, caresses them and kisses them... and then all begin to sing and dance, and the wanderer explains to them that the kisses, caresses, singing and dancing are a part of the divine service and that this gives God great joy and pleasure...

Soon the rumours about the "miracle-worker" multiplied among the peasants of the district. It was told that at the services held in the forests the strange wanderer did not content himself with caressing, fondling and kissing his "sisters," as he called his women followers... People whispered and told of revels that he holds with the women in the forests...

Awaken the Conscience of the World

Deputy Dr. Y. Thon writes in "Nowy Dziennik", among other things:
It is an indisputable fact — we have no other weapon. I will put it in the most brutal way: our strongest and sharpest weapon is the outcry; the louder the outcry, the surer it is.
With what else should we protect and defend ourselves? With our physical strength? When a force ten times greater or even more stands against us, and on top of that the enemy holds in advance all the safest strategic positions. We, however, meet with difficulties at every step even in the calmest times. The enemy has the further advantage that he comes to the attack completely fresh. We, however, are never sufficiently rested between two attacks that are carried out on us. There is never any time to rest and gather fresh strength. The attacker can choose the moment most suitable for himself, which is at the same time dangerous for the attacker [sic].
In a word — for a physical fight we are very poorly armed and prepared. Nevertheless, if it comes to a frontal fight, we still manage somehow, at least to the extent that we make the enemy's victory very hard, and he must also pay dearly for it. More than one Hitlerite or other Endek [National Democrat] has already felt on his own hard hide that Jewish muscles deal out by no means bad blows. So it could indeed be in a similar frontal fight. But the antisemitic "caste" is not suited to such a fight.
In this way we are completely helpless against the terrible and loathsome enemy — antisemitism. If we had in us even a little of its immorality, our act could become, for example, revenge, carried out in various ways and mostly with cold nerves. What is characteristic of antisemitism is that it always expects revenge from the Jews. It knows perfectly well that it would itself act this way and no other — it would take revenge, manipulating with treachery and other methods. The Jews do not possess such a capacity; when the wrong passes, their innate faith in man and in humaneness at once reawakens.
And whenever the world becomes a little looser, if some milder breeze blows in history, we are the first to greet it; and so every humanism, every step towards it, becomes a "Jewish invention", which our enemies mock and reject, staging "Jew-baiting" in German or pogroms in "Slavic", proving that the beast in man is still alive and well.
This is the deeper meaning of the constant, periodic outbreaks of antisemitic madness.
How can we protect and defend ourselves against [printed "negn", a misprint for "kegn"] these attacks?
Unfortunately we have no other weapon than the outcry. For when we raise our voice, we wake those who sleep and that which sleeps. We wake the lazy people, who above all want peace for themselves and do not want to meddle in other people's quarrels. They themselves are not antisemites and would not themselves do the loathsome things, but to hinder someone else from doing them — for that there is no longer any will. The Present Crisis and Our Children

[Education and family — article.] Should we tell our children about the depression, explain to them that times are bad and that therefore we must live differently, more frugally — or should we hide the truth from them, pretend that everything is as it was, that poverty is not knocking at our doors?
This important question has been raised by great pedagogues and psychologists. Until now the accepted opinion was that children should be kept away from social problems up to a certain age. The child, it was held, will still have time to find out that there is poverty, want and other troubles in the world. Meanwhile, as long as it is still young, let the child live in its own fantasy world and know nothing of the sad reality.
The depression, however, has posed the problem concretely, and evading[?] it with an ostrich policy has become impossible. Children at home, in the schools, in the streets — feel it. That things are [not?] as they used to be; in homes where the crisis has cut deeply into earnings, the child must feel on its own skin that father and mother are depressed. Parents try to hide the truth from the children. Fathers do not talk to them about the fact that earnings are considerably smaller and that one must therefore be more thrifty.
So what comes of it? On the one hand the parents take care that the children should, God forbid, not lack any of the things they are used to; on the other hand, when one is already forced to introduce economies, the children do not understand why it is so, and the parents become a riddle to them.
The theory of keeping children away from social problems is a false one; children live in a world where every phenomenon is of a social character, and guarding them from it is on the one hand impossible and on the other unhealthy. The present crisis has brought this very theory to complete bankruptcy, and everyone must now admit it.
What should parents do? The only answer is: tell the children the whole naked truth; however harsh and dark the truth may be, the lie is much worse. Leaving the children to discover the truth by themselves and to stand before it helpless, lost and frightened — that is surely a harmful tactic, which will do them, the children, no good. When a child has to find things out by itself, it often crawls off into a dark corner, and this affects its character for its whole life.
It is absolutely unnecessary to instil fear in the children. Tactfully and with understanding one lets them understand that what two years ago was an ordinary thing in life is now a luxury. The father must tell the children how far his income has been cut and how the expenses must now be cut.
For the children it will be no tragedy. On the contrary, they will have the feeling that they must help their parents get through the hard times. In general children very much like to know about grown-up matters, especially what concerns their parents. They become more mature, and their childhood is not, God forbid, diminished because of it.
The upshot is that parents who choke and torment themselves in order to hide from the children the truth that times are bad for them commit a great folly. On the one hand they do themselves harm, and on the other they do the children no good. Have fewer secrets from the children about the crisis, enlighten them about your own situation and about the general one, and you will see how clever children are, how they will understand you and will themselves be ready to help you bear the hard times. But if they find out unprepared, the moment will be a tragic one for them and will affect the whole course of their later life.

When a Woman Grows Older (A Sketch)

[Literature — sketch.] By Lili Kaufman (?).
Iza tossed her head back and burst into mischievous laughter. In fact she did not feel like laughing at all, and there was nothing to laugh about — but she did it simply out of habit, knowing that mischievous gaiety suited her; yet lately, quite often, a thought would leap up in her:
— They are laughing at me...
And the laughter suddenly choked in her throat. It broke off on the last mischievous note.
Ever since Ida [sic] had happened to overhear the conversation of those two young girls, it seemed to her all the time that everyone was talking about her and criticizing her, that everyone knew she was already well into her forties, and that everyone knew with what difficulty she was keeping up her fading beauty. Before, she used to think that this was her personal secret, her hidden secret, which nobody would ever find out. But those two young girls, proud of their youthfulness, without a drop of pity for wrinkles (?) on other people's faces, had held this conversation between them:
— Iza apparently thinks that if she puts on a tight dress she will hide her flabby figure.
The other one burst out laughing and said:
— I simply don't understand how a woman can still flirt and coquette at her age! Can it be that at such an age one still wants to please?
That evening Iza tried to be as quiet as possible, not to catch anyone's eye, and she even threw a little shawl over her shoulders. Somehow it turned out that while the young crowd danced, she — the leading dancer — sat right by the wall together with the rest of the mothers... And the worst of it was that this surprised nobody at all; only her own husband, passing by her, remarked with a yawn:
— Perhaps we had better go home to sleep now, Iza?
Iza had lived an interesting life. She had had what is called — success. Everyone liked her. God had given her beauty, charm, elegance and — what men like more than anything — femininity. That all this might one day vanish, she had never thought. Among men she always felt like a fish in water. In their presence she would suddenly become light, witty, enchanting. She did not like women; she was bored with them; but she did love to read in their eyes envy of her, of her young figure and her fresh little face. When she noticed that she was being looked at with envy, she knew that she was interesting now, that the dress suited her face...
No gossip about her was ever heard — she did not allow that. Whether she really was close to any of her admirers — nobody knew; she was considered simply a happy woman, pampered by men.
Age crept up on her quietly, on tiptoe, like a thief. Iza wrestled with it secretly, waged a quiet but stubborn, untiring war, and would by no means give in. She used every means she knew of; with dread, however, she saw that not everything can be hidden...
• • •
A merry outing in the woods, spring, spring in nature and in the women's dresses; with the men the spring is in their eyes, their hands hold on longer than they should — to the women's fingers.
Iza appears last; she always liked to come last, so as to show herself to everyone at once, to read on all sides enthusiasm and envy in their eyes, and to draw tens of hearts on invisible threads, to make them flutter and to carry on a flirtation — a merry, light, springlike flirtation.
She peers into the faces of the men and the ladies. The men look indifferently at her figure; the ladies tenderly "encourage" (?) her spring dress... In her heart bitterness gathers; she no longer hears the song of the birds, no longer sees the milky-blue sky with its airy little clouds. It seems to her that all this will never come back, never, lost forever, lost...
Unnoticed, she steps away from the rest of the company and goes off into the depths of the wood. She is afraid the tears will give her away; she feels that something is wrong with her... and nobody, nobody can understand her...
The voices grow ever more distant and muffled, and suddenly Bernard's voice is heard (he was once in love with her):
— Ha-oo! I-za! I-za! Where are you? What are you looking for there? What have you lost?...
She wants to call out something joyful, playful, coquettish, but instead a hoarse, cracked sound tears out of her throat, then a laugh. Then once more that sound — God, she has had a fit of hysterics!
When people run up to her, she is already laughing and crying at the same time, and the more she tries to hold herself back, the more she laughs and cries. Someone suggests she drink a little water, loosen her corset; meanwhile she hears someone behind her shoulders say:
— It's nothing, it will pass; you know, a woman of a certain age...
"We Want to Go to Cheder"

[Będzin — education and kehilla; demonstration of the Talmud Torah children.]
With this slogan hundreds of poor Jewish children demonstrated in front of the kehilla offices.

As our readers already know, barely 3 weeks have passed since the premises of the local Talmud Torah were closed, and the great crowd of poor children is going astray.
During this time meetings supposedly took place, but it is not the element that drums in the streets that Judaism is in danger if the town does not take on 20-year-old young lads as ritual slaughterers...
Such a meeting also took place last Saturday night (motsei Shabbat). At the meeting Mr. M. Dafner gave a survey of the present state of the Talmud Torah and pointed out that it happened only because they would on no account allow the Talmud Torah's administration to include representatives who are not from the Agudah camp.
One of the present gabbaim, Mr. Neitark [?], tried to weaken the accusations which Mr. Dafner had hurled at the address of the "Agudah", and said: "That one cannot entrust the Wygodzkis and the like with giving an opinion on religious studies"..
After a discussion it was resolved that the present administration should resign and that a fund-raising collection should be organised throughout the town, so that the lessons could take place again.
All these resolutions remained, as always, on paper, and the several hundred children are being brought up in the street...
In connection with this, last Sunday morning a children's procession formed, which, accompanied by a large number of parents, marched through the town up to the gmina [the kehilla building], where the little crowd expressed its protest against the kehilla administration and against those who have taken over the Talmud Torah.
The large gmina hall, which was packed full of the little "revolutionaries", resounded with the stormy cries: "We want to go to cheder! Open the doors of the Talmud Torah again! We want to learn!"
At that moment the administration member Mr. Plessner was in the gmina; he tried to calm the children's tempers, but they were not satisfied with Mr. Plessner's answer and demolished the gmina office. They overturned the tables and chairs, tore the green tablecloth, and everything that came into the children's hands was broken and wrecked.
Having done the job, the procession went off to the premises of the "Yesodei HaTorah", where the children's fathers demanded that the poor children too be admitted to the Agudah cheder.
Against this "insolence" stepped out the mashgiach (ba'al musar) Mr. Nate Guter, who shouted at the parents: "You have defiled our Torah".
Soon police appeared in the corridor of the cheder and drove away the "impudent" parents, in the course of which Mr. Dawid Ratmensz received heavy blows from the police.
Mr. Ratmensz came to us at the editorial office and showed the black marks on his body from the police blows.
The overturned tables and benches remained "untouched" until Monday evening, until the meeting of the kehilla administration on the situation of the Talmud Torah.
In the course of Sunday and Monday hundreds of curious people visited the gmina premises to view the picture "after the revolution"...

A second delegation, from the Radomsko Rebbe, Rabbi Chameides of Katowice and others, called on the prosecutor last Monday.

He Never Got the Promised Dowry.

(The ugly defeat of an old bachelor-bridegroom. A. Fortune-Seeker).

When Maniek of Sosnowiec first saw the Częstochowa young lady (panna) Genia N., he jumped at the match at once, like at a roast.

And why indeed should he not have been eager for this match? [—] Her finely chiselled little face shone like the bright sun in a clear sky, and when, in white ankle socks and a short childish dress with her long braid hanging down, she looked like a young hovering angel.

As for the dowry too, it seemed, there was nothing to be stubborn about. After all, Maniek was led into a house — a real palace, into an apartment — royal salons, where every corner gleamed with wealth and ampleness; and when the in-law himself, the magnate so to speak, offered him a whole 10 thousand live dollars, with a splendid trousseau and a comfortably furnished apartment —

he did not ponder any longer, quickly agreed, and within a month he had already reached the morning after the wedding.

On that day, sitting with the household and the closest relatives of both sides at a richly served breakfast, the father-in-law suddenly puffs himself up like a turkey and in an angry tone turns to the young son-in-law —

— Maniek, what is going to be the outcome?

This so unexpected "reception" completely confused Maniek, and not understanding what was going on, he asked him: —

— I don't understand, what does father-in-law mean by that?

— What is there not to understand? I mean something very simple — the old man answered calmly, like a cold-blooded robber. — You got married, took — so be it — the wife, and that's that, off you go.

— Fine. But where shall we go, when we have no apartment, the business is not yet set up, and we have not yet received a penny of dowry either — Maniek tried to appeal to his father-in-law's hardened conscience.

— What? — the father-in-law takes a firm stand — maybe you expect me to rent you an apartment, set you up in business, and if not, you, bachelor-bridegroom, won't go to the wedding canopy? Did you ever hear such a thing — he lets loose further — he even wants a dowry! That I should count it out to him — he stands on the mortgage, after all! A wife is too little for him, what I gave him?

In short, from this conversation it became clear enough to Maniek that the old man had led him into a pit. Incidentally, he also found out that old N. was not the father of his wife Genia at all, but barely an uncle, and that all along she had been no more than a simple servant girl at his house.

But it was too late to turn the wagon back. Maniek ground his teeth in shame and, having no choice, made peace with his fate.

For the few hundred złoty that he had barely managed to wrest from old N. after long quarrels, the couple rented a little room, put in a few belongings, and expected to begin leading a poor life.

But it so happens that Maniek wakes up on the second day on his own straw mattress and casts a glance at his young pretty little wife — and suffers a severe fainting fit:

Her charming, chiselled, fresh little face had suddenly turned into a worn-out, freckled rag, her alluring figure — into a plain wisp of straw, and the whole young hovering angel had turned overnight into an old, dishevelled[?], ugly hag.

Here is what turned out: Genia was a left-on-the-shelf[?] and quite[?] neglected girl. That is why her deep forties had spread out comfortably over every corner of her face. Her rich uncle very much wanted to clear this "stale chametz" out of the house, so he promised a gang of matchmakers a fat morsel, and they slipped the lucky match to Maniek. At the same time they ordered Genia's physiognomy to be adapted to his taste. Genia therefore became a daily subscriber at a local beauty parlour. There they indeed freshened her up and made a presentable person of her. She kept up appearances until after the wedding. Later she no longer had the possibility of covering up both[?], and soon the glamour faded and what was left was a mask.

This new discovery crushed Maniek completely. For years he had kept picking and choosing matches, had looked specifically for a "pot of fat" and for the capital itself to be appealing as well. In the person of Genia N. he had been sure he had at last found both ideals.

And here, suddenly, one disappointment after the other. True, the first disappointment hit him even harder. But he understands that nothing can be done about it. As for the second disappointment, he might perhaps even have forgiven her; but he is sure that it gives him a sufficient legal ground to get entirely rid of the wife he bargained for.

So Maniek is indeed knocking on the doors of all the lawyers, begging them to find in the codes a paragraph on the basis of which he could bring, and win, a divorce suit on the grounds stated.

As we have already written, the income from the Będzin shechita has fallen considerably.
Because of the situation, the kehilla administration finds it necessary to cut the slaughter fees by half.
The question will be decided at the administration meeting taking place next Sunday.
At the same time it is planned to raise the (fee for) slaughter of oxen, because instead of 4 head of cattle one ox is slaughtered.

Christian trader shot dead in Łagisza over a theft of 20 zł.
A thief got into the little shop of Jan Sroka[?] in Łagisza and started packing up the bit of merchandise that was in the shop; in the middle of the job the owner came in.
The thief, seeing that he was trapped, began shooting and badly wounded Sroka. A few hours later he died in the Będzin hospital.
After the murder the thief took the bit of merchandise worth 20 zł.

Great success of Bronisław Gimpel.
A great sensation for the music lovers in Zagłębie were the concerts of the violin virtuoso Bronisław Gimpel.
Bronisław Gimpel is no new face here. We have already appreciated his musical abilities several times. Nevertheless the concerts in Będzin and Sosnowiec showed again that Bronisław Gimpel has greatly perfected himself in his field. He is one of the musical geniuses in the musical world. His tone is lyrical, velvet-soft, and touches the depths of the soul.
After every number the audience presented the great artist with stormy ovations.
He was very finely accompanied by Mr. Koszlik[?], a well-known pianist from Katowice.

Będzin Revisionists Celebrate the Housewarming of New Premises

The Będzin Revisionists, who until now have had no „resting place“ (that is why they fight for a Jewish kingdom...), last Sunday celebrated the opening of their own premises on Kołłątaja Street.
Invited to the opening were representatives of the local Zionist Organization, of „Keren Hayesod“, of the Keren Kayemet, and ordinary guests who are[?] always to be seen at national celebrations.
At the festive opening of new, handsome premises, and especially in the present hard crisis, the saying „there is no joy without sorrow“ was fulfilled once again.
During the greetings the Zionists and the Revisionist representatives displayed such „mutual love“ that it very nearly came about that the dispute for the sake of Heaven led both sides to „kiss each other heartily“...
—_—
The opening was conducted by Mr. Kisner, and the chair was handed over to Mr. D. Hofer.
After the singing of „Hatikvah“ the representative of the Central Committee (C.C.), Dr. Wdowiński (Bielitz), delivered a greeting in which he set out the main problems and resolutions of the last world conference in Vienna.
On behalf of „Keren Hayesod“ greetings were given by Mr. Nate Landner, on behalf of the Keren Kayemet by Mr. A. Liwer. The latter stressed that they believe „with perfect faith“ that in future the Revisionists will „repent“ and work together for the benefit of the above-mentioned funds.
Mr. Klarman, just back from the Vienna conference, where he had absorbed a fair dose of „fascism“, replied sharply, and the upshot was that Messrs. Landner, Wygodzki and Liwer later left the hall.
On behalf of „Tse'irei Mizrachi“ greetings were given by Mr. Ch. M. Zylberberg, of „Herzliya“ — Olszewski, and of the Sosnowiec „Masada“ — Mr. Tajchman.
With this the official part came to an end.
In the second part one first saw clearly the „fascist danger“ of the Revisionists. And even more — of the Betarim... With great zeal they „fought“ — for a glass of wine and a piece of cake...
Having dispensed with the material things (very quickly...), those present had a spiritual treat from the violinists Mandelbaum and Unger.
Also taking part were the „commandant“ Chaim Triger (song) and above all little Łazinger (song). Mr. Pesachzon had great applause for his recitation „Legion“.
The celebration went on until late at night.
Memorial Service for the Airmen Who Perished

In the presence of the local rabbi, kehilla representatives, town councillors, the deputy mayor, the police commandant and others, a mourning memorial service was held last Sabbath in the Dąbrowa synagogue in memory of the airmen who perished, Żwirko and Wigura.
After speeches by the rabbi, chairman Neufeld and town councillor Bernard Rechnic, the deputy mayor Mr. Czenszmiech[?] gave thanks on behalf of the town administration.
The young cantor Gershon Lejtner with a choir led the prayers beautifully at the reader's desk and conducted the memorial.
Great Tishri Campaign of the JNF in Sosnowiec

The Keren Kayemet LeIsrael in Sosnowiec is conducting the Tishri campaign on a very large scale. The campaign begins on Friday, the eve of Rosh Hashana, through specially authorised pairs who will visit the Jewish population with rich JNF materials such as „Leshana Tova“ cards, pocket calendars, etc.
At the same time attention is drawn to the fact that the JNF has received from the Head Directorate in Jerusalem large wall calendars with very rich and valuable content; the calendars will be distributed free of charge to the houses of prayer and minyanim. From Sport

2 victories for Będzin „Hakoach“.
A great impression was made in local sports circles by the results „Hakoach“ achieved on its tour in Radomsko, beating the local „Hakoach“ there 7:0 and on the second day defeating the strong Polish club „Korona“ by a score of 7:1.
On the first day the „Hakoach“ players took the field without Gutman and Hampel; despite this they held a great superiority throughout the game.
All the players were in good form; Matil Rozen especially distinguished himself, scoring 5 goals by himself. With their play the Hakoach men left a very good impression, and the Radomsko Jewish public was highly satisfied. The referee was Mr. Winer — good.
On the second day the match against „Korona“ aroused colossal interest in sports circles there. A crowd of over 2 thousand people gathered for the match. For this match „Korona“ specially brought down players from Kraków, but it helped very little. In this match the „Hakoach“ players proved that today they are one of the strongest Jewish clubs in Poland.
Throughout the game the „Hakoach“ players had the upper hand. After the match the enthusiastic Jewish public carried the „Hakoach“ players shoulder-high.
—o—
„Gwiazda“ (Będzin) — „Jaworznik“[?] (Żychlin) 4:0
On Saturday the last championship match of Class „C“ took place on the „Hakoach“ ground. Throughout the match „Gwiazda“ held a great superiority, but up to half-time they managed to score no more than one goal, through Zawader. After half-time they managed to raise the score to 4:0. The goals were scored by Szwajcer 2 and Lindbaum 1. Best on the field: Lewkowicz. Referee Szabas — excellent.
—o—
On the first Jewish Winter Sports Games in Zakopane.
In accordance with the resolution of the „Maccabi“ Union convention held in July of this year in Vienna, the first „Maccabi“ Winter Sports Games will take place in Poland, in Zakopane, from 2 to 5 February 1933.
The programme includes: ski racing, sledging, hockey and others. The relevant programmes for the special sections have already been sent out to the sports unions.
The organisation of the whole event in Zakopane is in the hands of a specially created committee with its permanent seat in Kraków. The Polish government has promised the organisers the most far-reaching assistance.
A. Wrocławski.

In Klein-Wysoka [?] a local inhabitant poisoned with arsenic a whole family, with whom he had had a quarrel over a share of an inheritance.

In Murcki a 26-year-old young man threw himself into a chimney [?] of a house and was asphyxiated there by the fumes. The reason is that the suicide had been ill for several weeks with consumption and, seeing that he was incurable, he put an end to his life.

Paid with His Life Trying to Save Another.

From "Hakoach".

From "Betar".
On Saturday evening "Betar" held in the Artisans' Hall a festive academy in honour of the 15th anniversary since the creation of the Jewish Legion, with the participation of Mr. Klarman. A longer introductory speech is given by Mr. Chmielnicki, who among other things draws a parallel between the Jewish Legion and other left-wing Zionist groupings. Then Mr. Klarman gives a lecture on the topic "Fifteen Years of the Jewish Legion". The closing word then goes to Mr. Chaim Krahn, who gives a short but very interesting lecture interwoven with sayings of the Sages, discussing the great importance of "Betar", and expresses himself among other things: "This is the youth for whom we have waited more than two thousand years".

A "Hazkarah" (Memorial Service).
On Sunday morning a "hazkarah", organised by "Betar", took place in the town synagogue for the tragically killed Polish aviators Żwirko and engineer Wigura. Taking part in the memorial were the rabbi and representatives of the authorities, headed by the starosty's officer for Jewish affairs, Mr. Żurkowski. After the cantor, Mr. Unger, had sung several chapters of Psalms, the choir of the Jewish public elementary school, conducted by Mr. Lejzerowicz, sang the Polish anthem, and the "Betar" choir sang "Hatikvah". With an "El Male Rachamim" for the tragically killed, the memorial service came to an end.
