On the Eve of a Catastrophe (XII) — With a Quiet Conscience Our Representatives Consider Who Is to Blame for the Danger of the Moment

[Editorial — economy; the Jewish Sejm deputies; series, part XII.]
With a quiet conscience our representatives consider who is to blame for the danger of the moment.
A polemic has only just begun in the Jewish press among 2—3 Sejm deputies about the economic ruin of Polish Jewry, or, better said, the polemic is not really being conducted over the matter itself. People merely want to reach a conclusion and establish who is to blame for this ruin, which of our representatives allowed things to be brought to this sad state, to this catastrophic situation.
Is it not an incitement [hetze] that at a time when Jewish poverty, when want and distress take hold of everything from top to bottom, when Jewish property and possessions have become a heap of ruins forever [tel olam], when the waters have truly come up to the soul — people should have the patience and time and courage and strength to stand up and preach, to sermonize about the cause of how it came to this, while meanwhile, meanwhile everything goes on sinking as it sinks, as if this were a normal phenomenon, as if this is how it had to be.
It is truly an injustice crying to heaven that people who rose to the highest pedestal of their lives, people who with the help of Jewish votes, with the help of our recognition, attained a career, wanted only to argue and philosophize about seats and about politics and about everything in the world, while the economic "weaknesses" they wanted to leave to God's providence. Is that a small injustice? Could it really be tolerated?
For some time now, ever since the writer of these lines had occasion to speak in a narrow circle of writers about the terrible economic situation and about the specifically Jewish oppressions in the country, some of them clutched their heads on hearing in what a sad state the Jewish citizens find themselves; and then one of them asked whether this was the plain truth, whether it was not a little exaggerated, painted a little too vividly; and then he expressed [the misprinted word ארויסגעדרוגגען — ?] the view that since the Jewish Sejm deputies do not react with the utmost sharpness to the catastrophic situation, they surely do not go — as we do — among the broad strata of the popular masses; otherwise they would surely have had to storm, otherwise they would surely have had to do everything in the world so as not to let their brethren fall into the nethermost pit [she'ol tachtiyah].
Yes, about everything in the world they polemicized, about everything they haggled and quarrelled, and with everything they somehow managed among themselves; they merely forgot that one needs a livelihood, and that this very piece of bread is being systematically torn from one's mouth. And on top of that, on top of that the tax offices and assessment commissions and bailiffs worked ever more energetically. The last thing was carried out of the home for this or that tax; the workshop and the machine and the last piece of merchandise were taken from the citizen, and he had to close his shop, lock his workshop and shut down his little factory, because he had nothing to take in money from, nothing to sell and nothing to work with.
And these silent tragedies, which have driven people into the deepest abyss, to suicides and ruin and helplessness, none of our spokesmen and popular representatives has seen, or did not feel them on their own shoulders — perhaps that is why they remained at a distance. Yes, our Sejm deputies, whoever they may be, do not live together with the popular strata, are not found in their ranks, do not breathe their air, and therefore cannot feel their sufferings or see their pains.
Moreover, we do not have our own professional bodies that would understand their tasks and stay in contact with the representations, which could and should have prevented things from being brought to this brokenness, to these defeats.
One by one Jewish livelihoods are being taken away. Position after position, Jews are being pushed out of their branches of trade; systematically everything is being taken from us, so that we are left hanging in the air; and whoever still somehow runs a little business or a workshop cries out that he will have to liquidate everything because of the new regulations on bookkeeping, which he cannot afford. He does not earn for himself while he toils hard and bitterly, day and night, with his family — how then is he to provide a living for a bookkeeper who should keep the proper books for him? When one meets the worried Jews and hears their complaints, how they come to the conclusion that they have no way out and must capitulate, one is beside oneself on seeing how deep is the tragedy into which the whole Jewish people is sinking.
In the big cities one sees life in the streets, people walk, drive, and it seems that everything is alive; in the homes, however, one sees the poverty and the suffering and the hunger. Much more strikingly, however, one sees the oppression in the small towns. There everything has died out. Both the home and the street. People who played a role and were mighty rich men [gvirim adirim] do not have enough for a piece of bread and are hungry in the true sense of the word. There everything has died out and a common hunger reigns, a uniform want; on top of that antisemitism rages in all its size and strength.
And at such a time, in such a depressed mood, in such dark days, people have the courage and strength to stand and consider how we came to these dark times and who is to blame for it? Can one really allow oneself this luxury at the present time? May one today remain indifferent to everything that is happening around our economic situation and look on at it with apathy as if nothing were the matter, so that nothing more is left to do than merely to consider in what way the terrible catastrophe was brought about and who is to blame for it? Is that how one expects to heal the wound, which has already penetrated so deeply into the healthy body? May one stand at a distance on seeing that a fire is flaring up which can destroy everything, and then philosophize about where the fire came from? Must one not at such a moment first of all set about energetically to put out the fire, and only afterwards consider how and who caused the disaster? And why do our Sejm deputies have the courage, at such a serious moment, to sit down and consider the causes of how things became bad, at a time when it is getting constantly worse and worse?
Why do they not, first and foremost, take measures so that the catastrophe should not take further dangerous steps and that everything should not be burned up in the blaze? Why do they not [זענען — ?] first of all rescue what has not yet been burned completely to coal? At such a moment one must set about radical work as fast and as energetically as possible; one must with full seriousness and boldness set about saving the building, which still stands somehow on chicken legs and which must not be allowed to be completely undermined, completely destroyed.
Time is short; every day in which nothing is done brings enormously great damage and suffering to the Jewish citizens in Poland, who are living beyond their strength, beyond human endurance; and therefore our communal representatives must not delay, for the whole Jewish people has the right to blame them if they remain indifferent to the want and suffering of their poor and oppressed brothers and sisters.
— Let them remember that "well"
All for Me.

[Feuilleton.] For whom do they all take such trouble, if not for me?
How does it go in the Gemara?
See, my child, you have woken from sleep, rubbed your eyes, taken a look at the bright world. Whom has the dear sunbeam touched with a tickle? You! For whom does the peasant plough, sow and reap in the field? For you! For whom has the baker baked the warm roll, the gentile woman plucked the little red berries, the hen laid the fresh eggs, the cow let herself be milked of the sweet milk? All for you!
So says the Gemara, and there is a commentary to it as well:
For whom has an "Arban"[?] prepared municipal buses? For me! For whom has the magistrate [town council] laid sharp stones in the middle of the street, to tear one's feet on? For me! In whose ears do the newspaper boys shout till one goes deaf? Surely for me!
———
But I am not out to be clever. I mean it seriously: although by Darwin's theory it turns out that man is nothing less than a close[?] relative of the frog from the mud, nevertheless I see that in the small world that surrounds us man is, after all, the chosen of creatures, the mighty one, the aristocrat, the ruler and conqueror. And man — that is me.
With all my senses I feel that everything that is done in the world — tilled, traded and changed, bartered and brokered, babbled and blathered, all the wars with all the peaces, all the thefts with all the honesties, all the murders with all the justices, all the congresses and conferences and pre- and pre-pre-conferences — everything, everything is done only for my sake, to ease and improve my life.
Once it was thought that only the Almighty Himself, so to speak, could hand me the little plate from heaven: that He should by His grace transfer His almighty power to the king on earth; and the king, receiving the crown from God, broke borders like potsherds, seized countries like birds' eggs, stirred up peoples like porridge in a soldiers' kettle, with the hands of his thousands of servants drew out the goods of the earth and hurled them from one ocean to the other — and all for me, to feed and clothe and shoe me, to give me drink and load me with every good thing.
Then came the war and made a mess — and the little plate from heaven? Probably also buried deep in the earth, not to be found. So what will become of me? Where will I go on enjoying all the good things of the world? And if not I — then who?
That is the question that has tormented all mankind for 14 years now, that now hurls the great ones as from a sling from Geneva to Lausanne, from Lausanne to Berlin and Paris, that draws from their mouths 99 measures of talk — all for me, for my pleasure's[?] sake.
For when God's grace withdrew from the kings, they fell like tin soldiers. People picked up from the ground the rolling crowns and handed them to the new rulers, who rule "by grace from below"; and again they stitched the borders together — a border beside a border and a border within a border — and broke the empires up into tiny little states, and put fetters on their own feet, so as not to walk further than a Sabbath limit, and laid chains on their hands, so as not to reach further than their own pocket, and set dogs at every gate, so that no foreign foot should cross the threshold — all for me, for my pleasure's sake.
———
And I, poor man, for whose sake all the ministers confer, all the typewriters clatter, all the radios resound and all the newspaper boys in the streets shout like hoarse sirens; I, poor man, for whose sake the imperial thrones have been exchanged for benches in the Sejm and the governors' medals — for [?] tokens[?]; for whose sake all engineers build tanks and all chemists manufacture poison gases and all lawyers become diplomats, and communists and chauvinists become one fellowship — to provide me with houses I did not build, with money I did not gather and with all good things I did not toil for — I, poor man, stand disappointed and dishevelled, oppressed and ashamed, stand tottering on the edge of the narrow today, without a yesterday and without a tomorrow; I stand and ask, with my mouth gaping wide open, like the simple son of the Haggadah:
— What is this? Who are they, all these hearty caretakers of mine: nannies or policemen? Brothers or wolves? Guides or forest robbers? And what are they doing there so long, in all those Genevas? Do they really still want to bring down the little plate from heaven for me, or are they digging a grave for all my hopes?
If they are taking all this trouble for my sake, then why do I stand so bewildered and shattered on the brink of 7 abysses — war behind, war in front, financial crises to the right and to the left, political demonstrations, boycotts, barricades, spiced with antisemitic attacks — all on my poor head?
What do they want of me?
You Have the Floor — Honourable Voters!

[Będzin — Kehilla.] In the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" you asked us what has become of the elections of May 1931, and why we do not react to the fact that in the Jewish community (gmina), in which we ought to be sitting today, others are the masters, and the management there is such that the community is meanwhile [?] being utterly ruined.
Your question is a very important one, and it calls for an answer — and a clear answer at that...
You are right. After 16 months the matter of the kehilla elections really should have been settled long ago. These elections have cost too much time and energy, so that even today one has to talk about the election story; but the blame, of course, is not on our side.
We cannot compete with our opponent, the "Agudah"; we cannot bid ourselves down into the minus, as [?] they strive to keep us, the majority, from being admitted to the kehilla. The difference between them and us is this: we demand what is ours. We have a majority in the kehilla and we want to take it over as such — we demand what is ours clearly and proudly — whereas our opponent begs, cadges, bows double, and of course the lord (poritz) is more inclined to the "Moshkes" who bow than to the Jew who speaks proudly and openly. Here, after all, is reflected the struggle between the national camp and the Agudah, which supplies from its ranks the well-known "Ma Yafit"-niks; the Agudah trembles and flutters lest the kehilla be ruled by the national part of Polish Jewry, because then there will be an end to the various machinations of filling kehilla posts with "our own people". Then, when the national dozores [board members] take over the kehilla, one may at last begin to care, besides the mikveh and shechita, also for some cultural matters — and that is what they are afraid of.
It is truly a farce when one recalls that since May 1931 we, the elected representatives of the public, have been dragged some 10—12 times to the kehilla premises to hold elections of the presidium, and it is a disgrace to tell how we were treated: when the "mighty" Agudah president wished, elections took place; when he did not wish, 18 dozores had to waste their time for nothing and go home empty-handed. When he wished, he called a session precisely at a time when Jews must look for a livelihood (in the middle of the week, before noon). In a word, he is the "almighty" president. He may do anything, because he is the representative of the Agudah, of the "Ma Yafit"-niks, who feel strong — very strong.
Let us take a look back and we shall see that the Będzin kehilla elections strongly remind us of the tales of Chelm. The elections gave the national lists a majority of 11 against 7 of the Agudah (already counting their allied artisans). It is simply accepted in the whole civilized world that a majority takes over power. In Będzin, however, it is different. They bring in the well-known R' Leybele, and he takes great pains to diminish the result of the elections, and on 31 May the Będzin starosta [district head] orders a constituent session according to a count different from the one the election commission confirmed in its protocol, and the mighty and "honourable" president of the old gmina closes the session without any "why" — only because the great dignity of R' Leybele had been offended. A few days later, by order of the authorities, a second session takes place, this time again according to the count of the election commission — and again the "president" does not agree to it and again closes the session. The count — he says — is not right. A few days later the order is given again to call a session, again according to the count against [?] the election commission. So we went to the session, elected our president and vice-president, and sent the starosta's count to the Kielce voivode, who recognized that we were right and returned the 2 mandates which the starosta had taken from us. We thought that since we already had a presidium of the council, things would now run in order. Nothing gets started. The presidium elections of the board far surpass the council elections in their spectacle. That here too we would not have much joy we saw [?] already from the fact that the starosta refused to confirm, in the election commission (on which Messrs. Rozin, Fiszel and Strachlic sat), the former vice-president [deputy mayor] of Będzin, Mr. L. Rubinlicht. We swallowed this at once and elected another in his place, just to settle the election matter once and for all; and after a series of various tricks, which already belong to history, we finally received an order to elect a board on 30 September (Wrzesień) of last year. And in these elections too the Agudah came out defeated. Of 12 dozores we obtained 7. Thus, a decisive majority.
And it will be very interesting to tell that when the Będzin starosta ordered the board to elect a presidium on 24/10 of last year, the Agudah was badly frightened, ran wherever necessary, begged and cadged, until the same Mr. Starosta withdrew his own order, and the session again did not take place and everything was forgotten. There were no elections, there is no majority — quiet, hush — until the year 1931 came to an end.
Only on 27/1 of this year did they somehow remember and order new elections for a board presidium.
About the session of 27 January (Styczeń) alone it would be necessary to write a great deal, but it will suffice to point out that the session took place illegally — simply without a quorum. Of 12 persons 6 were present, and yet the authorities in Będzin confirmed this very session, because an Agudah president was elected at it...
A few days later, however, a new story develops: for some formal reasons the presidium elections in several towns, Będzin among them, were annulled, and the voivode ordered new elections, which indeed took place on 10 July (Lipiec) of this year, and a presidium of the majority was elected.
Two months have already passed, and we do not know whether the election affair has really ended. One thing, however, we can tell you, honourable voters: we are not to blame for this whole matter. We will not bow, we will not go "begging"; we have a majority and we do not want to give this majority away to anyone; we do not want to cede your votes to anyone; we will not cede the trust you have given us in favour of the Agudah — never, never.
We have patience; we know that the struggle is not a local one; we know that the struggle is the struggle for our rights, and therefore we must have endurance.
True, the kehilla is meanwhile being broken, everything is going under, a deathly stillness reigns in every corner.
What can we do about it when the authorities tolerate the situation that after 16 months there still sit there, in the kehilla office, dozores who pursue nothing but Agudah politics? If the authorities tolerate it, we must sit quietly and wait; one must have patience and endurance. True, patience. It has a limit [?]; it is possible that a day will come when we, the majority, will renounce our mandates and no longer wish to take over the kehilla, which is no more than a skeleton of bones, because the skin and flesh have rotted and wasted away; we shall forgo the honour of taking over a desolate ruin...
The Agudah was promised that the kehillot would be handed to it on lease; in Będzin this did not succeed. The Jewish voter in Będzin, the national voter, understood to whom to entrust the kehilla — so they are trying by other ways to ignore public opinion. That is indeed the reason why we cannot take over the kehilla, and a few rulers sit there against the will of the majority of the Jewish population of Będzin.
Our majority has hit the Agudah hard — our majority is a bone in their throat, our majority does not let them sleep peacefully, our majority has roused all their "shtadlonim" and "askonim", who knock on every door and beg for mercy that we not be let into power.
But we will wait calmly until we nevertheless obtain our rights as the majority and can work for a productive kehilla, which will serve and help the whole Jewish population, not only the privileged and the "court" people.
We will not withdraw from the front. Nor will we go along with the various machinations proposed to us from various sides.
Our motto is: patience and endurance — that is our answer, honourable voters.
This is the clear answer you demanded of us. Now judge for yourselves who is right and who is to blame. Now you can judge who are the destroyers of Jewish life — of Jewish work.
You have the floor — honourable voters.
Elazar Rubinlicht, A. Liwer, Nata Lander, Cwi Kitner, Dow Herszlewicz, Abraham Isachar Rechnic, Chaim Dawid Rozin, Cwi Strachlic, Mosze Kajzer, Lejbl Goldsztajn.
The Development and Significance of Vocational Schooling

[Article — Education, vocational schools.]
Our school bodies, in supporting the idea of vocational education, quite rightly point out that our society shows a greater inclination towards a one-sided general education.
At a time when other Western nations have for several years already placed the question on entirely different foundations, mostly economic ones, and have thereby succeeded in developing their trade and industry, as well as in attaining their economic prosperity, the statistics show a disproportionate overgrowth of general schooling in relation to vocational schooling. This proves most clearly that our society does not really give itself an account of the fact that a country such as Poland, whose economy depends exclusively on work in the fields of agriculture, trade and industry, needs specially trained vocational forces in order to exploit the enormous natural riches of our country, as well as to realise the brilliant economic opportunity. To this day we still have very few well-prepared forces for this, forces that only the vocational schools can supply us with. Only vocational schooling will show us the proper way not only to general prosperity but also to the true independence of the state.
In the present moment of a mounting economic crisis, the question of choosing a profession is becoming ever more topical. More than once this burning matter has been dealt with in the columns of this newspaper. To the correct arguments expressed there we will permit ourselves to add a few more remarks, whose aim is purely practical — to solve the above-mentioned question.
Ever louder, yet still rather faintly, one hears among us the voice of propaganda for vocational schooling; regrettably, the great role of this kind of school is still not appreciated here in Poland.
Springtime releases from the elementary schools and the gymnasia tens of thousands of girls and boys who, after so many years of effort and toil [?] on the school bench, are not fitted for life, and stand helpless on their thorny path in search of a purpose.
We shall not be far from the truth if we say that only 10 percent of the graduates know what to do with themselves, which path they should choose, for what they truly have an inclination. For the most part we are dealing here with chance or with financial possibilities; as a result the ranks of the dissatisfied grow, when the thought comes to them that they have wasted their abilities on entirely alien work to which they never aspired. Not only does this or that person become a tragic cripple in life — such a state of affairs does even more harm to society itself and to the state, because the work of such a person cannot be taken into account in the general balance sheet of society.
One must take up propaganda more energetically, so as properly to enlighten the interested parties, i.e. the parents and the educators, that the general gymnasium, although it swallows up so much time and energy, gives only the possibility of entering university, and the matura certificate obtained is no certificate of maturity for getting work.
Young people themselves are, of course, unable during their school years to give themselves an account of the future that awaits them, but the parents or educators commit an outright crime against their children by sending them to the gymnasia, which in the end give no preparation for life, and needlessly bring upon themselves so many material hardships. If, however, young people were shown the right path at the proper moment and were put to study in such types of vocational schools where each could find the true place for his aspirations and abilities, then our youth would indeed be ready to enter life laden with useful knowledge and sciences, so as to be able to wage the struggle for existence; thereby we would be freed of so many dissatisfied and unemployed people, and the well-trained professional element would multiply.
It must also be stressed that graduates of the vocational secondary schools are treated, when obtaining posts in government and local-government institutions, like the graduates of the general gymnasia; moreover, one notices the phenomenon that the above-mentioned institutions, when filling posts, gladly take professionally trained staff (employees) rather than holders of the matura [?] who are not at all prepared for the work.
The period of study is much shorter in the vocational school. A 7-grade elementary school or a gymnasium cycle of education suffices to enter such a school. Completing the higher type of vocational school gives the right to shorten the period of military service as well as to obtain officer's rank. We have various types of vocational schools, such as technical, agricultural and mining-industry schools, horticulture, handicrafts and dairy farming. We also have a large number of commercial schools, which train office clerks well versed in a range of useful fields.
We see, then, that great is the field of our work. But if everyone's heart is set above all on securing his own sure piece of bread, one should nevertheless not forget that the development of vocational schooling is closely bound up with the development of the whole social economy, and therefore we must develop the interest in this direction.
R. Lewi,
teacher at the commercial school of M. Bojarska in Będzin.
Don't Lock the Gates Before 11

[Short article — Tenants and caretakers.]
From 1 October the gates of the houses will again be locked at 10 in the evening.
If this happens, it will be a harsh decree for the residents. There is no concrete reason why the gates should have to be locked so early. There is only one reason: so that the house caretakers can earn a few złoty for opening the gates. Earnings for the caretakers may be a very sympathetic reason, but the convenience of the residents also has something to say here.
There are today hundreds of people who truly cannot afford to pay 10 or 20 groszy a night, and such people are forced to run home before 10, or — when they come after 10 — to be cursed by the caretakers (stróże), who have a quite "peculiar" attitude towards the poor tenants. Often this leads to rows and fights, depending on the "temperament" of the parties; it often happens that already at 10 o'clock a tenant has to stand at the gate for a good while in the snow and in the rain until His Excellency the caretaker deigns to open the gate.
We think that the tenants' association, if it cannot come to terms with the house owners, could perhaps nevertheless come to terms with the caretakers, if it were, for instance, to take the proper steps in good time, such as turning to the competent authority with the necessary memorandum.
Instead of at 10, the gates should be locked as hitherto — at 11 in the evening.
Baruch Spinoza — His Life and Work

[Culture — philosophy; Spinoza's 300th birthday.] (Dedicated to the International Philosophical Congress, which opens these days in The Hague on the occasion of Spinoza's 300th birthday)

Baruch Spinoza was born on 24 November 1632 in Amsterdam. His father, Michael Spinoza, came from a Portuguese Jewish family that had escaped the Inquisition to Holland, the only country in Europe where all those persecuted and hounded for their faith found protection. When Baruch Spinoza was 6 years old his mother died, and his father some time later married a second wife.

Baruch Spinoza received his first education at the Amsterdam Talmud Torah, which was very well organised for various subjects, because the rich Sephardi community of that time spared no money to set the teaching on a proper level. In this Talmud Torah Spinoza received an excellent Jewish education, and when he finished the Talmud Torah he knew the whole Tanakh by heart. He also had a great knowledge of grammar and knew Talmud and the codifiers (poskim) exceptionally well. Spinoza, who from his youth was physically very weak and sickly, distinguished himself — as very often happens with such children — by his intellectual abilities. He finished the Talmud Torah at 13, and afterwards studied with the local rabbi, R' Saul Morteira.

At the same time Spinoza became acquainted with medieval Jewish literature, read the Jewish poets of the Spanish period, took an interest in Jewish philosophy and also in the various commentators on the Torah. A great influence on him was exercised by the commentary of "Ibn Ezra" on the Pentateuch with its "secrets" — its veiled allusions. Spinoza, however, was not content with this alone; he also studied languages: German, Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch and especially Latin. The Latin language, which then had the greatest importance for science, Spinoza studied thoroughly with a certain teacher, Van den Enden.

Various biographers of Spinoza tell of a love affair that Spinoza had in his youth with a daughter of this teacher, a certain Clara Maria, who assisted her father and often substituted for him in teaching the pupils. On this subject the German Romantic Berthold Auerbach even wrote quite a large novel, in which Spinoza is depicted tragically, because his love was an unhappy one.

Later research, however, has shown that the "unfaithful" Clara Maria married in 1671, when she was 23 years old. It follows, then, that Spinoza would have fallen in love with her at a time when he was no longer in Amsterdam — he left that city in 1656, that is, when she was 12 years old. Besides, it is known that Spinoza's calm character and his philosophical attitude to life were not at all given to such things.

The developments Spinoza went through, his studies in philosophy and in Kabbalah, awakened in him various thoughts about God and the world. He therefore gradually distanced himself from the religious outlook that prevailed in the fanatical Sephardi community in Amsterdam. One must not forget that this community consisted for the most part of former "Anusim" (Marranos) or children of Anusim, who had suffered many, many troubles for their faith, and therefore they were strong fanatics. Although they did permit the study of poetry and philosophy, which was the finest heritage of the former Spanish golden age.

About the frictions Spinoza had with the heads of the community in Amsterdam, which led to his being placed under a herem (ban), various biographers, especially non-Jews, have told unfounded tales.

And indeed the newest research has proved that these are all mere old wives' tales, for in reality Spinoza never broke off his relations with Jews. Baruch Spinoza remained a faithful Jew to his last day. Incidentally, it is worth mentioning that as long as his father was alive he conducted himself very Jewishly; even after his father's death he often came to synagogue and was called up to the Torah. The frictions between him and the community leaders were therefore not so much due to a religious standpoint as to personal reasons. It is also worth noting that at that time the Amsterdam community often made use of the "herem" in order to carry out its policy in this way.

But whatever the story may be, it is a fact that as soon as the Amsterdam community learned that Spinoza was going about with free thoughts concerning certain laws of the Torah, they summoned him before the community board and demanded that he repent...

Spinoza at once replied with a detailed letter in which he explained his views on faith and politics and showed that they did not contradict the Jewish religion. But the community leaders did not accept this and gave him 30 days to reconsider. When the time was up and he had given no answer, on the 6th of Av in the year 1656, when he was 24 years old, he was cast under the herem.

Spinoza protested against the herem with a long letter in Spanish sent to the heads of the community, but he could no longer stay in Amsterdam, because the community had prevailed on the authorities to expel him from the city. He therefore settled in Rijnsburg.

In his enforced solitude Spinoza found good friends — Jews and non-Jews — who took an interest in his philosophy.

By that time he already had wide acquaintance with scholars and friends in various countries. By nature Spinoza was a quiet man, who confided his philosophical views only to learned people. Even to his pupil (printed "talmud") Albert Buren [as printed] he entrusted only René Descartes's philosophy, which he thoroughly explained and interpreted and afterwards published.

Of his own works Spinoza published during his lifetime only the well-known work, the "Theological-Political Treatise", which deals with the question of the relationship of the state to religion.

In this book Spinoza speaks at length about the matter of faith and politics and shows that the state has no business meddling in religious matters. This book, which appeared under a false name, raised a tremendous storm throughout Holland. Curses and insults were showered on the author from all sides. The anger grew even stronger when it finally became known who the author was.

At the same time the Elector Karl Ludwig of the Palatinate offered Spinoza the post of professor at the University of Heidelberg. Spinoza, however, declined, giving as his reason that he had no intention whatever of becoming a professor, because that would prevent him from devoting himself wholly to philosophy.

In 1670 Spinoza settled in The Hague, where he lived very solitarily, lodging with a certain painter: Van der Spijck. Sometimes Spinoza would not leave the house for 4–5 days. By day he used to grind lenses for spectacles for a certain apothecary — a craft by which he earned his living. By night, in turn, he occupied himself with his scholarly work.

He lived very frugally and dressed very plainly, so as not to benefit from strangers. His hard life and work had a strong effect on his weak health, which later turned consumptive. His friends tried as far as possible to cure him, but his way of life made his illness ever worse.

A year later he became very seriously ill and died on 21 February 1677, at the age of 44, in the city of The Hague — lonely, quietly, like a lost dove; even his friends and neighbours were not in the house at the time.

His life and his death will remain a model of fine integrity and philosophical calm.

Of the works he wrote, as I have already mentioned above, only the "Theological-Political Treatise" was printed in his lifetime. Only after his death were his works published, the most important of which is the "Ethics", which encompasses his whole philosophy. Later his letters also appeared, which he wrote to various friends on philosophical matters. Then a book "On Politics" and a book: "On the Improvement of the Human Understanding", as well as a Hebrew grammar, which remained unfinished. Then a work "On God, Man and His Happiness", as well as a sizeable work on the "Rainbow".

Some of his friends maintain that Spinoza also wrote a Dutch translation of the Torah, but it was not found among his writings; possibly he burned it before his death.

Of Baruch Spinoza we may boldly say: "There has not arisen another like him."

Kraków, September 1932.
When the assessors assess...

[Taxes — the assessment commission.] In the days when Jews begin to tremble like fish in water.
Elul.
Jews tremble like fish in water.
They tremble and pray for a good "kvitl" [a good inscription in the Book of Life], for a merciful verdict.
There come days when the assessors begin to assess, and Jews take fright.
Between man and God it is only half a misfortune; for that there is an old Jewish remedy: repentance, prayer and charity. The Days of Awe are approaching, and Jews will somehow manage, so as to obtain a good year.
Much worse, however, is the matter between man and man — with the assessors who are not in heaven but on earth.
This week the assessment commission at the tax authority began its work, and they are about to set about measuring out the income taxes. The fate of hundreds of Jewish families is being decided. Jewish merchants and Jewish shopkeepers know this and came to us at the editorial office to ask that we remind the Jewish members of the commission that they must remember not only to fulfil their duties and attend the sessions — not to miss them, not to come late and not to neglect them — but also to stand on guard, so that the judgment be a just one, that everyone be properly assessed and that no one, God forbid, be over-assessed.
We remind them of this, and remind them too that, unfortunately, it has happened more than once that, owing to neglect by the members of the commission, many Jews were very badly wronged.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Nitzavim-Vayelech)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Nitzavim-Vayelech
"And they that handle the Torah knew Me not" [Jer. 2:8].
Those who "grab God by the coat-tails", the official mitzvah-grabbers — "knew Me not": they know God least of all...
Rabbi Shmuel of Karov.
—o—
The Portion
a) "Then the Lord thy God will turn thy captivity" (30:3)
"The Lord thy God will return" — yes, God too must repent. He too is not entirely in order with us. He too has sinned a tiny bit against us... But only if we repent will we remind Him that He too must repent...
Zera Kodesh (Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz).
—o—
b) "And thou shalt return... with all thy heart and with all thy soul" (ibid. 2)
Usually the verse says "with all thy heart and with all thy soul and with all thy might [means]". With repentance, the "with all thy might" is missing. Must one not, then, repent — return to God — with one's money too?...
But here the subject is the repentance that will bring the redemption ("and will gather thee from all the nations"), and then, at the time of redemption, there will be no repenting with money, because "the son of David will not come until the last penny is gone from the purse" — the soul will not have a single grosz then...
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
c) "And the Lord thy God will put all these curses upon thine enemies and on them that hate thee, which persecuted thee" (ibid. 7)
Jews deserve the curses: Jews swindle, steal. "Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark", "Cursed be he that perverteth judgment". All this is found among Jews — but who is to blame? — Our enemies, who persecute and torment us and do not let us reach an honest livelihood; that is what drives us to swindling, to theft. Therefore all these curses surely belong to them, for our whole sin stems from that "which persecuted thee".
Kiflayim le-Tushiyah.
—o—
d) "It is not in heaven" (ibid. 12)
The Torah is not to be found among the official "heaven-Jews".
From the mouth of the people.
—o—
e) "And it shall come to pass, when many evils and troubles are befallen them, that this song shall testify before them as a witness" (31:21)
Why does he need a witness, a proof of the troubles? Does he not feel them himself?
What is meant here is "many evils": spiritual wickedness, moral decline — and that, indeed, one does not feel oneself. One can come to feel it only through "this song shall testify": when one goes back to study, one feels how empty one has been..
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
"Many evils and troubles".
The Talmud (Berakhot 5) relates:
Rabbi Yochanan fell ill. Rabbi Chanina came in to him and asked him: "Are your sufferings dear to you?" He answered him: "Neither they nor their reward."
Rabbi Meir'l could not understand this: would Rabbi Yochanan turn up his nose at suffering?...
But Rabbi Yochanan meant this: I will have the sufferings anyway — after all, in heaven they do not ask my opinion whether I want to accept them.. If I do not accept them with love, I will have only sufferings without reward... So it is better to accept them with love, for "neither" — if not — "they nor their reward": I will be left with just the sufferings and no reward. Let me at least have a reward for them...
Margenita de-Rabbi Meir.

The Jews will be redeemed because they will be so badly off that it cannot get any worse... But the nations will not know this; to them the redemption will be a glory for the Jews. They will not know that God must redeem them precisely because they have already fallen so low...
Ahavat Yehonatan.

g) "What is yours is mine and what is mine is yours — an ignoramus" (5:[10])
On this Bartenura says: "An ignoramus — who benefits and gives benefit equally, and this is the settling of the land".
The author of "Solet la-Minchah" wonders:
"What is yours is mine and what is mine is yours" is surely the genuine communist idea, and Bartenura even calls it "and this is the settling of the land" — does that mean that this must be the world's way out, "mine is yours and yours is mine"?..
How Does the World Crisis Stand?

By Dr. Herman Frank
In the last several weeks a strong revival can be observed in the business world of raw materials in America and Europe.
On the New York exchange the prices of the most important raw materials, such as cotton, metals and rubber, are rising. The staple foods, such as wheat and meat, have also risen sharply in price over the last months, and such "fallen" commodities as sugar, coffee and cocoa have gone up sharply since the end of June, when their prices stood at a level lower than ever before in the course of the long world crisis.
•
There is no lack of voices, both here in Europe and in the "New World", i.e. in America and Australia, which are already about to say Kaddish over the world crisis!?
The world's stock exchanges are in an optimistic mood. They believe in an improvement of the economic situation throughout the world. "Wall Street", the centre of the American financial world, and "Lombard Street", the heart of the London business world, are even prepared for still greater, still merrier happenings on the commodity and securities exchanges.
The great bankers and exchange magnates want to draw into the game the largest possible masses of new investors, that is, small and middling capitalists who are now looking for opportunities to earn quickly and handsomely from their "free" or saved-up money.
Is the present revival on Wall Street nothing more than a political trick to help the rich and strong political party in its election campaign in favour of President Hoover, or is the good mood in America's financial world really a proof and a guarantee that the world is gradually recovering from its long and grave illness?
We shall try here to give a short assessment of the situation.
Until a short time ago all commodity markets suffered from a terrible overproduction. The warehouses were full, prices fell to the ground, and customers had to be searched for with a candle. That was the situation for several years, and from year to year the condition grew worse.
Only some time ago did a slight improvement set in: the stockpiled reserves of raw materials, such as cotton, wool, grain and metals, are beginning to shrink, and consequently prices are rising too, and the desire returns to speculate again, or generally to buy goods for the factory or for the shop.
True, even today there is still more than enough of raw materials and finished goods, such as textiles, machines, sugar etc., which wait in vain for buyers; and of the most important article of daily use — wheat — there is far more than the whole world needs. But the mood on the commodity market is nevertheless better, that is a fact.
Where does it come from?
Simply, in recent years the world has gone thoroughly hungry for many goods, and people are beginning to demand goods. Do not forget that nowadays people everywhere are, after all, used to a better standard of living than 50 and 100 years ago: one wants sugar and coffee every day, white bread with butter and cheese, meat, a nice garment, a comfortable flat, not to speak of radios, cinema and other such "luxury items", which one wants to have day in, day out.
Apart from wheat, there is in the world practically no product in such colossal quantity that we need fear, God forbid, that there will not be enough buyers. True, the public lacks money to buy everything it wants and everything it needs, but that is not yet "overproduction". On the contrary, if the goods do not sell today, they will sell tomorrow, provided only that the consumers, the users, exist; but for the time being they lack ready cash. There is in the world an overproduction of bread, but not of other products.
And so we indeed see that large branches of trade, wholesale and retail, are now gradually reviving. The end of summer has always been the season when merchants fill their warehouses and shops with new goods. Nowadays, when the public notices that commodity prices are rising, the big businessmen and shopkeepers throw themselves with even more appetite onto the commodity market, so as not to put off the necessary purchase until tomorrow, when the goods will probably become even dearer.
That is the reason why the market for all important commodities except grain is now reviving.
A Tax Seizure at Night.

(A topical scene in 2 acts.)
Characters: the husband, his wife, her lover, the tax bailiff (egzekutor), a policeman.
Act One.
A lovely moonlit night. The lover and the wife sit on a bench in the New Market and talk.
She: (to the lover) My dear, my beloved, I think of you all the time, I long for you all the time.
Lover: I feel I am going out of my mind. I cannot sleep a single night through; I keep remembering that you must spend your life with your shlimazl, while my burning heart thirsts so for you, for your smile, for your tenderness...
She: Well, what am I to do, my dear, when I can do nothing else? I ask him to go away for a rest, and lately he doesn't want to go...
Lover: My pretty little canary! You know that tomorrow it will be exactly 3 years since we met and spent time together in Bystra...
She: I would so like to recall all that and live it again...
Lover: So would I! It would be a great happiness for me!
She: Then give me some advice, my dear, how to get rid of my shlimazl for tomorrow night.
Lover: I am thinking, indeed!
She: (thinking) I have a plan!
Lover: What sort of plan? Tell me, my dear.
She: Since my shlimazl owes a tidy sum in taxes, and lately they go around at night searching the homes for money, you come tomorrow at one o'clock at night and knock hard on our door; my carcass will think it's the bailiff knocking, so he'll run away — and then we can be together undisturbed...
Lover: (surprised) A splendid plan, but what if he doesn't believe you?
She: Leave that to me. I'll prepare him for it, only see that you're not late.
Lover: At one at night sharp I'll knock hard on the door.
She: Then remember not to be late.
They part.
Act Two.
After midnight. The husband sits at the table, leaning back and dozing; his wife lies in bed and looks nervously at the clock.
She: Listen to me, go to sleep, he won't come tonight; besides, I've left the lower passage open, so that as soon as you hear knocking you can run away.
Husband: Yes, run away — but I can't get undressed. I won't be able to put my shoes on that quickly.
She: Then lie down in your shoes; I can't fall asleep while you're sitting at the table.
Husband: I won't be able to sleep anyway, because the picture keeps coming before my eyes of how last night they took the last possessions of a widow — probably her daughter's dowry.
She: Who searched her place?
He: The bailiff.
She: Well, what are they to do? If they can't find people in by day, they have to search at night.
He: As I see it, you think they're right, and you're pleased about it.
She: Why are you picking on me, and what do you want from me? What do you mean, I'm pleased?
He: You said yourself they were right.
She: Why have you latched on to me, you shlimazl, what do you want — that I should cry, scream, upset my sick nerves? — Oy, my head.
He: All right, enough! Forgive me; you know, my dear, all day long one talks oneself hoarse with the Ślązaks [Silesians] just to take in something for a living; my only pleasure used to be the night, the good bed and the dear home, and now they want to take that from me too. What does one do? Where does one start? Where does one run, how does one save oneself from this misfortune?
She: (embraces and strokes him) Don't worry, my dear, it won't be like this forever; you know I'm terribly ill, nervous — so why do you have to upset me?
He: All right, no more. (He nestles up to her and wants to doze off. Suddenly a loud knocking is heard at the door; he jumps up like someone scalded and runs off.)
(On the threshold stands her lover; she runs to meet him joyfully with open arms.)
He: I knocked well, eh?
She: Very well! Your knocks frightened even me. (She laughs.) You should have seen how my shlimazl ran — grabbed his trousers and off he went! (Both laugh.)
He: (takes a small bottle of wine out of his pocket and puts it on the table) We drank this wine back then, when we were in Ustroń; today I bought the same one. If you remember, we drank from the bottle, I poured it right into your mouth! Ah, how good that was!
She: As I recall, there was such an ottoman in the boarding house; I lay on it and you[?] knelt beside me, my dear (they strike the same pose).
He: Open your pretty little mouth, and I'll give you wine to drink — the witness of our passionate love.
She: (boldly) Here, pour, my beloved! Tonight I want to get drunk and forget my cheated life (he pours into her mouth; he drinks too; both sing a song).
Scene 3.
The door opens and in come the bailiff and a policeman. "He" and "She" don't notice them. Only when the bailiff calls out her husband's name do they both jump up in fright. He wants to run to the door; the policeman stops him; she stammers helplessly.
She: That is... that's my husband.
Bailiff: (to the policeman) Guard the citizen [obywatel], he has to pay 495 zł. and 18 groszy in taxes!
Policeman: Hands up!
He: But I'm not able to pay so much for... such a... for...
Policeman: No more talk — taxes must be paid!
She: (strokes him) My dear! Calm down, you have to pay, otherwise there'll be a scandal.
He: What are you saying, it's my entire fortune, I don't have any more than that.
She: And me? You love me, don't you?
He: Yes, but I have, after all...
She: I beg you, don't upset me, I'm going to faint (she starts screaming and having spasms).
The policeman searches him and finds the money on him. The bailiff gives him a receipt; she is in spasms; he stands bewildered, holding the receipt in his hand.
(Curtain)
Sh. E.
Thousands of Cannons Thundered at the Announcement of World Peace (Memoirs of a Participant in the Making of Peace on the Western Front)

[History — First World War memoirs, signing of the Treaty of Versailles; series, part 6.]
6.
French mob wants to lynch the German peace delegates.
For almost a month the German delegates worked on the substantive remarks on the peace treaty, which were sent to the chairman of the Peace Congress in Versailles.
On 17 June the German delegation received word that it would be sent the final text of the peace treaty, which it would now have to sign.
That same day the French colonel („polkovnik“), accompanied by an officer, came to the delegation and demanded that the chairman go with them.
The French officer took the German delegate Simons to the Hotel Trianon. There the secretary-general handed over the final text of the peace treaty, giving 3 days for an answer whether it is accepted or not.
The German delegation once again walked out with a protest against such a short deadline, and the secretary-general of the Peace Conference took note of the protest.
Returning to the hotel, the German delegation sat down to consider whether such a harsh treaty could be signed, or whether they should try to consult the central government in Berlin.
At that moment a special courier appeared in the hall of the hotel, sent by the chairman of the Peace Conference, Clemenceau.
The courier brought an ultimatum letter, in which there was a demand that the German delegation give, within the shortest time, an answer whether it signs the Versailles Treaty or not. The deadline was set at 5 days.
Thereupon the chairman of the German delegation declared that he was leaving, together with the other delegates, for the session of the National Assembly in Weimar, where he would present the text of the peace conditions.
Preparations for departure were made very quickly; only the cases with the documents were taken along. The French colonel Agri[?], who was assigned to serve the delegation, sent automobiles to take the German delegation to the railway station at Nevi[?]. There a special train was to take the German delegates to Germany.
Soon, however, a rumour spread that the Germans were going home without signing the peace conditions. By the „Hotel Reservoir“, where the Germans were staying, a large crowd of Frenchmen began to gather. The mob grew more and more incited by agitators and took a threatening attitude towards the delegates, who had already loaded all their belongings onto the automobiles. Not a single policeman was to be seen, not for love or money.
By the hotel the alarmed members of the „League of Patriots“ gathered, and their „fighting squads“ („boyuvkes“) were getting ready for an attack on the German delegation.
The lower officials of the German delegation took their seats in the first automobiles. A second group, with the chairman of the German delegation, Count Brockdorff-Rantzau, left a little later.
As soon as the car with the German foreign minister appeared in the street, the assembled mob fell into a terrible fury; stones were torn from the pavement and hurled at his car. The windows of the automobiles were smashed, and the mob chased the departing automobiles, throwing stones without stop.
The French escorting officers ordered the chauffeurs to drive the cars at full power; at last the cars reached the station and the train left for Germany.
(To be concluded).
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Jewish Parents Demand That Their Children Study in the "Jewish" Public Schools

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday 22 Elul 5692 — 23 September 1932.)
Będzin

Jewish parents demand that their children study in the "Jewish" public (powszechne) schools.
On Saturday night a parents' meeting took place at Public School No. 2, at which, among other things, the question of sending Jewish children to the Christian public schools was discussed.

In this connection the guardians (opiekunowie) of School No. 4, Messrs. Tuchszneider and Wajberman, and on behalf of the parents Mr. Pfefer, called on the school inspector, who promised to settle the question favourably.

On Sunday evening, when the beadle (shammes) of the beth midrash, Mordechai Wajntrepach [?], was closing the gate of the beth midrash, he was attacked from behind by a ruffian, who struck him on the head with a brick.

In Memory of the Fallen Aviators

An End to Malicious Acts.
The new Penal Code, which came into force on 1 September, has introduced a whole series of new concepts concerning crimes, which ought to interest above all the broad public of merchants.
Lately, when bankruptcies multiply from day to day, it has become very much the fashion to transfer businesses and property to other names; the main question is always whether the debtor has not taken precautions so that nothing can be collected from him; quite often it also happens that one already comes with the bailiff [komornik] and nothing can be done; there are even cases where the debtor's shop is packed with goods, and yet the debt cannot be collected from him, because formally he is only a hired man employed by his wife, his mother-in-law or just by a good friend; everyone knows full well that this is a fiction, but by legal means it is hard to prove the fiction.
The new Penal Code will put an end to this abnormal state of affairs.
Under the new law, making such fictions in order not to pay debts will be punished with imprisonment of up to 5 years, regardless of the way in which the debtor protected himself against the creditors. The same penalty applies to transferring property to a stranger's name, staging a fictitious auction, hiding the goods, etc. In order to deter the public in practice from making fictions, the Penal Code lays down a penalty of up to 3 years' imprisonment for helping someone evade paying debts. A penalty thus threatens everyone who takes part in a fictitious auction, as well as the person in whose name the business is registered, etc.

[Olkusz — town council; antisemitism.] At Monday's session of the Olkusz town council it was once again plainly demonstrated that we Jews are only the givers and others the takers...
On the agenda of the session was the approval of the budget for 1932/33 in the sum of 1,537,280 zł. While 10 thousand zł. were being allotted to the Christian orphanage, Councillor Mr. Blum put forward a motion to allot 5 thousand zł. to the Jewish charitable society in Olkusz.
The Polish councillors, wishing to do away with the motion, also put forward a counter-motion to allot 5 thousand zł. to the Christian “Dobroczynność” [Charity].

Councillor Mr. Blum then took the floor, unmasked the true faces of the antisemitic councillors and left the session in protest.
The Jewish councillors also expressed their solidarity with him.
Regional Assembly of “HaNoar HaTsiyoni” in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism; youth movements.] Last Sunday an assembly of the council of the Zagłębie district (galil) of the Zionist youth organization “HaNoar HaTsiyoni” took place in Będzin. Delegates took part from: Sosnowiec, Będzin, Miechów, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie, Częstochowa, Chaszniców[?] [printed “Khashnitse”], Działoszyce, Koszyce, Wiślica, Wolbrom, etc., as well as the delegate of the Central Committee, Mr. Yitzchak Sztajger.
Mr. Buszewski[?] gave a report on the activity to date. From the delegates' reports on their work in the present situation it could be seen that the Zagłębie district numbers over 1500 members, who conduct a ramified activity in the field of education in the spirit of full pioneering (halutziut) and General Zionism.
After the reports a lively discussion developed, in which there took part: Śmietana (Sosnowiec), Brandes (Działoszyce), Gutman (Będzin), Lewit (Miechów), Buszewski (Sosnowiec), and others.
A longer lecture was given by Mr. Yitzchak Sztajger on the ideological foundations of the movement; he outlined the programme of work for the future, in which the necessity of educating our youth in the spirit of one-hundred-percent pioneering was especially stressed.
Finally it was resolved:
a) to unite both districts, of Zagłębie and of Silesia, into one large district under the management of the persons Miss Urbach (Będzin), Buesky [so printed here] (Sosnowiec) and Bitler (Bielsko). The district has been divided into 3 sub-districts with seats in Będzin, Miechów and Bielsko. b) to strengthen pioneering activity in all localities and to create new hachshara (training) points. c) to support with all forces the Tishri campaign for the Keren Kayemet (JNF). d) to strengthen the shekel campaign for 5693, which is utterly neglected and belittled by almost all Zionist parties. e) to begin a large campaign with the aim of activating the Zionist Organization in every town.
With the singing of “HaTikva” the assembly was closed.

Set Himself Up a Flat in the Cemetery

[Gołonóg — miscellany; crime.] In the night from Saturday to Sunday the police in Gołonóg carried out a round-up, in the course of which a search was also made in the local cemetery, where thieves hide.
When the police were in the cemetery they saw light shining out of a grave. How surprised they were when, approaching the spot, they saw a living man sleeping “comfortably” in a dry coffin.
As it turned out, the tenant is a professional beggar, born in Kutno, and having no place to spend the night, he set himself up a flat in the cemetery.
For this purpose he removed a corpse [bar-minan, “far be it from us”] from a large coffin, laid hay and straw in it, and did not have to pay any rent...
The “tenant” of the strange flat has been handed over to the investigating authorities.

„Hakoach“ — „Zagłębianka“ 1:4
After the victories that „Hakoach“ [Będzin] won last week in Radomsko, the Jewish sporting public in Zagłębie awaited their appearance in Będzin with great interest.
But the numerous public was greatly surprised by the Saturday match; such weak play had not yet been seen from „Hakoach“ this year. The forward line hardly existed on the field, and weakest of all was the defence (except Nunberg in goal). The defence of „Hakoach“ has lately been in very weak form, and by its play it created very many critical moments in front of its own goal.
„Zagłębianka“ kicks off and sets a very sharp pace, and owing to the weak play of „Hakoach“ has a slight advantage in the first 15 minutes. Already in the 2nd minute „Zagłębianka“ has a „corner“, which it does not use. „Zagłębianka“ is constantly at the „Hakoach“ goal, but does not exploit its advantage because of the poor shots its forwards aimed at the Hakoach goal. During this time „Zagłębianka“ failed to use as many as 5 „corners“.
In the 20th minute „Zagłębianka“ scores the first goal from a free kick.
„Hakoach“ carries out a fine attack, and Richter, who has a good chance to equalise, shoots it out.
For a „foul“ in the „penalty area“ the referee awards an „eleven-metre“ [penalty] to „Zagłębianka“, which it converts into a goal. „Zagłębianka“ leads 2:0.
After half-time „Zagłębianka“ scores 2 more goals within 10 minutes. From now on „Hakoach“ has a slight advantage. For a hand in the penalty area the referee awards an „eleven-metre“ to „Hakoach“, which Gutman converts into a sure goal. Because of an insult the referee sends off a player of „Zagłębianka“. The latter refuses to submit to the decision, on account of which the referee is forced to break off the match; this conduct of the „Zagłębianka“ player deserves strong condemnation.
„Hakoach“ — „Policyjni“ 4:0
The next day, Sunday, „Hakoach“ played a friendly match with the „Police Club“ and won by the high score of 4:0. One simply could not believe one's own eyes that this was the same „Hakoach“ that a day earlier had managed to lose so shamefully to a much weaker team. The „Hakoach“ forward line fulfilled its task properly; the defence, on the other hand, again played very weakly, and only thanks to Nunberg in goal, who was in good form that day and kept goal very finely, did „Policyjni“ fail to score a single goal.
„Hakoach“ kicks off and at once carries out several fine attacks on the opponents' goal. In the 20th minute Gutman succeeds in scoring the first goal. „Hakoach“ again has a slight advantage and the forwards fail to use many important moments; „Policyjni“, with the help of its right wing, several times brings the ball to the „Hakoach“ goal, but Nunberg in goal is on guard.
After half-time „Hakoach“ has a strong advantage, and Gutman scores the second with a „header“ [główka]. The third and finest goal of the day is scored by Beril Szyjek. „Hakoach“ carries out several more attacks, and from one such attack Kalman scores the fourth goal. Referee Moszkowicz — good.
