Have They Nothing to Say?

(What we call a crisis. — Unemployment and the Jewish element. — The "machers" [fixers] and our institutions.)
Whatever one touches, whatever question one wishes to deal with, one always bumps into the painful wound that has lasted so long already, that has already entered the phase of a chronic illness and that people have grown so used to calling by the common, shortened name: crisis.
Under the common name "crisis" we understand all our pains and aches, all our sufferings and ailments. If there is a crisis, if a standstill reigns in economic life, then who suffers from it as much as we Jews — both as the most mobile element in the economic-financial field on the one hand, and as Jews on the other.
Granted, when times were still normal, when the general situation in the country was a bearable, a normal one, when the struggle for existence made its way[?] on possible and normal foundations, the Jewish citizen too held his own alongside the great machine, thanks to his agility and understanding in this field, thanks to his quick orientation and competitiveness.
Now, the moment the great machine has stopped, the moment other living conditions have set in in the country, it is self-evident that it is first and foremost we Jews who suffer from it; for if we in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia lived around the factories, ironworks and coal mines, if we drew our hard little bit of livelihood from their workers and officials, this has now become a fantasy, for who could live as before from this element, which is mostly unemployed? And those who do work, those who have not yet been laid off, have such earnings that they are left only to buy the very most necessary, the very most urgent — so who can profit from them as before? It is therefore self-evident that the Jew suffers most here, that we here are the most tormented.
True, those who are unemployed, the workers who have no employment, have it bitter, and it is truly sad to see the state they are in; nevertheless they are better off than the Jew in that their civic obligations do not reach the measure that ours, the Jews', do.
The worker or factory official, if he earns hardly anything, is free of the great number of taxes that the Jew pays. Whoever has the smallest little shop, even if he takes in nothing, must keep paying all sorts of taxes, both new ones and arrears, from which he can never free himself.
They live[?], after all, in quite different conditions, so that as soon as they have no employment they can cut their expenses down to a minimum; for while the Jew living in town keeps bearing his rent expenses, the worker or official lives next to the factory, where the flat costs him nothing and where he also has a bit of field or garden, from which, incidentally, he also has a little livelihood. The Jew, however, cannot even dream of such economic notions: in town he must buy both the biggest and the smallest products; nor can he close the shop and stop declaring the "patent" [annual trade licence], even if he could catch up on a good sleep in his shop every single day.
So we live in entirely different conditions, in which we cannot cut any of our expenses. On top of that, the tax question does not get any smaller, because in the [tax] offices[?] we still make quite tidy turnovers, and our incomes are of course colossal. There is a sign, after all: the patent is bought and the shop is open every day.
Now that the Day of Judgment below has drawn near, one truly trembles far more than before the Day of Judgment above.
Besides all this, there are whole ranks of institutions that care for easing the living conditions of the working element and the officials — something that for us Jews is out of the question. The Jewish shopkeeper and artisan — he may be without employment, he may wander about without a scrap of work, his workshop may rust, he may starve in the true sense of the word — the bailiff (executor) demands his due from him, and if he has nothing to pay with, be the poverty at the very highest degree, they take away his machine or his workshop, if they have not already seized it once before.
Yes, on top of that antisemitism rages in all its length and breadth: for instance, a quiet and open[?] boycott agitation is carried on everywhere, that now that the school season has begun a Christian should not buy any book from a Jewish bookseller — at a time when Jewish children are not ashamed to go into the Christian bookseller. When the Christian comes from the village into town for whatever book, he looks the bookshop over carefully and checks whether he has not by chance fallen in with a Jew. One sees[?] that in the village he has been agitated and taught to go only "do swego" [Polish "to one's own" — the boycott slogan].
And we — what do we do in the face of this hard situation in which we find ourselves? What do our communal activists and professional institutions do to ease our enormously hard living conditions, in which we have now been living for such a long time?
Yes, we have all sorts of institutions that are supposed to see to improving our situation: the merchant has his "Merchants' Association", the shopkeeper — his Small Traders' Association, and the artisan — his Artisans' Associations, which all together do nothing; at best one can get a petition (prośba) written there — something the "machers", who nowadays multiply at every step, now do far more successfully. Do we then also have communal institutions in which the Jew has, nonetheless, more trust? May one really remain as indifferent to the members as the said institutions have managed to be, whose only merit is perhaps[?] that they have produced from among themselves a sufficient number of machers? Unfortunately we see no other activity there. We see nothing at all with which these institutions might come to the rescue, ease the members' need, reduce the citizens' taxes.
Had these institutions been set up on normal foundations, on a firm basis, would they then have cut such a figure both with the members and with the authorities? Could they not have achieved much, much in the interests of the citizens? And so, so the citizens were misled by their associations: for at the time when the member was sure that his association was doing something to improve his situation, to reduce his tax, it did nothing for it, and thanks to that a sizable amount of tax arrears piled up with everyone, for which they are now seizing his cupboard [shop fittings]. Is that not a responsibility? Does it not mean that the communal institutions have, with their own hands, helped aggravate the already hard enough situation of the average citizen, who believed so much in the power of society, in the power of his association and in the power of his representation?
Are our communal institutions then entirely in order, when they see[?] what their activity has helped bring about, and in the present hard situation they stand like helpless statues with folded hands and do not see in which direction everything has been turned? Have they really nothing at all to say to anyone and nothing at all to do?
R. Lem.
For Great Is the Day of Judgment... (A Political Letter)

[Political letter — Rosh Hashana 5693; the world economic crisis.]
To my dear friend, our teacher R' Shlomo, may his light shine!
If the nations of the world had listened to me, they would have had to stand up together with us and pray now for a good new year... For, in fact, we pray for a good new year, and at the same time we draw up a balance of the past year...
Only in these last years will others, too, understand us and feel with us... After all, they could never understand why we weep on Rosh Hashana... Very well, on Yom Kippur we pray for the forgiveness of sins, but Rosh Hashana — what have tears to do with it? With them, on the contrary, people rejoice when the new year arrives..
Now, I believe, they will understand us... For there is something to shed tears over... We bewail the past year and pray with bitter tears that the coming year should at least not be worse than the past one...
For great is the Day of Judgment..
And greater still is the fear for the fate of mankind, when you begin to reflect on all the troubles that have encircled us, both as Jews and as human beings...
As is the way of the world, on the eve of the New Year one looks around: how things stand in the world, where it is heading... But how should we now be accustomed to look around? It is a superfluous thing. Everyone knows well, feels well, how bad things are around us and around the whole world...
For great is the Day of Judgment...
And if in all previous years we used to draw up a balance before Rosh Hashana, listing precisely the most important events in Jewish life and dwelling above all on the specifically Jewish calamities and troubles throughout the world, now it is superfluous to do so... For the latest troubles make one forget the earlier ones. The latest trouble — the economic world crisis — outweighs all other misfortunes.. On the contrary, one has the impression that on the antisemitic front it has become somewhat quieter, at least in the last weeks, but the consequences of the crisis are all the more terrible...
What does the liturgical poet say? "And the stone shall cry out from the wall in judgment, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it in judgment"... Even the stones cry out... Not only does man now go about worried, darkened, despairing, carrying on himself the heavy burden of troubles — even the stones, dead nature, weep too over the destruction of the world...
For is there now, my friend, a single little corner in the world where man does not suffer from the plague of the crisis?
From all ends of the world come, day after day, terrible reports about the economic crisis; heart-rending news reaches us of cruel unemployment. Also from Argentina, Germany, England, Canada, Mexico, Brazil, Egypt, Japan, etc. And we in Poland are, of course, no exception either... Like a rope, it tightens around the neck of the world, ever narrower, and it seems that at any moment the whole world will be strangled, without even managing[?] to say its last confession...
And for this reason, my friend, I say that never yet have the nations of the world hit the mark as they do now, when they stand together with us and pray to God for better times...
"And of the countries it shall be said on it"... Yes, wrath has been poured out on all countries, the end of which nobody can yet see... Some scholars even try to console themselves with certain theories about "laws of crises"... They want to prove that the crisis must come to an end — would that it were so! Master of the Universe, the sooner the better; but for the time being it is getting sharper, and where does one find the strength to endure it?
And great is the calamity of the crisis, worse even than famine; for in time of famine, God forbid, bread used to be sent to the stricken countries from those places that had not suffered from famine, but now the whole world is seized by the crisis as by a hellish fire...
For great is the Day of Judgment...
A terrible Day of Judgment is passing over the world. Man, who for years has sinned against the Divine and also against his own fellow men, must pay for his sins... A time is coming of reckoning for all the deeds of delusion that men have committed, trampling underfoot all divine and human laws of compassion, honesty, justice and truth.. And this very Day of Judgment arrives with a great noise... And happy is the people that will come out acquitted in judgment.
Yes, my friend, mankind is now writhing in convulsions, like a dangerously sick man, like one in his death throes, God forbid, and the expert professors stand around the bed and argue over the causes of the weakness... One blames progress, mechanisation, which pushes thousands of workers out of their positions; a second explains it by accidental causes; a third by causes of an individual character in each country... In short — the patient is not relieved by it...
And when we say today in our prayers "And of the countries it shall be said on it: which for the sword and which for peace, which for famine and which for plenty", we really mean the crisis, for because of hunger and unemployment wars often break out, and conversely, plenty is a shield against war...
And we want to and must pray, especially this year, not only for ourselves but for the whole world.
"And may they all form one band" — help, Master of the Universe, the whole world... Let things become good not only with us but also in America... If it is good in Poland, the German Jews will benefit too; if the situation improves in Argentina, the Romanian[?] Jews will feel it too; if we live better, we will come to the aid of the Jews of other countries... If everyone lives well — how good that is.
And likewise concerning all people...
One great misfortune has struck the whole world, and all must pray for the annulment of the decree[?]...
Let us hope that the coming year will not be a year of drought (5692), but a year of gathering strength, material and spiritual, for the good of the Jews and of all mankind.
A. M.
From Year to Year

A short survey of Jewish social life in the year 5692 [1931/32] in Zagłębie.
5692.
A year of shadow in Jewish social life. The departing year has convinced us once again that in Jewish life in Zagłębie our traditional bottom line still comes out — a great social deficit.
Kehilla.
In first place stand the Jewish kehillas in Zagłębie, which cannot come forward with their balance sheets and show that they accomplished anything during the whole year; nothing positive was done in any field whatsoever.
The only work that those at the helm of the Będzin kehilla had was to drive the "harmful" elements out of the kehilla, and to see to it that the representation elected in 1931 — should not come to power. All these machinations caused the authority of the kehilla to be dragged down; lawlessness reigns along the entire front, "every man does what is right in his own eyes" — whatever one wants, he does, because from the "little seeds" that the Aguda [Agudas Yisroel] has sown no healthy growths can come up.
A great "asset" is shown us by the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec. There the "retreat" is even greater. After 16 months of quarrels, brawls and desecration of God's name they are still at Genesis... only now are they thinking about when the electoral commission should be set up for the new:
— kehilla elections...
An exception in this field — is the kehilla in Dąbrowa. What elsewhere was "treyf" became in Dąbrowa, with help "from above":
— kosher...
The newly elected kehilla rulers have received the government.
City Council.
"Habit is second nature" — when the city councils in Będzin and in Sosnowiec were dissolved, "those in the know" proved that within a few months there must take place
— elections to the city council.
"Practice," however, has proved otherwise. Two years have already passed and there is no end to the rule of the commissarial councils.
The administration of the municipalities is run according to the will of the commissioners. The "remnant" of the Jewish councillors wail out an opposition, but it is "a voice of crying in the camp": no one listens to their words, to their protests, and it stays just so
— as the commissioner wants...
One of the greatest injustices that the municipality, together with the "Dozór Szkolny" [school board], has committed against the broad Jewish masses is:
— the school system.
For several years now the "Dozór Szkolny" has been striving continuously to give a different form to the "Jewish" character, so to speak, of the powszechna [public elementary] schools.
They began with Christian teachers, and today it has already come to Jewish and Christian children studying together.
The "opposition"[?] has been very successful: first of all they abolished the premises for Jewish children in the town and gave everyone a single place — "and they all became one band"... and if the premises cannot take in all the Jewish children — open to them are the doors of:
— the Christian schools.
The economic situation.
The process of decline of Jewish trade grew even stronger this year.
The tax screw, which has been pressing on the Jewish population since Grabski's times, squeezed even harder this year. It has gone so far that Jewish firms and Jewish merchants have come down in the world, long-established businesses have gone under, the number of empty shops is great, and those that still hold on have had to go bankrupt.
The most striking proof of poverty is the great number of recipients who this year applied for maos-khitim [Passover relief].
Unemployment has grown from day to day, workshops are closing, Jewish artisans go about without a stitch of work, and the Jewish masses are reduced to starving.
Culture and education.
In this field absolutely nothing at all was done. There were only countless badge sales, ostensibly for "cultural purposes," but there is nothing positive to show.
Shul-Kult wanted to "compete" with YSHO [the Yiddish secular school organisation], held several meetings, collected a fund, but the work stayed standing in the same place as YSHO, and no school was founded.
In one respect there was a lively season. This year the number of "homespun" "dramatic sections" multiplied. Each section has its "board of directors" and impresarios, and since there is no shortage of societies and associations among us, hardly a week went by without some "hit play" being staged...
In the institutions.
Never before have the institutions found themselves in such a difficult state as this year.
In the merchants' institutions the crisis became even more entrenched this year. No signs of activity show. To blame in great measure are the members themselves, who regard the associations merely as a "clinic" [lecznica], to which one turns in a time of trouble for "medical advice"...
The philanthropic societies are in their death throes, because the first economic savings are made at the expense of the charitable institutions. The subsidies from the municipality are being shrunk, and the monthly payments have also been reduced.
Nevertheless we see that with goodwill and earnest devotion great deeds can be done. This was shown by the opening of the "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home] in Sosnowiec, the splendid building, which was built thanks to the energy of a few quiet communal workers.
A gladdening chapter will also be the dedication of the orphanage in Będzin. Here too, thanks to several philanthropists, they succeeded in bringing the building to this stage. For the time being one part is being opened. The "face" of the house still has the form of a skeleton, but it is to be hoped that the strength of the Będzin Jewish community will help the building soon to receive its true form...
Sport.
The Jewish sports movement has grown stronger, both in quantity and in quality; new sports clubs have arisen, whose main aim is — football.
We had hoped that in the end the sport of football was a passing phenomenon, especially [among] the Jewish public. The "wise and understanding people" would gradually shake off this game of chance, but we were mistaken: football has become a cult, a holy thing, and every match has more chance of success than the greatest artistic performance...
— — —
The overall total is, as we see, apart from small exceptions, very negative; but nevertheless we hope and believe that in the new year a better economic conjuncture will come, and only then will the great creative power of the folk-rooted Jewish Zagłębie reveal itself.
Bankruptcy (A Short Feuilleton)

(A short feuilleton)
I don't know why the doctors have not included in their lexicon, among the contagious diseases, the disease called bankruptcy as well.
It seems that no illness is as infectious as bankruptcy.
This malady spreads, after all, as fast as the rays of the sun reach us.
Only a few years ago symptoms of the disease began to show on Modrzejowska Street in Sosnowiec, and in Będzin on Kołłątaja Street, on Warsaw's Nalewki, on Łódź's Piotrkowska — and now it has already reached the very summit of the globe, the League of Nations. All the newspaper headlines are [?] now saying that "the League of Nations is bankrupt."
Don't think this is mere rhetoric — it is plain bankruptcy, with all the bells and whistles.
The League of Nations used to do favours; as a rich man does for his [?] poor relative, it used to endorse bills of exchange for states.
With such a favour-bill a state used to get money; such a bill could be discounted at a quite small rate of interest — is the League of Nations a trifle? It means the whole world, in person, has put its name on the left [back] side of the bill — can there be a better guarantee?
Who could have expected that even the mighty League of Nations would go bust and be unable to pay up on an endorsement?
One might as well take the "Szmargal" [?] and hand it over to the enforcement apparatus of the Dąbrowa "Kupiecki" bank [Merchants' Bank]...
What indeed will the League of Nations do if a bailiff (komornik) comes and seizes the pair of tables with the armchairs at which the foreign ministers of the whole world sit?
Finished with the League of Nations, finished with peace conferences, finished with disarmaments, finished with treaties, finished with political swindles.
Even with the pair of tables, the League of Nations was already a customer of the burial society: Germany says that to make cannons it needs nobody's consent, and the rulers of the Far East even claim that they begrudge the expense of travelling so far to the sessions...
So the creditors, poor things, have landed in a nasty mess. Now they know that the endorsement is worth nothing; the League has neither the say nor the means — it is merely a round rubber stamp, carrying as much weight as the stamp of a "Linat ha-Holim" society in Pogoń...
Yosef.
A Good New Year with All the Bells and Whistles!...

Pini Ba'al Lashon.
It is hard, very hard nowadays to say a new word in honour of a new year, my dear friends.
For ever since years have been turning over among us, we have already said plenty to them, just like that, into the years; and... they go their own way!
And yet, how can we Jews let go of an old, worn-out year that is already breathing its last breath and departing into eternity — without any funeral and without any eulogy? And how can we let in a new, young, fresh and lively year that is coming to us with pomp and charm — without any reception and without any greeting?
True, the world has persuaded itself that a year is really nothing.
No more than this: the globe has turned with us yet again some three hundred and sixty-five times.
Nevertheless we see that when these three hundred and sixty-five "circuits" come to an end, all people put down a full stop and reflect for a moment: ah, a year gone!
A year, then, is really nothing; but a normal person does not want to give up these nothings on any account.
On the contrary, everyone wants these nothings to be as many as possible, and as beautiful and good as possible!
But even granting that among other nations a year really is nothing — for us, our dear little brethren the children of Israel, a year is already a very long time.
All nations simply live through the year, sometimes better, sometimes worse; our people, however, you understand me, "drags itself through" the year in torment!
And not for nothing do we call it "tekufat ha-shanah", the turning-over of the year. And oh, my friends, what it takes before a year turns over with us!
Who else, like us [?], knows so well the true meaning of it;
The Jewish people knows what it means to turn and twist. Our people does not simply live just like that; neither do they let it, nor can it do so by itself. It must keep turning. It keeps turning constantly. In the world, with the world, for the sake of the world, and — in spite of the world!
And that is precisely why "tekufat ha-shanah" has a quite different meaning for us.
And that is precisely why we have also made the New Year a quite different sort of holiday, and we greet it in a quite different way.
Despite the fact that we are almost the merriest people in the world, at the beginning of the New Year we are very serious.
All the nations of the world greet their New Year with revelry, gorging and boozing.
And we greet our New Year with repentance, prayer and charity.
They make noise and we make noise too; but what a difference!
They make noise with drums and trumpets, fire bullets, break bottles, "smash teakettles".
And we make noise with the shofar — tekiah, shevarim, teruah — to confound Satan the destroyer, to awaken hearts, to elevate human thought.
And then we pray not only for ourselves, selfishly, but also for all of mankind, that "all creatures of the world shall become one band, and the rule of violence shall vanish from the earth, and all the inhabitants of the world shall be illumined with divine beauty."
In short, both our reckoning of the year lived through and our greeting of the coming year are entirely different.
A year with us is quite a long period. What we live through in one year, others do not live through in a whole jubilee.
And therefore, my dear tormented Jews, with us, when an old year departs, we see it off with groans and sighs. And our New Year we [printed: "mi"] always receive with awe and with fear and with prayer.
But one thing we possess that others do not — and that is hope!
This little bit of hope of ours gives [?] us at once courage and strength, and we remain again a cheerful people that laughs off all its troubles.
In this no nation in the world can compare with us.
A new year — and new hopes, new prospects, new plans and new dreams.
We never live with the "present", only with the "future". The "now" we dismiss at once if we don't like it, and we already look to the "later".
Our life consists of dreams and strivings — and dreams and strivings are, after all, always bound up not with the present moment but with the coming one.
And so a year goes and a year comes, and we groan and sigh, lament and weep — and we hope again, and we laugh off everything that was, and again we are a lively, cheerful people.
And that, perhaps, is indeed the the secret of our vitality.
And therefore, my dear exhausted Jews, let us take leave of the old, lived-out year 5692, and let us give it a fine funeral and deliver a fine eulogy: that "it could have been even worse, and thanks to it for not having been"... (never mind — with us they give fine funerals and eulogies to commoner persons too!) And let us send it off to its eternal rest and wish ourselves that ones like it should never come back again!
And for the new, young, fresh and lively year, let us hold our fine Rosh Hashanah banquet and tell it in harsh words:
— Listen here, you young 5693, you are coming to us and no doubt want us to love you and praise you — then keep up to standard! Send the crisis with all its troubles and terrors away at once, so that not a trace of them remains, and bring with you the true bundle of plenty and success, and indeed a little truth and justice too for the whole [printed: "garer"] world, and for [?] us as well, and may everyone be utterly satisfied with you!
In short: a good New Year with all the bells and whistles!...
In Honour of Rosh Hashanah.

Torah sayings and anecdotes
Collected and styled by Yehuda.

a) Rosh Hashanah, Satan and Esau.
"On Rosh Hashanah Satan comes before the Holy One, blessed be He, and brings the sins of Israel. The Holy One, blessed be He, takes the sins of Israel and places them upon the guardian angel of Esau. The angel says: What strength have I, that I should bear all these sins?" — Midrash Rabbah.
People want to load all the Jewish sins onto Esau. He is to blame for everything; it was from him that the Jews learned all this evil — "They mingled with the nations and learned their deeds." But when they come to him on Rosh Hashanah with the bundle of Jewish sins, he cries out: "What strength have I, that I should bear all these sins?" Why do you throw all the Jewish sins onto me? After all, among them there are such as baseless hatred, insolence and the like, which are not found with me at all — those I, if anything, learned from them, from the Jews.
— Rabbi Yehonatan Eybeschütz.

b) Without God's seal.
"Three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah. The completely righteous are inscribed and sealed at once for life. The completely wicked are inscribed and sealed at once for death. The intermediate ones are held in suspense: if they merit it, they are inscribed for life, etc." — so says the Gemara.
The question arises: why is it said of the completely wicked and the completely righteous "inscribed and sealed," while of the intermediate ones, if they "merit it," only "inscribed for life," without "sealed"?
But the intermediate ones are, after all, dealt with in loving-kindness — "abounding in kindness: [He inclines] towards kindness." The intermediate are those who have half merits and half sins; well, one allows oneself to give a little push to the pointer of the scales towards the right while Satan is looking the other way... So they win only through God's kindness and not through truth, and "the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth." It follows that if they merit it, there can be no seal of God — "truth" — upon it; therefore the "sealed" is missing...
— Yerach la-Mo'adim.

c) The vowel points.
In the liturgical poem there is the expression: "And today three books are opened, pointed [with vowels]." Why pointed?
Because the intermediate ones are written down as "lechaim" (for life) without vowel points; only if they "merit it" is the lamed of "lechaim" later pointed with a sheva, which means: to life; but if they "do not merit it," the lamed is pointed with a patach, which means: to not-life (see Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, §582, subsection 5, in the Magen Avraham there). So everything depends on how the word is pointed, and on the vowel points depends a person's life..
— Ya'arot Devash.

d) Measure for measure.
"When there is no advocate to plead for us against the accuser of sin, declare to Jacob the word of statute and judgement."
And if there is nothing with which to defend the sinner, we argue before the Master of the Universe: "Declare to Jacob the word of statute and judgement" — settle accounts with us measure for measure: we too perform many commandments for which we know no reason or sense whatever; so You may also forgive us without reason or sense...
— Shemen ha-Mor.

e) A cantor without a word...
To the Rabbi of Liska, Rabbi Tzvi Hirsh (author of the book "Ha-Yashar veha-Tov"), once came the following case for a rabbinical court:
A Jew, a cantor, had hired himself out to lead the prayers in a village. Then a second village came and hired him away — they gave him more money. The village Jews of the first village summon him to Liska for a din Torah. The cantor argues that they have no claim on him at all: he had only given them his word, nothing more...
"Well," says Rabbi Tzvi Hersh, "if you gave your word, your speech, in the first village, then how will you be able to pray in the second?... Will you pray without speech?..."

f) Inscribe us in the book of livelihood and sustenance.
At the house of the author of "Toldot Yaakov Yosef," a Hasid, while saying "Our Father, our King, inscribe us in the book of livelihood and sustenance," sighs piously:
"Well, we ourselves are to blame, after all. 'I have corrupted my deeds and forfeited my livelihood' (Kiddushin 14 [Mishnah 4:14]). Because one is not pious, there is no livelihood."
"Yes," answers the "Toldot," "the Tanna stresses 'I have corrupted my deeds,' and you stress 'forfeited my livelihood'... You are sighing over the latter, and the Tanna means the former..."

g) Between God and the wealthy.
"They shall exalt You in the congregation of the people, and those far off shall hear and come and give You the crown of kingship" (in the liturgical poem "Ve-ye'etayu").
A rich man does not want people to praise him as a good man, a giver of charity: he is afraid that people will come running to him from all sides.
God, however, does want to be praised as such. On the contrary: "those far off shall hear and come" — let people come from all sides...
— Or ha-Me'or.

h) What they mean...
"But if he survives a day or two days, he shall not be avenged, for he is his money" (Exodus 21) [printed: "a day in days"].
When Jews stand and press God hard for "a day or two days" during the Days of Awe — "for it is his money": all they mean is money, nothing more..
— Rabbi Mendele of Dynów.

• • •

At Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce's, a Hasid led the Rosh Hashanah prayers before the lectern. When he came to the liturgical poem "These and those with order arrange, these and those with song break forth," etc., he got somewhat tangled up in the Hebrew. Rabbi Naftali shouts at him:
"Why do you babble so much: 'with song break forth,' 'with order arrange'? Out with it plainly: Master of the Universe, give money..."

i) "If he repents at once, You accept him."
Rosh Hashanah is the season of repentance, and in season people snatch up all kinds of goods and are not very particular whether they are not sometimes defective...
— Eser Nifla'ot (before the Rebbe of Warka).
With a Full Mouth — Remarks on the Eve of Rosh Hashana

[Feuilleton — remarks for the eve of Rosh Hashana.] May you be inscribed for a good year. This is a heartfelt wish, short and sharp, but not on the "tip of the tongue" — only with a full mouth.
• • •
Melekh elyon and melekh evyon [the Supreme King and the beggar-king]. Many former "melekh elyons", people who stood at the very top, became "melekh evyons" in the past year — great paupers.
• • •
Once people used to say "melekh evyon" quietly; today there are former rich men who have come to such a pass that they are not ashamed to cry it out about themselves aloud.
• • •
Once "Hineni he-ani" ["Here I am, poor in deeds"] was a prayer for cantors only; today many former rich men can say it.
• • •
When eating a ram's head or a fish head on the night of Rosh Hashana we say: "May it be Thy will that we be at the head." Many believe that they have brought this about, and proclaim themselves heads, leaders and providers for the community.
• • •
Kings. Kings have been dwindling in the world in recent years; in the past year a few more were deposed — it is possible that "and Thou alone, O Lord, shalt reign" is drawing near. But for the time being we must still pray hard for it, because dictators are no better for us Jews than kings, and in some particulars even worse.
• • •
Happy is the people that knows the trumpet-blast — because this is the people that can trumpet, that can make a din, raise a "and they cried out". Yes, thank God, we can do that; but what is the use, if we are heard like the tomcat?
• • •
"But repentance, prayer and charity avert the evil decree." The three words "repentance", "prayer" and "charity" are interpreted as "fasting, voice, money" — that is: fasting, praying and giving charity. All three words add up to one and the same number — one hundred and thirty-six. This means, then, that fasting, praying and giving charity stand on one level. But there are Jews who hold by the first two and not by the last. They will fast, pray and "gulp down" plenty of mahzor, but give "charity" — that, no.
• • •
This Rosh Hashana, it seems, people will pray with fervour, with ardour; the thermometer, they say, shows ninety-eight.
—o—
On the Military Tax.
[Taxes — military tax.] The military tax was introduced under the law of 23.5.1924, amended by the decree of the President of the State of 29.XI.1930, and implemented on the basis of the regulation of the Council of Ministers of 24.8.31 (Dz. U. 89).
The regulations provide for a basic tax and a surtax on the income tax. The former amounts to 10 zł a year for reservists and for those exempted under art. 38E of the law of 1924; 15 zł a year — for those exempted on the basis of art. 38D of the said law; and 20 zł — art. 38C.
Exempt from the tax are only those who are maintained by the self-government bodies or by philanthropic institutions, or who are unable to work.
The tax is paid up to the age of 40 by reservists and by those exempted under art. 38E; — up to 50 by all others.
The basic tax is collected by the self-government bodies; the surtax on the income tax — by the Treasury (Skarb).
Payment orders (nakazy) are sent out by 15.X each year; the tax is payable on 1 November (listopad).
Appeals against the assessment of the basic tax are lodged with the voivodeship offices (time limit 14 days) through the communal offices. Appeals against the surtax — with the Treasury Chambers (Izba Skarbowa) (time limit 30 days) through the tax offices (urzędy skarbowe).
Splitting into instalments, deferment of the payment date and remission belong:
a) for the surtax — to the Minister of the Treasury.
b) for the basic tax — to the self-government offices.
The law does not provide for any limitation (przedawnienie) of the tax.
R.
Forgive Me!...

[Satirical feuilleton — asking forgiveness for the Days of Awe.] Listen, my dear communal workers, nag-riders, do-gooders, parnasim, town councillors, dozors [members of the kehilla board], presidents of every kind and in general all sorts of busybody "cooking-ladles"!
Since it is known to me that you bear me a grudge, that it annoys you greatly that for a whole year I have roused, woken, pricked and pinched you with my pen; and since you are, after all, not just any old nobodies but elected personalities, bigwigs, real "knackers"; and since moreover it is now the time of the Days of Awe, when not only you and I but even a fish in the water trembles — I have therefore decided to ask your forgiveness. What has been shall be no more! I forgive you, you forgive me, and may we have prayed for ourselves a good year!
Forgive me!
Forgive me, Panie "Mehikha Teisi" ["whence would it come"], you are a town councillor — may we have a better year! I have nothing against you. The sessions, by the way [?], which take place, what is done there and how the magistrate in general carries out your decisions, this way or that — as long as we have a "town council" and you are the ones there who "have a say". So what do you think, Panie "Mehikha Teisi", wouldn't it be better if you — may we have a good year — spat on the whole business and simply sat at home?...
Forgive me, Reb Bim-Bam! You are a dozor — truly, a gem! Upon my word, how I regret ever having thrown a word at you!... With such a "head" and such "humanity" as you possess, you could, upon my life, have been not only this year in the holy community of Będzin, but even something bigger, and somewhere else... But since the Będzin kehilla has been privileged to have you — may we all have a better year than you look in the eyes of all of us; but how are you to blame, poor thing, Reb Bim-Bam! Every kehilla has the dozors it deserves!...
Forgive me, Panie Ku-Ku, for having passed over in silence your activity in the society! I know it annoys you that I did not write at length about you, and about your "tireless, hard and self-sacrificing work", which has already saved more than one member from .. which — do you know from what? I also know that the members are so pleased with you that they actually take pity on you and beg you to sit and rest at home. But your shepherd's heart does not let you leave the little sheep without such a guardian as you are. I know all this very well, so do forgive me, Panie Ku-Ku, for having kept silent about it all! Rest assured, God willing, I will yet make you famous!...
Forgive me, Panie Pif-Paf, for having entirely overlooked your synagogue activities! A man like you, who still needs to go to heder himself and nevertheless runs a synagogue, truly deserves to be immortalized in history. But I could not do it, because I don't know how one does that in your language... So do forgive me for that, and at the same time perhaps you would forgo and worry less about the Talmud Torah children! Upon my life, it would be healthier for you, Panie Pif-Paf, and better for them!
Forgive me, Panie Pepper-Snake: if I ever picked on you, it was not my fault; I simply had no time to busy myself with you alone. With you, I admit, I should have taken more trouble, since after all you are a bigwig, a crooked person. Emigration.

Never before has the problem of emigration among the Jewish masses been as burning as it is today, because never before have want and despair looked so pitilessly, so terrifyingly and so brazenly into the eyes of almost the entire Jewish community (kibbutz) in Poland. The sources of livelihood are being stopped up from day to day; all possibilities of existence are being undermined — according to a well-worked-out strategy — and one can state with certainty that ninety percent of the Jewish population in Poland are without a livelihood. There has therefore arisen a declassed element many millions strong, which is spat out of the bourgeois sphere while the proletarian one does not want to take it in. A tragic situation has been created, in which it is impossible to discern even one single ray of light on the leaden-heavy, dark horizon.
The middle class is being consumed by the tax press, and it is not enough that the ruling factors do not care where it is to draw its income from — on the contrary, the ground is torn out[?] from under its feet and everything is done to ruin it; our working intelligentsia is not admitted to any state or municipal post, and our workers are not taken on in any factories.
True, there are a few fawning little Jews (ma-yafis) who want to persuade the world that this is not a purely specifically Jewish phenomenon, but one would have to be blind not to see that Jewish livelihoods are being taken away without any why or wherefore.
It is therefore no wonder that the word emigration has become the magic spell of millions, the one and only hope of tearing oneself out of a vegetating condition that is neither life nor death, in order to pass over to a normal way of life.
But where to emigrate?
Almost all the countries of the whole world have firmly shut their gates to emigration, and there is no prospect whatsoever that they will be reopened in the near future. Erets Yisrael, because of the prevailing conditions, is not able to still the colossal hunger for emigration; so there remain a few countries in Central and South America. Among us, however, complete ignorance reigns, an absolute neglect of the matter of emigration.
It very often happens that people gather together their last bit of property and emigrate to a country in Central or South America, and on arriving there they cannot by any means settle in, for climatic, social and other reasons. That is because the emigrant had not been well informed beforehand about the conditions there. The result is that whoever has money for expenses comes back and falls into even greater despair, and whoever does not have money for expenses remains exposed to the “mercy” of the half-savage population.
Therefore advisory offices for emigration matters must without fail be set up in the larger Jewish centres, where everyone will be able to get information from experts, specialists in the field — about everything that concerns the country in question to which one wants to emigrate. Every emigration candidate must get a clear picture of the geographical and ethnographic situation, of the climatic, social and political conditions prevailing there, etc. Only then is there a certain guarantee that whoever decides to emigrate will settle in somehow and will not be disappointed.
Emigration, however, by no means signifies resignation; it does not mean that we renounce our rights here. The struggle for our existence, for our right to work, must be taken up at a stepped-up tempo. Only this struggle, in parallel with a well-organized emigration, gives hope that it will be possible to tear Polish Jewry out of the extraordinarily desperate situation in which it finds itself today.
S. Rozenberg.
The Main Causes of a Bad Family Life.

— Who is to blame for so many family lives being broken?
This very question was raised at the congress of scientists held recently in New York.
At the last session Dr. Paul Popenoe read a rather long document on the marriage question.
This scientist is connected with the Institute of Family Research in Los Angeles. There, over a long period, many cases of bad, unsuccessful family lives were recorded and investigated.
There are three main causes that make family lives get torn apart. First, the inability to live together like two good friends — the quarrelling; second, bad housekeeping; and third, the fact that husband and wife do not know what to do with their idle time.
The first cause of discord and dissatisfaction arises from a series of things. Here physical conditions must be taken into consideration.
Discord sometimes also results from the husband not understanding that today’s woman cannot be kept the way the grandmother of old was...
Sometimes it comes from little education. She does not understand him and he does not understand her. Sometimes it comes from bad habits.
Sometimes it arises from their characters being completely different. But it is not right when the husband, at the first quarrel with his wife, says to himself: “Well, we will never come to terms, we are different people.” The truth is that absolute difference of character is rare; in most cases it is merely a mask, an excuse. In many cases the causes of quarrelling can be removed.
A great role in the breakdown[?] of a home is played by bad housekeeping; one must know how to manage a household life.
The third cause of a bad family life is that husband and wife do not know what to do with their free time.
A free day comes, one sits at home and is bored, and when one has nothing to do one begins to brood; and when a man sits at home and broods, he remembers the old grievances[?] he has against his wife, and so this very memory is refreshed in her too; and so it turns out that couples quarrel on Saturdays and Sundays more than on the other days.
Therefore husband and wife ought to know how to make use of their free time. One must look for new and fresh interests in life, and every person can find something with which to spend free time, and not bore each other.
In connection with home life it should be noted that quarrels sometimes arise from fear: when the wife grows older, she begins to fear that her husband will leave her... and therefore she picks on him.
Another time people quarrel over the children. The husband always likes to come up with brand-new ideas on how to bring up the children, and the end is — a quarrel.
As can be seen, these are all causes that could be greatly reduced if people approached them with the necessary intelligence.

The Jewish Woman, the Director and the Passport

[Humour — a sketch: a scene in a local bank.]
A scene in a local bank.
A Jewish woman with a cheque: Panie dyrektorze [Mr. Director], I have a cheque for 50 zł.
Director: Do you have a passport?
Woman: A passport? To cash 50 zł. one needs a passport? A pity, I didn't know about it. My daughter sent it to me from Prossen[?] so that I should buy myself a new wig for the High Holidays... Well, so you really won't give me the money? Must I first go all that way for the passport?
Director: Without a passport you cannot get the money.
Woman: What a pity! Well yes, how should the bank know me? Money matters were always handled by my late husband, may you live long; he even went to the market himself with the basket to do the shopping. A golden soul was my husband. Must I really, absolutely have the passport? Perhaps a letter would do, a bill from the electricity works, a receipt from the landlord?
Director: The bank recognizes no documents whatsoever. Paragraph 18, letter c, part 6 of the statute [ustawa] provides that a passport can be replaced only by a military booklet.
Woman: Where would I get a military booklet? My husband was in the Turkish war and fought at Constantinople — he had a military booklet, but me? Where shall I get you a military booklet now, where from?... To cash a cheque of 50 zł. must I really go all that way now for my passport? You don't know me, true, but I know you very well. You live on the second floor, on the left, and I on the third. I am the grandmother of the two boys, the łobuzy [rascals], but it's the cinemas with the cowboys that are to blame. This morning, when you left home, your wife came out after you onto the stairs and shouted after you:
— Zygmuntsze — she shouted — if you want to stuff yourself with dinner today, then at least leave 10 zł.
— There, and leave me alone! — that is how you answered [printed: "I answered"]. Even the Rosenblatts from the first floor were amazed that such an "osoba" [personage] as you, a so-called intellectual, should speak like that to his own wife; and when you came home yesterday evening drunk as Lot, the whole house...
Director: Enough, enough, where is your cheque? Give me your cheque!
Woman: But the passport...
Director: Not necessary, no passport needed, nothing needed. Give the cheque. (Shouts to the cashier:) Panie kasjerze [Mr. Cashier], be so kind and pay out this Jewish woman at once, but as fast as possible, the 50 zł.
Thousands of Cannon Thundered at the Proclamation of World Peace (Memoirs of a participant in concluding the peace on the Western Front)

[Memoirs — the Peace of Versailles, 1919; part 7, final.]
7.
At the beginning [of the month], on the 19th, 1919 [so printed, month missing], the train with the German delegation arrived in Weimar, and the arrivals submitted a report on the work together with a proposal that such harsh conditions should not be signed by the National Assembly.
The next day a conference was held of all the military commanders of the fronts, chaired by the War Minister Noske; they deliberated about putting up armed resistance, and in the end they sent to ask Generalissimo Hindenburg [printed "Hinrenburg"] what should be.
Field Marshal Gen. Hindenburg then answered thus:
— "If we resume military operations, we can take back the Posen region and hold the German borders.
On the Western Front, in case of a serious attack by the Entente army, it will not be possible to put up any proper resistance, since the Entente armies are much larger and better equipped than the German; therefore it is very doubtful whether the Germans will be able to win. As a soldier, however — Hindenburg answered — I would rather die with honour than have such a shameful peace."
Having received such an answer, the War Minister Noske rose from his seat and said:
— Here among us sit 15 heroes — supreme commanders; but there is also the German people, starved, brutalized and impoverished, and in such a situation the 15 heroes here can achieve nothing.
And the delegate Erzberger added:
"Let us not be obstinate; let us not wait until the French bring into the German towns the black Negroes, who will violate our wives and daughters."
To Weimar there came at that time the French professor "Enar" [perhaps Émile Haguenin], who tried to mediate between the parties.
Several more days went by in weighing the chances for and against signing — in the end the German government adopted a decision to sign the peace terms.
On 28 June 1919 the German peace delegates again arrived at Versailles, and in the same Hall of Mirrors of the sessions at Versailles the German envoy, Foreign Minister Müller and Justice Minister Bell, signed the peace agreement.
On that evening thousands of cannon of the fortresses around Paris saluted with firing the moment of the signing of the peace terms.
All over France the day of victory over Germany was celebrated with great parades. The American soldiers then staying in Paris, out of great joy, put women's hats[?] on their helmets and together with the French soldiers held revels and dances in the streets.
At the same time all of Germany was in mourning. The flags were lowered to half-mast as a sign of national mourning; the Peace of Versailles was received in Germany with great sorrow and pain.
(The end.)

On Doctors' Practice

[Poland — medicine and legislation.] In one of the latest issues of "Dz. Ustaw" [Dziennik Ustaw, the law gazette] there has appeared, in the form of a decree of the President of the State, an ordinance on doctors' practice, which comes into force as early as the 15th of this month and introduces very important changes into the system in force until now.
According to the ordinance, the right to practise belongs only to Polish citizens: a) who hold a diploma issued or recognised by any medical faculty of a Polish university, b) who after receiving the diploma have practised for a year in a hospital, and c) who are entered in the membership list of the Chamber of Physicians (izba lekarska).
The right to practise does not belong to those who, on the basis of a court sentence, have lost their public and civil rights.
Persons who have no right to practise in Poland and are entitled to practise in other countries have only the right to take part in consultations (consilia) at the invitation of Polish doctors.
Every doctor who wants to begin practising must carry out the following formalities: 1) register with the relevant voivodeship, enclosing his documents; 2) report to the Chamber of Physicians. Only after the registration and entry in the list of the Chamber does the doctor have the right to begin practice.
From now on doctors will be called "lekarz"; the title "doctor" belongs only to those who received their diploma before 30 June [czerwiec] 1930.
The law provides that in case of epidemics or mass diseases every lekarz up to 35 years of age can be called up to public health service.
The ordinance also regulates the question of doctors' fees, professional secrecy, apparatus and operations.
The purpose of the ordinance, and especially of the Chamber of Physicians, the nearest future will show us.
R. R.

Politicking among the Jewish artisans

[Poland — Jewish artisans; opinion piece.] For the last twelve years we have been seeing in Poland how the Jewish artisans are being transformed more and more from a social group into a political-party group. Had this process been the outcome of the rising political development of the Jewish artisan, one could only have welcomed the phenomenon.
Unfortunately, the political transformation of the Jewish artisan is the outcome not of a healthy, normal political development, but of the demagogic doings of certain political parties, which strive to influence the Jewish artisans through their organizations and, above all, through their so-called "leaders," who mostly pursue a "politics" of their own and strive for their own personal aims...
This demagogic road of the politicking Jewish artisans already leads them onto the political line of "going with the government" — no matter which one... One goes "with the government" that agrees to reward the "leaders of the Jewish masses" for dragging these masses onto the well-trodden assimilationist path... One unites with other such "leaders" of the Jewish merchants and with the "leaders of the Jewish working masses," who cannot reach the votes of these masses at elections. One unites — disregarding all the "heresy" — with a section of the pious Jews who want to exploit the poor masses and the government for themselves...
In this way a bought-and-paid-for rabble (erev-rav) is formed, which shouts and makes a din for everyone on the Jewish street, promising, supposedly in the name of the government, mountains and hills.
Day in, day out, these "leaders" "intervene" with the government, which "has taken an interest in the matter and has promised to settle it in the best possible way," yet the situation of the Jewish masses keeps getting worse, ever more desperate! For that reason the situation of the said "leaders" keeps getting better and better...
This politicking on the part of people who are, at best, interested in the Jewish artisan for political-party reasons, has in recent years done the artisans great harm, muddling their heads with all kinds of political chatter and "bit[?] culture" that has nothing whatsoever to do with culture.
Every party "Khlestakov" seeks in his own way to fool the artisans into the sack, in order to... exploit their votes at elections and ballots.
Worst of all, however, is that this leads the Jewish craftsman (ba'al melakha) away from the right path, from caring for his professional needs and from striving to perfect himself in his work. Every artisan trade, like every one of the free professions, represents a kind of work that is in constant improvement and is always evolving towards better achievements, finer forms and cheaper prices. If a craftsman stays put with what he once learned, he becomes, as time goes on, an ever weaker and more backward competitor for his fellows. A good craftsman must keep track of all the changes and improvements that the constant development of his trade brings with it; all the more so is this important for the Jewish artisan, who has to withstand the worst competition — under unequal conditions the Jewish craftsman, in order to be able to compete, for example, with the Polish artisan, must be a better, more highly qualified worker.
Where, among the Jewish craftsmen in Poland, are their leaders who should keep them in constant contact with the progress of their trade? Where are the trade journals that should spread among the artisans, in an understandable form, the necessary professional knowledge? Where are the evening courses that should acquaint them with all the novelties? Where are the more or less permanent exhibitions, travelling or local, where the artisan could learn? Where are the special instructors who should from time to time give the craftsman further training? Who cares for such a vital question for the Jewish craftsman as the question of widening the field of work of this craftsman?
Of all these and other professional novelties, only a tiny part is provided by the artisans' organizations, which are heavily occupied mainly with politicking, with elections, with the fight for seats and the like.
In this decline of the artisans' organizations from the right path lies also the main reason for the poor attendance of the supplementary courses by the Jewish apprentices (terminators) — which so gravely threatens the whole future of the Jewish artisan in Poland!...
Dr. Y. Wygodzki.
Long Live Gandhi!...

(A short feuilleton.)
Gandhi fasted one hundred and forty-nine hours.
The whole world was stirred up. Telegrams flew, ministers conferred and millions of Hindus wept bitter tears.
My old acquaintance and neighbour Reb Ozer does not understand: what exactly is all this fuss about? What is everyone so impressed by? He fasted one hundred and forty-nine hours. Well, what is all this about? What is the remedy for it? Which Jew does not keep such fasts? And for that the whole world is shaken! He himself, my dear Reb Ozer, fasts all the BeHaB fasts, Shovavim and „tsirufim“[?] and every eve of the New Moon; then comes the Holy Day [Yom Kippur], Tisha b'Av, the Tenth of Tevet, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the Fast of Gedaliah and the Fast of Esther. Then come days when there is not a single grosz in the house at all, the last penny is gone from the purse — and then Reb Ozer fasts, his wife fasts, the children fast. Add all that up and you will convince yourselves that Reb Ozer's smallest child is a bigger faster than the great Gandhi.
And yet Gandhi is a great man. A teacher, a guide, and as long as he has not patented his invention, one should use it and get rid of many troubles.
Our Będzin communal leaders should follow his example:
Take, for instance, our kehilla president, Reb Avraham Liwer. Why shouldn't he do exactly like Gandhi: sit down in the kehilla office and declare a fast, not eat until the Jews of Będzin pay in the budget [the communal tax, „etat“]. Imagine what a stir that would cause in town! Jews would pawn their pillows and bring the budget-tax to the kehilla.
The Jewish merchants of Będzin are not decent folk; they don't care that their merchants' bank is in a bad state — well, let such loyal merchants' activists as President Rubinlicht and Director Tenenbaum declare a hunger strike, not eating as long as the Jewish merchants do not reconsider[?] and become decent people.
Imagine what an uproar that would cause among the Jewish merchants of Będzin when they learn that their two darlings have stopped eating!
The same should also be done by „dazar“[?] Landner, the head of Keren Hayesod in Będzin. What does it mean — this one and that one won't sign any pledges, and what do people think? A Keren Hayesod bill of exchange is allowed to go to protest — a hunger strike! Now imagine how Keren Hayesod pledges would start pouring in if Nute Landner refused to eat; even the Revisionists would make peace with him.
The workers too can do the same: instead of striking against low wages they had better declare a hunger strike.
What a „blow“ that would be for the factory owners. With tears in their eyes the factory owners would come to the workers and plead: have mercy, children, don't embitter our lives, put something in your mouths! Perhaps a glass of coffee with pastries? Perhaps a little schnapps with a snack? Perhaps a quarter of goose[?] with compote? But the workers would be stubborn and shout: no, no, we're not eating! We are starving!...
And that is exactly what should be done not only by communal leaders and workers, but by all the Jews of Zagłębie.
Enough running around the government offices [urzędy][?], enough struggling with the tax-bailiffs, enough worrying about a livelihood, enough being torn apart; let there be an end to it, let it be over — we'll turn to the Master of the Universe: let us declare a hunger strike against Him.
Fast, fast for so long until the Old One gives in and on this Yom Kippur signs for all of us a „gmar chatima tova“ [a good final sealing].
A. Szwarcer.

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ha'azinu
The Portion
—o—
a) "Corrupt — his children are not his" (Deut. 32:5)
Usually a man wants his children to be more pious than he is; he himself may do every kind of evil, but the children — so he wants — should be pious. In fact, however, when "shiḥet" — when a man is corrupt — then "lo lo banav": the children no longer belong to him; they quickly learn from the father to be corrupt... Ezrat Yisrael.
• •
The prophet Jeremiah lamented: "Woe, those who say to a piece of wood: You are my father!" (woe to those who call a piece of wood "father") — and today's children turn it around and call their father: "You're a piece of wood"... Ibid.
—o—
b) "The Lord alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him" (ibid. 12)
In the time to come God alone will rule the world; today, unfortunately, other idols rule together with God — even in the world of Torah and piety: money, honour... Mi Shalaḥ.
—o—
c) "And the Lord saw and spurned, because of the provoking of His sons and His daughters" (ibid. 19)
"And the Lord saw" — every Jew believes in God. And if "He spurned" — if he nevertheless sins, it is "because of the provoking of his sons and daughters": his sons and daughters have brought him to that... But just as poverty "makes a man transgress the will of his Maker" (poverty drags a man down from faith), so it is today with children [?]...
Rabbi Moshe of Kobrin.
—o—
d) "And He said: I will hide My face from them" (ibid. 20)
They do not believe in God, today's generation. So God says: if so — "I will hide My face from them"; let them help themselves, let them be the clever ones. By all means, let us see... Imrei Shefer.
—o—
e) "And My sword shall devour" (ibid. 42)
God's sword, with which He strikes the Jews, will break sooner than the Jews will perish... "My arrows are spent, but they are not spent" — all 98 (numerically "ḥitzei", "My arrows") curses of the Tokheḥah will run out, and the Jews will still remain... Or Penei Moshe.
—o—
Haftarah: Shuvah
f) "Return, O Israel" (Hosea 14)
"Repentance preceded the world" —
Repentance was created before the world and now stands outside the world; so when one wants to repent, one must truly place oneself outside the world, outside the web of hypocrisy and wickedness that is called "world"...
Ramatayim Tzofim (Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk).
• • •
"And the Lord your God will return your captivity" —
Well, if you do not want to repent, God will have to repent for you... "And the Lord your God will return (ve-shav) your captivity"...
Rabbi Yeḥezkele of Kuzmir.
—o—
Yom Kippur
g) "Let us lift up our palms to our hearts" —
On Yom Kippur we all hold out our hands to one another [?], but "let us lift up our palms to our hearts" — let our hearts be with our hands...
Maḥshavah le-Tovah.
—o—
h) "For on this day He shall atone for you... before the Lord you shall be clean."
Yom Kippur does indeed atone, but "before the Lord you shall be clean" — you must first cleanse yourselves...
Kli Yakar.
—o—
i) "And this shall be an everlasting statute for you."
Regarding all the commandments the prophets rebuked the people for performing them as "a commandment of men learned by rote", merely out of habit, merely as a "statute" [?]. On Yom Kippur, by contrast, the Torah wishes: would that the festival remained merely a "statute" [?]; would that Jews did not sin and Yom Kippur were celebrated merely out of habit...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
—o—
j) "And you shall afflict your souls."
On the eve of Yom Kippur it is a mitzvah to eat. But it is much easier to fast two days for the sake of Heaven than to eat one day for the sake of Heaven...
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
Jabotinsky to the Jews of Zagłębie on the Yom Kippur Campaign

[Keren Tel Hai — letter to the editor; Revisionist Zionism.]
Jabotinsky [Ze'ev Jabotinsky]
To the Jews of Zagłębie on the Yom Kippur campaign
Dear Mr. Editor!
I see a dispute over the fact that Keren Tel Hai intends to hold collections during the month of Tishrei. I am very sorry if this is unpleasant to anyone, but I believe that in public life one must reckon not only with established claims (chazakot), but also with justice and the real interest of society.
Keren Tel Hai carries on, within the limits of its modest means, important work. It partly supports a youth movement in which many Jews see a joy and a hope for the future of national Jewry. It supports in general Jewish defence sport ("Wehrsport") — a task in which many Jews see the only means against "emunot"[?] in Eretz Israel and everywhere. All this is work that is just as important as all the other national-Jewish work. Such work must be helped and not hindered.
There are in Jewry other funds that do very important work in other fields, but in this particular field — supporting defence sport specifically — there is no unified world institution, with the sole exception of the Tel Hai Fund. Naturally it cannot yet maintain the youth movement that devotes itself to defence sport in many countries, and therefore from time to time local collections are also needed, which do not bear the name of Keren Tel Hai, and those collections too Jewish society must support. But in many countries this youth has agreed to refrain from local collections during certain periods, in order to help carry out the Tel Hai campaign. One of these periods is the month of Tishrei; and I ask every Jew to remember that Keren Tel Hai has an important task and deserves everyone's support.
It would be particularly unwise to present the Tel Hai campaign as a kind of conflict with the Keren Kayemet. Hundreds of young supporters of the Tel Hai Fund work energetically in every country for the Keren Kayemet as well, and in many places they even stand in first place in this respect. They do so because they believe that both funds can exist in parallel, and that the Keren Kayemet will not be made into an instrument of struggle against the Tel Hai Fund. The worst service one could render the Keren Kayemet would be to repel from it fresh young forces who love it and are ready to keep helping it — but on condition that it not be used against the interests of the Tel Hai movement.
The Zionist Congress has nothing to do with this. Defence sport is important not only in Eretz Israel, and the Tel Hai Fund must work in all countries. Just as a collection to help ruined Jews in various countries cannot be subordinated to the jurisdiction of the Congress, so one cannot demand it of a collection that seeks to protect Jews in various countries from the danger of being ruined.
The Zionist Congress naturally has the right to demand that the party-Zionist and purely Palestinian funds should not hold parallel collections at the same time, but this does not mean that the Congress has assumed the right to demand that at certain times such funds be boycotted as do not belong to the party-Zionist category and are [sic; probably "are not"] subject to its jurisdiction. Such a right the Congress has certainly not assumed, and it cannot assume it at all. If, God forbid, [tomorrow?] a collection is made for the "ruined", no one will have the right to misuse the name of the Congress in order to preach a boycott of such a collection; and if one must make a collection for a cause that is the only means against the ruin of Jews, one may also not invoke the Congress in demanding a boycott. That would mean: misusing the name of the Congress.
Precisely this year Keren Tel Hai faces especially important tasks. In the last weeks of 5692 (TRTZ"B), courses for defence-sport instructors were held with its help in Latvia. In the coming weeks such courses will be organised in Poland with the support of Keren Tel Hai. From the autumn Keren Tel Hai will open its central school for instructors in Paris (due to take place this winter — note of the K.T.H. headquarters in Poland). These are all tasks that deserve general sympathy. I am sure that the Jewish public in Zagłębie will understand this and will give its support.
Respectfully,
Ze'ev Jabotinsky.
