What Is New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Section heading.]
What is new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 7 / 7 / Tishrei 5693 — piątek 7 października 1932 [Friday, 7 October 1932].)
Będzin
The Community Tax Must Be Assessed According to the Income Assessments. — Notice from the Starosta to the Kehilla Boards.

[Zagłębie — kehillot, taxes.]
In connection with the fact that the completion of the new kehilla budgets is now actually on the agenda, the starosta (district head) has ordered the boards of the Jewish communities in Zagłębie that the assessment of the new etat (community tax) be made within the framework of the law, which provides for a levy of 10 percent according to each person's assessed income.
On the Eve of the Festive Opening of the Orphanage.

[Będzin — welfare, orphanage.]
As our readers know, on the 2nd day of Chol HaMoed [Sukkot] the orphanage on Sienkiewicza Street in our town will be opened.
For the time being only the official part will be opened, which contains, besides [the part] on the ground floor[?], 3 large, splendid halls where the orphans will eat and sleep.
In connection with the opening, a meeting took place on Tuesday evening under the chairmanship of Dr. Weinzieher, at which the programme of the festive opening was discussed.
Among other things, the programme also provides that all donors to date will be published in the report.
There is, however, a large part of the local Jewish population who to this day have not yet given their pledged donations for this important purpose, and especially those who have not yet pledged at all.
It was therefore decided to turn with an appeal to the above-mentioned to fulfil their sacred duty, so that at the opening they may figure on the list of donors.
Agitation Among Jewish Merchants over the Recall of Mr. Rubinlicht from the Tax Commission.

[Będzin — taxes, merchants.]
The report in our paper that Mr. L. Rubinlicht had suddenly been recalled as a member of the tax commission has, for understandable reasons, aroused strong agitation in Jewish merchant circles.
In the course of Friday dozens of merchants turned to us for information as to the reasons why Mr. Rubinlicht had been disqualified as a member of the tax commission.
At the close of Rosh Hashanah a meeting took place at the Merchants' Association, attended by the board of the Merchants' Association, representatives of the small traders, artisans and others.
After discussion of this question a resolution was adopted to react to the injustice committed against the Jewish merchant community in Będzin by the recall of Mr. Rubinlicht from the commission for assessing the income tax (podatek dochodowy).
—o—
[Będzin — Artisans' Association; statement.]
From the Artisans' Association in Będzin
Modrzejowska 83
On Monday, 3 October [?], a general meeting took place, at which the gossip printed in „Express Zagłębia“ of 29 September concerning Mr Klajnman was considered. We state that it is not true that Mr Klajman wanted [?] to have [—] which were abused [?] in the Artisans' Association while he was treasurer (skarbnik), for this was established by the prosecutor at the District Court on 31 December, ref. Ds. 587/311 [?]. It is also not true that Mr Klajman was expelled from the association, for on 15 May 1931 Mr Klajman submitted a letter of resignation to the board, and together with 400 members he withdrew, and we founded a new Artisans' Association. Mr Klajman was convicted only because he could not produce before the court the document on the basis of which Mr Klajman signed an artisan's card (karta rzemieślnicza) for Mr Strobel [?], because the document is held in the old Artisans' Association; against this Mr Klajman has lodged an appeal. We continue to place our trust in Mr Klajman as treasurer [?] of our association. Incidentally, we must remark that Klajger [?] has no right to call [upon] shoemakers and tailors, because the guild, and the board as well, are in our association.
On behalf of the board,
Chairman Chaim Dawid Grosman.
[Ad 422]
The Gates Are Now Locked at 10 O'Clock. — What Does the Tenants' Association Say to That?

[Będzin — housing, municipality.]
A few weeks ago we pointed out that from 1 October the gates should also be closed, as until now, at 11 in the evening. We justified our opinion by the fact that there are hundreds of people who truly cannot afford to pay 10 or 20 groszy a night, and because of this they are forced to run home before 10. It often happens that already at 10 o'clock a tenant has to stand at the gate for quite a while in the rain and snow until His Excellency the house watchman deigns to open the gate.
The matter, however, was passed over in silence by those who ought to be concerned with it. The Tenants' Association too treated it with indifference, and the result is that from the 1st of this month the gates are already locked at 10 o'clock.
It is interesting that the Association of House-owners and Plot-owners has decided to react to this and has applied to the magistrate (municipality) with a request that until December (grudzień) of this year the gates should stay open as until now, until 11 o'clock.
The “Kurier Zachodni” Wants to Kill Two Hares with One Shot...

[Będzin — municipality, press, antisemitism.]
In Wednesday's issue of the “Kurier Zachodni” a rather large item was printed devoted to the economy system of the Będzin magistrate (municipality).
In the item the bad management conducted by the present town administration is censured, but the essence of the item is that in the registration (meldunki) department there works the daughter of a “rich” mill-owner, and in the power station (elektrownia) there is an official who is at the same time a partner in a cinema.
In our opinion the paper is after something else; the anger at the officials is only because they are Jews...
The “Work” for the Talmud Torah...

[Będzin — religious education, charity.]
Last Tuesday a badge sale was to have taken place for the benefit of the “Talmud Torah”. Because there were no volunteers to sell the badges, the event (impreza) did not take place..
As we are told, the “Bnos” (girls) of the “Agudah” [Agudath Israel] refused to take part in the badge sale for the benefit of the religious institution.
On Giving Receipts to Tenants

[Będzin — housing.]
The Association of House-owners and Plot-owners asks us to point out that every house-owner is obliged to give receipts for the sum received as rent. Failure to give receipts carries the threat of a heavy fine.
Sign Up for the Evening Courses!

[Będzin — Education.] The evening courses, which were closed at the beginning of the current school year, have been reopened. One can register for the courses at the office of Public (Elementary) School No. 2.
An Accident with a Police Agent.

[Będzin — Accident.] The following accident happened at the Sławków railway station. As the train began to move off, a police agent from Olkusz jumped onto it. The jump, however, failed; the agent fell under the wheels, which cut off his right hand.
In serious condition the agent was taken to the local hospital.
—o—
The 'Birth Pangs' of Forming a Board for 'Hakoach'.
[Będzin — Societies and Sport.] Over the last few weeks several general meetings were held at 'Hakoach' [the Jewish sports club] with the aim of electing a board. But each time a 'black cat' runs across the path and everything stays as it was.
The same thing repeated itself at the general meeting held on the evening after Rosh Hashanah, chaired by the advocate Dr. Rechtman.
This meeting was actually lucky: a board was elected, and normal activity would already have begun, had it not been for the proposal of the Right Poale Zion that 'Hakoach' should not be affiliated with the world union 'Maccabi'.
When the proposal was rejected, several board members resigned their mandates, and —
'Hakoach' is once again without a board.
—o—
Heavy Fines for Unsanitary Conditions.
[Będzin — Municipal / Sanitation.] Recently the sanitary commission has been carrying out inspections in the shops and in the courtyards.
For the shops found in poor sanitary condition, reports are drawn up against the owners.
This week a number of house-owners were punished with arrest and fines because the sanitary state of their houses is poor.
Sosnowiec. The Englard–Markowicz Trial — Postponed.

[Sosnowiec — Court.] On Friday, the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the trial against Mr. A. Markowicz was to have taken place; as our readers know, he was sued by Rabbi Englard, who had been insulted by a leaflet signed by Mr. Markowicz.
29 witnesses were summoned to this trial, of whom 7 did not appear.
When the court proceedings were about to begin, Markowicz's advocate, Mr. Krzymuski [?], turned to the judge with a motion that, 1) because the principal witnesses are missing, and 2) because the trial falls on the eve of Rosh Chodesh, when it is very inconvenient for the Jewish witnesses to take an oath, the trial should be postponed.
Mr. Englard's advocate, Mr. König, opposed the motion and demanded that the trial go ahead; the judge, however, inclined to the motion of advocate Mr. Krzymuski, and the trial was postponed.
Young Jewish Woman Throws Herself from the Third Floor and Is Killed.

[Sosnowiec — Tragedy.] On Mościckiego [?] Street a terrible suicide took place, committed by the 30-year-old woman Rachel Binental.
The suicide lived in Czeladź. On the tragic day she came to her parents, who live on the third floor of a house on Mościckiego Street.
At a certain moment Binental fell out of the window and caught hold of the electric wires, which snapped, and the suicide fell down onto the pavement.
In a very serious condition she was taken to the Jewish hospital, where she breathed her last an hour later.
Rachel Binental has left a husband with 2 small children.
Employing Young Journeymen Will Be Punished.

[Sosnowiec — Labour.] At the local labour inspector's office a conference took place with the participation of Będzin shoe-upper makers.
The conference was called on the basis of information the inspector had received that in the workshops of the Będzin shoe-upper makers the working hours prescribed by law (ustawa) are not observed and young journeymen are employed.
Regarding the latter question the inspector declared that an inspection of the workshops will be carried out and that the master craftsmen who employ underage journeymen will be punished.
The shoe-upper makers raised the question of being permitted to work on Sunday, since because of the Sabbath they have to rest two days a week.
The inspector replied that on this matter they should apply to the Ministry of Labour.
So This Is Called 'Domestic Peace'... — Wrecked the Flat and Then Set It on Fire.

[Sosnowiec — Crime.] At Kilińskiego 7 lives the couple Falk Zachar [?], in whose home there is no domestic peace. Last Saturday a quarrel broke out between the couple, which led to the husband wrecking the flat, pouring flammable material over the furniture and then setting it alight.
The neighbours, seeing smoke billowing from the flat, broke the flat open and saw the terrible sight.
Thanks to the quick rescue the fire was put out. The arsonist was taken out scalded (burned).
The Kehilla's Supplementary Budget Is Ready.

[Będzin — Kehilla.] This week the supplementary budget, amounting to 40 thousand złoty, was sent off for approval.
The income of this budget is designated for buying a plot for a cemetery.
—o—
Piechowicz's Murderer Sentenced to 10 Years' Hard Prison.
[Będzin — Court.] In the month of July the local merchant Piechowicz was murdered in Olkusz.
The murderer, who stood this week before the local district court, was sentenced to 10 years of hard prison.
—o—
A Large Communist Trial.
[Będzin — Court.] Yesterday a large communist trial began at the local district court. In the dock sit 30 young people from the Zagłębie region, who are accused of communist activity.
The trial will last several days.
—o—
Poisoned by Goose Meat
[Sosnowiec — Health.] On the second day of Rosh Hashanah several Jewish families suddenly suffered terrible stomach pains. The doctors established that they had been poisoned by eating goose meat. One of the sick, a certain Dzięwięcki [?], was taken to hospital; the rest were left to be treated at home.
—o—
A Son Seriously Wounded by His Father.
[Sosnowiec — Crime.] In the night from Saturday to Sunday the shoemaker Kaczmarczyk attacked his sleeping son, aged 19, and seriously wounded him with a knife.
The 'hot-tempered' father has been arrested.
—o—
New Prices for Bread and Flour
[Sosnowiec — Economy.] The price commission at the local magistrate (municipality) held a meeting at which new prices for bread and flour were set: a kilo of rye bread — 30 groszy; wholemeal (razowy) — 24 gr.; rye flour 65 per cent — 30 gr.

[Zagłębie — Transport.] With the participation of representatives of the local self-governments of Zagłębie, a conference was held the day before yesterday in Katowice, at which the tram directorate's project to extend the tram network in Zagłębie was considered.
No concrete decisions were adopted at the conference.
—o—

Yesterday the inspectors of the Urząd Skarbowy (tax office) set out across the town and checked the trade licences (patents) in the shops and in the artisans' workshops.
Wherever things were not „kosher“, the inspectors wrote up reports.
—o—
[Będzin — Municipality; Warning.] On the advertisements concerning foreign loans.
On the basis of a rescript of the Kielce voivodeship office, the Będzin magistrate asks us to draw attention to the need to be careful and not to let oneself be misled by such advertisements about obtaining foreign loans; by means of these advertisements certain sums are swindled out of those who believe that they will receive the loans.
—o—
[Zagłębie — Unemployment.] The Kielce voivode in Zagłębie.
Until yesterday noon the Kielce voivode stayed in Zagłębie; he took an interest in the question of the further relief action for the unemployed.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Zionism.] From „Masada“ in Sosnowiec.
On Sunday, the 2nd day of Sukkot, a literary evening will take place in the premises of the Revisionist org. with the participation of the violinists Unger and Mandelbaum. The programme also includes lectures, recitations, singing, etc.
—o—
[Będzin — Zionism.] From the Będzin „Gordonia“.
In the premises of the Będzin „Gordonia“ the annual general meeting took place.
After hearing the reports, the new leadership was elected, consisting of: Reuven Liwer, Avraham Federman, Avraham Feldberg, Rachel Bukowska, Shlomo Cymerman, Matek Krzesiwo[?] and Asher Gitler.
—o—

On Monday, the first day of Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of Sukkot), a general meeting will take place in the premises of the Będzin Talmud Torah with the aim of electing a board from all strata of the Jewish population, in order to restore the institution to its proper level.
—o—
[Taxes.] Last date for paying the ryczałt instalment.
We draw our readers' attention to the fact that the 15th of this month is the last date for paying the instalment of the ryczałt obrotowy (lump-sum turnover tax). Everyone must pay the sum stated in the nakaz (payment order).
Merchants and shopkeepers who are unable to pay the entire ryczałt instalment by the deadline should make efforts to have it accepted from them in 2—3 instalments.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Accident.] A Jewish girl run over.
On Wednesday, in broad daylight, Sala Szwimer was run over on 3 Maja street in Sosnowiec and was seriously injured.
The reckless carter has been arrested.
Our explanations concerning the legal answers

[Będzin — Editorial notice; Legal advice.]
1) In connection with the fact that many of our readers and subscribers send in written questions about legal advice, we announce that the answers can, on request, be printed under the pseudonyms given; on the other hand, the editorial office must have the exact address of whoever wishes to receive the advice, otherwise we will not be in a position to deal with the questions.
2) Seeing that the free legal advice brings great benefit, and that we receive many letters of thanks full of appreciation — because in these present hard times we have taken upon ourselves the burden of giving every reader, entirely free of charge, all kinds of legal advice through our specially engaged lawyer — we have decided to accommodate our readers still further, so that they can make use of the benefits even more easily and practically.
For this purpose our lawyer will devote
2 hours a week specially to the readers of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“.
So every Sunday from 3 to 5 p.m. all readers can visit the office of our lawyer in Będzin, Kołłątaja 27, where they will be received at once and served on presentation of our certificate.
The editorial office of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“.

Notes of the Week

[Notes of the week — abroad.] In Germany a monarchist coup is being prepared. The Bavarian crown prince is to become king of Bavaria and Austria.
—o—
In France an express train came off the rails. 7 passengers were seriously injured. 2 of them have died.
—o—
France comes forward with a proposal to the League of Nations that a peace be concluded for 10 years.
—o—
In Wołkowysk Jewish Yevseks [members of the Yevsektsiya, Jewish communists] burst into the synagogue and relieved their physiological needs there..
—o—
In England a disaster occurred in a coal mine. 19 workers were killed.
—o—
Police, the Jewish self-defence and soldiers, numbering 3,000 men, kept order in Vienna on Yom Kippur.
—o—
In Italy there were great floods which caused great damage.
Who Is Not Liable to the Military Tax?

[Poland — taxes; army.] Recently the Ministry of the Interior, in agreement with the Ministry of Military Affairs, issued a circular to all voivodes and starostas, explaining which of the older age-classes are not liable to the military tax:
The tax is not paid at all by the age-classes 1883—1897, because these classes served at the time of the mobilisation.
Of the later classes, i.e. from 1898 and younger, exempt from the tax are those who reported for the draft [pobór] after the year 1925 and are:
1) invalids, both of the Polish army and of the former Russian, Austrian or German armies, since their ailments arose in connection with military service; 2) former soldiers of the former Russian, German or Austrian armies, if they served more than 5 months. The regulation on exempting from the tax those who reported for the draft after the year 1925 does not apply in Upper Silesia to the classes 1903 and younger, and in Galicia — 1900 and younger.
R. R.
Yom Kippur Eve in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — Yom Kippur; community.] Yom Kippur eve passed in fine weather. Because of this, and also because it fell on a Sunday, the cemeteries were packed full. The entrance to the new cemetery was besieged by the beggars. This time the beggars introduced a „reform“: they seated a cashier, who was guarded by 2 watchmen, and every visitor to the cemetery had to pay a lump sum...
———
At the kapparot the first „kapparah“ was the kehilla treasury. The „revolutionary“ shochet R' Yechezkel, who had been arrested for a certain time last Friday, was busy the whole night from Saturday to Sunday. Because of the watching of „evil eyes“ he slaughtered in several places, but everywhere he was besieged by hundreds of women and children, who shouted after him:
— „Slaughter mine already!“...
———
The Sosnowiec society „Tomchei Aniyim“ „lost“ its prayer leader for Kol Nidrei. The members, all of them poor porters, had hired Mr. Z. Federman to lead the prayers for them for 50 zł. Mr. F. handed the sum over to a certain rebbe. Half of the sum the porters gave before Rosh Hashanah, and the other half they wanted to add on Yom Kippur eve; and when they (through no fault of their own) were late with the obligation, the prayer leader did not come to Kol Nidrei, but only sent a messenger in the name of the rebbe (so we are told) that a pledge should be sent...
Night fell, the congregation waits and the prayer leader does not come. Only then did a Varsovian take pity on them, a certain Mr. Altman of Warsaw, who delighted the porters as a fine prayer leader.
———
In all the synagogues and minyanim the greatest decorum prevailed. The only exceptions were the synagogues in Pogoń and Old Sosnowiec, where the solemnity of Yom Kippur was weakened...
—o—
Paid with his life for a bit of coal.
The 12-year-old Skański in Strzemieszyce jumped onto a freight wagon with the aim of stealing a bit of coal. The leap, however, was a fatal one. Skański fell under a wagon, which wounded him mortally.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
They “Cannot”...
The great coal magnates of Upper Silesia, whose pensions amount to more than 100 thousand zł. a year per director, have decided not to reduce the price of coal for the winter. They declare that “they cannot”, because the population consumes little coal.
—o—
When One Leaves the Flat Unguarded...
The Mysłowice resident Yitzhak Mendel Korn went with his family to Sosnowiec, where they spent Yom Kippur.
The thieves took advantage of the opportunity and removed clothes, linen and other belongings from Korn's flat. The theft is estimated at 3 thousand zł.
—o—
Smuggled German Patterns.
The “Border Guard” has uncovered an affair of patterns for ladies' dresses that were smuggled from Germany. The patterns were smuggled to Katowice and from there they used to be sent on as parcel post to Warsaw.
At the head of the smuggling stood a certain Rozalia[?] Sal of Katowice and a Mrs. Leben (Warsaw).
—o—
Meeting of the Unemployed.
In Bogucice a meeting was held of the laid-off workers of the “Ferdynand” coal mine.
The meeting proceeded calmly.
—o—
A Victim of a Wild Car Race.
A car tore through the streets of Mysłowice at a wild speed and ran over a cyclist. The result was a terrible one: the cyclist was killed on the spot.
—o—
Catastrophe in a Coal Mine.
In the “Mysłowice” coal mine a lump of coal buried several workers. One of them was killed on the spot. The others were lightly injured.
—o—
An Interesting Trial.
The “7 Groszy” [Siedem Groszy] brings a report from the German press that on Friday the 28th of this month a military court will hear the trial of the man who shot Mr. Winterstein in Mysłowice. A number of witnesses who were present at the incident in Mysłowice are being summoned to the trial.
—o—
Siemianowice Engages a Rabbi.
The kehilla in Siemianowice, which is developing, has decided to engage a rabbi. The first candidate under consideration is Rabbi Halpern of Kraków (“Mizrachi”).
A Father Shoots His Only Son and Then Puts an End to His Own Life.

[Grójec[?] — a family tragedy.]
A Terrible Family Tragedy.
On First of May Street in Grójec[?] lived the official of the Grójec “Gez.”[?] [abbreviation unclear], Janaska, with his family, among whom quarrels often broke out.
Last Friday the following tragedy took place in the family: after one such family row Janaska shot his only son [printed “einzig yerign” — apparently garbled], who was sleeping in a cradle.
Having carried out the cruel murder, he shot himself with the same revolver and fell dead on the spot.
Several letters were found in the suicide's pocket, in which he takes leave of his friends and family.
A Flood of Laws

[Poland — law and legislation; interview.]
An assessment by Adv. Berenson.
In connection with the new decrees the famous advocate Leon Berenson declared in an interview:
— Everyone is complaining now about the flood of laws [ustawy] with which the country is now being inundated. There prevails among us a kind of morbid mania for two things: laws and uniforms. They would like to push a person into a machinery of regulations that would lead him by the hand from the cradle to the grave. Everything is to be foreseen, everything to be codified, everything to be encircled with an armour of prohibitions and penalties, or at the very least the citizen is to be dressed in a garment of articles and paragraphs. This surplus of regulations creates such chaos that not only a simple man but no specialist jurist either will master it. Every month we sit before a high mountain of new laws and torment ourselves in vain to swallow and digest them. If it goes on like this, “jur.”[?] [jurisprudence] will soon become such a mysterious science that only magicians will understand it.
An Important Law Concerning Shoemakers in Poland.

[Poland — crafts and economy.]
The Opinion of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
The Ministry of Commerce has drawn up an important draft law, which has now been sent out to the interested organizations in order to obtain the expert opinion. The law concerns shoemaking. As is known, the shoemakers now find themselves in a very difficult situation; because of mechanization and foreign competition many workshops are closing, and the shoemakers are left without a piece of bread.
The new law has the purpose of restricting the advance of mechanization and restricting the import of foreign footwear into Poland.
The law is directed against mechanical production, which is neither cheaper nor better than hand manufacture.
The Kielce Chamber of Crafts has received this draft, in order to state its opinion on it.

Pilica.

[Pilica — obituary; cultural life.]
A Young Cultural Activist Has Died.
The local Jewish youth, the lovers of the Yiddish word and of Jewish culture, have suffered a heavy loss with the untimely death of the young cultural activist Yosef Wasserman. There was not a single social or cultural institution in which the ever-cheerful Yosef did not want to be an active collaborator. He was the pioneer in creating a library here named after Y. L. Peretz, he created a drama circle and was the director of his own one-act play “The Deaf Widower”, which was performed many times with great success.
Yosef Wasserman possessed great creative powers; seeing the development of sport, he created a Jewish sports club.
With the death of Yosef Wasserman the youth of our town has been orphaned; there is no one else who could take his place in our Jewish cultural life.
S. S.[?]
When a Fantasy Becomes a Reality — On the Festive Opening of the Children's Home in Będzin

[Będzin — institutions; the orphanage.] L. Szpigelman.
And now the moment is drawing near when one can reap[?] the fruits of what was planted. Already on the 2nd day of Chol HaMoed the Jewish orphanage will be opened in Będzin. True, the building is not yet entirely finished inside, so that at the present moment only the lower part is being opened, where, however, 2 thirds of the children will already be accommodated. True, the joy is not so great, and the opening, by the way, will also not take place with all the splendour and glitter one would have been entitled to allow oneself if the whole building had already been finished; but then, we are Jews after all, so we must always have certain obstacles, for never have our paths been planted with flowers. In building this structure too we met, as usual, with no few difficulties; on top of that came the severe prevailing crisis, this catastrophic situation, which has hit us Jews most of all. After all, in the course of time [many?] solid firms have gone under, and yet there were stubborn people among us who said to themselves: come what may, we will not budge from our place, we want to know of nothing, we must do our part. We must realise our ideal in life, we will not stop before anything or for anything. Our part we must carry out — and it is simply to be admired under what conditions the building committee worked in these hardest moments. The people simply felt instinctively that they stem from the people called a stiff-necked people, and with that strength, with that willpower, the useful work was carried on.
The building, we say, is not yet finished, and we cannot celebrate its official opening, so for the time being only the rear wing [„oficyna“] is being realised — of which, by the way, we have nothing to be ashamed. It is a magnificent four-storey building with huge halls that give much light and air, executed according to the latest building technique; and that we have been privileged to move the children from cramped, stuffy little rooms into these [bright?] halls, where the children will breathe differently, move differently, eat differently — that is already a great gain for the town. At the same time it must not be forgotten that there still remains to be dealt with the greatest part of the building, i.e. the whole front, which consists of a huge four-storey building that will remain an eternal monument to Jewish Będzin, and which ought to be called, instead of „orphanage“, a „home for forlorn Jewish children“.
Let us not forget that this is the first grandiose modern public building, which belongs to the whole town and in which all without exception must take part. Now a part of this work, being realised before our eyes, is being opened, and at this half-official opening the committee is supposed to give us a report on its activity, an account of its income and expenditure — but we do not accept the account at all. We do not want to allow the committee for a single minute to rest from its intensive activity, in the midst of which it stands. A report is given only when everything is complete and finished. We therefore do not want to allow the committee to rest in the middle of this work, and regardless of the fact that they have now realised one part, we hold that we stand in the middle of the work, which must be continued at any price; and only then, when we are privileged to hand the whole building over to the town, will we accept the report and hear[?] the account.
When it was decided in its time to build this children's home, we said that we would not let the pen out of our hand until the town understood that out of this fantasy a reality must come. Now that the fantasy has almost been realised and [nothing remains?] but to finish the front, we, together with the committee, will certainly not cease to awaken the conscience of our citizens, who will help to complete this huge work.
The front must be finished inside, for outside everything is ready, the roof is covered. So that in all no more than several tens of thousands of złoty are needed. We know how hard the times are today, we are aware of the difficult situation we find ourselves in in the country at present, we know that this is not the time to come to the greater part of the impoverished people and tell them that they must help realise what is in the middle of the work, at a time when at home even the most necessary is lacking. We know all this, and we would therefore appeal to the somewhat better-situated elements that they should truly put themselves in the position of the impoverished masses, whom they must represent at the present moment, and add one more brick to the great building, which is already about to be finished — and the matter will be settled, the question will be solved. For after all, for the community, for the great Jewish society, a few tens of thousands of zł. play no role.
We have known it all along, and not only among us is it known, that the Jews of Będzin give money as soon as one comes to them — not to speak of when it concerns an already completed building, which is located right in the town itself.
Yes, Będzin is a town that gives much charity, one cannot deny it; it has long since made a name for itself by this. But the truth must be told: there are still among us such Jews who, thank God, are able to give and yet, unfortunately, have not lifted a finger for this building. They stand aloof, these egoists, and do not want to know what is being created in their generation for the poor community.
And therefore one must remind this element [printed „שלעמענט“] of the crime they commit if they continue to stand aloof and do not take part in the mitzvah, in the holy work. Perhaps they will think better of it and come at the third bell with their material support.
It goes without saying that the building committee, which spared no trouble and effort — and, by the way, money too — has great merit; but we will not say thanks to them: we would like them to be able to thank you, Jewish citizens, for having given them the opportunity to realise this magnificent monument.
Let us therefore remember at the present celebration that we may make no pause, that we are still in the middle of the work, which with a little effort will make it possible to finish the whole building.
But be that as it may, and if one also takes[?] into account the critical situation that befell us right in the middle of the work — much, much has been done for the town, much, much has been accomplished for the forlorn little orphans; and therefore let us rejoice in the present realisation, that we have the strength to create grandiose things in our hardest moments, when the people find themselves in such a difficult economic situation.
For that is why we are a people that hopes and believes, so that in the hardest moments we take upon ourselves the most incredible strength, with which we smash walls and work wonders.
This building too we must complete in all its size and splendour, not stopping at any stumbling blocks that lie on our way. And therefore we may take pride in the celebration taking place at the present opening.
Political Letters.

[World politics — satirical political letter: the Geneva disarmament conference and the Far East.] Dated "the portion of 'Tabernacle of Peace'"...
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
I have received your letter. You want my opinion on the present political situation in general and on the disarmament conference in particular? Then listen to me:
You surely remember the joke that the satirist Yitskhok-Yoyel Linetski once told.
"My father," he told, "once sat at the table and was expounding Torah. He dwelt for a long time on a verse and raised a question: why does it say 'vayomer' and not 'vayedaber'. He preached for a whole half hour, and afterwards it turned out that it does indeed say 'vayedaber'."
Almost the same thing is now happening in Geneva.
Everyone talks about disarmament, sermons are held on the danger of war, and it seems quite clear that the conference booklet says "vayomer" ("and he said"); in the end it turns out that he said nothing, that they are only at the beginning, and that for the time being there can be no talk of any complete disarmament.
Well, fine. They have already got through[?] the official and semi-official speeches, they have already handed out all the necessary honours, peppered with all sorts of compliments. But they have not yet, for the time being, got down to the main thing.
First of all the old argument was put forward — and the eternally new one — that not everyone can disarm at the present moment, because there are countries that lie "between the straits", i.e. among hostile countries, and therefore must arm.
Of course there is a certain truth in this argument, for there is a view that even those countries that do not lie among hostile states are in the same danger; but on the other hand one cannot deny that, when all is said and done, it is an argument — if one may say so — "not of the kind claimed".
If one thinks like that, one will never disarm, because one will always be able to say that one is afraid of the others.
And one more point must be taken into account: the "great ones of the generation", the great powers, have very scant interest in disarming. On the contrary, it is a matter of life for them to increase their armament more and more, because, firstly, one cannot give up at all such a golden idea as being well armed all the time. It comes in handy against any trouble, may it not come. A well-armed state somehow commands quite a different kind of respect. And, secondly (so say some connoisseurs among the lovers of militarism), one simply cannot give up[?] armies — what will one do with so many millions of people? It would only swell the number of unemployed even more.
In short, arguments and motives have already been found to pepper up[?] the anti-disarmament questions.
And were I not afraid, I would say that I suspect some participants of the Geneva conference of having agreed among themselves (perhaps in a silent language) to talk and talk but say nothing at all — for what, after all, according to their view, is the practical difference between armament and disarmament? This way all are equal, and the other way round, too, all are equal.
It recalls the episode of the dowry.
Two in-laws once sat together and held a conversation about the dowry. The groom's father demanded that the dowry be paid at once. The other in-law, the bride's father, argued that he did want to pay, gladly, and that he could do it, but that he simply considered it foolish to pay out the dowry, for either way: if the children marry, the money belongs to both of them anyway and there is no need to rush and pay it; and if, God forbid, they do not — then what is there to talk about? May God guard and save us. How can one even come up with such a terrible thought?
The same, R' Shlomo, is now happening between the parties in Geneva.
They talk about "settling" (getting rid of) the weapons. But some in-laws come and argue: either way — if there will be no need to fight on the battlefields, it does no harm for everyone to keep his weapons, and why waste time on empty talk about disarmament? And if — what then? — war will have to be waged after all, then weapons are certainly needed, and "whoever does more is praiseworthy"...
You already understand what kind of peace can come out of such talk. And meanwhile a hellish fire is flaring in the Far East.
The Japanese keep pushing forward, and the road ahead remains open to them. Not for nothing is there now talk of preparations on Russia's side in the Far East. The danger of a new war between Russia and Japan hovers there. True, in the circles of the political sages it is said that precisely at the present moment it is not good[?] for Russia to enter a war with Japan. But who can know how all these preparations will end?
Such, apparently, is the fate of peace. As soon as one begins to speak of peace among nations, the Prince of War comes and laughs devilishly at all this talk.
On the whole, we are still very far from contentment and peace among the nations.
Y. M.
“And Thou Shalt Rejoice in Thy Feast” (Sukkot Thoughts)

[Holidays — Sukkot; reflective essay.]
Mikri.
If one wishes to characterize the whole series of impressions, thoughts and feelings that the Jew lives through from Rosh Chodesh Tishri until Sukkot, one can find no better comparison than with a great polyphonic (many-voiced) musical work, with a symphonic poem that begins in the key of “Sal” [sic; presumably “Moll”, minor] (serious) and ends in “Dur” [major] (cheerful, lively).
Seriousness and joy, religious awakening and cheerfulness of spirit are united and fitted together in the month of Tishri into a single whole. Not for nothing did our ancients — who found for every phenomenon of our spiritual and moral life a fitting allusion, a characteristic designation — call the month of Tishri “saturated with commandments” (mushba be-mitzvot), for one holiday comes right after another, and one demand after another is placed before our religious feeling: “Shofar, within it atonement, within it sukkah, within it lulav, within it willow.”
After the echo of the shofar with its call to moral awakening comes the supreme, solemn concentration of our exalted Yom Kippur, and right after it — the holiday of Sukkot with all its hubbub: sukkah, lulav, the four species, hoshanot. All of this is bound and woven one into the other and runs like a single line, like one harmonious melody.
A solemn voice awakens us at Rosh Hashanah and calls on us to contemplate our life, to reflect on our conduct and ways during the past year. The holy, exalted day of Yom Kippur compels us to acknowledge our whole human weakness, our worthlessness, but at the same time shows us the way and the means by which our stained soul may regain its tikkun: the radiance and the purity that were dimmed by ourselves. And now comes the holiday of Sukkot and calls on us, on the contrary, to joy, to zest for life, to rejoice with all our own, with the household servants, with the stranger, without distinction of their social standing: “And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite, the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that are within thy gates”; and also in everything we have earned by our toil and labour (from the threshing floor and from the winepress) we must rejoice, in a joyful, cheerful mood (“and thou shalt be altogether joyful”).
Seven days in a row we must rejoice — this is expressly demanded several times in various places of the Torah! In this categorical commandment the whole optimism of our religion indeed finds expression. This principle of cheerfulness we — and the non-Jewish world as well — must recognize as one of the highest cultural values of our Torah, of the Jewish conception of life. For we are the only people, and our faith the only religion, that has adopted “simcha” — joy and cheerfulness of spirit — as a basic principle of our world-view. Can we picture in our imagination what forms such a religious command would have taken among the nations of the world, had their religious code prescribed for them a seven-day and interrupted [sic; read: uninterrupted] merrymaking! What bacchanalia it would have provoked, what unbridled carousing would have broken out, what excesses would have taken place!
Jewish simcha, however, is a pure, genuine, cheerful state of mind, because it springs from a crystal-clear source and — rests on the laws of nature!
According to the Torah we must rejoice in the harvest, in the gathering of our crops in the fields, of our fruits in the orchards and vineyards, in the result of our heavy, hard labour!...
True, among us Jews too things were merry and lively during the days of Sukkot, as can be seen from our ancient literature, from the Mishnah and Midrash, and also from later descriptions that have come down to us of the “Simchat Beit HaShoevah”, that genuine folk festival, during which our greatest Tannaim, our most famous Geonim and leaders used to abandon themselves completely to the intoxication of the “simcha shel mitzvah” and simply astonish the many-thousand-headed crowd of pilgrims with their gymnastic feats and acrobatic skill.
We also find authentic reports of the lively tumult and din when, on Hoshana Rabbah, the lulavim used to be destroyed in the “Azarah” [Temple court] — a custom that still finds its echo to this day in our synagogues in the “beating of the hoshanot” — but, as already mentioned, with all this the merriment and joy never crossed the bounds of the permissible and never took on the forms of Dionysian carousing or orgiastic wantonness, because the joy was inspired by a higher spirit; it was pure and natural.
Only in a later epoch, after we had lost our political independence, when we were torn from our own land, driven from our fields and gardens, winepresses and barns — did we lose our bond with nature, and consequently the holiday of Sukkot, that agricultural holiday “par excellence”, lost its true original character. Its liveliness and cheerfulness, and took on an entirely different meaning and character, both in literature and in the popular consciousness.
Living in foreign lands, among foreign peoples with foreign cultures, we became acquainted with the cult and mysticism of the surrounding nations, and little by little religious-mystical conceptions penetrated to us, especially from the Kasdim (Chaldeans) and Babylonians, and these were carried over onto our holiday of joy and gladness as well. And so the sukkah — the former merry “summer tent” in which the whole season of harvest and fruit-gathering was joyfully spent — is transformed into the mystical notion of a “dirat arai”, a temporary dwelling, meant to remind us symbolically of the brief span of our life in this world; the splendid bouquet, the four species, with which our forefathers used to appear in the house of study as a symbol of the greatest crops and fruit — now acquire a highly mystical meaning and are matched to various parts of the human body: the etrog to the heart, the myrtles — to the eyes, the willow — to the mouth, and the lulav — to the spine. A while later the custom arises of reading on Sukkot — the Book of Ecclesiastes: in the midst of the joy of the holiday we hear a voice of despair, of scepticism, of ironic, biting criticism, of negation of all human life and striving, and of the questionable worth of all our labour. For: “All is vanity, vanity of vanities.”
And our whole beautiful holiday of joy and cheerfulness, the whole express demand of the Torah — is lost to us, and the “season of our rejoicing” takes on an almost alien character.
But the true basic character of the holiday of Sukkot cannot nevertheless be denied, even in exile and under the influence of the mystical spirit. Too clearly are its fundamental principles marked out in the Torah, and too vividly do the memories of our old home, of our natural, agricultural life “every man under his vine and under his fig tree”, still live in our memory, for them to let themselves be dimmed by the later scepticism and by the mystical tone that disturbs the beautiful harmony of the harmonious chord between Judaism and the life of nature.
And in this sense, in this future togetherness in our reviving old-new home, we can even today call out to one another: “And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast!”
Some Own a Pearl...

[Poetry — folk song, in Yiddish translation.] H. N. Bialik. (Folk song)
Some own a pearl,
and some a diamond,
and some only six fingers
on their hand.
—
And I have three daughters
like pines in the forest,
with bosoms like towers,
and braids — no end of them.
—
They demand what is their due —
only give them a husband;
there's not a single dress,
shoes — none to be had.
—
As if the young men
had all struck a deal [“blat” ?]:
a dowry in cash —
put it straight into their hand.
—
Bridegrooms keep turning up,
one after another —
in the heart an ache,
on the face shame.
—
The “refreshments” take a stroll,
the very same ones, of course,
from the cupboard to the table,
from the table to the cupboard.
—
The pair of oranges,
almost dried up already,
the witnesses, the mute ones,
of nights “on watch”.
—
The same pistachios,
without any change at all —
youth is already running away,
bridegrooms — still far off.
—
And youth is already running away
like this, year after year, —
on the eldest one's head
a hair is already turning silver.
—
And the oranges
dried out and shrivelled,
pistachios worm-eaten,
the samovar ashamed.
—
It's all just a matter of luck:
who has a diamond,
who has a sixth finger
on the hand.
—
And I have three daughters — —
— — — — — — —
Yiddish: A. L. Pajans.
The Disrupted Simchat Beit HaShoevah

[Hasidic tale — Sukkot.] A terrible tale: how a leaseholder [arendar] came to ask for help from the Shpoler Zeyde [the Grandfather of Szpoła, R. Aryeh Leib of Shpola], who promised him that he would get lashes from the poritz [the landowner]
Once a leaseholder came to the Shpoler Zeyde and related with pleas that the poritz, from whom he holds the lease, wants to evict him from the tavern [kretshme] if he does not bring him two hundred gulden by the first day of Chol HaMoed Sukkot.
Says the Shpoler Zeyde to the leaseholder: And if you do not bring the money, what will he do to you, the poritz?
— What do you mean, what will he do to me? — repeats the leaseholder — I already told the Zeyde: he will throw me out of the village!
— Ay, one doesn't throw out so quickly — says the Shpoler Zeyde, — nowadays one doesn't throw out; at most one gets a few lashes, and so what — nobody dies of that yet...
The leaseholder stands and ponders and does not know what to say: he comes to ask for salvation, and the Shpoler Zeyde promises him lashes... His heart grows very gloomy; he takes his leave and drives home; well, we shall see — what will be, will be. Worse than bad it can no longer be.
The story happened between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Having come home to the village, the leaseholder was afraid to tell his wife what answer he had received from the Rebbe, and he went about very worried. Meanwhile Yom Kippur approaches; the leaseholder drives, as is the custom, into the shtetl for the minyan, and to all who ask him in the shtetl what answer he received from the Shpoler Zeyde, the leaseholder replies that he received no answer at all...
Well, Jews understand from this that the leaseholder must be a great sinner; they shake their heads over his luck, and that's all. Lost — when God wants to punish a person, it is bitter, poor thing...
On Yom Kippur, at prayer, the leaseholder wept very hard and pleaded, and for a whole twenty-four hours did not sit down for a minute to rest. His heart was very sad. Any moment now, another day or two, and the poritz will throw him out of the village — and as if that were not enough, he will also catch lashes. And the proof: the Shpoler had promised it to him, after all...
Ay, the Shpoler Zeyde himself said that one doesn't throw out so easily; well, if he said one doesn't throw out, then surely [?] one doesn't give lashes either...
A leaseholder's logic!
At the end of Yom Kippur the leaseholder drove home to the village and, as is the way of a pious Jew, first of all set about building a sukkah. Well, we shall see; until the first day of Chol HaMoed is still a long way, a miracle may yet happen.
During both first days of Sukkot the leaseholder did not say a word about Simchat Beit HaShoevah; while among Hasidim a whole measure of joy shines, our leaseholder was sunk in gloom, for he is certain he will get lashes and will be evicted from the lease as well — pleading does not help, after all...
But in Shpola the Zeyde sat and saw what was going on...
At the close of the first days of the festival a farmhand [parobek] arrived at the leaseholder's and ordered him to come to the poritz at once, immediately.
When the leaseholder heard this, a great dread fell upon him. Out of sheer fright he even forgot to say goodbye to his wife and children; only on the way to the poritz did he quietly recite the confession [viduy], certain that it was all over for him, because, you must know, in those days such things happened: when a poritz — may no Jew ever suffer it — ordered twenty-five lashes to be given, one could really lose one's life from it...
When he came in to the poritz, the latter lets out a shout at him: You Jew, swindler, what do you imagine — that you won't pay any lease and will sit at your ease? I'll show you what I can do. You so-and-so...
The poritz flew into such a rage that even the farmhands standing around trembled. “Biedny żydek” [Polish: poor little Jew], they whispered quietly to one another — he won't get out of here alive...
The poritz's anger grows greater by the minute. He shouts, stamps his feet; any moment, it seems, he will order the farmhands to lay the Jew down on the flogging bench and send gentiles to the leaseholder's wife and children to throw them out into the street with their few belongings. But it only seems so, because the poritz runs around the room, hurling and throwing himself about, God preserve us, but he does no more than threaten... He rages so long that a fit seizes him; one can see that the whole business has simply become loathsome to him. He no longer has the strength to rage; suddenly he gives a last stamp of his foot and shouts:
— Take the Jew and give it to him...
Everyone was sure he would say at least fifteen lashes, but to everyone's astonishment the word burst from the poritz's mouth: five lashes...
Well, what shall I tell you, the poritz himself was ashamed of the word: five lashes — a big deal, even a child could have withstood such a small punishment. About eviction from the lease he did not drop a single word. Out of shame the poritz ran off; lost — it does not befit him to take back his word; so they lay the Jew down and count them out to him one by one — five lashes, and a wonder: it seemed to the leaseholder that his father was striking him with the strap [kanczuk], such light little lashes — truly nothing at all [“chew and spit”]...
But do you think the story ends with that? It hasn't even begun: after the Jew got down from the flogging bench, the poritz suddenly came in once more and said to the leaseholder:
— Listen here, “żydek”, you caught five lashes. Therefore I give you in return five years of lease free of charge and five years of pasture for the cattle for nothing...
The leaseholder was astonished and dumbfounded. Out of joy he simply could not utter a word; he ran at once to his wife and told her the story, and only now did he tell her the secret: the Shpoler Zeyde had told him in advance that he would get lashes.
Ben-Zion Grinbojm.
The First Pogrom against Jews in Ancient Times. A new chapter of Jewish history of which nothing was known until now.

[Jewish history — antiquity; essay.] By Dr. Z. Kadish.
Until the twentieth century it was believed that the first incitements and pogroms against Jews by an enraged [?] mob took place in Alexandria, which was the largest Jewish community in the world in the times of the Second Temple. Now, however, we know that long before Alexandria was even built there had already been incitement and an attack on Jews in Egypt too — but far in the south of the country.
That first attack on Jews that we know of is a new chapter of Jewish history, which was dug out from under the earth only at the beginning of our century, in Elephantine and in Aswan.
Elephantine is the name of an island in the river Nile, at the very southern border of Egypt. On the bank of the river, on the eastern side, there still lies to this day the old town of Aswan, which is mentioned in Ezekiel ("the tower of Syene", ch. 30, verse 6). Since Greek times the island has borne the name Elephantine, because in former times the main market for the ivory trade was there. For in the southern part of Egypt there used to be many elephants. That island was therefore the centre of the ivory trade — a material from which the Egyptians had made all kinds of costly luxury articles since the most ancient times. In older times the fortified town on this island was the capital and the trading centre of that region. Later Aswan became the main town (the Egyptians called the island "Yeb", because "Yeb" meant an elephant in Egyptian).
It was right here, in Elephantine, that the first attack on Jews in the whole of Jewish history took place, as far as we know it today. Of course, what is meant here are only attacks on Jews in the lands of their dispersion, where they lived among a gentile population.
• • •
The Jewish community in Elephantine and Aswan was a very interesting one. It was a colony of professional Jewish soldiers who served the Egyptian government ("ḥayla yehudaya" — the Jewish force — they are called in the papyri). The members of the colony were obliged to go to war and to guard the Egyptian border on the southern side, next to Ethiopia.
For us today it is hard to imagine Jews who make a living by hiring themselves out as soldiers. In those days, however, Jews were famous as horsemen, archers and fortress guards. When a kingdom wanted capable, reliable soldiers to guard a fortress on a border, it hired Jews for the purpose. As generals and commanders, too, Jews played a great role under the Ptolemies, the Greek kings of Egypt.
The population of Elephantine is divided in the papyri into two classes: "ba‘alei qiryah" and "ba‘alei degel", that is: town citizens and soldiers; the Egyptians were the citizens and the Jews — the soldiers.
When exactly the Jewish military colony in Elephantine was founded we do not know, but most scholars hold that it happened even before the first destruction of Jerusalem, in the time of the Egyptian king Psamtik, the father of Pharaoh Necho, who is mentioned in the Bible.
• • •
The most sensational news, however, that the excavated papyri have brought us is that those Jewish soldiers at the farthest point of southern Egypt had a Temple, in which they offered sacrifices to the Jewish God; and that this Temple was destroyed in a pogrom that took place in Elephantine at the time of the Persian kingdom, when the Persian Empire ruled over the Near East and over Egypt as well.
The pogrom was made by the local inhabitants, the native Egyptians, who had a temple there for the Egyptian god Khnum, and they made it not directly on the Jews, but on their Temple.
Egypt was at that time a province of the Persian Empire, which stretched from India to Ethiopia ("from Hodu to Kush"). A Persian satrap, a governor-general, ruled over the country, and the Egyptians were subjected to a foreign rule. The soldiers of the Elephantine garrison, however, were a privileged class and aroused the hatred and jealousy of the local population, whom they served [?] in Upper Egypt.
Evidently the Egyptians, and especially their leaders, the priests of the god Khnum, looked very askance at the foreign, privileged soldier-colonists of the garrison. There were soldiers of various peoples in the garrison, but the Jews surpassed all the others there in number and importance. Therefore the incitement was directed mostly against them. On top of that, the Jews slaughtered sheep as sacrifices in their Temple at Elephantine, and in many regions of Egypt slaughtering sheep was a great sin. The priests of the god Khnum probably said that the Jews slaughtered rams and goats in their Temple to spite the Egyptians, to desecrate the holiness of their god, who was represented in the form of a he-goat or a ram.
The Jews there were protected by the Persian power, and as long as the Persian satrap was at his post in the capital of Egypt, people were afraid to attack the Jews and their temple. They therefore waited for a suitable opportunity. And the opportunity came in the year 410 before the Christian era, 34 years after Nehemiah had built the wall around Jerusalem.
The Persian satrap of Egypt had then gone away to the Persian capital, to the king; so the priests of the god Khnum fell upon it with an armed mob and smashed and destroyed the Temple of the Jews. It was not hard for them to carry this out, because the governor of Elephantine and the commander of Aswan were hand in glove with them in their conspiracy against the Jews.
It appears that the Persian satrap of Egypt, when he came back, merely punished those guilty of the assault on the Jews, but he did not permit their Temple to be rebuilt, because he did not want to stir up the fanaticism of the pious Egyptians who worshipped the god Khnum. The Jewish community of Elephantine therefore turned to the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem, to the High Priest Johanan and his colleagues (this is the same Johanan who is mentioned in Ezra and Nehemiah).
The Jewish leaders of Jerusalem, however, did not respond to the request of their brethren in Egypt; the Elephantine community therefore sent a second letter to Bagohi, the Persian governor of Judah. In addition, with the same messenger, they also sent a letter to Delaiah and Shelemiah, who are described as sons of "Sanballat, governor of Samaria" [printed "סנאכלעט פחית שמרין"] (Sanballat, the governor of Shomron).
The letters that were sent the second time, simultaneously to Bagohi and to Sanballat's sons, had a good effect. Bagohi and Delaiah strongly interceded with the Persian satrap in Egypt on behalf of the request of the Elephantine Jews; but whether all these efforts achieved their goal, and whether the Persian satrap really permitted the Temple in Elephantine to be rebuilt — that the papyri [printed "פאסירונגען"] do not tell us, and we do not know it.
Incidentally, the Elephantine Jews promised the governor Bagohi a sum of money for the good word he would put in for them with the satrap of Egypt.
Thus a new, remarkable chapter of Jewish history has been dug out from under the earth, of which until now there was not the slightest knowledge.
Lux in tenebris... [Light in the darkness]

[Essay — spiritual poverty in Jewish society.]
We are living through a time when life streams by with such speed that there is truly no time to dwell on questions that are old [?] and have already been dealt with many times, but which demand constant vigilance.
— I want to say a few words here about the spiritual poverty that has seized our little world under the current trademark of "intelligentsia-ness" and also of a specific "secularism".
— Incidentally, I do not wish here to touch at all on this or that political tendency, nor on the multiplicity of languages; the latter I leave to the various "fighters" against "shmendrikism" [shmendrik = a nincompoop] and assimilation, who have sprung up like mushrooms after the rain.
There was a time in our life when a father prided himself on his "vilkenrishe" [?] children, when the bookcase of sacred books occupied the place of honour in every Jewish home — today, however, the place of the former bookcase has remained empty.
— In our life, during the "Sturm und Drang" years after the World War, many bridles were broken, many sanctities were trampled and spat upon in the name of "secularism". But the ruins are far from having been rebuilt and filled with new values.
— One is seized with horror, and it is no secret to any of the leaders of the political tendencies what spiritual emptiness and even political ignorance [am-haaratzut] reign among the broad party masses.
— The youth is far from the book, far from any kind of thinking, and above all the earnestness with which people once used to treat problems and sacrifice themselves to realise them has left them.
— Everything that was once holy, and even what is holy now, has been exchanged for small groszy, cheapened.
— The Sabbath-and-holiday quality has vanished from our life, our struggle and our way of creating. — There has come a chain of grey, overcast years through which not a single ray of morning light penetrates.
— Many will explain this by saying that we live in a twilight time between two cultures, on the edge of two worlds. But here too it must be said that the road to this new life is still long, shrouded in thick darkness. All the more must all those who toil along the stony byways of present-day life let ring out [?] the call to carry light into the darkness.
Lux in tenebris...
Ab. Zh.
On a New Book in Yiddish Literature.

[Book review — Yiddish literature; travel narrative.]
(From the book table)
B. Y. Yahalom
"I Want to Go Home!.." ["Ikh vil aheym!"]
A. Gitlin Publishers,
Warsaw 1932.
The author's name is a new one, and the book he has brought into Yiddish literature is his first debut. But it is enough to read through the first few chapters and one is at once drawn into the countless travel pictures of the Orient with which the book is full.
What does the new, unknown writer tell us in this book? And does he have anything to tell at all?
It is the story of a young Jewish wanderer who, after spending some time in the Land of Israel, after various kinds of physical labour, nevertheless could not acclimatise, and without a grosz in his pocket set off to wander across the wide world. And it is only here that all the hard experiences, dangers and adventures of the young vagabond begin.
Right at his first departure from the Land of Israel, while still riding in the train that cuts through the desert to Egypt, he is detained by an Egyptian official; unable to show to whom he is travelling, he is taken off the train in the middle of the desert and driven by a black policeman to the only hut, ringed with wire, which serves as a lock-up for thieves, robbers and tramps. And when, exhausted, after long hours of trudging through the glowing sands of the desert, he is brought into the dark hut and falls down broken and exhausted, he is woken in the middle of the night by a pitiful howling of jackals which have burst into the hut by the dozen, smelling food. That is the first reception.
Later, when he is released from prison and steals aboard a ship standing ready to sail in the nearby port, he is detained as a "stowaway", and now the police will no longer let him go. Taking him for a dangerous criminal, he is thrown from one ship to another and no port will let him in.
Always half-hungry, never having slept enough, eaten through by wind, cold and damp at night and scorched by the eastern sun by day, but brave enough and strong in himself, neither broken nor fallen — from quarantine to prison there unroll before our eyes, as on a film, countless people, lives, foreign ways of life, encounters, clashes and brotherly devotion, which only need itself can in certain cases bring people closer to one another.
Touching is the picture when he has already been sitting for three days in a [prison in] Cairo without food, without drink, and nobody even looks at him, and only now does something happen: the homeless vagabond, the wanderer [na-ve-nadnik], bent down, and from his patched pocket fell two photographs of his father and mother — the father a dignified Jew with a venerable face, the mother too makes a good impression — and these pictures bring about a reversal in the attitude of the warder toward the prisoner: he orders him released at once and given something to eat. The author tells us that while the police officer stood and looked respectfully at the photographs of the prisoner's parents, he asked himself without words:
"Are the father's pleading [?] eyes now interceding for his child? Does the mother's tender look move him to have pity on her flesh and blood? Yes, their mute lips speak... One hears their weeping voices from afar... Across distant seas and mountains the looks and the sounds penetrate, as if they were pleading for their child who is so far away and lonely."
The merit of the book is that the writer has not "over-literarised" his work; in simple, healthy [?] and flowing language he gives us in compressed form pictures of all these various experiences and struggles, of hunger, thirst, pain, which hardened him enough — for example the picture in Cairo, where the police want to lead him forcibly [?] through the streets in chains, and when ten policemen throw themselves on him to lead him by force — he stretches himself out to his full length and they have to carry him.
As already said above, the book is written very warmly, vividly; it works through the plain truth that breathes from every page, and we follow the narrator with quiet suspense, very often delighting in the fine short nature sketches that the author has scattered here and there.
If one is to reproach anything, one must reproach the author for having given it a very unsuccessful title. The title says nothing. The book absolutely deserves a fine title, and in the second edition the author should bear this in mind.
Yiddish literature has gained a fine, vividly written book that deserves to be read by everyone.
G. Sternberg, Warsaw.
“Der Pitum” — Humour and Satire in Honour of Sukkot by Ben Amotz: Laws of the Sukkah

[Humorous feuilleton — “Der Pitum”, for Sukkot.] Temporary dwellings.
The essence of the sukkah is temporariness. And the essence of Jewish life is also temporariness.
Jewish wealth, Jewish livelihoods are only for the time being; a Jew is rich only as long as the “urząd” [the (tax) office] does not find out his address...
Present-day trade, too, is indeed only for the time being: when taking a parcel of goods one puts on a serious face, signs the bills of exchange with devotion, and until the due dates arrive — one goes bankrupt in the meantime...
Blessing the etrog.
All through Sukkot one blesses the etrog — one blesses it that it may live out its eight days, and a hole in the head [i.e. and nothing more].
The etrog must be taken with clean hands, and those who do not have clean hands, namely the “ro'ares” [?], who have shown that one “needs” the little shochtim [?] — must not be trusted with the etrog in their hands...
Putting up sukkahs.
The “tshvok” [the nail, i.e. the crux] of the sukkah is the peg; no great work is involved, one only has to be well organised so that the “enemy” has no strength — and the peg already sits firm.
A sukkah consists of four walls. One may also make use of a neighbour's “blind” wall; but if that neighbour is a sympathiser of the Arabs and a reader of the little “Folkstsaytung” [the Bundist paper], better not to start with him. A great quarrel may yet grow out of that “wall”.
What I Wish...

[Humorous feuilleton — “Der Pitum”, New Year wishes.] To the “Agudah” [Agudat Yisrael] “be-be” I wish, in the name of “Ma'avar Yabok” [the burial-society prayer book],
that our teacher R' Rubinlicht may sniff Gerer snuff,
eat liver with onion every Sabbath,
and in time to come be gabbai in the big Gerer shtibl.
To “Beth Jacob” I wish that, besides morals and ethics,
the girls be taught the Torah of cosmetics too,
so that they please the starosta [district head].
Therefore my blessing is a simple one:
Holy “panny” [young ladies]! You are, after all,
like a golden watch
with a diamond chain —
may you merit wearing a waved [ondulé] wig.
To walk in the ways of your “nauczycielka” [teacher],
to be with G-d “Shmelke shebeshmelke” [?],
to speak Polish like the editor of “Żydowskie Echo”
and be called Natasza — instead of Gecha.
To the “Hitachdut” and “Gordonia”
I wish with irony
that their party
get two more lawyers [printed “arvokatn”, misprint for “advokatn”].
To “Hashomer Hatzair” (though ideologically I am far from them)
I wish them in Hebrew:
Towards the social revolution — be strong and of good courage!
To Betar I send to its place,
since I am, after all, somewhat of the circle:
may Psachowan [?] hear “sergeant” under the command of Weisel [?]
in the Jewish Legion.
Now — pardon,
I am already tired as a fly;
next year we shall improve —
today is enough...
Z. I—k.
Polish Grammar. A Lesson for the Young Ladies of Zagłębie in Honour of Sukkot

[Humorous feuilleton — “Der Pitum”, language and women.] Seeing how our daughters, poor things, break their teeth speaking Polish and wage a merciless war with grammar, “Der Pitum” has decided to teach the Zagłębie “panny” [young ladies] the science of grammar.
Etymology and syntax.
When a wife says to her husband: “Apostate, treyfnyak, kiełbasa, may-his-name-be-blotted-out, good-for-nothing, shlimazl” — that is called “etymology”. But when she says, for example: “May you be my atonement, for me and for all Israel, amen” — that is called “syntax”.
The three genders.
There are three genders: masculine, feminine and neuter (“rodzaj męski, żeński i nijaki”); e.g. “żona” [wife] is “rodzaj żeński”, “przyjaciel domu” [friend of the house] — “rodzaj męski”, and “kino” — “rodzaj nijaki”. But what will “żona z przyjacielem domu w kinie” [the wife with the friend of the house at the cinema] be? — That will be “rodzaj ordynarny” [the vulgar gender].
Elements of speech.
Our language divides into various elements, such as: main words [nouns], side words [adverbs], time words [verbs] and vulgar words:
For a young man who gets engaged out of love, the main word is “dowry”, “bride” is a side word and “wedding” is a time word: he has time to get married.
For a deputy, a “concession” is the main word, “the public good” a side word, and “Sejm” a time word: he sees it every first of the month.
Nouns divide into concrete and abstract. Concrete nouns are those one can see, and abstract ones those one cannot see; e.g. when the Sosnowiec municipality builds a sewer system, the “hills”, “holes” and “swamps” are concrete nouns and “sewer system” is an abstract noun; when the Będzin kehilla takes “dollars” on the little shochtim, that is a concrete noun. For the Zagłębie textile merchants, “bill of exchange” is a concrete noun and “money” an abstract noun. For our Zagłębie “mężatki” [married women], “rekolt” [misprint for “dekolt”, décolletage] is a concrete noun and “modesty” an abstract noun.
The Będzin “panny” have their own division of our words; with them it goes like this: “dżeczownik” [garbled “rzeczownik”, noun], spódnik, paskudnik, klinek i tak dalej [and so on].
Issued by our Chair of Grammar at the “Mockery” [?] University of Prof. Józek.

A Jewish woman sits and prays: “Master of the Universe, see to it that my neighbour Pesele has a good livelihood, that she should never lack money.”
Another woman asks: — Why are you praying so for the neighbour?
— In the whole building — the woman answers — there is no one to grab an interest-free loan from except Pesele; and if she too has nothing, what will become of us?...
2.
Another Jewish woman sits and prays: “Master of the Universe, dear Father, see to it that my sister-in-law in America grows fat and broad.”
Another woman asks her: — Why are you praying so for your American sister-in-law?
— Every year she sends me a parcel of old clothes, and they are narrow and tight on me...
3.
A widow sits on the eve of Yom Kippur on her husband's grave and cries: “My dear husband! You went away and left me alone. At least one comfort has remained to me: at least I know where you spend your nights...”

Sleep, my child, my comfort, my dear one,

Ay, lyu—lyu—lyu.

Your mother is an official
At the rich skarb [state treasury],
Runs around like one poisoned,
Gathers basket to basket[?]

Until she scrapes a sum together
She has no rest,
So as to come with it to the treasury,
Ay, lyu—lyu—lyu.

— Sleep — for you money is still mud,
I carry you in my arms,
You know nothing of the crisis surcharge,
You need no trade licence.

You sequestrator, you!
Again you open your eyes,
Ay, lyu—lyu—lyu.

Never may I forget
That I carry a yoke,
Never slept enough, never eaten enough,
Only pay, pay and pay!

How much blood and time I squander,
All that I run and do!
Sleep — or I'll call the sequestrator,
Ay, lyu—lyu—lyu.

The Pedigree of the Etrog.
Why is the etrog the most important of the 'four species'? After all it is just one on its own, while the lulav has two more belonging to it: the myrtles with the willows. Nevertheless, people make a whole to-do about the etrog; one does not ask, 'Have you already said the blessing over the lulav?', but precisely, 'Have you already said the blessing over the etrog?'
That is why it is a man of pedigree — because it is not bound up with the 'Agudah' [pun: the lulav's binding and the Agudat Israel party].

As we have already written, next Tuesday, the 2nd day of Chol HaMoed, the official[?] [opening] of the orphanage on Sienkiewicz[?] Street („Shenkevitsh gas“) will take place.
At Tuesday's meeting, held under the chairmanship of President Dr. Weinzieher, the programme of the festive opening was set.
Invited to the opening, besides representatives of the municipal and administrative authorities, are also those who helped the building with their donations.
Since great interest is expected from the Jewish public, the building committee has decided to point out to those not invited that they will be able to visit the premises on the same day and also on the following days; one should therefore hold back and not insist on being at the opening, because the hall is not big enough to hold hundreds of people.
In connection with the opening, the head (kierownik) of Public School No. 2 approached the heads of the other Jewish public (powszechne) schools with a proposal that the day be proclaimed „the Day for Orphans“.
The proposal was accepted with satisfaction by the teaching staff, and a programme for the „Orphans' Day“ is being worked out.
Among other things it was also decided that every child must donate a few groszy to the „Beit HaYetomim“. So let Jewish parents not forget on Tuesday morning to give their children the modest donations for this purpose.

The Fröbel school „Gan Yeladim“, which was founded in our town on the initiative of the women's association „WIZO“, is being run from the new school year by a first-class Fröbel teacher who has great merits in this field. The Fight over the Slaughtering Post in Pogoń
A Będzin shochet sits locked up for several hours in the police station
Last Friday an incident took place in Pogoń which illustrates how far the lawlessness in the field of shechita has already gone.
For quite some time now the Będzin shochet R' Berish Makower has not been content with his fixed pension of 8,500 złoty a year, and comes to Pogoń, where he slaughters poultry in secret.
The local Jewish Community, which is wronged by this, has already warned the shochet several times through the press, and sent a protest to the starosta and to the voivode, but R' Berish the shochet stops at nothing and comes to encroach on the territory of the Pogoń shochet.
The slaughtering naturally takes place secretly, because the Pogoń police, informed by the interested party, had their eye on him and had indeed already drawn up several reports.
The finale of the secret shechita took place last Friday morning: as soon as R' Berish arrived in Pogoń he was arrested by the police, and after the first "cut" he was led away, escorted by three policemen, to the police station, where after many interventions he was released only at 12 noon.
The arrest, however, did not yet stop the shochet from coming to Pogoń; on Saturday night, the eve of Yom Kippur, at the time when the crush at the kaporos slaughtering in Będzin was enormous, at a time when children were being crushed in the throng, R' Berish again travelled to Pogoń to slaughter kaporos...
The "work" was this time disturbed; a "strong hand" took up the slaughtering question this time and —
R' Berish went back to Będzin.

Thefts

Jews Beaten
Hooliganism is so strongly developed in Zawiercie that at night it is impossible to go out into the street. Jewish Society Must Not Tolerate This!
(A letter to the editor)
As everyone knows, there exists in Będzin an association by the name of „Muza“. I will not dwell here on the merits of this association, because that is not within my competence; I only wish to report to the Jewish public the deeds of the persons who have the audacity to come to Jewish society for support.
It happened this past Yom Kippur, when in the premises of „Muza“ a great feast was prepared with all the trimmings; they ate, drank and caroused like real drunkards, so that the Jewish neighbours in the building should see and hear their „anti-religious demonstration“...
When I, as the owner of the building, and several tenants reacted against such base licentiousness, we were met with the vilest curses and abuse, as befits „cultured people“.
Still more regrettable is that the Yom Kippur feast was attended also by those who call themselves „Right Poale Zion“; these people too openly revelled and made merry at the ball...
No, such licentiousness must not be tolerated, and Jewish society must not forget it.
Respectfully,
Chaim Gotfried (house owner).

A Jewish woman with small children left under the open sky after an eviction by the Magistrat

A Jewish woman with small children wanders under the open sky because of an eviction by the Magistrat.
In a flat on Podzamcze. Street in Będzin, Mrs. Strupel[?] lived for many years with her four small children.
The building commission of the Będzin Magistrat (municipality) determined that the flat was about to collapse, but instead of providing the poor, unprotected family with another flat, it evicted her out onto the street, and they wander about without a roof over their heads.
