The First Days of Sukkot in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — Sukkot; synagogues.] This year's "Season of our Rejoicing" began "stormily" in the Sosnowiec synagogue. The 13-year-old chorister Nunberg [?] wanted to lead the first evening (Maariv) service. In his honour a large Hasidic crowd came to the synagogue. The gabbais, however, dug in their heels and did not let the boy lead the prayers. As a result a scandal broke out, with... blows, from which the antisemitic newspapers derived great satisfaction...
—
In the Będzin synagogue it was not quiet either. The difference is this: in the Sosnowiec synagogue people fought over a boy who wanted to lead the prayers, while in Będzin the worshippers stormed because Mr. Danziger refused to lead the prayers over a few złoty which the kehilla did not want to pay out.
—
A pretty "flower" is presented to us by a group of tenants of the house at 3 Maja Street 12 in Dąbrowa. The Jewish landlord of the house has, as is the custom, disputes with his tenants, and he decided to take "revenge" on them precisely on Friday evening, the first night of Sukkot.
To avoid unpleasantness, some of the tenants waited until the landlord had left the sukkah after his meal, and then they went into the sukkah, which, incidentally, was the only one in the house.
But the landlord had an answer to this too. He "delegated" his Christian maidservant into the sukkah, where, during the tenants' meal, she put out the candles and also wanted to remove the tablecloth...
That was not yet the end of it. During the meal a stone "flew" into the sukkah and hit Cukrowski on the head...
Who the stone-thrower was is not clear. But be that as it may, the Jewish residents of the street had something to talk about...

Exhibition of "Hashomer Hatzair"

[Sosnowiec — youth movements; culture.] (S.) On Sunday the 16th of this month, in the presence of an honorary committee consisting of Messrs. Dr. S. Melodysta [?], W. Stawski, B. Tencer and A. Chlewicki [?], the exhibition of "Hashomer Hatzair" was opened in the premises of the Sosnowiec "Merchants' Association" (Kowalska 2).
The ceremony is opened by Zvi Fergricht, and Messrs. Dr. S. Melodysta and B. Tencer give speeches on topical matters.
The choir under the direction of Boruszykowski [?] sings several Hebrew and Yiddish songs. Miss Hinda Jasna also sang a very successful solo with guitar accompaniment.
Dr. S. Melodysta cuts the ribbon and the guests move on to the second hall, where the exhibition is located.
The exhibition shows that among the members of "Hashomer Hatzair" (mostly young children) there are several talents who, after proper training, could grow into artists; unfortunately the organisation "Hashomer Hatzair" does not have the material means to support the beginners.
Thus, for example, Boroykowski [?] stands out with his portrait paintings, which are very successful (great acclaim went to the portrait of the well-known Cukerman — the shammes of the German synagogue in Sosnowiec. (The portrait was indeed soon sold), very beautiful and successful are the sculptures by Gliksman, as well as the geological collections of Shlomo Strauch. There are also various handicrafts, clowns (puppets), embroidery work, etc.
At the exhibition a prominent place is also taken by diagrams, pictures and statistics of "Tarbut", Keren Kayemet and of the Shomer movement.
The exhibition is a success and admission is free.

From Sport.

„Hakoach“ — „Maccabi“ 1:1 (half-time 0;1).
Despite the cold weather this match drew a fairly large crowd. „Hakoach“ took the field without Rosen I, „Maccabi“ without Prachtzweig and Schmid (the latter is said to have withdrawn from active sport altogether).
From the very start „Hakoach“ had a slight superiority, and so it stayed until the 20th minute. The „Hakoach“ forwards fatally missed many sure chances. Only in the 30th minute did the „Hakoach“ forwards manage to carry out a fine attack, from which Richter shot a splendid goal. „Hakoach“ leads 1:0. „Maccabi“ replies with several counter-attacks, but the attacks are not dangerous.
After half-time „Hakoach“ again has a great superiority, but they cannot by any means score a goal because of the brilliant play of the „Maccabi“ goalkeeper Hirsch and the defender Radzik. In this match Hirsch proved that he is one of the best goalkeepers in Zagłębie, and „Maccabi“ owes it to him alone that it came out of the match with a draw.
For unsporting behaviour on the field Beryl Szywek is sent off by the referee and „Hakoach“ plays with 10 men. „Maccabi“ carries out several attacks, and from one such attack „Maccabi“ shoots the equaliser.
Despite the efforts of both teams nobody succeeds in changing the score.
Referee Moszkowicz — very good.
The match „Hakoach“ — „Sarmacja“, which was to have taken place on Sunday, did not take place because of the downpour that lasted a whole day. For the same reasons the tennis tournament did not take place either.
W—ski.

How Do We Save Ourselves?

[Zagłębie — economy and taxes; article.]
(The bitter situation has already reached its culmination point. — Necessity breaks iron. — What next?)
We live in very hard conditions nowadays. The economic problems are so worrying[?], the worry for tomorrow — or, more correctly said, for today — is so heavy, that nobody could even have dreamt that it would take up so much of the time of our everyday worries[?].
We could not have imagined that we would ever have to spend so much strength before we see the clean groszy earned[?] for a piece of bread.
Once, when the petty burgher earned something, he knew that the "something" that fell into his hands through his hard toil was there for his loaf of bread. Today all this has changed radically. Today, when he earns his few groszy, he still[?] has nothing to eat, because first of all he has not fulfilled his civic duties, and these civic duties are so heavy, so complicated, that there is no way he can carry them on his exhausted shoulders.
For first of all such a citizen has all kinds of taxes: government, municipal, etc. It goes without saying that one cannot demand of him that he pay them punctually and honestly on the due date, because, firstly, he is helpless. He does not remember when and what he has to pay; and secondly, even if he did know, he is not in a position to meet his obligations according to the regulations, for material reasons alone: he does not earn even for the barest necessities, the day goes by and he and his family have to go half-hungry. So how can one demand of such a person that he be able to meet his civic obligations according to even the most minimal regulations, which, by the way, are very, very complicated, and from which one can never get out?
Granted, the larger firms, those that keep clerks and run offices, are at least in a position to deal with tax questions and to see to complying with them according to the proper regulations and all sorts of supplementary ordinances. But what are they to do, those who are not in a position to employ clerks and who run their businesses somehow on the smallest scale, in the most minimal way? How are they to comply with and fulfil the most varied tax regulations and all sorts of supplementary ordinances, which are already so obscured, so complicated, that with the best will and the most energetic efforts one cannot extricate oneself from them and be sure that everything has been fulfilled according to law and custom. Not to mention when one's head is spinning and there is still nothing to pay the little bill of exchange with.
The world says that necessity breaks iron. We know that there are such citizens who first of all saw to it that they were in order with their tax affairs; they trembled before the bailiff (tax executor). They did not want to set eyes on him, and so they carried the first guldens (złoty) to the Treasury (skarb) and to the magistrate (municipality), and what was left after that was handed to the housewife for household use, for domestic expenses. But all this was good once, when one earned and there was something to pay the imposed taxes with; but what now, when the situation has changed so enormously that earnings have shrunk to a minimum, and in parallel with these minimal earnings the tax expenses have, on the contrary, grown steadily? How then could this honest citizen adapt himself to conditions that are abnormal for him and still meet his civic obligations concerning taxes? How could he pay one tax after another, one instalment after the other, when he went about idle and empty-handed and forgot that he has a business in which a groszy of real cash is supposed to come in; and if he gave the goods on bills of exchange, he was certain that after the few weeks had passed he would see a protest; and in general, how could this small, more or less average citizen give away his goods on unsafe bills, which, even if they actually had been paid, — since for all his expenses he had to have cash: bread and meat and the cheder fees and the taxes and for the flat and for water and light, for everything he needed live guldens — one understands how hard it was for him until he got money for these bills. How much he had to lose on the bills, which were supposedly as good as cash. For today there is no bank where he would have credit and where he could go in to discount his little portfolios of bills. So that, however careful he tried to be, he had to end up at the "bas"[?], at the usurers, and they already laid him out on the salting bench, and he had to dance as they played for him, since, having no choice, he had no other way out. So what was he to do? What way out did he have once he saw that the slaughter-knife was lying on his neck and already choking him; and then one understands what his earnings could look like, when the cream had been skimmed off by usury.
And here came the ruin: how could he in such a period honour the Treasury and all the other taxes, when the situation was such that he had nothing to get through the day with, and when he sold his bit of goods there was a loss instead of a profit, even when the bill actually was paid. And in comparison with all this, in comparison with the hardest living conditions of the average citizen, which changed enormously from day to day for the worse, to the most catastrophic, the tax matters, on the contrary, grew and became more complicated in such a way that great lawyers and famous jurists state that they cannot make head or tail of them, that they cannot chew them through.
Yes, necessity, says the world, breaks iron; and when these downtrodden citizens of all classes and sorts were already utterly crushed and had no way out any longer, they had to drop the reins. So that they were no longer[?] in a position to observe and pay punctually their taxes, which swelled in the blink of an eye into colossal sums, and to pay them has therefore remained a fantasy. And nowadays this citizen cannot wash himself clean of all sorts of taxes, which weigh on him like a heavy press, and consequently he cannot trade and run his business on a normal basis either. The situation has thus now reached its culmination point, and if no way out is found that would rescue the citizens from this dangerous situation, things are very bad indeed.
Willy-nilly, the big question mark arises: what do we do next? How do we rescue ourselves from the dangerous situation in which we have been so tightly clamped?
It goes without saying that finding a way out is anything but easy; we have already sunk so deep into the depths of the witches' wheels that one cannot conceive how one will ever be able to get out of the dangerous depths into which life, the conditions of life and the situation have hurled mankind. Yet one must not remain indifferent to all this.
After all, we are a people of patience and endurance, of hope and initiative — so let us awaken and rise up to the bright light. Enough have our suffering and weak languished in the dark want, of whom broken shards have been made and who have remained incapable of work, incapable of adapting to the existing, prevailing conditions of life. And yet we cannot remain standing as if between heaven and water, unable to breathe, unable to continue[?] the thread of life.
Is our whole society really to be so dulled that there will no longer be anyone to cry out to, anyone to wake, anyone in whom to arouse feelings of mercy and compassion? One must after all use every possible means so that those elements awaken which must stand on guard and protect the interests of the people, the interests of the citizens who live beyond natural strength, beyond human understanding.
— One must therefore think seriously about how we can be rescued from the difficult situation into which we have been drawn.
R. Lew.
A Little Letter to a Będziner in Bucharest

[Feuilleton — a letter to Bucharest.] II.
And so, my dear friend, I am writing you this second letter in reply to the letter I wrote to you in the "Zagl. Tsayt." [Zaglembier Tsaytung]. You write to me about the fiasco of Ludwig Zakh's [probably the actor Ludwig Satz] latest guest tour; truly, he fully deserved it. Let it be underlined once and for all that artists of broad scope, people who have something to say, should not misuse their talent and bring nonsense before the public; above all, the American star-advertising is coming to an end — it no longer has any success with us.
Next you ask me how things are going here in the world of literature and art. As for literature, you already know the Romanian joke "ki kli" (meaning: everything head-down). By the way, I am the only one who has just published, like an "only child", a book of my own called "Tablets of a Gypsy", in which I showed that besides the tablets given on Mount Sinai there are tablets given in Bucharest by the Gypsies on the Kiseleff Chaussée, and may I have such a year as those tablets are good; for secretly singing a Gypsy song and planting a robber's kiss on a girl or a woman in the middle of "Calea Victoriei" is also a very good commandment.
Further, I now recall the swimming baths, that is, the year-round "canopies" [beach tents] of "Mamaia" at Constanța on the Black Sea.
I have worked all this into my book "Tsigayner Fleyt" [?]. In the Writers' Association, however, they say it is the best book I have written to date, because today the world holds by wine and women more than ever.
You ask me about art? I can report to you — and you should pass it on to all the theatre people in Bucharest — that the theatre season is in full swing, the papers are full of advertisements for all sorts of "dishes": revues, dramas, folk plays, and perhaps the new year will bring something in that direction; I am, as always, a strong sceptic. And now a little economics — it is now just before the holiday.
The Warsaw market squares and shop windows are truly full of every good thing: oranges, grapes, bananas, fish and meat; the crowd pushes its way there, but instead of coming into the shop it stands outside with worried looks and gazes in through the window like someone who has been flogged.
You are surely interested to know, my friend, what our kehillas are doing at present?
Oh, they are doing a lot. They are now renovating mikvehs, refreshing bathhouses and quarrelling over which of the dead communal workers in the Warsaw cemetery should get a tombstone first.
Otherwise everything goes on as usual. Except for one small piece of news: the kehillas have started awarding literary prizes. But I fear this is only some seasonal work, a fashion, a cold that will last a while, and perhaps the Będzin kehilla will catch this cold too (truly, I wish the Będzin kehilla that, if it is fated to catch a cold, then rather than wanting day and night to provide people with a mikveh and a bath, it should catch the literary-prize disease from Warsaw).
That is, for now, the most important thing I wanted to answer you and all the poor emigrants in Bucharest who would like to receive greetings from here.
Now I hear that in Bucharest, on the Jewish lower street "Calea Văcărești", they have taken down the witchcraft machines — that is, Jewish girls no longer go to the sorcerers to ask whether they will marry this year or not; that the Spanish [Sephardi] synagogue has stopped holding confirmations for thirteen-year-old Jewish girls; and that Bucharest will soon live to have a Jewish newspaper, at the head of which will stand our dear friend, the former editor of "Unzer Lebn" in Warsaw, S. Hochberg. Do give him my best regards, and greet Sternberg if you like.
I also ask you to convey my heartfelt greetings to the members of the Russian Club in Bucharest, with the wish that they truly spread the Yiddish word.
Warm regards to your dear wife.
———
The letter is addressed to: Hershile Tenenboym, Mihail Ginka [?] 75, Bucharest.
In Honour of Sukkot

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the last days of Sukkot — collected and styled by Yehuda.
Hoshana Rabba, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah
a) Why we beat the hoshanot
The four species symbolise the strata of the people. The etrog has taste and smell — corresponding to the elite of the people; the lulav has taste and no smell — corresponding to the charitable, who however have no "smell" of Torah; the myrtle has smell and no taste — corresponding to those who possess Torah without good deeds; the willow has neither taste nor smell — corresponding to the dregs of the people.
From all four species one has some pleasure: this one smells, that one has taste. Only the willow is empty, without taste and without smell — but for that very reason it has a voice: on Hoshana Rabba it makes itself heard...
A parable — to what may this be likened?
To that ox and the rooster who stood in the stable. The rooster began to crow. The ox asked him: "Why are you crowing?"
"I'm hungry," answers the rooster. "I'm hungry too," answers the ox, "and yet I don't shout."
— "The story is this," answers the rooster. "You, ox, cost a lot of money, you are important, and even if you keep silent the master will remember you. I, a rooster — if I don't shout, they will forget about me"...
So with the willow. The simple man must always make himself heard, because otherwise he will be forgotten...
Ezrat Yisrael.
b) A scientific reason
An original scientific reason for beating the hoshanot is reported in the name of the well-known scholar A. S. Hirschberg, who received the prize of the Warsaw kehilla for his work on the Talmudic era.
The ancient peoples regarded the willow as a goddess of the earth's fertility. In a year of famine they kissed the willow and prayed to it to wet the earth and make it fertile, and they called their land "Erev" after the name of their goddess: arava (willow).
This custom prevailed in Egypt, and therefore at the Feast of Ingathering — the festival of gathering in the crops (see Sukkah 44), when praying for rain — they beat with willows, to show that it is not the willow that bestows rain and fertility.
c) Rejoice and be glad on Simchat Torah
If only one side is happy at a celebration, it is a bad sign. "Rejoice and be glad on Simchat Torah": that you rejoice with the Torah — that is still too little. See to it that the Torah should rejoice too... that she too should have reason to be merry with you...
Rabbi David Fajans (Białystok).
d) The sacrifice of Shemini Atzeret.
Seventy sacrifices do Jews bring during all seven days of Sukkot, for the seventy nations. Only after we have already taken care of everyone, have sacrificed for all the nations of the world, do we bring on Shemini Atzeret a sacrifice for ourselves alone... For ourselves we sacrifice last of all, and sometimes in the end — not at all...
Hegyonot ha-RaMaH.
e) Atzeret
To rejoice is indeed a mitzvah the whole festival. But the pleasure is bound up with a mitzvah: with the sukkah, with the lulav. When the last days come, there is only joy without any mitzvah at all. So precisely then one must take stock. "Atzru alai" (hold back for Me) — don't gallop away...
Ktav Sofer.
Kohelet
f) They sought to hide away the Book of Ecclesiastes.
"The sages sought to hide away the Book of Ecclesiastes... And why did they not hide it away? Because its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah" (Shabbat 30).
Does that mean that because the beginning is good and the end is good they did not hide away Kohelet, although in the middle there are things that are not right?
Kohelet's words are incomprehensible only to ordinary people. And these people in any case learn only the beginning and the end... They skip from "in the sight of all Israel" and start again at "In the beginning". More than that they don't learn anyway..
R' Zvi Wolf of Goniądz.
g) One generation passes away and another comes.
Just like that swindler who deals in counterfeit goods: he carries them from town to town, because if he stays long in one town it will turn out that the clothes people made from his goods are already torn. So he must keep clearing out of the town where he made his takings.
That is his miracle — the Evil Inclination's: "one generation passes away and another comes" — before a man can convince himself that he has gone astray all his life, he already dies.
Kol Yaakov.
h) A man to whom God gives riches and wealth.
First he praises "the man to whom God has given", for that one is content with his lot — "a man to whom He gave", the one who is satisfied with what he has been given. Unhappy is only the one "to whom He will give", who always wants to be given anew, for whom everything is too little...
Kli Yakar.
i) And I find the woman more bitter than death.
Of a good wife it is said: "Whoso findeth (matza) a wife findeth a good thing" — matza, past tense. Of a bad one it is said: "u-motze" (and I find) — present tense, because the bad is felt all the time... To the good one quickly grows accustomed, but the bad is felt every moment...
The Vilna Gaon.
j) Riches kept for their owner to his hurt.
If "riches are kept for their owner" — if the wealth is guarded for its owner himself, if[?] he himself does not want to enjoy it — that is a sign that it is "to his hurt", that he acquired the wealth by dishonest means. He does not want to enjoy it, because he himself feels subconsciously that it is not honest, that it is not his...
The Dubno Maggid.
Jewish Troubles (A Short Feuilleton)

I tell you, if a week of aggravation is fated, it comes into the house by itself. My heart told me right at the start of the week that something was going to happen.
And sure enough, a little chain of aggravating events soon began to weave itself.
In the morning, I've barely opened the shop when the door bursts open noisily and a gentile lad in a little cap walks in without a "good morning" and fires off: — "Prąd przerwany!" [Polish: "Power cut off!"]
In my great surprise I didn't even understand what he meant, but I soon realised that yesterday we had been late at the cash desk of the power station (elektrownia), and this morning someone had gone to pay. Meanwhile the paid bill is brought in to me. But the lad won't hear of anything: disconnected is disconnected, and he shouts as if swearing by all that's holy!
While he is still speaking, in comes a "briefcase" (an official).
— Good morning — good morning, what's up[?]
— I have come to inform you that yesterday you did not pay the advance (zaliczka).
A little while passes; the postman comes in with a letter. I read: from a provincial customer.. Since he owes taxes, and under the new law they can search him in the street and take whatever he has on him, he was afraid to go to the bank with money to pay the bill of exchange, and the bill went back with a protest. Even very logical. But what do I get out of it? Meanwhile I have a protest.
First thing, I run off to pour out all my wrath at the power station. Such a scandal! All the time paid punctually, just once late at the cash desk by a few minutes — and already they order: pay a fine!
I come into the office of the power station — packed full of people. All with the same complaints and shouting, but it doesn't help: one weeps and pays the fine.
At the end of the week, I was just busy with a customer, when an elegantly dressed young man comes into my shop with a fat wallet (portfel) and a little suitcase in his hand. I immediately recognised in him the type of the travelling salesman (wojażer), surely from a Łódź firm.
I excuse myself, a little busy, and ask him to sit down. Meanwhile he examines the shelves, feels through the goods like an expert. I think to myself: oh well, let him fill the shelves with his goods — only one mustn't rush to give him the order; let him beg a little, get better terms.
— Well, now I have time for you, — I go up to him with courage (kuraż). — From which firm?
— What do you mean, from which firm? From the Urząd Skarbowy [tax office]!
I stand there as if doused with cold water.
— For the advance that you have not paid, I have distrained the shelf of goods, and you are not allowed to sell it.
He left me a writ and went away.
After such a week — I lived to see the Sabbath. I want to forget all my troubles, so I take up the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" to have a look at what's new with us.
But wherever I cast my eye — everywhere Jewish troubles. It seems to me as if I were in a house full of mirrors, and wherever I look, everywhere I see only myself.
Oh well, a trouble shared by many is indeed half a consolation, but where does one get the other half of the consolation?
Michel Sztupler

The Moment Missed

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — satirical poem; a Hoshana Rabba legend.]
(A Hoshana Rabba legend)
By Ma-Yafis.

Between the Euphrates and the river Tigris
stand seven date palms, —
there an assembly
of communal activists gathered.

Guardians of the public, who hold
the reins of the nation in their hands,
sat down to devise
counsel for the people of Israel.

Speakers gave reports there
and debates were held there:
this one says “no”, and that one says “yes” —
and there is still no money.

And great men,
experts and connoisseurs,
proposed many[?] plans —
each one finer than the next;
[—]
And the need grows by the hour,
and the counsels grow too —
and there is still no money...

So they sat
seven days and seven nights,
and what remained, unanimously,
was a resolution — that things are bad! —

At last it was proposed:
on Hoshana Rabba at twelve at night,
when the heavens split open
and are opened for prayers,
one should lie in wait for the moment,
the fateful moment,
and cry in a prayer,
as is needed for the community.

One should ask “kol tuv” [all good] for the Jews,

and the angel up in heaven
will surely know what is needed.
But it is easier said than done...
Easy to say: “be content”! —
There is, thank God, a language question
even among Jews. —

And in voting on the question
a hot battle broke out:
it was only after the evening prayer
on the night of Hoshana Rabba.

At once half a dozen
left-wing speakers stepped forward
and demanded that one cry
not “kol tuv” but “aldos guts” [Yiddish: all good]!

— Down — they boiled —
with the dead language of the siddur!
“Kol tuv” is dark reaction,
“aldos guts” in Yiddish, brothers!

The other side defended
precisely the “kol tuv” resolution,
they quarrelled, cursed each other,
and wallowed as in mud.

And midnight draws nearer, nearer,
here — the last moments are flowing.. —
Flim-flam! And a sword of fire
tore through the heavens.

And the angel up above
heard a torrent of abuse:
— Ham[?]!... Reactionary!... Traitor!..
and the moment was gone...

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Festive Opening of the Jewish Orphans' Home in Będzin

[Head of the local page; Będzin — welfare and philanthropy.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, H.R. [Hoshana Rabba][?] / 21 Tishrei 5693 — piątek 21 października 1932 [Friday, 21 October 1932].)
Będzin
Festive opening of the Jewish orphans' home in Będzin.
Last Tuesday, the second day of Chol HaMoed, a bright chapter was added to the history of communal work in the town of Będzin. On that day the saying "nothing stands in the way of the will" was once again fulfilled — there is no hard thing, if only there is will.
At a time of terrible economic crisis, at a time when the foundations of the financial world are breaking down day after day, thanks to the tireless energy of a few people grouped around the charity society, and [thanks to] the generosity of a handful of donors, those who take first place [printed: "dem bereyshis"] in every philanthropic and communal action — the gigantic project, which was proclaimed on 10 June [czerwiec] of the year 1928, has been realised, and a warm home has been opened for orphans and unprotected children.
True, only the first part, the only one[?], has been opened, but seeing the great interest of the Jewish public in the celebration, it is to be hoped that very soon the real celebration will take place, the true dedication of the whole four-storey building.
With the participation of the rabbinate headed by the rabbi, the Katowice rabbi Dr. Vogelmann, Starosta Mr. Baksa[?], Commissioner Mr. Rzeczkowski[?], the former town council, Jewish councillors, representatives of the Będzin and Dąbrowa kehilla presidiums and a large number of invited guests, the elite of our town, the festive opening took place on Tuesday at midday.
The 40 children, boys and girls in new clothes, are led to the sounds of the orchestra of Public School 2 into their new home. The mood in the street is a festive one; crowds of people stream to the building, but entry is by invitation only.
When the guests have gathered in the large dining room, the celebration opens with "Ma Tovu" and "HaNoten Teshua", sung by the Sosnowiec cantor Mr. Yitzchak Lajchter and his choir.
The orchestra under the direction of Mr. Berenblat plays the Polish and the Jewish anthem. Cantor Lajchter and his choir sing the same, and after the official opening by vice-president Mr. Goldfeld the rabbi receives the first word; he thanks all those who helped for the benefit of the building.
The president of the charity society, Dr. Weinzieher, gives a long historical survey of the founding of the orphans' home, points out the importance of the celebration, thanks to which 55 children receive surroundings of their own, a normal upbringing, so that the orphans grow up to be loyal citizens and good Jews.
Dr. Weinzieher reads out the list of donors. In first place are Messrs. Jakub Gutman, Eng. Weinzieher and President S. Fürstenberg (we give the donors' names elsewhere).
In conclusion Dr. Weinzieher announces that precisely on that day falls the 70th birthday of the donor Mr. Jakub Gutman, and he hands over in his name a donation of 1000 zł.
A fine greeting in Polish and Yiddish is delivered by the Katowice rabbi Dr. Vogelmann. Today's celebration — he says — falls on the festival when the Jewish people went out of Egypt and became independent. In the name of the Katowice rabbinate and the kehilla the speaker expresses thanks to the initiators and the donors.
Then come greetings: in the name of the magistrate — the town commissioner; of the homeowners' and merchants' associations — Mr. Rubinlicht; of Fürstenberg's gymnasium — Director Einhorn; and the "mother" of the orphans, Mrs. Cesia Szajn. She appeals especially to the women to keep helping to realise the great work.
A fine impression is left by the greetings of the children of the public schools [szkoły powszechne] no. 2, 4 and 8. In every school a collection was held that same day for the benefit of the orphans' home.

From Whom Money May Be Sought in Their Pockets During Distraint

[Poland — Taxes.] The Ministry of Finance has now published in book form the latest regulation on tax enforcement (distraint) together with explanations. We consider it necessary to reproduce here the explanations from the official edition concerning personal searches.
A personal search on the premises of the taxpayer or anywhere else may be carried out only as a last resort, when all other enforcement measures have been of no avail, or when there is a well-founded suspicion that the debtor is hiding property.
It is forbidden to search the pockets and clothing of other persons, not even of the tax debtor's closest relatives; even when there is proof that they hold property and money belonging to the tax debtor, they may still not be searched. Against such close relatives about whom there is a well-founded suspicion that they are hiding valuables and money belonging to the tax debtor, criminal proceedings may be brought for frustrating the enforcement.
We note in this connection that in such criminal proceedings a penalty of up to 2 years is threatened under Art. 285 of the Kodeks karny (Penal Code).

Large Factory of Counterfeit German and Polish Coins Discovered in Wolbrom.
[Zagłębie & Upper Silesia — Crime.] For some time now counterfeit 10-złoty coins have been circulating both in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia, so well imitated that it was hard to recognise them as false.
At the same time counterfeit 5-mark pieces were circulating in Upper Silesia.
The police undertook an operation to discover the source of the false money, but without result. Only a few days ago the investigation office in Katowice received information that the Garbachnik[?] brothers, residents of Dąbrowa, were the distributors of the counterfeit German and Polish coins.
Further investigation made it clear that the factory was indeed in Wolbrom, at the home of a certain Stanisław Gęgał[?], where a well-equipped factory was found. On the spot were found 653 silver five-mark pieces, 125 Polish 10-złoty pieces, 15 5-zł. and 23 2-zł. pieces, and a great deal[?] of material for producing the counterfeit money.
The manufacturers and the distributors (all Christians) have been put in prison.

„I Will Not Agree to Any Compromise Regarding the Closed Bakeries“

[Będzin — artisans; bakeries and sanitation.] So declares Dr. Ridel [Rydel?].
In connection with the strict regulations — almost impossible to carry out at the present time — that are being issued by the district (powiat) physician Mr. Ridel, a second conference took place on Wednesday evening at the Będzin Artisans' Association with the participation of the above-mentioned doctor.
The initiators of the conference hoped that „at home“ the doctor would be a little softer and that they would succeed in hearing from him words that would somewhat ease the sad situation of those who have now been [harmed?], and especially of the bakers left without a livelihood, whose bakeries the doctor has closed.
The conference is opened by the president of the Artisans' Association, Mr. Goldshtein [Goldsztajn], who welcomes the guest and sets out the aims of the conference.
In reply the doctor speaks about the binding regulations for bakers, confectioners, food shops etc., and declares: „I will not agree to any compromise.“ The bakeries must remain closed; only as regards the confectioners and chocolate-makers am I prepared to grant certain concessions, but only when a delegation negotiates with me for the benefit of the community as a whole; on the other hand, people should not turn to me with individual matters.
Then a short polemic takes place between Mr. Steinbrecher [Sztajnbrecher] and the doctor, and the latter leaves the conference.
After the doctor had gone a discussion developed, and it was decided that separate delegations of the bakers and of the confectioners should negotiate with the doctor.

On Shemini Atzeret a Jewish Mother Goes to Convert with Her 2 Children

[Zawiercie — conversion; town gossip.]
Zawiercie is seething over the conversion story.
Last Saturday, Shemini Atzeret, the conversion took place in Zawiercie of the 36-year-old woman Dvoyre Fayner and her 2 children, Golde, 14 years old, and Shmuel, 9 years old.
The story of the conversion is as follows: in the year 1916 Dvoyre Kutner married a young man from Dąbrowa, a certain Fayner, with whom she lived several years and bore the two children.
The couple had frequent family quarrels, which led to the husband leaving her and abandoning her with the 2 children.
Dvoyre Fayner searched for her husband for a long time, but without success. Once she received word that her "intended" was in Zagłębie.
She kept an eye on him and indeed caught him at the Będzin railway station. The woman, wishing to take revenge on him, doused him with vitriol, but luckily he came out of it unharmed.
But he could no longer get rid of her, and she succeeded in obtaining a get [religious divorce] from him.
After the divorce Dvoyre Fayner, the present apostate, began to occupy herself with selling goods to workers on instalments.
She ran this business for several years and... fell in love with a railway worker. When her family, especially her mother, who lives in Zawiercie, learned of her daughter's relations with the Christian, they began to work on her to break off the relations with the Christian, but without success. What is more, she demanded money from them and threatened that if she did not receive a certain sum of money from them she would convert herself and the children.
And she indeed carried out what she had said. The conversion ceremony took place on Shemini Atzeret and the next day, Sunday, the "ślub" [wedding] with the railway worker took place.
The godfather was a close in-law, the well-known apostate Halenderski[?], who spared no money as long as he could also "save" the souls of the 2 children.
The conversion has stirred up the whole Jewish population of Zawiercie, and the talk of the day is the sensational conversion.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
On the Autonomy of Upper Silesia.
This Sunday a large rally took place in Katowice with the participation of Sanacja deputies. This rally, at which Colonel Sławek also spoke, had great political significance.
The aim of the rally was to prepare the ground for restricting the autonomy of Upper Silesia. A resolution to this effect was also adopted.
The opinion was also expressed that the Kraków and Zagłębie coal districts should be merged into the Silesian voivodeship.
—o—
A Bailiff Sentenced to 3 Months in Prison.
In April of this year a bailiff [sequestrator] of the Königshütte tax office [Urząd Skarbowy] collected 660 zł. from several taxpayers, to whom he issued provisional receipts. Later it turned out that the bailiff had not handed the money over to the office. For this he was sentenced this week to 3 months in prison.
—o—
Young Jewish Man Commits Suicide.
On 3 Maja Street in Königshütte, 22-year-old Moshe Aharon Nisenbaum hanged himself in a lavatory. The doctor who was called confirmed the death.

Interesting Trial over Smuggling.
In the dock of the Katowice court sat the editor of a Warsaw newspaper, Mr. Książek, who had been sued by the firm "Mundus" in Katowice, which the editor had accused of smuggling.
Before the court the defendant submitted a document confirming the content of the accusation. Because of this the editor was acquitted.
—o—

The Katowice pilots Olszewski and Kanszin[?] fell from a height of 50 metres behind Będzin and were killed.

From the Second Days...

[Będzin, Sosnowiec, Czeladź — Simchat Torah.]
(A brief summing-up).
The weather — actually a fine one, truly festive, better than on the first days [of the holiday]. Perhaps because Jews no longer had to sit in the sukkah...
The mood — a festive one; Hasidim kept to the tradition, went round to kiddush, took a little glass of liquor, because:
What we are,
we are,
but Jews we are,
and a Torah
we have,
and Jews indeed "rejoiced" with the Torah.
The greatest "rejoicing" took place in Bożnicza lane [the Synagogue lane] in Będzin. Men, women and children came running together to hear the ringing of the smashed window-panes and the hysterical voices, and to see the blood-smeared stones...
The police were on the spot and dispersed the "Simchat Torah" Jews; at the hospital the wounded were given the necessary medical help, and as the saying goes:
— "As the Christians do, so the Jews do.
———
In the synagogue [the Great Synagogue, "di shul"] the honour of the Torah was this year even "stronger" than in all past years. In the middle of the hakafot the Anshei Polish came in, went up to the Holy Ark and proclaimed:
— The hakafot belong to us..
"Power" was taken over by them without "casualties"; they ruled over the hakafot, and those whom the new government did not impress — left the synagogue and heard hakafot elsewhere...
———
In the Kielce "shtibl" on Kołłątaja street this year's Simchat Torah was disrupted because of a landlord's revenge on a tenant.
The landlord has for quite some time had a dispute with one of his tenants over rent, and since obtaining an eviction is not among the easy things, the landlord decided that if he cannot evict his tenant, he would take revenge on him in another way: he would not give him any... hakafah.
And so it was: first he locked the "shtibl", but seeing the "people's wrath" he reopened the premises — yet the tenant did not get any hakafah...
———
The "Adas Yeshurun" society ought to change its present name; the most fitting title for them is — "Rodfei Shalom" [Pursuers of Peace].. for what do they not do, especially the gabbaim, for the sake of peace? Truly, even the League of Nations would not have managed to do such a thing as what happened this Simchat Torah.
On Simchat Torah morning several were left "hakafah-less", because the hakafot they had received on Shemini Atzeret were not regarded by them, the elected ones[?], as full "portions". Well, a "va-yitz'aku" [an outcry] broke out: is it possible[?]? What are we? Simchat Torah without hakafot? After all, the winter season is coming, one must take fresh "pekelekh" [bundles]...
Well, what did the gabbaim do? Hear and be amazed! — they started all over again, said "Atah hor'eita" once more and stilled the anger of the "hakafah-less"...
———
The holiday report from Sosnowiec could bear the same title as Remarque's war book, "All Quiet on the Western Front". Along the whole "front" there reigned calm and order; a slap even fell, because someone had been honoured with the "Ozer dalim"... but in general it was hush-quiet; even the "burning Balkans" in Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec] this year took a mouthful of water...
———
It was cosy in the suburb of Pogoń. Mighty upheavals took place there. "Governments" changed several times in the course of the day, just like the weather...
The course of the two days was as follows:
On Simchat Torah eve the "radio" announced that "Zweigenhaft's government is at the helm and Friedman's side has withdrawn".
The next morning Friedman's army received reinforcements, and because of this, in the presence of the police, Zweigenhaft stepped down from the amud [prayer-leader's] position...
At Minchah Zweigenhaft rose to the surface again, and as we are informed at the "last minute", Zweigenhaft holds "power".
In Czeladź a war has been going on for quite some time against those who think and work for the good of the Land of Israel. As soon as anything appears on the walls of the beis-midrash that bears a sign concerning Eretz Israel — it at once vanishes, even on the Sabbath, because the Czeladź zealots have "realised" that "the fight against Zionists overrides the Sabbath"..
This Simchat Torah the holy war intensified: a series of "regulations" was prepared against the "sinners", and to be on the safe side they made sure that there would be police during the hakafot.
———
As we see, no heed was paid to the economic crisis — this year's Simchat Torah report is no poorer..
When Winter Knocks on the Windowpane

[Editorial — winter relief.]
The winter is already knocking on our windowpanes; in the air one can already hear the melody of "Af bey"[?] in its elegiac Jewish rendering, which depicts the sad situation of the Jew in the ghetto in the face of the coming winter and ends with the melancholy-resigned refrain: "And still there is no money!"
And the sad situation has still not improved, because we are still sitting in the ghetto, although lately we have been straining with all our strength to get out of it.
We may pursue a policy of struggle, of the sharpest opposition, or of the Aguda [Agudat Israel], of shtadlanut [intercession] — whoever holds the say in the country keeps the gates of the ghetto firmly shut and does not let us out of there. Only in our own sauce may we stew, only within our own four cubits may we sit. Only our own air may we breathe, and when the air is used up — then let us suffocate!
And indeed we are suffocating, and when winter comes it becomes altogether impossible to live.
So the feeling of national self-protection ought to prompt us how to save ourselves from ruin, how the stronger should support the weaker and not let him fall.
The individual does this by instinct, but for the many, awareness must take the place of instinct, because the danger to the many is not so conspicuous, not so much on the surface, as the danger to the individual. Here someone can always imagine that he himself is still far from the danger.
When an individual has nothing to put in his mouth, his stomach feels it at once; but when one limb of a community is hungry, the other limb, the rich and sated one, does not feel it — unless awareness prompts him that if he does not ward off the troubles in good time, they will later reach him too.
In our society most of the work is done out of inertia. Public providers[?] happened to take an interest in a certain field of philanthropy, of social welfare, of cultural activity, threw themselves into it with all their altruism and work with self-sacrifice. People are ready to fight with opponents, with the "competition", to tear down worlds for their own "institution", and do not even give a thought that at the present moment one ought perhaps to put other work aside and help precisely the "competitor", because helping him is the command of the hour.
Winter is approaching now, people's needs have grown, and livelihood becomes smaller and scarcer from day to day — how is one to save oneself?
The first answer is philanthropy, cheap kitchens, coal campaigns, clothing campaigns — so that the poor man does not lack a spoonful of cooked food, a piece of coal, a piece of clothing on his body. And this activity cannot be dismissed with a wave of the hand; whatever our view of charity may be — as long as there are still people in society who have nothing to give and can only take, it is our duty to keep them alive and healthy, and so this activity must indeed be strengthened at the present moment, and everyone who can must help.
But on a higher level stands help for those masses who can still give to society, can be productive, creative, but lack the means for it, which they can obtain by way of credit.
Gone are the times when we could lean on the shoulders of our American uncles, or when we at least had illusions about it; America is itself poor, it already has its own unfortunates, who built skyscrapers so as to be able to throw themselves down from the 30th floor.
We are thrown back on our own help, and we must state that, however bad and bitter things are for our whole community, there are nevertheless still not a few among us who can stretch out a helping hand to their brother.
The only defect is our apathy, our inertia — among the public activists and among the givers alike. The communal workers once worked out a pattern for themselves and spin their activity on it. The givers, for their part, know that there is a Tabernacle and there is a Calf, and for everything people come demanding and for everything one must give.
So awareness must be called to help.
The most important work at the present moment is — to help the little man stay on his feet, to struggle with the difficulties of the coming winter. With a small loan of a hundred gulden [złoty] he can be saved. And the institutions that do this must be supported in the widest measure.
We need not point to any addresses here; we only want to remind those of our brothers who are not pressed by direct want and by the basic necessities, that they should keep in mind the smaller and weaker, and when they are approached for help for them, let them know that this help is the command of the present hour, when winter knocks on the windowpane.
P. K.
An End to Silence.

[Opinion — Polish Jewry; economic distress.] This is the last distress signal of a sinking ship. Regardless of one's attitude towards the state to which the sinking ship belongs, every ship that finds itself at sea must come to help, and often even put itself in danger, in order to rescue the sinking ship. We Jews here have now reached that stage — we are on the brink of ruin. Not even speaking of our political lack of rights, economically we are already further gone than “on the eve of ruin”. All the Nowaczyńskis-Dmowskis are already getting ready to dance a wild demons’ dance on our graves — and among us all is quiet. Our own leaders, our political and economic leaders of every kind, are busily pursuing behind-the-scenes politics, which helps nothing — always, and especially now. Suffice it to point out that in our struggle for survival things have already come to such a pass that the Galician Jewish leaders have begun to see the picture of misery among Polish Jews — but the ice still does not move. People do talk about starting to talk, but so far nothing has got further than a newspaper article.
One position falls after another; the last 2 years have broken the record of our collapse — and among us, among our shtadlonim, activists and advisers, it is as quiet as in a cemetery. True, today it is no longer a matter of a war of words, but practical care for us has not yet even begun; decrees pour down, each more terrible than the last. Today they no longer speak of ruining the Jewish merchant and artisan, but of pushing him out[?] altogether. And you, gentlemen deputies, communal workers, public representatives — where are you?
Remember, then, that sooner or later you will have to answer for your silence, whether you can help or not. But your voice ought to have been heard now — and not to relate so patiently and “finally”[?] still sated, as you do, to the cry of despair of all the Jews in Poland. Today you must stop being salon representatives; today you must organize the Jewish masses in Poland, so as to be able to begin, with success, some action or other for the improvement of the Jewish situation. Take an example from the peasants’ representatives in Poland. The peasant — who even now lives far better than the Jew — yet as soon as his situation is not so favourable[?], his representatives organize even strikes. Must one still wait, and can one still wait at all? You yourselves already admit that “the waters have come in unto the soul” [Psalm 69:2]; so how long? Know that Jewish society will condemn you not because you achieved nothing, but solely because you did not begin to act. Long enough have you quarrelled over higher and lower mandate ranks. Later you were exhausted by that “struggle” — you needed your “rest”; but when will your silence finally end? Terms of office will not last for ever. We remind, call and warn you: begin to fulfil your duty, do not look on so calmly at the S.O.S. signals of the sinking Jewish ship.
P. Goldkranc.
No More Wars!

[Feuilleton — satire; birth control.] When Pharaoh wanted to exterminate the Jews, he had two means: throw all the boys into the river, or order the midwives to smother the boys on the birthing stool[?]. That was a kind of birth control, Pharaonic style.
In later years, when people wanted to avoid the “Jewish danger” and in doing so not use Egyptian brutality, another means was applied: Jews were not allowed to marry. If one does not marry, it goes without saying, one cannot have children.
That is how the old world was able to control births: either not marrying, or killing the newborn. Over the mystical time between the wedding night and the birth, when the little foetus lies hidden in its natural fleshly fortress, they then had no control. As soon as a couple was allowed to come together, there was no longer any way to be rid of the fruit of human love — unless one became a murderer and killed a living creature.
Modern times have found a civilized means: not to hinder man in his natural desires and at the same time not to apply any brutal, murderous means against a small innocent creature, but merely to remove the bud by a medical operation, before the fruit has come...
But the world will not tolerate that either. The world argues that whoever wants to go sledding must also be willing to drag the sled, and whoever goes to the wedding canopy must also be ready for a circumcision...
Man, however, argues that he is not obliged to pay for a minute of pleasure with a lifetime of suffering, and that the prohibition “Thou shalt not kill” cannot apply to a creature that has not yet been born.
So a dispute goes on between the official law and the citizen, who already has his theorists[?] and his agitators, demanding that the law permit what life itself dictates.
And “the world goes its way” — the law does not allow it, and man does not obey. It began with a two-children system, moved on to a one-child system, and is now already at a half-child system, that is: one only son for two couples...
Now the governor of an American little state, Puerto Rico, has come along and proposed that his government apply the same modern means to the whole people.
Since, he says, the country is short of land and has a weak industry, it will have to live on imports — and how can one import if one has nothing to export? It is therefore more sensible to introduce a numerus clausus for births. Each year no more people may be born than died that year, and once the quota of births is filled, no more children shall be let out into the bright world: there is no room, so go back where you came from!
Not only should birth control be permitted — it should become a compulsion, a duty, a holy service to the state.
And one must believe that the wisdom of the Puerto Rican governor will catch on all over America.
For, reckon it up: since the gates are closed and no one is let in from the old world into the new world, why should the gates be open to let out the uninvited guests from that world?
And why, pray, let in exactly as many births as there are deaths? Why not deduct the 12 million unemployed who wander about the world and are worse off than the dead?
This, it seems, is the only means to regulate the economy of the countries and avoid the crisis.
It is not even news. All the bells are already ringing that there will be no other way to get rid of the crisis in the world except through a new world war, which will lay low several tens of millions of people; then there will be enough work and bread for everyone, and people will live in the world as in paradise. And when a few years pass and the world multiplies again, they will once more resort to the same means.
As if people let themselves a little surplus blood every time...
Today, again the same story. Why resort to such brutal means as war? Why kill fathers of children and bridegrooms of brides, why stir up bad blood at all, rouse hatred between people and people, country and country, in order to arrive at the longed-for war — when it can be done prettily and politely, without hatred, without diplomacy, without coalitions with Leagues of Nations, but simply through a doctor and his surgery, with the help of his sharpened little lancet.
And there will be another advantage: they will not kill off specifically the males, so that afterwards old maids remain on the shoulders of their fathers, who among the gentiles must go into a convent and among Jews travel to the Land of Israel. The numerus clausus of birth control will apply to both sexes equally.
One must therefore reckon that from America this new plan will be adopted in the whole world too, and then we shall be insured against wars and against revolutions and against crises and against all kinds of calamities.
All thanks to the wisdom of the modern Pharaoh, the Puerto Rican governor.
A-Gus.
It's Autumn...

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — feuilleton for Shabbat Bereshit.] In honour of Shabbat Bereshit. By Ben Amotz.

Unannounced, autumn has come. The sky is already covered with black, dense clouds, angry winds blow and carry with them half-yellow leaves that fall, abandoned, onto the pavement. The departing summer still wrestles with all its strength against the attacking enemy — autumn, but autumn defeats it and takes its place...
We sit in the editorial office, looking through the window at the street, at the dripping rain, at the falling leaves... and we listen to the words coming from the mouth of a well-known Sosnowiec public figure, which make us even sadder, even angrier, because we had believed that after so many years of struggle against the foolish petty servility, against all sorts of spiritual worms that devour [?] our people's soul — our horizon would become brighter, happier; but we are ever more disappointed. As if out of spite, the wind starts to howl harder like evil spirits, the rain falls more thickly, and
— it is autumn...
— There is — he says — in Sosnowiec a Polish girls' gymnasium, and as is the custom, Jewish daughters occupy an honourable place there. The attitude of the Jewish mothers and the Zionist fathers towards this gymnasium is a very correct one; they, the Jewish parents that is, will God forbid not say a crooked word even when their daughters attend Sabbath services —
— in church [kościół]...
But that is not what we are after now; we mentioned that little flower only in passing, on the way to the heart of the matter, to what our informant tells us:
— The management of the gymnasium — he says, a very liberal one, by the way — still holding to the old Polish traditions, has engaged a Jewish teacher.
— What? A Jewish teacher in a Polish gymnasium? Is that true?
— It is true, but
— But what?
— But it would have been much better for the Jewish pupils of that gymnasium had they not received the "gift" of the "Jewish" teacher...
— Why do you say so?
— Because she is a creature without any human dignity whatsoever; her conduct regarding Jewish traditions and Jewish culture is far worse than that of the worst enemy of Israel; her greatest pleasure is that she has the opportunity to besmirch what is holiest to Jews, to degrade the honour of the Jewish people, and in public, at school, during lessons, to make the blood of the Jewish pupils run cold, as they have to listen to the foolish chatter of this servile creature that
— she has nothing whatever in common with the "Zhids" [Polish slur for Jews]...
— — — — — — — — —
Outside the wind howls harder, yellow leaves fall and roll about on the pavement.
— Autumn...
* * *
Autumnal and grey, too, was this year's Simchat Torah night in the Będzin synagogue.
The same synagogue, the same brightness, only the order — a different one
— it is autumnal...
The Holy Ark is open. Beside it stand the gabbaim handing out the hakafot. Jewish life is so monotonous, so sad, so gloomy; the joy of old is gone, the singing is wrapped in sorrow. Everything is done perforce. One sings not because one wants to, but because — one must...
Right in the middle, when the congregation forgets for a while its everyday worries, when a higher thought awakens in the mind — a group of drunks bursts into the synagogue, plants itself insolently by the Holy Ark and
— takes over power...
Hurriedly, angrily, the congregation leaves the synagogue. Memories of the past float up, when joy, harmony and brightness always reigned in the synagogue.
And today?
— lawlessness, hooliganism, fists, and all around one can sense —
— autumn...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bereshit)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bereshit
The Portion
—o—
a) "In the beginning God created" (Gen. 1:1)
The Torah begins with a Bet and not with the first letter, Aleph. Every tractate of the Gemara, too, begins with folio 2 (Bet) and not with folio 1 (Aleph), so that a person should know that he is not yet even at the beginning, that he has not yet even reached the Aleph...
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdychiv.
• • •
A prodigious young man comes to the author of "Chidushei HaRim". The Gaon asks him:
— Can you learn?
— A little, — he answers humbly.
— And who, then, can do more than a little?... — the Gaon retorts.
—o—
b) "God created."
The Midrash relates that before creating the world, God took counsel with the angels. Truth was against creating the world, because "it is all falsehood". So God threw Truth into the earth and said: "It is My will that truth rise up from the earth, as it is said: Truth shall spring out of the earth."
Truth grows out of the earth; no one tends it, no one sows it — it grows out of the earth by itself...
Divrei Shaul.
—o—
c) "Herb yielding seed after its kind" (ibid., 12)
"When Moses our Teacher saw the grasses and the plants and saw the destruction — at once he wept." (Midrash Peliah).
Moses saw the world's "grasses and flowers", the flowers of the world, its culture, civilization, humanism, "and saw the destruction" — and at the same time he also saw how this very world perishes and slaughters thousands of innocent Jews, while all the grasses and flowers, the flowers of the human spirit, civilization and culture, go on shining upon man — at once he wept, he burst into tears...
Rabbi Yitzchak Shuster, Skałka[?].
—o—
d) "And the Lord God formed man" (2:7)
In a Lithuanian shtetl there lived a Jewish apothecary and his mother, about whom people told very ugly stories... Once there was a custom that every daybreak the town shammes knocked three times on the shutters of all householders, waking them for prayers. And when someone had died, the shammes knocked on the shutters only 2 times.
The said apothecary, however, asked the shammes not to knock on his shutters; there was no need to wake him for prayers — unless someone died, then he should knock.
The shammes obeyed. He did not knock on his shutters; only when someone had died did he knock several times. The next morning the apothecary asks him:
— Why did you knock more than twice?
The shammes answers him:
— The meaning of the three knocks is that a person has three partners: God, father and mother (Niddah 31a); so one calls upon the powers of all three to the service of the Creator. And therefore, when someone dies, one knocks only twice, to hint that only two partners remain with their share. The third partner, God, has taken back His share from the person. That is said of all Jews, who have only three partners. But you (hinting at his mother's conduct...) — who knows how many partners you have... So I knocked without number...
Ezrat Yisrael.
—o—
e) "And put him into the Garden of Eden to work it and to keep it" (ibid., 15)
"To work it — this is a positive commandment; and to keep it — this is a negative commandment." Midrash.
God made an experiment: so that man would be pious, He placed him in the Garden of Eden — let him be well and comfortable and he will not sin. And precisely there, in the Garden of Eden, Adam committed the first sin.
Divrei Chachamim.
—o—
f) "And the man hid himself" (3:8)
A grandson of the Rebbe, Reb Baruch, was playing hide-and-seek. Suddenly he comes in to his grandfather crying. What is the matter? He had been hidden in a cupboard for a long time, and his playmate forgot about the game and did not look for him.
Reb Baruch sighs:
— God, too, hides from His children so that they should seek Him — and they forget to seek Him...
Botzina Denehora.
—o—
g) "He shall bruise thy head" (ibid. 15)
The evil inclination grabs you only by the "head" (rosh): by talking you into believing that you are a "rosh" [a head, a leader]. That is the easiest way to let yourself be fooled...
Imrei Yoav.
—o—
h) "And in process of time Cain brought an offering unto the Lord" (4:3)
"In process of time" (literally "at the end of days"): in his old age, after everything, Cain turns pious and brings "an offering unto the Lord"...
Be'er Mayim Chaim.
—o—
The Haftarah
i) "Bring My sons from far, and My daughters from the ends of the earth" (Isaiah 43)
"From far" — from how far away will the Jewish sons have to be dragged home, to their own, at the time of the Redemption: from foreign lands, from afar... What is happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The outcry of the Jewish bakers and confectioners

What is happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday 28 Tishrei 5693 — Friday 28 October 1932.)
Będzin
The outcry of the Jewish bakers and confectioners.
On Monday evening a meeting of the Jewish bakers and confectioners took place in the premises of the Artisans' Union.
At the meeting the cries of woe of those assembled were heard; they told of outrageous facts about the chicanery and persecution they have lately been suffering at the hands of the sanitary authorities, which fine the bakers because a loaf of bread does not bear the firm name of the bakery, and the like.
It was resolved to intervene with the district (powiat) physician so that he should moderate the fines imposed on the bakers and confectioners.
The new 'etat' will be assessed as it has been until now.

As is well known, the 'etat' (communal tax) for the year 1933 was to have been assessed within the framework of the income tax. According to the latest 'Dziennik Ustaw', the law is being held back for one more year, i.e. the 'etat' for the coming year will be assessed according to the system in force until now.
Tenants in the 'Blocks' resolve to pay 30 per cent less rent.

Some time ago the tenants in the 'Blocks' held a meeting on the question of reducing the amount of rent. At the meeting it was resolved that, because of the bad economic situation, which leads to continual reductions of pensions, the management of the block-houses should reduce the rent by 30 per cent.
The resolution was sent to the management, but the latter pretended not to know and 'did not hear' the tenants' demand.
For this reason a second meeting took place last Sunday, at which the conduct of the management was discussed, which did not even find it necessary to give an answer, and it was resolved to pay the rent into the management's account at 30 per cent less than until now.
The new kehilla budget is already under discussion.

The kehilla administration is already setting about completing the new kehilla budget, which must be submitted to the authorities at the end of next month.
At yesterday's meeting of the administration the agenda included the budget question and the improper conduct on the part of the shochtim (ritual slaughterers).
A presidium of the 'Dozór Szkolny' elected.

On Tuesday evening the 'Dozór Szkolny' (school board) held a meeting in the municipal council (magistrat), at which the following presidium was elected: chairman — Commissioner Mr. Wszeszkowski[?], vice-chairman — the local priest, and secretary — headmaster (kierownik) Mr. Rapaport.
At the meeting a penal commission was also elected, whose task is to punish parents who neglect their children with regard to compulsory schooling.
The commission includes 2 Christians and the nominated member in the 'Dozór Szkolny', Mr. G. Rechnic.
The dispute with the caretakers — still continues.

At the labour inspector's office in Sosnowiec a conference took place, at which the dispute between the house-owners and the caretakers (stróże) concerning the renewal of the new agreement was discussed.
The conference produced no result.
The Talmud Torah is being reorganised.

The new committee (va'ad) of the Talmud Torah is holding regular meetings, at which resolutions are being adopted on how to reorganise and revive the local Talmud Torah, so that it may fulfil its tasks with regard to the education of the children of the Jewish masses.
Great weight is also being placed on the introduction of secular studies, so that the children who learn in the Talmud Torah may at the same time be exempt from the compulsory (state) schools.

Several weeks ago a group of residents of Mandoszewer [?] Street came to the editorial office and told us that Reb Shlomo the shochet (ritual slaughterer) does not want to take in his one-and-a-half-year-old grandson, who has been left without father and mother.

District Doctor Orders the “Mizrachi” School Closed

[Sosnowiec — Professional organisations.] In connection with the new accountants' law, which is soon to come into force and which is directed mainly against Jews, an organising meeting took place on Sunday evening in the premises of the Sosnowiec Merchants' Association (Kowalska 2), chaired by Mr L. Merchants of the third and fourth category must keep commercial books.
[Taxes — Turnover tax.] Beginning with the new year, retail merchants and small traders holding patents (trade licences) of the third and fourth category will pay only three per cent turnover tax. Only those merchants, however, who keep commercial books according to the simplified bookkeeping will be able to enjoy this relief.
Craftsmen who hold the proper rights will pay 1 per cent turnover tax; they are exempt from keeping commercial books. This will be a great relief for small traders, with the exception of the colonial-goods (grocery) branch, which will continue to pay 2 per cent turnover tax, even if they do not keep commercial books.
Small merchants and traders who, from the beginning of the new year 1933, do not wish to keep books according to the simplified bookkeeping will have to continue paying two and a half per cent turnover tax.
In this connection the merchants' organisations should undertake a campaign aimed at informing small merchants and traders about using their rights in accordance with the amendment (novella) on the turnover tax.

Theatre and Music Notes

The beginning has been made.
Very little has music been cultivated among Jews, notwithstanding that among the great composers Jews occupy a very respected place, to say nothing[?] of Jewish artists of world renown who have brought honour to the world of music — and yet the field of Jewish folk music has remained neglected. A very large part of the folk songs, which characterise the former Jewish way of life, its dreams and hopes, are being lost and forgotten.
Gone too are the times when the Jewish street had patrons who funded ethnographic expeditions through the Jewish towns and shtetls to collect material on the Jewish way of life. And the treasure of Jewish folk music waits[?] until the enthusiasts are found who will create pure music from it — in contrast to the atmosphere of cheap, banal jingling[?] that reigns today, which is really only a result of the spiritual chaos (tohu va-vohu) reigning in the world today.
Therefore one must welcome the initiative of that group of lovers of Jewish music which, regardless of the hard economic times and the oppressive apathy, nevertheless created such an important institution, which in the course of its 7 months of existence has grown into an institution of 300 members, possessing a good choir and a fine symphony orchestra.
The society has set itself the task of popularising Jewish music, performing works by Jewish artists, and creating the place that will enable young talents to advance.
The beginning has been made. Jewish society in Będzin must relate with more seriousness and love to such an important institution, which has set itself lofty goals.
M. B.

He kissed a pretty girl and got paid for it too.
On Tuesday around 7 in the evening a heavy rain suddenly fell, and people hurried to take shelter in the gateways. Tsach. And.[?] a sizeable group of boys and girls sheltered from the rain in the gateway of the „Hotel Centralny“, where there is a photographic studio.
So the boys stand there, eyeing the „Backfische“ [teenage girls], exchanging winks, and suddenly a „brilliant“ idea is born: who will have the nerve to go up to the prettiest gymnasium girl, Z., and give her a kiss on her [—] lips?
And at once someone on the spot finances this kiss expedition: he puts up a whole 2 złoty, to go to whoever dares to do it.
And one of the gang turned up, a certain S., who declared himself ready, saying: two złoty don't walk on foot [i.e. are not to be sneezed at].
And as soon as the rain eased and the girls began to slip out of the gateway one by one, S. made a firm leap[?], blocked girl Z.'s way, extorted a kiss on her lips and... stretched out his hand for the couple of złoty.
The girl ran away confused and did not even want to look back. When the bold lad ran after her and kept apologising to her that it had been a bet and he had had no choice...

The Trial of Lieutenant Kucharski before the Military Court in Kraków

[Courts — Będzin and Mysłowice.] The military district court has in recent days heard the trial against Lieutenant (porucznik) Kucharski of the 23rd Regiment in Będzin, who shot dead Mr. Winterstein of Mysłowice.
The events took place as follows:
On 29 June (czerwiec) of this year Lt. Kucharski came to Mysłowice together with several friends. While the company was on the veranda of the restaurant at the Mysłowice stadium, at a neighbouring table sat a certain Winterstein and his friend Wójcik of Mysłowice, who behaved provocatively towards Lt. Kucharski's company and at the same time expressed themselves in insulting words. Winterstein and his friend also did not stop insulting the officers, even when it was pointed out to them that these were Polish officers and must not be insulted.
When Lt. Kucharski reacted to the insults, Winterstein struck him in the face.
Kucharski then shot at Winterstein, killing him on the spot.
The district court, having heard a whole series of witnesses who confirmed the provocative conduct of Winterstein and his friend, after the examination of experts and the speeches of the defence, handed down an acquittal for Lieutenant Kucharski.

From Arthur Szyk's Exhibition in Katowice

[Katowice — art.] In Katowice the exhibition of Arthur Szyk's illumination works has been open for a week now, together with a whole series of further works created only recently, such as — besides the Statute of Kalisz — the epic of Simón Bolívar, George Washington in his time, the Covenant of the League of Nations, illustrations to Ludwig Lewisohn's work "The Last Days of Shylock", and others.
The exhibition is visited mainly by non-Jews, from all political camps — thus Korfanty supporters or members of the Sanacja come, and all are full of praise. Arthur Szyk himself is very pleased with this, because through the understanding of art comes also the understanding of other aims.
Arthur Szyk is an artist gifted by God; all his works are technically refined, and his love of a complete and pure line is very deep. His miniatures lift us so high and keep us in constant suspense. His figures are from the Middle Ages, and yet his creative art is so new. His works carry us away and bring us to ecstasy. Every picture is a world of its own.
In the future a new work by Arthur Szyk will appear: the Haggadah, which will be fully illustrated. The edition will be a facsimile one, so that everyone will be able to buy it. The work will take 2 years.
For this purpose a committee has already been formed, which includes Messrs. Wiktor Chajes, Hermann Horowitz, Rudolf Beres and our fellow townsman Szymon Fürstenberg.
H. Reldirf.
