On Guard Before a Catastrophe. XIV. (The Old Stock and the Student Youth. — Our Backwardness and Its Causes)

[Opinion / economy — crafts and trade.] L. Szpigelman.
It is no longer news to anyone, since we have said more than once and shown several times, that we are losing position after position, that our economic situation is already so deeply depressed, has fallen so unbearably, that in the prevailing situation we have no way out and we do not know how to save ourselves, how to remain standing on our feet.
We therefore must not remain indifferent to this chaos and look on as the branches of our economic tree-trunk — a field in which we were once of the noble lineage (yikhes) — break off systematically, and the ancient tree begins to stand bare and its roots begin to dry out, so that the tree stops yielding its fruit.
At such a moment one must surely take stock: where we stand and where the wind is tossing us. The older generation is no longer fitted to today's conditions; it cannot chase after the current, which spreads out broadly over a large area with tremendous speed and swallows up everything around it, so that one begins to lose one's way and sees no way out.
A large part of the Jewish population consciously realised this, and that was the reason why whoever had the means gave his children a secondary-school education, and with the matura people began to head for the temple of learning; they wanted to attain higher education, but the gates of the universities remained almost firmly shut to us Jews, and with that we are left without a way out: the older generation has begun to lose the ground from under its feet, and the coming generation, the youth already grown up, has no prospects at all, and the future looks to it very, very pessimistic, very, very sorrowful and clouded.
Well, as long as the years were still normal and business was still normal, the young gave up their studies and took up, some office work and some other white-collar professions. Now, when the times have become highly complicated, extraordinarily abnormal, there is nothing to be achieved in that field either; the youth wander about idle, and the element that until now was somewhat better situated has already forgotten how one can, under the prevailing conditions, earn both a livelihood and the most necessary needs that must figure in today's budget. The situation is thus without a way out, and one must not leave it hanging in the air; it must be resolved somehow, and one must adopt all possible and impossible means in order to examine this most dangerous situation in its full size and breadth, in its full light and nakedness. We must conceal nothing from the sad reality, however terrible and cruel it may be.
First of all it must be said that we underrate what we possess in the things we are occupied with. We know, for instance, that the Jewish craftsman finds it hard to make a living in the present bitter times; he goes about without a stitch of work, and when he does manage to obtain, after great interventions and string-pulling, employment — it happens that he cannot come out even with his capital; he has to put extra money into his undertaking and stays stuck in the middle.
Why is this so? Because he cannot calculate, he has not gone through any school, he is not qualified, and for that reason he cannot work out his accounts.
And something else: we quite often hear people complain that one should not deal with any craftsman; for thus — people say — it is well known that the artisan goes about without work and is simply happy when he gets something to do, yet as soon as he takes on a piece of work there is no getting along with him. One hour he works, and for two days he leaves the client stuck in the middle of the job. Of course this should not happen, but it is a rare thing for a craftsman to keep his word. Give him a piece of work, and though he has no work, he will drag you along for days and weeks and will never keep to the deadline. How often we hear people say that they never want to order [made-to-measure] what one can get ready-made in a shop, only because they are sick of begging for the goods or article to be finished at last, so that the customer already surely[?] gives up on the better finish and settles for a simpler[?] job, just so as not to have to waste time and effort in vain.
Our craftsmen do not progress in this field; they do not move with the times, they do not take conditions into account, they do not want to modernise their businesses, and because of this they suffer materially. People give them a piece of work only when there is no other way out.
If we think that things are better with us in another field, we are greatly mistaken. Trade in the shops and in small manufacturing, too, is inferior in the same way. They too cannot calculate and never know how to work out their accounts, and here too the fault, of course, is the school they did not go through. That school is missing for people at every step, and they suffer for it their whole life. That is why they overpay taxes, fall into debt, put money into the costing, and can never get out of it with whole bones. How many times do Jews pay taxes twice, and unjustified taxes, only because one time he does not have the receipts, and another time because he does not know what sort of tax he is paying.
At the same time the big industrialist or another large enterprise will not overpay a single grosz, because there the receipts are kept in proper order and an incorrect tax will never be paid, since they have specialists in this field, officials, who guard it like the apple of their eye. The poor craftsman (printed "bet melokhe" — a misprint for "bal melokhe"), on the other hand, or the small trader, overpays two- and threefold only because he has nobody to keep his tax assessments ("nakazy") and the receipts for sums he paid long ago; he pays a fine for it as well, so that he is reduced to poverty merely because of this disorder and lack of punctuality.
But what can these little people do so as not to overpay unnecessary sums two- and threefold? Can these people persuade themselves that they could hire people to keep all this for them as it is kept by big industrialists or in large commercial houses? Of course they cannot even dream of such fantasies, and therefore there is no way out here. Yes, it would have been quite a good way out if we were organised, if the organisation of every trade stood at the proper level — then it would be quite an easy matter.
But it turns out that socially we are still far from developed; people here are still far from understanding what communal responsibility, social accountability, is — which has been created all over the world in order to benefit the community, to help those who cannot help themselves.
How to remedy these dangers, both in the field of private commerce and in the sense of social life — in the next chapter.
Lawlessness and Fear (Sketches)

[Essay — Jewish public life in Poland.] Lately a heated debate has broken out in the Jewish press about our present political-social conditions and, especially, about the — — lawlessness! that has seized our entire life, about the takifes [the rule of the strong-arm bosses], in its various and most loathsome[?] forms, which floods the whole Jewish political-social life in Poland.
Something can be felt in this debate: that the tragedy of our situation has reached its — — culmination point! And that the conviction has ripened that one must at last say openly to the Jewish public that things cannot — — go on like this! That the coming tomorrow must be different from today, and that one must think over what is to be done.
And yet, even now, not everything is being said in this debate; even now the close connection between — — lawlessness and — fear! is still passed over in silence. In it lies our whole misfortune, the main source of our terrible helplessness, up to a boundless despair.
When we look closely at everything that goes on in and around us, we see that the entire Jewish political-social life is wrapped through and through with a — — spider's thread! which stretches from on high, runs through all our institutions and organisations, and by this barely visible but very strong — — thread! everything is bound together, everything entangled, and through it are firmly united the — — lawlessness! at the top of our political-social life and the — — fear! in the localities, in every town and shtetl.
The Jewish masses, the Jewish artisan, small trader and merchant, who on various occasions and in various circumstances happen to meet their various representatives — city councillors, kehilla parnassim, leaders of various organisations and all other kinds of — — „cooking spoons“ [busybodies who stir every pot]! — see and feel perfectly well what these — — representatives and providers! stand for with regard to the interests of the Jewish masses. They see and feel very well that in our present Jewish life, shattered to its foundations and poisoned as never before, a special — — caste! has taken root, of conscienceless careerists and swindlers who shamelessly build their personal — — prosperity! at the expense of the general Jewish — — misery and want! — closely bound to one another by one common slogan: — — „Guard me — and I'll guard you!“
We Jews, however, in our present inner brokenness and dejection, have moreover become, regrettably, isolated individuals[?]: each one thinks only of himself, and no one says a word out loud, because one is — — afraid!
And from this and because of[?] this there grows ever more, in all spheres of our political-social life, the — — lawlessness! This unbearable, oppressive and humiliating — — fear! takes hold, day by day, of ever broader strata of the Jewish population, and together with it the — — lawlessness! also grows ever greater in its scope and aspirations, thus creating a united front, over the whole of Jewish political-social life, of — — lawlessness and — fear!
And, fundamentally, — it is not at all impossible, and even not so very hard, to tear apart the — — spider's thread! that unites the — — lawlessness and — fear! that are so unbearable in our life. All that is needed is a little more courage, a little more understanding of the reality in which we find ourselves, and especially — of the slogan we so absolutely need: — — One for all and — all for one! And with common strength, at every step and stride, to stand up against the takifes, against careerism and machinations at the expense of Jewish — — troubles and — want!
And when we, stubbornly, sparing no one and nothing, bring into our — — extinguished and — trampled! political-social life small — — sparks! and a courageous struggle for our existence and human dignity, this will of itself become a great — — flame! that will burn up all the falseness and all the filth of our Jewish political-social life; and then life will change its heavy, dark forms of — — lawlessness and — fear!, under whose heavy yoke we are now so unbearably oppressed.
And when there is now so much talk about the necessity of mounting strong resistance to the — — lawlessness! at the top of our political-social life, there must at the same time also be proclaimed a merciless war against the takifes and the — — fear! in the localities, in every town and shtetl.
A. M. T. [„Emes“ — Truth]

World Antisemitism

[Essay / opinion — world antisemitism.]
By J. I. Segal [י. י. סיגאל]

The antisemites in all countries are now singing in one chorus. And among them there are all sorts of voices and little voices. And among them there are voices such as we had never heard anywhere before. We even wonder: do such ones really exist? Each time another one raises his lion's roar, or his still small voice, rises above the chorus and sings solo, shows what he can do. At times it becomes a real Katzenjammer of roaring and growling, nothing like that of any civilized — beasts. If the brilliant Wagner were alive now, he might perhaps have created a new work out of it. He might perhaps have caught signs of "revolution" and these black crow-croakings. God forbid that I should touch the honour of the genius, but falling into the ranks of the "song" of antisemitism, I remembered that he too, the great Wagner, had something against us; I grabbed hold of him like a drowning man at a straw, for one gets sick of dealing only with antisemitic nonentities like the present ones, who make a din up to the ceiling of the whole world-palace — so at least I grabbed hold of one decent person, of whom the antisemites themselves threw it up to us that he too is not alien to — Jewishness. At least [printed "patsh", read "khotsh"] we know that in him, in Wagner, there perhaps takes place a "and they struggled together" [Gen. 25:22], a Jacob-and-Esau fight, and when Wagner shouts and rails against Jews, we will assume that it is Esau inside him clenching [?] his fists, and when Wagner — plays, then it is "the voice is the voice of Jacob". That's how it must come out — how else? But, joking aside, antisemitism now sings in chorus. There are still a few countable countries that — keep silent. There is a supposition that they too are not silent. They murmur and hum under their breath everything the "chorus" says.

The only "luck" in this misfortune is merely that it is not the only hatred now raging in the world. The world is flooded with enmity and wickedness of one toward another. The measure of iniquities has been overfilled, of "sins" against the little bit of good and justice that has grown up on the black swamp of human malice and baseness. I do not know whether we ought to seek comfort for ourselves in this reason; it is a lamentable consolation, but it can somewhat still our burning sorrow, for it is hard to be alone in sorrow. It is a little easier when one sees broader, more distant causes and does not fall into too-deep self-accusation. Especially at such moments, when the beast has been let out of its cage and it races through streets and cities and overturns whatever comes in its way.

And we, in our great misfortune, are always in the beast's way; it will no longer let us pass, even if it has to make many detours in order to block our way — that is now its "manoeuvre".

And to this day we have not found any proper means of defending ourselves against it. After all we are speaking among ourselves, and the sad truth we may tell ourselves, even while holding our heads bowed in sorrow over our fate: we have, it seems, also lost a little of our certainty in political redemption. The last few years — such bitter disappointments in our protectors. But — something has become clearer to us: a certain feature on the face of world politics that has had a fatal effect on our national mood and consciousness. We have seen how we ourselves become a blind political instrument in the hand of a power that has only itself in mind and cares little about our existence. That is "something" more than disappointment and discouragement.

And now, in the antisemitic chorus, almost along the whole length of a world-line, with all the economic upheavals and the eve of upheaval, it follows the Judeophobic course; under every flag it grows. To the conservative [misprinted] camp it sends its black courier, and to the liberal, to the fascist and to the so-called socialist one, for a social-fascist is after all also a socialist. And a Jew — is treyf to it like a bourgeois. A Jewish person [misprint "mshnsh"] who works is not yet to be found in the world. All Jews are money-magnates. And if one does not see it on many of them, they hide their treasures. Where? About Jews one doesn't ask — who knows their hiding places, who can get to the bottom of their secrets. About Jews it is permitted to believe the worst and the most terrible. For the benighted masses there is an easy, elementary means: one incites them, one tells them tales of murders of Christian children, without whose blood Jews can by no means hold a seder or have a kosher Passover — that is for the mob. For the so-called intellectual a tale has already been invented about a kind of Sanhedrin, Elders of Zion, who sit and ponder plans for how to steal the world out of the hands of the goyim and run away — where to? — unless to the next world. Inquisitions there are indeed no longer today; we are, after all, a good few hundred years away from those — means; but other, sublimated ways have been found to burn the ground under one's feet. Hitler is the sheygets, the one who need not suffer any disgrace and really does not know what such a thing as shame is. Behind him, however, are silent those for whom Hitler is indeed their ugly plague, their disgrace, and their silence is perhaps fear. But we have already seen cases where the honest and humane knew no fear of the inhuman and came out openly and bravely against it and struck terror into the black gangs.

If even the better ones have already hidden themselves in a corner — perhaps we should not hold it too much against them; perhaps we should also put ourselves in their position, for they too are "guilty" in the eyes of the black forces. And in us too the instigator means not so much the Jew as the human being who bears the great sin of having thrown a spark of a higher moral feeling into the swarming vermin [?] of those crawling within themselves — destroying one another. We are often his bad conscience, and he might perhaps have loved us better if, along the roads of history, he had had before his eyes the grandiose picture of a whole crucified people instead of merely one single son of its own [printed: "zun irn"]. Antisemitism is still the most bloodthirsty in the forest of human settlement. It is only the savage that is still sometimes afraid to show itself in the ridiculousness of crawling on all fours, of climbing smooth walls, just to bark, growl and neigh at Jews, who hinder it a little from being an open beast; and — the poor thing, on top of all troubles, busies itself manicuring its nails with a little "scientific" file, when it sets about digging them into the body of a Jew, of the whole people.

We are now going through one of the antisemitic periods in history [...]
“Yo-Yo” (A Short Feuilleton)

[Feuilleton — the yo-yo craze.]
In the street and in the garden, in the restaurant and in the pastry shop, in the theatre and in the cinema, in the kitchen and in the parlour — everywhere a game of “yo-yo” is going on; whole houses, whole streets, whole towns — everything is being seized and swallowed up by the “yo-yo”.
And although an editor must be a “kol-boynik”, a know-it-all, an expert on everything in the world, my readers will have to forgive me if I sincerely confess that I have no notion what the “yo-yo” game actually means.
Two coloured half-rounded spools on a string.
A lady comes into a shop.
— Proszę jo-jo dla mojej córeczki [Polish: A yo-yo for my little daughter, please].
Got it.
Another lady.
— Proszę jo-jo dla mojego synka [Polish: A yo-yo for my little son, please].
Got it.
A moment later both ladies are already walking in the street, flinging the little “yo-yos” with their hands.
Why were they ashamed in the shop and, as it were, excuse themselves by saying they were buying the game for their children?
A young miss sits in the garden, a young man passing by throws her a thirsty glance — and there she is already jiggling her little hands —
— “Yo-yo”.
A fine means of understanding…
And now the new topics of conversation! The fresh virtues attributed to the young men!
— Wiesz, Heniek umie robić pięćdziesiąt razy! [Polish: You know, Heniek can do it fifty times!]
— A mój Leon robi sto razy! [And my Leon does it a hundred times!]
— Mój Dudek jest wspaniały, on to robi bez przerwy. [My Dudek is marvellous, he does it non-stop.]
And another young miss complains:
— A real big shot, that Bolek, but only with his mouth; when it comes to the “yo-yo” — he can’t.
And among the young people rumours go from ear to ear, with a lustful little smile on their lips:
— Lola has taken to the “yo-yo”… ah, she knows the craft!
— Liza jiggles — a delight! And Regina soon lets…
A father tells me:
— I hear a commotion in the other room! He shouts: Again! Again! And my daughter accompanies: Let go! Let go! One opens the door — there sits my daughter with her sweetheart, and they are enjoying themselves with the “yo-yo”.
An acquaintance, a colleague, a journalist and by nature something of a philosopher, explained the “yo-yo” to me from the standpoint of eternity: what, after all, is the whole of human life if not a wheel turning in the world? A circle; people torment themselves, despair — and the “yo-yo” says to them:
— Hold on, people, firm and cheerful, pull lightly on the string and remember that the world is a little wheel!
And something more:
that if life is sometimes bad, so bad that the sky seems to be lying down on the earth, one must still not lose heart; one light pull and you are up high again.
And what does the whole art of the “yo-yo” game consist of?
Both spools must go down only to a little before the end and then up high again; but if the spools go down to the very end it is no good — you are a bad player.
And after all these interpretations and explanations, do you now know what is meant by “yo-yo”?
It seems to me that —
no, — no.
Yankele.
Amnesty Troubles.

[Humour and satire — the general amnesty.]
— Good evening! — this week a gang of some twenty men burst into the editorial office with a great noise and racket. — Is this where the editorial office lives? — they all shouted together and pushed closer to me, fixing their eyes on me as if to swallow me up.
— Yes — I answered them, trembling all the while, as if a fever were shaking me. — And what on earth do my dear gentlemen wish? — I turned to them very politely and did not take my eyes off them for a minute.
— Is it true? — one of the gang moved forward right opposite me, his sparkling eyes darting back and forth.
— What do you mean, true — say I — what could possibly be a lie here, when you can plainly see that this is a real editorial office.
— Is it true, what the papers are writing? — thundered my “chwat” [Polish: daredevil], shoving his hands into his trouser pockets.
— It’s like always — I answered him, completely flustered — it is a business matter after all, and if one wrote only the truth we would look like butter in the sun.
— So — the whole crowd came out with a growl — and about the “mnesty”, is it true, or did you just make it up as a “granda” [Polish: prank, racket]?
— Aha! If that’s what this is about, that’s something else entirely — I began to speak to them in a different tone — in such matters one does not make “grandas”; about that one must write only the truth, without any tricks.
— My name is Meir Kiełbaśnik — said the little man who spoke for the whole bunch, thrusting out his rough hand and squeezing mine so that I almost fainted.
— Very pleased — I pushed a bench towards him with a pained little smile — please be seated!
— What? — he pulled his hands out of his pockets in a rage — how do you know I have to go and sit [in prison], eh? And the “mnesty” is a stillborn child?
— You are mistaken — I began to calm him — God forbid I want to put you inside; take a seat, please, you needn’t strain your feet.
— As you see us — my angel of death began, pulling the bench over — we are one “towarzystwo” [Polish: society, gang]; all of us have to go and sit or have “sprawy” [Polish: court cases] against us, and that is exactly why we have come to you, Panie Redaktorze.
— And how can I help you — I put on a God-fearing little face while my heart pounded like a robber’s — after all I can’t go and serve time for you; I have a wife and little chicks.
— Listen — the chief speaker gave me a slap on the shoulders, “po przyjacielsku” [Polish: in a friendly way] — you can go on sitting quite calmly in the editorial office. We only want you to “reform” [sic; i.e. inform] us exactly what this “mnesty” is and how we can come off in such a business.
— How long do you have to serve? — I asked very cautiously.
— Around 30 years — Meir Kelbaśnik answered me, and lowered his head in shame.
— What? — I jumped up, unnerved — 30 years? And for that you want an amnesty? The amnesty applies only up to 6 months’ imprisonment! Be so good as to go in good health, because if you could have got 30 years I am afraid to talk to you and want nothing to do with you.
— Panie Redaktorze! — the whole crowd suddenly began to shout — all, all of us together have to go for a thirty; we won’t let anyone go and sit alone, we are “solid” comrades and “nasz-brats” [from Polish nasz brat: “our own kind”].
Hearing that, I finally felt easier and began to talk with each one separately.
— Panie Maor [sic, for Meir] Kiel… Kielb…
— Well, “Kiełbaśnik” — he helped me out in a flash.
— Why and for how long do you have to go and sit?
— Going to sit is out of the question — Meirke answered me at once — I only got 4 months for wanting to do a “left” [crooked] deal, in which they caught me by the hand in time, eh? Came off really badly, Panie Redaktorze, true?
— You are free, Panie Kiełbaśnik! — I cried with great pathos, and shook his hand like a “przyjaciel” [Polish: friend].
— And me — pushed through the whole crowd a short creature with a red head of hair and a face full of freckles — I got three times three. One for that business — and he made a twist with his little hand behind his back. The second time I don’t remember exactly anymore, and lastly a policeman gave me, over a trifle, a “zbenk” [a hard whack] into the shoulder blade [Polish łopatka]; I made as if I were crying and shouted “boli” [Polish: it hurts], until he wrote me down in his “notes” [Polish: notebook], for which I later got 3 months.
— Free! — I showed him the door with my hand.
— My name is Reb Zalman Yekele — a tall [printed “hoyfer”], thin Jew with a neatly trimmed blond little beard began tugging me by the lapel. — A misfortune befell me, may it not happen to you, “Pan Redaktor”: ever since they introduced “colonization” [malapropism for canalization, i.e. sewers] in our town, there is no place in broad daylight where a person in the street can pop in. Well, never mind — besides being a Jew, one is a human being too… A policeman grabbed me by the collar and wrote, shouted… wrote, shouted… and after a few weeks a paper came to go and “sit”.
— Free, free! — I flung his hands off my coat-tails and moved aside.
Within one minute the whole remaining gang threw themselves on me together, pulling me and pinching me from all sides; with great effort I managed to tear myself out of their hands, leaving them all, one after another, a kind of ransom [“letst gelter” — ?]: free, free!
Help! Why did the government have to issue an amnesty, and what good to me are the troubles I have suffered in recent days from those “solid” fellows, who come to visit me in the editorial office every day.
Lux.

In the further part of the article the author mocks Opatoshu, relating various tales of how J. Legal Matters. New Laws.

[Law — legislation in Poland.] In the latest numbers of the "Dz. Ustaw" [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws] a series of new laws has appeared which fundamentally change the antiquated legislation:

a) The law on the organization of the bar unifies the organization in all parts of the country, makes it possible for advocates to transfer freely from one district to another, and reorganizes the governing bodies as well as disciplinary responsibility and state supervision.
The law came into force on 1 November [Listopad].

b) The law on the enforcement system introduces throughout the country the offices of komornicy [court bailiffs], subordinates them to the municipal courts, reorganizes the supervision over the komornicy, "introduces very important changes such as, for example, written information, judicial liability of the state jointly and severally with the komornicy for damages, etc.
The law simplifies the procedure and precisely defines the competences of the komornicy — it comes into force together with the new Code of Civil Procedure on 1 January [Styczeń] 1933.

c) From the same date the regulations on court costs come into force, which reduce the court fee from 3 per cent to 2.5 per cent and fundamentally change the fee for various court suits and petitions [podania].

d) The law on the Supreme Administrative Tribunal introduces very important changes in the organization of the Tribunal. The law comes into force on the 15th of this month and provides (Art. 115) that in all matters filed with the Tribunal before 1.4.1932 the interested parties must, within 3 months, submit declarations as to whether they maintain their complaints; otherwise the complaint is annulled.

e) The law on associations (Prawo o stowarzyszeniach) also comes into force on 1 January 1933, in place of the decree of 3 January 1919, and radically changes the regulations in force until now.
Because of its importance for public life, it calls for detailed treatment (in the next number).

f) The military penal code, which also comes into force on 1 January 1933.

g) Besides the laws, various decrees of the President of the State have appeared on income tax, amendments to the teachers' service statute [pragmatyka] of 1 July [Lipiec] 1926, etc.

h) The decree on amnesty in connection with the introduction of the new penal code.

D. R-n.
From the Book Table

[Book review.]
"Fun undzer altn oytser" ("From Our Old Treasure") — pearls gathered from our ancient sources and from various books, from the Rishonim and the Acharonim, arranged by the weekly Torah portions; collected and edited by B. Yeushzohn, two volumes. Warsaw 5692 [1932].
Shrewd wit is a Jewish trait; in no field of creativity does the Jew stand out as much as in the field of humor. Jewish humor has no equal in its sharpness, depth and originality — and yet among us the least effort has gone into cultivating and collecting Jewish flashes of wit, the learned Talmudic small talk that is a whole Torah in and of itself; these sparkling diamonds have been left to gather dust in the old bookcases.
And now a Jewish writer has come, in whose hands the keys to our old treasure had not yet rusted, who saw with pain how the gates [printed "tu ern"] of this treasure open ever more rarely — and he saw it as a need of the hour to throw the treasure-gates wide open, to pick out the most brilliant pearls, dust them off, polish and grind them, and present them to the Jewish reader: here, see what you possess and what you knew nothing about.
We said: a "need of the hour" [printed "tsorekh ha-sore"] — so the author calls it in the preface, and rightly so: the young generation is a stranger to the works and creative treasures even of our modern scholars, let alone of our ancients.
And that it was a need of the hour is shown by the interest the thousands of readers have shown in it — something a sefer or a book rarely merits nowadays.
The work is not exhausted; among other nations such a work is done by an academy; such an exhaustive, enormous work takes years, and the author indeed intends to publish a series of such collections.
To praise Yeushzohn's style, his masterly yet sharply apt simplicity, is superfluous for the better Jewish reader; his place in journalism and the feuilleton speaks for itself. It is only worth remarking that with this peculiar simplicity (simplicity borders on genius — someone once said) he breathes life into the words of our ancients; it is true that they therefore sometimes take on a different appearance, a more understandable one, a more apt one, without losing anything of the content, of the original idea — and that, the right measure between the two [printed "beyre" for "beyde"], is no small matter at all.
In any case, in no Jewish home where a Jewish sefer or book ever enters may the "Old Treasure" be missing, for it is in the category of "turn it over and over, for everything is in it."
Y. Leyzer.

Jewish Personalities.
Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov.
The creator of the Hasidic teaching and movement, Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov, was born in the year 1700 to poor parents, on the border between Podolia and Wallachia. He was orphaned early, and at 12 he was already an assistant (behelfer) to a melamed in his shtetl. Already in his youth he was strongly drawn to delving into the Kabbalah books, while to studying Gemara and the codifiers he paid little attention.
At 20 he leaves his home and arrives in Brody, where he becomes the brother-in-law of the well-known rabbi, Rabbi Gershon Kutover. He does not stay long in the Galician town, but goes off with his wife into the Carpathian Mountains, works hard digging clay and immerses himself in thoughts about the world, God and man. Such a life lasts 7 years, and later Rabbi Israel comes to a shtetl in eastern Galicia, Tłuste, where he becomes a shochet, cantor and melamed. At 36 he "revealed himself" to the world, first as a miracle-healer and later as teacher and comforter of troubled and unlearned souls, a leader of thousands of thirsting souls, a support and help for the simple folk, who longed for a warm word of instruction, encouragement and purification of the soul.
Soon Rabbi Israel becomes famous and receives the name "Baal Shem Tov", in order to distinguish [?] him from many other "miracle-workers" and healers, who used to go about among the people and heal only the physical sufferings of the poor.
In the year 1740 he settles in Międzybóż, a shtetl in Podolia, and from there he begins to spread his new teaching.
After Rabbi Israel's death, in 1760, his famous disciples and rabbis continued his work.

How the Bear Hunt Goes

[Children's page — nature and knowledge.]
Several hunters get together to go on a bear hunt, and when they come upon him they surround him and provoke him, and when he approaches them, the boldest of the hunters receives him, stretching out toward him his left hand, which is fitted on both sides into two thick pieces of wood. And at the moment the bear seizes the hand to bite it, the hunter thrusts into his side the long knife he holds in his right hand, and at that same moment the other hunters rush up to him and kill him.
But they do not always succeed in killing him this way. It happens that the bear understands instinctively that the hunter who stretches his hand toward him has an evil intention, especially when he notices the knife in the other hand, and instead of seizing the hand he first snatches the knife and breaks it to pieces with his strong paws. And in an instant he falls upon the hunter, giving the other hunters no time to approach him and kill him.
The bear — as a rule — will not attack a person who does not provoke him. Unless he is very hungry, or the she-bear [printed "בעריכטע"] has little cubs. And remarkably, it has never yet happened that a bear attacked a woman, and so the women of Kamchatka go without the slightest fear into the forests where the bears live.
The bear also shies away from a dead body, not touching it, and many hunters have saved their lives when they were in danger by throwing themselves to the ground and playing dead.
The Kamchatkans kill bears every winter, when they are sleeping, and although [printed "פאטש", read "כאטש"] they have little use of their meat — because of their leanness — the pelt of winter bears, on the other hand, is much more valuable than that of summer bears.

The Sky Is Burning!

[Children's corner — story.]
(From the cycle "Lemele").

Sabbath, toward evening.
The day had been a splendid summer one, a hot one, a very hot one.
Now it is stealing out slowly, the Sabbath, through door and window, through market and town, like a thief on tiptoe...
It is lovely now in the little town; everything is so idyllically dreamy, so full of longing...
Jews, young and old, with their wives, children and grandchildren rest on the thresholds of their blue-whitewashed houses. Pious women, hands clasped in prayer, heads thrown back and eyes fixed on the sky, bow with simple faith into the flaming sunset, and from pale lips rise sweet, longing prayers, melting into the [oppressive?] air — — — — — —
— God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob — — — — — — —
And [exhausted?] children on their mothers' tired laps plead so dreamily and with childlike gentleness:
— Mommy, say it louder, say more —
Reb Leybele the shochet [ritual slaughterer], Lemele's grandpa, now sits on the porch of his half-collapsed inherited house, and he, Lemele, his six-year-old grandson, rides mischievously on his lap, and from time to time casts a childish, pensive glance at the flaming western sky...
Lemele's clever little brain is still not ripe today to grasp such deep, unclear things as come into his mind.
Suddenly he cries out in fear in his little voice:
— Grandpa, my crown, the sky is burning!!
— What won't you think of next, Lemele dear — the grandpa smiles and gives Lemele a kiss on his little red lips.
— Well, then why is it so red there?
— Because that's just how it is — the grandpa wants to be rid of Lemele's questions.
— Why is it just how it is?
— Because a little boy like you doesn't ask difficult questions — says the grandpa with a smile into his long white beard.
Lemele's little cheeks redden and his deep-brown little eyes sparkle. A thought flashes in his mind. And he asks again:
— Grandpa, may one light a fire on the Sabbath?
The grandpa laughs: — No, one may not.
— Then who lit the sky?
— God Himself.
— God?
— Of course God, who else? God may do everything He wants.
— Why?
— Because everything belongs to Him.
— Dear grandpa — says Lemele again — where does God live?
— God lives everywhere.
— Is God a person?
The grandpa gets angry at his stubborn grandson — you are talking nonsense again. I've already told you a little boy mustn't be a [rascal?].
Lemele does not let up. He points with his little hand at the sky and asks once again:
— Right up there, does God live there?
The grandpa gives him a slap on the little hand:
— One must not point at God with a hand.
Lemele cries.
The grandpa wants to make up with him, but he, Lemele, is now cross with his grandpa, because he never wants to tell him some [—] [true?] little story; he always fobs him off, he thinks that he, Lemele, doesn't know that he, his grandpa, is fooling him.
Lemele's grandma, Kreyne-Golde "the Shlayserin" [keeper of the keys?], is nicer to him; she always tells him such lovely, wonderful little stories that it is a delight to listen to them..
So Lemele now tears himself out of his grandpa's hands and runs into the house to his grandma, who sits by the window and is now whispering a Sabbath evening prayer — — —
— Why are you crying, Lemele, my little crown? — the grandma takes him on her lap and cuddles him close.
— I'm afraid, because there's a fire burning in the sky! The sky is burning!!!
— You little silly, don't you know that this is how they drive the bad people, the wicked, back into Gehenna? Lay down your little head, my treasure, and I'll tell you a story —
And Kreyne-Golde the Shlayserin, wife of Reb Leybele the shochet, takes her grandson Lemele and tells him one of her enchanting stories about the wicked in Gehenna, about the righteous in Paradise, so broadly and so long, until Lemele falls asleep in a sweet childish sleep...
Leyzer Shikman.
A Delegation to the Starosta

[Będzin — trade and decrees.] [Section banner: “What's New in Zagłębie?” — Friday, 12 Cheshvan 5693, piątek 11 listopada 1932. Będzin.]
A delegation to the starosta [district head] — concerning the decree against the shopkeepers whose shops are together with their dwellings.
As our readers know, an official announcement has been published in Zagłębie that, in accordance with the law, shops selling articles of prime necessity may not be together with private dwellings.
The deadline for carrying this out is the 15th of this month.
It goes without saying that, in the present severe crisis, the decree has caused despair among hundreds of shopkeepers and fruit dealers of Będzin, Sosnowiec and the surrounding area, and it was resolved that a delegation should turn to the starosta with a request that he, as the protector of the town, use his influence so that the harsh decree be eased within the bounds of what is possible.
The delegation, which consisted of the town councillors and presidents of the Sosnowiec and Będzin small traders' associations, Messrs. Herman Aliner and Dawid Gutensztajn, and the merchants Anszel Openhajm, Kalman Hajda and Józef Kurc. [The sentence is left unfinished in the original.]
Messrs. Aliner and Gutensztajn described to the starosta the critical situation in which part of the shopkeepers find themselves, and the ruin facing hundreds of families if the law is applied against them.
The starosta took the facts submitted to him under serious consideration. “I am fully aware,” said the starosta, “what consequences the application of this law may have, but I shall endeavour by every possible means to find a way out that will satisfy both the legislation and those concerned.”
The starosta asked the delegation that all the material be handed to him in the form of a memorandum, and he will give an answer on the matter before the 15th.
———
On the same question a delegation of Polish merchants from Czeladź intervened with the district physician; the latter told the delegation that he cannot change the ministerial law, and refused the request.

[Będzin — societies, health.] A few weeks ago the youth society named “Tse'irei Mishmurei Cholim” [Young Watchers of the Sick] opened sanitary [medical-orderly] courses under the direction of several local doctors.
Next Sunday before noon a festive academy [ceremonial gathering] will take place at the “Nowości” in connection with the official opening of the sanitary courses at the above-mentioned society.
The academy, which has a rich programme, will, it is to be hoped, be well attended.
A Concert for Charitable Purposes.

[Będzin — charity, culture.] On Monday the 14th of this month a concert with a rich programme will take place at the “Nowości”. The participants are gifted musical talents from Upper Silesia and Zagłębie.
The proceeds go to the benefit of the local charitable society and to the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital.
It is to be hoped that the event will be supported as it deserves.

The new kehilla budget will be reduced by 10 percent.

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla — Budget.] Under the chairmanship of vice-president Mr. Wendel, a meeting of the kehilla board took place on Sunday. On the agenda was the draft of the new kehilla budget.
On this question a discussion developed, which was conducted within the framework that the new budget must be reduced.
Against this spoke dozór (board member) Nachemja, who declared that the Zionist group is against the reduction.
Dozór Reznik gives a statement that, although on all questions he goes hand in hand with the Zionists, nevertheless on this point he will vote for the reduction.
Before proceeding to the vote, the secretary, Mr. Lewenhof, takes the floor and declares that he agrees to a 10-percent reduction of his pension.
The proposal is put to the vote, and by a majority of votes it is adopted that all pensions above 200 zł. shall be reduced by 10 percent.
The same reduction will also be applied to the subsidies.
The management of Schön's factory threatens that all workers will be dismissed.

[Sosnowiec — Labour — Strike.] The strike at Schön's factory is still going on. On Tuesday the management published a notice that from that day on the factory is shut down for an unlimited time, and at the same time all workers are released from work.
The workers received the notice very calmly, knowing in advance that the notice is merely a simple threat.
The League of Nations, England and the Jewish question. Dr. Soskin's visit to Zagłębie.

[Sosnowiec — Zionism — Revisionists.] As is known from the press, the vice-president of the World Union of Revisionist Zionists, Dr. Soskin, has come to Poland — the political referent on behalf of the Revisionist Executive at the League of Nations in Geneva, where Dr. Soskin has his seat.
Dr. Soskin's coming to Poland is connected with the forthcoming events anticipated in the Zionist movement. On his tour of the larger cities of Poland the distinguished guest will visit Zagłębie, where he will hold consultations with the nationalist activists in order to inform them about the situation that has arisen in the Zionist world.
This coming Sunday Dr. Soskin will be in Sosnowiec, where he will lecture before a narrower circle of invited nationalist activists on the topic "The League of Nations, England and the Jewish question".

Instead of a Cure, She Met a Tragic Death

[Dąbrowa — accident.] On Poniatowskiego Street in Dąbrowa [Górnicza] lived the 70-year-old Christian woman Kwapisz [?], who suffered from internal pains. One of her acquaintances advised her to massage herself with warm kerosene mixed with salt.
The old woman followed the advice, warmed up kerosene, sat down by the stove and began massaging herself. At a certain moment a little kerosene spilled onto the hot metal plate of the stove and a fire broke out.
In the flames the old woman was so badly burned that a few hours later she died.

For Taking Newspapers to Read, Newspaper Vendors Will Be Deprived of Their Livelihood.
[Press — regulations.] The downright criminal practice of those who take a newspaper from the newspaper vendors in order to read it through [and return it] is deeply rooted, and the many measures adopted against it have almost all remained without result.
As it appears, however, an end will now be put to it.
Apart from the fact that giving out a newspaper to be read through harms the editorial offices and undermines the existence of the newspapers, it is also a spreader of contagious diseases.
The sanitary department of the Warsaw magistrate has already turned its attention to this and has resolved that, should a read newspaper be found in a newspaper kiosk, the vendor will have the kiosk concession taken away from him and will, moreover, also be fined.
As we learn, the sanitary departments of the Zagłębie magistrates have also resolved to follow the example of the Warsaw magistrate.

[Będzin — local news: trade, municipality, kehilla.]

Through the fault of the Będzin magistrate — Jewish children go hungry.
As we have already written, women's committees have been formed in the public (powszechne) schools in Będzin, engaged in the important campaign of providing free lunches for the poorest children of the schools.
Such a campaign is also being run in public school no. 8, under the direction of Mrs. Brojda. The women's committee has fulfilled its task and collected what was needed, but unfortunately the poor little children still cannot get the lunches
— And why, do you think?
— Because the magistrate, which should have been the actual initiator of the campaign, only creates difficulties and to this day refuses to hand over the requested premises in the „Piast“ for the kitchen.
About this, besides the school management, the parents' committee also intervened, but the magistrate will not give in to the demand and advises setting up the kitchen in Ważny's little room...
It goes without saying that for various reasons the kitchen cannot be at Ważny's, and thanks to that poor Jewish children go hungry...

Month of the Yiddish Book in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — culture, Yiddish books.] (Organised on the initiative of the Jewish PEN Club in Poland.)
The cooperative book depot „Kult-Bukh“, which is carrying out technically the campaign for the Yiddish book that the PEN Club proclaimed for the month of November 1932, has delegated the well-known publisher Y. Jaczkowski and the long-time distributor of the Yiddish book Ch. Lewiner to organise the Month of the Yiddish Book in the Zagłębie region.
The delegates have already been in our town for several days and are in contact with the communal circles and with the lovers of Yiddish literature in our town. They have already succeeded in putting together a committee which will lead this campaign and assist the delegates in their hard work for the spread of the better Yiddish book.
The committee consists of the following persons:
M. Gold, H. L. Goldsztajn, M. Gertner, B. Grojbard, A. Hampel, Y. Wygodzki, Dr. S. Weinzieher, A. Wajcenberg, Dr. [printed „R״R“] Y. Silberschatz, Prof. Elster, Y. Frejlich, Y. Pesachson, Dr. Ch. Perel, M. L. Kozłowski, L. Ratner, M. B. Rotenberg, Adv. R. Rechtman, A. Szwarcbaum, Eng. D. Szniderman and Ed. L. Szpigelman.
The committee has compiled a list of local citizens who will be visited by the delegates, and thereby reminds of the duty of every citizen to help Yiddish publishing and the Yiddish writer by buying books.
Every citizen who has a library at home must use the opportunity and enrich it from the large selection and at such cheap prices as have never been before; the others must acquire libraries for themselves on this occasion and thereby adorn their homes.
A warm response will give Yiddish publishing the possibility of getting out of the difficult situation in which it now finds itself and of attaining the possibility of further fruitful work.
Respectfully,
The Campaign Committee
in Zagłębie.

Reb Yeshaya Ratner, of blessed memory

Craftsmanship and the Intelligentsia

[Będzin — artisans; opinion.] The wish expressed at one of the board meetings of the Będzin Artisans' Association, that the intelligentsia should take an interest in the fate of the Jewish artisan masses, must have caused great surprise, and it is truly a curiosity of our public life that deserves careful examination.
Within some artisans' associations, a few years ago, the slogan arose that only an artisan can understand and defend an artisan. This slogan was turned into a system, and, with small exceptions, all non-artisans were pushed out of the associations and removed from any work on behalf of Jewish crafts. It went so far that the doors of the artisans' organizations were in practice closed to the Jewish intellectual, the student and the academic, the engineer, etc.
True, we never heard here the well-known cry "Down with the intelligentsia", but at every opportunity all means were used, even the harshest, to remove the intelligentsia and push it far away from the artisan. Whether this was a fight against supposed competitors, or an effort to remove better-informed collaborators — is a secret. The fact is that an abyss was created between the intelligentsia and the artisan class.
This tactic did great harm to the artisan class in general and to the provinces in particular, because while in the larger centres there are still artisans with professional education who can give the masses a certain minimum of education and organization, in the provinces there are almost none. Cooperation with the intelligentsia — engineers, doctors, technicians, etc. — which[?] in other societies has achieved much for the artisan, both in professional training and in organization, education and general culture, is sorely missing for our artisan masses, and this is without doubt one of the most important reasons for the decline of our crafts in favour of others, who have managed to coordinate the work of the two strata: intelligentsia and craft.
We are witnesses to how various trades that were almost exclusively in the hands of our artisans are being taken over by others, who organize themselves quietly and waste no energy on fighting their own intelligentsia.
And therefore now, when for various reasons there is no season for political work, nobody takes any interest in the artisan masses — and the artisans' apprentice youth is almost without supervision: there are no preparatory courses for the examinations, no trade schools and not even any courses. Only a minimal number of Jewish candidates sit the artisan examinations, the general trade schools are ignored by our youth, and we shall soon see the sad consequences of this situation, but then it will be too late: time always works against the neglected, and the positions that are abandoned or lost will never be regained.
If even now, for the majority in some branches of the crafts, the influence of our artisans in the guilds, and especially in the chambers of crafts, is minimal — one can imagine what times are still to come.
One thing is certain, though: had intelligent forces been active in the organizations, the ruin in the artisans' ranks would not have taken on such a sad character.
We want to believe that the situation of the artisan class has convinced the more conscious elements, who now stand at the head of the artisans' organizations, that there is an urgent necessity to change the tactics used until now.
It is in this sense that we wish to understand the wish of the Będzin artisans. The matter must be said clearly: for the sake of the artisans themselves, the way to the artisans and their organization must be reopened to the Jewish intelligentsia. The intentions must be serious and sincere. Guarantees must also be found that, at the first opportunity, people with the best intentions and the goodwill to work for the welfare of the artisan masses will not be shown the door so that they should not "disturb" — whether in petty internal struggles of ambition or in external wars over mandates.
The main goal of organizing the crafts in the present difficult time is first of all: professional education, both of the artisans and of the apprentice youth.
We are far from belittling political problems, but who knows whether it is not more correct to turn attention to creating great ranks of skilled tradespeople, trained and educated masters, instead of fighting for political offices of questionable value.
Cooperation of the intelligentsia with the artisan class is a necessity for us, if we do not want to allow skilled competition to push our craftsman out of the positions he holds and then ruin him.
The fight against the intelligentsia is pointless and harms first of all the artisan masses themselves.
An Intellectual.
The P.E.N. Club Again Proclaims a Month of the Yiddish Book — To All Friends of Yiddish Literature

[Culture — Yiddish literature; public appeal.] Once again the Yiddish P.E.N. Club turns to you. Once again we are organizing a Month of the Yiddish Book. Once again we remind you that Yiddish books are as good as not bought at all, that Yiddish publishers are not able to bring out new books, and that Yiddish book production hardly exists.
The difficult economic situation can in no way justify what is now happening on the Yiddish book market. After all, a book is not a luxury but spiritual bread, and it is a fact that books are indeed read and bought — but not Yiddish ones. The Jewish reader is gradually drifting away from the Yiddish book, without himself feeling how great his guilt is towards Jewish culture and towards himself.
Such a state of affairs cannot and must not be tolerated. The Yiddish P.E.N. Club, as the representative body of Yiddish literature, has therefore now decided to renew its campaign and to proclaim from the 1st to the 30th of November of this year a Month of the Yiddish Book. During this time everything must be done to rescue Yiddish book production from ruin and to reawaken interest in the Yiddish book, and consequently in Jewish creativity.
The P.E.N. Club again proclaims a Month of the Yiddish Book in the conviction that all sincere friends of Jewish culture, wherever they may be, will actively help in the campaign undertaken, will create purchase funds and the like. It must be a debt of honour for all to whom Yiddish literature is dear to help ensure that the Yiddish book, the main nerve of modern Jewish culture, should again take its place and be found in the bookcase of every educated Jewish home.
Friends of Yiddish literature, do your duty!
The Yiddish P.E.N. Club in Warsaw.
Warsaw, 1 November 1932.
My New Partner (Monologue of a Będzin Merchant)

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton.]
(Monologue of a merchant from Będzin.)
How do you like my new partner? May all bad, wild dreams fall on my enemies' heads! How do you like that business? He hasn't put a penny into the firm and wants to be a partner in all my businesses — so he is my guardian... He even has the nerve to come to my home and search; he rummages in every corner in case he finds some scrap of a document showing that, God forbid, I sold my goods at a high price and declared a lower price to him. Everything is "his grandmother's worry" [i.e., everything is his business] — otherwise the business of being my partner wouldn't pay him...
In my life, since I became a merchant, I have had several partners, and I had to put up with trouble from them too: my first partner, R' Berl, was not such a great intellectual either; he tore from the dead and the living, but it was still bearable — one could manage against him... My second partner, R' Velvl, did it in a very refined manner: he was polite to me and spoke only in the language of request: "bitte" here and "bitte" there, so that at times my mouth turned bitter from all his "bittes"...
But such a bitter partner as I have now hit upon is truly unbearable. One's gall could, God forbid, burst! If I don't pay [?] him the profit on the spot, he gets downright angry, draws up an account and charges himself percent upon percent... I don't know where he learned to reckon so fast. He never wanted to study, always just liked to play horsies, make a "bosat"[?] and the like — and suddenly he has become a complete master of arithmetic!...
It's useless to argue with him: why have you fallen in love with my bones? You joined as a partner with empty hands, and you know very well that I don't make such fortunes — where will I get the money to pay the debts... But he listens to me like the cat; he tears pieces of flesh from me alive, and, thank God, he lacks no lean ones; he sends in to me the wife with the children, the whole family with the servants...
I've already tried to protest against my partner's "pirekhtsn"[?] [antics/demands], wanted to summon him to a rabbinical court, but the rabbi warned me to run from my adversary to where the pepper grows [i.e., as far as possible], because in the end I'll still have to pay the partner the court fee.
Kundes.
Bloody Shooting on a Coal Train — 2 Coal Thieves Killed

[Poland — crime and accidents.]
On Saturday night, when the coal train travelling from Katowice to Łódź was a kilometre from Piotrków, several dozen people fell upon the train and began throwing coal off the wagons. The police travelling with the train fired several rifle shots into the air. Everyone scattered except 2 persons: a father and son kept standing on a wagon throwing lumps of coal. Having no other way out, the police fired a few more shots at the attackers. The father was seriously wounded by the bullets. The son, for his part, jumped off while the train was moving, but fell under the wheels of a wagon and was killed on the spot. Only when the train stopped at Widzew was the father found dead.
The names of the two attackers could not be established, as no documents were found on either of them.

Unemployment — The New Ruler of the World

[Essay — economy and society, unemployment.] By W. Zukerman.
One must not forget that unemployment is not merely an economic question; it also has a psychological and spiritual side. People are not machines or animals that need only be fed in order to be kept alive. People also have other needs besides physical work, and spiritual want is exactly the same kind of thing as economic necessity. People need something to be occupied with, and if society robs millions of people of their occupation, it must give them something else instead. This is as necessary as relief or charity.
Already in the most ancient times, in old Rome, the Caesars knew that the people must have "bread and spectacles". Food and entertainment — and the entertainment is as important [printed "ווילכטיג"] as the food, and without such entertainment (to fill people's idle time) the average person is just as restless as without food.
The modern Caesars (the governments) have also begun to realise this, and in various countries of Europe attempts are now being made to do something in this respect, because they are coming to the conviction that unemployment affects people as badly spiritually as economically.
People who go about for a long time without work and have no other occupation with which to fill their idle time become degenerate and even desperate; their condition can bring a country to the greatest misfortunes. Those who have experienced in their lives going about idle for several months (or, God forbid, several years) can testify what a terrible spiritual degradation idleness can be and how it can drive people to despair.
But what does the difficulty of this problem consist of? Why should it be so hard to find something with which to fill people's idle time? Is there a lack of entertainments and amusements in our time — do we not have enough theatres, films, radio, concerts, libraries, sports grounds, educational institutions and similar establishments with which people's idle time can be filled?
Those who ask such questions look at this modern problem with the eyes of a bygone time. All these means with which we are accustomed to fill our idle time are means of a different period, and they do not fit into the present time. A famous English professor, who has long studied this question, has now written a book about it, and he shows that all the entertainments with which we are used to filling our idle time are adapted chiefly to people who work a whole day and want a little entertainment in the evening.
All our entertainments are therefore mostly p a s s i v e, i.e. we ourselves do nothing, but let other people entertain us, as is the case in the theatre, cinema, concerts, etc. Everything is based on the principle that a person has worked a whole day (or for a certain time) and now comes to rest; his entertainment must therefore be an easy one and must not strain him. He himself need do nothing. Even when he does do something (as, for instance, when he plays cards), that too is light work, which must not tire him out physically.
But people today demand something quite different. They need a kind of entertainment that will take the place of their work; they need not to rest in their entertainment, but to work; not to be passive, but active; not to watch others play, but to play themselves — and to that we are not yet accustomed. Our world is wholly adapted to the old system of hard work, of "in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread". Our whole way of life, our thoughts, our morality and our entertainment — everything is based on that.
Now, however, we live in a different time. Hard work is disappearing from the world, disappearing forever, unless the world consciously decides to commit suicide or to destroy all machines. The present ideal of work will disappear. From a working world we shall become a workless world. Unemployment will in future be not an accident or an abnormal phenomenon, but the ordinary condition of the greater part of humanity.
People will therefore have to change their whole way of living and thinking in order to adapt to the new situation. Instead of work filling the greater part of our time, and entertainment being no more than a kind of rest and preparation for further work, entertainment will fill all our time.
We shall therefore have to find quite different forms of entertainment from those we have now. Entertainment will have to stop being passive and merely a means of passing the time easily and pleasantly. Our amusements will have to become creative ("schöpferisch"); they will have to fill the greater part of our time and become our most important occupation.
How this is to be done, this is not the place to tell. In England and in Germany very great and important experiments are now being made in this field, and the greatest minds of Europe are engaged in them. What is important for us to know is that from a hard-working world it is becoming a world of idleness and entertainment. Unemployment calls on us to rethink our life not only economically, but also spiritually.

[Poland — law, amnesty.] More about the latest amnesty decree.
Offences prosecuted by private complaint.
Article 11 of the latest amnesty decree is understood by many people to mean that the concessions of this decree apply only to offences prosecuted by the public prosecutor's office, administrative bodies or on some other official initiative, whereas they can have no application to offences that are tried only on the basis of a so-called private complaint.
Such an assumption does not agree with the actual state of affairs.
The validity of the amnesty does not depend on whether the proceedings against an offence committed must be undertaken on official or on private initiative.
The point here is only this: the criminal proceedings against offences arising from private complaints — although they belong to the category of so-called "wykroczenia" [petty offences] and therefore, in accordance with paragraph 2 of article 3 of the cited amnesty decree, should actually [?] have been annulled — must nevertheless be continued and carried through to a verdict.
Only then can the provisions of the amnesty be applied to this category of offences.
Fines.
There are many people sentenced to fines for petty offences committed before the cut-off date of the amnesty who, however, wishing to avoid the costs of enforcement, voluntarily paid the fines in question after the first of September. These people think they are entitled to reclaim the fines they paid which were later amnestied.
Their reckoning, however, is wrong, because the published amnesty does not relate to offences at all, but to the penalties for offences, and even then only insofar as the penalties have not yet been carried out.
It is a different matter when it concerns an amnestiable fine that had already been paid in a certain part before the publication of the amnesty, with the remainder due to be paid only after the publication of the amnesty.
Such remainders, not yet paid, have been remitted on the basis of the amnesty.
Supplementary penalties.
When speaking of the validity of the amnesty with regard to penalties, it must be established that it applies only to principal penalties (imprisonment, arrest, fine) but not to the so-called supplementary penalties (loss of public rights, civic rights of honour, professional rights, parental or guardianship rights, confiscation of objects and instruments, publication of the verdict), which are a consequence of criminal sentences passed for certain offences.
Offences to the detriment of the State Treasury.
Point 6, part 1, art. 6 of the amnesty ordinance is understood by some people to mean that those who committed offences to the detriment of the "State damage" [sic, "מלוכה-שאדן"; read: State Treasury] cannot enjoy its favours.
This interpretation is correct insofar as it concerns officials, but it is wrong when it concerns ordinary citizens.
Fiscal ("skarbowe") offences.
The amnesty does not apply to offences to the detriment of the State Treasury even when committed by ordinary citizens, if those offences belong to the category of so-called fiscal ("skarbowe") offences and are provided for in the Fiscal Penal Act of 28 March 1932.
In this respect, therefore, offences come into consideration that consist in violating the provisions:
1) on customs payments in the trade of goods with foreign countries; 2) on the tobacco monopoly; 3) the spirits monopoly, the taxation of vinegar essence and pressed yeast; 4) on the salt monopoly; 5) the match monopoly and the taxation of cigarette lighters; 6) the State lottery; 7) the tax on beer; 8) the tax on wine and mead; 9) the tax on coal; 10) the tax on playing cards; 11) the excise licence and 12) the trade of goods with Danzig [Gdańsk].
Y. A.

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayera

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Vayera and the Haftarah.] The portion.
A) "And he ran to meet them" (18:2)
The Gemara (Bava Metzia 86) says that the angels saw Abraham busy bandaging himself, so they went back out, and he chased after them.
The question arises: if so, it should have said "and he ran after them," not "to meet them"—
Rather: a folk aphorism says: "The poor are driven to a second door" — if a poor man comes in through one door, he is thrown out through the other. But Abraham, in whose house there were so many doors, when he saw the three men withdrawing through the door — "and he ran to meet them": he ran out through another door to cut off their way, so that, God forbid, they should not leave... Devarim Nehmadim.
B) "Meal, fine flour" (ibid., 6)
It is written "meal" and it is written "fine flour" — hence a woman is grudging toward guests (Bava Metzia 87).
The wife of Rabbi Shimshon Sukhakhalier[?] was renowned as a great scholar and an even greater miser. When Rabbi Shimshon used to bring guests home, she was not pleased. Rabbi Shimshon once said to her:
— You see, Lifshe, you prove that the sages were right when they said: "A woman's eye is grudging toward guests."
— With a rabbi that is not what is meant, because if a rabbi wanted to have a good "ayin" [eye; also the Hebrew letter ayin], then RAV would become R-A-'-V [ra'ev, hungry]...
(The meaning of this sharp-witted wordplay is that if he behaves too generously he will go hungry).
—o—
Learned sayings of famous women:
Rabbi Naftali Hirsch Meiselish, the Radver[?] rabbi, had a sister, Perl, a learned woman; she once said:
— "He who finds a wife finds good," because "it is not good for man to be alone"; therefore if he "finds a wife," he "finds good" — he gets the "good" back...
—o—
The widow of Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipman Heller, author of "Tosafot Yom-Tov," after his death took a second husband, also named Yom-Tov. She remarked on it with the Talmudic dictum:
— "The second Yom-Tov compared to the first is like a weekday"...
C) "That he may command his children and his household after him" (ibid., 19)
The Gemara says in Shabbat (119) that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the neglect of Torah study by the youth. There is a well-known saying: "The German schoolteacher defeated the French army." A land or a people is destroyed when its youth is not brought up in the purity of the holiness of the land. Tal le-Yisrael.
—o—
In Midrash Tanhuma it is said: "This lad has grown and has not been educated; there is another place a little distant from here where lads are educated; I shall take him and educate him there."
Abraham already sensed that only on Mount Moriah, only in the Land of Israel, is it possible to give youth a full national education. Rabbi Yitzhak Nissenbaum.
D) "Righteousness and justice" (ibid.)
Everywhere in the Bible justice is mentioned together with righteousness [tzedakah, also charity], because only such charity is dear to God if it stems from honest, just sources. Ohel Yaakov.
E) "This one came to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge" (19:9)
In Sodom too there were laws. Laws such as how to rob, how to plunder... and Lot was, as is known, their judge. And when they saw that their judge was hospitable to guests, they grew angry:
— You will yet, God forbid, teach the whole people to walk in your crooked ways, God forbid... The Dubno Maggid.
F) "Behold the fire and the wood" (22:7)
The Midrash says that Abraham was given the choice of what he wanted for his children: Gehenna or exile? He preferred to choose exile.
But in the end we have both, both Gehenna and exile.. "Behold the fire (Gehenna) and the wood (— Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon)." Nehmad mi-Zahav.
G) "And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. Because [ekev]..." (ibid., 14)
That the nations will envy the Jews will only be at the "ekev" [heel; end] — in the end, someday there... Meanwhile, unfortunately, it still stands at "pisht[?]. derbi"... Or Pnei Moshe.
Haftarah
H) "He is a holy man of God" (II Kings 4)
The Gemara (Berakhot 10) asks about this: how did she recognize that he was holy?
It appears that a truly holy man is indeed not recognized so easily... outwardly he makes nothing of himself. Peninim Yekarim.
